Question: A 50-year-old man presents to the ED with a rash and mouth pain. He developed oral ulcers several weeks prior to the onset of the rash, and they have persisted despite antiviral and antifungal therapy. His vital signs are unremarkable. On physical exam, flaccid blisters and erythematous erosions are noted across his trunk and extremities that spare the palms and soles. There are erosions on the buccal mucosa and hard palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Pemphigus vulgaris is a life-threatening, autoimmune blistering disease characterized by flaccid blisters and erosions of the skin and mucous membranes due to intraepidermal deposition of autoantibodies. Autoantibodies target desmogleins, which are transmembrane glycoproteins involved in maintaining tissue integrity, leading to acantholysis, or loss of cell-cell adhesion between keratinocytes. It most commonly presents in adults ages 40–60 and affects male and female patients equally. Almost all patients with pemphigus vulgaris have mucosal involvement, which may precede the development of cutaneous blisters. Mucosal lesions are typically painful erosions, and intact blisters are rarely seen. The oral cavity is the most common site of mucosal lesions, but the esophagus, conjunctiva, nasal mucosa, anus, labia, and vagina can be involved. Pain from severe oral erosions can lead to decreased oral intake, dehydration, and malnutrition. Over half of patients will also develop cutaneous manifestations. The classic skin lesions are flaccid blisters that easily rupture, leading to painful erosions that may ooze or bleed. Cutaneous blisters can affect any part of the body and are often widespread, but the palms and soles are typically spared. Without treatment, loss of the epithelial barrier can result in mortality from fluid losses and secondary bacterial infection.

The diagnosis is made through the combination of clinical findings, lesional biopsy for histopathology, perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence, and detection of serum autoantibodies. The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids. Steroid-sparing agents are often added, including azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin. Prior to the use of systemic corticosteroids, pemphigus vulgaris was usually a fatal disease. With current treatment, mortality ranges from 5–15%.



Bullous pemphigoid (A) is an autoimmune blistering disease of older patients, characterized by tense, pruritic blisters, as opposed to the painful, flaccid blisters of pemphigus vulgaris. A minority of patients with bullous pemphigoid have mucosal involvement.

Erythema multiforme (B) presents with a characteristic targetoid rash and variable mucosal involvement. The classic target lesions have a dusky central area of necrosis surrounded by a lighter area of edema and an outermost area of erythema.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) (D) is an important diagnosis to consider in any patient presenting with a painful rash and mucosal lesions, as it is life-threatening. However, SJS has a rapidly evolving course. The fact that this patient had oral ulcers for several weeks prior to the onset of the rash makes this diagnosis unlikely. Additionally, a patient with SJS who has progressed to widespread cutaneous involvement will appear ill, often with abnormal vital signs.

Question: Which of the following is most commonly associated with erythema nodosum?
ExplanationEN:
Erythema nodosum, thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a systemic disease or medication, is a vasculitis involving the venules and veins of the skin. It affects young adults primarily in their second to fourth decades, with women affected almost four times as often as men. A prodrome of nonspecific symptoms, including fever, malaise, and myalgias, is followed by the development of subcutaneous nodules, primarily on the anterior tibial surfaces. Lesions may also be seen on the forearms, trunk, and thigh. The nodules are often erythematous, well-circumscribed, and very tender. While many cases are found to be idiopathic, the most commonly implicated disease is a preceding streptococcal infection. Patients may give a history consistent with preceding streptococcal infection (e.g., fever and sore throat), and an antistreptolysin O titer should be checked. Treatment includes symptomatic care with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Inflammatory bowel disease (A), particularly Crohn disease, has been implicated in cases of erythema nodosum but not as commonly as streptococcal infection.

Patients with sarcoidosis (B) are at increased risk for developing erythema nodosum, but this is not as common of a preceding illness as a streptococcal infection.

Tuberculosis (D) has also been associated with the development of erythema nodosum, but preceding streptococcal infection is more common.

Question: Which of the following conditions is the rash seen above associated with?
ExplanationEN:
The image represents impetigo, a pustular eruption most commonly seen in preschool children. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis results from an antecedent infection of the skin or throat caused by nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis usually occurs 1–2 weeks after pharyngitis and 3–6 weeks after skin infection. The incidence is decreasing in the United States but is still common in some rural areas. It appears to result from the deposition of circulating immune complexes in the kidney. This leads to decreased glomerular filtration, allowing proteins to flow freely into the urine. Urinalysis shows significant blood and protein with RBC casts in 60% of cases. Pyuria with granular or hyaline casts also may be found.



Impetigo is not associated with arthritis (B). Other skin conditions, such as psoriatic arthropathy, occur in up to 20% of patients with psoriasis.

Clostridioides difficile (C) bacteria proliferate when the normal bowel flora is substantially reduced by antibiotic therapy. If the bacteria produce sufficient quantities of toxin, colitis develops.

There are a number of cutaneous manifestations of secondary syphilis (D). Lesions may be erythematous or pink macules or papules, usually with a generalized symmetrical distribution.

Question: A 7-year-old boy presents with a distinctive nonblanching rash on his buttocks and lower extremities and mild bilateral knee pain. He has no other concerns at this time. He appears nontoxic and his abdominal exam is benign. What test should be performed at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) is an IgA-mediated vasculitis of unknown etiology that commonly causes nephritis, and a screening urinalysis should be performed in the emergency department when the diagnosis is suspected. Patients with HSP are typically 3–10 years of age and present typically with palpable purpura on the buttock and extensor surfaces of the lower extremities. They also may have arthralgias or arthritis. These children appear nontoxic and have no mucous membrane involvement. The main predictor of long-term outcomes is the development of kidney involvement. Children should be screened by urinalysis on diagnosis and followed for 6 months.



An abdominal radiograph (A) would be an appropriate test if the patient presented with abdominal pain. Children with HSP can develop abdominal sequelae including intussusception and bowel perforation. Should sepsis with bowel perforation be a consideration, blood culture, abdominal radiographs, and empiric antibiotics would be appropriate. Generally, the standard test for intussusception is an abdominal ultrasound with radiological-assisted reduction in cases in which bowel perforation is not suspected. Children with free air on the abdominal radiograph should be immediately referred to surgery.

Blood cultures (B) are not useful in uncomplicated HSP as the disease is immune-mediated.

Platelet counts (C) in HSP are expected to be normal. If the diagnosis is in question, a platelet count may be of value.

Question: A 7-day-old boy presents to the emergency department with a fever, irritability, and a peeling skin rash. The parents report some nasal congestion and redness in the eyes but no oral lesions. The physical exam reveals the findings above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by infection with Staphylococcus aureus. It is most common in young children and newborns in the first week of life. Patients present with a fever and diffuse erythroderma and blisters with scaling of the skin. Patients will also experience conjunctivitis. Areas of high mechanical stress, such as the flexural areas, will blister and slough off. Patients often appear ill. Management is centered on resuscitation with crystalloid fluids, blood cultures, and antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus. It is appropriate to cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and narrow the coverage spectrum later. Patients require admission to a burn unit for care.



Cellulitis (A) presents with warmth, erythema, and tenderness at a focal site of infection. The diagnosis can be made clinically, though ultrasound may demonstrate edema and cobblestoning. It is not associated with diffuse erythroderma and skin peeling.

Necrotizing fasciitis (B) is a lethal diagnosis with a rapidly progressive skin infection, fever, tenderness, and possibly crepitus (if a gas-producing organism is present). Often, areas of dark necrosis can be seen on exam, which is not present in this patient. Patients may demonstrate hemodynamic instability that rapidly worsens.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) is associated with medication exposure, though infections and other antigens may lead to this condition. Patients present with erythema and blistering of their skin that is similar in appearance to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. A differentiating factor is mucosal surface involvement, which is not found in this patient.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the ED with a rash. It began 1 week ago with a single patch that was about 5 cm on his stomach, and has now worsened and spread along his back. It is mildly pruritic and only involves the torso. He has no fevers, cough, or other symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Pityriasis rosea is a common benign rash that occurs in children and young adults. It is recognized by the appearance of a herald patch 5–10 days before a widespread systemic eruption that is most prominent on the trunk and proximal limbs. The lesions are usually round, about 1 cm, and slightly raised. The widespread rash follows cleavage lines, giving it the appearance of a Christmas tree or a fir tree pattern on the back.

It is thought to be caused by a virus, debatably attributed to a reactivation of human herpesvirus 6, 7, or 8. It can often be mistaken for tinea corporis. Secondary syphilis can have a similar appearance, especially when considering that pityriasis rosea occasionally appears on the palms or soles. Treatment for asymptomatic patients is simply reassurance. Some patients have itching that is worse at night, which can be treated with a bland emollient or lubricating lotion with menthol or camphor, with or without an oral antihistamine.



There is limited evidence that acyclovir (A) or ultraviolet light causes more rapid resolution, but the data is weak and these therapies are only recommended in severe cases.

Fluconazole (B) is appropriate for tinea corporis but not pityriasis rosea. If the presentation is not clear, tinea corporis can be differentiated from pityriasis by a positive potassium hydroxide preparation on skin scrapings, best taken from the border of a plaque.

The rash from syphilis is usually diffuse, symmetric, and macular or papular and includes the palms or soles. It can have a similar appearance but often includes additional systemic symptoms and is treated with penicillin (C).

Question: A 27-year-old man with AIDS has the rash shown in the picture above. What type of isolation is required if he is admitted?
ExplanationEN:
Varicella-zoster virus (human herpesvirus 3) is the causative agent in both chickenpox and shingles. Herpes zoster, shown in this patient, occurs from reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus that has been dormant in a dorsal root nerve ganglion since an episode of chickenpox. Most reoccurrences occur in older (> 55 years) and immunocompromised patients. Prior to the onset of rash, patients experience tingling or hyperesthesia in the dermatome. Painful, vesicular lesions then appear on the skin along the distribution of the dermatome. Patients are considered infectious from 5 days before the appearance of the rash until 5 days after the appearance of the vesicles. If the patient is immunocompromised with localized herpes zoster, standard precautions plus airborne (negative pressure room) and contact precautions should be followed until disseminated infection is ruled out.



Droplet precautions (B) are indicated for viruses with larger respiratory particles. These precautions include a mask worn when entering a patient’s room. One of the most common indications for droplet precautions is influenza.

Positive pressure (C) precautions involve positive air pressure such that the air inside the patient’s room is forced out of the room into the surrounding environment. This type of isolation is sometimes used in patients with neutropenia.

Standard precautions (D) are universal for every patient in the hospital setting and are not unique to any particular disease entity.

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with herpes zoster (shingles) and should have appropriate pain control started, such as acetaminophen. Herpes zoster results from the reactivation of dormant varicella-zoster virus developing in patients with a history of chickenpox. Risk factors for the development of herpes zoster include advanced age, immunocompromised status, and chronic lung or kidney disease.

Typically, pain in a dermatomal distribution precedes the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the same dermatome. The vesicles are cloudy at first and progress to crust formation later in the course. The pain associated with the disease is often severe and debilitating. Patients may not initially see a dermatitis and may report unilateral deep burning or stabbing chest pain. If no obvious rash is initially present, a chest X-ray or ECG may be performed to rule out cardiovascular concerns, both of which are typically unremarkable in patients with herpes zoster.

The mainstay of treatment is pain control and oral antiviral medications, depending on the timing of symptom onset and comorbidities. Orally administered corticosteroids were commonly recommended in the treatment of herpes zoster, but given recent clinical trials showing variable results, they are not typically recommended.



Antibiotics such as cephalexin (B) are only indicated if there is a superinfection of the lesions.

Antihistamines such as fexofenadine (C) have not been shown to hasten the rate of healing or aid in symptom relief in patients with varicella-zoster.

Nitroglycerin (D) is used for patients with anginal chest pain or pain associated with acute coronary syndrome.

Corticosteroids such as prednisone (E) have not been proven to be beneficial, although when combined with antivirals, such as valacyclovir, they may help with pain reduction.

Question: A 15-month-old girl presents due to a progressive rash and fever. She has had thick white nasal discharge and some left eye crusting with discharge for the preceding week. Fever as high as 103.3°F (39.6°C) has been present for the past 3 days. Areas of the skin are red with superficial peeling and crusting present on the face and upper chest, as shown above. She has been fussy, and the parents note that she is uncomfortable when held. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her findings?
ExplanationEN:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) occurs following the release of exotoxins (epidermolytic toxin A and B) associated with a focal infection due to Staphylococcus aureus that results in a generalized indurative or sunburn-like erythema (erythroderma) of the skin accompanied by marked skin tenderness. The exotoxins produce a split high within the superficial layers of epithelium, resulting in superficial skin peeling, blistering, and crusting.

These skin findings are especially pronounced around the mouth and nose or within the axillary and inguinal regions where skin friction plays a role in skin breakdown and peeling (positive Nikolsky sign). Mucous membranes are typically spared in SSSS. The outer two-thirds of the lip (dry surface) is keratinized and may manifest with superficial peeling, while the inner one-third of the lip is not keratinized and thus is not involved. Other mucous membranes (e.g., intraoral) are not keratinized and remain unaffected, which is an important clinical differentiator between SSSS and other mucocutaneous syndromes.

Treatment includes the use of a first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin), penicillinase-resistant penicillins (nafcillin or oxacillin), and vancomycin in areas with a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus.



Impetigo (A) is a localized infection due to S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is not accompanied by fever or other signs of systemic illness.

The mucous membrane findings in Kawasaki syndrome (B) include coarse vascular injection of the eyes with deep hemorrhagic crusts of the lips and mouth.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) is marked by deeper skin erosions, blistering, and desquamation due to inflammatory cleavage at the epidermal-dermal junction. Significant involvement of mucous membranes is characteristic of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, not SSSS.

Question: A 65-year-old man presents to the ED with a painful rash on his right upper arm that he first noticed 2 days ago. It has since rapidly progressed to involve his lateral upper arm and anteromedial axilla and has spread inferiorly near the elbow and antecubital fossa. His vital signs include a BP of 90/45 mm Hg, HR of 115 bpm, and T of 38.3°C. There is erythema, warmth, and exquisite tenderness to palpation over the site. Which of the following additional findings would support a diagnosis of a necrotizing soft tissue infection?
ExplanationEN:
Necrotizing soft tissue infections are caused by microbial invasion of the skin, fascia, and muscle. Two types of infection have been described. Type 1 infections comprise up to 75% of cases and are polymicrobial, including aerobes and anaerobes. Type 2 infections comprise 20–30% of cases and are monomicrobial, with the most common isolates including group A Streptococcus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Less common etiologies, such as Vibrio vulnificus or fungi, more commonly affect immunocompromised patients. As sanitation efforts have improved, Clostridioides species have become uncommon. Older age or a history of diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney or liver disease, heart disease, active malignancy, immunocompromised state, intravenous drug use, alcohol use, frequent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory use, or chronic skin infection or decubitus ulcers is a risk factor for the disease. In the early stages, infections may present with pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, followed by rapid tissue destruction and toxin release. The diagnosis of necrotizing soft tissue infections is clinical, and a high index of suspicion should be maintained in patients with bullae formation, crepitus (though only seen in up to 50% of patients), and necrotic skin. Evidence of systemic illness (e.g., tachycardia, hypotension, mental status changes) may represent an evolving bacteremia, which is seen in 25–30% of cases. Imaging may demonstrate soft tissue gas, though this is not required for the diagnosis. The presence of inflammatory laboratory results (e.g., C-reactive protein elevation, leukocytosis, anemia, hyponatremia, creatinine elevation, and hyperglycemia) embodied by the well-known laboratory risk indicator for necrotizing fasciitis score support the diagnosis. Prompt surgical exploration (i.e., incision and debridement) is the mainstay of diagnosis and treatment. Early empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy should include a carbapenem (e.g., imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) or piperacillin-tazobactam, an agent with anti-MRSA activity (e.g., vancomycin or linezolid), and clindamycin due to its antitoxin effects. Despite early antibiotic therapy and surgical intervention, the mortality rate remains up to 10% in the United States.



Erythema with a dusky center (B) is a common finding in erythema multiforme, which is a circumscribed erythematous area with central dusky or purplish skin, depending on the patient’s baseline skin tone. A positive Nikolsky sign (C) is present when there is a separation between layers of keratinocytes, which is nonspecific and can be seen in a variety of mostly immune-mediated skin disorders (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris). Raised tender nodularities (D) describe the lesions of erythema nodosum. Silver patches and plaques (E) are the characteristic examination findings of plaque psoriasis.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents with concerns of a progressive rash developing over the past 3 days. He reports no fever, headache, or arthralgia. His vital signs include blood pressure of 124/78 mm Hg, heart rate of 96 bpm, respiratory rate of 14 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation of 99%, and temperature of 99.0°F (37.2°C). ExplanationEN:
This patient has erythema multiforme, an acute immune-mediated self-limited rash characterized by target-shaped skin lesions. The most common known causes include reactivated herpes simplex, Mycoplasma pneumonia, and upper respiratory tract infections. Rarely, it can be associated with allergens, drugs, connective tissue diseases, and internal malignancies.

While it can present with multiple forms, such as red macules and papules, urticarial-like lesions, vesicles, and bullae, most of these will evolve over 24–48 hours to form 1–3 cm target lesions. Lesions appear in crops, resolve in 2–4 weeks, and often involve the palms and soles. Involvement of oral mucosa differentiates erythema multiforme major from erythema multiforme minor. Question: A 55-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents to the emergency department with diffuse sloughing of his skin with blisters that extend easily when lateral pressure is applied to them. The lesions cover his entire torso and back and are also found within his mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with findings covering roughly 36% of his body (using the rule of nines) suggestive of a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a life-threatening autoimmune condition of the skin that presents with diffuse sloughing of the skin covering at least 30% of the body with associated mucosal lesions. Potential causes of toxic epidermal necrolysis include drugs (such as allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs), and infections (such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae). The disorder can also occur spontaneously without a known trigger. Minor pressure can be applied to blisters resulting in sloughing (Nikolsky sign). The treatment of toxic epidermal necrolysis is typically admission to a burn center, supportive therapy, and possibly immunomodulators (though there is not sufficient evidence to suggest this is standard of care). Patients will require pain control, nutritional support, and meticulous wound care. Currently, there is no clear evidence suggesting a benefit of steroids in toxic epidermal necrolysis, and treatment requires an emergency dermatology consult. The mortality of this condition is high (> 30%).

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (B) presents with macular erythema and widespread exfoliation typically in the setting of fever and tachycardia with tender skin and mucosal sparing.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (C) is essentially a less severe form of toxic epidermal necrolysis and presents with dermatologic lesions or skin detachment on < 10% of the body. Using the rule of nines, this patient’s lesions cover his chest and back, meaning that 36% of his body is covered, suggesting a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Question: A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the ED, brought in by family, with altered mental status, fever, and a “female problem” that has rapidly evolved over 12 hours. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and alcohol use disorder. Current medications are lisinopril and metformin, but the patient is chronically noncompliant. On exam, the patient’s vital signs include an oral T of 102.5°F (39.2°C), BP of 84/66 mm Hg, HR of 120 bpm, and RR of 24/min. Her peripheral capillary blood sugar is 350 mg/dL. She appears to be seriously ill, is pale, and has delayed capillary refill. The labia and perineum are significantly swollen bilaterally and deeply erythematous with a very indurated texture. There is a 2 cm blackened area on the inferior aspect of the left labia majora. Swelling does not permit visual inspection of the vagina or cervix. Of the options below, which best describes your clinical diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Fournier gangrene is a type of necrotizing fasciitis that is commonly thought to be specific to male genitalia. However, the term includes female labial and perineal necrotizing fasciitis as well. The most common predisposing factors are diabetes and excessive alcohol use, but other factors include extremes of age, malignancy, chronic steroid use, cytotoxic drugs, malnutrition, drug use, human immunodeficiency virus, and other causes of immunocompromise. This patient has two of these factors (diabetes and alcohol use disorder). Common findings of Fournier gangrene include abnormal vital signs, severe site pain or pain out of proportion to physical findings (at least early in the course), severe swelling, site warmth and woody induration, altered mental status, hemorrhage, rapidly advancing infection, crepitus, hemorrhage, sloughing, and blistering. The disease may begin gradually and often originates from local skin infections or trauma. Colorectal causes include local infections of the perineum, anal fissures, colon rupture, rectal carcinoma, and perianal surgery. Urologic causes include chronic urinary tract infections, neurogenic bladder, and epididymitis. Additional sites of origin for women include Bartholin gland abscess, episiotomy, hysterectomy, and septic abortion. Pediatric sites of origin include insect bites, burns, trauma, and circumcision. About 25% of all cases are judged idiopathic. Resulting inflammation and edema lead to the destruction of affected tissue via endarteritis. Infection tends to dissect along perifascial planes, permitting rapid extension and progression to gangrene. Fascial necrosis in Fournier gangrene can advance at 2–3 cm per hour. Mortality rates, even with aggressive treatment and early identification, are generally 20–40%. The most common microorganisms include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant varieties), and Bacteroides fragilis. Most cases are polymicrobial, with group A Streptococcus being the most common organism in monomicrobial cases.



Bartholin gland abscess (A)and cellulitis (B)are incorrect. Both entities can be the site of origin of Fournier gangrene, but the pathognomonic findings of tissue necrosis, widespread tissue involvement and rapid spread, and severe, woody induration plus risk factors are concerning for progression to necrotizing fasciitis.

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens(D) is incorrect. Findings may be similar, but this disorder is caused by ileofemoral vein thrombosis, which may be extensive enough to result in arterial insufficiency and gangrene. Workup should identify the presence of thrombosis.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 days of myalgias, headache, and low-grade fever. Today, he noticed the lesion on his nose, as shown above. What is the next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, a potentially sight-threatening infection, is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion. Patients often present with a prodrome of fever, headache, malaise, and hypesthesia in the affected eye and forehead, followed by a vesicular rash along the trigeminal dermatome. Discharging with acyclovir (A) is the appropriate treatment for uncomplicated herpes zoster involving a trunk or extremity dermatome.

Question: A 40-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension presents with a large mass on her back. She states that it has been there for roughly 1 year, and the appearance is bothersome to her. She reports no fevers, pain, or restricted motion. On examination, the patient has a 3 cm skin-colored, soft, mobile mass on her back overlying the right scapula. There is no tenderness, induration, or punctum. What is an ultrasound of this mass most likely to show?

Options.text: Anechoic poorly defined structure with collections of internal echogenic fluid
Hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement
Hypoechoic free fluid separating subcutaneous tissue and fat
Hypoechoic well-circumscribed mass with pulsation on color Doppler
Well-circumscribed circular hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic rim

CorrectAnswer: Hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a lipoma. A lipoma is a mass consisting of mature fat cells enclosed in a thin fibrous capsule. Lipomas are typically diagnosed clinically by their appearance as soft, skin-colored, painless nodules ranging from 1 cm to > 10 cm. Occasionally, an ultrasound may be needed to differentiate a lipoma from other skin lesions such as epidermoid cysts or ganglion cysts. Ultrasound commonly shows a hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement. It is important to note that while the majority are hyperechoic or isoechoic, they can occasionally be hypoechoic. Lipomas are benign and do not need to be removed unless bothersome to the patient. Generally, the removal of lipomas requires a surgical referral.



Anechoic poorly defined structure with collections of internal echogenic debris (A) best describes an abscess. Anechoic coloring is due to fluid that does not reflect ultrasound waves, and echogenic debris may represent purulence. In this patient without overlying erythema, pain, or fluctuance, abscess is unlikely.

Hypoechoic free fluid separating subcutaneous tissue and fat (C) describes cobblestoning. Cobblestoning on ultrasound represents edema in the subcutaneous tissue, which may represent cellulitis or simple edema.

Hypoechoic masses with pulsation on color Doppler (D) may represent pseudoaneurysms. In this patient with a mass, one should always evaluate the mass under color Doppler before any incision to ensure the mass does not have pulsatile, arterial blood flow. These most commonly are associated with femoral or radial artery procedures, so this mass over the scapula is most likely not a pseudoaneurysm.

Well-circumscribed circular hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic rim (E) describes an epidermoid cyst. These cysts can be difficult to differentiate from lipomas, as they are also skin-colored and mobile, so ultrasound is the first-line tool used to differentiate the two.

Question: A 74-year-old man presents to the ED with blistering on his extremities. On physical exam, tense bullae are noted on the arms and legs. Nikolsky sign is negative. There is no oral involvement. Which of the following is part of the appropriate treatment for this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms and physical exam findings consistent with bullous pemphigoid. Bullous pemphigoid is a chronic bullous disease that involves IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane (subepidermal). It is the most common bullous disease and is classically seen in adults > 60 years. It may be caused by repeated skin trauma and the presence of other inflammatory skin conditions such as psoriasis. However, it is often idiopathic.

Signs and symptoms include a pruritic rash that evolves into tender, tense bullae occurring most often over the legs, forearms, and axillae. Mucosal involvement is uncommon. Nikolsky sign is negative. Diagnosis is made by needle biopsy to discriminate from pemphigus vulgaris. However, it may be differentiated clinically based on the differences between the two, as pemphigus vulgaris includes oral involvement, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, while bullous pemphigoid does not.

Initial management includes general wound care, steroids (topical or systemic), and doxycycline. This disease process often improves and relapses spontaneously. Dapsone and immunomodulators such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, and methotrexate may be needed for refractory cases. Mortality, though rare, is most commonly caused by sepsis. Overall, bullous pemphigoid has a relatively good prognosis when compared to pemphigus vulgaris.



Burn center admission (A) would be appropriate if this patient had Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). However, there is no evidence of recent infection or medication use and no description of sloughing skin. Additionally, Nikolsky sign is positive in SJS and TEN. Patients with bullous pemphigoid more often follow a prolonged, relapsing and remitting course, and general wound care is recommended instead of burn center care.

Clindamycin (B) would be appropriate for necrotizing fasciitis, which may exhibit blistering but is also characterized by pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, and gas in the tissues. These patients also tend to be febrile and have abnormal vital signs.

Vancomycin (D) would be appropriate for inpatient treatment of severe cellulitis. This would be warranted if he had vital sign abnormalities or had not improved with outpatient treatment for cellulitis. Vancomycin should be reserved for instances of concern regarding methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Question: A 82-year-old patient with history of advanced dementia presents with altered mental status. As part of a full physical evaluation, you note a 4 x 6 cm area of ulceration over the sacrum with exposed adipose tissue and areas of granulation tissue but no visible bone or muscle. A small area of eschar is noted at the superior aspect of the wound. There is no purulent drainage or fluctuance. What is the best next step in management of this pressure injury?

Wet to dry dressing and intravenous antibiotics

ExplanationEN:
Pressure ulcers are graded on a scale of 1 to 4 based on the involvement of various tissues. Stage 3 pressure ulcers are characterized by full thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat may be exposed but bone, muscle, and tendons are not. Granulation tissue is often visible and there may be areas of eschar or slough present. Treatment of pressure ulcers of all stages includes proper positioning of the patient to avoid prolonged pressure in any area, pain management, and optimization of nutrition. Although all ulcers are colonized with bacteria, only those wounds with evidence of active infection should be cultured and treated with antibiotics. Specific wound management varies based on the stage of the ulcer. Stage 3 ulcers should be covered with a dressing that keeps the wound moist while the surrounding skin is kept dry. This can be accomplished with saline-moistened gauze or hydrogel dressing. As necrotic tissue impedes wound healing, surgical consultation for debridement should be requested for patients with ulcers that have overlying necrotic tissue and eschar.



A stage I ulcer consists of intact skin with nonblanching erythema. These ulcers can be covered with a transparent film (A) and special attention should be paid to proper positioning and nutrition to prevent continued injury. Debridement of eschar in the emergency department followed by application of an occlusive, dry dressing (B) is incorrect because wounds should be kept moist to facilitate reepithelialization. Intravenous antibiotics (D) are not indicated in this patient because there is no evidence of superimposed infection, such as surrounding erythema, warmth, foul odor, or purulent drainage.

The infestation of the skin by a female Sarcoptes scabiei mite can cause scabies, an infectious and intensely pruritic illness. The mites mate on the skin surface, and the female then burrows into the skin, creating a shallow well, which she then extends by a few millimeters every 24 hours while laying eggs. The eggs hatch within a few days, and the mite dies in the burrow within a few weeks. Mites not on the skin die within a few days, so transmission is usually through close contact, not through fomites. The mite, mite feces, and eggs cause a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is extremely itchy.

The classic illness is first recognized about a month after primary inoculation by 1–2 mm red papules. The burrows of the female mite are sometimes visible but other times difficult to see due to excoriation. Extreme itching is universal and worse at night. The rash is most prominent in the webs of the fingers, flexor aspects of the wrists, extensor aspects of the elbows, anterior axillary folds, waist, umbilicus, and the lower buttocks and adjacent thighs.

Unusual manifestations are crusted scabies, which occur in immunocompromised patients. It is more severe and diffuse and presents with a prominent scale that becomes almost wart-like with crusts and fissures, but it does not itch. Small infants also often lack the interdigital manifestations with lesions mostly on the trunk.

The treatment for scabies is a permethrin 5% cream, which should be applied to the scalp and entire body from the neck down. This should be left in place for 8–14 hours (depending on the reference text) before rinsing. This should be reapplied in 1 week in a similar fashion. Alternative therapies include sulfur ointment, crotamiton lotion, or lindane lotion. Lindane lotion can cause neurotoxicity (especially in children), should be avoided whenever possible, and is contraindicated in children with poorly controlled seizures. Immunocompromised children are sometimes also treated with oral ivermectin.

Question: A 20-year-old woman is started on lamotrigine after she was diagnosed with epilepsy. She presents to the emergency department with a new-onset rash 10 days after initiating the antiepileptic therapy. She notes that preceding the onset of the rash, she had fevers, malaise, and anorexia. The patient’s temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), blood pressure is 136/73 mm Hg, heart rate is 101 bpm, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical examination reveals multiple exfoliative skin lesions, tender erythema, bullae formation, and mucositis involving approximately 40% of her total body surface area. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Supportive treatment and transfer to a burn center

CorrectAnswer: Supportive treatment and transfer to a burn center
ExplanationEN:
This patient has toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), a potentially life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction that is characterized by exfoliative skin lesions, tender erythema, and bullae formation involving > 30% of total body surface area (TBSA). It is more severe but less common than Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), which typically involves < 10% of TBSA. The most frequent triggers for TEN/SJS are medications, including allopurinol, lamotrigine, antibacterial sulfonamides, nevirapine, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). After medications, the next most common trigger is Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Patients often exhibit a prodromal phase of fever, malaise, and anorexia for 1–2 weeks. The onset of the characteristic rash can occur anywhere from 4 days to 4 weeks after continuous use of the medication. The majority of cases of TEN/SJS have mucosal lesions. Treatment includes cessation of the suspected offending medication and supportive treatment, including intravenous fluid resuscitation, electrolyte replacement, wound care, infection prevention, and pain control. Patients with signs of infection should be promptly covered with antibiotics. However, prophylactic antibiotics are not generally recommended. After supportive treatment is initiated, definitive care should be continued at a burn unit, if available.



Dermatology consultation (A) and surgical debridement (D) are not routinely indicated in the initial, acute treatment of TEN/SJS. The use of corticosteroids (B) in the management of TEN is controversial as there is conflicting evidence regarding improvement in mortality and complication rates associated with their use.

Question: A 5-month-old male infant presents to the ED, brought by his parent, for a severe rash. She states the baby has been teething recently and has been having several loose stools per day. The baby is in daycare, and the childcare workers are not able to change his diapers as frequently as he is stooling. On examination, he has an erythematous perianal rash with denuded skin but no satellite lesions. Which of the following is the recommended first-line therapy?
ExplanationEN:
Diaper dermatitis is a common pediatric problem and is caused and exacerbated by overhydration of the skin from prolonged skin contact with feces and urine. Peak incidence is 9–12 months of age. Simple measures can be taken to improve and prevent diaper dermatitis. Infant skin benefits from diaper-free periods, allowing the skin to air dry. Cleaning is best done by patting the skin (as opposed to vigorously scrubbing) with a soft cloth and using lukewarm water. Commercial wipes impregnated with fragrance, alcohol, or other chemicals may further irritate the skin. Superabsorbent disposable diapers help maintain a dry environment. Additionally, a protective barrier ointment or paste containing either zinc oxide or petroleum should be used at every diaper change. Other options for complex cases include low-potency topical corticosteroids and sucralfate, which has antibacterial properties. Some rashes may become secondarily infected with Candida species and require topical antifungal therapy. Candida lesions are typically well-demarcated, erythematous lesions with smaller satellite lesions that are separate from the larger areas of dermatitis. Parents should be educated about these measures to prevent further instances of diaper rash. An acronym to remember these is ABCDE: air, barrier, cleansing, diaper, education.



Betamethasone cream (A) is a higher-potency topical corticosteroid that is not safe for infants’ thin skin.

Mupirocin ointment (B) is used to treat impetigo due to gram-positive skin flora.

Topical clotrimazole (C) is an azole antifungal that may be required for secondary fungal infection from Candida species. However, this is not typically the first-line treatment for a rash that does not appear to have fungal elements.

Question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for oral lesions for 3 weeks. She has multiple oral lesions that are painful to the touch and with oral intake of food and fluids. She has not had similar symptoms in the past. She had negative serum HIV viral load, oral herpes simplex virus, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis tests 1 week ago. She reports no other associated symptoms. Physical examination shows over 50 ulcers that are 0.5–1 cm in diameter and well-defined with a thin ring of erythema and a white base. There is no significant oral edema, intolerance of secretions, or stridor. A full surface skin examination reveals no other lesions. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Aphthous ulcers (commonly called canker sores) are defined as discrete, painful, 3–5 mm oval ulcers with a rim of erythema and a white or yellow adherent central exudate located in the oral cavity. Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) is the regular recurrence of multiple ulcers that last up to 14 days. Some patients present with complex RAS, when the lesions last 4–6 weeks, occur more frequently, may be associated with similar genital lesions, and are larger in diameter. RAS can be treated with topical agents. Clobetasol 0.05% gel three times daily and sucralfate rinse four times daily are the most commonly available, effective, and tolerated treatments. Patients with complex RAS rarely achieve control of symptoms with topical therapies. Patients with a large number of ulcers (like this patient), a history of recurrence, or symptoms lasting longer than 14 days (also this patient) are likely to require a 4–7 day course of oral prednisone 20–40 mg once daily. Furthermore, for patients with refractory disease not controlled by topical therapies, oral corticosteroids are best.



Oral lidocaine suspension (B) would likely provide relief of this patient’s symptoms in the short term but is not a sustainable treatment. Oral lidocaine suspensions require frequent redosing, are less effective than corticosteroids, and may be associated with methemoglobinemia in the setting of overuse. Intravenous corticosteroids (C) are unnecessary for the treatment of aphthous stomatitis. Oral treatment is sufficient. Topical corticosteroids (D) are the best initial treatment for patients with RAS who do not have features of complex disease. This patient’s numerous ulcers and duration of symptoms suggest that systemic treatment would be beneficial.

Question: A 17-year-old boy with a history of asthma presents with an itchy, scaly rash on his arms and legs. He states he has had the rash on and off for years but has never been on treatment for it. The itching is severe and keeps him up at night. Vital signs include a BP of 112/74 mm Hg, HR of 68 bpm, RR of 16/minute, and a T of 98.8°F. Physical examination reveals erythematous areas to the bilateral antecubital and popliteal fossae, which are thick and leathery with excoriations. What management is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with an exacerbation of atopic dermatitis requiring topical corticosteroid treatment. It is a common dermatologic condition. It is often referred to as eczema or chronic dermatitis. Patients with atopic dermatitis have abnormal humoral and cell-mediated immunity, but the exact mechanism of the disease is unknown. There is an increased risk of atopic dermatitis in individuals with a personal or family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis.

Atopic dermatitis may be acute or chronic. Acute disease usually presents as intensely pruritic erythematous skin lesions with papules, vesicles, exudation, and crusting. The lesions of chronic atopic dermatitis are still erythematous and pruritic but with associated scaling, excoriations, and lichenification (skin thickening). In infants ages 0 to 2 years of age, the lesions are most commonly on the face, trunk, or extensor surfaces. In adolescents and adults, the flexor surfaces (i.e., antecubital and popliteal fossae), wrists, ankles, face, and hands are most likely to be involved. It is a chronic disease that waxes and wanes and is often worse in the winter, when the weather is cold and dry, and when the skin is exposed to irritants such as certain soaps, lotions, detergents, or cleaning products.

In general, treatment is directed at controlling inflammation, dryness, and itching. The mainstay of treatment for patients’ atopic dermatitis is topical corticosteroids, including hydrocortisone, desonide, fluocinolone, and triamcinolone. Antihistamines may also be necessary for symptomatic relief. In addition, patients should be advised to avoid scented products, wear lightweight clothing, avoid hot baths, and wash clothing in dye-free, unscented detergent.



Oral cephalexin (A), a first-generation cephalosporin, may be used for cellulitis or other bacterial infections. However, atopic dermatitis is not caused by bacteria, and thus cephalexin is not indicated for its treatment. Cellulitis is associated with acute erythema, warmth, and edema of the skin but does not appear in a symmetrical pattern or chronically over many years.

Oral steroids, such as prednisone (B), are rarely used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis, as topical agents are adequate, and systemic corticosteroids are associated with more adverse effects and risk of rebound of symptoms after discontinuation. Oral prednisone may be used if symptoms are severe and require rapid relief during acute exacerbation. This patient does not have symptoms that are severe enough to warrant systemic corticosteroids.

Topical clindamycin (C) is an antibacterial agent that may be used for the treatment of acne vulgaris or rosacea but is not useful for atopic dermatitis. Acne vulgaris presents with comedones, pustules, or papules, most commonly on the face, upper torso, or proximal arms. Rosacea is associated with facial erythema and papules, pustules, telangiectasia, or rhinophyma.

Topical silver sulfadiazine (E) is a topical antibiotic that is most often used for burn wounds but is not useful for the treatment of atopic dermatitis. This patient has no history of a burn.

Question: A 12-year-old boy presents with intermittent abdominal pain and a rash as seen in the image above. There is no fever. Which of the following is a complication of this disease?
ExplanationEN:
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a small vessel vasculitis caused by the deposition of immune complexes in blood vessels. In approximately half of cases, it is preceded by an upper respiratory infection. It is also induced by vancomycin, cefuroxime, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. HSP is characterized by palpable purpura as well as gastrointestinal and kidney symptoms. The disease almost always occurs under the age of 20, and children < 5 years are more frequently affected. Classically, symptoms appear 1–2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. The triad of signs and symptoms is purpura, arthralgias, and abdominal pain. The purpura typically affect dependent regions of the body and thus are seen on the legs and buttocks. Patients develop colicky abdominal pain and may even have hematochezia due to gastrointestinal vasculitis. Rarely, intussusception occurs. Kidney manifestations include glomerulonephritis presenting with hematuria, red cell casts, and azotemia. Treatment is supportive.



Aseptic meningitis (A) is not associated with HSP.

Coronary artery abnormalities (B) are a complication of Kawasaki disease in children. Signs of Kawasaki disease include fever for > 5 days, strawberry tongue, cervical adenopathy, conjunctivitis, and desquamation.

Diarrhea (C) is not a classic complication of HSP. Approximately 30% of children develop bloody stool from gastrointestinal vasculitis and may even show obstructive symptoms if they develop intussusception.

Question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the ED with tender erythematous nodules on the anterior surface of the lower extremities, as shown above. She was ill 3 weeks ago with a headache, fever, and sore throat that lasted 4 days. She had been doing well until the nodules appeared yesterday. What is the most appropriate treatment for her symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Ibuprofen is the most appropriate treatment because the patient presents with erythema nodosum, which is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. NSAIDs help reduce pain, swelling, and inflammation in the subcutaneous fat, which is the hallmark of erythema nodosum.

Erythema nodosum is an inflammatory condition that affects the dermis and subcutaneous fat, characterized by tender, erythematous or violaceous nodules, most often located on the anterior shins. These nodules may also appear on the arms or trunk and are frequently preceded by fever or joint pain, especially in the ankles or knees. As the nodules evolve, they often take on a yellow-purple hue and may resemble bruises. The condition is more common in women aged 30–50 years.

Erythema nodosum is associated with various underlying conditions, including infections (streptococcal pharyngitis, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis), inflammatory diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease), pregnancy, malignancy, and medications (oral contraceptives, sulfonamides such as sulfasalazine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, penicillins, cephalosporins, minocycline, phenytoin, NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen, bromides, and methotrexate). Despite these associations, about half of all cases have no identifiable cause.

Treatment focuses on identifying and treating the underlying etiology. Supportive care includes leg elevation, rest, and use of elastic stockings to relieve discomfort and swelling. NSAIDs can help alleviate pain, and in more severe cases, potassium iodide may be prescribed. The condition is self-limited, resolving within 3 to 8 weeks.



Amoxicillin (A) would be appropriate if she had an ongoing streptococcal infection, but her prior illness resolved 3 weeks ago, so antibiotics are not indicated now.

Azithromycin (B) is used for atypical bacterial infections like Mycoplasma, which is not the cause here, especially with a classic history of recent Streptococcus-like illness.

Prednisone (D) may be considered in severe or refractory erythema nodosum, but it is not first line and should be avoided unless necessary due to potential immunosuppressive effects.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, diabetes, and coronary artery bypass graft presents with a rash. This morning, she awoke with a fever of 101.2°F (38.4ºC) accompanied by right leg myalgias. An erythematous rash subsequently appeared on her right calf and has begun to rapidly spread up her leg. She states that the rash is intensely painful. Physical exam reveals an erythematous rash with overlying bullae. What additional finding would best support the diagnosis of erysipelas rather than necrotizing fasciitis?

Options.text: Pain out of proportion to exam

ExplanationEN:
Erysipelas is an infection of the superficial lymphatics and upper dermis. It is characterized by profound erythema and marked dermal edema resulting in well-demarcated borders. It may also present with a peau d’orange appearance, as well as with vesicles, bullae, and lymphangitis. The rate of spread is often rapid, and accordingly, early necrotizing fasciitis must be ruled out. Risk factors for erysipelas include lymphatic dysfunction, venous insufficiency, edema, and immunocompromise. While erysipelas is classically thought of as occurring on the face, 80% of cases will present in the lower extremities. Group A streptococci are responsible for most cases of facial erysipelas, and a history of pharyngitis preceding the infection is not uncommon. Alternatively, lower extremity infections are more likely to include group B, C, F, and G Streptococcus. Penicillin is the antibiotic of choice for mild cases of erysipelas. However, more severe cases require cefazolin or vancomycin.



Crepitus (A) occurs with necrotizing fasciitis, not erysipelas. The sound of crepitus is crackling under the skin due to gas-forming organisms like Clostridium perfringens.

Pain out of proportion to the exam (B) is always a concerning finding for soft tissue infections and is suggestive of a severe infection. It can be present in necrotizing fasciitis. However, anesthesia to touch can also be present depending on the stage of infection.

Skin sloughing (C) occurs more often with necrotizing fasciitis. However, erysipelas can have areas of necrosis, and in the resolving phase, desquamation can occur.

Question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a painful rash in her axilla. Physical examination reveals the finding above. She notes she has had episodes of this same rash for the past 2 years. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Hidradenitis suppurativa is a relapsing and remitting inflammatory condition in the areas where there are apocrine glands (most commonly the axillary region). It presents with painful, recurrent nodules and abscess formation, often with cellulitis. It is more common in individuals who have an overweight BMI. The diagnosis is made based on the clinical picture of relapsing and remitting symptoms. Treatment is focused on prevention with good hygiene, including antibacterial soaps and topical antibiotics such as clindamycin. Oral antibiotics are indicated when cellulitis is present. Incision and drainage should be performed if a large abscess is present. However, given the chronic nature of this condition, incision and drainage should be used judiciously, as scarring can occur if performed regularly.



Cellulitis (A) presents with redness, warmth, and tenderness to palpation of the skin with cobblestoning seen on ultrasound. While cellulitis may be present in this patient, the underlying cause of their relapsing symptoms is better explained by hidradenitis suppurativa.

Necrotizing fasciitis (C) presents with erythema, warmth, tenderness, crepitus (if a gas-producing organism is present), fever, hemodynamic instability, and rapidly progressive symptoms. Remarkable tenderness to palpation is noted on exam, and patients are often ill appearing.

Pyoderma gangrenosum (D) is associated with autoimmune conditions (such as inflammatory bowel disease) and malignancy. It may present with a seemingly pyogenic wound (though no infection is present) with ulceration and a violaceous border. Treatment is focused on addressing the underlying cause.

Question: A 69-year-old woman presents with a rash on her arm that began with several “very itchy spots” about 2 weeks ago. She is concerned since it appears to be getting worse and more widespread. Her skin examination is shown above. Her oropharynx is clear. She reports no fevers, travel, or sick contacts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Bullous pemphigoid is a type of blistering disease of the skin. The typical patient is between 60 and 80 years old, and there is an equal incidence in men and women. It is an inflammatory autoimmune disease due to immunoglobulin G autoantibodies against proteins in the basement membrane zone between the dermis and epidermis. Thus, the cleavage point is relatively deep, yielding thick, tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign (lateral pressure on normal skin adjacent to a lesion does not dislodge the epidermis). Bullae develop from significantly pruritic urticarial plaques and papules on normal or erythematous skin over a period of weeks to months. This disease can persist for years, and the bullae eventually rupture, resulting in crusts and erosions. The trunk and extremities are the sites most often involved, while mucous membrane involvement is uncommon. Autoantibodies can be detected in most patients and about half will show blood eosinophilia. Diagnosis requires histopathology and immunofluorescence studies in consultation with a dermatologist.

Treatment includes high-potency topical steroids if the disease is localized or oral prednisone or doxycycline for extensive disease. Immunosuppressant medications such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, and methotrexate are also used. Many patients require treatment for years to achieve long-term remission. The course of the disease is usually benign, although fatalities are possible, usually due to sepsis from infection or treatment complications.



Pemphigus vulgaris (B)is a life-threatening autoimmune blistering disease with an intraepidermal cleavage plane producing large, fragile bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign. Most patients have mucous membrane involvement.

Pustular psoriasis (C) usually presents with large amounts of small vesicles filled with whitish fluid on erythematous, tender skin. Patients are often febrile and acutely ill, particularly if the lesions are generalized.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (D)is a poorly understood life-threatening condition, most likely representing the same process as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and erythema multiforme, but involving > 30% of the body surface area. Large, flaccid bullae may develop within hours on erythematous, tender skin, which leads to shedding of the epidermis in large sheets. The Nikolsky sign is positive and mucous membrane involvement is common and extensive.

Question: An otherwise healthy 38-year-old man reports 6 days of a painful boil on his upper back. Vital signs are BP of 128/82 mm Hg, HR of 70 bpm, RR of 16/min, and T of 98.6°F. He has been applying warm compresses to the area, but it is increasing in size and the pain is worsening. On exam, you palpate a 1 x 1 cm erythematous, tender, fluctuant abscess without induration or surrounding cellulitis. What is the most appropriate treatment?

Options.text: Continue warm compresses and discharge home
Perform incision and drainage and prescribe IV antibiotics
Perform incision and drainage and prescribe oral antibiotics

ExplanationEN:
Incision and drainage only are the recommended treatments for simple abscesses in otherwise healthy patients. Abscesses are formed by collections of pus in the dermis and deeper layers of the skin most often as a result of infection, usually Staphylococcus aureus. They present as painful, erythematous, fluctuant, and tender nodules with or without surrounding erythema that may spontaneously drain purulent material. Systemic symptoms are uncommon.

Furuncles and carbuncles are two forms of abscesses caused by infected hair follicles that occur most commonly in areas of friction and perspiration, such as the axillae, buttocks, back of the neck, and face. A furuncle is a single small abscess in the subcutaneous tissue that develops as a result of an infected hair follicle, while a carbuncle consists of a collection of several infected hair follicles that produce a single abscess. Larger furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses require incision and drainage.

Untreated abscesses may lead to cellulitis and systemic infections. Recurrent infections in the same location are usually the result of a local defect such as a cyst, hidradenitis suppurativa, or a retained foreign body, but immunodeficiency should be considered in a patient with recurrent infections arising in multiple sites.

Incision and drainage

Warm compresses (A) are recommended and usually sufficient for small skin abscesses. Most small abscesses will drain spontaneously and resolve without further intervention. Treatment with warm compresses failed in this case.

IV antibiotics (B) are indicated only in the most severe cases in immunocompromised individuals or when there are signs of serious systemic infection. In these cases, IV antibiotics are started prior to incision and drainage. Appropriate IV antibiotics include vancomycin and daptomycin.

Oral antibiotics (C) are indicated when there is surrounding cellulitis, in immunocompromised individuals, or when there are signs of systemic infection. Appropriate oral antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and minocycline.

Only prescribing antibiotics (E) is not an effective therapy for a simple abscess since incision and drainage optimizes the likelihood of cure.

Question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pruritus of his skin. He went camping yesterday evening and noticed symptoms this morning. He reports wearing sunblock appropriately. His T is 98°F (36.7°C), BP is 120/81 mm Hg, HR is 72 bpm, RR is 14/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. The physical exam is shown above. This skin finding is primarily on his extremities but is also found on the face and torso. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

Options.text: Topical emollients and topical triamcinolone with oral prednisone

CorrectAnswer: Topical emollients and topical triamcinolone with oral prednisone
ExplanationEN:
Allergic contact dermatitis is a hypersensitivity reaction (type IV) that occurs when exposed to certain antigens. Allergic contact dermatitis presents with erythema and vesicles and is often confined to the site of exposure, with some minor spreading beyond this area. This patient is likely experiencing allergic contact dermatitis based on his exposure to plants while camping. Irritant contact dermatitis presents similarly but is more directly confined to the site of exposure, and dry skin and scaling may be additional features. It is more commonly associated with chemical exposures.

Common exposures that lead to allergic contact dermatitis include detergents, fragrances, makeup, nickel, poison oak, and poison ivy. Patients will often present with intense pruritus in the distribution of exposure. A dermatologic exam will reveal vesicles, bullae, and scaly plaques that are erythematous. Patients with limited symptoms may be treated with symptomatic therapy involving topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines for symptom control. Facial involvement can be treated with topical tacrolimus. Topical emollients are also recommended as an adjunct to mitigate symptoms. Severe cases with symptoms affecting a large percentage of the total body surface area (such as in this patient) should be treated with systemic steroids (prednisone) and often require a 2- to 4-week course to control and avoid rebound symptoms. Patients should be advised to find the underlying cause and avoid further exposure.



Topical emollients (A) are a part of the therapy for contact dermatitis. However, they are more strongly recommended when treating irritant contact dermatitis, not allergic contact dermatitis. In any case, topical emollients alone would not be appropriate, as contact dermatitis typically involves treatment with topical corticosteroids. Given this patient’s severe symptoms and significant total body surface area involvement, topical therapy alone would not be appropriate.

Topical emollients and oral cephalexin (B) would be appropriate if contact dermatitis and skin breakdown led to secondary cellulitis. Cellulitis presents with warmth, tenderness, and erythema of the skin. Antibiotics are not given empirically for patients with contact dermatitis.

Topical emollients and topical triamcinolone (C) is the appropriate management of limited contact dermatitis without severe symptoms. This patient’s involvement of his torso, face, and extremities would not make this the best treatment regimen.

Question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the ED with 2 days of bloody diarrhea and a lower extremity rash. The patient is well-appearing and interactive on exam. Vital signs are within normal limits. Her abdominal exam is benign. She has palpable purpura on her lower extremities. Laboratory evaluation reveals a creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL and proteinuria. Which of the following kidney pathologies is most likely responsible for her condition?
ExplanationEN:
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is an IgA vasculitis seen in school-aged children and young adults. Classic manifestations include purpura, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and kidney disease. Glomerular involvement leads to elevated creatinine, hematuria, proteinuria, and nephritis in up to 50% of cases. Permanent kidney injury may occur in up to 2% of children.

Patients suspected of having IgAV should have a urinalysis and creatinine ordered. Kidney manifestations of IgAV include microscopic or gross hematuria, proteinuria, and nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic-range proteinuria, elevated creatinine, and hypertension are present in a minority of patients, but they are concerning for significant kidney involvement and are associated with an increased risk of disease progression. Treatment is mainly supportive and includes rest, hydration, and pain control. Nephrology consultation is indicated for kidney involvement. Steroid therapy may improve the severity of kidney involvement but does not decrease its incidence.



Interstitial (B) kidney injuries can be infectious (e.g., pyelonephritis, kidney abscess) or drug-induced (e.g., penicillin) or due to systemic illnesses (e.g., lupus, sarcoid).

Prerenal (C) causes of acute kidney injury include those that lead to renal hypoperfusion. These include volume loss (e.g., hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea), low cardiac output, renal artery stenosis, and medication toxicities (e.g., NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors).

Tubular (D) kidney injuries include acute tubular necrosis from ischemia or hemorrhage or toxin exposure (e.g., aminoglycosides, ethylene glycol) that leads to an inability to concentrate urine.

Question: A 30-year-old man presents with a genital rash. He had a similar rash in the same location several years ago while being treated for a skin infection. It is painless, and he has no systemic symptoms. He recently started taking doxycycline for acne. On physical exam, there is a solitary, reddish brown, nonulcerating macule on the glans penis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is a cutaneous delayed hypersensitivity reaction defined by single or multiple lesions that recur at the same anatomic location upon reexposure to the drug. Common triggering medications include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, tetracyclines, penicillins), antimalarials, and anticonvulsants. The characteristic rash is a single or multiple well-demarcated, dusky, brown to red ovoid macules that may blister or ulcerate. Patients may be asymptomatic or have associated pruritus and burning. The rash can occur anywhere on the body, but the most common anatomic sites are the extremities, lips, genitals, hands, and feet. Onset is typically days to weeks upon initial exposure to the inciting agent and minutes to hours after reexposure. Upon reexposure, the rash characteristically recurs at the same anatomic location. Clinical variants include generalized FDE, which involves disseminated lesions on the trunk and extremities that may mimic erythema multiforme, and bullous FDE, which can be localized or generalized and may mimic Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The diagnosis is made clinically based on the characteristic appearance and history and may be difficult to diagnose on the first presentation. The mainstay of treatment is withdrawal and avoidance of the offending agent. The rash typically resolves within 7–10 days but often leaves residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines can be used for symptomatic treatment. This patient’s typical-appearing rash on the genitals, in combination with the history of rash in the same location during treatment for a skin infection for which he presumably was prescribed a tetracycline, suggests FDE.



Chancroid (A) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi that presents with multiple painful genital ulcers and regional lymphadenopathy. While FDE on the genitals can mimic a sexually transmitted infection when it ulcerates, the presence of a single painless, nonulcerating lesion suggests against chancroid. Contact dermatitis (B) occurs in response to a localized exposure and is usually intensely pruritic. In contrast, FDE is less pruritic and more clearly demarcated and hyperpigmented. Additionally, there will be a history of similar rash in response to systemic, as opposed to local, exposure. Primary syphilis (D) presents with a painless genital ulcer and may be confused with FDE that ulcerates, especially on the first presentation. The lack of ulcer and history of similar rash suggest against syphilis.

Options.text: Defer antimicrobial therapy until microbiological testing is performed
Oral analgesics and local wound care

ExplanationEN:
Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus species. It is known to be contagious and typically affects children ages 2–5 years. It can be primary due to direct bacterial invasion of normal skin or secondary due to associated minor skin trauma. Impetigo typically occurs in warm, humid conditions and spreads via close contact with infected individuals. The rash of impetigo is most common on the face and other exposed areas and begins as a single pustule that progresses to multiple lesions that form a golden-yellow crust. Pruritus and regional lymphadenopathy may be present but pain is usually not. Fever and other systemic infectious signs are usually absent as well. Diagnosis is made clinically, but microbiological testing may be obtained to rule out other potential causes, such as herpes simplex virus and superficial fungal infections, but treatment can be instituted prior to results of these tests being available.

For simple, uncomplicated cases of impetigo, topical antibiotics are used as first-line therapy. Mupirocin and bacitracin are the two most frequently used drugs for this purpose, while minocycline, retapamulin, and ozenoxacin are alternate options. Oral antibiotics are indicated for patients with severe, extensive lesions or lesions at multiple sites. First-line oral antibiotics are cephalexin and dicloxacillin, but doxycycline, clindamycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be used in cases when methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is suspected. Fortunately, impetigo generally resolves in 3–6 weeks even without treatment, but it can be complicated by poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.



Microbiological testing (A), often in the form of bacterial Gram strain and culture or viral PCR, may be obtained for definitive diagnosis, but treatment can be instituted prior to the results of these tests returning. The patient’s facial lesions are classic for impetigo and less suspicious for herpes simplex virus, so acyclovir (B) would not be the first-line empiric therapy in this case. Because the lesions are not painful, oral analgesia (C) would be of little benefit in this patient, and failure to treat with antibiotics could result in a longer disease course and potential complications (e.g., poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis). Oral cephalexin (D) may be used for the treatment of impetigo when systemic antibiotics are indicated, but this patient’s single site of infection and relatively mild disease do not represent such indications. Topical antibiotics would be an appropriate first step.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents to the ED with areas of hair loss that have been progressively enlarging for several weeks. His physical examination demonstrates scattered areas of alopecia with peripheral scaling. There is no fluorescence under Wood lamp examination. What is the most appropriate management?
ExplanationEN:
Tinea capitis describes the fungal infection of the hair shaft and stratum corneum of the scalp skin. The most common isolated dermatophytes are from the Trichophyton genus, followed by Microsporum. Clinical findings include patchy, nonscarring areas of hair loss with peripheral hair breakage and scaling. Associated inflammation may cause lesions to be indurated, boggy, or tender, and lymphadenopathy may be present. Secondary permanent scarring and alopecia may develop in patients with long-standing infection. Wood lamp examination will fail to fluoresce if the dermatophytic infection is related to Trichophyton. Microsporum does fluoresce. The diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by a positive potassium hydroxide preparation. Fungal cultures take 3–4 weeks for results and are typically not pursued. Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungal therapy, and first-line agents include oral terbinafine or oral griseofulvin.



Oral itraconazole (A) is used to treat a variety of fungal infections, but there is limited evidence to suggest that it sufficiently treats Trichophyton or Microsporum species. It also is not approved for the treatment of dermatophytes in the pediatric population. If used, it would be recommended after failure of griseofulvin or terbinafine. Topical griseofulvin (C) may be used to treat other types of tinea (e.g., tinea pedis, tinea cruris) but is insufficient in treating tinea capitis. Topical permethrin (D) is useful in the treatment of many arthropod infections affecting the scalp (e.g., pediculosis capitis, scabies) but not tinea capitis.

Question: A 32-year-old woman presents with tender lower extremity nodules, as shown above. Which of the following is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Sarcoidosis is associated with the most likely diagnosis of erythema nodosum, which presents as tender, erythematous subcutaneous nodules on the shins.

Erythema nodosum is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction that most commonly presents as bilateral, erythematous, subcutaneous, and tender nodules on the anterior and lateral aspects of the lower extremities, especially over the pretibial region. The condition affects the female population aged 10–40 years old and may be preceded by nonspecific systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, headache, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Joint pain or swelling, particularly in the ankles, may also occur.

In over one-third of cases, no identifiable cause is found. When a cause is identified, common etiologies include systemic inflammatory conditions (e.g., sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease), medications (e.g., oral contraceptives, sulfonamides), pregnancy, and infections. Infectious triggers include streptococcal pharyngitis, Salmonella, and certain fungal pathogens such as Coccidioides, Histoplasma, and Blastomyces species.

The diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the lesion and the patient’s history. Skin biopsy is rarely needed but may be considered in atypical presentations. Laboratory tests such as a throat culture, chest radiograph, or stool studies may be warranted to identify underlying causes.

Treatment focuses on treating the underlying condition when known and providing supportive care. Recommended interventions include rest, leg elevation, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain relief. The nodules resolve spontaneously within 2–8 weeks without scarring, although recurrence may occur if the underlying trigger persists.



Human leukocyte antigen B27 seropositivity (A) is associated with psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis, and reactive arthritis.

Intravenous drug use (B) is a risk factor for developing cellulitis and abscesses due to inadequate cleaning of skin or dirty needles. It is also a risk factor for developing infective endocarditis, which may present with cutaneous findings such as Janeway lesions and Osler nodes.

Tick bite (D) is associated with Lyme disease, which may present with erythema migrans, classically described as a bull’s-eye rash.

Question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to pain with eating. For the past 3 weeks, he has had painful ulcers in the mouth that wax and wane in quantity and severity but never completely resolve. He has also been experiencing vague abdominal cramping and constant diarrhea. His HR is 80 bpm, BP is 145/90 mm Hg, RR is 16/min, and SpO2 is 98% on room air.
