ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with severe aphthous stomatitis based on the description of the lesions. Aphthous stomatitis can result from transient and benign autoimmune and infectious processes but may also be the result of a more severe underlying disease. Behçet syndrome is a rare form of autoimmune vasculitis that affects vessels of all sizes. It most commonly presents in men between 20 and 40 years of age. Numerous and recurrent painful aphthous ulcers are the most common manifestation. Similar lesions appear on the scrotum or vulva of up to 75% of patients with Behçet syndrome. Bilateral uveitis (sometimes with hypopyon), skin lesions, and cutaneous lesions are the other most obvious physical exam findings that are highly associated with the diagnosis. If untreated, Behçet syndrome can lead to retinal damage, large vessel aneurysms, severe venous thromboembolic disease, and damage to the cerebral parenchyma. Treatment of oral and genital ulcers with topical corticosteroids and sucralfate mouthwash is recommended. Symptoms in other organ systems should prompt specialty referral as recommendations change based on the severity of the disease. Ocular, gastrointestinal, and vascular manifestations often require prompt treatment with systemic glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing therapies.



Erythema nodosum (A) is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is associated with streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, and tuberculosis. It is also one of the possible cutaneous manifestations of Behçet syndrome but is uncommon compared to genital lesions. A pericardial friction rub (B) is most commonly seen in the setting of pericarditis. Behçet syndrome rarely leads to significant cardiac involvement. Symmetrical small joint arthritis (D) is not a common feature of Behçet syndrome. Arthritis in the setting of Behçet syndrome is typically asymmetric and affects more proximal joints. Unilateral uveitis (E) would not be expected in the setting of a systemic inflammatory condition such as Behçet syndrome. Uveitis is more likely to be bilateral.

Question: A 59-year-old woman presents to the ED with a rash. She initially developed small blisters in her mouth, and a few weeks later a rash appeared on her skin. She reports that the rash has been progressively worsening and is now painful when the skin rubs off. She has a history of hypertension and takes lisinopril. She lives alone in her rural home in the southwestern United States. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Her skin exam shows scattered flaccid, thin-walled bullae on an erythematous base, predominantly involving the trunk and proximal extremities. What is the mechanism underlying this patient’s most likely disease process?

Options.text: Blister formation from underlying viral infection and intranuclear inclusion body formation
Bullae and blister formation from deposition of immunoglobulin G autoantibodies
Toxin-mediated blister formation and sloughing of skin
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to a medication

CorrectAnswer: Bullae and blister formation from deposition of immunoglobulin G autoantibodies
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s story and physical exam are consistent with pemphigus vulgaris. This is a generalized, mucocutaneous, blistering disease characterized by the presence of vesicles or bullae throughout the body. The blistering lesions also involve the mucous membranes. The blisters start out clear and tense. After 2–3 days, the bullae become flaccid and cloudy. Then they rupture, causing extreme pain. The ruptured lesions are often prone to infection. The Nikolsky sign, removal of intact superficial epidermis by shearing forces, is positive in pemphigus vulgaris. It is important to obtain an accurate history to be able to differentiate this rash from other blistering diseases. Pemphigus is an autoimmune disorder characterized by bullae and blisters that develop from the deposition of immunoglobulin G autoantibodies in the epithelial cell surface. A biopsy is required to make an official diagnosis.

Treatment includes care of volume depletion and electrolyte imbalance, typically in a burn unit. Oral glucocorticoids should be administered. Other therapeutic options include immunosuppressive treatments, intravenous immunoglobulins, immunoadsorption, or rituximab. Antibiotics should be reserved for patients who have lesions complicated by infection.



Blister formation from underlying viral infection and intranuclear inclusion body formation (A) is the pathophysiology behind infection with the herpes simplex virus. This patient’s bullous, blistering disorder is not characteristic of herpes simplex infection.

Toxin-mediated blister formation and sloughing of the skin (C) is the pathophysiology behind staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. This syndrome is a bacterial exotoxin-mediated skin disorder characterized by skin erythema and desquamation. The skin resembles the look of a deep red sunburn. As the disease progresses, patients develop flaccid bullae and a wrinkled skin appearance, accompanied by sloughing of the skin in areas subjected to friction forces. This rash is different from pemphigus in that it does not involve the mucous membranes.

A type IV hypersensitivity reaction to a medication (D) can present with a spectrum of rashes including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis exhibit skin erythema, bullae formation, mucous membrane involvement, and subsequent skin exfoliation. Question: A 32-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with rapid swelling and foul-smelling discharge from the right lower extremity. Systemic illness commonly occurs, leading to fever, tachycardia, and septic shock. Type II infections are monomicrobial and are most commonly caused by group A streptococci, but community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus accounts for a subset of cases. Question: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a rash. She has felt generally fatigued for a week and developed a rash yesterday that has rapidly worsened. Physical exam is as shown above, and the patient also has lesions in the mouth. Which of the following medications is most likely to be the cause of the patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s rash is consistent with a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) due to the use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. TEN is a severe dermatologic disease characterized by tender erythema, bullae formation, mucous membrane lesions, and skin desquamation. There are multiple causes, but the most common is medications. Sulfa and penicillin antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and oxicam anti-inflammatories are most frequently implicated. Malignancy and human immunodeficiency virus infection can also cause TEN, although an etiology is not always identified.

TEN can develop in patients of all ages and is thought to be a more severe form of Stevens-Johnson syndrome that involves > 30% of body surface area. Patients will present as systemically ill and may experience a 1- to 2-week prodrome of malaise, anorexia, fevers, and arthralgias. Skin signs typically begin with warm erythema involving the eyes, nose, mouth, and genitalia, but the areas can rapidly become tender and confluent. This is followed by the development of flaccid bullae that demonstrate a positive Nikolsky sign. The epidermis is then shed in large sheets, resulting in widespread skin desquamation. The average time of onset after exposure to an inciting agent is 2 weeks, but cutaneous extension can demonstrate rapid, extensive progression. Similar to Stevens-Johnson syndrome, patients will have mucous membrane involvement that may lead to airway compromise due to sloughing of the airway and respiratory epithelium. Mucous membrane lesions may precede the skin manifestations by 1–3 days. The discomfort from oral lesions can impair oral intake, leading to hypovolemia. Ocular involvement may lead to conjunctivitis, painful erosions, and potential blindness. Anogenital lesions are also common manifestations of mucous membrane involvement.

The mortality rate in TEN is as high as 30%, with the primary causes of death being infection and hypovolemia with electrolyte disorders. Factors associated with a poor prognosis include extensive body surface area involvement, increased age, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum urea, bicarbonate, creatinine, and glucose levels. Treatment requires hospitalization in an ICU or burn unit, airway management as needed, management of hypovolemia and electrolyte imbalances, and antibiotic administration for infection. Prophylactic antibiotics are generally not recommended. If an offending agent is identified, it should be immediately discontinued. Steroids should be avoided, as their use can lead to worse outcomes.



Colchicine (A) is not typically associated with TEN, but cases have been attributed to the use of allopurinol, which is also used to treat gout.

Lamotrigine, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are anticonvulsants that have often been involved in cases of TEN. However, an association with levetiracetam (B) is much less common.

Anti-inflammatories are often implicated, but the oxicam anti-inflammatories, such as meloxicam, are more characteristically associated with TEN than naproxen (C). Ibuprofen and diclofenac have also been identified as causative agents in case reports.

Question: A 15-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with redness and a rash on her face. This patient presents with impetigo, a contagious superficial bacterial infection most frequently found in children. It usually occurs in warm, humid conditions and is highly transmissible from one individual to another. It is most often found on the face, neck, and extremities. Risk factors for the infection include poverty, crowding, poor hygiene, minor cutaneous trauma, and underlying scabies. Systemic symptoms, such as fever, are uncommon. The rash of nonbullous impetigo appears as papules that progress to vesicles with surrounding erythema. Over a few days, the lesions become pustules, enlarge, and break down, forming a characteristic golden crust. Bullous impetigo is similar, but instead, the lesions begin as large, flaccid bullae. Diagnosis is based on the clinical exam. Treatment is with topical or oral antibiotics. Topical therapy includes mupirocin or retapamulin. Extensive lesions can be treated with oral cephalexin or dicloxacillin.



Mycobacterium leprae (A) is the cause of leprosy, not impetigo. The rash of leprosy presents as macular, erythematous, anesthetic lesions that are well-defined and possess a raised margin. They are often found on the arms, legs, and face. This patient’s rash is not characteristic of leprosy.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (B) is not a common cause of impetigo.

Although impetigo can be caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci, such as Streptococcus pyogenes, it is not caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (D).

Question: What is the most common cause of erythema multiforme?
ExplanationEN:
Erythema multiforme is an acute, immune-mediated dermatologic condition characterized by a distinct rash that occurs most frequently in young adults aged 20–40 years. Most cases result from infection, with herpes simplex virus being the most commonly implicated. A mild prodrome, if present at all, may consist of fever, myalgias, and malaise. The rash starts as maculopapular lesions that develop into distinct target lesions with three components: a central, dark papule surrounded by a pale zone surrounded by a halo of erythema. The lesions are often symmetrically found on the extensor surfaces and spread in a centripetal pattern. The palms and soles are also commonly involved. Oral mucous membrane involvement occurs in nearly three-quarters of patients. The rash appears over a few days and typically resolves in 2 weeks. Patients with mild disease and minimal mucosal involvement may be treated symptomatically with oral antihistamines and topical steroids. Those with more extensive disease, especially involving the mucous membranes, may be treated with a course of systemic steroids.



Mycoplasma pneumoniae (B) is another common cause, although less frequently noted than herpes simplex virus, especially in children.

Medications account for about 10% of cases of erythema multiforme, with two frequently implicated drugs being nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications (C) and sulfonamides (D).

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents with a rash on his back for 1 week. He states the rash started as a single patch and then spread to the rest of his back. The rash is itchy, but otherwise, the patient is asymptomatic. What management is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with pityriasis rosea and should be treated symptomatically with antihistamines and topical corticosteroids, as the condition is self-limiting. Pityriasis rosea presents as scaly, salmon-colored, oval papules or plaques 1–2 cm in diameter on the trunk and proximal extremities. It usually presents in children and young adults.

Classically, the diffuse rash is preceded by a herald patch 1 week prior. This lesion is larger (2–5 cm in diameter) than the others that form. Patients may also initially have a fever, malaise, or lymphadenopathy prior to the appearance of a rash, but this is rare. The diffuse form of the rash has a fir tree-like distribution following the cleavage lines of the skin.

Pityriasis rosea is a self-limiting disease but may take 8–12 weeks to completely resolve. The causative agent is unknown, but a virus is suspected (human herpesvirus 7). There is no specific treatment for the disease, so care should be directed at relieving symptoms, most commonly itching, with topical corticosteroids. Triamcinolone is a medium- to low-potency topical steroid that has a lower side effect and risk profile and is appropriate for this patient.



Cephalexin (A) is a first-generation cephalosporin with activity against many Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species, which are not implicated in pityriasis rosea.

Oral prednisone (B) has not been shown to reduce symptoms or duration of pityriasis rosea. Risks of prednisone use include immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, mood changes, weight gain, and adrenal suppression.

Topical clobetasol (C) is a super-high-potency topical steroid and is reserved for recalcitrant, chronic dermatoses such as psoriasis and lichen planus.

Although tinea infections are on the differential diagnosis for pityriasis rosea, a fungal etiology has not been shown to be causative of the disease, and topical econazole (D) or other topical antifungals do not play a role in treatment.

Question: A 21-year-old man presents with dysuria. He states that he noted dark-colored urine 4 days ago and was concerned he had developed a urinary tract infection. He attempted to treat himself at home by taking some old antibiotics he had lying around. Despite trying cephalexin, sulfamethoxazole, and amoxicillin, his symptoms have not improved. Yesterday, he started to note dysuria and reports ulcers on his penis and a rash on his abdomen. Physical exam reveals superficial ulcers to the urethral meatus and scrotum. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. An erythematous macular rash with a purpuric center is present on the abdomen without vesicles or bullae. Urinalysis is negative. What is the best next step in clinical management?
ExplanationEN:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome is an autoimmune type IV hypersensitivity reaction that affects the skin and mucous membranes. Stevens-Johnson syndrome exists on a continuum with toxic epidermal necrolysis in which Stevens-Johnson syndrome is defined as < 10% total body surface area (TBSA) affected, while toxic epidermal necrolysis involves > 30% TBSA. The rash occurs most often on the trunk and is classically described as macular and target-like with two zones of color: purpuric at the core with surrounding erythema. However, the rash can also be vesicular, bullous, and necrotic. Ruptured bullae and desquamation place the patient at risk for secondary infection, which is the leading cause of death. Stevens-Johnson syndrome can also affect the kidneys, liver, and lungs. Mucosal involvement is often present as well, affecting the genitals, mouth, and eyes. Up to half of all patients will have eye involvement and early ophthalmologic consultation is necessary for patients with ocular symptoms. Risk factors include antibiotics (e.g., penicillins and sulfonamides), anticonvulsants (e.g., carbamazepine and phenytoin), and infection (e.g., upper respiratory infections). Treatment consists of stopping the offending agent and supportive care. These patients are often best cared for at burn centers.



The decision to admit for broad-spectrum antibiotics (A) is not appropriate as there is no evidence of infection, and prolongation of antibiotics will likely worsen this patient’s condition.

Ceftriaxone IM and doxycycline orally (B) is a common antibiotic regimen used to treat sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea, chlamydia, and chancroid. However, these diseases do not present with the rash described here.

Ciprofloxacin (C) can be used to treat urinary tract infections and prostatitis. While the patient’s urine could be falsely negative from antibiotic use, his initial symptoms are not in keeping with a urinary tract infection and his rash and mucosal ulcerations are concerning for Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

EM is a hypersensitivity reaction triggered by various factors, including herpes simplex virus, certain medications (sulfa drugs, penicillins, barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and NSAIDs), bacterial infections such as Streptococcus or tuberculosis, and fungal infections like dermatophytosis, histoplasmosis, or coccidioidomycosis. The differential diagnosis includes conditions such as urticaria, pemphigus, pemphigoid, viral exanthems, and scalded skin syndrome.

The condition is acute and often self-limited. It is characterized by symmetrically distributed erythematous or violaceous macules, papules, vesicles, or bullae, with a predilection for the palms, soles, and extensor surfaces. Target lesions with three distinct color zones are pathognomonic. Treatment involves identifying and treating the underlying cause. Mild cases without systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement typically resolve within 2 to 3 weeks. More extensive disease, especially involving the trunk or occurring in immunocompromised patients, may warrant systemic corticosteroids and urgent dermatologic evaluation.



Borrelia burgdorferi (A) is the cause of Lyme disease and is associated with erythema migrans. While erythema migrans also has a target-like appearance, it is commonly characterized by a local, expanding, erythematous plaque with central clearing. Untreated Lyme disease may cause fever, headache, meningitis, adenopathy, arthropathies, myopathies, and neuropathies. Doxycycline and amoxicillin are the antibiotics of choice for Lyme disease.

Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (B) is the cause of scarlet fever, which is characterized by exudative pharyngitis, a strawberry tongue, and a fine, palpable sandpaper rash. Penicillins are the antibiotics of choice for scarlet fever.

Neisseria meningitidis (D) is a life-threatening cause of meningitis and sepsis and is associated with a petechial rash. Broad-spectrum cephalosporins, such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, are the antibiotics of choice.

Question: A 34-year-old previously healthy patient presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen abscess on the thigh that they noticed today. On examination, the 0.8 cm abscess is shallow, fluctuant, and accompanied by surrounding erythema and warmth. There is no lymphatic streaking. ExplanationEN:
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a strain of Staphylococcus that has developed resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics. This resistant strain is often health care-associated but is also found in the community.

Topical therapies are only appropriate for nasal decolonization or very small localized abscesses without systemic symptoms.

For limited community-acquired infections not requiring hospitalization, patients may be treated with oral antibiotics. A tetracycline, such as doxycycline, is an acceptable choice to treat community-acquired MRSA. Clindamycin or a sulfa drug (such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) are other acceptable alternatives.

Health care-associated strains of MRSA are typically not susceptible to these oral antibiotics and will require IV vancomycin. Additional indications for IV therapy include severe or deep infection, severe systemic symptoms (hemodynamic instability, sepsis), or the inability to tolerate oral medications.



Oral amoxicillin (A), an aminopenicillin beta-lactam antibiotic, is ineffective against MRSA. Patients with skin abscesses should receive empiric therapy that covers S. aureus, including MRSA.

While vancomycin has good activity against MRSA and is the IV antibiotic of choice for MRSA infection, oral vancomycin (C) has very little GI absorption and is not helpful for MRSA treatment as an outpatient.

Although clindamycin is a suitable choice for the treatment of some MRSA infections due to its effectiveness against the bacteria, topical clindamycin (D) is generally not appropriate as the sole treatment for MRSA cutaneous infections, especially if the infection is associated with a fever.

Topical mupirocin (E) may be appropriate for superficial MRSA skin infections like impetigo or small localized abscesses in patients without systemic symptoms such as fever.

Question: An 87-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with failure to thrive. He has not gotten out of bed in 6 days due to generalized weakness. On examination, he is noted to have an open sacral pressure ulcer with a red and pink wound bed. What stage is this ulcer?
ExplanationEN:
Pressure ulcers are damage to the skin and underlying tissue, typically in an area overlying a bony prominence, that result from localized pressure to the area. Risk factors for pressure ulcers include immobility, chronic steroid use, malnutrition, and advanced age. Pressure ulcers are graded on a scale of 1–4, depending on the involvement of various tissues. The ulcer described above involves partial-thickness loss of skin with exposed dermis consistent with a stage 2 ulcer. There may be an intact fluid-filled vesicle or the wound bed may be pink or red, but there is no exposed adipose tissue. Treatment of pressure ulcers depends on the stage of the ulcer but includes proper positioning of the patient to minimize prolonged pressure in any one area, local wound care with debridement and antibiotics as necessary, optimal nutritional support, and pain control.



Stage 1 ulcers (A) are characterized by intact skin with a localized area of nonblanchable erythema. Stage 3 ulcers (C) penetrate into the subcutaneous fat and represent full-thickness loss of skin. Stage 4 ulcers (D) also involve full-thickness loss of tissue with exposure of fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone.

Question: A healthy 3-month-old male infant presents to the emergency department with a painful, red rash in the diaper area. His parents state that he has been ill with a runny nose and diarrhea for the last 4 days. They report no fevers. His vital signs are within normal limits. Your examination shows an erythematous, tender, macular rash in the diaper area concentrated within the folds of the groin, with several smaller macular lesions scattered around it. Which of the following is the best topical therapy?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with Candida diaper dermatitis. It is often caused by C. albicans, which can proliferate in response to chronic exposure of the skin to moisture. This is often the case with children who wear diapers. The rash characteristically presents as a beefy, erythematous, and painful rash concentrated within skin folds. The presence of satellite lesions can also aid in diagnosis. The treatment for Candida diaper dermatitis includes topical antifungals such as nystatin. Patients should be evaluated for concurrent thrush and, if found, treated with oral nystatin as well.



Topical clotrimazole-betamethasone (A) and other combination antifungal and steroid preparations should be avoided since the diaper area is more sensitive to adverse side effects of steroids, such as skin atrophy and striae.

Topical hydrocortisone (B) would be the treatment of choice for seborrheic or atopic diaper dermatitis. Seborrheic diaper dermatitis presents as salmon-colored patches with yellow, greasy scales. In individuals with darker skin tones, scaly, hypopigmented macules and patches may be seen. Atopic dermatitis presents as irritation in areas that are in direct contact with the diaper and spares the inguinal folds. When needed, low-potency corticosteroid preparations are recommended no more than twice daily for short periods.

Topical zinc oxide (D) is an effective choice to create a moisture barrier and protect the epidermal layer in the diaper area. However, this patient has already developed a fungal infection, and zinc oxide alone will not treat all of his symptoms.

Question: A 44-year-old neurosurgeon presents to the ED for evaluation of the rash shown above. He reports no fever, injection drug use, new food ingestion, or medication changes. He has a history of epilepsy and has been taking levetiracetam for the last 7 years with no dose adjustment. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this skin finding?
ExplanationEN:
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is the most likely cause of this rash, which is characteristic of erythema multiforme (EM). The rash features classic targetoid lesions and surrounding erythema. Lesions are often distributed on the extremities, particularly the extensor surfaces, but may also involve the palms and soles.

EM is an acute, self-limited inflammatory condition that presents with iris- or target-shaped macules. It can affect both children and adults. Most cases are associated with HSV type 1 or 2, and a history of recent or recurrent HSV infection is the most common risk factor. Less commonly, EM may be triggered by other diseases, such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, and coccidioidomycosis, and by viral illnesses such as influenza or hepatitis. Although certain medications (e.g., NSAIDs, sulfonamides, penicillins, barbiturates, and anticonvulsants) have been reported as triggers, these are more often associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome rather than true EM.

Approximately half of all EM cases are idiopathic. The rash typically has an abrupt onset and may be associated with a burning or stinging sensation. Pruritus can also occur but is less prominent. Lesions may enlarge or coalesce but generally remain well demarcated.

EM is usually self-limited and resolves within 2 to 3 weeks without scarring. Treatment is supportive. Reassurance is often sufficient. For symptom relief, oral antihistamines or topical corticosteroids may be used. The role of systemic corticosteroids is controversial and generally reserved for severe or refractory cases, particularly those with significant mucosal involvement.



Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (B), formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is a separate entity with a separate pathophysiology from EM. It causes palpable purpura, kidney disease, and arthralgia.

Levetiracetam (C) is not known to cause EM. Barbiturates, phenytoin, and valproic acid have been associated with EM, but drugs are more likely to cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis than EM.

Solid organ neoplasms (D) are a much less common cause of EM than HSV.

Question: A 12-year-old boy develops a raised, itchy rash, shown above. It has been progressive over the past 12 hours. He is not experiencing any difficulty with breathing or swallowing and reports not feeling lightheaded. He has had a cough with congestion over the past week and a low-grade fever, for which he has taken several doses of acetaminophen. At a health care visit 4 days ago, he was diagnosed with otitis media and placed on amoxicillin, and he took a total of eight doses prior to developing the rash. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this rash?
ExplanationEN:
The raised erythematous plaques in the image above are consistent with urticaria. Urticaria are classified as acute when present for < 6 weeks and chronic when signs and symptoms recur most days of the week for ≥ 6 weeks. In children, infection is associated with 40–80% of cases of acute urticaria, with most of these due to viral upper respiratory tract infection. Urticaria are circumscribed, raised, erythematous plaques that may be round, oval, or serpiginous in shape. They may occur in small clusters or be present in large, coalescent plaques. They are typically itchy. Urticaria are mediated by histamine and other vasodilatory factors released by mast cells and basophils in the superficial dermis. Second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine and loratadine are preferred over diphenhydramine for the treatment of urticaria, as they cross the blood-brain barrier to a lesser extent, resulting in less overall sedation.



An IgE-mediated, type I immediate allergic reaction often involves urticaria that appear within minutes to 2 hours after exposure to the suspected allergen. It would not typically appear after multiple doses of medication like acetaminophen (A) or amoxicillin (B). Detergents (C) are more likely to cause contact dermatitis than urticaria.

Question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the ED with the rash shown above, which is limited to his face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The image shows erythematous, scaly, and crusted lesions on the cheeks of a young child, classic for atopic dermatitis. It commonly affects the face in infants and often presents as dry, itchy, inflamed skin.

Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disorder that affects individuals across all age groups but commonly begins in infancy or early childhood. It is part of the atopic triad, which also includes asthma and allergic rhinitis, and is frequently associated with a personal or family history of atopy.

In infants, atopic dermatitis begins between 4 and 6 months of age and primarily affects the face, particularly the cheeks, forehead, and scalp. As children grow, the distribution of the rash changes. In children < 12 years old, lesions are often found on extensor surfaces such as the elbows and knees. In adolescents and adults, the distribution shifts to the flexural surfaces (e.g., antecubital and popliteal fossae), neck, wrists, and ankles. This age-specific pattern helps distinguish atopic dermatitis from other pediatric dermatoses.

The hallmark symptom is intense pruritus, which can be severe and disrupt sleep. Chronic scratching leads to secondary changes, including lichenification, excoriations, and hyperpigmentation, particularly in individuals with darker skin tones. During acute flares, lesions may appear erythematous, vesicular, and oozing, while chronic lesions are more likely to be scaly, dry, and thickened. The skin barrier is impaired, leading to increased transepidermal water loss and vulnerability to environmental irritants, allergens, and secondary bacterial infections, most commonly with Staphylococcus aureus.

Flares are often triggered by cold, dry weather, increased body temperature, sweating, emotional stress, irritating fabrics (e.g., wool), harsh soaps, and allergens. Routine bathing with harsh cleansers can exacerbate dryness, and proper skin care is essential to minimize flares.

Treatment of atopic dermatitis is primarily supportive and aimed at restoring skin barrier function and reducing inflammation. First-line treatment includes regular use of emollients to maintain hydration and topical corticosteroids during flares to reduce inflammation. In mild cases, low-potency corticosteroids are preferred, while moderate to severe flares may require medium- or high-potency agents for short-term use. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) may be considered for maintenance therapy or use on sensitive areas like the face and intertriginous zones. Antihistamines may help relieve itching, especially at night, though they do not alter the disease course. In cases with signs of secondary infection, topical or systemic antibiotics may be necessary. Severe, refractory disease may warrant referral for systemic therapies, including biologics like dupilumab or phototherapy.



Impetigo (B) is found most commonly on the face and other exposed areas. It usually begins as a single pustule that develops into multiple lesions. When the pustules break, they leave erythematous erosions covered with a characteristic golden-yellow crust.

Psoriasis (C) is a chronic, multisystem inflammatory disorder. The most common skin manifestations are scaly erythematous macules, papules, and plaques. Typically, the macules are seen first and progress to maculopapules and ultimately well-demarcated, noncoherent silvery plaques overlying a glossy, homogeneous erythema.

Urticaria (D) can occur on any part of the body and appear as edematous plaques with colorless centers and erythematous borders.

Question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a scaly scalp lesion. The lesion is shown above, and the central area is tender and boggy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a kerion that is caused by a severe tinea capitis infection. This is a fungal infection of the scalp that presents with a pruritic area of scaling hair loss. It is most commonly caused by Trichophyton and Microsporum dermatophytes. A kerion is a severe inflammatory response with a suppurative lesion. Initial treatment is with an oral antifungal (e.g. griseofulvin, terbinafine, fluconazole). Topical treatments such as selenium sulfide, ketoconazole, or ciclopirox shampoo may increase cure rates.



Impetigo (A) is a superficial bacterial infection of the skin common in children. Its appearance will typically evolve from papules to vesicles to pustules that will break down and form a golden-colored crust.

Lipomas (C) are painless, soft subcutaneous nodules that typically appear on the trunk or upper extremities.

Psoriasis (D) is characterized by plaques with silvery scales and erythematous papules.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ED 4 days after a cesarean section. The procedure was uneventful, and she has no significant medical history. Today, she is experiencing fever, chills, and pain at the surgical site. She has a T of 102.0°F (38.9°C), BP of 114/74 mm Hg, HR of 122 bpm, RR of 19/min, and SpO2 of 99% on room air. Physical exam reveals erythema and induration surrounding the incision, which is tender to palpation with a small amount of associated purulence. Which of the following is the most likely infectious etiology of this patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Postpartum wound complications of a cesarean section include infection, hematoma, seroma, and wound dehiscence. This patient presents 4 days after a cesarean section with systemic symptoms (fever, tachycardia) and localized signs of surgical site infection (erythema, induration, and purulence). These features are most consistent with a superficial wound infection. Given its high virulence and frequent colonization of the skin, Staphylococcus aureus is the most likely pathogen in this context.

The timing of symptom onset is critical in narrowing the differential. Early wound infections, those occurring within the first 24 to 48 hours, are often caused by group A or B beta-hemolytic Streptococcus and are characterized by high fever and nonpurulent cellulitis. However, beyond this early window, particularly after 48 hours, infections are more likely to involve Staphylococcus aureus or Staphylococcus epidermidis, gram-negative organisms such as Escherichia coli or Proteus mirabilis, and anaerobes or cervicovaginal flora in polymicrobial infections.

The presence of purulent drainage in this case supports an etiology involving S. aureus, a common pathogen in postoperative wound infections, especially in otherwise healthy patients. Treatment involves inspecting and irrigating the wound, using sterile dressings, and administering IV antibiotics. If there is any suspicion of an underlying abscess (such as purulence), a CT scan may be required to determine the extent of the infection. The obstetrician who performed the procedure should also be consulted for further care, and the patient should be admitted.

Other potential complications after a surgical procedure include a postoperative hematoma and seroma (collection of serum). These appear within a few days of the surgery and may present with localized swelling, pain, and possibly drainage. Small seromas and hematomas will resolve with expectant treatment alone. Larger collections may need to be drained and can predispose the wound to infection or separation.

Finally, wound dehiscence is a possible complication postoperatively and is more common in patients with vascular risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. It will appear as a wound that has separated or is failing to heal. Treatment often involves general wound care, including packing if the wound is minor (involving only the skin and subcutaneous tissue). On the other hand, if the wound fails to heal or extends to or involves the fascial layer, it may require surgical repair in consultation with the operating surgeon.



Clostridium perfringens (A) causes gas gangrene, a rapidly progressive and necrotizing infection. Findings such as crepitus, severe pain out of proportion to exam, and signs of tissue necrosis are characteristic. The absence of these features and the presence of purulence point against this diagnosis.

Escherichia coli (B) is a common pathogen in intra-abdominal or urinary infections, particularly postpartum endometritis. While it can be part of polymicrobial infections after cesarean section, it is less likely to be the primary pathogen in a superficial surgical site infection, especially with purulence and localized findings. Its role increases when infections are polymicrobial or originate from deeper pelvic structures.

Staphylococcus epidermidis (D) is increasingly associated with later postoperative infections due to its biofilm-forming capacity, especially in the presence of foreign material, but it is less virulent than S. aureus and more commonly associated with chronic or indolent infections. This patient’s acute symptoms and marked systemic response make S. aureus the more likely culprit.

Streptococcus pyogenes (E) causes early-onset wound infections (within the first 48 hours) and presents with rapidly spreading cellulitis and systemic toxicity rather than localized purulence. This patient’s infection is past that time frame and exhibits localized signs suggestive of S. aureus.

Question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ED with joint swelling and abdominal pain. His skin condition is shown above. Vital signs are a T of 99.4°F ( 37.4°C), BP of 140/90 mm Hg, HR of 108 bpm, RR of 18/min, and SpO2 of 96% on room air. Which of the following serum laboratory tests is associated with the most serious complication in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), now more accurately referred to as immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV). IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting children and is characterized by immune complex deposition of IgA in vessel walls. It presents with a classic triad of palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, and abdominal pain. The purpura is nonthrombocytopenic, meaning the platelet count remains within normal limits or elevated, which helps distinguish HSP from thrombocytopenic purpuras such as immune thrombocytopenia.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, but several laboratory tests are useful for assessing the extent of organ involvement. The most serious complication of IgA vasculitis is kidney involvement, which occurs in up to 40% of cases and can range from mild hematuria and proteinuria to acute glomerulonephritis. As such, serum creatinine, urinalysis, and blood pressure monitoring are essential in the evaluation. Findings may include elevated creatinine, hematuria, proteinuria, and, in rare cases, gross hematuria. Approximately 1% of patients may progress to end-stage kidney disease. Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are often elevated but nonspecific.

Additional features of IgA vasculitis can include colicky abdominal pain, bloody stools, and arthritis, most commonly affecting the knees, ankles, wrists, and elbows. Scrotal edema may also occur in male patients. Abdominal pain, especially when severe or persistent, raises concern for ileoileal intussusception, a known complication of IgA vasculitis, and warrants evaluation with abdominal ultrasound.

Treatment is generally supportive, as most patients experience spontaneous resolution of symptoms within 4–6 weeks. NSAIDs may be used for joint symptoms, but should be used cautiously or avoided in patients with evidence of kidney involvement. Corticosteroids may be considered for patients with significant kidney involvement, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, or scrotal involvement.

Hospital admission is recommended for patients with severe arthritis or arthralgia limiting mobility, evidence of intussusception, or kidney involvement, including significant hypertension, elevated serum creatinine, or substantial proteinuria. Close follow-up is crucial to monitor kidney function, as late-onset kidney complications can occur.



Bicarbonate (A) would be a potentially important laboratory test in pyloric stenosis, as these patients may develop hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

Platelets (C) would be useful if the patient were exhibiting signs or symptoms of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or disseminated intravascular coagulation. IgA vasculitis may be confused with these disease processes at times, but this patient has clear dependent lower extremity purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis, which are far more suggestive of IgA vasculitis.

Sodium (D) would be important if this patient were exhibiting signs or symptoms of altered mental status or volume changes.

Question: A 34-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period presents to the emergency department with generalized itchiness and a rash for the past 2 days. The itching has been driving her crazy, but she has been too nervous to take medications for fear of side effects on her developing fetus. She reports no difficulty breathing, nausea, or vomiting. You note hives covering most of her abdomen, back, and neck. Her vital signs are normal, her airway is patent, and no wheezing is appreciated on examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment plan?
ExplanationEN:
Urticaria, or hives, is a commonly encountered condition that is characterized by intensely pruritic erythematous plaques that are often described as wheals. Urticaria can be associated with angioedema secondary to swelling in the deeper skin layers, but the involvement of additional organ systems (e.g., wheezing, vomiting) should be considered anaphylaxis instead of urticaria. Urticaria is an IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity reaction, causing degranulation of cutaneous mast cells, leading to the release of vasodilatory substances and histamine, which are responsible for localized swelling and pruritus, respectively. While most cases of urticaria are self-limited, if treatment is initiated, it should be tailored to the severity of the symptoms.

H1 blockers (e.g., cetirizine) are first-line therapy for urticaria and should be used for mild symptoms. Second-generation H1 blockers like cetirizine are generally preferred to first-generation H1 blockers (e.g., diphenhydramine) due to their decreased risk of anticholinergic side effects and sedation. For moderate to severe urticaria, an H2 blocker (e.g., famotidine) can be added. Steroids were previously thought to be beneficial for severe urticaria. However, recently the largest randomized controlled trial to date showed no benefit to the addition of a steroid burst to H1 blocker therapy for isolated acute urticaria. Steroids may still have a role when urticaria is associated with prominent angioedema. Furthermore, steroids are associated with fetal cleft lips and palates and should generally be avoided if possible in the first trimester of pregnancy, especially in the treatment of self-limited conditions like urticaria.



Cetirizine (A) is a second-generation H1 blocker and is considered first-line therapy for mild urticaria. However, with this patient’s hives covering nearly 40% of her body surface and the distress that the itching is causing her, she would likely benefit from more aggressive treatment including an H2 blocker.

Cetirizine, famotidine, and prednisone (C) would be considered appropriate urticaria associated with angioedema in a nonpregnant patient. However, given prednisone is associated with birth defects when used in the first trimester and that this patient has not yet tried any other therapies, a trial of H1 and H2 blockers without prednisone would be prudent. She also has no evidence of angioedema on exam.

Cetirizine, famotidine, prednisone, and epinephrine (D) are not all indicated in the treatment of this patient. Epinephrine is a first-line therapy in the management of anaphylaxis. This patient has isolated urticaria without signs of anaphylaxis.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 45-year-old man presents with a lump on the back of his neck. He reports the lump has been there for a few months and occasionally is sensitive to touch but usually is not painful. He reports no fevers, drainage, or similar lesions in the past. On examination, you note a 2 cm, tense, skin-colored, mobile lump on the back of the neck to the right of midline. There is a small indentation in the center of the mass. Notably, there is no fluctuance, erythema, or tenderness to palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
An epidermoid cyst is the most likely diagnosis, given the presence of a slow-growing, mobile, skin-colored nodule with a central punctum on the back of the neck.

Epidermoid cysts are benign, slow-growing subcutaneous nodules that result from the proliferation of epidermal cells within the dermis. These cysts are filled with keratinous debris and develop from a blocked pilosebaceous unit. Common locations include the face, neck, scalp, upper trunk, and back.

Diagnosis is clinical and based on characteristic features: a well-circumscribed, skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule, often with a central punctum. These lesions are usually asymptomatic but may become inflamed or secondarily infected. When noninfected, they may drain a thick, malodorous, cheese-like material composed of keratin. If signs of infection are present (such as erythema, tenderness, fluctuance, or purulent drainage), the cyst may be acutely inflamed or abscessed.

Treatment is not required for asymptomatic epidermoid cysts. However, patients may request removal for cosmetic reasons or due to discomfort. Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice to prevent recurrence. This involves removing the cyst wall in its entirety. For noninflamed cysts, a small incision can be made to express the contents, followed by careful extraction of the cyst wall. Mild, isolated inflammation of an epidermoid cyst is not a contraindication to primary excision, but excision may be technically more challenging during inflammation. Alternatively, a short course of NSAIDs and antibiotics can be used to reduce inflammation, with excision deferred until the area is quiescent.



A ganglion cyst (B) is a fluid-filled swelling over a joint or tendon sheath. These are found on the dorsum of the wrist or other extremities. These lesions will also transilluminate due to being filled with clear, mucinous fluid.

A lipoma (C) is a collection of mature fat cells in a fibrous capsule. These are usually soft and painless and can grow to be over 10 cm. The tense umbilicated lesion in this patient is not consistent with a lipoma, but if in doubt, ultrasound can help differentiate the two.

Molluscum contagiosum (D) is an umbilicated lesion caused by a poxvirus that is common in childhood or immunodeficient states. These papules are usually numerous and only 2–5 mm in diameter.

Pilar cysts (E) are similar in appearance to epidermoid cysts, as they are firm, slow-growing nodules. The main differentiation is these cysts grow from the root of the hair follicle, so they are most often located on the scalp.

Question: A 49-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer, hypertension, and diabetes presents to the emergency department with malaise, decreased appetite, and mild abdominal cramping for 5 days. Vital signs are within normal limits, and examination is remarkable for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. Diagnostic testing is notable for glucose 244 mg/dL and calcium 13.3 mg/dL. Other laboratory values are unremarkable. What is the most appropriate initial care for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Hypercalcemia is seen in many patients with advanced cancer, particularly patients with breast cancer, lung cancer, or multiple myeloma. The most common mechanism whereby malignancy produces hypercalcemia is when a solid tumor produces a parathyroid hormone-related protein that is structurally similar to parathyroid hormone and binds to parathyroid hormone receptors, thereby mobilizing calcium from bones and increasing reabsorption of calcium. Hypercalcemia can also develop from enhanced osteoclastic activity from bony metastases. In lymphomas, vitamin D analogs are produced, leading to hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia does not always require treatment, particularly in asymptomatic patients. Patients with symptoms, which generally include lethargy, confusion, anorexia, nausea, and constipation, or with calcium > 14.0 mg/dL should be treated with intravenous isotonic saline at a rate adjusted to the ability of the patient’s cardiovascular system to tolerate the volume load. The initial priority in these patients is restoration of intravascular volume. Typically, patients are given a fluid bolus of 1–2 L followed by 200 mL/h. Further pharmacologic management should ensue once the patient has been admitted to the hospital and once appropriate hydration has been completed.



Intravenous normal saline plus calcitonin (B) has a limited role in treating malignancy-induced hypercalcemia. Calcitonin may lower plasma calcium levels within 2–4 hours, but it may cause a hypersensitivity response, and tachyphylaxis develops within 3 days, so the beneficial effect is short-lived.

Intravenous normal saline plus furosemide (C) would only be indicated in patients who cannot tolerate the volume load due to heart failure or kidney insufficiency. It has little additive effect when given to patients with malignancy with normal cardiac and kidney function.

Intravenous normal saline plus pamidronate (D), a bisphosphonate, is recommended in malignancy-induced hypercalcemia, but it is generally not initiated in the emergency department or until adequate intravenous hydration has been completed.

Question: A 55-year-old man with stage III chronic kidney disease presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He reports cramping and weakness in his arms and legs for 2 days. A 12-lead ECG obtained in triage is shown above. Which of the following therapies should be initiated immediately?
ExplanationEN:
Muscle weakness and paralysis, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and cardiac dysrhythmias are the most serious clinical manifestations of hyperkalemia. Peaked symmetrical T waves with shortened QT intervals and ST-segment depression are the earliest ECG changes seen in patients with hyperkalemia. Worsening hyperkalemia results in progressive lengthening of the PR interval and QRS duration, disappearance of the P wave, and ultimately, widening of the QRS complex into a sinusoidal pattern. The muscle and cardiac manifestations of hyperkalemia are a result of impaired neuromuscular transmission due to the persistent depolarization caused by elevated extracellular potassium levels. This leads to the inactivation of the sodium channels, causing decreased membrane excitability, which manifests as muscle weakness and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Symptomatic hyperkalemia is typically seen in patients with underlying acute or chronic kidney disease but can also be seen in conditions that cause increased tissue breakdown such as tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and crush injuries. Treatment of hyperkalemia includes antagonizing the membrane effects of potassium, driving extracellular potassium into cells, and removing potassium from the body. Calcium directly antagonizes the effect of potassium on cell membrane excitability, decreasing the cardiotoxic effects of hyperkalemia. While immediate administration of calcium gluconate or calcium chloride does not alter potassium levels, calcium helps prevent potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities or dysrhythmias until the excess extracellular potassium can be driven into cells or out of the body. Treatment can then be initiated with agents to drive excess potassium intracellularly. These include insulin (with glucose), beta-2 agonists such as albuterol, and occasionally sodium bicarbonate. These treatments act quickly to decrease the extracellular potassium level until treatments such as dialysis, loop or thiazide diuretics, or cation-exchange resins can be initiated to remove excess potassium from the body.



Aspirin (A) is indicated in suspected or confirmed cases of acute coronary syndrome. While early hyperkalemia may cause ST-segment depression, this is not an indication of cardiac ischemia and aspirin will not resolve the problem.

Dialysis (C) and furosemide (D) are important for removing excess total body potassium from the body in cases of hyperkalemia, but calcium therapy for cardioprotection and fast-acting transient therapies that quickly reduce extracellular potassium levels should be initiated first, especially in cases with proven ECG abnormalities.

Question: A 2-year-old previously healthy boy presents to the emergency department with a seizure. He has been increasingly sleepy over the past 24 hours, which developed into confusion and seizure. He has had no fevers, and his serum glucose is 92 mg/dL. His seizure does not stop with two appropriate doses of intravenous lorazepam but stops after a bolus of normal saline. His serum sodium returns at 168 mEq/L. A review of his chart shows a weight gain of 6.6 lbs (3 kg) since a clinic visit a month ago. After hydration, his urine osmolality remains higher than his serum osmolality, and his fractional excretion of sodium remains > 2%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypernatremia?
ExplanationEN:
Hypernatremia is a serum sodium of > 150 mEq/L and is most commonly caused by gastrointestinal losses from vomiting and diarrhea. Depending on the ratio of free water and sodium loss, vomiting and diarrhea could instead result in hyponatremia. Other causes of hypernatremia include free water loss from increased insensible losses due to fevers, prematurity, phototherapy, tachypnea, or renal losses from an arginine vasopressin disorder (also known as diabetes insipidus). These causes of hypernatremia typically result in significant weight loss due to the large amount of water lost that has not been replenished.

Salt poisoning is an uncommon cause of hypernatremia, but unlike other causes, it is associated with weight gain due to thirst. It can be a form of child abuse or can be caused by incorrect formula preparation. Children who are young or have developmental delays are at risk for salt poisoning, as they are not able to communicate their thirst and rely on others for access to water. Table salt ingestion is unpleasant and rarely voluntary. One teaspoon of salt contains 100 mEq of sodium and can raise the serum concentration of a 10 kg child by as much as 15 mEq/L. Such an ingestion results in a rapid increase in serum osmolality and can present with neurologic symptoms such as weakness, lethargy, coma, and seizures. Seizures are unlikely if the change from baseline is gradual. A high fractional excretion of sodium after water replacement is virtually diagnostic of salt poisoning, as it is usually low in rehydrated patients with hypernatremia from water losses.



Patients with an arginine vasopressin disorder (A) typically have weight loss from excessive water losses and will have a urine osmolality lower than the serum osmolality, which is not seen above.

Patients with gastroenteritis (B) usually have a history of vomiting and diarrhea, but even if this is not given in the history, these patients usually have weight loss and a urine osmolality lower than serum osmolality after rehydration, which is not seen above.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (D) secretion usually presents with hyponatremia due to excessive water reuptake, not hypernatremia.

Question:
A patient presents to the ED with dyspnea. An arterial blood gas is drawn with the following results:

pH: 7.50

PCO2: 25 mm Hg

PO2: 102 mm Hg

Bicarbonate: 23 mEq/L

Which of the following conditions could this patient have?

Options.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease without exacerbation

ExplanationEN:
When reviewing an arterial blood gas, first the pH should be assessed to determine if acidosis or alkalosis is present. This patient has an alkalosis, given the pH is > 7.45. Next, the PCO2 can be evaluated. It is expected that when a metabolic alkalosis is present, the PCO2 would be elevated to compensate. However, the patient’s PCO2 is lower than the normal range, suggesting it is contributing to the pH imbalance and that a respiratory alkalosis is present. Next, the bicarbonate should be reviewed. If a respiratory alkalosis is present (as was just determined was likely in this patient), the kidneys should be wasting bicarbonate to compensate, resulting in a low bicarbonate when the respiratory alkalosis has been ongoing. However, this patient’s bicarbonate level is normal, suggesting that it is not correcting for the alkalosis. Thus, this patient has acute respiratory alkalosis.

To remember the expected compensation for bicarbonate reduction in acute and chronic respiratory alkalosis, you can use this mnemonic: acute two, chronic four or more. This phrase helps you recall that in acute respiratory alkalosis, for every 10 mm Hg decrease in PCO2, there is about a 2 mEq/L decrease in bicarbonate. And in chronic respiratory alkalosis, for every 10 mm Hg decrease in PCO2, expect a decrease of about 4–5 mEq/L in bicarbonate.

In the example above, a panic attack could result in tachypnea and hyperventilation, leading to respiratory alkalosis. Given this is an acute event, the kidneys would not have time to compensate, and the bicarbonate would be normal.



Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease without exacerbation (A) would present with a normal pH, an elevated PCO2 (from COPD), and an elevated bicarbonate (from kidney compensation).

Septic shock (C) could present with metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis due to hypoxia, suggesting impaired oxygen exchange.

In severe asthma exacerbation (D) or status asthmaticus, a normal or high PCO2 level is seen. In the early stages of an acute asthma exacerbation, patients tend to hyperventilate, leading to a reduction in PCO2 (respiratory alkalosis). However, as the exacerbation becomes more severe, leading to significant airflow obstruction, the ability to exhale carbon dioxide decreases. This can result in PCO2 returning to normal levels and, if the obstructed airflow is severe enough, can lead to hypercapnia (elevated PCO2).

Question: A 25-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the ED for vomiting. Her initial blood tests are notable for a glucose of 473 mg/L, pH of 7.19, sodium of 130 mEq/L, potassium of 2.7 mEq/L, chloride of 95 mEq/L, and bicarbonate of 10 mEq/L. She is given potassium supplementation and lactated Ringers solution, and she is started on an insulin infusion once her potassium is corrected. Several hours later, blood tests are notable for a glucose of 190 mg/L, pH of 7.26, sodium of 135 mEq/L, potassium of 4.1 mEq/L, chloride of 100 mEq/L, and bicarbonate of 15 mEq/L. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Continue insulin infusion and add 5% dextrose to fluids
Continue insulin infusion and administer sodium bicarbonate
Continue insulin infusion and fluids and administer insulin SC
Continue insulin infusion and fluids and allow the patient to eat
Discontinue insulin infusion and add 5% dextrose to fluids

CorrectAnswer: Continue insulin infusion and add 5% dextrose to fluids
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s initial lab results demonstrate hyperglycemia, low serum bicarbonate, acidosis, and an elevated anion gap, which is most consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The key components of DKA management include fluid resuscitation, correcting electrolyte abnormalities, correcting metabolic derangement, and treating the underlying cause. Fluid resuscitation with normal saline or lactated Ringers solution should be initiated as soon as a diagnosis of DKA is suspected. Hypokalemia should be corrected prior to initiating an insulin drip. Insulin can be administered with or without a 0.1 units/kg bolus followed by a 0.1 units/kg/hr drip. Glucose should be corrected at a rate of 75 mg/dL/hr. Once the glucose is < 250 mg/L, the insulin infusion should be continued at half the rate, and 5% dextrose should be added to the fluids. The endpoints of therapy are glucose < 200 mg/L, normalization of the anion gap, bicarbonate ≥ 18 mEq/L, and pH > 7.3. Once these occur, the patient should be transitioned to subcutaneous insulin with at least 2–4 hours of overlap when the insulin infusion remains on. At this point, the patient may begin eating, and dextrose supplementation can be stopped. For this patient, her repeat lab values show a glucose level of 190 mg/L, so 5% dextrose should be added to her fluids. Her anion gap is still elevated (135 mEq/L – (100 mEq/L + 15 mEq/L) = 20 mEq/L), bicarbonate is low, and pH is < 7.3, indicating that her DKA has yet to fully resolve and her insulin infusion should be continued.



Continuing the insulin infusion is the appropriate treatment for this patient who continues to have an elevated anion gap, low pH, and low bicarbonate. However, sodium bicarbonate (B) is only indicated in DKA when the pH is < 6.9. Transitioning to subcutaneous insulin (C) and allowing the patient to eat (D) should occur once the acidosis, anion gap, and bicarbonate have normalized. Discontinuation of the insulin drip and adding 5% dextrose to fluids (E) would worsen this patient’s DKA.

Question: A 43-year-old man presents to the ED with abdominal pain. His medical history includes type 1 diabetes and nonischemic cardiomyopathy, for which he takes subcutaneous insulin, metoprolol, losartan, and empagliflozin. He states he ran out of his insulin 4 days ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Laboratory results show a serum glucose of 204 mg/dL, bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L, potassium of 5.6 mEq/L, and anion gap of 19 mEq/L. A 1 L bolus of crystalloid is given IV. Which of the following should be administered as the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: IV insulin bolus of 0.1 U/kg followed by infusion of 0.1 U/kg/hr
IV insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/hr and IV 5% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hr
IV potassium 20 mEq in a 1 L lactated Ringer bolus prior to insulin administration

CorrectAnswer: IV insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/hr and IV 5% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hr
ExplanationEN:
Diabetes-related ketoacidosis (DKA) is a serious, acute complication of diabetes resulting from insulin deficiency and glucagon excess, which produce hyperglycemia, dehydration, acidosis, and electrolyte derangements. It commonly results from cessation of insulin therapy, such as running out of medications, or in response to physical or emotional stress, as with infection or other serious illness. The patient’s lack of insulin for several days is the most likely precipitating factor in this scenario.

DKA should be suspected in any patient presenting to the ED with hyperglycemia, with greater suspicion after cessation of insulin use or with an acute stressor. Serum glucose is typically > 350 mg/dL. Euglycemic DKA (glucose < 300 mg/dL) occurs in nearly one-fifth of cases, with greater incidence in patients who take sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, such as this patient’s empagliflozin. Because the patient’s glucose is < 300 mg/dL with other evidence of DKA (i.e., anion gap elevation, low serum bicarbonate), his case is classified as euglycemic DKA. Diagnostic workup for all patients should include serum glucose, an electrolyte panel, including phosphorus and magnesium levels, and a venous blood pH. Serum keto acid levels are commonly measured but not essential to make the diagnosis.

Initial management of euglycemic DKA is similar to that of DKA with hyperglycemia but for one key difference: simultaneous administration of dextrose and insulin. Insulin is critical in suppressing ketogenesis, but lesser degrees of hyperglycemia increase the risk of consequent hypoglycemia without the administration of dextrose. Fluid resuscitation and adequate potassium replacement, when indicated, remain key factors of management in euglycemic DKA.



Initial fluid resuscitation is important in managing DKA, but administering additional fluids (A) should not delay insulin administration, as it is critical in suppressing ketogenesis and definitively treating the condition.

A bolus of IV insulin followed by an infusion (B) is no longer recommended. The American Diabetes Association now recommends initiating a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/hr, up to 10 U/hr. Furthermore, this patient needs a concomitant dextrose infusion.

Potassium supplementation (D) is required for patients with approximate serum potassium levels < 5.5 mEq/L but is not necessary with levels above this threshold.

Question: An 82-year-old woman is transferred to your emergency department from another hospital. She presents with confusion, lethargy, trouble speaking and swallowing, and profound weakness in all extremities. Her condition is most consistent with a complication from the treatment of which electrolyte abnormality?
ExplanationEN:
The treatment of severe hyponatremia (defined as a serum sodium level < 120 mEq/L with central nervous system abnormalities) is a delicate and challenging affair. Several variables guide the approach: the severity of clinical symptoms, the rate of onset, the current serum sodium level, and the volume status of the patient. It is essential to keep in mind that in the treatment of severe hyponatremia, the rate of correction should never be > 0.5–1.0 mEq/L/hr or 1–2 mEq/L/hr if the patient is having seizures. The goal is to raise the sodium level to > 120 mEq/L and see improvement in neurologic symptoms. The initial treatment includes hypertonic saline (3%) at 25–100 mL/hr and furosemide 20–40 mg IV. After each 100 mL infusion of 3% hypertonic saline, the serum sodium level requires repeat measurement. Improvement is often seen after raising the serum sodium level by 4–6 mEq/L, and the level should not be raised by more than 8 mEq/L in the first 24 hours.

This patient is presenting with osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), formerly known as central pontine myelinolysis. The change in name pays tribute to the discovery that demyelination is in the pontine in about 50% of cases, whereas the remaining cases are extrapontine or a combination of the two. This devastating condition is caused by a too-rapid correction of hyponatremia. Several factors place the patient at an increased risk for developing ODS, such as very low initial serum sodium (well below 120 mEq/L), concurrent hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia, malnutrition, alcohol misuse, cirrhosis, and chronic heart failure. The symptoms usually start within 24–48 hours after rapid correction, beginning with dysarthria, dysphagia, confusion and lethargy, and profound weakness, progressing to paraparesis or quadriplegia, seizures, coma, and death. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain will reveal ODS lesions, though their time of appearance may vary and be delayed. The prognosis of ODS was at one time bleak, but in recent years complete recovery has been achieved more frequently. The treatment includes 5% dextrose in water at 3 mL/kg/hr and desmopressin, which reintroduces hyponatremia. Additional measures, including corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin, are still being explored, with some reports of success.



Too rapid correction of hypernatremia (A) may lead to cerebral edema manifesting with severe headaches, declining mental status, respiratory depression, and seizures. Paraparesis or quadriparesis are not usually the presenting symptoms.

Treatment of severe hypocalcemia (B) with intravenous calcium can lead to vasoconstriction and ischemia.

Overtreatment of hypomagnesemia (C) may result in hypermagnesemia presenting with nausea, somnolence, hyporeflexia, respiratory depression, hypotension, and heart block.

Question: Which of the following findings can distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
ExplanationEN:
Primary adrenal insufficiency, or Addison disease, is the failure of the adrenal gland to produce cortisol or aldosterone. The most common cause is autoimmune destruction of the gland. Other causes include adrenal hemorrhage, infections (e.g., tuberculosis), cancer, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. While the adrenal gland fails, the remainder of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis remains intact. Therefore, cortisol levels will be low or absent, but adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH) levels will be elevated.

Clinical features of adrenal insufficiency (both primary and secondary) include weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, abdominal cramps, hyponatremia, and hypotension. Hyperkalemia, often associated with mild hyperchloremia acidosis, is due to mineralocorticoid insufficiency and will be seen in primary disease 65% of the time. As secondary adrenal insufficiency is the result of a problem either at the level of the hypothalamus or pituitary gland, patients will have normal aldosterone levels and, more often, normal potassium levels.



Hyponatremia (B) and hypotension (D) are frequently seen in both primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency.

Hypopigmentation (C) is not seen in either primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency. However, patients with primary disease will display hyperpigmentation.

What causes hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency?

A lack of cortisol results in elevated production of adrenocorticotropic hormone and its precursor, proopiomelanocortin (POMC), by the anterior pituitary. POMC is also a precursor to melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which stimulates melanocytes and leads to hyperpigmentation.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department reporting “leaking from my breasts” for 2 weeks. She is not currently breastfeeding or taking any hormonal therapies. She also reports slight visual disturbances and mild headaches. Her last menstrual period was 6 months ago. Prior to this, they were regular. Her vital signs are within normal limits and her urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for her condition?
ExplanationEN:
The combination of galactorrhea and amenorrhea in a female patient suggests a pituitary tumor, which is a suprasellar mass, as the primary etiology. The pituitary gland is continuous with the hypothalamus by way of the infundibulum and hypophysial stalk, and it is seated within the sella turcica. It is divided into an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis). Hormones and releasing hormones that are generated in the hypothalamus are delivered to the pituitary gland through neurovascular tracts and then released into the hypophysial portal system. Patients with pituitary tumors often experience visual symptoms due to the gland’s proximity to the optic nerves, optic chiasm, and optic tracts. Pituitary adenomas (hormone-secreting tumors) represent approximately 10–15% of all primary intracranial tumors. Most pituitary tumors are benign and slow-growing. In young adults, the most common pituitary tumors are noncancerous. Tumors can be either secreting (microadenomas or macroadenomas) or nonsecreting. The most common secreting tumor is a prolactinoma. Common conditions caused by secretory tumors include acromegaly (growth hormone), hypo- or hyperthyroidism (thyrotropin hormone), Cushing disease (adrenocorticotropic hormone), and galactorrhea and amenorrhea in women or impotence in men (prolactin). Diagnosis of these tumors may be incidentally made with imaging or may present with features secondary to mass effects such as headache, visual disturbances, cranial nerve dysfunction, personality changes, autonomic dysfunction, sleep disturbances, temperature dysregulation, or hormone hypersecretion sequelae.



An adnexal malignancy (A), such as secretory ovarian cysts, would cause negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary gland to decrease prolactin secretion. Amenorrhea may be present, but galactorrhea would be absent.

An adrenal nodule (B) would not cause galactorrhea but may lead to amenorrhea.

An intraductal papilloma (C) may cause galactorrhea but would not explain amenorrhea.

Question: You are treating a patient who has been diagnosed with thyroid storm. The patient reports a headache. Which of the following is contraindicated during acute thyroid storm?
ExplanationEN:
Thyroid storm is a rare event caused by severe thyrotoxicosis. This hypermetabolic state involves multiple organ systems. The mainstay of therapy includes adrenergic blockage with beta-blocker therapy. Propranolol is preferred since it also partially blocks the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, in addition to its beta-blocking properties.

Additional therapy includes antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil and methimazole), iodide (inhibits release of stored thyroid hormone), and corticosteroids (decrease peripheral conversion of T4 to T3). Aspirin is contraindicated during thyroid storm because it displaces T4 from binding proteins, leading to increased serum levels of T4 and T3 potentiating the thyrotoxicosis.



Acetaminophen (A) has no direct effects on thyroid hormone levels and is an appropriate analgesic agent for a patient with a headache.

Metoclopramide (C) is often used in the management of acute headaches. Most commonly, metoclopramide is used intravenously for patients with migraine headaches. There is some antidopaminergic effect of the medication, and this is often abortive for a migraine headache. There are no contraindications to this medication in patients with thyroid storm.

Prednisone (D) reduces the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, promotes vasomotor stability, and can possibly treat an underlying relative adrenal insufficiency. It is not contraindicated in thyroid storm.

Question: A 19-year-old woman with a history of depression presents via EMS to the ED after a suicide attempt during which she ingested a full bottle of aspirin approximately 1 hour ago. Her vital signs include a BP of 90/58 mm Hg, HR of 112 bpm, and RR of 30/min. An arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.50, pCO2 of 30 mm Hg, and bicarbonate of 22 mEq/L. What is the underlying pathophysiology responsible for this patient’s arterial blood gas findings?

Options.text: Direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center

CorrectAnswer: Direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center
ExplanationEN:
Salicylate toxicity occurs with the ingestion of readily available products such as aspirin, oil of wintergreen, and bismuth subsalicylate. They are rapidly absorbed and can lead to detection in the serum within 30 minutes. Mild symptoms are seen at salicylate doses < 150 mg/kg, while more severe manifestations arise at serum levels > 300 mg/kg. Serum toxicity typically arises when values reach ≥ 40 mg/dL. The peak effect occurs approximately 6 hours after absorption. Initially, salicylates stimulate the respiratory center of the medulla, leading to increased ventilation, decreased pCO2, and elevated pH, all consistent with respiratory alkalosis.

Salicylates also uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, leading to anaerobic metabolism and the development of metabolic acidosis, often with an anion gap secondary to lactate production, though a normal anion gap does not exclude this development. This leads to a mixed acid-base disturbance, depending on the timing of the patient’s presentation. Other clinical features include nausea and vomiting due to stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, hyperthermia due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation, altered mental status, tinnitus, dizziness, and dyspnea (e.g., secondary to pulmonary edema from increased pulmonary vascular permeability).

The initial resuscitation of these patients involves addressing the airway, breathing, and circulation. Decontamination may be pursued if the patient presents immediately (e.g., oral charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation). Alkalinization of the plasma and urine through an intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion is indicated at serum salicylate values > 35 mg/dL to improve kidney elimination and prevent further diffusion across the blood-brain barrier. If severe neurologic symptoms (e.g., altered mental status, seizure), pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, or a pH < 7.20 develop or initial or persistently elevated salicylate levels are present, then hemodialysis should be pursued.



Conversion of salicylate into metabolites (A) and impaired cellular aerobic metabolism (C) lead to anaerobic metabolism and metabolic acidosis. After metabolite accumulation, a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis will be evident, but as respiratory failure ensues, metabolic acidosis will prevail and should signal impending hemodynamic collapse. Impaired kidney bicarbonate reabsorption (D) describes the pathophysiology of a nonanion gap metabolic acidosis such as renal tubular acidosis, which presents with failure to thrive and growth delay. Recurrent episodes of diarrhea (E) may lead to the loss of bicarbonate ions in the gastrointestinal tract, ultimately causing a nonanion gap metabolic acidosis.
