Question: A 1-year-old girl presents to the ED with a fever for the last 6 days. Physical exam reveals conjunctival injection, oral fissures, a rash with peeling on two fingers, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following tests is most appropriate?

Options.text: C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate

ExplanationEN:
Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is a life-threatening vasculitis most common in children. The diagnostic criteria for classic Kawasaki disease include fever for 5 days in addition to at least four of five other physical exam findings. These findings include conjunctival injection; oral mucosa membrane changes such as fissured lips, injected pharynx, or strawberry tongue; peripheral extremity changes including erythema of the palms or soles, or edema of the hands or feet; a polymorphous rash; and cervical lymphadenopathy. Of note, the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease can be made in a patient with a fever for 4 days if they meet all other diagnostic criteria. Patients who meet classic Kawasaki disease diagnostic criteria do not require further laboratory testing to confirm the diagnosis. The next step is to perform echocardiography to evaluate for potentially devastating coronary artery aneurysms. Additionally, patients who develop peeling need an echocardiogram because peeling is usually a later finding.

Some patients may have incomplete Kawasaki disease. The diagnosis of incomplete Kawasaki disease requires a fever for at least 5 days plus two to three of the physical exam findings of Kawasaki disease. These patients should also have laboratory evidence of inflammation characterized by an elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Additional laboratory evidence of incomplete Kawasaki disease includes a WBC count ≥ 15 x 109/L, normocytic, normochromic anemia for age, platelet cell count ≥ 450,000/microL, pyuria (≥ 10 WBCs/high-power field), serum alanine aminotransferase level > 50 units/L, and serum albumin ≤ 3 g/dL. Alternatively, patients with incomplete Kawasaki disease and elevated inflammatory markers can undergo echocardiography instead of further laboratory testing. Children with atypical Kawasaki disease should have at least three laboratory abnormalities consistent with the diagnosis.

The treatment of Kawasaki disease and incomplete Kawasaki disease includes intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin. The dreaded complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment needs to be initiated immediately to prevent this complication.



Blood cultures (A) would be appropriate in a child suspected of sepsis. However, this child meets the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease. Blood cultures would not be the most appropriate study but should be considered in any child with a fever.

Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (B) are markers of inflammation that help in the diagnosis of atypical or incomplete Kawasaki. However, this patient already meets complete Kawasaki diagnostic criteria so these tests are not indicated.

A urinalysis (D) should be considered in any female child with a fever. However, while this is an appropriate study in a patient with Kawasaki disease, an echocardiogram is the most appropriate test.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents with an itchy rash and joint pain, which appeared suddenly this afternoon. His parent is concerned because he ate peanuts earlier this morning, although he has had them in the past without problems. He also developed a cough and rhinorrhea 2 days ago and is taking amoxicillin for an ear infection diagnosed 8 days ago. He has not had any vomiting or difficulty breathing. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), and his exam is remarkable for only the rash shown above. His fever and joint pain resolve quickly with acetaminophen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Serum sickness is an immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity reaction seen after the administration of one of the few medications derived from animal serum. Immunoglobulin M antibodies can develop about 7–14 days after exposure to animal serum, which forms complexes with any remaining animal serum depositing in tissues, activating complement and causing mast cells to degranulate. Symptoms include a urticarial rash, lymphadenopathy, and sometimes fever and arthralgias. The rash often appears as annular, sharply marginated, coalescing plaques, as seen in this patient. Severe cases of true serum sickness can include blurry vision from anterior uveitis, splenomegaly, diarrhea, neuropathy, and even Guillain-Barré syndrome. Symptoms usually resolve within 2 weeks of removal of the causative agent.

A serum sickness-like reaction is a similar but less severe illness that occurs after the administration of a medication or vaccine. This does not result in the formation of measurable immune complexes but otherwise has similar symptoms. When fever and joint pain are present, they are usually mild. The most common medications that cause a serum sickness-like reaction are cefaclor and amoxicillin. The most frequent vaccines that cause it include the influenza, pneumococcal, and tetanus vaccines. Other common medications include penicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and the list of uncommonly implicated medications is extensive.

Patients with symptoms of serum sickness without a clear cause should be evaluated for a poststreptococcal infection by testing serum creatinine and complement C3 and C4, and performing a urinalysis. Those with serum sickness usually have mild thrombocytopenia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein level, and occasionally, mild proteinuria or microscopic hematuria.

Treatment is symptomatic care with the removal of the offending agent and acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fevers and joint pain. While there is little evidence to support the use of glucocorticoids, a short course is frequently used in severe cases, such as those with a fever > 38.5°C (101.3°F), severe joint pain, or an extensive rash.



Patients with anaphylaxis (A) usually do not present with a fever and typically have more than one system involved, most frequently GI symptoms with an urticarial rash. It also usually, but not always, happens quickly after exposure to a potential allergen. While anaphylaxis is still a possibility, it is less likely to be the cause than a serum sickness-like reaction in this case.

IgA vasculitis (B) typically presents with palpable purpura, which is more painful than itchy and is located in gravity-dependent areas. It can also present with joint pain, but fever is uncommon. It is also more frequent in slightly older children between 3 and 15 years of age.

The rash due to a viral exanthem (D) can vary, but it often has a blanching, erythematous-to-purplish macular appearance with less urticaria.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a burning sensation in her chest that is worse when she lays flat at night. She has had this sensation before but finds her symptoms have been worsening. Review of systems is notable for fatigue and difficulty manipulating household items, such as utensils, due to stiffness in her hands. Her vital signs are within normal limits and physical exam is notable for taut, thickened skin and mild edema of the hands with stiffness on range of motion testing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Scleroderma is a systemic connective tissue disease that occurs secondary to the pathologic formation or production of collagen. Scleroderma can present with dermatologic findings (tight and smooth skin), joint pain (which is typically mild and symmetric), pulmonary findings (including pulmonary fibrosis and hypertension), cardiac findings (restrictive cardiomyopathy), and kidney abnormalities (with scleroderma renal crisis as the most life-threatening sequelae). Gastrointestinal symptoms occur secondary to dysmotility, which can cause severe reflux disease and small bowel bacterial overgrowth from stasis, which causes chronic diarrhea. The most common gastrointestinal complication of scleroderma is gastroesophageal reflux disease (burning sensation in the chest when lying flat), which occurs secondary to fibrosis and dilation of the lower esophagus resulting in decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone.



Rheumatoid arthritis (A) presents with symmetric joint pain in a middle-aged woman that is typically worse in the morning and improves with activity. Other symptoms include fever, fatigue, malaise, weight loss, and anemia.

Sjögren syndrome (C) presents with dry eyes, dry mouth, arthritis, and dyspareunia.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (D) presents with many different presentations including arthralgias, fever, fatigue, malaise, serositis, oropharyngeal ulcers, photosensitivity, anemia, kidney injury, psychosis, and a malar or discoid rash.

Question: A 25-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents to the ED with a dry cough and dyspnea for the past 2 weeks. Her vital signs are within normal limits, and an ECG is unremarkable. Her X-ray is shown above. Which of the following findings would best support this suspected diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely has sarcoidosis, a multi-organ inflammatory condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas. The lung is the most commonly affected organ.

Other commonly affected organs include the skin, eyes, and liver. The etiology is not fully understood but is thought to be due to an immune reaction related to a prior insult, such as chemical exposure or infection earlier in life. The disease occurs in young, otherwise healthy adults > 18 years old. Symptoms depend on the organ involved and may range from asymptomatic to organ failure.

Constitutional symptoms include fever, fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss. Respiratory symptoms commonly include prolonged cough and dyspnea. Cutaneous symptoms include erythema nodosum, hypo- and hyperpigmentation, and maculopapular lesions. Lupus pernio is pathognomonic for chronic sarcoidosis and is characterized by indurated, raised skin lesions around the nose, beneath the eyes, and on the cheeks. Ocular manifestations include retinitis and anterior or posterior uveitis, which may cause eye pain, photophobia, blurry vision, and increased tearing.

Diagnosis is made clinically, with the assistance of blood work and imaging. Patients may have elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels, hypercalcemia due to increased granuloma production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and an increased CD4:CD8 ratio in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

A chest X-ray classically shows hilar lymphadenopathy, as seen in this patient. A CT scan may show granulomatous lesions. Diagnostic tools such as biopsy, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis, and PET scan are also used to assist diagnosis outside the emergency department.

Treatment includes corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy, depending on the degree of organ involvement.



Decreased bronchoalveolar fluid CD4:CD8 ratio (A) is not expected in sarcoidosis. Instead, the ratio is increased due to a predominance of CD4+ helper T cells in the granulomatous inflammation.

Elevated serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate (C) may be seen in many inflammatory conditions, but it is not specific and does not point toward sarcoidosis over other causes.

Hypocalcemia (D) would not be expected. Sarcoidosis often leads to hypercalcemia due to increased 1-alpha hydroxylase activity in granulomas.

Question: A 2-year-old girl presents with intermittent episodes of abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. An abdominal ultrasound image is provided above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis associated with?
ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely has intussusception, as evidenced by her symptoms and abdominal ultrasound showing the classic bullseye lesion, reflecting telescoping bowel, which is a highly sensitive and specific sonographic finding. Intussusception is associated with IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura. IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting children between 2 and 11 years of age, caused by the deposition of IgA immune complexes. The etiology of the immune complex deposition is unclear, but there appears to be an association with a preceding upper respiratory infection. The classic triad of symptoms includes abdominal pain, arthritis, and a palpable purpuric rash, most commonly involving extensor surfaces of the lower extremities and buttocks. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding occur in 50–75% of cases. IgA vasculitis is also associated with IgA nephropathy, a glomerulonephritis caused by immune complex deposition in the renal mesangium. IgA nephropathy is a nephritic syndrome that may present with hypertension, azotemia, hematuria, proteinuria, and edema. Treatment for IgA vasculitis is supportive. Consultation with a pediatric nephrologist is recommended in patients with kidney involvement. The treatment for intussusception is an air contrast enema.



Appendicitis (A)typically presents as right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Ultrasound findings suggestive of appendicitis include a noncompressible appendix > 6 mm in diameter, periappendiceal fluid, and wall thickness ≥ 3 mm. Appendicitis is rarely associated with intussusception.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (B), formerly known as Churg-Strauss syndrome, is a small-vessel vasculitis that predominantly affects the skin and lungs, and it is rarely associated with intussusception.

Zenker diverticulum (D) is a pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum that presents as dysphagia, halitosis, and neck mass. Patients are at risk for aspiration and esophageal obstruction, which is not associated with intussusception.

Question: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, malaise, blurry vision, and extremity pain, with diminished upper extremity pulses. Vital signs are significant for a T of 100.9°F (38.3°C) and BP of 170/95 mm Hg. Her blood work shows an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 81 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 210 mg/L. MRI shows inflammatory thickening of the vasculature. Which of the following is most likely to be affected in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely has Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis. Takayasu arteritis affects the aorta and its major branches, including the subclavian and carotid arteries, in contrast to giant cell (temporal) arteritis, which predominantly affects patients over 50 years old and has a predilection for the temporal artery.

Patients with Takayasu arteritis may present with nonspecific constitutional symptoms such as fever, malaise, and weight loss. Large artery inflammation and damage can lead to decreased upper extremity pulses, unequal blood pressures in the arms, tenderness over the carotid arteries, bruits, hypertension, retinopathy, and limb claudication.

Diagnosis is made via MRI, which shows inflammatory thickening of affected arteries. CT angiography can also be used and would show stenosis, occlusion, and dilation of arteries.

Since Takayasu arteritis is an inflammatory condition, patients may have elevated inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Treatment is dependent on the severity of the disease and includes corticosteroids and immunosuppressive medications.



Coronary artery (B) involvement can occur in Takayasu arteritis, but it is not the primary or most commonly affected vessel. Coronary involvement is a secondary consideration. It is a feared complication of Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis seen in children who present with fever (for > 5 days), conjunctival injection, desquamating rash, cervical adenopathy, oral mucositis (strawberry tongue), and edema of the hands and feet.

The middle meningeal artery (C) is a branch of the maxillary artery and is not typically involved in large-vessel vasculitis. Takayasu arteritis affects the aorta and its major branches, not small intracranial vessels.

Temporal artery (D) involvement is characteristic of giant cell arteritis (GCA), not Takayasu arteritis. GCA affects patients > 50 years old and has a predilection for the external carotid branches, including the temporal artery.

Question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for serum sickness?
ExplanationEN:
Immune complex-mediated reactions (type III hypersensitivity) occur when IgG or IgM antibodies bind to antigens and form a soluble complex that then causes a local inflammatory reaction. Serum sickness is an example of this type of reaction. Classic serum sickness occurs after administration of a nonhuman protein antigen (e.g., venom antitoxins, rabies antigen). Serum sickness-like symptoms are more commonly seen in children and occur after administration of various medications, such as amoxicillin, cefaclor, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Patients present with fever, polyarthralgias, polyarthritis, and a rash usually 1–2 weeks after starting a new medication. Symptoms may start sooner and be more severe when the patient has been exposed to the antigen previously.

Treatment consists of supportive care and discontinuation of the offending agent. Resolution of symptoms generally occurs within 2 weeks.



Cell-mediated hypersensitivity (type IV) (A) occurs when sensitized lymphocytes detect an antigen and start an inflammatory reaction, such as in erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Cytotoxic antibody reactions (type II) (B) occur when IgM or IgG antibodies bind to membrane-bound antigens, resulting in complement activation.

IgE-mediated hypersensitivity (type I) (C) is responsible for most anaphylactic reactions.

Question: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea on exertion. He has had worsening dyspnea for the last 4 days, which has been most noticeable when climbing stairs, but reports no chest pain. His medical history includes a heart transplantation 10 months ago for cardiac amyloidosis. He now takes mycophenolate daily but notes that he ran out roughly 1 week ago and was unable to refill the prescription due to travel. Vital signs are within normal limits. A chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the best management of this condition?

Options.text: Continuation of his home mycophenolate dose and admission for observation
IV dobutamine infusion and admission to the cardiovascular ICU
IV furosemide and close monitoring of urine output
IV methylprednisolone and cardiology consultation for endomyocardial biopsy

CorrectAnswer: IV methylprednisolone and cardiology consultation for endomyocardial biopsy
ExplanationEN:
Acute cardiac allograft rejection remains a prominent complication of heart transplantation despite recent advances in immunosuppressive therapy. All cardiac transplant recipients are at risk, but the risk increases in the presence of several known donor and recipient factors, including recipients who are younger (< 24 years) and female, donors who are female, and the presence of recipient antibodies against donor antigens. Nonadherence to immunosuppressive therapy is another prominent risk factor that is thought to underlie many cases of rejection in adolescent and young adult recipients (age 17–24 years).

Patients often undergo routine surveillance after cardiac transplantation due to high rates of asymptomatic rejection. Reported clinical symptoms range from mild heart failure and palpitations to cardiogenic shock. Atrial dysrhythmias are a common manifestation. Acute rejection should be suspected in patients in the first year post-transplantation presenting with new cardiac symptoms or objective findings, and endomyocardial biopsy should be performed in cases of high suspicion. While biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis, many patients will be started on empiric treatment, commonly in the form of corticosteroids. Severe rejection is characterized by hemodynamic compromise and shock and is typically treated with antithymocyte globulin. Hemodynamic support in the form of inotropic or vasopressor agents may also be required in such cases. Additionally, patients who receive high-dose corticosteroids or antithymocyte globulin should be given prophylaxis for opportunistic infections. This often consists of clotrimazole for candidiasis, acyclovir for herpesviruses, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii.



Transesophageal echocardiogram (A) has higher sensitivity than transthoracic echocardiogram for conditions such as atrial thrombus and vegetations in endocarditis but is not useful in the diagnosis of acute rejection.

Though this patient will eventually require the continuation of his immunosuppressive regimen (B), he requires high-dose corticosteroids or antithymocyte globulin to treat his acute rejection.

Cardiogenic shock in the setting of acute rejection would warrant inotropic agents and ICU admission (C), but these would not be indicated in cases of mild rejection, such as in this patient.

IV furosemide (D) may be a useful adjunctive therapy in the treatment of this patient’s rejection, but corticosteroids are the most important step in definitive treatment and should be instituted at this time.

Question: A 7-year-old boy presents with fever for 6 days. Examination reveals an uncomfortable child with erythema around the lips with cracking, bilateral conjunctivitis, a generalized rash, and swelling of the hands. Lab tests show an elevated platelet count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Which therapy should be initiated?
ExplanationEN:
Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is a common vasculitis in childhood. Clinicians should consider the diagnosis in any child presenting with prolonged fever. Classic Kawasaki disease is diagnosed based on the presence of fever for > 5 days and four of the five following signs: unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, mucous membrane involvement (strawberry tongue, lip fissures), extremity changes (edema, erythema, pain, desquamation), bilateral conjunctivitis, and nonvesicular rash.

Laboratory tests will often show a number of abnormalities, including thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, anemia, increased inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate), and elevated liver function tests. Treatment is with aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Additionally, patients should have an echocardiogram performed looking for coronary artery aneurysms.



Antibiotics (A) play no role in the management of Kawasaki disease.

Corticosteroids (B) are controversial and currently not recommended.

Long-term anticoagulation (D) is often instituted after admission but acute treatment is with high dose aspirin and IVIG.

Question: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a fever and malaise. Her medical history includes end-stage kidney disease due to systemic lupus erythematosus with a subsequent kidney transplant. She underwent transplantation 4 months ago, at which time the deceased donor allograft was transplanted into the right iliac fossa. Her postoperative course thus far has been uncomplicated, and she has been taking mycophenolate daily. Which of the following findings on physical exam and laboratory testing most strongly suggests a diagnosis of acute allograft rejection?

Options.text: Gross hematuria and red blood cell casts
Low urine output and the presence of granular casts
Right costovertebral angle tenderness and nitrite-positive urine
Right lower quadrant tenderness and elevated serum creatinine levels

CorrectAnswer: Right lower quadrant tenderness and elevated serum creatinine levels
ExplanationEN:
While its incidence has decreased with advances in antirejection therapy, acute allograft rejection remains a fairly common, serious complication of kidney transplantation that threatens graft survival. The introduction of calcineurin inhibitors and antiproliferative agents reduced the incidence of one or more episodes of acute rejection in the first 5 years following transplantation, going from 50–60% in the 1980s to just 8% in 2017. Risk factors for acute rejection include presensitization, human leukocyte antigen mismatches, blood group incompatibility, and age < 18 years. Deceased donor allografts carry a slightly higher risk of acute rejection than living donor grafts.

The majority of episodes of acute kidney rejection occur within 6 months of transplantation, and episodes occurring after the 12-month mark are usually due to aggressive reduction in or nonadherence to an immunosuppressive regimen. Most cases produce no clinical symptoms, but when symptoms are present, they can include fever, malaise, oliguria, and graft pain or tenderness. The location of this patient’s pain is helpful in identifying an issue with the graft, as transplanted kidneys are usually transplanted into the iliac fossa rather than the anatomic location of native kidneys. Given the lack of symptoms, many cases are identified only by laboratory findings, which include elevations in serum creatinine levels, pyuria, and new or worsening proteinuria. Creatinine elevation is considered a late finding of the disease course and is often associated with a high degree of histological damage.

New or worsening hypertension, proteinuria, and elevation in creatinine levels should all raise suspicion for acute rejection, but the definitive diagnosis is made via kidney biopsy. In the absence of frank rejection, a biopsy will also aid in excluding other causes of similar presentations, such as glomerular disease and interstitial nephritis. Treatment of acute allograft rejection typically involves an increased immunosuppressive regimen with glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive agents. However, some patients will not regain full function of the graft kidney even with maximal immunosuppression, and each episode of acute rejection threatens long-term graft survival, as acute rejection is a major predictor of more chronic complications.



Gross hematuria and the presence of red blood cell casts (A) suggest a glomerular source of bleeding, which is not part of the expected pathophysiology of acute allograft rejection.

The combination of hematuria and proteinuria (B) is not typical of acute allograft rejection, as hematuria is not expected.

Oliguria is common in symptomatic cases of acute rejection, but granular casts (C) suggest acute tubular necrosis, which is a separate pathologic entity.

Tenderness at the costovertebral angle and nitrite-positive urine (D) is consistent with pyelonephritis of a native kidney. Symptoms related to complications of the transplanted kidney would be expected in the lower abdomen, where most grafts are placed during transplantation.

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a rash on her arm and face. She burned her forearm on a curling iron 1 week ago and has been applying a topical antibiotic to the burn. She has since developed redness and itching on the forearm that spread to her eyelids. Her vital signs are normal. On physical exam, there is a well-demarcated, weeping, erythematous rash on the right forearm and red papules on the bilateral eyelids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory skin reaction resulting from direct contact with an allergen or irritant. Allergic contact dermatitis is a T cell-mediated, delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Common allergens include nickel, topical antibiotics, fragrances, preservatives in soaps and cleansers, rubber, and plants of the Toxicodendron species (e.g., poison ivy). Irritant contact dermatitis presents similarly to the allergic form, but it is not immune mediated. Common irritants include industrial solvents and detergents. Acute contact dermatitis presents with well-demarcated, erythematous, pruritic papules, plaques, or vesicles, often with linear streaking. In severe cases, there may be bullae and edema. If left untreated, it can progress to a chronic form, characterized by lichenification, scale, and fissures. The rash is distributed in the areas exposed to the trigger but can become generalized due to secondary transfer. The hands, face, and eyelids are the most common areas involved, as they are most likely to come in contact with the environment. Other common clinical scenarios include involvement of the neck and chest due to fragrances, the scalp and adjacent skin due to hair dyes or shampoos, the tops of the feet due to rubber in shoes, and the hands due to occupational exposures. In a patient with suspected contact dermatitis, a careful history regarding the patient’s occupation, hobbies, and new exposures or products, along with the timing and distribution of the rash, can provide clues to the diagnosis and etiology. Long-term exposure to a previously tolerated allergen does not exclude it as the cause, as sensitivities can change over time. When symptoms persist and the trigger is not easily identified, patients should be referred for patch testing. Treatment includes avoidance of the offending agent and controlling inflammation with steroids. Low-potency topical steroids should be used on the face, anogenital region, and flexural areas, while medium- to high-potency topical steroids can be used in other locations. In cases of extensive, severe rash, systemic steroids are first line. Oral steroids should be prescribed as a 3-week taper to prevent rebound worsening symptoms. This patient likely developed allergic contact dermatitis in response to the topical antibiotic that she applied to the burn. Secondary eyelid involvement is common, as the contact allergen is easily spread to the face by the hands. Neomycin and bacitracin, which are often combined with polymyxin B in triple antibiotic preparations, are common contact allergens.



Cellulitis (A) presents with localized erythema and induration and can be confused with contact dermatitis. However, cellulitis does not typically itch, and the presence of pruritus suggests against infection. Additionally, cellulitis should not spread to noncontiguous areas, such as the eyelids. Dyshidrotic eczema (C) is a form of eczema characterized by a pruritic, vesicular eruption on the hands and feet, particularly the palms and soles. It is not found on the forearms or face. Seborrheic dermatitis (D) presents with pruritic, greasy plaques with yellow scale, commonly affecting areas rich in sebaceous glands, including the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and less commonly the trunk. It does not typically present on the arms.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with gradually worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, and a nonproductive cough, which started 7 months ago. He now feels short of breath even with minor exertion. The patient has a 50 pack-year smoking history, but he has not smoked for several years prior to his left lung transplant, which occurred 2 years ago. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 157/98 mm Hg, heart rate is 90 bpm, respiratory rate is 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Physical exam is notable for unilateral expiratory wheezes on the patient’s left side. Forced expiratory volume in 1 second is performed, demonstrating a decline of 20% from his forced expiratory volume in 1 second performed 1 year ago by his outpatient clinician. A chest radiograph is notable for hyperinflation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Bronchiolitis obliterans may have a multifactorial etiology, but it is generally thought of as a manifestation of chronic lung transplant rejection. Early in the pathology, a submucosal lymphocytic inflammation can disrupt the epithelium of the small airways, followed by an ingrowth of fibromyxoid granulation tissue into the airway lumen, leading to the obliteration of the airway lumen. The presentation of bronchiolitis obliterans can be vague but presents in the setting of a lung transplant with dyspnea on exertion, nonproductive cough, and possible wheezing. This presentation occurs gradually with a slow onset of loss of pulmonary function, which differentiates it from other possible etiologies such as infection.

A key diagnostic clue to diagnosing bronchiolitis obliterans is the change in forced expiratory volume in 1 second. In bronchiolitis obliterans, a chronic decline in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second or forced expiratory volume in 1 second:forced vital capacity ratio can be seen supporting this diagnosis in the setting of a lung transplant. The diagnosis can be confirmed with a biopsy. Imaging is generally not useful in confirming the diagnosis, but radiography can be ordered to rule out other etiologies of the patient’s decline in pulmonary function including infection. Treatment should involve the consultation of the transplant service and can include long-term azithromycin therapy, changing immunosuppressive medications, and plasmapheresis, among other therapies, after initially stabilizing the patient.



Acute graft rejection (A) typically presents within the first 6 months of transplant with symptoms that could be similar to bronchiolitis obliterans. Symptoms can be nonspecific and include low-grade fever, shortness of breath, and cough. Patients can also be asymptomatic, and the diagnosis can be supported with surveillance transbronchial biopsies.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C) typically presents with dyspnea, wheezing, a barrel chest, intercostal hypertrophy, and hypoxia in a patient with a significant smoking history. This patient has not smoked since before the transplant, so it is unlikely that inhalation of smoke has destroyed the elastic tissue in his new lung.

Pneumonia (D) presents with a fever, cough, and possible interstitial infiltrates or lobar consolidation on chest radiography. This presentation would be more sudden and less likely to occur over a 7-month period in the setting of a lung transplant.

Question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for chest pain. She reports no other symptoms. The pain began several hours after she was lifting weights at the gym. Her vital signs are HR 74 bpm, BP 128/84 mm Hg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99%, and T 36.9°C. She is in no acute distress, and her physical exam is unremarkable. She has a medical history of systemic lupus erythematosus and takes prednisone daily. She has no history of deep vein thrombosis, does not use hormonal medications, and reports no recent surgeries or trauma. She does not have a family history of cardiac disease. Her ECG shows normal sinus rhythm and normal intervals and does not demonstrate any PR or ST segment changes. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms that sound most consistent with costochondritis or musculoskeletal chest pain. However, her medical history is notable for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The inflammatory process caused by SLE causes accelerated atherosclerosis and a hypercoagulable state, which predisposes individuals to atherosclerotic and thromboembolic disease. Early coronary artery disease is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SLE. The risk of myocardial infarction is markedly higher in patients with SLE, particularly for young premenopausal women relative to healthy women of the same age group. In addition to coronary artery disease, patients with SLE are prone to other cardiac manifestations such as pericarditis, myocarditis, and endocarditis. While this patient’s presentation may be considered reassuring and low risk in an otherwise healthy, young patient, there should be a low threshold to evaluate for cardiac pathology in the setting of SLE. Therefore, cardiac enzymes should be obtained.



Discharging with NSAIDs and colchicine (A) may be appropriate if this patient had pericarditis. Typical ECG findings in pericarditis include widespread concave ST segment elevation, PR depression, and downsloping of the TP segment. Bedside ultrasound may also be used to evaluate for pericardial effusion. While pericarditis should be considered during the initial evaluation of patients with SLE who present with chest pain, this patient’s ECG does not demonstrate findings concerning for pericarditis, and further lab tests and imaging are indicated to assess for other cardiac manifestations. Initiating anticoagulation (B) would be appropriate for acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism. However, the diagnosis should be confirmed before initiating therapy. Further testing should be obtained for this patient before such an intervention. If this patient did not have SLE, reassurance and discharge (D) may be considered, given the absence of traditional risk factors, family history, and ECG changes. Despite lacking traditional risk factors, this patient’s medical history is categorized as high risk, and further testing should be obtained. Patients taking chronic steroids are at risk of adrenal insufficiency, often due to physiologic stressors (such as infection) or if glucocorticoid medication use is discontinued. Stress-dose steroids (E) should be administered if there is clinical suspicion of adrenal insufficiency or sepsis. This patient does not have signs or symptoms of adrenal insufficiency or infection.

Question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department due to dyspnea. She notes progressive dyspnea with associated cough and intermittent hemoptysis for the past 3 weeks. Her medical history includes a kidney transplant 5 months ago due to chronic interstitial nephritis. She takes mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus daily. She has never lived outside of the United States and has no history of experiencing homelessness or incarceration. She has had no recent travel or known sick contacts. Lab results show a white blood cell count of 1,200/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm3. CT imaging is recommended to further evaluate possible pneumonia found on a chest X-ray, and the image is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely causative pathogen?
ExplanationEN:
Infection is a significant obstacle in achieving disease-free survival for patients following solid organ transplantation. With improving immunosuppressive regimens and longer graft survival, the incidence and spectrum of infection complications have grown. The risk of developing infectious complications results from the interplay between epidemiologic exposure of the patient and the overall immunosuppressive state. The risk of infection with a specific pathogen varies by post-transplant timing. A patient 1–6 months post-transplant, such as this patient, is at particular risk of opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus, parasites, and endemic mycoses, including Aspergillus.

A patient within 1–6 months post-transplant who presents with respiratory symptoms and a cavitary lesion on imaging (shown above in the right lung) is highly suspicious for fungal infection or tuberculosis. Given this patient’s lack of risk factors for tuberculosis, such as experiencing incarceration or homelessness, a fungal etiology like Aspergillus fumigatus is the most likely cause. More specifically, this patient would likely be diagnosed with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, given the evidence of angioinvasion in the form of hemoptysis. This patient’s neutropenia should further raise suspicion for a fungal etiology. Definitive diagnosis is achieved via tissue sampling and biopsy, but positive fungal testing such as serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan assay help support the diagnosis. Polymerase chain reaction testing for Aspergillus DNA in bronchoalveolar lavage samples may also support the diagnosis.

Voriconazole is the treatment of choice for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, with echinocandins indicated as well in severe cases. However, voriconazole has significant interactions with calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus, so dose reductions of the immunosuppressive agents or using an alternate antifungal, such as posaconazole, is typically warranted. Patients at high risk for fungal infections are often treated with antifungal prophylaxis following transplant.



Cytomegalovirus (B) commonly complicates the post-transplant course for patients but would not be expected to cause a cavitary lung lesion. Tuberculosis (C) would need to be ruled out in this patient with neutropenia and a cavitary lung lesion but is less likely to be the cause than an endemic fungal infection, as this patient has no risk factors for tuberculosis. Respiratory symptoms in a transplant patient should raise suspicion for respiratory syncytial virus (D), but a cavitary lesion would not be expected in this case. Typical community-acquired infections, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae (E), are possible during the 1–6 month period but are more common after 6 months, and this would be more likely to cause lobar consolidation rather than cavitation.

Question: A 20-year-old man presents to the ED after a bee sting. He has a diffuse urticarial rash. Physical exam reveals wheezing bilaterally. Which of the following medications is most appropriate?
ExplanationEN:
Anaphylaxis is an acute IgE-mediated immune response that can be triggered by food, drugs, insect stings, or other antigens. Anaphylaxis is defined as a serious allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction that can progress rapidly and may cause death. It is characterized by involvement of multiple organ systems including the skin (urticaria or rash), mucosa (swelling of the lips or tongue), GI (vomiting), cardiovascular (tachycardia and hypotension), and respiratory (difficulty breathing and wheezing) systems. Skin and mucosal findings occur in up to 90% of patients.

Several diagnostic criteria have been recognized. Anaphylaxis should be suspected in a patient with a history suggestive of a recent allergen exposure who develops symptoms within several minutes to hours of exposure. Any patient with signs or symptoms involving at least two organ systems should be suspected of anaphylaxis. Cutaneous manifestations are the most common, which can help establish the diagnosis.

The treatment for anaphylaxis is intramuscular epinephrine. Antihistamines and steroids are often given, but they do not provide a mortality benefit.



Albuterol (A), diphenhydramine (B), and methylprednisolone (D) can be used as adjunctive therapy for anaphylaxis. The only medication shown to have a mortality benefit is epinephrine. All adjunct treatment for anaphylaxis is mainly given for symptomatic treatment but does not directly treat the underlying disease process.

Question: Which of the following is the most common major manifestation found in patients diagnosed with rheumatic fever?
ExplanationEN:
Acute rheumatic fever most commonly affects children between 5 and 15 years of age and follows a streptococcal pharyngitis infection. The five major manifestations (i.e., Jones criteria) of acute rheumatic fever are carditis, arthritis, central nervous system involvement (e.g., Sydenham chorea), subcutaneous nodules, and erythema marginatum. Arthritis is common, most often involves the large joints, and is usually migratory and polyarticular. Carditis is usually subclinical but found in well over one-half of patients with rheumatic fever and is also one of the most common major manifestations (along with arthritis).

An echocardiogram is typically necessary to diagnose carditis. Consider getting an echocardiogram on patients with large joint migratory polyarthritis and fevers, as this can diagnose rheumatic fever. The four minor manifestations of rheumatic fever are arthralgia, fever, elevated acute phase reactants (i.e., erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR], C-reactive protein [CRP]), and a prolonged PR interval on ECG. A fever is defined as 38.5°C, elevated ESR at 60 mm/hr, and elevated CRP at 3 mg/dL. The diagnosis of rheumatic fever has two sets of criteria for different populations depending on risk. Initial acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed with evidence of streptococcal infection plus two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria. Patients who previously had rheumatic fever follow the same diagnostic criteria but can also be diagnosed with three minor criteria alone.



Erythema marginatum (B) and subcutaneous nodules are found in fewer than 10% of people with rheumatic fever.

Fever (C) is a minor manifestation of rheumatic fever but is very common on presentation.

Sydenham chorea (D) usually presents months after the diagnosis of rheumatic fever but can occur in as many as one-fourth of patients with this disease.

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents with diffuse joint pain and a rash, which is shown above. She is febrile to 101.1°F (38.4°C). Which of the following antibodies is the most specific for the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease considered a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which cells and virtually every organ may be damaged via tissue-specific autoantibodies and immune complexes. Though the disease etiology is unknown, a subtype of lupus is drug-induced. Commonly implicated drugs include procainamide, hydralazine, and isoniazid. Approximately 90% of patients with SLE are women of reproductive age. SLE affects nearly every organ in the body, so patients may have various presentations. Classic signs and symptoms include a characteristic malar or discoid rash, arthralgias, and fever. Patients may also have serositis, hematologic disorders such as cytopenias, hypercoagulability disorders such as antiphospholipid syndrome, oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers, photosensitivity, neurologic disorders such as seizures and psychosis, cardiopulmonary disease such as pleuritis, pericarditis, myocardial infarction, or endocarditis, and kidney disease. Diffuse proliferative nephritis is the most common and severe kidney disease associated with SLE. The most common causes of death in patients with SLE are cardiovascular disease, infection, and kidney disease. About 98% of patients with SLE have positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA), making it a valuable screening tool. Anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for SLE and thus help confirm the disease. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, immunosuppressive therapy, and hydroxychloroquine.



Anticardiolipin antibodies (B) are seen in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune hypercoagulability disorder associated with SLE.

Antihistone antibodies (C) are sensitive for drug-induced SLE due to medications such as procainamide and hydralazine. There is no mention of a medication that this patient is taking.

Antinuclear antibodies (D) are sensitive but not specific for SLE, thus they are used to screen patients for SLE. Antinuclear antibodies are seen in various autoimmune conditions including Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, mixed connective tissue disease, and autoimmune hepatitis.

She had a kidney transplant 2 weeks ago. On examination, her heart rate is 112 bpm, blood pressure is 155/100 mm Hg, and temperature is 101.3°F (38.5ºC). Which of the following describes the pathophysiology of the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Acute inflammation or infection due to luminal obstruction
CD4+ T-cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in proliferation of the vascular intima and fibrosis of renal vessels causing marked decrease in lumen size
CD8+ T-cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in leukocyte infiltration of graft vessels impairing perfusion
Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells or basophils causing histamine release

CorrectAnswer: CD8+ T-cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in leukocyte infiltration of graft vessels impairing perfusion
ExplanationEN:
CD8+ T-cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in leukocyte infiltration of graft vessels impairing perfusion is the mechanism of acute rejection following kidney transplant. This is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction similar to a tuberculosis skin test, or contact dermatitis (poison ivy, poison oak). It is a delayed T-cell mediated attack against foreign major histocompatibility complexes in the donated organ. It can occur within weeks of transplant and up to approximately 3 months after. It results in microvascular lesions via leukocyte infiltration of the graft vessels impairing perfusion to the graft.

Patients may present with fever, swelling, and tenderness over the allograft and decreased urine output. A subtle rise in creatinine is important to note. A renal ultrasound should be performed to rule out obstruction, abscess, vascular thrombosis, and perirenal collections of blood. Early consultation with the patient’s transplant team or a nephrologist is important. Acute rejection is often managed by high-dose methylprednisolone.



Acute inflammation or infection due to luminal obstruction (A) describes the pathophysiology of acute appendicitis. Given the patient’s history and presentation, acute rejection following a kidney transplant is the most likely diagnosis.

CD4+ T-cell mediated process resulting in the proliferation of the vascular intima and fibrosis of the renal vessels causing a marked decrease in lumen size (B) describes the pathophysiology of chronic rejection following kidney transplant. It is a combination of type II and type IV hypersensitivity reactions. This process occurs over months to years resulting in nephrosclerosis.

Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells or basophils causing histamine release (D) describes the pathophysiology of anaphylaxis. This is a form of type I hypersensitivity.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department for facial swelling. He states that symptoms started 1 hour prior to arrival after being slapped on the right side of his face. He reports that symptoms started with mild right-sided facial swelling but has progressed to involve his entire face as well as his mouth. He has no history of allergies. He does not use any medications. When asked, he notes that his father and paternal grandfather have had similar episodes in the past but were never formally diagnosed. On exam, he has bilateral facial swelling with edema noted in the lips, tongue, and uvula. There are no rashes on the skin exam. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
ExplanationEN:
The patient is presenting with hereditary angioedema and should be given fresh frozen plasma. Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant disorder that is characterized by a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor. Patients will present with recurrent acute bouts of angioedema without urticaria or pruritus. Minor trauma can trigger episodes, but oftentimes a clear trigger is not identifiable. Hereditary angioedema can be diagnosed by obtaining serum C4 levels.

Normal treatments for anaphylaxis and allergic reactions, such as epinephrine, corticosteroids, and antihistamines, are ineffective at treating hereditary angioedema. Assessment and protection of the airway is the most important aspect of management, as asphyxiation from laryngeal edema is the most common cause of death. First-line medical treatment involves the administration of either plasma-derived or recombinant C1 esterase inhibitor. Bradykinin B2-receptor antagonists and kallikrein inhibitors are also effective treatments. However, these therapies are often unavailable, so fresh frozen plasma is the therapy of choice.



Cryoprecipitate (A) is prepared from plasma and has a role in treating many bleeding disorders but is not efficacious in treating hereditary angioedema.

Epinephrine (C) is a first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, which can also present with angioedema, but is ineffective in hereditary angioedema.

Diphenhydramine (B) is effective at treating histamine-mediated allergic reactions but has no role in hereditary angioedema.

Question: A 12-year-old girl presents with joint pain and fevers. She reports that over the past week, she has had pain in multiple joints, starting in the shoulders, then moving to the left knee. Today, her parent noticed that she had a fever and a rash. She has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin, and on review of systems, she notes a sore throat for several days 1 month ago. On a physical exam, there is a slightly raised macular rash in a serpiginous pattern with central clearing on her trunk. She has no murmur on auscultation. Her left knee is tender with an effusion. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms concerning for acute rheumatic fever. Primarily a disease of childhood, rheumatic fever occurs 2–6 weeks after an initial group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus infection. Antibodies subsequently form and then invade host tissues. Patients usually present with nonspecific systemic symptoms early in the disease course, then develop more focal symptoms as the disease progresses. There is a specific constellation of symptoms that is characteristic of rheumatic fever that confirms the diagnosis. The Jones criteria were developed to establish a diagnosis of rheumatic fever in conjunction with evidence of an antecedent streptococcal infection. The major Jones criteria are carditis (including a new or changing murmur, congestive heart failure, or pericarditis), chorea, migratory polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules. The minor criteria are fever, arthralgias, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, or prolonged PR interval. Two major criteria or two minor criteria with one major criterion suggest a high probability of acute rheumatic fever.

The most common symptom of acute rheumatic fever is a fleeting polyarthritis that is migratory and involves the large joints. The most serious manifestation is carditis and typically involves valvulitis with a murmur. The mitral valve is most commonly involved. Erythema marginatum is rare but specific for rheumatic fever and is described as bright pink macules or papules in a serpiginous pattern, sometimes with central clearing that is not pruritic or painful and does not involve the face. Sydenham chorea is defined as involuntary jerking movements of the hands, feet, face, and tongue. Patients should be admitted to the hospital and started on antibiotics until the diagnosis is confirmed.

Intramuscular penicillin G or oral penicillin is the preferred antibiotic. Cephalosporins can be used for those with a history of a mild reaction to penicillin. Azithromycin is an acceptable alternative for those with anaphylaxis to penicillin. Many patients must remain on prophylactic antimicrobial therapy for years or even for life. The arthritis in acute rheumatic fever responds remarkably well to NSAIDs.



First-, second-, or third-generation cephalosporins can be used in acute rheumatic fever. Cefuroxime (B) is a second-generation cephalosporin that is used to treat rheumatic fever in those with mild penicillin allergies. However, this patient has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin, so other options should be used.

Ciprofloxacin (C) is not recommended for the treatment of acute rheumatic fever.

Doxycycline (D) has poor activity against Streptococcus and is not a viable option for acute rheumatic fever. It is used to treat Lyme disease, and while erythema migrans can be somewhat similar in appearance to erythema marginatum, they are distinct entities.

Question: Which of the following findings differentiates rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?

Options.text: Involvement of the proximal interphalangeal joints

ExplanationEN:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) share a number of features, but constitutional symptoms are only seen in RA. RA is a chronic inflammatory disease that is more common in women and has a peak onset between the ages of 30 and 59.

Patients with RA often present with fatigue, fever, malaise, weakness, and musculoskeletal pain lasting for weeks to months. Arthritis involves symmetric joints of the hands, wrists, and elbows. Morning stiffness is common and usually lasts for about an hour. Inflammation may affect other organs, leading to hepatitis, scleritis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and pleuritis. Atlantoaxial subluxation may also occur, and cervical spine precautions should be maintained during intubation.



Both RA and OA often involve the proximal interphalangeal joints (A), making this nonspecific for RA.

Joint pain worsening with activity (B) is characteristic of OA, which is exacerbated with mechanical stress compared to RA, in which pain and stiffness often improve with activity as inflammation decreases.

The morning stiffness (C) associated with RA lasts > 30 minutes and often lasts many hours. The joint pain and stiffness associated with OA are generally worse in the evening, but it may also be worse first thing in the morning.

RA is often polyarticular (D), but it may manifest as persistent monoarthritis of a large joint such as the knee, wrist, hip, or ankle. OA can also involve multiple joints, especially in older adults, or may be monoarticular. The key difference is the inflammatory nature of RA, while OA is more degenerative, with wear-and-tear changes.

Question: What test is helpful in ruling out the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus?
ExplanationEN:
The antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is highly sensitive, as it is present in nearly all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disorder. The disease results in organ inflammation, dysfunction, and eventually destruction. Patients can present with a wide variety of clinical presentations, including nephritis, thrombosis, carditis, pneumonitis, pulmonary hypertension, and stroke.

The workup of patients with signs or symptoms concerning for SLE involves a number of serum tests, all of which are imperfect. However, nearly all patients with the disease will have ANA present on testing. The absence of this antibody virtually rules out the disease. Unfortunately, it is also present in up to 50% of patients without SLE, so a positive test does not clinch the diagnosis.



Anti-ribosomal P protein antibody (A) is highly specific for SLE but has a low sensitivity, so a negative result does not rule out SLE.

Anti-Smith antibody (B) is a more specific antibody for SLE, but it is not present in all patients with the disease.

C-reactive protein (D) does not typically rise in response to increased disease activity and may be within reference range in 10–15% of patients.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (E) is frequently elevated in SLE but may be within normal limits in up to 30% of patients.

Question: Which of the following is a minor rather than a major Jones criterion in the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever?
ExplanationEN:
Rheumatic fever is a known delayed sequela of infection with group A streptococcal infection. The Jones criteria, created in 1944 and updated in 1992, are used to diagnose acute rheumatic fever (ARF). Rheumatic heart disease is an important yet uncommon sequela of rheumatic fever. ARF incidence is declining in the US and other resource-rich countries and is reported to be < 20 cases per 100,000 individuals in school-aged children.

Diagnosis of ARF is possible using one major plus two minor Jones criteria or two major Jones criteria. Major criteria include carditis (new murmur), polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum (nonpruritic, erythematous rings found on the trunk and inner limbs), and subcutaneous nodules (painless collagen collections on the back of wrists, elbows, and knees). Minor criteria include fever, arthralgias, prolonged PR interval on ECG, and elevated acute phase reactants (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein).



Erythema marginatum (A) refers to a nonpruritic rash involving the trunk and extremities, sparing the face, and is one of the major Jones criteria.

New murmur (C) represents carditis, or valvulitis, which is a major Jones criterion.

Polyarthritis (D) and arthritis are considered major Jones criteria, and they most often affect large joints such as the knees, ankles, and elbows. Polyarthralgia and monoarthralgia are part of the minor Jones criteria.

Subcutaneous nodules (E) are painless and firm nodules located over bones or tendons, and they are part of the major Jones criteria.

Question: A 63-year-old woman with a prior orthotopic kidney transplant who takes tacrolimus and levothyroxine presents with a new skin rash. The rash developed yesterday with painless “blood blisters” that formed on her buttocks and arms. Since then, she reports that when the blisters pop, they leave behind a “disgusting pit in my skin.” She reports no new exposures to foods or skin products, changes in her medications, or fever. Her exam is as shown above. What therapy should the patient receive to treat her condition?
ExplanationEN:
This immunocompromised patient presents with hemorrhagic bullae that give way to necrotic ulcers, most concerning for ecthyma gangrenosum, which should be treated immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics with double antipseudomonal coverage. Ecthyma gangrenosum is a rare, rapidly progressive skin manifestation of bacteremia, usually from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Bacteria invade perivascular structures and lead to diffuse ulcerative lesions from ischemic necrosis. The lesions develop in < 18 hours and progress rapidly. Patients are usually immunosuppressed. They can present with sepsis or other signs of bacteremia, but patients with ecthyma gangrenosum often present without other constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis is made clinically and confirmed by blood culture.



Cutaneous mucormycosis is another infection that leads to rapidly progressing skin necrosis and is treated with systemic antifungals (D). However, cutaneous mucormycosis is usually limited to a single lesion and does not develop from hemorrhagic bullae.

Pyoderma gangrenosum can also lead to necrotic skin ulceration and can be treated with steroids (B) in addition to antibiotic therapy. Necrosis in pyoderma gangrenosum is very tender and evolves more slowly.

Methotrexate (C) can be used for cutaneous manifestations of certain vasculitides or psoriasis but should not be used in this patient with a likely serious bacterial infection.

Question: A 47-year-old woman with a history of Raynaud phenomenon presents to the emergency department with pain in her second and third fingers of both hands. She also reports a pale color and paresthesias. She has felt this way since yesterday and has not been able to relieve the symptoms with her typical maneuvers. Her primary care clinician has indicated that, at some point, she may need medication to help with the symptoms. What is the recommended first-line oral medical therapy recommended for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Raynaud phenomenon is a disorder characterized by exaggerated vasoconstriction of the digital arteries in response to cold temperature or emotional stress. The disease may be a primary disorder not associated with other symptoms, or it may be associated with other autoimmune disorders, such as systemic lupus erythematosus or systemic sclerosis. The phenomenon is most often found in the hands. Typically, patients report sudden-onset cold fingers, paresthesias, aching fingers, and hand clumsiness, and they have sharply demarcated skin pallor due to constricted blood flow. The skin can become cyanotic, which suggests tissue hypoxia. Typically, an attack begins in one finger and then spreads to other digits symmetrically. The thumb is often spared. There are no diagnostic tests used to diagnose Raynaud phenomenon. The diagnosis is based on symptoms, including fingers sensitive to the cold, changing color when exposed to the cold, and turning white or blue. The only testing that is recommended is to determine whether the patient has Raynaud phenomenon associated with an underlying autoimmune disorder. Patients with primary Raynaud phenomenon often have transient symptoms that eventually completely disappear. Patients with secondary Raynaud phenomenon are more likely to have progressive, unremitting disease, and they may develop digital ischemia requiring aggressive interventions.

The initial management of Raynaud phenomenon includes lifestyle modifications, such as avoidance of the cold, keeping the body and the digits warm, avoiding trauma to the fingertips, limiting emotional stress, avoiding vasoconstricting drugs and medications, and smoking cessation. If nonpharmacologic measures do not relieve the patient’s symptoms, pharmacologic therapy can be instituted. Long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as nifedipine and amlodipine, are the recommended first-line therapy for the disease. Patients should be started on a low dose and gradually increased as needed. If calcium channel blockers are not tolerated by the patient, then other treatment options include a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor such as sildenafil, topical nitrates such as 2% nitroglycerin ointment, angiotensin II receptor blockers such as losartan, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine.



Beta-blockers such as metoprolol (A) are not indicated for the treatment of Raynaud phenomenon. While topical nitrates can be used in patients who have not tolerated oral calcium channel blockers, oral nitroglycerin (C) is not recommended for Raynaud phenomenon. Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as verapamil (D) or diltiazem, have not been effective for Raynaud phenomenon.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with finger pain. The patient was shoveling snow when her symptoms began. These symptoms have happened to her before and typically start with severe pain in her hands, followed by color changes in her fingers. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Primary Raynaud phenomenon occurs secondary to vasospasm, typically of the digits, and presents with severe pain and a color change in the fingers, which is typically seen as white discoloration of the fingers (initial vasospasm), followed by cyanosis (tissue hypoxia), and then rubor (reperfusion). These episodes are painful and can be precipitated by stressors, such as exertion, emotions, or cold weather (environment).

Secondary Raynaud phenomenon is seen in association with other connective tissue diseases, such as scleroderma. Thus, a new diagnosis of Raynaud phenomenon warrants outpatient follow-up to ensure that a systemic connective tissue disease is not present. The treatment of Raynaud phenomenon is a calcium channel blocker, such as nifedipine. If the patient cannot tolerate a calcium channel blocker, other interventions include sildenafil, topical nitrates, losartan, and even botulinum toxin injections. Outpatient treatment of anxiety or any mood disorders is also important, given the correlation of symptoms with stressors.



Iloprost (A) is a prostaglandin analogue and vasodilator that is used in thromboangiitis obliterans, which presents with digital ischemia typically in men who smoke. It is not the best treatment for Raynaud phenomenon.

Phentolamine (C) is an alpha-1 blocker that has limited data supporting its use in Raynaud phenomenon. Phentolamine is a potential initial blood pressure medication used in pheochromocytoma.

Sildenafil (D) is a vasodilator that is used to treat erectile dysfunction. However, it is also used in some refractory cases of primary Raynaud phenomenon with symptomatic improvement. It is not the best initial treatment for primary Raynaud phenomenon.

Question: A 54-year-old woman presents after a fall. She notes she usually walks with a cane but did not have it handy today. You notice contractures of the fingers bilaterally, and her skin is thick and hard. When you range her elbows, you can hear what sounds like crepitus along the triceps tendon during extension. ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with systemic sclerosis, also known as scleroderma. This disease is caused by excessive accumulation of collagen and matrix in various tissues. Skin involvement is the most clinically apparent feature, manifesting as skin thickening and hardening. Scleroderma also affects the musculoskeletal system, leading to arthralgia, arthritis, and tendon friction rubs. The disease leads to widespread complications with problems in multiple organ systems, from interstitial lung disease to kidney impairment, to gastrointestinal dysmotility, and then vascular disease. Raynaud phenomenon is virtually always present in patients with scleroderma and is characterized by reversible vasospasm in the digital arteries of the hands and feet. This is often triggered by cold or stress and causes a characteristic white, red, and blue discoloration.

A rectovaginal fistula (D) may be a complication of cancer, radiation, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department for generalized fatigue and weakness. He had a kidney transplant 7 weeks ago and is currently on immunosuppressive therapy. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 167/108 mm Hg, heart rate is 90 bpm, respiratory rate is 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for tenderness over his transplanted kidney. Laboratory values reveal a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L and a creatinine of 2.9 mg/dL from a baseline of 2.0 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Acute kidney graft rejection typically occurs within the first 6 months after transplantation (secondary to T cell activity) and may present in an asymptomatic patient or with weakness, fatigue, fevers, or tenderness of the transplanted kidney. The diagnosis is typically suggested by an increased creatinine (which is a late manifestation) or proteinuria. The incidence of acute rejection has been reduced since the introduction and use of immunosuppressive agents, but patients who do not take their medication are at particular risk for rejection. The diagnosis of acute rejection should be suspected if there are any of the following: a new increase in serum creatinine of ≥ 25%, worsening hypertension, proteinuria > 1 g/day, or plasma donor-derived cell-free DNA > 1%. Imaging is not required to make the diagnosis, but ultrasonography may show increased graft size, loss of the corticomedullary junction, and decreased echogenicity of the renal sinus. The only test that can confirm the diagnosis is a biopsy, but prior to performing such an invasive measure, other etiologies of the elevated creatinine should be worked up, including calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, thrombotic microangiopathy, recurrent primary disease, transplant renal artery stenosis, urinary obstruction, infections, and new-onset glomerular disease. Patients with a suspected rejection can initially be given steroids, and the transplant service should be promptly consulted.



Chronic rejection (B) occurs months to years following a solid organ transplant and is associated with T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, and antibodies with histological findings of scant inflammatory cells and interstitial fibrosis.

Hyperacute rejection (C) occurs secondary to preformed antibodies and presents with vascular thrombosis within minutes leading to near-immediate graft rejection. This can be prevented with ABO and lymphocytotoxic matching.

Subacute rejection (D) is not a term typically used to describe graft rejection.

Question: A 12-year-old girl presents to the ED with hematuria. Her parent states that the patient had a recent sore throat but has been otherwise healthy. Vital signs are BP 140/95 mm Hg, HR 105 bpm, and T 99.4°F (37.4°C). Which of the following conditions may precede the development of the most likely disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Acute glomerulonephritis following acute group A streptococcal infection is characterized by the sudden appearance of hematuria, red blood cell casts in the urine, edema, and hypertension with or without oliguria. The classic presentation of edema, hematuria, and hypertension makes up the constellation of findings in nephritic syndrome. Laboratory testing will reveal elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen. An antistreptolysin O titer should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow either streptococcal skin infection (impetigo) or streptococcal pharyngitis. This condition typically affects children aged 2–12 years. A latent period always occurs between the streptococcal infection and the onset of signs and symptoms of acute glomerulonephritis. In general, the latent period is 1–2 weeks after a throat infection and 3–6 weeks after a skin infection. Dark urine is often the first clinical manifestation of the disease. Periorbital edema typically follows with the sudden onset of puffiness of the face or eyelids. Finally, many patients will develop diffuse edema. Management is primarily supportive. Indications for dialysis include life-threatening hyperkalemia and clinical manifestations of uremia.



Otitis media (B), pneumonia (C), and sinusitis (D) are all frequently caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae as opposed to a group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection.

Question: A 17-year-old girl presents with shortness of breath, rash, and nausea after an insect bite. Her vital signs are T 97.7°F (36.5°C), HR 128 bpm, BP 85/56 mm Hg, RR 28/min, and SpO2 93%. Exam reveals diffuse hives and posterior pharyngeal swelling. Which of the following should be immediately administered?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with anaphylactic shock from an insect bite and requires immediate administration of epinephrine. Epinephrine is potentially life-saving in severe anaphylactic reactions. During an anaphylactic reaction, mast cells degranulate, leading to the release of histamines and other immune mediators. These mediators lead to the hallmark symptoms of allergic reactions, including hives, nausea and vomiting, airway edema, bronchoconstriction, and hypotension.

Epinephrine acts immediately on adrenergic receptors to reverse these symptoms. Inhaled beta-agonists can also be given to rapidly reverse bronchoconstriction. Many of the other treatments in anaphylaxis have a delayed onset of action. Diphenhydramine (H1 receptor blocker) acts by blocking the effect of histamine on H1 receptors, mainly in the skin. Ranitidine, famotidine, and other H2 blockers can mitigate some of the GI symptoms caused by histamine, as well as some of the cutaneous manifestations. Steroids mainly act by stabilizing mast cells from further degranulation, but this effect is usually delayed 4–6 hours after administration. Steroids also increase the expression of beta-receptors in the lung, increasing the efficacy of inhaled beta-agonists. Epinephrine should be given as 300–500 mcg IM in the anterolateral thigh. This dose equates to 0.3–0.5 mL of the 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) preparation.



Giving epinephrine 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) 0.3 mL IV (B) is a massive overdose and can cause dysrhythmias and cardiac ischemia. Cardiac epinephrine (1:10,000 concentration or 0.1 mg/mL) comes in vials of 10 mL for a total of 1,000 mcg of epinephrine.

Epinephrine 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) 0.3 mL IM (C) is a tenfold underdose, as this amount only contains 30 mcg of epinephrine.

Giving epinephrine 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) 10 mL IV (D) would also not be appropriate dosing for anaphylaxis, as IM administration is preferred, and giving 10 mL at this concentration would result in an overdose of epinephrine (1 mg total). This would be the appropriate dose used for cardiac arrest.

Question: Which of the following criteria, in addition to high-grade fever for 5 days, is sufficient to diagnose complete Kawasaki disease?

Options.text: Conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash, and altered mental status
Conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash, and swollen hands and feet
Conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, lymphadenopathy, and altered mental status
Conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, lymphadenopathy, and swollen hands and feet

CorrectAnswer: Conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, lymphadenopathy, and swollen hands and feet
ExplanationEN:
Kawasaki disease is a type of vasculitis and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children. The cause of Kawasaki disease is unknown. Kawasaki disease affects children with a peak at 2 years of age but can present in children up to 10 years of age. Diagnosis can be made clinically if the presentation is complete or classical. The criteria for diagnosing the complete presentation include 5 days of fever in addition to four of the following: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, erythema of the lips or oral mucosa, various skin changes of the extremities such as swelling or peeling of skin, and a rash. The fevers are usually abrupt and high-grade.

On the other hand, a diagnosis of incomplete Kawasaki disease is made in conjunction with blood work. The patient will present with 5 days of fever and have two signs from the list above instead of four. Additionally, patients must have an elevated C-reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate and three of the following laboratory findings: anemia, leukocytosis, low albumin, elevated alanine aminotransferase, elevated platelets, or pyuria.

Maintaining a high index of suspicion for Kawasaki disease is crucial because patients with Kawasaki disease have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death due to the formation of coronary artery aneurysms. Initiating treatment within the first 10 days of the disease decreases the risk of coronary artery aneurysms fivefold. Patients with Kawasaki disease should be admitted to the hospital and treated with aspirin and IV immunoglobulin infusion.



The differential diagnosis for Kawasaki disease is broad. The diagnosis of the complete form of Kawasaki disease requires four of the criteria listed above. Therefore, the other answer choices are incorrect. Sore throat (A and B), especially with exudative pharyngitis on exam, is more consistent with streptococcal pharyngitis.

Altered mental status (A and C) is not a clinical feature of Kawasaki disease. Altered mental status in the setting of a fever should prompt a workup for meningitis.

Sore throat can also be seen with infectious mononucleosis, which is characterized by generalized lymphadenopathy (C and D) as opposed to cervical lymphadenopathy that is seen in half of the patients with Kawasaki disease.
