Question: A 29-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents to the ED with mouth pain and the findings shown in the image above. What should be recommended to the patient based on this finding?
ExplanationEN:
Corticosteroid medications are used to treat a wide range of medical conditions, including many autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, adrenal insufficiency, asthma, and certain types of hematologic malignancies. The adverse effects of corticosteroids are manifold. Hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, leukocytosis from demargination, Cushing syndrome, cataracts, and acute psychosis are among the many complications that present with long-term corticosteroid use.

The mechanism of action of corticosteroids is suppression of B-cell and T-cell function by decreasing inflammatory cytokine gene transcription. Corticosteroids cause decreased activation of neutrophil adhesion molecules, which inhibits the ability of neutrophils to transmigrate from the vasculature to sites of inflammation. This leads to neutrophilia.

Inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone and budesonide are common (and often first-line) therapies for chronic asthma and other chronic lung diseases. Patients taking these medications are at risk for developing thrush (oropharyngeal candidiasis). Thrush is caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, and is only found in neonates, immunocompromised patients (e.g., those with AIDS), and those taking prolonged antibiotic or glucocorticoid therapies.

Thrush appears as white or gray plaques on the tongue, gingiva, and buccal mucosa on an erythematous base. These plaques are able to be scraped off with a wooden tongue depressor. Patients may report sore throat, tongue burning, or an abnormal taste in their mouth. To prevent thrush, patients with asthma taking inhaled glucocorticoids should be advised to rinse their mouth after use or use a spacer with their metered-dose inhaler. Other therapies include antifungal agents such as nystatin or azole antifungals (e.g., fluconazole).



Chlorhexidine mouthwash (A) is not the treatment of choice for candidiasis. Antifungals like nystatin or fluconazole are more appropriate, and chlorhexidine may cause mucosal irritation with chronic use.

Discontinuing the current therapy (B) would risk worsening asthma control. Instead, improving inhaler technique or using a spacer is safer and more effective.

Screen for malignancy (C) is unnecessary unless there are chronic, nonhealing lesions or other signs suggesting malignancy. In this case, the etiology is almost certainly related to corticosteroid use.

Question: Which of the following is an appropriate treatment for a patient with acute rheumatic fever who has a severe penicillin allergy?
ExplanationEN:
Nearly all patients with acute rheumatic fever have evidence of an antecedent group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis infection either by history or serology. Diagnosis is made using two major or one major and two minor Jones criteria. The five major Jones criteria include carditis, polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, and chorea. The Jones criteria were updated in 2015 to include subclinical carditis based on echocardiography. The four minor criteria were also updated and include arthritis (monoarthralgia in high-risk populations), fever, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, and a prolonged PR interval on ECG. There must be evidence of prior group A streptococcal infection for diagnosis. All patients with rheumatic fever should receive antibiotics to treat group A streptococcal infection of the pharynx, usually with penicillin, amoxicillin, or cephalexin. For patients allergic to penicillin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, or clindamycin are recommended.



Cephalexin (A) is a cephalosporin that will treat group A streptococcal pharyngitis. However, it has cross-reactivity with penicillin, so is not recommended for use in those with a severe penicillin allergy.

Ciprofloxacin (B) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) are not recommended, as penicillins have a narrow spectrum, lack the development of resistance, and are more cost-effective. Clindamycin has also shown a high eradication rate for Streptococcus compared to other antibiotics.

Question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 weeks of decreased urine volume. Her medical history is notable for a kidney transplant 3 months ago. She stopped taking all her medications last week because they make her nauseous. Her vital signs on arrival are T 38.5°C, HR 120 bpm, RR 18/min, BP 190/110 mm Hg, and SpO2 98% on room air. Her lab work shows a doubling of her baseline serum creatinine, and her urinalysis is notable for 3+ proteinuria and > 182 WBC/hpf. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient’s disease process?
ExplanationEN:
The patient is presenting with symptoms of acute rejection. This diagnosis is suggested by rising serum creatinine, worsening proteinuria, and worsening hypertension in a patient who is < 1 year post-transplant, especially if she is off immunosuppressant medications. In patients who are not taking their immunosuppressants, graft pain, fever, malaise, and decreased urine output can occur. Most patients with acute rejection are asymptomatic, and the diagnosis is made through routine laboratory surveillance. Laboratory findings consistent with acute rejection include a rise in serum creatinine, pyuria, and new or worsening proteinuria. Biopsy with histological analysis is needed for a definitive diagnosis. In acute rejection, the histological analysis will show lymphocytic infiltration of the transplanted tissue. Patients with evidence of allograft rejection should be admitted, and early communication with the patient’s transplant surgeon regarding the initiation of antirejection medications should be considered.



Fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis (A), and tubular atrophy describe the mechanism of chronic graft rejection. While biopsy is necessary to definitively differentiate between acute and chronic rejection, chronic rejection is rare before 3 months post-transplantation. It would also be atypical for chronic rejection to present with fever and signs of inflammation. Massive capillary thrombosis (D) describes the pathogenesis of hyperacute rejection, which occurs secondary to immunohistochemical incompatibility between the donor and recipient. Hyperacute rejection is humorally mediated and occurs within minutes to hours of transplantation due to vascular destruction. Transplant patients are at increased risk for infection secondary to immunosuppression (B). The increases in creatinine and proteinuria, though possible with infection, are more in line with transplant rejection as the etiology of the patient’s symptoms, especially given her history of medication discontinuation.

Question: A 53-year-old woman presents reporting severe acute neck pain at the base of her skull, intermittent occipital headaches, bilateral paresthesias in her arms, and vertigo when she looks down. She has a longstanding history of progressively worsening symmetric painful swelling in her joints. Her vital signs are temperature 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure 129/70 mm Hg, heart rate 93 bpm, respiratory rate 17/min, and oxygen saturation 100%. Which condition is the most likely underlying etiology of her symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic inflammatory disorder that has a predilection for the atlantoaxial joint. Instability and subluxation of the atlantoaxial joint may be spontaneous or related to minor injury. Many patients with atlantoaxial instability have no symptoms. Flexion and extension of the cervical spine are contraindicated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and may precipitate symptoms of acute cervical myelopathy. Symptoms suspicious for instability or subluxation include severe cervical pain that radiates occipitally, upper limb paresthesias and vertigo, and other signs of vertebrobasilar ischemia. Additional complications of rheumatoid arthritis may include inflammatory manifestations throughout the body such as constitutional symptoms, symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, skin lesions, interstitial lung disease, inflammatory cardiac conditions, vascular disease, hematologic manifestations, and Sjögren syndrome. Cervical CT scan may reveal fracture or subluxation, but MRI is required to assess the extent of spinal cord involvement in symptomatic patients.



Giant cell arteritis (A)is a chronic inflammatory vasculitis of the large vessels and commonly affects older patients (mean age of 70 years). Headaches associated with giant cell arteritis are temporal due to the involvement of the temporal artery. Patients may have neurological symptoms from the involvement of the carotid and vertebrobasilar arteries, resulting in transient ischemic attacks, vertigo, hearing loss, gait disturbance, and focal neurological deficits. Severe neck pain and bilateral paresthesias suggest cervical spine pathology in this patient. Polyarteritis nodosa (B) is a vasculitis of the medium-sized muscular arteries. Neurological symptoms associated with polyarteritis nodosa are typically due to ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke and are likely to be unilateral and focal. Transverse myelitis (D) is a rare acute inflammatory condition that affects a focal area of the spinal cord, commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Symptoms are progressive and include weakness, back and limb pain, sensory alterations, and autonomic dysfunction. Occipital headache and vertigo is an unlikely presentation for transverse myelitis.

Question: A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with elevated blood pressure. She had a kidney transplant 18 months ago. On examination, her heart rate is 80 bpm, blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg, and temperature is 98.3°F (36.8ºC). Which of the following describes the pathophysiology of the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Acute inflammation or infection due to luminal obstruction
CD4+ T cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in proliferation of the vascular intima and fibrosis of renal vessels causing marked decrease in lumen size
CD8+ T cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in leukocyte infiltration of graft vessels impairing perfusion

CorrectAnswer: CD4+ T cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in proliferation of the vascular intima and fibrosis of renal vessels causing marked decrease in lumen size
ExplanationEN:
CD4+ T cell mediated process resulting in the proliferation of the vascular intima and fibrosis of renal vessels causing a marked decrease in lumen size describes the pathophysiology of chronic rejection following a kidney transplant. Chronic rejection occurs over months to years following transplant. It involves a combination of type II and type IV hypersensitivity reactions against donor tissue that look like self-tissue presenting a foreign antigen. This process ultimately results in intimal thickening and fibrosis, leading to systemic hypertension and ischemia to the graft. Over time, the ischemia causes tubular and glomerular atrophy, which is noted clinically with rising blood pressure, proteinuria, and elevated creatinine. Chronic rejection is a slow progressive decline in organ function, while acute rejection is a more rapid decline. The mainstay of treatment is aimed at prevention using immunosuppressive therapy.



Acute inflammation or infection due to luminal obstruction (A) describes the pathophysiology of acute appendicitis. Given the patient’s history and presentation, chronic rejection following a kidney transplant is the most likely diagnosis.

CD8+ T cell mediated process against donor tissue resulting in leukocyte infiltration of graft vessels impairing perfusion (C) describes the pathophysiology of acute rejection following a kidney transplant. The timeline provided, along with the history and laboratory analysis, is more consistent with a diagnosis of chronic rejection.

Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells or basophils causing histamine release (D) describes the pathophysiology of anaphylaxis. This is a form of type I hypersensitivity.

Question: A 34-year-old man arrives by ambulance with shortness of breath and hives. He is allergic to peanuts and was given two doses of epinephrine by the medics en route to the hospital without significant improvement. Vital signs include a respiratory rate of 24/min and a blood pressure of 85/52 mm Hg. On exam, he has diffuse hives, lip swelling, and bilateral wheezing. His medical history includes hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and gout, for which he takes metoprolol, metformin, and simvastatin. What is the best next step in the management of this patient's condition?
ExplanationEN:
Anaphylaxis encompasses both immunologic (IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated) and nonimmunologic (mast cell and basophil degranulation in the absence of immunoglobulins) immediate hypersensitivity reactions, both of which can produce the same rapidly fatal disease process. Common causes include foods, insect stings, medications, latex, and allergen immunotherapy. Exposure causes rapid degranulation of mast cells or basophils with the release of inflammatory mediators. Symptoms occur within minutes to hours following allergen exposure but may occur in the absence of a known exposure. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on the involvement of two or more organ systems: skin or mucosal involvement, respiratory compromise, hypotension or cardiovascular collapse (e.g., syncope), and persistent abdominal cramps or vomiting.

The treatment of choice for anaphylaxis is epinephrine, a mixed alpha and beta-agonist. Treatment should not be delayed when anaphylaxis is suspected, even in the absence of hypotension or airway compromise. Patients like this one who are taking a beta-blocker, whether for hypertension or other conditions, are at risk for severe refractory anaphylaxis resistant to epinephrine and should be treated with glucagon. Glucagon produces inotropic and chronotropic effects not mediated through beta-receptors. Glucagon and epinephrine can both be repeated every 5–10 minutes as needed, followed by IV infusions as needed. Other therapies that are commonly given but have less supporting literature include corticosteroids, H1- and H2-antihistamines, and nebulized albuterol. Cimetidine should be avoided as it may prolong the metabolism of many drugs, including beta-blockers.



Albuterol (A) is a good second-line therapy for wheezing in anaphylaxis, but it is not as critical as glucagon in patients on a beta-blocker who are hypotensive despite epinephrine.

Icatibant (C) is a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist used in the treatment of hereditary angioedema. It has also been used for angioedema caused by angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, a drug class commonly used for hypertension. Angioedema can present with lip swelling and shortness of breath. However, in cases with diffuse hives such as this one, the lip swelling is more likely due to an allergic reaction, not a bradykinin-mediated mechanism.

Methylprednisolone (D) is commonly given in allergic reactions to help prevent the biphasic reaction, but it is not as critical in the immediate management as epinephrine and glucagon.

Question: An 8-year-old boy presents with a fever for the last 6 days. He has been fussy, has decreased activity, and has had daily vomiting and diarrhea. He has not had any upper respiratory symptoms since recovering from COVID-19 4 weeks ago. He had eye redness 4 days ago, and his lips are a brighter red than usual per the parents. He has no rash or lymphadenopathy. His C-reactive protein is 41 mg/dL, platelet count is 82,000 cells/mm3, D-dimer is 2,200 ng/mL, and high-sensitivity troponin T is 320 ng/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
COVID-19 usually only causes a mild illness in children, with a few days of fever and tachycardia and occasionally croup. However, a postinfectious overactive inflammatory response can occur 2–6 weeks later in a small group of children, and it is called multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C). This illness is poorly understood and occurs almost exclusively in patients who did not develop COVID-19 pneumonia and are instead in a period of viral recovery. While it has some features similar to Kawasaki disease, it is thought to be a distinct illness. Kawasaki disease historically was hypothesized to be associated with coronavirus, but this was never proven.

MIS-C was more common early in the COVID-19 pandemic. The average age of patients with MIS-C is about 8–11 years, but it can occur in any individual < 18 years old recovering from a COVID-19 infection. There are some hypotheses that there is a genetic predisposition in some children to excessive cellular inflammation in response to viral RNA, but the evidence so far is limited. As more people are immunized or infected with COVID-19, the demographics of MIS-C are expected to change.

The presenting symptoms for MIS-C vary widely. Most patients will have persistent fevers and GI symptoms like this patient. Many will have a rash, conjunctivitis, mucous membrane involvement, headaches, or respiratory symptoms. Few will have a sore throat, myalgias, swollen hands or feet, or lymphadenopathy. Severe cases will show end-organ dysfunction such as confusion or shock and may appear like sepsis.

Laboratory testing usually shows extremely elevated inflammatory markers, including a C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, D-dimer, fibrinogen, ferritin, and procalcitonin. Cardiac involvement is common, and many will have an elevated troponin, elevated basic natriuretic peptide, or decreased left ventricle function on echocardiogram. Many will have hypoalbuminemia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

Treatment depends on the severity. Follow guidelines for sepsis or shock if present and treat with aspirin if the patient meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease. Intravenous immune globulin is used for both Kawasaki disease and MIS-C. Some institutions add glucocorticoids, tissue necrosis factor inhibitors (e.g., infliximab), and low-molecular-weight heparin in severe cases.



Kawasaki disease (A) is also a disease of systemic inflammation that can result in organ dysfunction and vascular damage. The findings of Kawasaki disease are not all present at the same time but should include at least four of the following: conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, peripheral extremity changes, rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. This patient only has two of those features. Laboratory findings that suggest incomplete Kawasaki disease include thrombocytosis, not thrombocytopenia.

A pulmonary embolism (C) is often suspected when a patient has an elevated D-dimer but is unlikely in a child without a history of injury or immobilization, and this patient’s significant inflammatory response is more likely to represent that seen in MIS-C in this child with prolonged fevers.

Viral gastroenteritis (D) is a common cause of vomiting and diarrhea but uncommonly causes fevers, and patients are more likely to show electrolyte disturbances than marked elevation in inflammatory markers.

He returns to the ED with fevers, arthralgias, rash, and malaise 1 week later. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Serum sickness, a type III hypersensitivity reaction occurs when IgM-containing immune complexes deposit in membranes, fix complement, and cause tissue damage. Patients with serum sickness present with fevers, polyarthralgias, polyarthritis, rash, and malaise typically 7–14 days after initial exposure. This patient was bitten by a crotalid snake and likely treated with the antivenin Crotalidae polyvalent immune fab due to his significant local and systemic effects, which led to serum sickness. Other causes of serum sickness include therapeutic antibodies such as rituximab and infliximab.

Treatment of serum sickness is cessation of offending medication and supportive care with NSAIDs and antihistamines. Severe cases may require corticosteroids. Other examples of type III hypersensitivities include polyarteritis nodosa, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, Arthus reaction, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.



Type I hypersensitivity (A) is an IgE antibody-mediated hypersensitivity that occurs within 1 hour of antigen exposure due to degranulation of sensitized mast cells. Examples include anaphylaxis, angioedema, and drug/food allergies.

Type II hypersensitivity (B) is an IgG/IgM antibody-mediated hypersensitivity against cellular or extracellular antigens. Examples include autoimmune hemolytic anemia (red blood cells), Goodpasture syndrome (glomerular basement membrane), Graves disease (thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor), immune thrombocytopenia (platelets), and myasthenia gravis (muscle acetylcholine receptor).

Type IV hypersensitivity (D) is a cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity involving T cells and macrophages that release cytokines and trigger an immune response. Examples include allergic contact dermatitis, type I diabetes mellitus, Hashimoto thyroiditis, multiple sclerosis, and tuberculin reaction.

Question: A patient with Hodgkin lymphoma presents to the ED with tingling and burning in his hands and feet after starting a new chemotherapy agent. This agent acts by binding beta-tubulin and inhibiting the polymerization into microtubules, thus preventing mitotic spindle formation and arresting the M phase of the cell cycle. Which of the following medications does this describe?
ExplanationEN:
Vincristine and vinblastine are chemotherapeutic agents classified as vinca alkaloids, derived from the periwinkle plant (Catharanthus roseus). Their primary mechanism of action is the inhibition of microtubule polymerization, which is essential for the formation of the mitotic spindle during cell division. Microtubules are structural components of the cytoskeleton and play a crucial role in mitosis, intracellular transport, and maintenance of cell shape. By preventing microtubule assembly, these agents disrupt mitotic spindle formation, thereby arresting the cell cycle at the metaphase stage and leading to apoptosis of rapidly dividing cells.

Clinically, vincristine and vinblastine are used to treat a range of hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Vincristine is commonly used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Wilms tumor, and neuroblastoma. Vinblastine is used primarily in Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular cancer, and Kaposi sarcoma. Despite their similar mechanisms, they differ significantly in their toxicity profiles: vincristine is associated with neurotoxicity, particularly peripheral neuropathy, and autonomic dysfunction, which can manifest as constipation or even paralytic ileus. In contrast, vinblastine is more myelosuppressive, leading to bone marrow suppression, which limits its dose in clinical use.

Other chemotherapeutic agents that target microtubules include taxanes, such as paclitaxel and docetaxel, which stabilize microtubules and prevent their depolymerization. Unlike vinca alkaloids, which inhibit assembly, taxanes inhibit disassembly, also disrupting mitosis. Taxanes are widely used in the treatment of ovarian, breast, and non-small cell lung cancers. Eribulin, a non-taxane microtubule inhibitor, is a synthetic analog of halichondrin B and is used in metastatic breast cancer and liposarcoma. It inhibits microtubule growth without affecting shortening, leading to irreversible mitotic blockade and apoptosis.

Together, these agents form a critical part of modern chemotherapy regimens, particularly for rapidly dividing malignancies. However, their efficacy is often balanced against significant side effects, requiring careful monitoring and dose adjustments.



Busulfan (A) is an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA and is used prior to bone marrow transplantation. It causes myelosuppression, pulmonary fibrosis, and skin hyperpigmentation.

Etoposide (B) inhibits the enzyme topoisomerase and leads to increased DNA breakdown. Alopecia is a common side effect.

Methotrexate (C) is a folic acid analog that inhibits DNA synthesis by inhibiting thymidine synthesis. It is used to treat malignancies such as leukemia, lymphoma, choriocarcinoma, and non-neoplastic conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.

Question: A patient presents to the ED with an anaphylactic reaction to peanuts and receives epinephrine. The beta-2 agonist effect from epinephrine has which one of the following primary actions?
ExplanationEN:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, dramatic type-1 hypersensitivity reaction (i.e., immunoglobulin E-mediated) that can progress rapidly and may cause death if not recognized and treated early and appropriately. Definitions vary from source to source as to the criteria for anaphylaxis. It should be suspected when a patient exposed to a known allergen develops hypotension. Anaphylaxis is associated with urticaria; generalized flushing or itching; or swelling of the tongue, lips, uvula, or skin within minutes to hours after allergen exposure, along with either respiratory distress or hypoxia, hypotension, or other organ dysfunction (e.g., syncope, incontinence). Finally, the presence of two or more of the following within minutes to hours after allergen exposure is diagnostic of anaphylaxis: skin or mucosal changes, respiratory symptoms, symptomatic hypotension, vomiting or persistent GI cramps.

Anaphylaxis occurs when IgE interacts with mast cells and basophils, causing them to degranulate and release their contents (inflammatory mediators), beginning a cascade of inflammatory responses. These contents include histamine, tryptase, and cytokines (e.g., tumor necrosis factor-alpha). Prostaglandins and leukotrienes are downstream products of this cascade. Physiologic changes that occur in response to these inflammatory mediators include vasodilation, bronchial secretion, tachycardia, bronchoconstriction, and increased vascular permeability.

Epinephrine is the mainstay of therapy and acts on alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. Activation of alpha-1 receptors decreases mucosal edema and induces peripheral vasoconstriction, improving hypotension. Beta-1 receptor activation leads to increased heart rate (chronotropy) and contractility (inotropy). Beta-2 receptor activation leads to bronchodilation and stabilizes mast cells and basophils to limit the further release of inflammatory mediators. The dose of epinephrine for anaphylaxis is 0.3–0.5 mg to be given intramuscularly in the anterolateral thigh.



The alpha-1 (not beta-2) activation from epinephrine leads to decreased mucosal edema (A).

Increased chronotropy (B) and inotropy (C) are the result of beta-1 (not beta-2) receptor activation.

Question: A 26-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with joint pain. She reports no medical history and does not know if her immunizations are up to date. Her pain began approximately 1 week ago in her left knee and ankle. However, today, the pain is also in her right knee, so she came to the emergency department for evaluation. Vital signs show HR 109 bpm, BP 116/70 mm Hg, RR 12/min, and T 38.9℃. On examination, significant findings include a faint cardiac murmur and mild tenderness and swelling to her left ankle joint and both knee joints. She has good range of motion in those joints. No rash is evident. What preceding symptoms and illness are the risk factors for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms that fit the criteria for a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever, which is a nonsuppurative sequelae that occurs 2–4 weeks after group A Streptococcus infection, most often from pharyngitis. Thus, the important information to ask this patient is whether she had a sore throat a few weeks ago that might suggest she had pharyngitis. A diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is established on clinical grounds using the revised Jones criteria. This patient meets the criteria for a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever based on a new murmur, polyarthritis, and fever.



Infection from group A Streptococcus is the only infection associated with acute rheumatic fever. Viruses and other causes of pharyngitis do not lead to acute rheumatic fever. Streptococcus pneumoniae, which would cause a cough suggesting pneumonia (A), would not lead to acute rheumatic fever.

Along the same lines, group B Streptococcus can lead to urinary tract infections and cause dysuria (B) but is not a risk factor for acute rheumatic fever.

Streptococcal skin infections suggesting impetigo (C) have been more closely linked to glomerulonephritis. There is a risk of acute rheumatic fever but at much lower rates than Streptococcus pharyngitis infection.

Question: A 25-year-old man presents to the ED with joint and back pain. He was diagnosed with urethritis 2 weeks ago. On physical exam, he is noted to have joint effusions of his right ankle and left knee. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Reactive arthritis is an inflammatory asymmetric oligoarthritis that develops soon after or during an infection elsewhere in the body. It can occur after urethritis, secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis, or after gastrointestinal infections caused by organisms such as Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter. Clinical manifestations include symptoms of preceding enteric or genitourinary infections, peripheral arthritis, dactylitis, and low back pain. Extra-articular signs and symptoms include conjunctivitis, dysuria, urethritis, cervicitis, and prostatitis. Classically reactive arthritis presents with conjunctivitis, spondyloarthropathy, and urethritis, the majority of patients do not present with this triad of symptoms.



Gout (A) is an inflammatory arthritis that most commonly affects the great toe. Diagnosis is made through the identification of uric acid crystals in synovial fluid. Oligoarthritis is an uncommon presentation of gout.

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder that commonly affects the wrist and hands. It is more common in middle-aged women and would be rare in a young man with preceding urethritis.

Septic arthritis (D) is a local joint infection that leads to rapid joint destruction. Risk factors for septic arthritis include immunocompromised states, history of joint replacement, and joint injections. Septic arthritis rarely affects multiple joints.

Question: A 55-year-old woman presents to the ED with a rash on her left arm. She was stung by a wasp while attempting to destroy a nest in her garage. On examination, she has diffuse urticaria and biphasic wheezes. She says this happened to her when she was a child. She begins to vomit while you are examining her. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening type I mast cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction and is the likely diagnosis when any one of the following criteria is met: (1) hypotension after exposure to an allergen, (2) onset of illness involving the skin or mucosal surfaces with accompanying respiratory compromise or hypotension, or (3) two of the following after exposure to a suspected allergen: skin or mucosal tissue involvement, hypotension, respiratory compromise, or GI symptoms.

Anaphylaxis is often underdiagnosed and undertreated. Urticaria and bronchospasm do not need to be present for anaphylaxis to be diagnosed. The consequences of missing the diagnosis may include rapid clinical deterioration and death due to circulatory collapse or airway obstruction. Food is the most common trigger among children, and insect stings and medications are the most common causes among adults. The approach to any patient with anaphylaxis begins with an assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.

If anaphylaxis is suspected based on the above criteria, intramuscular epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg of 1:1,000 solution should be given (0.01 mg/kg 1:1,000 for children). The dose may be repeated every 5–15 minutes, depending on how the patient responds. For refractory cases, intravenous epinephrine may be indicated to prevent hemodynamic compromise or cardiac arrest. The severity of illness and response to medication should guide ED management. Patients with mild to moderate symptoms should be monitored for up to 6 hours, whereas patients with severe symptoms or shock require intensive care admission. Discharged patients should receive recommendations about allergen exposure prevention and should be given a prescription for an epinephrine autoinjector.



Hymenoptera sensitization (B) is the initial exposure to the allergen (e.g., venom), which creates IgE antibodies. After subsequent allergen exposure, mast cell and basophil degranulation occur, resulting in histamine-release reactive symptoms such as pruritus, urticaria, nausea, vomiting, and throat swelling. Sensitization does not result in anaphylaxis.

Systemic mastocytosis (C) is a clonal expansion of mast cells that may be malignant or nonmalignant and may present with similar features as anaphylaxis (e.g., urticaria, gastrointestinal symptoms, cardiovascular collapse). It is diagnosed with bone marrow biopsy.

Anaphylaxis is a type I rather than a type II hypersensitivity reaction (D). Examples of the latter include Goodpasture disease and ABO blood incompatibility reactions.

Question: An 8-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with facial swelling. She has asymmetric, nonpitting, non-gravity-dependent edema, as shown above. Which of the following history and exam findings most suggests this patient has C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?
ExplanationEN:
Angioedema is caused by the local extravasation of fluid into the interstitial tissues. It tends to affect the face, extremities, and genitals. When it occurs on the face, it tends to involve the airway, including the lips, mouth, uvula, larynx, and pharynx. It tends to be rapid in onset, asymmetric, and not to involve gravity-dependent areas. It can be mast cell mediated or bradykinin mediated. When mast cell mediated, it is often seen as a component of allergic symptoms, which range from mild to anaphylaxis. This type is associated with bronchospasm, itching, flushed skin, hypotension, and urticaria. It has an onset within hours and resolves within 1–2 days.

Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, such as from angiotensin inhibitor use or C1 esterase deficiency, has no allergic symptoms and has an onset within 1–2 days and resolution within 3–4 days. This type frequently affects the gastrointestinal tract, with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. C1 esterase deficiency results in bradykinin-mediated angioedema and can be inherited or acquired. Angioedema from C1 esterase deficiency presents without allergic symptoms. Hereditary angioedema usually presents in childhood and only involves one site at a time. There is an association between C1 esterase deficiency and autoimmune disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroiditis, and glomerulonephritis.



Wheezing (A), skin flushing (B), and hypotension (D) are associated with allergic symptoms, which suggests a mast cell-mediated angioedema and not bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

Question: A 3-year-old boy presents to the ED with a fever for 6 days. His T is 103°F (39.4°C), BP is 85/50 mm Hg, HR is 142 bpm, RR is 23/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. CorrectAnswer: Echocardiography, IV immune globulin, and aspirin
ExplanationEN:
Kawasaki disease, or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is a medium-vessel vasculitis that usually presents in children < 5 years of age. The diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease include a fever for ≥ 5 days and four out of the following five criteria: cervical adenopathy, polymorphous rash, conjunctival injection, oral membrane changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), and extremity changes (erythema and a desquamating rash of the palms and soles).

The management of Kawasaki disease includes echocardiography, IV immune globulin, and aspirin. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels are often elevated in this condition and can help support the diagnosis. A broad infectious workup should take place, and admission is necessary. Coronary artery aneurysm and thrombosis is a possible life-threatening complication of this condition.



In addition to giving ceftriaxone and vancomycin (A), a broad infectious workup should be done that includes a viral panel, blood cultures, chest imaging, and urinalysis. These constitute reasonable management to ensure that a bacterial infection is not the etiology of the patient’s symptoms. However, the overall constellation of symptoms is most consistent with Kawasaki disease, and antibiotics are not the appropriate treatment.

Providing reassurance, oral hydration, and primary care follow-up (C) is the appropriate treatment for a viral syndrome. Given the persistence of this patient’s fever and meeting the criteria for Kawasaki disease, reassurance alone would not be appropriate.

Vitamin A (D) could shorten the course of measles in some patients. Measles presents with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, a maculopapular rash, and Koplik spots, which is not consistent with this patient’s presentation.

Question: Which of the following is an expected history or exam finding of serum sickness?
ExplanationEN:
A true serum sickness reaction is uncommon due to the decrease in the use of medications made with animal serum. It was first described when antitoxins from horse serum were used to treat diphtheria and scarlet fever in the early 1900s. In serum sickness, nonhuman proteins form immune complexes, causing a variety of allergic symptoms a few weeks after administration (i.e., Gell and Coombs type III hypersensitivity). Many drug reactions to antibiotics have a similar appearance, timeframe, and duration and are thus called serum sickness-like reactions, despite being thought to be caused by a different mechanism. The most common symptoms of serum sickness are a rash, fever, malaise, and polyarthralgias. Fever and malaise are nearly universal, but rigors are uncommon. Nearly all patients will have a pruritic rash that resembles hives and does not involve the mucous membranes. Some of the lesions may appear urticarial but may include palpable purpura, papules, or macules or be morbilliform. Ulcers, scarring, and secondary bacterial skin infections suggest an alternative diagnosis. Most patients will also have simple arthralgias without joint swelling, most commonly in the extremities. Myalgias are uncommon. The symptoms subside over time after removal of the causative agent. Theoretically, anaphylaxis can occur with repeat administration of the causative agent.



Angioedema (A) does not occur in serum sickness or serum sickness-like reactions and suggests an alternative diagnosis such as urticarial vasculitis. Joint swelling (C) is uncommon in serum sickness and suggests a different diagnosis such as rheumatic fever. Myalgias (D) are much less common in serum sickness and suggest a different process such as a viral infection (prominent in influenza and dengue fever) or an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis.

Question: Which of the following findings is consistent with scleroderma renal crisis?
ExplanationEN:
The hallmark of scleroderma, also known as systemic sclerosis, is an uncontrolled accumulation of collagen affecting nearly every organ in the body, and widespread vascular involvement. It is an autoimmune disorder that more commonly affects women than men with a peak age of onset between 30 and 50 years of age. Kidney disease is the most common cause of death in patients with systemic sclerosis. Scleroderma renal crisis affects up to 20% of patients with systemic sclerosis and occurs early in the course of the disease, often within 5 years of diagnosis. It is characterized by acute onset of oliguric kidney failure, moderate to marked hypertension, and a urinalysis that is often normal or may show only mild proteinuria. Additional findings may include signs and symptoms related to malignant hypertension (e.g., retinal hemorrhages, altered mental status), microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The treatment of choice is prompt blood pressure control with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and close monitoring of kidney function.



The vascular involvement with scleroderma affects medium-sized vessels, sparing the preglomerular vessels. This explains the lack of significant abnormalities on urinalysis other than mild proteinuria and possibly microscopic hematuria. Gross hematuria (A) and nephrotic-range proteinuria are not expected.

New-onset hypertension or acute worsening of hypertension above baseline levels is the most common presentation of scleroderma renal crisis. However, some patients do present with normal blood pressure and these patients have a worse prognosis. However, hypotension (B) is not consistent with renal crisis.

Scleroderma renal crisis is most often found in patients with widespread skin involvement (C). Skin induration, edema, hyperpigmentation or depigmentation, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias are all common skin manifestations. Glucocorticoid use is also a risk factor for the development of acute renal crisis.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with the above physical exam finding, which he states he has experienced before. His primary care clinician recently treated him for an infection, but the patient cannot recall the name of the drug. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with findings and a history suggestive of a fixed drug eruption. A fixed drug eruption is believed to be associated with CD8+ T-cell activity and presents with a fixed lesion that typically occurs in the same area when exposed to an offending agent. The presenting dermatologic finding is typically an oval or circular hyperpigmented lesion that can be erythematous, edematous, and may demonstrate central blistering and necrosis. The lesions typically fade when the offending agent is removed and may leave a hyperpigmented lesion behind. The treatment of a fixed drug eruption is typically symptomatic therapy involving oral antihistamines and topical steroids.



Contact dermatitis (A) occurs secondary to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction when exposed to certain antigens, such as poison ivy, and presents with fluid-filled lesions that are highly pruritic and occur in the distribution of the exposure or where the contact took place.

Erythema multiforme (B) is an immunologically triggered hypersensitivity reaction that presents with a target lesion with possible mucous membrane involvement.

Urticaria (D) occurs secondary to the release of histamine, prostaglandins, and bradykinin and presents with urticarial wheals with erythematous swelling with central pallor. The lesions can feel warm or pruritic, and treatment involves avoiding the offending agent and antihistamines, H2 blockers, and, in more severe cases, steroids.

Question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with dark-colored urine. He has no significant medical history and is fully immunized. His symptoms started yesterday evening, and his parent initially thought he was dehydrated. A review of systems reveals a recent rash with a yellowish crust that was treated with topical antibiotics 3 weeks ago. The rash has since resolved. Vital signs are remarkable for a BP of 140/89 mm Hg and an HR of 90 bpm. Physical examination demonstrates puffy eyes and bilateral lower extremity edema. Microscopic urinalysis reveals 2+ protein and red cell casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a kidney disorder that is caused by a prior infection of specific nephrogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause of acute nephritis in children worldwide, with it being more common in resource-poor areas. It has a bimodal distribution affecting the young, between 5 and 12 years of age, and those ≥ 60 years. It is twice as common in male patients compared to female patients. Clinical features range from being completely asymptomatic or having microscopic hematuria to having full-blown acute nephritic syndrome. Acute nephritic syndrome is characterized by red or brown urine, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and an elevation in serum creatinine. Classically, streptococcal pharyngitis occurs between 1 and 3 weeks before the onset of symptoms and a streptococcal skin infection occurs 3–6 weeks before the onset of symptoms. The most common symptoms include generalized edema, gross hematuria, and hypertension. However, patients may only have microscopic hematuria or patients may develop a hypertensive crisis with minimal urine abnormalities.

The diagnosis is made on clinical findings suggestive of acute nephritis (noted above) with an antecedent group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection. A positive throat culture, skin culture, or positive serological tests (anti-streptolysin O) can confirm a recent infection. The complement protein, C3, can also be measured, and in the majority of patients, this will be significantly depressed during the first 2 weeks of disease before slowly recovering. The acute management and treatment for poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is largely supportive care, particularly caring for the complications of fluid overload. Lasix or other loop diuretics help provide prompt diuresis with a reduction in blood pressure. Hypertensive encephalopathy or other hypertensive crises may occur and warrant an emergent reduction in blood pressure with nicardipine or nifedipine. Hemodialysis may be required in severe cases of acute kidney failure in which severe metabolic or electrolyte derangement (pulmonary edema, heart failure, hyperkalemia, or uremia) are present. Antibiotics should only be used if an infection is currently present. Most patients recover without any significant long-term sequelae and rarely progress to end-stage kidney disease. If patients do not eventually recover, further evaluation into other forms of glomerulonephritis is warranted.



Alport syndrome (A) is also known as hereditary nephritis and is a form of progressive nephritis that is also associated with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities. Alport syndrome can be X-linked, autosomal recessive, or autosomal dominant. Patients with X-linked and autosomal recessive inheritance have disease states that progress rapidly to end-stage kidney disease with associated deafness and ocular abnormalities. The autosomal dominant form also has these clinical features but tends to occur more gradually. Both gross and microscopic hematuria may be present, with either form of hematuria almost always being present by the age of 10. The complement protein C3 will be normal in patients with Alport syndrome. Alport is a progressive disease that does not improve with time and does not typically have antecedent streptococcal infection.

Goodpasture disease (B), also known as anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, is caused by circulating antibodies that are directed at the basement membrane of the glomerulus. This results in acute or rapid progression of glomerulonephritis and is also commonly associated with pulmonary hemorrhage. Clinical presentation is that of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with acute kidney injury with proteinuria demonstrated on urinalysis. Alveolar hemorrhage also occurs in patients with Goodpasture disease which can manifest as dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, and pulmonary infiltrates on X-ray. Patients usually will not have associated fevers, malaise, weight loss, or arthralgias and, if present, should prompt investigation into a concurrent vasculitis. Patients will not have an antecedent streptococcal infection and typically acutely worsen without any improvement.

Wegener granulomatosis (D), also known as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, is an antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody vasculitis that results in kidney and nasopharyngeal clinical manifestations. Wegener granulomatosis more commonly affects older adults but has been reported and can affect all age groups. Both male and female patients are equally affected. Ear, nose, and throat manifestations occur in the vast majority of patients with Wegener granulomatosis, including nasal crusting, sinusitis, otitis media, earache, otorrhea, rhinorrhea, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, oral or nasal ulcers, and polychondritis. Patients can frequently develop sensorineural hearing loss which progresses rapidly and is irreversible. Glomerulonephritis occurs in most patients with the diagnosis. Hematuria, elevated creatinine, edema, proteinuria, and hypertension can all occur as with other causes of glomerulonephritis. C3 is not affected in Wegener granulomatosis, nor is there a preceding streptococcal infection.

Question: A 20-year-old man with a medical history of asthma presents with a rash and difficulty breathing. His symptoms started shortly after taking the first dose of an antibiotic that he was prescribed for cellulitis. Vital signs are a T of 98.5°F (36.9°C), BP of 89/50 mm Hg, HR of 130 bpm, RR of 22/min, and SpO2 of 92% on room air. On physical exam, he appears anxious and has diffuse urticaria. He is using accessory muscles and has wheezing on lung exam. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient, who presents with urticaria, bronchospasm, and signs of shock, has anaphylaxis, which is a serious allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction that can progress rapidly and may cause death. Common triggers include foods, medications, and insect stings. Patients can present with a range of symptoms and disease severity, from mild wheezing and urticaria to shock and complete airway obstruction. Most patients present with mucocutaneous involvement, including urticaria, pruritus, lip and oropharyngeal swelling, periorbital edema, and conjunctival injection. Lower respiratory symptoms include wheezing and shortness of breath, while upper airway involvement can present with stridor, voice changes, throat tightening, and airway obstruction. GI symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. If there is hypotension, patients may have dizziness or syncope.

The diagnosis is based on the clinical history and exam findings. According to the World Allergy Organization diagnostic criteria, anaphylaxis is likely in a patient with an acute onset of illness with mucocutaneous involvement and at least one of the following: respiratory compromise, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms. In the absence of skin involvement, anaphylaxis is likely in those presenting with hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement (e.g., stridor, voice changes) after exposure to a known or likely allergen.

The mainstay of treatment for anaphylaxis is intramuscular epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.5 mg) administered in the anterolateral thigh. Epinephrine acts on the alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors to decrease mucosal edema and increase systemic vascular resistance, increase inotropy and chronotropy, and promote bronchodilation, respectively. Epinephrine is the only medication that has been shown to be effective in treating anaphylaxis, yet it is underused in emergency settings. This is likely due to the fear of causing unwanted side effects such as cardiac ischemia, especially in older patients. However, when administered at the correct dose, intramuscular epinephrine is safe and should not be withheld due to concerns about side effects. The initial dose of epinephrine can be repeated at 5-minute intervals. For patients requiring multiple doses or who have persistent shock, an intravenous infusion of epinephrine should be started, along with fluid resuscitation.

Adjunctive medications include glucocorticoids and antihistamines, both H1 and H2 blockers. These medications are routinely administered, but there are no high-quality data showing that glucocorticoids or antihistamines are effective for the acute management of anaphylaxis. Use of these medications should not replace or delay the administration of epinephrine. Inhaled bronchodilators can also be used adjunctively in those with wheezing. Patients who have an adequate response to intramuscular epinephrine can be discharged after a period of observation with a prescription for an epinephrine autoinjector. Practice patterns vary, but in general, prescriptions for glucocorticoids or antihistamines are not necessary and may cause unwanted side effects.



Intravenous epinephrine (B) may be used in the patient with refractory symptoms or shock after multiple doses of intramuscular epinephrine. However, most patients will respond to intramuscular epinephrine, which can be administered quickly and without intravenous access, and it has fewer potential adverse effects compared to the intravenous route.

Intravenous methylprednisolone (C) may be used adjunctively for the treatment of anaphylaxis, but it is not the first line and should never replace epinephrine. Steroids take several hours to take effect and thus have no role in treating the acute, life-threatening reaction. They may theoretically reduce the rate of a biphasic reaction, although there is no evidence to support this.

Nebulized albuterol (D) is the first-line therapy for wheezing secondary to asthma. This patient does have a history of asthma, but the history of recent antibiotic use and the presence of urticaria and hypotension make anaphylaxis the more likely cause of the wheezing. Epinephrine is more effective than albuterol in treating bronchospasm from anaphylaxis.

Question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the ED with shortness of breath. Chest radiograph reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and evidence of pulmonary fibrosis. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is associated with this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of sarcoidosis. It is characterized by the formation of noncaseating granulomas composed of helper T cells and other inflammatory cells such as macrophages. Only 5% of patients with sarcoidosis are asymptomatic, and half of them have pulmonary or systemic concerns, which manifest later in the disease process.

When patients become symptomatic later in the disease process, they have constitutional symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, polyarthritis, or myositis and respiratory symptoms such as cough, dyspnea on exertion, or hemoptysis. Patients may also have peripheral neuropathies, skin lesions such as erythema nodosum, lymphadenopathy, or uveitis.

Sarcoidosis is fatal in 10% of patients due to pulmonary fibrosis or extensive organ involvement. Diagnosis is with chest radiograph, which reveals hilar lymphadenopathy. As the disease progresses, there will be findings of pulmonary fibrosis. Laboratory testing reveals leukocytosis with eosinophilia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, and hypercalcemia. Biopsy of the involved organ is the most definitive diagnostic procedure, but it is infrequently performed.

Treatment of sarcoidosis is most often with steroids or cytotoxic medications. Lung transplantation may be considered for patients with severe, refractory disease.



Hyponatremia (B) is not associated with sarcoidosis. It is often caused by gastrointestinal losses such as vomiting and diarrhea, volume overload syndromes such as heart failure and cirrhosis, or the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone.

Metabolic acidosis (C) is classified as anion gap or non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis is most often caused by gastrointestinal losses, diuretic use, or renal tubular acidosis. The causes of anion gap metabolic acidosis include metformin, methanol, uremia, diabetes-related ketoacidosis, paraldehyde, iron, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, and salicylates, which can be summarized by the MUDPILES mnemonic.

Respiratory alkalosis (D) is caused by hyperventilation states and can be seen in salicylate overdoses in association with a metabolic acidosis.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents to the ED with left knee pain and swelling. Review of systems is notable for the presence of penile discharge and a recent history of bloody diarrhea. In addition to mild swelling and discomfort with range of motion of the left knee, the physical examination shows bilateral conjunctival erythema. Which of the following is most likely to be found on synovial fluid analysis in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Reactive arthritis is a form of spondyloarthritis that characteristically occurs following an infection. The classic triad of reactive arthritis is asymmetrical polyarthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. A mnemonic used to remember these symptoms is “can’t see (conjunctivitis), can’t pee (urethritis), can’t climb a tree (arthritis).” Reactive arthritis typically follows enteric infection, with Yersinia, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter being the most commonly implicated. While less common, infections with Escherichia coli, Chlamydia, and Clostridioides difficile may also lead to the development of reactive arthritis.

Importantly, although reactive arthritis follows an infection, no organisms are noted on synovial fluid Gram stain and culture (the recovery of an organism is suggestive of septic, rather than reactive, arthritis). Synovial fluid analysis also shows increased leukocytes, typically from 2,000–64,000 cells/mm3.

First-line treatment of reactive arthritis is the use of NSAIDs. Steroids can be used as second-line treatment, and if NSAIDs and steroids do not work, patients may require treatment with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.



Gram-negative diplococci (A) on Gram stain would indicate septic arthritis, likely Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Patients with disseminated gonococcal infection can present with penile discharge and septic arthritis. However, the patient's other symptoms of conjunctivitis and recent bloody diarrhea would make reactive arthritis more likely.

Negatively birefringent crystals (B) are suggestive of a diagnosis of gout. Crystal arthropathies such as gout should be in the differential for this patient but are less likely than reactive arthritis given the patient’s other symptoms of conjunctivitis and penile discharge following a diarrheal illness.

Positive bacterial culture (C) is indicative of septic arthritis. While septic arthritis is on the differential for this patient, it is less likely than reactive arthritis, which is suggested by the history of diarrhea and the presence of a triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. Gram stain and culture of the synovial fluid in reactive arthritis typically reveal no organisms.

Question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the ED with fever, eye redness, and rash. On physical exam, you note bilateral conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, fissured lips, and a diffuse nonvesicular rash. Which of the following is the most serious complication of this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease most commonly affects children < 5 years. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in the developed world, surpassing rheumatic heart disease.

Signs and symptoms of Kawasaki disease include a fever for ≥ 5 days, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy > 1.5 cm, mucous membrane involvement (e.g., strawberry tongue or fissured lips), extremity changes (e.g., edema or erythema), bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis without iritis, and nonvesicular rash.

Diagnosis is clinical. Fever ≥ 5 days must be present and at least four of the five aforementioned features. If there are fewer than four signs present, diagnosis may be made with evidence of coronary artery disease on echocardiography or by a constellation of laboratory tests.

Imaging includes echocardiography to evaluate for complications related to Kawasaki disease, including coronary artery aneurysms, which are detected in 25% of untreated and 5–10% of treated patients, valvular incompetence, ventricular wall motion abnormalities, or pericardial effusion. Laboratory testing may reveal thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, leukocytosis with left shift, anemia, elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and abnormal liver function tests.

Complications of Kawasaki disease include coronary artery aneurysms, which may result in myocardial infarction or congestive heart failure.

Treatment of Kawasaki disease includes aspirin and intravenous gamma globulin. Corticosteroids are controversial and not currently recommended. Patients should be admitted to the hospital, and cardiology consulted early in their course.



Aortic dissection (A) is closely associated with Marfan syndrome, which is characterized by tall, thin stature and vascular wall abnormalities.

Multi-system organ failure (C) is associated with toxic shock syndrome, which presents with diffuse erythroderma without ocular or mucous membrane involvement.

Rheumatic fever (D) is associated with streptococcal pharyngitis and presents with carditis, diffuse migratory arthritis, Sydenham chorea, serpiginous rash, and subcutaneous nodules.

Question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the ED with daily fevers for 6 days. She was initially seen at an urgent care and diagnosed with a viral illness. However, her parent says the fever will not come down. On exam, the child has a fever and tachycardia. You notice injected conjunctiva and dry mucous membranes with cracked lips. If not treated appropriately, what complication can this child most likely develop?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms that are characteristic of Kawasaki disease or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is a generalized systemic vasculitis that is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in North America. It affects infants and young children. The diagnosis is clinical and is based on criteria including fever for ≥ 5 days, bilateral conjunctivitis, oropharyngeal erythema, a diffuse nonspecific rash with erythema or edema of the hands and feet, and cervical lymphadenopathy. The disease can look like many other illnesses, so it should be considered when other causes, such as viral illnesses, are excluded. After having 6 days of fever it is more likely this patient has a more severe underlying illness besides a viral infection.

Cardiac complications are the most severe manifestations of the disease and the classic complication is coronary artery aneurysms. Children can also develop myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular dysfunction, and dysrhythmias. Treatment of Kawasaki disease is directed at reducing inflammation and preventing cardiac complications. Administration of intravenous immune globulin results in rapid and dramatic symptomatic improvement and prevents aneurysm formation in the majority of patients. Additional treatment with aspirin has a synergistic effect.



Glomerulonephritis (B)can be a complication associated with streptococcal infection. Although this patient has a sore throat with redness and cervical lymphadenopathy with fever, the rest of her presentation is more characteristic of Kawasaki disease.

Mitral valve stenosis (C)can also be a complication of streptococcal infection and presents as rheumatic fever. Again, this patient's presentation may be misinterpreted as streptococcal pharyngitis but her signs and symptoms are more characteristic of Kawasaki disease.

Nonischemic cardiomyopathy (D) can be a complication from infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, a parasite that can lead to Chagas disease. This patient’s presentation is not at all similar to parasitic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi. Patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy present with typical heart failure symptoms of dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, palpitations, dizziness, and lower extremity edema. Many patients may even be asymptomatic.

Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas that can affect any organ system, the underlying mechanism for which remains undetermined. Some individuals are more likely to develop Löfgren syndrome, which is comprised of erythema nodosum, polyarthralgias, and bilateral perihilar lymphadenopathy. Sarcoidosis has a predilection for the lymph system and lungs but also commonly affects the skin, eyes (e.g., uveitis), and heart (e.g., dysrhythmias and heart failure). Cutaneous manifestations include erythema nodosum and lupus pernio, a rash with violaceous plaques and nodules affecting the cheeks, nose, forehead, and ears. Lupus pernio is pathognomonic for sarcoidosis. Other findings that support a diagnosis of sarcoidosis include bilateral perihilar adenopathy or infiltrates on chest X-ray, hypercalcemia (due to macrophage production of calcitriol), and elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme. Due to its variable presentations and similarity to other diseases (e.g., lupus and tuberculosis), sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion. Treatment is often unnecessary in asymptomatic individuals and consists of NSAIDs for milder symptoms like arthralgias. More advanced disease requires corticosteroids or other immunosuppressant medications, which places these patients at high risk for infection.



Elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) (A) causes increased calcium reabsorption by the kidneys. Pathological causes of elevated PTH include parathyroid cancer, vitamin D deficiency, and kidney failure.

Kidney involvement (B) in calcium homeostasis is comprised of calcium resorption and calcitriol synthesis. However, in sarcoidosis, excess calcitriol is produced by macrophages.

Osteolysis (D) is uncommon in sarcoidosis and is not the principal cause of hypercalcemia in these patients. Osteolytic hypercalcemia is seen in breast cancer, lung cancer, and multiple myeloma.

Question: Which of the following infections should be ruled out by pretreatment screening before initiating treatment with a tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor?
ExplanationEN:
Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors have become cornerstone therapies for treating chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, plaque psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. TNF-alpha is a proinflammatory cytokine central to the immune response, playing a key role in the activation of macrophages, recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes, and formation and maintenance of granulomas, which are critical for containing infections like tuberculosis.

Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody composed of both human and murine components, and it binds to both soluble and transmembrane forms of TNF-alpha, neutralizing its biological activity. By suppressing TNF-alpha, infliximab and other TNF-alpha inhibitors effectively reduce inflammation and halt disease progression. However, this immunosuppression presents at the cost of impaired host defense, especially against intracellular pathogens that are controlled by granulomatous responses. This includes Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Histoplasmosis, and other opportunistic fungal infections.

Because of this, all patients should be screened for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), using a tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, before initiating TNF-alpha inhibitors. If positive, appropriate treatment for LTBI should be started before initiating biologic therapy. Additionally, screening for hepatitis B and C is recommended, as reactivation of chronic viral hepatitis can occur under immunosuppression.

Other contraindications or cautions include active or chronic infections, such as untreated herpes zoster, invasive fungal infections, and nonhealing infected skin ulcers. TNF-alpha inhibitors are also generally avoided in patients with moderate to severe heart failure (class III/IV) due to an observed increased risk of worsening cardiac function. Patients should be monitored closely for signs of infection throughout treatment, and live vaccines should be avoided during therapy due to the immunosuppressive effects.



Hepatitis A virus (A) causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is not associated with reactivation risk or chronic carriage, making pretreatment screening unnecessary.

Legionella (B) is a cause of atypical pneumonia and does not persist in a latent form, so screening before immunosuppressive therapy is not relevant.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (C) can cause skin and soft tissue infections, but is not a latent infection requiring pretreatment evaluation in patients starting TNF-alpha inhibitors.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right knee pain for 4 days. He reports no trauma to the knee. He works in construction and typically has back pain, but that has also been worse over the last few days. What preceding symptoms would suggest that this patient’s knee pain is due to reactive arthritis?
ExplanationEN:
Reactive arthritis is a spondyloarthropathy that presents with acute, asymmetric oligoarthritis approximately 2–6 weeks after an infectious illness. The classic presenting triad of reactive arthritis includes joint pain, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. All three components are not necessary for the diagnosis but are highly suggestive of it. When considering this disease on your differential for a patient with arthritic pain, the patient should be questioned regarding a previous enteric infection and for symptoms of urethritis. Common organisms that are associated with reactive arthritis include Chlamydia trachomatis, Yersinia, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter. Less common organisms associated with reactive arthritis include Chlamydia pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Mycoplasma genitalium.

Patients with reactive arthritis are usually young adults, and they typically report arthritis in the lower extremities, most often the knees. Back pain is also a frequent concern. Additionally, patients may have dactylitis. Conjunctivitis occurs in approximately one-third of patients with preceding urethritis and occurs in over half of patients with preceding enteritis. Arthritis usually develops approximately 4 weeks after the preceding infection. Synovial fluid analysis demonstrates an inflammatory profile. Treatment of the arthritis itself is with NSAIDs. If the patient has preceding urethritis, the patient should be treated for the genitourinary infection. Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated enteric infections. Most patients with this disorder have arthritis for 3–5 months, but most remit completely after that. Some go on to develop chronic arthritis.



Joint swelling and fever (B) is more suggestive of septic arthritis.

A rash and palpitations (C) is suggestive of Lyme disease, not reactive arthritis.

Sore throat and fever (D) is more suggestive of poststreptococcal arthritis.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED with swelling to her tongue. She indicates that the right side of her tongue and cheek became swollen immediately after eating a spice on her taco. She also developed some itching around her neck. She reports no difficulty swallowing or difficulty breathing. Her vital signs show HR 72 bpm, BP 125/72 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and T 37.3°C. On exam, the right side of her tongue has mild edema. She also has mild swelling of her right cheek near the corner of her lip. There is no swelling of her posterior pharynx. She has no notable skin changes. She does not have any stridor, and her lungs are clear. What is the most appropriate next step at this time?

Options.text: Intravenous diphenhydramine plus methylprednisolone plus famotidine
Intravenous diphenhydramine plus methylprednisolone plus famotidine plus subcutaneous epinephrine

CorrectAnswer: Intravenous diphenhydramine plus methylprednisolone plus famotidine
ExplanationEN:
This patient is having an acute hypersensitivity reaction or type I immunoglobulin E-mediated reaction to a specific food allergen. Adverse reactions to foods are more common. Much like allergic reactions to other substances, a wide range of symptoms, including local edema and urticaria to widespread angioedema and anaphylaxis, can develop. It is the clinician’s job to determine the severity of the illness and treat it accordingly. It is common for people with food allergies to develop local urticaria and angioedema where the food touches the skin. This is the case in this patient since only part of her tongue and part of her cheek are swollen. Clearly, these symptoms can progress to widespread angioedema of the tongue, lips, and face, which has the potential for airway compromise with anaphylaxis, so treatment needs to be initiated. The mainstay of treatment for any allergic reaction is avoidance of the offending agent, observation for airway compromise, and treatment with antihistamines and glucocorticoids. This patient is not showing signs of airway compromise or anaphylaxis. Thus, she should be treated with intravenous diphenhydramine plus methylprednisolone plus famotidine.



Although it is important to monitor this patient’s airway since she may develop widespread angioedema, her localized swelling without other significant findings does not suggest that she needs emergent intubation for airway protection (A).

As already mentioned, patients with allergic reactions should be treated with antihistamines and corticosteroids, but only patients with impending or apparent anaphylaxis should also be treated with epinephrine. This patient is not presenting with significant airway compromise, does not have respiratory distress, is not hypotensive, and does not have symptoms of end-organ damage. She does not have anaphylaxis. Therefore, she does not need subcutaneous epinephrine (C) added to her regimen at this time.

Some patients who present to the ED with angioedema of the tongue may have angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor-induced angioedema or hereditary angioedema. This patient developed symptoms after ingesting food, and there is no mention of a history of hereditary angioedema. However, if there were a concern for hereditary angioedema, treatment would include subcutaneous ecallantide (D).

Question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the ED by his parent due to a fever and rash for 1 week. Physical exam is notable for conjunctival injection, dry-appearing lips, a generalized rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
ExplanationEN:
Kawasaki disease is a febrile, exanthematous, multisystem vasculitis of the small- and medium-sized vessels thought to be caused by an immune response to a respiratory infection. Left untreated, it can lead to coronary artery aneurysms and other abnormalities. It typically affects children < 5 years of age and has a male predominance.

Classically, Kawasaki disease is diagnosed in a child with a fever for ≥ 5 days and at least four of the following five symptoms: bilateral conjunctival injection, red and cracked lips or strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, palmar or plantar erythema and edema or periungual desquamation, and a polymorphous generalized rash.

Complications of Kawasaki disease include myocarditis early on during the disease and coronary artery dilation with subsequent development of aneurysms in the later phase of the illness. These can lead to myocardial infarction with all its complications.

In addition to supportive care, treatment consists of aspirin and IV immune globulin to decrease cardiac inflammation.



Treatment with corticosteroids (B) is not recommended as a first-line option. It may have a role in refractory cases.

Ibuprofen (C) is relatively contraindicated, as it may antagonize the antiplatelet effect of aspirin.

Plasma exchange (D) is not a standard therapy for Kawasaki disease.

Question: A 57-year-old woman presents with weakness and a rash, as shown above. She states she initially had difficulty rising from a seated position and recently noticed difficulty washing her hair. On exam, she has bilateral 3/5 strength with shoulder shrug and extension at the knee. Blood work is significant for a creatine kinase level of 502 U/L. Which of the following is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with proximal muscle weakness and a violaceous rash on the eyelids (heliotrope rash), classic for dermatomyositis. Her elevated creatine kinase supports muscle inflammation. Occult malignancy is a key associated condition in adults with dermatomyositis, especially those over age 50. Cancer screening is essential due to the strong paraneoplastic link.

Dermatomyositis is a systemic autoimmune perimysial inflammatory myopathy with cutaneous manifestations. Myopathy more often affects women and presents with progressive, symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Patients often report difficulty rising from a seated position or climbing stairs due to quadriceps or gluteal muscle weakness and difficulty washing their hair or reaching overhead due to deltoid and shoulder muscle weakness. Cutaneous findings include a malar rash similar to systemic lupus erythematosus but distinguished by involvement of the nasolabial fold. Additional cutaneous findings include heliotrope sign (violaceous erythema on the upper eyelid), shawl sign (erythematous patches and plaques in a shawl-like distribution), Gottron papules (erythema on interphalangeal joints), and mechanic’s hands (hyperkeratotic papules along the thumb and index finger). Patients may also have extracutaneous and extramuscular manifestations such as interstitial lung disease, arthralgias, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and occult malignancy. Malignancies associated with dermatomyositis include hematopoietic malignancies and solid tumors such as breast, lung, ovarian, colorectal, gastric, and pancreatic tumors.

Clinical findings, cutaneous features, electromyographic studies, imaging, and laboratory evaluation are useful in initial diagnosis, although there is no gold standard for diagnosis. Patients with dermatomyositis have elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase) due to underlying myopathy. In the ED, in addition to muscle enzymes, patients should receive a urinalysis to assess for myoglobin, which may provide rapid data on the presence of muscle damage, and an ECG and troponin level to assess for myocardial involvement. Treatment involves assessment of the potentially affected organs, cancer screening, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressive therapy.



Hypercalcemia (A) may be seen in patients with the autoimmune disorder sarcoidosis due to increased granuloma production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

Hypercoagulability (B) is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, which may be seen in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (D) is associated with giant cell (temporal) arteritis, a large-vessel vasculitis that may lead to permanent blindness.
