Question: A 50-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with weakness. She has been having trouble walking up the stairs. On physical exam she is noted to have erythematous papules on the dorsal aspect of her hands. Which of the following is the best test to determine her condition?
ExplanationEN:
Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory polymyopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness as well as various cutaneous manifestations. Proximal muscle weakness is a common feature and may be present in up to 90% of patients. Common muscles affected include the deltoids, hip flexors, and neck flexors. Patients may present with difficulty standing from a seated position, climbing stairs, or holding children. The muscle weakness is usually gradual, progressing over months. However, patients may develop symptoms that prompt an emergency department evaluation. Characteristic cutaneous findings include Gottron papules and a Gottron sign. Gottron papules are erythematous papular lesions located on the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. A Gottron sign describes erythematous macules, patches, or papules on extensor joint surfaces. Other skin findings consistent with dermatomyositis include heliotrope eruptions, which are erythematous to violaceous eruptions on the upper eyelids, and facial erythema similar to that seen in patients with lupus. Elevation of creatine kinase is the most sensitive and specific enzyme abnormality in patients with dermatomyositis. The diagnosis is made based on history, elevated muscle enzymes, and autoantibodies such as anti-Jo-1.



An elevation in C-reactive protein (CRP) (A) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (C) may be seen in patients with dermatomyositis. However, a normal ESR or CRP does not rule out the diagnosis. In addition, some patients with dermatomyositis can have normal inflammatory markers.

A urinalysis may reveal urine myoglobin (D), but in a patient with a physical exam and history consistent with dermatomyositis, serum creatine kinase would be a more appropriate test in establishing the diagnosis.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents with ankle pain. He recently started taking an antibiotic for a sinus infection. He reports pain and swelling overlying the back of his ankle. Physical exam reveals tenderness, swelling, and mild erythema overlying the Achilles tendon. Which of the following antibiotics is most likely responsible?
ExplanationEN:
Tendinitis is the inflammation of a tendon, typically manifesting as an overuse injury. However, tendinitis may also occur due to overloading, trauma, infection, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, and fluoroquinolone use. Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are commonly implicated, but all fluoroquinolones come with the risk of tendinitis and rupture. Accordingly, these antibiotics are increasingly being used as a treatment of last resort. Fluoroquinolone-related tendinitis affects the Achilles tendon in 90% of cases, with the rotator cuff and quadriceps tendons accounting for most of the remaining cases.

Symptom onset can occur within hours of antibiotic initiation or as late as 6 months after completing a regimen. Risk factors for fluoroquinolone-related tendinopathy include age > 60 years, steroid use, kidney disorders, and rheumatic disease. Fluoroquinolones should be immediately discontinued in patients with signs of tendinopathy.

Patients with tendinitis, regardless of etiology, present with symptoms of pain, particularly with range of motion and weight-bearing. Physical exam may reveal tenderness to palpation, swelling, and erythema. Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging are useful adjuncts in cases when the diagnosis remains in doubt.

General treatment for acute tendinitis starts with rest, ice, and NSAIDs. More severe cases may require immobilization. Once the inflammation has begun to improve, the patient should start gentle stretching with graded progression to normal exercise.



Clarithromycin (A), like many antibiotics, has gastrointestinal manifestations as its most common side effect. Tendinitis is not a side effect of this medication.

Clindamycin (B) can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia, but it does not cause tendinitis.

Doxycycline (C) can cause photosensitivity and exfoliative dermatitis but is not implicated in tendinitis.

Question: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the ED with left ankle pain that started 2 days ago. He reports no trauma, falls, fevers, or chills. Physical exam reveals a palpable effusion and limited range of motion due to pain. Arthrocentesis shows positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals, 10,000 WBCs/mm³ with 60% polymorphonuclear cells, and no bacteria on Gram stain. What is the pathophysiology behind the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Age-related loss of cartilage and bone density
Coagulation factor deficiency leading to intra-articular hemorrhage
Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the synovial space
Excess uric acid leading to precipitation in the synovial space

CorrectAnswer: Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the synovial space
ExplanationEN:
Pseudogout is a crystalline arthropathy that mimics gout but arises from the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the synovial space. The related immunologic response leads to inflammatory changes in the joint, causing patients to experience pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth of the joint. Arthrocentesis should be performed, which would demonstrate positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals, as seen in this patient.

The acute treatment of pseudogout involves local (e.g., intra-articular glucocorticoids) and systemic anti-inflammatory agents for symptomatic management. Oral anti-inflammatory medications can include a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), colchicine, or a glucocorticoid.



Osteoporosis manifests as age-related loss of cartilage and bone density (A) that is seen on X-ray as the loss of joint space, accompanied by sclerosis and osteophyte formation.

In individuals with hemophilia, genetic coagulation factor deficiency leading to intra-articular hemorrhage (B) can occur spontaneously or after minor trauma. Arthrocentesis demonstrates red blood cells without crystal formation.

Gout arises from excess uric acid leading to monosodium urate crystal precipitation in the synovial space (D), appearing as needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.

Inflammatory arthritis (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) leads to immune complex-mediated synovial inflammation (E).

Question: A 12-year-old girl presents to the emergency department for knee pain and limp for 3 days. The parents and patient cannot recall a traumatic incident prior to the onset of her pain. An X-ray of her knee is unremarkable, and an X-ray of the pelvis is shown above. What is the most appropriate step in management?

Options.text: Full body evaluation for other signs of child abuse
Nonsurgical and conservative management with hip brace placement
Orthopedic evaluation in the emergency department
Prepare the patient for a knee arthrocentesis

CorrectAnswer: Orthopedic evaluation in the emergency department
ExplanationEN:
The finding of asymmetry between the femoral epiphysis and femoral neck is diagnostic of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). SCFE is idiopathic. However, risk factors include male sex, puberty, obesity, and hypothyroidism. It is diagnosed two times more often in boys than girls and typically appears at the onset of puberty, with peak incidences at 13 years old for boys and 11 years old for girls. Diagnosis is made with anterior-posterior or frog leg pelvis X-rays that will show apparent posterior and inferior displacement of the femoral head (as shown above). If the diagnosis is made, the contralateral hip should be evaluated, as up to half of cases can be bilateral. Patients will commonly present with an atraumatic, painful limp and referred knee pain that localizes on exam to one or both hips. Management is with non-weight-bearing recommendations and orthopedic evaluation for surgical fixation to avoid further slippage. Despite treatment, many patients will be left with some degree of limitation in range of motion.



SCFE is an idiopathic slipping of the femoral epiphysis and is not associated with child abuse (A).

Legg-Calve-Perthes is an idiopathic disorder characterized by avascular necrosis of the femoral head. It presents similarly to SCFE with idiopathic limping in young boys. However, they tend to be pre-pubescent between the ages of 5 and 7 years old. Treatment for Legg-Calve-Perthes is conservative and nonsurgical commonly with hip brace placement (B). However, the mainstay of treatment for SCFE is surgical fixation to avoid further epiphyseal slipping.

An arthrocentesis (D) has no role in the diagnosis or management of SCFE.

Sacroiliitis is an inflammatory disorder of the sacroiliac joint in the posterior pelvis. It is a feature of spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis. Referral to a rheumatologist and treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are recommended. Emergent causes of low back pain (e.g., spinal cord compression, spine infection, trauma) should be considered and screened with a directed history and physical examination. Concerning features of back pain include history of trauma, recent surgery, intravenous drug use, old age, history of cancer, fever, focal neurologic deficits (e.g., weakness, numbness), urinary or bowel dysfunction, and unexplained weight loss. Question: A 48-year-old woman is concerned about a month of increasing difficulties getting out of a chair and walking up the stairs. She also reports some difficulties with swallowing. On exam, her thighs are diffusely tender, and she seems symmetrically weak in her proximal upper and lower extremities. Which of the following additional findings would be expected on further evaluation?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has polymyositis, a rare inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal weakness and muscle pain that progress over weeks to months. Weakness affects the proximal limbs, trunk, and neck. It is often manifested as difficulty getting out of a chair, walking up stairs, or reaching overhead. Occasionally, there can be dysphagia, cardiomyopathy, or dyspnea if the respiratory muscles are involved. Sensation, reflexes, and ocular muscles are usually spared. Abnormal labs include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase (CK), aldolase, aminotransferases, and myositis-specific autoantibodies.

It is important to start systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants early to avoid irreversible muscle damage. Hospitalization should be considered for patients with rhabdomyolysis, respiratory distress, or profound muscle weakness. Otherwise, outpatient follow-up within a week with neurology or rheumatology is appropriate.

In contrast to myopathies, neuropathies tend to cause distal weakness and may affect sensation and reflexes. Polymyositis does not affect reflexes.

Dilated and nonreactive pupils (B) with proximal descending weakness is typical of botulism, in which a toxin irreversibly binds to the presynaptic membrane of cranial and peripheral nerves, inhibiting the release of acetylcholine.

Improved strength with sustained exercise (D) is a unique exam finding seen in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, an autoimmune disorder affecting calcium channels at the axon nerve terminal and inhibiting acetylcholine release. The syndrome is associated with lung cancer in about half of cases. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness. They may also have decreased pupillary and deep tendon reflexes, along with autonomic dysfunction like dry mouth and impotence from muscarinic cholinergic deficiency.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents with right-sided elbow swelling and pain. He works as a plumber and has no specific injuries. The elbow pain and swelling developed rapidly and became worse over the last 2 days despite applying ice and using over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications. His vital signs are HR 104 bpm, BP 110/60 mm Hg, RR 18/min, and T 100.2°F (37.9°C). On physical exam, his right elbow is swollen and tender to touch, with redness and fluctuance isolated to the posterior tip of the elbow. He refuses full flexion of the elbow on exam due to pain but allows passive pronation and supination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Septic bursitis refers to a bacterial infection that seeds in one of the bursas. The superficial location of the olecranon bursa at the posterior tip of the elbow makes it susceptible to septic bursitis. The most common mechanisms of infection involve percutaneous inoculation of skin organisms from trauma, prolonged pressure on the elbow such as from leaning on a hard surface, or from overlying cellulitis. Iatrogenic causes can also lead to septic bursitis following joint injections or other joint procedures. Hematogenous spread of infection is a rare cause of septic bursitis. Staphylococcus aureus is responsible for the majority of cases, accounting for up to 80% of them. Patients present with fluctuance, erythema, warmth, and tenderness of the overlying area. More specific features include the rapid onset of pain and swelling, as well as fevers and limited joint mobility. Diagnosis is confirmed with synovial fluid analysis. A yellow or serosanguineous fluid usually indicates nonseptic bursitis, while a purulent cloudy fluid may indicate infection or crystal formation. Cell count revealing a WBC of 5,000–100,000 cells/mm3 with 90% neutrophils may indicate a septic bursa. In addition to the use of oral or IV antibiotics, treatment may involve drainage of bursa in the operating room, but this is not a common intervention.



Lateral epicondylitis (A) and medial epicondylitis (B) are tendinopathies that affect the distal humerus and occur secondary to repetitive motion and overuse. Lateral epicondylitis is more common than medial epicondylitis and typically affects tennis players. Medial epicondylitis occurs more often in those who golf. Both of these conditions present with an insidious onset, will lack fevers, and will not have severely limited motion of the elbow.

Olecranon bursitis (C) can be distinguished from septic bursitis by history and physical exam as well as fluid analysis. Patients with olecranon bursitis will lack significant tenderness and erythema overlying the bursa and will not have fever. Passive range of motion should be normal. If the diagnosis is in question, bursal fluid should be aspirated for analysis.

Question: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with low back pain. He has had chronic low back pain for several years but reports worsening pain over the last 4–5 days. There was no preceding trauma or other inciting factor prior to this worsening. His pain extends into his legs when he stands up and walks, so he takes breaks during walking and leans forward on furniture and other objects for support. His medical history is significant for hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine daily. Physical examination shows full, symmetric patellar and Achilles reflexes. Strength and sensation are normal in his lower extremities. Peripheral pulses are full and symmetric in all extremities. There is no midline or paraspinal lumbar tenderness, and straight leg raise testing is negative bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Spinal stenosis refers to a narrowing of any part of the spine, including the spinal canal, intervertebral foramina, and nerve root canal, and is a prominent cause of chronic back pain. It typically develops as a result of degenerative processes, such as osteoarthritis and degenerative disc disease, that cause narrowing and compression of nearby neurovascular structures. Spinal stenosis typically first becomes clinically apparent between ages 50 and 60 years.

Spinal stenosis typically causes chronic low back pain but may come to clinical attention in the emergency department due to an episode of acute worsening. While some patients will have no symptoms and stenosis will be diagnosed incidentally on imaging studies, those with symptoms often report low back pain that is exacerbated by standing up and other movements requiring lumbar extension and improved with forward flexion (e.g., leaning forward). Many patients report low back and lower extremity pain with walking that mimics vascular claudication. Therefore, it is termed “neurogenic claudication” or pseudoclaudication. Physical examination is often normal, and findings of neurologic abnormalities such as abnormal reflexes should raise suspicion for an alternate diagnosis.

Diagnosis of spinal stenosis is primarily made clinically via thorough history and careful physical examination to rule out cord compression syndromes. CT and MRI can confirm the diagnosis and further evaluate for cord compression and osseous abnormalities if the clinical assessment is equivocal. Once serious and emergent diagnoses have been ruled out, patients with spinal stenosis can be treated similarly to nonspecific, musculoskeletal back pain with pharmacologic therapy such as NSAIDs and supportive measures like heat and ice. Duloxetine has been shown to be an effective medical therapy for chronic back pain, while gabapentin and pregabalin have not, though they are still often used. All patients with chronic back pain should have appropriate primary care follow-up to ensure proper chronic management of their pain.



Cauda equina syndrome (A) and conus medullaris syndrome (B) are specific epidural compression syndromes differentiated by their specific location of cord compression and subsequent presenting signs. A normal neurologic exam throughout the lower extremities effectively rules out both of these conditions, as each would be expected to show some degree of impairment of reflexes, strength, or sensory function. Acute nonspecific back pain, also known as lumbago, lumbar strain (C), and mechanical back pain, is a common, nonthreatening cause of back pain usually associated with a minor inciting trauma or exertional event. The improvement of this patient’s pain with leaning forward (i.e., flexion) and lack of inciting event is more typical of spinal stenosis. Lumbosacral radiculopathy (D) usually causes back pain with radiation into the lower extremities due to nerve root compression by disc herniation. Negative straight leg raise testing in this patient makes this diagnosis unlikely.

Question: A 35-year-old man with no medical conditions presents with 1 week of right elbow pain. He reports a 3-month history of intermittent right elbow pain, but it typically goes away with ibuprofen and ice packs. He is an avid daily climber and has not been able to climb for a few days due to the pain. Which physical exam finding is most consistent with the likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Nontender egg-size swelling at the olecranon with normal range of motion
Normal-appearing elbow with pain medially elicited by resisted pronation
Swollen, warm, exquisitely tender elbow with painful range of motion
Visible deformity of elbow with no range of motion possible

CorrectAnswer: Normal-appearing elbow with pain medially elicited by resisted pronation
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s daily athletic activities put him at risk for overuse syndromes. He has no medical conditions, and there is no history of trauma. The timing of the injury is subacute to chronic, and it is exacerbated by climbing. The most likely injury in this scenario is overuse tendinopathy of the elbow. Repetitive athletic movements, especially involving eccentric and sudden forceful contraction, as in rock climbing, predispose individuals to tendon injury.

Once tendon injury has occurred, ongoing stress and repetitive movement can create tendinosis, in which the tendon tissue is infiltrated by disorganized tissue and vasculature. These injuries are not significantly inflammatory and typically present with pain to palpation and with range of motion (ROM) rather than warmth or swelling.

This patient’s activity predisposes him to medial elbow tendinopathy, which presents as pain at the medial epicondyle near the origin of the proximal tendons of the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis. Physical exam maneuvers that activate these muscles, such as resisted wrist flexion or pronation while the elbow is in extension, can elicit the pain. Management includes NSAIDs, physical therapy, and activity modification.



A nontender egg-size swelling at the olecranon with normal ROM (A) is suggestive of olecranon bursitis. Swelling and inflammation of the bursa may develop due to direct trauma, inflammatory conditions such as gout, or infection. Chronic bursitis often presents with swelling but minimal to no pain.

A swollen, warm, exquisitely tender elbow with painful ROM (C) is concerning for inflammatory arthropathy. The differential also includes joint infection, crystal disease, autoimmune or osteoarthritis, and traumatic injury.

An elbow that is visibly deformed with no possible ROM (D) is most likely dislocated. Fractures typically allow some mobility or crepitus, but dislocated joints are often nonmobile.

Question: A healthy 16-year-old boy presents to the ED with several weeks of atraumatic right thigh pain. The pain, initially mild, has rapidly progressed to severe intensity, is worse with walking and at night, and is associated with a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. Vital signs: T 100.4°F (38°C). Exam reveals a tender, palpable 8 cm mass in the mid-right femur without loss of range of motion in the hip or knee. X-ray shows concentric layers of periosteal elevation at the diaphysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient's clinical scenario is most consistent with Ewing sarcoma. Ewings sarcoma is sarcoma arising commonly in the diaphysis (shaft) of long bones in children aged 5–25 years. The most common bones affected are the femur, pelvis, tibia, and fibula. These patients present with weeks to months of pain localized to a fixed, hard mass. The mass is often tender and can have surrounding swelling. This can be associated with a cytokine-induced fever, loss of joint motion if the tumor is obstructing the joint, and weight loss from the metabolic demand of tumor growth.

Plain radiographs are the initial imaging modality of choice and will often show classic onion skinning periosteal reaction at the diaphysis to help differentiate it from other neoplastic diseases or causes of pain. Treatment requires additional imaging and biopsy for staging, surgery, and likely chemotherapy.



Osteochondroma (B) is a benign cartilaginous tumor, also presenting in children of similar age but is typically painless and would show an irregularly shaped mass on imaging. These typically do not require treatment unless they obstruct range of motion.

Osteomyelitis (C) is a bony infection that could present with fever and pain but typically has a more acute presentation, without weight loss, mass, or imaging findings noted above. These patients would require admission for antibiotics and possibly surgery.

Osteosarcoma (D), would present similarly but can be differentiated on X-ray. Osteosarcoma presents with a sunburst pattern on X-ray due to osteoblast activity and most commonly affects the distal femur or proximal tibia. It is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with posterior ankle pain for the past week. He runs cross-country for his school. The pain is worse with running or trying to go up the stairs. He has not had any known injury. On examination, there is slight swelling noted to the distal Achilles tendon with associated tenderness to palpation. There are no overlying skin changes, and the Thompson test is negative. Ankle X-ray reveals soft tissue swelling to the posterior ankle with no bony abnormality. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Rest, ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity modification
Splint in 15 degrees plantar flexion, non-weight bearing with crutches

CorrectAnswer: Rest, ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity modification
ExplanationEN:
Achilles tendinitis is an overuse injury most commonly seen in those participating in running or jumping activities. The cause of Achilles tendinitis is often multifactorial due to biomechanics, equipment, and environmental factors (uneven terrain, concrete). Patients often report pain to the posterior ankle with weight bearing or stair climbing. Physical examination often reveals mild to moderate swelling along the Achilles tendon with associated tenderness to palpation. Often there is pain with passive stretching of the Achilles tendon with dorsiflexion of the ankle. The Thompson test is used to evaluate the integrity of the Achilles tendon. With the patient prone and feet hanging over the edge of the bed, squeezing the calf at its widest point should result in passive plantar flexion of the Achilles tendon if it is intact. A positive Thompson test would result in no passive plantar flexion of the Achilles tendon signifying concern of a tear in the Achilles tendon. Rest, ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity modification are the most appropriate initial treatment for Achilles tendonitis.



Orthopedic consultation (A) is not indicated in the emergency department for Achilles tendonitis.

Splinting in 15 degrees plantar flexion, non-weight bearing with crutches (C) is the initial treatment for a suspected Achilles rupture, which is not the diagnosis in this patient since he has a negative Thompson test.

Steroid injection (D) is not recommended for Achilles tendinitis as it can lead to rupture.

Question: A 35-year-old man presents to the ED with finger pain. He sustained lacerations to his right hand 5 days ago during a bar fight, and 2 days ago, he started to notice pain and swelling in the right third finger. On exam, his finger is diffusely swollen, erythematous, slightly flexed at rest, and tender along the palmar surface, and he has increased pain on the palmar surface with passive extension of the finger. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

Options.text: Incision and drainage by a hand surgeon
Incision and drainage in the ED

CorrectAnswer: Incision and drainage by a hand surgeon
ExplanationEN:
Flexor tenosynovitis is an infection in the flexor tendon sheath and is diagnosed by the four cardinal signs of the Kanavel criteria, including the finger held in passive flexion, symmetric swelling of the digit that is commonly referred to as a sausage digit, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain with passive extension of the finger. The combination of these signs is very sensitive and fairly specific for flexor tenosynovitis. Infectious tenosynovitis, including flexor tenosynovitis, usually occurs from direct traumatic inoculation or spread from nearby soft tissues but can also occur from hematogenous spread.

Treatment includes IV antibiotics, usually vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and surgical drainage by a hand surgeon.



Admission for IV antibiotics (A) is appropriate in all cases of suspected flexor tenosynovitis. However, it is definitive treatment only in the most mild cases involving only mild pain and local inflammation. These patients can be given vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin and admitted to monitor progression and the need for surgical intervention. Once there is severe pain, diffuse swelling, and limited passive range of motion, surgical intervention is warranted for definitive management in addition to IV antibiotics.

Incision and drainage in the ED (C) is appropriate for simple abscesses but not infections involving complex structures like the flexor tendons of the hands, which require specialist intervention.

Oral antibiotics (D) are not appropriate for the treatment of flexor tenosynovitis, given the high likelihood of progression to require surgical drainage, even in mild cases. Patients with mild signs and symptoms may be admitted for IV antibiotics and monitoring. Individuals with more advanced presentations, like this patient, should undergo surgical drainage by a hand surgeon.

Question: Which clinical feature is most sensitive for cauda equina syndrome?

Options.text: Diminished strength in bilateral lower extremities

ExplanationEN:
Cauda equina syndrome results from lesions compressing the conus medullaris and the nerve roots extending from it (the cauda equina). These lesions most commonly are herniated discs, bone fragments, hematomas, epidural abscesses, tumors, or vascular insufficiency. Spinal epidural abscess is a rare but important infection of the central nervous system (CNS) that requires emergent consideration, diagnosis, and treatment. Spinal epidural abscesses are most commonly found in the thoracic or lumbar areas, where the epidural space contains more infection-prone fatty tissue in a larger area. Risk factors for a spinal epidural abscess include epidural catheter placement, paraspinal injections, diabetes mellitus, alcohol use disorder, HIV, trauma, bacteremia, intravenous drug use, and hemodialysis. The classic triad of symptoms of spinal epidural abscess is fever, spinal pain, and neurologic deficits (may be consistent with cauda equina syndrome). Patients with other forms of cauda equina commonly report low back pain, lower extremity pain, paralysis or paresthesia, saddle anesthesia, impotence, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. Once paralysis is present, it quickly becomes irreversible, thus early recognition and treatment are crucial. Urinary retention is the most consistent finding with a sensitivity of 90%.

A thorough history regarding recent spinal procedures, trauma, anticoagulation, intravenous drug use, and history of malignancy helps aid in determining the cause. Physical examination of the lower extremities may demonstrate sensory or motor deficits. Frequently, clinical features are asymmetric with unilateral signs and symptoms being present. Absent or decreased rectal tone and bulbocavernosus reflexes may also be found. A palpable distended urinary bladder may be appreciated secondary to urinary retention. Laboratory examination may reveal an elevated or normal white blood cell count, and may therefore not be helpful with the diagnosis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) lab values are typically obtained for evaluation with both being elevated in the majority of cases. However, several studies have found that the ESR has better sensitivity and specificity compared to CRP.

Patients with a suspicious history and physical or lab results concerning for cauda equina require emergency MRI imaging. CT myelogram may be utilized in patients unable to have an MRI performed. A bedside postvoid residual of 100–200 mL without a history of voiding difficulties suggests a neurologic etiology. Treatment relies on early surgical decompression. If a spinal epidural abscess is found, antibiotics should be started as soon as the diagnosis is strongly suspected or confirmed. Vancomycin plus cefotaxime or ceftriaxone are appropriate empiric antibiotics. If Pseudomonas is thought to be a possible organism, then cefepime or ceftazidime should be used in place of cefotaxime or ceftriaxone.



Diminished deep tendon reflexes (A), diminished strength in bilateral lower extremities (B), and positive straight leg raise (D) may or may not all be present in cauda equina syndrome. However, none of these clinical features are the most sensitive for cauda equina syndrome.

Question: An otherwise healthy 13-year-old boy with a history of obesity presents to the ED with 1 day of hip pain. On exam, you note an antalgic gait and a right leg held in external rotation. Question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with ankle pain. He has a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and diabetes. He states his ankle started hurting after a weekend with friends. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination is significant for a right ankle that is edematous and erythematous with exquisite tenderness with active and passive range of motion of the joint. The remainder of the exam is unremarkable. Synovial fluid analysis shows a WBC of 45,000/μL, normal glucose, and negatively birefringent crystals. What is the cause of the patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Gout is a type of crystal-induced synovitis that is caused by uric acid crystals. These crystals are negatively birefringent and needle-shaped. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness. The joints most commonly affected are the great toe, tarsal joints, and knee. Crystal-induced synovitis generally affects middle-aged and older patients. Both gout and pseudogout, as well as rheumatoid arthritis, Lyme disease, and lupus, can all cause inflammatory arthritis that is defined and confirmed by synovial fluid analysis. Synovial fluid for inflammatory arthritis will have a white blood cell count between 200 and 50,000/μL with > 50% neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance with crystals being present if gout or pseudogout is the cause. Treatment consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine. Corticosteroids can be used in patients with kidney disease, in those who cannot take other forms of treatment, or those who have been found to be refractory to other treatments. Corticosteroids should be avoided in those with uncontrolled diabetes.



Osteoarthritis (B)is a chronic, symmetric polyarticular destruction of joints distinguished by the lack of constitutional symptoms. Patients may present with acute monoarticular exacerbations that consist of joint pain and inflammation. Synovial fluid for osteoarthritis will demonstrate a white blood cell count of < 3,000/μL with < 25% neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be clear and transparent in appearance without crystals present. Treatment consists of rest and analgesics.

Pseudogout (C)is a type of crystal-induced synovitis that is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. These crystals are positively birefringent. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness. The joints most commonly affected are the knee, wrist, ankle, and elbow. Synovial fluid for inflammatory arthritis will have a white blood cell count between 200 and 50,000/μL with > 50% neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance with crystals being present if pseudogout is the cause.

Septic arthritis (D) is a condition that, if left untreated, leads to rapid irreversible joint destruction. The presentation typically involves swelling, erythema, and warmth over one joint. Patients may present with associated chills, fevers, and malaise, although the absence of one or all of these symptoms does not exclude the diagnosis. One way to help differentiate septic arthritis from infections surrounding the joint is joint compression, which will reproduce symptoms for arthritis and not infections of surrounding tissues. True arthritis produces joint pain that is exacerbated by both active and passive range of motion. Lab tests such as the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein can be helpful in increasing the suspicion for the diagnosis but are neither specific nor sensitive enough to rule in or rule out the diagnosis. If the diagnosis is suspected based on clinical features synovial fluid analysis via arthrocentesis should be performed to confirm or rule out the diagnosis. Synovial fluid for septic arthritis will demonstrate a profound white blood cell count of > 50,000/μL with > 50% neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance without crystals present.

Question: Which of the following patients requires radiologic imaging for back pain?

Options.text: A 26-year-old woman with unilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, fever, and dysuria
A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks gestation with lumbosacral pain that radiates down the right posterior thigh
A 30-year-old woman with midline lumbar pain and tenderness, fever, and difficulty urinating
A 35-year-old woman with bilateral lumbar-level back pain after lifting furniture that is worse with movement and alleviated with rest
A 40-year-old woman with lumbar-level pain and tenderness that radiates to her left anterior thigh and unremarkable findings on neurologic exam

CorrectAnswer: A 30-year-old woman with midline lumbar pain and tenderness, fever, and difficulty urinating
ExplanationEN:
This patient has symptoms suspicious for a spinal epidural abscess. Patients at risk for spinal epidural abscess include those with diabetes, malignancy, recent spinal procedure, alcohol use disorder, immunocompromise, and IV drug use. The classic triad is severe back pain, fever, and neurological deficits. In this patient’s case, urinary retention is her deficit, which by itself is worrisome for cauda equina syndrome.

The diagnostic test of choice is an MRI. Epidural abscess may require evacuation by a spine surgeon. Patients are often on IV antibiotics for many weeks. Empiric antibiotics are indicated in patients with neurological deficits or signs of sepsis and in cases in which surgery is delayed. Two sets of blood cultures should be drawn prior to antibiotics administration.



Pyelonephritis (A) is an infection of the kidney parenchyma and upper collecting system. In an otherwise healthy, young patient, treatment can be performed on an outpatient basis with 10–14 days of oral antibiotics. Radiographic imaging is not needed unless there is suspicion of an infected kidney stone.

Pregnancy-related low back pain (B) is a common occurrence, particularly in the second half of pregnancy due to changes in posture, weight distribution, and ligament laxity. It can lead to discomfort, radiating pain down the posterior thighs, and pain worsening at night. It is managed conservatively without imaging, but radiologic studies are indicated for cases with alarm symptoms such as severe pain that interferes with function, systemic symptoms, significant neurological deficits, and pain that worsens with cough or Valsalva.

Nonspecific back pain (D) in the absence of red flags (e.g., fever, neurologic deficit, IV drug use, trauma) does not require radiographic imaging and can be managed symptomatically with resumption of usual daily activities as soon as possible. Bed rest has been shown to prolong the duration of pain, as have back exercises. Most nonspecific back pain resolves in 4 to 6 weeks.

Radiculopathy (E) or nerve impingement syndrome may be caused by a disc herniation or other irritation of the nerve root. Given the location of symptoms, compression of the L4–L5 nerve root should be suspected, but without worrisome features, imaging in the emergency department is not indicated. If her symptoms do not resolve in 4 to 6 weeks, an MRI of the lumbosacral spine may be warranted.

Question: Which of the following wounds is a potential candidate for primary closure?

Options.text: Facial laceration from a dog bite
Forearm laceration from a human bite
Laceration on the sole of the foot after stepping on an unknown object in a stream
Laceration over the metacarpophalangeal joint sustained during a fistfight
Puncture wounds on the foot due to a dog bite

CorrectAnswer: Facial laceration from a dog bite
ExplanationEN:
Although dog bite wounds pose a high risk for infectious complications, those that are cosmetically deforming are often closed primarily, especially on the face. Dog bites are at high risk for infection from organisms commonly found in the dog’s mouth, which include Staphylococcus aureus, Pasteurella multocida, and viridans group streptococci. All bite wounds must be thoroughly irrigated and cleansed.

Although controversy exists over the management of animal bite wounds, it is generally agreed that those that are cosmetically deforming (including those on the face) should be repaired primarily. Wounds on the extremities and those that are not as much of a cosmetic concern are generally left open or loosely approximated in this situation.



Certain lacerations are best managed when left open or closed in a delayed fashion. These include human bites (B) and animal bites that are not cosmetically significant, lacerations that are heavily contaminated or have extensive associated tissue damage, and contaminated lacerations on the bottom of the feet. A laceration on the plantar aspect of the foot sustained on an unknown object while walking in a stream (C) would be considered contaminated.

Lacerations over the metacarpophalangeal joints (D) that occur during a fistfight are considered human bites and should not be closed primarily.

Puncture wounds on the foot (E) from a dog bite are considered high risk for infection but are not cosmetically significant. Thus, they should not be closed primarily.

Question: A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department concerned about severe left shoulder pain. His medical history is significant for smoking and a chronic cough. He reports that he has had a persistent ache in that shoulder for several weeks. Today, he was walking through a crowded entrance and hit his shoulder on a door jamb. Since then, he has had severe pain in his shoulder. Minimal active or passive motion causes pain. No deformity is appreciated on exam. The X-ray reveals the above finding. What is the most likely reason for the patient’s findings?
ExplanationEN:
Pathological fractures are fractures that occur with an inconsistent or minor mechanism due to a pathological weakening of the bone. Pathological fractures are most frequently caused by metastatic cancer from solid organ tumors (most commonly breast, lung, and prostate) or myeloma. Metastatic bone lesions typically affect the axial skeleton (e.g., skull and spine) and the proximal limbs. Metastases have a predilection for areas of bone with high vascularity. Metastases can cause constant pain without deformity, and in the setting of pathological fracture, the pain may be severe. The image above shows a fracture through a lytic “moth-eaten” bone lesion, which is consistent with a metastatic lesion. Other radiographic findings can include periosteal abnormalities and areas of irregularly increased density. Additional radiographic modalities that may be useful are a CT scan with IV contrast and reconstructions, an MRI for smaller lesions, and a total-body radionuclide bone scan to screen for other areas of metastasis. Treatment includes pain management, radiation therapy, and surgical repair.



Osteoporosis (B) may cause pathological fractures. However, the X-ray would reveal decreased bone density without a lytic lesion. Osteoporosis is more common in postmenopausal women and men > 65 years. Osteoporosis-related pathological fractures most commonly occur in the hips and spine. Pathological fractures within lytic lesions are less commonly due to Paget disease (C), a localized disorder of bone metabolism. Paget bony lesions more commonly affect the axial skeleton, pelvis, and long bones of the lower extremities. Primary sarcoma (D) may also present with a lytic bone lesion and fracture but not as commonly as metastatic disease.

Question: A 21-year-old man who works as a chef recently cut his hand with a knife. Which of the following clinical findings suggests a diagnosis of infectious flexor tenosynovitis?

It is most commonly caused by penetrating trauma to the digit, including bites from animals or humans.

Question: A 9-year-old boy presents with 2 days of high fever and severe focal left leg pain. He refuses to bear weight, and examination shows warmth, swelling, and marked tenderness over the proximal tibia. X-ray shows focal cortical destruction. Which of the following bacteria is most likely to be isolated upon bone biopsy and culture?
ExplanationEN:
Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone that can affect patients of any age. In children, most cases are due to hematogenous spread. The initial bacteremia may be from a skin lesion, infection, or trauma. In adults, it is more likely to be seen in a compromised host due to immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, chronic illness (diabetes mellitus), or debilitation. It may also be seen in adults with an iatrogenic postsurgical prosthesis complication. Osteomyelitis can occur in any bone, but is most common in long bones in children, especially the metaphysis of the tibia or femur.

Typical symptoms of osteomyelitis include pain, overlying skin changes (erythema, warmth), fever, limp, or inability to bear weight, or refusal to use the extremity. Laboratory analysis will often reveal an elevated white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein. Blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when feasible. The gold standard and definitive test used to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment of osteomyelitis is a bone biopsy and culture.

Radiographic evidence of osteomyelitis lags behind the clinical picture. Plain radiography may not show the characteristic findings of lucent lytic areas of cortical bone destruction until approximately 2 weeks. Approximately 50% of the bone mineral must be lost for detection on plain radiographs. Other imaging adjuncts include computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and bone scan (Technetium-99m).

The most common bacteria causing osteomyelitis in all age groups, except neonates, is Staphylococcus aureus. These patients tend to have more abrupt symptoms as this patient. Compared with other organisms that cause more indolent disease in younger children, Staphylococcus aureus more often produces high fever, significant pain, and an ill appearance. Other bacteria, besides the other choices above, include group A Streptococcus, Enterobacter species, Kingella kingae, and Haemophilus influenzae type B. Tuberculosis may also cause osteomyelitis (known as Pott disease if in the vertebrae) along with some systemic fungal infections (Candida, Aspergillus, Blastomyces, or Cryptococcus). A prolonged treatment with intravenous antibiotics or antifungals is recommended, sometimes with surgical drainage and debridement.



Group B Streptococcus (A) is a common cause of osteomyelitis in neonates. In neonates, the most common bacterial causes of osteomyelitis are group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus epidermidis.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (B) is not a common cause of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in an otherwise healthy school-aged child. It is more commonly associated with osteomyelitis due to puncture wounds to the foot through rubber-soled shoes.

Salmonella enterica (C) osteomyelitis should be strongly considered in children with a history of sickle cell anemia. There are no indications that this patient has sickle cell anemia and even in children with sickle cell anemia, Staphylococcus aureus is the more common cause of osteomyelitis.

Streptococcus pyogenes (E) can cause invasive musculoskeletal infection, including osteomyelitis, but it is much less common that Staphylococcus aureus. These infections also tend to be rapidly progressive to systemic toxicity.

Question: A 28-year-old woman presents with pain in the heel of her right foot that has been bothering her for the past week. She has been training for a marathon but does not recall any specific injury to the area. She states her pain is worse in the morning when taking her first steps. The pain improves throughout the day but then worsens after a long day on her feet. The pain is reproducible with dorsiflexion of the great toe. What is the next step in management?

Options.text: Immobilize the foot using a surgical boot
Inject steroids and bupivacaine in the heel of the foot
Obtain an MRI of the ankle and foot

ExplanationEN:
Plantar fasciitis is a condition that leads to pain in the sole of the foot secondary to degenerative or inflammatory changes in the fascia of the plantar surface of the foot. It is caused by overuse, making it a condition that affects young athletes, especially long-distance runners. Other risk factors include flat or high-arched feet, limited ankle dorsiflexion, and prolonged walking or standing on hard surfaces. Patients report pain in the heel of the foot that is typically worse with the first step of the day. The pain improves initially but recurs at the end of the day. On physical exam, patients have tenderness on the medial plantar tubercle of the calcaneus and pain with toe dorsiflexion. There is an absence of swelling, warmth, or redness to the heel. Radiographs are not required and can be deferred until after conservative treatment. Radiographs can be considered in patients showing no improvement to look for a stress fracture of the metatarsal or other more serious conditions such as cancer and osteomyelitis. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for 2–3 weeks, heel cushion use, and upgrading to shoes that have impact-resistant heel and arch support. Additionally, patients can be instructed to reduce activity and increase stretching exercises.



Immobilizing the foot using a surgical boot (A) is not recommended. While patients are advised to reduce the amount of activity, total inactivity may slow the healing process. Injecting steroids and bupivacaine in the heel of the foot (B) is a treatment option reserved for refractory cases that do not respond to conservative measures. However, before steroid injections, other diagnoses must be excluded. Obtaining an MRI of the ankle and foot (C) would be the best imaging option in terms of excluding other serious conditions for refractory cases but is not needed at this time.

Question: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with progressive muscle weakness and difficulty walking. He reports no prodromal illness, recent infection, overexertion, or any current medications. The examination is significant for 2+ bilateral patella and Achilles reflexes, normal strength with ankle flexion but weakness with both neck and hip flexion, a normal sensory examination, and no difficulty urinating. Laboratory studies are significant for a creatine kinase of 1,500 IU/L. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation, with proximal muscle weakness without changes in sensation or reflexes and mildly elevated creatine kinase (CK), is most consistent with polymyositis. Polymyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with a gradual onset, most commonly affecting the proximal muscles of the hips, shoulders, and neck. Patients may experience myalgias and will have a normal sensory and reflex examination. The diagnosis can be suggested in patients with a classic presentation and elevated muscle enzymes and may be confirmed with electromyography or muscle biopsy. Patients with mild weakness may be started on glucocorticoids with outpatient neurology follow-up. Those with severe weakness should be admitted for further evaluation and treatment.



Ciguatera (A) is a fish-derived toxin that may cause neurologic and gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea and vomiting, hot-cold reversal (cold allodynia), and ataxia. Guillain-Barré (B) is an immune-mediated ascending paralysis that also presents with diminished reflexes. Transverse myelitis (D) is an inflammatory disorder that causes paraplegia at the affected spinal level with sensory and autonomic effects, depending on the level involved.

A Pott puffy tumor is an uncommon condition that encompasses subperiosteal abscess or osteomyelitis of the frontal bone that results from the contiguous spread of frontal sinusitis. Question: In which setting is initiating allopurinol inappropriate in the treatment of gout?
ExplanationEN:
Gout is caused by the deposition of uric acid crystals in the synovium, bursae, tendon sheaths, skin, heart valves, and kidneys, which can lead to arthritis, tophi, kidney stones, and gouty nephropathy. Typically, patients present with acute, exquisitely tender, monoarticular arthritis. The joint is usually warm and erythematous. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is most commonly affected. Detecting negatively birefringent, needle-like crystals in the synovial fluid from an arthrocentesis confirms the diagnosis.

Allopurinol is a urate-lowering medication used for the long-term prevention of gout attacks, but it should not be initiated during an acute gout flare if the flare is not yet controlled. Starting allopurinol can rapidly shift serum urate levels, which may worsen or prolong the acute attack. The preferred approach is to first treat the flare with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids until symptoms improve. Once the acute attack is resolved and inflammation is controlled, allopurinol may be started with prophylactic colchicine to reduce the risk of flare during initiation.

The risk of triggering or aggravating a flare occurs because changes in uric acid concentrations destabilize urate crystals within joints. Therefore, guidelines emphasize stabilizing inflammation before initiating a urate-lowering agent. If a patient is already on allopurinol at the time of a flare, the medication should not be discontinued, but starting it during an active, uncontrolled flare is inappropriate. After resolution, allopurinol can be initiated at a low dose and titrated upward as tolerated.



While caution and dose adjustments are required, allopurinol is not contraindicated in chronic kidney disease (B). Proper dosing and monitoring can safely facilitate its use in gout management for patients with impaired kidney function, so it would not be inappropriate to start in a patient with a GFR stage of G3a.

Ethanol metabolism blocks kidney excretion of uric acid, which increases the risk of developing gouty arthritis. However, allopurinol is not contraindicated in individuals who consume ethanol (C).

Hyperuricemia (D) is present (usually > 8 mg/dL) in patients with gout, and when symptomatic, these patients should be treated. Allopurinol is used to decrease uric acid production, thus managing hyperuricemia effectively, and there is no contraindication based on the level of serum uric acid.

Colchicine (E) can be used in combination with allopurinol to help decrease the likelihood of a gouty flare while the uric acid level decreases after an acute attack has subsided. Colchicine decreases inflammation associated with lactic acid production and phagocytosis of urate. It terminates most gouty attacks within 6–12 hours but is limited by GI side effects.

Question: Which one of the following physical examination findings suggests cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy rather than a musculoskeletal cause for a patient’s neck pain?

Options.text: Focal point tenderness near the cervical spine
Neck pain alone in response to the Spurling test
Shock-like paresthesias upon flexion of the neck

CorrectAnswer: Shock-like paresthesias upon flexion of the neck
ExplanationEN:
Shock-like paresthesias upon flexion of the neck (known as the Lhermitte sign) suggest cervical myelopathy, indicating spinal cord involvement. This symptom is a hallmark of central nervous system pathology and helps differentiate neurologic causes from musculoskeletal neck pain.

Neck pain is a frequent presenting symptom in the ED and a leading cause of chronic musculoskeletal disability in the United States. The etiologies are diverse, ranging from benign musculoskeletal strain to life-threatening spinal or infectious pathology.

The differential diagnosis of neck pain includes a wide array of conditions: traumatic injury, degenerative spine disease, muscular strain, facet joint arthritis, discitis, meningitis, spinal epidural abscess, spinal tumors, herniated intervertebral discs, epidural hematoma, and transverse myelitis. Among neurologic causes, cervical radiculopathy involves compression or irritation of the nerve root, whereas cervical myelopathy refers to dysfunction of the spinal cord itself. This distinction is clinically critical, as spinal cord lesions typically require urgent or emergent evaluation and intervention to prevent permanent neurologic deficits.

While many cases of neck pain are due to benign soft tissue strain or degenerative changes, certain red flags should prompt immediate consideration of more serious pathology. These include Lhermitte phenomenon, unilateral or bilateral hand weakness, gait instability, new bowel or bladder symptoms, fever, unexplained weight loss, known immunosuppression, history of malignancy, or intravenous drug use. The presence of these features necessitates prompt laboratory workup and advanced imaging.

While plain radiographs of the cervical spine may identify gross bony abnormalities or alignment issues in trauma, they are typically of limited use in nontraumatic presentations of cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy. MRI is the preferred modality for evaluating the spinal cord, intervertebral discs, and soft tissues, and it is critical for identifying compressive lesions, inflammation, infection, or neoplasms. When infection is suspected, additional evaluation with complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and blood cultures may be warranted.



Focal point tenderness near the cervical spine (A) is more indicative of a localized musculoskeletal issue, such as a strain or facet joint irritation, not neurologic disease.

Increased pain with shoulder abduction (B) reflects musculoskeletal or rotator cuff pathology rather than cervical nerve root or spinal cord involvement.

Neck pain alone in response to the Spurling test (C) is nonspecific. A positive Spurling sign suggests radiculopathy only when it reproduces radiating arm symptoms, not just localized neck discomfort.

Question: A 16-year-old healthy boy presents to the ED for 6 weeks of progressive, dull, atraumatic pain just proximal to his right knee. Examination shows a full range of motion of the right knee without effusion, and there is a tender, palpable mass in the distal femur. X-ray is as shown above, and laboratory evaluation is significant for alkaline phosphatase of 225 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This X-ray shows a destructive, sclerotic lesion with periosteal reaction and sunburst pattern, characteristic of osteosarcoma. This is the most common primary bone malignancy in adolescents, often affecting the metaphyseal region of long bones like the distal femur. This patient’s age, presentation with localized pain and mass, and elevated alkaline phosphatase all support this diagnosis.

Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant bone tumor with a bimodal age distribution. It most frequently affects adolescents between 16 and 18 years old during periods of rapid skeletal growth, and a second peak occurs in adults > 60 years old, often in the setting of predisposing conditions. Known risk factors include genetic syndromes such as hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1 gene mutation), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 mutation), Paget disease of bone, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation or alkylating chemotherapy.

The tumor most commonly arises in the metaphyseal regions of long bones, with the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus being the most frequent sites. Patients present with localized, progressively worsening bone pain that may be accompanied by swelling or a palpable, tender mass. Symptoms may develop gradually or be noticed following minor trauma. Despite the aggressive nature of the tumor, constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats are uncommon and may suggest alternative or advanced disease.

Initial evaluation should include plain radiographs, which often reveal classic findings such as a mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion with periosteal elevation, producing a characteristic sunburst or hair-on-end appearance due to aggressive periosteal bone formation. The Codman triangle, another radiographic feature, represents subperiosteal new bone formation at the tumor margin.

Laboratory findings may include elevated alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, both of which correlate with tumor burden and may have prognostic significance. Definitive diagnosis requires a biopsy, ideally performed after consultation with an orthopedic oncologist to prevent compromising future surgical margins. Staging with chest imaging (CT scan) and bone scintigraphy or PET scan is essential, as the lungs are the most common site of metastasis.

Treatment involves a multidisciplinary approach, typically starting with neoadjuvant chemotherapy to shrink the tumor and address micrometastatic disease, followed by wide surgical resection. Limb-salvage surgery is preferred over amputation when feasible. Postoperative (adjuvant) chemotherapy is administered to reduce the risk of recurrence and improve long-term survival, which varies depending on factors such as tumor size, location, response to chemotherapy, and metastatic status at diagnosis.



Chondroblastomas (A) are benign tumors of the cartilaginous epiphyseal plate. They affect a similar area, most commonly the distal femur and proximal tibia, but present with restricted range of motion due to epiphyseal involvement, and X-ray findings show a well-circumscribed lytic lesion without periosteal reaction. Treatment often involves surgery to eradicate joint obstruction.

Ewing sarcoma (B) is another malignant neoplasm of the diaphysis of long bones that presents with pain, fever, and a hard mass. It can be differentiated on X-ray with classic onion skinning of the periosteum. Treatment would be similar, with surgery and chemotherapy.

Osteomyelitis (C) is an infection of the bone, which would typically present with fever, acute-onset pain, and elevated white blood cell count. An X-ray may show cortical destruction in advanced disease. Treatment would require intravenous antibiotics and orthopedic evaluation.

Question: An 8-year-old previously healthy boy presents with back pain and fever for 4 days. He reports pain in the lower back that is increased with bending and twisting. The pain radiates down into his left leg. He reports no trauma. The physical exam is remarkable for tenderness to palpation over the lumbar spine. What management is indicated?

Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms consistent with discitis, and he should have an MRI to make the diagnosis. Discitis is a rare infection of the nucleus pulposus and can involve the cartilaginous endplate and vertebral body. It can occur spontaneously or after surgical procedures. Typically, patients present with severe pain localized to the spinal level of involvement. Any movement of the spine exacerbates the pain. Children often present with sudden onset of back pain and refusal to walk. The lumbar spine is most commonly involved, and the average age of patients is 7 years. Radicular symptoms are common (present in 50–90% of cases). Fever rates have ranged in multiple studies, with percentages from 50–90% of patients being febrile. Neurologic deficits are uncommon. Serious pathology should be suspected in any pediatric patient presenting with back pain. MRI is the best study for diagnosis and can also rule out other critical diagnoses, including epidural abscess. Laboratory studies are nonspecific and insensitive but typically have an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. White blood cell counts are frequently within the normal range.



Symptomatic treatment with ibuprofen and follow-up (A) is inadequate care because of the higher likelihood of serious pathology in pediatric patients presenting with back pain in comparison to adults. Furthermore, this patient reports a fever with the pain.

Plain radiographs of the spine (C) are unlikely to be helpful early in the clinical course but may reveal disk space destruction after 2–4 weeks of symptoms.

Urinalysis (D) is not indicated, as the patient does not have symptoms consistent with a urinary tract infection.

Question: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hip pain. Examination of the hip reveals pain with passive range of motion and a restricted range of motion. A radiograph is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Avascular necrosis (AVN) occurs when there is a disruption of the blood supply to the bone, leading to cell death, necrosis, and collapse of the bone. The condition most commonly affects the femoral head. There are many causes for AVN, including sickle cell disease, Gaucher disease, steroid use, excessive alcohol consumption, kidney disease, HIV infection, trauma, and idiopathic (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease in children). Initially, AVN may be asymptomatic. But as the condition progresses, it can lead to groin, thigh, or buttock pain (especially during weight-bearing activities), limited range of motion, and stiffness of the hip joint.

Diagnosis of AVN typically involves imaging studies such as X-rays, which may show changes in bone structure in later stages, MRI scans that are sensitive to early bone changes and blood flow loss, and CT scans that provide detailed images of bone structure. Treatment focuses on preventing further bone loss, relieving pain, and maintaining joint function. This can include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain, physical therapy, and reduced weight-bearing on the affected hip. Medications like bisphosphonates may slow disease progression. Surgical options range from core decompression, which reduces bone marrow pressure, to total hip replacement in advanced disease. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for preserving the hip joint and preventing further deterioration.



Femoral neck fractures (B) may occur after trauma and present with a shortened and externally rotated lower extremity. Imaging would show cortical disruption and a shortened, impacted femoral neck.

Osteoarthritis (C) presents with joint pain worsened by movement and weight-bearing activity. Imaging reveals a narrowed joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts.

Septic arthritis (D) presents with a red, hot, warm, and painful joint. Pain is worsened with passive range of motion. Imaging cannot be relied upon to make the diagnosis, but an effusion may be seen. The diagnosis is confirmed through arthrocentesis.

The subacromial space is an area between the coracoacromial arch and the greater tuberosity of the humerus. It contains the long head of the biceps tendon, the supraspinatus tendon, and the subacromial bursa. Subacromial bursitis is most often an overuse injury due to chronic impingement. Patients who participate in frequent overhead activity are most at risk. The most common symptoms are pain with overhead movement and difficulty finding a comfortable position at night due to pain. On physical examination, they likely will have a positive Neer impingement sign (pain with arm in 180 degrees forward flexion, followed by internal rotation) and Hawkins impingement sign (pain with arm in 90 degrees abduction, elbow flexed at 90 degrees, followed by internal rotation). Initial treatment is conservative with rest, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity modification. Some patients may need additional physical therapy or a subacromial bursa steroid injection. Those with continued pain may proceed to further imaging with ultrasound or MRI and consideration of decompression surgery with orthopedics.

It follows an injury to the shoulder, most often a direct or blunt hit to the shoulder. It results in a significant global loss of active and passive range of motion of the shoulder (forward flexion, abduction, external rotation, and internal rotation). It can occur following an injury or spontaneously in those with autoimmune disorders such as diabetes or hypothyroidism.

Question: A 9-year-old child presents to the ED with left groin pain and knee pain. Parents report no fever or trauma. Lower extremity pulses are intact. X-rays reveal avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Which of the following is most likely to be associated with this diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the pediatric proximal femoral head due to repeated episodes of ischemia. It occurs more commonly in prepubertal boys (4:1 male predominance), and 80% are from 3–11 years of age. The most common presentation is insidious onset of hip pain radiating to the groin, thigh, or knee with a limp. Pain is worse at the end of the day and with activity and is relieved with rest. Quadriceps atrophy, calf atrophy, and buttock atrophy due to disuse, along with leg shortening, may also be present on exam. Internal rotation of the hip and hip abduction may be decreased.

The disease is bilateral in 10–15% of cases, and up to 10% of cases are familial. Subchondral stress fractures and subluxations from femoral head flattening are common complications. X-rays may reveal femoral head flattening and widening of the cartilage space of the affected hip, but may initially be negative. Therefore, a high index of suspicion is needed, and additional imaging such as MRI may be needed for diagnosis. Patients should be non-weight-bearing, and orthopedic follow-up should be arranged.



Prepubertal male individuals are four times more affected than female individuals (A).

Question: What treatment should be initiated for a patient who presents with a crush syndrome and rhabdomyolysis?
ExplanationEN:
Patients with crush injuries and rhabdomyolysis should be aggressively resuscitated with intravenous fluids. Rhabdomyolysis is a life-threatening condition characterized by skeletal muscle breakdown and the release of intracellular contents into the circulatory system. Muscle damage leads to third spacing of fluid into muscles. Intravascular volume contraction from this sequestration, in turn, leads to acute kidney failure. In rhabdomyolysis, aggressive fluid resuscitation and volume expansion are critical to avoid myoglobin-induced acute kidney failure. Volume expansion results in increased blood flow to the kidneys and increased glomerular filtration. In turn, the kidneys excrete the toxins from cellular breakdown, including myoglobin, into the urine.



Acetazolamide (A) and furosemide (B) are diuretic agents that can increase urine output, but they also lead to further intravascular volume depletion.

Sodium bicarbonate (D) administration can be used in certain types of rhabdomyolysis (severe creatine kinase elevation or muscle injury) but does not take priority over fluid rehydration.

Question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department with knee pain. This morning he slipped on the ice and felt a pop in his knee. An osteochondroma is a benign bone lesion. It is an outgrowth of the growth plate and is made up of bone and cartilage. It often develops in childhood or adolescence and grows larger over time until skeletal maturity is reached. Osteochondromas are the most common benign bone tumor. Many lesions are asymptomatic and incidentally found on radiographs. Some may present with a painless mass while others may develop mechanical symptoms, such as a catching sensation. On X-ray, osteochondromas appear as a sessile or pedunculated outgrowth along the surface of the bone. They are most often seen in the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal femur, and proximal humerus. Treatment most often is observation. However, osteochondromas may be surgically resected if symptomatic.

Osteoid osteoma (C) is a benign bone lesion seen on X-ray as intensely reactive bone around a radiolucent nidus most often in the lower extremities.

Question: A 19-year-old man who is employed in construction presents with pain in his thumb and wrist for 4 months. He states the pain worsens while he is working. Examination reveals pain along the radial surface of the wrist with forced ulnar adduction. What initial management is indicated?

Options.text: Corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment
Surgical release of the dorsal extensor compartment
Wrist X-ray with ulnar deviation view

ExplanationEN:
De Quervain disease is a repetitive strain injury that is often work-related. In this disorder, the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons found in the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist are inflamed and enlarged. Patients commonly present with pain on the radial surface of the wrist, which is increased with movement of the thumb or ulnar deviation at the wrist. Patients may have decreased grip strength as well.

Finkelstein test is considered to be pathognomonic for de Quervain disease. It involves ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb in full flexion. This movement creates severe pain over the radial styloid. First-line treatment is with rest, splinting (thumb spica splint), and NSAIDs.



A corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment (A) may be offered by an orthopedic surgeon if conservative measures are not helpful in alleviating symptoms, but it would not be a recommended first-line treatment and would not be performed in the ED.

MRI of the wrist (B) is not necessary to diagnose de Quervain disease, but it is useful if a scaphoid fracture is suspected.

Surgical release of the dorsal extensor compartment (D) is indicated for patients with refractory symptoms.

Wrist X-rays with ulnar deviation (E) are not often indicated for patients with nontraumatic wrist pain but may be helpful in patients with trauma. Ulnar-deviated wrist X-rays are used to image the scaphoid.

ExplanationEN:
Legg-Calvé-Perthes is a pediatric disease characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of one or both femoral heads. It most commonly occurs in prepubescent boys with a 4:1 incidence compared to girls. Ages tend to range from 4 to 10 years old. There are no specific risk factors known for the disease. The mainstay of diagnosis is a pelvic radiograph. Frog leg views are controversial as they may cause further injury in another pediatric femoral disease, slipped capital femoral syndrome, that presents very similarly to Legg-Calvé-Perthes. Normal radiographs do not preclude the diagnosis. Timely diagnosis and treatment equate to good functional outcomes.

Patients commonly present with an insidious onset of limping with hip, thigh, or knee pain. Examination may reveal limited hip abduction and internal rotation and, in severe cases, limb length discrepancies. SCFE is more likely in puberty-aged boys who have overweight BMIs or have hypothyroidism.
