Vital signs are a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 142/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 16/min, temperature of 98.6°F (37°C), and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. On physical examination, the right hip appears swollen and tender, with a limited range of motion due to pain. Laboratory results include the following:

Hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL

White blood cell count: 7,200/μL

Platelets: 220,000/μL

Sodium: 140 mEq/L

Potassium: 5.8 mEq/L

Phosphorous: 5.8 mg/dL

Calcium: 7.6 mg/dL

Blood urea nitrogen: 38 mg/dL

Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL

Glomerular filtration rate: 60 mL/min/1.73 m2

Creatine kinase: 1,520 U/L

Which of the following results are more likely to be seen in this patient’s urine dipstick and microscopy examination?

Question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with ankle pain for the last 2 days. He recently underwent surgical repair of a right ankle fracture sustained when he tripped on a hike. He was discharged 2 weeks ago with no apparent complications at the time. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes a basal-bolus insulin regimen. His most recent hemoglobin A1C was 8.2%. T is 100.9°F (38.3°C), HR is 90 bpm, RR is 20/min, and BP is 126/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a healing surgical wound with no purulent drainage. There is significant point tenderness over the medial malleolus. Laboratory studies show elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Which of the following is the best next step in the treatment of this patient’s most likely condition?

Options.text: Discharge with oral analgesia and close orthopedic follow-up
Give intravenous vancomycin and a normal saline bolus
Hold antibiotics and consult orthopedic surgery for emergent washout and debridement

ExplanationEN:
Normal bone tissue is typically fairly resistant to infection except in the circumstances of trauma, foreign body, disruption of blood flow, or large inocula of microorganisms. These circumstances can result in the development of osteomyelitis, an infection of bone and the medullary cavity. Osteomyelitis occurs either by hematogenous spread or direct extension from a contiguous infectious site, with the latter accounting for approximately 80% of cases. Hematogenous spread is commonly associated with long bone infection in pediatric patients and vertebral osteomyelitis in adults. Patient risk factors for osteomyelitis influence the likely causative pathogen(s) and thus the recommended empiric therapy. For instance, patients with sickle cell disease are at increased risk of infection with Salmonella species, thus requiring treatment with ciprofloxacin. The two most prominent organisms in cases of postoperative osteomyelitis are Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci. Patients with diabetes often have polymicrobial infections, including S. aureus, Streptococcus agalactiae, and Streptococcus pyogenes, among others.

The clinical signs and symptoms of osteomyelitis vary, but pain is a prominent feature that may not be present in patients with diabetic ulcers since they often have sensory neuropathy. Patients may also present with fever, rigors, and other systemic features. Examination may show point tenderness with associated swelling and erythema, but the presence of these findings is variable. Diagnostic evaluation of patients with osteomyelitis may show leukocytosis and elevation of inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality, but X-ray is more readily available and commonly the only imaging modality used. Definitive diagnosis is achieved with microbiological testing of infected bone through sampling via fine-needle aspiration or surgical resection.

As stated above, the choice of initial empiric therapy for osteomyelitis should be guided by the suspected pathogen. This patient’s diabetes puts him at risk of a polymicrobial infection, which warrants combination therapy with both vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, but imipenem may be used in place of piperacillin-tazobactam. Had this patient’s only risk factor been his recent operation, recommended empiric therapy would be vancomycin alone for coverage of S. aureus and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species. The most common complications of acute osteomyelitis are bacteremia and sepsis, but local extension of invasive infections can result in pneumonia or empyema, meningitis, brain abscess, cord compression, and septic arthritis. Chronic osteomyelitis and pathologic fractures can develop as well. In children, osteomyelitis can damage the developing skeleton, and permanent alterations in growth can occur when the epiphysis is involved.



This patient's presentation strongly suggests osteomyelitis, and he requires antibiotic therapy. Treatment only with oral analgesia and close follow-up (A) would not be appropriate. Intravenous crystalloid fluids and vancomycin (B) are the initial empiric therapy for sepsis in a patient without risk factors for a polymicrobial infection. This patient does not have sepsis and should be treated for polymicrobial osteomyelitis. Vancomycin and ciprofloxacin (C) is the recommended regimen for patients with osteomyelitis in the setting of sickle cell disease to cover Salmonella species rather than diabetes mellitus. This patient may ultimately require surgical washout and debridement (E) by orthopedic surgery, but he should be started on appropriate antibiotic therapy pending orthopedic evaluation and determination of definitive care.

Question: Which of the following physical exam findings is expected to be diminished in a patient with impingement of the L4 spinal nerve root?
ExplanationEN:
Radiculopathy is an impingement of a nerve root that leads to pain and paresthesias in the area of distribution that the nerve supplies. Nerve impingement can occur anywhere along the route of the nerve fibers. Patients with radiculopathy mostly report pain, but their symptoms can progress to include neurologic deficits such as motor or sensory impairment. A targeted physical exam can determine the location of the impingement. In this case, impingement of the L4 spinal nerve root would result in decreased knee jerk reflex. Of note, the spinal cord ends at the T12–L1 vertebral level, but the nerve fibers continue in the conus medullaris until they exit at their corresponding level. Therefore, symptoms involving the L4 nerve distribution may also be originating from lesions anywhere above the L4 vertebral body. Disc herniation is the most common cause of radiculopathy in the lumbar region. However, more serious diagnoses can be present (such as cauda equina, epidural abscess, or metastatic cancer) and should be investigated further according to the history and physical.



The ankle jerk reflex (A) and the rectal tone (D) are controlled by the S1 nerve root. It is not necessary to perform a rectal exam on every patient reporting radiculopathy or low back pain unless the history or physical exam contains concerning features for a serious diagnosis.

Dorsiflexion of the great toe (B) is supplied by the L5 nerve root.

Question: A 12-year-old girl with a history of obesity presents to your ED with left thigh pain over the last 2 weeks causing her to limp. While stepping off a curb, the pain suddenly worsened, and she is now unable to walk. She reports no recent trauma, fevers, or other ill symptoms. Your exam shows a normal exam except for pain over her anterior left hip and decreased range of motion at the left hip. You obtain a complete blood count that is normal, as well as an anteroposterior view of the pelvis that shows a slight widening of the physis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Crutches with weight bearing as tolerated
Joint aspirate of the left hip

ExplanationEN:
A slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the most common adolescent hip disorder and is caused by a relatively weak proximal femur physis (i.e., growth plate) that cannot support the child's weight. It may slip slowly, presenting in an ambulatory patient with weeks of knee, thigh, or hip pain, acutely in a patient now unable to bear weight, or a combination of the two. Trauma can worsen an SCFE, causing an acute or chronic picture, but the trauma is typically minor for the degree of symptoms as seen in this patient. An anteroposterior view of the pelvis may show only mild widening or irregularity of the physis. A SCFE is best visualized with a frog-leg view of the pelvis, which shows displacement of the femoral epiphysis, often described as the image of ice cream falling off a cone. If you are concerned about an associated pelvic fracture, obtain a cross-table lateral image instead, which can show the posterior displacement. These patients should be kept non-weight bearing and admitted for surgical pinning by orthopedic surgeons.



A patient with an SCFE should not be allowed to bear weight so sending the patient home with crutches with weight bearing as tolerated (A) can worsen the slip.

A joint aspirate of the left hip (C) is appropriate when ruling out a septic joint but is less likely than an SCFE in this patient based on the lack of fever and normal complete blood count.

An MRI of the pelvis (D) is useful if you suspect osteomyelitis and would make the diagnosis, but it is unnecessary in this patient as the presentation is more consistent with SCFE.

Question: A 48-year-old woman presents to the ED with progressive neck pain over the last 6 weeks. The pain radiates down her posterior arm to the dorsum of her forearm. She reports numbness and tingling of the forearm and third digit. On examination, she has mild weakness with pronation of the forearm and decreased triceps reflex. What is the likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The distribution of symptoms (posterior arm and forearm radiation, numbness of the third digit, triceps reflex reduction, and pronation weakness) is characteristic of C7 radiculopathy. C7 innervates the triceps and contributes to wrist extension and finger extension. Involvement of the third digit is highly suggestive of C7 nerve root compression.

Cervical radiculopathy refers to a constellation of neurologic symptoms, most notably pain, sensory disturbance, and motor weakness, resulting from compression or irritation of one or more cervical nerve roots. This condition most frequently arises from intervertebral disc herniation, degenerative spondylotic changes, or a combination of the two. Less common causes include foraminal stenosis, facet joint osteophytes, trauma, and space-occupying lesions such as tumors or abscesses.

The cervical nerve roots exit the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina above their corresponding vertebral bodies (e.g., the C7 nerve root exits between the C6 and C7 vertebrae). Posterolateral disc herniation is the most common anatomical cause of root compression and typically occurs at the C5–C6 and C6–C7 levels. These herniations can result in both axial neck pain and referred or radicular pain, sometimes accompanied by occipital headache due to upper cervical involvement.

The C7 nerve root is the most commonly involved and characteristically produces radiating pain from the neck through the posterior arm and forearm to the dorsum of the hand and third digit. Patients may also report discomfort along the medial border of the scapula, reflecting referred pain from the affected nerve root. Sensory deficits typically involve the dorsum of the forearm and the middle finger. Motor findings include weakness in forearm extension and pronation, due to involvement of the triceps and wrist flexors. A diminished or absent triceps reflex is a hallmark physical examination finding.

Evaluation begins with a thorough neurologic examination, focusing on sensory mapping, myotomal strength testing, and deep tendon reflexes. While plain radiographs may show degenerative changes or reduced disc height, MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice due to its superior ability to visualize soft tissues, including nerve roots, intervertebral discs, and spinal cord.

Most cases of cervical radiculopathy are self-limited and improve over weeks to months with conservative treatment, including physical therapy, NSAIDs, and activity modification. Corticosteroids, either systemic or via epidural injection, may be used for more severe symptoms. Surgical intervention (e.g., anterior cervical discectomy and fusion) is reserved for patients with intractable pain, progressive neurologic deficits, or spinal cord compression.



C5 radiculopathy (A) would affect the deltoid and biceps, leading to shoulder pain and decreased biceps reflex, not triceps weakness or third digit symptoms.

C6 radiculopathy (B) presents with pain radiating to the lateral forearm and thumb, with biceps and brachioradialis reflex involvement.

C8 radiculopathy (D) affects the medial forearm and fourth and fifth digits, often impairing finger flexion and grip but not pronation or third-digit sensation.

Question: A 22-year-old man presents with chronic back pain. He notes it has gone on for his whole life and is the most severe in the morning. As he exerts himself or lifts boxes at his job, he notes his symptoms improve. Physical exam reveals reduced mobility in all directions of the spine with no midline tenderness. An erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 35 mm/hr. A radiograph is performed, and the results are shown above. The patient is requesting a work note for a month off from work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a rheumatologic cause of back pain more common in young men. It classically presents with back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and relieved with exertion and exercise. AS may also affect peripheral joints and other areas, including the eyes (uveitis), heart, lungs, and kidneys. Patients will have reduced mobility of the spine. Initial diagnostic workup may include plain films of the lumbar spine (demonstrating a bamboo spine) or sacroiliac joint (demonstrating sacroiliitis). The most accurate diagnostic test is an MRI of the sacroiliac spine. Human leukocyte antigen B27 testing can also support the diagnosis. Inflammatory markers can be elevated in AS. Treatment is centered on exercise and physical therapy. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, and immunomodulators, such as infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept, can be used to control symptoms.



Malingering (B) should be suspected when a patient has concerns that do not line up with the exam or normal physiology and the patient is seeking secondary gain. While this patient is requesting a work note (secondary gain), his reduced spinal mobility and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate suggest against this diagnosis.

A muscle strain (C) is the most common cause of back pain after heavy lifting and is worsened by lifting, bending, and twisting. There may be palpable tenderness over the muscles. This patient’s symptoms improve with lifting rather than worsen.

Spinal epidural abscess (D) is a life-threatening cause of back pain that is more common in immunosuppressed patients and patients who use intravenous drugs. Patients will present with back pain, malaise, and fever and will have elevated inflammatory markers. While this patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate is elevated, his other symptoms suggest a diagnosis of AS, and he lacks risk factors for spinal epidural abscess.

Question: A patient presents to the emergency department for a painful, swollen finger. Which of the following features, if present, would be most consistent with a diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis?

Options.text: Localized swelling along the flexor tendon
Pain on passive extension of the affected finger
Percussion tenderness isolated to the distal phalanx

CorrectAnswer: Pain on passive extension of the affected finger
ExplanationEN:
Flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency that requires rapid bedside diagnosis to expedite appropriate care. Penetrating trauma precedes most cases, although the injury itself may have been innocuous, leading to bacterial seeding of the deep tendon sheath. Skin flora, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus spp, are most commonly identified. On examination, Kanavel signs may be identified that can help with the diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis: pain on passive extension of the affected finger (often the first finding), finger held in partial flexion, tenderness of the full tendon sheath, and fusiform swelling of the digit. These findings are due to progressive inflammation of the tendon sheath. Kanavel signs have a sensitivity of approximately 90% in the diagnosis of flexor tenosynovitis. Patients with findings concerning for this diagnosis should rapidly be treated with intravenous antibiotics such as vancomycin plus extended-spectrum penicillins. They should have emergent hand surgery consultation, as this infection can rapidly spread through the fascial planes of the hand. Inappropriate management of flexor tenosynovitis can lead to loss of function in the affected hand.



Fingers are typically held in partial flexion rather than full extension (A) in flexor tenosynovitis.

Fusiform or symmetric swelling, rather than localized swelling (B), would be seen in flexor tenosynovitis.

Percussive tenderness will involve the full length of the digit and tendon sheath and will not be isolated to the distal phalanx (D).

Question: A 15-year-old boy presents with 2 days of finger pain and swelling after pulling off a hangnail. The pain has progressed and he is having difficulty performing simple tasks. The finger is shown above. On exam, there is tenderness of the distal phalanx with a small area of fluctuance. He is able to articulate the finger at both the metacarpal and interphalangeal joints with no significant discomfort. He reports no fevers, nausea, nor diarrhea. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this condition?

Options.text: Surgical washout of the tendon sheath

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with paronychia, a soft tissue infection of the fingernail. Paronychia is the most common hand infection in the United States and begins as cellulitis of the paronychium but can progress to an abscess of the deeper structures, which necessitates incision and drainage. The most typical causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include finger trauma such as nail biting, manicure, or forcibly removing hangnails. Diagnosis is made with clinical exam. When paronychia involves abscess, the purulent material should be drained to facilitate healing. Untreated infections can spread to deeper structures such as the pulp (felon) or the flexor tendon (flexor tenosynovitis).



Antibiotics (B), either oral or topical, are often used in the treatment of paronychia. In simple cases of isolated cellulitis, antibiotics are sufficient. However, progression to abscess requires drainage as the first step in management.

Warm compresses (D) and soaks are the traditional treatment for mild paronychia limited to cellulitis. However, there is little evidence to support their efficacy.

Surgical washout of the tendon sheath (C) is indicated for flexor tenosynovitis, which also presents with finger swelling and pain. However, this patient’s symptoms are localized to the distal finger and he does not have pain with range of motion of the digit or along the flexor tendon.

Question: Which of the following symptoms is most consistent with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?
ExplanationEN:
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) is characterized by fever, arthritis, and rash occurring in children up to 16 years of age. All sexes are affected equally. The fever, present in > 95% of patients, is described as quotidian (one high spike of fever per day followed by normal temperatures for the rest of the day). Constantly elevated temperatures should prompt investigation for an alternative diagnosis. Arthritis typically affects more than one joint. While the wrist, knees, and ankles are most commonly affected, any joint can be involved. An erythematous, macular rash is also commonly seen and is most noticeable when the child is febrile. Although not diagnostic of sJIA, patients will often have leukocytosis, reactive thrombocytosis, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Diagnosis can only be made after excluding other etiologies of the patient’s symptoms (e.g., septic arthritis). Fever must be present for > 2 weeks and arthritis for > 6 weeks before a definitive diagnosis can be made.



Lymphadenopathy (B) can be seen in sJIA but is only present in one-third of patients.

The arthritis is polyarticular or oligoarticular in the vast majority of patients. Monoarthritis (C) is much less commonly seen.

The classic rash in sJIA is a faint, erythematous macular rash which is typically present when the patient is febrile and recedes when the patient has defervesced. A purpuric rash (D) is not characteristic of sJIA.

Question: A 26-year-old man presents with 1 day of muscle aches, dark urine, and fatigue after intense exercise yesterday. Which of the following would be expected on laboratory analysis?
ExplanationEN:
Rhabdomyolysis is a potentially life threatening condition caused by the breakdown of skeletal muscle and the release of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. This causes a cascade of metabolic abnormalities which include increased creatine kinase, increased serum and urine myoglobin, and hyperkalemia. The increase in potassium can lead to life threatening dysrhythmias and death. The elevated myoglobin can overwhelm the glomerulus and cause acute kidney injury. The myoglobin forms casts in the glomeruli which is worsened by volume depletion and the subsequent renal vasoconstriction, thus causing tubule obstruction. Complications of rhabdomyolysis can be viewed as early or late findings. Compartment syndrome, acidosis and electrolyte disorders, hypovolemia, and liver dysfunction are all early findings. The late complication of myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury is the main focus of treating a patient with rhabdomyolysis. Aggressive fluid administration and urine alkalinization are necessary to maintain filtration at the glomerular level.



Although the urine would be strongly positive for blood on a urine dipstick, you would not see 51–100 RBC/hpf (A) in the urine. Myoglobin contains a heme compound which will be detected as blood on a urine dipstick, but there will be few, if any, red blood cells in the urine.

Bicarbonate (B) would be low because of the metabolic acidosis that occurs during rhabdomyolysis.

Uric acid (D) is elevated from the breakdown of muscle nucleic acids and, along with lactate, contributes to metabolic acidosis.

Question: A 12-year-old boy with a history of obesity presents with groin and proximal anterior thigh pain. He has no pain below the knee. Physical examination shows a significant decrease in internal rotation of the affected hip. Radiographs show a widened growth plate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Atraumatic pediatric hip pain or limp is usually caused by acute transient synovitis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, or slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). SCFE is a fracture in the physis (growth plate) of the femoral head, which leads to slippage of the overlying epiphysis. It usually occurs during adolescent growth spurts. Predisposing factors include male sex, obesity, and increased sports activities. The typical age range is 10–14 years for girls and 11–16 years for boys.

Patients present with pain in the anterior proximal knee or thigh that is exacerbated by activity. On exam, there is a loss of hip internal rotation, particularly with the hip flexed. Patients typically walk with the involved extremity externally rotated. Anteroposterior and frog-leg radiographs show “ice cream falling off the cone.” All cases warrant urgent orthopedic evaluation for stabilization surgery. Patients should be non-weight-bearing and restricted to bed rest until then. Complications of untreated disease include chondrolysis and osteonecrosis.



Acute transient synovitis (A) is considered the most common cause of childhood hip pain or limp. It is most common in boys aged 3–6 years. Radiographs are normal. Treatment includes NSAIDs and relative rest.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (B) is a group of arthritic conditions affecting children, which typically presents with joint swelling and pain over a longer duration and does not involve widening of growth plates.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (C) is avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head. It occurs more commonly in boys aged 4–10 years. Radiographs show a small, sclerosed femoral head and widened joint space.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (D) is a common adolescent condition in those active in sports. Repeated microtrauma occurs at the apophyseal cartilage between the anterior tibial tubercle and the secondary ossification center of the patellar tendon. These patients present with anteroinferior knee or superior shin pain and tender tibial tuberosities.

Question: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left knee pain and swelling. He has a medical history significant for heavy alcohol use, hypertension, gout, diabetes mellitus, and stage III kidney disease. On exam, vital signs are HR 90 bpm, BP 145/90 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and T 38.5ºC (101.3ºF). The patient’s left knee is significant for joint effusion, erythema, and increased warmth. He experiences excruciating pain with both active and passive range of motion. Which findings on synovial fluid analysis are most consistent with the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 34,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, negative birefringent crystals present on analysis
Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 45,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, positive birefringent crystals present on analysis
Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 90,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, no crystals present on analysis
Transparent, yellow in appearance, 2,000 WBC/µL without a predominance of neutrophils, no crystals present on analysis

CorrectAnswer: Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 90,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, no crystals present on analysis
ExplanationEN:
Septic arthritis is a condition that can rapidly lead to irreversible joint destruction if inadequately treated. Patients typically present with monoarticular arthritis and may have associated fevers, chills, and malaise, although the absence of these symptoms does not exclude the diagnosis. Arthritis should be differentiated from a more focal periarticular inflammatory process such as cellulitis, bursitis, and tendinitis. True arthritis produces joint pain that is exacerbated by both active and passive range of motion. Synovial fluid analysis confirms the diagnosis.

Synovial fluid for septic arthritis will demonstrate a profound white blood cell count of > 50,000/µL, often with > 75% being neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance without crystals present. Synovial fluid cultures are positive a little over half the time and provide the causative organism. Admission for parenteral antibiotics and repeated needle aspiration, arthroscopy, or open surgical drainage is required. Vancomycin and ceftriaxone should be administered empirically until cultures have returned.



Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 34,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils and negative birefringent crystals present on analysis (A) is most consistent with gout. Gout is a type of crystal-induced synovitis caused by uric acid crystals. These crystals are negatively birefringent and needle-shaped. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness but should not have a fever. If fever is present, the clinician should be more concerned about septic arthritis. The joints most commonly affected are the great toe, tarsal joints, and knee.

Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 45,000 WBC/µL with a predominance of neutrophils and positive birefringent crystals present on analysis (B) is most consistent with pseudogout. Pseudogout is a type of crystal-induced synovitis that is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. These crystals are positive birefringent and rhomboid-shaped. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness. The joints most commonly affected are the knee, wrist, ankle, and elbow. Crystal-induced synovitis generally affects middle-aged and older adults. Both gout and pseudogout, as well as rheumatoid arthritis, Lyme disease, and lupus, can all cause inflammatory arthritis that is defined and confirmed by synovial fluid analysis. Synovial fluid for inflammatory arthritis will have a white blood cell count between 200 and 50,000/µL with > 50% being neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance with crystals being present if gout or pseudogout is the cause. Treatment consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine. Corticosteroids can be used in patients with kidney disease. They should be avoided in those with uncontrolled diabetes.

Synovial fluid that is transparent, yellow in appearance, 2,000 WBC/µL without a predominance of neutrophils and no crystals present on analysis (D) is consistent with osteoarthritis, a chronic, symmetric polyarticular destruction of joints distinguished by the lack of constitutional symptoms. Patients may present with acute monoarticular exacerbations that consist of joint pain and inflammation. Synovial fluid for osteoarthritis will demonstrate a white blood cell count of < 2,000/µL with < 25% being neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be clear and transparent in appearance without crystals present. Treatment consists of rest and analgesics.

Question: A marathon runner presents with diffuse muscle aches and weakness. The symptoms began after he ran his first marathon 3 days ago. His urine is dark and shows 3+ blood on dipstick with 5 RBC/hpf on microscopy. Which of the following tests is most likely diagnostic for this patient’s disorder?

Options.text: Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms consistent with rhabdomyolysis, which can be diagnosed by an elevated creatine kinase (CK). Rhabdomyolysis describes the breakdown of skeletal muscle with the release of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. These contents include CK, aspartate transaminase, lactate dehydrogenase, myoglobin, aldolase, and electrolytes. Muscle breakdown leads to swelling, edema, increased compartment pressure, and ischemia. The entry of intracellular components into the bloodstream can lead to kidney impairment, insufficiency, and irreversible damage. There are four major etiologies of rhabdomyolysis: impaired muscle adenosine triphosphate production, disruption of nutrient delivery to skeletal muscle, increased metabolic demands of skeletal muscle, and direct muscle damage.

Patients typically report swelling and tenderness of muscle groups, as well as cramping and pain. Tea-colored urine often prompts clinical evaluation. The disease is commonly suspected by a urine dipstick positive for blood, with the absence or only a minimal number of RBCs on microscopy. The positive dipstick is the result of myoglobinuria. Elevated CK levels are diagnostic of rhabdomyolysis. The enzyme rises over 12 hours and remains elevated for 5 days. Treatment of rhabdomyolysis focuses on identifying compartment syndrome, correcting electrolyte disorders, and instituting fluid resuscitation to correct kidney impairment, if present.



Direct assay for urine myoglobin (A) is rarely used in clinical practice, and myoglobinuria lacks sensitivity as a test for rhabdomyolysis.

A noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (B) would be indicated for the diagnosis of urolithiasis, which presents with hematuria. However, this patient does not have a clinical scenario consistent with this disease.

Serum myoglobin (D) is useful in the early presentation of rhabdomyolysis, but the level returns to normal within 24 hours.

Serum potassium (E) may be elevated in rhabdomyolysis due to kidney impairment and myocyte breakdown, but it is not diagnostic.

Reveal Answer:

Question: What is the most common site of osteosarcoma in children?
ExplanationEN:
Osteosarcomas are the most common primary bone tumor in children with a peak incidence between the ages of 13 and 16 years, which corresponds to the typical time for an adolescent growth spurt. Boys are more commonly affected than girls. Osteosarcomas can also occur in adults, but are often considered secondary and attributed to sarcomatous transformation of Paget’s disease of the bone, previously irradiated bone, or bone infarcts. While it can be found in any bone, the majority of osteosarcomas occur in the long bones with the distal femur most commonly affected.

Patients present with persistent bone pain that worsens at night or with activity. There may be localized swelling and tenderness of the affected area. Pathologic fractures are an uncommon presentation in children. Plain radiographs often show a lytic lesion with cortical destruction near the metaphysis. The classic radiographic finding is the “sunburst” appearance of the periosteal reaction. Diagnosis requires biopsy for confirmation. There are no laboratory markers for osteosarcoma although alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase may be elevated. Treatment includes limb-sparing resection and chemotherapy.



While unusual in children, the axial skeleton, which includes the skull, ribs, sternum, and vertebral column (including lumbar vertebrae) (B), is often affected in adults with osteosarcoma. However, as with children, the long bones are still the most commonly affected bones in the adult population.

The proximal femur (C) can also be affected, but is less common.

The proximal tibia, not the proximal fibula (D) is second only to the distal femur as the most likely site involved.

Reveal Answer:
The lungs.

Question: A 7-day-old baby boy presents with his parent for evaluation of left hip clicking that was noticed while changing his diaper. On exam, he has positive Barlow and Ortolani tests. The palpable clunk felt during the Ortolani maneuver is due to which one of the following?

Options.text: Femoral head relocating anteriorly into the acetabulum
Femoral head relocating posteriorly into the acetabulum

CorrectAnswer: Femoral head relocating anteriorly into the acetabulum
ExplanationEN:
Developmental dysplasia of the hips can range from mild acetabular dysplasia to irreducible hip dislocation. Risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, and family history of hip dysplasia. It is usually unilateral. The diagnosis can be heralded within the neonatal period by two physical exam maneuvers: the Barlow provocative test and the Ortolani reduction test. If these maneuvers are not performed at birth, the diagnosis (and management) can be delayed. These tests become less accurate after 4–6 months of age. The Barlow provocative test is performed by stabilizing the pelvis of the supine infant, adducting and flexing the hip, and applying posterior (downward) pressure at the acetabulum to test for subluxation or dislocation of the hip, which is felt as a palpable clunk as the femoral head dislocates posteriorly. The Ortolani reduction test is performed by abducting the infant’s hip and applying upward (anterior) pressure with the thumb and index fingers at the greater trochanter to reduce the posteriorly dislocated or subluxated hip. The femoral head relocating anteriorly into the acetabulum is recognized as a palpable clunk. Other physical clues include asymmetries in the groin, buttock, or thigh skinfold, leg length discrepancies, or abnormal range of motion of the hips. Radiographs are of little utility in infants, but hip ultrasonography can help confirm the diagnosis. Infants with easily subluxable or dislocatable hips should be referred for orthopedic evaluation promptly. Management should be initiated immediately upon diagnosis and involves immobilization with a Pavlik harness or other device that keeps the infant’s hips in flexion and abduction. The goal is to allow the hip to correct any dysplastic features as the bone and cartilage of the hip joint mature with age.



The femoral head dislocates posteriorly (B), not anteriorly (A), during the Barlow provocative test, not the Ortolani reduction test. During the Ortolani reduction test, the femoral head relocates anteriorly, not posteriorly (D), into the acetabulum.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ED by his mother for evaluation of left hip pain and a limp that started suddenly yesterday. On exam, he is well appearing, sitting with his left hip preferentially abducted and externally rotated. Although uncomfortable, he is able to tolerate full passive range of motion of the hip. He has a low-grade fever, and his mother says he has had a cold for the past few days. Laboratory studies are significant for a WBC count of 15,000 cells/microL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hr. Bedside ultrasound shows an effusion of the left hip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Transient synovitis of the hip, as the name implies, is a self-limited inflammatory condition of the hip joint that usually lasts 3–7 days and tends to follow a viral syndrome. Transient synovitis is the most common cause of hip pain in children < 10 years old and usually presents with sudden-onset unilateral hip pain and an associated limp. Patients may have a low-grade fever or be afebrile, and on exam, they classically hold the affected hip in abduction and external rotation and have preserved passive range of motion.

Leukocytosis and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate are both possible, so they cannot be used to distinguish transient synovitis from septic arthritis, though they are typically significantly lower than in septic arthritis. If there are concerns for septic arthritis either by history, exam, or laboratory studies, arthrocentesis should be performed. Synovial fluid in transient synovitis is transudative and will have no organisms on Gram stain. Treatment is rest and NSAIDs.



Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (A) is a form of avascular necrosis of the hip that commonly occurs in children 4–9 years old. As compared to the abrupt onset of pain in transient synovitis, hip pain in Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is usually gradual in onset, as repeated episodes of ischemia lead to necrosis and ultimately stress fractures.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (B) is an inflammatory condition of the tibial tuberosity at the insertion of the patellar tendon. It develops from repetitive stresses, most commonly in adolescent boys who are active in sports that involve running or jumping. It is not associated with hip effusions.

Septic arthritis (C) can also cause hip effusions, fever, leukocytosis, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Older children are usually ill-appearing, have high fevers, and hold their hip in abduction and internal rotation. Intermediate levels cannot be used to exclude septic arthritis, and this patient should likely have an arthrocentesis performed to exclude this diagnosis. Given that he appears well, he only has a low-grade fever, and his symptoms started suddenly in the wake of a viral illness, his effusion is most likely related to transient synovitis.

Question: A 13-year-old girl presents to the ED after feeling a pop in her knee while playing soccer at school. She states it occurred after she attempted to score a goal. The patient has been unable to ambulate since the event and was wheeled into the exam room. Which positive finding is most consistent with the knee X-ray noted above?
ExplanationEN:
Injuries to the quadriceps muscles and tendons are common among athletes and active adults. The quadriceps is composed of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. These four muscles come together distally to form a common tendon known as the quadriceps tendon, which continues down and envelopes the patella. From the patella, the tendon transitions into the patellar tendon, which inserts on the tibial tuberosity. The main function of these tendons is knee extension. However, the quadriceps is also responsible for numerous actions, some of which include pelvis stabilization during gait, hip flexion, and knee stabilization along with the hamstrings.

Patellar tendon ruptures are more common than quadriceps tendon ruptures and tend to be acute, sudden, and follow a strong contraction. With complete tears, patients may experience a sudden pop or tearing sensation. This is followed by the inability to bear weight and significant swelling. Knee extension is absent with complete tears and limited with partial tears. Patients with a complete tear cannot maintain a straight leg and cannot raise the leg against gravity while lying supine. An avulsion fracture is often seen with a complete patellar tendon rupture. A high-riding patella (as seen in this patient) suggests the diagnosis of patellar tendon rupture. Prompt diagnosis and referral to orthopedics for repair are crucial to improve outcomes. Rest, ice, elevation, and compression of the affected extremity are the focus of initial therapies with crutches and immobilization until follow-up with orthopedics.



The Lachman test (B) involves flexing the knee to 30° and then stabilizing the distal femur with one hand while pulling the proximal tibia anteriorly with the other hand. This tests anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and suggests an anterior cruciate ligament tear.

The McMurray test (C) assesses both the medial and lateral meniscus. To test the lateral meniscus, the clinician applies one hand to the knee along the lateral joint line and holds the foot and ankle with the other hand with the knee flexed. Internal rotation of the foot and varus stress at the knee while slowly extending the knee is then performed. To test the medial meniscus, the clinician applies one hand to the knee along the medial joint line and holds the foot and ankle with the other hand with the knee flexed. External rotation of the foot and valgus stress at the knee while slowly extending the knee is then performed. Pain along the lateral or medial joint lines is a positive finding and is suspicious for a respective meniscus tear.

Valgus laxity (D) is performed by applying a medial force at the knee’s joint line, attempting to “bow” the knee. This tests the integrity of the lateral collateral ligament, with increased laxity being a positive exam.

Question: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to weakness. The parent notes that in the past week, the child has had increased difficulty getting up from the floor after playing. She describes her having to push with her hands on the legs, from knees to hips, in order to stand upright. She also notes that she has had increased fatigue, myalgias, and a low-grade fever. On physical examination, what other finding is likely in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Juvenile dermatomyositis is an inflammatory autoimmune myopathy similar to polymyositis but also presents with classic dermatologic findings. Affected children are usually 5–10 years of age, and the disease disproportionately affects girls. Proximal muscle weakness is the predominant symptom and manifests clinically as Gower sign, pushing with hands on the legs, from knees to hips, in order to stand upright. There may be tenderness with palpation of the proximal muscles, but atrophy is a late finding. In addition to weakness, patients display a variety of skin findings including a heliotrope rash (reddish or violet coloring of the skin, most commonly seen on the eyelids and periorbital area), Gottron papules (violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints), and nail fold telangiectasias. Patients often have constitutional symptoms, such as fever, weight loss, fatigue, and headache, as well. Electromyography and muscle biopsy are used to confirm the diagnosis. Oral corticosteroids are the mainstay of initial treatment.



On the differential for a patient who presents similarly to this one would be Guillain-Barré syndrome. This acute inflammatory polyneuropathy presents with paresthesias, ascending weakness, and diminished reflexes or areflexia (A). While patients with juvenile dermatomyositis may have decreased reflexes in proportion to their weakness, they are not typically areflexic. Additionally, this patient did not report any sensory symptoms or paresthesias.

This patient presented with Gower sign, which is caused by proximal muscle weakness, not distal muscle weakness (B).

Ophthalmoplegia (D) can be seen in botulism, a toxin-mediated illness that results in descending symmetrical paralysis. Initially, it often involves the cranial nerves and bulbar muscles, and patients will have symptoms of diplopia, dysarthria, and dysphagia before generalized weakness develops.

One Step Further
Question:
When children with juvenile dermatomyositis develop respiratory compromise, how does their presentation differ from other illnesses that lead to respiratory compromise?

Reveal Answer:
Children with respiratory muscle weakness in the setting of juvenile dermatomyositis develop hypercarbia rather than hypoxemia and increased work of breathing that are found in other disease states.

Question: An 8-year-old healthy boy presents to the emergency department for nontraumatic left hip pain that has been progressing over several weeks and is worse with exertion. On examination, the patient has normal vital signs and reduced internal rotation of the left hip, and he is able to bear weight, although he has pain when doing so. An X-ray of his hip is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Avulsion fracture of the anterior inferior iliac spine

CorrectAnswer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation and imaging are consistent with avascular necrosis of the femoral head, or Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. Commonly seen in boys ages 4–8 years, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease presents with gradual, nontraumatic hip pain due to poor blood supply to the developing femoral head. Symptoms may be bilateral in 10% of cases. Patients should be able to bear weight but will have reduced abduction and internal rotation on exam and, in severe cases, may develop limb shortening.

X-ray is the preferred initial study, although it has a low sensitivity for early cases. In early cases, widening of the growth plate or osteopenia may be seen, followed by a crescent-shaped lucency of the superior femoral head (Caffey sign). Magnetic resonance imaging or bone scans have higher sensitivity and may be used following nondiagnostic X-rays when there is a high index of suspicion. Patients should be made non-weight-bearing on the affected leg and have urgent orthopedic follow-up scheduled for further care.



An avulsion fracture of the anterior inferior iliac spine (B) will present with acute, severe hip pain and weakness in adolescent athletes following explosive rectus femoris contracture. X-ray will reveal the avulsed iliac spine, and treatment requires immobilization.

Septic arthritis (C) is more common in toddlers, and they will have fever, refuse to bear weight, and have pain on active and passive range of motion of the joint. The Kocher criteria are used for screening (elevated white blood cell count, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, refusal to bear weight, and fever), and treatment requires intravenous antibiotics and orthopedic admission.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (D) also presents with progressive, nontraumatic hip pain that may radiate to the knee in adolescents with obesity. X-ray in these children will be significant for an abnormal Klein line or widening of the physis.

Reveal Answer:
Chronic steroid use and bisphosphonates (isolated to the jaw with bisphosphonates).

Question: What is the most common extra-articular manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis?
ExplanationEN:
The most common extra-articular manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis is uveitis. It presents with eye pain, redness, photophobia, and blurred vision and can be recurrent. Up to 40% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis may experience uveitis during their disease, making it the most frequent systemic involvement.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder primarily affecting the axial skeleton, particularly the sacroiliac joints and spine. It belongs to the group of seronegative spondyloarthropathies and is strongly associated with human leukocyte factor B27 positivity. The condition predominantly affects men aged 20–40 years.

Patients often report an insidious onset of low back pain that is worse in the morning and associated with prolonged stiffness, especially after periods of inactivity. Unlike mechanical causes of back pain, symptoms improve with exercise and worsen with rest, with some patients noting increased severity in the evening or overnight.

On physical examination, findings may include reduced lumbar flexion, loss of spinal mobility, and a positive Schober test, which assesses lumbar flexion. As the disease progresses, ankylosis of the spine may lead to a characteristic stooped posture with limited chest expansion due to costovertebral joint involvement.

Beyond axial symptoms, ankylosing spondylitis frequently involves extra-articular manifestations, with acute anterior uveitis being the most common. Uveitis presents with the sudden onset of unilateral eye pain, photophobia, lacrimation, and blurred vision, often requiring urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. Other extra-articular features may include enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertions), peripheral arthritis, aortitis, conduction abnormalities, and restrictive lung disease from apical pulmonary fibrosis or reduced chest wall compliance.

Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and laboratory findings. Early radiographic changes include sacroiliitis, best visualized with MRI, while later stages show vertebral body squaring, syndesmophyte formation, and bamboo spine appearance on plain radiographs. Inflammatory markers such as elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein may be present, although they are not specific.

First-line treatment involves NSAIDs for symptom control and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors or interleukin-17 inhibitors for patients with inadequate response or severe disease. Regular physical therapy and exercise are essential components of long-term treatment to preserve spinal mobility and function.



Aortic regurgitation (A) can occur in long-standing disease due to aortic root dilation, but it is far less common than uveitis.

Inflammatory bowel disease (B) is associated with spondyloarthropathies but is not as prevalent in ankylosing spondylitis as uveitis.

Psoriasis (C) is linked to psoriatic arthritis, another spondyloarthropathy, but is not a common feature of ankylosing spondylitis.

Question: Which of the following antibiotics is associated with spontaneous tendon rupture?
ExplanationEN:
Fluoroquinolone drugs, including levofloxacin, have been associated with spontaneous tendon ruptures. Fluoroquinolones are a commonly prescribed antibiotic class. The class includes ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and levofloxacin. The fluoroquinolone class of drugs has a number of side effects, the most serious of which are prolongation of the QT interval and spontaneous tendon rupture. Tendon rupture appears to be more common in patients > 60 years of age and those also taking systemic glucocorticoids. These drugs are discouraged for use in pregnant patients and children secondary to their effect on cartilage.

An Achilles tendon rupture typically presents with a sudden, sharp pain in the back of the ankle or calf, often described by patients as feeling like a “pop” or being kicked. This is usually followed by swelling, bruising, and an inability to bear weight or push off the foot while walking. Patients may have difficulty standing on their tiptoes on the affected side. Physical examination often reveals a palpable defect in the tendon above the heel. The Thompson test is commonly used to diagnose an Achilles tendon rupture. In this test, the patient lies prone, and the calf muscle is squeezed. A normal response would be plantar flexion of the foot, but in the case of a rupture, the foot remains still. Imaging, such as ultrasound or MRI, may be used to confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the rupture.



Amoxicillin (A), a penicillin antibiotic, is not associated with tendon rupture. It is commonly used to treat bacterial infections such as streptococcal pharyngitis, pneumonia, and ear infections. Its adverse effects are usually mild, including gastrointestinal upset and allergic reactions.

Doxycycline (B) is a tetracycline antibiotic, and this class of antibiotics does not have a known association with tendon rupture. It is used in the treatment of a variety of bacterial infections, such as sexually transmitted infections, skin and soft tissue infections, Lyme disease, certain respiratory tract infections, and acne vulgaris. Common side effects include photosensitivity and gastrointestinal discomfort.

Erythromycin (C), a macrolide antibiotic, is not associated with an increased rate of spontaneous tendon rupture. It is used to treat infections like respiratory tract infections and skin infections. Common side effects include gastrointestinal upset and the potential for QT interval prolongation.

Sulfamethoxazole (E) is part of a combination antibiotic often used with trimethoprim. This combination is effective against a variety of bacterial infections but does not cause tendon ruptures. Adverse effects may include allergic reactions and the potential for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially in susceptible individuals.

Question: A 35-year-old man presents with severe muscle pain after running a marathon. His creatine kinase level is 55,000 U/L. Intravenous normal saline is initiated. What is the goal of therapy?
ExplanationEN:
Rhabdomyolysis is the result of the breakdown of skeletal muscle, releasing the intracellular contents into the bloodstream. In minor cases, patients are asymptomatic, but in severe cases, the condition is life-threatening, with severe electrolyte disturbance and kidney failure. The ultimate final pathway in rhabdomyolysis is the accumulation of intracellular cytoplasmic calcium, which leads to myocyte destruction. This occurs as a result of direct cell membrane damage and adenosine triphosphate depletion. The hallmark of diagnosis is the presence of elevated serum creatine kinase and myoglobinuria. Management of rhabdomyolysis involves treating or removing the underlying cause, correcting electrolyte abnormalities, and preventing kidney failure. Intravenous fluid administration is the mainstay of therapy titrating to a goal urine output of 2–3 mL/kg/hr.



Standard therapy previously included the alkalization of both serum and urine with the administration of sodium bicarbonate. The goal alkaline pH of urine (A) was > 6.5. This is no longer the targeted endpoint of rhabdomyolysis treatment. Intravenous fluids should be continued until clearance of the plasma creatine kinase.

Precise guidelines do not exist, but the goal creatine kinase level should be < 1,000 U/L, not 15,000 U/L (B).

A creatinine < 1.0 mg/dL (C) is not a standard goal of hydration for rhabdomyolysis. If kidney failure is present, hydration will continue until improvement, although no specific value is identified as the target.

Question: A 34-year-old handyman presents to the ED with a rapid onset of severe right forefinger fingertip pain and swelling over the last 24 hours. He states that he has been working around fiberglass for the last several days. He does not recall any specific injury. His hands and forearms have numerous small nicks and irritated areas. The pad of the right forefinger is tensely swollen, erythematous, and extremely tender to palpation, especially over a fluctuant area of the pad. These findings do not extend proximally past the distal interphalangeal joint. The cuticles are not swollen and the fingernail is not abnormally dark colored. There has been no drainage. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with a felon, an infection of the finger pad of the distal phalanx. Pain and swelling develop over hours to a few days and pain is severe. Usually, there are signs of minor injuries such as small cuts, splinters, or other embedded materials in the area, but a specific injury or retained foreign body may not be identifiable. The swelling and erythema do not extend proximally across the distal interphalangeal joint because the pad contains numerous fibrous septa that contain the infection to the distal phalanx. These septa attach to the periosteum of the distal phalanx. Inadequate treatment can result in osteomyelitis.



While a distal tuft fracture (A) distal tuft fracture could be present in addition to the felon, it does not account for all of the findings suggestive of infection in this patient and would likely be associated with a specific injury incident, which this patient does not have.

Paronychia (C) is an infection of the skin around the fingernail rather than in the pad of the finger. It is also usually triggered by minor trauma but is much less painful than a felon.

There is no visible subungual hematoma (D) between the nailbed and the lower nail surface, and no specific traumatic event is recalled. Thus, a subungual hematoma does not explain the localization of the worst symptoms.

Question: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset back pain after lifting a box. The pain radiates down to the mid-thigh and is worse with bending and walking. Physical exam reveals left paralumbar muscular tenderness without spasm. Which of the following exam maneuver(s) has the highest sensitivity and specificity for sciatica, respectively?

Options.text: Crossed straight leg raise, straight leg raise
Straight leg raise, crossed straight leg raise

CorrectAnswer: Straight leg raise, crossed straight leg raise
ExplanationEN:
Sciatica is a lumbosacral radiculopathy that is caused by compression of the spinal nerve root(s). Approximately 90% of all cases are due to disc herniation, although spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and piriformis syndrome are other notable causes. Symptoms typically develop suddenly during physical activity and consist of back pain radiating down the leg, though the pain may radiate bilaterally. Weakness and numbness in the affected limb may also be present. The straight leg raise (SLR) is a good screening test for sciatica, with 92% sensitivity and 28% specificity. The patient’s affected leg is extended and passively elevated. Pain elicited in a sciatic nerve distribution past the knee indicates a positive test. Pain elicited in the back alone is not considered positive.

The crossed straight leg raise compliments the straight leg raise well in that it has a sensitivity of 28% and specificity of 90%. The crossed straight leg raise is performed by passively elevating the extended unaffected leg. A positive test is signified by pain evoked in a sciatic nerve distribution in the affected leg. Atraumatic sciatica does not necessitate imaging. Imaging should be sought when there is concern for infection or malignancy or when significant neurologic deficits are present (e.g., marked weakness, numbness, or bowel or bladder dysfunction). MRI is the preferred imaging modality in these cases. Treatment of sciatica is largely symptomatic with the use of nonnarcotic analgesics, preferably nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity as tolerated. Steroids and neuropathic pain medications have not shown significant efficacy in sciatica. With conservative management, most patients’ symptoms resolve after 6 weeks. Surgical treatment via discectomy is reserved for patients who do not improve with conservative care. However, while studies have shown short-term improvement in pain control after surgery, no difference in long-term pain control has been found between conservatively and surgically treated patients.



Crossed leg raise alone (A) has good specificity but poor sensitivity.

Crossed straight leg raise and straight leg raise (B) should be used together. However, the straight leg test has the highest sensitivity and the crossed straight leg raise has the highest specificity.

Straight leg raise alone (C) has good sensitivity but poor specificity.

Question: Which of the following results of synovial fluid analysis is most consistent with septic arthritis?

Options.text: Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 25,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and positively birefringent crystals present on analysis
Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 48,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and negatively birefringent crystals present on analysis
Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 85,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and no crystals present on analysis
Transparent, yellow in appearance, 1,000 WBCs/µL without a predominance of neutrophils, and no crystals present on analysis

CorrectAnswer: Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 85,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and no crystals present on analysis
ExplanationEN:
Septic arthritis is a condition that can lead to rapid irreversible joint destruction if inadequately treated. Patients typically present with a monoarticular arthritis and associated fevers, chills, and malaise (but absence of these symptoms does not exclude the diagnosis). Arthritis should be differentiated from a more focal periarticular inflammatory process such as cellulitis, bursitis, and tendinitis. True arthritis produces joint pain that is exacerbated by both active and passive range of motion.

If septic arthritis is suspected based on clinical features, an arthrocentesis should be performed, and synovial fluid should be obtained. Synovial fluid should be sent for cell count, Gram stain, crystal analysis, and culture. In septic arthritis, the synovial fluid will typically demonstrate a WBC count > 50,000 cells/µL with > 50% neutrophils. The synovial fluid will be cloudy and yellow in appearance without crystals present. Cultures of the synovial fluid will be positive in most cases and provide the causative organism.

Patients with septic arthritis should be admitted for IV antibiotics. Orthopedic surgery should be consulted because patients often require surgical washout. Vancomycin and ceftriaxone should be administered empirically until cultures have returned.



Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 25,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and positively birefringent crystals present on analysis (A) is most consistent with pseudogout. Pseudogout is a type of crystal-induced synovitis that is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. These crystals are positively birefringent and rhomboid shaped. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness. The most commonly affected joints are the knee, wrist, ankle, and elbow. Synovial fluid in inflammatory arthritis will have a WBC count of 200–50,000 cells/µL with > 50% neutrophils and can appear cloudy or yellow in appearance secondary to the presence of crystals.

Cloudy, yellow in appearance, 48,000 WBCs/µL with a predominance of neutrophils, and negatively birefringent crystals present on analysis (B) is consistent with gout. Gout is a crystal-induced synovitis caused by uric acid crystals. These crystals are negatively birefringent and needle shaped. Patients will present with joint pain, swelling, and redness. The most commonly affected joints are the great toe, tarsal joints, and knee. Synovial fluid in inflammatory arthritis will have a WBC count of 200–50,000/µL with > 50% neutrophils and can appear yellow or cloudy because of the presence of crystals.

Synovial fluid that is transparent and yellow in appearance with 1,000 WBCs/µL without a predominance of neutrophils and no crystals present on analysis (D) is consistent with osteoarthritis, a chronic, symmetric polyarticular destruction of joints distinguished by the lack of constitutional symptoms. Patients may present with acute monoarticular exacerbations that consist of joint pain and inflammation. Synovial fluid in osteoarthritis will demonstrate a WBC count < 3,000/µL with < 25% neutrophils and will be clear and transparent in appearance without crystals present. Treatment consists of rest and analgesics.

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the ED with left leg pain. He began limping a week ago and is now unable to bear weight on his left leg. He has a BMI of 40 kg/m2. He has a negative straight leg raise test. He reports no recent trauma, new activities, or respiratory illness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The differential diagnosis of atraumatic pediatric hip pain or limp includes slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, Osgood-Schlatter syndrome, transient (toxic) synovitis, septic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, acute rheumatic arthritis, and rarely, tuberculosis of the hip. SCFE is the most common cause of hip disability in adolescents. Most patients have obesity. The classic presentation is an adolescent with an elevated BMI who experiences nonradiating, dull, aching pain in the hip, groin, thigh, or knee with no history of recent trauma. Typical age range is between 8 and 15 years old. However, any child may develop SCFE during a growth spurt.

Atypical SCFE is possible in patients with no obesity or patients with juvenile arthritis, endocrinopathies, kidney failure, or previous irradiation or chemotherapy for malignancy. SCFE may be acute, chronic or acute-on-chronic. Acute injuries are often severe and require surgical reduction and fixation. Patients may report hip pain or groin pain that radiates to the thigh or knee. Patients often walk with a limp, and the affected limb may be flexed and externally rotated. Since delaying the diagnosis can portend significant morbidity, adolescents with chronic hip, groin, thigh, or knee pain should have bilateral hip X-rays to evaluate for SCFE. Bilateral disease is common, so bilateral X-rays are essential.

X-rays classically show posterior displacement of the epiphysis from the femoral neck that resembles ice cream falling off a cone. However, SCFE may be radiographically silent, and an MRI may be required to visualize early or subtle slippages. Orthopedic surgery should be consulted if the diagnosis is confirmed or highly suspected. Management includes non-weight-bearing and timely operative management.



Approximately 80% of patients with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (A) (i.e., avascular necrosis of the femoral head) are between the ages of 4 and 9 years at onset. It is caused by repeated episodes of ischemia and necrosis that lead to a subchondral stress fracture. Onset is insidious, and patients report hip pain and may walk with a limp.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (B) is an apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, seen in children who are usually 10–15 years old. It is caused by repetitive stress or overuse (e.g., running, kneeling, squatting, or climbing stairs) that results in microavulsions of the ossification center of the tibial tuberosity. Patients have tenderness over the tibial tuberosity.

Transient synovitis (D) is a noninfectious, self-limited inflammatory process of the hip that occurs most commonly in children < 10 years of age, with a peak incidence between 3 and 6 years old. Most cases are thought to be postviral and are managed with rest and NSAIDs.

Question: A 13-year-old boy presents with progressive right knee pain over the past 6 weeks. He reports no history of significant trauma. The pain is worse at night and with activity. On examination of the right knee, there is swelling and tenderness of the distal femur with no overlying erythema. There is no knee joint laxity or effusion. His X-ray is shown above. ExplanationEN:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in children with a 5-year survival rate of 60–80% if localized at the time of diagnosis. Incidence peaks during adolescence, particularly after a growth spurt. Patients often present with persistent bone pain that is worse at night and with activity. There may be a localized area of swelling and tenderness at the site involved. The distal femur is the most commonly involved site, followed by the proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. The axial skeleton is unlikely to be involved in pediatric cases but can be seen in adults with osteosarcoma. Plain radiographs will show a lytic lesion with an associated “sunburst” appearance of the periosteal reaction. Pathological fractures are an uncommon presentation in kids. There are no serum markers for osteosarcoma, but patients will often have an elevated alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase. Diagnosis is made by biopsy. Treatment includes limb-sparing surgery, when possible, and chemotherapy.



Osgood Schlatter disease (A), also known as osteochondritis of the tibial tuberosity, primarily affects children ages 9–14 years of age who have recently undergone a growth spurt. Patients report anterior knee pain that is worse with activity and relieved by rest. Examination findings include swelling and tenderness of the anterior tibial tuberosity where the patellar tendon inserts.

Septic arthritis (C)should be considered in patients with pain, swelling, and erythema of a joint. Fever is often present. On examination, there is typically exquisite pain with range of motion.

Stress fractures (D) can certainly cause persistent bone pain but do not appear as a lytic lesion on a radiograph.

ExplanationEN:

The most common extra-articular manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis is unilateral uveitis which presents with eye pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. While no laboratory study is diagnostic for ankylosing spondylitis, there is a strong association with the presence of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 and the disease.

His examination reveals a right metatarsophalangeal tophus. Which of the following regimens represents appropriate medical therapy for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Crystal-induced arthropathy includes gout and pseudogout. Gout is caused by monosodium urate (uric acid) crystals, and pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Gout is a monoarthropathy that most commonly affects the great toe (podagra) and ankle and more commonly affects men than women. Pseudogout is more likely to affect the knee or other large joints. Other risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Arthralgia usually develops over hours. Diagnosis can only be made with arthrocentesis of the affected joint and synovial fluid analysis with polarizing light microscopy. Uric acid crystals are negatively birefringent (i.e., appear yellow when light is parallel to the crystal), and calcium pyrophosphate crystals are positively birefringent (i.e., appear blue when light is parallel to the crystals). Serum uric acid levels have little utility in the acute diagnostic workup of gout, as up to 30% of patients having an acute gout attack will have normal levels.

First-line therapy includes a 5–7 day course of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as indomethacin or naproxen. Therefore, naproxen and topical ice is the most appropriate therapy for this patient. Patients who have kidney insufficiency should not be treated with NSAIDs. Colchicine is also an alternative agent for patients with normal kidney and liver function. For patients with contraindications to NSAIDs, pain may be treated with opioid analgesics. Additionally, prednisone is considered a first-line therapy but must be used with caution in those with diabetes and patients with hypertension and congestive heart failure. Allopurinol and probenecid are not useful for acute gout flares. Rather, they are used for long-term therapy and prophylaxis to reduce and prevent uric acid crystal formation. Patients should also be counseled on avoiding gout-inducing medications (e.g., thiazide diuretics), foods rich in purines (e.g., seafood, red meat), and alcohol.



Aspirin (A), along with loop and thiazide diuretics, are contraindicated in gout management because they increase uric acid formation.

Prednisone and colchicine (C) along with triamcinolone injections (D) may be used if a patient is unable to tolerate NSAIDs, and care must be taken when providing corticosteroids to those with diabetes due to the risk of hyperglycemia.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 21-year-old woman with a history of anorexia nervosa presents to the emergency department with 1 week of progressive, activity-induced foot pain that has become constant. The pain is relieved with rest, and she reports no acute trauma. She is the star on her college track and field team, preparing for a national competition. On exam, she has tenderness to the fifth metatarsal with associated edema. An X-ray is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Stress fractures occur due to increased muscle activity on bones that cannot tolerate the additional forces. Causes include using worn-out athlete’s shoes, running on hard surfaces, and a recent increase in activity, as can be assumed in this patient preparing for a national competition. Risk factors include female sex (two times higher than in male patients) and eating disorders, as the chronic underlying electrolyte imbalances in these patients lead to demineralized, weakened bone. About 50% of all stress fractures occur in the tibia. However, other sites, such as the metatarsals, tarsals, and fibula, are common. Patients typically have activity-induced pain at the site of the fracture that is relieved by rest.

On physical exam, patients may have tenderness to palpation over the fracture site, edema, and increased pain with weight-bearing on the affected bone. Diagnosis is made with imaging. X-rays may be negative on initial presentation. Thus, they cannot be used to rule out a stress fracture. X-rays taken 10–15 days after injury may show evidence of a healing fracture such as periosteal elevation or demineralization at the former fracture line. Treatment of suspected or confirmed stress fractures generally includes cessation of activity and varies based on fracture location. Some may require prolonged immobilization.



Exertional compartment syndrome (A) presents as activity-induced aching, squeezing, or cramping, often in the anterior compartment of the leg.

Jones fracture (B) is a fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. The stress fracture in this patient is more distal than would be expected with a Jones fracture.

A pseudo-Jones fracture (C) is a nondisplaced avulsion fracture of the fifth metatarsal tuberosity.

Reveal Answer:
A spiral fracture of the proximal fibula associated with a medial malleolar fracture or deltoid ligament injury and a distal tibiofibular syndesmosis tear.

Question: Which of the following tests performed during physical examination would lead one to diagnosis de Quervain tenosynovitis in a patient?
ExplanationEN:
De Quervain tenosynovitis is an entrapment syndrome of the tendons contained within the first dorsal compartment at the wrist. It presents with pain during thumb motion. Any thickening of the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis from acute or repetitive trauma restrains gliding of the tendons through the extensor retinaculum. It is most common in women ages 30–50 years old. It is also common in parents of infants as the repetitive lifting of the baby contributes to friction tendonitis. Patients usually present with tenderness over the radial styloid. The Finkelstein test consists of flexion of the thumb across the palm and then ulnar deviation of the wrist. Sharp pain at the dorsal compartment suggests a positive test and a diagnosis of de Quervain tenosynovitis.



The Hawkins-Kennedy test (B) is used in the evaluation of shoulder pain. A positive test suggests subacromial impingement syndrome. The patient is examined while sitting with their shoulder flexed to 90° and their elbow flexed to 90°. The clinician grasps proximal to the wrist and elbow and then quickly rotates the arm internally. Pain located below the acromioclavicular joint with internal rotation is considered a positive test result.

The Phalen test (C)is used to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome by force-flexing the wrists for 30–60 seconds. Burning, tingling, and numbness suggest a positive test.

The Thompson test (D) is used to diagnose a ruptured Achilles tendon in the lower limb. The test is performed with the patient lying face down with feet hanging off the edge of the bed. The test is positive when there is no movement, or plantar-flexion, of the foot on squeezing the corresponding calf, signifying likely rupture of the Achilles tendon.
