Question: A 64-year-old man reports pain and paresthesias in his right hand intermittently for several weeks. He works in a factory putting together electronics. On exam, he has decreased sensation of his right first through fourth digits and an atrophied thenar eminence. What test in the ED will help diagnose his condition?

Options.text: Percussion of the right volar wrist

CorrectAnswer: Percussion of the right volar wrist
ExplanationEN:
This patient has median mononeuropathy, also known as carpal tunnel syndrome, a compression neuropathy of the median nerve as it traverses under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist. The median nerve provides sensation primarily to the palmar aspect of the first, second, third, and radial side of the fourth digits. When it is compressed, the patient experiences pain, paresthesias, and numbness in that distribution.

The Tinel test is performed by lightly tapping the volar surface of the wrist over the median nerve. This should elicit a sensation of tingling or pins and needles in the distribution of the median nerve. The Phalen test consists of maximal flexion of the wrist for 60 seconds to see if symptoms are elicited. Carpal tunnel syndrome is first treated with wrist splinting and initiation of a more ergonomic work environment. If symptoms do not improve, the patient should be referred to a hand specialist who may elect to perform a carpal tunnel release procedure.



CT scan of the head (A) would be useful if there was suspicion that this patient’s symptoms were from a central process such as an acute stroke. However, his numbness is in a peripheral nerve distribution and not dermatomal.

Electromyography (B) is used most commonly by neurologists to confirm damage to peripheral nerves and is the appropriate outpatient confirmatory test. It may be used for carpal tunnel syndrome if the symptoms do not resolve with conservative management.

Ultrasound of the median nerve (D) can be helpful in patients with a suspected structural abnormality at the carpal tunnel and those who have atypical symptoms that do not fit with electrodiagnostic findings. It is not routinely needed in patients with typical carpal tunnel syndrome presentation.

A variety of heavy metals are associated with peripheral neuropathy (lead, mercury), but these require special serologic testing, not a urine drug screen (E). The patient is at risk for occupational exposures because he works in a factory, but most heavy metal poisonings are associated with other symptoms.

Question: A 52-year-old woman presents to the ED for finger pain. She is a dentist and thinks she scratched her finger at work a few days ago but cannot remember how. Since then, her finger has become red and swollen. During your examination, you note erythema, fluctuance, and severe pain with palpation of the distal finger pictured above. She has full range of motion of her finger. What is the most effective treatment for this patient's condition?

Options.text: Incision and drainage and trimethoprim-sulfamethaxozaole and amoxicillin-clavulanate

CorrectAnswer: Incision and drainage and trimethoprim-sulfamethaxozaole and amoxicillin-clavulanate
ExplanationEN:
A felon is an abscess that spreads through the compartments of the distal finger pad. This produces a fluctuant and painful mass, most commonly with overlying cellulitis, as seen in the picture above. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common bacterial pathogen. Thus, the most effective treatment is incision and drainage and antibiotics, typically trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. However, as in this case, if an anaerobic infection is favored given the patient's history and risk factors, such as diabetes, immunosuppression, or intravenous drug use, the addition of clindamycin or amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended. Care must be taken to ensure a single longitudinal incision (from proximal to distal) across the fluctuance to avoid the more lateral digital nerves. Fishmouth, through and through, and deep incisions, as well as incisions abutting or through the flexor crease, may inadvertently predispose the patient to flexor tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, nerve damage, soft tissue necrosis, and osteomyelitis. A culture should be obtained from the expressed fluid, as these infections may be difficult to treat due to the highly compartmentalized septa in the finger.



It is common to confuse a felon for herpetic whitlow, a viral infection of the distal fingers typically caused by herpes simplex viruses 1 or 2. These lesions will appear as white vesicles overlying an erythematous base and are treated with acyclovir (A, C). Incision and drainage is not indicated in cases of herpetic whitlow.

Flexor tenosynovitis is a potential complication of an untreated felon and presents with a flexed finger and pain with passive extension. This condition is treated with surgical debridement, ampicillin-sulbactam, and admission (B).

Question: Which one of the following is classically seen in infectious flexor tenosynovitis?

Options.text: Extended position of the involved digit
Flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint alone
Vesicular eruption over the flexor surface

ExplanationEN:
The flexor tendons of the fingers are covered by a double layer of synovium to promote gliding of the tendon underneath. Infections in the synovial spaces of the hand tend to spread along the course of the flexor tendon sheaths and may extend proximally to the hand. Infections are usually due to penetrating trauma involving the sheath but occasionally from hematogenous spread.

Four cardinal signs of acute flexor tenosynovitis are usually present to help distinguish tenosynovitis from other hand infections. These criteria are referred to as the Kanavel signs. Flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency. Consultation with a hand surgeon is warranted, along with intravenous antibiotics.



The affected digit is held in a flexed, not extended (A), posture.

Flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint (B) alone is known as a mallet finger. With infectious flexor tenosynovitis, the entire digit is in a flexed posture.

The tenderness is over the flexor sheath, not extensor (D).

Vesicles (E) are not commonly associated with flexor tenosynovitis. A localized herpes simplex infection may cause vesicles to form on a digit.

Question: A 5-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with a limp, which his parent noticed 2 days ago. On exam, the patient appears well. Vital signs are significant for fever with a temperature of 38.1°C (100.6°F). Heart rate and blood pressure are within normal limits. The patient demonstrates an antalgic gait, and there is warmth and tenderness to palpation of the soft tissues in the distal thigh. Lab tests show a WBC count within reference range and elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Plain radiographs of the femur show soft tissue swelling in the distal thigh, as well as a periosteal reaction in the distal femur. Knee radiographs are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely infecting organism?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has osteomyelitis of the distal femur. Osteomyelitis, which is a pyogenic infection of the bone, occurs via hematogenous seeding (most common in children), a contiguous source of infection (e.g., diabetes-related foot ulcer), or direct inoculation (e.g., puncture wound, orthopedic procedure).

Children will most often present with acute osteomyelitis (< 2 weeks) with signs of systemic infection such as fever and irritability, in addition to localized bone pain and swelling. Adults commonly present with subacute or chronic osteomyelitis and will have pain, swelling, and nonhealing ulcers more frequently than fever. Plain radiographs are the initial imaging choice in patients with osteomyelitis, though fewer than one-third of patients will have any abnormalities in the first 7–10 days of admission. Periosteal reaction is the earliest osseous finding. The most common infecting organism in osteomyelitis for healthy hosts in all age groups except neonates is Staphylococcus aureus. Patients with sickle cell have an increased risk of osteomyelitis overall, especially from Salmonella spp. Additionally, Salmonella spp are the most common pathogens identified in patients with sickle cell presenting with osteomyelitis.



Clostridium spp (A) are anaerobic bacteria known for causing myonecrosis (i.e., gas gangrene), tetanus, and gastrointestinal infections. They do not commonly cause osteomyelitis.

Haemophilus spp (B) used to be the second most common cause of osteomyelitis. However, this is no longer true due to the advent of the Haemophilus vaccine.

Klebsiella spp (C) and other anaerobes are rarer causes of osteomyelitis and are more frequently associated with chronic osteomyelitis, as in patients with diabetes and nonhealing foot ulcers.

Pseudomonas (D) infection should be considered when osteomyelitis develops following a penetrating injury through a surface colonized with Pseudomonas (e.g., the sole of a shoe).

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with finger pain that prevented him from sleeping. He has noticed increased swelling of his finger over the last several days. He is holding his hand elevated, which he says improves the pain. The distal pad of the middle finger is significantly swollen, red, and tender. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Digital block with incision and drainage
Oral antibiotics covering skin bacterial flora and discharge

CorrectAnswer: Digital block with incision and drainage
ExplanationEN:
The soft, fleshy pads of the distal segment of the fingers are supported by fibrous tissue that divides the space into multiple compartments. An abscess within one of these compartments is called a felon. A felon causes significant pressure and pain and can lead to necrosis of surrounding tissue, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and flexor tenosynovitis. Felons most commonly occur after a neglected minor puncture wound. Early infections can be treated with warm soaks, elevation, and oral antibiotics. Infections with abscess formation require a digital block and an incision and drainage to reduce the pain and for treatment in some cases. Once a definitive felon is suspected, a digital block with incision and drainage is required. The incision should be made at the point of maximal tenderness. When unclear, the recommended incision sites are directly through the pad longitudinal to the distal phalanx or along the edge near the nail, also longitudinal to the distal phalanx. The initial method spares the finger’s lateral and medial neurovascular bundle but can result in a scar on the pad of the finger. The latter method may sever the finger’s neurovascular bundle. Frequently, the infection is more extensive than the clinical appearance suggests, and surgical consult for operative drainage may be required.



Oral antibiotics covering skin bacterial flora and discharge (B) is appropriate when there is an early infection, but incision and drainage is required once abscess formation is suspected.

Specialist consultation for operative drainage (C) may be necessary in advanced disease.

X-ray of the affected finger (D) is appropriate if there is history of trauma or suspected foreign body, neither of which is noted in this patient.

Question: A 24-year-old mechanic presents to the ED with severe pain and swelling of his left middle finger. He thinks he may have injured it while removing a nail from a tire a few days ago. Which of the following is consistent with the diagnosis of infectious flexor tenosynovitis?

Options.text: Localized distal swelling of the digit

ExplanationEN:
Infectious flexor tenosynovitis is an infection of the flexor tendon sheath of the finger. It is most often caused by penetrating trauma, but patients may be unaware of a specific traumatic incident. It is a surgical emergency, as failure or delay in diagnosis and management can lead to spread of infection to deep spaces, tissue necrosis, and adhesions.

The diagnosis is made clinically using the four cardinal signs of flexor tenosynovitis from the Kanavel criteria, which include a digit flexed at rest to minimize pain, uniform (fusiform) swelling of the affected digit, intense pain with passive extension of the digit, and tenderness to palpation along the flexor tendon sheath.

The most commonly isolated organism is Staphylococcus aureus, but infections may be polymicrobial. Because infection can spread rapidly into the deep hand spaces, early intravenous antibiotics (including coverage for methicillin-resistant S. aureus) are indicated along with consultation from a hand surgeon.



Flexor surface tenderness rather than extensor surface tenderness (B) is a cardinal finding of infectious tenosynovitis.

Localized distal swelling of the digit (C) is seen in other hand infections such as felons and paronychias.

The digit is uniformly swollen in flexor tenosynovitis. Patients have pain with passive extension rather than pain with passive flexion (D) of the affected digit.

Question: A 26-year-old man is training for a marathon and presents to the ED with right knee pain. The pain began during a run yesterday and has become progressively worse. He is unable to ascend stairs without significant pain. Palpation below the medial joint line of the knee elicits pain. You suspect anserine bursitis. The tendon of which of the following muscles is affected with this diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The tendons of the gracilis, sartorius, and semitendinosus muscles insert onto the medial tibia below the knee joint and overlie the pes anserinus (Latin for goose’s foot) bursa. Pes anserine bursitis occurs commonly in runners, female individuals with obesity and osteoarthritis, and those with overuse syndromes. It is thought to be due to tight hamstrings, leading to increased friction and irritation of the bursa.

Patients report anterior medial knee pain below the joint line (upper medial tibia) and tenderness to palpation over the bursa. Symptoms may worsen with overuse or with certain activities such as squatting, running, or ascending or descending stairs. It usually is not symptomatic when walking on flat surfaces. Diagnosis is clinical. Management consists of rest, ice, proper stretching, and NSAIDs. The condition is self-limiting, and most athletes are able to return to play after a period of conservative therapy.



The biceps femoris (A) muscle is part of the hamstring muscle group that arises from the ischium and femur and attaches to the lateral aspect of the tibia and fibula. It is more commonly associated with lateral knee pain due to strain or tendinopathy in athletes.

The gastrocnemius (B) muscle has medial and lateral heads that originate on the medial and lateral femoral condyles, respectively, and attach to the calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. Injury to this muscle or its tendon would typically result in calf pain rather than medial knee pain.

The rectus femoris (D) and vastus medialis (E) muscles are part of the quadriceps muscle group of the anterior thigh that extends the knee. Its tendons join those of the other quadriceps muscles on the patella to form the quadriceps tendon, which envelops the patella and inserts onto the anterior proximal tibia. Quadriceps tendinopathy may result in pain with knee flexion and diminished knee extension.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents with low back pain and stiffness that appeared insidiously. He works at a department store and has difficulty reaching the top shelves due to pain and decreased range of motion. The pain usually improves somewhat as the day progresses but returns at night. He notices that sitting with his right foot on his left knee causes significant pain in his left posterior pelvis. On exam, he has a kyphotic back, tenderness over the posterior pelvic joints bilaterally, and mild tenderness over his Achilles tendons bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This young patient with low back pain and morning stiffness that improves with exercise most likely has ankylosing spondylitis. Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory arthritis that primarily affects the spine and is associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA-B27). Diagnosis is made using a combination of clinical symptoms, lab testing, and radiographic findings suggestive of sacroiliac joint pathology. Classically, X-ray imaging shows fusion of vertebrae (“bamboo spine”) as the peripheral fibers of the intervertebral annulus fibrosus discs ossify. However, symptoms can be present up to 10 years before radiographic evidence of the disease is apparent. Patients generally present with arthritic symptoms most apparent in the lower back but can also have enthesopathy (as in this patient’s Achilles tendon pain), uveitis, and fibrosis of the upper lobes of the lung. The sacroiliac joint can be tested by flexing, abducting, and externally rotating one leg (FABER test). If pain is elicited on the posterior contralateral side, it is suggestive of sacroiliac joint pathology. If pain is elicited on the anterior ipsilateral side, it is suggestive of pathology within the hip. The mainstay of treatment is nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and tumor necrosis factor antagonist medications.



Osteoarthritis can also cause back pain but generally affects older patients and usually improves with rest rather than worsening. The sacroiliac joints are rarely affected.

Rheumatoid arthritis (D)can cause arthritic pain in younger individuals with morning stiffness but usually affects small joints (hands, feet, and cervical spine).

Osteofibrous dysplasia (C) is a fibrovascular defect of the long bones that leads to the replacement of cortical bone with fibrous tissue. The disease is usually painless and spinal involvement is extremely rare.

Question: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the ED for a limp. Her parent notes that she seems to limp in the morning but has not reported any pain. The limp seems to improve throughout the day. The parent also reports that the child’s left knee is swollen. Which of the following features is associated with a diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile arthritis?
ExplanationEN:
Uveitis is a well-known and serious complication of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), particularly in young girls with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test. It can be asymptomatic and insidious, which is why routine ophthalmologic screening is critical in these patients.

Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype of JIA, defined by involvement of five or fewer joints during the first 6 months of disease. It typically affects girls more frequently than boys and has a peak onset at 2–3 years of age, with rare onset > age 10. The condition is characterized by insidious onset of joint stiffness, swelling, or a painless limp, most often affecting the large joints, particularly the knees and ankles. Unlike systemic JIA, constitutional symptoms such as fever, rash, or weight loss are absent.

On physical examination, the affected joints are usually swollen and tender, but erythema and warmth are uncommon, helping to distinguish this from septic arthritis or systemic inflammatory conditions. Despite the lack of systemic symptoms, chronic inflammation can silently cause joint damage and growth disturbances.

Laboratory findings often include positive ANA in up to 80% of cases, while erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are within normal limits or only mildly elevated. Rheumatoid factor is negative in oligoarticular JIA.

The most significant complication is chronic anterior uveitis, which occurs in up to 25% of patients and is often asymptomatic in early stages. Routine screening with slit lamp ophthalmologic examinations is essential to detect early uveitis, particularly in children with a positive ANA diagnosed under age 6, who are at highest risk. Additional complications include temporomandibular joint arthritis, which may lead to jaw asymmetry and dysfunction, and leg-length discrepancy, especially when the disease is unilateral.

Treatment focuses on NSAIDs for mild disease. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are often effective for rapid symptom control. In cases of persistent or refractory inflammation, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs such as methotrexate or biologic agents may be necessary. Regular monitoring by pediatric rheumatology and ophthalmology is critical to prevent long-term complications.



Gottron papules (A), violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, are a feature of juvenile dermatomyositis. Other signs and symptoms of this disease include proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, and nail fold telangiectasia.

Hepatosplenomegaly (B), quotidian fever, arthritis (in the knees, wrists, and ankles), and a macular rash are all characteristics of systemic juvenile arthritis.

Negative ANA (C) is seen in systemic juvenile arthritis, while patients with oligoarticular and polyarticular juvenile arthritis will have a positive ANA test.

Question: A 67-year-old man with a history of gout presents with atraumatic left knee pain. He reports the pain began suddenly yesterday and has progressively worsened. He reports no history of any recent trauma. His vital signs include a temperature of 102.0°F, a blood pressure of 102/62 mm Hg, a heart rate of 89 bpm, and a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min. Physical examination reveals an effusion with overlying warmth and erythema. There is marked tenderness with passive range of motion. What is the appropriate next step?

Options.text: Obtain a radiograph of the knee
Obtain arthrocentesis of the affected joint
Order a serum uric acid level

CorrectAnswer: Obtain arthrocentesis of the affected joint
ExplanationEN:
Septic arthritis is a bacterial or fungal infection of a joint that typically spreads hematogenously unless there is direct bacterial contamination. The synovium is highly vascular and lacks a basement membrane, which facilitates bacterial seeding and rapid joint destruction if untreated. Risk factors for septic arthritis includes diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, immunocompromised state, alcohol dependence, and preexisting joint disease like rheumatoid arthritis or gout. The knee is the most commonly involved joint, and infection can lead to irreversible cartilage damage within days.

Clinical presentation includes acute onset of monoarticular joint pain, swelling, and decreased range of motion. Pain with passive range of motion is a common finding because it indicates inflammation within the joint capsule itself. Fever is present in less than half of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. On physical exam, joints are typically erythematous, warm, and tender, often with a large effusion.

Diagnostic evaluation for septic arthritis includes arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis, which should be obtained before initiating antibiotics to preserve culture yield. Synovial fluid in septic arthritis typically has a white blood cell count > 50,000/µL, is neutrophil predominant, and may show organisms on Gram stain. Culture is essential for directing antibiotic therapy. Management includes prompt initiation of empiric intravenous antibiotics after fluid collection, followed by tailoring antibiotics to culture results, and often surgical drainage or serial aspirations for source control.



Indomethacin (A) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent commonly used in the treatment of acute gout. Its mechanism of action is cyclooxygenase inhibition, which decreases prostaglandin synthesis and thereby reduces inflammation and pain. While effective in managing crystal-induced arthritis, it does not address septic arthritis.

A radiograph of the knee (B) may show chronic degenerative changes associated with gout, such as tophi or erosions, but they will not help to differentiate gouty arthritis from septic arthritis. Both conditions can present with monoarticular swelling, warmth, and erythema, so imaging cannot confirm or exclude infection.

A serum uric acid measurement (D) does not reliably correlate with the presence or absence of an acute gout flare. Levels may be normal during an acute episode and elevated in asymptomatic individuals. Gout results from monosodium urate crystal deposition due to uric acid overproduction or underexcretion, and diagnosis is made by identifying negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid.

Starting empiric intravenous antibiotics (E) without first obtaining joint analysis can sterilize the fluid and reduce diagnostic yield, making it more difficult to confirm the diagnosis and guide targeted therapy. While antibiotics are ultimately indicated in patients with confirmed or highly suspected septic arthritis, they should only be administered after synovial fluid analysis, including Gram stain, cell count, crystal analysis, and culture, are obtained. Exceptions to initiating antibiotics prior to diagnosis would include a patient who is hemodynamically unstable or has systemic signs of sepsis.

Question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism presents with left hand numbness that woke her from sleep. She reports no headache, slurred speech, blurred vision, or extremity weakness. She has diminished sensation in her fifth finger and the medial side of her ring finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cubital tunnel syndrome is a compressive ulnar mononeuropathy caused by compression of the ulnar nerve as it traverses through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow. It is the most common ulnar mononeuropathy. The ulnar nerve innervates the skin of the medial palm, the fifth digit, and the medial aspect of the fourth digit. Repetitive stress, trauma, and inflammation are all causes of cubital tunnel syndrome. Classic features include paresthesias of the fifth and medial fourth fingers, and it often occurs in the middle of the night as the elbow is flexed during sleep. Over time and in severe cases, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hand may occur.

Several provocative tests can help with diagnosis. Tapping on the cubital tunnel may elicit symptoms, suggesting the diagnosis. If symptoms are produced within 3 minutes of holding the elbow in flexion with the wrist in extension, cubital tunnel syndrome is more likely (positive elbow flexion sign). Pain is typically not part of the syndrome, but anti-inflammatory medications may aid in relieving symptoms. Emergent imaging and consultation are not required in the acute setting. However, outpatient orthopedic follow-up may be appropriate if symptoms are severe or affect activities of daily living. Patients should be counseled on reducing repetitive use and eliminating habits that create pressure or stress on the elbow.



Carpal tunnel syndrome (A), or median mononeuropathy, is the most common acute mononeuropathy and affects the median nerve at the wrist, leading to impaired motor and sensory function of the thumb, index finger, and long fingers and the radial (lateral) aspect of the ring finger. Risk factors include hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, amyloidosis, obesity, overuse of the hand and wrist, and rheumatoid arthritis.

De Quervain tenosynovitis (C) is an inflammatory condition of the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis tendons as they travel along the radial styloid. It is commonly caused by overuse of the wrist or thumb, and patients often report wrist pain radiating to the thumb.

Meralgia paresthetica (D)is a compressive mononeuropathy of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve that causes numbness or pain in the anterolateral thigh. Risk factors include pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, obesity, intraabdominal or pelvic mass, or external compression with a belt or tight-fitting clothing.

Question: Which of the following is a common complication of the fracture seen above?
ExplanationEN:
Avascular necrosis (AVN) is a process of ischemic bone death. It is also known as aseptic necrosis, ischemic necrosis, and osteonecrosis. Over time, the ischemia will lead to a collapse of the bone, causing pain, swelling, and decreased range of motion. The average age at the time of diagnosis is 37 years. Causes include trauma, chronic corticosteroid use, chronic alcohol use, and an underlying hemoglobinopathy (sickle cell anemia). However, AVN may be deemed idiopathic in up to 20% of patients. Treatment ranges from supportive treatment (observation, immobilization, physical therapy, and anti-inflammatory drugs) to surgical procedures. If the cause is thought to be iatrogenic, eliminating the source should lessen the progression of bony destruction. The X-ray above demonstrates a scaphoid fracture, which is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Due to the distal blood supply to the scaphoid, it is at risk for AVN following a fracture.



Kienböck disease (B) is a condition involving AVN of the lunate. It is most often seen in men ages 20–40 years. Patients present with dorsal wrist pain, and treatment includes both conservative and surgical management.

Thenar eminence atrophy (C) may be seen as a complication of untreated carpal tunnel syndrome. It may also be seen as a complication of a more proximal neuropathy to the median nerve.

Ulnar nerve injury (D) is a potential complication of fractures to the hamate, pisiform, or medial epicondyle. Patients will have decreased sensation of the fifth digit or have a claw hand with unopposed extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fourth and fifth digits along with unopposed flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joints.

Question: A 39-year-old woman presents to the ED concerned about pain and swelling in her distal index finger. On exam, you note her finger, as seen in the above image. There is mild tenderness and full range of motion at the distal interphalangeal joint. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The lesion seen above is herpetic whitlow, secondary to herpes simplex infection. This is the most common viral infection of the hand. It is usually caused by direct inoculation of the virus into an open wound or broken skin. It is often reported in adult women who also have genital herpes, children with coexistent herpetic gingivostomatitis, and health care workers who are exposed to orotracheal secretions. The infection usually involves a single finger and begins with localized pain, pruritus, and swelling, followed by the appearance of clear vesicles. Systemic symptoms are usually absent, but secondary bacterial infection of the vesicles can occur. Over 2 weeks, the vesicles coalesce to form an ulcer, at which time the lesion may be difficult to distinguish from other common finger infections, such as a felon or paronychia. The lesions will resolve spontaneously over 3–4 weeks. The lesions should be kept covered. The role of oral acyclovir is not clear in immunocompetent individuals but should be administered in those who are immunocompromised or have recurring infections.



An eponychia (A) is a localized soft tissue infection, similar to a paronychia (D), but it occurs under the eponychium aspect of the nail. Both present with swelling, erythema, and tenderness at the respective nail fold. A felon (B) is an infection of the fingertip pulp. The fingertip is separated into small closed spaces by vertical septa. Infection can easily spread along these compartments.

Question: A 37-year-old man presents to the ED with right shoulder and neck pain that has been ongoing for the past 3 weeks. He reports no trauma. On physical exam, the right-sided arm pain is reproduced when pushing down on his head while his neck is extended and leaning toward the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with right-sided, subacute, nontraumatic neck and shoulder pain, a common but nonspecific presentation. The differential diagnosis is broad and includes muscle strain, cervical spondylosis, facet arthropathy, rotator cuff pathology, and more serious conditions such as cervical radiculopathy or spinal cord compression. Careful history and physical examination are key to narrowing the differential.

The physical exam maneuver described is known as the Spurling test (or Spurling sign), a provocative maneuver used to evaluate for cervical radiculopathy. It is performed by applying a downward axial load on the patient’s head while simultaneously extending and laterally flexing the neck toward the side of symptoms. A positive test reproduces radicular pain, described as sharp, burning, or electric shock-like, that radiates into the ipsilateral arm in a dermatomal distribution. This test is highly specific (approximately 90%) but only moderately sensitive, meaning a positive result is strongly suggestive of cervical nerve root involvement, but a negative test does not exclude the diagnosis.

Among the diagnostic considerations listed, cervical disc herniation is the only option that may directly cause cervical radiculopathy by impinging on an exiting nerve root. Disc herniations commonly occur at the C5–C6 or C6–C7 levels and can result in radiating pain, sensory disturbances, and weakness consistent with the affected nerve root. Other causes of radiculopathy include osteophyte formation, foraminal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis, but disc herniation is more commonly implicated in younger patients with acute or subacute presentations.

Prompt recognition of cervical radiculopathy and correlation with clinical findings such as a positive Spurling sign can guide appropriate diagnostic imaging (e.g., MRI of the cervical spine) and treatment, which often includes conservative therapy such as physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and activity modification. Severe or progressive neurologic deficits may warrant surgical referral.



A rotator cuff tear (B) would present with shoulder pain that is worse with movement. The painful arc test is performed by having patients actively abduct the arm. If pain is reported in 60–120°, then the patient likely has impingement syndrome. If pain is reported beyond 120°, then an acromioclavicular joint injury is more likely.

Impingement syndrome (C) is a common cause of shoulder pain that occurs secondary to excessive overhead activity. The Neer and the Hawkins-Kennedy tests are useful in diagnosing impingement syndrome.

Thoracic outlet syndrome (D) is diagnosed with a positive Adson test. It is performed by checking the radial or ulnar pulse while the patient’s upper extremity is abducted overhead. A decrease in heart rate during the maneuver indicates a positive test.

Question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the ED with right hip pain. His mother states that he had just gotten over a cold 1 week ago and has been doing well. However, for the last day, he has developed acute hip pain and a limp. Vital signs show a temperature of 37°C, heart rate of 100 bpm, and blood pressure of 90/60 mm Hg. On physical exam, he has full range of motion of the hip, but with pain. Laboratory studies show a WBC count of 10,000/µL, a C-reactive protein of 2 mg/L, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 10 mm/hr. X-rays show no abnormalities. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Discharge patient home with limb rest
Obtain an MRI of the hip

CorrectAnswer: Discharge patient home with limb rest
ExplanationEN:
Transient synovitis of the hip is a self-limiting disease, characterized by inflammation of the synovium. Peak incidence is usually from 3–6 years of age. The cause of transient synovitis is unknown, but it is often seen as a sequela of a viral infection. Patients usually present with sudden-onset hip pain. On exam, patients will generally have a good range of motion, even though significant pain may be present. Laboratory workup is usually unremarkable, but patients can sometimes have a mildly elevated white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Imaging is usually normal but can also show a small effusion.

Although transient synovitis is a benign disease, it can sometimes be difficult to differentiate from a septic arthritis, which is an orthopedic emergency. In septic arthritis, patients usually have significantly decreased range of motion. They may also present with fevers and more elevated laboratory studies when compared to transient synovitis. If there is some concern, an arthrocentesis can be performed. However, a patient with a reassuring exam and normal laboratory findings can be treated as transient synovitis. If there are laboratory abnormalities or an effusion noted on imaging, an arthrocentesis should be performed to help differentiate the diagnosis.

Management of transient synovitis is with limb rest and NSAIDs. Patients can be safely discharged home for follow-up with their primary care clinician in 2 weeks.



Applying a long leg splint (A) is appropriate for many lower extremity fractures but would not be appropriate to treat transient synovitis.

An MRI of the hip (C) would be useful if the patient is suspected to have osteomyelitis, but it would have little utility in diagnosing transient synovitis.

An arthrocentesis (D) is often necessary to rule out septic arthritis. However, if the patient has a reassuring exam and normal laboratory findings, it is unnecessary.

Question: A patient presents with muscle pain, weakness, and rash. Which of the following exam findings would be most consistent with dermatomyositis?

Options.text: Midface erythema that spares the nasolabial folds
Scaly erythematous papules on extensor surfaces of the hands

CorrectAnswer: Scaly erythematous papules on extensor surfaces of the hands
ExplanationEN:
Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy associated with both skeletal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings. It is more common in women than men and the peak incidence is between the ages of 40 and 50 years. Proximal, symmetric muscle weakness is the most common finding and may be accompanied by myalgias. The deltoids and hip flexors are typically affected while distal muscle weakness, if present, is mild and does not cause functional impairment. The proximal muscle weakness often makes it difficult to get up from a seated position or climb stairs. The onset of weakness is often gradual over a period of several months. Gottron papules and a heliotrope rash are the hallmark cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis. Gottron papules are scaly erythematous papules found on the extensor surfaces of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. The heliotrope rash is an erythematous rash on the upper eyelids. Laboratory studies will show an elevation in creatine kinase as well as other muscle enzymes, although the levels can vary and a negative test does not rule out the disease. Antinuclear antibodies are present in up to 80% of patients. Electromyography and muscle biopsy confirm the diagnosis. Treatment is oral steroids. Refractory cases may be managed with azathioprine and methotrexate.



Cranial nerve weakness (A) is not typical in dermatomyositis but can be seen with botulism, which presents with descending, flaccid paralysis and findings of ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia.

The hallmark of dermatomyositis is symmetric, proximal muscle weakness, not distal weakness (B).

Midface erythema (C) is also common in dermatomyositis, but unlike the malar rash of systemic lupus erythematosus, it involves the nasolabial folds. The rash is often photosensitive.

Question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with 3 days of back pain and leg weakness. Her vital signs are within normal limits for her age. She has no meningeal signs or midline bony tenderness on examination. Which of the following findings on history or physical examination is concerning for cauda equina syndrome?
ExplanationEN:
Cauda equina syndrome is a neurologic emergency and is the result of external compression of the cauda equina by a tumor, abscess, herniated disc, expanding hematoma, or other mass. Because the cauda equina is composed of spinal nerve roots, compression results in peripheral neuropathy instead of central neuropathy. Signs and symptoms include back pain, urinary retention (measured by a post-void residual bladder volume usually > 100 cc), overflow urinary incontinence, saddle or perianal anesthesia, and lower motor neuron findings such as lower extremity hyporeflexia and flaccidity, which are usually unilateral. Patients with findings concerning for cauda equina syndrome need emergent neurosurgical consultation and advanced imaging with MRI.



Conus medullaris syndrome is another neurosurgical emergency that may present with similar features as cauda equina syndrome, including saddle anesthesia and bladder incontinence. However, because the conus medullaris is the terminal spinal cord and, by definition, a central structure, exam findings will be consistent with upper motor neuron deficits such as lower extremity spasticity (B), hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign.

A positive Romberg test (C) indicates dorsal column involvement, which is absent in cauda equina syndrome.

A post-void bladder volume < 100 cc (D) is not concerning for cauda equina syndrome. Residual bladder volumes > 100 cc suggest urinary retention and, in the context of back pain and neurological findings, are concerning for cauda equina syndrome.

Question: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with difficulty walking. Her parents have noticed she has extreme difficulty getting up or down stairs. She has not had any fevers and began walking at a normal age. Her exam shows vital signs within normal limits for her age. She has symmetric proximal muscle weakness in her arms and legs, along with weakness of her anterior neck and abdominal muscles. She has a purple rash over her upper eyelids and a scaly erythematous rash on her knuckles. Lab results show mildly elevated creatine kinase and aldolase. Which of the following is this patient at risk for if her most likely diagnosis remains untreated?
ExplanationEN:
Juvenile dermatomyositis is a rare rheumatologic myopathy and capillary vasculopathy that presents in childhood with proximal muscle weakness and a characteristic rash. It affects girls twice as often as boys. The muscle weakness is proximal and can also involve the neck flexors and abdomen. The commonly seen rash is a heliotrope rash, a purple-to-lilac discoloration over the eyelids or, less commonly, periorbitally. Erythematous macules or papules are also frequently found over the extensor surfaces of joints and may be scaly. Dermatomyositis in children differs from that in adults, as there is more prominent vascular inflammation, it is rarely associated with malignancy, and it usually has no detectable autoantibodies. Muscle enzymes are often elevated (including creatine kinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, and transaminases), but should be interpreted carefully, as not all are specific to muscle inflammation.

Patients with untreated dermatomyositis are at risk for diaphragm weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and atelectasis. These patients may present with bacterial pneumonia or aspiration pneumonitis. Patients with steroid or immunomodulator treatment may develop complications of osteoporosis, gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, and rarely hypertension or dysrhythmia.



Cardiac involvement in juvenile dermatomyositis can manifest as acute congestive heart failure (A), myocarditis, dysrhythmias, and complete heart block, though these often remain unrecognized due to lack of overt clinical manifestations. However, these occur infrequently.

Patients with dermatomyositis usually have an elevated creatine kinase but not the fivefold elevation and myoglobinuria seen in rhabdomyolysis (C).

Uveitis (D) is associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis but is not typically seen with dermatomyositis.

Question: A 61-year-old man presents to the emergency department by paramedics after being found down in a neighbor’s yard. He has slurred speech and smells of alcohol. Laboratory tests reveal sodium 146 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L, chloride 119 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL, creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, glucose 210 mg/dL, and creatine kinase 22,000 U/L. Which of the following is indicated at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Rhabdomyolysis is characterized by skeletal muscle breakdown from any process that injures myocytes or their membranes. This breakdown leads to the release of intracellular contents, including uric acid, potassium, and lactate dehydrogenase. Myoglobinuria and acute kidney failure may occur. Laboratory findings include hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated serum creatine kinase, urea nitrogen, creatinine, transaminases, and lactate dehydrogenase. Alcohol and drug use are the most common causes of rhabdomyolysis. Other causes include head injuries, trauma (e.g., crush injuries), strenuous muscular activity, heat injuries, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and seizures. Multiple causes are found in most patients. Management involves early and aggressive intravenous resuscitation with crystalloid boluses followed by maintenance fluid therapy for a goal urine output of 3 cc/kg/hour or 200–300 cc/hr to prevent acute kidney failure. Therapy may need to be continued for up to 72 hours.



Insulin bolus and infusion (B) is appropriate therapy for diabetes-related ketoacidosis (DKA). While hyperglycemic, this patient has a normal anion gap of 6 mmol/L and a bicarbonate level > 15 mmol/L, so it is unlikely that he has DKA.

Oral rehydration therapy (C) is an inadequate resuscitation method for the management of rhabdomyolysis. Patients require aggressive intravenous crystalloid fluid therapy.

Rasburicase (D) is a recombinant urate oxidase used to treat hyperuricemia in cases of tumor lysis syndrome.

Question: A 12-year-old healthy boy is brought to the ED with several weeks of aching right knee pain with exercise that improves with ibuprofen and acetaminophen. He reports no fever, trauma, or weight loss. On physical examination, the patient has normal vital signs, normal strength, and full range of motion of the right leg, with a tender mass noted on the proximal right knee. An X-ray of the femur is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This child’s presentation and imaging findings are most consistent with a diagnosis of osteosarcoma, the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents. Osteosarcomas arise during periods of rapid skeletal growth, most often in children aged 10–20 years, and they are characteristically located in the metaphyseal regions of long bones, with a predilection for the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. Risk factors in pediatric populations include hereditary retinoblastoma (associated with RB1 gene mutations), Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and prior therapeutic radiation exposure.

Patients frequently present with an insidious onset of localized bone pain that progresses over weeks to months, occasionally accompanied by swelling or a firm, tender soft tissue mass at the affected site. Despite the malignant nature of the tumor, systemic signs such as fever, fatigue, or weight loss are uncommon. In some cases, symptoms may be precipitated or noticed after minor trauma. Notably, up to 20% of patients have evidence of metastatic disease at diagnosis, most commonly involving the lungs or other skeletal sites.

Initial diagnostic imaging begins with a plain radiograph, which may reveal pathognomonic findings such as a sunburst pattern from radiating periosteal bone spicules or a Codman triangle, formed by reactive subperiosteal bone at the tumor margin. These findings reflect aggressive periosteal reaction and cortical bone destruction. Additional imaging, including MRI of the primary site, is essential to assess local extent, neurovascular involvement, and surgical planning. Chest CT and bone scans or PET imaging are indicated for staging and detection of metastases.

Definitive diagnosis requires a biopsy, which should be performed at a center experienced in sarcoma treatment to avoid compromising future surgical resection. Emergency department treatment includes adequate pain control, limitation of activity to prevent pathologic fracture, and expedited referral to orthopedic oncology and pediatric oncology for further evaluation and treatment planning.

The mainstay of therapy involves multiagent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-sparing surgery when feasible, or amputation in select cases with extensive disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy is administered postoperatively. The treatment strategy is tailored based on factors such as tumor location, response to initial chemotherapy, and the presence of metastatic disease, all of which influence long-term prognosis.



Ewing sarcoma (A) presents similarly, with localized pain and swelling. However, these tumors have a predilection for the diaphysis and appear as “onion skinning” of the periosteum on X-ray.

Giant cell tumors (B) are benign tumors of the long bones that appear as lytic lesions with a “soap bubble” appearance.

Osteochondromas (C) are benign, pedunculated lesions of the external bony surface, most often seen in male patients in their teens and twenties. These lesions rarely cause severe symptoms unless they lead to a restricted range of motion.

Question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the ED with right hip pain. His mother reports no history of trauma but states he had a cough and runny nose last week. Vital signs are within normal limits, and a physical exam reveals a flexed right lower extremity. He is noted to have a limp and favors his right side when ambulating. Hip X-ray and white blood cell count are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate test at this point?

Options.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein

CorrectAnswer: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
ExplanationEN:
An erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) may help determine if further diagnostic testing is necessary for a child presenting with hip pain. Hip pain in a child who can bear weight, a history of a recent upper respiratory infection, plus a normal hip X-ray and WBC count suggest transient synovitis. Transient synovitis is an inflammatory response of the synovium of unclear etiology but may be secondary to recent or active infection, trauma, or allergic hypersensitivity. Common manifestations include hip pain, groin pain, limp, or refusal to walk. A physical exam may reveal a child with a flexed and externally rotated leg. A child who can bear weight and who has a normal hip X-ray and WBC count < 12,000 is unlikely to have septic arthritis if the ESR is < 40 mm/hr and the CRP is < 20 mg/L. In children with a negative workup and symptom improvement with NSAIDs, close outpatient follow-up is an appropriate management strategy.



Arthrocentesis (A) may be necessary in children presenting with limp or hip pain if septic arthritis is suspected. However, in children with a history, physical exam, WBC count, and hip X-ray consistent with transient synovitis, an ESR and CRP would be helpful in determining the need for arthrocentesis.

An MRI (C) is ideal for the assessment of bone or joint infection because it can assess bones, joint spaces, and surrounding structures with great detail. However, MRI is time-consuming, difficult to perform in young children, and often unnecessary in most cases of hip pain.

Ultrasound (D) may reveal an effusion in 60–70% of patients with transient synovitis, but this can also be seen in other causes of hip pain. Ultrasound can be used to guide joint aspiration if arthrocentesis is necessary.

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the ED with leg pain for 2 weeks. He reports no recent illness or trauma. His symptoms are exacerbated during basketball practice at school. He has point tenderness over his right anterior tibia. There is no evidence of patellar dislocation or knee instability. His muscular compartments are soft. His lower extremity muscle strength and reflexes are intact. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Pediatric orthopedic concerns are common in the emergency department. Adolescents (ages 10–15 years old) who present with anterior lower leg pain due to an increase in activity or during periods of increased growth should be suspected to have Osgood-Schlatter disease, or tibial apophysitis. It results from overuse or repeated stress of the patellar tendon at its site of insertion at the tibial tubercle. Overuse, commonly from running or jumping sports, can result in microavulsions of the ossification center and cartilage without avascular necrosis. The patellar tendon becomes inflamed and creates an overlying indurated, tender, and prominent tibial tuberosity. Boys are more commonly affected than girls, and symptoms are usually bilateral, chronic, and intermittent. Activities such as kneeling, squatting, jumping, or stair climbing exacerbate symptoms and rest improves symptoms. The patella is not dislocated and there should be no knee joint effusion. The knee examination is otherwise unremarkable. Imaging is not necessary and only shows nonspecific tibial tuberosity changes. Management is conservative and involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, ice after exercise, and quadriceps and hamstring strengthening. Complete cessation of activity is contraindicated because it can lead to quadriceps atrophy.



Reactive arthritis (A)is a clinical syndrome characterized by iritis, urethritis, and polyarthritis that follows either an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal illness.

Superficial thrombophlebitis (B) does not cause bony findings (e.g., tenderness, swelling) and usually presents with redness, warmth, and tenderness over the affected vein.

Transient synovitis (D) is a noninfectious inflammatory condition of the hip that typically affects children younger than 10 years of age.

Question: An 81-year-old man injured his left hand while using a table saw. He presents to the emergency department 5 days after the incident with pain and swelling of his left middle finger. His vital signs are T 100.5°F (38.1°C), HR 98 bpm, RR 12 breaths/minute, BP 135/80 mm Hg, and SpO2 100% on room air. On physical examination, the patient’s left middle finger appears circumferentially swollen. He has pain with passive extension of the digit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The patient has clinical signs of flexor tenosynovitis, a deep space infection of the hand involving the flexor tendon sheath of the digit that requires prompt diagnosis and management, as delay will lead to digit- or limb-threatening morbidity. The four cardinal Kanavel signs of flexor tenosynovitis are finger fixed in a flexed position at rest, fusiform swelling of the digit, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and pain with passive extension. Clinicians should have a high index of suspicion for the diagnosis, as delay in care can be devastating. Most patients will require surgical irrigation and debridement due to the multiplanar involvement of the hand and digits. Flexor tenosynovitis is most commonly caused by penetrating trauma to the fingers. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism to cause infection. Signs and symptoms include extreme pain, fever, erythema, and the cardinal signs noted above. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical in care.



Compartment syndrome (A) is a clinical phenomenon in which an anatomic compartment (e.g., abdomen, lower leg, forearm) experiences an intracompartmental pressure that leads to neurovascular compromise and warrants emergent compartmental decompression. Clinical features include pressure, pain, pallor, paresthesias, poikilothermia, and pulselessness.

Dactylitis (B) is sausage-like digits seen in patients (more often children) with sickle cell disease. It is a vaso-occlusive crisis of the digits that causes pain and fusiform swelling.

De Quervain tenosynovitis (C) is an inflammatory condition of the lateral forearm tendons, notably the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. It causes pain with thumb and wrist motion and often occurs from repetitive stress or direct trauma, but may also occur in pregnancy or thyroid disorders.

Question: You perform an arthrocentesis on a patient with knee pain. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 128/81 mm Hg, heart rate of 89 bpm, respiratory rate of 19/min, oxygen saturation of 100% on room air, and a temperature of 99.9°F. Synovial fluid analysis reveals a WBC of 5,000 cells/µL with 70% polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The analysis of synovial fluid is essential for identifying crystalline and suppurative causes of acute arthritis. The WBC count dictates the inflammatory class of the fluid. However, an analysis is often difficult because there is significant overlap between entities. A very high fluid WBC or polymorphonuclear leukocyte pleocytosis indicates infection, but a modest elevation does not exclude it. Therefore, cell counts should be used as a guide rather than definitive diagnosis. WBCs between 2,000/µL and 75,000/µL are often categorized as inflammatory. However, a WBC over 50,000/µL has a likelihood ratio of 7.7 for septic arthritis.

Inflammatory arthritis encompasses several types of arthritis characterized by inflammation of the joints, leading to pain, swelling, and stiffness. Rheumatoid arthritis is a common form, in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, often leading to joint deformity and dysfunction. Ankylosing spondylitis primarily affects the spine, causing inflammation and potential fusion of the vertebrae. Psoriatic arthritis occurs in some patients with psoriasis and involves both skin and joint symptoms. Other types include gout, resulting from uric acid crystal deposition in the joints, and lupus arthritis, part of systemic lupus erythematosus, in which joint involvement is one aspect of a broader autoimmune disorder.



Hemorrhagic effusions (A) are caused by trauma to the knee or coagulopathy. The fluid is grossly bloody and may contain fat droplets (lipohemarthrosis).

Noninflammatory arthritis (C) such as osteoarthritis will have < 3,000 WBCs/µL on arthrocentesis.

Normal synovial fluid (D) is a clear, pale yellow, and viscous liquid that serves as a lubricant and cushion within joint cavities. It is produced by the synovial membrane and contains hyaluronic acid, proteins, glucose, and minimal cellular content. Typically, it has < 150 WBC/µL, mostly mononuclear, with negligible neutrophils, indicative of its noninflammatory nature.

The likelihood ratio for septic arthritis (E) increases as the joint WBC count rises. A WBC count < 25,000/µL has a likelihood ratio of 0.32, > 25,000/µL has a likelihood ratio of 2.9, and > 50,000 has a likelihood ratio of 7.7/µL.

Question: Which of the following is the most common finding in patients with septic arthritis?
ExplanationEN:
Bacteria in the joint capsule is a true surgical emergency requiring prompt drainage, joint washout, and antibiotics to prevent permanent joint damage. It is typically monoarticular, occurring through hematogenous spread. It is most common in the lower extremities and larger joints, with the knee and hip being most commonly affected. The bacteria isolated depend on age, immunization status, and region. Due to vaccines for Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most commonly isolated organism is currently Staphylococcus aureus in all age groups.

True bacterial arthritis has a variable presentation depending on the organism, but virtually all patients with septic arthritis will have resistance or pain with active or passive range of motion due to the associated joint effusion. The challenge for the clinician is to determine if this pain is due to septic arthritis or another cause such as viral, autoimmune, or other (e.g., transient synovitis, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease). Many patients with septic arthritis will have additional findings such as fever, inability to bear weight, limp (when in the lower extremity), leukocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers. However, some patients with septic arthritis have none of these additional findings. Due to the high risk of morbidity, expert consultation is recommended when findings are equivocal.



The majority of cases of septic arthritis are the result of hematogenous spread making findings of extremity trauma (A) less likely. Penetrating joint injuries may result in unusual pathogens as the cause of infection.

Fever (B) is present in most but not all patients with septic arthritis, especially when they present early in the illness.

Subtle joint findings without appreciable warmth or swelling (B) are relatively common, especially in the hip as it is deeper than other joints. Exam findings are also subtle in patients with primary osteomyelitis as the metaphysis is located deeper than the primarily infected synovium. All patients with a fever and a limp should receive an evaluation for septic arthritis including laboratory evaluation for leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and affected joint ultrasound.

Question: A 58-year-old man with a medical history of diabetes presents to the emergency department for pain in his right second finger after working in his garden 2 days ago. On exam, there is a small puncture wound to the palmar surface of the finger with uniform swelling to the digit. The finger is flexed and the patient has intense pain when the finger is passively extended. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Flexor tenosynovitis is considered a true surgical hand emergency. The flexor tendons are covered by a layer of synovium to promote proper hand movement. An infection into this space can lead to adhesions and permanent loss of hand functioning if left untreated. The majority of patients will have an associated penetrating trauma that introduces an infection. Diagnosis is clinical and based on a group of exam findings called the Kanavel cardinal signs. These include fusiform swelling of the finger, flexed posture of the finger, pain with passive extension, and tenderness along the entire flexor tendon sheath. However, all four signs may not be present in an early infection, thus a normal exam may not rule out flexor tenosynovitis. Some small studies have shown that bedside ultrasound may be used to help with diagnosis. Treatment is immobilization, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergent hand consultation for surgical debridement.



There are many other types of hand infections. Cellulitis (A) is the most superficial infection of the hand and can usually be treated in the outpatient setting with oral antibiotics. However, a thorough examination of the compartments on the volar surface must be done to evaluate for a deep space infection. Felon (B) is an infection of the fingertip pulp that may need incision and drainage by an emergency physician but does not extend across the entire length of the finger. Septic joints (D) will be red, tender, and swollen overlying a specific joint. Septic joints should be treated with antibiotics and early orthopedic consultation.

Question: A 38-year-old man presents to the ED with muscle aches and fatigue. After finding that the patient is a bodybuilder who also used methamphetamine and ecstasy this weekend, you check laboratory work that reveals a creatine kinase level of 26,760 U/L. Other laboratory work shows creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, potassium 5.0 mEq/L, and calcium 8.3 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis, a syndrome caused by muscle injury leading to the release of intracellular contents, including myoglobin, creatine kinase (CK), potassium, and phosphate, into the bloodstream. The most common causes include trauma, exertion, drug use (such as stimulants like methamphetamine and ecstasy), and muscle compression. The hallmark laboratory finding in rhabdomyolysis is an elevated CK level, often exceeding 5,000 U/L, and myoglobinuria can contribute to acute kidney injury. The cornerstone of treatment in the emergency department is aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids, primarily normal saline or lactated Ringer, to promote kidney perfusion, dilute myoglobin, and prevent tubular obstruction.

Rhabdomyolysis presents with a triad of muscle pain, weakness, and dark urine (myoglobinuria), though many patients do not exhibit all three symptoms. Laboratory abnormalities in this case, including an elevated CK and acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL, confirm the diagnosis. Hyperkalemia (potassium 5.0 mEq/L) and metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 18 mEq/L) are common complications, reflecting cellular breakdown and impaired kidney excretion. Hypocalcemia, often seen due to calcium binding with released phosphate, is typically transient and does not require immediate correction unless symptomatic.

Early and aggressive IV fluid administration is the most effective initial intervention, as it prevents further kidney damage by increasing urine output and flushing out myoglobin. While urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate and osmotic diuresis with mannitol have been proposed, they lack strong evidence for improving outcomes compared to volume resuscitation alone. In severe cases with refractory hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, or significant kidney injury requiring kidney replacement therapy, hemodialysis may be necessary, but it is not the first-line treatment.



Hypocalcemia in rhabdomyolysis is typically transient and results from calcium-phosphate precipitation in damaged muscle tissue. Routine calcium administration (B) is not recommended unless the patient has symptomatic hypocalcemia (e.g., tetany, seizures, or cardiac dysrhythmias). Empirical calcium replacement in asymptomatic patients can lead to rebound hypercalcemia during recovery.

Although hemodialysis (C) may be required in severe rhabdomyolysis with refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, or oliguric acute kidney injury, it is not the initial therapy. This patient does not yet have life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities, and early aggressive IV fluid therapy remains the first-line treatment. Dialysis should only be considered if conservative measures fail or if complications such as severe hyperkalemia or volume overload develop.

Mannitol (D), an osmotic diuretic, has been proposed to increase urine flow and prevent kidney injury, but evidence does not support its routine use over crystalloid hydration. It may also cause volume depletion if not carefully monitored. Fluid resuscitation with normal saline or lactated Ringer remains the primary intervention in rhabdomyolysis treatment.

While urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (E) has been suggested to reduce myoglobin toxicity and prevent kidney injury, studies have not consistently shown improved outcomes compared to IV fluid therapy alone. Furthermore, this patient has only mild metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 18 mEq/L), and alkalinization is generally reserved for severe cases or specific situations such as concurrent acidosis or severe hyperkalemia.

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the ED with an excruciatingly painful right knee. The patient reports no history of trauma, medication use, or recent illnesses. He is sexually active. The pain started this morning and has gotten worse over the past couple of hours. The patient is unable to bear weight on the knee. On physical exam, the knee is swollen, warm, and tender on palpation, with no overlying erythema. Which of the following organisms is most likely the cause of this infection?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has septic arthritis. The most likely cause of septic arthritis overall is Staphylococcus aureus, but a common cause in a sexually active adolescent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Septic arthritis is an infection of the joint space by various microorganisms, most commonly bacteria. The knee is the most commonly involved joint in septic arthritis.

Patients with septic arthritis usually present with fever, acute joint pain, swelling of the joint, and limited range of motion. Prosthetic joints, immunosuppression, and advanced age are risk factors for septic arthritis. Culture of the synovial fluid or of synovial tissue itself is the only definitive method of diagnosing septic arthritis. Obtain at least two sets of blood cultures to rule out a bacteremic origin of the septic joint. For possible gonococcal infection, obtaining cultures from the patient’s rectum, cervix, urethra, and pharynx and any skin lesions is appropriate. Imaging is not accurate for diagnosing septic arthritis. However, radionuclide bone scans are used to nonspecifically localize areas of inflammation and may be of use in diagnosing septic arthritis in relatively sequestered areas, such as the hip and sacroiliac joints.

Synovial fluid drainage in a sterile environment, along with 2–4 weeks of antibiotic therapy, is the standard treatment for septic arthritis. Choosing the proper antibiotics depends on the bacterial cause. However, the initial antibiotic choice should be empiric until the results and sensitivity patterns of the culture are known. An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein is useful in following response to therapy.



Infection of the sternoclavicular and sacroiliac joints with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (B) occurs almost exclusively in people who use intravenous drugs.

Salmonella (C) species are not commonly associated with septic arthritis in children without a history of sickle cell anemia.

Streptococcus agalactiae (D) is a group B Streptococcus species that is commonly observed in infants < 3 months.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (E) is a common cause of bacterial arthritis in children > 5 years of age, but would not be as common in this sexually active adolescent. The incidence of Streptococcus pneumoniae arthritis has significantly declined due to vaccination.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents with progressive back pain and stiffness that started 2 months ago. The pain is worse at night and when he wakes up in the morning, and it improves with exercise. In the last week, he has also noted pain and stiffness in the hips and ankles. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 118/72 mm Hg, heart rate of 64 bpm, respiratory rate of 17/min, oxygen saturation of 100% on room air, and a temperature of 98.2°F. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory condition primarily affecting the spine and pelvis. There is a strong association between the presence of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 and AS. Patients often present in their 20s to 30s with a 3:1 male predilection. Symptoms consistent with ankylosing spondylitis include an insidious onset of pain and stiffness (often present for 3 months or more) that is worse at night and the morning but improves with mild activity.

Pain typically affects the lower spine and hips, but it can involve peripheral joints as well, most notably the ankles and knees. Another classic finding is pain, stiffness, and tenderness at the insertion sites of ligaments and tendons to the bone (enthesitis). This is most commonly seen at the Achilles tendon attachment to the calcaneus and the plantar fascia. Diagnosis is made based on history and physical findings, the presence of HLA B-27, and radiographs consistent with disease (e.g., erosions or fusion of sacroiliac joints). First-line treatment is nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Symptoms of lumbar radiculopathy (B) include lower back pain with unilateral radiation to the leg. Patients often have numbness, weakness, and decreased deep tendon reflexes that reflect the particular nerve root involved.

Rheumatoid arthritis (C) typically affects older women and primarily involves the peripheral joints.

Spinal stenosis (D) is narrowing of the spine that results in chronic back pain that is worse with prolonged standing and back extension and is relieved by rest and forward flexion of the spine.

Spondylolisthesis (E) involves the slippage of one vertebra over another and may cause back pain, but it does not typically present with the inflammatory symptoms or joint involvement seen in ankylosing spondylitis.

Question: A 42-year-old woman with sickle cell disease presents to the ED with unilateral knee pain. You are worried she might have septic arthritis. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
ExplanationEN:
Septic arthritis is a joint infection that often presents with acute onset of joint pain, swelling, erythema, and fever. Patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) are at an increased risk of septic arthritis due to compromised splenic function (resulting in immunosuppression) and bone infarctions that predispose to bacterial seeding. While Salmonella spp is often remembered as an organism more likely to be involved in infection in those with SCD, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen causing septic arthritis in both the general population and patients with SCD. It has a high propensity for joint involvement and produces proteases and toxins that contribute to joint destruction.

Patients with SCD are also at risk for infections caused by encapsulated organisms such as Salmonella and Streptococcus pneumoniae due to functional asplenia. However, Salmonella is more commonly associated with osteomyelitis in this population, whereas S. aureus is more frequently implicated in septic arthritis. The clinical presentation of septic arthritis in these patients includes intense joint pain (often monoarticular), warmth, swelling, and limited range of motion. Systemic symptoms like fever may also occur. Diagnosis typically involves joint aspiration for synovial fluid analysis, including Gram stain, culture, and cell count, as well as blood cultures and imaging studies.

Treatment of septic arthritis involves prompt empiric antibiotics to cover likely pathogens and often surgical or needle-based joint drainage. Empiric regimens typically include vancomycin with or without a third-generation cephalosporin until specific cultures guide targeted therapy.



Escherichia coli (A) is primarily associated with septic arthritis in the setting of intra-abdominal or genitourinary infections leading to bacteremia. It is not a common pathogen for septic arthritis in patients with SCD. While patients with SCD are immunocompromised, their predisposition is not typically toward gram-negative organisms like E. coli in the setting of septic arthritis.

Pasteurella multocida (B) is associated with animal bites and may cause osteomyelitis but does not typically lead to septic arthritis.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (C) is a rare cause of septic arthritis and is typically associated with intravenous drug use, penetrating trauma, or joint surgery. While patients with SCD may have increased susceptibility to certain infections, Pseudomonas is not a common pathogen in this population’s septic arthritis cases.

Salmonella (D) spp are a significant cause of infections in patients with SCD due to their predilection for causing osteomyelitis. This occurs because bone infarctions create an avascular environment where Salmonella can thrive. However, Salmonella is a much less common cause of septic arthritis compared to S. aureus.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents with pain in his index finger. Which of the following is suggestive of flexor tenosynovitis?

Options.text: Grouped vesicles with an erythematous base
Swelling localized to the volar aspect of the finger

ExplanationEN:
Flexor tenosynovitis is an infection of the flexor tendon sheath of the finger. Most commonly, penetrating trauma to the actual sheath causes this infection, although direct spread from other areas of the hand may occur. Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci are the most common causative organisms.

The Kanavel signs are the four cardinal signs of acute flexor tenosynovitis and include tenderness along the flexor tendon, symmetric swelling of the finger (“sausage finger”), pain on passive extension, and flexed posture of the finger. These patients need antibiotic therapy and admission to the hospital for possible operative washout.



Delayed capillary refill (A) may be seen with significant swelling in a finger infection, but it is not a hallmark sign of flexor tenosynovitis.

Grouped vesicles with an erythematous base (B) around the paronychial folds, pad of the finger, or lateral aspect of the digit are observed in herpetic whitlow.

Typically, the pain of the infection is exacerbated when the finger is fully extended, and as a result, patients avoid holding the finger fully extended (C). More often, the finger will be flexed, and the pain is exacerbated on passive extension by the clinician.

Swelling is not localized to the volar aspect of the finger (E) but is more symmetric and uniform along the entire finger, creating the sausage-like appearance.
