Question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for worsening weakness in both legs that began this morning and has since progressed to an inability to walk this evening. There was no preceding trauma or other obvious inciting factor. Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and systemic lupus erythematosus, for which she takes metformin and hydroxychloroquine daily. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows 2 out of 5 muscle strength in the bilateral lower extremities. Her sensation is reduced below the level of the umbilicus. An MRI of the spine shows abnormal T2 signal hyperintensity within the spinal cord at the level of the T10 vertebrae and expansion of the visualized spinal cord. Lumbar puncture and CSF studies are pending. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Transverse myelitis is an inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord that results in a complete transection with resulting sensory deficits. The exact pathogenesis has not yet been identified, but it has a known association with infectious, autoimmune (e.g., lupus), and idiopathic conditions. Roughly 30% of cases occur following an acute viral infection, in which case it is termed “postinfectious myelitis.” The clinical syndrome of transverse myelitis depends upon the particular location of insult within the spinal cord, with the thoracic cord affected in 60–70% of cases. If the spinal cord lesions affect three or more spinal cord levels, it is termed “longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.”

The primary presenting features of transverse myelitis are sensorimotor deficits that correlate with the level of the lesion within the spinal cord. This patient’s lower extremity weakness and sensory level at the umbilicus suggest a lesion within the thoracic spinal cord, likely at or near the level of T10. Autonomic disruption and urinary and fecal disturbances are common as well, with both incontinence and retention as possible symptoms. Symptoms of transverse myelitis typically progress fairly rapidly, with two-thirds of cases reaching their point of maximal neurologic deficits by the 24-hour mark. However, symptoms can be somewhat protracted and progress over the course of days to weeks in some cases. MRI with contrast enhancement is the test of choice for diagnosis, with the most characteristic features being abnormal T2 signal hyperintensity and spinal cord expansion at the involved spinal cord level(s), such as in this case.

Few data exist to guide the treatment of known or suspected cases of transverse myelitis, but management is typically aimed at the underlying etiology. In this patient’s case, the underlying etiology is likely her systemic lupus erythematosus, and treatment of a lupus flare may be warranted. Though there are no good studies to support or refute their use, intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) are commonly administered. The clinical course and prognosis of transverse myelitis are highly variable, ranging from full recovery to permanent neurologic impairment and death. Patients with idiopathic cases generally display some degree of improvement, usually recovering the maximum degree between 3 and 6 months after the acute episode. The rate of 5-year mortality is approximately 15%.



Brown-Séquard syndrome (A) is characterized by a unilateral hemisection of the spinal cord that presents with sensory loss of pain, temperature, and light touch contralateral to and below the level of the lesion and loss of proprioception, vibration, and motor control ipsilateral to it.

The presence of neurologic deficits and the patient's age effectively rule out discitis (B) as the diagnosis since this is a rare cause of inflammatory back pain that almost universally presents without focal neurologic findings and most often occurs in children.

Spinal epidural abscess (C) can mimic some clinical features of transverse myelitis, including sensory level and other focal findings, but a lack of fever and an MRI that does not show an extrinsic cord lesion make this diagnosis unlikely.

Syringomyelia (D) is a spinal cord disorder in which there is formation of a cavitary lesion that causes sensory disturbances, gait dysfunction, motor weakness, and muscle wasting. The cavity formed in these cases is typically easily seen on MRI and is not present in this patient’s imaging.

Question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the ED with a severe headache. The headache is behind her right eye with associated right-sided lacrimation and rhinorrhea. She reports a long history of these headaches that come and go over the course of a few weeks before resolving for a few years. Which outpatient treatment may decrease the recurrence of this patient's most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cluster headaches are acute onset, unilateral headaches that are characterized primarily by their clustering of attacks. They tend to occur in young and middle-aged patients who use tobacco. While the underlying etiology of cluster headaches is unknown, abnormal trigeminal nerve firing is thought to be involved. The headaches most commonly are one-sided, surrounding the eye with associated ipsilateral autonomic dysfunction (i.e., ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, diaphoresis). Central neurologic deficit concerns and physical exam findings are absent. Clusters can occur suddenly, multiple times daily, and last up to weeks or months.

The mainstay of treatment is high-flow oxygen via a nonrebreather mask. Supplemental treatment with subcutaneous sumatriptan has also been shown effective. Given the clustering characteristics of these headaches, acute treatment is only the first step. Clinicians should ensure patients are discharged with adequate outpatient treatments to decrease the length of these clusters. Verapamil and corticosteroids have been used to decrease the length and number of clusters.



High-dose ibuprofen (A) has no role as an abortive or prophylactic treatment for cluster headaches. Home oxygen (B) and sumatriptan (C) are used as cluster headache abortives and may decrease emergency department visits during clusters. They have not been shown to decrease the length or frequency of attacks.

Question: A 6-month-old girl presents to the ED with her parents who are concerned about recurring incidents of shaking upon awakening. Per parents, she is unable to sit tripod and seems to lack any emotion. Electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia. What is the characteristic age range at presentation of this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with infantile spasms or West syndrome. Signs and symptoms of infantile spasms usually begin at age 2–8 months. Infants will demonstrate brief contractions of the neck, trunk, and extremities lasting 5–10 seconds each, occurring in clusters. Infantile spasms are defined by the triad of findings including clusters of myoclonic seizures on awakening, hypsarrhythmia pattern on EEG, and developmental delay. These children are most frequently diagnosed by the presence of the characteristic EEG finding of hypsarrhythmia, which has the appearance of high amplitude irregular waves and spikes in a background of chaotic and disorganized activity. Management of infantile spasms is primarily with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), prednisone, vigabatrin, and antiepileptic medications or combinations of these medicines.



1–2 years (A), 1–4 months (B), and 8–16 months (D) are not the typical age ranges for the presentation of children with infantile spasms.

Question: A 67-year-old man with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department with a headache. Shortly after the initial evaluation, he develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. An image from his scan is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary brain tumor. It is an aggressive malignant tumor with a poor prognosis of about 6 months after diagnosis. The median age of diagnosis is 64, with patients > 65 having a less favorable outcome than younger patients. There are no identifiable risk factors. Signs and symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, memory loss, personality changes, neurological deficits, and seizures, depending on the location of the tumor. Some patients may be asymptomatic until the tumor reaches a larger size. Diagnosis is made via biopsy, but a CT scan or MRI with intravenous contrast will show a tumor in the cerebral hemispheres that may cross the corpus callosum. A classically used term to describe the appearance of the tumor on CT scan is butterfly glioma. Treatment includes a combination of radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and surgical resection.



Hemangioblastoma (B) is a primary brain tumor of blood vessel origin associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome that is most often cerebellar.

Meningioma (C) is a slow-growing primary brain tumor that originates from the meninges and, as such, occurs near brain surfaces. Risk factors include exposure to ionizing radiation and a family history. Patients are often asymptomatic but may present with neurological deficits or seizures.

Oligodendroglioma (D) is a rare, slow-growing primary brain tumor that most often occurs in the frontal lobes.

Question: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a headache. His symptoms began 1 hour prior to arrival. He reports sharp, intense pain localized near the left temporal region and around his left eye. He reports no vision changes. He had similar symptoms the day prior and 1 year ago. Both resolved without treatment within 30 minutes. On exam, he appears uncomfortable and has difficulty sitting still. He has ptosis of the left eye, and his left pupil is constricted. Intraocular pressure is 19 mm Hg. There are no other focal neurologic abnormalities noted. What is the best next step in the management of this patient’s most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s symptoms are most consistent with a cluster headache. Cluster headaches classically present with severe, unilateral pain that is self limited, lasting up to 3 hours. Symptoms are often localized to the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Patients may be restless and uncomfortable appearing. Associated autonomic symptoms include ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, ptosis, miosis, and swelling. Cluster headaches are more common in men and occur in “clusters” of daily episodes before remitting for several months, often in a circadian or circannual pattern. Alcohol and vasodilatory medications can precipitate symptoms. The diagnosis is made clinically. Acute-onset cluster headaches should be treated with 7–12 L/min of oxygen via nonrebreather mask for 15 minutes. Subcutaneous sumatriptan is also effective but should be avoided in patients with cardiovascular disease.



Migraines often occur as throbbing headaches with or without an aura. Patients may have associated photophobia or phonophobia. Triptans are the first line for abortive therapy. NSAIDs and dopamine receptor antagonists such as ketorolac and metoclopramide (A) may be used in the emergency department if abortive treatment fails. This patient’s symptoms are not consistent with a migraine headache. Evaluation of headache in the emergency department requires recognition of signs or symptoms that are concerning for life-threatening conditions. Head trauma, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, sudden-onset headache, or severe uncontrolled hypertension should prompt consideration of the use of head CT without contrast (D) to evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage or structural abnormalities. Ptosis can be suggestive of arterial dissection or third cranial nerve compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, so it is reasonable to consider CT angiography of the head for this patient. However, his symptoms overall are more consistent with a cluster headache, and oxygen therapy would be the most appropriate next step. Lumbar puncture (E) should be performed if there is clinical concern for meningitis. Meningitis should be suspected if a headache is associated with fevers or signs of meningeal irritation. A lumbar puncture can also be performed to evaluate for xanthochromia if there is a concern for subarachnoid hemorrhage and the patient presents > 6 hours after the onset of symptoms. Emergent ophthalmologic consultation (C) should be obtained if there is a concern for acute angle-closure glaucoma. This patient does not have visual deficits, and his intraocular pressure is within normal limits, making acute angle-closure glaucoma unlikely.

Question: A 31-year-old woman presents to the ED with dizziness. She has had ringing in her ears intermittently, but the dizziness began a few weeks ago and has become worse over time. On physical exam, you note nystagmus at rest that does not fatigue and poor balance with ambulation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reveals an enhancing lesion in the region of the internal auditory canal. From which cranial nerve does this disease process arise?
ExplanationEN:
This patient likely has a vestibular schwannoma (VS) (acoustic neuroma), a benign tumor that arises from the vestibular portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). Symptoms include progressive dizziness, tinnitus, hearing loss, and balance issues. The lesion’s location in the internal auditory canal and enhancing appearance on MRI are classic for this tumor.

Though histologically nonmalignant, they can significantly impact quality of life due to hearing loss and imbalance. VS makes up most cerebellopontine angle tumors and is increasingly detected due to widespread use of neuroimaging. These tumors typically present in individuals around age 50 years, with unilateral hearing loss being the most common symptom. Bilateral cases are rare and usually linked to neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2-related schwannomatosis).

VS originates from Schwann cells and can compress nearby cranial nerves and brain structures. Early symptoms result from cochlear nerve compression, leading to hearing loss, tinnitus, and disequilibrium. As tumors grow, they may affect the trigeminal and facial nerves, causing facial numbness or weakness. In advanced cases, large tumors can compress the brain stem and fourth ventricle, resulting in signs of increased intracranial pressure such as headache or nausea.

Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss is the key clinical feature, although some patients have normal audiograms. These individuals often report tinnitus, ear fullness, imbalance, or facial symptoms. VS grows slowly, often about 1 mm per year, and the average time from symptom onset to diagnosis is about 1 year. Because of its slow progression and variable symptoms, diagnosis can be delayed, particularly in those with subtle findings.

Differential diagnoses for asymmetrical hearing loss include Ménière disease and cerebellopontine angle meningiomas. Ménière disease tends to cause intermittent tinnitus and episodic vertigo, unlike the persistent imbalance of VS. Meningiomas may cause similar symptoms but more commonly result in facial weakness or trigeminal nerve deficits, helping distinguish them from VS.

Diagnosis typically involves an outpatient MRI, which is highly sensitive and allows for earlier detection and improved treatment outcomes. Audiometry is also performed, although CT is less useful due to poor resolution in the posterior fossa. Treatment depends on tumor size, symptoms, and patient factors and includes observation, surgical removal, or stereotactic radiation. Observation may suit older adults with small tumors, but most growing tumors eventually affect hearing. Surgery is favored for tumors > 3 cm, while smaller lesions may be treated with either surgery or radiation with similar long-term outcomes.



The facial (A) nerve may be compressed by the tumor, leading to facial weakness, but it is not the nerve of origin in VS.

Glossopharyngeal (B) nerve lesions would more likely cause dysphagia or impaired gag reflex, not dizziness or tinnitus.

Trigeminal (C) nerve involvement could cause facial numbness or pain, but not the vestibular and auditory symptoms described here.

Question: A 44-year-old man presents to the emergency department with weakness in his legs. He is generally healthy and went on a long hike 5 days ago in the woods. Today, he has gradually worsening difficulty walking and weakness in his legs. He has no other medical conditions. Physical exam reveals 3/5 strength in the bilateral lower extremities. His reflexes in the Achilles tendon and patella are reduced. Which of the following is the most appropriate method of supporting the diagnosis?

Options.text: MRI of the brain with and without contrast

ExplanationEN:
Tick paralysis is caused by a neurotoxin produced by certain ticks. This neurotoxin inhibits acetylcholine release. The classic presentation is an ascending flaccid paralysis with ataxia. Symptoms can progress to involve the respiratory muscles as well. When this diagnosis is suspected, a thorough dermatologic exam should take place to locate and remove the tick. Tick removal involves clasping the tick as close to the head as possible with forceps without crushing the body. The site should then be irrigated, and any retained parts should be removed. Symptoms will improve gradually once the tick is removed but may take hours to days for full symptom resolution.



Electromyography (B) can be used to diagnose many neuromuscular disorders, including traumatic peripheral nerve injury or myasthenia gravis. While it might help in understanding the weakness's nature, it is not the most direct approach given the acute onset and environmental exposure.

Lumbar puncture (C) demonstrating albuminocytologic dissociation is seen in Guillain-Barré syndrome. Guillain-Barré syndrome presents with ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia and abnormal sensation. Also, it can affect the muscles of respiration. It occurs as an autoimmune phenomenon after infection, with Campylobacter jejuni being the most common culprit. This patient does not report sensory deficits.

MRI of the brain with and without contrast (D) is appropriate in the diagnosis of central nervous system disorders such as multiple sclerosis. Multiple sclerosis is more common in young (age 20–40) women, and it presents with neurological deficits separated by time and space. Paresthesias, weakness, mood changes, and bowel and bladder symptoms are common initial presenting symptoms.

Question: A 52-year-old man presents to the ED for a facial droop. He noticed mild right ear pain this morning. An hour prior to arrival, he developed weakness on the right side of his face, associated with paresthesias and increased sensitivity to sounds. On exam, you notice a right-sided facial droop that involves the forehead and lower face. What is the appropriate next step in care to evaluate for Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

Options.text: Obtain a brain MRI with contrast
Order a CTA of the head and neck
Order serum varicella-zoster virus IgG and IgM titers

ExplanationEN:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, leading to a painful vesicular rash of the external ear and ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis. It is often more severe than Bell palsy and has a lower rate of complete recovery. This patient presents with ear pain, unilateral facial paralysis, and hyperacusis, which raises suspicion for Ramsay Hunt syndrome. The best next step is to perform an otoscopic examination to evaluate for vesicles on the external ear, ear canal, or tympanic membrane, which are hallmark findings of Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Vesicular lesions may also be present on the tongue or soft palate.

Distinguishing Bell palsy from Ramsay Hunt syndrome is important because treatment differs slightly. Bell palsy is typically idiopathic or associated with herpesvirus infection, whereas Ramsay Hunt syndrome is due to VZV reactivation. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is often more severe than Bell palsy and less likely to resolve completely, even with treatment. Patients with Ramsay Hunt syndrome require both corticosteroids and antivirals. Treatment should include valacyclovir or acyclovir and prednisone. Eye protection is also crucial due to incomplete eyelid closure.



MRI (A) is useful for evaluating central causes of facial nerve palsy, such as brain stem strokes, multiple sclerosis, or facial nerve tumors, but it is not the first step in evaluating Ramsay Hunt syndrome. MRI may show enhancement of the facial nerve in both Bell palsy and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, but this is not specific. A simple physical exam (otoscopy) is much faster, cost-effective, and specific for Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

A CTA (B) is indicated for stroke evaluation, particularly if there are concerns for large-vessel occlusion, but this patient’s presentation is more consistent with peripheral facial nerve palsy. A stroke that causes facial weakness typically spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation. In contrast, peripheral facial nerve lesions (such as Bell palsy or Ramsay Hunt syndrome) affect both the upper and lower face. Since the patient has no focal limb weakness, speech deficits, or other stroke symptoms, a CTA is not warranted.

While VZV is the causative agent of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, serologic testing for VZV (C) is not useful in acute diagnosis. Most adults will have positive IgG titers from prior VZV exposure (chickenpox or vaccination), and IgM titers do not reliably indicate acute reactivation. Instead, the diagnosis is clinical, based on facial paralysis, otalgia, and vesicular lesions in the external ear or mouth.

While lumbar puncture (LP) (D) can help diagnose infectious or inflammatory causes of facial paralysis (e.g., Lyme disease, VZV meningitis, or Guillain-Barré syndrome), it is not necessary for diagnosing Ramsay Hunt syndrome. The diagnosis is clinical, based on facial paralysis and vesicular eruptions in the ear or mouth. LP should only be considered if there are signs of meningitis, encephalitis, or other central nervous system involvement, which are not present in this case.

Question: A 93-year-old woman is boarding in the ED after being admitted to the hospital for a urinary tract infection. She is receiving IV ceftriaxone. The nurse notifies you that the patient is becoming increasingly agitated. She is not cooperative with a repeat examination and attempts to pull out her peripheral IV and climb out of the stretcher. What is the most appropriate pharmacologic agent for this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s change in mental status is due to delirium, which is characterized by a fluctuating course with impaired cognition, attention, or perception. Features of hyperexcitation or hypoactivity may be observed. The fluctuating course of delirium distinguishes it from other entities such as depression or dementia. Delirium most commonly occurs in the older patient population and is usually triggered by toxins, medications, metabolic derangement, infection, trauma, intracranial disease, or surgery. The primary management of delirium should be focused on addressing the underlying cause. Symptomatic care includes frequent reorientation, preserving sleep-wake cycles, limiting noise, and minimizing the use of medical equipment (catheters, wires, etc.). If nonpharmacologic measures are unsuccessful, pharmacologic therapy may be used.

The use of antipsychotics or sedatives in older patients should be done with caution, and age-adjusted doses should be used. Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine are appropriate first-line therapies. Olanzapine is available in oral, intramuscular, and intravenous forms. Typical adult dosing for hyperactive delirium is 5–10 mg IM or IV, but for older patients, dosing should be started at 2.5–5 mg. Physical restraints should be avoided unless all other options are exhausted and the patient continues to pose a threat to themselves or others.



Haloperidol (A) is a first-generation antipsychotic commonly used for the treatment of acute agitation in the ED. However, first-generation antipsychotics are associated with more side effects when compared to second-generation medications. If used for an older patient with hyperactive delirium, the starting dose should be 0.5–1 mg IM.

There is extremely limited evidence for the use of ketamine (B) in treating hyperactive delirium in older patients. Thus, it is not a preferred treatment.

Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam (C) and midazolam (D) may worsen delirium and should be avoided in the older population.

Question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with gradually worsening weakness. This morning, she had minimal symptoms but noticed after going on a hike that she felt fatigued and had double vision. Her T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 115/80 mm Hg, HR is 83 bpm, RR is 11/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. While waiting in the emergency department, she notices her symptoms are resolving. Physical exam reveals 5/5 strength in all extremities, and the patient is able to ambulate. However, after repeat exertion in the ED by having her walk around, she reports repeat weakness in the lower extremities and has 4/5 strength on exam. Which of the following is most likely to benefit this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) occurs secondary to autoantibodies that bind the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing neurotransmission. With repeat exertion, patients will have worsening weakness. The diagnosis is often made with electromyography and antibody testing. Treatment of mild and moderate episodes includes monitoring respiratory status and giving acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine. Pyridostigmine increases acetylcholine levels in the synaptic cleft, thus improving weakness. It is indicated in mild and moderate flares but is avoided in myasthenic crisis, as it could worsen respiratory symptoms.



Ceftriaxone and metronidazole (A) are unrelated to the treatment of MG symptoms and are typically used for bacterial infections, which do not align with this patient's clinical presentation.

Intubation (B) and plasmapheresis (C) are indicated in the management of a myasthenic crisis, which presents with severe weakness and respiratory failure not found in this patient. Patients often require early intubation, initial avoidance of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, and early plasmapheresis.

Question: A 45-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera presents to the ED with a severe headache for the past 3 days. He describes it as a persistent, worsening pressure that is different from his usual migraines. He also reports mild confusion, and he thinks he had a seizure yesterday. His vital signs are BP 155/95 mm Hg and HR 98 bpm. His neurological exam reveals mild dysarthria but no focal deficits. Noncontrast head CT is unremarkable. What is the best next step in care?

Options.text: Discharge home with headache precautions and outpatient neurology follow-up
Obtain CT venography of the head

CorrectAnswer: Obtain CT venography of the head
ExplanationEN:
Cerebral vein sinus thrombosis (CVST) can present with a subacute headache, seizures, and altered mental status, particularly in patients with hypercoagulable states such as polycythemia vera. While noncontrast head CT may be normal, the next step in evaluation is CT venography or MR venography, which can directly visualize thrombus within the venous sinuses. CT venography is often preferred in the emergency setting due to its rapid availability.

CVST occurs when thrombosis obstructs venous outflow, leading to intracranial hypertension, venous infarction, and sometimes hemorrhage. Risk factors include hypercoagulable conditions (e.g., malignancy, thrombophilias, pregnancy, polycythemia), infections (e.g., sinusitis, mastoiditis), trauma, and dehydration. The clinical presentation varies widely but commonly includes headache, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and altered consciousness. If left untreated, CVST can lead to progressive cerebral edema and brain herniation.

In the emergency department, once CVST is diagnosed, the cornerstone of treatment is anticoagulation. Neurosurgery or neurology consultation is required for severe cases, particularly if there is extensive thrombosis or impending herniation. Patients are admitted to a monitored setting for serial neurological assessments, and further workup for underlying thrombophilia is warranted. Long-term anticoagulation is typically continued for several months.



Although the patient has elevated blood pressure, it is not in the range of a true hypertensive emergency (≥ 180/120 mm Hg with end-organ damage). More importantly, the primary pathology in CVST is venous thrombosis, which this patient is at risk for based on his history of polycythemia. The pathology is not uncontrolled hypertension, making antihypertensive therapy with labetalol (A) inappropriate as the primary treatment.

Given the presence of new-onset seizures and persistent symptoms in a high-risk patient, immediate further evaluation is warranted. Discharging (B) the patient would delay diagnosis and increase the risk of worsening thrombosis and neurological deterioration.

While meningitis can cause headache and altered mental status, this patient lacks fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness. Additionally, CVST-related intracranial hypertension increases the risk of herniation following lumbar puncture (D), making this a potentially dangerous choice.

Thrombolytics (E) (e.g., tPA) are contraindicated in CVST because the underlying issue is venous, not arterial, thrombosis. Moreover, CVST-related infarcts are frequently hemorrhagic, increasing the risk of catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage if tPA is administered. While this patient has neurologic concerns that could be confused with acute stroke, his primary symptom is headache, and he is at risk for venous thrombosis.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents to the ED with right sided facial droop and slurred speech. Which of the following signs or symptoms most suggests a central etiology?

Options.text: Decreased taste on the anterior tongue

ExplanationEN:
The presence of bilateral forehead wrinkling suggests that the patient’s symptoms are most likely from a central source, such as an acute stroke. The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) innervates the muscles of facial expression. The peripheral nerve exits the skull base through the stylomastoid foramen and then splays into five segments within the parotid gland.

The motor nucleus of CN VII receives dual innervation from the bilateral cerebral cortices to supply the upper face but only unilateral innervation for the lower face. Any supranuclear lesion will cause deficits of the lower face, while the upper face will be spared. Therefore, patients who present with unilateral facial droop or facial asymmetry who are unable to wrinkle both sides of the forehead may be quickly ruled out as having an acute intracranial process as the cause of their facial asymmetry.



Decreased taste on the anterior tongue (B) may occur as the result of a peripheral facial nerve palsy. The chorda tympani nerve is a branch of the facial nerve that relays taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

Palatal vesicular lesions (C) suggest herpes zoster, which affects the peripheral cranial nerves, particularly the trigeminal nerve.

A positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver (D) suggests benign paroxysmal peripheral vertigo and should not be performed when a patient presents with stroke-like symptoms.

Question: A 10-year-old girl presents in the early fall with right leg weakness. Her parent first noticed the weakness yesterday, but this morning, the patient could not get up to get dressed and was choking and coughing while eating. She had symptoms of a mild gastrointestinal virus last week but has not had a fever or headache. She is well-appearing and alert, and her vital signs are within normal limits for her age. She has received all of her childhood immunizations. A detailed neurologic exam shows asymmetric bilateral leg weakness that is worse on the right. She also has right arm weakness and subtle weakness on the right side of her face compared to the left. She has decreased reflexes but no sensory deficit. Her head CT is within normal limits, and her CSF shows a total nucleated cell count of 400 cells/µL, a protein of 147 mg/dL, and a glucose of 84 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) is an acquired disorder of the motor neurons in the brain stem and spinal cord due to a viral infection. Outbreaks tend to occur in the late summer and early fall and most commonly affect children between 7 and 11 years of age. Most recently, enterovirus D68 and A71 are thought to cause most outbreaks, which tend to peak every other year on even-numbered years in the United States. Less commonly, flaviviruses and adenoviruses have been identified as causative agents.

Symptoms and testing are similar to poliomyelitis. Patients with AFM typically have symptoms of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal illness within the last few weeks. The weakness begins gradually and progresses over hours to days. The location of weakness varies but is most common in the legs and is usually asymmetric. It can involve cranial nerves VI and VII and include bulbar weakness. Patients may have double vision, facial weakness, difficulty speaking, and difficulty swallowing. Some present with bowel or bladder dysfunction, and rarely, there will be sensation changes.

Similar to polio, the virus is not typically found in the CSF. Instead, the virus is transmitted through the fecal-oral route and can be identified using a nasopharyngeal swab. CSF testing will show a mild pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein but normal glucose. MRI can identify lesions within the anterior horns of the spinal cord, which indicates this diagnosis over others.

Treatment is mostly supportive, and patients are often treated with steroids and intravenous immune globulin. Outside of the United States, some children have been given a medication called pleconaril, which has some effect against RNA viruses but is not available in the US. Unfortunately, some degree of paresis on recovery is typical.



Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) (B) is a peripheral nerve disorder typically triggered by a recent infection and has a similar presentation as AFM. Typically, these patients have a gradual onset of lower extremity weakness and lack of deep tendon reflexes. However, patients with GBS have a longer course of onset of weakness (8 instead of 3 days) and symmetric ascending weakness, and they frequently have sensory deficits.

Poliomyelitis (C) is also an acquired peripheral nerve disorder but is caused by poliovirus, which is an enterovirus and should be considered in any patient who has symptoms similar to AFM. Fortunately, the incidence of polio has been reduced significantly through vaccination. Two of the three wild polioviruses no longer circulate, and the final one is limited to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Mozambique, and Malawi. Polio cases caused by the use of live virus vaccines are ten times higher than those caused by wild polio.

A spinal cord infarct (D) can present with weakness and sensory loss in the arms and legs, and the severity and type of deficits depend on the affected area. However, a spinal cord infarct diagnosis is nearly always symmetric.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents to the ED secondary to altered mental status and left-sided weakness for the past hour. The patient has a history of hypertension and diabetes. An ECG shows sinus rhythm without any acute abnormalities. A chest X-ray reveals no acute process. A noncontrast CT of the brain shows no evidence of hemorrhage. Thrombolytic therapy is considered. Which of the following is a relative contraindication to thrombolytic therapy if found in this patient?

Options.text: Observed seizure at stroke onset with postictal neurologic deficits
Systolic blood pressure of 180 mm Hg

CorrectAnswer: Observed seizure at stroke onset with postictal neurologic deficits
ExplanationEN:
Thrombolytic therapy, such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), can be initiated in specific patients experiencing an acute stroke. The traditional inclusion criteria was a symptom onset of 180 minutes (3 hours). This has been expanded for a select population to 4.5 hours. Several absolute contraindications exist for the administration of tPA. An observed seizure at stroke onset is a relative contraindication as the patient's symptoms may be due to a postictal state or suggestive of an intracranial hemorrhage.



A stroke within the past 4 months (A) is not a relative contraindication. Instead, a stroke within the past 3 months is an absolute contraindication.

A platelet count < 100,000/µL (C), not 150,000/µL is an absolute contraindication.

A systolic blood pressure ≥ 185 mm Hg (D) or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mm Hg is an absolute contraindication.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a pulsating headache that she describes as severe. The headache has persisted for approximately 2 hours and is associated with vomiting. She usually gets these headaches and notes that her symptoms are preceded by visual spots, which she is experiencing today. Physical examination, including a detailed neurological exam, reveals no abnormalities or focal deficits. Which of the following is the best treatment at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Migraine headaches present with the classic symptoms of headache, nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and possible aura. On occasion, migraines may be associated with neurological deficits in conditions such as a hemiplegic migraine. The diagnosis of migraine is made clinically with careful attention to rule out or consider life-threatening differentials such as a subarachnoid hemorrhage. For moderate to severe migraine headaches, the three classes of medications recommended as initial parenteral therapy are antiemetic dopamine receptor antagonists, such as droperidol, metoclopramide, or prochlorperazine; migraine-specific agents, such as triptans and dihydroergotamine; and parenteral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, such as ketorolac.

Upon discharge from the emergency department, more than half of patients will experience residual headache, with an increased likelihood of headache recurrence within the first 3 days after discharge. It is advisable to include a prescription for abortive medications as part of the discharge plan for patients diagnosed with migraine in the ED (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, and combination therapies like sumatriptan-naproxen). Also, patients should be given a neurology referral for chronic and preventive migraine care.



100% oxygen via nasal cannula (A) is appropriate management of a cluster headache. Cluster headaches are more common in men and present with a focal, severe headache with an “ice pick” quality and unilateral tearing and rhinorrhea.

Acetaminophen (B) is often included in mild migraine headache treatment regimens. While administering acetaminophen to this patient is a reasonable approach, its effectiveness may be lower compared to treatments specifically tailored for migraines.

Sphenopalatine blocks (D) are not necessarily first-line treatments for migraine but can be highly effective in some patients. The sphenopalatine block procedure is indicated for patients experiencing migraine headaches who have not responded well to other treatments or who are seeking alternative options for treating their symptoms. It may be particularly useful for those with severe or refractory migraines or for patients who cannot tolerate or prefer to avoid systemic medications due to side effects or contraindications.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED with abnormal movements for the past 2 days. His partner brought him to the ED after noticing odd movements of the patient’s right arm. The patient states he noticed them but that they did not cause him any concern. He reports no personal or family history of neurologic disorders. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical exam shows brief, irregular right arm movements with otherwise normal findings on sensorimotor exam. Which of the following, if present, most likely contributed to this patient’s current condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is displaying hyperkinetic movements consistent with chorea, which is a movement disorder characterized by random, brief, irregular muscle contractions. It can be idiopathic, primary due to hereditary causes, or secondary from a variety of contributing causes such as drugs, infections, and structural lesions. The most common hereditary cause of chorea is Huntington disease, resulting from trinucleotide repeats within the huntingtin gene, while other hereditary causes include Wilson disease, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and ataxia-telangiectasia. Drugs are a commonly implicated acquired cause, with antidopaminergic agents (e.g., antipsychotics, certain antiemetics) being of particular importance. Haloperidol is an example of a first-generation antipsychotic with antidopaminergic properties that may contribute to the development of movement disorders, including chorea. Levodopa also causes drug-induced movement dyskinesias, including chorea, in up to one-half of patients who receive it.

Choreiform movements are most common in the distal extremities and face but can affect muscles involved in respiration and phonation. Patients are often unaware or unbothered by these movements, and they are often brought to clinical attention by family members. Evaluation of a patient with chorea should be aimed at a potential underlying cause via careful history to identify both hereditary and environmental risk factors. Chronic, progressive chorea is typically due to hereditary causes, while acquired causes more commonly cause acute or subacute symptoms. A basic workup for secondary causes should include a complete blood count, serum electrolytes and glucose, vitamin B12 and parathyroid levels, liver and thyroid function tests, and a pregnancy test in appropriate patients. Neuroimaging, preferably with MRI, should be obtained in cases of suspected structural lesions, such as with focal or unilateral chorea, but it may also identify changes related to more systemic or neurodegenerative disorders.

Management of secondary chorea primarily involves cessation of the offending agent, which is haloperidol in this case. Second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine, risperidone) are associated with fewer movement-related symptoms and can be considered as an alternative in appropriate patients. Acute management of dangerous or distressing symptoms may include pharmacotherapy with agents such as anticholinergics (e.g., benztropine), benzodiazepines, or dopamine agonists. The primary management strategy for patients with hereditary chorea is genetic counseling with symptomatic management for symptoms that produce functional impairment or social embarrassment.



Rarely, carbon monoxide toxicity (A) can cause movement disorders, including chorea, but this is much less likely than movement disorders caused by typical antipsychotic medications.

Ondansetron (C) is an antagonist at serotonin receptors rather than dopamine. It is not associated with the development of chorea.

Huntington disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by trinucleotide repeats on chromosome 4p (D) that causes hereditary chorea, but it is not likely in this case given the acuity of symptom onset and the lack of family history to suggest this diagnosis.

Question: A 66-year-old woman with an unknown medical history presents with burning in her hands and feet and stumbling when she walks. She reports taking multiple medications but is unable to name them. Her presenting symptoms are most likely caused by a regular medication used to treat which of the following conditions?
ExplanationEN:
Isoniazid (INH) is an antimicrobial with selectivity against mycobacterial infection (e.g., tuberculosis). It is usually used in combination with other antimycobacterial drugs such as rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. It competes with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) as a cofactor for neurotransmitter synthesis. One of the known side effects of INH is peripheral neuropathy. Other neurologic side effects include ataxia and paresthesias. These side effects are more common in patients with risk factors such as increased age, chronic liver disease, malnutrition, HIV infection, kidney failure, diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, pregnancy, breastfeeding, or pediatric patients. Treatment of neuropathy secondary to INH toxicity is with high-dose pyridoxine (100–200 mg/day). Other side effects of INH include hepatotoxicity, altered mental status, and status epilepticus.



Treatments used for atrial fibrillation (A) have not been found to have side effects of peripheral neuropathy. There are reports of peripheral neuropathy with amiodarone and dronedarone use, but these are not as regularly prescribed for atrial fibrillation. Treatments for hypothyroidism (B), such as levothyroxine and liothyronine, carry adverse effects such as tachycardia, dysrhythmias, heat intolerance, and tremors. Ferrous compounds (e.g., ferrous sulfate and ferrous fumarate) used to treat iron deficiency anemia (C) can cause nausea, vomiting, gastric bleeding, lethargy, and gastric outlet obstruction if taken in an overdose but do not usually cause adverse side effects at therapeutic levels.

Question: A call comes into the emergency medical service patch phone from a paramedic on the scene of a 13-year-old boy who has been having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure for the past 5 minutes. Paramedics have been unable to obtain IV access and ask for advice on medical management. Which of the following is the best advice?

Options.text: Continue attempts at IV access then administer lorazepam
Obtain intraosseous access then administer lorazepam

ExplanationEN:
Status epilepticus is defined as a prolonged seizure or recurrent seizures lasting > 5 minutes without regaining consciousness. While most seizures last < 5 minutes and do not require treatment, treatment of status epilepticus is associated with improved neurologic outcomes and is easier when treatment is initiated early. Benzodiazepines are the first-line medications for the treatment of status epilepticus. When IV access is easily and quickly obtainable, lorazepam is generally considered the benzodiazepine of choice, given its longer duration of action and better side-effect profile. However, when IV access would result in a delay in treatment of status epilepticus, other benzodiazepines are available and can be given via nonintravenous routes. Diazepam can be given rectally, and midazolam can be given either intranasally or intramuscularly. In 2012, a landmark paper about the RAMPART trial demonstrated that high-dose intramuscular midazolam is superior to IV lorazepam for the treatment of prehospital status epilepticus. This appears to be secondary to a significantly reduced time to medication administration. As such, intramuscular midazolam should be considered for the treatment of status epilepticus when IV access has not been obtained, especially in the prehospital setting.



Administering intramuscular lorazepam now (A) is not advised because the onset of action of lorazepam is too long when given intramuscularly to be of use in status epilepticus.

Continuing attempts at IV access and then administering lorazepam (C) would waste precious time for a patient who has status epilepticus. The benefit of intramuscular midazolam over IV lorazepam for the treatment of status epilepticus is likely due to its quicker administration time, which leads to faster resolution of seizures.

Obtaining intraosseous access and then administering lorazepam (D) can be considered, but it is an unnecessary procedure when alternative medications and routes of administration are available. Midazolam can be given intramuscularly and intranasally, and diazepam can be given rectally as well.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a headache, nausea, and vomiting. His symptoms are intermittent and improve when he lies down. The patient has a history of a central nervous system shunt but is otherwise healthy. He is currently afebrile and is reporting a headache. A CT scan is performed, as seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Neural and vascular changes causing headache

ExplanationEN:
Overdrainage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via a shunt can cause functional shunt failure resulting in slit ventricle syndrome. The pathophysiology is related to overdrainage of CSF, which reduces the size of the ventricles (making them appear slit-like on head imaging), causing the catheter to press against the ependyma and choroid plexus. These tissues subsequently block the holes in the catheter, decreasing its efficacy. This obstruction causes intraventricular pressure to increase (causing symptoms of headache and vomiting), resulting in expansion of the ventricles and reopening of the shunt, thus starting the cycle over again. Intermittent narrowing of the ventricles can subsequently cause fibrosis, which decreases ventricular ability to expand. This leads to suboptimal changes in ventricular size when CSF is produced. Treatment typically involves a neurosurgery consultation and possible replacement of the shunt.



Bacterial infection of the meninges (A) describes meningitis, which presents with a fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and a positive Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, and jolt accentuation of headache.

Bacterial infection of the shunt (B) can present in a patient who is asymptomatic or who has a low-grade fever and signs of increased intracranial pressure from shunt obstruction. Infection is also more likely in the first few months after shunt placement. Hydrocephalus would be a more likely finding on head imaging (due to obstruction of the shunt) rather than slit-like ventricles.

Neural and vascular changes causing headache (C) describes a migraine headache, which presents with a unilateral or pulsatile headache that can be associated with an aura such as vision changes or weakness. The headache onset will typically be gradual and is associated with a normal head CT.

Question: A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents with a headache. Yesterday she had a lumbar puncture performed as part of an outpatient evaluation for multiple sclerosis, and today she developed a severe headache. The headache is worse with standing and improves when lying flat. She has tried over-the-counter medications without relief. Her vital signs are unremarkable. She appears uncomfortable but has no neurologic deficits. What is the most effective management of this condition?
ExplanationEN:
The patient presenting with a positional headache after a lumbar puncture (LP) has a postdural puncture headache, for which the definitive treatment is an epidural blood patch. The exact cause of postdural puncture headache is unclear, but it is thought to be due to continued leakage of CSF from the puncture site resulting in decreased intracranial pressure and increased traction on pain-sensitive areas of the brain and meninges. Procedural factors that may increase the rate of postdural puncture headache include the use of a larger needle, the use of a cutting needle, multiple attempts, and orientation of the needle perpendicular as opposed to parallel to the longitudinal axis of the spine. Patient factors that are associated with a higher incidence of postdural puncture headache include female sex, pregnancy, history of prior headaches, and ages 18–50 years compared to extremes of age. Patients typically present within 72 hours of an LP or epidural anesthesia. The headache is classically worse with standing and improves when lying flat. Patients with minor symptoms can be treated supportively with oral medications and intravenous fluids, and the headache usually resolves within 1 week. The treatment of choice for those with severe, debilitating symptoms is an epidural blood patch. An epidural blood patch is performed by injecting the patient’s venous blood into the epidural space. While the exact mechanism of action of epidural blood patching is not known, clotted blood may plug the dural puncture site and stop the continued leakage of CSF. Relief from an epidural blood patch is usually immediate, and reported success rates range from 65–98%.



While intravenous fluids and bed rest (B) may help alleviate symptoms, these supportive measures should be reserved for the patient whose headache is relatively minor, as they are not as effective as epidural blood patching. Ketorolac and metoclopramide (C) are preferred agents for the treatment of migraine headache. While they can be used as an adjunct for the treatment of postdural puncture headache, they are not as effective as epidural blood patching. Morphine (D) may provide temporary relief but is not definitive management, and the headache will likely persist after the medication has worn off.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a headache. He also reports neck stiffness and chills at home for the past day. Vital signs are T 101.1°F (38.4°C), BP 132/74 mm Hg, HR 86 bpm, and RR 18/min. There is nuchal rigidity and a positive Brudzinski sign on exam. Which of the following features, if present, would warrant empiric treatment for a fungal etiology of meningitis?

Options.text: Concomitant dermatologic infection of the face

ExplanationEN:
Fungal agents are of increasing concern in recent years due to a higher incidence of fungal meningitis. This increase may be due to higher numbers of immunosuppressed patients in the setting of organ transplants and autoimmune disease. It is estimated there are > 1 million cases annually in the United States, most commonly caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, with species of Candida and Aspergillus implicated as well. In addition to iatrogenic immunosuppression, other risk factors for fungal meningitis include HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancy, and immunosuppression from chronic disease, though some agents (e.g., Coccidioides) can infect immunocompetent hosts. Cases of Candida infection are usually associated with candidemia or implanted neurosurgical hardware.

Fungal meningitis usually occurs via hematogenous spread but can result from direct invasion, especially in cases of fungal sinusitis (e.g., mucormycosis). Clinical presentation is similar to that of infectious meningitis with other causes and includes headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity, though these may occur on a subacute or chronic basis. Findings on CSF analysis usually include normal or low glucose, total cell count < 500/µL, and protein > 200 mg/dL. Initial Gram stain will be negative due to a lack of bacterial organisms, but both bacterial and fungal cultures should be sent. India ink stain showing encapsulated organisms is the test that is classically positive in cases of Cryptococcus.

Antifungal therapy should be initiated empirically in cases of suspected meningitis with specific risk factors for fungal agents. Patients with advanced or untreated HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancies, and other chronic diseases causing immunosuppression, or who use immunosuppressive drugs, should be considered at high risk for fungal meningitis, and empiric treatment should be initiated. Initial therapy often consists of amphotericin B and flucytosine, with step-down to tailored therapies when appropriate. Common complications of fungal meningitis include abscesses, seizures, invasive bone infections, and ocular abnormalities.



Dermatologic infections of the face (A), IV drug use (B), facial trauma (C), and prior intracranial hemorrhage and craniotomy (D) all carry an increased risk of complications, some involving the CNS like herpes meningitis or other serious bacterial illnesses. However, these risk factors are not specifically associated with a higher incidence of fungal meningitis and do not warrant empiric treatment.

Question: A 65-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with his daughter, who is concerned he has had a stroke. She last saw him at his baseline 4 days ago. His CT is notable for hypoattenuation of the medial aspect of the right frontal cerebral cortex. Which of the following physical examination findings would be expected in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Ischemic strokes are the most common type of stroke and can be caused by thrombosis, embolism, and hypoperfusion. Thrombosis is the most common cause of ischemic stroke. Risk factors for ischemic stroke include smoking, increasing age, male sex, diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. The middle cerebral artery is the artery most commonly affected by ischemic strokes. Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) infarcts are rare due to collateral blood flow supplied by the anterior communicating artery. The ACA supplies the frontal (superior and medial aspects), prefrontal, and supplementary motor cortex. Symptoms of an ACA infarction include contralateral lower extremity weakness and sensory loss with sparing of the upper extremity and face. CT is poorly sensitive for the diagnosis of ischemic stroke in the first 48 hours, and MRI is the test of choice. Early CT findings in ischemic stroke include hypodensity, loss of gray-white differentiation, and effacement of sulci.



Arm weakness and aphasia (A) is consistent with infarction in the territory of the middle cerebral artery, which supplies the temporal lobe, parietal lobe, internal capsule, and the posterior portion of the frontal lobe. Symptoms depend on what area of the artery is involved as well as which lobe is dominant in the patient. Typical symptoms include contralateral hemiparesis (involving both the arm and leg, in contrast to an ACA stroke), facial droop, and sensory loss. Involvement of the dominant lobe will result in aphasia, which may be expressive, receptive, or both.

Ataxia, nystagmus, and dysarthria (B) is consistent with a stroke involving the posterior circulation, the territory supplied by the vertebrobasilar system. Strokes of the posterior circulation vary in symptoms depending on which area of the posterior circulation is involved.

Hemianopsia (C) is concerning for infarction in the territory of the posterior cerebral artery, which supplies the occipital lobe. Symptoms of a posterior cerebral artery stroke are subtle and may include ataxia, vertigo, contralateral motor weakness, and visual field cuts.

Question: A 64-year-old man is brought to the ED by his spouse due to a rapidly progressive cognitive decline over the past 6 weeks. He has developed frequent muscle jerks and gait instability, and he is now intermittently mute. He has no significant medical history and has not traveled recently. Neurologic examination reveals increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and startle-induced myoclonus. MRI of the brain shows hyperintensity in the caudate nucleus and putamen on diffusion-weighted imaging. Bedside EEG reveals periodic sharp wave complexes. What is the most likely prognosis for this condition?

Options.text: High risk of recurrence after initial response to corticosteroids

ExplanationEN:
This presentation is classic for sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion-mediated neurodegenerative disorder characterized by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, characteristic MRI diffusion restriction in the basal ganglia, and periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG. The disease course is uniformly fatal, with most patients dying within 6–24 months of symptom onset.

CJD has several variants, including sporadic CJD (most common, due to spontaneous prion misfolding), familial CJD (inherited mutations), and iatrogenic CJD (transmitted via contaminated medical instruments or biologic products). Variant CJD is acquired from bovine spongiform encephalopathy-contaminated beef and typically affects younger patients with prominent psychiatric symptoms early.

Sporadic CJD is not acquired through typical infection or person-to-person transmission. It arises from spontaneous misfolding of the normal cellular prion protein PrPC into the abnormal pathogenic form PrPSc. This misfolded protein induces further misfolding of normal prion proteins, leading to neuronal loss, spongiform change, and rapid neurodegeneration. Unlike variant or iatrogenic CJD, there is no history of exposure to contaminated food or medical instruments.

A definitive diagnosis is established by neuropathologic confirmation, which demonstrates prion deposition and spongiform encephalopathy in brain tissue (obtained through autopsy or biopsy). In clinical practice, a diagnosis of probable CJD is made based on the characteristic clinical syndrome, together with supportive tests such as MRI showing cortical and basal ganglia diffusion restriction, CSF biomarkers, and EEG findings.

There is no effective disease-modifying treatment, and treatment is supportive and palliative.



Gradual decline over 10 years (B) is characteristic of neurodegenerative dementias such as Alzheimer disease or frontotemporal dementia, which develop over many years. In contrast, CJD progresses rapidly, often within weeks to months. This patient’s 6-week history of worsening cognitive function, myoclonus, and akinetic mutism is too fast for typical dementias, and his imaging and EEG findings strongly support a diagnosis of prion disease.

Chelating agents (C) are used to treat heavy metal toxicity, such as lead or mercury poisoning. While those conditions may cause cognitive changes or tremor, they do not produce the MRI findings seen here, nor do they cause periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG. Additionally, the rapid progression to mutism and the presence of startle-induced myoclonus are not features of heavy metal toxicity but are classic in CJD.

High risk of recurrence after initial response to steroids (D) refers to autoimmune encephalitis, such as limbic encephalitis or steroid-responsive encephalopathies like Hashimoto encephalopathy. These may initially improve with immunosuppression and sometimes relapse. However, CJD does not respond to steroids and is relentlessly progressive. The MRI findings and EEG pattern are also not typical for autoimmune encephalitis.

Rapid recovery after ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting (E) is possible in normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). It presents with a triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline, and may improve dramatically with VP shunting. However, NPH is not associated with myoclonus, startle reflex, or basal ganglia hyperintensities on MRI. The EEG in NPH is usually unremarkable. In contrast, CJD leads to inexorable deterioration, and surgical interventions such as VP shunting offer no benefit.

Question: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a headache and associated nausea and dizziness that started last night (14 hours ago) while she was jogging. She indicates this is the worst headache she has ever had, and it has not improved after taking acetaminophen and ibuprofen. She has a history of migraines and a previous ectopic pregnancy. Her medications include acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and sumatriptan for her headaches. Her examination is normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic evaluation for this patient?

Options.text: Noncontrast CT of the head followed by CTA of the head if the initial CT is negative

CorrectAnswer: Noncontrast CT of the head followed by CTA of the head if the initial CT is negative
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a headache that could be consistent with spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Her headache is different than previous headaches, is the worst headache she has ever had, and is associated with symptoms of nausea and dizziness that can be found in patients with SAH. Additionally, patients with SAH frequently develop symptoms while engaged in activities that cause increased blood pressure, such as exercise.

The imaging modality of choice when SAH is suspected is a noncontrast CT of the head. The sensitivity of CT in diagnosing SAH is highest shortly after symptoms begin and is estimated to be 98–100% within 6 hours of the onset of symptoms. Sensitivity decreases to about 91% at 24 hours and continues to decline rapidly thereafter, reaching 50% at 1 week. For suspected SAH, a negative head CT is typically followed by a lumbar puncture (LP) or CTA of the head to evaluate for an aneurysm. Given the life-threatening nature of this disease and the fact that head CT is not 100% sensitive for SAH after several hours, further evaluation after an initial normal noncontrast head CT is required.



As already mentioned, a noncontrast CT of the head (C) would not complete the workup for a patient suspected of SAH if she had symptoms for > 6 hours. Newer generation CT scanners have improved capability in detecting SAH, especially within 6 hours of the onset of symptoms and in those with focal neurological signs. However, a negative head CT in a patient suspected of having SAH 14 hours after symptom onset should be followed by an LP or CTA of the head.

Similarly, CTA (A) can help diagnose SAH in a patient suspected of the diagnosis who presents for evaluation > 6 hours after symptom onset. However, this test would only be performed after negative noncontrast head CT imaging.

MRI of the brain (B) is another option but has limited utility. The major disadvantages of MRI are availability, time to perform the examination, and cost.

Question: A 24-year-old man who emigrated from Mexico 5 years ago presents to the ED via EMS after he had a seizure at home. His spouse noticed tonic-clonic activity that lasted about 1 minute. The patient has no significant medical history. Vital signs are BP 138/89 mm Hg, HR 105 bpm, T 37.7°C, RR 18/min, and SpO2 100% on room air. He is somnolent but responds to verbal commands and is moving all four extremities purposefully. A CT scan is obtained and seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cysticercosis is caused by the larval form of the tapeworm Taenia solium, a common CNS pathogen found in many tropical areas. It is acquired by humans who swallow eggs found in the feces of a person who has an intestinal tapeworm. The adult worm matures in the small intestine. The larval form may penetrate through the gut wall and end up anywhere in the body. The most common sites include the CNS, muscle, and soft tissue. In the brain, the larvae form an expanding cyst that induces an intense immunologic reaction from the host. Neurologic symptoms begin when the involved neural tissue cannot accommodate the enlarging cyst. Seizure activity often is the first indication of cysticercosis, which should be considered in any adult patient with undiagnosed seizures, especially immigrants. CT scan with contrast or MRI may reveal a ring-enhancing lesion. These lesions may mimic a CNS abscess, metastasis, or primary tumor. Benzodiazepines are used to treat an actively seizing patient. Albendazole is the treatment of choice for Taenia solium. Corticosteroids may be necessary if there is edema due to CNS cysts. Neurologic consultation is recommended for neurocysticercosis because obstructive hydrocephalus is a complication.



Meningioma (B) is a benign tumor that is usually asymptomatic when < 2.0 cm in size. It is typically an incidental finding on neuroimaging that is located near the inner surface of the skull or tentorial dura. Herpes encephalitis (A) can present with fever and seizures. However, a ring-enhancing lesion would not be present on imaging. HSV encephalitis is associated with CT scan changes in the temporal and frontal lobes. Toxoplasmosis (D) is a protozoan infection by Toxoplasmosis gondii. This typically leads to focal encephalitis in patients with AIDS, most commonly with a CD4 count < 100 cells/µL. Contrast-enhancing CT typically shows ring-enhancing lesions with toxoplasmosis as well.

Question: A 29-year-old woman presents with 4 days of ascending weakness in both legs. She reports difficulty walking, with symptoms beginning in her feet and progressing to her thighs. She has no fever, headache, or neck stiffness. Her deep tendon reflexes are absent in the lower extremities. On review of the record, she had an ED visit 2 weeks ago for diarrhea. Which diagnostic study is recommended next based on the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy characterized by rapidly progressive, symmetric, ascending muscle weakness. Most patients report symptoms beginning in the distal lower extremities with subsequent progression to involve proximal muscles, upper extremities, and sometimes respiratory or bulbar muscles. Reflexes are typically diminished or absent. Antecedent infections, especially GI or respiratory illnesses (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus), are commonly reported 1–3 weeks before symptom onset.

CSF analysis is essential for the diagnosis of GBS and often reveals albuminocytologic dissociation, characterized by an elevated protein concentration with a normal WBC count. This finding typically occurs after the first week of symptom onset. Thus, a normal CSF early in the disease process does not always exclude the diagnosis. In the ED, CSF evaluation via lumbar puncture is a crucial step in the initial diagnostic workup, particularly when clinical suspicion is high, as it helps distinguish GBS from mimics, including infectious and structural CNS conditions.

Acutely, the priority is rapid recognition of GBS, assessment of respiratory function (including forced vital capacity), and early neurology consultation for further diagnostic and treatment decisions.



A brain MRI (A) is useful in evaluating central causes of weakness such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, or transverse myelitis. However, GBS is a peripheral demyelinating condition, and MRI findings are often normal or nonspecific. Although MRI may be performed to exclude other conditions, it is not confirmatory for GBS. This patient’s clinical features, including absent reflexes and ascending symmetric weakness, make a central cause less likely.

Electromyography (EMG) (C) and nerve conduction studies can confirm GBS by showing demyelination and decreased conduction velocity. However, these tests are typically not performed in the ED and may be normal in early disease. EMG is more useful for subtyping and confirming chronicity but is not the first-line diagnostic test for suspected GBS during the initial evaluation.

Like EMGs, nerve conduction studies (D) support the diagnosis of GBS but are rarely available in the acute care setting and require specialized equipment and personnel. Additionally, abnormal findings may not appear until several days after symptom onset. Therefore, while useful for confirmation and prognosis, they are not the best initial test.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a headache and confusion. He is currently in a group living situation focused on coding and computer science. His T is 103°F (39.4°C), BP is 75/40 mm Hg, HR is 132 bpm, RR is 25/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals the rash above. Manipulation of the head causes significant pain and discomfort. The patient is not able to follow commands. Head CT imaging is normal. Despite intravenous fluid infusion and vasopressors, the latest BP is 88/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen for the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Bacterial meningitis is a condition with high morbidity and mortality if not recognized and treated early. In healthy adults aged 18–50 years, common causes of meningitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae. Neisseria meningitidis is more common in patients who live in close quarters and have contact with others, such as college students or military recruits. When disseminated, life-threatening meningococcemia can occur. It peaks in winter. In the US, the mortality rate is 40%.

Meningococcemia symptoms vary from mild fever to rapid, fatal disease progression. Common symptoms include fever, headache, irritability, lethargy, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, and runny nose. About 27–77% of patients show classic hemorrhagic skin lesions, potentially escalating to purpura fulminans, hypotension, adrenal hemorrhage, and multiorgan failure. The standard treatment for confirmed meningococcemia involves penicillin G for adults and a weight-based dose of penicillin for children, with low penicillin resistance observed in the U.S. Although penicillin is a first-line therapy, initial treatment for suspected meningococcal sepsis or meningitis often includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime due to their efficacy, safety, and broad coverage. Chloramphenicol is an alternative for patients allergic to penicillin and cephalosporins. For fulminant cases, treatment may require airway management, IV fluids, vasopressors, monitoring for cardiovascular and electrolyte issues, and possibly hemodialysis or fresh frozen plasma for complications. The use of steroids in meningococcemia without meningitis is debated, with current recommendations suggesting consideration only for patients with persistent shock after other treatments.



Acyclovir and vancomycin (A), while effective against a range of viral and bacterial pathogens, are not tailored to the likely bacterial cause suggested by the patient's symptoms and living situation. Additionally, there's no indication of herpes encephalitis (e.g., focal seizures, temporal lobe abnormalities on imaging) that would necessitate acyclovir.

Ampicillin and gentamicin (B) provide coverage against Listeria monocytogenes, a concern in neonates, patients > 65 years, and those who are immunocompromised, and some gram-negative bacteria, but it is not the first-line therapy for suspected meningococcal meningitis in a young adult.

Vancomycin and hydrocortisone (D), while likely to be included when empirically treating meningitis, do not provide appropriate coverage for Neisseria meningitidis. Vancomycin provides coverage against resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis.

Question: A 17-year-old boy from New Jersey presents with a 1-day history of facial droop. He also reports a headache. The cutaneous image above represents a rash the patient described having 3 weeks prior to arrival. In addition, you note mild nuchal rigidity. A noncontrast head CT is performed, and findings are normal. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a rash consistent with erythema migrans and facial nerve palsy, indicating a likely early disseminated Lyme disease infection. Serologic testing should be performed.

Lyme disease is primarily transmitted via the Ixodes scapularis tick. The disease manifests in many phases, beginning with early Lyme, which typically demonstrates (in 90% of cases) the classic erythema migrans rash. The rash begins at the site of the bite and progresses outward. It typically exhibits central clearing. During this time, patients may also experience nonspecific, flu-like symptoms. Acute disseminated infection occurs after the hematogenous spread of the spirochete and can result in neurologic, cardiac (heart block), rheumatologic, and ophthalmic manifestations. The most common neurologic manifestation is meningoencephalitis with superimposed cranial neuropathies.

Diagnosis of Lyme disease often starts with serologic testing, but clinicians should interpret the results carefully and in the correct clinical context. Antibodies to the spirochete take 3–6 weeks to develop, which means false-negative results can occur early in the disease process. Additionally, false-positive results are common because serologic cross-reactivity can occur with other spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum. It is recommended to pair serum serologic testing with CNS evaluation in patients with neuroborreliosis. A lumbar puncture will show lymphocytic pleocytosis with a moderately elevated protein level. However, most patients with this patient's clinical presentation will test positive for Lyme disease through serum serology, making lumbar puncture unnecessary. Neuroborreliosis is treated with ceftriaxone. Empiric treatment should begin immediately after serologic testing is done.



Acyclovir and corticosteroids (A) are often prescribed for Bell palsy but are not effective in Lyme disease.

Lumbar puncture (B) is not always needed in an individual with the classic erythema migrans rash who resides in an endemic area and presents with CNS manifestations. Although it is recommended to pair CNS evaluation with serum serologic testing, most patients will test positive for Lyme disease on serum serology. If clinical suspicion is high and a patient tests negative on serum serology, lumbar puncture is recommended.

An MRI of the brain (C) is unnecessary, as this lesion does not represent a central cranial nerve lesion.
