Question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the ED with 4 days of rapidly worsening vision in the right eye associated with severe eye pain that is worse with eye movement. She reports decreased color vision and photophobia. Examination reveals markedly reduced visual acuity in the right eye, a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and pronounced optic disc edema with peripapillary hemorrhages. Brain MRI is normal. Orbital MRI shows long-segment enhancement of the right optic nerve extending from the globe to the orbital apex without optic chiasm involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with severe optic neuritis characterized by rapid vision loss, intense pain with eye movement, and prominent optic disc edema with peripapillary hemorrhages. These findings favor myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD). MOGAD-associated optic neuritis is frequently anterior and is associated with marked disc swelling in approximately 70–80% of cases, often more severe than that seen in multiple sclerosis (MS).

MRI findings further support this diagnosis. MOGAD commonly demonstrates long-segment optic nerve enhancement, often extending over much of the nerve, while sparing the optic chiasm. In contrast, MS-associated optic neuritis involves shorter segments of the retrobulbar optic nerve. A normal brain MRI is also typical at initial presentation in those with MOGAD. A positive serum MOG-IgG in the appropriate clinical and MRI context confirms the diagnosis.

MOGAD is a distinct inflammatory demyelinating disorder that often presents with optic neuritis in adults aged 20–30 years. Recognition is important because patients respond well to high-dose corticosteroids, though relapses are common, and long-term immunotherapy may be required.



Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (A) primarily affects children and presents with encephalopathy and multifocal neurologic deficits. Brain MRI demonstrates widespread demyelinating lesions rather than isolated optic neuritis.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (B) presents with headache and bilateral papilledema due to elevated intracranial pressure. It does not cause painful eye movement, unilateral vision loss, or optic nerve enhancement on MRI.

MS (C) presents with retrobulbar involvement and minimal or absent optic disc edema. MRI of the orbit typically shows shorter segments of optic nerve enhancement, and brain MRI often reveals periventricular or juxtacortical demyelinating lesions, which are lacking in this case.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) (E) and related optic neuritis is often bilateral, severe, and more likely to involve the optic chiasm. It is associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies rather than the imaging pattern seen here. The lack of chiasmal involvement makes NMOSD less likely.

Why is differentiating myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) from multiple sclerosis (MS) important in regard to treatment decisions?

Reveal Answer:
MOGAD is treated with corticosteroids and long-term immunosuppression, while MS requires disease-modifying therapies that are ineffective or harmful in MOGAD.

Question: A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with numbness and weakness in his left hand. He states that he slept on a bench last night and awoke this morning with these symptoms. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation over the first, second, and third digits, and a wrist drop is present. What is the next step in the care of this patient?

Options.text: Noncontrast CT scan of the head
Orthopedic referral for carpal tunnel release surgery
Wrist splint and follow-up with neurology

CorrectAnswer: Wrist splint and follow-up with neurology
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a radial nerve palsy likely caused by direct compression. He should have a wrist splint placed and be prescribed follow-up with a neurologist. The radial nerve arises from the C5–T1 roots, exits the brachial plexus, and passes into the spiral groove behind the proximal humerus. It bifurcates at the antecubital fossa. This nerve controls the extension of the fingers, thumb, and wrist and sensation over the dorsum of the first, second, and third fingers.

Compression of the radial nerve in the axilla occurs secondary to the improper use of crutches or from an extended period of unconsciousness with prolonged compression. This pathology is typically called a Saturday night palsy. Patients with radial nerve palsy present with weakness in extension of the fingers and wrist. Spontaneous recovery often occurs but may take 2–4 months. During this time, the wrist should be splinted with 60° of volar extension to prevent atrophy and contractures.



CT of the cervical spine (A) may be indicated in a patient suspected of having a cervical radiculopathy. The patient may have pain in the neck that radiates into the arm.

MRI of the brain (B) and CT scan of the head (C) are not indicated, as this is a peripheral nerve injury, not a disease of the central nervous system. A patient presenting with hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffman sign, or other symptoms suggestive of central nervous system disease (e.g., vision loss, ataxia) should undergo neuroimaging.

Orthopedic referral for carpal tunnel release surgery (D) would be appropriate for a patient with severe carpal tunnel syndrome. Carpal tunnel syndrome presents with numbness and tingling involving the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger. Patients may also experience symptoms that radiate up the arm and usually have nighttime symptoms that can awaken them from sleep. There may be clumsiness of the hand, weak thumb abduction and thumb opposition, and atrophy of the thenar eminence.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with painful unilateral vision loss. She states it started this evening and has persisted. The patient has no significant medical history and is not currently taking any medications. Her vital signs and an initial ECG are within normal limits. When the patient’s neck is flexed, she feels an electrical pain down her neck and back. An afferent pupillary defect is present in the affected eye. Which of the following is the best initial treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disorder. Demyelination can cause seemingly unrelated symptoms, including paresthesias, weakness, urinary or bowel incontinence, and loss of pain or temperature sensation. Ophthalmoplegia can be seen in this condition, which presents with an inability to adduct the affected eye. Other unique symptoms include optic neuritis (which can present with a painful unilateral loss of vision) and the Lhermitte sign (which presents with electrical pain that radiates down the neck and spine when the head is flexed). Diagnosis can be supported with MRI (preferred) or lumbar puncture demonstrating oligoclonal bands, and the best initial treatment in an acute exacerbation is a steroid such as high-dose methylprednisolone.



Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and dexamethasone (A) is an appropriate initial antibiotic regimen for bacterial meningitis, which would present with fever, headache, photophobia, jolt accentuation of headache, and a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign.

Plasmapheresis (C) may be indicated in conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, which would present with a loss of deep tendon reflexes and ascending weakness or paralysis that could affect the diaphragm after a viral or diarrheal illness.

Riluzole (D) is an appropriate treatment for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which can present with limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, emotional lability, limb muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, dysarthria, dysphagia, and difficulty with mastication.

Question: A 67-year-old woman presents with a gradual-onset headache that has been present for several days. Examination is notable for tenderness over the left temple. Vital signs include a BP of 126/84 mm Hg, HR of 80 bpm, RR of 17/minute, SpO2 of 99% on room air, and T of 98.8°F. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test to order?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s symptoms suggest temporal arteritis. Temporal arteritis, also known as giant cell arteritis, affects large- and medium-sized vessels. Temporal arteritis occurs most commonly in patients > 50 years of age.

The pain may occur anywhere on the head but is usually localized to the temporal region. Up to half of patients may report a history of jaw claudication with chewing due to vascular insufficiency of the masseter and temporalis muscles. It can also affect vision, typically with transient monocular vision loss called amaurosis fugax early in the disease process, and there is a risk of permanent vision loss.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are markedly elevated in most patients. ESR and CRP are not specific for temporal arteritis, but they are helpful in ruling out temporal arteritis if both are within normal limits and are most appropriate as the initial diagnostic study. A definitive diagnosis is made with a temporal artery biopsy. Treatment is with long-term high-dose steroids and should not be delayed pending biopsy. Untreated temporal arteritis leads to visual loss in 50% of patients.



Lumbar puncture with opening pressure (B) is an important part of the evaluation for patients with suspected meningitis or idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not temporal arteritis.

MRI of the brain (C) is is used to evaluate central nervous system pathologies such as tumors, strokes, or demyelinating diseases. High-resolution MRI with MRA may be performed as part of the evaluation of temporal arteritis, but laboratory studies are typically obtained first.

Noncontrast head CT (D) is indicated in the evaluation of headaches suspicious for subarachnoid hemorrhage, mass, traumatic injury, or ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction. It is also indicated in the workup of a suspected acute stroke to help differentiate ischemic versus hemorrhagic stroke.

Temporal artery biopsy (E) is recommended to confirm the diagnosis of temporal arteritis, but it is not the initial diagnostic study. Additionally, obtaining the biopsy should not delay treatment to reduce the risk of permanent blindness.

Question: Which of the following would be the best pharmacologic treatment option for managing acute delirium and agitation in an older patient?
ExplanationEN:
Delirium is characterized by a disturbance in attention and awareness that develops over a short period of time (hours to days) and can fluctuate in severity during the day. There are also disturbances in cognition, including memory, language, visual-spatial ability, or perception. Comorbid illnesses, especially previous stroke, dementia, or Parkinson disease, advanced age, male sex, and medications are all predisposing factors in the development of delirium. Any acute systemic or central nervous system stressor can be a precipitating cause. Although the exact pathophysiology of delirium has not been determined, it is often associated with an alteration in cholinergic transmission.

The management of delirium centers on screening for and treating any possible underlying etiologies. Pharmacologic treatment of agitation is also frequently necessary. The drug of choice should have a low incidence of side effects, a short half-life, little to no effect on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, and be easy to administer. Haloperidol, a dopamine-blocking agent, meets these criteria and is the primary medication used for the management of acute agitation in older patients. Extrapyramidal side effects and prolongation of the QT interval are potential adverse effects but the incidence of both is relatively low.



Diazepam (A), a benzodiazepine, should be avoided due to its long half-life and risk of drug accumulation with multiple doses.

Diphenhydramine (B) has anticholinergic side effects and is thus not recommended in older patients.

Unless agitation is deemed to be due to pain, morphine (D) and other opioid analgesics should not be given for the treatment of delirium.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Yes. QT prolongation is more likely with intravenous administration.

Question: A 31-year-old man presents to the ED with right-sided facial pain. He recently moved to a cold environment from a warm, humid environment and has noticed debilitating pain along his right cheek whenever he is exposed to cold wind. He reports the pain lasts anywhere between a few seconds to a few minutes and feels sharp. He is currently pain-free, and his exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is most likely to improve his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is describing symptoms suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia, a disorder of cranial nerve V. This illness tends to cause paroxysmal episodes of severe, unilateral facial pain often triggered by innocuous sensory stimuli on that part of the face. Examples of triggers can include facial hygiene, chewing, and exposure to hot or cold temperatures. Attacks are unpredictable, and the duration is typically brief, lasting a few seconds to a few minutes. Autonomic symptoms, such as tearing and rhinorrhea, may be present. The diagnosis is primarily based on history in the presence of a normal exam with no neurologic deficits.

First-line management of trigeminal neuralgia is sodium channel blockers, such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. Surgical evaluation for microvascular decompression or stereotactic radiosurgery is an option if medical management fails.



Acetaminophen (A) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories are unlikely to prevent or manage painful episodes of trigeminal neuralgia.

High-flow oxygen inhalation (C) is first-line treatment for cluster headache, which is not this patient’s diagnosis. Cluster headaches are characterized by unilateral head or facial pain accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms and restlessness. The duration of cluster headaches is longer than trigeminal neuralgia, lasting between 15 and 180 minutes.

Sumatriptan (D) can be used in the management of migraine, not trigeminal neuralgia. Typical migraine headaches are pulsatile, associated with nausea and photophobia or phonophobia, and can last hours to days.

Question: A 56-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia undergoing chemotherapy is brought to the ED with 1 week of progressive headache, photophobia, and confusion. He is febrile and somnolent but arousable. Physical exam reveals neck stiffness and no focal neurologic deficits. Brain MRI shows basilar meningeal enhancement without mass lesions. CSF analysis reveals elevated protein levels, low glucose levels, and predominance of lymphocytes. CSF fungal cultures are pending, but galactomannan is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is immunocompromised and presents with a subacute meningoencephalitic syndrome, CSF findings of fungal meningitis, and positive galactomannan in the CSF, which strongly supports the diagnosis of Aspergillus meningitis. Galactomannan is a polysaccharide component of the Aspergillus cell wall that is released during active infection. While it can also be detected in serum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid in pulmonary aspergillosis, detection in CSF is highly specific for CNS aspergillosis, especially in patients with risk factors such as hematologic malignancy and neutropenia.

Clinical signs and symptoms of Aspergillus meningitis include subacute headache, fever, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits, seizures, and cranial nerve palsies. Symptoms often progress insidiously and may be accompanied by stroke-like features due to fungal angioinvasion, causing cerebral infarction.

MRI findings may include basilar meningeal enhancement, infarcts, or parenchymal lesions due to angioinvasion. CSF culture is often negative, making antigen detection essential for early diagnosis.

Treatment requires prompt initiation of antifungal therapy, with voriconazole as first-line treatment due to superior CNS penetration and improved survival. Liposomal amphotericin B is an alternative, particularly in cases of intolerance or resistance. Combination therapy may be considered for patients with severe or refractory disease. Treatment also includes reversal of immunosuppression when feasible, close neurologic monitoring, and neurosurgical consultation for abscesses or obstructive hydrocephalus.



Candida meningitis (B) can cause meningitis in patients with neutropenia, but galactomannan testing is not the primary diagnostic modality for candidiasis. Candida meningitis is diagnosed by mannan antigen and antimannan antibody testing or direct culture. The CSF galactomannan positivity in this patient points specifically toward Aspergillus.

Coccidioidal meningitis (C) is unlikely without endemic exposure history (southwestern US, parts of Central or South America). Coccidioidal meningitis is diagnosed by CSF anti-Coccidioides antibodies and Coccidioides antigen testing, not by galactomannan testing.

Cryptococcal meningitis (D) is less likely despite being common in patients with a weakened immune system. The positive CSF galactomannan specifically indicates Aspergillus, as galactomannan testing does not detect Cryptococcus. Additionally, cryptococcal meningitis would be diagnosed by cryptococcal antigen testing.

Tuberculous meningitis (E) remains in the differential diagnosis for any patient with basilar meningeal enhancement, elevated protein, low glucose, and lymphocytic predominance. However, the positive CSF galactomannan strongly favors Aspergillus over tuberculosis.

Vital signs and physical examination, including her neurologic and fundoscopic evaluations, are unremarkable. What is the best next step to obtain the diagnosis?

Options.text: CT noncontrast of the head followed by lumbar puncture
MRI of the brain with venography

CorrectAnswer: MRI of the brain with venography
ExplanationEN:
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is a challenging diagnosis to make due to the nonspecific symptoms along with the age group it most commonly affects. The incidence is increasing secondary to improved detection related to more advanced imaging modalities being used within the emergency department. Risk factors include prothrombotic states, oral contraceptives, pregnancy or peripartum period, malignancy, infection, and head injury. Clinical features most commonly include headaches with or without vomiting, visual problems, papilledema, focal neurological deficits or seizures, mental status changes, stupor, or coma.

Diagnosis is made with neuroimaging identifying thrombosis of one of the cerebral venous sinuses. MRI with MR venography is the most sensitive and preferred imaging modality to make the diagnosis. If this is not available, the next best imaging study is the CT venogram.

Anticoagulation is the treatment of choice, with the current recommendation being low-molecular-weight heparin. If the patient develops neurological worsening, then endovascular thrombolysis or thrombectomy may be required.



CT noncontrast of the head (A) is the initial evaluation for ischemic stroke, not for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. The patient above does not have any neurologic deficits, and although this may be the initial test performed, a head CT will be normal in 30% of patients.

CT noncontrast of the head followed by lumbar puncture (B) is the sequence of tests that should be performed if one is concerned about subarachnoid hemorrhage. A noncontrast CT has been shown to be sufficient to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage if it is performed within the initial 6 hours of symptoms. If a patient presents after this timeframe, a lumbar puncture evaluating for xanthochromia should be performed. This patient has had a headache for 2 weeks and does not have presenting symptoms typical of a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Lumbar puncture with opening pressure (C) is performed to make the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Previously known as pseudotumor cerebri, idiopathic intracranial hypertension is defined as a condition of increased intracranial pressure with normal CSF analysis and no other causes evident on neuroimaging or other evaluations. Patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension will demonstrate papilledema on funduscopic exam or have a dilated retinal sheath on ultrasonography of the eye suggestive of papilledema.

Question: What is the most common cause of an intracranial neoplasm?
ExplanationEN:
Intracranial neoplasms encompass a diverse group of conditions characterized by the abnormal proliferation of cells within the cranial cavity. These neoplasms can be broadly classified as primary, originating from brain tissues, or secondary (metastatic), arising from cancer cells that have spread from other body sites. Primary brain tumors include gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary adenomas. Clinical presentations can vary based on tumor location, size, and growth rate, with common symptoms including headaches, seizures, cognitive or sensory deficits, and personality changes.

Metastatic disease (primarily from lung cancer) is the most common cause of an intracranial neoplasm. These secondary neoplasms arise from the hematogenous spread of malignant cells from primary sites elsewhere in the body, with other common sources including breast, melanoma, and kidney cancers. MRI with contrast is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosis, allowing detailed visualization of the lesions and surrounding edema. Treatment strategies often involve a combination of surgery, radiation therapy (such as whole-brain radiotherapy and stereotactic radiosurgery), and systemic chemotherapy or targeted therapies, depending on the tumor type and primary cancer.



Acoustic neuromas (A), also known as vestibular schwannomas, are benign tumors that originate from the Schwann cells of the eighth cranial nerve. The most common clinical presentation is unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which may be accompanied by tinnitus. They are less common than brain metastases.

The malignant gliomas, anaplastic astrocytomas (B) and glioblastoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase-wildtype (glioblastoma multiforme), are the most common glial tumors. These are located in the cerebral hemispheres.

Meningiomas (C) are generally benign, slow-growing tumors that originate in the meninges.

Pituitary adenomas (E) are tumors originating from the pituitary gland and are often first noted when the patient exhibits decreased vision from compression of the optic chiasm. Pituitary adenomas can also present with decreased libido and erectile dysfunction in male patients and menstrual cycle disorders in female patients.

Hunt and Hess scale classifies severity of subarachnoid hemorrhage to predict mortality
Treatment is supportive (blood pressure control with IV agents), euvolemia, and nimodipine (prevents vasospasm and other neurologic complications)

A head CT confirms the presence of subarachnoid hemorrhage. What is this patient’s grade, according to the Hunt and Hess classification of subarachnoid hemorrhage?

Question: A 10-year-old boy returns to the ED for the second time in a week, reporting a right-sided headache. He was also seen for a right-sided headache 5 days ago and had thick nasal drainage and a fever. A diagnosis of acute sinusitis was made, and he was discharged on amoxicillin-clavulanate, nasal spray, and decongestants. Today, he returns for continued pain above his right eye, fever, vomiting, and confusion. Vital signs are T 39.4°C, BP 85/40 mm Hg, HR 130 bpm, and RR 32/min. His exam is notable for drowsiness, confusion, and yellow nasal discharge from both nares. Which of the following findings confirms the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Elevated leukocytes, low protein, and normal glucose in the cerebrospinal fluid
Elevated white blood cell count with left shift
Ring-enhancing lesion seen on CT scan of the head with IV contrast

CorrectAnswer: Ring-enhancing lesion seen on CT scan of the head with IV contrast
ExplanationEN:
This child has an intracranial abscess caused by local spread of infection from his frontal sinus. The imaging modality of choice is CT or MRI with contrast, which may show one or more ring-enhancing lesions. The ring of contrast enhancement is the inflammatory capsule surrounding the abscess. The infection reaches the brain via three mechanisms: contiguous spread from the middle ear, sinus, mastoid, or teeth; directly from trauma or neurosurgery; or hematogenously (cardiac, skin, pelvic, intra-abdominal, and pulmonary infections.) The most common symptom is headache, with one-third of patients also having fever and a focal neurologic deficit. Other symptoms stem from increased intracranial pressure and include hemiparesis, seizure, vomiting, and confusion.



Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (A) are also nonspecific markers of inflammation and cannot be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Cerebrospinal fluid with increased leukocytes (B) raises the suspicion of a CNS infection but does not confirm the diagnosis. If there is a high clinical suspicion that an intracranial abscess is present, a lumbar puncture should be avoided due to the increased risk of brain herniation.

An elevated white blood cell count (C) is nonspecific and cannot confirm the diagnosis.

A concomitant influenza infection (D) is possible but does not explain all of the patient’s findings.

Question: A 2-month-old infant presents to the emergency department with loss of consciousness and tonic-clonic activity that is ongoing for 10 minutes in the upper and lower extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to administer at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Status epilepticus (SE) in pediatrics is a neurological emergency characterized by a prolonged seizure or a series of seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them. Recent guidelines consider SE as any continuous seizure activity lasting > 5 minutes or two or more seizures between which there is incomplete recovery of consciousness.

In children, SE can have various causes, including febrile seizures (common in children aged 6 months to 5 years), infections such as meningitis or encephalitis, epilepsy syndromes, metabolic disturbances (including electrolyte imbalances, hypoglycemia, and inborn errors of metabolism), brain injury (resulting from trauma, hypoxia, or stroke), toxins, and drug withdrawal.

SE can manifest as convulsive SE (characterized by visible, continuous convulsive movements and is the most common and recognizable form) and nonconvulsive SE (characterized by a change in behavior and consciousness without overt convulsions, which can be harder to recognize without electroencephalography).

The management of SE in children is a stepwise approach aimed at stopping the seizure as quickly as possible, identifying and treating the underlying cause, and preventing recurrence. Key steps include initial stabilization (assessing and managing the airway, breathing, and circulation to ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation and establishing intravenous access) and pharmacotherapy. The first-line treatment includes the administration of benzodiazepines, such as lorazepam or diazepam. Later-line therapies (if seizures persist after initial benzodiazepine treatment) include agents such as fosphenytoin or phenytoin, levetiracetam, and valproate. In refractory SE, intensive care management, including continuous EEG monitoring and potential anesthetic agents, like propofol or pentobarbital, may be required.

In treating pediatric SE, the choice and administration route of benzodiazepines are tailored to the clinical setting. Lorazepam is preferred for intravenous use due to its longer action within the central nervous system. Midazolam is recommended for intramuscular, intranasal, or buccal routes when IV access is challenging, offering rapid absorption and effect. Diazepam is suggested for rectal administration, especially when other routes are not feasible. The prognosis depends on the underlying cause, age of onset, and the duration of the SE. Early recognition and prompt treatment are crucial to reduce the risk of long-term neurological damage and improve outcomes.



Levetiracetam (B), phenobarbital (C), and phenytoin (D) are all later-line agents for SE and would not be given first line. These agents would be tried once benzodiazepines have failed.

What is the mechanism of action of phenobarbital in terms of seizure control?

Reveal Answer:
Increases the duration of gamma-aminobutyric acid type A channel opening and reduces N-methyl-D-aspartate activity.

Question: A 37-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a right-sided facial droop. He states over the past 3 days, it has been more difficult moving the right side of his face. In addition, he also noticed he is more sensitive to sound and is having difficulty closing his right eye. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals paralysis of the right side of his facial muscles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?

Options.text: Peripheral nerve palsy of cranial nerve VII

CorrectAnswer: Peripheral nerve palsy of cranial nerve VII
ExplanationEN:
The patient is experiencing facial droop involving the forehead which is the typical presentation for Bell palsy also known as peripheral palsy of the seventh cranial nerve. Other symptoms can include hyperacusis and decreased tear production. An important distinction to make during the exam is the involvement of the forehead. The innervation of the upper facial muscles is bilateral and that of the lower facial muscles unilateral. If the patient has weakness in the lower half of his or her face but not the upper half, an intracranial process should be suspected. Most often the cases are idiopathic with no known cause. The prognosis of Bell palsy is excellent, with 85% of patients regaining function within 3 weeks.



Clinicians should have a low threshold to suspect a stroke (C) especially if there is forehead sparing, involvement of other cranial nerves, weakness or numbness of arms or legs, headaches, visual deficits, or nausea and vomiting. Ischemic stroke is the second leading cause of unilateral facial paralysis after Bell palsy. However, there usually are comorbid conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, or cardiovascular disease to increase your suspicion.

Lyme disease (A) often presents with other symptoms preceding facial paralysis such as erythema migrans, heart block, or arthritis. Often times patients do not recall exposure to a tick. This patient has no rash, heart block, or joint pain.

Trigeminal neuralgia (D), also known as tic douloureux, is a severe unilateral pain in the trigeminal nerve lasting only seconds. It is usually associated with a headache and most commonly occurs in middle-aged women. Patients have normal neurological examinations.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for Bell palsy?

Reveal Answer:
Currently, the recommended treatment regimen for Bell palsy is prednisone, 60–80 mg per day, for 1 week. Antivirals are indicated in severe cases.

Question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to thrombolytic therapy in a patient presenting with acute ischemic stroke?

Options.text: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the preceding 21 days

CorrectAnswer: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the preceding 21 days
ExplanationEN:
The idiom “time is brain” underscores the importance of swift action in the diagnosis and treatment of acute stroke. The stroke subtype needs to be identified and an appropriate course of treatment implemented without delay. Because ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage require drastically different treatment strategies, rapid identification of each subtype is critical. Acute ischemic stroke represents 87% of all stroke events and may occur due to in situ thrombosis or embolic events. Ischemic strokes affect either the anterior or posterior circulation, and the resulting neurologic deficits depend highly upon the anatomic regions of the brain supplied by the occluded vessel and the degree of collateral circulation present.

The characteristic patterns of presentation depend upon the particular location of the lesion. When strokes occur in the anterior circulation, a combination of motor weakness, sensory deficits, facial asymmetry, language deficits (e.g., aphasia), and ocular abnormalities (e.g., visual field deficits) can be expected. Strokes of the posterior circulation are often more subtle in presentation and may cause gait ataxia, dizziness, headache, and sensorimotor deficits. Patients with suspected stroke should be evaluated clinically via the NIH stroke scale followed by noncontrast CT of the head to rule out hemorrhagic stroke prior to determining their eligibility for reperfusion therapy.

Patients with acute ischemic stroke should be considered for thrombolytic therapy (e.g., tissue plasminogen activator), for which there exist several inclusion and exclusion criteria. The three primary inclusion criteria for thrombolytic use are age ≥ 18 years, measurable diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke, and symptom onset < 4.5 hours prior to thrombolytic administration. Examples of absolute contraindications to thrombolytic therapy include platelets < 100,000/mm3, INR > 1.7 or prothrombin time > 15 s, gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the preceding 21 days, current use of direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors, history of prior intracranial hemorrhage, symptoms to suggest subarachnoid hemorrhage, known intracranial neoplasm or arteriovenous malformation, and recent intracranial or spinal surgery. Examples of relative exclusion criteria or warnings include blood glucose < 50 mg/dL, age > 80 years, pregnancy, and major trauma or surgery in the preceding 14 days.



There is no maximum age criterion for excluding thrombolytic use, so age > 90 years (A) is not a contraindication. However, age > 80 years is a relative contraindication or warning, especially 3–4.5 hours after symptom onset.

There is no threshold of anemia (C) that excludes patients from eligibility for thrombolytic therapy.

Thrombocytopenia with a platelet count (D) < 100,000/mm3 is an absolute exclusion criterion for thrombolytic administration.

A blood glucose < 50 mg/dL (E) is a relative contraindication to the use of thrombolytics, as low blood glucose can be the sole cause of neurologic findings. Patients with hypoglycemia should have the abnormality rapidly corrected and have a neurologic reassessment. If neurologic deficits remain with a normal blood glucose level, thrombolytic administration may be indicated.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 38-year-old man with a history of underlying psychiatric disease presents to the ED with strange facial and tongue movements. He was recently started on a new medication, but he cannot remember the name. He has difficulty describing his exact underlying psychiatric condition, and the friend with him does not know the details regarding the patient’s chronic medical issues. On exam, the patient is smacking his lips periodically and twisting his tongue in and out of his mouth. He is also holding his head stiffly and tilted to the left. What neurotransmitter imbalance is responsible for the development of this syndrome?

Options.text: Altered calcium channel gating, leading to an excess accumulation of calcium and thus hypermetabolism
Decreased circulating dopamine and gamma-aminobutyric acid, leading to a surplus of acetylcholine and glutamate
Dopamine receptor blockade, leading to increased cholinergic activity

CorrectAnswer: Dopamine receptor blockade, leading to increased cholinergic activity
ExplanationEN:
The clinician should recognize this patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction, a medication-induced movement disorder characterized by sudden, involuntary muscle contractions that cause abnormal postures or repetitive movements. These reactions commonly involve the muscles of the face, neck, and head, such as tongue twisting, lip smacking, cheek puffing, blepharospasm, torticollis, and oculogyric crisis. Other presentations may include shoulder shrugging, finger splaying, toe extension, hip thrusting, and rocking or swaying. In contrast to tardive dyskinesia, which tends to affect the entire body and occurs with prolonged exposure, acute dystonia appears within hours to days of starting or increasing the dose of a dopamine-blocking agent.

The most frequently implicated medications are first-generation antipsychotics (such as haloperidol) and antiemetics with dopamine antagonism (such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine). Less commonly, other agents such as certain antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and antimalarials may contribute. The underlying mechanism involves an imbalance between dopaminergic and cholinergic neurotransmission in the basal ganglia. Dopamine receptor antagonism results in reduced dopamine activity, which disinhibits acetylcholine release, leading to excessive cholinergic activity and resulting motor symptoms.

Diagnosis is clinical and based on the characteristic timing and presentation in the setting of a known offending agent. Rapid recognition is essential, as the symptoms can be distressing or even dangerous.

Treatment involves immediate administration of anticholinergic agents such as diphenhydramine or benztropine, which restore the dopaminergic-cholinergic balance and usually relieve symptoms within 30 minutes. Benzodiazepines can also be used as adjuncts to reduce anxiety and muscle rigidity. Because the half-life of most causative agents exceeds that of the anticholinergics, repeated dosing or a short course of scheduled anticholinergics may be necessary to prevent recurrence.

Once stabilized, patients should discontinue or switch from the offending agent to prevent future episodes. Alternative medications with lower extrapyramidal side effect profiles, such as second-generation antipsychotics, may be considered based on the underlying indication for therapy.



Altered calcium channel gating, leading to an excess accumulation of calcium and thus hypermetabolism (A), is the pathophysiology of muscle rigidity found in patients with malignant hyperthermia. This is a life-threatening clinical syndrome of hypermetabolism involving skeletal muscle. It is triggered in susceptible individuals who receive certain types of anesthetic agents or succinylcholine. Malignant hyperthermia occurs in patients with an inherited disorder that puts them at risk for the syndrome. These patients typically present in the operating room with tachycardia, rigidity, increasing temperature, myoglobinuria, and hyperkalemia. Treatment is with dantrolene and supportive care.

Decreased circulating dopamine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), leading to a surplus of acetylcholine and glutamate (B), is found in patients with Parkinson disease. It can be difficult to differentiate Parkinson disease from drug-induced parkinsonism. Dopamine receptor antagonists are implicated in drug-induced parkinsonism. Symptoms include rigidity, akinesia, and tremor. However, in true Parkinson disease, the dopamine receptors are not blocked. Instead, there is a deficiency of dopamine and GABA, leading to an imbalance in acetylcholine and glutamate. Treatment for Parkinson disease is with levodopa, the chemical that is converted to dopamine.

Excess circulating serotonin (D) produces a life-threatening syndrome called serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome presents with mental status changes, hyperactivity, tremors, clonus, muscle rigidity, and hyperreflexia. These patients will also have hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia. Serotonin syndrome generally occurs when patients either overdose on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or combine these medications with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Treatment is with benzodiazepines and supportive care.

Reveal Answer:

Question: Ventriculoperitoneal shunts are used in the setting of hydrocephalus to divert cerebrospinal fluid from the cerebral ventricles to the abdominal cavity. Which of the following time intervals best identifies when most ventriculoperitoneal shunt infections occur following placement?
ExplanationEN:
Approximately 50–70% of infections of CSF shunts will occur within the first month following surgical placement and in most cases are due to coagulase-negative staphylococci or Staphylococcus aureus likely acquired in the perioperative period. Fever is generally present, but additional signs and symptoms are nonspecific. Meningeal symptoms or findings may not be observed because communication between the infected ventricles and the meninges is altered by the presence of the shunt. Thus, the time course of fever and associated illness symptoms in relation to surgical placement is a key feature in the identification of a CSF shunt infection.



Late-occurring ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection, such as those occurring > 1 year (C) or > 5 years (D) following placement, represents a minority of all infections. It is often associated with peritonitis that may arise as a complication of appendicitis or, less commonly, due to catheter end perforation of the bowel leading to ascending infection. Ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection rarely occurs within the first week (B) following placement.

One Step Further
Question:
When did the modern era of surgical ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement begin?

Reveal Answer:
Around 1960, when the combined invention of artificial valves and silicone led to a worldwide therapeutic breakthrough in the development of implanted shunts achieving long-term success.

Question: Which of the following features, in addition to progressive cognitive decline, is most consistent with a diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies?
ExplanationEN:
Dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most common cause of degenerative dementia. Cognitive dysfunction is often the first presenting symptom but, unlike Alzheimer disease which presents with memory loss initially, it is more often characterized by early impairment in attention and executive and visuospatial function. Memory impairment usually comes later in the disease process.

The presence of progressive cognitive decline, in addition to at least two of the core clinical features - fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism - are essential for a probable diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. Visual hallucinations occur in up to two-thirds of patients, as opposed to those with Alzheimer disease who rarely have visual hallucinations. The symptoms of parkinsonism (e.g., bradykinesia, rigidity, gait disorder) typically begin concurrently or shortly after the onset of cognitive decline.



Autonomic dysfunction (A) and delusions (C) can also be found in patients with dementia with Lewy bodies but are not considered core features of the disease.

Cerebrovascular disease (B) is more often associated with focal neurologic deficits and abnormal neuroimaging, which are not hallmarks of dementia with Lewy bodies.

Deposition of beta-amyloid protein and neurofibrillary tangles.

Question: A 66-year-old man presents to the ED with loss of vision and weakness on his left side lasting about 1 hour. The patient has a medical history of hypertension and dyslipidemia and is currently taking no medications. His vital signs show BP 170/90 mm Hg, and the neurological exam on presentation is normal. An ECG and noncontrast head CT are within normal limits. Which of the following is the best next treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a temporary reduction or cessation of blood flow to the CNS that results in neurologic dysfunction without acute infarction. Symptoms are transient and may have resolved by the time the patient presents to the emergency department. The etiology can be secondary to cardiogenic and noncardiogenic sources.

Noncardioembolic TIAs can occur secondary to atherosclerosis, plaque rupture, and a hypercoagulable state, among many other etiologies. The American Heart Association recommends that treatment of a noncardiogenic TIA is short-term dual antiplatelet therapy, including aspirin and clopidogrel, as first-line agents for high-risk patients with TIA who present within 24 hours of symptom onset. This patient qualifies as high-risk given his presentation with both motor weakness and visual symptoms. Treatment should be initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset and continued for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy.

On the other hand, cardiogenic causes of a TIA are usually secondary to atrial fibrillation. The treatment of cardiogenic causes of TIA is typically anticoagulation.



Heparin (B) may be an appropriate initial measure for a cardiogenic TIA as a bridge to therapy with warfarin.

Rivaroxaban (C) is a novel anticoagulant that can be used when there is a cardiogenic source of a patient’s TIA but is not indicated early in those with a noncardiogenic TIA.

Warfarin (D) may be appropriate after initial therapy with heparin in a patient with atrial fibrillation.

Question: Which of the following is the most common presenting sign or symptom of a primary brain tumor in a 3-year-old child?
ExplanationEN:
Pediatric primary brain tumors are the most common solid tumors in children and a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality in childhood. Peak incidence is in children 5–10 years old. Supratentorial tumors are more common in children < 1 year of age and > 10 years of age. Infratentorial tumors are more common in children 1–10 years old. Children are also more likely to have histologies tied to developmental biology rather than environmental exposures or metastatic disease.

Common tumor types include medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymoma, and diffuse midline glioma (H3K27 altered). Each has a characteristic age distribution, location, and growth pattern, which heavily influences both presentation and management. Presenting signs and symptoms vary based on tumor location, but children may present with signs of increased intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, papilledema), ataxia, cranial nerve deficits, or more subtle symptoms such as behavioral changes or loss of developmental milestones. Macrocephaly is the most common presenting sign in children < 4 years old with brain tumors, presumably due to the plasticity of the skull in children and the relative volume that the tumor occupies.

Diagnosis is typically made with advanced brain imaging. A CT scan of the head can be performed in the ED setting, but carries the risk of radiation exposure. In otherwise stable patients without neurologic deficits, a risk-benefit discussion with parents can be used to determine the best testing to perform. Ideally, an MRI with contrast, which allows detailed evaluation of tumor location, cystic versus solid components, and involvement of critical structures, would be performed to avoid radiation exposure. However, this is not often readily available in the ED. Therefore, patients with suspected brain tumors may require close outpatient follow-up or admission to the hospital, depending on the physical exam, presenting symptoms, caregiver comfort, and access to timely follow-up.

Management typically requires multidisciplinary care involving neurosurgery, oncology, radiation therapy, and supportive services. Maximal safe surgical resection is pursued whenever feasible, as the extent of resection is a major prognostic factor for most pediatric tumors. Therapy is then tailored by tumor type and molecular profile and ranges from observation (pilocytic astrocytoma after complete resection) to chemotherapy-first approaches in very young children to delay radiation and combined chemoradiation for malignant or metastatic tumors such as medulloblastoma.



The anterior fontanel normally closes between 9 and 18 months of age, and the posterior fontanel typically closes by 3–4 months of age. A bulging fontanel (A) can be associated with prematurity, hypothyroidism, hydrocephalus, increased intracranial pressure, and brain tumors. Although a bulging fontanel can be seen in young children with brain tumors, it occurs much less frequently than macrocephaly and would not be expected in a 3-year-old child because the fontanels would likely be closed.

Headache (B) is the most common presenting symptom of a brain tumor in children ≥ 4 years old and occurs in 33% of these children. Headaches from pediatric brain tumors often show progressive frequency or severity and are classically worse in the early morning due to overnight carbon dioxide retention and increased intracranial pressure. They may be accompanied by recurrent vomiting without nausea, particularly on awakening, and can temporarily improve after emesis. Red flag features include nighttime awakening, positional worsening (especially with Valsalva), and association with neurologic deficits, behavior changes, or decline in school performance.

Nausea and vomiting (D) occur in approximately 30% of all children with brain tumors, which is still less common than macrocephaly. However, recurrent vomiting without nausea, especially when this occurs in the morning, is more concerning for a primary CNS lesion.

Seizures (E) are one of the most common presenting symptoms of brain tumors in adults, and the type of seizure depends on the location of the tumor. However, seizures are much less likely to be the presenting symptom in children with brain tumors.

Question: A 65-year-old woman presents with a headache. She describes 2 months of headache, which has been intermittent and worse in the cold weather. The pain is throbbing and located at the left temple. On physical examination, she has tenderness over the left temple. Which of the following diagnostic tests should be obtained next?

Options.text: C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate

CorrectAnswer: C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with classic symptoms of giant cell arteritis and should have a C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) sent to help confirm the diagnosis. Giant cell arteritis or temporal arteritis is a systemic inflammatory syndrome of small and medium sized arteries. The disease affects women more frequently than men and occurs later in life (average age 71). Headache is the most common initial presentation. It is typically subacute and temporally located. Jaw claudication is often seen as well. Physical examination often reveals tenderness over the scalp and temporal artery. A CRP and ESR, if markedly elevated, help to confirm the diagnosis. ESR is typically > 100 mm/hr. Definitive diagnosis is obtained by biopsy of the artery. However, when the history is convincing for the disease, corticosteroids should be started if the biopsy will be delayed, as vision loss frequently occurs in untreated patients.



CT scan (B) and MRI (D) are not necessary or helpful in the diagnosis. Lumbar puncture (C) is also not necessary as the symptoms are not consistent with a subarachnoid hemorrhage or infectious etiology.

Question: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute right arm ataxia and right leg weakness suggestive of a stroke. Which of the following is most likely to elucidate the etiology of this patient’s stroke?

Options.text: Deep venous ultrasound of the lower extremities

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms suggestive of an acute ischemic stroke, which can be secondary to thrombotic or embolic events. He has two neurologic deficits that can be localized to two different arterial supplies. Multiple simultaneous infarcts suggest an embolic source of an ischemic stroke, and localization should focus on finding a common potential source of the embolisms.

First, his right leg weakness is suggestive of a lesion in the distribution of the left anterior cerebral artery, which originates from the left internal carotid artery. The anterior cerebral arteries supply the most frontal and medial aspects of the brain, including motor and sensory function of the legs, as can be visualized in the cortical homunculus.

The patient’s second neurologic deficit is his right arm ataxia, which is suggestive of a right-sided cerebellar lesion. Cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral deficits due to a double crossing of fibers. The cerebellum gets its vascular supply from the vertebral arteries, which usually originate from the subclavian arteries. As such, this patient has two lesions, one in the distribution of the right vertebral artery and one in the distribution of the left internal carotid artery. The most proximal source that gives rise to these two vessels is the heart, which is best visualized with echocardiography.



Brain CT scan (A) would show the locations of the two ischemic events, but these would only be considered the source in the setting of a thrombotic stroke, which, as noted above, is considered less likely in the setting of multiple simultaneous infarcts. CT findings might not be as sensitive as MRI for detecting small or posterior fossa infarcts.

Carotid Doppler (B) or CT angiogram of the neck is often used to evaluate for carotid artery plaques that are at risk for embolization. Left carotid artery stenosis would put this patient at risk for his left anterior cerebral artery embolism and associated right leg weakness. However, given that the cerebellum is supplied by the vertebral arteries, which arise proximal to the carotid arteries (and in this case, on the contralateral side), the source of embolization is expected to be proximal to the aortic arch and not elucidated with imaging of the carotid arteries.

Deep venous ultrasound of the lower extremities (C) is often used to evaluate embolic strokes in young patients or patients whose workup has revealed no other source of the embolism. A deep venous thrombosis can cause a stroke if there is a patent foramen ovale or other septal defect allowing venous thrombi to cross to the systemic arterial circulation. This is a relatively rare cause of embolic strokes, especially in the older patient population.

Question: A 49-year-old man presents to the ED after being found unconscious in his house. He was immediately intubated in the field by EMS for airway protection. A head CT in the ED shows subarachnoid hemorrhage that is likely aneurysmal. The patient is awaiting transfer to the neuroendovascular suite to secure the aneurysm via pipeline embolization. Vital signs are BP of 155/85 mm Hg, HR of 110 bpm, and T of 38.2°C (100.8°F). Other notable lab results include hemoglobin 9 g/dL, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 3,000 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

Options.text: Initiate nicardipine for systolic blood pressure goal < 140 mm Hg
Start nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours via nasogastric tube after obtaining enteral access
Transfuse red blood cells for hemoglobin goal > 10 g/dL

CorrectAnswer: Start nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours via nasogastric tube after obtaining enteral access
ExplanationEN:
In patients presenting with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH), prompt initiation of nimodipine, a second-generation dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, has been shown to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI). After aSAH, significant morbidity is related to cerebral infarction and DCI. Extravasated blood in aSAH is believed to cause inflammation, sympathetic nervous system activation, microthrombosis, and cerebral autoregulatory failure. Evidence suggests that nimodipine can reduce the risk of morbidity and mortality related to this phenomenon.



Administration of four-factor prothrombin concentrate (A) has demonstrated efficacy in the rapid reversal of warfarin and direct oral anticoagulant-associated intracranial hemorrhage. This intervention does not improve outcomes in patients with aSAH who are not taking anticoagulants.

While the risk of rebleeding in aSAH is associated with increased blood pressure, decreasing blood pressure via a titratable infusion for blood pressure control (B) also increases the risk of DCI. Current American Heart Association/American Stroke Association guidelines recommend gradual reduction of systolic blood pressure (SBP) in patients with SBP > 180–200 mm Hg with strict avoidance of hypotension, as this can lead to reduced cerebral perfusion. Often, the treatment goal is SBP < 160 mm Hg. Ideally, this should occur after blood pressure response to nimodipine has been evaluated. In any case, this patient’s SBP is already < 160 mm Hg.

Although red blood cell transfusion (D) may improve brain tissue oxygenation, blood transfusions are associated with multiple adverse effects, and their utility in patients with aSAH and noncritically low hemoglobin is not robustly validated.

Question: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents with severe, increasing lower back pain. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 136/82 mm Hg, heart rate of 70 bpm, respiratory rate of 17/min, oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and temperature of 98.8°F. His lower extremity strength is 4/5 bilaterally. He has no bowel or bladder dysfunction and no perianal anesthesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate imaging test?

Options.text: CT myelography of the thoracic and lumbar spines
CT scan without contrast of the lumbar spine
MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spines

CorrectAnswer: MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spines
ExplanationEN:
With a history of cancer and increasing low back pain, the most worrisome diagnosis is spinal cord compression. When cancer becomes metastatic to the spine, the tumor can extend into the epidural space, causing compression of the spinal cord. Additionally, tumors compress the venous plexus, leading to inflammation and vasogenic edema. The most common cancers associated with cord compression are breast, prostate, and lung.

Classic symptoms include pain, motor deficits, and bowel or bladder dysfunction. Bowel and bladder symptoms are late symptoms, and their absence does not rule out the possibility of cord compression. Pain is the initial symptom in 95% of patients. The gold standard for diagnosis is MRI and should include both the lumbar and thoracic spine since there are often lesions at both levels.



Bone scanning (A) is helpful in identifying bony metastasis of the entire skeleton in one imaging study. The radionuclide test identifies metastases with increased blood flow or new bone formation, potentially missing disease without that (e.g., multiple myeloma). The study also does not give any information about the thecal sac necessary for the diagnosis of cord compression.

While CT myelography (B) can provide detailed images of the spinal canal and cord, it is more invasive than MRI and typically not the preferred imaging modality. It is considered a second-line option when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., presence of certain electromagnetic cardiac devices) or if MRI is unavailable.

CT scan without contrast of the lumbar spine (C) is helpful in the evaluation of the bony architecture of the spine and identification of metastatic disease but does not give information about the cord or thecal sac.

Radiographs of the lumbar spine (E) may identify metastatic disease with less sensitivity than the other modalities mentioned. Metastatic disease is necessary for cord compression. However, the lower sensitivity does not allow for sole evaluation with plain films.

Question: A 3-year-old previously healthy, fully immunized boy presents after a seizure that occurred 2 hours prior to arrival. He has never had a seizure before. Today, he experienced a 35-second generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He had a postictal period of 20 minutes and is now at his neurologic baseline. EMS was called, and he had a blood glucose level of 84 mg/dL on the scene. He has had a cough and runny nose for the past day. Shortly before the seizure, he developed a fever of 39.3°C. On exam, he is a well-appearing boy with a supple neck, no rashes, normal tympanic membranes, a normal pharynx, clear lungs, and a soft abdomen. What diagnostic study should be obtained on this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Febrile seizures occur in 2–5% of the general pediatric population. Simple febrile seizures are defined as a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting < 15 minutes associated with a fever in a child 6 months to 5 years of age occurring only once in a 24-hour period. Febrile seizures are the most common type of pediatric seizure. The American Academy of Pediatrics states that no diagnostic studies are needed specific to a febrile seizure.

The goal of the evaluation should be to identify the source of the fever. In this child with a benign exam, rhinorrhea, and a cough, a viral upper respiratory infection is the likely cause of the fever. Less than half of children will experience another febrile seizure, and the risk of developing epilepsy is similar to the general population risk.



A basic metabolic panel (A) is only necessary to monitor for electrolyte abnormalities in patients who have had persistent vomiting or diarrhea or have signs of dehydration.

Electroencephalogram (B) is not indicated in the evaluation of a child with a febrile seizure who does not have any neurologic abnormality.

Lumbar puncture (C) should only be performed when there is concern for meningitis or encephalitis, such as if the child is not up to date on immunizations or has an altered level of consciousness, nuchal rigidity, or petechial rash.

Noncontrast CT scan (D) is not indicated for a child with a routine febrile seizure. Imaging with a head CT or MRI should be obtained in patients with persistent neurologic deficits or signs of increased intracranial pressure such as headache, vomiting, vision changes, or altered mental status.

Question: A 35-year-old woman with a history of migraines and polycystic kidney disease presents to the emergency department with a severe, diffuse headache. The onset was abrupt, approximately 1 hour prior to arrival. Her vital signs are within normal limits. She has photophobia and phonophobia, as well as pain with extraocular movements. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) accounts for approximately one-third of all hemorrhagic strokes. Atraumatic SAH is due to ruptured aneurysms. A history of polycystic kidney disease is a risk factor for developing berry aneurysms, which may spontaneously rupture and cause a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Other medical conditions associated with SAH include Marfan syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, and fibromuscular dysplasia.

Classic symptoms include an abrupt “thunderclap” headache that is maximal in severity at onset. Patients often have signs of meningeal irritation secondary to blood in the subarachnoid space. These include nuchal rigidity, painful extraocular movements, photophobia, and a positive Brudzinski or Kernig sign. Subarachnoid blood appears white on noncontrast head CT and most often appears in the cerebral cisterns within which lies the vessels that compose the circle of Willis. Management includes supportive care, including airway management as needed, blood pressure control, nimodipine, and neurosurgical consultation.



A classic migraine (A)presentation is gradual in onset, often unilateral, and does not include classic signs of meningeal irritation.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (B), or pseudotumor cerebri, is most commonly seen in females with obesity and hypertension or those who take oral contraceptive pills. Papilledema is a common exam finding. These headaches are gradual in onset and may be present for weeks before patients seek care.

Meningitis (C) is an infectious process of the leptomeninges that presents with fever, altered mental status, gradual onset headache, nuchal rigidity, and other signs of meningeal irritation.

Question: Which of the following is most likely present in a patient with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome?
ExplanationEN:
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is characterized by a combination of acute hypertension and endothelial dysfunction, which results in bilateral symmetric vasogenic edema. While it typically affects the posterior regions of the brain, other areas may be affected as well. Conditions associated with PRES include hypertensive encephalopathy, acute or chronic renal disease, eclampsia, immunosuppression, autoimmune disorders, and vasculitis, among others. Although it is termed reversible, outcomes depend on timely recognition and treatment, and delays can lead to hemorrhage, infarction, or persistent neurologic deficits.

Symptoms evolve fairly rapidly over hours to days, and hypertension, which is typically moderately elevated except in cases of malignant hypertension, is a common finding. Patients present with a combination of four characteristic complaints: headache, altered mental status, visual disturbances, and seizures. The headaches are often constant and nonlocalizing. Altered mental status can range from mild confusion to coma. Hemianopia, visual hallucinations, cortical blindness, and auras are possible visual findings. Lastly, seizures occur in the majority of patients and are typically generalized.

Neuroimaging will show white matter edema in the bilateral posterior cerebral hemispheres. In contrast to acute strokes, imaging abnormalities are not typically confined to a single vascular territory. Treatment involves the gradual lowering of the blood pressure using a titratable parenteral medication. Initiation of antiseizure medication is also indicated except in the setting of eclampsia. Symptoms are often reversible in days to weeks following blood pressure control and treatment of any underlying causes.



Focal neurologic deficits such as ataxia (A), facial droop (B), or limb weakness (C) are not typical of PRES.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents to the ED with weakness and abnormal gait. He has a medical history significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He states his symptoms started 3 days ago when he noticed he kept stubbing his toes when he walked. Today, he required an ambulance ride into the emergency department because he was unable to walk. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination is remarkable for 5/5 strength in bilateral upper extremities, 5/5 strength in the proximal lower extremities, 1/5 strength with plantar and dorsiflexion of the ankles, and 0/5 strength in bilateral feet. Sensation appears to be normal, but deep tendon reflexes are diminished at the ankles. Which of the following is the most common cause of his most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy that is most often characterized by an acute monophasic paralyzing illness. It is thought to result from an immune response that occurs secondarily to a preceding infection that causes a crossreactivity between the peripheral nerve component due to molecular mimicry. Campylobacter jejuni infections are the most commonly identified infections preceding GBS, although other infections are also known to cause GBS. Classically, the clinical features include progressive and symmetric ascending muscle weakness that is accompanied by decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes. Weakness ranges from being mild with only minor walking difficulties to full-blown paralysis. Weakness generally starts in the lower extremities and ascends, but weakness can also start in the upper extremities in a small subgroup of patients. The weakness can ascend and affect the facial, respiratory, and bulbar muscles. Severe respiratory muscle weakness can occur, requiring mechanical ventilation.

Sensory deficits are present in GBS, but they are usually less prominent than motor deficits. While they are typically mild, the complete absence of sensory symptoms is not required to diagnose GBS. The initial diagnosis is made on clinical presentation. The diagnosis is then supported if cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies and electrodiagnostic studies demonstrate abnormalities. Albuminocytologic dissociation is found on CSF analysis, which is defined as an elevated protein with a normal white count. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography can be valuable in helping confirm the diagnosis, as they can demonstrate axonal or myelin disease processes.

Treatment focuses on stabilization and supportive measures to ensure intact airway, breathing, and circulation and hemodynamic integrity. Patients should also undergo either plasmapheresis or intravenous immune globulin, as both of these treatments accelerate the recovery. Respiratory failure can occur in GBS, so patients should be closely monitored for this.



Epstein-Barr virus infection (B), influenza infection (C), and Zika virus infection (D) are all known to cause GBS as a preceding infection. However, none are as common as Campylobacter jejuni.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A healthy 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a headache. She has been having chronic, daily headaches for the last 4 months that have been worsening in severity. Yesterday, she developed ringing in her ears but no hearing loss. She has also been having intermittent blurred vision. Physical exam reveals normal findings on neurologic exam. Findings from the funduscopic exam are shown above. BP is 135/80 mm Hg, HR is 76 bpm, and T is 98.5°F (36.9°C). Which of the following is most likely to establish the definitive diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) that can be confirmed by the presence of elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture (LP). IIH, formerly known as pseudotumor cerebri, most commonly affects women with obesity between the ages of 20 and 44 years. Most patients with IIH will have headaches, while other symptoms include visual changes, back pain, and tinnitus. Complete vision loss is a less common symptom, but untreated IIH may lead to permanent decreased vision.

The diagnostic criteria include papilledema (as shown in the funduscopic image above) with otherwise normal findings on neurologic exam and elevated opening pressure on LP (> 250 mm H2O [25 cm H2O] in adults and > 280 mm H2O [28 cm H2O] in children). Papilledema is characterized by blurring of the optic disc with a surrounding grayish halo (as shown above), and there may be obscuration or loss of the major vessels as they leave the disc. The CSF studies should otherwise be within normal limits, and neuroimaging will typically be benign or demonstrate nonspecific findings.

There is a variant of IIH that does not present with papilledema but has either unilateral or bilateral sixth (abducens) nerve palsy, resulting in a lateral gaze palsy on exam. Neuroimaging may show an empty sella, flattening of the posterior aspect of the globe, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without a tortuous optic nerve, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. At least three of the neuroimaging findings can be diagnostic of IIH in the absence of papilledema or abducens nerve palsy. An LP is necessary to make the diagnosis of IIH and may also provide therapeutic relief of a patient’s symptoms by removing a volume of CSF. After an opening pressure is determined, CSF can be removed in multiple aliquots, with a target pressure of 150–200 mm H2O (15–20 cm H2O). In general, the removal of 1 mL of CSF will lower the CSF pressure by about 10 mm H2O (1 cm H2O).

Oral acetazolamide is the first-line treatment for lowering intracranial pressure and decreasing symptoms of IIH, with a typical starting dose of 250–500 mg twice per day. Increased doses can have significant side effects and should be prescribed only under the supervision of a neurologist or ophthalmologist. Long-term interventions include CSF shunting and optic nerve sheath fenestration to treat failing or lost vision.



A head CT (A) is likely to be obtained before performing an LP to rule out any other intracranial abnormality, but it will often be benign in IIH. There may be findings on CT that are suggestive of a diagnosis of IIH, but they do not negate the need for an LP to establish a definitive diagnosis. This patient’s funduscopic exam shows papilledema, which is often indicative of increased intracranial pressure, but a patient with IIH is expected to have normal intraocular pressure measurements (C). An ultrasound of the optic nerve (D) sheath can help determine the diameter of the nerve and whether the patient has elevated intracranial pressure. A diameter > 5 mm is consistent with increased intracranial pressure. However, this does not provide a definite diagnosis of IIH.

Question: A 64-year-old woman presents to the ED with a headache. She also reports nausea with no vomiting. Her medical history includes breast cancer, for which she underwent a double mastectomy 3 months ago and is currently receiving chemotherapy. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no focal neurologic findings. A CT of the head is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV followed by 4 mg IV every 6 hours
Levetiracetam 2 g IV followed by 750 mg PO twice daily
Metoclopramide 10 mg IV plus ketorolac 15 mg IV
Radiation oncology consult for whole brain radiation therapy

CorrectAnswer: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV followed by 4 mg IV every 6 hours
ExplanationEN:
Headache and other symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) can develop with both primary CNS tumors and metastatic disease. The most common primary CNS neoplasms associated with symptoms of elevated ICP are meningioma, glioblastoma, pituitary adenoma, and primary CNS lymphoma, while brain metastasis causing elevated ICP is most often a consequence of melanoma or breast, lung, or gastrointestinal cancer. This patient’s medical history of likely metastatic breast cancer and new symptoms of potential elevated ICP are highly suspicious for intracranial metastases. The headache caused by intracranial neoplasms arises from two mechanisms: mechanical traction on pain-sensitive structures (e.g., meninges) and elevation of ICP.

Isolated headache is a rare presentation of intracranial neoplasm, but this diagnosis should be considered in any patient with a new persistent headache, especially in patients > 50 years old. Symptoms are often initially only present in the morning, with progressive worsening to become more constant, and are often worse with coughing or Valsalva and associated with other symptoms of elevated ICP such as nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, and seizures. Neuroimaging should be performed in any patient in whom intracranial neoplasms are suspected, preferably with MRI, though CT with contrast is sufficiently sensitive for many neoplastic lesions. Noncontrast head CT is insufficiently sensitive except in the case of large masses or those with associated hemorrhage. This patient has multiple round, well-circumscribed hemorrhagic masses near the gray-white junction with surrounding edema, which is an appearance that strongly suggests metastatic disease.

Management of intracranial metastases is multifactoral, targeting both the acute symptoms and the underlying chronic disease process. ED management should focus on treating symptoms and limiting complications posed by potential elevation of ICP. IV corticosteroids are commonly used to reduce tumor-associated edema and can provide dramatic relief of symptoms. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV followed by 4 mg every 6 hours is a commonly used regimen, while NSAIDs may also provide some symptomatic relief, but only if lesions are nonhemorrhagic. Patients with seizures should be given anticonvulsant medications, usually levetiracetam, but these should not be given prophylactically in the absence of seizures. Symptomatic patients should be admitted to a facility with specialty care to manage symptoms and complications of elevated ICP, warranting transfer to such facility if not immediately available. Neurosurgery consultation is warranted in patients with any intracranial neoplasm, including metastases that are large or symptomatic tumors, such as those causing elevated ICP.



Levetiracetam (B) is often the drug of choice for many patients with seizures, including those from intracranial neoplasm, but this patient has no reported history of seizures, so anticonvulsant drugs are not recommended.

IV dopamine antagonists and NSAIDs (C) are recommended in the treatment of patients with migraine headache, which is not present in this case. Furthermore, NSAIDs would not be a good treatment choice for this patient with hemorrhagic lesions.

Radiation oncology consultation and whole brain radiation therapy (D) may be involved in this patient’s treatment course but would likely happen during the inpatient hospitalization, as it is not an appropriate first step in treatment.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents with new onset weakness 1 hour prior to arrival. On examination, he is unable to lift his right arm. He can lift his right leg against gravity but not resistance, and he has expressive aphasia. Thrombosis of which of the following vessels is the likely cause of his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Stroke is the leading cause of long-term disability in the United States. Most strokes are ischemic in origin and can be due to in situ thrombosis, embolic obstruction, or hypoperfusion. The vessel involved results in a recognizable pattern of symptoms. The middle cerebral artery is the vessel most commonly involved in ischemic stroke and results in hemiparesis, facial weakness, and sensory loss contralateral to the affected cortex. The face and upper extremity are typically affected to a greater extent than the lower extremity. Aphasia, both expressive and receptive, is seen if the dominant hemisphere is affected (most commonly the left hemisphere in right-handed patients and the majority of left-handed patients). If the nondominant hemisphere is involved, the patient may show signs of neglect, inattention, and dysarthria. Homonymous hemianopsia (loss of half of the field of vision on the same side in both eyes) can also be seen. There may be a gaze preference toward the affected hemisphere.



Anterior cerebral artery (A) involvement results in hemiparesis with the lower extremity affected to a greater extent than the upper extremity and face. Posterior circulation strokes can cause a wide variety of symptoms making them more difficult to diagnose. Ataxia, nystagmus, vision loss, confusion, nausea, and posterior headache can be seen in patients with posterior cerebral artery (C) occlusion. Vertebrobasilar artery (D) strokes present with unilateral limb ataxia, nystagmus, cranial nerve V signs, and gait ataxia.

Question: A 14-year-old girl with a history of obesity presents with a headache. She states that the headache has been on and off for weeks and has a moderate intensity. She also states that she has had intermittent loss of vision for seconds at a time for the last 2–3 days. Physical examination reveals the above image. A noncontrast head CT scan is normal.
