Options.text: CTA of the head and neck

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms and signs consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) and should have a lumbar puncture with an opening pressure performed to make the diagnosis. The pathophysiology of IIH is not completely understood but is thought to be due to an imbalance of CSF production and reabsorption. Patients typically present with a generalized headache of gradual onset. The headache is worsened by the Valsalva maneuver or bending over. Patients may also present with visual changes that are transient or continuous. Patients may have visual field defects or frank vision loss. The hallmark physical exam finding is papilledema, as seen in the patient above. It is typically bilateral and symmetric. Sixth cranial nerve (abducens) palsy may also be present. The diagnosis of IIH is made by a lumbar puncture with an increased opening pressure. Making the diagnosis is critical as it affects management and appropriate management can avoid the most common complication which is vision loss.





Acetazolamide (A) and corticosteroids (B) are treatments for IIH but should not be started until a definitive diagnosis is made.

CTA of the head and neck (C) could be performed if there was concern for acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), which presents with an acute onset headache sometimes associated with neurologic deficits. This patient's intermittent headache is not characteristic of acute SAH.

Symptomatic management and follow-up (E) should not be the next best step as a diagnosis is critical in those with IIH.

Question: Which of the following is the most sensitive laboratory test for diagnosing a spinal epidural abscess?
ExplanationEN:
Spinal epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis, and discitis are life-threatening infectious causes of back pain. Spinal epidural abscess has a particularly high mortality when untreated. Risk factors for spinal epidural abscess include intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and recent spinal procedures or hardware. The diagnosis of spinal epidural abscess can be challenging to make as often patients only present with back pain and possibly vague viral symptoms. The C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate levels are often elevated in this condition as these are sensitive but not specific markers for this condition. When this diagnosis is suspected, an MRI of the spine with and without contrast should be obtained. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started, and spine surgery should be consulted for further care.



Procalcitonin (B) can be elevated in bacterial infections and may be used by inpatient services to aid in determining when to discontinue antibiotics. It is not as sensitive as inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate in the diagnosis of spinal epidural abscess.

The sodium level (C) can be low in acute systemic infections such as severe sepsis and septic shock. It is neither sensitive nor specific in the diagnosis and workup of spinal epidural abscess.

White blood cell counts (D) may be elevated or normal when spinal epidural abscess leads to systemic infection. It is a less sensitive marker than inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. In a retrospective study of patients presenting to the emergency department, only 60% of those diagnosed with spinal epidural abscess exhibited leukocytosis at their initial visit.

Question: A 52-year-old man is brought to the ED by his shift supervisor because of right-sided facial droop and speech difficulty. Onset was approximately 30 minutes prior to arrival. The patient’s symptoms have now resolved. Findings on his neurological exam are normal, and a noncontrast head CT shows no acute findings. Which of the following interventions is indicated at this time?
ExplanationEN:
The patient experienced a transient ischemic attack (TIA), which is defined by the presence of transient focal neurologic symptoms without evidence of acute infarction on neuroimaging. TIAs are clinical emergencies that require urgent evaluation and risk stratification because they often precede more severe cerebrovascular events. Prompt diagnosis involves a noncontrast head CT to exclude hemorrhage and major infarction, followed by MRI for greater sensitivity in detecting subtle ischemic changes. Vascular imaging, such as carotid ultrasonography or CT angiography of the head and neck, is critical for identifying large-vessel stenosis or occlusion. Additional workup includes electrocardiography and continuous cardiac monitoring to evaluate for dysrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation, and basic blood work to assess for contributing metabolic or hematologic abnormalities.

Treatment of TIA focuses on preventing recurrent stroke. First-line therapy includes antiplatelet agents, with aspirin the most commonly used. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel may be initiated in high-risk patients within 24 hours of symptom onset and continued for a short duration, up to 21 days, to reduce early recurrent stroke risk. Monotherapy with either aspirin or clopidogrel is also acceptable and is often chosen based on individual patient factors such as history of gastrointestinal bleeding, allergy, drug cost, and overall bleeding risk. Aggressive risk factor modification is essential and includes blood pressure control, lipid-lowering therapy with statins, smoking cessation, glycemic control in patients with diabetes, and lifestyle interventions that address diet and physical activity.

Atrial fibrillation is a well-recognized independent risk factor for cardioembolic stroke and TIA. However, in patients who present with new or suspected atrial fibrillation, the decision to initiate anticoagulation in the ED must be made cautiously. The risk of recurrent embolic events without anticoagulation is relatively low in the first 48 hours, while the risk of hemorrhagic transformation of an undetected infarct is highest during this same period. For this reason, starting anticoagulation in the emergency setting is generally avoided unless imaging definitively rules out infarction and a comprehensive evaluation has been completed. In most cases, initiation of oral anticoagulation can be deferred to the inpatient setting or outpatient follow-up once the diagnosis and risk profile have been fully assessed.

Long-term treatment strategies should be individualized and coordinated with neurology and primary care follow-up. Patients with significant carotid artery stenosis may require surgical intervention, such as carotid endarterectomy or stenting, depending on the degree of stenosis and timing of symptoms. Ultimately, early recognition and comprehensive treatment of TIA can significantly reduce the risk of subsequent stroke and improve patient outcomes.



Heparin followed by warfarin (B) is not currently recommended for TIA treatment because the risk of intracranial hemorrhage outweighs the benefit of preventing future ischemic strokes.

Lumbar puncture (C) is not indicated in the treatment of TIAs. This procedure is used to aid in the diagnosis of meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Patients with normal findings on neurologic exam and without other findings to suggest either of these diagnoses do not require a lumbar puncture.

Reassurance and neurology follow-up (D) is inappropriate treatment, as up to 10% of patients with a TIA will have a stroke within 90 days. Neurologic consultation should be made in the emergency setting for further recommendations and possible admission for further testing.

Question: Which of the following CSF studies is most helpful to differentiate viral from bacterial meningitis?
ExplanationEN:
Viral meningitis may be clinically indistinguishable from bacterial or fungal meningitis, with a few exceptions. For example, patients with bacterial meningitis may have certain risk factors like recent neurosurgery, odontogenic infection, dormitory living, CSF leak, or splenectomy. Risk factors for fungal meningitis may include AIDS, malignancy, or another immunocompromised state. It may also present with seizures.

Headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity are the most common presenting symptoms of meningitis. Common viruses responsible for meningitis include enteroviruses (coxsackievirus and echovirus), HIV, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, adenovirus, and cytomegalovirus. Enteroviruses cause > 90% of cases.

Immunoassay and PCR of the CSF for specific viral species is the gold standard for the diagnosis of viral meningitis, but this can be time-consuming and may not be immediately available at some institutions. In viral meningitis, opening pressure is typically normal but can be increased. Other common CSF findings include normal glucose, normal or increased protein, a negative Gram stain, and 100–1,000 WBCs with a lymphocytic predominance.

Because definitive diagnosis is often delayed while awaiting culture results, empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis is usually started by the ED clinician. Ultimately, the mainstay of therapy for most cases of viral meningitis is supportive care. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty or in ill-appearing patients, admission should be secured until cultures have resulted.



Beta-2 transferrin (A) is a protein found in CSF and is helpful in diagnosing a potential CSF leak. It can be useful in patients with rhinorrhea after facial trauma or intracranial or facial surgical intervention, but the results often take several days, so this test is not useful acutely.

CSF cell count (B) alone is not sensitive or specific enough to differentiate viral meningitis from other causes of meningitis.

Procalcitonin (D) is largely used to differentiate bacterial causes of pneumonia from other respiratory illnesses (e.g., influenza or viral pneumonia).

Question: A 22-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought to the ED after having brief, seizure-like activity that spontaneously resolved prior to arrival. On initial evaluation, he is noted to be protecting his airway with stable vital signs but appears somnolent. Blood glucose is unremarkable, and IV access is established. Family notes no recent illnesses or injuries, but they are concerned that he has been unable to afford his prescriptions recently. Shortly thereafter, he begins to exhibit generalized convulsions that do not spontaneously resolve after several minutes. Which of the following medications should be given next?
ExplanationEN:
Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency commonly encountered in the ED. It is defined as seizure activity lasting more > 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without a return to baseline mental status between episodes. Prompt recognition and intervention are critical to reduce morbidity and mortality.

Initial treatment should focus on stabilization, beginning with assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation, along with rapid exclusion of mimics such as hypoglycemia. All patients should be placed on a cardiac monitor with continuous pulse oximetry, and a fingerstick glucose should be obtained immediately. Intravenous access should be established, and laboratory studies should be sent promptly.

The first-line treatment for status epilepticus is a benzodiazepine, with IV lorazepam preferred when access is available. Lorazepam has demonstrated superior efficacy due to its rapid onset (peak effect in 3 minutes) and longer duration of action (4–24 hours) compared to diazepam (15–60 minutes), making it ideal for initial seizure control.



IV diazepam (A) is another benzodiazepine that can be used for aborting status epilepticus. However, diazepam’s slower onset to peak and tendency to redistribute into adipose tissue outside the central nervous system make it a less desirable option than lorazepam.

IV levetiracetam (B) is given over 15 minutes (loading dose of 60 mg/kg) and is recommended as a second-line agent.

IV phenytoin (D) is also a treatment for status epilepticus but is not currently recommended as a first-line agent.

Question: A 53-year-old woman presents to the ED after being found unresponsive on the floor at her home. Her medical history includes hypertension and atrial fibrillation, for which she takes amlodipine and warfarin daily. Vital signs include a T of 97.3°F (37.2°C), BP of 192/104 mm Hg, HR of 94 bpm, RR of 14/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. Physical examination shows a leftward gaze deviation. The patient is unable to follow commands, precluding a comprehensive neurologic examination. A CT of the head without contrast is as shown above. Which of the following, in addition to blood pressure control and neurosurgery consultation, is the best next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

Options.text: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K
Fresh frozen plasma and IV vitamin K

CorrectAnswer: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K
ExplanationEN:
Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) accounts for 10–15% of all acute stroke events and carries a significant risk of resulting morbidity and mortality, with up to 50% 30-day mortality and one-half of those patients dying within the first 2 days. Either hypertensive vasculopathy or cerebral amyloid angiopathy underlies most cases of spontaneous ICH, each with its characteristic pattern of hemorrhage. Hypertensive ICH tends to affect deep regions of the brain, such as the basal ganglia and thalamus, while amyloid angiopathy classically affects the lobes of the cerebral hemispheres. Less common etiologies include arteriovenous malformations, aneurysmal rupture, and sympathomimetic drug use (e.g., cocaine).

Spontaneous ICH characteristically presents with severe hypertension and an associated sudden onset of headache, vomiting, and focal neurologic deficits. There commonly are sensorimotor deficits contralateral to the side of the lesion. However, many patients will not have the classic symptoms, and their presentation will be indistinguishable from an acute ischemic stroke. It is for this reason that, after examining the patient and calculating a baseline NIH stroke scale score, a CT of the head without contrast is typically obtained as the first step in the diagnostic evaluation of patients with suspected stroke. Additionally, CT angiography is used in many settings to detect underlying vascular lesions that may be contributing to the bleeding and identify patients with a higher risk of hematoma expansion.

Treatment for spontaneous ICH varies considerably from that of acute ischemic stroke, so rapid identification of acute hemorrhage on noncontrast CT is crucial for both diagnosis and management. The primary goals of initial management are to prevent expansion of the hemorrhage and reduce secondary brain injury by stabilizing the airway, respiratory system, and circulatory system. For patients taking anticoagulants for other conditions, such as warfarin for this patient’s atrial fibrillation, these medications should be discontinued and appropriate reversal agents given immediately. Appropriate reversal for warfarin, specifically, consists of four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) and vitamin K, as the former acts rapidly while the latter provides longer-acting antagonism. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can also be used but is less preferred given its longer onset of action and greater volume of infusate, which increases the risk of volume-related complications (e.g., pulmonary edema).



Andexanet alfa (B) was the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban and apixaban. However, as of December 2025, it has been removed from the U.S. market due to manufacturing and supply issues. It is no longer a viable treatment option in clinical practice, and is not a recommended reversal agent for warfarin.

FFP (C) contains all coagulation factors and is used to reverse vitamin K antagonist (e.g., warfarin)–induced bleeding. It has a slower onset, requires large volume transfusion, and carries risks such as transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and therefore, 4F-PCC would more rapidly reverse this patient's anticoagulation.

Idarucizumab (D) is a new agent used for anticoagulant reversal in patients taking direct-acting oral anticoagulants that are direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g., dabigatran), but it is not useful for reversing vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin.

There is a high likelihood that IV vitamin K (E) will be initiated in this patient, but immediate steps should include a more rapid-acting reversal agent such as 4F-PCC.

Question: A 35-year-old woman with a known history of seizure disorder is actively seizing in the ED. Which of the following is the best first-line medication and route to treat her seizure?
ExplanationEN:
In an actively seizing patient, attention is always directed to the airway first. A patient having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure has a suppressed gag reflex and is prone to aspiration of gastric contents. Therefore, patients should be placed in the left lateral decubitus position.

First-line pharmacologic treatment for an actively seizing patient is a parenteral benzodiazepine. Benzodiazepines directly enhance gamma-aminobutyric acid-mediated neuronal inhibition, affect clinical and electrical manifestations of seizures, and are highly effective at terminating seizure activity. Benzodiazepines have been shown to be more effective than phenytoin at terminating status epilepticus. They are as effective as parenteral phenobarbital, but phenobarbital is associated with a higher risk of hypoventilation and hypotension. The intravenous route is the preferred route to administer an antiepileptic because this has the quickest onset of action. Therefore, intravenous midazolam is the preferred agent from the choices listed above. Midazolam’s onset of action is within 1 minute. In addition to the intravenous preparation, it is available in both intranasal and buccal formulations. It also has the least cardiovascular effects among benzodiazepines.



Fosphenytoin (A) is a water-soluble prodrug form of phenytoin. Unlike phenytoin, fosphenytoin can be administered intramuscularly. Although fosphenytoin can be infused more rapidly than phenytoin, the time to a therapeutic concentration of the active drug is the same as for intravenous phenytoin.

Levetiracetam (C) is used in the treatment of status epilepticus as a second-line treatment following benzodiazepines. Levetiracetam should be administered intravenously, not orally.

Lorazepam (D) is considered a first-line agent for an actively seizing patient and is the most popular agent used. However, oral medications are contraindicated in an actively seizing patient due to the prolonged onset of action and risk of aspiration.

Diazepam (E) is also a first-line agent for an actively seizing patient and is most commonly used as a rectal preparation in the pediatric population in which intravenous access is not readily available.

Question: Which of the following is the preferred imaging option when neurocysticercosis is the suspected cause of a patient’s symptoms?

Options.text: CT angiography of the head and neck
CT head with contrast and MRI brain with contrast
MR venogram of the head and neck

CorrectAnswer: CT head with contrast and MRI brain with contrast
ExplanationEN:
Cysticercosis refers to the clinical manifestations of infection caused by the larval stage of the Taenia solium tapeworm and can be further stratified into neurocysticercosis and extraneural cysticercosis. Neurocysticercosis is the most common parasitic infection of the CNS globally and the most common etiology of brain abscess in Latin America and those who have emigrated from Latin America. Infection occurs via ingestion of T. solium eggs with cysticerci developing within host tissues over a period of 3–8 weeks.

The most common clinical manifestation of neurocysticercosis is new-onset partial seizures that may or may not have secondary generalization. Elevated intracranial pressure and its associated sequelae may develop, especially when lesions are located in ventricles or subarachnoid space, while focal neurologic deficits may be apparent with intraparenchymal lesions. Definitive diagnosis of neurocysticercosis is complex and requires consideration of clinical, neuroimaging, and epidemiological features. When possible, both CT of the head and MRI of the brain with contrast should be obtained, but the specific appearance of lesions varies by location and stage of infection. A well-performed thin-slice CT scan with contrast can be as good as an MRI in disease detection. MRI of the spine should also be obtained when there is basal subarachnoid involvement. Serology and molecular testing may also be useful in patients with suspected cases in which neuroimaging findings are nonconfirmatory.

Anticonvulsant therapy is indicated for all patients presenting with seizures due to neurocysticercosis, but there is some debate about whether all patients require anthelmintic therapy. Generally, cystic lesions within the brain parenchyma warrant anthelmintic treatment. Patients with one or two intraparenchymal cysts can be treated with albendazole alone, while three or more cysts warrant the addition of praziquantel. Systemic corticosteroids are often added prior to initiation of anthelmintic therapy to reduce the host inflammatory response to dying parasites.



Vascular imaging in the form of CT angiography (A) and MR venography (D) would not be routinely indicated in the evaluation of suspected neurocysticercosis and would only be warranted in specific cases of suspected vascular compromise. CT of the head (C) is indicated but should be obtained with contrast or with MRI when possible, rather than alone.

Question: A 25-year-old man presents to the ED with a headache, fever, and malaise for 3 days. He is nontoxic-appearing, oriented, and able to follow commands. His mucous membranes appear dry. A lumbar puncture is performed with an opening pressure of 18 cm H2O. Cerebrospinal fluid results are WBC 5/µL, 10% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 80% lymphocytes, 10% monocytes, glucose 70 mg/dL, protein 60 mg/dL, and RBC 10/µL. Gram stain shows few lymphocytes and no organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the treatment of this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and clinical presentation suggest a diagnosis of viral meningitis. Treatment of viral meningitis is supportive in nature and may include IV hydration, antipyretics, and analgesics. Viral meningitis is most commonly caused by enteroviruses (echovirus, coxsackievirus) but may also be caused by mumps, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus (HSV), adenovirus, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The CSF generally shows a WBC count < 1,000/µL, with a lymphocytic predominance, although neutrophils may dominate in the first 24 hours. Glucose is > 40 mg/dL, and protein is < 200 mg/dL. Gram stain is negative for organisms. Viral meningitis is usually self-limited, resolving without complications in 7–10 days.



Ceftriaxone and vancomycin (A) are used to treat bacterial meningitis. CSF in bacterial meningitis typically shows a greater predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes, with low glucose and high protein.

CT of the head (B), when needed, should be performed prior to lumbar puncture. It is not recommended in uncomplicated cases and is a poor indicator of raised intracranial pressure. Inappropriate imaging may cause an unacceptable delay in the administration of antibiotics and the treatment of bacterial meningitis, leading to higher rates of mortality and morbidity. There are a few cases in which lumbar puncture has led to cerebral herniation, but a normal neurological exam should lead one to perform an LP, not a CT scan.

Dexamethasone (C) is a steroid shown to improve outcomes in patients with pneumococcal meningitis when given before or concurrently with antibiotics. There have been no trials demonstrating benefit in patients with viral meningitis.

Valacyclovir (E) is used to treat genital HSV and herpes zoster. Acyclovir is an antiviral medication used to treat suspected HSV meningitis in newborns and meningoencephalitis in children and adults. When encephalitis is present, the gray matter is affected, causing cognitive and psychiatric symptoms, which is not the case in this patient. This patient exhibits no confusion or cognitive deficits, making herpes encephalitis unlikely.

Question: A young woman presents with a bilateral headache. She describes it as a band-like pressure from her forehead to her neck, feeling as if her head is in a vice. She reports no prodromal symptoms, nausea, or photophobia. Cervical spine range-of-motion and skull palpation do not reproduce the headache. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Tension-type headache is the most common type of recurring headache other than migraine and the most common type overall. Tension headaches present as bilateral with pain in the frontal and occipital regions in a band-like distribution. The headaches are exacerbated by stress, fatigue, glare, or noise. They also often involve contraction of the scalp and posterior neck muscles, with a normal neurologic exam. Tension-type headaches are commonly addressed through a combination of pharmacological and nonpharmacological strategies.

First-line pharmacotherapy typically includes over-the-counter analgesics such as acetaminophen and NSAIDs. Ergotamines may also be used. Preventive treatments may involve tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline. Nonpharmacological approaches are essential and include stress management techniques, cognitive behavioral therapy, and relaxation exercises. Identifying triggers and encouraging lifestyle modifications such as regular sleep, hydration, and physical activity are also key components of a comprehensive treatment plan.



Cervicogenic headache (A) is a secondary headache disorder resulting from pathology in the cervical spine or soft tissues of the neck. It typically presents as a unilateral headache, often starting from the neck, with pain radiating to the frontal and temporal regions. It is often associated with pain exacerbated with neck movement and restricted range of motion in the neck.

Cluster headache (B) has a predilection for male patients and is associated with excruciating periorbital pain, ipsilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation, and nasal discharge.

Unilateral, throbbing headache with nausea and photophobia is much more indicative of migraine headache (C)​. These symptoms are absent in tension-type headaches.

Occipital headaches (D), sometimes called occipital neuralgia, C2 neuralgia, or C2 headaches, are characterized by sharp, shooting, electric-like occipital pain that radiates cephalad, retro-orbitally, or in the distribution of the greater and lesser occipital nerves. This pain typically worsens with upper cervical spine range of motion. A common exam finding of occipital headaches is the reproduction of radiating pain during palpation of the occipital nerves as they exit the ligamentum nuchae at the base of the skull.

Question: A 26-year-old woman without significant medical history presents to the ED with progressive headaches associated with nausea and intermittent bright sparkles of light in her visual fields bilaterally. She has had minimal relief with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at home. She reports no history of trauma. On examination, she is alert and oriented. There is bilateral papilledema, but visual acuity and the remainder of the examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following diagnostic findings would be consistent with the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: CSF with elevated protein and 150 WBCs/hpf
Distended cavernous sinus with a filling defect on contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain
Hydrocephalus on noncontrast CT scan of the brain with opening pressure 8 cm H 2 O

ExplanationEN:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, previously known as pseudotumor cerebri, is a disorder most commonly seen in young women with obesity and is thought to be the result of imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid production and reabsorption. The most prominent symptom is a headache, which is gradual in onset and often worse with bending forward or Valsalva maneuver. It may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Visual disturbances, including transient visual obscurations, are common and can be bilateral or unilateral.

On examination, papilledema, generally bilateral, is the hallmark sign of idiopathic intracranial hypertension. A sixth cranial nerve palsy, characterized on exam by limited abduction on extraocular testing, or visual field defects are also possible but much less common findings. Any patient with findings of papilledema and headache requires neuroimaging to rule out a structural lesion or hydrocephalus. In idiopathic intracranial hypertension, the ventricles and brain appear normal on MRI or CT. Lumbar puncture is the diagnostic test of choice and will be positive for elevated opening pressures, > 25 cm H2O in adults and > 28 cm H2O in children. Cerebrospinal fluid studies will be otherwise unremarkable.



CSF with elevated protein and 150 WBCs/hpf (A) is consistent with meningitis. Patients present with headache, fever, and neck stiffness. Papilledema and cranial nerve palsies would not be typical of viral meningitis.

Distended cavernous sinus with a filling defect on contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain (B) would be diagnostic of cavernous sinus thrombosis. These patients can also present with headache and focal neurologic symptoms but also typically have orbital signs such as chemosis, periorbital swelling, and exophthalmos on exam.

Hydrocephalus on noncontrast CT scan of the brain with opening pressure 8 cm H2O (C) would be consistent with a diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus. The classic presentation consists of dementia, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence in patients typically > 60 years. Neuroimaging will show hydrocephalus and opening pressures will be in the normal range (7–18 cm H20).

Question: A 67-year-old woman is evaluated after multiple falls at home. On exam, she has no obvious injuries but has a slow, wide, shuffling gait with a normal arm swing. Cranial nerve exam is normal. She has a history of obesity, headaches, hypertension, diabetes, and urinary incontinence. Her family reports that she drinks alcohol daily and that, over the past 6 months, she has become more forgetful, depressed, and slower to respond to questions. What is the most likely underlying cause of her symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient likely has normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), a potentially reversible cause of dementia resulting from impaired CSF absorption across the subarachnoid villi. The problem can be idiopathic or secondary to scarring from a prior injury, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or meningitis. Diagnosis is made based on enlarged ventricles on CT scan and normal opening pressure on lumbar puncture. The CSF accumulation in the ventricles is termed hydrocephalus. It affects the periventricular white matter tracts, especially those serving the frontal lobes. The classic triad of symptoms involves cognitive impairment, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. Gait difficulty is the most prominent early clinical feature and is classically described as the feet being “stuck to the floor.” Cognitive impairment commonly involves psychomotor slowing and apathy. Urinary urgency progresses to incontinence later in the disease course. Symptoms are usually reversible with shunt placement. Before shunt placement, an MRI should be done to rule out structural causes obstructing CSF outflow, such as a Chiari malformation. In addition, lumbar puncture helps confirm the diagnosis with a favorable clinical response to CSF removal.



Dopamine depletion in the substantia nigra (A) is seen in Parkinson disease. The gait can look similar to that of NPH in that they both involve a slow, shuffling gait. However, in Parkinson disease, the foot base is narrow, the arm swing is diminished, and the patient is more responsive to visual cues. Parkinson commonly involves a resting tremor and autonomic dysfunction. Both diseases can include urinary incontinence.

NPH does not have increased intracranial pressure (C). High opening pressure on lumbar puncture (at least 25 cm H2O) is used in the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension, previously called pseudotumor cerebri. It presents with headache and vision problems, not gait disturbances.

Thiamine deficiency (D) is associated with malnutrition and heavy alcohol use. It can lead to Wernicke encephalopathy. The clinical triad includes altered mental status, ataxic gait, and oculomotor dysfunction. This patient’s cranial nerve exam is normal.

Question: A 28-year-old man presents to the ED one evening with restlessness and intermittent head turning. He was seen earlier that day for agitation and was discharged after he was treated with medication and cleared by a psychiatrist. On examination, he has frequent muscle spasms of his neck and bizarre ocular movements. He is alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy at this time?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction from the medication he received earlier for his agitation, likely an antipsychotic. Typical antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol) can cause adverse effects, the most common of which seen in the emergency department is an acute dystonic reaction. Patients may have intermittent, uncontrollable muscle spasms of the face, neck, or back. Oculogyric crisis (a phenomenon in which the eyes deviate up or away and do not return to neutral) or laryngospasms may occur. This is caused by excess cholinergic activity, and treatment is with either benztropine 1–2 mg IV or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV. If either of these treatments fails, benzodiazepines may be used.

Typical antipsychotics can also prolong the QT interval, potentially leading to malignant tachydysrhythmias like torsades de pointes. Other side effects of antipsychotic medications include akathisia (motor restlessness), anticholinergic syndrome (e.g., constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, acute delirium, dry mouth and skin), drug-induced Parkinson syndrome (e.g., cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, bradykinesia), and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.



Cyproheptadine (A) is an antiserotonergic agent used to treat serotonin syndrome, which presents with cognitive, autonomic, and neuromuscular dysfunction. Classic features include agitation, altered mental status, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, and muscle rigidity.

Dantrolene (B) is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia, a pharmacogenetic disorder characterized by a hypermetabolic state triggered by certain anesthetic agents (e.g., succinylcholine, halothane). It typically presents during or after anesthesia.

Haloperidol (D) is a typical antipsychotic that can cause (not treat) acute dystonic reactions.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department with back pain for the past 2 days. He initially thought he had slept awkwardly but became concerned when the pain persisted and worsened in severity. He reports no lower extremity numbness or weakness. Vital signs show T of 102.1°F (38.9°C), HR of 104 bpm, RR of 18/min, BP of 132/80 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 99% on room air. Physical examination shows point tenderness over the L1 and L2 vertebrae. Patellar reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. MRI of the spine is pending. Which of the following, if detected in this patient's history, most likely contributed to his current condition?
ExplanationEN:
Spinal epidural abscess (SEA) is an infectious process in which pyogenic material accumulates within the adipose tissue of the dorsal epidural space. Incidence has been increasing in recent decades, presumably due to an increased prevalence of major risk factors for the condition, which include spinal surgery, intravenous drug use, and immunosuppression. Some 15–22% of cases are considered iatrogenic through spinal surgery or other invasive instrumentation. SEAs can arise via hematogenous spread or direct extension from adjacent infected tissue, with the former being the more common route. Infections frequently implicated in hematogenous spread include urinary tract, skin and soft tissue, and respiratory infections. However, SEA can occur in patients without any specific risk factors, so a high index of suspicion should be maintained for patients presenting with classic findings.

The characteristic triad of symptoms for SEA consists of back pain, fever, and neurologic deficits, though only a minority of patients present with the entire triad. The location of back pain is variable, depending upon the particular location of the SEA, with the thoracic and lumbar spine most commonly affected, due to a wider epidural space and richer venous plexus. Patients with SEA often progress through a range of symptoms with initially milder neurologic findings consisting of radicular pain and hyperreflexia. Incontinence, frank motor weakness, and paralysis represent advanced stages of disease. MRI with contrast is the gold standard imaging modality for SEA, while CT myelography is a reasonable alternative. However, CT myelography has limited utility in surgical planning and differentiating an abscess from a mass, so it is not preferred. Elevations in erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are nonspecific, but sensitive, findings that support the diagnosis. Leukocytosis may also be seen. Blood cultures should be sent, but lumbar puncture should not be performed, due to the risk of traversing the abscess and inducing meningitis or subdural infection.

Management of all cases of SEA should involve immediate neurosurgical evaluation for potential decompression, as there is a significant risk of cord compression and permanent neurologic deficits if not promptly treated. If these services are unavailable, the patient should be transferred for definitive care. Some patients may be candidates for CT-guided aspiration of the abscess, but decompressive laminectomy is the definitive form of surgical management. Patients not being taken for immediate surgical management of SEA should be started on empiric antibiotic therapy consisting of vancomycin and an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime or meropenem. For some patients, such as those with no neurologic deficits at the time of presentation or those with deficits for > 72 hours, conservative treatment with antibiotics and close observation may be appropriate. Complications of SEA are severe and include sepsis, permanent neurologic deficits, and death, as well as potential complications from related surgical intervention.



Acquired hypercoagulable states (A), such as in systemic lupus erythematosus, could be an underlying risk factor for spinal cord infarction. However, spinal cord infarctions are extremely rare and would not be expected to cause the characteristic triad of epidural abscess symptoms. Some familial syndromes (B) can be the underlying etiology of CNS tumors, such as in neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and tuberous sclerosis, but such tumors are more common in the brain. Spinal tumors are more likely to be metastases, and this patient’s constellation of symptoms is the classic triad for a spinal epidural abscess. Spinal epidural abscesses are associated with intravenous drug use but have no known association with intranasal drug use (C). Tobacco use (E) has many well-known adverse health effects but is not known to be directly related to the development of spinal epidural abscesses.

Question: A 39-year-old man with a history of epilepsy is brought to the ED for breakthrough seizures. He has had multiple seizures several minutes apart without returning to his baseline mental status. Vital signs are BP of 163/98 mm Hg, HR of 118 bpm, RR 20/min, and SpO2 of 92%. On exam, he is not protecting his airway. His seizures persist despite the administration of lorazepam and levetiracetam. Which of the following induction agents is most appropriate for intubating this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has status epilepticus. Status epilepticus is defined as a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting > 5 minutes or two or more seizures without return to mental status baseline in between events. General management of status epilepticus includes benzodiazepines (first-line) and antiepileptic agents such as levetiracetam. For ongoing status epilepticus, definitive airway management may be needed. First-line induction agents include propofol or midazolam, as both have antiepileptic properties. Paralysis may be achieved with either succinylcholine or rocuronium. Succinylcholine is shorter-acting but may precipitate hyperkalemia in patients who have seizure-related rhabdomyolysis. Rocuronium is longer-acting but has a more favorable safety profile and can be reversed with sugammadex.



Diazepam (A) is a first-line medication for seizures but is not commonly used for induction, as it has a longer time of onset.

Etomidate (B) is commonly used for induction and has a reasonable safety profile, but it does not have antiepileptic properties.

Ketamine (C) has some anticonvulsant properties and can be used as an adjunct with propofol or midazolam. However, it can cause hypertension, making it less favorable for this patient who has an elevated BP.

Pentobarbital (D) is a third-line agent for refractory status epilepticus and should not be used until other agents are first attempted, as it can be difficult to titrate and prolongs time on the ventilator.

Question: Which of the following patients most likely has dementia?

Options.text: A confused 65-year-old man brought from a house fire who exhibits good long-term recall, no recall of immediate events, normal vital signs, and carboxyhemoglobin level of 7%
A confused 65-year-old man brought from a house fire who exhibits poor long-term recall, no recall of immediate events, normal vital signs, and carboxyhemoglobin level of 25%
A confused 80-year-old man brought from home with fever, back pain, and urinary retention
A confused 80-year-old man brought from home with fever, cough, and hypoxia
A confused 80-year-old man brought from home with increased thirst, increased urination, and blood sugar monitor that reads high

CorrectAnswer: A confused 65-year-old man brought from a house fire who exhibits good long-term recall, no recall of immediate events, normal vital signs, and carboxyhemoglobin level of 7%
ExplanationEN:
Dementia results from a gradual loss of mental capacity with the preservation of motor and speech. Dementia generally occurs in older patients. Remote memories are often preserved. The most common types of dementia are Alzheimer disease and vascular dementia, both insidious in onset. Symptoms may worsen acutely because of a concurrent medical condition. Physical exam and laboratory workup are generally unrevealing. Of the choices, a confused 65-year-old man brought from a house fire who exhibits good long-term recall, no recall of immediate events, normal vital signs, and a carboxyhemoglobin level of 7% is most likely to have dementia.



The other patients described all have organic causes of delirium. Carbon monoxide poisoning (B) causes confusion, headache, vomiting, and syncope, similar to the patient in the vignette. A febrile illness (pyelonephritis (C) or pneumonia (D)​) or severe metabolic derangement (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (E)) can also lead to delirium in older patients. In the evaluation of all such patients, it is critical to differentiate acute delirium, which is a confusional state where functions of cognition and attention are impacted due to an underlying medical cause, from chronic dementia.

Question: What is the most sensitive test for ruling out delirium in the ED?
ExplanationEN:
The Delirium Triage Screen (DTS) is the most sensitive bedside test for ruling out delirium, with a sensitivity of 98% and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.04. This makes the DTS an ideal, highly sensitive rule-out test in the two-step approach to delirium screening in the ED. When the DTS is negative, delirium can be confidently excluded, allowing clinicians to avoid unnecessary further testing.

When the DTS is positive, it should be followed by a more specific confirmatory tool, such as the Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM) or the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), to establish the diagnosis. Routine delirium screening in older adults and high-risk patients in the ED improves early recognition, facilitates prompt evaluation for reversible causes such as infection or metabolic disturbances, and is associated with better patient outcomes.



The bCAM (A) is a validated and efficient tool to diagnose delirium in patients in the ED. However, it is most useful as a confirmatory diagnostic tool, not a screening tool. Compared with DTS, bCAM is more specific but less sensitive. For this reason, bCAM is better used following a positive DTS screen rather than to rule out delirium.

The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (C) is a cognitive function test commonly used to assess dementia. However, it is not reliable for diagnosing or excluding delirium. It lacks sensitivity and specificity for detecting the acute cognitive changes and fluctuations characteristic of delirium, particularly in patients with baseline cognitive decline. It is also time consuming and does not assess key delirium features, such as inattention and altered consciousness.

The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) (D) is a validated tool to assess a patient’s level of arousal and is a component of both the DTS and bCAM. However, RASS alone does not assess attention or cognition and cannot independently rule out delirium. While a nonzero RASS score raises concern for delirium, normal findings do not exclude it without further assessment.

Question: Which of the following is characteristic of myasthenia gravis?

Options.text: Improvement of muscle strength with repeated stimulation

ExplanationEN:
Myasthenia gravis is caused by the autoimmune destruction of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. As a result of this autoantibody destruction, over time, fewer total receptors are available. At the remaining receptors, the autoantibodies compete with acetylcholine for the binding sites. With repeated stimulation, fewer receptor sites are available because of destruction, competition, and receptors remaining in the refractory period. As a result, muscles weaken and fatigue, which is the disease's hallmark. Most commonly, the first manifestation of the disease is ocular symptoms including ptosis, diplopia, and blurred vision. Over the course of the disease, involvement of the respiratory and bulbar muscles may develop. Symptoms of myasthenia gravis improve with cooling; thus the ice bag test is a diagnostic bedside maneuver. The ice bag test is based on the physiologic principle of improving neuromuscular transmission at lower muscle temperatures. The eyelid muscles are the most easily cooled by the application of ice. After the application of the ice bag, the distance between the lids is remeasured to assess for a difference.



Descending paralysis (A) is classic for botulism in which the botulinum toxin irreversibly binds to presynaptic membranes preventing the release of acetylcholine into the synapse. Botulism occurs in three forms to cause disease in humans: food-borne, wound botulism, and infant botulism. Improvement of muscle strength with repeated stimulation (B) is characteristic of Lambert-Eaton syndrome. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies target the presynaptic calcium channels which results in a reduction of acetylcholine release. With repeated stimulation, more acetylcholine is released from the intact portions of the synapse from calcium accumulation causing improvement of muscle strength. In myasthenia gravis, ptosis worsens over the course of the day, not in the morning (D).

Question: A 47-year-old man presents with acute onset of severe unilateral headaches. The headaches start behind his left eye and last approximately 45 minutes. Over the past 3 days, he has had roughly 10 such episodes. During the headaches, his eyes get blurry and “tear up,” and his nose “runs like a faucet.” He has tried acetaminophen, indomethacin, and cold compresses without relief. On exam, the patient has left-sided eyelid edema and conjunctival injection. His cranial nerves are intact, and he has no nuchal rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient with unilateral, retro-orbital headaches accompanied by lacrimation, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema has cluster headaches. Cluster headaches are four times more common in men than women. Little is known about the pathophysiology of the headache, though 85% of patients smoke cigarettes chronically. However, quitting smoking does not appear to alter the disease course. Diagnosis is made by clinical criteria with the International Classification of Headache Disorders and includes at least five headaches, severe unilateral pain, and associated sympathetic symptoms. Lab testing is unrevealing. Acute episodes are treated with high-flow oxygen by a nonrebreather mask, which relieves over 70% of headaches. Sumatriptan can be used for those who do not show clinical improvement with oxygen.



Paroxysmal hemicrania (B) has a similar presentation, with unilateral headaches and autonomic symptoms. However, paroxysmal hemicrania has a female predominance, attacks last < 30 minutes, and the vast majority of patients respond to indomethacin.

Primary stabbing headache (C) can also present as a unilateral headache but usually involves a distinct area of the scalp, lasts < 15 seconds, and does not have accompanying autonomic symptoms.

Trigeminal neuralgia (D) is similar to primary stabbing headache, with attacks that generally last < 15 seconds and follow the trigeminal distribution. Autonomic symptoms are less common in trigeminal neuralgia and V2 and V3 nerve branches are more often affected than V1.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 21-year-old woman presents with progressive headaches for 1 month. She also reports intermittent blurred vision bilaterally and increased headache with coughing. Direct ophthalmoscopy findings are shown above. What abnormality is typically found on lumbar puncture in patients with this presentation?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with a diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), which can be diagnosed by an increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture. IIH, previously called pseudotumor cerebri and benign intracranial hypertension, is a relatively common disease. It is typically seen in female patients with obesity. The exact pathophysiology of the disease is not fully understood, but it seems to result from a decreased outflow of CSF and increased brain water content.

The headache is typically generalized and gradual in onset. It may be worsened by eye movement or the Valsalva maneuver (or other maneuvers that increase intracranial pressure). Visual symptoms are common and can range from transient blurring of vision to vision loss. The headache may also be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Physical examination reveals papilledema, and patients may also have visual field defects. Diagnosis is made by an increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture. Opening pressure will be elevated > 250 mm H2O (25 cm H2O).



CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (A) are observed in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). While MS commonly presents in women around the age of 30 years, the common clinical manifestations are fatigue, sensory disturbances, visual impairment (often due to optic neuritis), incoordination, and weakness. Physical exam may demonstrate hyperreflexia and ocular abnormalities such as a relative afferent pupillary defect and internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Papilledema is not a common finding.

Decreased glucose (B) and an elevated white blood cell count (E) are typically seen in bacterial meningitis. Patients with bacterial meningitis present with an acute onset of fever, nuchal rigidity, and headache.

An elevated red blood cell count (D) is found in subarachnoid hemorrhage. Patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage present with a sudden, severe headache, which may be associated with loss of consciousness, vomiting, and meningismus signs.

Question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy presents to the ED after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 60 seconds. She reports running out of her valproate prescription 4 days ago. She reports no recent illness, trauma, or substance use. On examination, she appears mildly slow to respond, is oriented to person, place, and time, and has no focal neurologic deficits. What is the best management plan for this patient once she has returned to her baseline?

Options.text: Admission for observation and intravenous valproate administration
Discharge home with refills of her valproate prescription after a loading dose in the ED
Infectious, toxic, and metabolic laboratory evaluation
Noncontrast computed tomography of the brain

CorrectAnswer: Discharge home with refills of her valproate prescription after a loading dose in the ED
ExplanationEN:
In patients with a known seizure disorder who have returned to their neurologic baseline and have a clear explanation for a breakthrough seizure (e.g., missed antiepileptic dosing in this patient), it is reasonable to discharge these patients home. They should be given a dose of their home antiepileptic medication in the emergency department, though the route of administration may be either by mouth or intravenous. According to the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) policy on the management of seizure, patients with a known seizure disorder in which resuming their antiepileptic medication is appropriate, the route of administration does not impact seizure recurrence. Patients should be advised regarding the importance of medication adherence and provided with appropriate refills of antiepileptic medications. Discharge instructions should include the avoidance of driving and bathing or swimming alone and an expedited follow-up with their outpatient neurologist.



Admission for observation and intravenous valproate administration (A) might be considered if this patient had not returned to her neurologic baseline.

EEG and neurology consultation (C) are appropriate as a part of the outpatient follow-up for first-time unprovoked seizures in patients who have returned to their neurologic baseline. EEG and specialty consultation are unlikely to be of additional yield for a patient with a solidified epilepsy diagnosis and established outpatient neurology care.

Infectious, toxic, and metabolic laboratory evaluation (D) aids in the evaluation of a first-time seizure to delineate whether provoking factors (e.g., electrolyte disturbance, substance withdrawal) are present. If this patient had not returned to baseline, completion of this laboratory evaluation would be appropriate.

Noncontrast computed tomography of the brain (E) is indicated for patients with a first-time unprovoked seizure, immunocompromised state, a history of alcohol use disorder, focal neurologic deficits, or a first-time focal seizure.

Reveal Answer:
No, but it may reduce the rate of seizure recurrence.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED with a fever and a headache. The patient states he experienced a severe headache starting this morning as well as subjective fevers and malaise. He noticed that bright lights aggravated his symptoms. His BP is 127/68 mm Hg, HR is 120 bpm, RR is 24/min, T is 103°F (39.4°C), and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for jolt accentuation of the patient’s headache. Which of the following is the appropriate management?

Options.text: Ampicillin, vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and dexamethasone administration
IV fluids and repeat neurological exams to monitor recovery

ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of bacterial meningitis. Bacterial meningitis typically presents with a fever, stiff neck (meningismus), headache, phonophobia, and photophobia. Physical exam maneuvers include the Kernig sign (inability to extend the leg when the hip is flexed), Brudzinski sign (spontaneous flexion of the hips during passive flexion of the neck) and the most sensitive maneuver: jolt accentuation of headache (induced headache with horizontal rotation of the head at a rate of two to three times per second). The best initial step in management is early lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis.

Antibiotic therapy should also be promptly started. In immunocompetent patients aged 1 month to 50 years, empiric coverage for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis is mandatory. The preferred agents are ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and dexamethasone.

Dexamethasone is given as it reduces inflammation, mortality, and neurologic sequelae, including impaired mental status, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and sensorineural hearing loss in particular when the infectious agent is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Acyclovir can be added to cover for herpes simplex virus as part of initial empiric therapy.



Ampicillin, vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and dexamethasone administration (A) would be appropriate empiric treatment of bacterial meningitis in a patient ≥ 50 years. Ampicillin is added to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

Ceftriaxone and vancomycin administration (B) is an appropriate antibiotic regimen for bacterial meningitis for a patient between the ages of 1 month and 50 years. However, empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis of unknown etiology must have dexamethasone added to reduce mortality and the incidence of permanent neurologic sequelae (typically secondary to Streptococcus pneumoniae).

IV fluids and repeat neurological exams to monitor recovery (D) is the appropriate management of viral meningitis that is not due to herpes simplex virus (a potential cause of encephalitis) as these infections resolve on their own. It is inappropriate to only offer supportive therapy without a lumbar puncture demonstrating a clear viral etiology.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the preferred empiric antibiotic regimen for meningitis in an immunocompromised patient?

Reveal Answer:
Vancomycin, ampicillin, and cefepime or meropenem to cover for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes, and aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa).

Question: Which of the following requires chemoprophylaxis for meningitis exposure?

Options.text: Breastfeeding mother of an infant with Escherichia coli meningitis

Respiratory therapist (vaccinated) for a 10-year-old with Haemophilus influenzae meningitis
Roommate of a 19-year-old with Neisseria meningitidis

CorrectAnswer: Roommate of a 19-year-old with Neisseria meningitidis
ExplanationEN:
Chemoprophylaxis with rifampin is recommended for all high-risk contacts of patients with documented meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis. High-risk contacts include household members, school contacts in the prior 7 days, and patients with direct exposure to secretions. Patients given chemoprophylaxis should be advised to seek medical treatment immediately if they develop signs or symptoms of meningitis.



E. coli (A) rarely causes meningitis outside of the newborn period. Chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for these contacts.

S. pneumoniae (B) meningitis does not require chemoprophylaxis for contacts.

H. influenzae (C) meningitis is rare now that the H. influenzae vaccine is prevalent in the population. Vaccinated health care workers do not require chemoprophylaxis. However, chemoprophylaxis is recommended in confirmed cases of H. influenzae meningitis when the exposed person has not received vaccination.

Question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the hospital with sudden weakness. On exam, she has aphasia, leftward gaze preference, right facial droop, and right upper and lower extremity weakness. Her family reports she was last at her baseline 8 hours ago, where she was functionally independent. Her NIH Stroke Scale score is 11. A head CT head shows no acute hemorrhage, and CT angiography shows a left proximal middle cerebral artery occlusion. Which clinical decision-making tool is most useful for determining the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with an acute ischemic stroke, and she has a large vessel occlusion (LVO) of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). While she is outside the window for thrombolytic therapy, she is a candidate for mechanical thrombectomy since she is presenting within 24 hours of symptom onset.

The decision to pursue mechanical thrombectomy for LVO depends on if there is a significant amount of salvageable tissue, known as penumbra. Since infarcted tissue is not salvageable, patients with large volumes of infarcted tissue are less likely to benefit from mechanical thrombectomy. The ratio of penumbra to infarcted tissue can be determined with computed tomographic perfusion (CTP) or with the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS).

The ASPECTS score is based on radiologic findings from the initial noncontrast head CT. To calculate the score, 1 point is subtracted from 10 if there is radiographic evidence of ischemic change in designated regions of subcortical structures and the MCA cortex. Lower scores represent a greater extent of infarction. Patients with ASPECTS ≥ 6 are more likely to benefit from mechanical thrombectomy.



The congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, stroke, vascular disease, sex category (CHA2DS2-VASc) score (B) is used to stratify risk of thromboembolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation and determine which patients would benefit most from anticoagulation. This score does not have a role in determining the management of acute ischemic stroke.

The modified Rankin Score (mRS) (C) quantifies the degree of disability in patients who have sustained a stroke. It is used over time to assess functional outcomes. While prestroke functional status is important to consider when determining the best intervention, it is not the primary means of determining eligibility for thrombectomy.

The secondary intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) score (D) is used for patients with intracerebral hemorrhage to predict the likelihood that the hemorrhage was caused by a vascular etiology. In the setting of intracranial hemorrhage with a negative CT angiogram, higher sICH scores may be used to support a decision to pursue cerebral angiography. The sICH score does not have a role in ischemic stroke management.

The thrombolysis in cerebral infarction (TICI) score (E) is used to grade reperfusion after thrombectomy. TICI 3 indicates normal perfusion after thrombectomy, while TICI 0 indicates no reperfusion. TICI scores are not used prior to intervention.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents after a seizure at home. His spouse notes that he has been acting strangely for the last few weeks, yelling at family members for minor things and missing appointments. He also reported a headache each of the last three mornings. He has no significant medical history and has always been healthy, according to his spouse. Which of the following will most likely be found on brain imaging?

Options.text: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema
Solid, homogeneous mass in the midline of the posterior fossa
Temporal lobe mass with central necrosis and peripheral enhancement

CorrectAnswer: Temporal lobe mass with central necrosis and peripheral enhancement
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms concerning for a malignant brain tumor. Glioblastomas are the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. Patients often present with a fairly short duration of symptoms including headache, vomiting, neurologic deficits, personality changes, and seizures. Headaches are often dull, worse in the morning, and exacerbated by bending over or the Valsalva maneuver.

On imaging, glioblastomas appear as heterogeneous lesions with central necrosis and peripheral enhancement. There is often associated edema and mass effect present. The term “butterfly glioma” comes from the preferential spread of tumor along white matter commissural tracts, such as the corpus callosum. The overall survival rate is 10–12 months after diagnosis despite treatment, which can include surgical resection, radiation therapy, and adjuvant chemotherapy.



An extra-axial dural-based mass (A) describes a meningioma, the most frequently encountered primary brain tumor, the majority of which are benign. They are very slow growing and are often found incidentally in asymptomatic patients. Depending on their location, they can cause focal neurological findings or seizures. Given the rapid progression of this patient’s symptoms, glioblastoma is more likely.

Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema (B) would be seen in a patient with cerebral toxoplasmosis. This is almost exclusively a disorder found in significantly immunocompromised individuals (e.g., AIDS patients with CD4 counts < 100 cells/µL) and presents with headache, fever, altered mental status, and seizure.

A solid, homogeneous mass in the midline of the posterior fossa (C) would be characteristic of medulloblastoma, a highly invasive neuroepithelial tumor. They are the most common malignant brain tumors found in children. Presenting signs and symptoms are related to increased intracranial pressure (e.g., vomiting, headache) and cerebellar dysfunction.

Question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the ED with numbness. She states that she has had reduced facial sensation for the past 2 days. She reports a similar episode of sensory change approximately 2 years ago in which her hand and forearm were affected, but she did not seek medical attention at that time. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows reduced sensation to pinprick in the right face and flattening of the nasolabial fold with intact movements of the upper face. Which of the following is the most appropriate test for diagnosing this patient’s most likely condition?

Options.text: CT of the head without contrast
CTA of the head and neck
MRA of the head and neck
MRI of the brain and spinal cord with contrast
MRI of the brain and spinal cord without contrast

CorrectAnswer: MRI of the brain and spinal cord with contrast
ExplanationEN:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system (CNS), the etiology of which has not been explicitly identified. It is thought to result from an autoimmune mechanism triggered by environmental stimuli in patients with an underlying genetic susceptibility. This causes inflammatory demyelination in discrete regions within the CNS, with relative sparing of axons. The clinical features of MS are highly variable, but they are defined by recurrent episodes of neurologic symptoms that progress over days and gradually resolve over weeks. The specific symptoms vary based on the location of underlying CNS lesions but may result from injury to any of the cranial nerves, sensory or motor pathways, cerebellar pathways, or structures involved in such functions as cognition, bowel and bladder control, and sexual function. Optic neuritis is the presenting diagnosis in up to 30% of patients. This patient is describing both a current and prior episode of sensory pathway involvement, affecting distinct locations within sensory pathways that are highly suspicious for MS, given her demographics.

Given the heterogeneity of symptoms caused by MS and that most ED clinicians do not evaluate these patients longitudinally, the diagnosis is challenging to make in the ED. MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium enhancement is the best initial imaging study for new suspected cases of MS and for evaluation of disease severity in exacerbations. MS lesions typically occur in multiple locations, though the periventricular white matter is the most common. Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis is also a useful diagnostic test for suspected MS, though definitive diagnosis typically requires more specialized CSF testing than is commonly available in the ED. Prompt, accurate diagnosis is crucial in cases of MS, as it carries the risk of significant disability if neurologic symptoms and deficits become permanent. If diagnosed, treatment with high-dose steroids should begin to reduce the duration of symptoms, typically in consultation with a neurologist.



While potentially useful in ruling out other serious neurologic conditions (e.g., stroke, intracranial hemorrhage), CTA (B) and noncontrast CT of the head (A) are not helpful in the diagnosis of MS.

The pathogenesis of MS does not involve cerebral vasculature, so an MRA (C) would be of limited utility.

Gadolinium enhancement is crucial in identifying CNS lesions of MS, so MRI without contrast (E) would be insufficient.

Question: A 22-month-old patient whose immunizations are up to date presents after a generalized seizure. Her parent reports one seizure lasting < 5 minutes. She has had rhinorrhea for the last 2 days and has a temperature of 102.0°F (38.9°C). On exam, she is well appearing and has returned to baseline. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
ExplanationEN:
Febrile seizures are defined as the presence of seizures in a febrile child without a CNS infection (e.g., meningitis). They are a common cause of seizures in children and most commonly occur between 6 months and 5 years of age, with a peak occurrence between 14 and 18 months. The risk of seizure is thought to correlate more with the absolute temperature rather than the rate of rise.

A simple febrile seizure is brief, single, and nonfocal or generalized. Complex febrile seizures are prolonged, recurrent, or focal. Evaluation of the simple febrile seizure is dictated by the evaluation of the fever and not the seizure. Patients should receive supportive care for the postictal state and their underlying illness.



Anticonvulsant therapy (A) has no role after a single febrile seizure.

CBC and blood culture (B) is not indicated in this patient. In fully vaccinated children aged 3–36 months, routine laboratory testing is not part of the diagnostic algorithm. A urinalysis and culture are considered in female patients < 24 months.

CT scan and EEG (C) are unnecessary in most patients with febrile seizures. Neuroimaging should be considered in children who have abnormal findings on neurologic exam that persist after the seizure ends. Children with prolonged or focal complex febrile seizures may benefit from a delayed EEG to evaluate for the presence of underlying epilepsy.

Lumbar puncture (D) is suggested by the American Academy of Pediatrics for children with the following criteria: signs of meningeal irritation, incomplete immunization, or history of prior antibiotic therapy. It is also more strongly considered in children with complex seizures or those < 12 months of age.

Reveal Answer:
Yes, slightly. The risk is 1–2% instead of 0.5–1% in the general population.

Question: A previously healthy 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with headache and neck stiffness. On examination, he appears ill. His HR is 110 bpm and BP is 110/70 mm Hg. He experiences pain with flexion of his neck. A lumbar puncture is performed and shows a CSF WBC count of 110 cells/µL, glucose of 60 mg/dL, protein of 60 mg/dL, and opening pressure of 7 cm H2O. Which of the following represents the most likely etiology of the patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with viral meningitis most likely secondary to enterovirus. Enterovirus represents the most common cause of aseptic meningitis in children. Symptoms are similar to bacterial meningitis and include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. In older children, meningeal irritation can be elicited by the Kernig or Brudzinski signs. Etiologies and clinical manifestations are different in the neonatal period and are not discussed here.

Patients with suspected meningitis should receive a lumbar puncture as part of their evaluation. Typically, patients affected by viral meningitis will demonstrate a slightly elevated CSF cell count and protein with normal CSF glucose and opening pressure. Antibiotics should be initiated until CSF cultures can confirm viral meningitis. Acyclovir should also be initiated as this is the only treatable etiology of viral meningitis (for herpes simplex virus [HSV]). Serology for HSV and enterovirus should be obtained. Treatment of confirmed non-HSV viral meningitis is supportive care.



Mycobacterium tuberculosis (B) should be suspected in patients with risk factors, including known exposure. However, CSF glucose would be expected to be < 40 mg/dL and CSF protein would be more significantly elevated in this type of infection.

Respiratory syncytial virus (C) is not a typical cause of viral meningitis.

Streptococcus pneumonia (D) is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in this age group. However, CSF findings would include an elevated opening pressure, cell count, and protein and decreased glucose.

Question: A 6-year-old girl with a mature ventriculoperitoneal shunt due to congenital hydrocephalus has had 3 days of fever and increasing seizures at home. She presents along with her parents for evaluation. She is not currently seizing but appears altered from baseline. What is your next step?

Options.text: Obtain a CT of the head without contrast

CorrectAnswer: Obtain a CT of the head without contrast
ExplanationEN:
A CT of the head is the next priority in the case of a suspected failed or infected shunt, as it can reveal worsening hydrocephalus or possible shunt fracture. Shunts most often fail shortly after being placed but can fail at any time due to the growth of the patient, trauma, or CNS infection. Shunt failures most commonly lead to symptoms such as progressive headaches, altered mental status, new or increasing seizures, or fever, and require a broad differential and workup to include lab studies and imaging.



Once all causes of infection and shunt failure have been addressed, a neurology consult (A) is appropriate to ensure that patients with seizure disorders are medically optimized. However, if there is an indication of a shunt failure or infection, a neurosurgeon should be consulted to consider surgical intervention. Fevers and infections lower the seizure threshold, so it is important to rule out other causes of fever with a chest X-ray and blood cultures (C), but imaging is the immediate priority in such cases. A suspected infected shunt should be tapped by a neurosurgeon instead of a lumbar puncture (D), if at all possible.

Question: A 46-year-old woman presents to the ED for urinary symptoms and is diagnosed with a UTI. Her medical history includes schizoaffective disorder, for which she receives a monthly long-acting depot injection of haloperidol. The patient displays repetitive lip-smacking movements and twisting motions of the hands. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathogenesis of this patient’s abnormal movements?

Options.text: Axonal demyelination within the central nervous system
Dysregulated dopaminergic signaling within the basal ganglia
GABAergic neuronal dysfunction within the brainstem and cerebellum
Increased serotonergic stimulation within the central and peripheral nervous systems
Neurodegeneration within the striatum due to mutant huntingtin protein

CorrectAnswer: Dysregulated dopaminergic signaling within the basal ganglia
ExplanationEN:
Drug-induced movement disorders are a prominent adverse effect of drugs with anti-dopaminergic activity and include dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. The pathogenesis of these disorders is not entirely known but likely involves impaired dopaminergic signaling, particularly within the basal ganglia, due to the dopamine-blocking effects of neuroleptic medications. The most prominent of such medications are the first-generation antipsychotics, which include haloperidol, though second-generation antipsychotics and the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine have been implicated as well.

Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a specific form of drug-induced movement disorder characterized by choreiform or dystonic movements primarily of the lips, mouth, and tongue, though the trunk, limbs, and respiratory muscles can be affected in severe cases. These symptoms present months to years after initiation of the causative agent and can even develop after drug cessation. Typical movements of the face include tongue protruding, lip smacking, chewing, and blepharospasm. Truncal and limb movements can include twisting and spreading motions of the hands and fingers and shoulder shrugging, while tachypnea and irregular breathing patterns can manifest when respiratory muscles are involved.

Primary treatment of TD is cessation of the offending agent, but abrupt withdrawal should be avoided, as this can induce worsening of symptoms. In cases in which continued antipsychotic therapy is needed, patients should be transitioned to an atypical antipsychotic, as these carry a lower risk of movement disorders compared to typical antipsychotics. Valbenazine is approved for pharmacologic treatment, and some studies have shown benefit with other agents such as valproic acid, anticholinergics, and botulinum toxin injections. Movements of TD can persist after withdrawal of the offending agent and become permanent in some cases, making effective treatment difficult.



Multiple sclerosis is caused by axonal demyelination within the CNS (A), which is not associated with the movements in this patient, while dysfunction of GABAergic neurons in the brainstem and cerebellum (C) contributes to the pathogenesis of essential tremor.

Increased serotonergic stimulation within the central and peripheral nervous systems (D) and striatal neurodegeneration (E) describe the pathogenesis of serotonin syndrome and Huntington disease, respectively. Serotonin syndrome presents with tachycardia, agitation, pressured speech, diaphoresis, mydriasis, and hyperreflexia. Huntington disease presents with choreiform (writhing) movements with cognitive and behavioral decline.
