Question: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a fever and confusion. His T is 104°F (40°C), BP is 112/63 mm Hg, HR is 132 bpm, RR is 25/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals a confused young man who does not follow commands. The patient has 1,500 mL of urine in his bladder. He does not withdraw his upper or lower extremities to painful stimuli. MRI of the brain and cervical spine is presented above. The patient is started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following would most appropriately improve outcomes for this patient based on the symptoms and MRI findings?
ExplanationEN:
The MRI reveals an extensive hyperintense T2 and short tau inversion recovery signal spanning from C1 to C7 within the spinal cord accompanied by swelling of the cord. The diagnosis is transverse myelitis when there is inflammation that affects an entire transverse section of the spinal cord. There are many possible causes, including autoimmune conditions (multiple sclerosis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis), infectious conditions (herpes simplex virus, syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus, West Nile virus), and malignancy (paraneoplastic syndromes, neurosarcoidosis). Patients will present with sensory, motor, and autonomic dysfunction below the level of the lesion. Management involves first working up and addressing any underlying causes, particularly infectious causes. The diagnosis is supported by an MRI with and without contrast. Intravenous steroids, such as methylprednisolone, are the first-line treatment for this condition. Additional treatments may be considered based on the underlying cause (e.g., antiviral therapy for viral infections, immunotherapies for autoimmune diseases, plasma exchange, or plasmapheresis when patients do not respond adequately to high-dose corticosteroids).



Acyclovir (A) is an antiviral medication effective against herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus. There is no direct evidence in this patient suggesting a herpes simplex virus infection that acyclovir would treat. No rash is mentioned. Further testing is recommended.

Neurosurgery consultation for decompression (C) would be appropriate management of an epidural abscess, which may present with a fever, neck pain, back pain, neurological deficits, and possible sepsis. MRI would demonstrate an abscess rather than spinal cord edema.

Tenecteplase (D) is the appropriate treatment for an acute ischemic stroke, which would present with focal neurological deficits isolated to a vascular distribution. One of the contraindications to tenecteplase is a more likely alternative diagnosis, such as meningitis and transverse myelitis, as is present in this patient.

Question: Which of the following is suggestive of dementia rather than delirium?

Options.text: Sudden onset and offset of symptoms
Symptoms associated with disturbance in the sleep-wake cycle

ExplanationEN:
Dementia presents with gradual-onset memory loss. Early in the disease course, patients may present with minor forgetfulness that can be confused with normal memory loss of aging. As it progresses, patients will forget names and addresses and lose the ability to perform acts of daily living. Dementia is a gradual-onset process that slowly worsens over months to years. As the condition progresses, patients may struggle to find words and communicate. In contrast, delirium is a sudden-onset process. Patients with dementia are more prone to delirium, as are patients with advanced age. Infection, change in environment, loss of a hearing aid, dehydration, or any physiological disturbance can cause delirium. Delirium has a rapidly fluctuating course, and patients may be suddenly agitated and confused with possible delusions and hallucinations. Symptoms are more common at night and when the sleep-wake cycle is disturbed. Management is centered on treating any underlying medical cause. Regular sleep and a healthy diet are also protective. A familiar environment and family can also reduce delirium.



Sudden onset and offset of symptoms (B), symptoms associated with disturbance in the sleep-wake cycle (C), and symptoms associated with infection (D) would all be more suggestive of delirium rather than dementia.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a headache. He has a history of diabetes mellitus type 1, hypertension, and alcohol use disorder. He states he started feeling unwell 3 days ago, and the headache started this morning. He also reports having blurred vision and nausea without vomiting and no chest pain or shortness of breath. Vital signs are remarkable for a T of 39°C (102.2°F), HR of 115 bpm, BP of 100/60 mm Hg, RR of 23/min, and SpO2 of 97%. Physical examination is remarkable for a man who appears lethargic. Upon passively flexing the patient's neck, he flexes at the hips and knees. Which of the following sequences is the best next step in this patient’s care?

Options.text: Administer ceftriaxone and vancomycin; CT head; lumbar puncture
Administer ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin; CT head; lumbar puncture
CT head; lumbar puncture; administer ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin
Lumbar puncture; administer ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin

CorrectAnswer: Administer ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin; CT head; lumbar puncture
ExplanationEN:
Meningitis is due to meningeal infection and inflammation, and the diagnosis should be considered in patients with a headache who present with an associated triad of fever, altered mentation, and neck stiffness. However, the entire triad is rarely seen. Thus, a high index of suspicion should be maintained in patients presenting with any combination of these. Meningitis can be viral, bacterial, and, less commonly, fungal or parasitic. A lumbar puncture (LP) for analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid should be obtained in patients with features concerning for meningitis. Bacterial meningitis will demonstrate a low glucose, high protein, and a significant elevation of WBCs in the CSF that is often > 100 WBCs/µL.

In patients presenting with features concerning for elevated ICP, such as altered mental status, neurological deficits, seizures, or papilledema, a CT scan of the head should be obtained before LP due to the risk of herniation. In any situation, antibiotics should be administered first, as a delay worsens the prognosis and mortality risk, and this is especially the case in patients who require a head CT first. The recommended antibiotics include ceftriaxone and vancomycin in patients beyond the neonatal period and up to 50 years. In neonates and patients > 50 years old, ampicillin should also be administered to cover Listeria monocytogenes. This recommendation should also be provided to patients who have alcohol use disorder or are immunocompromised, including those with HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancies, end-stage kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and those being treated with tumor necrosis factor medications.



Administering ceftriaxone and vancomycin; CT head; lumbar puncture (A) would have been an appropriate treatment sequence if the patient did not have a history of diabetes mellitus and alcohol use disorder. Due to this history, the patient is considered immunocompromised, and ampicillin should be added for Listeria monocytogenes coverage until cultures return.

CT head; lumbar puncture; administering ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin (C) is incorrect due to the worsened prognosis with antibiotic delay.

Lumbar puncture; administering ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and vancomycin (D) is incorrect as the patient has visual changes and appears lethargic, which could suggest papilledema and increased intracranial pressure. Head CT is required.

Question: A 61-year-old man presents to the ED with intermittent shock-like spasms of pain in his right cheek. The pain only lasts a few seconds at a time but recurs frequently. He notes that shaving each morning causes intense spasms of pain, as does chewing. What is the first-line treatment for his likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Trigeminal neuralgia is a chronic pain condition characterized by sudden, severe, unilateral, electric shock-like paroxysms of pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, most commonly the maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions. Episodes are brief, typically lasting seconds to minutes, and can occur spontaneously or be triggered by everyday activities such as chewing, brushing teeth, speaking, shaving, or exposure to wind or temperature changes. Pain is often described as stabbing or burning and may occur in clusters, with symptom-free intervals in between.

The condition is usually caused by vascular compression at the root entry zone of the trigeminal nerve, often by an aberrant loop of the superior cerebellar artery. This compression leads to demyelination and hyperexcitability of the nerve fibers. Less commonly, trigeminal neuralgia may result from multiple sclerosis, tumors, or brain stem infarcts, especially in patients < 65 years old or those with bilateral symptoms. Women are affected more frequently than men, and it typically presents after age 50.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on a detailed patient history and characteristic features of the pain. A thorough evaluation is essential to exclude other causes of facial pain, such as dental infections, temporomandibular joint disorders, sinusitis, or postherpetic neuralgia. Neuroimaging, typically with MRI, is often performed to assess for secondary causes like tumors or multiple sclerosis plaques and to evaluate for vascular compression of the nerve root.

First-line pharmacologic treatment is carbamazepine, which is initiated at 100 mg twice daily and titrated as needed for symptom control, typically up to 1,200 mg/day. Oxcarbazepine is an alternative with a similar mechanism of action and fewer side effects. Patients on carbamazepine require periodic monitoring of complete blood counts and liver function tests due to the risk of hematologic toxicity and hepatotoxicity. If medication is ineffective or poorly tolerated, second-line options include other anticonvulsants (e.g., gabapentin, lamotrigine).

Overall, early recognition and effective treatment of trigeminal neuralgia are important to reduce the impact of this debilitating pain disorder on quality of life. Treatment plans should be individualized, with a focus on symptom control and minimizing adverse effects.



Baclofen (A) has been used in the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia, although there is limited evidence of its efficacy.

Botulinum injections (B) may be useful in patients with pain that is refractory to medical options.

Diazepam (D) is not used in the management of trigeminal neuralgia.

Question: A 17-year-old girl with a history of migraines presents to the emergency department with a severe headache. She reports the pain is her typical migraine pain consisting of unilateral severe head pain with photophobia and flashes of light. Her trial of acetaminophen and sumatriptan at home has not resulted in any relief. Her physical exam is normal. Which of the following is the most effective next step in the management of her headache?
ExplanationEN:
A migraine is a severe disabling recurrent headache often accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia, and vomiting. No genetic markers have yet been identified as the cause of migraines despite that such headaches frequently run in families. The once well-known theory of a vascular origin of migraines has been shown to be incorrect. The current leading theory is one of primary neuronal dysfunction but is yet to be proven. Treatment includes identifying triggers with a headache calendar, sleep, and a trial of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs which are often effective for mild symptoms. In the emergency department, one of the most effective solutions includes an intravenous normal saline bolus given with intravenous prochlorperazine and ketorolac.



Dexamethasone (A) and other corticosteroids have not been shown to be effective in the treatment of acute migraines in children in the emergency department setting.

Meperidine (B) and other opiates should be avoided in the treatment of headaches as they are less effective and have a strong potential to promote chronic migraines.

While sodium valproate (D) has historically been used in the treatment of migraines, there is limited evidence for its use in children.

Question: A 48-year-old man with a history of hypertension and nonadherence to his medications presents with a severe headache that began 8 hours before arrival. His neurologic exam is nonfocal. CT scan is shown above. His pain is resolved after intravenous fluids and parenteral medications. Vital signs include a BP of 195/96 mm Hg, HR of 92 bpm, RR of 16/minute, and T of 98.6°F (37°C). Which of the following is the best next step in patient care?

Options.text: Check an ECG, urinalysis, and basic metabolic panel

ExplanationEN:
Nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is an important cause of headache with a 30-day mortality of almost 50% and potentially devastating complications. It is usually caused by a ruptured berry aneurysm, which is a focal arterial pouch in areas of bifurcation on the circle of Willis. Diagnosis within the first 6–12 hours can often be made by a noncontrast CT scan, which shows hyperdense material filling the subarachnoid space.

Blood pressure should be lowered immediately. Systolic blood pressure < 160 mm Hg is a reasonable initial target according to a national guideline. Definitive therapy involves urgent endovascular coil embolization or surgical clipping of the aneurysm to prevent rebleeding. If the patient has acute hydrocephalus with increased intracranial pressure, they may also require urgent ventriculostomy.

Even if symptoms resolve, patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage should be treated in the ICU due to the risk of complications, such as delayed vasospasm with ischemia. Other serious potential complications include seizures, hyponatremia, stress cardiomyopathy, dysrhythmias, and other organ dysfunction. Oral nimodipine is proven to improve neurologic outcomes if started within 4 days of symptom onset and continued for 21 days.



Checking an ECG, urinalysis, and basic metabolic panel (A) is sometimes done to screen for complications of poorly controlled hypertension. Obtaining a baseline creatinine prior to an angiogram is also reasonable. However, addressing the blood pressure is more important in the initial treatment of this patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Discharging with close follow-up (B) would not be appropriate for this patient, even if asymptomatic, as he still needs evaluation for a possible ruptured aneurysm.

While lumbar puncture (D) could be performed in a patient highly suspected of having a subarachnoid hemorrhage after a negative head CT, this patient’s imaging shows a hemorrhage and requires further intervention.

One Step Further
Question:
Should patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage receive seizure prophylaxis?

Reveal Answer:
Not usually, unless hemorrhage is extensive with cortical involvement. Specifically, prophylaxis with phenytoin has been shown to cause worse outcomes.

Question: A 76-year-old man presents with acute onset of sustained vertigo and nystagmus. Which of the following findings on examination would be concerning for a central cause of his symptoms?

Options.text: Absent skew deviation with alternate eye covering
Fatigability of nystagmus with repeated Dix-Hallpike testing

ExplanationEN:
Patients presenting with acute vertigo and nystagmus pose a challenge to the emergency clinician. While the majority of these patients will have a peripheral etiology for their symptoms, a small percentage will have a central cause such as a cerebellar stroke. The HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) exam is a bedside test that can help differentiate between peripheral and central causes of vertigo. It should only be used in patients with acute, sustained vertigo and nystagmus. The head impulse test is performed by quickly and unpredictably turning the patient's head from side to side while instructing them to maintain focus on a distant target. A patient with central vertigo will have a normal head impulse test, characterized by the patient’s eyes remaining on the target. In a patient with a peripheral cause of vertigo, the eyes are dragged off the target followed by a corrective saccade. This is considered an abnormal head impulse test and is reassuring for a peripheral cause of vertigo such as vestibular neuritis.



Evaluation of nystagmus is the second component of the HINTS exam. A patient with peripheral vertigo will have unidirectional, horizontal nystagmus (D), while a patient with a central cause will have bidirectional nystagmus (i.e., the fast component of nystagmus beats in the same direction as the gaze).

The Dix-Hallpike test is not a part of the HINTS exam but is a positional test that can confirm the diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. One of the classic findings of positional vertigo is fatigability of nystagmus with repeated Dix-Hallpike testing (B).

The test of skew is the final component of the HINTS exam. Patients with peripheral vertigo will have absent skew deviation with alternate eye covering (A), while vertical ocular misalignment is concerning for brainstem stroke.

One Step Further
Question:
Should both the Dix-Hallpike and the head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (HINTS) exams be performed on the same patient?

Reveal Answer:
No. The Dix-Hallpike test should be done on patients who present with episodic vertigo and nystagmus that occurs with certain movements of the head while the HINTS exam is reserved for patients with sustained vertigo not associated with position changes.

Question: A 60-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with weakness. The patient has a medical history of hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, and low back pain. She states that she has been well other than a recent upper respiratory infection. She started noticing difficulty with ambulation 3 days ago. She also thinks she now has a urinary tract infection, and she reports urinary urgency with the sensation of incomplete voiding. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination is remarkable for 0/5 strength in bilateral lower extremities that are notably flaccid, numbness in the perineum, and paresthesias and numbness noted encircling the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus. Laboratory studies reveal sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 105 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 75 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, calcium 2.4 mmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 25 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 20 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 50 IU/L, WBC 12 x 10⁹/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 20 mm/hr. A postvoid residual reveals 400 mL of urine retained in the bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Acute transverse myelitis is a rare acquired neuroimmune spinal cord disorder that results in several neurological concerns and deficits. It is considered a mixed nervous inflammatory disorder and affects white matter, gray matter, axons, and myelin sheaths and is thus not considered a demyelinating disorder. It can occur independently, usually as a postinfectious complication, or as a continuum of neuroinflammatory disorders. Clinical features include motor, sensory, or autonomic dysfunction with an acute or subacute onset. Motor symptoms include a rapidly progressing paresis that can include both the lower and upper extremities. This paresis typically starts as a flaccid paralysis that is followed by increased spasticity. Patients will also have a sensory level that is noticeable on exam as well as on MRI. Sensory symptoms include pain, sensory deficits, dysesthesia, and paresthesia. Autonomic symptoms can also occur and include urinary urgency, bladder and bowel incontinence, difficulty or inability voiding, incomplete bowel evacuation, and sexual dysfunction. The onset of urinary retention may be the first sign of transverse myelitis and should raise suspicion for the possibility of myelopathy.

The diagnosis should be suspected in all patients who present with acute or subacute symptoms suggestive of myelitis but without evidence of cord compression. Thus, transverse myelitis requires excluding a cord-compressing lesion, usually by MRI, and confirming an inflammatory lesion. This lesion is typically revealed on a gadolinium-enhanced MRI or lumbar puncture. CSF will be abnormal in approximately one-half of patients and will demonstrate a lymphocytosis and an elevated protein level. Glucose will be normal and oligoclonal bands are not typically present. Intravenous high-dose glucocorticoids are the treatment of choice for all adults and adolescents diagnosed with transverse myelitis. Plasmapheresis is performed in refractory cases in conjunction with continuing intravenous glucocorticoids.



Cauda equina syndrome (A)results from lesions compressing the conus medullaris and the nerve roots extending from it (the cauda equina). Patients with cauda equina syndrome commonly report low back pain, lower extremity pain, paralysis or paresthesia, saddle anesthesia, impotence, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. However, patients will not have a sensory level on exam, making cauda equina less likely in this case.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (B)is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy that is most often characterized by an acute monophasic paralyzing illness. Clinical features include progressive and symmetric muscle weakness that is accompanied by decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes, with sensory deficits not typically present, and when present, they should prompt further investigation into other causes. This patient does not have a history of ascending paralysis and is also experiencing sensory deficits, making this diagnosis less likely.

Spinal epidural abscesses (C) are a rare but important infection of the central nervous system that requires emergent consideration, diagnosis, and treatment. Spinal epidural abscesses are most commonly found in the thoracic or lumbar areas. Risk factors include epidural catheter placement, paraspinal injections, diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, HIV, trauma, bacteremia, intravenous drug use, and hemodialysis. The classic triad of symptoms for a spinal epidural abscess is fever, spinal pain, and neurologic deficits (may be consistent with cauda equina syndrome). A complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein lab values are typically obtained for evaluation, with elevation noted in the majority of cases. This patient has a normal sedimentation rate, no fever, and no back pain, making spinal epidural abscess less likely.

Reveal Answer:
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation on warfarin presents to a rural emergency department at 11:00 AM with a left-sided facial droop and left upper extremity weakness. She reports the symptoms began at 7:00 AM while making her coffee. Her National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale is calculated to be 10. Blood work is performed and significant for an INR of 2.5. A CT scan is performed and shown above. Which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Administer tPA then transfer to a stroke center
Initiate aspirin and high-dose statin therapy
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Transfer to a stroke center for possible mechanical thrombectomy

CorrectAnswer: Transfer to a stroke center for possible mechanical thrombectomy
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s symptoms and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) are concerning for an acute cerebrovascular accident (CVA). Her CT scan shows focal hyperdensity of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), known as the dense MCA sign, an early indication of MCA ischemic occlusion. While her presentation puts her in the appropriate time window for tPA administration (0–4.5 hours), her daily warfarin use and INR ≥ 1.7 is an absolute contraindication for tPA administration. Patients with evidence of large artery occlusion, such as an internal carotid artery or MCA occlusion, who have absolute contraindications to tPA or are ineligible for tPA due to the time of symptom onset, are candidates for mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours from the time they were last seen well. Additional criteria depending on the time from onset include functional independence at baseline, and the area of ischemia should be < one-third the MCA territory. These patients should be transferred to a stroke center for a CT angiogram or MR angiogram to quantify the occlusion further and be evaluated for mechanical thrombectomy.



Patients presenting with an acute stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset who do not have any contraindications should receive tPA. Administering tPA and then transferring to a stroke center (A) is incorrect in this case as the patient has an absolute contraindication to tPA administration. Absolute contraindications include neurosurgery, head trauma, or stroke in the last 3 months; uncontrolled hypertension (> 185 mm Hg systolic BP or > 110 mm Hg diastolic BP); history of intracranial hemorrhage; known intracranial arteriovenous malformation, neoplasm, or aneurysm; active internal bleeding; suspected or confirmed endocarditis; blood glucose < 50 mg/dL; and known bleeding diathesis (platelet count < 100,000, heparin administration within last 48 hours and elevated aPTT, current use of oral anticoagulant with an INR ≥ 1.7, or current use of direct thrombin inhibitors or direct factor Xa inhibitors). Initiating aspirin and high-dose statin therapy (B) is incorrect. While these agents play a well-documented role in reducing the risk of recurrent CVAs, they are not indicated in the acute treatment phase. Inconclusive CT imaging (including CT angiogram) may be followed up with magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (C). This patient has a dense MCA sign on her CT imaging, highly specific for MCA occlusion.

Question: If a child is brought to the ED with a fever and seizure activity, establishing characteristics of the seizure activity via talking to parents or caregivers is key to making a correct diagnosis. Which of the following is most consistent with a simple febrile seizure?

Options.text: Focal seizure activity with postictal neurological abnormalities

ExplanationEN:
Characteristics of a simple febrile seizure include seizure duration < 15 minutes, generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity, and one seizure in a 24-hour period. These characteristics must be present, along with a lack of postictal neurological abnormalities, to diagnose a simple febrile seizure. Individually, they are nonspecific. Proof of fever prior to arrival may not be available at the ED, but fever in the ED or descriptions of suspected fever signs may suffice. Other useful past and recent medical history elements include a history of previous seizures and associated diagnoses, patient medications and allergies, recent head trauma, family medical history including siblings of the patient, and the type, dose, method, and last administered time of antipyretics, if administered.



Age < 6 months (A) is incorrect, as simple febrile seizures occur in children 6 months to 5 years of age.

Focal seizure activity with postictal neurological abnormalities (B) is incorrect since the presence of focal seizure activity and postictal focal neurological abnormalities are both signs of complex febrile seizures.

Multiple seizure-like episodes within 24 hours (C) is incorrect, as a history of multiple seizures within 24 hours is not consistent with simple febrile seizures.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the role of antipyretics relative to febrile seizures?

Reveal Answer:
Antipyretics have not been found to prevent febrile seizures in subsequent febrile episodes. They may be administered to increase patient comfort.

Question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with a sudden onset of severe headache, nausea, and progressive right-sided weakness. His blood pressure on arrival is 200/110 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate study to perform next in this patient?

Options.text: CTA of the head and neck
MRI of the brain with contrast

ExplanationEN:
Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a medical emergency characterized by bleeding into the brain parenchyma without trauma. The initial and most crucial imaging study in the emergency department for suspected ICH is a noncontrast CT head. This modality offers rapid availability, quick scanning times, and high sensitivity for detecting acute hemorrhage, appearing as hyperdense (white) areas on the CT scan.

Key risk factors for ICH include hypertension, anticoagulant use, amyloid angiopathy, and vascular malformations. Symptoms often include sudden severe headache, nausea, vomiting, focal neurologic deficits, and altered mental status. A noncontrast head CT should be the first study performed on patients with these acute symptoms, even if acute ischemia is higher on the differential diagnosis.

On CT, besides the hyperdensity of blood, there might be signs of intraventricular extension or mass effect. CTA is useful after the diagnosis of ICH to assess for underlying vascular anomalies or aneurysms and to evaluate for the risks of continued hematoma expansion, but it not the first-line imaging due to time and contrast concerns.

Emergency management focuses on airway, breathing, and circulation stabilization, lowering blood pressure (typically aiming for SBP < 140 mm Hg in acute settings), reversal of anticoagulation if present, and considering neurosurgical intervention for hematoma evacuation or management of increased intracranial pressure.



Carotid Doppler ultrasound (A) is excellent for evaluating extracranial carotid artery stenosis but does not provide information about intracranial pathology or acute hemorrhage. Although vascular risk factors like carotid stenosis might contribute to stroke risk, the primary concern in this patient is the acute hemorrhage within the brain, which requires intracranial imaging.

CTA of the head and neck (B) is indeed valuable following the initial diagnosis of ICH to investigate potential vascular abnormalities like aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations that could be the source of the bleeding. However, it involves contrast, which is not necessary or optimal for the initial rapid assessment when the primary goal is to confirm or rule out hemorrhage without delay. CTA would be a secondary step after confirming hemorrhage with a noncontrast CT scan.

Lumbar puncture (C) is contraindicated when there is a high suspicion of raised intracranial pressure due to the risk of herniation. It is not used for diagnosing ICH directly but might be considered if subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected and initial imaging is negative. In this case, with clear neurological deficits and hypertension, the priority is to image the brain for hemorrhage directly using CT without risking further complications from an LP.

While MRI with contrast (D) provides detailed imaging of brain parenchyma and can be very useful for diagnosing conditions like ischemic strokes or certain tumors, it is not the first choice in acute ICH due to its less availability in emergency settings, longer scan times, and potential issues with patient safety and stability in an MRI environment. MRI's sensitivity to acute hemorrhage is lower than CT in the very early phase, which is critical for rapid assessment and management decisions in the ED.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with his spouse for a headache that began after sexual intercourse 3 hours ago. The pain is diffuse, severe, and pressure-like in nature. He has no focal neurologic deficits or meningismus on physical examination. The CT scan of his head is normal. Due to continued high clinical suspicion, a lumbar puncture is performed, and it does not show xanthochromia or measurable RBCs in the sample fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?
ExplanationEN:
Acetaminophen is an appropriate therapy for patients with acute headache. This patient likely has a postcoital headache, which could be a common inciting event for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Therefore, an appropriate workup should be completed to rule out emergent and life-threatening causes of the headache. However, in the absence of focal neurologic findings, normal initial head CT imaging, and normal cerebrospinal fluid studies, SAH can reliably be ruled out. At this time, the best next step is pain control.



CT angiography (B) is an imaging modality that may be appropriate to identify cerebral aneurysms in lieu of performing a lumbar puncture, but its utility, in this case, is low given a negative noncontrast head CT, which has a high sensitivity for detecting SAH (~ 100% if performed within 6 hours of symptom onset), in addition to normal appearing cerebrospinal fluid analysis.

Intravenous thrombolysis (C) is indicated only for acute ischemic strokes in a very select patient population. Patients must have measurable neurologic deficits, which are absent in this case.

Neurosurgical consultation (D) is not indicated in the absence of surgical pathology.

Question: A 69-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset left leg weakness that began 7 hours ago. His examination is notable for 3/5 strength in his left lower extremity and diminished sensation to light touch. Speech and arm strength are normal. Which of the following is the most sensitive modality for the detection of this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
MRI is the most sensitive modality for the detection of early ischemic stroke and is particularly effective within 6 hours of symptom onset. Diffusion-weighted imaging, a specialized MRI sequence, can detect cytotoxic edema caused by ischemia within minutes, making it an invaluable tool for confirming stroke when clinical signs are subtle or evolving. MRI is notably superior to noncontrast-enhanced CT in the detection of acute infarcts. It is also more effective at visualizing infarcts in the posterior fossa, brain stem, and cortical regions, which are often difficult to assess on CT due to bone artifact or small lesion size.

Although MRI provides more detailed imaging of brain tissue and pathology, it is not necessary for the administration of tissue plasminogen activator. The decision to initiate thrombolytic therapy is primarily based on clinical presentation and the exclusion of hemorrhage, which can be rapidly achieved with a noncontrast CT scan. As such, CT remains the standard initial imaging modality in the emergency evaluation of patients with suspected acute stroke, allowing for quick triage and treatment decisions. This approach minimizes delays in therapy, which is critical for optimizing outcomes in ischemic stroke.

MRI is typically performed after CT in patients with acute stroke symptoms, given its limited availability in many emergency settings, higher cost, and longer acquisition times. Additionally, MRI has several contraindications, including the presence of certain metallic implants, pacemakers, or severe claustrophobia, which may preclude its use in some patients. Nonetheless, when available, MRI offers significant advantages for more detailed evaluation, especially in complex or uncertain cases.

Beyond its role in detecting infarcts, MRI is useful for distinguishing stroke from transient ischemic attack, which by definition lacks radiographic evidence of infarction. It also aids in identifying stroke mimics such as migraines, seizures, demyelinating disorders, and functional neurologic conditions. Advanced MRI techniques, including MR angiography and perfusion imaging, can further assess vessel patency, collateral circulation, and the extent of salvageable brain tissue. These capabilities are increasingly important in determining eligibility for endovascular intervention and refining prognostic assessments.



Contrast CT of the head (A) is not the initial imaging choice in suspected acute stroke due to limited sensitivity for ischemia and risk of contrast-related complications.

CT angiogram (B) is useful for evaluating vascular occlusion or stenosis but is less sensitive than MRI for detecting small or early parenchymal infarcts, particularly in the anterior cerebral artery territory.

Noncontrast CT of the head (D) is commonly used in the acute setting to rule out hemorrhage, but it has low sensitivity for detecting early ischemic stroke, especially in small cortical areas.

What are the MRI findings in ischemic stroke?

Reveal Answer:
Diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging and corresponding low signal on apparent diffusion coefficient maps, often with T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities that develop over time.

Question: A 55-year-old woman without significant medical history presents to the ED with right-sided facial weakness that began acutely 1 hour prior to arrival. She woke up from sleep this morning with a dry right eye and is now unable to move the right side of her mouth. You ask the patient to smile and raise her eyebrows, and you note a right-sided facial droop and no forehead wrinkling on the right side. Her neurological exam and vital signs are otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

Options.text: Administer a small dose of edrophonium, followed by a full dose, and observe the patient for improvement of her symptoms
Obtain a blood glucose level, basic laboratory work, and CT scan of the head
Obtain a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, bring the patient to the CT scanner, and consult a neurologist
Provide prescriptions for corticosteroids, antivirals, artificial tears, and an eye patch and have the patient follow up with her physician

CorrectAnswer: Provide prescriptions for corticosteroids, antivirals, artificial tears, and an eye patch and have the patient follow up with her physician
ExplanationEN:
This patient has Bell palsy, partial or complete paralysis of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). Typical symptoms include sudden onset of unilateral facial paralysis, including the forehead, decreased tearing, hyperacusis, and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue that can progress over 1–7 days. Many patients describe a viral prodrome. The physical exam is key in the diagnosis to establish the presence of a peripheral rather than a central seventh nerve palsy. Upper and lower facial weakness is present in the peripheral nerve palsy. In central seventh nerve palsy, common in stroke syndromes, only the lower facial weakness is present. The forehead is spared because of bilateral hemispheric innervations to the forehead muscles. Treatment includes corticosteroids, antivirals (for patients with severe to complete paralysis), artificial tears, and eye protection.



Administration of edrophonium (A), a short-acting acetylcholine esterase inhibitor, was historically useful for suspected cases of myasthenia gravis (the Tensilon challenge test) and can help distinguish exacerbations from cholinergic crises. Although myasthenia gravis often involves facial (especially ocular) muscle weakness, systemic symptoms are not uncommon and, unlike Bell palsy, deficits tend to worsen with activity.

Prochlorperazine (B) is often used in the treatment of migraine headaches but has no role in the management of Bell palsy.

Obtaining a blood glucose level (C) is important to rule out hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia as a cause of the neurological deficit and would be reasonable in this case, but further laboratory or radiographic evaluation is not necessary. Imaging should be considered in patients with an atypical presentation, which is not the case with the patient above. The

National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (D) helps to classify the severity of deficit in the setting of an acute stroke and should be obtained in all suspected cases. However, this patient had clear evidence of peripheral seventh nerve palsy, so a stroke scale is not needed.

Question: A 38-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with headache and lethargy. She reports no recent travel or sick contacts. Her family history includes what she describes as a “blood disorder” and asthma, but she is otherwise healthy. Her headache began 4 days ago, has progressively worsened, and does not change with posture. Her vital signs are within normal limits for her age. She has no papilledema or other focal neurologic findings on examination. Non-contrast computed tomography of the brain does not show any abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cerebral venous thrombosis is a rare cause of headache. Patients at risk include peripartum individuals, those with recent surgery, and those with hypercoagulable states such as oral contraceptive use, Factor V Leiden mutation, or protein C or S deficiency. Presenting features may range from an insidious headache over days to weeks to an abrupt, explosive headache. Seizures or stroke symptoms may accompany the headache.

Other life-threatening causes of headache (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke) should be sought first with noncontrast CT scan, which can often be performed without delay in the emergency department, but this study can be negative in up to 30% of patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The modality of choice for diagnosis of a central venous thrombosis is a magnetic resonance venogram (MRV). The absence of flow in the affected cerebral venous sinus or sinuses is present on MRV. If done, a CT of the brain with contrast will show an empty delta sign.



Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (B) is common in women with obesity and causes headache, visual disturbances, and tinnitus. Patients will have papilledema on physical exam and an elevated opening pressure (> 25 cm H2O) on lumbar puncture with normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies.

Intracranial hypotension (C) is caused by low CSF volume and is most commonly due to recent dural penetration (e.g., recent lumbar puncture). Patients often have worsening of symptoms with sitting up or standing and improvement with lying down. The opening pressure is usually < 6 cm H2O.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus (D) is more commonly found in older patients and is characterized clinically by urinary incontinence, personality changes, and gait abnormalities.

Question: A 27-year-old woman presents with a concern about transient vision loss in her right eye. She states that she has had multiple similar episodes in the past 6 months. She also reports incomplete bladder emptying, intermittent tremors, and intermittent weakness in her left arm. Which of the following is the best diagnostic test for the suspected diagnosis?

Options.text: CSF testing for myelin basic protein
CT scan of the brain and spine

CorrectAnswer: MRI of the brain and spine
ExplanationEN:
MRI of the brain and spine is the diagnostic modality of choice for multiple sclerosis (MS), a disease characterized by demyelination of axons within the CNS. Patients present with symptoms that are scattered in time and space, meaning that they have intermittent symptoms in anatomically disparate locations. Patients may have patchy motor and sensory deficits and bladder dysfunction. Optic neuritis is a common initial presentation. Spinal cord lesions typically involve the posterior columns, lateral spinothalamic tracts, and corticospinal tract. Brain and spinal MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice because it can be used to rule out causes of cord compression while also showing lesions diagnostic for MS.



CSF testing for myelin basic protein (A) can be used in an MS diagnosis but is of questionable accuracy, and no CSF test is entirely specific.

CT scan of the brain and spine (B) does not aid in diagnosis. MRI has a better sensitivity and specificity for detecting MS lesions.

CSF oligoclonal bands, not serum (D), are also helpful. Oligoclonal bands are found in the CSF of most patients with MS.

Evoked potentials (E) are infrequently used in the diagnosis of MS. Somatosensory evoked potentials assess the electrical conduction of sensory pathways in the CNS coming from the limbs to the brain.

Question: A 5-month-old girl presents to the ED with her parents who are concerned about brief episodes of whole-body muscle contraction. On physical exam, the child has poor head control and absent palmar grasp. Her electroencephalogram shows hypsarrhythmia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with infantile spasms or West syndrome. Infantile spasms are defined by the triad of the following findings: clusters of myoclonic seizures on awakening, hypsarrhythmia pattern on electroencephalogram, and developmental delay. Signs and symptoms of infantile spasms usually begin at 4–8 months of age but are rare beyond 1 year of age.

Infants will demonstrate brief contractions of the neck, trunk, and extremities lasting 5–10 seconds each, occurring in clusters. These episodes may be accompanied by a cry. Imaging of the brain with CT or MRI is often abnormal. However, it is not diagnostic of infantile spasms. These children are most frequently diagnosed by the presence of the characteristic electroencephalogram finding of hypsarrhythmia, which has the appearance of high amplitude irregular waves and spikes in a background of chaotic and disorganized activity. A lumbar puncture should also be considered and performed to rule out meningitis or encephalitis. Management of infantile spasms is primarily with adrenocorticotropic hormone, prednisone, and vigabatrin.



Cerebral palsy (A) may present with seizures and developmental delay. However, the child will also typically have other findings, including muscular spasticity. Hypsarrhythmia is also nearly pathognomonic for the diagnosis of infantile spasms.

Kernicterus (C) will usually present with jaundice and hypotonia.

Tay-Sachs disease (D) presents with muscle atrophy beginning at age 6 months and an abnormal funduscopic exam with blindness.

Tetanus (E) typically presents with muscle stiffness and spasms, often starting with the jaw and progressing to other muscles. Additional findings include autonomic dysregulation, stiff neck, and apneic periods.

Question: What is the most likely cause of a patient presenting with bilateral facial nerve palsy?
ExplanationEN:
Bell palsy is a paralysis of the peripheral seventh cranial nerve. Clinically, one is able to distinguish a peripheral from a central cause of facial motor weakness by involvement of the forehead in a peripheral palsy. The forehead receives bilateral innervation centrally and a stroke syndrome will not interfere with upper facial strength because of the contralateral innervation. In Bell palsy, the seventh nerve is affected after leaving the brainstem and weakness is seen on the entire side of the face. Bilateral Bell palsy occurs simultaneously very rarely. Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative organism of Lyme disease and Lyme is one of the few causes of bilateral Bell palsy. Other causes include Guillan-Barre syndrome, sarcoidosis, meningitis, or bilateral neurofibromas.





The list of possible causes of Bell palsy is quite extensive and includes infectious etiologies, structural abnormalities, trauma, and toxic etiologies. Herpes simplex virus (B), leukemia (C), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (D) are all possible causes of acute Bell palsy but Lyme disease is most likely to cause bilateral symptoms.

Question: Which of the following is the most common cause of status epilepticus in a patient with known epilepsy?
ExplanationEN:
The most common cause of status epilepticus in a patient with known epilepsy is discontinued medication. In patients with an established seizure disorder, abrupt withdrawal of antiseizure medications or subtherapeutic drug levels is the leading precipitating factor for breakthrough seizures and progression to status epilepticus.

Nonadherence may occur due to missed doses, inability to obtain medications, adverse effects, or intentional discontinuation. Loss of steady-state antiseizure medication levels lowers the seizure threshold and can result in prolonged or recurrent seizures without recovery of baseline mental status.

In contrast, in patients without a prior seizure history, acute structural, metabolic, or infectious etiologies are more frequently implicated.



Hypoglycemia (A) is a well-recognized cause of acute symptomatic seizures and can precipitate status epilepticus in patients with and without a prior seizure disorder. However, in patients with known epilepsy, it is not the most common cause of status epilepticus. Hypoglycemia is more frequently seen in patients with diabetes mellitus who use insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents or in those with critical illness, alcohol use disorder, or sepsis. While glucose should always be checked in any patient with seizures because it is a reversible and life-threatening cause, it is less common than discontinuing the medication in patients with established epilepsy.

Meningitis (C) can cause seizures due to cortical irritation from infection and inflammation, and it may lead to status epilepticus in severe cases. However, meningitis is more commonly a cause of new-onset seizures in patients without a prior seizure history rather than the most common cause of status epilepticus in patients with known epilepsy. Patients with meningitis present with additional findings such as fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, or photophobia. In contrast, patients with known epilepsy who develop status epilepticus most often have a precipitating factor related to medication nonadherence or subtherapeutic drug levels rather than a new central nervous system infection.

Trauma (D) can precipitate seizures due to structural injury, intracranial hemorrhage, or cortical irritation. Acute trauma is a recognized cause of new-onset seizures and may lead to status epilepticus, particularly in patients with severe head injury. However, in patients with known epilepsy, trauma is not the leading cause of status epilepticus unless there is a clear history of recent head injury. In the absence of such a history, breakthrough seizures due to discontinued medication are much more common.

Question: A 3-year-old boy with no significant medical history presents with a seizure. His parent states that he had a cough and a fever for the last day, and then they witnessed him having 45 seconds of tonic-clonic movements. In the emergency department, the patient’s vital signs are within normal limits except for a temperature of 102.0°F (38.9°C). Physical examination reveals a well-appearing boy who is playful and interactive. He has no neurologic findings. What management is indicated?

Options.text: Noncontrast CT scan of the head
Observation, reassurance, and follow-up with a pediatrician

CorrectAnswer: Observation, reassurance, and follow-up with a pediatrician
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a simple febrile seizure, and the parents should be reassured and instructed to follow-up with the child’s pediatrician. Febrile seizures are defined as a seizure occurring in the presence of a fever without central nervous system infection or other cause. A simple febrile seizure describes a brief (< 15 minutes) generalized seizure in a developmentally normal child between the ages of 6 months and 5 years. A complex febrile seizure occurs when there are multiple seizures during the same illness, the seizures are prolonged, or the seizures are focal.

Febrile seizures are common and occur in 2–5% of children. Children who experience a febrile seizure are likely to have a recurrence (30%) and are at a 2–3% risk of developing epilepsy. Seizure activity usually ceases on its own without specific management, but if the child has a seizure in the ED, they can be treated with benzodiazepines. Children with simple febrile seizures do not require any specific testing beyond a good history and physical examination. Administration of antipyretics has not been found to reduce the likelihood of recurrence but can be used to treat the fever. Reassurance and follow-up with their pediatrician are the most important aspects of care.



Admission for electroencephalography monitoring (A) is unnecessary after a simple febrile seizure.

Administering a benzodiazepine (B) is appropriate for a child who is actively seizing in the ED. This is unnecessary in a child who has already stopped seizing and is back at baseline.

Likewise, a CT of the head (D) and lumbar puncture (C) are not necessary if the patient’s physical examination is unremarkable.

Question: What is the mechanism of action of phenytoin?
ExplanationEN:
Phenytoin is an antiepileptic medication widely prescribed for long-term management of partial and generalized seizures and is a second-line drug in the management of status epilepticus. It works as a sodium channel antagonist resulting in decreased firing of the action potential. The onset of action is 10-30 minutes.

Fosphenytoin, the prodrug form of phenytoin, is preferred for intravenous administration due to the lower risk of cardiovascular side effects as well as the ability to administer the drug at a faster rate than phenytoin. Fosphenytoin can also be administered intramuscularly. Adverse effects of phenytoin include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, rash, and ataxia.



Benzodiazepines and phenobarbital, also used in seizure management, are gamma-aminobutyric acid receptor agonists (A) resulting in enhancement of GABA-mediated neuronal inhibition.

Flumazenil is a gamma-aminobutyric acid receptor antagonist (B).

Phenytoin is a sodium channel antagonist, not a sodium channel agonist (C).

Question: A previously healthy and fully immunized 10-year-old boy presents with difficulty walking. His symptoms started 1 week ago and have progressively worsened. When he walks into the room, you note an unstable, ataxic-appearing gait. A head CT is performed and is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Central nervous system (CNS) tumors include nonmalignant and malignant tumors of both the spinal cord and brain and are the leading cause of death from childhood cancer. Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood and occur exclusively in the cerebellum. Clinical manifestations of CNS tumors are dependent on the location of the tumor and the age of the child. Since medulloblastomas occur exclusively in the posterior fossa, clinical features are consistent with those of cerebellar dysfunction and increased intracranial pressure. Nausea and vomiting, headache, disturbances in gait and coordination, papilledema, and abnormal eye movements are common features. Patients presenting with persistent headaches, particularly those occurring early in the morning, should prompt further evaluation. Headache with associated symptoms of vomiting, vision impairment, unsteady gait, changes in behavior or school performance, sleep disturbances, growth impairment, signs of increased intracranial pressure, or localizing neurological features should cue further investigation into intracranial pathology. The mainstay of treatment in CNS tumors includes a multimodal approach with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Therefore, prompt diagnosis and urgent referral to appropriate specialists are vital.



Craniopharyngiomas (A) are historically located adjacent to the optic chiasm and classically result in visual symptoms and endocrine abnormalities. These tumors are not more common than medulloblastomas and are not located in the posterior fossa.

Ependymomas (B) are uncommon and account for < 10% of CNS tumors, with the fourth ventricle being the most common location with extension into the subarachnoid space. Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure are common, with headaches being a common presenting concern. Although these tumors can present in a similar location to medulloblastoma, they are far less likely than medulloblastoma.

Glioblastoma (C) is a high-grade, malignant tumor that presents with headaches, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Glioblastomas are more commonly found in adult patients and are typically located in the supratentorial region.

Question: What is the most common tumor of the cerebellopontine angle?
ExplanationEN:
The posterior cranial fossa, containing the cerebellum, pons, and medulla oblongata, with the foramen magnum at the center of the space, has the potential to house a multitude of benign and malignant neoplasms due to the diversity of structures with varying anatomic makeups within the region. Presenting signs and symptoms depend upon the etiology and location of the developing lesion, with the cerebellopontine angle as the most common site of tumors in the posterior fossa. The vast majority of tumors at this site are benign with approximately 90% of lesions at this location being vestibular schwannomas or acoustic neuromas.

Regardless of etiology, the most common presenting symptom of all cerebellopontine angle tumors is hearing loss, seen in over 95% of cases. Vestibular schwannomas similarly present in this manner with patients reporting gradual loss of hearing and tinnitus over a period of years due to cochlear nerve involvement. Additional symptoms may arise depending on further nerve involvement, including gait instability and vertigo associated with vestibular nerve disturbances, as well as facial numbness and pain resulting from trigeminal nerve disruption. If there is clinical suspicion based upon sensorineural hearing loss with or without concomitant cranial nerve abnormalities, MRI with gadolinium is the diagnostic study of choice with 1–2 mm sections through the internal auditory meatus, which will optimally visualize the region and determine the degree of cerebellopontine angle involvement.



An ependymoma (A) is a tumor arising from the neuroepithelial lining of the ventricular system of the brain and spinal cord. The majority of cases occur in the pediatric population, with half of these lesions seen in children < 3 years. They are most commonly seen in the fourth ventricle, where obstruction of the flow of cerebrospinal fluid may produce hydrocephalus.

Glioblastoma (B) is an aggressive malignant brain tumor that is most commonly located in the frontal and temporal lobes and may present with progressively worsening headaches, vomiting, neurologic deficits, and stark personality changes.

Of the malignant lesions that develop in the posterior fossa, medulloblastomas (C) are the most common primary brain malignancy in children, arising from the medullary velum and typically extending into the fourth ventricle, with symptoms developing due to worsening obstructive hydrocephalus.

ExplanationEN:
The head CT scan shows a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Most SAHs are caused by a ruptured berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis. CT scan is the initial imaging modality to detect SAH and may (as with this example) show an accumulation of blood in the subarachnoid space. However, if the CT scan is negative after 6 hours from symptom onset, a lumbar puncture (LP) or CTA can be performed to better assess the presence of SAH. If LP is performed, comparing RBC count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) across tubes helps diagnose SAH over a traumatic lumbar puncture.

If the first and last tubes both have a significant number of RBCs, SAH is most likely. A large difference in RBC numbers (first tube >> last tube) indicates a traumatic tap. No definitive number of RBCs needs to be present in the CSF to diagnose SAH. The pathology can also be detected by identification of xanthochromia, a yellow appearance of the CSF due to blood breakdown and release of bilirubin. Xanthochromia may take up to 12 hours to develop and remains present for several weeks. Xanthochromia can be detected by direct visualization or, preferably, via spectrophotometry.



Tube 1: WBC 5/µL, RBC 4,000/µL; tube 2: protein 70 mg/dL, glucose 60 mg/dL; tube 3: RBC 50/µL (A) is most likely due to a traumatic LP. There is a large difference in the number of RBCs from tube 1 to tube 4.

Tube 1: WBC 80/µL, RBC 3/µL; tube 2: protein 60 mg/dL, glucose 60 mg/dL; tube 3: RBC 0/µL (C) is CSF indicative of aseptic meningitis, with elevated WBCs, mildly elevated protein, and normal glucose.

Question: A 65-year-old man with a history of alcohol-related cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with sudden onset left arm weakness and facial droop. Which of the following studies is required prior to administration of tissue plasminogen activator in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
The administration of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with suspected ischemic stroke. Due to the relatively high risk of catastrophic bleeding associated with tPA, patients must be evaluated carefully for indications and contraindications for tPA. A blood glucose level obtained by fingerstick should be obtained prior to the administration of tPA. A fingerstick blood glucose < 50 mg/dL is a relative contraindication to the administration of tPA. This is because both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia can mimic the symptoms of a stroke. If symptoms persist after correction of hypoglycemia, tPA can be administered in the absence of contraindications. Head imaging must be performed prior to the administration of tPA to rule out hemorrhagic stroke. In the emergency department, this is typically done with a noncontrast CT scan.

Liver function tests (C) do not have to be performed or resulted prior to the administration of tPA.

Question: A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with urinary incontinence. His partner also notes frequent falls, an abnormal gait, and forgetfulness that have occurred over the past week. His urinalysis is unremarkable. A computed tomography image is provided above. What is the pathophysiology of this patient’s most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Decreased cerebral volume and neuronal atrophy
Obstruction of ventricular cerebrospinal fluid circulation

ExplanationEN:
The CT shows enlarged ventricles without cortical atrophy, consistent with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). The triad of urinary incontinence, gait disturbance (magnetic gait), and cognitive decline is classic. NPH is caused by impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations, leading to ventricular enlargement.

Despite the term “normal pressure,” intracranial pressure may be intermittently elevated or exhibit a high reference range, particularly during CSF dynamics testing. The expansion of the ventricles causes compression and stretching of periventricular white matter, particularly affecting the corona radiata, where motor and cognitive fibers pass. This disruption leads to the clinical symptoms: gait instability, often the earliest and most prominent feature, is characterized as a magnetic gait, in which the feet seem stuck to the floor despite forward propulsion of the upper body. Urinary incontinence tends to follow and may start with urgency or frequency. Cognitive impairment is mild to moderate and includes slowed thinking and impaired executive function rather than the profound memory deficits seen in Alzheimer disease.

Etiologies of NPH may be idiopathic, particularly in older adults, or secondary to conditions that affect CSF pathways, such as subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, traumatic brain injury, or intracranial surgery. It is considered one of the few reversible causes of dementia, making a timely diagnosis critical.

Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuroimaging and CSF studies. CT scan or MRI of the brain reveals ventriculomegaly that is out of proportion to cortical atrophy, with no evidence of obstruction at the level of the third or fourth ventricles. A high-convexity sulcal effacement and disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus are additional MRI findings that may support the diagnosis. Lumbar puncture is often diagnostic and therapeutic: removal of a large volume of CSF (30–50 mL) followed by transient improvement in gait or cognition, referred to as a tap test, supports the diagnosis.

Treatment involves referral to neurosurgery for ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, which can dramatically improve symptoms in appropriately selected patients. Repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures may provide temporary relief in those who are not surgical candidates. While gait abnormalities are the most likely to improve with shunting, improvements in urinary and cognitive symptoms are also possible, particularly with early intervention.

Long-term outcomes depend on early recognition and intervention, as prolonged ventricular dilation and white matter damage can reduce the likelihood of symptom reversal. Therefore, maintaining a high index of suspicion, particularly in patients > 65 years with progressive gait disturbances and cognitive decline, is essential for identifying NPH.



Decreased cerebral volume and neuronal atrophy (A) cause increased CSF on imaging, referred to as ex vacuo ventriculomegaly. Etiologies include Alzheimer disease, Pick disease, Huntington disease, and advanced HIV.

Obstruction of ventricular CSF circulation (C) is seen in noncommunicating hydrocephalus due to a tumor, a colloid cyst that blocks the foramen of Monro, or stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius.

Shearing of bridging veins (D) is the pathophysiology behind subdural hematomas. CT imaging would show a crescent-shaped density.

Question: Which of the following features is most highly associated with a positive biopsy result in a patient with suspected giant cell arteritis?
ExplanationEN:
With a mean age of onset of 70 years, giant cell arteritis is a systemic vasculitis that affects medium-sized vessels. Although primarily known for affecting the temporal artery, it can also affect the subclavian, aortic, vertebral, and iliac arteries. Patients present most frequently with a new onset localized headache in association with nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, low-grade fever, and weight loss. There may be tenderness with palpation of the temporal artery in addition to a decreased temporal artery pulse. Jaw claudication occurs in half of patients and is the symptom most highly associated with a positive biopsy. The most feared complication is visual loss, which can be sudden and painless, partial or complete, and involve one or both eyes. Criteria for diagnosis of giant cell arteritis include age > 50 years, new onset localized headache, temporal artery tenderness or decreased pulsation, erythrocyte sedimentation rate > 50 mm/hr (although often > 80 mm/hr), and abnormal biopsy results. Patients meeting two or fewer criteria require a biopsy for confirmation of the diagnosis. Any patient in whom the diagnosis is suspected should be started on high-dose corticosteroids while arranging for a temporal artery biopsy.



While common symptoms like a fever (A) and headache (B) are associated with giant cell arteritis, they do not increase the likelihood of a positive temporal artery biopsy.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (C) presents with symptoms of morning stiffness and aching in the shoulders, hip girdle, and neck. About half of patients with giant cell arteritis will be diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica, but it is not associated with an increased likelihood of a positive biopsy.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents to the ED with fever, headache, and altered mental status. His partner reports the patient has been confused and irritable for 2 days and today had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Vital signs show T 38.9°C (102.0°F), BP 144/90 mm Hg, and HR 111 bpm. Physical examination shows agitation, disorientation to time and place, and a right-sided facial droop. A head CT without contrast shows no acute findings. An MRI of the brain is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV

ExplanationEN:
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis is the leading cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in the United States and requires prompt recognition and initiation of treatment to limit morbidity and mortality. HSV type 1 (HSV-1) is the most common causative agent in immunocompetent children and adults, while HSV-2 is implicated more often in neonates and immunocompromised patients. The classic clinical presentation includes fever, altered mental status, new-onset seizures, and focal neurologic deficits, often progressing rapidly. The virus demonstrates a neurotropism for the temporal lobes. MRI findings of asymmetric temporal lobe hyperintensity strongly support the diagnosis, and temporal lobe hypodensities may even be seen on CT in rare instances. CSF findings typically include a lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein level, and normal glucose level. However, initial CSF findings within normal limits do not rule out early HSV encephalitis, and MRI findings and clinical judgment should guide early empiric treatment while awaiting confirmatory testing.

Empiric treatment with intravenous acyclovir at 10 mg/kg every 8 hours is the standard of care and should be initiated immediately when HSV encephalitis is suspected, even before confirmatory CSF PCR results are available. Delaying acyclovir administration significantly increases the risk of severe neurologic sequelae or death. The recommended dose of 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours is based on pharmacokinetic studies ensuring adequate CNS penetration and viral suppression. Acyclovir therapy is typically continued for 14–21 days, depending on clinical response and PCR clearance.



A dose of 5 mg/kg of IV acyclovir (B) is inadequate for HSV encephalitis in adults. While this dose may be used for other indications, such as HSV mucocutaneous infections or in some pediatric settings, it does not achieve the necessary CNS levels for effective treatment of encephalitis.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV (C) is appropriate empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis but does not treat HSV. While bacterial causes must be considered in encephalopathic patients with fever, the focal findings and temporal lobe MRI abnormalities in this case are more consistent with HSV encephalitis, requiring antiviral rather than antibacterial therapy as the first priority.

Ganciclovir (D) is used primarily to treat cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections, especially in immunocompromised patients. HSV is not reliably treated with ganciclovir, and this patient is immunocompetent, presenting with findings most consistent with HSV, not CMV, encephalitis.

Loading doses of levetiracetam (E) are appropriate for treating or preventing seizures, and this patient had a witnessed seizure. However, antiseizure therapy does not address the underlying viral cause. Although adjunctive levetiracetam may be appropriate, it is not the best treatment for this patient.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents to the ED for an acute onset of slurred speech. His daughter states he suddenly began slurring his words about 30 minutes prior to arrival. His medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals drooping of the lower left side of his face with mild dysarthria. The initial NIH stroke scale score is 3. A CT of the head without contrast shows no acute intracranial hemorrhage. On reassessment 20 minutes later, the patient’s dysarthria and facial droop have resolved, and the NIH stroke scale score is 0. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Administer alteplase and admit to the neurointensive care unit
Administer clopidogrel and aspirin and admit to the neurology service
Initiate apixaban and follow up with neurology in 1–2 weeks
Initiate aspirin and atorvastatin and follow up with neurology in 24–48 hours
Initiate aspirin monotherapy and follow up with primary care in 24–48 hours

CorrectAnswer: Administer clopidogrel and aspirin and admit to the neurology service
ExplanationEN:
Transient ischemic attack (TIA) was previously defined as temporary symptoms of acute cerebral ischemia with an arbitrary duration of no more than 24 hours. However, patients with symptoms < 24 hours may have ischemic lesions on MRI. Many patients with TIA have symptoms lasting only minutes to hours, so definitions have moved away from time-based characterizations. More recently, an endpoint of cerebral infarction (i.e., ischemic stroke) has been used to differentiate TIA from permanent cerebral ischemia, or stroke.

TIA often will not be differentiated from acute ischemic stroke in the emergency department, so patients ultimately diagnosed with either should be evaluated and treated similarly. This begins by using an NIH stroke scale to assess for neurologic impairment due to the associated ischemia. Noncontrast CT of the head should then be obtained to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, and advanced neurovascular imaging (e.g., CT angiography) may also be employed. Neurology, if available, should be involved early in the evaluation and management, either in person or via tele-stroke services, depending upon the capabilities of the presenting facility.

The age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration of symptoms, and diabetes (ABCD2) risk score is an evidence-based tool used to identify patients with TIA who have a high risk for developing acute ischemic stroke in the short term. While subsequent studies have questioned its performance, this tool uses features of the presenting symptoms and medical history to risk-stratify patients. The resultant score can help clinicians identify patients who require inpatient admission and dual antiplatelet therapy versus those who may be appropriate for expedited outpatient follow-up with aspirin monotherapy. This patient would have a score of at least 5 and be considered moderate to high risk, with a 7-day risk of acute ischemic stroke ~6%. This warrants admission to a stroke service and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel. Patients with an ABCD2 score of ≤ 3 are considered low-risk. However, in patients with a low baseline stroke risk, an even lower score (0–2) correlates with a < 1% risk of stroke within the next week. These patients may be appropriate for aspirin monotherapy and expedited outpatient evaluation.



While not an absolute contraindication to the administration of thrombolytics with subsequent ICU admission (A), minor or rapidly improving symptoms of acute cerebral ischemia warrant consideration for more conservative approaches.

Anticoagulation therapy with apixaban (C) or other direct-acting oral anticoagulants is used for secondary stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, which is not relevant for this patient.

Aspirin and statins plus neurology follow-up (D) will all likely be included in the treatment course, but this patient’s high ABCD2 score indicates that the initial steps should include dual antiplatelet therapy after excluding intracranial hemorrhage.

Aspirin and primary care follow-up (E) would be suboptimal management for a first-time ischemic event in this patient with risk factors for a repeat event.

Question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the ED with acute-onset left-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. She reports difficulty closing her left eyelid and excessive tearing. On exam, she has incomplete closure of the left eyelid. Neurologic examination findings are otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate eye care recommendation for this patient?

Options.text: Apply an eye patch at night only
Apply artificial tears during the day and an eye patch at night
Wear an eye patch all of the time

CorrectAnswer: Apply artificial tears during the day and an eye patch at night
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell palsy), as evidenced by facial weakness that includes the forehead and impaired eyelid closure. In cases of incomplete eyelid closure, the cornea is at risk for exposure keratopathy due to impaired blinking and tear film distribution. Preventing corneal injury is a key component of treatment.

During the day, artificial tears should be applied regularly to maintain moisture, typically four times daily (or more often, as needed). At night, the patient should apply a lubricating ophthalmic ointment and either tape the eyelids closed or use an eye patch to protect the cornea during sleep. This combined regimen is effective in reducing the risk of corneal drying, abrasion, and ulceration.

Studies demonstrate that all patients benefit from drops throughout the day and a thicker lubricant at night, with eyelid-stretching techniques providing additional benefit by mechanically disrupting cross-linked myosin bridges in the levator palpebrae superioris, though this effect lasts only 8 hours and requires repeated application.



An eye patch at night alone (A) does not guarantee full eye protection and can leave the cornea exposed to drying and damage during the day.

Using antibiotic ointment before bed (C) does not provide sufficient lubrication and is not indicated unless there is concern for an active infection. This option does not adequately address the risk of exposure-related injury during the day.

Using an eye patch all the time (D) without concurrent lubrication is insufficient for protecting the cornea. Continuous patching may also impair visual function.
