Question: A 34-year-old pregnant woman at 10 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. On examination, the patient’s cervical os is closed. A transvaginal ultrasound confirms an intrauterine pregnancy but is unable to detect cardiac activity. What classification of spontaneous abortion does the patient have?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with a missed abortion, a type of spontaneous abortion. A spontaneous abortion is defined clinically as a pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of gestation. Although spontaneous abortions can occur unprovoked, common risk factors include maternal age, previous history of miscarriage, inherited thrombophilias, obesity, and other concurrent medical conditions such as diabetes and thyroid disease. A missed abortion refers to intrauterine fetal death prior to 20 weeks gestation in a patient with a closed cervical os and retention of the pregnancy. The patient may or may not have symptoms such as vaginal bleeding or pelvic pain. Management of missed abortions often depends on patient preference and condition but can be cared for with surgical uterine aspiration, medical uterine evacuation, or expectant management.



An incomplete abortion (A) refers to cases in which a patient presents with vaginal bleeding and has a dilated cervical os with incomplete passage of products of conception.

An inevitable abortion (B) refers to cases in which there is an impending miscarriage. Patients present with vaginal bleeding with a dilated cervical os on exam but no passage of fetal tissue.

A threatened abortion (D) is the most common cause of vaginal bleeding in pregnancy and refers to cases in which patients may or may not progress to an inevitable, incomplete, or complete abortion. Patients may also progress to have a normal pregnancy. These patients present with vaginal bleeding with a closed cervical os on exam.

Question: A 26-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department with a headache. She is 4 weeks postpartum. She reports having a severe posterior headache and also reports seeing flashes of light in her vision. Her vital signs include T 37.0°C, HR 90 bpm, BP 160/90 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 100%, and she is unchanged after rechecking multiple times. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
The patient is presenting with postpartum preeclampsia with severe features and requires medications to prevent progression into eclampsia. Preeclampsia refers to a complication in pregnancy characterized by new-onset hypertension and signs of end-organ damage with or without proteinuria ≥ 20 weeks gestation up to 6 weeks postpartum. Risk factors for preeclampsia include nulliparity, multifetal gestation, obesity, and diabetes mellitus. Delayed-onset postpartum preeclampsia can occur > 2 days and up to 6 weeks postpartum. Patients often present with symptoms of headache, visual changes, abdominal pain, or stroke. A patient is considered to have preeclampsia with severe features if they present with systolic blood pressure ≥ 160 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mm Hg and proteinuria, signs of end-organ damage, platelet levels ≤ 100 x 109/L, or pulmonary edema. These patients are at high risk of developing a stroke or progressing to eclampsia.

Acute management includes immediate administration of intravenous magnesium to prevent seizures (4 g IV loading dose, followed by 1–2 g/hour). This is considered first-line therapy for all cases of preeclampsia and eclampsia. It relaxes the smooth muscle, leading to some decrease in peripheral and cerebral vascular resistance, limiting cerebral edema formation, and it has central anticonvulsant activity. However, its antihypertensive effects are modest. Thus, additional treatment is typically needed to control the blood pressure, but this would occur after administration of magnesium. Options include IV labetalol or hydralazine. Nicardipine is an alternative treatment option. Nifedipine is given orally and is also an option for preeclampsia with severe features according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.



Giving nifedipine (B) would be appropriate to treat this patient's hypertension, but preeclampsia with severe features should be treated with IV magnesium first.

Consulting obstetrics (C) would be appropriate, but resuscitation of the patient should be performed first.

Obtaining a head CT (D) would be appropriate for patients with a headache and neurological findings, but control of the patient’s blood pressure and potential transition to eclampsia should be attempted first.

Question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with continued vaginal bleeding 1 hour after a home birth of her first child at 41 weeks gestation. She estimates she has lost about 750 cc of blood since the birth. Abdominal examination reveals a soft and boggy uterine fundus. Vaginal examination reveals active bleeding from the cervix but no masses or lacerations. She brought the placenta to the emergency department, and it appears intact. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate, in addition to OB/GYN consultation and hemodynamic resuscitation?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with postpartum hemorrhage, defined as blood loss > 1,000 mL after delivery or bleeding associated with signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of the birth process. The most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage is uterine atony, as in this patient. Physical examination reveals a soft and boggy uterus. Uterine atony is a diagnosis of exclusion, as uterine rupture, retained products of conception, and uterine inversion should be ruled out. The patient lacks signs or symptoms of these conditions.

Treatment consists of aggressive resuscitation, OB/GYN consultation, two-handed uterine massage, and oxytocin IV. It can be given as a 5-unit IV bolus or 10–40 units in 1 L of IV fluid. Additional uterotonic agents that may be used include methylergonovine, carboprost, and misoprostol.



Digital internal uterine examination (A) is indicated if retained products of conception are the suspected cause of postpartum hemorrhage. However, this patient has no abnormalities on vaginal examination, and the placenta appears intact, so this is less likely.

Terbutaline IV (D) and magnesium IV (B) are tocolytics, medications used to decrease contraction strength and frequency, and would likely worsen the bleeding in this patient.

Question: A 33-year-old G5P4 woman presents to the ED in active labor. Physical exam reveals the baby's head crowning at the introitus. After two pushes, the head is delivered with the umbilical cord wrapped around the neck. Reducing the cord over the head is unsuccessful. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Administer tocolytic agents to allow time for an obstetrician to arrive
Clamp and cut the cord, then rapidly deliver the baby
Push the infant back into the vaginal canal until there is enough slack to reduce over the head
Rotate the baby within the vaginal canal to unwrap the cord

CorrectAnswer: Clamp and cut the cord, then rapidly deliver the baby
ExplanationEN:
Precipitous deliveries in the ED are dangerous for both the mother and the infant. Emergency physicians must be comfortable with the basic maneuvers required for both uncomplicated and complicated deliveries. One of the common complications during delivery is a nuchal cord. A nuchal cord refers to a looped umbilical cord around the infant's neck.

Often a loose nuchal cord can be reduced by sliding it over the infant's head at the perineum. If reduction at the perineum cannot be accomplished, the cord should be clamped and cut. After the cord is clamped, the infant no longer receives oxygen-rich blood from the placenta, and therefore delivery should be expeditious.



Administering tocolytics (A) is relatively contraindicated after the cervix is dilated 5 cm.

Pushing the infant back into the vaginal canal (C) is not indicated and is likely to harm the infant.

Rotating the infant within the vaginal canal (D) is difficult and also likely to harm the infant.

Question: A 21-year-old woman presents to the ED with severe right upper quadrant pain for 2 days. She was recently diagnosed with chlamydia, but never picked up her antibiotics. The pain is severe, constant, and radiates to her right shoulder. She has continued to have significant, yellow vaginal discharge and dyspareunia since her diagnosis of chlamydia. On pelvic exam, she has significant cervical motion tenderness and yellow discharge from the os. Which of the following is the most common finding in this condition?

Options.text: Laparoscopic evidence of hepatic fibrinous exudates

CorrectAnswer: Laparoscopic evidence of hepatic fibrinous exudates
ExplanationEN:
This patient likely has perihepatitis in the setting of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), or Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome. This syndrome is a rare complication of untreated, long-standing PID. It is characterized by inflammation of the liver capsule and subsequent adhesions formed between the capsule and the right upper quadrant peritoneum. While diagnosis is clinical, evidence of hepatic fibrinous exudates on laparoscopy confirms the diagnosis. Other, noninvasive imaging is not required or reliable for diagnosis. Patients commonly present with right upper quadrant pain and referred right shoulder pain in the setting of clinical signs and symptoms consistent with PID. Treatment is geared toward treating the underlying PID with antibiotics like ceftriaxone and doxycycline.



Abnormal right upper quadrant ultrasound (A) and significantly elevated liver function tests (D) are not expected, as Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is inflammation of the liver capsule and does not involve the liver parenchyma. If liver function tests are elevated, the elevation is only mild.

A positive pregnancy test (C) is not expected in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.

Question: A 37-year-old woman just birthed an infant and the placenta in the ambulance en route to the ED. EMS reports that the patient is tachycardic with a significant amount of bleeding. On vaginal examination, the vaginal vault immediately fills with active bleeding. What is the most common cause of this hemorrhage?
ExplanationEN:
Postpartum hemorrhage may occur immediately within the first 24 hours after a delivery (primary) or up to 6 weeks after delivery (secondary). Cumulative blood loss in excess of 1,000 mL or bleeding associated with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth, regardless of the delivery route, defines postpartum hemorrhage.

Uterine atony is the most common cause and is responsible for 75–90% of postpartum hemorrhages. If the uterus does not contract appropriately after delivery, the exposed spiral arteries at the site of placental implantation will continue to bleed. On physical examination, the uterus is described as a soft, boggy mass. Initial management may involve bimanual massage and oxytocin.



Coagulopathy (A) is a possible acquired complication of delivery. Patients may develop disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) after placental abruption, eclampsia, amniotic fluid embolism, and postpartum infections or secondary to volume resuscitation. In the evaluation of a secondary hemorrhage, the presence of retained products of conception can also lead to the development of DIC.

Maternal birth trauma (B) is the second most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Trauma is possible along any aspect of the birth canal and includes lacerations of the cervix, perineum, rectum, urethra, vagina, and vulva.

Retained products of conception (C) cause approximately 10% of cases of postpartum hemorrhage. The retained products prevent full contraction of the uterus and may lead to immediate or delayed bleeding.

Question: A 27-year-old woman presents with persistent nausea, vomiting, and a 5-pound weight loss over the past week. She is currently 8 weeks pregnant with twins. Blood work shows hypokalemia, normal glucose, and ketonemia. She is unable to tolerate oral fluids. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous fluid choice for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Nausea and vomiting occur in about 90% of pregnancies. Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, defined as intractable vomiting, dehydration, and weight loss. The presence of abdominal pain should raise suspicion for another diagnosis, as this is highly unusual in hyperemesis gravidarum. Risk factors include multiple gestation, prior history of hyperemesis gravidarum, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Laboratory values consistent with hyperemesis gravidarum include hypokalemia and ketonemia, reflective of prolonged vomiting and volume depletion.

Treatment includes thiamine supplementation to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, a potentially irreversible and life-threatening neurologic complication, and intravenous fluid resuscitation with 5% dextrose in lactated Ringer solution or 5% dextrose in normal saline to reverse ketonemia. Antiemetic therapy is also added to control symptoms. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends a stepwise approach to nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. In patients who can tolerate oral intake, the first-line antiemetic treatment is PO doxylamine with pyridoxine, as they are both pregnancy category A medications. It may be necessary to treat patients in the ED with intravenous antiemetics if they cannot tolerate oral intake. In these scenarios, a discussion should take place with the patient about the potential fetal risks of administering other antiemetics such as ondansetron and metoclopramide. Patients unable to tolerate oral intake after intravenous antiemetics and fluid resuscitation, or with significant hypokalemia, should be admitted.



While 0.9% normal saline (A) helps restore intravascular volume and corrects hypovolemia, it does not address the patient’s ketosis and caloric deficit. This patient has ketonemia due to starvation, which requires dextrose for reversal. Administration of saline alone without glucose would not halt ketone production.

Lactated Ringer solution (B) lacks dextrose, so it will not correct ketosis or caloric depletion. For this patient with ketonemia and ongoing emesis, isotonic saline with dextrose and thiamine is preferred to provide both hydration and carbohydrate repletion.

Although thiamine and 5% dextrose in water (D) provides thiamine and glucose, it lacks sodium and other electrolytes necessary to correct the hypovolemia and hypokalemia seen in this patient. The hypotonic nature of 5% dextrose in water can lead to hyponatremia if administered in significant volumes. The inclusion of 0.9% saline ensures both electrolyte and volume restoration while safely addressing ketosis.

Question: A 34-year-old G4P2 woman at 37 weeks gestation presents to the ED with vaginal fluid leakage for the past 2 hours. Which of the following exam findings is consistent with a diagnosis of prelabor rupture of membranes?

Options.text: Cervical dilation of 2 cm on sterile vaginal examination
Vaginal secretions with a pH of 4
Yellow coloration of nitrazine strip when exposed to fluid

ExplanationEN:
Prelabor rupture of membranes (PROM) is rupture of the amnion and chorion > 1 hour prior to the onset of labor, defined as contractions resulting in cervical change. If this occurs prior to 37 weeks gestation, it is termed preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM). If labor does not begin within 18 hours of membrane rupture, it is termed prolonged prelabor rupture of membranes, which carries a significant risk of infection and maternal and fetal mortality.

Patients with rupture of membranes typically present with leakage of clear or blood-tinged fluid, most notable with maneuvers that increase intra-abdominal pressure such as straining or Valsalva. Risk factors for PROM include infection, trauma, fetal anomalies, polyhydramnios, and multiple gestations. Examination findings suggestive of rupture of membranes include fluid pooling on speculum examination, dark blue coloration of the nitrazine strip on exposure to fluid, and ferning on microscopic evaluation of fluid.



Cervical dilation (A) in the presence of contractions is indicative of labor, and prelabor rupture of membranes occurs before labor rather than during it.

Vaginal secretions with a pH of 4 (C) is a normal finding. The pH of amniotic fluid is generally 7.0–7.4.

Yellow coloration of the nitrazine strip (D) is indicative of an acidic fluid such as vaginal fluid or urine. In the case of prelabor rupture of membranes, the nitrazine strip should turn a dark blue color in the presence of amniotic fluid.

Often, the uterine size is larger than expected for dates in molar pregnancy and the beta-human chorionic gonadotropin is higher than expected for dates. Diagnosis is based on characteristic findings on ultrasound. Hydropic vessels within the uterus cause a snowstorm appearance. Because of the potential for complications and the nonviability of the pregnancy, dilation and curettage is recommended. Once a hydatidiform mole is diagnosed, a chest X-ray should be obtained as trophoblastic tumors metastasize to the lung, liver, and brain.

Question: A 16-year-old girl with lupus presents with heavy vaginal bleeding, passing large clots daily for the last 12 days. She states that, although her periods are usually regular and heavy, she has never had one this long. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Her lab results are remarkable for a hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL. Which of the following is the best approach to her treatment?
ExplanationEN:
Patients with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) have a period that is unusually long, occurs at irregular intervals, or is heavy (> 80 mL). Heavy vaginal bleeding is difficult to measure, but a history of passing clots > 2.5 cm, bleeding through clothing, and needing to change sanitary protection overnight suggest heavy bleeding. A speculum examination should be considered, as it can rule out the rare nonuterine sources of bleeding. However, in adolescents who are not sexually active, it is acceptable to defer until after a trial of medical therapy.

AUB can be idiopathic or caused by pregnancy complications (e.g., spontaneous abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy), polycystic ovary syndrome, cervical or uterine abnormalities (e.g., cervical outlet obstruction, ovarian mass), coagulation disorders (e.g., von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia), pelvic inflammatory disease, hyper- or hypothyroidism, or congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A reasonable workup includes a complete blood cell count, liver function tests, pregnancy test, sexually transmitted infection testing, pelvic ultrasound, and orthostatic vital signs. Consider hormone studies and a workup for common coagulation disorders.

Treatment depends on the severity of the bleeding. Those with mild anemia who have no symptoms and a hemoglobin > 12 g/dL can be treated with routine oral contraceptives. Those with moderate anemia (hemoglobin 10–12 g/dL) should be treated with an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive every 6 hours until the bleeding stops, along with iron and a stool softener. Those with severe bleeding, hemoglobin < 10 g/dL, and continued brisk hemorrhage should receive volume resuscitation and intravenous conjugated estrogen. A blood transfusion should be considered for these patients.

While an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive would be a good option for a patient like this one, estrogen is contraindicated in patients at risk for thromboembolism, such as those with a history of deep vein thrombosis or lupus. In these cases, medroxyprogesterone or norethindrone can be given every 6 hours for up to 4 days until the bleeding stops. This is tapered to three times per day for 3 days, then two times per day for 2 weeks. Recurrence of uterine bleeding during the taper should be expected, and the taper should be continued.



Intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 hours (A) is recommended for patients with severe anemia from AUB and continued bleeding. It contains estrogen and should not be used in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies, prothrombotic disorders, lupus, or a history of thromboembolism.

Intravenous desmopressin (B) is used for patients with hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease. While reasonable to try, it is less likely to be effective than hormone therapy in treating AUB unless von Willebrand disease is confirmed. It should be noted that testing for von Willebrand disease should be done before starting hormone therapy, as it can falsely elevate the level.

Oral ethinyl estradiol-norgestrel every 6 hours (C) is recommended for patients with moderate anemia from AUB, like this patient. However, it also contains estrogen and is contraindicated in this patient who has lupus.

Question: A 26-year-old woman without previous prenatal care presents to your small, rural ED with a precipitous vaginal delivery. The woman is unclear about the date of her last menstrual period. She reports no previous medical history, but this is her fifth pregnancy. The infant is hemodynamically stable at this time, and you are awaiting the transfer of the patient and newborn. However, during the waiting period, the patient continues to have heavy vaginal bleeding. Vital signs show HR 110 bpm, BP 90/56 mm Hg, and RR 20/min. What is the most likely cause of bleeding in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Postpartum hemorrhage is an obstetrical emergency and has been a major cause of maternal mortality. Timely diagnosis and management are important to prevent death. Usually, hemostasis is achieved after vaginal delivery because of contraction of the myometrium, which compresses the blood vessels leading to mechanical hemostasis, and because of local hemostatic factors that lead to clotting. If there is a dysfunction of one of these mechanisms, then women are at risk for hemorrhage.

The most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage is uterine atony or lack of contraction of the myometrium. The diagnosis is usually made when the uterus does not become firm after delivery, the bleeding is greater than expected, and the bleeding results in signs or symptoms of hypovolemia. To treat uterine atony, the clinician should begin with uterine massage and give oxytocin. Resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood products, if needed, should be performed next. Obstetrical services should be sought emergently.



Coagulopathy (A) is a cause of postpartum hemorrhage in women with an acquired or inherited bleeding diathesis or in women who have had complications during pregnancy such as preeclampsia with hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome. This is not the most likely cause of postpartum hemorrhage in this patient.

Retained products of conception (B) is a more common cause of secondary postpartum hemorrhage or hemorrhage that occurs 24 hours after delivery and up to 12 weeks postpartum.

Vaginal lacerations (D) may develop during a natural delivery or may be related to clinician interventions. They are not the most likely cause of postpartum hemorrhage in this case.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED with lower abdominal pain and intermittent vaginal bleeding since last night. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. Vital signs show HR 88 bpm, BP 124/70 mm Hg, and T 37.3°C. She has mild suprapubic tenderness on exam without peritonitis. Her urine pregnancy test is positive, and her serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level is 1,000 mIU/mL. No gestational sac or intrauterine pregnancy is found on transvaginal ultrasound, but no masses are found either. What is the most appropriate treatment and disposition of this patient?

Options.text: Consult obstetrics for initiation of methotrexate since the patient has crossed the discriminatory zone and ectopic pregnancy is the diagnosis
Consult obstetrics for surgical evaluation since the patient has crossed the discriminatory zone, no masses are seen on ultrasound, and ectopic pregnancy is the diagnosis
Discharge home with obstetric follow-up in 1–2 weeks for repeat ultrasound
Discharge home with obstetric follow-up in 48–72 hours for repeat ultrasound and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level

CorrectAnswer: Discharge home with obstetric follow-up in 48–72 hours for repeat ultrasound and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s story and evaluation are consistent with an extrauterine pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy. Patients with ectopic pregnancy typically present to the ED with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain during the first trimester of pregnancy. The most common time to be diagnosed with an ectopic pregnancy is 6–8 weeks after the last menstrual period. Patients may present with a ruptured or unruptured ectopic pregnancy. Those with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy more commonly present with acute, severe abdominal pain and hypotension from life-threatening hemorrhage. The majority of patients with an ectopic pregnancy present unruptured.

Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy include use of an intrauterine device, prior tubal ligation, and in vitro fertilization. However, these risk factors are not a requirement for an ectopic pregnancy since studies have shown that many female patients with ectopic pregnancy do not have any prior risk factors.

The diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy is made by using a combination of serum quantitative human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels and findings on transvaginal ultrasound in a pregnant patient. Once a patient is found to be pregnant, a serum beta-hCG level should be obtained to determine whether it is above the discriminatory zone. The discriminatory zone is the serum beta-hCG level at which a gestational sac should be visualized by transvaginal ultrasound. Many institutions use a discriminatory zone of approximately 2,000 mIU/mL. However, some laboratories and institutions set a discriminatory zone of 3,500 mIU/mL. The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology also supports a discriminatory zone of 3,500 mIU/mL.

If a patient’s serum beta-hCG level is above the discriminatory zone and no intrauterine pregnancy or gestational sac is found on transvaginal ultrasound, the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy is highly likely. In such a patient, the emergency clinician can discuss further management with obstetrics because treatment for ectopic pregnancy could be initiated without finding a definite mass. However, if the emergency clinician is making this decision alone, it is recommended that a repeat transvaginal ultrasound be performed in 2 days instead. This patient has not crossed the discriminatory zone, which means there is a chance that an intrauterine pregnancy will be found on repeat imaging. Appropriate treatment and disposition of this patient is to discharge her home with obstetric follow-up in 48–72 hours for repeat ultrasound and beta-hCG level. Strict return precautions should be given.



Since this patient has not crossed the discriminatory zone, no matter the institution, it would be inappropriate to initiate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at this point. Therefore, consulting obstetrics for the initiation of methotrexate (A) is not appropriate. In this hemodynamically stable patient, the only time that methotrexate could be considered is in an unwanted pregnancy.

For the same reason, consulting obstetrics for surgical evaluation (B) is also not the best course of action. Consultation for surgery would be indicated if this patient were hemodynamically unstable with suspected ectopic pregnancy.

Discharging home with obstetric follow-up in 1–2 weeks for repeat ultrasound (D) is also inappropriate since ectopic pregnancy has not been ruled out as a diagnosis in this patient. Since ectopic pregnancy remains a consideration, this patient needs appropriate follow-up in 48–72 hours for repeat ultrasound and beta-hCG testing to determine whether there is a pregnancy in the uterus and to see if the pregnancy is progressing normally.

Question: A 23-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding that began 6 hours ago. She reports that she is pregnant and concerned about her baby. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. A pelvic exam reveals a closed cervical os with a small amount of blood. A urine pregnancy test is positive and transvaginal ultrasound reveals an intrauterine embryo with cardiac activity. ExplanationEN:
Concern regarding miscarriage is a common reason for presentation to the emergency department. Half of women who experience bleeding during their first trimester eventually miscarry. There are different classifications of abortion, based on the history and examination, for first-trimester vaginal bleeding. A threatened abortion is characterized by vaginal bleeding in the first 20 weeks of pregnancy with a closed cervical os and no history of passed products of conception. A completed abortion describes a closed cervical os and a history of having passed products of conception. An ultrasound will show no evidence of intrauterine pregnancy and the uterus will be contracted. Transvaginal ultrasound is the cornerstone of evaluating first-trimester bleeding. Confirming the presence of embryonic cardiac activity on ultrasound provides reassurance to the mother and useful information regarding prognosis. When embryonic cardiac activity is confirmed after vaginal bleeding, the risk of miscarriage is estimated at 5%.



An incomplete abortion (A) describes an opened cervical os with partial passage of products of conception. There may be visible products of conception in the cervix or vagina. Placenta previa (B) is a common cause of bleeding in the second and third trimesters. It is caused by the placenta implanting over the cervical os and classically presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Placental abruption (C) is a common cause of bleeding and pregnancy loss in the second and third trimesters. Classically, it presents as painful vaginal bleeding in a woman with a history of chronic hypertension, cocaine use, preeclampsia, or abdominal trauma.

Question: A 26-year-old woman who is 5 days postpartum presents to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain and fever. Her vital signs show HR 123 bpm, BP 102/65 mm Hg, and T 38.7°C. She has lower abdominal tenderness and a foul-smelling vaginal discharge on exam. What is the most common factor that puts this patient at risk for the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Any female patient who is up to 2 weeks postpartum and presents to the emergency department with fever, tachycardia, and lower abdominal pain should be suspected of having endometritis. Other symptoms may include malaise, headache, anorexia, and purulent vaginal discharge. Although most cases are mild and improve with antibiotic therapy, if not treated appropriately, patients can develop peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscess, or sepsis. Postpartum endometritis is usually a polymicrobial infection with a mixture of two to three aerobes and anaerobes. Sexually transmitted infections, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, are uncommon causes of postpartum endometritis. Cesarean delivery is the most important risk factor for developing this infection. Prophylactic antibiotics given before cesarean delivery reduce the frequency of postpartum endometritis, particularly if the cesarean section is performed electively. Postpartum endometritis after vaginal delivery is uncommon. Diagnosis is usually made based on clinical history and physical exam. Treatment is with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. The most commonly used treatment regimen is clindamycin plus gentamicin.



Other risk factors to consider when determining the likelihood of postpartum endometritis include internal fetal monitoring (B), multiple cervical examinations (C), prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes (D), manual removal of the placenta, a large amount of meconium in the amniotic fluid, low socioeconomic status, and comorbidities, such as diabetes or HIV infection. Although any of these risk factors can be associated with postpartum endometritis, the primary risk factor is cesarean delivery.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED for 24 hours of worsening nausea, abdominal pain, and abdominal distention. She recently began hormone-based assisted reproductive therapy, received an injection 5 days ago, and has not yet had oocyte retrieval and fertilization. She has a BP of 85/55 mm Hg and HR of 120 bpm. Which of the following steps is contraindicated for this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with classic ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), evidenced by her recent hormone-based assisted reproductive therapy (5 days postinjection), abdominal pain, nausea, distention, and hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia). Bimanual pelvic examination is contraindicated in OHSS because the ovaries are significantly enlarged and fragile, creating a substantial risk of ovarian rupture or torsion with manual manipulation.

OHSS can lead to hemoconcentration, liver failure, electrolyte derangements, coagulopathies, and kidney failure, resulting in multiorgan system failure, so the emergency physician should have a high index of suspicion in even a stable-appearing patient. The mainstay of emergency department treatment of OHSS is to replenish volume, identify and correct electrolyte derangements, and consult a gynecologist or fertility subspecialist.

Given the significant risk of venous thromboembolism in OHSS (due to hemoconcentration and hypercoagulability), prophylactic anticoagulation should be considered in patients with severe disease, particularly those requiring hospitalization.

OHSS is treated supportively and resolves as human chorionic gonadotropin levels decline. Pregnancy may prolong the condition, but it is not terminated as a treatment.



Anticoagulation (A) is indicated, not contraindicated, in severe OHSS. Venous thromboembolism is one of the most dangerous complications of OHSS due to hemoconcentration and hypercoagulability.

CT scan (C) is not contraindicated and may be used as a problem-solving tool when ultrasound is inconclusive or when evaluating for complications. The concern about radiation exposure to potential early pregnancy exists, but this patient has not yet had oocyte retrieval and fertilization, so pregnancy is not a factor.

Pelvic ultrasound (D) is the recommended imaging modality for OHSS diagnosis and monitoring. It can assess ovarian size, follicle number, and detect ascites and pleural effusions.

Question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the ED with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping. She is 16 weeks pregnant by ultrasound dating. What physiologic changes can be expected with a normal pregnancy?

Options.text: Renal blood flow decreases as placental blood flow increases
The afterload increases due to an increase in systemic vascular resistance
The respiratory rate increases to > 20 breaths/minute
The uterine fundus grows outside the pelvis into the abdomen at 12 weeks gestation
The white blood cell count is generally > 20,000/µL

CorrectAnswer: The uterine fundus grows outside the pelvis into the abdomen at 12 weeks gestation
ExplanationEN:
There are several physiologic and anatomic changes that occur in a normal pregnancy. The uterine fundus grows up out of the pelvis at approximately 12 weeks gestation and becomes an intra-abdominal organ. It characteristically reaches the umbilicus at 20 weeks gestation. As the uterus grows, it places pressure on the inferior vena cava, causing decreased blood return to the heart. This can result in supine hypotension as the uterus places more pressure on the inferior vena cava while the patient is lying flat. Rolling the patient into the left lateral decubitus position may relieve this hypotension by increasing venous return to the heart.

With regard to the cardiovascular system, cardiac output increases by increasing blood volume and increasing resting heart rate by 10–15 bpm. Systemic vascular resistance is decreased overall with diastolic blood pressure decreasing primarily during the first trimester. In regard to the respiratory system, the tidal volume increases while the functional residual capacity decreases due to elevation of the diaphragm. However, the respiratory rate remains relatively unchanged.

Within the gastrointestinal system, gastric reflux is common secondary to delayed gastric emptying and decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone. There is also an increased risk of gallstones during pregnancy. The renal and metabolic systems experience an increase in kidney size, kidney blood flow, and glomerular filtration rate, and there is also increased peripheral resistance to insulin in pregnancy. Pregnant patients with diabetes prior to pregnancy are more prone to diabetes-related ketoacidosis. Pregnancy affects the hematopoietic system by causing a decreased hemoglobin secondary to volume dilution, while the leukocyte count is increased, although only mildly.



Renal blood flow (A) increases rather than decreases during pregnancy.

In a normal pregnancy, the afterload decreases with pregnancy due to decreased systemic vascular resistance (B), which occurs due to systemic vasodilation and the high-flow, low-resistance circuit in the uteroplacental circulation.

The respiratory rate (C) remains relatively unchanged despite increased tidal volume and decreased functional residual capacity.

While the white blood cell count increases slightly during pregnancy, a very high white blood cell count, such as > 20,000/µL (E), would still be abnormal.

Question: What are the cardinal movements of fetal descent during uncomplicated labor?

Options.text: Descent, engagement, flexion, internal rotation, external rotation, extension, expulsion
Engagement, descent, extension, external rotation, internal rotation, flexion, expulsion
Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, expulsion
Flexion, internal rotation, engagement, descent, extension, external rotation, expulsion

CorrectAnswer: Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, expulsion
ExplanationEN:
The cardinal movements of the second stage of labor are engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, and expulsion. During engagement, the fetal head enters the pelvic inlet. Subsequently, it descends into the pelvic cavity and flexes (the fetal chin moves toward its chest, reducing the presenting diameter of the head and facilitating movement through the birth canal) and internally rotates (most commonly into the occiput anterior position) due to compression from the birth canal. When the fetal head crowns, it extends as it emerges. The clinician may apply gentle downward pressure over the fetal head to prevent rapid expulsion, which could lead to perineal tearing. Once the head is delivered, the shoulders rotate into an anterior-posterior position, and the head externally rotates (also known as restitution) to maintain alignment. During the expulsion stage, after checking for a nuchal cord, the clinician may provide gentle downward traction to facilitate delivery of the anterior shoulder, followed by upward movement to deliver the posterior shoulder, completing the delivery of the neonate. Throughout the process, careful monitoring and gentle maneuvers are essential to minimize the risk of trauma to both the mother and neonate. After the delivery, immediate assessments of neonatal health are performed, alongside supporting maternal well-being, including ensuring the uterus is contracting to prevent postpartum hemorrhage.



The sequence of descent, engagement, flexion, internal rotation, external rotation, extension, and expulsion (A) is not in the appropriate order. Engagement should occur before descent. Engagement involves the fetal head entering the pelvic inlet, which logically precedes descent into the pelvis.

Engagement, descent, extension, external rotation, internal rotation, flexion, and expulsion (B) is a sequence of movements that is also out of order. After descent, flexion should occur, allowing the fetal head to align optimally for movement through the birth canal.

The sequence of flexion, internal rotation, engagement, descent, extension, external rotation, and expulsion (D) incorrectly starts with flexion before engagement and descent. Engagement must occur first, in which the fetal head enters the pelvic inlet, followed by descent.

Question: A 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with uncontrolled nausea and vomiting daily for > 2 weeks. She has been taking the first-line medicine recommended by her obstetrician, but it does not seem to help. She reports no diarrhea and has not had any abdominal pain. She reports no vaginal bleeding. However, she has started to lose weight. Vital signs show HR 128 bpm, BP 110/72 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and SpO2 100% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and she vomits during the exam. She is able to give a small amount of urine for testing, and it shows moderate ketones. At this stage of illness, which of the following is the best option for control of this patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy generally occur within the first 12 weeks. Severe nausea and vomiting that is associated with volume depletion and laboratory abnormalities is found in approximately 2% of pregnancies and is known as hyperemesis gravidarum. The finding of ketonuria in this patient is important because it is an early sign of starvation and suggests volume depletion and potential electrolyte abnormality. Treatment consists of intravenous fluids containing 5% glucose in either lactated Ringer solution or normal saline. In addition, texts recommend the administration of thiamine to prevent progression to Wernicke encephalopathy. Any number of antiemetic drugs are available to help treat the symptoms. The antiemetic medication that is recommended in a particular situation depends on the volume status and severity of symptoms in the patient. Risks to the pregnancy should also be considered.

For patients who present to the emergency department with refractory nausea and vomiting with dehydration, nonoral routes of medication administration are recommended, and ondansetron is the first-line agent. Ondansetron has been compared to other medications including promethazine and metoclopramide. Promethazine is as effective as ondansetron but comes with sedating effects and potential dystonic reactions. Ondansetron has been shown to be superior to treatment with metoclopramide for hyperemesis gravidarum.



Other medications can be used for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, but their use depends on the severity of symptoms. Diphenhydramine (A), along with meclizine and dimenhydrinate, are second-line therapies for nausea and vomiting. They can be used when the first-line therapy, doxylamine with pyridoxine (B), fails to control mild vomiting in pregnancy. However, these medications are not as effective for severe symptoms of hyperemesis gravidarum that is associated with weight loss as this patient reports.

Methylprednisolone (D) is given to patients with refractory symptoms who also do not improve with the use of ondansetron. Corticosteroids should only be given in conjunction with the patient’s obstetrician, especially if the patient is < 10 weeks pregnant, since corticosteroids pose a slightly increased risk for oral clefts.

Question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for recurrent pelvic pain. She reports a long-standing history of spotting between periods and dysmenorrhea. She has tried birth control pills and shots in the past without improvement. She reports that this current episode is severe and has been intermittent over the past 3 days. It is located on both sides of her pelvis and radiates to her back. The pain commonly worsens with bowel movements. She has no contributory surgical or family history. On pelvic exam, she has significant rectovaginal nodularities but no visible structural abnormalities. Which of the following conditions is this patient most at risk for, given the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Endometriosis is due to ectopic endometrial tissue, most commonly within other pelvic organs. It is most commonly diagnosed during the evaluation of dysmenorrhea or infertility. A clinical diagnosis may be used to begin treatment. However, confirmation can be obtained via pelvic ultrasonography, laparoscopy, and tissue biopsies. Patients present with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, intermittent low back pain, and infertility. Physical exam may reveal rectovaginal nodularity or adnexal masses. An endometriosis mass may be noted on pelvic exam, but this is extremely rare. Treatment is with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents and hormonal contraceptives to control pain and swelling. Surgical resection is reserved for patients who continue to have severe symptoms and those with infertility despite medical management.



Endometrial cancer (A)has not been shown to be more common in patients with endometriosis. Ovarian torsion (C)may be more common in patients with endometriosis lesions on the ovaries, allowing the ovary to torse. However, this is not the most common complication overall. Catamenial endometriosis is when ectopic endometrial tissue is found in the thorax. These lesions are extremely rare and can lead to spontaneous pneumothorax (D).

Question: You diagnose lactation mastitis in a postpartum 17-year-old adolescent. She is currently breastfeeding her healthy newborn. She has no allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment in addition to local cool compresses and ibuprofen?
ExplanationEN:
In lactating female patients, mastitis typically presents within a few weeks postpartum and occurs in 2–10% of breastfeeding women. The infection is almost always unilateral. The most common causative agent is Staphylococcus aureus, which originates mainly from the newborn’s pharynx. The antibiotic of choice for nonsevere disease is a penicillinase-resistant agent, such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin. If the patient has beta-lactam sensitivity, clindamycin is recommended. If there is concern for maternal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus colonization, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin is recommended. If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, inpatient intravenous vancomycin should be initiated after local wound and blood cultures are obtained.



Aztreonam (A) and penicillin (D) are antibiotics that do not properly cover staphylococcal infections.

Although metronidazole (C) is a common treatment for many gynecologic conditions, it is ineffective against Staphylococcus aureus. However, it should be administered if mastitis is associated with subareolar abscess and nipple retraction.

Question: A 30-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum from an uncomplicated vaginal birth presents to the emergency department with pain and redness in her right breast for 2 days. She has continued nursing her baby girl, but the redness seems to be spreading, and she now feels malaise and chills. On physical examination, she is afebrile with normal vital signs and a nontoxic appearance. Her right breast is engorged with redness and tenderness streaking laterally from the areola. The area is indurated but not fluctuant. The patient would like to continue nursing her infant. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This woman is presenting with signs and symptoms of acute mastitis. Lactational mastitis is common in the first 3 months of breastfeeding and presents as a red, swollen, and painful breast. It can also be associated with malaise and fever. It is more common in women with poor drainage or breast engorgement. Initial treatment involves symptom control with NSAIDs and cool compresses, along with complete emptying of the breasts. If symptoms do not improve within 12–24 hours or if systemic symptoms are present, antibiotics should be started.

Most cases of lactational mastitis are caused by Staphylococcus aureus, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is becoming an important pathogen in these infections. In the setting of nonsevere infections, empiric treatment against Staphylococcus aureus should be initiated unless the patient has risk factors for carrying MRSA, such as recent hospitalization, previous MRSA infection, or close contact with someone who has MRSA. Dicloxacillin is the recommended first-line therapy. Cephalexin is also a good option.



In the setting of severe infection, evident by hemodynamic instability or worsening disease while on antibiotic therapy, intravenous vancomycin (A) should be initiated, and the patient should be admitted to the hospital. Breast milk and blood cultures should be sent to help tailor antibiotic management. However, this patient is stable and without other signs of severe infection.

In the setting of nonsevere infection but risk factors for MRSA, the patient should be started on clindamycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (C). It is important to remember that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should not be used in nursing mothers due to the risk of kernicterus. This patient would like to continue nursing, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole would not be a good option at this time.

If the patient is nursing a child who was born full term and is older than 1 month, then trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole could be used. Topical bacitracin (D) may help the healing process or prevent severe infection when the breasts are cracked and dry, but this therapy alone will not improve lactational mastitis.

Question: Which of the following is an appropriate treatment for the painful genital lesions pictured above?
ExplanationEN:
The picture depicts the characteristic ulcerative lesions seen in genital herpes, the most common cause of sexually transmitted genital ulcerations in the United States. Lesions may be grouped, fluid-filled vesicles or ulcers on an erythematous base. Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) accounts for the majority of cases of genital herpes, but it may also be caused by herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1).

Clinically, genital herpes manifests as either a primary infection or a local recurrence from the reactivation of dormant virus in the spinal cord ganglia. Primary infection tends to be more severe with systemic symptoms, more copious genital lesions, and a prolonged clinical course. The diagnosis is largely clinical, although it can be confirmed with serologic testing, viral culture, or antigen retrieval from the lesions. The Tzanck test, once the mainstay of diagnosis, is no longer widely performed due to its lower sensitivity compared with newer tests.

Although outbreaks are self-limited and resolve spontaneously, treatment with antiviral medication may shorten symptom duration, reduce viral shedding (and thus infectivity), and reduce recurrences. It is also important to provide pain relief and educate the patient about sexually transmitted infections.



Azithromycin and ceftriaxone (B) is an appropriate treatment for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and chancroid. Chlamydia and gonorrhea primarily affect the mucous membranes, like the urethra or cervix, and do not present with crops of genital lesions. Chancroid presents as a tender bump that evolves into an open sore, which bleeds easily and is often associated with significant groin lymphadenopathy.

Benzathine penicillin (C) is an appropriate treatment for primary or secondary syphilis. Latent syphilis requires two additional treatments, each 1 week apart. Primary syphilis typically presents with an isolated painless genital lesion, not painful lesions.

Doxycycline (D) would be the appropriate treatment for chlamydia and lymphogranuloma venereum. Lymphogranuloma venereum is less common and presents with erythematous, friable ulcerative lesions and is associated with large, painful unilateral groin lymphadenopathy.

Question: A sexually active, healthy 19-year-old woman presents to the ED with vaginal pain and discharge. She has had multiple recent sexual partners and uses a progestin intrauterine device for contraception and desires to continue this therapy. Her exam is significant for cervical bleeding after being swabbed, as well as thick, white mucus discharge from the cervical os. A bimanual exam does not reveal any masses or tenderness. Her urine pregnancy test is negative. After swabbing for microbiology samples, which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Ceftriaxone IM, doxycycline PO, and metronidazole PO
Intrauterine device removal, ceftriaxone IM, and azithromycin PO

CorrectAnswer: Ceftriaxone IM, doxycycline PO, and metronidazole PO
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms and exam findings of acute cervicitis. Pelvic pain, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and post-coital bleeding are all common findings of cervicitis. Additionally, on exam, cervical motion tenderness (highest-sensitivity finding) and friability (bleeding after minor trauma) would be expected. Current guidelines do not call for any change in management in a patient who has an intrauterine device and desires to keep it. The patient should receive ceftriaxone and doxycycline (first-line in nonpregnant patients; in pregnant patients, azithromycin should be substituted for doxycycline) to cover Neisseria gonorrhea and Chlamydia trachomatis. Current standards also recommend that women be treated empirically with metronidazole for the treatment of potential Trichomonas vaginalis, as this can also be a cause of purulent cervicitis. Metronidazole will also treat potential bacterial vaginosis. All patients should follow up for re-evaluation. If the patient is not improving at follow-up, device removal may be advised.



Doxycycline (B) would be appropriate for the treatment of chlamydia, but empiric treatment of gonorrhea and trichomoniasis is indicated as well.

Device removal (C) is not required as part of the treatment, and device removal alone would not be sufficient to clear the bacterial infection.

Device removal, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin (D) is not appropriate therapy as the patient can continue to use the device if she desires and have a favorable outcome with antibiotic therapy alone. Also, azithromycin would only be appropriate in a pregnant patient. Doxycycline is preferred in this patient. She should also be treated for possible trichomoniasis.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Her parent first noticed the discharge 3 weeks ago, and it has progressed to thick pus with a small amount of blood over the last few days. There is no history of trauma. The girl has not had any fevers, vomiting, pain with urination, behavior changes, or other ill symptoms. Her primary care clinician performed a urine nucleic acid amplification test for gonorrhea and chlamydia a week ago, which was negative. A frog-leg position exam shows thick drainage coming from her vagina but normal-appearing vaginal tissue. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Oropharyngeal swab for group A Streptococcus
Procedural sedation for thorough pelvic examination
Repeat the urine nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia
Warm water vaginal irrigation using a syringe and small feeding tube

CorrectAnswer: Procedural sedation for thorough pelvic examination
ExplanationEN:
Vaginal discharge in prepubertal girls is an uncommon presenting concern. The most common vaginal discharge in prepubertal girls is from nonspecific vaginitis, which can be seen on exam as irritation, soreness, and sometimes thin discharge and is thought to be due to harsh soaps (including laundry soaps) or bubble baths. Thick, purulent discharge with normal-appearing vaginal tissue, as in the above patient, is more suggestive of a vaginal foreign body or bacterial infection. The most common foreign body is toilet paper, which can be removed by simple warm water vaginal irrigation after applying topical lidocaine jelly to the hymen. This should only be performed when the foreign body is visible. Sometimes a pelvic X-ray can identify a vaginal foreign body and direct the need for transfer if the current setting is not equipped for sedation or does not have the appropriate subspecialist.

When a vaginal foreign body is suspected but not identified on external visual examination, a pelvic exam should be performed under procedural sedation, preferably by a pediatric gynecologist or pediatric surgeon when available. This identifies and treats the vaginal foreign body. When a foreign body is not found, it also allows the clinician to obtain a quality specimen for additional testing, such as for Trichomonas or fungus on a vaginal pathogen smear. Some of the more challenging vaginal foreign bodies to remove are round objects, which sometimes also require a digital rectal examination with outward pressure. A pelvic exam in prepubertal girls should not be performed without appropriate sedation.



Group A streptococcal vaginitis can produce acute purulent vaginal discharge, which usually presents with a fiery red appearance of the skin, not mentioned in this patient. Throat cultures with an oropharyngeal swab for group A Streptococcus (A) are positive most of the time, but vaginal cultures can be obtained under procedural sedation when a vaginal foreign body is also probable.

Repeating urine nucleic acid amplification for gonorrhea and chlamydia (C) will not rule out a vaginal foreign body, even if positive. In addition, sexual abuse in children is often accompanied by behavioral changes not described above, such as changes in bladder or bowel habits, sleep disturbances, and abnormal sexual behavior for age.

Warm water vaginal irrigation using a syringe and small feeding tube (D) after application of lidocaine gel is appropriate for small visible foreign objects such as toilet paper but is not recommended for objects that are not visible on external physical examination.

Question: Which of the following is the most effective emergency contraception?
ExplanationEN:
Emergency contraception is used to decrease the risk of pregnancy. Methods include administration of oral medications such as levonorgestrel, mifepristone, combined estrogen-progestin, and ulipristal, or insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD). Insertion of a copper intrauterine device (IUD) following unprotected sexual intercourse has the lowest pregnancy risk (0.1%) and is therefore considered the most efficacious emergency contraception method. Further advantages of a copper IUD include its efficacy up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse, at any point in the menstrual cycle, and regardless of body mass index (BMI).

A disadvantage of copper IUD for emergency contraception is that it requires an appointment with a gynecology-trained clinician for insertion. This disadvantage limits its use in the emergency department. Therefore, patients who present to the emergency department with indications for emergency contraception are generally prescribed ulipristal, as it is the most effective oral emergency contraception method.



Levonorgestrel (B) is an oral emergency contraceptive option that has the advantage of being available over the counter. However, it is less effective than both a copper IUD and ulipristal. It may be used up to 3 days after unprotected intercourse.

The combination of levonorgestrel and estrogen (C) is an oral emergency contraceptive option with decreased efficacy and increased side effects compared to levonorgestrel alone.

Ulipristal (D) is the first-line oral emergency contraceptive option, as it has the lowest pregnancy risk and may be used up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse. However, it is less effective than insertion of a copper IUD. Question: A 29-year-old woman who is G2P1001 at 13 weeks gestation presents to the ED for vaginal bleeding. Her vital signs are in the normal range. On exam, her cervical os is closed, and there is moderate bleeding. Ultrasound examination demonstrates an intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart rate of 130 bpm. Her blood test results demonstrate a hemoglobin of 14.6 g/dL, an O Rh-negative blood type, and a beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level of 60,576 mIU/mL. What is the best next step in management?

ExplanationEN:
Vaginal bleeding with a closed cervical os at < 20 weeks gestation is characteristic of a threatened abortion. Blood should be obtained for a type and screen for pregnant patients > 12 weeks gestation who presents with vaginal bleeding. Those with Rh-negative status should be treated with Rh D immune globulin to prevent Rh isoimmunization and hemolytic disease of the newborn or fetus in subsequent pregnancies.

In 2024, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists published a guideline update that shows findings from recent studies suggest there is a low risk of Rh alloimmunization associated with abortion or pregnancy loss at < 12 weeks gestation, and many expert guidelines no longer recommend routine anti-D immune globulin prophylaxis for abortion or pregnancy loss at < 12 weeks gestation because of the lack of evidence to support benefit. However, emergency medicine textbooks still recommend administering anti-D immune globulin in the ED to all pregnant patients with bleeding. If anti-D immune globulin is administered, a 50–120 μg dose can be used during the first trimester and a full 300 μg dose after the first trimester.



Hemodynamically stable patients who present to the emergency department with threatened or complete abortion may typically be discharged with close follow-up and do not require admission (B).

Emergent obstetrics consultation (C) is indicated for threatened abortion in the event of hemodynamic instability.

Discharge with close obstetrics follow-up (D) is appropriate after administering Rh D immune globulin in patients > 12 weeks gestation like this patient. Those who are stable and < 12 weeks gestation can also be discharged with close obstetrics follow-up.

Question: A 27-year-old woman, 8 weeks since her last menstrual period, presents to the ED with vaginal bleeding, an open cervical os, and ultrasound showing an intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal pole but no heartbeat. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The key distinguishing feature in this case is the open cervical os combined with vaginal bleeding and an intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal pole but no cardiac activity. Inevitable abortion is defined by an open cervical os with vaginal bleeding in the setting of a nonviable or failing pregnancy, indicating that pregnancy loss is imminent and cannot be prevented.

Spontaneous abortion before 20 weeks of gestation is the most common serious complication of pregnancy. Most spontaneous abortions occur in the first trimester of pregnancy, and almost all occur before 20 weeks gestation. Many pregnant patients experience bleeding during pregnancy, so the evaluation of threatened abortion is common.



Incomplete abortion (A) refers to partial expulsion of products of conception, with residual pregnancy tissue remaining in the uterus after some tissue has already passed. On ultrasound, this appears as irregular heterogeneous echoes within the endometrial cavity, often with internal vascularity, rather than an intact gestational sac with a fetal pole as described in this case. The patient has not yet expelled any tissue.

Missed abortion (C) or embryonic demise refers to a nonviable pregnancy with an embryo ≥ 7 mm crown-rump length without cardiac activity, but critically, the cervical os remains closed. The patient has no symptoms of active spontaneous abortion, and the pregnancy tissue is retained. Also, an open cervical os excludes missed abortion.

Threatened abortion (D) is defined by vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy with a closed cervical os and a viable intrauterine pregnancy (with cardiac activity present). This patient has both an open os and no fetal cardiac activity, excluding this diagnosis.

Question: A 31-year-old G1P0 woman at 8 weeks gestation presents to the ED with intractable nausea and vomiting. She is lightheaded and has been unable to tolerate anything by mouth. Which of the following confirms your suspected diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of hyperemesis gravidarum. Nausea and vomiting affect 70% of pregnancies during the first 12 weeks. However, hyperemesis gravidarum occurs in only 2% of pregnancies. Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterized by intractable vomiting accompanied by weight loss, dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, ketonuria, and ketonemia). Diagnosis of hyperemesis gravidarum includes laboratory testing with CBC, electrolytes, kidney function, and urinalysis.

The management of hyperemesis gravidarum is done with 5% dextrose in lactated Ringer solution or normal saline to restore volume and reduce ketosis. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) alone or combined with doxylamine has emerged as the antiemetic of choice. Second-line options are typically antihistamine medications including diphenhydramine, meclizine, and dimenhydrinate. Third-line options include promethazine, prochlorperazine, and metoclopramide. Ondansetron is considered a third or fourth-line option. Indications for admission for hyperemesis gravidarum include persistent vomiting, persistent acidosis, severe electrolyte abnormalities, or weight loss > 5–10% of pre-pregnancy weight.



Decreased serum sodium (A) may be a marker of dehydration. However, it is not definitively associated with the diagnosis of hyperemesis gravidarum. The electrolyte abnormalities most associated with hyperemesis gravidarum are hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia.

Weight loss, not weight gain (D), is common with nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. Patients with severe hyperemesis gravidarum may lose so much weight that they are well below their pre-pregnancy weight.

There is no definitive number of times that one must vomit (C) in a day to meet the diagnostic criteria for hyperemesis gravidarum.

Question: A 34-year-old woman who is 8 days postpartum presents to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain and a fever of 100.7℉ (38.2℃) at home. She reports continued vaginal bleeding since delivery of the baby. She mentions there were no complications during vaginal delivery, but her obstetrician had to manually remove the placenta. Vital signs in the emergency department are within normal limits. On pelvic exam, you find suprapubic abdominal tenderness, bloody discharge in the vaginal vault without a foul smell, and no cervical motion tenderness. You speak with her obstetrician regarding the diagnosis, and she recommends an intravenous dose of antibiotics followed by outpatient therapy. The obstetrician will see the patient first thing in the morning. The patient wishes to take medicine that will allow her to continue nursing the new baby. What is the most appropriate outpatient treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Postpartum endometritis is a common cause of postpartum fever, especially within the first week after delivery. Cesarean delivery is the most important risk factor for endometritis, but other risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple cervical examinations, internal uterine monitoring, manual removal of the placenta, colonization with group B Streptococcus, low socioeconomic status, and preterm birth. The diagnosis is largely clinical and based on fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, cervical motion tenderness, and elevated white blood cell count, but these can be nonspecific findings.

Postpartum endometritis is typically a polymicrobial infection, and therapy should be directed to cover aerobes and anaerobes. Any patient with signs of sepsis should be admitted to the hospital, but many infections, especially those considered late in onset (1–6 weeks postpartum), are mild and can be treated on an outpatient basis if appropriate follow-up is ensured. Furthermore, even patients who are admitted to the hospital for parenteral therapy are eligible for early discharge if they are clinically improved and afebrile.

This patient is presenting with late-onset endometritis, and she has normal vital signs with a relatively reassuring exam. First-line treatment is usually clindamycin plus gentamicin. However, there is a trend toward the use of broad-spectrum oral monotherapy even without the use of parenteral antibiotics. From the above options, the best oral therapy that would also allow this patient to continue nursing would be amoxicillin-clavulanate. Patients with a penicillin allergy can take clindamycin instead.



Clindamycin (B) would be appropriate coverage for gram-positive organisms and anaerobes, but it is not the best treatment option. Additionally, clindamycin resistance among anaerobic bacteria is emerging, and amoxicillin-clavulanate or ampicillin-sulbactam are recommended therapies instead.

Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia and gonorrhea are uncommon causes of postpartum endometritis. Therefore, treatment with ceftriaxone intramuscularly plus doxycycline (C) would not be an appropriate therapy for this patient. Additionally, doxycycline is not recommended in lactating women.

Finally, levofloxacin (D) could be used as monotherapy to treat endometritis. However, it is not recommended for lactating mothers.

Question: A 28-year-old woman at 37 weeks gestation presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her vital signs are normal and she has uterine tenderness on palpation of her abdomen. What is the most important diagnosis to rule out given this presentation?
ExplanationEN:
Abruptio placenta is the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall occurring in 1% of pregnancies. Abruption occurs spontaneously (associated with hypertension, cocaine use, previous abruption, multiparity, increased maternal age, smoking) or as a result of trauma. Patients experience an abrupt onset of bleeding, often with abdominal pain. The uterus is tender with contractions. The clinician should defer the pelvic examination in the third trimester until placenta previa has been ruled out by ultrasound. Abruption may be diagnosed on ultrasound, but the sensitivity is poor due to similar echogenicity of blood to the placenta. Therefore, it is usually a clinical diagnosis. Depending on the size of the abruption, patients may lose a significant amount of blood. Laboratory analysis may show markers of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Immediate consultation with an obstetrician should be obtained.





Placenta previa (B) is the implantation of the placenta over the cervical os. Patients present with painless vaginal bleeding. Risk factors include multiparity, previous cesarean section, advanced maternal age, and smoking. Ultrasound is 95% sensitive and must be performed prior to the vaginal examination as bleeding may increase with digital or speculum exam. Subchorionic hemorrhage (C) occurs during the first trimester and is the accumulation of blood between the chorionic membranes and uterine wall. Patients may have vaginal bleeding. The presence of a subchorionic hemorrhage increases the chance of spontaneous abortion. Vasa previa (D) occurs when fetal vessels within the membrane (but unsupported by the umbilical cord) pass across the internal os ahead of the presenting fetal part. Patients may experience painless vaginal bleeding. These patients require emergent C-section.

Question: A 35-year-old G3P2 woman at 32 weeks gestation presents to the ED following a motor vehicle collision. Her history is significant for two prior cesarean deliveries. She has severe abdominal pain, continuous uterine contractions, and decreased fetal movement. She reports no vaginal bleeding or gush of water. Her vital signs upon arrival are T 37.2°C, HR 130 bpm, BP 80/50 mm Hg, and RR 24/min. A fetal heart rate by bedside Doppler is 100 bpm. Physical exam reveals a rigid, tender uterus and ecchymosis over the site of the seatbelt. Which of the following best describes the cause of the patient’s symptoms?

Options.text: Hemorrhage between the uterine decidua and the placenta
Placental invasion into the uterine myometrium
Rupture of membranes resulting in infection by urogenital microflora
Separation of the uterine myometrium at the site of prior surgery

CorrectAnswer: Hemorrhage between the uterine decidua and the placenta
ExplanationEN:
Placental abruption, also known as abruptio placentae, is bleeding at the interface of the placenta and the uterine decidua, causing complete or partial detachment of the placenta from the uterus before delivery of the fetus. It is one of the most common causes of vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks of gestation, and risk factors include maternal trauma, cocaine use, multiple gestation, antiphospholipid antibodies, hypertension, preeclampsia or eclampsia, tobacco use, and previous abruption.

Placental abruption typically presents with late pregnancy bleeding accompanied by uterine pain or contractions. However, almost 20% of placental abruptions do not present with vaginal bleeding because the blood accumulates between the placenta and the uterine wall. Retroplacental hematoma is the most classic finding of placental abruption on ultrasound. Other findings include echogenic debris in the amniotic fluid or placental thickening. However, while specific, ultrasound has poor sensitivity for placental abruption, and a normal ultrasound does not exclude the diagnosis. The diagnosis of placental abruption is clinical, and high suspicion must be maintained for any woman with late pregnancy vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain.

Physical examination may show a uterus that is tense, tender, and larger than expected for gestational age. Fibrinogen levels lower than 200 mg/dL have the best correlation with severe maternal hemorrhage. The complications of placental abruption include placental or uterine insufficiency leading to fetal demise, maternal coagulopathy with disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hemorrhagic shock. Management of placental abruption depends on maternal and fetal status as well as gestational age. Hemodynamically stable mothers and fetuses with reassuring heart rates may be observed and monitored, and those at term may attempt a vaginal delivery. Mothers with unstable vital signs or those with fetuses with nonreassuring heart rates should proceed to emergent cesarean section.



Placental invasion into the uterine myometrium (B) describes the pathogenesis of placenta accreta. This condition results when placental tissue implants in the myometrium rather than the decidua of the uterus. This is associated with postpartum hemorrhage but does not typically cause hemodynamic compromise in the antepartum period and is not exacerbated by traumatic mechanisms, as above. Additionally, this condition is typically seen on ultrasound as myometrial thinning, abnormal placental vascularity extending into the myometrium, or loss or irregularity of the hypoechoic area behind the placenta.

Rupture of membranes resulting in infection by urogenital microflora (C) describes the pathogenesis of chorioamnionitis. This condition is an infection of the fetal membranes typically caused by an ascending urogenital infection. Findings suggestive of chorioamnionitis include maternal fever and uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, and evidence of membrane rupture (such as a gush of water, oligohydramnios, or pooling of fluid on vaginal speculum examination). While maternal trauma can cause a rupture of membranes, this patient does not have any evidence of this, and both maternal and fetal vital signs are not consistent with infection.

Separation of the uterine myometrium at the site of prior surgery (D) describes uterine rupture. This rare condition can be precipitated by maternal abdominal trauma. Physical examination findings consistent with this diagnosis include palpation of fetal parts in the maternal abdomen and loss of fetal station (if the rupture occurs during labor). Imaging for uterine rupture is not routinely done, as this is an obstetric emergency needing emergent surgical intervention. However, ultrasound findings consistent with a diagnosis of uterine rupture include disruption of the myometrium, fetal parts outside the uterus, free peritoneal fluid, and anhydramnios.

Question: A 26-year-old woman presents to the ED in labor. She reports that she is 39 weeks pregnant, her water broke 2 hours ago, and she is having contractions every 3 minutes. On physical exam, she is gravid with a palpable uterine fundus just under the xiphoid process and appears uncomfortable. A digital cervical exam is performed. The patient is dilated to 6 cm, and a pulsatile umbilical cord is palpable. Which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Administer oxytocin to strengthen uterine contractions and expedite delivery
Ask the patient to urgently push with the next contraction
Attempt to reduce the prolapsed cord
Place a hand in the vagina to elevate the fetal head

CorrectAnswer: Place a hand in the vagina to elevate the fetal head
ExplanationEN:
Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetrical emergency that occurs when the umbilical cord slips ahead of the fetal head (or other presenting part) and prolapses through the cervical os into the vagina. With each contraction, the umbilical cord can become compressed by the fetus, which leads to decreased fetal blood flow and oxygenation. This can occur with any pregnancy, but risk factors that lead to increased risk include breech presentation, preterm birth, multiple gestations, multiparity, and polyhydramnios. In the ED, fetal heart monitoring is not likely to be available, but severe, prolonged fetal bradycardia and variable decelerations are common on tracings. If an umbilical cord is palpated on cervical exam, the patient should be placed in Trendelenburg position and the physician should place a hand in the vagina to elevate the fetal head and reduce compression on the umbilical cord. An emergent obstetrics consultation should be placed, and the hand should remain in place until an emergency cesarean section is performed.



Once an umbilical cord prolapse has occurred, any attempt to vaginally deliver the fetus will cause damage to the umbilical cord and fetal hypoxia. Therefore, the administration of oxytocin to strengthen uterine contractions and expedite delivery (A) and asking the patient to urgently push with the next contraction (B) will cause fetal harm.

An attempt to reduce the prolapsed cord (C) should not be made by the ED physician. Although there have been several case reports when this has been successful, these were performed on an obstetrics ward with fetal monitoring available at all times.
