Use verbal techniques and remove the patient from an agitating environment
Physical restraints only when necessary

Question: A 72-year-old patient with COPD presents to the ED with significant respiratory distress requiring intubation. A postintubation arterial blood gas is obtained, revealing a pH of 7.10, PCO2 of 94 mm Hg, PO2 of 94 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 95%. Which of the following ventilatory changes should be considered first to improve this patient’s blood gas analysis?
ExplanationEN:
Increasing the respiratory rate is the most appropriate first ventilatory change to address this patient’s severe respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia. This patient has severe respiratory acidosis (pH of 7.10, PCO2 of 94 mm Hg) but adequate oxygenation (PO2 of 94 mm Hg, SpO2 of 95%). The primary goal is to increase carbon dioxide elimination by augmenting minute ventilation. The product of tidal volume and respiratory rate determines minute ventilation, which predominantly affects PCO2 and pH.

Increasing the respiratory rate is preferred over increasing tidal volume in this patient with COPD for several important reasons. First, patients with COPD already have reduced functional lung capacity and are at risk for ventilator-induced lung injury from overdistension. Evidence supports lung-protective ventilation with tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight while keeping plateau pressures below 30 cm H2O.

The respiratory rate can be safely adjusted to achieve acceptable PCO2 and pH levels without the risks associated with high tidal volumes.



Decreasing positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) (A) would not address the hypercapnia and would potentially worsen oxygenation. While this patient currently has adequate oxygenation, PEEP serves critical functions in mechanically ventilated patients. PEEP maintains alveolar recruitment, prevents atelectasis, and reduces the cyclic opening and closing of alveoli. In patients with COPD specifically, appropriate PEEP can counteract intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP) that develops from air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation. Decreasing PEEP does not increase minute ventilation or carbon dioxide elimination, so it would have no beneficial effect on severe respiratory acidosis. The primary problem is inadequate carbon dioxide clearance, not oxygenation.

Decreasing tidal volume (B) would worsen the respiratory acidosis by further reducing minute ventilation and carbon dioxide elimination. Low tidal volume ventilation is associated with hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis. While lung-protective ventilation with tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight is standard for preventing ventilator-induced lung injury, further reducing tidal volume in a patient with already severe acidosis (pH of 7.10) would be harmful. Severe hypercapnic acidosis can cause pulmonary hypertension, altered cardiac function, and other adverse effects.

Increasing tidal volume (D) would increase minute ventilation and carbon dioxide clearance, but it also poses significant risks of ventilator-induced lung injury in patients with COPD and would not be the best first-line intervention. Patients with COPD have reduced lung compliance, air trapping, and dynamic hyperinflation, making them particularly vulnerable to barotrauma and volutrauma from excessive tidal volumes.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most appropriate ventilator adjustment to make to reduce the risk of dynamic hyperinflation in a patient with an acute COPD exacerbation?

Reveal Answer:
Prolonging expiratory time is the most appropriate ventilator adjustment to reduce the risk of dynamic hyperinflation in a patient with acute COPD exacerbation. This can be achieved by decreasing respiratory rate, reducing inspiratory time, or both, allowing more time for complete lung emptying before the next breath.

Question: A 62-year-old man presents with acute onset of chest pain with radiation to the shoulders and nausea while walking his dog. On examination, he is diaphoretic with HR 94 bpm, RR 20/min, BP 92/59 mm Hg, and SpO2 96% on room air. His ECG reveals 2 mm ST elevation in lead aVR with 1 mm ST elevation in lead V1 and ST depressions in leads I, II, and aVL. Which coronary artery is most likely diseased and responsible for this patient’s presentation?
ExplanationEN:
ST segment elevation in lead aVR > 1 mm or greater than the ST elevation seen in lead V1 is most concerning for occlusion or subocclusion of the left main coronary artery. In addition to elevation in aVR, diffuse horizontal ST depression will be seen, most prominently in leads I, II, and V4–6. The degree of ST elevation in aVR correlates with increased mortality and also distinguishes left main coronary artery occlusion from left anterior descending artery occlusion with a sensitivity and specificity of approximately 80%. This ECG pattern can also be seen in proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion (although this is less likely), severe three-vessel coronary artery disease, and diffuse subendocardial ischemia (e.g., postcardiac arrest). There is conflicting opinion on whether the lesion that leads to ST elevation in aVR is due to an acute occlusion or to either subocclusion or complete occlusion with collateral blood flow. Recent evidence suggests that many patients have the latter. However, at this time, ST elevation in aVR is considered a STEMI-equivalent and is an indication for emergent cardiac catheterization if present in the setting of ischemic chest pain. It is essential to discuss this case further with the cardiology consultant.



The left anterior descending artery (A) supplies the anterior wall and septum. Occlusion of this artery presents with ST elevations in V1–4.

Occlusion of the left circumflex artery (B) results in ST elevation in leads I, aVL, and V5–6, indicative of a lateral myocardial infarction.

The right coronary artery (D) supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle in most patients. In the remainder of patients, the inferior wall is supplied by the left circumflex artery. ECG findings of an inferior wall myocardial infarction include ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.

One Step Further

What ECG findings are consistent with a posterior myocardial infarction?

Reveal Answer:
Horizontal ST depression with tall, broad R waves, and upright T waves in leads V1–3.

Treatment
Percutaneous coronary intervention: gold standard
Thrombolytic therapy
Aspirin
P2Y12 receptor blocker
Beta-blocker
Anticoagulation

Question: A 25-year-old man presents to the ED as the unrestrained front-seat passenger involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision that resulted in significant front-end damage. The patient reports severe pelvic pain. His vital signs are within normal limits for his age. His pelvis is stable to bimanual internal compression. He has blood at the urethral meatus and suprapubic tenderness. A bedside pelvis X-ray is negative for acute fractures. Which of the following will have the best diagnostic yield for these findings?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has blood at the urethral meatus following blunt trauma in a motor vehicle collision, an important clinical sign that suggests urethral injury, most likely an anterior urethral injury (often bulbar) or a posterior urethral disruption in the setting of high-energy trauma.

In patients with suspected urethral injury, especially in the setting of perineal trauma, pelvic pain, inability to void, or blood at the urethral meatus, the first diagnostic test should be a retrograde urethrogram. This imaging study involves instilling contrast into the urethra, followed by X-ray, allowing direct visualization of any extravasation, strictures, or complete disruption.

Importantly, catheterization should be avoided until urethral injury is excluded, as blind catheter placement can worsen existing injuries. Patients with posterior urethral injuries often require bladder drainage by means of suprapubic catheterization followed by delayed operative repair. Penetrating anterior urethral injuries require surgical exploration.



Kidney ultrasound with Doppler (A) is used to assess kidney perfusion or hydronephrosis, not urethral integrity. It provides little to no diagnostic value in the setting of suspected urethral trauma.

Pelvis CT scan (B) is excellent for detecting pelvic fractures and intra-abdominal injuries, but it is not diagnostic for urethral injury. This patient’s pelvic X-ray is already negative for acute fractures, and CT would not provide the same level of urethral visualization as a retrograde urethrogram.

Peritoneal lavage (C) is used to detect intra-abdominal bleeding, not genitourinary tract injuries. This is neither indicated nor informative in this context.

Reveal Answer:

Question: Which of the following is the most appropriate location to perform a thoracentesis?

Options.text: Anterior in the lateral one-third of the clavicular line second intercostal space
Anterior midclavicular line second intercostal space
Midaxillary line in the tenth intercostal space
Posterior midscapular line in the eighth intercostal space

CorrectAnswer: Posterior midscapular line in the eighth intercostal space
ExplanationEN:
A thoracentesis is both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure that can be used to remove fluid from the pleural space. The most common locations chosen for the procedure include the posterior midscapular line or the midaxillary line. The location of the thoracentesis should be guided by ultrasound to determine if there is a deep fluid pocket and no other structures that could be damaged. It is crucial to ensure that the site of insertion is above the ninth rib (eighth intercostal space), as penetrating below this rib heightens the danger of injuring the diaphragm, liver, or spleen.

This procedure is done under sterile conditions with local anesthesia. The needle and catheter are advanced until there is pleural fluid pulled back. A sample can then be pulled off and sent for analysis, and the apparatus can be connected to a vacuum container. If a large volume of pleural fluid is removed, patients may experience irritation and coughing toward the end of the procedure. Moreover, the removal of a large volume of fluid can also lead to reexpansion pulmonary edema. Other complications that can occur are trauma to local structures, infection, injury to the lung parenchyma, and pneumothorax (most common).



Anterior in the lateral one-third of the clavicular line (A) or anterior midclavicular line (B) would not be appropriate or common locations for a thoracentesis.

Midaxillary line in the tenth intercostal space (C) risks entering the abdominal cavity. If a bedside ultrasound clearly shows a deep fluid pocket with no abdominal structures, perhaps a lower rib level could be used, though this would not be typical.

Question: An 89-year-old man with chronic dementia, hypertension, diabetes, recent stroke, and congestive heart failure is brought to the emergency department from his nursing home because his recently placed percutaneous gastrostomy tube was inadvertently pulled out last night. You learn from the nursing home notes that the patient underwent percutaneous gastrostomy tube placement in another hospital approximately 10 days ago. There is no other information regarding the tube. The patient appears chronically debilitated and cachectic with normal vital signs. You see a very small open tract over the left upper quadrant of the abdomen without any drainage or bleeding and minimal surrounding skin erythema. What is the most appropriate action at this time?

Options.text: Admit to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics
Consult gastroenterology to emergently replace the gastrostomy tube before discharging back to the nursing home
Place a Foley catheter into the tract and refer the patient to his gastroenterologist for tube replacement
Replace the gastrostomy tube at the bedside and discharge back to the nursing home

CorrectAnswer: Admit to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics
ExplanationEN:
Gastrostomy tubes are often used for patients with underlying neurological conditions such as dementia, cerebral palsy, or multiple sclerosis; obstructions such as esophageal cancer; and other conditions such as malnourishment secondary to cancer and those with short bowel syndrome. Complications of gastrostomy tube placement can be minor, such as bleeding, or major, such as necrotizing fasciitis. A more common complication, particularly in combative patients or those with dementia, is inadvertent tube removal. If the gastrostomy tract has had time to mature, a replacement tube or Foley catheter may be placed through the gastrostomy tract. Remember, the tract will begin closing within hours of tube dislodgement. However, it takes at least 1 week for a stable tract to form, and patients with delayed healing (those with diabetes) may not have a fully mature tract for at least 3 weeks. The information presented in this case shows that this patient had the gastrostomy tube placed approximately 10 days ago. Therefore, the gastrostomy tract might not have matured and, at this point, a replacement tube should not be placed at the bedside. Patients who have inadvertently removed their tubes before 3–4 weeks postprocedure should be admitted to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics and monitoring for signs of peritonitis. The gastrostomy tract site can heal over the next several days, and a new site can be used to place another tube.



Consulting gastroenterology to emergently replace the gastrostomy tube and discharging the patient back to the nursing home (B) would not be appropriate since there is a chance this patient could develop peritonitis. Intravenous antibiotics should be administered and the patient should be observed. Additionally, replacing the tube is not an emergency and gastroenterology should not be called for emergent replacement.

Placing a Foley catheter into the tract and referring the patient to his gastroenterologist for tube replacement (C) would also be inappropriate since the Foley catheter could be placed into the peritoneal cavity when going through an immature gastrostomy tract.

Similarly, replacing the gastrostomy tube at the bedside and discharging the patient back to the nursing home (D) would also be inappropriate at this early date.

Question: A 74-year-old woman presents with right-sided epistaxis that started 1 hour ago. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 86 bpm and blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg. After asking the patient to blow her nose and expel any clots, visualization of the right septum shows a small area of active bleeding. What is the next step in management?

Options.text: Application of silver nitrate to the bleeding site
Instillation of oxymetazoline spray and holding bilateral pressure on the nasal septum
Placement of a double balloon nasal catheter in the right nare
Placement of a nasal tampon in the right nare

CorrectAnswer: Instillation of oxymetazoline spray and holding bilateral pressure on the nasal septum
ExplanationEN:
The vast majority of epistaxis events are the result of an anterior source of bleeding. Kiesselbach plexus, formed by the superior labial branch of the facial artery, the anterior ethmoidal artery, and the terminal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, is found on the anterior nasal septum and is the source of 90% of anterior bleeding. Features that make a posterior source more likely include older patients, hemorrhage from bilateral nares with significant blood seen in the posterior pharynx, and bleeding that can not be controlled with vasoconstrictors and anterior packing. Initial care of patients presenting with epistaxis includes having the patient gently blow their nose to expel any clots in the nares. This allows for better visualization of a potential bleeding site. Oxymetazoline, a vasoconstrictor, should be sprayed in each nostril and bilateral pressure on the nasal septum should be held for 10–15 minutes. Alternatives to oxymetazoline spray include the placement of pledgets soaked in cocaine or lidocaine with epinephrine. Once temporary hemostasis is achieved, the nares should be reexamined. If a site of bleeding is identified, it should be cauterized with silver nitrate. If bleeding persists, a nasal tampon or balloon epistaxis catheter should be placed.



Application of silver nitrate to the bleeding site (A) prior to the instillation of a vasoconstrictor is often unsuccessful as active bleeding interferes with the chemical cautery. When using silver nitrate, the site of bleeding should be cauterized starting at the periphery of the lesion toward the center. Cautery of both sides of the septum is contraindicated due to the potential risk of septal necrosis. Patients with posterior epistaxis typically require the placement of a double-balloon epistaxis catheter (C) to control the bleeding. The catheter is placed in the nose, the posterior balloon is inflated, and the catheter is pulled anteriorly. The anterior balloon is then inflated. Placement of a nasal tampon (D) is an appropriate treatment for anterior epistaxis that is not responsive to nasal pressure, vasoconstrictors, and chemical cautery. Anterior nasal packs should stay in place for 2–3 days before being removed by an otolaryngologist.

One Step Further
Question:
Is antibiotic prophylaxis indicated in patients who require nasal packing for management of epistaxis?

Reveal Answer:
Although frequently given, there is no evidence that antibiotics prevent the development of toxic shock syndrome or sinusitis in these patients.

Question: A 45-year-old man with dialysis-dependent end-stage kidney disease and hypertension presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and fatigue. He states he had missed a couple of dialysis appointments, and his symptoms started earlier today. On exam, the patient has distended neck veins, normal breath sounds bilaterally, faint heart sounds without murmur, abdominal distention, and cool, clammy extremities. His blood pressure is 70/55 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, and his ECG is shown above. Which of the following would be the best next step for this patient's condition?

Options.text: Needle insertion at left midclavicular line between second and third ribs
Needle insertion at left sternal border between fifth and sixth ribs
Tube insertion at left anterior axillary line between fifth and sixth ribs

CorrectAnswer: Needle insertion at left sternal border between fifth and sixth ribs
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting in shock with hypotension and tachycardia. Given his symptoms of hypotension, muffled or distant heart sounds, and jugular venous distention (Beck triad), as well as ECG findings of electrical alternans and narrow pulse pressure, the most likely diagnosis is cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade occurs from fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac which impedes cardiac filling. It can be the result of blunt or penetrating trauma, malignancy, kidney disease, or restrictive changes to the pericardium. In a hemodynamically unstable patient, the definitive treatment is pericardiocentesis with needle insertion at the left sternal border between the fifth and sixth ribs. An 18-gauge spinal needle with a large volume syringe utilizing ultrasound is the preferred method.



Dobutamine infusion (A) or other inotropes have not been shown to benefit patients with tamponade physiology. Dobutamine is a beta-agonist used in heart failure and sepsis to increase cardiac output, but would not help with the mechanical obstruction of an effusion.

Inserting a needle in the midclavicular line between the second and third ribs (B) is the correct location for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax, which also presents with tachycardia and hypotension but can be differentiated by decreased breath sounds on the affected side. Tension pneumothorax is most often seen in trauma or patients on positive-pressure ventilation.

Inserting a needle in the anterior axillary line between the fifth and sixth ribs (D) is the location for a thoracostomy tube, which would be indicated for a large pleural effusion or pneumothorax, both of which could be differentiated from pericardial effusion by decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side.

Question: A 79-year-old woman is brought into the ED by her family for chest pain and diaphoresis. After being placed on the cardiac monitor, she develops wide complex tachycardia with no palpable pulse. Chest compressions are initiated, and she is defibrillated at 200 J. She is intubated for airway protection while cardiopulmonary resuscitation continues. Which of the following medications can be administered endotracheally?
ExplanationEN:
During the resuscitation of patients in cardiac arrest, high quality chest compressions and time to defibrillation (when appropriate) are essential to improving outcomes. Intravenous (IV) or intraosseous (IO) access should be obtained as soon as possible so that antidysrhythmic medications and other medical therapies (e.g., IV fluids) may be administered. When IV or IO access is not rapidly achieved, but an endotracheal tube is present, certain medications can be administered endotracheally. These include lidocaine, atropine, naloxone, and epinephrine, remembered by the mnemonic LANE. Epinephrine is the most commonly administered drug by the endotracheal route. Drugs are typically double or triple the IV dose and diluted with 3–5 mL of normal saline. Several positive pressure ventilations with a bag-valve mask should be administered after the medications are delivered. Further attempts at obtaining IV or IO access should continue while administering endotracheal medications as outcomes are inferior compared to drugs administered either IV or IO. Many other medications used in advanced cardiac life support, including adenosine, amiodarone, calcium chloride, and sodium bicarbonate, are not administered endotracheally.



Adenosine (A) is not used for cardiac arrest but rather for supraventricular tachycardia with both diagnostic and therapeutic utility. It cannot be administered endotracheal.

Amiodarone (B) may be used for cardiac arrest caused by ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation but also cannot be administered endotracheal.

Epinephrine, but not norepinephrine (D), can be administered endotracheally during cardiac arrest.

Question:
What therapy should be administered during cardiac arrest caused by torsade de pointes?

Reveal Answer:
Defibrillation, as torsade de pointes in the absence of a pulse is treated as pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

Question: A 30-year-old man with a history of daily alcohol use since age 15 presents with epigastric abdominal pain and vomiting. He has been vomiting for 2 days with an inability to keep anything down. Today he developed chest pain and palpitations, and he had a near syncopal episode. Vital signs show HR 104 bpm, BP 184/100 mm Hg, RR 16/min, T 37.1°C, and SpO2 99% on room air. He appears to be in pain and has epigastric tenderness on exam. An electrocardiogram is obtained and is shown above. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s near syncope and palpitations?
ExplanationEN:
The electrocardiogram in this question shows sinus tachycardia with an important finding of a prolonged QT interval. The long QT syndrome is associated with an increased risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, also known as torsades de pointes. The long QT syndrome may be congenital or acquired, and the most common symptoms include palpitations, syncope, seizures, and sudden cardiac death. On an electrocardiogram, the QT interval is measured and then corrected for heart rate. The equation to calculate the QT interval is somewhat complex, but generally it is accepted that measurements, including those by machines, are abnormal when a corrected QT interval is > 500 milliseconds. The corrected QT interval on this patient’s electrocardiogram is 650 milliseconds.

The diagnosis of acquired long QT syndrome can be made with an electrocardiogram and a clinical scenario associated with prolonged QT. This patient has a history of alcohol use and is presenting with signs and symptoms of pancreatitis and alcohol withdrawal. Although laboratory work is not available yet, it is likely this patient has hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, both of which prolong the QT interval. Another major cause of acquired prolonged QT syndrome includes medications such as antidysrhythmics, antiemetics, antipsychotics, and antimicrobials like fluoroquinolones and macrolides. Treatment of a prolonged QT interval includes treating the underlying problem, correcting electrolyte abnormalities, and stopping all medications that precipitate the problem.



The electrocardiogram findings in aortic stenosis (A) may be entirely lacking or show nonspecific left ventricular hypertrophy and left atrial enlargement. There are many different criteria for determining left ventricular hypertrophy, but an easy one to remember is tall R waves in left ventricular leads such as aVL. Additionally, patients with aortic stenosis generally present with chest pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion. This patient’s story and electrocardiogram are not consistent with aortic stenosis.

The electrocardiogram in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (B)classically shows large dagger-like septal Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads, and criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy is generally present. Additionally, patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy present with chest pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, and dyspnea on exertion, if they have any symptoms at all. This patient’s story and electrocardiogram are not consistent with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

The electrocardiogram in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (D)would show a short PR interval and a delta wave or slurring of the upstroke of the QRS complex. Additionally, patients with ongoing symptoms from Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome generally present with palpitations, fast heart rate, and lightheadedness. This patient’s story may suggest Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, but his electrocardiogram does not.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 19-year-old man presents with a stab wound to the left chest. While he is being transferred to your stretcher, he loses his pulse. Which of the following is most likely to result in return of spontaneous circulation?
ExplanationEN:
Patients with penetrating trauma who lose a pulse in transport or the emergency department should be considered for resuscitative thoracotomy. The vast majority of ED thoracotomies are performed on penetrating trauma patients. The survival rate for patients undergoing resuscitative thoracotomy after cardiac arrest from penetrating trauma is roughly 15%. Unfortunately, the survival rate with blunt trauma is much less. In general, ED thoracotomy should only be considered in patients who have signs of life at some point after their trauma. Thoracotomy allows for exposure of the major organs of the chest. The main goals of resuscitative thoracotomy are the identification and treatment of pericardial tamponade or cardiac defect, cross-clamping of the aorta, and internal cardiac massage.



External chest compressions (A) have never been shown to be beneficial in patients with traumatic arrest.

A left chest thoracostomy tube (B) can be placed simultaneously while a thoracotomy is performed, but it is unlikely to be helpful alone in restoring spontaneous circulation.

Pericardiocentesis (C) is suboptimal in comparison to thoracotomy for relief of pericardial tamponade in an arrest situation.

Question:
Where should the incision be made into the pericardium during resuscitative thoracotomy?

Reveal Answer:
The incision should be made at the apex near the diaphragm anterior and parallel to the left phrenic nerve.

Question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an assault. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. He reports no loss of consciousness and only has severe right eye pain. His vital signs are within normal limits. There is significant right periorbital swelling and proptosis. His right pupil is dilated and nonreactive. Intraocular pressures are 42 mm Hg for the right eye and 12 mm Hg for the left eye. Visual acuity for the right eye is shadows only and 20/40 in the left eye. What is the best next step in management for this patient’s suspected condition?
ExplanationEN:
An emergent lateral canthotomy is indicated, as this patient has elevated intraocular pressures and evidence of optic neuropathy. When acute orbital compartment syndrome is suspected, no further testing or treatments should delay immediate lateral canthotomy. An emergent ophthalmologic consultation should be called but should not delay treatment. Retrobulbar hematomas, either from surgery or direct ocular trauma, are the most common cause of acute orbital compartment syndrome. However, orbital cellulitis, orbital emphysema, and tumors are possible etiologies. The most common physical exam findings of acute orbital compartment syndrome include acute unilateral optic neuropathy with evidence of changes in visual acuity and abnormal pupillary reflexes, limited extraocular movements, elevated intraocular pressures (typically > 30–40 mm Hg), proptosis, or any combination of the above.



Further imaging and treatments, such as fresh frozen plasma administration (B) or orbital computed tomography scan (D), should not delay a lateral canthotomy.

Homatropine drops (C) are a common treatment for traumatic iritis, which may occur after trauma but does not present with increased ocular pressure or evidence of optic neuropathy. The pathognomonic physical exam finding is consensual photophobia.

Reveal Answer:
First the inferior lateral canthal tendon and, if decompression does not occur, the superior lateral canthal tendon.

Question: A 35-year-old man is diagnosed with a right-sided peritonsillar abscess. Which of the following is a contraindication to performing drainage in the ED?
ExplanationEN:
For proper visualization during incision and drainage of a peritonsillar abscess, the patient must be able to open his or her mouth widely. Therefore, severe trismus is a contraindication to performing needle aspiration or incision and drainage. Trismus occurs due to irritation of the pterygoid muscle by local infection or inflammation. Maneuvers to optimize visualization include having the patient sit up with his or her head in the sniffing position, using a tongue depressor, and using a headlamp, which allows for better illumination and use of both hands. Other contraindications to ED drainage of a peritonsillar abscess include recurrent peritonsillar abscess (indication for tonsillectomy), evidence of deep neck tissue extension, significant coagulopathy, and airway obstruction.



Drooling (A), otalgia (B), and voice changes (D) occur as the abscess expands in size but are not contraindications to performing a drainage of a peritonsillar abscess.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 14-year-old boy with a history of pacemaker placement for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy presents to the emergency department with fatigue and dyspnea. He appears pale and diaphoretic. His HR is 45 bpm and BP is 70/50 mm Hg. The patient’s rhythm strip is shown above. A chest radiograph shows displacement of the ventricular lead as compared to previous chest radiographs. Which of the following represents the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This child requires emergent transcutaneous cardiac pacing to restore cardiac output. Indications for pediatric pacemakers are complex, and common reasons include bradycardia secondary to sinus node dysfunction, acquired or congenital heart block, long QT syndrome, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. This patient had a pacemaker placed for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is experiencing a common complication in which the pacemaker is generating an impulse that is not captured and thus unable to depolarize myocardial tissue. This can sometimes occur secondary to lead fracture, detachment, insulation breakdown, or myocardial fibrosis, which are common, given that the lead is the most vulnerable part of the pacing system. One common site for lead fracture is between the clavicle and the first rib. This can be evaluated with a chest radiograph. An ECG may show a heart rate below the programmed rate or an irregular heart rate following pacemaker spikes.

Other common complications include failure to pace and failure to sense. If the leads are intact, the battery or programming may be the underlying issue. In this case, the patient is hemodynamically unstable with a malfunctioning pacemaker secondary to a malpositioned lead. Epinephrine can also be used to increase the heart rate, but if unsuccessful, transcutaneous pacing should be pursued in conjunction with urgent cardiology consultation. Transcutaneous pacing pads should be applied to the right of the sternum and on the left lateral chest in patients with typical cardiac anatomy. The pacing rate should be set to an age-appropriate rate with maximum output. Sedation and analgesia should be provided, if possible.



Knowledge of the pacemaker type, baseline settings, and manufacturer should be reviewed. It may be helpful to call the pacemaker manufacturer (B) to interrogate the pacemaker if a programming malfunction is suspected. However, consultation with a pediatric cardiologist trained in pacemaker programming is required, and it is not appropriate to have a representative from the pacemaker manufacturer download the device information without a trained cardiologist available to help guide management. Furthermore, this patient is hemodynamically unstable, and there is no time to wait for pacemaker interrogation.

Electrolyte abnormalities (C) may change pacemaker function by changing the depolarization threshold and should be evaluated. However, this patient is known to have a dislodged ventricular lead that is more likely causing their symptoms.

Patients with pacemakers are at risk for the development of thromboses and should be evaluated for these. However, anticoagulation (D) is not indicated at this time.

Question:

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 65-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary hypertension presents to the ED via EMS with shortness of breath for 2 days. She has associated jugular venous distension, bilateral lower extremity edema, and abdominal distension. She is not having chest pain and has not had recent fever, cough, congestion, or rashes. She has been taking her bosentan as prescribed. Her initial ECG is shown above. Her chest X-ray shows prominent pulmonary vasculature, but her lungs are clear bilaterally. Her D-dimer is 0.15 mg/L, and her initial troponin I is < 0.4 ng/mL. What is the most likely etiology of this patient’s ECG findings?
ExplanationEN:
A right bundle branch block (RBBB) is characterized by a prolonged QRS complex (i.e., > 0.12 ms) in the limb leads, an RSR′ pattern in V1 (often seen through V3) with discordant ST depression or T wave changes in V1 through V3, and a slurred S wave in V6. Etiologies include right ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular failure, pulmonary embolism, ischemia, rheumatic heart disease, myocarditis, and cardiomyopathy. Any ST segment elevations, ST depressions outside of V1–V3, or T wave inversions outside of V1–V3, are abnormal in RBBB and should prompt evaluation for associated ischemia. In this patient with known pulmonary hypertension and an acute worsening of her symptoms despite taking her home medications, progression to right ventricular failure should be considered the most likely diagnosis and is supported by the presence of an RBBB and signs of volume overload (e.g., jugular venous distention, abdominal distension, and lower extremity edema).



Coronary ischemia (A) should be suspected if the patient is having chest pain, if troponins are elevated, or if there are ST depressions outside of V1–V3, T wave inversions outside of V1–V3, or any ST segment elevation. Myocarditis (B) secondary to underlying infection should be considered in a patient with flu-like symptoms (e.g., fever, fatigue, myalgias), chest pain, new-onset heart failure symptoms (e.g., dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, signs of volume overload), elevated troponins, and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction on echocardiography. Pneumonia (C) should be suspected in patients with fever, dyspnea, cough, sputum production, chest pain, and infiltrates seen on chest X-ray, but a new RBBB would be unusual. A pulmonary embolism (D) may demonstrate nonspecific ECG findings consistent with right-heart strain (e.g., RBBB, right axis deviation, T wave changes in leads II, III, aVF) but an elevated D-dimer would likely be present.

Question: A term infant presents limp and apneic after a precipitous delivery. Stimulation and bag-mask ventilation with 21% FiO2 is given. There is no chest rise and no respiratory effort. After repositioning the airway, there is still no chest rise or respiratory effort and the heart rate remains at 50 bpm. Which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Decompress the chest with a needle

ExplanationEN:
The resuscitation of neonates requires a different approach from typical Advanced Life Support guidelines. Newborns are in a unique transition state as their gas exchange shifts from the placenta to the lungs. Most infants who require resuscitation at birth are experiencing respiratory failure and have hypoxia and carbon dioxide accumulation. Stimulation alone is sufficient when the newborn is delivered in the early stages of respiratory failure. Those who are delivered in the later stages often recover with adequate positive-pressure ventilation alone. This is why the focus of neonatal resuscitation is on providing adequate ventilatory support.

Infants who are born with poor tone or apnea should be briefly dried and stimulated. A pulse oximeter should be placed when bag-mask ventilation is started. If there is no chest rise, efforts should be made to optimize positive pressure by adjusting the mask, repositioning the head, clearing the mouth and nose, and increasing pressure. This should be accomplished within the first 60 seconds after birth. If this is unsuccessful, the best next step to ensure adequate ventilation is endotracheal intubation. Endotracheal intubation is strongly recommended in newborns whose heart rate remains < 100 bpm with positive-pressure ventilation and can be performed quickly with a laryngeal mask airway. This should be performed before chest compressions, even if the heart rate is < 60 bpm.



Continuous positive airway pressure (A) is only effective in those with a respiratory effort. It is instrumental in the neonate when there are signs of respiratory distress such as retractions or tachypnea after birth. It is not effective in children with apnea.

Chest compressions (B) should be initiated in newborns when the heart rate remains < 60 bpm, after ensuring adequate ventilation with endotracheal intubation or laryngeal mask ventilation.

The oxygen saturation should remain 21% FiO2 for term newborns until chest compressions are started, at which time the FiO2 is increased to 100% (D).

After chest compressions are started on a newborn, an emergent umbilical line should be placed to administer epinephrine. After epinephrine is administered, additional reversible causes should be addressed, such as hypovolemia or a pneumothorax, by administering volume or by decompressing the chest with a needle (C). These can be addressed earlier in the resuscitation if identified as the cause (e.g., known hemorrhage or asymmetric chest rise with positive pressure ventilation), but no cause is evident in this patient.

Question: Which of the following scenarios is a cricothyrotomy relatively contraindicated in?
ExplanationEN:
Cricothyrotomy is considered the last-line therapy in the classic cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate, cannot ventilate scenario. Before considering this option, every other method for airway management should be attempted, including orotracheal intubation with multiple attempts from multiple physicians. Contraindications for performing cricothyrotomy are age < 10–12 years (varying by reference text), tracheal transection, larynx fracture, and obstruction beneath the cricothyroid membrane.

The procedure begins by locating the cricothyroid membrane. In the traditional technique, a vertical incision is made to locate this structure. Next, a horizontal incision is made across the membrane, and a finger is inserted into the space. A stylet or bougie is then introduced, and then the endotracheal tube is fed over the stylet or bougie.



A 15-year-old patient (A) would be an appropriate candidate for this procedure, as a patient this age would have a more adult-like anatomy.

A known challenging intubation (C) would still warrant attempts at orotracheal intubation. However, this is the patient population that will typically require a cricothyrotomy.

Severe asthma (D) is not among the contraindications for cricothyrotomy. The procedure can be used as a last resort in an emergency asthma airway failure scenario.

Question: A 27-year-old gravid woman is brought in by EMS after a motor vehicle collision. On arrival, she loses her pulse. CPR is continued for 3 minutes, and the decision is made to proceed with a perimortem cesarean section. What abdominal incision is made?
ExplanationEN:
Perimortem cesarean section is a rare procedure since maternal cardiac arrest only occurs in 1 out of 30,000 pregnancies. Additionally, in order to have any reasonable chance of fetal survival, the procedure is ideally done within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest also limiting how often the procedure is performed. The goal of a perimortem cesarean section is to save the infant, but also potentially the mother as removing the fetus increases maternal cardiac output by 30%, potentially providing the necessary circulatory support.

When the decision is made to proceed with the procedure, a large, midline vertical incision is made extending from the pubic symphysis to the xiphoid process. The incision must go through all layers of the abdominal wall into the peritoneum. The abdominal wall is retracted laterally and the bladder is retracted inferiorly to expose the uterus. A small incision is made with a scalpel on the uterus and scissors are used to extend the incision vertically. The infant is delivered and suctioned, and the cord clamped. Preparations should occur simultaneously for newborn resuscitation.



The high transverse (A) and low transverse (B) incisions will not provide adequate exposure to the uterus in this emergent situation. Even in the nonperimortem cesarean section, obstetricians use a vertical incision for emergent deliveries and preserve the low transverse for a routine or stable delivery.

The Pfannenstiel incision (D) is the very low transverse incision along the top of the pubic hair used in nonemergency cesarean sections. The outcomes of this incision are cosmetically appealing to women.

Question: Which of the following is the most appropriate prescribing practice when initiating opioid therapy for acute pain in the emergency department?

Options.text: Avoid prescribing opioids altogether, regardless of pain severity
Combine immediate-release and extended-release opioids for optimal pain management
Initiate therapy with immediate-release opioids to manage acute pain episodes
Prescribe extended-release or long-acting opioids to provide consistent pain control
Prescribe the highest effective dose of immediate-release opioids to ensure adequate pain relief

CorrectAnswer: Initiate therapy with immediate-release opioids to manage acute pain episodes
ExplanationEN:
The third recommendation of the CDC’s 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline advises clinicians to prescribe immediate-release opioids instead of extended-release or long-acting opioids when initiating opioid therapy for acute, subacute, or chronic pain. Immediate-release opioids have a shorter duration of action, allowing for better control over dosing and a reduced risk of accumulation, which can lead to overdose. This approach is particularly pertinent in the ED, where the goal is to manage acute pain effectively while minimizing potential harms associated with opioid use.

In the ED setting, best practices for opioid prescribing emphasize using the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary. Nonopioid therapies, such as acetaminophen and NSAIDs, should be considered first-line treatments for many types of acute pain due to their favorable safety profiles. Opioids should be reserved for cases of severe pain for which nonopioid options are insufficient. When opioids are deemed necessary, immediate-release formulations are preferred to manage acute pain episodes effectively.

Complications associated with opioid prescriptions include the risk of misuse, development of opioid use disorder, and potential for overdose. Extended-release and long-acting opioids carry a higher risk of these complications due to their prolonged effects and potential for accumulation in the body. By adhering to guidelines that recommend immediate-release opioids for acute pain and emphasizing nonopioid therapies when appropriate, clinicians can mitigate these risks and promote safer pain management practices in the ED.



While nonopioid therapies are preferred, completely avoiding opioids (A) regardless of pain severity may not be appropriate. Opioids can be considered when the anticipated benefits outweigh the risks, particularly in cases of severe acute pain unresponsive to other treatments.

Combining immediate-release and extended-release opioids (B) is not recommended for initiating therapy in acute pain scenarios, as it complicates the dosing regimen and increases the risk of adverse effects without clear evidence of additional benefit.

Prescribing extended-release or long-acting opioids (D) for acute pain is discouraged because these formulations are designed for chronic pain management and pose a higher risk of overdose due to drug accumulation.

Initially prescribing the highest effective dose (E) is inappropriate. The guideline recommends starting with the lowest effective dose to minimize risks and titrate as necessary based on patient response.

Question: A 52-year-old man presents to the ED with left flank pain for the past 24 hours. He has a history of recurrent ureterolithiasis and says his current symptoms are similar. A point-of-care ultrasound image is shown above. Which of the following techniques can help to differentiate the diagnosis from normal renal anatomy?

Options.text: Apply color flow Doppler to the hypoechoic areas
Have the patient urinate and repeat the ultrasound after
Scan from the upper to the lower pole of the kidney in the transverse plane
Scan the contralateral kidney and compare

CorrectAnswer: Apply color flow Doppler to the hypoechoic areas
ExplanationEN:
Color flow Doppler is a valuable adjunct to point-of-care ultrasound in the ED when evaluating the kidney. This ultrasound image displayed here shows a dilated renal pelvis consistent with early hydronephrosis. However, the anechoic and hypoechoic areas within the renal sinus in early hydronephrosis can resemble intrarenal vasculature or normal collecting system structures. Applying color flow Doppler helps distinguish these structures by identifying blood flow. If color is present, the structure is likely a vessel, while the absence of flow suggests urine-filled spaces consistent with hydronephrosis.

Point-of-care renal ultrasound is performed using a curvilinear probe placed in the posterior axillary line with the patient in the supine or lateral decubitus position. The kidney is scanned in both longitudinal and transverse planes. A normal kidney appears as a bean-shaped structure with a hypoechoic cortex, echogenic renal sinus, and central echogenic hilum. The renal pyramids may appear hypoechoic and triangular. In contrast, hydronephrosis appears as anechoic dilations of the collecting system starting in the renal pelvis and extending into the calyces.

Hydronephrosis on ultrasound is graded as mild (dilatation of the renal pelvis only), moderate (pelvis and calyces), or severe (marked dilatation with thinning of the renal parenchyma). In the emergency setting, causes of hydronephrosis include obstructing ureteral calculi, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and rarely external compression from masses or retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Management depends on severity and symptoms but typically includes analgesia, antiemetics, IV fluids, and urologic consultation if infection or severe obstruction is suspected. In stable patients with uncomplicated nephrolithiasis, outpatient follow-up may be appropriate.



Having the patient urinate and repeating the ultrasound (B) may help clarify whether bladder obstruction is contributing to hydronephrosis, but it does not assist with interpreting intrarenal hypoechoic structures. Therefore, it does not help to differentiate between blood vessels and the renal collecting system.

Scanning through the kidney in both planes (C) is a routine part of renal ultrasound and helps visualize the full extent of the collecting system. However, it does not distinguish between vessels and collecting system structures. Without color Doppler, hypoechoic areas could be misinterpreted, especially in early hydronephrosis or in kidneys with prominent vessels.

While comparing both kidneys (D) is good ultrasound practice, it does not help confirm whether a hypoechoic structure in the renal sinus represents a vessel or a dilated collecting structure. Early hydronephrosis may be unilateral, and anatomical variation between kidneys limits the diagnostic specificity of this comparison.

Question: A 40-year-old man is brought to the ED after being assaulted during a bar fight. He has proptosis of the right eye with a measured intraocular pressure of 50 mm Hg. A lateral canthotomy is started. Once the Kelly clamp is released from the lateral canthus and the overlying tissue incised, what is the appropriate next step?

Options.text: Cut the inferior crus of lateral canthal tendon
Cut the superior crus of lateral canthal tendon

CorrectAnswer: Cut the inferior crus of lateral canthal tendon
ExplanationEN:
A lateral canthotomy is performed to relieve intraocular pressure from a retrobulbar hematoma, or postseptal hemorrhage, which creates orbital compartment syndrome and requires immediate decompression. This is an ophthalmologic emergency. The most common cause is blunt trauma to the eye. Abrupt postseptal hemorrhage increases intraocular pressure and decreases optic nerve blood flow, leading to ischemia and vision loss if not corrected in a timely fashion. Exam findings include proptosis, difficulty with extraocular movements, eye pain, decreased visual acuity, and elevated intraocular pressure (> 40 mm Hg). A lateral canthotomy begins with anesthetizing the lateral canthus with lidocaine with epinephrine, followed by crushing it with a straight Kelly clamp for 1–2 minutes. This will also help minimize further bleeding. When the clamp is removed, the next step is cutting the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon. The procedure is successful if intraocular pressure is lowered and pain and visual acuity improve. If not, the superior crus of the lateral canthus can be cut to allow for further decompression. Ophthalmology should be consulted in all cases.



There is no indication to clamp the medial canthus (A) when managing a retrobulbar hematoma.

One may need to cut the superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (C) if cutting the inferior crus does not relieve intraocular pressure.

Before rechecking intraocular pressure (D), the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon should be cut to complete the lateral canthotomy.

Question: A 16-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of difficulty breathing. The history and physical is consistent with a spontaneous pneumothorax, which you confirm by a chest X-ray. You decide to place a thoracostomy tube, as the pneumothorax is large and the patient is in severe distress. You insert the tube at the fifth intercostal space along the midaxillary line. Which direction should you direct the tube during the procedure?
ExplanationEN:
A thoracostomy tube (i.e., chest tube) is indicated in patients who require drainage of the pleural space to allow for lung inflation. This is most common in patients with a large pneumothorax, a hemothorax, or large pleural effusion. There are no absolute contraindications during a life-threatening event such as a tension pneumothorax, but anticoagulation or coagulopathy can cause significant bleeding and complicate the procedure.

The standard approach is under sterile technique at the mid- or anterior axillary line in the fifth intercostal space. The procedure is painful, even with appropriate local analgesia, and additional sedation may be required for awake patients. A 1–2 cm incision is made, and a tunnel is bluntly dissected using a Kelly clamp. Care should be taken to avoid the neurovascular bundle beneath each rib. Inserting a finger can confirm proper placement inside the thorax before the tube is inserted with the Kelly clamp. The thoracostomy tube should be inserted posteriorly and superiorly for best fluid drainage if it is being inserted for trauma or hemothorax. The thoracostomy tube should be inserted anteriorly and superiorly for best air drainage if inserting the tube for a pneumothorax alone. The tube should be sutured in place and attached to a one-way Heimlich valve or water seal device to allow continuous removal of air or fluid. Alternative methods using a Seldinger technique with smaller bore tubes or using a pigtail catheter may be appropriate in certain circumstances. An additional technique using an anterior approach at the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is described as more comfortable and may be acceptable to drain a pneumothorax when seen clearly on X-ray and when a smaller catheter can be used.



Inserting the tube inferiorly such as anteriorly and inferiorly (A) or posteriorly and inferiorly (C) risks insertion into the mediastinum or lung parenchyma and can result in significant injury. In a case when the tube is inserted into the lung fissure, it should be removed and replaced as necessary, as it is unlikely to provide the intended drainage.

Inserting a thoracostomy tube posteriorly and superiorly (D) is appropriate positioning but is best for drainage of fluid. Placement anteriorly and superiorly is best for drainage of air, as in this patient.

Question: A 47-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ED with persistent right eye pain and swelling after finishing antibiotics for an eye infection. His eye hurts when moved. He has right periorbital edema and erythema, pain on lateral gaze, a dilated nonreactive right pupil, and intraocular pressures of 42 mm Hg (right eye) and 12 mm Hg (left eye). Visual acuity is shadows (right eye) and 20/40 (left eye). What is the best next step in treatment?
ExplanationEN:
An emergent lateral canthotomy is indicated as this patient has elevated intraocular pressures and evidence of optic neuropathy. When acute orbital compartment syndrome is suspected, no further testing or treatments should delay immediate lateral canthotomy. Retrobulbar hematomas, either from surgery or direct ocular trauma, are the most common cause of acute orbital compartment syndrome. However, orbital cellulitis, orbital emphysema, and tumors are possible etiologies. In this case, the patient most likely has postseptal cellulitis leading to compartment syndrome of his left eye.

The most common physical exam findings of acute orbital compartment syndrome include acute unilateral optic neuropathy with evidence of changes in visual acuity and abnormal pupillary reflexes, limited extraocular movements, elevated intraocular pressures (typically > 30–40 mm Hg), or any combination of the above.



While an emergent ophthalmologic consult (B) should occur immediately, this consult should not delay the procedure and can be called by an extra team member. As noted above, no further imaging or treatments, such as an orbital computed tomography scan (C) or parenteral antibiotics (D), should delay a lateral canthotomy.

Question: An 8-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after they discovered a tick attached to his right armpit. What is the best way to remove the tick?

Options.text: Coat the tick in petroleum jelly
Grab the tick’s head with forceps and pull upward
Immerse the tick in isopropyl alcohol
Immerse the tick in normal saline
Tie a suture around the tick’s body and pull upward

CorrectAnswer: Grab the tick’s head with forceps and pull upward
ExplanationEN:
Although many techniques have been described over the years for removing a tick, the correct method is to use tweezers or forceps, grab the tick’s head as close to the skin as possible, and gently pull upward. The goal is to avoid crushing or tearing the tick’s head or body because this can induce regurgitation of infectious contents or leave behind its body parts, a possible nidus for infection or granulomatous reaction.



Immersion of the tick in an irritating, suffocating, or anesthetizing solution, such as petroleum jelly (A), alcohol (C), or saline (D), has been studied and found ineffective.

Tying a suture around the tick’s head can be attempted, but tying it around its body (E) increases the risk for transmission of infectious matter from the tick as it is killed or from residual embedded body parts.

Question: A 57-year-old man with a history of morbid obesity, cirrhosis, hypertension, and COPD presents to the emergency department with confusion, cough, and hemoptysis. His oxygen saturation is 60% on room air and 100% on a nonrebreather. He does not respond to painful stimuli, and naloxone has no effect. The decision is made to intubate the patient. Which of the following most supports using video laryngoscopy rather than direct laryngoscopy during intubation in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Emergency physicians are experts in managing critical and challenging airways. Any patient presenting with a need for intubation should be preoxygenated to allow optimal time during the procedure and minimize hypoxia. Appropriate setup should include bag-mask ventilation; suction (sometimes double suction); medications (often a sedative and a paralytic); postsedation medications, fluids, or vasopressors if hypotension exists; and appropriate primary and secondary methods of intubation. Studies on the use of video laryngoscopy have evidence to support an increased rate of first-pass intubation. It is generally the preferred method of intubation in patients with a predicted difficult airway, which may include a history of challenging intubation, a short or immobile neck, a Mallampati score of class 3 and above, and significant maxillofacial trauma. It is important to have multiple intubation methods readily available, including a rigid stylet, bougie, and surgical airway kit. Calling for help prior to intubation when patients have known difficult airways is also optimal care.



Active bleeding into the airway (A) may be one of the few instances in which video laryngoscopy may be a worse option, given that blood and secretions may obstruct the camera.

A history of multiple intubations (C) does not necessarily suggest that video laryngoscopy would be superior to direct laryngoscopy. Rather, a history of multiple intubations without documentation of a challenging airway may suggest the patient is easy to intubate.

A severe obstructive lung disease exacerbation (D) is more concerning for challenges with ventilation and oxygenation while on the ventilator. In an obstructive lung disease exacerbation, breath stacking may occur, and ventilation may be particularly challenging. A prolonged expiratory phase and lung-protective volumes may be indicated, and a slower respiratory rate may be needed to allow for full exhalation.

Question: A 21-year-old woman presents with left shoulder pain and limited range of motion. Her examination reveals the left arm to be completely abducted with the elbow flexed and the hand behind her head. Which of the following maneuvers will bring therapeutic relief?
ExplanationEN:
Luxatio erecta is an inferior glenohumeral (shoulder) dislocation. The mechanism of this injury is extreme abduction that is sometimes accompanied by downward force on the humeral head, causing it to break through the weak inferior glenoid rim. The arm is then positioned in full abduction with elbow flexion and the hand is held behind or on top of the patient’s head. The humeral head may be palpable in the lateral chest wall. Reduction is usually successful with upward (cephalad) axial traction in line with the humerus, along with countertraction. An audible clunk signifies successful reduction. The arm is then immobilized at the patient’s side. This type of shoulder dislocation is rare and often associated with significant soft tissue trauma or fractures of the proximal humerus. Concomitant rotator cuff injuries are also common. Operative management may be required if the dislocation is irreducible. For successful reductions, orthopedic follow-up is needed.

Downward (caudal) axial traction (B) is not feasible, as the arm is fixed in abduction and will not be successful in reduction.

Question: Which of the following is associated with an increased risk of postlumbar puncture headache?

Options.text: Sitting the patient upright after the procedure

ExplanationEN:
A lumbar puncture is the access into and removal of CSF from the spinal canal. It is a common procedure in emergency medicine, as it is the gold standard for diagnosing meningitis. Less common indications include evaluation of encephalitis, intracranial hypertension, and demyelinating conditions. Contraindications include skin infection overlying or near the puncture site, significant lumbar spine trauma, platelets < 20 x 109/L, and cranial mass with elevated intracranial pressure.

The procedure can be performed with the patient sitting upright or in lateral decubitus. The latter is preferred, as it allows for measurement of the opening pressure. The patient’s L4–L5 intervertebral space is then identified. After appropriate sterilization and anesthesia, the needle, with the bevel up if in the lateral position, should be inserted perpendicular to the patient and directed toward the umbilicus. Once past the “popping” sensations, which should be the ligamentum flavum and dura, the stylet should be removed and CSF should be drained. After collection of 1 mL of CSF into each of all four tubes, the stylet should be replaced before removal of the needle. An adhesive bandage can be placed over the insertion site. Common pitfalls include nonoptimal patient positioning, not truly directing the needle toward the patient’s umbilicus, and withdrawing the needle without the stylet in place. The most common complication is a postlumbar puncture headache. Use of a cutting needle (Quincke), use of a larger bore needle (e.g., 18-gauge), and multiple attempts have been associated with postlumbar headaches. Laying patients flat after the procedure and removing less CSF have not been shown to prevent postlumbar puncture headaches.



Low opening pressure (A) and sitting the patient upright after the procedure (B) have not been found to be associated with postlumbar puncture headaches.

The use of a noncutting needle (D) has been shown to decrease the likelihood of postlumbar puncture headaches.

Question: A 34-year-old man presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision reporting severe right hip pain and inability to move the limb. His X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate reduction technique?
ExplanationEN:
Posterior hip dislocations account for 90% of traumatic hip dislocations and are typically caused by high-energy trauma, such as dashboard injuries in motor vehicle collisions, in which axial force is transmitted through a flexed knee to the femoral head. Risk factors include unrestrained vehicle occupants, prior dislocations, and total hip arthroplasty. Clinically, the affected leg is classically shortened, adducted, and internally rotated, distinguishing it from anterior dislocations, which present with external rotation and abduction. Diagnosis is confirmed by X-ray, and a CT scan is recommended after reduction to assess for occult fractures or intra-articular fragments.

In the ED, prompt recognition and reduction within 6 hours is critical to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Procedural sedation is typically required. Neurovascular examination should be performed before and after reduction, with special attention to the sciatic nerve, which is at risk of injury in posterior dislocations.

The Allis maneuver is a commonly used and effective method for reducing posterior hip dislocations, particularly in patients without associated fractures. The patient is positioned supine, and after appropriate sedation and analgesia, an assistant stabilizes the pelvis by applying downward pressure on the anterior superior iliac spines. The physician then applies longitudinal traction on the flexed hip and knee, gradually increasing the force until the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum, often with an audible or palpable clunk. The leg is then extended and abducted slightly. This method is widely used in emergency settings due to its high success rate and relatively low risk of complications when performed correctly. After successful reduction, post-reduction films and advanced imaging guide further orthopedic care.



The Kocher maneuver (B) is used for anterior shoulder dislocations, not hip dislocations. It involves a sequence of external rotation, adduction, and internal rotation, which would be anatomically inappropriate and dangerous in a hip dislocation, risking fracture or vascular injury.

The Milch technique (C) is another method for reducing anterior shoulder dislocations, involving abduction and external rotation. It has no role in hip reduction and would not address the pathophysiology of a femoral head dislocated posteriorly from the acetabulum.

Spaso technique (D) is a shoulder reduction technique in which the patient is supine and the arm is flexed to 90 degrees with vertical traction and external rotation. It is not indicated for hip dislocations.

The Stimson technique (E) is most often used to reduce anterior shoulder dislocations, typically performed in the prone position with traction provided by a hanging weight. It can be done for posterior hip dislocations, but requires multiple assistants to ensure patients do not fall off the bed and can be challenging to use due to difficult patient positioning. It would not be the most appropriate technique for this patient.

Question: What is the likely diagnosis based on the above echocardiographic findings?
ExplanationEN:
Point of care echocardiography in the emergency department has benefits in terms of aiding in diagnosis and guiding treatment plans. The clinician is able to identify pericardial effusions, estimate ejection fraction, and assess for right heart strain. The video in the question stem shows a four-chamber view of the heart in which the right and left ventricles, as well as the right and left atria, are viewed from the apex of the heart. The mitral and tricuspid valves are in view as well. The right ventricle appears to be equal or even larger in size compared to the left ventricle. Additionally, the septum appears to be flattened, and the right ventricular systolic function is diminished. All of these findings are consistent with right heart strain. Right heart strain can occur in the setting of pulmonary embolism.



Point of care ultrasound is capable of identifying an aortic dissection (A). However, a CT angiography is a more optimal study. With an ultrasound, a suprasternal view of the aortic arch or a parasternal long-axis view of the thoracic aorta may visualize a dissection flap.

Cardiac tamponade (B) can be clinically diagnosed by the triad of hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and jugular venous distension. On bedside echocardiogram, patients with tamponade will have a pericardial effusion with right ventricular collapse during diastole.

Patients who develop acute mitral regurgitation (C) can be critically ill, especially in the setting of acute ischemia leading to papillary muscle rupture. Echocardiography is vital in making a quick diagnosis and will show a prolapse of the mitral leaflet into the left atrium.

Question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a facial laceration after a fall. He has a 2-cm linear laceration extending vertically through his left lower lip, crossing the vermilion border. Which of the following is the most appropriate method of analgesia for his repair?
ExplanationEN:
Facial lacerations are among the most common traumatic injuries treated in the emergency department, and adequate anesthesia is essential for proper wound preparation and repair. Three primary modalities exist: local infiltration, topical anesthetics, and regional nerve blocks. Local infiltration with lidocaine (with or without epinephrine) is the most commonly used method and is appropriate for most simple facial lacerations. Topical anesthetics such as LET gel (lidocaine 4%, epinephrine 0.1%, tetracaine 0.5%) are particularly valuable in pediatrics, as they eliminate the pain and anxiety associated with needle injections and are recommended as a first-line option for simple facial and scalp lacerations in children. Regional nerve blocks, including the supraorbital, infraorbital, and mental nerve blocks, are indicated when local infiltration would cause unacceptable tissue distortion (e.g., at the vermilion border or eyelid margin), when large wounds would require potentially toxic doses of local anesthetic, or when infiltration would be particularly painful. The mental nerve block is performed by everting the lower lip, identifying the mental foramen below the second premolar, and injecting 1–2 mL of local anesthetic (e.g., 0.25% bupivacaine or 1–2% lidocaine) after aspiration. [3-4] Contraindications to regional nerve blocks include local infection at the injection site, known allergy to the anesthetic agent, and distorted anatomy (e.g., from prior fractures). Contraindications to topical LET include application to mucous membranes and areas of end-arterial supply (nose, ears, digits, penis) due to the risk of epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction.

Complications of facial anesthesia are generally uncommon but include local anesthetic systemic toxicity from inadvertent intravascular injection or excessive dosing, allergic reactions, hematoma formation at the injection site, and temporary nerve injury. Aspiration before injection during nerve blocks is essential to prevent intravascular delivery. Topical LET has been associated with rare adverse effects, including mydriasis, when applied near the eye. Regional nerve blocks may fail to achieve complete anesthesia, while tissue distortion from local infiltration represents a significant practical limitation when repairing lacerations at cosmetically important areas, such as the vermilion border, hairline, or eyebrow. Each of these limitations should be considered when choosing a route of anesthesia for wound management.



While nitrous oxide (A) can reduce pain and anxiety during laceration repair in children, it provides anxiolysis and mild analgesia rather than true local anesthesia. It would be insufficient as the sole anesthetic for suturing a through-and-through lip laceration and does not address the need to avoid tissue distortion at the vermilion border.

Although local lidocaine with epinephrine (B) is the most commonly used method for facial lacerations in general, local infiltration at the vermilion border causes tissue edema and distortion that obscures the precise skin-vermilion junction, making accurate alignment and cosmetically optimal repair significantly more difficult.

Topical lidocaine-epinephrine-tetracaine gel (D) is an excellent first-line topical anesthetic for simple pediatric facial and scalp lacerations. However, it is contraindicated for mucous membranes, and a laceration that crosses the vermilion border involves the mucosal surface of the lip.

Question: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks gestation with a history of obesity presents to the emergency department in active labor. The obstetrics team is paged, but the woman begins delivering. You direct her to push with contractions and deliver the baby’s head in an occiput-anterior position. A nuchal cord is quickly reduced, but the baby’s head retracts back tightly against the perineum despite the mother bearing down and you providing gentle downward traction. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Attempt internal rotation of the fetus
Instruct the mother to get on her elbows and knees to push
Instruct the mother to hyperflex her thighs against her abdomen

CorrectAnswer: Instruct the mother to hyperflex her thighs against her abdomen
ExplanationEN:
This delivery is complicated by shoulder dystocia, an arrest of delivery in which the fetal shoulders fail to deliver after the fetal head. Shoulder dystocia occurs in around 1% of vaginal births with an increasing risk as birth weight increases (up to 9% of vaginal births of fetuses weighing over 4 kilograms). Other risk factors include maternal obesity, post-term delivery, and prolonged labor. Fetuses often present with a “turtle sign” in which the fetal head is drawn back against the perineum. Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency, as the birth canal compresses the umbilical cord and can lead to hypoxia and neurologic damage. The management of shoulder dystocia should begin with hyperflexion of the mother’s thighs against the abdomen. This is termed the McRoberts maneuver and straightens the sacrum to improve the mechanics of contractions and help the posterior fetal shoulder pass over the pubic symphysis. This maneuver is the most effective single maneuver and relieves between 40 and 90% of shoulder dystocias. Suprapubic pressure can also be applied.



Internal rotation of the fetus (A) can be attempted if maternal thigh hyperflexion and suprapubic pressure do not relieve the dystocia. It involves rotating the posterior fetal shoulder past the sacrum.

If internal rotation also fails to release the fetus, mothers can roll onto their knees and elbows (B) in an “all fours position,” which uses gravity to help optimize the posterior fetal shoulder’s passage over the sacrum.

Episiotomy (D) can be considered if other maneuvers fail but does not address the underlying problem of bony impaction.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shoulder pain after being tackled. A radiograph reveals an anterior shoulder dislocation. The patient is unable to undergo reduction without sedation. Propofol and fentanyl are given until the patient is adequately sedated. During the procedure, the above capnography waveform is seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Procedural sedation is commonly performed in the emergency department to facilitate procedures such as joint reduction, fracture reduction, and cardioversion, among others. There are many agents used for procedural sedation in the emergency department, including propofol, ketamine, etomidate, fentanyl, and midazolam. The emergency physician should titrate the depth of sedation to the procedure being performed. Managing the airway is the most critical component. During procedural sedation, the patient should be connected to the monitor and have ongoing pulse oximetry and capnography. Capnography is a tool for detecting how rapidly and deeply the patient is breathing. It is more sensitive and specific for detecting ventilation than pulse oximetry. A normal capnography amplitude should be around 40 mm Hg. The physician should also assess the respiratory rate, which usually is around 12–20 breaths/minute. During sedation, it is common to see a reduction in the capnography waveform and the respiratory rate.

Apnea is a prolonged period in which the patient is not breathing, and capnography will show a prolonged absence of waves. This is more common during deep sedation. If the patient becomes apneic or is hypoventilating, then stimulating the patient by performing the planned procedure or a jaw thrust technique is appropriate. If this does not improve respirations, the patient may need bag-mask ventilation. Finally, if the physician is unable to improve the patient’s oxygenation and ventilation, intubation may be indicated as a last-line measure. It is always important to use common sense when relying on capnography. Some patients preferentially breathe through their mouth, and leads placed in the nose will make capnography appear as if the patient has apnea. When an abnormal finding is seen on capnography, first perform an exam and assess whether the patient is breathing.



Hypoventilation secondary to oversedation (B) would be seen with breathing that is inappropriately slow. The waveform will maintain the same amplitude while the patient breathes, but the waves will be longer in duration.

A normal breathing pattern during sedation (C) would involve a regular capnography waveform with regular intervals between each wave. It is expected during sedation to have slightly slower breathing and slightly smaller waveforms than those seen during the awake state.

Tachypnea caused by pain (D) would present with more frequent waves of a shorter duration seen on capnography. This is common during sedation when a painful procedure is occurring. More sedation may be needed if the patient is in too much pain or is too awake or alert.
