Question: A 32-year-old man with a history of heroin use, who is now on a methadone maintenance program, presents to the emergency department with muscle aches and abdominal pain. He indicates he has not had his usual methadone 60 mg dose in 2 days and thinks he is in opioid withdrawal. He was able to obtain methadone 10 mg last night but does not feel like that helped. The patient is mildly agitated and does not sit still in bed. Vital signs show HR 96 bpm, BP 123/72 mm Hg, and T 37.2°C. On examination, his pupils are large but equal in size. His abdomen is diffusely tender, but he does not have any focal tenderness or peritoneal signs. What is the best option for treating his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Opioid drug use and use disorder are widespread across the United States. Rapid cessation of opioid drug use leads to uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms within 6–12 hours if short-acting opioids are used or within 24–48 hours if long-acting opioids, such as methadone, are used. While naturally occurring opioid withdrawal usually does not pose a life-threatening emergency, iatrogenic withdrawal with a reversal agent, such as naloxone, can lead to a catecholamine surge and hemodynamic instability that may be life-threatening. Reversal agents should only be utilized in a patient with life-threatening respiratory compromise. Symptoms of opioid withdrawal include restlessness, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, myalgias, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Signs of opioid withdrawal include dilated pupils, yawning, diaphoresis, increased bowel sounds, and piloerection. It is rare for these patients to have vital sign abnormalities, unless they have severe volume depletion. Their mental status is usually preserved. Patients who present to the emergency department with abnormal vital signs and mental status changes should be evaluated for other medical problems or other withdrawal syndromes. There are several options for treating opioid withdrawal. If confirmed with his treatment center, continuation of treatment with methadone is the best option for this patient if it is available, as he is on methadone regularly.



Buprenorphine (A) can be difficult to use in the emergency setting because its partial agonist properties can worsen withdrawal symptoms if the patient recently used opioids. This patient used methadone less than a day prior to presentation and is already prescribed methadone regularly, so buprenorphine would not be the best treatment option.

The best nonopioid treatment agents include alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, such as clonidine (B) or lofexidine. These agents can be used as adjuncts to treatment with buprenorphine or methadone or in cases of iatrogenic withdrawal. Clonidine may be administered orally every hour until symptoms are resolved. The optimal maximum daily dose in this setting is unknown, but experts do not recommend more than 1.2 mg per day. The addition of benzodiazepines can help calm the patient. Promethazine is a good antiemetic due to its anticholinergic properties, and loperamide or octreotide can be used to control diarrhea.

Previously, it was thought that calcium channel blockers, such as nifedipine (D), could be used to treat opioid withdrawal. However, studies have not shown this to be true.

Question: Withdrawal syndromes from which one of the following can be life-threatening?
ExplanationEN:
Withdrawal is manifested by either a characteristic withdrawal syndrome for the substance, or the use of a substance or one that is closely related to relieve withdrawal symptoms. Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine that binds to the gamma amino-butyric acid (GABA) receptor. When any chronically ingested substance with GABA activity is withdrawn, inhibitory control of excitatory neurotransmission is lost. This results in the clinical syndrome of withdrawal manifested by CNS excitation (tremor, hallucinations, seizures) and autonomic dysregulation (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis). Severe withdrawal from GABA agonists (e.g., ethanol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates) can result in death.



Cocaine (A) does not produce a withdrawal syndrome but rather a postintoxication condition often described as the crack crash, washed-out syndrome, or cocaine blues. It is associated with lethargy, hypersomnolence, movement disorders, and irritability.

Morphine (C) withdrawal, unlike that of benzodiazepines or barbiturates, is not fatal by itself. Clinically, it is associated with piloerection, irritability, dysphoria, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, vomiting, diarrhea, and insomnia.

Phencyclidine (D) or PCP is a hallucinogen that can produce anxiety and paranoia from chronic use or “bad trips.” There is generally no withdrawal syndrome associated with phencyclidine.

Question: What act, when performed by the person experiencing abuse, most increases the chances for death when in a relationship of intimate partner violence?

Options.text: Attempting to fight back with physical force
Being discovered to have other medical conditions

ExplanationEN:
Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a pattern of assault or coercive behavior perpetrated by someone who was, is, or wishes to be involved in an intimate relationship with another individual, with the aim of establishing control over the individual. IPV can include physical injury, psychological abuse, sexual assault, intimidation, stalking, and progressive social isolation.

IPV occurs in every race, culture, geographic location, and type of religious group and affects individuals of all socioeconomic and educational backgrounds. IPV can be difficult to identify in the ED, as it does not always present with signs of abuse. Frequently, IPV presents with other health-related consequences of the violence. Therefore, screening programs should be established, and all individuals should be asked about abuse at home and suicidal or homicidal behavior.

Patients should be interviewed alone so they have an opportunity to be more forthcoming about abuse concerns. Once intimate partner violence has been identified, it is important to ensure the safety of the patient. To this end, it is important for the clinician to understand that the most dangerous time for people experiencing abuse occurs when the abuse is disclosed and when they attempt to leave the relationship.

This fear of death frequently plays a role in why a patient may choose to return to an unsafe environment rather than attempt to leave. While in the ED, patients should be provided information about IPV and given options for social support. The clinician should also stress that any type of violence, abuse, and intimidation is not normal in a healthy relationship. Most states do not require reporting of IPV, but many states require reporting of injuries that result from firearms, knives, or other weapons. ED clinicians should be aware of these reporting requirements and inform the patient accordingly.



Attempting to fight back with physical force (A) can sometimes escalate an encounter, but the strongest predictor of death is leaving or attempting to leave, not retaliatory force.

Becoming pregnant (C) is a known risk factor for IPV, as violence often begins or escalates during pregnancy, but it does not independently increase the risk of homicide to the same degree as separation from the relationship.

Being discovered to have other medical conditions (D) may increase dependency and vulnerability, but it is not a primary predictor of lethal outcomes in IPV.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 27-year-old woman presents to the ED after experiencing an episode of her heart racing and a sense that she was losing control of her own body. She was at her friend’s house approximately 3 hours ago when they used an illicit substance that was given to them. Her friends remark that initially she seemed to have a very elevated mood and claimed to be seeing sounds, which then progressed to a panic attack within 40 minutes of taking the drug. Her initial vital signs are within normal limits other than a heart rate of 115 bpm. Physical exam is unremarkable other than mild agitation. The patient is observed in the ED and 8 hours later, her symptoms improve. Which of the following agents is the most likely etiology of this patient’s presentation?
ExplanationEN:
Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) intoxication presents with a heightened perception of sensory input, a distorted sense of time, euphoria, synesthesia (blending of senses), and a sensation of being out of one’s body with a sense of mystical or spiritual experiences. Unwanted complications can include panic, dysphoria, and a sense of dread, with some patients experiencing psychosis. The half-life is roughly 3 hours. Thus, symptoms tend to improve rapidly in the ED. Other hallucinogens that can cause similar symptoms include mescaline and psilocybin.

Hallucinogens alone typically do not lead to ED visits. However, when crossed with other substances, including alcohol, marijuana, and other illicit chemicals, there is an increased likelihood of complications. Use of LSD can lead to an increased risk of serotonin syndrome (presenting with altered mental status, neuromuscular abnormalities, and autonomic hyperactivity).

In general, the management of hallucinogens includes cardiac monitoring and correction of any electrolyte derangements. It is imperative to ensure that the patient is safe, which may require sedation, restraints, or closer observation.



3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (A) (also known as MDMA or ecstasy) intoxication presents with increased alertness, increased energy, and a sensation of increased physical and mental abilities with euphoria. It can present similarly to an LSD ingestion. However, the symptoms of MDMA tend to be more often associated with a pleasant experience with a lower incidence of panic attacks (though anxiety is a common complication). The duration of action of this drug is shorter than LSD and is closer to 4–6 hours. This patient’s symptoms resolving over 8 hours, the intensity of symptoms, and synesthesia make LSD a more likely intoxication, though MDMA is certainly on the differential.

Cocaine (B) intoxication presents with tachycardia, increased energy, and agitation with a shorter duration of symptoms when compared to amphetamines, which present similarly. Mydriasis may be seen on physical exam. Significant hypertension and tachycardia are more common findings in cocaine and amphetamine intoxication when compared to LSD intoxication.

Phencyclidine (D) presents with acute and violent behavior with psychosis. Patients will often need both chemical sedation and physical restraints depending on the severity of their symptoms. Presenting findings may include hypertension, tachycardia, aggression, and rotary nystagmus.

One Step Further

Reveal Answer:
Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment, followed by alpha-blockers such as phentolamine.

Question: A 21-year-old college student arrives at the ED at 1:00 am with crushing, substernal chest pain. Vital signs are BP 170/80 mm Hg, HR 110 bpm, RR 16/min, and T 99°F (37.2°C). An ECG demonstrates ST-segment elevations. The patient states that he was at a party. The patient is emergently taken to the cardiac catheterization lab. The results of which lab test would likely explain the patient's presentation?
ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely has sustained a cocaine-induced myocardial infarction (MI). Cocaine causes coronary vasoconstriction and increases myocardial oxygen demand. In addition, cocaine increases platelet aggregation, leading to a prothrombotic state. As a result, coronary insufficiency can result, leading to myocardial ischemia or infarction. In a patient with an MI, the first step in management is emergent cardiac catheterization. MIs can have many etiologies. Up to 25% of nonfatal MIs in patients 18-45 years old were related to cocaine use. It has also been found that concomitant use of alcohol enhances the effects of cocaine through the metabolite cocaethylene. Therefore, a urine drug screen should be obtained to test for the use of cocaine by the patient.



A cholesterol panel (B) and hemoglobin A1c (C) should be ordered to investigate any underlying cardiac disease, but in this patient, a urine drug screen is more likely to elucidate the cause in this previously healthy, young individual.

If no etiology is discovered, a cardiac stress test (A) could be performed to further evaluate this patient’s cardiac status but should never occur during an active MI.

Question: Which of the following is consistent with a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa?
ExplanationEN:
Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors, most commonly self-induced vomiting.

Repeated vomiting leads to loss of gastric hydrochloric acid, resulting in metabolic alkalosis. Additionally, volume depletion from fluid loss activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, promoting sodium and water retention at the expense of hydrogen and potassium excretion. This process produces contraction alkalosis, a hallmark laboratory finding in patients with ongoing purging behavior. It is called contraction alkalosis because the alkalosis results from a contraction (reduction) of extracellular fluid volume, not just from loss of acid.

The combination of metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, and volume depletion is classic for bulimia nervosa. Patients may also develop complications, including dental enamel erosion, parotid gland enlargement, and electrolyte abnormalities.

Recognition of contraction alkalosis is important because it reflects both the underlying behavior and associated physiologic consequences.

This finding helps distinguish bulimia nervosa from other eating disorders. For example, patients with restrictive eating patterns without purging are more likely to have different metabolic disturbances, such as those related to malnutrition rather than vomiting-induced alkalosis.



Heart failure (B) is not a typical or defining feature of bulimia nervosa. While severe electrolyte abnormalities, particularly hypokalemia, can predispose patients to cardiac dysrhythmias, structural or functional heart failure is not commonly seen. Cardiac complications in bulimia are more often related to arrhythmogenic risk rather than pump failure. Therefore, heart failure does not align with the expected presentation.

Hyperkalemia (C) is not seen in bulimia nervosa. Patients with bulimia nervosa who engage in vomiting develop hypokalemia. Potassium is lost both directly through emesis and indirectly through renal excretion driven by aldosterone activation in response to volume depletion. Hyperkalemia would suggest a different process, such as kidney failure or medication effects, which are not characteristic of bulimia.

Hypothermia (D) is more commonly associated with severe malnutrition and low body mass, as seen in anorexia nervosa. Bulimia nervosa patients often maintain a normal body weight, and thermoregulatory disturbances are less prominent. The physiologic effects of bulimia are primarily related to purging behaviors rather than chronic caloric restriction. While mild temperature changes could occur in extreme cases, hypothermia is not a typical or distinguishing feature.

Question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the ED with shortness of breath. He had a recent sore throat that resolved, but has had dark urine and puffy eyes for the past few days. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse rales. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a mild pericardial effusion. Vital signs are a T of 100.2°F (37.9°C), BP of 90/60 mm Hg, HR of 100 bpm, RR of 18/min, and SpO2 of 90% on room air. Urinalysis reveals red blood cell casts, moderate proteinuria, and hematuria. Loop diuretics are administered with no improvement in symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
This child presents with signs of fluid overload (dyspnea, rales, low oxygen saturation, pericardial effusion) following a recent sore throat and development of dark urine and facial edema, suggesting acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN). The failure to respond to loop diuretics indicates that his kidney function is too impaired to manage the fluid overload, making hemodialysis the most appropriate treatment to rapidly remove excess fluid and correct uremia or electrolyte imbalances.

APSGN is an immune-mediated kidney disorder that classically presents 1 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal infection. It is most commonly seen in children aged 2 to 12 years, although it can occur at any age. APSGN can follow either streptococcal pharyngitis or streptococcal skin infections, such as impetigo. The condition results from immune complex deposition in the glomeruli, which activates the complement system and leads to inflammation and damage.

The hallmark features of APSGN include the sudden onset of gross hematuria, often described by caregivers as “tea-colored” or “cola-colored” urine, red blood cell casts in the urine, mild to moderate proteinuria, edema, and hypertension. Edema often begins periorbitally, particularly noticeable in the morning around the eyelids, and may progress to generalized edema involving the face, extremities, and abdomen. Oliguria (reduced urine output) may be present, reflecting decreased glomerular filtration. These findings represent the classic picture of nephritic syndrome: hematuria, hypertension, and edema, often accompanied by impaired kidney function.

Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and supported by laboratory findings. Urinalysis reveals hematuria, red blood cell casts, and proteinuria. Serum complement levels, particularly C3, are decreased due to complement consumption. Evidence of recent streptococcal infection should be sought with tests such as antistreptolysin O titers, anti-DNase B, or streptozyme tests. Kidney function should be monitored with serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, and blood pressure should be closely followed.

Treatment is primarily supportive, as the condition is usually self-limited in children. Antihypertensive therapy, such as calcium channel blockers or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, may be required to manage elevated blood pressure. Diuretics can be used to address volume overload and edema. Antibiotics, such as penicillin, may be given to eradicate any residual streptococcal infection, although they do not alter the course of the glomerulonephritis itself. Immunosuppressive agents, corticosteroids, and plasmapheresis are not indicated in uncomplicated APSGN.

Indications for hemodialysis include severe and refractory volume overload, life-threatening hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and clinical signs of uremia, such as encephalopathy, pericardial effusion, or pulmonary edema not responsive to medical therapy. Most children recover fully with supportive care, but adults and patients with more severe disease may have a prolonged course or progress to chronic kidney disease. Regular follow-up is essential to monitor for persistent hypertension, proteinuria, or kidney dysfunction.



Furosemide-induced diuresis at higher doses (A) is not effective if the kidneys are failing to respond, as indicated by no improvement with standard dosing.

High-dose corticosteroids (C) are used in immune-mediated nephritis, such as lupus nephritis or minimal change disease, not in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis when supportive care is the mainstay.

Plasmapheresis (D) is used in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or conditions like Goodpasture syndrome, but not in postinfectious glomerulonephritis.

Question: Which one of the following overdoses is most commonly managed with dialysis?
ExplanationEN:
The indications for dialysis include severe fluid overload, refractory hypertension, severe hyperkalemia that cannot be managed medically, severe acidosis, uremia, and certain intoxications and overdoses. Toxicity from toxic alcohols, such as methanol or ethylene glycol, often requires dialysis. Any initial ingestion should first be managed by administration of fomepizole (or ethanol if this is not available) to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase and stop the ultimate formation of formic acid (with methanol ingestion) or glycolic acid (with ethylene glycol ingestion). This temporizes the patient until they can receive dialysis to ultimately remove the toxic compounds. Indications for dialysis with toxic alcohol overdose include severe metabolic acidosis that is refractory to treatment, kidney insufficiency, worsening vital signs, refractory electrolyte abnormalities, and visual abnormalities (in methanol toxicity).



Amitriptyline (A) toxicity is determined by the width of the QRS complex on ECG and is treated with sodium bicarbonate.

Amlodipine (B), a calcium channel blocker, is highly protein-bound and is not amenable to elimination by hemodialysis. Treatment of calcium channel blocker toxicity includes calcium, glucagon, high-dose insulin therapy, and lipid emulsion therapy.

Ethanol (C) toxicity is managed with supportive therapy only and observation of the patient until sober. Withdrawal can be managed with phenobarbital or diazepam, which can be gradually tapered.

Question: A 30-year-old man presents to the ED with left groin swelling and discomfort. He reports a history of unprotected sexual contact with multiple male partners. About 1 week ago, he noticed a small, painless, purplish ulcer on his penis that resolved on its own within a few days. Over the past 3 days, he has developed increasing pain and swelling in his left groin. He reports no fever, chills, urethral discharge, or dysuria. On physical exam, he has tender, fluctuant left-sided inguinal lymphadenopathy with overlying erythema but no current genital ulcer. Rectal exam is normal, and there is no rash or oral lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy following resolution of a painless genital ulcer, a presentation characteristic of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV). LGV is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the L1, L2, and L3 serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis. It is more commonly seen in tropical and subtropical regions, but outbreaks have also been reported in urban centers, particularly among men who have sexual intercourse with men (MSM).

The primary stage begins with a small, painless papule or ulcer at the site of inoculation, often on the genitalia, rectum, or cervix. The lesion is frequently transient and may go unnoticed, as it resolves within a few days and is often asymptomatic. The secondary stage develops 1 to 4 weeks later, characterized by painful, unilateral inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy, sometimes referred to as buboes. These lymph nodes may become tender, fluctuant, and drain spontaneously, leaving sinus tracts or scarring. The so-called groove sign may be seen, when the inguinal ligament separates two enlarged lymph node groups. Constitutional symptoms such as fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, and arthralgias may accompany this stage.

The tertiary stage, or anogenitorectal syndrome, seen more commonly in MSM, can result in proctocolitis with rectal pain, tenesmus, discharge, and bleeding. Chronic inflammation may lead to strictures, fistulae, and lymphedema, particularly in untreated cases. Rarely, LGV can result in systemic complications such as meningoencephalitis.

LGV can mimic other causes of genital ulcers and inguinal lymphadenopathy, including syphilis, chancroid, herpes simplex virus, and granuloma inguinale (donovanosis). Important distinguishing features include the biphasic progression, transient primary lesion, and delayed but prominent lymphadenopathy. The painless ulcer of LGV contrasts with the painful ulcers of chancroid and herpes, and the suppurative lymphadenopathy differentiates it from syphilis.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, especially in resource-limited settings. Laboratory confirmation may involve nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis from lesion swabs, lymph node aspirates, or rectal specimens, though serotyping is often unavailable. First-line treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days.

Alternative options include erythromycin or azithromycin. Buboes may require needle aspiration or incision and drainage to relieve pain and prevent rupture. Sexual partners should be evaluated and treated. Patients should abstain from sexual activity until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved.



Chancroid (A) is caused by the bacteria Haemophilus ducreyi and presents as a painful erythematous papule with bilateral tender and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Granuloma inguinale (B) is caused by the bacteria Klebsiella granulomatis and presents as a beefy, painless genital ulcer that bleeds easily due to increased vascularity of the lesion.

Primary syphilis (D) is caused when the bacteria Treponema pallidum presents with a single painless chancre and bilateral, nontender, rubbery lymphadenopathy. In contrast, this patient has unilateral, tender, fluctuant lymph nodes with overlying inflammation, which is more consistent with LGV.

Question: A 36-year-old man presents to the ED with a painful erection for 14 hours. Workup in the emergency department reveals ischemic priapism. What is the first-line treatment for this patient?

Options.text: Cavernosal aspiration of blood and injection of phenylephrine
Corpus cavernosum irrigation with cold sterile saline

CorrectAnswer: Cavernosal aspiration of blood and injection of phenylephrine
ExplanationEN:
After establishing a diagnosis of ischemic, or low-flow, priapism from supporting history, physical examination, and blood gas analysis, a time-sensitive treatment approach should be employed. First, analgesics should be administered as this condition is painful. Anesthesia through a dorsalpenilenerveblock or a circumferential penile ring block is recommended for patient comfort.

A single corpus cavernosum should be accessed with a large-bore needle (19 g at least) attached to a syringe, either longitudinally through the glans penis or perpendicularly to the shaft. The first-line treatment is aspiration of blood until fresh red arterial blood is obtained and injection of phenylephrine. This may require aspiration of approximately 50 mL of blood. Phenylephrine is the preferred agent due to its alpha-1-selective agonism, demonstrated efficacy, and limited systemic cardiovascular side effects compared with other sympathomimetics. Blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored during administration.



If detumescence does not occur after aspiration and the instillation of phenylephrine, irrigation with cold, sterile saline (B) can be attempted. This is done by instilling 25 mL of cold sterile saline into the corpus cavernosum and aspirating the fluid after 20 minutes if detumescence is not achieved. Cold saline has been shown to be more effective than room temperature saline, but it is not recommended as first-line treatment. The combination of intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection and corporal aspiration is successful in 70–100% of cases, whereas conservative measures alone (including ice packs and cold saline instillation) are much less effective (1–55%).

Intracavernosal injection of methylene blue (C) has been shown to be a potential therapy for ischemic priapism in two studies, but there is a lack of evidence in comparing treatment with methylene blue to other priapism therapies. At this time, it is not recommended as a standard treatment option.

Oral sympathomimetics such as terbutaline (D) have shown only modest efficacy compared to intracavernosal phenylephrine and are not recommended as first-line therapy for established ischemic priapism. These agents may have a limited role in prolonged iatrogenic erections of < 4 hours but should never replace definitive treatment when emergent detumescence is required.

Question: Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for the development of contrast-associated acute kidney injury?

Options.text: Exposure to contrast more than once in 48 hours

ExplanationEN:
The greatest risk factor for the development of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) is preexisting kidney insufficiency, with patients having a serum creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL at greatest risk.

Exposure to radiocontrast agents is a common cause of hospital-acquired acute kidney injury. Kidney perfusion can be decreased for up to 20 hours following radiocontrast exposure. The ensuing injury can range from a mild nonoliguric rise in serum creatinine to severe kidney failure requiring hemodialysis, which is less commonly seen.

A rise in serum creatinine > 25% of baseline occurs within 3 days of exposure and resolves within 10–14 days. The risk of developing CA-AKI is nearly negligible in patients without any risk factors.

However, patients with risk factors such as preexisting kidney insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, age > 65 years, volume depletion, and multiple myeloma have a significantly greater risk of developing kidney injury (up to 10–20%).



Age > 65 years (A) makes patients more susceptible to CA-AKI if there are other comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, but age alone is not an independent or primary risk factor. The decline in kidney function with age is gradual and does not universally predispose patients to injury unless other contributing factors, such as underlying kidney disease, are present.

Diabetes mellitus (B) is frequently cited as a risk factor, but its significance diminishes when controlling for baseline kidney function. Patients with diabetes are at increased risk, primarily because of coexisting diabetes-related nephropathy. In the absence of kidney dysfunction, diabetes alone does not substantially elevate the risk of CA-AKI.

Repeated contrast exposure within a short time frame (C) may elevate risk, particularly in susceptible individuals. However, this factor is situational and less predictive than underlying kidney disease. While cumulative nephrotoxic effects can occur, preventive strategies can mitigate this risk, and many patients tolerate repeated studies without incident if baseline kidney function is intact.

Question: A 56-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents with penile and prepuce redness, swelling, and discharge as pictured above. The symptoms have been ongoing for several days. When the foreskin is not routinely cleaned, the buildup of sweat, debris, exfoliated skin, and bacteria or fungus can occur, leading to inflammation. Candidal infection is the most common cause, especially in patients with diabetes. In this situation, empiric treatment with topical clotrimazole cream is warranted.

Topical mupirocin cream (D) would be indicated if streptococcal or staphylococcal infection was suspected. Severe cases could be treated with oral cephalexin. There is not a good way to differentiate typical candidal inflammation from streptococcal or staphylococcal causes so it's essential to evaluate risk factors. One might consider treatment with topical mupirocin if topical clotrimazole fails in this patient.

Question: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the ED with a painless abdominal mass and hematuria. On physical exam, a unilateral right-sided abdominal mass is palpated inferior to the liver. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic modality for the most likely condition?

Options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

ExplanationEN:
This child presents with signs and symptoms suggestive of a Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common kidney malignancy in children and the second most common abdominal malignancy of childhood after neuroblastoma. Wilms tumors affect children < 5 years old, with a median age at diagnosis around 3.5 years. The tumors arise from embryonic kidney tissue and are often associated with mutations in genes regulating kidney development, such as WT1 and WT2 on chromosome 11.

Wilms tumors may occur sporadically or in association with congenital syndromes, such as WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary abnormalities, and range of developmental delays), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and Denys-Drash syndrome. In syndromic cases or those with known genetic predisposition, screening with regular abdominal ultrasounds is recommended.

The most common presenting symptom is a painless, palpable abdominal mass, noted by caregivers or during routine physical examination in about 80% of cases. Other signs and symptoms may include abdominal pain, hematuria, hypertension (due to increased renin production by the tumor), fever, anemia, and symptoms related to lung metastases, such as cough or respiratory distress. Wilms tumors can also rupture spontaneously or during handling, leading to intraperitoneal seeding and worsened prognosis.

The initial imaging modality of choice is kidney ultrasound, which is noninvasive and radiation-free, and it readily identifies intrarenal masses. If a mass is confirmed, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and chest is performed to evaluate the extent of the tumor and detect lung metastases, which are the most common site of distant spread.

Treatment involves a multimodal approach, beginning with surgical nephrectomy and followed by chemotherapy tailored to the tumor stage and histologic features. Radiation therapy may be added for higher-stage disease, anaplastic histology, or incomplete resection. The overall prognosis is excellent, with 80–90% survival rates due to effective risk-adapted therapy.

Staging is based on surgical findings and imaging, ranging from stage I (tumor confined to the kidney and completely resected) to stage V (bilateral kidney involvement). Children with bilateral disease may undergo nephron-sparing surgery when feasible to preserve kidney function.



CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (A) is useful for staging and surgical planning but is not the first-line diagnostic tool due to radiation exposure, especially in young children.

MRI of the abdomen (B) provides excellent detail but is more expensive and time consuming. It is generally used for further characterization or surgical planning, not as an initial test.

Paracentesis with peritoneal fluid analysis (C) is not appropriate for a solid kidney mass and does not aid in diagnosing a Wilms tumor.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with painful urination and urethral discharge. He is sexually active. ExplanationEN:

The diagnosis is made clinically and supported by using nucleic acid amplification tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis on first-catch urine. These results generally take several hours to a day to complete, so presumptive treatment for both Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is appropriate in sexually active postpubertal male patients with urethritis. Urethritis can also be caused by chemical irritation (e.g., bubble baths), medications (e.g., ceftriaxone, ticarcillin, penicillin), local injury, hypercalciuria, labial adhesions, or urethral strictures. A thorough history and exam are especially needed for prepubertal children with urethritis to evaluate for the possibility of sexual abuse.

Question: A 43-year-old man presents to the ED with urinary retention along with penile and abdominal pain. He reports that although he feels an urge to urinate, he has been unable to do so for the past 12 hours. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. On physical examination, there is suprapubic abdominal tenderness to palpation, and findings on the genitourinary exam are as shown in the photo above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Discharge with oral antibiotics and topical triamcinolone
Hold firm pressure followed by manual reduction

CorrectAnswer: Hold firm pressure followed by manual reduction
ExplanationEN:
Phimosis and paraphimosis are related urological disorders that occur in uncircumcised male patients. While phimosis refers to an inability to retract the foreskin from the glans penis, paraphimosis occurs when the retracted foreskin cannot be replaced past the penile corona. Paraphimosis represents a urologic emergency because the associated venous congestion can lead to urinary obstruction and penile necrosis. It most commonly develops due to chronic inflammation underneath the redundant foreskin, leading to contracture of the prepuce. When retracted, the tight ring formed by the prepuce constricts the penis proximal to the glans, which can lead to occlusion of both the urethra and the vasculature.

On physical examination, there will typically be significant penile pain and a swollen, edematous glans. Patients usually have swelling of the retracted foreskin, and the rest of the penis is not affected. In cases of ischemia, discoloration of the glans may occur, and it can become hard and firm rather than soft, which can lead to necrosis if left untreated. In infants, it is important to differentiate paraphimosis from tourniquet syndrome, which can present in a similar fashion.

Reduction should be performed as soon as possible to prevent ischemia. Manual reduction should be attempted initially, in which firm circumferential pressure is applied to the distal penis and glans for 5–10 minutes. Once the swelling has subsided and lubricant has been applied, manual reduction of the foreskin over the glans is often easily accomplished by pushing on the glans and simultaneously gently pulling the foreskin back into place. If swelling prevents manual reduction, the use of ice, compression bandages, or osmotic agents such as sugar or mannitol may reduce edema and aid in reduction. These agents should not be used in patients who already have signs of ischemia or necrosis. Urology should be consulted if manual reduction is unsuccessful, as the patient may require more advanced procedures, such as dorsal slit reduction, followed by full circumcision when the inflammation has subsided.



Manual reduction is often successful and should be attempted before urology consultation (A).

Oral antibiotics and topical steroids (B) are often used in the management of balanitis, which can predispose patients to phimosis and paraphimosis but would not treat this patient’s condition.

Dorsal slit reduction (D) is only indicated in cases of failed manual reduction and is best performed by a urologist, followed by delayed circumcision.

Question: A 37-year-old man with no significant medical history presents to the ED with sudden onset back pain radiating to his left groin. He reports dysuria and hematuria that began this morning. Vital signs are T 98.5ºF (36.9ºC), HR 103 bpm, RR 12/min, BP 125/85 mm Hg, SpO2 99% on room air. He appears uncomfortable and cannot sit still. A bedside ultrasound is obtained and is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The patient’s history is concerning for symptomatic urolithiasis and his renal ultrasound illustrates severe hydronephrosis. When kidney stones become obstructed in the ureter, they cause swelling of Gerota fascia of the kidney, causing flank pain. Pain can also be caused by renal pelvic stones that obstruct the proximal ureter or migrating ureteral stones. Patients with obstructive uropathy appear to be writhing in pain and have a hard time finding a position of rest. The location of the stone commonly corresponds with clinical symptoms. For example, proximally obstructing stones tend to cause flank pain, whereas midureteral obstructing stones tend to cause lower quadrant abdominal pain. Pain is intermittent and colicky with radiation to the groin. Approximately half of patients experience nausea and vomiting, and pain may also result in tachycardia, hypertension, and diaphoresis. Hematuria is present in approximately 85% of cases, meaning that up to 15% of patients with nephrolithiasis will not have hematuria.

Risk factors for developing kidney stones include obesity, diets rich in meats and sodium, gout, family history of kidney stones, inflammatory bowel disease, certain bowel surgeries, and hyperparathyroidism. Two conditions that may mimic symptomatic nephrolithiasis that should be considered are ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm and renal artery thrombosis and infarction. Ultrasound may help diagnose kidney stones, proximal and distal ureteral stones, and hydronephrosis, but it is relatively insensitive for diagnosing midureteral stones. For first-time presenters, noncontrast CT imaging is generally recommended for the detection of stones as it is the most sensitive and specific imaging technique.



Benign prostatic hyperplasia (A) can cause acute urinary retention and lower abdominal pain. However, older men are most commonly affected rather than young men. Furthermore, BPH rarely causes hydronephrosis.

Pyelonephritis (C)is an upper urinary tract infection involving the renal parenchyma and pelvicalyceal system. It is associated with fever, chills, nausea and vomiting, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (D) should be considered in any older patient (> 60 years) presenting with symptoms suggestive of obstructive uropathy with or without a history of kidney stones. While a ruptured aneurysm can cause hydronephrosis, it is less likely in young, otherwise healthy, patients.

Question: A 22-year-old woman with no medical history presents with constant left-sided flank pain, worsened by hematuria today. She reports no fever, dysuria, or abdominal pain. Exam shows left costovertebral angle tenderness. CT scan reveals multiple small kidney and liver cysts but no kidney stones. Urinalysis shows 6–10 leukocytes, many red cells, few bacteria, and few squamous cells. What is the likely pathophysiology behind her hematuria?
ExplanationEN:
Polycystic kidney disease is a genetic disorder characterized by multiple kidney cysts that develop from nonfunctioning renal tubules. However, cyst formation is not limited to the kidneys and can also be seen in the liver, pancreas, and spleen. Polycystic kidney disease can occur at any age, as the autosomal dominant form requires a mutation in the normal allele to cause cyst formation. Symptoms include flank pain, abdominal pain, hematuria, and urinary frequency. The disease can be complicated by hypertension (typically diastolic), portal hypertension, kidney insufficiency, kidney cyst infection, heart valve infection (owing to abnormal valves), ventral hernia, and cerebral aneurysms. The diagnosis of polycystic kidney disease can be made by the number of cysts present in a patient with a family history of the disease. Alternatively, the diagnosis may be made in an individual with appropriate symptoms and imaging findings (e.g., multiple kidney and liver cysts).

Patients presenting with worsening pain should prompt investigation for cyst expansion or rupture. Excessive angiogenesis around the cysts results in fragile vessels that can rupture from even minor trauma such as vigorous exercise. The resultant bleeding may travel to the renal collecting system (manifesting as hematuria), be confined to the kidney capsule, or rupture the kidney capsule causing peritoneal irritation. Infection is another important consideration, as the cysts themselves may become infected. The diagnosis of a pyocyst is suggested by a temperature of ≥ 38°C for > 3 days, costvertebral angle or liver tenderness, C-reactive protein > 5 mg/dL, and no evidence of cyst bleeding on CT scan. CT has notoriously low sensitivity for diagnosing a pyocyst, so high clinical suspicion is paramount. Cyst infection requires an extended duration of antibiotic therapy (5 weeks on average), which in isolation has a high treatment failure. Surgical drainage of the cyst is often also required.



Bladder wall inflammation (A) is due to cystitis, which can manifest as hematuria. However, this patient’s urine is not indicative of infection.

Glomerular inflammation (C) is seen in nephritic syndrome. Flank pain is not a typical symptom of nephritic syndrome. Patients typically present with hematuria, hypertension, and some degree of kidney insufficiency.

Radiolucent urolithiasis (D) can present with flank pain and hematuria. While some kidney stones (e.g., uric acid and struvite stones) are radiolucent on plain film imaging, the vast majority of stones can still be seen on CT scan, although with varying density. The exception is kidney stones secondary to protease inhibitors (indinavir) and pure matrix stones which are radiolucent on CT.

ExplanationEN:
Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) often present with dyspnea secondary to hypervolemia and associated pulmonary edema. In many cases, fluid overload results from inadequate volume removal during dialysis or as a consequence of missed sessions. However, previous myocardial ischemia can lead to depressed left ventricular systolic function and exacerbate the pulmonary congestion caused by hypervolemia. Symptoms are similar to pulmonary edema from other causes, commonly including dyspnea and orthopnea. However, recent weight gain above a patient’s dry weight is the most reliable clinical indicator, typically an increase > 5 lb (2.2 kg).

Strategies for treating pulmonary edema in patients with ESKD vary considerably from those with normal kidney function. Dialysis is the most reliable and rapid form of volume removal, and it is the definitive therapy that can occur in consultation with nephrology. Many patients with ESKD are anuric at baseline, and diuretics often have limited benefit, though they may be used at times for their vasodilatory effects.

Oral and IV nitrates are beneficial, as they rapidly decrease preload and afterload. Sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) can be administered quickly, and then an IV infusion is initiated and titrated to the desired effect. Other beneficial treatments include supplemental oxygen, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and bilevel positive airway pressure for patients with signs of respiratory distress. Response to the above therapies should be monitored closely, particularly in patients who present with severe respiratory distress, as they require endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.



Oral aspirin and cardiology consultation (A) are warranted in cases of acute coronary syndrome, which usually causes chest pain and possibly dyspnea. However, this patient’s clinical picture and chest X-ray suggest pulmonary edema, and in the setting of missed dialysis sessions, this is most likely secondary to volume overload.

Loop diuretics such as bumetanide (B) are often useful in the treatment of pulmonary edema but would have limited benefit in this patient, who is anuric.

Endotracheal intubation (D) and mechanical ventilation are sometimes indicated for patients with pulmonary edema who present in respiratory distress. However, this patient is improving on nasal cannula oxygen and has no increased work of breathing, so less invasive measures are initially indicated.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis. He also reports painful urination. Genital examination reveals multiple purulent-based, sharply defined, circular ulcers on the shaft of the penis and tender, enlarged, inguinal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

Options.text: A single dose of oral azithromycin
A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G
Weekly intramuscular injections of benzathine penicillin G for 3 weeks

CorrectAnswer: A single dose of oral azithromycin
ExplanationEN:
The patient is diagnosed with chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid is more common in resource-limited settings but may still occur sporadically in high-income countries, often associated with poor access to health care. Transmission occurs through direct contact with open lesions during sexual activity, and it facilitates the acquisition and transmission of HIV due to disruption of the epithelial barrier.

After an incubation period of about 3 to 10 days, chancroid begins with a painful papule or pustule at the site of inoculation that rapidly ulcerates. The resulting ulcers are multiple, deep, and painful, with ragged edges and a purulent, yellow-gray base. The ulcers often bleed easily and may be surrounded by erythema. When located near the urethral meatus, they can cause dysuria or urinary retention due to pain.

A hallmark feature of chancroid is painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, which may develop 1–2 weeks after ulcer formation. These enlarged lymph nodes can coalesce into buboes, which are fluctuant and tender and may spontaneously rupture, discharging purulent material. This distinguishes chancroid from syphilis, in which the primary chancre is painless, clean-based, and typically solitary, and from herpes simplex virus, which causes painful vesicles or shallow ulcers that are usually accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, as laboratory confirmation can be challenging. Haemophilus ducreyi is fastidious and requires special culture media, which are not routinely available. Diagnosis is typically made after ruling out syphilis and herpes using serologic testing and PCR or culture for herpes simplex virus, if available.

Empiric treatment should not be delayed. Recommended antibiotic regimens include azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose, ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly in a single dose, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days.

Patients should be counseled on abstaining from sexual activity until ulcers are fully healed, and their sexual partners should be evaluated and treated. Symptomatic improvement typically occurs within a few days, with full resolution in about 2 weeks. When buboes have formed, needle aspiration or incision and drainage may be necessary to relieve pain and prevent spontaneous rupture. Early recognition and appropriate treatment are crucial to avoid complications and interrupt transmission.



A 3-day course of oral nitrofurantoin (A) is used for urinary tract infections, not genital ulcer disease.

A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G (C) is the treatment for primary syphilis, which causes a painless chancre and nontender lymphadenopathy.

Weekly intramuscular injections of benzathine penicillin G for 3 weeks (D) are used for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, not painful genital ulcers like chancroid.

Question: An 8-month-old boy has a painless swelling on the right side of his scrotum since birth that gets worse with crying. Transillumination of this side of the scrotum reveals increased fluid and the child does not cry on palpation of the testicle, which lies in its normal position. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis, based on these findings?
ExplanationEN:
A hydrocele is a collection of fluid that accumulates in the tunica vaginalis. Communicating hydroceles result when the upper processus vaginalis fails to be obliterated, leaving an open tract between the peritoneum and the scrotum. The tract is closed in noncommunicating hydroceles. Most hydroceles are right-sided. Hydroceles may be present at birth, but they are usually painless and worsen with crying or exertion.

Hydroceles often resolve spontaneously by the age of 18 months. Examination reveals transillumination and enlargement of the scrotum. Patients with a hydrocele that has persisted for > 1 year or who are older than 18 months should undergo ultrasonography to ensure that the hydrocele is not a reactive hydrocele caused by a testicular tumor or inflammatory process.



Epididymitis (A) is inflammation of the epididymis, which is located along the posterior aspect of the testicle. The most common cause is infectious, and the etiology varies by age. Patients present with a painful, edematous scrotum and tenderness at the epididymis.

A non-incarcerated inguinal hernia (C) typically presents as a reducible mass that is not tender. It does not transilluminate, and it increases in size with a Valsalva maneuver.

Testicular torsion (D) presents with acute scrotal pain and swelling, an elevated testicle, and absence of the cremasteric reflex. Testicular torsion has been reported in all age groups, from the developing fetus to older patients, but is most common in adolescence.

A varicocele (E) is a collection of venous varicosities of the spermatic veins in the scrotum caused by incomplete drainage of the pampiniform plexus. Left-sided varicoceles account for 85–95% of cases, but varicoceles are rare in children < 10 years. Varicoceles do not transilluminate.

Question: A 40-year-old woman returns to the emergency department with continued fever and flank pain after discharge 5 days ago with a diagnosis of pyelonephritis. She indicates she has been taking her antibiotics (levofloxacin) as directed. Vital signs show HR 104 bpm, BP 114/70 mm Hg, T 101.7℉ (38.7ºC), and RR 16/min. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis shows a 6 cm intraparenchymal left kidney abscess. What is the most appropriate next action to take in this patient?

Options.text: Begin intravenous antibiotics and admit to the intensive care unit
Begin intravenous antibiotics and admit to the medicine service
Consult interventional radiology for percutaneous drainage of the abscess
Consult urology for surgical drainage and removal of the abscess

CorrectAnswer: Consult interventional radiology for percutaneous drainage of the abscess
ExplanationEN:
Most patients with pyelonephritis begin to see improvement in symptoms within days of starting appropriate antibiotic therapy. Patients who return with continued fever and pain are likely to have a complication from pyelonephritis, which can include a renal corticomedullary abscess. Antibiotic therapy alone for large kidney abscesses generally is not recommended, as mortality rates can be as high as 33%. However, antibiotic therapy can be attempted with small abscesses (< 5 cm) in hemodynamically stable patients. Patients with larger abscesses or with hemodynamic instability require a more invasive intervention such as percutaneous drainage. Surgical intervention with debridement has fallen out of favor due to the success of effective antibiotics and percutaneous drainage. Therefore, the appropriate next action in this patient with a 6 cm kidney abscess would be to consult interventional radiology for percutaneous drainage.



As mentioned, kidney abscesses are difficult to treat with antibiotics alone. Beginning intravenous antibiotics and admitting to the intensive care unit (A) would not be the correct action as patients requiring intensive care are likely hemodynamically unstable and would benefit from percutaneous or surgical intervention in conjunction with antibiotics.

Beginning intravenous antibiotics and admitting to the medicine service (B) might be a consideration for patients with hemodynamic stability and small abscesses (< 5 cm). However, this patient’s abscess is larger and requires further intervention.

Surgical debridement, drainage, and nephrectomy were widely used to treat corticomedullary abscesses. However, these invasive techniques have been replaced by successful percutaneous drainage and antibiotic therapy. Therefore, consulting urology for surgical drainage and abscess removal (D) would be reserved for severe, refractory cases.

Question: A 73-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with a failure to void for 3 days and lower abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals lower abdominal distension and moderate tenderness to palpation. His blood urea nitrogen to creatinine is 20:1.6. What management is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
The patient presents with symptoms and signs consistent with acute urinary obstruction requiring the placement of a Foley catheter to relieve the obstruction. Postrenal or obstructive kidney failure is a reversible cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) and should always be considered in patients with new azotemia. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a common cause of urinary obstruction. Treatment of obstructive uropathy focuses on relieving the obstruction. There is no contraindication to placing a Foley catheter in patients with BPH, and it should be done emergently to relieve the obstruction.



Emergency dialysis (A) should only be undertaken for pulmonary edema, severe uncontrollable hypertension, hyperkalemia, severe electrolyte or acid-base disturbance, specific overdoses, and severe symptomatic uremia. Intravenous fluids (C) to restore circulating volume are unnecessary in obstructive kidney failure. Suprapubic catheterization (D) should be attempted if the placement of a Foley catheter fails.

Question: An 18-year-old sexually active man presents with testicular pain for 3 days. The pain is constant and accompanied by fever. Examination reveals a mildly tender right testicle with a normal lie and no urethral discharge. Urinalysis shows 2+ leukocyte esterase, negative nitrites, and 10–25 WBC/hpf. What treatment is indicated?

Options.text: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular once and doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular once and levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 10 days
Ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice a day for 3 days
Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 10 days

CorrectAnswer: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular once and doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 10 days
ExplanationEN:
This patient has signs and symptoms consistent with epididymitis, which results from infection of the vas deferens, causing edema from passive congestion and inflammation. It usually presents with a gradual onset of scrotal pain, unlike torsion, which presents with a more abrupt onset of symptoms. Approximately 10–30% of patients present with urinary symptoms, and more than half of patients report fever. Early in the course, patients present with pain and tenderness localized to the epididymis, but symptoms quickly spread to the adjacent testicle. Classically, the Prehn sign (decrease in pain with elevation of the scrotum) is taught to indicate epididymitis, but this sign has a low sensitivity.

Urinalysis typically demonstrates signs of infection. Pyuria is common. If testicular torsion is suspected, scrotal ultrasound should be pursued. Antibiotic therapy should be tailored based on patient characteristics. In sexually active adults and adolescents, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections are the most common cause of epididymitis, particularly in younger patients (< 35 years). Therefore, treatment includes ceftriaxone and doxycycline. Older patients are more likely to have urinary tract abnormalities, predisposing them to epididymitis from typical urinary tract pathogens (e.g., Escherichia coli). However, if they are sexually active, coverage of C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae is also indicated.



Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (A) is insufficient treatment for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis.

Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular once and levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 10 days (C) is an appropriate treatment regimen for a patient with acute epididymitis with a history of insertive anal intercourse or a patient with risk factors for both sexually transmitted infections and urinary pathogens, like having obstructive uropathy or a recent urologic procedure.

Ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice a day for 3 days (D) is a treatment option for patients with an uncomplicated urinary tract infection, though it should not be used as first-line treatment when other options are available, as it has a boxed warning (tendinitis or tendon rupture, CNS side effects, peripheral neuropathy).

Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for 10 days (E) is an appropriate treatment for epididymitis in a patient who is not sexually active when only typical urinary pathogens are suspected.

Question: An 8-year-old girl presents to the ED with dark urine and swollen extremities. She is otherwise healthy outside of a recent sore throat. Which of the following laboratory tests will assist you in confirming the diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN). Acute glomerulonephritis following acute group A streptococcal infection is characterized by the sudden appearance of hematuria, red blood cell casts in the urine, edema, and hypertension with or without oliguria. The classic presentation of edema, hematuria, and hypertension make up the constellation of findings in nephritic syndrome. Laboratory testing will reveal elevated creatinine and BUN. An antistreptolysin (ASO) titer should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. APSGN may follow either streptococcal skin infection or streptococcal pharyngitis. This condition typically affects children aged two to twelve years. A latent period always occurs between the streptococcal infection and the onset of signs and symptoms of acute glomerulonephritis. In general, the latent period is 1–2 weeks after a throat infection and three to six weeks after a skin infection. Dark urine is often the first clinical manifestation of APSGN. Periorbital edema will then typically follow sudden onset of puffiness of the face or eyelids. Finally, many patients will develop diffuse edema. Management is primarily supportive. Indications for dialysis include life-threatening hyperkalemia and clinical manifestations of uremia.



Antinuclear antibody (A) is elevated most commonly in systemic lupus erythematosus, but can also be elevated in multiple other rheumatologic conditions. It may present with signs and symptoms consistent with nephritis; however, it will not usually be preceded by a sore throat and not often seen in the pediatric population.

Heterophile antibodies (C) are classically elevated with infectious mononucleosis. Patients will usually present with sore throat, malaise, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. They do not have renal manifestations.

Parvovirus B19 IgM (D) is elevated in acute parvovirus B19 infections. These are most concerning in pregnant patients and patients with sickle cell anemia as it may cause birth defects and aplastic crisis, in these respective patient populations.

Question: A 20-year-old woman presents to the ED with eye swelling. She has a history of drug-induced lupus, depression, and chronic sinusitis. She reports no painful eye movements, fever, trauma, vision changes, or nasal congestion. Her vital signs are a T of 97.9°F (36.6°C), BP of 179/93 mm Hg, HR of 90 bpm, RR of 12/min, and SpO2 of 100% on room air. She has bilateral periorbital edema and hand edema. Her urine studies include a glucose of 30 mg/dL and protein of 310 mg/dL, and a pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following most likely explains her symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Nephrotic syndrome is a glomerular disease characterized by heavy proteinuria, leading to hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia, although the latter two findings may be inconsistently present. It may be preceded by a viral upper respiratory illness, particularly in minimal change disease. Nephrotic syndrome includes several primary forms such as minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, and conditions with mixed features such as membranoproliferative and proliferative glomerulonephritides. Secondary causes include systemic lupus erythematosus, IgA vasculitis, sickle cell disease, drug or toxin exposure, and systemic infections.

The most common presenting symptom is edema, which may be localized (periorbital, dependent, scrotal), multifocal, or diffuse (anasarca). Pleural effusions may occur and lead to dyspnea, orthopnea, or cough. Patients are at increased risk of infection due to urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement and thromboembolic events due to a hypercoagulable state caused by loss of anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III.

Treatment focuses on recognition and diagnosis, assessment of intravascular volume status, treatment of acute complications, and treatment of associated infections or thromboembolism when present. Corticosteroids are a mainstay of therapy in selected etiologies, particularly minimal change disease, while steroid-resistant cases may require additional immunosuppressive or targeted therapies. Patients with severe edema, pulmonary involvement, infection, or thromboembolism should be admitted.



Cavernous sinus thrombosis (A) presents with periorbital edema and erythema, fever, and extraocular movement deficits, often progressing from unilateral to bilateral involvement due to retrograde spread from facial or sinus infections. It is frequently associated with sepsis.

Insulin resistance (B) causes type 2 diabetes mellitus, which causes glycosuria but does not include many of the findings seen in nephrotic syndromes, such as edema and hypoalbuminemia.

Primary hypothyroidism (D) is due to intrinsic thyroid gland dysfunction. Causes include autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, iodine deficiency, and infiltrative processes (e.g., amyloidosis, lymphoma), and it can also arise postsurgery or postradiation. Facial swelling and periorbital edema may be present. Laboratory evaluation will reveal abnormal thyroid studies and potentially hyponatremia and hypoglycemia.

Question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the ED with malaise and lower extremity edema that has progressed over the last 2 days. Her urine has been very dark, but there has been no dysuria or fever. She was treated 1 week ago with amoxicillin for a fever and sore throat. On examination, she is afebrile with a BP of 125/75 mm Hg, HR of 105 bpm, RR of 20/min, and SpO2 of 99% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation, and there is 1+ pitting edema of the legs bilaterally. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts and proteinuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a history and presentation consistent with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Fluid and salt restriction help control edema and prevent hypertension or volume overload.

PSGN occurs 7 to 14 days after a group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection, most often pharyngitis. It presents with nonspecific symptoms such as malaise and fatigue, along with more characteristic findings of gross hematuria, periorbital and generalized edema, and hypertension. The urine may appear tea- or cola-colored, a hallmark of glomerular bleeding. Edema often begins around the eyes and progresses to involve the extremities and abdomen due to fluid retention. Oliguria may also be present, reflecting impaired glomerular filtration.

Laboratory studies typically reveal hematuria with red blood cell casts, mild to moderate proteinuria, elevated antistreptolysin O titers indicating recent streptococcal infection, and low serum complement levels, particularly C3, due to complement consumption. Serum creatinine and BUN may be elevated depending on the severity of kidney involvement. Additional evidence of streptococcal infection may include elevated anti-DNase B or streptozyme titers.

Treatment is primarily supportive, as APSGN is self-limited in children. In mild cases, treatment involves fluid and sodium restriction to minimize fluid overload and reduce blood pressure. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, are effective in treating significant edema or pulmonary congestion. Antihypertensive therapy is indicated in patients with moderate to severe hypertension and may include calcium channel blockers or angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, though ACE inhibitors should be used with caution in patients with impaired kidney function.

Antibiotics, typically penicillin, may be administered to eradicate any residual streptococcal infection, though they do not affect the course of glomerulonephritis. Immunosuppressive therapy is not indicated unless there is an alternative or overlapping diagnosis. Most children recover fully, but follow-up is important to monitor for persistent hypertension, proteinuria, or kidney dysfunction. Rarely, some patients may progress to chronic kidney disease or end-stage kidney disease, particularly those with severe or atypical presentations.



Intravenous methylprednisolone (B) is used in nephrotic syndrome or immune-mediated nephritis like lupus, not in postinfectious glomerulonephritis.

Nephrology consultation for kidney biopsy (C) is reserved for atypical cases (e.g., prolonged symptoms, low complement levels that do not normalize), not standard first-line management.

Oral nifedipine (D) may be used if hypertension becomes severe, but this patient’s BP is mildly elevated and does not yet require pharmacologic treatment.

Question: Which of the following is the most common presentation of testicular cancer?

Options.text: Lower abdominal, perianal, and scrotal discomfort
Painless enlargement superior to the testicle that feels like a “bag of worms”
Swelling and tenderness of the entire testicle

ExplanationEN:
Although testicular cancer is the most common solid malignancy in young male patients ages 15–35 years, it accounts for just 1% of all cancers in men. These tumors are more common in those with undescended testicles and infertile patients. The most common presentation is that of a palpable, nontender solid nodule or mass that cannot be separated from the testicle. A mass that is palpable is more likely to be malignant than one found only via imaging. Acute onset of scrotal pain is unlikely in testicular cancers and should prompt an evaluation for other causes, such as testicular torsion or epididymitis. Patients may also present with symptoms related to metastasis including regional lymphadenopathy (found in 15% of patients at the time of diagnosis) or bone pain. All patients with a scrotal mass should undergo ultrasound imaging for further evaluation and prompt referral to a urologist.



Approximately 30–40% of patients present with lower abdominal, perianal, or scrotal discomfort (A). However, the most common presentation is the finding of a focal nontender testicular mass.

Varicoceles present as painless enlargement superior to the testicle (B). Palpation of a varicocele is often described as feeling similar to a “bag of worms.”

Swelling and tenderness of the entire testicle (D) is concerning for orchitis. The most frequent bacterial causes of orchitis in adults include N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, E. coli, and Klebsiella.

Question: A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with lower extremity swelling and dark urine for 1 day. According to his parent, he recently had streptococcal pharyngitis, but he completed his antibiotic treatment and seemed to be doing fine until this morning. He awoke early this morning with pain and tightness in his legs, and he noticed his urine was a different color. He reports no other symptoms, including shortness of breath, fever, or sore throat. Vital signs show HR 82 bpm, BP 156/90 mm Hg, and T 37.0°C. On exam, he has 1+ pitting edema in both ankles. What will most likely be found in this patient’s urinalysis?
ExplanationEN:
Acute kidney injury is defined as the deterioration of kidney function resulting in the accumulation of toxic waste and loss of internal homeostasis. Causes of kidney insults can be classified as prerenal, intrinsic, or postobstructive. Prerenal failure is associated with decreased renal blood flow. Restoration of circulating blood volume is usually sufficient to restore kidney function. Postobstructive kidney failure leads to an increase in tubular pressure followed by vasoconstriction to the kidney. Relief of the urinary obstruction promptly decreases tubular pressure and resultant vasoconstriction. Intrinsic kidney failure can occur with a wide array of disease processes and nephrotoxins that lead to tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, and interstitial nephritis. Signs and symptoms of kidney failure can include hypertension, decreased urine output, changes in urine color, lower extremity edema, and shortness of breath. The creatinine level is the mainstay of assessing kidney function, and an elevated level suggests insufficiency. The cause of a patient’s kidney failure can be discovered with a good history and assessment of risk factors, but the addition of a urinalysis can further narrow the differential diagnosis. The patient in this question is presenting with signs and symptoms of intrinsic kidney disease after being treated for streptococcal pharyngitis. This information suggests a diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can occur 1–3 weeks following infection. Urinalysis in this patient will reveal red cells and casts. In this particular patient, with a diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, there is no specific treatment. Management is supportive and focused on treating volume overload and hypertension.



Pigmented granular casts (A) would be found in patients presenting with acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxins. Common nephrotoxins include aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, radiocontrast dye, and chemotherapeutic agents. There is no mention of a nephrotoxic agent in this patient’s history, so urinalysis is unlikely to show pigmented granular casts. Renal tubular epithelial cells (C) are generally found in patients presenting with acute tubular necrosis from ischemic insults. This occurs after cardiac arrest and severe sepsis or with other causes of systemic hypotension. Renal tubular epithelial cells can also be found in kidney transplant patients with acute rejection. White cells and casts (D) are found in patients with acute interstitial nephritis. Acute interstitial nephritis is commonly found in patients with allergic reactions to certain drugs, autoimmune disorders, and in patients with kidney infections. Although this patient could be presenting with a new autoimmune disorder, his history should clue the physician into poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents with gradually worsening right testicular pain over the last 4 days. He is sexually active. On examination, his cremasteric reflex is normal. The testicle has a normal lie. There is tenderness focally over the epididymis. Which of the following tests should be performed next?
ExplanationEN:
Epididymitis is the most common inflammatory condition within the scrotum. The epididymis is a tubular structure on the posterior aspect of the testicle where sperm mature. The epididymis becomes infected when retrograde transit of an infection travels from the vas deferens. In patients who are sexually active, the organisms of sexually transmitted infections are likely etiologies. For these patients, testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia is indicated. For those not sexually active, urinary pathogens are more common, and a urine culture is indicated.

Patients develop gradually increasing pain in the testicle and classically present for evaluation later than patients with torsion, who experience severe onset of pain immediately. Patients with epididymitis may report lower abdominal or flank pain due to inflammation of the vas deferens. Up to 75% of patients have a fever. Pain begins in the epididymis and then spreads to the entire testicle. Over time, the ipsilateral hemiscrotum becomes edematous, erythematous, and tender. Improvement of pain with elevation of the testicle (Prehn sign) often describes a characteristic of epididymitis (although it is neither sensitive nor specific). If the clinical history and examination are unclear, an ultrasound of the scrotum will show hypervascularity of the affected epididymis (and testicle if it is involved). Antibiotic therapy is aimed at the most likely organism, which in this case would be empiric treatment for gonorrhea and chlamydia with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. Complications of epididymitis include orchitis and testicular abscess.



Epididymal aspiration (A) has been described as a mechanism to identify the causative organism of epididymitis. However, this has no role in the ED or office setting and may be performed later for those not improving with treatment and without positive urine or sexually transmitted infection testing.

A rectal exam (C) is usually obtained to evaluate for bleeding or to assess for tenderness related to prostatitis. Patients with prostatitis typically present with fever, myalgias, urinary symptoms, and perineal pain. In this case, the patient’s clinical symptoms are consistent with epididymitis, and he has no rectal bleeding. Thus, a rectal exam is not necessary.

A urine culture (D) is indicated in patients with acute epididymitis when there is clinical suspicion of a UTI or when the cause of epididymitis is unclear. It is particularly relevant in patients whose symptoms include dysuria, frequency, and urgency, suggesting a possible UTI. In younger patients, epididymitis is often due to sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia or gonorrhea, but in older patients, it can be associated with UTIs.

A urine wet mount (E), also known as a urinary sediment microscopy, is a diagnostic procedure in which fresh, uncentrifuged urine is examined microscopically to identify and evaluate various cellular elements and structures, including red blood cells, white blood cells, epithelial cells, bacteria, crystals, and casts. This test can be helpful in diagnosing urinary tract infections, glomerulonephritis, and other kidney pathologies. A urine wet mount is not indicated in the evaluation of epididymitis.
