Question: Which of the following is the most effective treatment for a 3-week-old infant with excessive crying in the evening without any other findings on history or exam?
ExplanationEN:
Infants cry the most during the first 3 months of life. Normal crying increases from birth and peaks between 2 weeks and 2 months of age but can last until as old as 5 months. Infants who excessively cry without an apparent reason are said to have colic. The degree of crying needed to define colic varies based on the reference textbook and journal article. Infants with colic generally resist soothing, have a pained look, and cry more in the evening. This is extremely distressful to a new family. When added to the exhaustion of caring for an infant in the early weeks of life, postpartum depression, and hormonal normalization, many new parents seek help to stop the crying.

The most important step to guide the treatment of a crying infant is the history and physical exam. Crying can be due to pain or distress from illnesses such as abstinence syndrome, ingestion, hair tourniquet, child abuse, glaucoma, corneal abrasion, thrush, otitis media, heart failure, supraventricular tachycardia, gastroesophageal reflux, incarcerated hernia, gonadal torsion, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, meningitis, or a urinary tract infection. When the history and exam of an excessively crying infant do not suggest a medical cause, empathy and reassurance should be given to the family. Interventions should focus on improving the infant-family relationship. Address feeding difficulties, provide education on colic, and reassure the family that the crying is not their fault and that their infant is not sick. Permit them to put the infant down in a safe space, tell them that feelings of anger, guilt, and helplessness are normal, and that they can always return for more support.



While massage has weak evidence of helping infants with colic, chiropractic manipulation (A) is generally considered unsafe in infants and should not be recommended.

There are no safe and effective medications to treat colic, and they are not recommended. Methylscopolamine (B) is neither effective nor safe and commonly causes drowsiness and confusion. The evidence to support probiotics (C) is weak and inconsistent, and some studies show an increase in the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis with their use in infants. Simethicone (E) has not been shown to be effective but has no known side effects.

Question: An 8-year-old girl presents with a lump on her neck. Her parent reports that the girl has had a cough, nasal congestion, and a sore throat for the last 3 days. She continues to eat and drink well. She is vaccinated, has no animal exposures, and has no ill contacts. Her temperature is 39.1°C, heart rate is 135 bpm, respiratory rate is 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On exam, she has a few 1–1.5 cm tender but mobile anterior cervical lymph nodes on the right without any skin changes or warmth and none on the left side. Which of the following is the best next step to care for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
The terms lymphadenitis and lymphadenopathy are often used interchangeably, but lymphadenitis is preferred when patients report pain, as this is more suggestive of inflammation. Uncommon questions that might lead to a diagnosis include asking about drinking unpasteurized milk (brucellosis), eating undercooked meat (toxoplasmosis), and exposure to cats (Bartonella), rabbits (tularemia), and prairie dogs (Yersinia). Be sure to examine the liver (Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV), eyes (adenovirus, Kawasaki disease), and mouth (periodontal disease).

Most children with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy or lymphadenitis have an illness caused by an upper respiratory virus. These tend to be mild, but testing for streptococcal pharyngitis or Epstein-Barr virus is appropriate when there is exudative tonsillitis and tender bilateral lymphadenitis.

In contrast, most children with unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy have an infection caused by group A Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus. Those without a fever who are well-appearing can be monitored with serial examinations for improvement. Those with unilateral lymphadenopathy who have a fever and tender lymph nodes (i.e., lymphadenitis) should be treated with a course of oral antibiotics. The antibiotic choice should depend on the local susceptibility of Staphylococcus aureus. Culture of any drainage to the skin or culture of the throat is not helpful in these cases, as patients can be colonized in both locations with Streptococcus or Staphylococcus. When an inflamed lymph node is erythematous or fluctuant, it may be suppurative, and needle aspiration may reveal a causative organism.

Patients with unilateral cervical lymphadenitis treated with oral antibiotics should have follow-up within 48–72 hours to evaluate for improvement. Patients occasionally worsen and need hospitalization for intravenous antimicrobials and incision and drainage.



Patients with severe unilateral cervical lymphadenitis that is fluctuant or erythematous can benefit from imaging of the affected lymph node. Imaging usually starts with an ultrasound, sometimes followed by a CT scan of the affected lymph node (A) if a fluid collection was discovered on ultrasound. While a bedside ultrasound is reasonable for this patient, those with mild to moderate illness and relatively small lymphadenopathy with only tenderness and fever are likely to be treated successfully with oral antibiotics and do not require advanced imaging.

Patients with unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy with mild symptoms and without fever can be monitored with serial examinations every few weeks (B), but those with fever and tenderness over the lymph node should receive oral antibiotics.

Testing for streptococcal pharyngitis (C) does not benefit patients with unilateral cervical lymphadenitis unless their symptoms are mild and it will impact the decision for oral antibiotics. Those with fever and tenderness over the lymph node, like this patient, should instead be treated with oral antibiotics that cover Streptococcus.

Question: A 29-year-old woman, who is 7 weeks pregnant by dates, presents to the emergency department with severe pelvic pain. Laboratory workup is notable for a serum hCG level of 7,000 IU/L. Ultrasound shows the image above. What is the appropriate next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
The patient is presenting with a pseudosac with surrounding free fluid, which is concerning for an ectopic pregnancy. An ectopic pregnancy refers to a pregnancy that implants outside of the uterus and is a leading cause of death in first-trimester pregnancies. The majority of ectopic pregnancies implant in the fallopian tubes but can also implant anywhere in the abdomen. Risk factors for ectopic pregnancies include a history of pelvic inflammatory disease, history of tubal surgery, conception with intrauterine device in place, smoking, and advanced maternal age. Patients most commonly present with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Diagnosis of an ectopic pregnancy is made by direct visualization with ultrasonography. Ectopic pregnancy can often be ruled out with the diagnosis of an intrauterine pregnancy (IUP). However, the possibility of a heterotopic pregnancy must be considered. In order to confirm an IUP, a gestational sac and a yolk sac must both be clearly visualized within the endometrial cavity. An empty gestational sac alone does not confirm an IUP. Furthermore, 20% of ectopic pregnancies may present with a pseudosac, which is a small fluid collection that is centrally located in the endometrial cavity. A small amount of free fluid in the pelvis of a woman can be a normal sonographic finding. However, significant free fluid, echogenic fluid, or complex fluid is never physiologic and would raise suspicion for an ectopic pregnancy. Given the presence of a pseudosac with surrounding free fluid in the pelvis in this patient, obstetrics and gynecology should be consulted.



Administering antibiotics (A) would be appropriate for pelvic inflammatory disease or sexually transmitted infections.

Administering misoprostol (B), which is often used to medically induce an abortion, would not be efficacious if the pregnancy is located outside of the uterus. For medical management of an ectopic pregnancy, methotrexate is preferred.

Discharging the patient home with expectant management (D) would be inappropriate, as an ectopic pregnancy is an obstetrical emergency. Sometimes, a missed abortion can present with an empty gestational sac on ultrasound and can be treated with expectant management. However, a pseudosac with surrounding free fluid in the setting of severe abdominal pain is more concerning for an ectopic pregnancy.

Question: A 45-year-old woman presents with low back pain. She states that she has had back pain for years, but it is worse today. She reports the pain is in the lower part of her back and radiates to her left foot. Physical examination reveals no midline tenderness to palpation of the lower back but a positive straight leg raise. She exhibits no weakness, and has a normal sensory exam. What diagnostic testing is indicated in the ED?

Options.text: CT scan of the lumbar spine

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms of sciatica, which may be due to a herniated disc and does not require emergent imaging. Sciatica describes lumbar radiculopathy commonly seen in patients who typically report sharp, burning, or shooting pain beginning in the back and radiating down the leg past the knee. There may be associated numbness or weakness or both on the affected side. The pain is often exacerbated with bending, straining, or sitting and relieved with lying supine. Physical examination often reveals tenderness in the sciatic notch and a positive straight leg raise. To perform a straight leg raise, start with the patient lying supine. The symptomatic leg is then passively raised with the knee fully extended. Eliciting back pain that radiates down the leg into the knee at 30–70 degrees of leg elevation suggests an L5–S1 radiculopathy. The straight leg raise has good sensitivity (91%) but poor specificity (26%). Sciatica symptoms are typically caused by lumbar disc herniation (~ 95% of cases). Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, ankle plantar flexion, and knee extension are common findings in lumbar disc herniation. Immediate imaging is not indicated in patients with symptoms consistent with disc herniation. Most of these patients will improve with conservative care alone.



CT scan (A) is an excellent modality for evaluating the presence of fractures in the vertebral column, but in the absence of trauma, the yield of this test is low.

MRI (B) is the definitive modality in the evaluation of possible cauda equina syndrome, spinal infection, or malignancy, but this patient’s presentation is not consistent with these diagnoses, and she does not have any sensory or motor concerns.

Plain radiographs (E) and ultrasound (D) generally do not play a role in the evaluation of low back pain because they contribute little to the care of these patients.

Question: What laboratory abnormality is an adverse effect of chlorthalidone?
ExplanationEN:
Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-like diuretic that can cause hypercalcemia. It decreases urinary calcium excretion and may consequently increase the serum calcium concentration. Although clinically significant hypercalcemia is uncommon, the effect may be more pronounced in patients with underlying primary hyperparathyroidism or excessive calcium intake.

Chlorthalidone inhibits the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. The resulting changes in sodium transport and mild intravascular volume contraction increase kidney calcium reabsorption. This results in hypocalciuria and can lead to a mild elevation in serum calcium concentration.

Other important adverse effects include hypokalemia (most common), hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Electrolytes and kidney function should be monitored after initiation and following dose adjustments.



Chlorthalidone typically causes hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia (B). Increased sodium delivery to the collecting duct promotes sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium secretion. Secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system from mild volume contraction further increases potassium loss.

Chlorthalidone can also cause hyponatremia rather than hypernatremia (C). Sodium loss from inhibition of the distal sodium-chloride cotransporter, combined with impaired urinary dilution and water retention, may reduce the serum sodium concentration. This adverse effect may develop shortly after the medication is started.

Chlorthalidone is associated with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis rather than metabolic acidosis (D). Volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, increasing distal hydrogen and potassium secretion. The resulting loss of hydrogen ions and chloride promotes an alkalemic state. Therefore, metabolic acidosis would not be the expected acid-base disturbance.

Question: Which of the following conditions is the most common cause of abdominal surgery in older patients?
ExplanationEN:
The most common indication for surgery in older adults is cholecystitis. Older patients in the ED with acute abdominal pain are at higher risk for surgical conditions and increased mortality. Their presentations can be misleadingly subtle, with an absence of peritoneal signs despite significant pathology. Additionally, nonabdominal causes such as myocardial infarction, pneumonia, or herpes zoster should be considered. Given the complexity of their presentations, clinicians must maintain a broad differential diagnosis and avoid relying solely on physical exam findings.

Diagnosis in older patients is often complicated by factors such as altered pain perception, immune system changes, medication effects, and an impaired febrile response. Some may only present with nonspecific symptoms like delirium, malaise, or dizziness, making recognition of an underlying abdominal condition challenging. Even with significant pathology, laboratory values may be within normal limits. Imaging, particularly CT, should be obtained with a low threshold to ensure timely diagnosis.

Vascular emergencies, including ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and acute mesenteric ischemia, are highly morbid and time-sensitive causes of abdominal pain in older adults. Sudden symptom onset should raise suspicion, even in the absence of the classic AAA triad of abdominal pain, shock, and a pulsatile mass. Mesenteric ischemia, often due to superior mesenteric artery occlusion, is more common than appendicitis or AAA complications in those over 75, with risk factors including cardiac dysrhythmias, atherosclerosis, and prothrombotic conditions.

Biliary tract disease is the most frequent cause of abdominal pain in older adults, with cholecystitis being the leading surgical indication. Up to one-third of older patients with acute cholecystitis may lack fever, leukocytosis, or significant pain, increasing the risk of complications such as perforation and emphysematous cholecystitis. Other common causes of abdominal pathology in older patients include appendicitis, which often presents atypically and is associated with a high rate of perforation, as well as peptic ulcer disease, diverticulitis, bowel obstruction, and malignancy. Hernias should also be considered, particularly in individuals with cognitive impairment who may not report symptoms.



Acute appendicitis (A) is more common in younger patients. In older individuals, presentation is often delayed and can be complicated by perforation. However, appendicitis is not the most common surgical emergency in this demographic.

Acute mesenteric ischemia(C) is a major concern in older patients with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis. Pain is out of proportion to the exam, and patients often have bloody diarrhea or metabolic acidosis. However, it is not the most common cause of abdominal surgery.

Perforated peptic ulcer (D) causes sudden, severe pain and peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity), and it is less common than cholecystitis as an indication for surgery.

Question: A 66-year-old man presents to the ED with shortness of breath and hypoxemia. Arterial blood gas on room air shows a pH of 7.38, PCO2 of 58 mm Hg, PO2 of 46 mm Hg, and bicarbonate of 32 mEq/L. The alveolar-arterial gradient is calculated to be normal for his age. After administration of 100% oxygen, his PO2 rises to 230 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s hypoxemia?
ExplanationEN:
This patient demonstrates hypoxemia with hypercapnia and a normal alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient, which is the hallmark of alveolar hypoventilation. Hypoventilation leads to decreased alveolar oxygen tension and increased carbon dioxide due to insufficient ventilation. Because the lung parenchyma and gas exchange surfaces remain intact, the A-a gradient stays within normal limits. Moreover, PO2 increases markedly with 100% oxygen, confirming that alveolar diffusion is not impaired.

This presentation is common in patients with COPD who develop acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure, especially during exacerbations or poor medication adherence. It also underscores the importance of evaluating both PCO2 and A-a gradient when determining the cause of hypoxemia.

Clinical signs of hypoxia include CNS effects like confusion, agitation, and seizures. Hyperventilation and tachypnea are common early signs, while severe hypoxemia may cause respiratory depression. Cyanosis is unreliable as a diagnostic sign. Patients may show signs of chronic compensation, such as polycythemia or cachexia in long-standing disease. Diagnosis primarily relies on pulse oximetry, which is generally accurate but can be misleading in the presence of abnormal hemoglobins like methemoglobin or carboxyhemoglobin.

The mainstay of treatment is ensuring a patent airway and giving supplemental oxygen to maintain PO2 > 60 mm Hg. Most causes of hypoxemia respond to oxygen therapy, except for right-to-left shunts. Understanding the underlying cause is essential, but initial treatment should always prioritize oxygenation and airway support.



Diffusion limitation (A) occurs when oxygen transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane is impaired, such as in interstitial lung disease or advanced emphysema. It results in a widened A-a gradient, especially during exertion, as the time available for gas exchange is shortened. In this case, the patient's A-a gradient is reported as within normal limits, and his PO2 improves significantly with 100% oxygen, which argues against diffusion impairment.

Right-to-left shunt (C) refers to blood bypassing the ventilated alveoli entirely, as seen in conditions like intracardiac shunts or acute respiratory distress syndrome. The hallmark feature is refractory hypoxemia, and PO2 remains low despite administration of 100% oxygen. In contrast, this patient's PO2 rose to 230 mm Hg with 100% oxygen, ruling out a significant shunt.

Ventilation-perfusion (V-Q) mismatch (D) is common in COPD and other lung diseases and does cause hypoxemia. However, it usually results in an elevated A-a gradient, which is not present in this case. Additionally, while V-Q mismatch does often improve with oxygen, the normal gradient combined with elevated PCO2 points more specifically to hypoventilation rather than regional mismatch.

One Step Further
Question:
How is the A-a gradient adjusted for age?

Reveal Answer:
The simple formula (commonly used) is [(age / 4) + 4]. For every decade a person has lived, their A-a gradient is expected to increase by approximately 1 mm Hg. The more detailed formula is [2.5 + (0.21 × age) ± 11].

Question: A 3-day-old boy who was born at 40 weeks presents to the ED with skin discoloration. On physical exam, you note jaundice. The child is afebrile with normal vital signs for age. A total bilirubin returns with a level of 23 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Admit and initiate broad spectrum antibiotics
Insert nasogastric tube for enteral nutrition
Observe and re-check the level in 24 hours

ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting physical exam findings consistent with neonatal jaundice. Jaundice is defined as discoloration of the skin and sclera caused by the accumulation of unconjugated or conjugated bilirubin. Jaundice presenting on days 2 or 3 of life is often physiologic jaundice. This is caused by the breakdown of fetal reticulocytes and decreased conjugation ability of the liver due to low uridine diphosphoglucuronyltransferase (UDPGT) activity. Physiologic jaundice may result in very high levels of bilirubin. The decision to initiate phototherapy is based on the bilirubin level for age, gestational age, and the presence of neurotoxicity risk factors. At 72 hours of age in this infant, phototherapy should be considered when the bilirubin level reaches 20 mg/dL in order to avoid the risk for kernicterus, which is defined as neurotoxic hyperbilirubinemia and can lead to motor and cognitive delays if not treated.

Phototherapy converts bilirubin into water-soluble isomers that can be excreted without conjugation. It is the mainstay of treatment for moderate hyperbilirubinemia and is highly effective in preventing progression to severe hyperbilirubinemia and its complications. The decision to initiate phototherapy is based on the infant’s age in hours, total serum bilirubin level, and risk factors (e.g., hemolysis, prematurity, sepsis). Complications of phototherapy include dehydration, temperature instability, and worsening hyperbilirubinemia.



Sepsis should be considered in any infant with jaundice, however is unlikely in a child that is afebrile, feeding well, and has normal vital signs. This makes broad spectrum antibiotics (A) unnecessary at this time.

Inserting a nasogastric tube for enteral nutrition (C) would be reasonable if the child would not feed via breast or bottle. However, it is too early in the course to determine that this child is unable or unwilling to feed, leading to jaundice.

Observing and re-checking the level in 24 hours (D) could lead to severe complications and a delay in appropriate therapy.

Question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a limp. The patient is up to date on all immunizations and has no known allergies. He has a history significant for obesity, but it is otherwise unremarkable. His parent states that the symptoms began approximately 6 days ago. He is active and currently in football season. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination reveals an unremarkable evaluation of the knee, but there is pain with both passive and active range of motion of the hip. An X-ray of the hip is obtained and is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is characterized by the displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck along the physeal plate. It is the most common cause of hip disorders in adolescent patients. Patients who develop SCFE typically have obesity and are 12–14 years of age, with a slight male predominance. In one-fifth to almost one-half of cases, both hips are affected, and nearly half of those with unilateral disease will develop contralateral SCFE.

The most common clinical features include pain and altered gait. Pain is most commonly located in the hip, although a small percentage of patients will present with knee pain. In these patients, the knee physical examination is unremarkable and should make the clinician think to evaluate the hip as a potential cause. Classically, an adolescent boy with obesity presents with hip, thigh, groin, or knee pain that is made worse with range of motion and physical activity.

The diagnosis of SCFE can be made most of the time with X-ray films. Films of bilateral hips should be obtained in the anteroposterior and lateral projections. On an anteroposterior film without SCFE, a line drawn along the superior femoral neck, the Klein line, will intersect the lateral portion of the femoral head. However, in patients with SCFE, the Klein line will pass outside the epiphysis or just at the superior edge. In early slips, plain films may only show a blurring of the junction between the metaphysis and the growth plate. If plain films are unremarkable but suspicion remains high, an MRI can demonstrate widening of the physis and surrounding edema suggestive of SCFE. Prompt referral to an orthopedic surgeon is required because the treatment for SCFE requires operative stabilization.



Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (A) is characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the hip. It typically affects children between the ages of 3 and 10 years, with a higher prevalence in male individuals. The etiology remains unknown, though there is a slight familial tendency. Classically, patients present with an insidious onset of a limp and mild pain. On examination, patients may have a limited range of motion, particularly with internal rotation and abduction. Initial radiographs are often benign but may show a denser and smaller epiphysis compared to the contralateral side, along with joint space widening. MRI or bone scans can aid in diagnosis if suspicion remains high and plain films are unremarkable. Patients should be made non-weight-bearing and referred to a pediatric orthopedist for treatment.

Osgood-Schlatter disease (B), also known as apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity, is an overuse syndrome seen in active adolescents, especially those involved in sports. Patients typically present with anterior knee pain that worsens over time and with increased activity. Pain is exacerbated by trauma, jumping, and running and relieved with rest. Physical examination reveals localized tenderness over the tibial tuberosity with soft tissue swelling.

Transient synovitis (D) is the most common cause of nontraumatic hip pain in children. Patients usually present with symptoms lasting 1 to 3 days, often following a viral upper respiratory infection. Children are nontoxic in appearance and usually afebrile. The condition most commonly affects children between the ages of 3 and 8 years, with a higher incidence in male patients. Pain is elicited with both passive and active range of motion without clear precipitation. Patients may hold their hip in a position of comfort, typically abduction and external rotation. Septic arthritis must be excluded before diagnosing transient synovitis. Inability to bear weight, fever, a C-reactive protein level > 2 mg/dL, or an erythrocyte sedimentation rate > 20 mm/hr should raise concern for septic arthritis and warrant further workup with hip arthrocentesis and synovial fluid analysis.

Question: A 77-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with weakness. She has a history of hypothyroidism and is on levothyroxine. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate 38 bpm, temperature 98.9°F, and respirations 18 bpm. She is oriented only to herself and is notably confused. An ECG reveals sinus bradycardia. Intravenous access is established. What is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN:
Sinus bradycardia on ECG is defined as a regular rhythm with ventricular rates < 60 beats per minute. The P wave morphology and PR intervals are normal and consistent. While asymptomatic sinus bradycardia does not necessarily require any treatment, if the patient is unstable with either hypotension, altered mental status, or signs of shock, then intervention is necessary. Initial interventions include atropine and transcutaneous pacing. Atropine is a nonselective muscarinic acetylcholinergic antagonist. Its cardiac effects include increasing the firing of the sinoatrial node and the conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node. The initial dose is 1 mg IV or IO, which can be repeated every 3–5 minutes up to a maximum of 3 mg. Transcutaneous pacing should be considered immediately in any unstable patient, especially those with high-grade AV blocks.



Beta-agonists, such as epinephrine (B) and dopamine (D), are considered second-line agents that can be considered if atropine is not successful.

Transvenous pacing (C) is the definitive treatment for persistent and symptomatic bradycardia, but it is time consuming and often difficult to start in the ED, so medications and transcutaneous pacing should be attempted first.

Question: A 52-year-old woman with a history of obesity and type 2 diabetes presents to the ED with medial knee pain for the past several weeks. She describes the pain as a dull ache that worsens with activity, particularly going up and down stairs. She reports no trauma, mechanical locking, or instability. On examination, there is tenderness over the anteromedial proximal tibia approximately 2–3 cm below the joint line, with pain elicited by resisted knee flexion. There is no joint effusion, erythema, or warmth. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

Options.text: Recommend quadriceps strengthening exercises and NSAID therapy

CorrectAnswer: Recommend quadriceps strengthening exercises and NSAID therapy
ExplanationEN:
This patient's exam is most consistent with pes anserine pain syndrome (PAPS), also known as pes anserine bursitis, a common cause of medial knee pain, particularly in middle-aged and older adults with risk factors such as obesity, osteoarthritis, and diabetes. The pes anserine bursa lies beneath the combined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles at the medial proximal tibia. Repetitive stress, valgus knee deformity, and poor biomechanics can contribute to its inflammation. The condition typically presents with anteromedial knee pain that worsens with activities such as climbing stairs or transitioning from sitting to standing. Unlike intra-articular pathology, PAPS does not cause significant joint effusion, instability, or mechanical symptoms like locking or catching.

The diagnosis is clinical, based on localized tenderness at the pes anserine bursa without significant joint involvement. Imaging is not routinely necessary unless an alternative pathology is suspected. First-line treatment includes conservative measures such as NSAIDs for pain relief, ice application, and most importantly, quadriceps and hamstring strengthening exercises. Strengthening the quadriceps reduces stress on the knee joint and improves biomechanics, which is essential for long-term symptom relief. Physical therapy emphasizing stretching and strengthening is highly effective in preventing recurrence. Most cases improve with these conservative measures, making this the best initial management step in the emergency setting.



Septic arthritis typically presents with acute-onset severe joint pain, warmth, swelling, and systemic symptoms such as fever and would be an indication to perform arthrocentesis (C) and initiate antibiotic therapy (A). Gout and pseudogout also usually cause acute-onset, severe joint pain with significant swelling, erythema, and warmth. This patient lacks these inflammatory findings. Her symptoms are chronic and localized without joint effusion, making infection and crystal disease highly unlikely.

Radiographs (B) are unnecessary unless there is trauma or significant concern for structural joint damage. This patient’s symptoms are localized to the pes anserine region and do not indicate acute bony pathology.

Immediate orthopedic consultation (D) is not necessary for PAPS, as it is a nonemergent, soft tissue condition that typically responds well to conservative management. Orthopedic referral is generally reserved for cases involving significant structural damage, such as ligamentous injury, complex meniscal tears, or fractures, none of which are present in this patient.

Question: A 67-year-old man is brought in from his care facility for a change in his behavior. The patient seems more confused and is not eating or drinking. He was dropped off by a caregiver who does not know his medical history. He is not answering questions on arrival. His T is 103°F (39.4°C), BP is 100/70 mm Hg, HR is 122 bpm, RR is 25/min, and SpO2 is 89% on room air. Physical exam reveals a confused-appearing man with increased work of breathing. Significant, diffuse muscle atrophy is noted. Fasciculations and hyperreflexia are also found on neurological exam, as well as a positive Babinski sign. Which of the following is used to treat this patient’s underlying condition?
ExplanationEN:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease of upper and lower motor neurons. Upper motor neuron dysfunction may cause symptoms that include spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign. Lower motor neuron signs include muscle atrophy, weakness, and fasciculations that are often asymmetric. It is unique when both upper and lower motor neuron symptoms are present, which helps differentiate this condition from other neuromuscular disorders. There is no definitive treatment for ALS. Supportive care and intubation in respiratory failure are the mainstays of therapy. Respiratory failure and pulmonary infections are common causes of death. The diagnosis can be made with electromyography along with the history and exam. Management may include disease-modifying agents such as riluzole.



L-dopa and carbidopa (A) is appropriate management of Parkinson disease. Parkinson disease is a disorder of the substantia nigra and dopamine-producing cells in the brain. Patients present with bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, hypomimia, micrographia, and difficulty performing acts of daily living. Methylprednisolone (B) is the appropriate management of an acute multiple sclerosis exacerbation. Multiple sclerosis presents with neurological deficits separated by time and space, including migratory paresthesias, weakness, vision changes, and personality or mood changes. Pyridostigmine (C) is a long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that can be used in the treatment of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis presents with weakness that worsens with exertion or repeat movement. Symptoms improve with rest.

Question: Which of the following disease entities can be treated with the Epley maneuver?
ExplanationEN:
The Epley maneuver is used to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) by repositioning displaced otoliths within the semicircular canals.

BPPV is a common cause of vertigo due to displaced calcium debris within the semicircular canals, most often the posterior canal. It leads to brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movements, such as turning in bed or looking up. While symptoms can be distressing, they usually respond well to particle-repositioning maneuvers like the Epley maneuver, which can be performed in an office setting or at home.

BPPV is more prevalent in older adults and women, with risk factors including osteoporosis, prior head trauma, vestibular disorders, and vascular conditions. Symptoms include recurrent vertigo lasting < 1 minute, often accompanied by nausea but not hearing loss. Diagnosis is confirmed by observing characteristic nystagmus during a positional test, such as the Dix-Hallpike maneuver for posterior canal BPPV or the supine head-roll test for horizontal canal involvement.

Treatment involves repositioning maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver for posterior canal BPPV or the Lempert (barbecue roll) and Gufoni maneuvers for horizontal canal BPPV. These maneuvers help move otolith debris out of the semicircular canals, resolving symptoms in most patients. Some individuals may experience residual imbalance, but this usually improves over time. Medications and vestibular rehabilitation play limited roles and are reserved for select cases.

While BPPV often resolves spontaneously, recurrence is common, with about one-third of patients experiencing another episode within 5 years. Risk factors for recurrence include older age, female sex, vascular risk factors, osteoporosis, and vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D supplementation may help prevent recurrence in those with low levels. Self-treatment with home-based maneuvers can be effective for recurrent episodes. Persistent or atypical cases warrant further evaluation with neuroimaging to rule out central pathology. In rare refractory cases, surgical interventions such as canal occlusion may be considered.



Ménière disease (B) is caused by excess endolymphatic fluid in the inner ear, leading to episodes of vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. Unlike BPPV, it is not positional and does not respond to repositioning maneuvers. Treatment focuses on salt restriction, diuretics, and vestibular suppressants.

Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (C) results from reduced blood flow to the brain stem and cerebellum, leading to dizziness, imbalance, and other neurological symptoms. Neck movements often trigger it, but it is not due to inner ear dysfunction. Treatment includes risk factor modification and vascular evaluation.

Vestibular neuritis (D) is an inflammatory disorder that affects the vestibular nerve. It causes prolonged vertigo and imbalance without hearing loss. It is not positional and does not benefit from the Epley maneuver. Treatment involves symptomatic treatment with vestibular suppressants and physical therapy.

Question: A 17-year-old student presents to the ED with unilateral hearing loss. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 110/72 mm Hg, heart rate of 60 bpm, respiratory rate of 14/min, oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and a temperature of 36.7°C (98.1°F). Weber and Rinne testing supports conductive hearing loss of the left ear. Otoscopic examination reveals a waxy-appearing polyp situated behind a normal-appearing tympanic membrane. There is no purulent discharge or tympanic perforation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cholesteatoma is an abnormal growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid process, most commonly affecting adolescents and adults < 65 years. Despite its name, it is unrelated to cholesterol or gallbladder pathology. This lesion results from chronic inflammation, negative middle ear pressure, or eustachian tube dysfunction, which leads to the retraction of the tympanic membrane and accumulation of keratin debris. The condition can be congenital, arising from embryonic epithelial remnants located medial to an intact tympanic membrane, or acquired, which is far more common and typically results from chronic otitis media or repeated infections, often starting at the pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane.

Patients present with progressive conductive hearing loss, which is the most common symptom due to ossicular chain erosion. Other associated symptoms may include a sensation of fullness in the ear, tinnitus, vertigo, imbalance, and in more advanced cases, facial nerve weakness or paralysis. Otoscopic examination may reveal a pearly white, waxy mass or debris behind a retracted tympanic membrane or a foul-smelling, white-pasty otorrhea if the tympanic membrane is perforated. Chronic inflammation may also produce polyps or granulation tissue in the middle ear, making the condition easily mistaken for chronic suppurative otitis media.

Cholesteatomas are locally invasive and can erode surrounding structures, including the ossicles, facial nerve canal, labyrinth, and even the cranial vault, potentially leading to life-threatening complications such as meningitis, brain abscess, or lateral sinus thrombosis. Therefore, early diagnosis is essential. Imaging with high-resolution CT of the temporal bone may be used to assess the extent of disease. Definitive treatment is surgical, involving microscopic excision via tympanomastoidectomy to fully remove the lesion, reconstruct damaged structures, and prevent recurrence. Long-term follow-up is often necessary due to the risk of regrowth.



Acoustic neuromas (A) present with sensorineural, not conductive, hearing loss. Furthermore, these masses occur in the inner ear and temporal bone on the vestibular nerve and would not likely be viewable during an otoscopic examination.

Otitis media (C) presents with otalgia, hearing loss, fever, and tympanic membrane abnormalities like erythema, bulging, or cloudiness. Although retrotympanic masses can result from chronic suppurative middle ear infections, current infection is unlikely in this patient.

Otosclerosis (D) involves abnormal bone growth of the footplate of the stapes and can cause conductive hearing loss, but it would not present with a polyp on otoscopic examination.

Squamous cell carcinoma (E) is an epithelial cell malignancy that typically occurs on the external, not the middle, ear due to prolonged sun exposure. It has an ulcerated, erythematous appearance with or without bleeding.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the ED with shortness of breath, palpitations, and muscle spasms in her hands. She appears visibly anxious and is breathing rapidly. She reports no chest pain, fever, or drug use. Vital signs are a T of 98.6°F (37°C), HR of 110 bpm, BP of 118/72 mm Hg, RR of 32/min, and SpO2 of 100% on room air. On examination, she is alert and oriented, with carpopedal spasm noted in both hands. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are normal. Despite reassurance and coaching, she remains anxious and vital signs are unchanged. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Provide rebreathing with a paper bag

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with tachypnea, anxiety, and carpopedal spasm, which are classic signs of respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation syndrome. Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, is an appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for acute anxiety-related hyperventilation. It acts quickly to reduce anxiety and restore normal respiratory rate and carbon dioxide levels.

Hyperventilation syndrome is a clinical condition in which a patient breathes more than necessary for their metabolic needs, leading to decreased PCO2 and respiratory alkalosis. This overbreathing is often associated with symptoms like dizziness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, and paresthesia in the absence of an identifiable organic disease. While commonly linked to anxiety or panic disorders, hyperventilation can also occur with other triggers and overlaps with conditions such as sighing dyspnea and dysfunctional breathing. From a physiologic standpoint, hyperventilation differs from tachypnea and hyperpnea. It is not just faster or deeper breathing, but breathing that lowers carbon dioxide more than needed. The resulting hypocapnia can cause cerebral vasoconstriction and electrolyte shifts, leading to neurologic symptoms like tingling and tetany. Physical findings may include carpopedal spasm.

Diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion. In patients with a low risk, classic symptoms, and normal exam and pulse oximetry, no further testing may be required. For those with atypical features, capnography, arterial blood gas, or point-of-care testing may be helpful. It is crucial to exclude serious conditions like pulmonary embolism, metabolic acidosis, pneumothorax, and cardiac ischemia before diagnosing hyperventilation syndrome.

Acute treatment of hyperventilation focuses on reassurance, explaining symptoms, removing stressors, and initiating breathing retraining. Patients should be guided to practice abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing by placing one hand on the chest and one on the abdomen, then adjusting their breaths so the abdomen rises more than the chest. They should slowly inhale over 4 seconds, pause briefly, and exhale over 8 seconds. Repeating this for 5–10 cycles reduces anxiety and eases symptoms. If symptoms persist despite breathing exercises, a short-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam 0.5–1 mg orally or IV may be given.



Fluoxetine (A) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used for long-term treatment of anxiety and depression, but it has no role in acute treatment. It takes weeks to reach therapeutic effect and is inappropriate for this urgent scenario.

IV calcium (B) is used for hypocalcemia with ECG changes, hyperkalemia, or calcium channel blocker overdose. While this patient has symptoms that mimic hypocalcemia (spasm), they are due to alkalosis-induced calcium binding, not true hypocalcemia. IV calcium is not needed at this point.

Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (D) is indicated for conditions like COPD exacerbation, pulmonary edema, or hypercapnic respiratory failure. This patient is not hypoxic or in respiratory distress from a mechanical issue, making this intervention unnecessary and potentially harmful.

Rebreathing with a paper bag (E) was historically used to treat hyperventilation by increasing inhaled carbon dioxide but is no longer recommended due to the risk of hypoxia. It should be avoided in favor of safer interventions like anxiolytics.

Question:
What is sighing syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Sighing syndrome is a breathing pattern disorder characterized by frequent, exaggerated deep sighs or the sensation of being unable to take a satisfying breath, often linked to anxiety or stress rather than lung disease.

Question: A 30-month-old boy presents to the ED after an accidental ingestion of amlodipine. The patient’s parent reports that he was playing with her pillbox, and she noticed a pill missing. She did not witness the ingestion event, and there were no episodes of choking. The parent is missing one amlodipine tablet, 5 mg in dosage. What vital sign abnormality is most characteristic of this overdose syndrome?
ExplanationEN:
Hypotension is the most characteristic and clinically significant abnormality in amlodipine overdose, especially in children.

Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are used to treat hypertension and cardiac dysrhythmias. The potential toxicity of these agents is substantial. The number of intentional and unintentional overdoses is high, and these drugs account for a large percentage of deaths from overdose. In children under 6 years of age, symptoms can develop from as little as 2.5 mg of amlodipine.

CCBs are divided into two major categories based on their predominant physiological effects. The dihydropyridines preferentially block calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, whereas the non-dihydropyridines selectively block calcium channels in the myocardium. Dihydropyridines include commonly used medications such as nifedipine, amlodipine, and nicardipine. They are potent vasodilators and have little negative effect on cardiac contractility. In contrast, non-dihydropyridines, such as verapamil and diltiazem, have depressive effects on cardiac contractility and are weak vasodilators.

Overdose of a dihydropyridine, such as amlodipine, results in arterial vasodilation, causing hypotension and reflex tachycardia. Otherwise, the patients are generally asymptomatic and, despite hypotension, may maintain a clear mental status. Maintaining circulation is the primary focus of treatment in a calcium channel blocker overdose. In this particular patient, intravenous fluids are the initial therapy of choice for hypotension. However, severely symptomatic patients may require additional treatment with calcium salts, vasopressors, high-dose insulin therapy, or lipid emulsion therapy.



Bradycardia (A) can be seen with non-dihydropyridine CCBs (like verapamil or diltiazem), but amlodipine more commonly causes reflex tachycardia due to vasodilation. Bradycardia may occur in severe poisoning, but it is not the hallmark finding.

Hypothermia (C) is not a characteristic feature of amlodipine toxicity. It may be seen in severe systemic illness or prolonged environmental exposure, but it is not associated with this ingestion.

Respiratory depression (D) is more common with opioids, sedative-hypnotics, or central nervous system depressants. Amlodipine does not typically cause primary respiratory depression.

Question:

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 35-year-old man with a history of hepatic steatosis presents to the ED with a tremor and gait instability. He says the tremor is worse when he attempts to do activities and when he walks. His vital signs are within normal limits. Upon first inspection, you notice golden brown circles around his corneas. On neurologic exam, he has a tremor when performing finger-to-nose testing that is particularly severe as he attempts to touch your finger. He does not have a resting tremor but seems fidgety and unable to sit still. He cannot tandem gait and is unsteady when attempting to walk on his own. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The patient in this question is presenting with an intention tremor but also has a history of transaminitis and a physical exam finding golden brown circles around the corneas that suggest Wilson disease. This disease is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder that leads to impairment of hepatocellular copper transport. Impaired biliary copper excretion leads to the accumulation of copper in several organ systems, including the liver, cornea, and brain. Although patients with Wilson disease may have a resting tremor, the majority have cerebellar dysfunction that leads to an intentional tremor, most often in the distal upper extremities. Other signs and symptoms that suggest Wilson disease include chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis, granular deposits of copper in the cornea called Kayser-Fleischer rings, psychiatric symptoms such as depression and irritability, dysarthria, gait ataxia, and cognitive impairment. Additionally, Wilson disease more often occurs in young patients. Treatment includes detoxifying tissues of copper and preventing reaccumulation. The primary chelator used is D-penicillamine, but trientine is another good agent that has fewer side effects. Prevention of reaccumulation can be achieved with oral zinc salts.

Tremor is defined as an involuntary rhythmic movement of a body part. It is the most common movement disorder and can occur occasionally in normal individuals. The type of tremor and distribution can help guide the clinician to an underlying diagnosis. Tremor is divided into resting versus action. Resting tremors are noticed when a patient is sitting still and supporting the affected body part. They are often suppressed by voluntary muscle contraction or action, so are sometimes considered less debilitating. Action tremors occur during voluntary movements or when assuming a specific posture. When associated with voluntary movements, they are often called intention tremors because the symptom worsens as the body part approaches its target. These tremors are often found with finger-to-nose testing, reaching, writing, eating with utensils, and pouring water into a cup.

Resting tremors are most often associated with Parkinson disease. Action tremors are associated with cerebellar disease, multiple sclerosis, or other demyelinating disorders. Tremors can affect a focal body part, such as one limb or the head, can be segmental in the upper or lower body, and can be one-sided or generalized, which can further narrow to a specific diagnosis. For instance, a head tremor is common in essential tremor but uncommon in Parkinson disease. When evaluating patients with tremor, it is important to obtain a detailed history, including questions regarding precipitating factors, relieving factors, and toxic ingestion. The physician should also note the age of the patient since certain disorders occur at either a young or old age.

A detailed neurologic examination is essential to identify features of the tremor and to detect other neurologic findings. Tremor is often due to an underlying neurologic illness, but it is important to remember to look for other examination findings that might suggest an alternative diagnosis such as hyperthyroidism or Wilson disease.



Essential tremor (A) is the most common neurologic disorder that causes an action tremor. It most often affects the hands and arms, but can also involve the head, trunk, and voice. This is a strong consideration in any patient with tremor, but our patient has other exam findings that suggest an alternative diagnosis. Additionally, essential tremor usually does not appear until over the age of 60.

Multiple sclerosis (B) is another neurologic disorder that can be associated with an intention tremor, particularly when other cerebellar findings are present. However, multiple sclerosis is often associated with other neurologic symptoms, such as sensory loss or visual loss, which were not evident in our patient. Additionally, our patient has Kayser-Fleischer rings that are associated with Wilson disease.

Parkinson disease (C) is associated with a resting tremor, which was not described in our patient.

Question: A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department with chest pain and shortness of breath while mowing his lawn. He felt diffuse chest pressure that radiated to his jaw and resolved completely when he sat down. The patient has had similar episodes of chest pain while mowing his lawn in the past. He has a medical history of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and smoking. The patient’s initial vital signs, ECG, and cardiac troponin are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Angina occurs when the oxygen demands of the heart cannot be met by the blood supply. This is caused by narrowing of the blood vessels secondary to atherosclerosis. Risk factors for heart disease and angina pectoris include diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, and inflammatory conditions (such as HIV or psoriasis). Stable angina presents with chest pain that is provoked by exertion. When an individual exerts themselves, their coronary arteries are not able to sufficiently dilate and supply blood (secondary to the narrowed and atherosclerotic vessels), thus provoking symptoms. Rest improves symptoms in these patients as the oxygen demand of the myocardium at rest decreases. As the disease progresses, patients may experience unstable angina (ischemic symptoms that occur with exertion or rest that are more frequent or more severe), which can subsequently progress to a myocardial infarction (occlusion of a coronary artery). The workup of stable angina should include lab tests including cardiac troponins and an ECG. The ECG is typically unremarkable and troponins are normal.



Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (A) presents with chest pain that can be exertional or occur at rest and is associated with an ECG that does not demonstrate ST elevation but laboratory values that demonstrate elevated cardiac troponins (which differentiates it from stable and unstable angina).

ST elevation myocardial infarction (B) presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, ST elevation on ECG, and elevated troponins.

Unstable angina (D) is a progression from stable angina and is worsening chest pain associated with exertion (a change from baseline), chest pain associated with less exertion than previously, or chest pain at rest. This reveals atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries that has reached a critical level such that perfusion may be insufficient even at rest, and these patients are at high risk for progressing to a full myocardial infarction.

Question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the ED with numbness. He notes a tingling sensation in his feet for the past few weeks. He takes metformin and his last hemoglobin A1c was 7.3%. He reports no alcohol or drug use. Physical exam reveals decreased sensation to light touch in his toes. Which of the following lab results is most likely to be beneficial in determining the etiology of his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Paresthesias are abnormal neurologic sensations occurring in the absence of stimulation. They may be described as numbness, tingling, or prickling. While most paresthesias are due to an insult of a peripheral nerve, the inciting cause may be found anywhere along the neural tract. Paresthesia can be caused by an almost innumerous litany of medical diagnoses. A brief list for consideration includes nerve compression (e.g., sciatica and carpal tunnel syndrome), demyelination (e.g., multiple sclerosis and Guillain-Barré), metabolic (e.g., hypocalcemia, hypothyroidism, and diabetes), malnutrition (e.g., vitamins B1, B6, B12, and E), and medications (e.g., amiodarone, statins, and levodopa). Patients with diabetes and paresthesias should be closely investigated, as diabetes-related neuropathy, although common, is not the only possible cause.

Metformin has been shown to cause vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with type 2 diabetes. The risk increases with the age of the patient, the dose, and the duration of treatment. Patients with type 1 diabetes are also at risk for vitamin B12 deficiency but by a different mechanism. The autoimmune nature of the disease puts patients with type 1 diabetes at increased risk of developing pernicious anemia, hypothyroidism, and celiac disease. B12 deficiency is typically treated initially with intramuscular cobalamin followed by oral cobalamin for life. The treatment for other causes of paresthesias varies and should be targeted to the underlying pathology.



Calcium (A)deficiency is associated with paresthesias, but this patient does not have any risk factors for this finding. Hypocalcemia can be caused by hypoparathyroidism, kidney injury, and hypoalbuminemia.

Magnesium (B)deficiency can cause muscle weakness and paresthesias, but this patient does not have any risk factors for hypomagnesemia.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (C)can help diagnose hypothyroidism, which can cause paresthesia, though the mechanism is not known. However, this is less likely to be the cause for this patient as he does not have any other symptoms of hypothyroidism and does have risk factors for B12 deficiency.

Question: A 78-year-old man is brought to the ED from his nursing home for confusion. His vital signs are within normal limits for his age. He is thin but unshaven and malodorous. He is awake, alert, and oriented only to person and place. His blood glucose is 89 mg/dL. What is the next most appropriate step in diagnosis after completing a head-to-toe examination?

Options.text: Contacting the patient’s family for further information
CT of the head without contrast

CorrectAnswer: Contacting the patient’s family for further information
ExplanationEN:
In a patient with altered sensorium, the next best step after obtaining as much information from the patient and prehospital personnel and performing a thorough physical examination is to attempt to contact the patient’s family to obtain further information that may elucidate the cause of the mental status change. Mental status is the clinical state of one’s emotional and intellectual function and can include appearance, behavior, attitude, thought content, perception, mood, affect, insight, judgment, and level of alertness.

Delirium is a transient alteration in attention and cognition that generally develops acutely (i.e., over days rather than weeks or months) and often has an underlying systemic, toxic, or primary neurologic cause. Symptoms are often intermittent, fluctuate throughout the day, and typically become worse at night. Clinical features that may be present include visual hallucinations, tremors, tachycardia, asterixis, diaphoresis, hypertension, and emotional outbursts. The primary method for diagnosis is obtaining history from family, caregivers, other health care providers, and spouses. Information obtained from these ancillary sources can help differentiate causes of delirium and may guide diagnostic and therapeutic intervention.



Further historical information should be gathered in any case of altered mental status or delirium prior to placing a consultation for admission (A).

Ordering a CT of the head without contrast (C) may be indicated, but a history and physical examination should be completed prior to neuroimaging in the absence of clinical findings that might suggest an acute stroke.

Similarly, serum chemistry and urinalysis (D) may be appropriate, but a thorough history should be obtained prior to diagnostic workup.

Question: A parent brings their full-term 3-day-old boy to the ED after noticing an episode of dark, tarry stool at home. The mother birthed the newborn vaginally with no complications. She follows a vegan diet and is breastfeeding. On exam, the patient is afebrile. His abdomen is soft with no palpable masses. Rectal exam reveals dark, tarry stool that is positive for guaiac. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
ExplanationEN:
Swallowed maternal blood is the most common cause of melena in otherwise healthy neonates. During birth or breastfeeding, infants may ingest maternal blood that later appears in their stools as dark, tarry, guaiac-positive material. Importantly, these infants remain well appearing, with normal vital signs and benign abdominal exam findings, distinguishing the condition from pathologic gastrointestinal bleeding. Recognition of this benign etiology prevents unnecessary invasive workup in otherwise stable neonates.

The Apt test differentiates fetal from maternal blood. The blood is mixed with alkali to detect the conversion of oxyhemoglobin to hematin. Fetal hemoglobin is more resistant to denaturation than adult hemoglobin. If the supernatant stays pink after the addition of alkali, the blood is fetal in origin (a positive test).

Differentiating swallowed maternal blood from true neonatal gastrointestinal pathology is crucial. Unlike necrotizing enterocolitis, Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, or malrotation with volvulus, infants with swallowed maternal blood are afebrile, nontoxic, and have soft, nondistended abdomens. Early reassurance and education for parents is key, while ongoing monitoring ensures that more serious conditions are not missed.



Anal fissures (A) are the most common cause of hematochezia in children and usually present with bright red blood streaking the surface of hard stools or on toilet paper after wiping. They are often associated with constipation and painful bowel movements. In this neonate, the stool is described as dark and tarry, not bright red, and the infant is exclusively breastfed at 3 days old, making constipation or fissures improbable. The guaiac-positive tarry stool also indicates digested blood, inconsistent with a superficial anal fissure.

Meckel diverticulum (B), a remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct, is most commonly diagnosed around 2 years of age. It occurs in approximately 2% of the population and often contains ectopic gastric mucosa, which can cause painless rectal bleeding. Diagnosis is confirmed with a Meckel scan.

Milk protein allergy (C) should be suspected after the introduction of a new formula. Infants who are breastfed are not immune to this condition if the mother consumes cow milk. Since this patient’s mother follows a vegan diet and is breastfeeding, it is unlikely that a milk protein allergy is responsible for the patient’s guaiac-positive stool.

Necrotizing enterocolitis (D) is a complication of premature infants and presents with abdominal distension, bloody stools, and feeding intolerance. Radiographs may reveal ileus and pneumatosis intestinalis.

Question: A man is found outdoors in freezing temperatures. EMS finds him conscious but not shivering, with impaired movement and decreased alertness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Apply active warming to lower extremities
Encourage movement and provide oral fluids
Handle gently, apply heat to the upper trunk, and insulate
Insulate, have the patient sit, and monitor for 30 minutes
Perform a 60-second pulse and breathing check

CorrectAnswer: Handle gently, apply heat to the upper trunk, and insulate
ExplanationEN:
This patient is demonstrating signs of moderate hypothermia, as indicated by impaired consciousness, lack of shivering, and lack of appropriate motor dysfunction in the setting of freezing outdoor temperatures. In moderate to severe hypothermia, aggressive but careful treatment is essential to prevent complications such as “afterdrop,” core temperature paradoxical drop, and dysrhythmias from rough handling.

The first step in treating moderate hypothermia in the field includes gentle handling, active external rewarming focused on the torso, and insulation to prevent further heat loss. Warming should prioritize the core (chest, neck, and head) over the extremities to avoid peripheral vasodilation, which can exacerbate core cooling (after-drop) and destabilize the patient.

These patients have a high risk of ventricular fibrillation with minimal stimulation, so they must be moved and treated with extreme caution. Heat packs applied to the upper trunk and insulation can help safely raise core temperature without redistributing cold peripheral blood to the core, which could worsen the condition.



Actively warming (A) the extremities before the core can lead to after-drop, a situation in which cold peripheral blood returns to the central circulation, causing a further drop in core temperature and an increased risk of cardiac instability.

Encouraging movement (B) increases metabolic demands and can be dangerous in moderate hypothermia. It also risks precipitating dysrhythmias. Additionally, patients with impaired consciousness or cold-induced ileus may not be able to safely swallow or absorb fluids, making oral hydration inappropriate at this stage.

Asking the patient to sit (D) and simply monitoring them is insufficient and potentially harmful. A patient with signs of moderate hypothermia needs active core rewarming, not passive observation. This approach may delay necessary interventions and lead to further deterioration.

Performing a 60-second pulse and breathing check (E) is used during cardiac arrest in hypothermic patients, not in conscious individuals. While hypothermia may significantly slow heart rate and respiratory rate, this patient is conscious, and thus, prolonged pulse checks are unnecessary and not indicated at this point.

Question: A newborn boy presents to the ED shortly after a home delivery. The mother had routine prenatal care and reports that he was due in 2 days. The patient appears term and vigorous but is in respiratory distress and gasping for air. His heart rate is 80 bpm. What percentage of oxygen should you initially use when providing positive-pressure ventilation to this patient?
ExplanationEN:
The principles of neonatal resuscitation differ from the resuscitation of infants. The distinction is the complications newborns experience as they transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life, which differ from those of infants born even for a few hours. Fortunately, most term infants only need to be dried, warmed, and stimulated. A small percentage will need positive pressure ventilation, and a rare minority will need significant resuscitation. Unfortunately, infants that present newly born to the emergency department are more likely to have high-risk deliveries, such as trauma-induced labor or unexpected pregnancies. If the infant is term, vigorous, breathing, and crying, they can be reunited with their mother but should be reevaluated frequently. Many clinicians will at least dry, warm, and stimulate the infant before reuniting them.

Unlike in infant resuscitation, if there is gasping, respiratory distress, or a heart rate < 100 bpm, the first step is positive-pressure ventilation. Standard practice has changed with studies showing improved survival for newborns resuscitated with room air compared to 100% oxygen. A pulse oximeter should be applied when administering oxygen or positive-pressure ventilation. In normal cases, newborns are expected to have a slow rise in their oxygen saturation, only reaching 85–95% at 10 minutes of life. Oxygen may be administered, blended with room air, and only to reach age-appropriate goals (in minutes). Of the above options, 21% oxygen or room air is the best initial choice for positive pressure ventilation.



The rule for neonates < 35 weeks gestation is slightly different, with a recommended initial oxygen saturation between 21 and 30% oxygen (C).

50% oxygen (D) is not recommended but may be needed in certain cases to reach age-appropriate goals.

100% oxygen (A) is recommended if the neonate remains bradycardic and chest compressions are required.

Reveal Answer:

Question: An 8-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a report of gradual-onset vague lower back pain and lower extremity paresthesias. Her symptoms are worse during gymnastics practice. The pain does not wake her at night. On exam, she does have some pain with extension of the back, but she has a normal gait, normal range of motion, and no point tenderness. Her back appears straight when bending forward, and there is no posterior pelvic tilt. She has normal sensation in her legs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN:
Careful attention is needed in young children with back pain as it is not a common concern and often signifies pathology. Back strains and lumbar herniation are less frequent in children compared to adults. However, an injury to the vertebral pars interarticularis is common. Spondylolysis is a fracture or separation from the pars interarticularis, commonly from overuse. When bilateral pars defects occur, the lumbar spine slips anteriorly in a process called spondylolisthesis. Occasionally, this can result in spinal cord compression or injury. It typically presents as a gradual onset of vague lower back pain and is frequently seen in patients with repetitive hyperextension of the back, such as figure skaters and gymnasts. They usually have normal range of motion and a reassuring exam, although pain on back extension is common. Spondylolisthesis is typically diagnosed with an X-ray of the lumbar spine.

Treatment varies based on the degree of lumbar slip, but most patients are treated conservatively with stretching exercises, ice, warm baths, and over-the-counter analgesics. They are usually followed as an outpatient by orthopedic surgeons. Only those with signs of cauda equina syndrome (e.g., urinary incontinence, saddle anesthesia) need emergent intervention. Back pain in children can also present due to neoplasm, bony metastasis, inflammatory arthritis, pneumonia, pneumothorax, nephrolithiasis, or a vaso-occlusive crisis in patients with sickle cell anemia, who are also at risk of osteomyelitis of the back. Rarely, back pain in children is due to an aortic aneurysm, most commonly seen in patients with Marfan syndrome. History and physical exam findings indicating a dangerous cause of back pain include children < 4 years of age, patients with associated fever, weight loss, worsening pain, pain at night, or those with evidence of neurologic dysfunction.



Back strengthening exercises (A) are not routinely recommended in children with back pain, but stretching exercises are sometimes used to provide relief in patients with spondylolisthesis.

An MRI of the lumbar spine (B) can rule out many serious diagnoses that cause back pain, but plain film radiographs are usually recommended as the initial starting point. An exception could be made when the history or exam suggests a spinal epidural abscess or hematoma, transverse myelitis, osteomyelitis, or a spinal cord lesion.

Back pain in young children is uncommon, and while the history and examination may suggest spondylolisthesis, the degree of lumbar slip will change treatment. Thus, reassurance and discharge (C) are less appropriate than an X-ray.

Question: Which of the following can cause reversible sensorineural hearing loss?
ExplanationEN:
Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from damage to the inner ear (cochlea), auditory nerve, or central auditory pathways. It accounts for approximately 90% of all cases of hearing loss, particularly in adults > 65 years. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is defined as a rapid-onset hearing loss ≥ 30 dB over at least three contiguous frequencies, occurring within 72 hours. Although SNHL is often permanent, certain ototoxic medications can cause reversible cases, particularly when identified early and discontinued.

Aspirin, especially at high doses (e.g., > 3 grams/day), can cause reversible SNHL. The mechanism is thought to involve alterations in cochlear blood flow or direct effects on outer hair cell function. This toxicity is dose-dependent and typically resolves upon discontinuation of the drug. In the acute setting, identifying medication-induced hearing loss is crucial, especially if the patient presents with no signs of infection or trauma. Prompt discontinuation of the offending agent often results in complete resolution of symptoms, underscoring the importance of a detailed medication history during evaluation.

Diagnosis of SNHL is primarily clinical and may be supported by bedside tuning fork tests (Weber and Rinne), audiometry, or urgent otolaryngology consultation. In cases of sudden SNHL without an identifiable and reversible cause, corticosteroids are often initiated promptly to improve outcomes. Complications of untreated SNHL include permanent hearing loss, communication difficulties, social withdrawal, and decreased quality of life. Therefore, timely recognition and management, particularly when a reversible cause such as aspirin toxicity is suspected, are paramount.



Cisplatin (B), gentamicin (C), and sildenafil (E) have all been associated with irreversible SNHL.

Lisinopril (D) is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor commonly used for hypertension, but it has no known association with SNHL or tinnitus. Its most common side effects include a dry cough, angioedema, and hyperkalemia. Loop diuretics like furosemide are frequently associated with ototoxicity and potential hearing loss. In cases where loop diuretics cause hearing changes, the effect is often related to changes in the ionic gradient of the stria vascularis.

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with pelvic pain for 4 days and right upper quadrant pain for 1 day. She had a vaginal delivery 5 weeks ago and was presumptively treated for group B Streptococcus. She reports chills but no fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On abdominal exam, she has tenderness in the suprapubic area and significant right upper quadrant tenderness with voluntary guarding. On pelvic examination, she has a yellow discharge and moderate uterine tenderness. Laboratory analysis is significant for a urinalysis with 1+ blood, white blood cell count of 13.2/µL, aspartate aminotransferase of 75 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase of 90 U/L. What diagnosis is the most likely cause of this patient’s transaminitis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s symptoms are most consistent with Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, or perihepatitis associated with chronic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome most often occurs from ascending infection from the vagina to the endometrium, through the fallopian tubes, and into the peritoneal cavity. Once this occurs, patients develop inflammation of the liver capsule, leading to right upper quadrant pain and adhesion formation.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome occurs in approximately 10% of patients with PID. Many organisms can cause the illness, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Streptococcus agalactiae, Gardnerella vaginalis, Escherichia coli, and Bacteroides species, but Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common organism. Clinicians must have a high index of suspicion for this illness since its signs and symptoms mimic other pathology in the right upper quadrant, including cholecystitis, pyelonephritis, and ascending cholangitis. Along with right upper quadrant pain that is typically worse with inspiration, patients with Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome also have pelvic symptoms.

Laboratory workup is commonly nonspecific, but patients can have mild transaminitis. Further imaging studies such as CT or pelvic ultrasound usually show PID, but CT imaging is better at showing perihepatic enhancement suggestive of inflammation. Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis. Treatment depends on the most likely causing organism. Typically, patients are treated with ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole.



Acute hepatitis B infection (A) usually presents with malaise, nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Patients will often also appear jaundiced. These patients will also have significant transaminitis with values > 1,000 U/L. This patient’s history, physical exam, and laboratory values are not consistent with acute hepatitis B infection.

Acute pyelonephritis (B) can sometimes present with right upper quadrant pain and suprapubic abdominal pain due to bladder inflammation, but these patients usually report flank pain, too. They do not have significant transaminitis. This patient has hematuria on laboratory results, but she does not have leukocytes in the urine to suggest infection.

The classic presentation for ascending cholangitis (C) is right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice. Patients with severe disease will also have mental status changes and hypotension. This patient’s history and physical exam are not consistent with ascending cholangitis.
