Question: A 62-year-old man with a history of epilepsy, a congenital brain abnormality, and alcohol use disorder presents to the ED acutely altered. He was found down outside a grocery store and initially was obtunded. On arrival, the patient now responds to stimuli but is unable to move the right side of his body, even with painful stimuli. He does not answer questions or follow commands and has an abrasion on his tongue. A head CT is performed and is unremarkable. A phone call with a family member suggests he was last seen acting normally 4 hours ago. His initial laboratory studies are unremarkable and re-evaluation demonstrates further improvement in his mental status. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
Todd paralysis is a mimicker of stroke that presents after a seizure with focal limb weakness or paralysis. It typically occurs during the postictal phase and should improve gradually with time, assuming there is no recurrence of seizures. It is more common in older patients and patients with a history of structural brain disease. Any patient presenting as altered with focal neurologic deficits after a seizure or in the setting of known epilepsy should be suspected of having a Todd paralysis.

The difficulty in this diagnosis is assuming a Todd paralysis is present in a patient without a clearly witnessed seizure episode or known history of epilepsy, in which case, stroke rises on the differential as the most likely underlying cause of symptoms. In the setting of a Todd paralysis, in particular without a known history of epilepsy, it is prudent to consult a neurologist to discern stroke from Todd paralysis.

Further workup should include the normal workup for stroke, including a blood glucose, and looking for other toxic, metabolic, or infectious causes and addressing those promptly to see if symptoms improve. A Todd paralysis should improve with time but may persist for up to 36 hours. Thus the patient should be observed until their neurologic symptoms resolve. If a patient’s symptoms resolve and their neurologic workup is negative, they can often be discharged if there is no other acute finding to explain their presentation.



Alteplase (A) could be indicated in the management of an acute ischemic stroke in a patient presenting without any contraindications within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. It is less likely this patient is presenting with an acute ischemic stroke, given his postictal state, history of epilepsy, and improving mental status.

Aspirin (B) would be appropriate as the next step in management for an acute stroke in a patient who does not meet criteria for tissue plasminogen activator, in addition to medical optimization, including smoking cessation, blood pressure control, and a statin.

An MRI brain (C) would be performed in the acute management of stroke after a decision has been made as to whether tissue plasminogen activator would be administered or not. It can delineate the extent of the stroke, confirm the diagnosis, and be useful in prognostication but would not be necessary in the setting of a Todd paralysis unless there was uncertainty about the diagnosis.

Question: What is the most common cause of pruritus ani in a pediatric patient?
ExplanationEN:
Patients with pruritus ani report an uncontrollable urge to scratch the perianal area. In the pediatric population, the pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) is the most common cause. In adults, the most common cause of pruritus ani is the presence of feces on the perianal skin.

A pinworm infection is transmitted by the fecal-oral route. After the eggs hatch and the worms mature in the colon, adult females migrate at night to the perianal area and deposit their eggs, triggering the itching. The presenting symptoms are nighttime itching that makes it difficult to sleep, or concern after the caregiver sees worms on the skin, underwear, or bedding.

The diagnosis is made by either directly observing the worms or by detecting eggs on a clear piece of tape swabbed from the anus. The exam during the day is normal, although worms can migrate to the vulva or vagina, causing vulvovaginitis. Treatment includes a single dose of albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate. Instruct the families to use good hygiene to prevent familial spread. The patient should get a repeat dose of the medication in 2 weeks as the medication kills worms better than eggs.



Candidal dermatitis (A) causes an erythematous, moist perianal rash, often with satellite papules or pustules and is a less common cause of pruritus ani in children.

Lichen planus (B) is an itchy, inflammatory dermatosis that involves the skin and mucous membranes but is uncommon in children. It usually causes violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules or plaques.

Perianal streptococcal dermatitis (C) causes a sharply demarcated perianal rash associated with pain and discomfort. It does not cause much itching.

Seborrheic dermatitis (E) usually affects sebaceous gland-rich areas of the scalp but is unusual in the genital region. It can cause pruritus ani but is less common than pinworms in the pediatric population. It is seen more commonly in adults.

Question: Which of the following best describes the Dix-Hallpike maneuver?

Options.text: With the patient lying down, turn the head 45 degrees to one side, sit the patient up and look for nystagmus. Repeat on the contralateral side
With the patient lying down, turn the head 90 degrees to one side, sit the patient up and look for nystagmus. Repeat on the contralateral side
With the patient sitting up, turn the head 45 degrees to one side, lie the patient down with head overhanging the edge of the bed and look for nystagmus. Repeat on the contralateral side
With the patient sitting up, turn the head 90 degrees to one side, lie the patient down with head overhanging the edge of the bed and look for nystagmus. Repeat on the contralateral side

CorrectAnswer: With the patient sitting up, turn the head 45 degrees to one side, lie the patient down with head overhanging the edge of the bed and look for nystagmus. Repeat on the contralateral side
ExplanationEN:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is caused by the presence of otoliths in the posterior semicircular canal. One procedure used to diagnose BPPV is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver (also known as the Hallpike test or Nylan-Barany test).

To properly perform this test, start with the patient sitting upright, positioned far back enough so that when you lay the patient down, their head overhangs the head of the bed. Have the patient turn their head 45 degrees in one direction and then rapidly lower the patient so that the head overhangs the head of the bed. A positive test result is one where nystagmus (not dizziness) is induced. The Epley maneuver, used to dislodge the otolith and relieve the symptoms of BPPV, should be performed in the ipsilateral direction where nystagmus was elicited.



The Dix-Hallpike maneuver starts with the patient sitting up, not lying down (A, B), and entails turning the patient's head 45 degrees to each side, not 90 degrees (B, D).

Question:

Reveal Answer:
(1) Unstable heart disease, (2) ongoing stroke or transient ischemic attack, (3) severe neck disease, and (4) high-grade carotid stenosis.

Question: A 2-month-old term male infant presents to the ED with trouble feeding. His mother reports it is taking longer for him to feed and he often seems like he is choking. She reports it began at birth and has been slowly worsening, and while the infant frequently spits up, it has been similar to her other two children. He has had no fevers, vomiting, or other ill symptoms. On exam the infant is well appearing with vital signs within normal limits for age. A complete exam, including of the oropharynx and oral mucosa, is normal. The patient is gaining weight well but has frequent coughing episodes on observed breastfeeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN:
Dysphagia is described as both difficulty with or abnormality with swallowing. Most pediatric patients with dysphagia have an associated infection, such as stomatitis, pharyngitis, or a peritonsillar abscess. When unrelated to infection, dysphagia is an uncommon problem in children and, unlike many other pediatric concerns, is usually associated with serious illness. A complete history and physical examination will suggest a diagnosis in most patients. Causes of dysphagia in infants and children include birth trauma from intubation or meconium aspiration, congenital anomalies (e.g., tracheoesophageal fistula, vascular ring, or choanal stenosis), extreme cases of gastroesophageal reflux, foreign body, anaphylaxis, airway obstruction, and botulism.

In this patient, a history of worsening dysphagia since birth suggests a congenital anomaly. When dysphagia presents at birth, passing an 8 F catheter through the nares and into the stomach can evaluate for choanal stenosis or esophageal obstruction such as esophageal atresia. This is often done with an X-ray to confirm placement in the stomach, followed by an upper gastrointestinal series with catheter removal to evaluate for an H-type tracheoesophageal fistula. An upper gastrointestinal series will also evaluate the esophagus for stenosis or an esophageal web.



A fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (A) involves threading an endoscopic camera through the nose to evaluate swallowing in real time. This is one method for screening for pre-esophageal disorders, but it does not detect congenital esophageal anomalies.

A trial of acid suppression, such as a limited famotidine trial (B), is reserved for infants with gastroesophageal reflux with significant symptoms (e.g., failure to thrive) and who do not improve with conservative therapy. Infants with gastroesophageal reflux typically present with frequent spit-ups, fussiness, and occasionally failure to thrive, not with dysphagia.

Children with dysphagia require further evaluation to determine a cause and to arrange definitive treatment, so reassurance and discharge (C) is inappropriate in this patient.

Question: A 50-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia, seizure disorder, chronic back pain, and hypertension presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), blood pressure is 174/89 mm Hg, heart rate is 112 bpm, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. On physical exam, he is agitated, diaphoretic, hypersalivating, and has mydriasis. Lower extremity hyperreflexia, rigidity, and clonus are noted. Review of his chart indicates that he was started on a cough medication 1 day ago. Which of the patient’s current medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s suspected diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening adverse reaction to serotonergic drugs and is one of many causes of drug fevers. Pathophysiology involves overstimulation of central postsynaptic serotonin receptors, particularly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A. The most common class of drugs associated with serotonin syndrome is antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI), serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRI), tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), and atypical antidepressants such as trazodone and bupropion. Several other drugs are associated with serotonin syndrome such as tramadol, lithium, linezolid, triptans, meperidine, and dextromethorphan.

Symptoms typically begin 2–24 hours after increasing the dosage of a serotonergic drug or adding a new serotonergic drug. This patient could be taking tramadol for chronic back pain and was recently prescribed a cough medication, most likely dextromethorphan, which triggered serotonin syndrome. Patients with serotonin syndrome present with a triad of cognitive, autonomic, and neuromuscular-related symptoms. Cognitive symptoms may manifest as altered mental status, agitation, or pressured speech. Autonomic effects cause vital sign abnormalities such as hyperthermia, hypertension, and tachycardia and symptoms such as diarrhea, mydriasis, and diaphoresis. Neuromuscular symptoms include tremors, hyperreflexia, rigidity, and clonus. Clonus is an important distinguishing feature of serotonin syndrome since it is uncommon in other similarly presenting causes of drug fevers. Treatment is immediate cessation of offending medications as well as supportive care. Benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine have activity as serotonin receptor antagonists and are often used for symptomatic management, although they have not been consistently shown to have a significant effect.



Haloperidol (A) is a typical antipsychotic that exerts its effect as a dopamine receptor antagonist. It is commonly implicated in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a drug fever that presents similarly to serotonin syndrome but without clonus.

Lisinopril (B) is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor implicated in angioedema. It is not associated with serotonin syndrome.

Phenytoin (C) is an antiepileptic medication implicated in Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome syndrome (formerly known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms [DRESS]).

Question: A young adult presents to the ED with a decreased level of consciousness. Paramedics state the patient is coming from a music festival and was found minimally responsive in the restroom by other concertgoers. His medical history is unknown. Vital signs are remarkable for HR 135 bpm, BP 105/70 mm Hg, RR 32/min, T 101.1℉ (38.4°C), and SpO2 92%. The physical exam is remarkable for fruity odor on the patient’s breath, 3 mm reactive pupils, diaphoresis, rapid, deep respirations, dry mucous membranes, and epigastric abdominal tenderness with guarding. What next step will help determine the etiology of the patient’s altered level of consciousness?
ExplanationEN:
Mental status is the clinical state of emotional and intellectual functioning of an individual. Altered mental status is a change from a patient's emotional or intellectual baseline due to one or multiple causes. Patients who present with a decreased or altered level of consciousness need to have a full evaluation looking into potentially reversible and irreversible etiologies. Etiologies include acidosis, toxic alcohols, substance misuse, polypharmacy, encephalopathy, electrolyte abnormalities, endocrinopathy, infection, hypoxia, uremia, trauma, shock, stroke, and psychogenic origins. Determining the onset and progression of symptoms can also help determine if the patient’s presentation is due to delirium (over days), dementia (insidious and progressive), or psychiatric disorder (sudden). This patient is demonstrating clinical features concerning for diabetes-related ketoacidosis (DKA) (e.g., altered mental status, tachypnea, fruity odor of breath, dry mucous membranes). A point-of-care glucose will demonstrate either an unreadable glucose or an elevated glucose. Promptly obtaining this information can help guide the clinician in how to treat and reverse the patient’s altered level of consciousness. The treatment for DKA includes insulin replacement therapy, reversal of acidosis, fluid resuscitation, and electrolyte replenishment. Infectious and ischemic processes and nonadherence are the most common causes of DKA, and all causes should be evaluated for in the workup.



Flumazenil (A) is the reversal agent for benzodiazepine overdose. It is rarely used secondary to the potential for inducing withdrawal seizures that are refractory to therapy. Typically, supportive care is the management of choice for benzodiazepine overdose. This patient is not demonstrating clinical features consistent with benzodiazepine overdose.

Naloxone (B) is the reversal agent for opiate, opioid, or narcotic overdose. This patient is not demonstrating clinical features concerning for such an overdose (pinpoint pupils or bradypnea/hypopnea/apnea). Thus, naloxone would have no effect on his presentation.

Oxygen therapy (C) benefits patients who develop an encephalopathy secondary to reduced cerebral oxygen. Oxygen would be unlikely to aid in determining the cause of the patient’s presentation, as he is not hypoxic.

One Step Further
Question:
Multiple redoses of naloxone are concerning for overdose of what substance?

Reveal Answer:
Methadone. Due to its prolonged half-life, patients who overdose on methadone commonly require a naloxone infusion and admission.

Question: A 53-year-old woman presents to the ED with confusion. She is unable to offer a history on arrival, so her partner is giving the information. She has a history of type 1 diabetes with multiple visits for diabetic ketoacidosis, as she does not take her diabetes medications. Her T is 101°F (38.3°C), BP is 102/81 mm Hg, HR is 122 bpm, RR is 32/min, and SpO2 is 96% on room air. The physical exam reveals a woman who is breathing rapidly and deeply. Dermatologic exam reveals the finding shown above. Bedside laboratory testing reveals a pH of 6.9, potassium of 5 mEq/L, blood glucose of 670 mg/dL, and bicarbonate of 8 mEq/L. The patient is started on IV fluids, insulin, and potassium. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for this patient?

Options.text: Vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, and surgical debridement

ExplanationEN:
Mucormycosis is a life-threatening fungal infection that is more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients and patients with diabetes. Other risk factors for mucormycosis include the use of medications such as deferoxamine and corticosteroids. The classic presentation is a black eschar with pain, tenderness, and systemic symptoms. The orbital and facial regions are commonly affected, which may lead to orbital and facial pain with vision loss.

When the diagnosis is suspected, liposomal amphotericin B and surgical consult for debridement should be initiated. Imaging, including CT and MRI, may be performed to determine the extent of the infection. However, patients with mucormycosis may be hemodynamically unstable and critically ill, so routine imaging depends on the clinical presentation.

Further management of mucormycosis involves treating the underlying disease, such as hyperglycemia and acidosis, and monitoring the patient in an ICU. Mortality is high in this condition.



Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and admission (B) would be appropriate management of a more extensive case of cellulitis that causes systemic symptoms or diabetic ketoacidosis. Cellulitis presents with warmth, tenderness, and erythema of the skin. This patient’s exam shows a much more invasive infection.

Cephalexin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and admission (C) could be considered appropriate management for cellulitis in a patient who is well-appearing enough to tolerate oral antibiotics. However, most patients who are being admitted to the hospital will be placed on IV antibiotics.

Vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, and surgical debridement (D) is appropriate management of necrotizing fasciitis. Necrotizing fasciitis presents with a fever, hemodynamic instability, and a rapidly spreading dermatologic infection. While it would be prudent to give this patient empiric antibiotics until the diagnosis of mucormycosis has been confirmed, mucormycosis is more likely given her physical exam, and she needs an antifungal agent.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 65-year-old man with a history of IV drug use presents with a fever and confusion. His only medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease managed with inhalers and steroids. His T is 103°F (39.4°C), BP is 65/20 mm Hg, HR is 142 bpm, RR is 28/min, and SpO2 is 95% on room air. The patient is given 3,000 mL of fluids with an unchanged blood pressure. He is started on maximal doses of norepinephrine and epinephrine with a blood pressure of 72/33 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment to administer?
ExplanationEN:
Septic shock is defined as persistent hypotension refractory to appropriate fluid resuscitation in the setting of systemic infection. Management should be centered on early lab testing, blood cultures, lactate, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Source control is paramount, such as draining an abscess or removing infected lines. In septic shock, the vasopressors given are typically norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin, and then phenylephrine (last-line). Steroids have a permissive effect on blood pressure and upregulate alpha-1 on the vasculature, thus increasing the effect of vasopressors. They are particularly important in patients with adrenal suppression, such as those chronically taking steroids or those with adrenal dysfunction. Generally, steroids with both mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid activity are given, such as hydrocortisone.



Dobutamine (A) is a beta-1 and beta-2 agonist that increases heart rate and contractility. It may be used in heart failure to augment cardiac output (though it is not the first-line medication in cardiogenic shock). Given the maximal doses of norepinephrine and epinephrine, dobutamine is unlikely to offer any benefit.

Dopamine (B) is a vasopressor that may increase cardiac contractility and output. In the treatment of shock, it is not clearly a first- or second-line vasopressor and may be dysrhythmogenic. It is unlikely to offer benefit in a patient on maximal norepinephrine and epinephrine. Furthermore, this patient’s history of chronic corticosteroid use should lead the clinician to steroid replacement therapy for refractory shock.

Phenylephrine (D) is a vasopressor and alpha-1 agonist. It is often used as a last-line vasopressor in septic shock. While it would be reasonable to start this medication, it is unlikely to have much effect without the permissive effect of steroids.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the emergency department after her family found her chasing a bat around a room. They are visiting from out of town and renting a cabin about 2 hours away. They found the patient jumping on her bed and trying to reach a bat that was on top of the curtains. She has no injuries or bites and otherwise appears well. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Administer rabies immunoglobulin now and the rabies vaccine over 2 weeks
Bring the bat in for 10 days of observation and treat the girl if the bat shows signs of rabies
Perform a skin exam and discharge if there are no bites or lesions

CorrectAnswer: Administer rabies immunoglobulin now and the rabies vaccine over 2 weeks
ExplanationEN:
This patient may have been exposed to rabies, a fatal viral infection. Once acquired, the mainstay of treatment is palliative care. Given the significant mortality of rabies, public health officials recommend aggressive treatment guidelines for possible exposure. As most animals’ rabies statuses are unknown, it has been determined which animals are most at risk and when to treat for rabies exposure empirically. Bites or saliva contact with raccoons, skunks, and foxes are commonly treated as presumed rabies exposure. Bats are responsible for the largest number of possible rabies exposure in the U.S. Thus, it is recommended that all patients with any exposure to bats be treated as presumed rabies exposure unless they can reliably report no bite or contact with the bat. As this patient is a young child, she should be considered an unreliable historian and be treated with postexposure prophylaxis for rabies. Treatment consists of the rabies immunoglobulin at the initial evaluation and the rabies vaccine dosed over 2 weeks (days 0, 3, 7, and 14).



Rabies postexposure prophylaxis consists of both rabies immunoglobulin (A) and vaccine. Unreliable patients in contact with bats should be treated as presumed rabies exposure.

While the bat may be collected for evaluation, the patient should be treated until the results return (C). Notably, wild animals are recommended to be immediately euthanized and evaluated rather than observed for 10 days, which is reserved for domestic pets.

A negative skin exam (D) is not an appropriate reason to withhold rabies prophylaxis, especially in patients who have been in contact with bats.

Question: A 45-year-old man with unknown medical history is brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious at a bus stop. The patient is protecting his airway and breathing 24/min with a blood pressure of 180/110 mm Hg. He is noted to have a fever of 39.5°C. He has no signs of trauma, and his pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. He localizes to pain but will not open his eyes spontaneously or speak beyond moaning. His CBC shows leukopenia and anemia. CT is unremarkable for acute bleeding or large mass. A lumbar puncture is performed and shows an elevated intracranial pressure of 25 cm H2O. On microscopic evaluation of the CSF, round encapsulated organisms are visualized. Which of the following medications is a first-line agent for the likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis, an opportunistic fungal infection most often seen in untreated patients with AIDS, particularly those with CD4 counts < 100 cells/µL. Typically, the course of cryptococcus is indolent, taking 1–2 weeks to become severe. Initial symptoms include fever, malaise, and headache. Expected findings of meningitis, such as stiff neck, photophobia, and vomiting, are present in only one-quarter to one-third of patients. Often, patients will develop lethargy, confusion, or altered mentation alongside a fever. After obtaining a CT to identify possible masses or herniation, a lumbar puncture should be done, which can provide a rapid diagnosis on India ink staining. Cryptococcus neoformans has a polysaccharide fungal capsule that does not take up the India ink stain, creating a halo-like appearance that looks like round white cells on a black background. Other options for diagnosis include cryptococcal antigen testing through serum and CSF. Treatment of cryptococcus involves three phases. The first phase, induction, uses flucytosine and amphotericin B together. Amphotericin works by binding to ergosterol in the fungal cell wall. Flucytosine inhibits fungal DNA synthesis.



Micafungin (B), a member of the echinocandin drug class, is also not a recommended therapy for Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis, as the echinocandins have been shown to have no in vitro activity against specific yeasts, including Cryptococcus.

Nitazoxanide (C) is an antiparasitic and antiviral medication used on Cryptosporidium parvum, an opportunistic pathogen associated with diarrhea.

Voriconazole (D) is not a recommended therapy for Cryptococcus neoformans. Another azole, fluconazole, can be used in conjunction with amphotericin B if flucytosine is not available. Fluconazole is also regularly used in later phases of treatment.

Question: Which description below is most consistent with the exanthem associated with rubella?

Options.text: Erythematous malar rash that starts on the face and spreads caudally into a reticular rash on the trunk and extremities
Erythematous, blanching maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads caudally with associated white lesions on the buccal mucosa
Maculopapular, blanching exanthem that starts on the trunk and neck and spreads to the face and extremities with an associated resolved fever
Pinpoint, pink, maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads caudally to the trunk and extremities with associated fevers

CorrectAnswer: Pinpoint, pink, maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads caudally to the trunk and extremities with associated fevers
ExplanationEN:
Rubella belongs to the togavirus family and is a single-stranded RNA virus. Prior to the advent of the rubella immunization, outbreaks occurred in the winter and early spring every few years. While effectively eliminated from the US, rubella still occurs in outbreaks in other countries, particularly resource-poor nations. Viremia occurs within the first 5–7 days, allowing the virus to spread throughout the body. Patients may shed virus and are potentially contagious for up to 1–2 weeks before clinical symptoms become evident.

Clinical features are generally mild and, in many cases, patients remain asymptomatic. Typically an acute onset of a maculopapular rash with minimal systemic symptoms is seen when symptoms are present. A fever may be present on presentation or may have preceded the rash. Classically, the rash is described as maculopapular, pinpoint, and pink, which starts on the face and spreads caudally to the trunk and extremities. A mild, nonexudative conjunctivitis and soft palate enanthem may also be present. The diagnosis is most commonly made by the detection of rubella-specific IgM antibodies. These specific antibodies can be detected as early as 4 days after the onset of the rash and can still be detected 6–8 weeks later. This test should be reserved for patients who have a suspicious history for rubella but are not demonstrating clinical features of other illnesses that can also cause the rash. Treatment for rubella consists of supportive care, as there is no specific treatment for rubella.



Erythematous, blanching maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads caudally with associated white lesions on the buccal mucosa (B) describes the classic rash associated with measles.

Erythematous malar rash that starts on the face and spreads caudally into a reticular rash on the trunk and extremities (A) describes the classic rash associated with erythema infectiosum from parvovirus B19.

Maculopapular, blanching exanthem that starts on the trunk and neck and spreads to the face and extremities with an associated resolved fever (C) classically describes roseola.

Question: A 20-month-old girl is brought to the ED with her parent for a rash. The patient is fully immunized and has no significant medical history. The parent states the rash started this morning. Which history is most suggestive of roseola?

Options.text: Abrupt resolution of high fever followed by a maculopapular rash that spreads from trunk to extremities
Fever for 5 days and associated nonexudative conjunctivitis, palm desquamation, lymphadenopathy, and mucositis
Low-grade fever followed by maculopapular rash that starts on face and spreads to the trunk
Maculopapular rash with associated conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea, and blue lesions on buccal mucosa

CorrectAnswer: Abrupt resolution of high fever followed by a maculopapular rash that spreads from trunk to extremities
ExplanationEN:
Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, is a viral illness that is characterized by high fever and a classic rash. Transmission in most cases occurs sporadically. However, horizontal transmission and secondary cases have been reported. Roseola is an illness that is associated with young children, with the peak prevalence between 7–13 months of age, with the large majority of cases occurring before 2 years of age. Boys and girls are equally affected, and cases occur throughout the year without a predominance in any part of the year.

Clinical features include a classic clinical course that involves the abrupt resolution of high fever followed by a maculopapular rash that starts on the neck and trunk before spreading to the extremities and face. The fever is high, commonly exceeding 104°F (40°C), and lasts for 3–5 days. During this period of time, the fever may be associated with irritability, lymphadenopathy, or erythematous tympanic membranes. However, most children are otherwise well-appearing, active, and alert. Less commonly, anorexia, upper respiratory tract symptoms, diarrhea, and cough may be present. The fever resolves abruptly and a macular or maculopapular rash develops, typically starting on the trunk and neck and spreading to the face and extremities.

Laboratory investigation is rarely needed unless the patient has an atypical presentation or concerning features for other disease processes, such as pneumonia, sepsis, or meningitis. The diagnosis is made clinically based on the presentation of symptoms described above.



Five days of fever and associated nonexudative conjunctivitis, palm desquamation, lymphadenopathy, and mucositis (B) are clinical features concerning for Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is considered a vasculitis without a known infectious etiology. It should be suspected in patients with ≥ 5 days of fever and at least four of the following symptoms: mucocutaneous inflammation, peripheral extremity changes (erythema and edema of palms and soles or desquamation of digits), polymorphous rash, oropharyngeal changes (erythema, fissures or cracked lips, strawberry tongue), bilateral conjunctival injection, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Coronary aneurysm is the most worrisome complication of Kawasaki disease and should be evaluated for with an echocardiogram if the diagnosis is suspected. Clinicians should also be aware of depressed cardiac contractility, heart failure, dysrhythmias, and peripheral arterial occlusion as potential complications.

Low-grade fever followed by a maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads to the trunk (C) are clinical features consistent with rubella. Patients who are unimmunized or underimmunized, with the findings noted above, should be evaluated for rubella.

Maculopapular rash with associated conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea, and blue lesions on the buccal mucosa (D) are clinical features concerning for measles, not roseola. Unimmunized or underimmunized patients with the findings noted above should be evaluated for measles.

Question: In late summer, many individuals are presenting to your ED over a few days with fever, headache, malaise, rash, nausea, and vomiting. Several neighborhood crows and jays have been found dead over the past week, and local news has reported an uptick in mosquito activity. Which of the following infections is most likely responsible for these patients’ illness?
ExplanationEN:
Dead corvids (e.g., crows, jays) in an urban area are a sentinel clue for West Nile virus activity. West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus most commonly transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Most infections are asymptomatic or cause a self-limiting febrile illness characterized by headache, myalgias, and GI symptoms.

A minority of cases develop neuroinvasive disease, such as meningitis or encephalitis, with risk increased in adults > 65 years old and individuals with certain immunocompromising conditions. West Nile virus is the leading cause of domestically acquired arboviral disease in the US, with transmission peaking during July through September.

Serum and CSF fluid IgM testing with a macrophage-attacking complex enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is recommended for diagnosis. If results are equivocal or cross-reactivity is a concern, plaque-reduction neutralization testing can be used for confirmation.

Treatment is supportive, including hydration, antipyretics, and pain control. Individuals with neuroinvasive disease may require hospital admission for airway protection, treatment of increased intracranial pressure, and seizure control. There is no approved antiviral therapy.



Hantavirus (A) is associated with exposure to aerosolized rodent excreta and can cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome rather than a mosquito-linked febrile illness with bird die-offs.

Histoplasma capsulatum (B) is a dimorphic fungus linked to soil enriched by bird or bat droppings, often causing pulmonary disease after soil disruption, not mosquito-borne citywide outbreaks with dead birds.

Influenza A virus (C) can produce abrupt fever and systemic symptoms but is not associated with mosquito exposure or sentinel bird mortality events in urban surveillance.

Zika virus (E) is a flavivirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes and is associated with fever, rash, arthralgias, and conjunctivitis, as well as congenital complications during pregnancy. It is not linked to urban corvid die-offs serving as a sentinel for West Nile virus activity.

Question: A parent presents with their healthy 18-day-old male infant for evaluation of a fever. They report that he was hot to the touch today and had a rectal temperature of 100.9°F (38.3°C) at home. The patient has no symptoms of cough, congestion, vomiting, or diarrhea. There are no known sick contacts. The child was born full term, and there were no complications with the birth or the pregnancy. The birth mother had no known history of herpes simplex virus. A complete physical exam reveals a well-appearing infant with no abnormal findings. HR is 174 bpm, SpO2 is 99%, and a rectal T is 101.1°F (38.4°C). Which of the following is the most appropriate workup for this patient’s fever?

Options.text: Obtain CBC, CMP, blood culture, and urinalysis
Obtain urinalysis and blood culture and perform a lumbar puncture

CorrectAnswer: Obtain urinalysis and blood culture and perform a lumbar puncture
ExplanationEN:
This patient is an infant between 8 and 21 days old with a temperature ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) and no evident source of infection. Therefore, the patient needs a septic workup, including a urinalysis, blood culture, and lumbar puncture (LP). Viral infections are the most frequent cause of fever in infants, but infants < 3 months of age are relatively immunodeficient and have an increased risk of serious bacterial illness. The most common bacterial infections are urinary tract infections, bacteremia and sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. When assessing an infant < 3 months of age presenting with a fever, it is important to review the pregnancy and birth history, use of peripartum antibiotics in the mother or infant, and maternal history of herpes simplex virus (HSV). Signs and symptoms of serious bacterial illness are typically nonspecific in infants < 3 months, thus the need for more thorough testing than may be indicated in older children. A full physical exam should be performed with the infant completely undressed to identify any focus of infection. Infants with meningitis frequently exhibit inconsolable crying or increased irritability when handled, while other signs of meningeal irritation, such as nuchal rigidity, are typically absent.

Since the 1980s, the epidemiology of bacterial infections in neonates and infants has shifted from gram-positive to gram-negative predominance, with Escherichia coli being the most common organism causing bacteremia. This has led to a need for improved decision models related to neonatal fever workups. Current guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend obtaining urinalysis, blood culture, and performing an LP on all infants 8–21 days old who are well-appearing, with no obvious source of infection, and temperature ≥ 100.4°F (38°C). Inflammatory markers such as procalcitonin, C-reactive protein, and absolute neutrophil count (included on a CBC) may also be considered. HSV studies should be sent if the mother has genital HSV lesions or fever 48 hours before or after delivery or the infant has vesicular lesions, seizures, hypothermia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated alanine aminotransferase levels, or CSF pleocytosis in the absence of a positive Gram stain result.

These patients should all be started on parenteral antibiotics, with the addition of acyclovir if indicated, and admitted to the hospital for observation. Commonly used antibiotic regimens are ampicillin and cefotaxime or ampicillin and gentamicin. The choice of antibiotic regimen should be based on regional susceptibilities for group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. Ceftriaxone should not be given to infants < 1 month old because it can displace bilirubin and worsen hyperbilirubinemia. Patients may be considered for discharge from the hospital when culture results are negative at 24–36 hours, the infant continues to appear clinically well or is improving, and there are no other reasons for hospitalization.



Admitting the patient to the hospital (A) is the correct disposition for the patient, but a septic workup needs to be performed prior to hospital admission. It is important to obtain blood work, including blood culture and urinalysis (B) as part of the septic workup, but in this age group, an LP is a necessary part of the evaluation. Given the risk of serious bacterial infections in infants < 3 months of age, reassurance and discharge home (D) is not an appropriate plan of care for this patient.

Question: What is the causative agent for the above rash?
ExplanationEN:
This image shows grouped vesicles on an erythematous base consistent with herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. HSV is a common virus affecting a considerable portion of adults. There are two variants of HSV that infect humans: HSV-1 typically affects nongenital sites, and HSV-2 typically affects the genital area and is transmitted by sexual contact.

HSV lesions typically present as painful, grouped vesicles that are localized in a nondermatomal distribution. Oral lesions are the most common site of HSV-1 infections. In addition to affecting the lips, they can also cause ulcerations to the gingiva, tongue, and mouth. Outbreaks can be accompanied by fever and lymphadenopathy.

A first episode of HSV can be treated with acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir for 7–10 days. These agents accelerate healing and reduce the length of viral shedding. Recurrent HSV may be treated with no intervention, episodic antiviral therapy, or chronic suppressive antiviral therapy.



Coxsackievirus (A) causes hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). These lesions may be macular or maculopapular but may also be vesicular and can be confused with HSV. HFMD lesions are typically not grouped, will be present on the hand or foot in addition to oral lesions, and are often accompanied by sore throat and fever.

Staphylococcus aureus (C) is the common causative organism of impetigo, which presents with macules, vesicles, bullae, and pustules with a yellow-gold crust. It may also cause other bacterial skin infections, such as folliculitis, cellulitis, and abscesses.

Varicella-zoster virus (D) is associated with chickenpox, which presents with a widespread vesicular rash in various stages (macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts) over the body, or shingles, which appears as a painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution. It does not typically cause isolated oral lesions like HSV.

Variola virus (E) is responsible for causing smallpox, which is now eradicated worldwide. Smallpox is associated with widespread lesions that begin as maculopapular and evolve into vesicular and then pustular lesions, as compared to the localized vesicular lesions with HSV.

Question: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED after he crashed his dirt bike going over a jump. He has a 5 cm wound to his right leg with a significant amount of dirt and debris in the wound. He does not think he has ever received a tetanus vaccine in the past, as his parents were against vaccinations. Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Tetanus immune globulin and tetanus vaccine

CorrectAnswer: Tetanus immune globulin and tetanus vaccine
ExplanationEN:
This patient is at risk for tetanus, a nervous system disorder that causes severe muscle spasms and hypertonia. Although it is an uncommon condition in the US because of universal vaccination, patients who are unvaccinated or from resource-limited countries are at risk. Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani, which is an anaerobic, motile, spore-forming, gram-positive rod that is found in soil, dust, and feces and is resistant to heat and chemicals. Most cases of tetanus are caused by wounds, including postoperative infections. The incubation time for tetanus is generally 3 days to 2 weeks. Signs and symptoms of tetanus include weakness, myalgias, dysphagia, hydrophobia, and drooling. Patients may also exhibit lockjaw, known as trismus (painful, intense spasms of the masseter muscles with the inability to open the mouth), risus sardonicus (facial muscle spasms), and generalized severe muscular spasms. Death is commonly secondary to laryngeal or respiratory spasms leading to respiratory failure and arrest. Patients may also exhibit autonomic dysfunction. There is no effect on mental status.

Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis. Management of tetanus infection is first supportive and includes minimizing stimuli and administering benzodiazepines and narcotics for the spasms. Intubation and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade may be necessary. These patients should be admitted to an ICU for further care. To eliminate toxin production, the wound should be cleaned and debrided, and IV metronidazole should be given. Additionally, IM tetanus immune globulin (TIG) injection should be given, as this may shorten the course and reduce the severity of the disease. TIG is safe during pregnancy and is not needed if the primary series of vaccines was completed (three or more tetanus toxoid vaccinations). TIG should also be given around the wound. TIG neutralizes circulating tetanospasmin and toxin in a wound but will not treat any toxin already fixed in the nervous system.

Tetanus immunization should be considered for all wounds in the ED. Adults who have not been previously vaccinated against tetanus should receive a series of three vaccines, with the second dose in 4 weeks and the third dose in 6–12 months. If the wound is dirty, administer the tetanus-diphtheria vaccine (Td) if > 5 years since the last booster. If the wound is clean, administer Td if > 10 years since the last booster. If the patient is allergic to Td, administer TIG and consider prophylactic antibiotics. TIG is needed for dirty wounds, as well as if the patient did not complete the primary series of vaccines as in this case. Vaccination is the only way to prevent disease, as a history of tetanus infection alone does not lead to immunity.



The diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis vaccine (A) is routinely recommended in children, not in adults. Children should get a booster dose of a vaccine containing tetanus toxoid at age 11–12, followed by Td or the tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis vaccine every 10 years throughout life.

Tetanus immune globulin (B) should be given to this patient, as the wound is dirty, and the patient is not vaccinated. However, he also needs a diploid tetanus vaccine since he has not been previously vaccinated.

Tetanus immune globulin and metronidazole (C) would be indicated if the patient had signs and symptoms of active tetanus to neutralize the toxin and treat the disease process.

Tetanus vaccine (E) should be given to this patient, as he has not been vaccinated previously and has a dirty wound. He should also be given TIG in combination with the diploid vaccine for the same reasons.

Question: Which of the following is typically the most common incubation period for Ebola virus disease?
ExplanationEN:
Ebola virus was first discovered as the causative agent of an outbreak of viral hemorrhagic fever syndrome in 1976 near the Ebola River in former Zaire, which is now the Democratic Republic of Congo. The 2014–2016 outbreak of Ebola virus disease in West Africa (Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea, and several other countries) was the largest outbreak of Ebola virus disease in history to date. In 2018, another Ebola virus outbreak was declared in Central Africa (Democratic Republic of Congo).

The Ebola virus is an enveloped RNA virus of the Filoviridae family (named for their characteristic filamentous form). Like almost all viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever, it is capable of spreading by an aerosol. Thus, it is feared for potential use in bioterrorism. There are four separate species of Ebola virus that cause disease in humans: Zaire Ebola virus, Sudan Ebola virus, Taï Forest (formerly Ivory Coast or Côte d’Ivoire) Ebola virus, and Bundibugyo Ebola virus. The Reston Ebola virus is of Asian origin and can infect humans but does not cause disease. The Zaire and Sudan variants are the most lethal, with mortality rates of up to 89% and 40–60%, respectively. Both the 2014–2016 and the 2018 outbreaks in Africa were caused by the Zaire Ebola virus.

Initial infection or primary exposure is thought to be due to contact with an infected animal, such as a nonhuman primate or bat. Although still unclear, fruit bats are recently thought to be a natural reservoir for the Ebola virus. Secondary exposure occurs via human-to-human contact. Transmission is by direct contact with blood or bodily fluids (urine, saliva, sweat, tears, feces, vomit, semen, breast milk, spinal fluid) via broken skin or mucous membranes. The virus survives for several hours on dry surfaces such as doorknobs or countertops, but it can survive for several days in blood and body fluid drops. The incubation period is anywhere between 2 and 21 days but typically and most commonly is between 3 and 12 days. The onset is usually sudden, and initial symptoms and signs include fever, fatigue, severe headache, myalgias, hiccups, and bilateral conjunctival injection. Sometimes a maculopapular rash may be seen on the trunk. Ebola virus disease quickly progresses with gastrointestinal involvement, particularly abdominal pain, vomiting and severe diarrhea, and hemorrhage in the form of ecchymosis, petechiae, mucosal hemorrhage, or frank bleeding. Pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, multiorgan failure, and septic shock often follow. Death during the latest outbreaks has typically occurred between day 6 and day 16 after symptom onset. As soon as a patient is symptomatic, they are infectious and require isolation, contact and droplet precautions, and use of personal protective equipment for any clinicians as well as immediate contact with the local public health authority, who will then determine with the Centers for Disease Control whether specific Ebola testing is indicated.

Earliest basic laboratory findings include leukopenia and pronounced lymphocytopenia as well as thrombocytopenia on complete blood count. Neutrophilia with a left shift and elevated liver enzymes may be observed a few days after onset. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time will be prolonged, and fibrin degradation products will be elevated, consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment is entirely supportive. An experimental vaccine shows promise against the Zaire Ebola virus. There are several potential long-term sequelae of Ebola virus disease, including persistent headaches and joint and vision problems, as well as mental health problems such as depression and post-traumatic stress disorder in survivors. The virus persists in some bodily fluids for a variable length of time (commonly months) in individuals who survive the acute infection.



An incubation period of 1–2 days (A) is uncommon. Although symptom onset within 2 days is possible (usually with primary exposure to an infected animal in an endemic area), the incubation period is on the shorter side (2–8 days).

An incubation period of 13–21 days (B) is seen but is less common than a 3–12 days period from exposure to symptom onset.

An incubation period of 22–45 days (C) is not seen with the Ebola virus.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 55-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents to the emergency department with scrotal pain. He notes a history of skin rash in his groin for a few days, and he has felt unwell for the past few hours. Temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), heart rate is 144 bpm, respirations are 22/min, blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg, and SpO2 is 99%. His rhythm on telemetry is irregularly irregular. His physical exam reveals an edematous, erythematous scrotum with a small area of crepitus. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Administer intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, and clindamycin
Obtain a CT of the abdomen and pelvis

CorrectAnswer: Administer intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, and clindamycin
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with vital sign abnormalities and skin findings that are concerning for necrotizing soft tissue infection. Risk factors include diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, or skin breach or trauma. Involvement of the perineum and groin is also known as Fournier gangrene. Crepitus on exam is caused by gas-forming bacteria, such as Clostridium perfringens. Other pathogens that are commonly implicated include group A Streptococcus or Enterobacteriaceae. Polymicrobial infections are common. Therefore, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy with agents like piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, and clindamycin is ideal. Clindamycin is particularly effective against bacterial toxins. Bedside ultrasound may show dirty shadowing from gas within soft tissue. Despite aggressive antimicrobial therapy, these infections can progress quite rapidly through tissues, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Definitive care involves prompt surgical debridement.



Intravenous metoprolol (A) is an atrioventricular-nodal blocking agent used in supraventricular tachycardias, such as atrial fibrillation. This patient’s atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is due to a severe infection causing a systemic inflammatory response and hyperadrenergic state. Rate control is not a priority in this case and may harm the acutely ill, septic patient.

Intravenous vancomycin (C) is an antibiotic that is particularly effective against gram-positive organisms, especially methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and can be used as an adjunct in critically ill patients. However, as most cases of necrotizing fasciitis are polymicrobial in origin, empiric antibiotics should be broad-spectrum.

Obtaining a CT of the abdomen and pelvis (D) can help confirm the diagnosis, identify gas in the soft tissue, and assist with surgical staging. However, this is a clinical diagnosis, and definitive care with prompt surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics should not be delayed to obtain imaging.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents with fever, headaches, and a rash. He started having fevers 3 days ago after returning from a hiking trip. The rash appeared yesterday on his hands and feet, before spreading to his ankles and wrists, and then to the rest of the body. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: A lumbar puncture should be performed to check for protein content in cerebrospinal fluid
An electrocardiogram should be obtained to rule out heart block
The body should be exposed and inspected
The patient should be isolated immediately

CorrectAnswer: The body should be exposed and inspected
ExplanationEN:
This patient likely has Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) and should be exposed to inspect for a tick bite. RMSF is a tick-borne disease caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, which are pleomorphic, obligate intracellular organisms. The tick carrier is the American dog tick Dermacentor. Zoonotic hosts include deer, rodents, horses, cattle, cats, and dogs. The triad of fever, rash, and a history of tick bite should raise suspicion for RMSF. Other nonspecific symptoms may occur, including myalgia, malaise, lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. If left untreated, the disease can cause meningitis, kidney failure, respiratory failure, and myocarditis. The fever can be the sole initial symptom. The rash begins to appear 2–4 days after the fever. The rash is composed of blanching pink macules or petechiae that appear distally on the extremities and spread to the trunk. The rash of RMSF involves the palms and soles. Patients will have normal white and red blood cell counts but will exhibit thrombocytopenia. The treatment of choice is doxycycline and is recommended for all age groups, even younger children.



A lumbar puncture to check for protein content in cerebrospinal fluid (A) should be performed in patients who you suspect to have Guillain-Barré syndrome which presents with ascending symmetrical paralysis.

An ECG should be obtained to rule out heart block (B) if you suspect Lyme disease. The classical rash in Lyme disease is erythema migrans, which presents as a raised plaque that has central clearing.

RMSF is contracted through a tick bite and is not contagious. Thus, the patient does not need to be isolated immediately (D).

Question: What is the vector for transmission of Zika virus?
ExplanationEN:
Zika virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes and is related to dengue, yellow fever, and West Nile viruses. In addition to vector transmission, Zika can be spread through sexual contact, vertically from mother to fetus during pregnancy, and rarely through blood transfusion.

Infection typically causes a mild, self-limited illness characterized by fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and malaise, and many patients are asymptomatic.

Although most cases are benign, Zika infection during pregnancy is associated with congenital Zika syndrome, including microcephaly and other severe fetal brain abnormalities. Rare neurologic complications include Guillain-Barré syndrome and meningoencephalitis.

Zika virus has been identified in Africa, Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and the Americas. In the United States, most cases have occurred in travelers returning from endemic regions, although limited local mosquito-borne transmission has been reported in Florida and Texas.

Diagnosis should be considered in symptomatic patients with recent travel or other exposure risk and requires specialized laboratory testing, including PCR and serologic assays, which may not be widely available.

There is no specific antiviral therapy for Zika virus infection. Management is supportive and includes rest, oral hydration, and acetaminophen for fever and pain. Aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be avoided until dengue infection is excluded due to the risk of hemorrhagic complications.



Ixodid ticks (B) are the vectors for transmission of Lyme disease and babesiosis. A bite from these ticks can also lead to tick paralysis, weakness, and ascending paralysis related to tick neurotoxin. Ixodid ticks do not transmit the Zika virus.

Reduviid bugs (C) are the vectors for transmission of Trypanosoma cruzi, which leads to Chagas disease.

The tsetse fly (D) is found in Africa, and its bite can transmit Trypanosoma brucei, a parasitic infection that leads to African sleeping sickness.

Question: A 62-year-old man who lives with his daughter and her family of four children presents with 3 days of fever, chills, and generalized weakness. His medical history includes end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis, chronic anemia, diabetes, and peripheral arterial disease. Vital signs include T 38.7°C (101.7°F), BP 102/62 mm Hg, HR 122 bpm, RR 20/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. A chronic ulcer is found on his left lower extremity. Blood cultures are drawn, and the initial Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. PCR testing is positive for methicillin resistance. Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of this patient’s current condition?

Options.text: Living with multiple other household members
Presence of a chronic indwelling hemodialysis catheter

CorrectAnswer: Presence of a chronic indwelling hemodialysis catheter
ExplanationEN:
The finding of gram-positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain is highly suspicious for Staphylococcus aureus, and modern PCR assays allow for rapid identification of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) strains. MRSA commonly colonizes skin and mucous membranes, and vascular catheters provide a direct pathway for bacterial inoculation into the bloodstream. Patients who undergo hemodialysis frequently experience repeated vascular access and skin barrier disruption, making catheter-related bloodstream infection a major route of MRSA invasion. Thus, hemodialysis performed through an indwelling catheter is among the strongest clinical risk factors for MRSA bacteremia, while other prominent risk factors include IV drug use, antibiotic use, HIV infection, and residence in a long-term care facility.

S. aureus expresses multiple virulence factors, including protein A, surface adhesion molecules, and cytotoxins, that facilitate attachment to indwelling devices and persistence within biofilms. These biofilms protect bacteria from antimicrobials and host defenses, making catheter-associated MRSA infection particularly difficult to eradicate. In patients with hemodialysis catheters, bacteremia often arises from colonization of the catheter hub or endoluminal surface. Such patients may report fevers, chills, or general malaise during dialysis sessions, as catheter access allows for further systemic dissemination of bacteria.

In the ED, evaluation should include promptly recognizing sepsis, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics, and administering empiric agents with reliable MRSA coverage, such as IV vancomycin. Hemodynamic support and source control (in this case, the removal or exchange of the infected catheter) are essential. Early infectious disease consultation improves outcomes, particularly because MRSA bacteremia requires prolonged antimicrobial therapy and surveillance blood cultures to confirm clearance. MRSA bacteremia carries high morbidity and may lead to metastatic complications such as vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, endocarditis, or epidural abscess.



Although anemia (A) is common among individuals receiving dialysis, it does not directly contribute to this patient’s risk compared with the far more significant factor of catheter-based vascular access. Anemia does not increase the risk of MRSA bacteremia and is not associated with an increased likelihood of invasive S. aureus infection.

Household crowding (B) may increase the prevalence of S. aureus colonization, but it is not a major clinical predictor of MRSA bacteremia in adults presenting to the ED. In this patient, systemic illness and the presence of a hemodialysis catheter far outweigh household factors in determining the likelihood of MRSA bloodstream infection.

Although peripheral arterial disease (C) increases the risk of skin ulceration and soft-tissue infection, it is not among the strongest predictors of MRSA bacteremia. This patient’s chronic ulcer may serve as a potential portal of entry for S. aureus, but the presence of an indwelling hemodialysis catheter poses a much higher risk for bloodstream infection.

Diabetes (E) increases susceptibility to skin and soft-tissue infection due to impaired host defenses, but it is not as strongly associated with MRSA bacteremia as hemodialysis catheter use. While diabetes may predispose a patient to colonization or local infection, the patient’s tunneled catheter provides a direct route for bloodstream invasion.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 27-year-old woman presents to the ED for evaluation of a rash and fever. She has a diffuse erythematous and vesicular rash that began as a single papule that evolved into an eschar. Before the rash, she had a prodrome of headache, myalgias, nausea, and vomiting. She reports no recent travel or outdoor activities but recently moved into a new apartment and has seen mouse droppings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The patient’s exposure to mouse droppings, prodromal symptoms, and progression of the lesion to an eschar with diffuse vesicles make rickettsialpox the most likely diagnosis.

Rickettsialpox is a zoonotic illness caused by Rickettsia akari, a member of the spotted fever group of Rickettsia. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mites, typically Liponyssoides sanguineus, which reside on house mice. Outbreaks are often linked to urban settings with rodent infestations, particularly in densely populated housing complexes. Following the bite, a painless, erythematous, indurated papule appears at the inoculation site, commonly on the trunk or extremities. Within a few days, this lesion evolves into a vesicle that ruptures and forms a black eschar, a hallmark of the disease. A rim of erythema surrounds the eschar and may be mistaken for the inoculation lesion of anthrax or other poxviruses.

Patients develop systemic symptoms within 3–7 days of the bite. These symptoms are nonspecific and resemble a viral prodrome, including fever, headache, malaise, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, photophobia, anorexia, and night sweats. Soon after, a generalized eruption appears (a diffuse, erythematous, papulovesicular rash resembling chickenpox). Lesions can involve the face, trunk, and extremities but often spare the palms and soles. Lymphadenopathy, particularly regional to the eschar, may be present. Unlike other rickettsial infections, severe complications are rare. Most cases are self-limited, but treatment with doxycycline accelerates recovery and shortens symptom duration.

The diagnosis is clinical, supported by a history of rodent exposure and characteristic eschar and rash. Serologic testing and polymerase chain reaction can confirm the diagnosis, though they are not always necessary for treatment. Rickettsialpox should be distinguished from varicella, smallpox, and other eschar-producing infections. Timely recognition is essential to avoid unnecessary testing or treatment delays. With appropriate antibiotic therapy, patients typically recover fully within 7–10 days without long-term sequelae.



Aspergillosis (A) is a fungal infection that begins as a pulmonary infection and remains isolated to the lungs. In immunocompromised individuals, systemic disease may develop, with dissemination involving the skin.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (B) is the most common form of leishmaniasis. It is caused by a parasite transmitted through bites of sandflies found in the tropics, subtropics, and southern Europe. The rash has more ulcerations than vesicles.

Tularemia (D) is most commonly transmitted through handling the animal tissue of rabbits, muskrats, and prairie dogs in the southwest central United States. The classic ulcerograndular tularemia has discrete skin ulcerations with regional adenopathy.

Question: A 10-year-old girl presents with a diffuse erythroderma, lethargy, headache, and hypotension 2 days after developing a pustule on her knee. Based on her history, exam, and laboratory evaluation, you begin treating her for toxic shock syndrome. Which of the following antibiotics should be administered to inhibit exotoxin production?
ExplanationEN:
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a severe, potentially fatal illness caused by exotoxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus and group A Streptococcus (GAS). Patients can present with fevers, pharyngitis, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, diffuse erythroderma, and rapid progression to hypotensive shock with multisystem organ dysfunction. Initial treatment consists of rapid volume resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics. Many children will require vasoactive agents and advanced airway management. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should treat both Staphylococcus aureus and GAS. Clindamycin should also be administered, as studies have shown it works to inhibit the production of bacterial exotoxin.



Both ceftriaxone (A) and nafcillin (D) may be acceptable choices in the chosen antibiotic regimen, but neither has an effect on toxin production.

Metronidazole (C) would not provide coverage for either Staphylococcus aureus or GAS and would not affect toxin production.

Question: A 21-year-old woman presents to the ED with a cough, fever, and headache. Symptoms started soon after returning from a mission trip to Rwanda. She has had intermittent fevers over the last 10 days, along with chills, headaches, and a nonproductive, sporadic cough. On physical exam, her vital signs are temperature 101.7°F (38.7ºC), heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, respirations 16/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen is soft and nontender with no organomegaly. Which of the following studies is likely to confirm the diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium ovales, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium knowlesi, and Plasmodium malariae. Malaria should be highly considered in patients with irregular fevers and a travel history. Most people contract malaria from being bitten by an infected mosquito from an endemic area. Other reported forms of transmission include blood transfusions, injection of drugs from contaminated syringes, perinatal transmission, and organ transplantation. Irregular fevers are seen in most patients with malaria. Other symptoms or clinical manifestations include anemia, headache, nausea, chills, lethargy, abdominal pain, and upper respiratory symptoms.

Infection with P. falciparum may lead to severe organ damage and death. Acute infection with P. falciparum may manifest as cerebral edema and encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, severe anemia, kidney failure, pulmonary edema, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death. The gold standard of diagnosis is the detection of the parasite on thick and thin blood smears.

Treatment depends on the severity, region, and particular parasite type. Uncomplicated malarial infections in Haiti, Dominican Republic, Central America, and areas of the Middle East may be treated with chloroquine phosphate. Chloroquine-resistant, uncomplicated malaria may be treated with quinine and doxycycline or proguanil-atovaquone. Complicated P. falciparum may be treated with intravenous artesunate. Primaquine may be used to treat the hepatic phases of P. ovale and P. vivax.



Chest X-ray (B) would not make the definitive diagnosis of malaria. In malaria, it may reveal pulmonary edema. It would be useful in ruling out pneumonia in the scenario above but would not confirm the more likely diagnosis of malaria.

Monospot testing (C) would be helpful in ruling in the diagnosis of mononucleosis. The clinical scenario above is more consistent with malaria.

Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test (D) is used to screen for syphilis. Some patients with malaria will have a false positive VDRL.

Question: A 56-year-old man presents to the ED with rapidly progressing pain and swelling of his right lower leg after a shark fishing trip the day prior. He states that he sustained a small cut on his leg from a large fishing hook that bled briefly but quickly stopped. His medical history includes cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C. Vital signs show a T of 38.9°C (102.0°F), BP of 86/52 mm Hg, HR of 118 bpm, and RR of 24/min. Examination shows diffuse soft tissue swelling and tenderness in the right leg with overlying hemorrhagic bullae. Which of the following is the most appropriate antimicrobial regimen to treat this patient’s most likely cause of infection?
ExplanationEN:
Vibrio vulnificus is a gram-negative, halophilic bacterium found in warm, brackish, or saltwater environments, most commonly along coastal regions such as the Gulf of Mexico. Infection can occur after ingestion of raw or undercooked seafood, particularly oysters, or following exposure of open wounds to seawater. Individuals with chronic liver disease, especially cirrhosis, are at significantly increased risk due to impaired iron metabolism and reduced immune defense. The organism thrives in high-iron environments, which may explain the heightened susceptibility and severity of infection among patients with liver dysfunction.

Clinically, V. vulnificus wound infections present within hours of exposure, with severe pain out of proportion to physical findings, rapidly progressive swelling, ecchymoses, and the formation of hemorrhagic bullae. Systemic toxicity with hypotension and multiorgan failure may develop quickly, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It can closely resemble necrotizing soft tissue infections, warranting prompt recognition and intervention. Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion in the appropriate epidemiologic setting, supported by culture of wound, blood, or tissue specimens.

Empiric treatment for V. vulnificus infection should begin as soon as it is suspected, with doxycycline 100 mg IV or PO twice daily plus a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours as the recommended regimen. Alternatives include a fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) alone in patients who cannot tolerate tetracyclines. Supportive care includes aggressive fluid resuscitation and early surgical consultation for debridement of necrotic tissue or fasciotomy if compartment syndrome is suspected. Delay in antibiotic initiation or surgical care is associated with high mortality, exceeding 50% in cases of sepsis or necrotizing fasciitis.



Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (A) is an appropriate regimen for V. cholerae and many community-acquired pneumonias but does not provide reliable coverage against V. vulnificus. In the context of severe cellulitis and sepsis after saltwater exposure, doxycycline combined with a third-generation cephalosporin is the recommended empiric treatment.

Ciprofloxacin with metronidazole (B) exhibits some activity against Vibrio species and anaerobes but is more suitable for polymicrobial intra-abdominal infections. Doxycycline with ceftriaxone provides superior targeted coverage and reduces mortality in severe V. vulnificus infections.

The standard regimen for Streptococcus pyogenes necrotizing soft tissue infections is penicillin G and clindamycin (D), but this is ineffective against V. vulnificus. The rapid progression of disease following seawater exposure in a patient with cirrhosis strongly suggests Vibrio infection, for which penicillin and clindamycin provide inadequate coverage.

Although broad-spectrum coverage with vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam (E) is commonly used for empiric treatment of severe cellulitis and necrotizing soft tissue infections, it does not reliably cover V. vulnificus. When marine exposure is part of the history, therapy should specifically include doxycycline and a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone.

Question: A 13-month-old boy presents with a rash that developed yesterday on his neck. His parent notes that he had a high fever for 3 days earlier in the week and resolved yesterday. The child has been a little fussier than usual but has otherwise been acting normally. On examination, he is afebrile. A diffuse maculopapular rash is noted on his face, trunk, and extremities. What is the likely cause of his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Roseola infantum, or sixth disease, is a benign febrile illness affecting children ages 6 months to 3 years. Human herpesvirus 6 is the most common cause of roseola. The illness starts with an abrupt onset of a high fever that lasts 3–5 days. During that time, the child may also have symptoms of malaise, conjunctival injection, inflammation of the tympanic membranes, or mild respiratory symptoms, but generally, the child is nontoxic in appearance despite the high fever. A key feature of the illness is that the rash starts when the fever resolves. The lesions are discrete, pink, blanching macules or maculopapules that start on the neck and trunk before spreading to the extremities and face. Roseola infantum is typically nonpruritic and lasts 1–2 days. No treatment is necessary.



Coxsackie virus (A) causes hand, foot, and mouth disease in children. Children present with low-grade fever, an oral enanthem consisting of small vesicular lesions on the oral mucosa, and a maculopapular or vesicular rash on the hands and feet. Hand, foot, and mouth disease may be complicated by dehydration due to oral pain and subsequent decrease in oral intake.

Parainfluenza virus (C) is implicated in a variety of respiratory infections and is the primary cause of croup in children.

Parvovirus B19 (D) is responsible for erythema infectiosum or fifth disease, a febrile illness affecting primarily school-aged children. After a prodrome of nonspecific symptoms of fever, malaise, coryza, and nausea, an erythematous malar rash appears with relative circumoral pallor, giving a slapped-cheek appearance.
