Question: A 34-year-old man presents to the ED with bilateral eyelid weakness and associated diplopia that began yesterday morning upon waking. Today, he noted weakness with his grip when attempting to eat breakfast and difficulty lifting his arms to dress. He has a history of polysubstance use and reports using intravenous fentanyl 2 days ago but otherwise has no chronic medical conditions and takes no daily medications. Physical examination reveals 5 mm pupils that are minimally reactive to light bilaterally, bilateral eyelid ptosis, dysarthric speech, and a weak gag reflex. There is no nystagmus. Upper extremity strength is 2/5 bilaterally, including shoulder abduction, biceps, triceps, and hand grip. Lower extremity strength testing shows 5/5 strength proximally and distally. Reflexes are 2+ throughout. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Botulism is a clinical syndrome caused by the anaerobic, spore-forming Clostridium botulinum bacteria commonly found in soil. There are several forms of botulism, such as wound-related botulism seen in this patient. Wound-related botulism occurs when a wound is contaminated with Clostridium botulinum (e.g., wounds contaminated by soil or intravenous drug use) and neurotoxin is produced in vivo. Infantile botulism occurs with Clostridial spore ingestion and subsequent gastrointestinal tract colonization with toxin release. Adult enteric botulism has a similar mechanism to infantile botulism, with toxin production occurring in the gastrointestinal tract, unlike food-borne botulism, in which the botulinum toxin is directly ingested via contaminated food. Inhalation botulism can occur if there is release in an act of bioterrorism.

Clinical features include symmetric cranial nerve palsies (e.g., symmetric dilated and nonreactive pupils) and symmetric descending weakness, though some patients may progress rapidly to experience respiratory arrest. Other generalized symptoms are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal cramping. Responsiveness and sensory functions are typically preserved. The initial diagnosis is made based on the history and physical examination. Additional testing, such as nerve conduction studies and electromyography, may aid in diagnostic uncertainty, with confirmatory findings including decreased compound muscle action potential amplitudes and rapid depletion of acetylcholine stores during repetitive nerve stimulation. Treatment includes supportive care, and human-derived botulinum immune globulin or botulinum antitoxin may be considered depending on the form of botulism.



Miller-Fisher syndrome (B) is an acute demyelinating peripheral nerve syndrome that presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and hyporeflexia or areflexia. It can be confused with botulism since the symptoms start near the head, but reflex testing can help differentiate the two entities.

Hypermagnesemia (C) may have inhibitor properties at calcium channels, leading to reduced voltage-gated calcium channel activity at the presynaptic terminal and impairing presynaptic acetylcholine release. Patients have diffuse muscle weakness and loss of deep tendon reflexes.

Hypocalcemia (D) can lead to reduced release of presynaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine secondary to reduced activity of the voltage-gated calcium channels that trigger their release. Like hypermagnesemia, resultant weakness from hypocalcemia is often generalized and does not follow a specific ascending or descending pattern.

Tick paralysis (E) occurs through tick-borne toxins that reduce presynaptic acetylcholine release, leading to fatigue, myalgias, muscle weakness, nystagmus, and ascending flaccid paralysis approximately 3–7 days after tick attachment.

Question: A 47-year-old man presents for evaluation of a whitish discoloration on his tongue for the last several days. He reports no fever or other systemic signs. Exam findings are seen in the image above. You are unable to scrape the base of the plaque off with a tongue depressor. Which of the following tests is likely to be positive?

Options.text: Gram stain demonstrating large, ovoid, gram-positive yeast

ExplanationEN:
This patient’s tongue demonstrates the white corrugated plaques of oral hairy leukoplakia. This is a disease of the lateral tongue caused by infection of the squamous epithelium with Epstein-Barr virus. Most commonly, the infection is localized to the lateral portion of the tongue, although in rare cases it may involve the floor of the mouth, palate, or buccal mucosa. Clinically, this may be difficult to differentiate from thrush caused by Candida. However, the lesions of oral hairy leukoplakia cannot be scraped off the surface. Although caused by Epstein-Barr, it is rarely seen in patients without HIV infection.



A positive anti-hepatitis C virus antibody (A) suggests hepatitis C. It remains unclear whether there is an association between hepatitis C and oral lichen planus. Oral lichen planus has a white, reticulated pattern commonly found on the buccal mucosa.

A Gram stain demonstrating large, ovoid, gram-positive yeast (B) is consistent with candidiasis, which can be confused with this patient’s findings but is not the correct diagnosis.

A potassium hydroxide prep (C) may also be used to identify Candida infections. On the prep, pseudohyphal elements will be seen microscopically.

A rapid streptococcal pharyngitis test (E) would not be positive in this individual. Streptococcal pharyngitis characteristically has a white exudate over the tonsils and posterior pharynx. When using this test diagnostically, it has high specificity but poor sensitivity, necessitating follow-up culture for negative rapid tests when suspicion is high.

Question: A 3-month-old vaccinated girl presents with a fever. She has no other symptoms. She has a rectal temperature of 39.2°C that began today. She is vigorous and appears well. The rest of her exam is unremarkable. Which of the following tests is most likely to reveal the source of this patient’s fever?
ExplanationEN:
A rectal route is the most reliable method to measure a temperature in infants, with a rectal temperature ≥ 38°C used by most clinicians to define a fever in infants. Axillary, temporal, and tympanic membrane measurements are not as dependable but should still be considered positive for a fever if > 38°C. Historically, parents were taught to add a degree to axillary measurements to compensate, as these are consistently lower than rectal temperatures, but this is not recommended, as axillary measurements vary too widely. Half of the patients with tactile fever have true fevers. Bundling should not be attributed as the cause of a fever in any infant. This will raise the skin temperature but does not raise the core temperature, especially when the ambient temperature is < 35°C and humidity is < 75%.

The most common cause of a fever without a source in young infants is a viral infection. While these can be serious, usually the severity is clinically apparent on physical exam. The most common invasive bacterial infection in infants > 60 days of age that is not apparent on a physical exam is a UTI. The University of Pittsburgh created a calculator that has outperformed other published guidelines and gives a likelihood of UTI based on age, maximum temperature, UTI history, sex, circumcision history, and fever duration. This calculator is a good reference to estimate the risk of a UTI in children < 2 years of age with a fever, but it should be noted that it is based on the patient population at the University of Pittsburgh. Other than possibly needing a urinalysis, appropriately immunized infants > 60 days of age who appear well and have a fever can be tested and treated based on history and physical exam findings alone.

Older studies before the conjugate vaccine era (the year 2000) show that children < 3 years old with a fever who do not have the currently available immunizations are at risk of occult bacteremia. Some experts recommend a more extensive workup in this group, including a CBC, urinalysis, urine culture, and serum procalcitonin. A blood culture should be sent if the white blood cell count is > 15,000/µL, and a chest X-ray should be obtained if it is > 20,000/µL. However, these more extensive workups are falling out of favor in more recent studies and guidelines.



A serum CBC (A) would show a WBC count, which can help to guide further testing in unimmunized children 2–36 months of age who have a fever, but it is not necessary for well-appearing immunized infants.

The prevalence of bacterial pneumonia has decreased enough in infants that obtaining a chest X-ray (B) is only necessary in immunized children with a fever who have abnormal focal lung sounds, respiratory distress, or hypoxemia. It is also much less likely than a UTI in infants with a fever.

Testing the CSF is not benign. False-positive or unclear results may lead to a longer hospital stay. A lumbar puncture is painful, costly to families, and causes a lot of parental anxiety. Obtaining a CSF cell count (C) is still encouraged in infants that do not appear well and in those at higher risk of meningitis, particularly those ≤ 28 days old with a fever. Bacterial meningitis is much less common than a UTI in any well-appearing vaccinated infant with a fever.

Question: A 35-year-old man who returned 1 week ago from a whitewater rafting trip in northern Chile presents with a severe headache, low-grade fever, chills, and severe myalgias. On exam, you note bilateral conjunctival redness without exudates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Leptospirosis is the most common bacterial zoonotic infection that occurs worldwide. It is found mostly in travelers in endemic regions of the world. It is caused by the spirochete Leptospira interrogans. Exposure generally occurs from contaminated freshwater (whitewater rafting in this case) where the spirochete infects through damaged or exposed mucous membranes. The acute phase lasts up to 1 week. Symptoms range from mild illness to abrupt high fever, chills, intense headache, and severe myalgias. A characteristic finding on exam is conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudates). Symptoms typically resolve after 1 week. Approximately 10% of those infected will go on to develop Weil syndrome (caused by circulating antibodies), which is a progression to aseptic meningitis, kidney failure, hepatitis, uveitis, rash, and circulatory collapse. Treatment reduces the severity and duration and may prevent the secondary phase. Mild disease can be treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline, although some prefer azithromycin as an alternative if the diagnosis is unclear. Doxycycline will also cover rickettsial disease like Rocky Mountain spotted fever. More severe cases require intravenous penicillin or ceftriaxone.



Coccidioidomycosis (A) is a pulmonary fungal infection found in the southwest United States.

Cysticercosis (B) (Taenia solium) is a cestode infection caused by contaminated pork. Findings consist of CNS cysts and new-onset seizures.

Leishmaniasis (C) is an intracellular protozoan transmitted by sand flies and generally occurs in Africa, Asia, the Mediterranean basin, and Central and South America. It most commonly presents as a cutaneous disease, but it may also involve the visceral organs (kala-azar, or black fever) and lead to weight loss, fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. Treatment is with antimonials, either sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate.

Question: A 21-year-old man presents to the ED after being bitten by an Ixodes scapularis tick on Cape Cod. He has no concerns and no rash. Based on history, you suspect that the tick was present for 48 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment plan?

Options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily x 21 days

ExplanationEN:
Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted to humans through tick bites from either Ixodes scapularis or Ixodes pacificus. The disease occurs throughout the United States but is endemic in the Northeast Coast, mid-Atlantic, and North Central states. Transmission of the spirochete occurs during feeding which happens approximately 2 days after attachment to the person. Early Lyme disease is characterized by a rash with some constitutional symptoms typical of a viral syndrome. The rash is erythema migrans, the classic “bull’s eye” or target lesion. This is an erythematous area associated with central clearing, sometimes with raised edges. Approximately 90% of patients with Lyme disease develop erythema migrans. A single dose of doxycycline 200 mg demonstrates effectiveness in preventing the development of Lyme disease if given within 72 hours and is recommended prophylactically in the setting of a known Ixodes tick exposure. The most recent CDC guidelines further note that prophylaxis should be given if the tick is estimated to have been attached for ≥ 36 hours (either by the degree of engorgement or time of exposure) and that the local rate of infection of ticks with B. burgdorferi is ≥ 20%. Nausea and vomiting are the most frequently cited adverse effects of treatment, occurring in up to 15% of patients.



Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM x 1 (A) is not used in prophylaxis. This medication and dose was previously used in the treatment of gonorrhea although the recommendation is now for 500 mg.

Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 14–21 days (B) is the recommended treatment course for early Lyme disease. In the case presented, the patient has no symptoms of early Lyme disease and should only receive a prophylactic dose.

Observation (D) for the development of a rash and constitutional symptoms was previously recommended until the evidence supporting a single dose of doxycycline.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fevers. Associated symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His symptoms started 3 days ago. He has no rash. He was hiking on the Appalachian Trail 2 weeks ago. His blood work shows leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Ehrlichiosis is a zoonotic, tick-borne infection caused by a number of gram-negative organisms that infect leukocytes. The Lone Star tick, Amblyomma americanum, is a primary vector for ehrlichiosis. The white-tailed deer is the main reservoir for this disease in the United States. Endemic areas include the southeast, southcentral, and mid-Atlantic regions of the United States. Symptoms develop 1–2 weeks after exposure to the tick bite. Patients present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, headache, malaise, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and arthralgia. A rash may be seen in about 30% of patients and is usually maculopapular. Laboratory studies will show leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases. Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by peripheral blood smear showing colonies of Ehrlichia ewingii within white blood cells. Lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase will be elevated as well. Treatment is with doxycycline. Complications may include kidney failure, respiratory failure, and encephalitis, although the majority of patients recover. Due to leukopenia, patients may present with opportunistic infections such as herpes simplex virus, candidiasis, and aspergillosis.



Hanta fever (B) is a zoonotic disease caused by the hantavirus. The deer mouse is the carrier and secretes the virus in feces, saliva, and urine. The virus is inhaled by humans and causes cardiopulmonary collapse similar to acute respiratory distress syndrome. The mortality rate can be as high as 60%.

Lyme disease (C) is also a tick-borne illness that initially causes erythema migrans, a circular erythematous plaque that has central clearing. As the disease progresses, patients may develop fever, adenopathy, cardiac abnormalities, neuropathy, and arthritis. Atrioventricular blocks and bilateral facial palsy are complications that can be seen in patients with Lyme disease.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever (D)is another tick-borne illness that presents with nonspecific generalized symptoms. The rash in Rocky Mountain spotted fever can help identify the disease as it involves the palms and soles and spreads inward to the torso.

Question: An 80-year-old woman presents from the local nursing facility with altered mental status. She is febrile, tachycardic, and hypotensive. Following adequate fluid resuscitation, she continues to be hypotensive, and the decision is made to initiate vasopressors. Which of the following is the most appropriate vasopressor for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Sepsis is a syndrome of dysregulated host response to an infectious agent, commonly resulting in end-organ dysfunction and significant morbidity and mortality. Sepsis is the most common cause of death in both medical and traumatic intensive care units worldwide. There is no gold standard or clearly outlined clinical criteria to define sepsis, though the use of the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is prevalent in clinical practice. Current guidelines for the management of sepsis recommend the continuous administration of crystalloid fluids as long as hemodynamic factors continue to improve. If the administration of fluids fails to achieve a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mm Hg, the use of vasoactive agents is recommended, with norepinephrine being the vasopressor of choice in septic patients. Norepinephrine is favored because of its dual alpha and beta effects, resulting in vasoconstriction as well as inotropy. Furthermore, its side effect profile is more favorable as it is less prone to cause dysrhythmias. In addition to hemodynamic resuscitation, prompt and aggressive source control is of utmost importance in the treatment of sepsis. This can be achieved through the administration of antimicrobials and, in some cases, through surgical intervention.



Dobutamine (A) is an inotropic agent with primarily beta-1 effects. It does not cause vasoconstriction and may actually result in worsening hypotension. It may be used in cardiogenic shock but is not a preferred agent in septic patients.

Dopamine (B) is a vasopressor with dose-dependent effects. It has fallen out of favor as a vasopressor in sepsis due to its propensity to produce cardiac tachydysrhythmias.

Vasopressin (D) is used as a second-line agent in treating shock in sepsis because trials have failed to show its benefit over norepinephrine as a first-line agent in septic shock.

Question: A 45-day-old boy presents to the emergency department with a fever and a cough that began yesterday. He was born at 38 weeks gestation at home, his mother did not receive prenatal care, and he was not given any immunizations. His temperature is 38.2°C, heart rate is 168 bpm, respiratory rate is 60/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. He has diffuse and moderate rhonchi and is head bobbing on exam. Which of the following is the reason this patient should be excluded from the use of the 2021 American Academy of Pediatrics guideline for febrile infants?

Options.text: He has a gestational age of 38 weeks at birth

ExplanationEN:
In 2021, the American Academy of Pediatrics published an updated guideline on the care of infants 8–60 days old with a fever (rectal temperature ≥ 38°C or 100.4°F). The guideline gives the clinician several options in the care of an infant with a fever. The options are supported by literature, but the guideline authors acknowledge that due to varying opinions on the level of acceptable risk and a changing bacteriology landscape, clinicians may have to deviate from them.

Since the risk of serious bacterial infection drops as infants age, separate guidelines were created for ages 8–21 days, 22–28 days, and 29–60 days. Infants should be well-appearing and should not have a clear source of infection to use the guideline. Infants who are 29–60 days old should have a urinalysis with culture, blood culture, and measurement of inflammatory markers. Elevated inflammatory markers include a temperature > 38.5°C, a C-reactive protein > 20 mg/L, an absolute neutrophil count > 5,200/µL (or > 4,000 if procalcitonin is available), and a procalcitonin > 0.5 ng/mL. Those with normal inflammatory markers do not need a lumbar puncture or antibiotics but should have close follow-up. Those with an identified UTI and normal inflammatory markers do not need a lumbar puncture and can be treated at home with oral antibiotics and follow-up within 24 hours. Most patients with elevated inflammatory markers should be given a dose of intravenous antibiotics. This group might benefit from a lumbar puncture, but even without one, they may be admitted for monitoring or observed closely at home.

Patients born at home who did not receive antibiotics or who have diarrhea, mild upper respiratory symptoms, or otitis media can be included in the guideline. Patients who should be excluded from the guideline are infants who were born before 37 weeks gestation, infants who have had a prenatal course complicated by maternal fever, and infants who show signs of clinical bronchiolitis, have signs of herpes simplex virus, have a focal bacterial infection, have had surgery, have congenital malformations, have received immunizations within the last 48 hours, or are medically fragile.

Several large studies have found no cases of meningitis or bacteremia in infants with a fever and clinical bronchiolitis. These infants, like this patient, should be treated for bronchiolitis with less focus on the fever. Some studies show a similar rate of UTIs in those with clinical bronchiolitis, so a urinalysis may still be indicated.



The 2021 guideline for infants 8–60 days old with a fever can be used in infants who are missing vaccinations (C) or were born at home (D).

The guideline can also be used for infants born after 37 weeks gestation (A), but those born before 37 weeks should be excluded.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 2-month-old term female infant is brought to an exam room in the emergency department, limp and apneic. She is febrile to 39.0°C, has a heart rate of 190 bpm, and a systolic blood pressure of 59 mm Hg. She has extremely delayed capillary refill and cold extremities. The patient is intubated and intravenous access is successful and she is given three 20 mL/kg normal saline boluses without improvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN:
Sepsis is a difficult-to-define but well-recognized systemic dysfunction of the inflammatory system in response to infection. It is defined as an abnormal temperature or leukocyte count and tachycardia (or bradycardia in children < 1 year) or tachypnea in the presence of infection. Septic shock includes cardiovascular organ dysfunction, as seen in this patient, despite administration of ≥ 40 mL/kg isotonic saline. Risk factors for septic shock include age < 1 month, serious injury, immunosuppression, large surgical incisions, in-dwelling lines, urinary tract abnormalities, and chronic, debilitating medical conditions. Most children in septic shock will present with “cold” shock, like this patient, with delayed capillary refill and poor extremity perfusion from vasoconstriction, high systemic vascular resistance, and low cardiac output. Initial treatment is with rapid infusion of normal saline in 20 mL/kg increments (up to three times) and prompt antibiotic administration. When septic shock is refractory to intravenous fluid and antibiotic administration, “cold” shock is best treated with intravenous epinephrine. Inotrope administration should not be delayed for central line placement and may be administered via a peripheral line while a central line is obtained.



Patients with fluid-refractory hypotensive shock should continue to receive fluid resuscitation unless there are signs of fluid overload. However, fluid administration with more than three intravenous normal saline boluses (A) without inotrope administration is associated with poorer outcomes.

Intravenous dopamine (B) was recommended as the first-line agent in children and is still considered an acceptable alternative. However, recent data suggests these patients are at higher risk of dysrhythmia and death when compared to epinephrine.

Intravenous norepinephrine (D) is the appropriate treatment for “warm” shock recognized by bounding pulses, pink extremities, and a flash capillary refill not seen in our patient.

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a new onset rash. She has no significant medical history but is known to the emergency department for the treatment of frequent sexually transmitted infections. She reports no preceding genital ulcers. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination is remarkable for the rash noted above, which appears pustular in nature. Which of the answer options below is the most appropriate treatment for her condition?

Options.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM daily for 2 days followed by cefixime BID for 1 week plus doxycycline BID for 1 week
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with azithromycin 1 g PO
Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once

CorrectAnswer: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM daily for 2 days followed by cefixime BID for 1 week plus doxycycline BID for 1 week
ExplanationEN:
Gonorrhea is the second most common sexually transmitted infection (STI). It is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which is a gram-negative diplococcus. Most gonococcal infections in women are asymptomatic and often coexist with chlamydial infections. Symptoms, when present, include lower abdominal discomfort and mucopurulent cervicitis. In contrast to women, men are typically symptomatic with dysuria and profuse, purulent penile discharge. Complications related to gonorrheal infections include ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and pelvic inflammatory disease. If left untreated, disseminated gonococcal infections can occur and present with petechiae or pustular acral skin lesions with an erythematous base, asymmetric arthralgias, tenosynovitis or septic arthritis, and fevers or malaise. This patient has a rash consistent with disseminated gonococcal infection and requires treatment with ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV daily for 2 days followed by cefixime BID for a minimum of 1 week. Other treatment options include ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily. Cefotaxime or ceftizoxime could be also used instead. Empiric treatment for chlamydia should also be given with doxycycline in nonpregnant patients. Azithromycin can be used for chlamydia coverage in pregnant patients. Patients with gonococcal arthritis rarely require surgical drainage and irrigation of the affected joints.



Acyclovir 5% topical (A) is a potential treatment option for herpetic whitlow. However, this has not been shown to improve outcomes or shorten the duration of the lesion and thus is not commonly used.

Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with azithromycin 1 g PO (C) is the standard treatment for cervicitis pregnancy, not disseminated gonococcal infections.

Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once (D) is the treatment of choice for secondary syphilis, which classically presents with painless lesions on the soles and palms of patients after the resolution of a painless genital lesion.

Question: Which of the following patients with flu is paired with the appropriate treatment?

Options.text: Amantadine: 9-year-old boy with 24 hours of symptoms
Baloxavir: 89-year-old man requiring hospitalization and 36 hours of symptoms
Oseltamivir: 24-year-old pregnant woman with 72 hours of symptoms
Zanamivir: 17-year-old girl with an asthma exacerbation and 24 hours of symptoms

CorrectAnswer: Oseltamivir: 24-year-old pregnant woman with 72 hours of symptoms
ExplanationEN:
Influenza is a highly contagious respiratory illness caused by the influenza virus. Cases tend to be seasonal, and influenza season extends throughout the fall and winter when dry air facilitates the spread of droplets that carry the infection. Patients can transmit the virus as early as 1 day before the onset of symptoms and up to 1 week after symptoms appear. The incubation period is 1–4 days. Those at increased risk of complications from influenza include patients < 5 years old or > 65 years old, nursing home residents, pregnant patients (up to 2 weeks postpartum), and those with COPD, asthma, congestive heart failure, diabetes, or immunosuppression. The full list of risk factors for influenza complications is extensive and can be located on the CDC website.

Symptoms of influenza include fever, cough, rhinorrhea, sore throat, headache, myalgias, vomiting, and diarrhea. Several rapid tests are available that can yield a result in as little as 15 minutes but with variable sensitivity. For example, rapid influenza diagnostic tests have a sensitivity of 50–70%, while molecular assays have a sensitivity > 90%. Once diagnosed, infected patients should be isolated with droplet precautions.

Antiviral treatment should be considered for otherwise healthy patients with symptoms for < 48 hours. However, antiviral therapy should be initiated as soon as possible for all patients with a risk for complications. Antiviral therapy has been shown to be beneficial in patients who require hospitalization and for those with severe or complicated illness, even in the presence of up to 5 days of symptoms. Similarly, pregnant patients treated with oseltamivir show benefit with up to 4 days of symptoms. Antiviral prophylaxis should be instituted for patients with < 48 hours of exposure to an infected individual and extended for 1 week after exposure ends. Vaccination is readily available and recommended for patients > 6 months of age.



Amantadine (A) and rimantadine are adamantane antivirals. They only have activity against influenza A, with no activity against influenza B. However, recent influenza strains have resistance to these medications and so they are not recommended for treatment.

Baloxavir (B) is not recommended in patients with severe disease (e.g., hospitalized patients) due to a lack of data in this population.

Zanamivir (D) is contraindicated in patients with underlying respiratory disease, such as COPD and asthma, owing to the risk of bronchospasm.

Question: Which of the following infections is most likely to lead to microcytic anemia?
ExplanationEN:
Necator americanus, a type of hookworm, causes infection when its larvae penetrate intact skin, through bare feet, in contact with feces-contaminated soil. The infection is most prevalent in warm, humid climates such as the tropics and the Southeastern United States. After skin penetration, larvae enter the bloodstream, travel to the lungs, ascend the trachea, are swallowed, and mature into adult worms in the small intestine. There, they attach to the intestinal mucosa and feed on host blood, leading to blood loss over time.

Clinical manifestations vary depending on the stage and intensity of the infection. Initial symptoms may include a localized pruritic erythematous rash at the site of entry, known as “ground itch.” Pulmonary migration may cause a dry cough, wheezing, and fever. Once the worms reach the gastrointestinal tract, patients may experience intermittent diarrhea, abdominal pain (especially epigastric), anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Chronic blood loss from mucosal attachment can lead to iron deficiency anemia, particularly in children, resulting in pallor, fatigue, and developmental delays.

Laboratory findings include eosinophilia and, in cases of significant blood loss, hypochromic microcytic anemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by identification of characteristic eggs in stool samples.

Treatment involves anthelmintic therapy, with albendazole or mebendazole being the drugs of choice. Iron supplementation may be needed for patients with anemia. Preventive strategies include improving sanitation and wearing protective footwear in endemic areas.



Entamoeba histolytica (A) infection is usually asymptomatic. In a minority of patients, it can result in abdominal cramps, bloody diarrhea, fever, and microcytic anemia. It is often described as amebic dysentery and is associated with the development of a liver abscess.

Enterobiasis (pinworm) (B) infection is most commonly seen in children and is the most common cause of pruritus ani. It does not produce laboratory abnormalities.

Isospora belli (C) is a parasitic infection most commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS. It causes profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting.

Question: Which of the following patients would have the lowest risk of contracting HIV?

Options.text: A medical staff member with an 18-gauge needlestick injury sustained while caring for a patient who uses intravenous drugs
A patient who had receptive penile-oral intercourse with a partner with HIV
A patient who has a sexual partner with HIV and takes no pre-exposure prophylaxis before intercourse
A patient who was penetrated vaginally by an unknown assailant

CorrectAnswer: A patient who had receptive penile-oral intercourse with a partner with HIV
ExplanationEN:
Oral intercourse (especially penile-oral contact) is associated with a significantly lower risk of HIV transmission compared to other forms of sexual or percutaneous exposures. While not zero, the estimated transmission risk per act of receptive oral intercourse is extremely low (generally < 0.01%) and is considered the least risky of common exposure types. Factors such as the absence of open sores or bleeding in the mouth further reduce the risk. In contrast, other exposure types, such as vaginal intercourse, receptive anal intercourse, or percutaneous injuries, carry much higher transmission probabilities.

The most effective strategies for reducing oral transmission risk include avoiding ejaculation in the mouth, treating any active oral infections, using barrier protection (e.g., condoms or dental dams), and ensuring the partner with HIV is on antiretroviral therapy with a suppressed viral load. These steps further reduce the already low baseline risk and are consistent with HIV prevention guidelines.



Needlestick injuries (A) involving hollow-bore needles carry a high HIV transmission risk. The estimated risk per exposure is approximately 0.3%, especially if the source patient is known or presumed to have HIV due to high-risk behavior such as injection drug use.

Intercourse with a partner with known HIV (C) is one of the highest-risk behaviors for HIV acquisition. The risk is significantly influenced by the type of intercourse (anal > vaginal > oral) and the partner’s viral load. In the absence of prophylaxis, barrier protection, or viral suppression, this exposure carries a markedly high risk.

Receptive vaginal intercourse (D) carries an estimated HIV transmission risk of about 0.08% per act. This risk may be higher in the context of sexual assault due to mucosal injury and inability to use barrier protection. If the assailant’s HIV status is unknown and considered high-risk, postexposure prophylaxis is indicated.

Question: A 36-year-old man with a several-day history of flu-like illness, nausea, vomiting, and shortness of breath presents to an ED in New Mexico. He states his symptoms began approximately 1 week after cleaning out his barn, where he noticed a large amount of mouse droppings. Which organ system most commonly fails in this illness, resulting in death?
ExplanationEN:
Hantavirus, a viral zoonosis caused in North America by the Sin Nombre virus. It is transmitted by a number of rodent types, with the deer mouse being the most common vector in the Southwest US. It is transmitted by inhalation of dried rodent excrement or, less commonly, by a rodent bite. It begins with a prodromal phase lasting 3–4 days with vague flu-like symptoms (typically including dyspnea without cough) and rapidly develops into hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, characterized by pulmonary edema, hypoxia, and hypotension. The mortality rate historically was as high as 60%, but with early recognition, this has improved to 30%. Treatment is supportive.



Multiple organ failure, including cardiac (A), hepatic (B), and neurologic (C) dysfunction, may also develop but are not the most common cause of death after infection by hantavirus.

Although typically presenting as acute kidney (E) insufficiency in the rest of the world, the hantavirus seen in the US most commonly results in death due to pulmonary complications.

Question: A 37-year-old man with a history of human immunodeficiency virus with a previous CD4+ count of 90 cells/µL presents to the emergency department feeling poorly with a mild headache, neck pain with stiffness, and nausea. He has not been taking his medications. Physical examination shows vital signs of HR 97 bpm, BP 133/70 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and T 99.0℉ (37.2ºC). The patient has noticeable meningismus. Head CT performed is unremarkable. Lumbar puncture is performed during the workup. The opening pressure is 40 cm H2O and results show WBC 75 cells/µL with 20% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, glucose 24 mg/dL, protein 290 mg/dL, and negative Gram stain. What further cerebrospinal fluid analysis should be performed to confirm the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Patients who are immunocompromised with entities such as AIDS are at increased risk for serious infections including meningitis. This is particularly true in patients with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/µL. Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS and ultimately affects 10% of patients with AIDS. As with other opportunistic infections, highly active antiretroviral therapy has dramatically decreased the incidence of cryptococcal meningitis. However, it remains a leading cause of mortality for people with HIV infection. It usually affects patients with a CD4+ count < 100 cells/µL. A lumbar puncture is diagnostic; elevated opening pressures are typical; and evidence of encapsulated yeast forms on staining of the cerebrospinal fluid with India ink can be found. Other CSF findings include elevated protein, low glucose, and moderately elevated WBC but < 500 cells/µL. Treatment is with amphotericin B and flucytosine.



Tuberculous, syphilitic, and aseptic meningitis caused by viruses such as herpes simplex virus can also be found in AIDS patients, but are not as common as cryptococcal meningitis. Tuberculous meningitis would be suggested by a positive acid-fast bacilli test (A). Herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR (B) would be required to diagnose aseptic meningitis due to HSV. A Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test (D) would help to diagnose secondary syphilis causing meningitis. The lumbar puncture results in this patient are not consistent with aseptic or bacterial meningitis. The results are similar to those found in tuberculous meningitis but, as already mentioned, tuberculous meningitis would not be the most likely cause of symptoms in this patient.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with agitation, confusion, hydrophobia, and left arm pain several weeks after returning home from a mission trip to Uganda, where he was bitten by a stray dog. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with late findings of rabies infection. Rabies is caused by a Lyssavirus that is transmitted through saliva, usually after a bite. After inoculation, the virus replicates locally in muscle, then enters peripheral nerves and travels to the central nervous system via retrograde axonal transport. It exclusively affects mammals and once clinical signs begin, the disease is nearly always fatal. Rabies is considered a neglected disease, with most cases occurring in Africa and Asia, particularly in rural communities with poor access to health care.

Rabies often begins with a nonspecific syndrome, then progresses to encephalitis or myelitis. Hydrophobia is virtually exclusive to rabies and is the key clue. Other clues are the dog bite, pain at the healed wound site, agitation, and confusion. There are two clinical syndromes associated with active rabies infection: furious and paralytic rabies. Furious rabies, as seen in this patient, includes hyperesthesia at the site of the initial trauma, progressive agitation, confusion, hallucinations, aerophobia, and hydrophobia. Paralytic rabies includes regional paresis of the muscles at the site of initial trauma with a progression to full-body paralysis. Both clinical syndromes can last 2–10 days and eventually progress to coma and death. Once symptoms begin, treatment is primarily supportive.

Rabies is vaccine preventable, and vaccinating dogs is the most cost-effective strategy for preventing rabies in people. Preexposure vaccination in humans is also effective and recommended for travel to endemic areas or for occupations at high risk of rabies exposure. Postexposure prophylaxis prevents virus entry into the central nervous system and consists of local wound care as soon as possible after exposure, rabies vaccination, and the administration of rabies immune globulin. Once neurological symptoms have developed, the disease is fatal, and supportive and palliative care should be discussed.



Acyclovir (A) is used for illnesses such as herpes simplex encephalitis, but this patient’s presentation is more consistent with rabies. The stem includes a stray dog bite in Uganda, pain at the healed wound site, agitation, confusion, and hydrophobia, which are classic clues for rabies encephalitis. Rabies should be considered in patients with encephalitis plus an animal exposure history, especially when neurologic findings include hydrophobia, dysphagia, or autonomic features. Herpes simplex encephalitis can cause fever, altered mental status, and seizures, but it does not characteristically cause hydrophobia or exposure-site paresthesias after a dog bite.

Human rabies immune globulin (B) is part of postexposure prophylaxis after exposure to rabies, but is not a treatment for symptomatic rabies. This approach is intended to prevent the virus from reaching the central nervous system. This boy already has hydrophobia and encephalopathy, so the window for immune globulin has passed.

Rabies vaccination (C) is also part of postexposure prophylaxis and is highly effective when given promptly after exposure and before clinical disease develops. Once a patient has confusion, agitation, and hydrophobia, vaccination is no longer effective as treatment. In this case, supportive critical care is the best next step because the patient already has clinical rabies.

Ribavirin (D) may sound attractive because it is an antiviral, but this patient’s illness is clinically rabies rather than a viral syndrome for which ribavirin would be considered. The combination of encephalopathy, hydrophobia, agitation, and pain at the site of a prior dog bite strongly points to symptomatic rabies. Ribavirin instead is recommended for the treatment of respiratory syncytial virus in immunocompromised patients, viral hemorrhagic fever, or a chronic hepatitis C infection.

Question: A 62-year-old man presents with fever, productive cough, and progressive confusion. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. He weighs 65 kg, and vital signs include T of 39.2°C (102.6°F), BP of 78/46 mm Hg, HR of 128 bpm, RR of 28/min, and SpO2 of 90% on room air. Capillary refill is delayed, and the skin is cool. Bedside lactate level is 5.1 mmol/L. The patient is given a 1 L bolus of lactated Ringer solution, and repeat BP is 85/53 mm Hg. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s current condition?

Options.text: Administer additional 1 L of lactated Ringer solution
Place a central venous catheter for central venous pressure monitoring and ScvO 2 measurement

CorrectAnswer: Administer additional 1 L of lactated Ringer solution
ExplanationEN:
Septic shock is defined as sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors despite adequate fluid resuscitation, along with serum lactate > 2 mmol/L. While no definite indicators for a source of infection are given in this patient, his presentation, including findings of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (e.g., fever, tachycardia), cough, and hemodynamic instability, prompts suspicion of sepsis with a potential pulmonary source. These features, along with findings of systemic hypoperfusion (e.g., elevated lactate, cool skin), require prompt recognition in order to institute appropriate resuscitative measures.

The primary pathophysiologic mechanism in septic shock is profound vasodilation driven by inflammatory mediators, resulting in reduced systemic vascular resistance and impaired organ perfusion. Initial resuscitative measures should include crystalloid fluids at a bolus dose of 30 mL/kg to alleviate relative and absolute hypovolemia. Given that this patient has received only 1 L of fluids, an additional 1 L should be administered to reach the recommended bolus volume. However, once preload is optimized, the vasodilation typically does not respond to further fluid resuscitation and vasopressors may be required. Norepinephrine is the recommended first-line vasopressor for septic shock because it increases systemic vascular resistance through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction while having minimal effect on heart rate, with vasopressin typically used as the second agent, when required. Starting norepinephrine early in appropriate patients improves survival and reduces the risk of complications (e.g., fluid overload).

In addition to appropriate empiric antimicrobials, prompt fluid resuscitation and early vasopressor therapy are essential because delays in restoring perfusion can lead to acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, and multisystem organ dysfunction. As soon as a patient with septic shock demonstrates persistent hypotension after appropriate fluid resuscitation, norepinephrine should be initiated. While this patient has not been adequately fluid resuscitated yet, the clinician should have a low threshold for starting vasopressors should the patient’s hemodynamics not improve with additional fluids.



Relative adrenal insufficiency is a potential feature of septic shock and is treated with IV hydrocortisone (B) but is not an initial step in resuscitation. IV fluids and vasopressors should be implemented first.

Vasopressors, such as norepinephrine (C) and vasopressin (D), may be required in patients who remain hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation but should not begin until after the patient has received adequate crystalloid fluids at 30 mL/kg.

Central venous pressure and ScvO2 monitoring (E) can help guide ongoing resuscitation in patients with various types of shock, but are not recommended as primary resuscitative endpoints in the initial management of septic shock. Thus, the next steps in resuscitating this patient should not be delayed for the placement of a central venous catheter.

Question:
A 35-year-old man diagnosed with HIV 5 years ago and who is not currently taking antiretroviral therapy presents to the emergency department with persistent, watery diarrhea associated with abdominal cramps and occasional nausea. The frequency of bowel movements is around six to eight times per day, and the diarrhea is not improving with over-the-counter antidiarrheal medications. Vital signs are blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 100 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, temperature of 38°C, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. The patient appears exhausted and malnourished, and there is mild abdominal tenderness on palpation. Laboratory findings show

Hemoglobin: 10.2 g/dL

Hematocrit: 32%

White blood cell count: 3,200/µL

Platelets: 150,000/µL

CD4 cell count: 80/µL

A fecal stool sample is shown above. What is the most likely cause of the diarrhea in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Cryptosporidiosis is a common and often severe diarrheal disease caused by the protozoan parasite Cryptosporidium, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV infection and a CD4 count < 100/µL. Cryptosporidiosis can lead to persistent and severe diarrhea, which is a hallmark symptom. The diarrhea is often watery and can last for an extended period, contributing to dehydration and malnutrition. Other associated symptoms may include abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Laboratory findings in individuals with Cryptosporidium diarrhea in the context of HIV infection may reveal the presence of the parasite in stool samples. Microscopic examination of stool samples using special staining techniques can help identify Cryptosporidium oocysts. In modified Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain, the oocysts stain red or pink and are usually 4–6 micrometers in diameter. Other diagnostic methods like polymerase chain reaction may be employed for more sensitive and specific detection. Treatment for Cryptosporidium diarrhea involves managing the symptoms and addressing the underlying immune deficiency.



Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (B) infection in those with HIV and CD4 < 100/µL will often present with persistent diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and weight loss. CMV can involve various organ systems, leading to complications such as colitis, retinitis, and pneumonitis. Diagnostic tests may include CMV PCR or viral cultures. In addition to gastrointestinal symptoms, CMV can cause systemic manifestations, such as fever and fatigue. Ophthalmologic examination may be necessary to assess for CMV retinitis, a severe complication. In this case, the absence of characteristic ophthalmologic findings and the presence of oocytes in the stool exam make Cryptosporidium more likely.

Giardia (C) infection presents with watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, bloating, and weight loss and can look similar to cryptosporidiosis. Laboratory findings may show peripheral eosinophilia, although this is not always present. Stool studies, such as microscopy or enzyme immunoassays, can detect Giardia lamblia cysts or trophozoites. Stool exams for both Giardia and Cryptosporidium involve microscopic examination of stained stool samples. They differ in the specific targets they are looking for: Giardia cysts or trophozoites are pear-shaped and approximately 10–20 micrometers in diameter, and Cryptosporidium oocysts are smaller and round.

Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) (D) often occurs when the CD4 T-cell count drops to < 50/µL. This opportunistic infection manifests as chronic, debilitating diarrhea and is accompanied by symptoms such as abdominal pain, weight loss, and fever. Laboratory findings typically reveal acid-fast bacilli in stool specimens, aiding in the diagnosis.

Question: A 39-year-old woman presents to the ED with rigors. She smokes marijuana and uses intravenous heroin. She has been living in a nearby shelter and became ill 2 weeks ago with a cough and night sweats. Her vital signs are T 101.4°F (38.6°C), BP 109/73 mm Hg, HR 110 bpm, RR 20/minute, and SpO2 94% on room air. She appears thin and has asymmetric breath sounds without wheezes. Her chest X-ray is shown above. Her condition is most likely a result of which of the following?
ExplanationEN:
Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the acid-fast bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is a non-spore-forming, non-motile, aerobic intracellular organism with humans being the sole known reservoir. The diagnosis of TB is not always straightforward, and clinicians should have a high index of suspicion in patients with significant risk factors. These include immigration from a TB-prevalent country, being without housing, poverty, substance use disorder, institutional living settings, urban overcrowding, or concomitant infection with HIV/AIDS. Any vague systemic symptoms or fever of unknown etiology may be TB. Constitutional symptoms are common, including weight loss, fever, weakness, fatigue, anorexia, headache, and chills. However, these are not specific and are seen in many other conditions. Night sweats are classic with TB because the fever usually develops later in the day and defervesces during the night while sleeping. Most patients will present with a cough that may be dry to mucopurulent and may include hemoptysis. A chest X-ray is useful in evaluating pulmonary TB. The classic finding is an upper lobar cavitary infiltrate, but these infiltrates can occur in any lobe. However, the additional finding of enlarged hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes strongly suggests the diagnosis. Sputum analysis for acid-fast bacilli should be obtained. The most common first-line agents for treating TB include a multidrug regimen of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.



Long-term tobacco use (B) can lead to lung cancer, which can present with similar signs and symptoms of TB such as cough, weight loss, hemoptysis, and lobar opacities on chest X-ray. However, there is no mention of tobacco use and the patient has other features that suggest TB: living in a shelter, fever, night sweats, and worrisome chest X-ray findings.

Noncaseating granulomas (C) occur with sarcoidosis, a systemic disease of unclear inflammatory etiology that primarily affects the lungs. Chest X-ray findings include pulmonary fibrosis with hilar lymphadenopathy.

Septic valvular embolization (D) from bacterial endocarditis can present similarly to pulmonary TB. Patients may report chest pain or shortness of breath and have other findings of endocarditis such as splinter nail hemorrhages, a new cardiac murmur, petechiae, Osler nodes, and Roth spots which this patient lacks. Additionally, the chest X-ray shown is more consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a non-spore-forming bacterium, so spore inhalation (E) is not the cause of this patient's condition.

Question: A 68-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with headache and right eye pain for 2 days. She reports the feeling of a foreign body sensation in her right eye with redness and blurry vision. On physical examination, you notice some blotchy redness on her forehead and the tip of her nose. She reports pain when you touch her skin in those areas. Her vision is 20/70 in her right eye and 20/50 in her left eye. Her right conjunctiva is injected, and she has photophobia. On fluorescein examination, you notice the above findings. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms characteristic of herpes zoster ophthalmicus, a serious condition of the eye. The condition is linked to varicella zoster virus reactivation within the trigeminal ganglion. Acute symptoms usually begin with headache, malaise, and fever with unilateral pain or hypesthesia in the affected eye and side of the forehead and face. Vesicular facial lesions on the nose are associated with a high risk of ocular involvement, as this signifies involvement of the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve. This nerve also innervates the globe. Patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus can develop conjunctivitis, episcleritis, or keratitis that may present with a pseudodendritic lesion. Early diagnosis and treatment is required to prevent vision loss. The standard approach is to treat with oral antiviral therapy with either acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. In addition, steroid ophthalmic drops help reduce inflammation, but they should only be initiated in conjunction with ophthalmology consultation. Patients who are immunocompromised and those with severe disease should be started on intravenous antivirals in conjunction with emergent ophthalmology consultation.



Oral cephalexin (B) would be the appropriate treatment for a patient presenting with facial cellulitis. This patient clearly has an ocular problem in addition to facial lesions.

Topical acyclovir plus topical cyclopentolate (C) has historically been thought to have better penetration of the globe and would be the recommended therapy for patients with herpes simplex keratitis. However, patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus require oral antiviral therapy. Cyclopentolate would only be used for additional pain management, especially for patients with iritis.

Topical ciprofloxacin (D) would be an appropriate therapy for patients with a bacterial corneal ulcer. The clinician should recognize the photo in this question as a pseudodendritic lesion and not a typical corneal ulcer, which would appear as a sharply demarcated lesion with gray, ragged borders.

Question: A 4-day-old infant born of a normal full-term pregnancy, labor, and delivery presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of 102.2°F (39°C) fever, poor feeding, irritability, and fitful sleeping. Parental and infant history is unremarkable, with the exception that the parent had a urinary tract infection at the end of their second trimester, which was not cultured, and low-grade fever after discharge from the hospital on day 2 after delivery. Physical examination of the neonate demonstrates pallor, mild jaundice, tachycardia, episodes of apnea, difficult arousal, and a bulging fontanel. Peripheral white blood cell count is 2,000/µL, mostly lymphocytes. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid demonstrates elevated protein, low glucose, very elevated white blood cell count (98% neutrophils), and a few red blood cells. Gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid reveals gram-positive cocci in chains. What is the most likely cause of the neonate's sepsis and meningitis?
ExplanationEN:
Streptococcus agalactiae, or group B Streptococcus (GBS), is currently the major cause of perinatal bacterial infection in the United States. As is the usual case with Escherichia coli and other bacteria that cause perinatal infections, the organism colonizes the birth canal and passes to the infant during labor and delivery. However, less frequently, there is also hematogenous spread from the mother.

Maternal manifestations of GBS include endometritis, chorioamnionitis, and urinary tract infections. Current recommendations to reduce the incidence of and mortality from GBS include screening with vaginal and rectal cultures at the end of the second trimester and between 35 and 37 weeks gestation. Women with positive cultures, a GBS urinary tract infection, or GBS bacteria should receive intrapartum antimicrobial prophylaxis with intravenous ampicillin.



Enterococcus spp (A), primarily E. faecalis and E. faecium, are increasingly recognized as significant pathogens in neonatal sepsis. These gram-positive bacteria can be part of the normal intestinal flora but may become opportunistic under certain conditions, leading to infection. Neonatal sepsis due to enterococci often occurs in premature infants or those with compromised immune systems.

E. coli (B), the second most common cause of perinatal infection, is even less likely because the Gram stain demonstrates gram-positive organisms in chains.

Currently, perinatal staphylococcal (C) infection is a rare cause of perinatal sepsis and meningitis, as is Streptococcus pyogenes (E), group A Streptococcus (GAS). It should be remembered that GAS was a major cause of puerperal fever and mortality prior to the discovery by Dr. Semmelweis in 1847 that hand washing between deliveries almost eliminated “childbed fever.”

Question:
What is the difference between early-onset and late-onset neonatal infections?

Reveal Answer:
Early-onset refers to infections in which symptoms develop within 7 days of birth (although some indicate within 72 hours after birth) and are acquired before or during delivery. Late-onset refers to infections that begin after 7 days of life and are caused by organisms from the hospital or community.

Question: A 3-year-old child presents with a harsh raspy cough that has progressed over 24 hours. On exam, they are somewhat agitated with moderate subcostal retractions. They receive nebulized racemic epinephrine and oral dexamethasone and are observed for 3 hours. Which of the following assessment areas would most likely help the clinician determine that this patient has significant ongoing disease and requires additional treatment and possible hospital admission?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with moderately severe croup. Oral dexamethasone and nebulized racemic epinephrine are appropriate treatments for this level of severity. A period of observation for 2–4 hours is typically recommended following treatment due to the short half-life of nebulized epinephrine and the time needed for oral dexamethasone to begin to exert its effect.

Patients with moderately severe croup, despite the initial treatment, may continue to exhibit good distal air exchange and normal pulse oximetry and may remain playful and interactive, displaying a relatively normal level of consciousness even though they have severe disease and might require further treatment and hospital admission.

Decisions regarding disposition are best guided by the clinical assessment of work of breathing and degree of stridor. This is shown well by the use of the Westley croup severity score. Patients who continue to exhibit signs of stridor (especially at rest), along with increased work of breathing, may need additional treatment and a more extended period of observation.



Patients with moderate croup and severe croup will have a frequent barking cough (A), and this assessment is unlikely to change the patient’s disposition plan.

While persistently abnormal vital signs in any situation should encourage pause before a final disposition plan, the heart rate (B) is not typically used to determine whether a patient with croup requires further inpatient care or can be sent home.

Patients with impending respiratory failure can exhibit signs of cyanosis. However, patients with severe croup can still have a normal oxygen saturation (C) in the setting of increased work of breathing. Thus, a work of breathing assessment is more likely to aid the clinician in disposition decisions.

Question: A 22-year-old man who works as a landscaper presents to the ED with a rash that began approximately 3 weeks ago. He says it started with a single bump on his right forearm that has been oozing fluid. He subsequently developed lesions tracking up the arm. The patient reports no joint pain, decreased range of movement, fever, numbness, or weakness. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, oxygen saturation of 96% on room air, and temperature of 98.6°F (37.0°C). On exam, the patient has an area of redness overlying a small papule and a rash spreading proximally, as depicted in the image above. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has sporotrichosis, a fungal infection transmitted by inoculation into the skin with the fungus Sporothrix schenckii. It is most commonly seen in gardeners, farmers, landscapers, and other agricultural workers. The infection is classically associated with a seemingly innocuous puncture wound from a rose bush thorn.

The characteristic rash begins with an ulcer or papule and then spreads proximally along lymphatic channels with skip lesions. Lymphocutaneous involvement, as depicted in the picture, is the most common manifestation. Treatment for this is 3–6 months of itraconazole.



Acyclovir (A) can be used for cutaneous zoster, which looks similar to this infection. However, zoster occurs in a dermatomal distribution and presents primarily with vesicles on an erythematous base.

Doxycycline (C) can be used to treat skin infections caused by Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, such as cellulitis. These infections typically present with acute onset of erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain and may be accompanied by systemic signs such as fever. Doxycycline is also used in the treatment of acne vulgaris, rosacea, and Lyme disease, which may present with erythema migrans.

Hydrocortisone (D) is used for various inflammatory and allergic conditions, such as eczema. It is not indicated for the treatment of sporotrichosis.

Permethrin (E) is commonly used in the treatment of scabies, an infection that can be identified by visualization of burrowing mites that appear as linear or S-shaped tracks in the skin, often accompanied by rows of small pimple-like insect bites. Scabies skin lesions are often found in crevices of the body, such as on the webs of fingers and toes, around the genital area, and under the breasts.

Question: A 26-day-old boy presents with a fever. He was born at 39 weeks gestation, and his mother received no prenatal care. He was not immunized at birth. He has a rectal temperature of 38.1°C (100.6°F), and his exam is otherwise unremarkable. He appears well and is feeding normally. Blood and urine cultures are obtained. The parents are not interested in him being admitted to the hospital. Which of the following additional conditions are recommended to be met to discharge this patient, according to the 2021 American Academy of Pediatrics febrile infant guidelines?

Options.text: Cerebral spinal fluid testing shows no pleocytosis
Nasal viral testing detects an alternative source of the fever
Serum white blood cell counts are within the reference range
Urinalysis identifies the source of the fever as a urinary tract infection

CorrectAnswer: Cerebral spinal fluid testing shows no pleocytosis
ExplanationEN:
The American Academy of Pediatrics released an updated guideline for the care of febrile children between 8 and 60 days of life in 2021. The authors recognize that the creation of the guideline was challenging due to a number of factors, including changing bacteriology, disagreements in what is considered an acceptable risk, and advances in testing. The guideline is expected to change as more data is obtained, especially around viral testing. It should only be used in infants who appear well and can be used if there are mild respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, otitis media, or positive viral testing results.

The new guideline should not be used in infants born at < 37 weeks gestation, those < 2 weeks old whose course was complicated by a maternal fever or infection, those with an obvious focal bacterial infection, those with clinical bronchiolitis, those who had surgery or previous infection, those with chromosomal or congenital abnormalities, those who are medically fragile, or those who received immunizations in the last 48 hours.

The previous guideline recommended that all infants < 60 days of life with a fever undergo testing and cultures of blood, urine, and cerebral spinal fluid. The new guideline recognizes that the risk of bacteremia and meningitis drops as infants age. Infants aged ≤ 21 days still should have blood, serum, and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Infants aged > 28 days do not necessarily need a lumbar puncture. Infants 22–28 days old are in a period during which the risk is dropping but not yet low enough to comfortably limit testing or monitoring. Parents who wish to avoid a lumbar puncture in this age group may do so, but if this is the case, it is recommended that they be monitored in the hospital. Parents who wish to avoid hospitalization in this group may do so, but only if a lumbar puncture is performed and the cerebrospinal fluid testing shows no pleocytosis. Such patients should be given parenteral antimicrobials and be reevaluated within 24 hours. If the lumbar puncture is traumatic or uninterpretable, current recommendations are that the patient be monitored in the hospital.



Nasal viral testing (B) is a relatively new test, and data regarding how it can best be used is still evolving. Currently, nasal viral testing results do not change testing recommendations. Instead of nasal viral testing, remember that children < 60 days with a fever who have clinical bronchiolitis are excluded from the guidelines and may not need a lumbar puncture, regardless of whether there is a positive viral test result.

A patient 21–28 days old with a fever should have normal inflammatory markers to be considered eligible for discharge. A C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and an absolute neutrophil count are considered inflammatory markers, not the white blood cell count (C). A C-reactive protein > 20 mg/L, absolute neutrophil count > 4,000/µL (or > 5,200/µL if procalcitonin is unavailable), procalcitonin > 0.5 ng/mL, or a fever > 38.5°C (101.3°F) are considered abnormal inflammatory markers. When present, this increases the risk of a serious bacterial infection in this age group, and a lumbar puncture should be performed. However, if these inflammatory markers are within reference range and the lumbar puncture shows no pleocytosis, these infants can be monitored at home or in the hospital. Caution is still advised in this group when a lumbar puncture is not performed, as many infants with bacterial meningitis will have inflammatory markers within the reference range.

A positive urinalysis (D) result showing a urinary tract infection does not change whether the infant in this age group needs a lumbar puncture or can be monitored at home.

Question: A 75-year-old man presents from the local nursing facility with severe lower extremity pain. His vital signs on arrival are T 39.3℃, HR 160 bpm, BP 72/40 mm Hg, and RR 40/min. Physical examination shows erythema and crepitus in the lower extremity. An X-ray of the extremity is shown above. Which of the following antibiotics is indicated for direct inhibition of toxin synthesis?
ExplanationEN:
Gas gangrene is a form of necrotizing soft tissue infection that is characterized by extensive soft tissue necrosis, systemic symptoms, and high morbidity and mortality. Risk factors for the development of gas gangrene include advanced age, diabetes mellitus, immunocompromise, alcohol use disorder, chronic cardiac or kidney disease, chronic skin infections, and intravenous drug use. Gas gangrene is categorized into types based on the infecting organism. Type I infections are more common and are polymicrobial, while type II infections are monomicrobial and more likely to occur in healthy hosts with a history of trauma. Necrotizing soft tissue infections spread rapidly and aggressively due to the release of bacterial exotoxins, leading to thrombosis, tissue ischemia, and liquefactive necrosis. Physical examination findings include erythema and tenderness out of proportion to physical exam findings. Crepitus is often present but is not necessary for diagnosis. An X-ray may show subcutaneous emphysema. Vital signs may show tachycardia out of proportion to fever. Signs of hemodynamic compromise should be treated aggressively with fluid resuscitation and vasopressors as needed. Patients should be covered with broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting both gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria as well as both aerobic and anaerobic species. Clindamycin should be included in the regimen due to its direct inhibition of bacterial exotoxin production, an important component of the pathogenesis of necrotizing fasciitis. Surgical consultation should be obtained as soon as possible. While the initiation of antibiotics is important, antibiotics alone are rarely effective, and immediate surgical debridement is the cornerstone of care.



Cefepime (A) is a fourth-generation cephalosporin with activity against a large spectrum of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas species. Like other cephalosporins, it works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall production through the prevention of peptidoglycan crosslinking. It has no effect on exotoxin production. Piperacillin-tazobactam (C) is a combination medication of an extended-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotic with a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It has activity against a large spectrum of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas species. It works through the inhibition of cell wall synthesis but has no effect on the production of bacterial exotoxins. Vancomycin (D) has activity against a large spectrum of gram-positive bacteria and, like cephalosporins and beta-lactam antibiotics, works through inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis. It, likewise, has no effect on bacterial exotoxin production.

Albuterol (A) does not routinely play a role in the treatment of croup.

Question: A 75-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis, and remote history of IV drug use presents with 3 days of progressive erythema and tenderness of the right lower extremity. Temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), heart rate is 114 bpm, respirations are 18/min, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 98%. He is awake, alert, and mildly diaphoretic but otherwise in no acute distress. Physical exam reveals a large area of indurated, erythematous skin along the medial aspect of his right calf that is warm and tender to palpation. In the center, you find an area of swelling and fluctuance. Which of the following is the most effective therapy against the suspected microorganism?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a soft tissue infection and systemic signs of toxicity. Despite fever and tachycardia, he appears to be hemodynamically stable. The presence of swelling and fluctuance suggests an underlying abscess. The patient has multiple risk factors for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), including a history of IV drug use and ongoing hemodialysis.

Optimal management of an abscess with overlying cellulitis involves incision and drainage of the abscess pocket, in addition to antibiotic coverage. Treatment with parenteral antibiotics is preferred over oral therapy in this case, due to vital sign abnormalities and the rapid progression and involvement of a large area of skin. IV vancomycin is the antibiotic of choice for the management of MRSA. Alternative antibiotics include daptomycin and linezolid.

Of note, if a patient is at risk for endocarditis, parenteral antibiotics are no longer required in patient's such as this prior to incision. Purulent material should be sent for culture and susceptibility testing. Patients with vital sign abnormalities should be admitted to the hospital.



Ceftriaxone (A) is a third-generation cephalosporin that has greater activity against gram-negative organisms and is not as effective against MRSA. Fifth-generation cephalosporins, such as ceftaroline, have broad-spectrum activity and can be used if the staphylococcal infection has reduced susceptibility to first-line agents (vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin).

MRSA soft tissue infections exhibit varying resistance patterns to fluoroquinolones, so levofloxacin (B) is not a good option. Furthermore, increasing evidence of significant adverse events (such as aortic dissection) with systemic fluoroquinolone use makes them a less attractive option if there are other treatment options available.

Clindamycin (D) is an effective antimicrobial agent against gram-positive and anaerobic organisms. It is an efficacious agent for treating MRSA infection, however, oral therapy is reserved for mild infection. This patient’s systemic symptoms warrant parenteral therapy.

Question: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of alcohol-related cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with rapid worsening of what he states began as a small cut on his hand 6 hours ago. The patient cut his hand shucking oysters, and his hand now appears diffusely erythematous with the presence of multiple hemorrhagic bullae. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
Vibrio vulnifcus is a free-living bacteria that occupies salty marine environments and causes illness in humans predominantly via wound exposure through marine animals (fish, oysters, and shellfish) or aquatic recreation. V. vulnificus can also cause primary septicemia (i.e., septicemia without an obvious source, such as a wound) in patients who have consumed raw oysters fished from V. vulnificus rich environments. Patients with underlying liver pathologyare at increased risk for serious infection. Serious infection often results in a clinical picture equivalent to necrotizing fasciitis. Thus, prompt recognition and management with appropriate surgical consultation is essential.



Pseudomonas aeruginosa (A) is associated with aquatic environments but would not present with the presence of multiple hemorrhagic bullae.

Similarly, a Staphylococcus aureus (B) infection would likely present as mild cellulitis and does not fit the context of this patient’s oyster exposure.

While Streptococcus pyogenes (C) is a known cause of necrotizing fasciitis, this patient’s clinical history and presentation are more consistent with a V. vulnificus exposure.

Question: A 32-year-old woman presents with acute onset of low-grade fever, pruritic rash, and joint pain in her hands and feet after returning from a trip to Brazil last week. Her vital signs are unremarkable other than a temperature of 100.2°F (37.9ºC). She has an erythematous maculopapular rash on the face, trunk, and extremities, as well as conjunctival injection without discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Zika virus is a flavivirus primarily transmitted by mosquitoes. It may also be transmitted from mother to fetus, as well as via sex, blood transfusion, and laboratory exposure. In 2018, there was an outbreak in South America, the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands. The incubation period lasts from 2 to 14 days, and approximately 20% of infected patients develop clinical symptoms. Low-grade fever; an erythematous, pruritic, maculopapular rash; arthralgias primarily affecting the small joints of the hands and feet; and nonpurulent conjunctivitis are all common symptoms. The presence of two or more of these findings in a patient with an appropriate exposure history is consistent with Zika virus infection. Diagnosis can be confirmed with reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction for Zika virus RNA or serology. Management is symptomatic with hydration and acetaminophen. Zika virus infection has been associated with congenital microcephaly, pregnancy loss, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.



Dengue fever (A) is also transmitted by a mosquito vector and causes similar symptoms to Zika virus. However, high fever, headache, and severe myalgias are more typical, while conjunctivitis is not.

Malaria (B) is characterized by cyclic fevers, nausea, myalgias, and anemia.

Yellow fever (C) presents with liver dysfunction, kidney failure, and coagulopathy. It is also transmitted by a mosquito vector and is found in the subSaharan region of Africa and South America.
