Question: A 35-year-old man with recently diagnosed human immunodeficiency syndrome presents for evaluation due to a positive tuberculin skin test of 5 mm. The patient feels well and reports no recent cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or hemoptysis. His CD4 count is 650/µL. He reports no previous diagnosis of tuberculosis. A sputum culture sent earlier was negative. His chest radiograph is normal. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months
Repeat chest radiograph and sputum culture in 3 months

ExplanationEN:
Tuberculosis (TB) is the world’s second leading cause of infectious death, with more than 8 million people acquiring active TB each year. There was a reemergence of tuberculosis in the 1980s due in large part to the epidemic of HIV/AIDS. Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis is typically contained by host defenses and can remain in a latent or suppressed state for a prolonged period of time. Patients with latent tuberculosis are those who are found to have a positive tuberculin skin test but who lack any findings of active disease. Depending on host factors, latent disease can develop into active disease. Patients at increased risk of developing active disease include those with HIV infection (at any stage), immunocompromised patients, including patients who have had a transplant or are undergoing chemotherapy, patients with lymphoma, leukemia, or head and neck cancer, and dialysis patients. As this patient has a positive tuberculin skin test but has no evidence of active disease, he has latent tuberculosis that should be treated as he is at increased risk of developing reactivation tuberculosis. The preferred treatment option, in this case, would be isoniazid and rifampin daily for 3 months. Oral rifampin for 4 months is another alternative.



Previously, isoniazid for 9 months (B) was the recommended treatment for latent tuberculosis, and it still remains an alternative regimen. However, patients have less toxicity and are more likely to complete treatment with dual isoniazid and rifampin therapy for 3 months. Therefore, this would not be the best treatment option. The emergence of multidrug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis guides the initial management of patients newly diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis. One of the basic principles in the treatment of active tuberculosis is that regimens must include multiple drugs to which the possible resistant organism is susceptible. First-line agents include isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol daily for 2 months (C), followed by isoniazid and rifampin for an additional 4 months. As this patient with HIV is at high risk for developing active tuberculosis, withholding treatment in favor of a repeat chest radiograph and sputum culture in 3 months (D) is not recommended. Persons with latent tuberculosis with no known risk factors for conversion to active disease should be considered for treatment if they have a positive tuberculosis blood test (e.g., interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)) or if the tuberculin skin test result was ≥ 15 mm.

Question: A biological attack has struck a nearby metropolitan area, and cases of smallpox have begun to develop outside the containment zone. A 52-year-old woman presents due to concern for exposure. She notes an episode of fever, myalgias, and vomiting starting 1 week ago. What is the earliest mucocutaneous finding expected to develop if her symptoms are due to smallpox infection?
ExplanationEN:
Smallpox, caused by variola virus, has a characteristic clinical progression that begins with a prodrome, followed by a staged rash. The prodromal phase lasts 2–4 days and includes high fever, malaise, severe myalgias, headache, and sometimes vomiting. This patient describes fever, myalgias, and vomiting 1 week ago, consistent with this initial viremic phase. The rash begins shortly after the fever resolves or begins to improve.

The earliest mucocutaneous manifestation of smallpox is an oral enanthem. Lesions first appear on the mucous membranes of the oropharynx and tongue as erythematous macules that rapidly progress to vesicles and ulcerations. These mucosal lesions precede the cutaneous rash by approximately 24 hours and are associated with high viral shedding, contributing to transmission. The presence of oral enanthem marks the transition from prodrome to eruptive phase.

After the enanthem, a centrifugal rash develops, starting as macules on the face and distal extremities, including the palms and soles, before spreading centrally. These lesions evolve synchronously from macules to papules, then vesicles and pustules. Thus, oral enanthem is the first visible lesion in the progression of smallpox.



Centrifugal macules (A) describe the initial cutaneous rash pattern of smallpox, in which lesions are more concentrated on the face and distal extremities than on the trunk. Although this is a classic feature of smallpox, these macules occur after the oral enanthem.

Forehead papules (B) represent a later stage of lesion evolution. Cutaneous lesions in smallpox progress in a predictable and synchronous manner: macules, then papules, then vesicles, and finally pustules and crusts. Papules specifically occur after the macular stage and after the enanthem has already developed. Thus, forehead papules would not be the earliest finding in the disease course.

Thoracic vesicles (D) are a subsequent stage in the evolution of the rash and develop after macules and papules. In addition, smallpox has a centrifugal distribution, meaning lesions are more prominent on the face and distal extremities than on the trunk. A thoracic-predominant vesicular eruption would be less typical and would also occur later in the disease progression.

One Step Further
Question:
How does the rash differ in smallpox versus chickenpox?

Reveal Answer:
In smallpox, lesions are in the same stage of development and spread centrifugally (face and extremities more than the trunk), whereas in varicella, lesions are in different stages simultaneously and are more concentrated on the trunk (centripetal distribution).

Question: A 36-year-old woman presents to the ED with a rash that began 1 day ago. She also reports lightheadedness and muscle aches. Her medical history includes chronic rhinosinusitis for which she underwent endoscopic sinus surgery 5 days ago. Vital signs are a T of 39.3°C (102.7°F), BP of 82/48 mm Hg, HR of 124 bpm, RR of 22/min, and SpO2 of 96% on room air. Physical examination reveals diffuse, confluent, blanching erythema over the trunk and extremities with conjunctival injection and bright red oral mucosa. Nasal packing is in place in both nares. Laboratory studies show elevated creatinine, elevated transaminases, and thrombocytopenia. Which is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s fever, hypotension, erythematous rash, and multiorgan dysfunction following recent nasal surgery with retained packing are highly suspicious for staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a systemic inflammatory syndrome classically associated with toxigenic variants of Staphylococcus aureus, though it has also been described with Streptococcus species. It was historically associated with high-absorbency tampons, though these have since been removed from the market, and now roughly one-half of cases are related to nonmenstrual causes. Prominent nonmenstrual risk factors include nasal packing, surgical wound infections, viral infections (e.g., varicella, influenza A), cancer, and chronic cardiopulmonary disease. Its pathogenesis involves exotoxins that function as superantigens, inducing massive, nonspecific T-cell activation and cytokine release, which causes increased capillary permeability, systemic hypoperfusion, and multiorgan dysfunction.

There are no clinical or diagnostic criteria with sufficient sensitivity or specificity to diagnose TSS. Overall clinical suspicion should guide diagnosis and treatment. Clinical suspicion should be high in patients presenting with fever, diffuse erythroderma, and hypotension, in the setting of appropriate risk factors, such as this patient’s nasal packing. A variety of laboratory derangements due to underlying organ dysfunction may be seen, including abnormal liver function tests (e.g., elevated transaminases, hypoalbuminemia, hyperbilirubinemia), kidney impairment, and hematologic abnormalities such as leukocytosis, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Blood cultures are positive in many cases of streptococcal disease but are usually negative in cases caused by S. aureus. The CDC has developed a case definition that includes both clinical and laboratory criteria, but it is intended for epidemiologic surveillance and should not be used for clinical diagnosis.

Treatment of TSS should consist of resuscitation, antibiotic therapy, and source control via surgical debridement or foreign body removal, if needed. Patients should be given IV crystalloid solutions for initial fluid resuscitation, with vasoactive infusions (e.g., norepinephrine) given to those who remain hypotensive despite fluid administration. Recommendations vary by source, but linezolid with clindamycin is a commonly recommended first-line regimen, as both agents suppress bacterial exotoxin production and provide coverage against methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). While challenging to ascertain during the initial evaluation, patients in whom infection with methicillin-sensitive S. aureus is known or suspected may be treated with nafcillin or oxacillin plus clindamycin. Without prompt recognition and intervention, TSS carries significant morbidity and mortality with complications, including new or progressing organ dysfunction, disseminated intravascular coagulation, shock, and death.



Ceftriaxone and azithromycin (A) is an appropriate regimen for community-acquired pneumonia but does not cover S. aureus effectively, particularly MRSA, and lacks antitoxin activity. This patient’s postoperative status, hypotension, and diffuse erythematous rash are more consistent with staphylococcal TSS than a respiratory infection.

Doxycycline and ceftriaxone (B) covers Rickettsia and Neisseria gonorrhoeae but lacks adequate S. aureus coverage and antitoxin suppression. This patient has no tick exposure or pelvic findings. Rather, the presence of nasal packing and shock suggests staphylococcal TSS.

While nafcillin and clindamycin (D) is an effective regimen for methicillin-sensitive S. aureus, MRSA cannot be initially excluded in most patients and this regimen is usually inappropriately narrow until later in the patient’s treatment course.

The treatment of choice for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is penicillin G and clindamycin (E), but this regimen lacks coverage against S. aureus and is, thus, inadequate in this case.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an abrasion on his right hand and painful lymph nodes in his right axilla. The patient sustained several scratches from his kitten on his hand. He has no other concerns and otherwise feels well. Exam reveals a small area of erythema over a scratch on his hand. Tender lymph nodes are palpated in the right axillary region. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
ExplanationEN:
Cat-scratch disease is most commonly caused after a scratch from a kitten leads to infection with Bartonella henselae. Patients may present with a small scratch, erythema (or signs of cellulitis), and tender lymphadenopathy proximal to the scratch. The diagnosis is generally made clinically. First-line treatment is azithromycin. Other treatments may include rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or ciprofloxacin second-line.



Eikenella corrodens (B) is a common cause of infection in human and animal bites. These bites require copious irrigation and are generally left open to avoid infection. Antibiotics should be administered for all human and animal bites, and amoxicillin-clavulanate is the preferred agent.

Staphylococcus aureus (C) is a common cause of cellulitis. Any patient with cellulitis and risk factors for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus should be started on antibiotics that cover both this organism and other common causes of cellulitis, such as Streptococcus pyogenes (D). The history of a cat scratch in this patient should guide the clinician toward B. henselae.

Question: An 8-year-old unvaccinated boy presents with a fever for 3 days. He had a fever, cough, and nasal congestion 2 days ago, and this morning, he developed a rash that started on his face. Vital signs are a T of 102.1°F, HR of 124 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 99%. Examination reveals red maculopapular lesions over the face, neck, and chest. You also note conjunctivitis. He otherwise appears well. What is the best course of action?

Options.text: Isolation of the patient from family

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms consistent with measles and requires supportive care. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness spread by infectious droplets. The incubation period for the virus is 10–14 days, and patients are contagious from 2 days prior to the onset of symptoms to 4 days after the rash appears. The rash is typically preceded by malaise and fever, which increases daily for 5–6 days. Cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis begin about 24 hours after the onset of fever. Koplik spots, a pathognomonic finding, appear on the second day of illness. They are small, bright red spots with blue-white centers appearing on the buccal mucosa. A rash follows on day 4 or 5 of the illness. The rash is characterized by maculopapular lesions beginning on the forehead and face and spreading to the trunk, arms, and legs.

Treatment for measles focuses on supportive care and recognition of bacterial complications. Isolation of infected patients is often not helpful, as exposure usually occurs prior to identification of the disease. Additionally, patients are not contagious after the rash has been present for 5 days. Administration of human immune serum globulin can modify the course of disease if given within 6 days of exposure. Live measles virus vaccine may prevent measles if given within 72 hours of exposure. The CDC recommends vitamin A for all patients with severe disease who require hospitalization.



Amoxicillin (A) is used to treat streptococcal infections, such as scarlet fever. Patients with scarlet fever have a sandpaper-like rash made up of small papules starting in the armpits and groin and spreading to the trunk. It is associated with circumoral pallor and Pastia lines.

Ceftriaxone (B) may be helpful if post-measles bacterial pneumonia is suspected. Otherwise, it does not play a role in treatment.

Doxycycline (C) is the treatment of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which is characterized by a rash that spreads centrally from the extremities.

Isolation (D) is likely to be unhelpful, as the family has already been exposed during the infectious period.

Question: Which of the following best describes the classic presentation of botulism?

Options.text: Cranial nerve palsies and descending motor weakness

CorrectAnswer: Cranial nerve palsies and descending motor weakness
ExplanationEN:
Botulism is a rare life-threatening neuroparalytic syndrome caused by Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin. Clostridium botulinum is a gram-positive, rod-shaped, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacterium that is found on vegetables, fruits, seafood, and in soil. When appropriate environmental conditions are present, including restricted oxygen exposure, low-acidity water, and temperatures between 25°C and 37°C, the spores germinate and grow into toxin-producing bacilli.

Botulinum neurotoxin targets motor and sensory neurons and blocks cholinergic neuromuscular innervation of striated and smooth muscle. Although still rare, the most common form of botulism is infant botulism. Most cases are thought to result from ingestion of environmental dust and soil containing Clostridium botulinum spores. Patients classically present with cranial nerve palsies and descending motor weakness. Neurologic symptoms will be symmetric, and the patient will remain responsive. No sensory deficits will be reported with the exception of blurred vision. Heart rate and blood pressure will be normal, and the patient will not have a fever. Clinicians must have a clinical suspicion for the illness to make a diagnosis. The diagnosis can be confirmed by the identification of toxin in serum, stool, vomitus, or food sources. Management includes close monitoring, as half of patients will develop respiratory symptoms requiring intubation due to diaphragm paralysis. Antitoxin is the main therapeutic option. Patients with wound botulism should have appropriate debridement.



A patient presenting with ascending paresthesias and motor weakness (A) would be typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome or potentially tick paralysis. A patient presenting with miosis, ptosis,and anhidrosis (C) is classic for Horner syndrome. Horner syndrome can be caused by a variety of illnesses including multiple sclerosis, tumors, encephalitis, trauma, cluster headache, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and carotid artery aneurysm. A unilateral seventh cranial nerve palsy (D) would be found in a patient presenting with Bell palsy, not botulism.

Should patients with suspected infant or food-acquired botulism be treated with antibiotics?

Reveal Answer:
No, because intraluminal lysis of bacteria increases the amount of toxin available for absorption.

Question: A 2-day-old infant presents to the emergency department with fever, poor feeding, and irritability. She was born at home at 38 weeks gestation. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen associated with this patient's illness?
ExplanationEN:
Neonatal sepsis can be classified as either early onset or late onset. Early onset sepsis typically develops within 7 days (some still use 72 hours) of birth and is due to vertical transmission of infection from the maternal genital tract or amniotic fluid to the infant. Risk factors for development include maternal colonization of group B streptococcus (especially if untreated during labor), premature rupture of membranes, prolonged rupture of membranes, prematurity, and maternal urinary tract infection. The most common pathogen associated with early onset neonatal sepsis is group B Streptococcus. Other frequently implicated pathogens include Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and coagulase-positive Staphylococcus. Infants may present with subtle, nonspecific findings such as irritability, poor feeding, jaundice, tachypnea, fever, and signs of septic shock. Infants presenting with signs and symptoms concerning for early onset sepsis should undergo a full diagnostic evaluation, including complete blood count, blood cultures, urinalysis, urine culture, and lumbar puncture. A chest radiograph is indicated if respiratory findings are present. Appropriate empiric antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin and gentamicin) should be started while awaiting culture results.



Enterococcus (A) is more commonly seen in neonatal sepsis in premature infants. It is unlikely in otherwise healthy-term infants. Listeria monocytogenes (C) is a less commonly implicated pathogen and is more likely seen during outbreaks of listeriosis. Staphylococcus aureus (D) is more commonly associated with late onset neonatal sepsis (i.e., presenting after 7 days [some still use 72 hours]). Late onset sepsis is the result of horizontal transmission from caregivers or the environment to the infant.

Question: Which of the following findings on history or physical examination is most consistent with Rocky Mountain spotted fever?
ExplanationEN:
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne illness caused by infection with Rickettsia rickettsii. The disease is most prevalent in the southeastern United States and is transmitted primarily by the American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis) and the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni). After introduction into the host, R. rickettsii invades the vascular endothelial cells, which leads to direct damage of the cells, increased vascular permeability, and activation of clotting factors. The host response to the infection also plays a role in the clinical manifestations of the disease. The vast majority of patients present with a fever and rash. The rash typically starts on the second to fourth days of the illness as a blanching erythematous macular rash that starts on the wrist and ankles. It spreads centripetally to involve the extremities and trunk. The rash becomes maculopapular and, eventually, petechial in appearance. The lesions may occasionally coalesce to form large ecchymotic areas.



Ascending flaccid paralysis (A) is characteristic of tick paralysis. Caused by a neurotoxin that is released by an attached tick, patients present 4–7 days after the tick attaches with ascending paralysis, ataxia, and loss of deep tendon reflexes. Symptoms improve within hours after removing the offending tick.

Colorado tick fever is a tick-borne viral infection with flu-like symptoms of fever, headache, myalgias, and nausea. A key characteristic of the infection is a biphasic fever (B), in which patients have symptoms for 2–3 days which resolve, only to recur a few days later. Treatment is supportive.

Prominent lymphadenopathy (D) is a key feature of tularemia which is caused by Francisella tularensis. The most common form of tularemia also involves ulcerations at the site of inoculation and fever. The treatment of choice is streptomycin.

Question: A 54-year-old man with a history of HIV and recent CD4 count of 85 presents with headache for 3 days. The patient’s sister says that he has been increasingly confused over the last 3 days. While in the Emergency Department, he has a seizure which resolves spontaneously. Electrolytes are within normal limits. A CT scan is performed and is shown above. Which of the following medication regimens should be given?
ExplanationEN:
The patient has toxoplasmosis, an opportunistic infection caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Patients at risk are those who are immunocompromised or have CD4 counts less than 100. Patients experience headache, confusion, lethargy and seizures. CT scan of the head reveals multiple, subcortical, ring-enhancing lesions. The lesions are usually present on non-contrast enhanced CT, but if clinical suspicion is high, a CT with contrast should be performed to increase detection. Definitive diagnosis requires a brain biopsy, however, treatment is recommended in patients with a compatible clinical presentation and CT findings. Empiric treatment for toxoplasmosis is pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin. CNS lymphoma also causes ring-enhancing lesions in patients with AIDS. However, the lesions are usually solitary and located in the periventricular white matter. In addition, symptoms in these patients are usually gradually progressive over months rather than days as in this patient.



Amphotericin B (A) is the treatment for cryptococcal meningitis. In this condition, the head CT is usually normal, and a lumbar puncture demonstrates leukocytosis and a positive cryptococcal antigen.

Ganciclovir and foscarnet (B) combination therapy is the treatment for CMV retinitis or encephalitis. CMV encephalitis usually causes multifocal micronodules and ventriculoencephalitis on MRI.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) may be used if the patient is unable to tolerate oral therapy, but the patient must be transitioned to the above therapy once able to tolerate oral treatment.

Question: A 17-year-old girl presents with the above rash a week after hiking in the woods. She reports no tick bite. She otherwise has no symptoms. What management is indicated?

Options.text: Cephalexin 500 mg three times a day for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 3 weeks
No treatment while awaiting diagnostic testing

CorrectAnswer: Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 3 weeks
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with erythema migrans, the typical rash seen in early Lyme disease. Lyme disease is an illness caused by the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria from a tick and is the most common tick-borne disease in the US, Canada, and Europe. The common vector is Ixodes scapularis. Transmission from tick to person requires attachment and feeding for > 48 hours. Thus, early removal of ticks can prevent transmission.

Typically, erythema migrans presents 7–10 days after infection and is preceded by nonspecific constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise, fatigue). Approximately 90% of patients report the presence of the rash. The rash begins as a small papule at the site of infection and gradually expands (1–2 cm/day). Typically, the rash will have central clearing, but this is not universal. Further hematogenous spread of B. burgdorferi can cause numerous symptoms, including arthralgias, neurologic manifestations, and heart block.

The diagnosis of Lyme disease is based primarily on clinical features, but serologic or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing can be used to confirm the diagnosis. Prompt treatment of early manifestations can both shorten symptom duration and prevent progression to later disease stages. Early Lyme disease should be treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg by mouth twice a day for 14–21 days. Amoxicillin and cefuroxime are alternatives to doxycycline. A negative pregnancy test should be obtained in all female patients of reproductive age before starting doxycycline.



Ceftriaxone (A) is a third-generation cephalosporin that should be used in patients with Lyme meningitis, moderate to severe cardiac manifestations, or arthritis.

Cephalexin (B) is not used in the treatment of Lyme disease. It is a good option for treating conditions such as cellulitis and other soft tissue skin infections not caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Chloramphenicol (C) is an alternative to ceftriaxone in the treatment of Lyme meningitis.

Withholding treatment while waiting for diagnostic testing (E) is not recommended because the diagnosis should be made clinically, and both serologic and ELISA tests have less-than-perfect sensitivity and specificity.

Question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with rash, fever, headache, and diffuse joint pain. He has a history of sickle cell anemia. On physical exam, his cheeks appear bright red. This infection places the patient at risk of developing which of the following serious complications?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with erythema infectiosum, better known as fifth disease. It is classically a mild illness caused by parvovirus B19. It typically occurs in school-aged children in the spring and winter months. Viremia occurs about 1 week after exposure to the virus and lasts 3–5 days. Symptoms include headache, fever, sore throat, coryza, pruritus, abdominal pain, and arthralgias. The characteristic rash develops abruptly with bright red cheeks giving the “slapped cheek” appearance. Subsequently, a maculopapular faintly pink rash develops over the trunk and the extremities, then clears in a lacy, reticulated pattern. The rash fades over several days but can reappear intermittently for several weeks, particularly when the skin is exposed to sun or a warm bath. The disease is self-limited in children and requires only supportive care. In children with sickle cell anemia, parvovirus B19 is associated with bone marrow suppression and aplastic crisis. Additionally, infection during pregnancy can result in fetal death or red blood cell aplasia with fetal hydrops.



Acute chest syndrome (A) will characteristically present with cough and fevers, similar to pneumonia. A chest X-ray should be performed to evaluate for an infiltrate. It is a vaso-occlusive event and these are not characteristically triggered by parvovirus infections.

Splenic sequestration (C) results when there is a sudden enlargement of the spleen from trapping large amounts of sickled red blood cells, resulting in a precipitous decline in hemoglobin. This may result in shock. It is most commonly seen in sickle cell patients < 5 years old as most undergo autosplenectomy by that time. Parvovirus is not a known cause of this pathology.

Vaso-occlusive pain crisis (D) is not commonly triggered by parvovirus.

Question: Which of the following substances interferes with laboratory testing for GI parasites?
ExplanationEN:
Enteric parasites commonly cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, flatulence, and abdominal distention, although symptoms may not occur until weeks to months after an exposure. Such parasites are relatively common in children, especially in resource-poor areas. Sources include foods (e.g., local or shipped produce from a high-prevalence region, raw meats), other children (e.g., daycare), pets, and livestock.

For many parasites, diagnosis is done through stool testing. PCR testing is highly sensitive but only available for a limited number of parasites. Direct visualization of the stool requires a microscopist. Some parasites, like Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora species, are not detected on an exam for ova and parasites. Additionally, children infected with an intestinal parasite will have variable shedding of eggs, cysts, and trophozoites. With these factors in mind, the sensitivity of a single stool sample is only about 70% in the United States. Up to three samples may be needed in complex cases.

Common materials that interfere with the visualization of ova and parasites and contribute to false-negative results include antacids, antibiotics, barium, bismuth, and mineral oil. Less common materials include antidiarrheal medications and gallbladder dyes. Patients taking or receiving these medications should wait at least 1 week before providing a stool sample for parasite evaluation.



Mercaptopurine (B) is used to suppress the immune system in inflammatory bowel disease and does not affect stool testing for parasites.

Ondansetron (C) is an antiemetic that does not affect stool testing for parasites.

Polyethylene glycol (D) is a laxative and bowel prep agent that does not affect stool testing for parasites.

Simethicone (E) is an antiflatulent that does not affect stool testing for parasites.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with the above rash. It does not itch and is minimally painful. It began about a week ago and has slowly been increasing in size. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the rash?
ExplanationEN:
A rash of erythematous concentric rings with central clearing and a central papule is classic for erythema migrans, the hallmark of early localized Lyme disease. Lyme disease is spread by the bite of an Ixodes genus tick infected with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. In the United States, this is usually Ixodes scapularis, also known as the deer tick. It is most frequently seen in the northeastern portion of the United States, along with states just west of the Great Lakes.

Erythema migrans is the first sign of Lyme disease, seen 7–14 days after the tick bite, and gradually expands over several weeks if untreated. Multiple smaller annular lesions are occasionally seen when patients have early disseminated disease and may be accompanied by peripheral facial nerve palsy, aseptic meningitis, or heart block. Most patients with late Lyme disease develop large joint arthritis weeks to months after the initial tick bite. Congenital Lyme disease is rare and inconsistent in presentation. The diagnosis of erythema migrans is pathognomonic in endemic areas. Nummular eczema, tinea corporis, granuloma annulare, and southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI) can appear similarly. When unclear, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for specific immunoglobulin antibodies is most commonly used to identify Lyme disease. This test is sensitive but not specific due to cross-reactivity with other spirochetal infections. Western immunoblotting is a specific test but is not as sensitive as ELISA. The preferred treatment is doxycycline (acceptable for those < 8 years of age if given for < 21 days) or amoxicillin.



Erythema marginatum (A) is a pink or faintly red lesion with a pale center and rounded or serpiginous margins. This rash usually is clustered, begins on the trunk, and is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. It is similar in appearance to erythema migrans, except it typically appears with multiple lesions and lacks a central papule.

Erythema multiforme (C) begins as round lesions that develop into target lesions, most commonly over the shins. They may have a central erosion with an edematous rim and a peripheral, erythematous halo. The cause is unclear, but Mycoplasma is associated with erythema multiforme.

Erythema toxicum (D)is a neonatal illness with diffuse, transient red macules with central, whitish-yellow papules and pustules that appear about the second day of life and resolve spontaneously over weeks to months.

Question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the ED with fever, productive cough, and confusion. He is hypotensive despite an initial 1 L crystalloid bolus given by EMS en route. His weight is 70 kg. Which of the following is the best initial intravenous fluid treatment strategy in the ED for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with sepsis and likely septic shock, with signs of infection, altered mental status, and hypotension. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends administering 30 mL/kg of crystalloid fluids within the first 3 hours of recognizing septic shock. For a 70 kg man, this amounts to 2,100 mL. EMS has already given 1,000 mL, so the ED should administer the remaining 1,100 mL.

A balanced crystalloid is preferred as it more closely approximates plasma electrolyte composition than 0.9% sodium chloride. Balanced solutions, such as lactated Ringer solution, are preferred over 0.9% normal saline based on evidence of reduced mortality, particularly when used for the entire resuscitation.



0.9% sodium chloride (A, B) might seem appropriate, especially if giving another 1 L, as a rounded figure after an initial liter, but it falls a tad short of the full 30 mL/kg dose. The remaining amount needed is 1,100 mL, not 1,000 mL. In addition, 0.9% sodium chloride is a nonbalanced crystalloid that contains a high chloride concentration, increasing the risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Balanced solutions like lactated Ringer solution are preferred in the management of septic shock.

Lactated Ringer solution 2,100 mL (D) represents the full 30 mL/kg dose for a 70 kg man, but it does not account for the 1,000 mL already administered by EMS. Giving an additional 2,100 mL would exceed the guideline-recommended dose, potentially leading to volume overload, especially in patients with reduced cardiac or kidney function. Although lactated Ringer solution is preferred, the volume should be adjusted to reflect prior fluid resuscitation.

One Step Further
Question:

Reveal Answer:
Target serum lactate ≤ 2 mmol/L (or a ≥ 20% decrease from initial level within the first 2–4 hours) as a marker of adequate resuscitation in sepsis.

Question: Which of these symptoms are most suggestive of Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

Options.text: Ear pain, facial paralysis, hearing loss

ExplanationEN:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by herpes zoster (HZ) and is characterized by unilateral facial paralysis, a herpetiform vesicular eruption, and vestibulocochlear dysfunction (hearing loss or hyperacusis). The vesicular eruption may occur on the pinna, external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, soft palate, oral cavity, face, neck, and as far down as the shoulder.

Although it shares some clinical features with Bell palsy, Ramsay Hunt syndrome is often associated with severe pain. Treatment includes steroids and antiviral therapy.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents with abrupt onset of fever, malaise, and headache 6 days ago. Yesterday, he noticed a red rash on his ankles which has since spread to his trunk. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.1°C. He has a diffuse petechial rash. He is alert and oriented with no nuchal rigidity and a normal neurological exam. Laboratory studies include a WBC count of 12 x 109/L, platelets of 100 x 109/L, and hematocrit of 48%. What is the likely cause of his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a febrile, tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium. It is the most common rickettsial illness in the United States. Unlike its name implies, it can occur anywhere in the US. The primary ticks involved in the transmission of infection include Dermacentor variabilis (the American dog tick) and Dermacentor andersoni (the Rocky Mountain wood tick). Symptoms typically begin 5–7 days after a tick bite with fever, headache (often severe), myalgias, nausea, and rash. The rash tends to start on the wrists, palms, soles, and ankles before spreading centripetally to the upper extremities and trunk. The face is usually spared. The rash starts as blanching discrete macules before becoming maculopapular and, finally, petechial in appearance. Diagnosis is based primarily on clinical presentation and can be confirmed by serology studies or skin biopsy. Laboratory abnormalities include thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia although these are nonspecific and can not be used to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Doxycycline is the drug of choice for treatment. An alternative to doxycycline is chloramphenicol.



Babesia (A) is the cause of babesiosis, a malaria-like illness transmitted by the Ixodes tick that is characterized by spiking fevers, headache, and anorexia. Unlike other tick-borne illnesses, rash is not a common feature in babesiosis.

Borrelia burgdorferi (B) is the spirochete transmitted by the Ixodes tick that is responsible for Lyme disease. Lyme disease is classified into three stages: early localized disease consisting of a flu-like illness and the appearance of erythema migrans; early disseminated disease, which commonly affects the nervous system and heart; and late disease, which is characterized by arthritis.

Francisella tularensis (C), a pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus, is the primary cause of tularemia. The most common form of tularemia is ulceroglandular tularemia which starts as a papule at the site of inoculation that then ulcerates. Regional lymphadenopathy and fever then develop. Streptomycin is the drug of choice for treatment.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the ED after being sexually assaulted 4 months ago. Today, she is concerned she may have a sexually transmitted infection. On physical exam, she is noted to have a diffuse macular rash and moist broad-based papular lesions on her external genitalia. Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption is the most specific test for the diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Patients with syphilis can present with variable clinical signs and symptoms depending on the progression of the disease. Syphilis is divided into primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages. In primary syphilis, patients will present with a painless chancre, which can often go unnoticed. If left untreated, patients with primary syphilis can ultimately develop secondary syphilis in the following weeks to months. Secondary syphilis presents with generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous membrane lesions, systemic symptoms, and a rash classically involving the palms and soles. Although typically maculopapular, the rash can appear scaly or pustular. Condyloma lata is an anogenital exam finding in patients with secondary syphilis (this patient). It can be described as a flat, moist, and broad-based papular lesion. Without treatment, patients with undiagnosed secondary syphilis can ultimately develop tertiary syphilis. Tertiary syphilis is characterized by cardiovascular manifestations, such as aortic aneurysms and aortitis, or gummatous disease. Before progression to tertiary syphilis, patients may have an indefinite asymptomatic period known as the latent stage.



An endocervical culture (A) would be an appropriate test for patients who are suspected to have disseminated gonococcemia. It can also present with a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles. A patient with disseminated gonococcemia is unlikely to have findings consistent with condyloma lata on physical exam.

A rapid plasma reagin (C) can be considered as an initial test for diagnosing syphilis. However, both rapid plasma reagin and venereal disease research laboratory tests are only 70–80% sensitive.

A tissue biopsy (D) is unlikely to help in the diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Dark-field microscopy has been used in the diagnosis of syphilis and may be useful in primary syphilis when serology testing is more likely to be falsely negative. However, dark-field microscopy relies on appropriate equipment and sampling techniques, which results in low diagnostic utility.

Question: An 18-month-old girl presents to the ED with a fever of 104.9°F (40.5°C). She tests positive for influenza and is discharged with a prescription for oseltamivir. Which of the following is the most accurate way to describe how this medication works?

Options.text: It blocks uptake of the influenza virus into healthy cells
It prevents the release of virus from infected cells
It stops the formation of a protein channel needed for efficient replication

CorrectAnswer: It prevents the release of virus from infected cells
ExplanationEN:
Antiviral agents are a new and important way to reduce the morbidity and mortality of influenza. The three classes of medications available are neuraminidase inhibitors, selective inhibitors of influenza cap-dependent endonuclease, and adamantanes. Release of virions from infected cells is mediated by neuraminidase. Oseltamivir, zanamivir, and peramivir are neuraminidase inhibitors that work by preventing the release of virions from the host cell. There is little resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors, and they are effective against both influenza A and B.

Oseltamivir is approved for use in patients older than 2 weeks of age. Zanamivir is an inhaled powder with poor oral bioavailability and is approved in children > 7 years of age but should be avoided in patients with COPD or asthma, as it is known to cause bronchospasm. Peramivir is a single-dose intravenous neuraminidase inhibitor approved in children > 2 years of age. Neuraminidase inhibitors are well tolerated, with the most common side effect being GI symptoms. Additional side effects include neurologic effects such as delirium, hallucinations, confusion, and abnormal behavior.



There are no currently approved drugs that block uptake of the influenza virus into healthy cells (A).

Baloxavir is a selective inhibitor of influenza cap-dependent endonuclease that works by inhibiting initiation of mRNA synthesis (B).

Amantadine and rimantadine are adamantanes that work by blocking the M2 protein of influenza A, stopping the formation of a protein channel needed for efficient viral replication (D).

It has been shown to decrease the symptom duration of influenza by approximately 17 hours. Oseltamivir may be used in the treatment of influenza at any age. However, it is generally felt that in healthy individuals, the benefit of reduced duration of illness does not outweigh the adverse effects of oseltamivir, such as nausea, vomiting, headache, and seizures. As such, oseltamivir is typically given to patients at high risk for developing complications, such as patients < 2 years of age or > 65 years of age and pregnant or immunocompromised patients, such as a patient on methotrexate.

The CDC also recommends treatment with oseltamivir in patients with chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular (except hypertension alone), renal, hepatic, hematologic (sickle cell anemia), metabolic (diabetes), or neurologic and neurodevelopmental conditions. A potential complication of influenza virus infection is a superimposed pneumonia, most classically with the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus. Oseltamivir has the greatest benefit if given within 48 hours of symptom onset, but it may still be beneficial up to 5 days after symptom onset.

Question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 2 days of fever and rash. His vital signs include a temperature of 100.9°F, a heart rate of 108/min, a respiratory rate of 22/min, a blood pressure of 96/58 mm Hg, and an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with findings consistent with erythema infectiosum, also known as fifth disease, which is caused by parvovirus B19. The virus infects and lyses erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow, which can lead to transient anemia, especially in children with hemoglobinopathies, hemolytic anemia, or immunodeficiency. In otherwise healthy children, the illness is typically mild and self-limited.

Clinical presentation may include a low-grade fever, malaise, or coryza, followed by the appearance of the characteristic rash. The exanthem is classically described as bright red malar erythema with circumoral pallor, giving a “slapped cheek” appearance. Days later, a lacy, reticular maculopapular rash may spread to the trunk and extremities, often waxing and waning with temperature or sun exposure. Children are usually well-appearing on exam, and systemic findings are generally mild.

Diagnosis of erythema infectiosum is clinical in most cases, based on history and examination. Lab testing for parvovirus B19 DNA or IgM antibodies is reserved for atypical or complicated cases, such as aplastic crisis or pregnancy exposure. Management is supportive with reassurance to caregivers, hydration, and fever control using acetaminophen or ibuprofen.



Cephalexin (B) is a first-generation cephalosporin commonly used to treat bacterial skin infections such as cellulitis or impetigo caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus. These conditions present with erythema, warmth, tenderness, or honey-crusted lesions.

Diphenhydramine (C) is an oral antihistamine used for urticaria, which presents with transient, pruritic, raised wheals that migrate across the body. It also provides relief of pruritus in allergic reactions and contact dermatitis.

Mupirocin (D) is a topical antibiotic effective against localized impetigo, which presents in children with honey-colored, crusted papules or pustules, often around the nose and mouth.

Topical corticosteroids like hydrocortisone (E) are useful in inflammatory and allergic skin conditions, such as atopic dermatitis, which presents with pruritic, scaly, erythematous patches often on flexural surfaces.

Question: A 42-year-old man with a history of HIV presents to the emergency department with acute vision loss. He reports noncompliance with his antiretrovirals, and review of his chart shows that his most recent CD4 count 1 year ago was 63 cells/mm3. Funduscopy shows white perivascular lesions with areas of hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for the suspected diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a serious ocular opportunistic infection and the most common cause of blindness in AIDS patients. It is considered an AIDS-defining illness associated with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm3. Patients may present with visual acuity changes, visual field cuts, flashes, floaters, eye pain, eye redness, and photophobia. Funduscopy findings include white perivascular lesions with areas of hemorrhage.

Patients with CMV retinitis should receive an early emergent ophthalmologic consultation. Systemic therapy with oral valganciclovir or intravenous foscarnet is indicated for disease that is not immediately sight-threatening. Sight-threatening disease, as seen in this patient with visual acuity abnormalities, or disease occurring close to the macula or optic nerve, requires combined intravitreal ganciclovir in addition to systemic therapy with oral valganciclovir.



Acyclovir (A) is an antiviral used in the treatment of herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses. It has no activity against CMV.

Tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz (C) is a common antiretroviral therapy regimen used in patients with HIV/AIDS. While this patient should be restarted on antiretroviral therapy to decrease his likely high viral load, it is not indicated in the acute treatment of CMV retinitis.

Zanamivir (D) is a neuraminidase inhibitor used to treat influenza A and B viruses, not CMV retinitis.

Question: A 12-year-old patient presents to the ED for evaluation of a swollen lump in the axilla, as shown above. The swelling has been present for about 3 weeks, is painful, and seems to be increasing in size. The patient has had intermittent fevers as high as 100.9°F (38.3°C) and increased fatigue. There is no one at home with similar symptoms. The patient lives with their parents, siblings, two dogs, and a kitten. The physical exam is notable for a 4 cm swollen area in the axilla that is tender to touch, erythematous, warm, and indurated. BP is 110/65 mm Hg, HR is 90 bpm, RR is 16/min, and T is 99.9°F (37.7°C). Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting typical findings of cat scratch disease (CSD), caused by the bacteria Bartonella henselae following a cat bite or scratch. Most cases occur in people < 20 years of age, and a history of recent contact with a cat (most often kittens or feral cats) is present in almost all cases. The incubation period may be 5–50 days before the appearance of skin findings or regional lymphadenopathy. Skin manifestations include a scratch or bite with surrounding pustules or papules, which can be small and easily overlooked. The most common physical exam finding is regional lymphadenopathy of 1–5 cm, present in almost all cases, and is most often a single node but can involve multiple lymph nodes in some cases. The involved lymph nodes are typically tender, erythematous, warm, and indurated. The axillary, cervical, submandibular, preauricular, epitrochlear, femoral, and inguinal lymph nodes are the most commonly involved sites. Patients may also experience symptoms of low-grade fever, malaise, fatigue, anorexia, and headache. CSD can rarely cause more severe symptoms of persistent fever, maculopapular rashes, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, hepatitis, pneumonia, microabscesses in the liver and spleen, osteolytic lesions, and thrombocytopenic purpura.

Lymphadenopathy from CSD typically lasts several months but may last up to a year. It tends to resolve spontaneously, but in patients with severe, painful lymphadenopathy, a 5-day course of azithromycin may decrease swelling and speed up resolution. Suppuration of involved lymph nodes can occur and may be drained with needle aspiration. Incision and drainage should be avoided due to the risk of fistula formation. For ill patients with systemic symptoms, antibiotic therapy with oral azithromycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or ciprofloxacin is often recommended. No treatment or quarantine of cats who transmit CSD is recommended, but patients should be counseled regarding hand washing after animal contact.



Sporothrix schenckii (B) is the causative organism in sporotrichosis infections. It is associated with a rash that can last weeks to months and may spread along lymphatic channels and cause lymphadenitis. This patient does not have a rash suggestive of sporotrichosis or the expected history of inoculation through agricultural exposure.

In cases of CSD, abscess formation with an involved lymph node may occur and can be confused for an abscess caused by Staphylococcus aureus (C). The clinical history of a longer duration of symptoms and the lack of fluctuance in a swollen lymph node suggest CSD rather than an acute abscess.

Streptococcus pyogenes (D) can cause cellulitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, and impetigo that may have mildly associated lymphadenopathy but not to the degree seen with CSD.

Question: A 3-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with decreased appetite and fever. Vital signs are a BP of 88/50 mm Hg, HR of 110 beats per minute, RR of 18 breaths per minute, and T of 101.9°F (38.3ºC). On physical exam, you note the oral lesions seen above. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). HFMD is a viral illness most often affecting children < 5 years. It is classically caused by the coxsackievirus A. Coxsackieviruses belongs to the Enterovirus family. Coxsackieviruses are transmitted primarily through direct or droplet contact from nasopharyngeal secretions.

Signs and symptoms include fever; oral ulcers and vesicles on the buccal mucosa, lips, and tongue; and a peripherally distributed, tender maculopapular rash that includes the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. HFMD is a self-limited illness.

Management is primarily supportive and includes antipyretics for fever, oral rehydration, and analgesia with over-the-counter medications, including acetaminophen. Oral rehydration may prove difficult with oral ulcerations, so topical oral anesthetics can be useful in aiding this endeavor.



Measles virus (B) is transmitted by respiratory droplets and causes measles (rubeola). Symptoms include fever, malaise, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Koplik spots, 1 mm bluish-white lesions with surrounding erythema, develop 2 days before the rash and are pathognomonic for measles.

Parvovirus B19 (C) is the causative agent responsible for erythema infectiosum, better known as fifth disease. This causes a fever and rash with the classic “slapped cheek” appearance and a morbilliform, maculopapular rash of the trunk and extremities.

Rickettsia rickettsii (D) is the causative agent responsible for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which results in high fever and a petechial rash beginning on the wrists and ankles, spreading to the palms and soles before moving centrally.

Treponema pallidum (E) is the causative agent responsible for syphilis, which is rare in a 3-year-old patient.

Question: Which scenario describes a patient with the highest likelihood of rapidly developing rabies?

Options.text: 12-year-old girl licked on intact skin by a fox while camping
25-year-old man scratched on the leg by a stray dog
30-year-old man bitten on the face by a raccoon
40-year-old woman bitten on the hand by a bat while exploring a cave

CorrectAnswer: 30-year-old man bitten on the face by a raccoon
ExplanationEN:
The scenario of a 30-year-old man who was bitten on the face by a raccoon is more likely to lead to a rapid onset of rabies due to the rich nerve supply in the facial area. Rabies is caused by the rabies virus, an RNA virus belonging to the genus Lyssavirus in the family Rhabdoviridae. Human rabies cases in the US are rare, with only two or three occurrences annually, often from non-dog vectors, organ transplants, or infections acquired abroad. However, rabies causes about 61,000 deaths worldwide each year, mostly in Asia and Africa. Globally, dogs are the primary reservoir for rabies. However, in the US, > 90% of cases result from exposure to raccoons, bats, and foxes. The virus migrates from muscle tissue to the peripheral nervous system through the neuromuscular junction, progressing to the spinal cord and brain.

The average incubation period for rabies infection is 1–3 months, with shorter durations observed in patients exposed in body areas richly supplied with nerves, such as the face, compared to those with exposures on the extremities. This is due to the virus migrating more rapidly to the brain. Two forms of clinical rabies, encephalitic and paralytic, have been identified, with the encephalitic form being more common, accounting for about 70% of all human rabies cases.

Encephalitic rabies progresses rapidly with anxiety, confusion, and delirium, leading to hydrophobia, aerophobia, and seizures, signaling impending death. Difficulty swallowing, hypersalivation, and characteristic drooling occur, with coma and death following within days. Paralytic rabies starts with headache and malaise, leading to muscle weakness and paresthesias at the bite site, followed by acute flaccid paralysis.

Postmortem examination of fresh brain samples is the definitive method for diagnosing rabies across all mammalian species. Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) for rabies should be administered to individuals exposed to the secretions of high-risk animals (raccoons, bats, skunks, foxes, coyotes, unimmunized dogs, and wild carnivores in rabies-endemic areas). The World Health Organization divides rabies exposures in enzootic areas into three categories. Category I involves nonexposure activities like touching or feeding animals and licks on intact skin, which do not require PEP. Category II includes minor nibbles or scratches without bleeding, for which vaccine administration is recommended promptly. Category III covers more severe exposures, such as bites, scratches that penetrate the skin, licks on broken skin, mucous membrane contact with saliva, and bat exposures, necessitating immediate and comprehensive PEP. PEP includes wound care, passive immunization with human rabies immune globulin (HRIG), and active immunization with rabies vaccine. A common approach is to inject HRIG directly into the wound area, administer any remaining into one deltoid muscle, and give the rabies vaccine in the opposite deltoid muscle.



A 12-year-old girl licked on intact skin by a fox while camping (A) includes a high-risk animal (fox). However, intact skin serves as an effective barrier against the rabies virus. Therefore, being licked on intact skin by a potentially rabid animal is considered a negligible risk for rabies transmission.

A 25-year-old man scratched on the leg by a stray dog (B) is a much lower-risk scenario compared to a bite. This is because scratches do not typically introduce saliva deep into the tissues.

A 40-year-old woman bitten on the hand by a bat while exploring a cave (D) poses a risk of rabies transmission for several reasons. Bats have small, sharp teeth that may cause bites that go unnoticed or are minimally traumatic but still capable of transmitting rabies. Also, bats are significant reservoirs for rabies virus in many parts of the world. However, virus from a bite on the hand migrates to the brain more slowly than from the face.

Question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after the parents saw a bat in his room when they went to wake him up this morning. The child has no symptoms. No obvious bite marks are seen on the child. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Give rabies immunoglobulin 20 IU/kg and the first dose of the rabies vaccine 1 mL IM with instructions to have repeat vaccine doses on days 3, 7, and 14
Give the first dose of the rabies vaccine 1 mL IM with instructions to have repeat doses on day 3, 7, and 14

CorrectAnswer: Give rabies immunoglobulin 20 IU/kg and the first dose of the rabies vaccine 1 mL IM with instructions to have repeat vaccine doses on days 3, 7, and 14
ExplanationEN:
Rabies is transmitted through exposure to saliva or nervous system tissue of infected animals such as bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes. Although still a possibility, the number of cases of rabies in domestic animals, such as cats and dogs, has significantly declined in the United States. Infection with the rabies virus results in a fatal disease characterized by headache, fever, encephalitis, and eventual death. However, infection can be prevented by post-exposure prophylaxis if given in a timely manner. Any patient who has had direct contact with a bat should receive post-exposure prophylaxis. Prophylaxis is also indicated in individuals who have been in a room with a bat and exposure can not be ruled out (e.g., a person sleeping who awakens to find a bat in the room, unattended children, and mentally disabled or intoxicated people). The lack of finding a bite mark on the skin does not rule out the possibility of exposure. For previously unvaccinated patients, post-exposure prophylaxis consists of rabies immunoglobulin 20 IU/kg followed by the first dose of the rabies vaccine 1 mL IM. Additional doses of the vaccine are given on days 3, 7 and 14. Rabies immunoglobulin should be given around the wound site, if possible. If there is no obvious wound, it should be given intramuscularly at a site distant from the rabies vaccination.



Discharging home with reassurance (A) is inappropriate care as this child may have been bitten by the bat despite not having any skin findings.

Rabies immunoglobulin (B) provides passive immunization. In a previously unvaccinated person, it would not be given without the vaccine.

Giving just the vaccine (D) alone without rabies immunoglobulin is only indicated in previously vaccinated patients.

Question: A 36-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-week history of fatigue, dry cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain. He recently returned from a camping trip in the California Central Valley. He reports night sweats and unintentional weight loss of 4 lbs (1.8 kg). Vital signs are normal except a T of 38.1°C (100.6°F). His chest radiograph is shown above. Basic laboratory studies are unremarkable. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the most likely diagnosis?

Options.text: Enzyme immunoassay for IgM and IgG antibodies
Fungal culture of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid

CorrectAnswer: Enzyme immunoassay for IgM and IgG antibodies
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a subacute febrile respiratory illness with dry cough, pleuritic chest pain, night sweats, and weight loss after recent travel to the California Central Valley, an endemic region for Coccidioides species. The X-ray shows patchy infiltrates in the right middle lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy, which is consistent with the disease process.

Coccidioidomycosis, also known as valley fever, is caused by the dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii, which are endemic to the southwestern US. Most cases present as subacute pneumonia with systemic symptoms and can mimic bacterial or viral infections. A key to diagnosis is a detailed exposure history, particularly travel or residence in endemic areas like Arizona and the California Central Valley.

The best initial and confirmatory diagnostic test for suspected coccidioidomycosis is serologic testing using enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for both IgM and IgG antibodies. This test is rapid, widely available, and sensitive in early disease. EIA for IgM can detect early infection within the first week of symptoms, while IgG indicates progression or disseminated disease. A positive EIA result may be followed by confirmatory immunodiffusion or complement fixation testing if needed.

Treatment depends on the severity of illness and the patient’s immune status. Most immunocompetent patients with mild or self-limited pulmonary disease recover without antifungal therapy, though symptoms may persist for weeks. Supportive care with rest, hydration, and analgesics is sufficient in these cases. Oral fluconazole or itraconazole is recommended for moderate or prolonged pulmonary disease, especially when symptoms last > 6 weeks, involve extensive pulmonary infiltrates, or cause severe fatigue or weight loss.

For disseminated disease or meningeal involvement, prolonged or lifelong antifungal therapy is necessary. High-dose fluconazole (400–800 mg daily) or itraconazole is a first-line option for disseminated infection, with fluconazole preferred for meningitis because of its superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration. In severe or rapidly progressive disease, initial treatment with intravenous amphotericin B may be required before transitioning to an oral azole for long-term maintenance.

Patients with immunosuppression, diabetes, or pregnancy are at increased risk for severe or disseminated infection and should be treated more aggressively. Close monitoring with serial serologic titers and imaging is essential to assess response and detect relapse, as the disease can be indolent and recurrent if not fully treated.



Acid-fast bacilli sputum stain (A) is useful in evaluating for tuberculosis, which can present similarly with chronic cough and weight loss. However, it does not detect fungal organisms and is not appropriate for diagnosing coccidioidomycosis. This patient’s exposure history makes coccidioidomycosis the more likely diagnosis.

CT-guided lung biopsy (B) is highly invasive and reserved for cases with atypical imaging, failure of serologic testing, or concern for malignancy. It is not the best initial or confirmatory test in most patients with suspected coccidioidomycosis.

Fungal cultures (D) are definitive but often take several days to weeks for results and may have a lower yield in mild disease. Invasive sampling, such as bronchoalveolar lavage, is not typically needed for uncomplicated pulmonary coccidioidomycosis and entails procedural risks.

Serum beta-D-glucan assay (E) detects fungal cell wall components but is not specific for Coccidioides species. It is most useful for invasive fungal infections, such as candidiasis and aspergillosis, and does not reliably detect coccidioidomycosis.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents to the ED, accompanied by his parents, with fever and headache. He has no significant medical history, takes no medications, and has not traveled outside of the US recently. He has been outdoors for much of the summer and frequently has mosquito bites. He reported myalgias and nausea 2 days ago, and last night, he developed a fever with a severe headache. Vital signs show HR 145 bpm, BP 112/70 mm Hg, RR 20/min, and T 38.8°C. He has photophobia with mild neck stiffness. You also notice a small morbilliform rash over his anterior chest wall. Out of concern that he may have meningitis, you perform a lumbar puncture. The CSF results show a WBC count of 502 cells/µL that are predominantly lymphocytes, a protein level of 51 mg/dL, a glucose level of 77 mg/dL, and a negative Gram stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with meningitis or encephalitis. The presence of fever suggests an infectious cause to his illness. There are many different organisms that cause meningitis. The clinician must rely on subtle physical exam signs, potential environmental exposures, lumbar puncture results, and recent travel history to determine the most likely cause of this patient’s infectious meningitis. The important aspects of this patient’s history and diagnostic evaluation are his exposure to mosquito bites, his lack of travel outside of the US, and CSF results suggesting a viral etiology to his illness.

In viral meningitis, the cell count is usually < 1,000–2,000 cells/µL, the protein is < 150–200 mg/dL, and the glucose level is normal. One of the most common viral causes of meningitis and encephalitis in the US is West Nile virus, an arbovirus. Mosquitoes, ticks, or flies transmit the arboviruses. Other common arboviruses include St. Louis encephalitis virus, eastern equine encephalitis virus, dengue virus, Zika virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus. These viruses often cause rash, myalgias, arthralgias, meningitis, encephalitis, and hemorrhagic fever. Most people who become infected with West Nile virus are asymptomatic. Those who do become symptomatic develop headache, malaise, back pain, myalgias, anorexia, and fever. Patients can also develop a morbilliform or maculopapular rash that is often found on the chest, back, and arms. West Nile virus can also lead to encephalitis or flaccid paralysis.

The illness is often self-limited and rarely leads to severe encephalopathy and death. It is most common during mosquito season in the summer and fall. Diagnosis is confirmed by identification of serum or CSF immunoglobulin M antibodies. Symptomatic management is the mainstay of treatment, but often these patients will receive antibiotics for presumptive bacterial meningitis during initial workup.



Japanese encephalitis (A) virus is the most common cause of viral encephalitis worldwide. It usually affects children in Asia. Most adults in Asia have been exposed to the virus and are immune to it. It is an uncommon cause of encephalitis in the United States.

Meningococcal meningitis (B) is an important consideration in this patient. It has a high mortality rate, so it is important to consider and treat. It is necessary to perform a lumbar puncture to evaluate for bacterial versus viral etiologies of meningitis. If this patient had bacterial meningitis, his CSF results would show > 1,000–2,000 white blood cells/µL, a high protein > 250 mg/dL, and low glucose at < 45 mg/dL. This patient’s CSF analysis suggests a viral etiology. Thus, meningococcal meningitis is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever (C) is an important illness characterized by fever and rash, but it is caused by a bacterial infection with Rickettsia rickettsii and is transmitted by the bite of a tick, which was not mentioned in this patient’s history. Additionally, the rash in Rocky Mountain spotted fever is petechial, starts in the wrists, palms, ankles, and soles of the feet, and spreads centrally. This patient’s rash is not characteristic of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

Question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a fever, cough, and malaise. He recently participated in a cultural event in which he played animal skin drums that were later discovered to be contaminated with Bacillus anthracis. The patient is well appearing, with vital signs that are normal for his age. The chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive spore-forming rod found in the soil and was the first recognized bacterial pathogen. It is a zoonotic disease that can be transmitted from infected animal products including hides, hair, wool, and meat. It causes distinct illnesses depending on its route of entry, which are cutaneous, gastrointestinal, inhalation, and injection. Outbreaks are most commonly seen by the ingestion of undercooked meat from infected animals, but inhalational anthrax can occur in drum makers or performers using instruments made with contaminated hides.

Due to the high mortality rate and insidious nature of inhalational anthrax, there is a high potential for chemical bioterrorism. In 1979, an inadvertent release from a bioweapons facility in the former Soviet Union resulted in the death of most of the victims. In 2001, almost half of the victims of contaminated mail attacks in the United States died. While Bacillus anthracis designed for bioterrorism can be created to be resistant to antimicrobials, naturally occurring disease is more likely to respond to treatments.

Inhalational anthrax is a biphasic illness. It first presents similarly to early pneumonia or any other influenza-like illness. It starts with nonspecific findings of cough, fever, and malaise. The incubation period can be as short as a day or as long as 43 days. The average incubation period is 7–9 days, but even this varies significantly depending on the reference text. When the disease becomes fulminant, it does so with a rapid progression of respiratory symptoms, resulting in death within 24 hours from hypoxemia and septic shock. Findings common to inhalational anthrax include tachycardia, high hematocrit, low albumin, low sodium, pleural effusions, and a wide mediastinum on X-ray.

The treatment of patients with inhalational anthrax is with intravenous broad-spectrum parental antibiotics, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends combination therapy with three antibiotics, including two bactericidal drugs plus a protein synthesis inhibitor (or RNA synthesis inhibitor), updated in 2023. The CDC recommendations still list use of one bactericidal drug plus one protein synthesis inhibitor as an option, but this option is less preferred than the three antibiotic combination. Thus, a proper treatment regimen includes meropenem plus either ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin and adding doxycycline. Antitoxin with raxibacumab or obiltoxaximab should also be given if available along with diphenhydramine to avoid a hypersensitivity reaction.

The greater challenge for the emergency clinician is differentiating inhalational anthrax from all of the other common respiratory viruses seen in children. While there is little evidence for this, symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sore throat suggest against inhalational anthrax, and high hematocrit, hyponatremia, or a wide mediastinum on X-ray are supportive of the diagnosis of inhalational anthrax.



Most Bacillus anthracis is not susceptible to cephalosporins like cefdinir (B) nor to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (C). It can easily become resistant to penicillins, although the addition of clavulanate is usually effective. Single antibiotic oral therapy is recommended for postexposure prophylaxis in patients without symptoms, and ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or doxycycline should be used.

While reassurance and discharge (D) is indicated for children with similar symptoms as this patient due to a viral infection, the potential for death from inhalational anthrax is extremely high. These patients have a short treatment window and should be started on broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics after blood and sputum cultures are obtained.

Question: A 20-year-old woman presents to the ED with a fever. Her vital signs are BP 70/40 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, and T 101°F (38.3°C). On physical exam, she has diffuse erythroderma. Which of the following physical exam findings would be most consistent with this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
Female patients with toxic shock syndrome should be examined for a retained vaginal foreign body such as tampons or female barrier contraceptives. Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a toxin-mediated infectious disease that leads to septic shock and multisystem organ failure. The pathogenesis revolves around Staphylococcus aureus exotoxins that act as superantigens.

These superantigens lead to massive activation of the immune system and cytokine release, leading to shock and multisystem organ failure. Classically, toxic shock syndrome presents with fever, hypotension, and skin rash. The initial skin finding is characterized by erythroderma formed by a diffuse confluence of macules, giving a sunburn appearance. Late cutaneous manifestations include desquamation of the palms and soles. The development of TSS is associated with tampon use, cellulitis, abscesses, and infected surgical and postpartum wounds. Treatment is directed at source control and antibiotic therapy with clindamycin or vancomycin in cases of methicillin-resistant toxic shock syndrome.



Crepitus (A) is a possible clinical finding in patients with necrotizing fasciitis. Skin findings with necrotizing fasciitis will be more localized and not diffuse as seen in toxic shock syndrome. Risk factors for necrotizing fasciitis include immunocompromised states, diabetes, postoperative wound infections, or cirrhosis.

A painless genital ulcer (B) is characteristic of primary syphilis. Secondary syphilis can present with a diffuse rash involving the palms and soles. Patients with secondary syphilis are not typically critically ill.

A positive Brudzinski sign (C) is a rare physical exam finding seen in patients with meningitis. The test is considered positive if the knees and hips flex upon flexion of the neck.

Question: A 7-year-old girl presents with a rash. Her parent states it appeared 7 days after hiking through the woods near their home in New Jersey. The patient has no known drug allergies. Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States. It is a tick-borne illness caused by the spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi. The early phase of the disease results in erythema migrans, a characteristic annular rash with central clearing.

Prednisone (E) is a corticosteroid that can reduce inflammation. It is not used in Lyme disease and is associated with worse outcomes in patients with facial palsy secondary to Lyme. Prednisone would be an appropriate treatment if the patient has severe dermatitis secondary to poison ivy.
