Question: A 72-year-old man living in a skilled nursing facility presents with altered mental status. He has a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg, oxygen saturation of 92%, and rectal temperature of 101.1°F (38.4°C). On physical exam, he is lethargic but responds to verbal stimuli. Which of the following, if found in this patient, would help to fulfill the criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome in this patient?

Options.text: Kidney dysfunction with creatinine of 3.8 mg/dL and urine output of 450 mL/day
WBC count of 13,000/µL with 76% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, and 12% bands

CorrectAnswer: WBC count of 13,000/µL with 76% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, and 12% bands
ExplanationEN:
The goal of sepsis care has evolved to include early recognition of sepsis and subsequent aggressive fluid resuscitation and antibiotic administration within 1 hour. The systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria were developed to capture patients who exhibit abnormal vital signs and laboratory data secondary to an infection. Although many screening tools have been developed since the advent of SIRS, the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines indicate that clinicians should not use the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment as a single screening tool over the SIRS criteria, National Early Warning Score, or Modified Early Warning Score. Thus, SIRS still plays a role in the early identification of acute systemic infection.

Patients meet the criteria for SIRS when two or more abnormalities are identified, which are listed in the illustration below. Thus, a finding of a WBC count of 13,000/µL with 76% neutrophils, 10% lymphocytes, and 12% bands helps meet SIRS criteria in this patient. When patients have SIRS plus a confirmed or suspected infection, sepsis is likely. It is important to recognize that other noninfectious conditions can be the cause of SIRS, including trauma, hemorrhage, pancreatitis, burns, and overdose.



A heart rate of 88 bpm (A) would not meet the criteria for SIRS. Rather, a heart rate > 90 bpm is one of the criteria.

Kidney dysfunction (B) is not part of the SIRS criteria, but it is part of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score in adults. A creatinine of 3.5–4.9 mg/dL or urine output of 200–500 mL/day gives 3 points in the kidney function portion of a SOFA score.

A measured lactic acid of 3.8 mmol/L (C) is not part of the SIRS criteria. Lactic acid has become an important marker of increased risk of mortality in patients with sepsis. As sepsis evolves and patients develop tissue hypoperfusion, levels of lactic acid increase in the blood. Once a patient has an elevated lactic acid level > 2.0 mmol/L, it is consistent with septic shock, as this is a marker of end-organ damage (e.g., impaired kidney function, coagulopathy, altered mental status). While performing aggressive resuscitation, serial lactic acid levels are measured to ensure its clearance. If initial fluid resuscitative efforts have not decreased lactic acid by 10%, additional fluid is indicated.

The respiratory rate must be > 20/min (D) to meet SIRS criteria.

Question: Which of the following patients meets systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria?

Options.text: 25-year-old woman with T 98.0ºF (36.7ºC), HR 94 bpm, RR 22/min, and BP 120/80 mm Hg
41-year-old woman with T 102.5ºF (39.2ºC), HR 85 bpm, RR 18/min, and BP 89/50 mm Hg
68-year-old woman with T 100.1ºF (37.8ºC), WBC count 15,000 cells/mm 3 , PaCO 2 35 mm Hg, and BP 100/70 mm Hg
90-year-old woman with T 99.9ºF (37.7ºC), PaCO 2 34 mm Hg, HR 100 bpm, and WBC count 7,000 cells/mm 3

CorrectAnswer: 25-year-old woman with T 98.0ºF (36.7ºC), HR 94 bpm, RR 22/min, and BP 120/80 mm Hg
ExplanationEN:
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. While bacteremia (the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream) can cause sepsis, not all cases of sepsis involve bacteremia. Risk factors include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, and recent hospitalization. Early recognition in the emergency department is crucial. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends early identification of sepsis and septic shock through screening tools such as quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), the National Early Warning Score, or the Modified Early Warning Score. Once identified, it is essential to begin antibiotic administration (within 1 hour), aggressive fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg IV crystalloid), and vasopressor support for persistent hypotension.

SIRS is defined as the presence of two or more of the following criteria: temperature > 100.4ºF (38ºC) or < 96.8ºF (36ºC), respiratory rate > 20/min or PCO2 < 32 mm Hg, HR > 90 bpm, WBC count > 12,000 cells/mm3 or < 4,000 cells/mm3, or > 10% band neutrophils on cell differential. SIRS is often caused by bacterial infections, but other causes include myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolus, diabetes-related ketoacidosis, gastrointestinal bleeding, thyrotoxicosis, severe allergic reactions, trauma, and acute adrenal insufficiency. The 25-year-old woman does not have a fever but she meets the SIRS criteria with HR 94 bpm and RR 22/min.



A 41-year-old woman with T 102.5ºF (39.2ºC), HR 85 bpm, RR 18/min, and BP 89/50 mm Hg (B) does not meet SIRS criteria despite having low blood pressure. Note that blood pressure is not part of the criteria for SIRS.

A 68-year-old woman with T 100.1ºF (37.8ºC), WBC count 15,000 cells/mm3, PCO2 35 mm Hg, and BP 100/70 mm Hg (C) only meets one criterion for SIRS with an elevated WBC count.

A 90-year-old woman with T 99.9ºF (37.7ºC), PCO2 34 mm Hg, HR 100 bpm, and WBC count 7,000 cells/mm3 (D) only meets the heart rate criteria for SIRS.

Question: A 21-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of right-sided hearing loss for 1 day. She also has severe vertigo associated with nausea and vomiting. The patient reports upper respiratory infection symptoms over the previous 3 days. Currently, she feels fullness and mild otalgia in her right ear and abnormal taste when she eats food. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 122/84 mm Hg, heart rate of 64 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, and a temperature of 36.7°C (98.1°F). On exam, you note a few vesicles anterior to her right ear. She has drooping on the right side of her face and cannot wrinkle the right side of her forehead. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?

Options.text: Head CT scan and neurology consult

ExplanationEN:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (also termed herpes zoster oticus) is an acute peripheral facial neuropathy associated with an erythematous vesicular rash of the skin of the ear canal, auricle, or mucous membrane of the oropharynx. It is caused by the reactivation of herpes zoster in the geniculate ganglion. This nerve cell ganglion is responsible for movements of the facial muscles, sensation of parts of the ear and ear canal, taste function of the tongue, and lubrication of the eyes and oral mucosa. Because the vestibulocochlear nerve is close to the geniculate ganglion, patients may report tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo.

Patients usually present with paroxysmal pain deep within the ear. The pain often radiates outward into the pinna of the ear and may be associated with a more constant, diffuse, and dull background pain. The onset of pain usually precedes the rash by several hours and even days. Poor prognostic factors for good functional recovery include age > 50 years, complete facial paralysis, and lack of cranial nerve VII excitability. Combined therapy with prednisone and acyclovir is the most commonly used treatment and is most effective if started within the first 3 days of symptom onset.



Antibacterial otic drops (A) are ineffective for a viral infection. In some cases, the ulcers from herpes zoster lead to a secondary bacterial infection, in which case, antibiotic otic drops may be necessary.

Doxycycline (B) is also ineffective for viral infections. It is an antibiotic medication belonging to the tetracycline class, widely used for treating a variety of bacterial infections. It is effective against common conditions such as respiratory tract infections, acne, urinary tract infections, and certain types of malaria. Doxycycline works by inhibiting protein synthesis in bacteria, preventing them from growing and replicating.

A CT of the head (C) is an appropriate workup when there is a clinical suspicion for a central cause of facial droop (occurs with forehead sparing). However, Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves a peripheral neuropathy, and CT imaging is not necessary.

Herpes zoster vaccine (D) is used to help stop the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. The vaccine is suggested in people aged ≥ 50 years but is strongly recommended for use in people aged ≥ 60 years to prevent zoster and has been shown to reduce the risk of shingles and postherpetic neuralgia. It does not have a role in the treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

Question: Which of the following is most consistent with a diagnosis of neurosyphilis?

Options.text: Reactive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test and rash on soles of feet
Reactive rapid plasma reagin titer and diminished visual acuity
Reactive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay and genital chancre
Reactive venereal disease research laboratory test and palpable epitrochlear node

CorrectAnswer: Reactive rapid plasma reagin titer and diminished visual acuity
ExplanationEN:
Syphilis has varying manifestations depending on the stage of the disease. After infectious exposure, primary and secondary syphilis develop within a few weeks to a few months. Although these early-stage symptoms typically resolve spontaneously even in the absence of treatment, up to 40% of untreated individuals can subsequently develop tertiary syphilis. In addition, both secondary and late-stage (tertiary) syphilis can result in neurosyphilis.

The early manifestations of neurosyphilis occur during the secondary stage and include headache, meningitis, stroke, hearing loss, and ocular findings. Eye involvement has been increasing in recent years, is most commonly secondary to posterior uveitis, and presents with diminished visual acuity. Urgent treatment is required for ocular syphilis to prevent retinal involvement and blindness. Early forms of neurosyphilis are most frequently observed in individuals with HIV.

CNS involvement in the late stages of syphilis includes general paresis and tabes dorsalis. General paresis (previously known as general paralysis of the insane) usually presents 10–25 years after the initial infection and is a progressive dementia that may or may not be accompanied by abnormal findings on physical exam (e.g., dysarthria, hypotonia, intention tremor).

Symptoms of tabes dorsalis, which is a disease of the posterior columns of the spinal cord and dorsal roots, include sensory ataxia, absent lower extremity reflexes, Argyll Robertson pupil (small, contracts to accommodation but not to light, lack of dilation to painful stimuli), and lancinating back, limb, or face pains. Common non-neurologic manifestations of tertiary syphilis include cardiovascular involvement (particularly aortitis) and gummatous syphilis, which typically involves nodular, granulomatous lesions of the skin and bones. Late syphilis is uncommon, and its incidence may have been reduced partially due to the use of antibiotics for other infections in asymptomatic individuals with untreated early syphilis.

Laboratory testing protocols vary. Nontreponemal tests, such as the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and the venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test, are based on the reactivity of serum to a cardiolipin-cholesterol-lecithin antigen. Although they are sensitive screening tests, there is an elevated false-positive rate associated with other conditions (e.g., pregnancy, recent immunization, rickettsial disease, autoimmune disorders, HIV). Nontreponemal tests have the advantage of being quantitative tests. As a result, the value of the titer may be helpful in determining whether an infection is acute and whether treatment is effective. However, nontreponemal tests may be nonreactive in very early or late syphilis, as well as in immunocompromised individuals (particularly HIV infected). In the case described above, ocular symptoms represent the secondary stage of syphilis but early stage of neurosyphilis, at which time a nontreponemal test would be expected to demonstrate an elevated titer, and a treponemal test would also be positive.

Treponemal tests, such as the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS), Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA), and microhemagglutination test for antibodies to Treponema pallidum (MHA-TP), are qualitative tests and are specific for syphilis. Treponemal tests remain positive after initial infection and thus are not able to clarify whether there is an acute infectious process present. Confirming the presence of active syphilis is based on the results of both a nontreponemal and treponemal test. Diagnosing neurosyphilis requires clinical suspicion and a spinal fluid examination, including a VDRL, lymphocyte count, and protein level. Consultation with laboratory or infectious disease experts is important in selecting appropriate diagnostic testing. The mainstay of treatment for all stages of syphilis is penicillin.



A reactive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test and a rash on the soles of the feet (A) is consistent with secondary syphilis. Even as the initial chancre heals, there is widespread dissemination of the infectious agent within the body. This sets the stage for progression to secondary, tertiary, and neurosyphilis. Approximately 25% of infected individuals will demonstrate systemic symptoms consistent with secondary syphilis, such as fever, rash, and adenopathy. The classic rash involves the entire trunk and extremities and is diffuse, symmetric, and macular or papular. Involvement of the palms and soles should alert the clinician to the possibility of secondary syphilis.

A reactive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay and a genital chancre (C) is consistent with primary syphilis, which generally presents with a painless papule at the site of inoculation. Subsequent ulceration reveals a 1–2 cm ulcer with a raised and indurated margin, the classic syphilitic chancre. Lesions develop at the site of inoculation, which is most frequently on the genitals. Other sites include the posterior pharynx, vagina, or anus. Since the chancre is typically painless, may not be visible, and heals spontaneously without treatment, it may go unrecognized by the individual and result in transmission to others.

A reactive venereal disease research laboratory test and a palpable epitrochlear node (D) is consistent with secondary syphilis. Palpable epitrochlear nodes indicate a disease process and, in particular, forearm or hand infection, secondary syphilis, lymphoma, tularemia, or sarcoidosis. In the context of syphilis, the epitrochlear nodes are typically firm, rubbery, and only minimally tender.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents with an acute onset of vomiting and diarrhea tonight. She thinks she ate some bad food earlier because she was well before and now she cannot control the vomiting. When she vomits, she ends up having diarrhea at about the same time. She reports crampy abdominal pain. She reports no fever or blood in her stool. On exam, she is clearly in distress and currently vomiting. Her abdominal exam shows diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs. What is the most likely bacterial agent causing her acute illness?
ExplanationEN:
Ingestion of foods contaminated with bacteria, viruses, parasites, chemicals, and biotoxins leading to foodborne illnesses is very common. Viruses are the most common cause, with norovirus leading the pack. There are different mechanisms by which microbes cause illness. Certain bacteria such as Bacillus cereus and Staphylococcus aureus produce preformed toxins that are capable of causing illness. These toxins are ingested and then release intestinal inflammatory cytokines that cause vomiting and diarrhea. Symptom onset is generally within 6 hours of ingestion of the toxins, which is consistent with the illness in this patient. Most patients with foodborne illness do not require diagnostic testing and the illnesses are often self-limited. Most patients do well with adequate oral rehydration.



Another method through which bacteria can cause acute illness is through the production of toxins after ingestion. These toxins interact with the intestinal epithelium, destroying receptors and wreaking havoc with the gastrointestinal osmotic gradients. This process leads to vomiting and diarrhea since fluid builds up in the intestine and can only be expelled through diarrhea. Bacteria such as Vibrio, Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (B), and Shigella (D) produce these symptoms within about 24 hours of ingestion.

Finally, direct invasion of the intestinal epithelium by organisms such as Salmonella (C), Campylobacter, and enteroinvasive Escherichia coli destroys the tissue and leads to malabsorption. This is frequently associated with bloody diarrhea. This patient’s symptoms are more acute, and she does not have bloody diarrhea to suggest enteroinvasive disease.

Question: A healthy 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a rash on his arm. He has had the rash for approximately 5 weeks and completed a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole without any improvement of his symptoms. He has not had any known bug bites and works as a florist. The patient’s vital signs are within normal limits, and physical exam reveals the rash shown above and some axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
This rash is due to sporotrichosis and is most appropriately treated with oral itraconazole. Sporotrichosis is a fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii, an organism most commonly found in soil, plants, flowers, and decaying vegetable matter. The disease is common among florists, gardeners, and agricultural workers. Inoculation most commonly occurs when a plant thorn or barb penetrates the skin. There are also reported cases of transmission from animals, particularly cats, in which the fungus inhabited claws.

The average incubation period is 3 weeks after inoculation, but symptoms may appear even a few days after the initial exposure. Most sporotrichosis infections are localized to the site of inoculation and may appear as a crusted ulcer or plaque, a subcutaneous nodule with associated lymphadenitis, or as an initial painless nodule or papule that then spreads along local lymphatic channels. The lymphocutaneous type is the most common skin manifestation, but all three types are typically painless and will show no improvement without appropriate treatment. Systemic illness is rare, but when it does occur, patients may have symptoms of monoarticular arthritis, tenosynovitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and osteomyelitis.

History and physical exam are sufficient for diagnosis. Fungal cultures and tissue biopsies may provide a definitive diagnosis. Laboratory findings are usually nonspecific but might include an elevated white blood cell count, eosinophil count, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice for localized and systemic infections, dosed at 100–200 mg daily for 2–4 weeks until all lesions have resolved.



Amphotericin B (A) may be used intravenously to effectively treat sporotrichosis but, due to side effects, should be reserved for disseminated disease that is not responsive to alternative treatments. Fluconazole (B) is an alternative antifungal treatment that may be used to treat sporotrichosis, but it is less effective than itraconazole and should be reserved for those who do not tolerate itraconazole. During an epidemic or in an endemic region, such as Central and South America or Africa, a saturated solution of potassium iodide (D) may be an effective low-cost treatment option. In this patient, an oral antifungal agent is the more appropriate choice of treatment.

Question: A 16-month-old boy presents to the emergency department with a rash. According to his parent, the child has been febrile and ill over the last few days. His fever was as high as 104.8℉ (40.4ºC) 2 days ago, but it has been improving. The child’s grandparent has been giving him an herbal medicine for his fussiness, but the only other medication the parent has been giving is acetaminophen for the fever. Now the child has a rash. The rash does not seem to bother him or itch. He does not have a fever today. He has been eating and drinking well today and behaving much more normally than the previous few days. What is the most appropriate treatment for this rash?

Options.text: Supportive care and acetaminophen as needed

CorrectAnswer: Supportive care and acetaminophen as needed
ExplanationEN:
This child is presenting with a history and physical examination that is consistent with roseola infantum, a viral illness caused by human herpesvirus 6. Most cases occur sporadically without a known exposure. It is an illness of young children and generally occurs before 3 years of age. The clinical course is characterized by 3–5 days of fever that resolves abruptly and is followed by a maculopapular rash. Classically, fevers are very high and may exceed 104℉ (40ºC). The fever is often accompanied by irritability but children are otherwise fairly well appearing. Roseola is a benign, self-limited disease. Treatment is supportive with fever control with acetaminophen.



Clotrimazole (A) would treat any fungal rash this child may develop. This child’s story and exam are not consistent with a fungal rash.

Frequently, children are diagnosed with otitis media and started on antibiotics during the febrile phase of roseola infantum. After initiation of any medicine in the setting of roseola infection, a rash can look like a drug allergy. In this particular case, the clinician might consider that the herbal medicine given to this child has caused a drug allergy. Features that can help distinguish roseola from a drug allergy include the duration of the rash (an allergic rash will last longer) and pruritus (present in a drug allergy and not roseola). Diphenhydramine (B) would be indicated for drug allergy, but this patient does not have features to suggest allergy.

Another diagnosis to consider in this patient is scarlet fever, which produces a diffuse, erythematous rash. However, in scarlet fever the rash is sandpaper-like and it usually occurs in conjunction with pharyngitis. Penicillin (C) would be indicated for scarlet fever.

Question: A 31-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for vaginal lesions. She has had them for 1 week and she thinks they are warts. She reports no pain. Physical examination shows flat, white, velvety, wart-like lesions on both sides of the vulva and perineum. You ask if the patient ever had a sexually transmitted infection or other types of vaginal lesions and she indicates “yes, but the lesion went away on its own a few weeks ago”. What is the appropriate test to perform to make a diagnosis in this patient?

Options.text: Biopsy a lesion and send for human papillomavirus testing

ExplanationEN:
The wart-like lesions presented in this patient are consistent with condyloma lata, lesions that are found in secondary syphilis. Syphilis presents in three phases: primary, secondary, and tertiary or latent syphilis. The disease may be diagnosed in any of the stages. Primary syphilis is characterized by a painless chancre with indurated borders on the penis or vulva. The lesion resolves spontaneously. The lesion that this patient reports previously was likely due to primary syphilis.

Secondary syphilis develops 3–6 weeks after the primary stage and is characterized by rash, nonspecific symptoms such as fever, sore throat, headache, and genital warts called condyloma lata. Condyloma lata are large, raised, flat, grey or white lesions. They appear in warm, moist areas such as the mouth and the perineum as a manifestation of the secondary stage of syphilis. The lesions can look very similar to condyloma acuminata but are usually more white and flat.

Tertiary syphilis develops in about one-third of patients after secondary syphilis and may occur 3–20 years after the initial infection. Manifestations of tertiary syphilis include meningitis, dementia, neuropathy, and thoracic aneurysm. The causative agent of syphilis is the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Nontreponemal tests include the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) and the rapid plasmin reagin (RPR) tests. These tests detect nonspecific antibodies to cardiolipins, which are released as a result of infection. The VDRL and RPR are used as screening tests. Tests may not become positive until approximately 1–4 weeks after the initial lesion, the chancre, appears.



Human papillomavirus (HPV) infections are very common and are the cause of a variety of cutaneous and mucous membrane lesions, including anogenital or venereal warts called condyloma acuminata. Condyloma acuminata are easily confused with condyloma lata. Therefore, a good history and physical examination is necessary. Venereal warts, found on the internal or external genitalia or perianal region, are hyperkeratotic, exophytic papules, either sessile or pedunculated, and are sexually transmitted. Biopsying a lesion and sending for HPV testing (A) is not appropriate as HPV testing is done through a Pap smear, not a biopsy of the lesion. Additionally, HPV is generally a clinical diagnosis and does not require further testing.

A rapid HIV test (B) would not provide an accurate diagnosis in this situation. HIV itself does not have cutaneous manifestations. However, patients with HIV are more likely to have another sexually transmitted infection, such as HPV. Additionally, immunocompromised patients are at risk for other opportunistic infections that produce cutaneous lesions including lymphoma and Kaposi sarcoma. Although the clinician would not be faulted for testing for HIV, the test would not provide accurate results to explain this patient’s wart-like lesions.

A Tzanck test (D) is used to determine whether lesions are caused by herpes simplex II virus (HSV). HSV causes genital herpes, a lifelong infection caused by exposure of mucosal surfaces or nonintact skin to the virus. Classic outbreaks of primary genital herpes infection begin with a prodrome that is characterized by localized pain, tingling, and burning. Next, symptoms of headache, fever, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy, anorexia, or malaise are common. As the disease progresses, papules and vesicles on an erythematous base become evident. The vesicles erode and then usually crust and re-epithelialize and heal without scarring. The lesions in this patient do not fit the description of herpes.

Question: A 2-week-old girl presents with a fever. She was born at 38 weeks gestation, and the pregnancy was complicated by being small for gestational age. Her birth was a planned C-section, and her delivery was uncomplicated. Her exam is remarkable only for a rectal temperature of 39.4°C (102.9°F). Serum blood cultures and a urine culture are obtained. Which additional tests are most likely to change the care of this patient, according to the 2021 American Academy of Pediatrics febrile infant guidelines?

Options.text: Cerebral spinal fluid cell count result
Serum white blood cell count value

CorrectAnswer: Cerebral spinal fluid cell count result
ExplanationEN:
In 2021, the American Academy of Pediatrics published an updated guideline for the care of febrile infants. The authors recognize the challenges of creating such a guideline, including the variation in what is considered acceptable risk among clinicians and parents, advances in testing, and the changing bacteriology landscape. These pathways are expected to change with further advances in testing and additional research. The guideline should only be used in infants who appear well, are older than 1 week of age, and were born after 37 weeks gestation. Infants with respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, otitis media, or positive viral test results can be included in the recommended pathway.

Infants with a fever are risk stratified by age, as the rate of bacteremia drops as they age. A separate management guideline is recommended for each age range, which includes ages 8–21 days, 22–28 days, and 29–60 days. A cerebral spinal fluid cell count and culture are strongly recommended in infants who are 8–21 days old and have a fever. The prevalence of bacterial or viral meningitis is highest in this age group, the results can be used to target the source of infection, and the results help in the decision to stop antibiotics when appropriate. Infants < 21 days old with a fever should be hospitalized and receive appropriate intravenous antibiotics. They may be sent home if all culture results are negative at 24–36 hours and if they have a negative herpes simplex PCR result.



Nasal viral testing (B) is a relatively new process that does not have enough evidence to be included in current pathways, but it may be useful to change management since more data is obtained. There is some evidence that rates of bacteremia are much lower in infants > 28 days old with a fever and positive viral testing during seasonal outbreaks, but this should not affect the decision on whether an infant < 28 days needs a lumbar puncture without more data.

Serum inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein (C) or procalcitonin, are recommended in infants > 28 days and, if negative, can now change whether a lumbar puncture is performed. While they may be obtained in infants < 22 days with a fever, they do not change how these patients receive care.

A serum white blood cell count (D) was one of the fundamental markers in previous guidelines in infants this age but now is only considered part of the measurement of inflammatory markers. This is thought to be due to the change in bacteriology, given that Escherichia coli has replaced group B Streptococcus as the primary pathogen. A differential that shows an absolute neutrophil count > 4,000/µL (or > 5,200/µL if a procalcitonin is not available) is still used to suggest inflammation similar to an elevated C-reactive protein or procalcitonin level, and it does not change care in infants.

Reveal Answer:

Question: A community is currently affected by a bioterrorist incident. Affected patients are presenting to the ED with high fevers, followed 1 to 2 days later by a maculopapular rash with lesions in the same stage of development. What is the most likely causative biological warfare agent?
ExplanationEN:
Rapid recognition of infections caused by biological warfare agents is critical to minimize spread within the community and among health care workers. The described presentation is classic for the most common and severe form of smallpox, variola major. Smallpox begins with a 2–4 day prodrome of high fever, malaise, headache, and myalgias before the development of a centrifugal maculopapular rash that progresses to vesicles and pustules. A key distinguishing feature is that lesions are all in the same stage of development, unlike varicella.

Smallpox is highly contagious through respiratory droplets and close contact, and each infected person may transmit the virus to multiple contacts in a susceptible population. Historically, case fatality rates for variola major were approximately 30%. Exposed individuals require monitoring for 17–21 days, corresponding to the incubation period, and quarantine may be necessary depending on exposure risk.

Smallpox is classified as a CDC category A bioterrorism agent due to its high mortality, ease of transmission, and potential for widespread public health impact. Other category A agents include Bacillus anthracis, Yersinia pestis, Clostridium botulinum, Francisella tularensis, and viral hemorrhagic fever agents (e.g., Ebola).

If smallpox or another high-risk biologic agent is suspected, the patient should be placed in airborne and contact isolation (negative pressure room), strict isolation precautions should be implemented, and hospital infection control and public health authorities must be notified immediately. Early coordination with infectious disease specialists and public health agencies is essential for containment and surveillance.



Anthrax (A) most commonly presents as cutaneous disease with a painless ulcer that develops a black eschar, not a diffuse maculopapular rash. Inhalational anthrax causes severe respiratory distress and mediastinal widening, not a vesiculopustular eruption. Lesions are not classically all in the same stage of development.

Tularemia (B) commonly presents as ulceroglandular disease with a skin ulcer and painful regional lymphadenopathy. It does not produce a diffuse rash with uniform lesion stages. Systemic forms cause fever and pneumonia or sepsis, not a smallpox-like eruption.

Yersinia pestis (D) causes plague. Bubonic plague presents with painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), not a generalized maculopapular rash. Pneumonic plague causes severe pneumonia and sepsis without a characteristic skin eruption. There is no classic, same-stage vesicle rash pattern, as seen in smallpox.

Question: Which of the following is the most common laboratory abnormality seen in ehrlichiosis?
ExplanationEN:
Human ehrlichiosis in the United States originally encompassed two diseases: human monocytic ehrlichiosis caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis and human granulocytic anaplasmosis caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Both illnesses are tick borne and have similar presentations and clinical findings. The diseases are now thought of as two separate diseases, but have similar presentations. The incidence of illness seems to be increasing with most cases occurring in the spring and summer months. Ehrlichia are gram-negative, obligate intracellular rickettsia-like coccobacilli. The main two vectors of infection are the Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americana) and the Ixodes tick which also transmits Lyme disease and babesiosis. The majority of patients provide a history of a tick bite with an average time between bite and symptom onset of 9 days. Patients present with abrupt onset of fever, chills, malaise, headache, and myalgias. Gastrointestinal symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, are less common. In contrast to other tick-borne illnesses such as Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever, only one-third of patients develop a rash, which can be macular, maculopapular, or petechial. The most common laboratory abnormalities, found in up to 90% of patients, include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases. Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical presentation. Treatment consists of a 10-day course of doxycycline.



Patients with ehrlichiosis may have elevated serum creatinine (A), although this is not the most common laboratory abnormality.

Hyponatremia (B) can be seen in patients with advanced Rocky Mountain spotted fever, especially those patients with central nervous system involvement.

Thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis (D) is a common finding in patients with ehrlichiosis. Decreased platelet counts can also be seen in Rocky Mountain spotted fever and can be a clue to the possibility of rickettsial disease.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fatigue, aches, and fevers that have been worsening over the past 7 days. He states his symptoms started after a vacation to Hawaii, where he participated in many outdoor activities. He is otherwise healthy. His T is 104°F (40°C), BP is 100/62 mm Hg, HR is 132 bpm, RR is 21/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. Physical exam reveals the finding pictured above, and the patient has mild jaundice. Infection with which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Leptospira interrogans is the causative organism for leptospirosis. Infection occurs after exposure to animal (particularly rodent) urine or contaminated water. Patients will initially present with fever, chills, headaches, and muscle aches. A conjunctival suffusion may be seen on examination. Other findings may include uveitis, elevated liver enzymes, proteinuria, and hematuria. Although patients with leptospirosis have similar symptoms as those with self-resolving viral illnesses such as influenza, they are often more ill-appearing. In some circumstances, this condition can progress to Weil syndrome, which presents with liver failure, kidney failure, meningitis, pulmonary failure, myocarditis, and rhabdomyolysis. The diagnosis of leptospirosis can be made with serologic testing. Treatment may include penicillin, doxycycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone. Since Leptospira interrogans is a spirochete, the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur once treatment is started.



Campylobacter jejuni (A) can cause colitis and infectious diarrhea, which are not mentioned in this case. Patients will present with abdominal pain, fever, and possibly bloody or purulent diarrhea. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a possible complication that occurs after the acute infection. It presents with ascending flaccid paralysis and the loss of reflexes.

Hepatitis A (B) infection is less likely associated with the acute onset following outdoor activities in freshwater exposure described in this case. The virus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. Patients may have jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. With supportive care, healthy individuals generally have spontaneous resolution of their symptoms.

Influenza virus (C) infection presents with fevers, fatigue, malaise, aches, chills, nausea, vomiting, cramping, and diarrhea. Respiratory symptoms are characteristic and are not seen in this case. Patients who are healthy can be treated with supportive care only.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a new-onset rash over 12 hours. He reports having a sore throat, malaise, and a mild cough for 2 days. He visited urgent care yesterday and was given an antibiotic for which he cannot remember the name. Today he developed a rash over his entire body. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. On examination, he has bilateral tonsillar swelling with diffuse exudates and erythema. He has bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. His airway is open and tonsillar swelling is symmetric. He has a diffuse morbilliform rash on his torso and extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis to explain the rash in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with symptoms of pharyngitis. The differential for pharyngitis most commonly includes viral versus bacterial causes. Viral causes of pharyngitis include rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, adenoviruses, influenza and parainfluenza viruses, and Epstein-Barr virus leading to mononucleosis, herpes simplex virus, rubeola, and coxsackievirus. Bacterial causes of pharyngitis include group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Corynebacterium diphtheriae. We can assume a clinician suspected a bacterial cause of this patient’s pharyngitis since he was treated with antibiotics. However, we do not have any other information regarding tests performed or the antibiotic used for treatment.

The majority of pharyngitis cases are caused by viruses. Pharyngitis is a prominent feature of Epstein-Barr virus infection. Symptoms also include fever, malaise, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Patchy pharyngeal exudates can be found and look extremely similar to those found in group A beta-hemolytic streptococci infections. Although empiric treatment for group A beta-hemolytic streptococci infection is not recommended in the setting of pharyngeal exudates since the signs and symptoms overlap so much with viral etiologies, it is still done. One of the more common complications of Epstein-Barr virus infection or infectious mononucleosis that is treated with antibiotics is a morbilliform rash following the administration of ampicillin or amoxicillin. The mechanism responsible is not understood. The development of this rash does not mean the patient has a penicillin allergy. This patient has most likely developed this complication of Epstein-Barr virus infection. Thus, the most likely underlying diagnosis is infectious mononucleosis.



As already mentioned, the morbilliform rash that develops after treatment of infectious mononucleosis with ampicillin or amoxicillin is not an allergic reaction to the antibiotic (A). A patient who has developed a true allergic reaction to an antibiotic is more likely to present with hives and itching.

Measles (C), or rubeola, is a viral infection of the respiratory system and is incredibly contagious. Symptoms include sore throat, cough, congestion, muscle aches, conjunctivitis, and white spots in the mouth also known as Koplik spots. A widespread morbilliform rash develops approximately 3 days after exposure to the virus. Measles could be a consideration in this patient, but usually, the pharyngitis from measles is not exudative. Additionally, widespread vaccination has reduced the number of measles cases, making this diagnosis less likely.

Scarlet fever (D) occurs at the same time or right after a group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection. However, the rash in scarlet fever is described as tiny bumps that feel like sandpaper. The rash in this patient is not this way. Patients will generally have a very bright red tongue also.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with the above lesion on his arm that he noticed 2 days ago. It does not hurt or itch. Initially, the lesion was small, but it has expanded, so he came to the emergency department for evaluation. He does not know of any new exposures. He was hiking with his children a few weeks ago but does not remember anything remarkable about the hike. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness that is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. The clinical manifestations of Lyme disease are divided into three phases: early localized, early disseminated, and late disease. Early localized disease is characterized by the appearance of a characteristic skin lesion, erythema migrans. This lesion usually presents itself within 1 month following a tick bite. Other manifestations of early localized disease include nonspecific viral symptoms. Erythema migrans occurs in about 80% of patients. The lesions are often found near the axilla, groin, popliteal fossa, or belt line. They are not painful but sometimes they burn or itch. Erythema migrans lesions are usually red spots that expand over days and weeks to form an area of central clearing and, as they grow even larger, they resemble a target or bull’s eye. Treatment of Lyme disease can be with oral doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime.



Erythema migrans can be confused with contact dermatitis (A), an allergic or irritant-induced inflammatory reaction that develops a few days after exposure. A carefully elicited history will help differentiate Lyme disease from contact dermatitis. Contact dermatitis presents as pruritic papules and vesicles on an erythematous base. A target lesion does not develop.

Cutaneous larva migrans (B)manifests as an erythematous, serpiginous, intensely pruritic cutaneous eruption from penetration and migration of various nematode parasites. The disease is mainly acquired in tropical areas. In comparison to erythema migrans, these lesions are linear moving lesions and are intensely pruritic.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) is a hypersensitivity reaction involving the skin and mucous membranes. A careful history will differentiate Lyme disease from Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The typical lesion has the appearance of a target, but in contrast to erythema migrans, the lesions of Stevens-Johnson syndrome have two tones of color instead of three. Additionally, lesions in Stevens-Johnson syndrome are multiple instead of singular.

Question: Which of the following patients may obtain the most benefit from treatment with oseltamivir twice a day for 5 days during influenza season?

Options.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of hypertension and high cholesterol diagnosed with influenza A after 3 days of symptoms
A 73-year-old woman with a history of arthritis diagnosed with influenza A after 3 days of symptoms
A 9-year-old healthy boy diagnosed with influenza A after 3 days of symptoms
An asymptomatic 35-year-old woman with two children at home who are ill with influenza A for 1 day

CorrectAnswer: A 73-year-old woman with a history of arthritis diagnosed with influenza A after 3 days of symptoms
ExplanationEN:
Influenza is a highly contagious orthomyxovirus that is transmitted through aerosolized respiratory secretions and large droplets. Infection with influenza is seasonal, typically peaking in the winter months. There are two primary forms of the disease: influenza A and influenza B, and influenza A is usually the more serious of the two. Influenza is one of the most common viral infections encountered in the emergency department. Mortality rates in the United States can vary between 5,000 to 50,000 deaths each year. The incubation period for influenza is typically 1–4 days. Patients report fever and respiratory symptoms, which usually resolve within about 1 week. Complications from the illness can include pneumonia, worsening chronic respiratory disease, myocarditis, meningitis, and bacterial superinfection. Individuals at greatest risk for these complications include the very young, the very old, and those with chronic medical conditions such as chronic obstructive lung disease, congestive heart failure, chronic kidney insufficiency, and an immunocompromised state.

Influenza can be diagnosed clinically, but testing is available with rapid antigen testing. Unfortunately, the sensitivity is low, but the specificity of the test is high. Most patients, particularly healthy individuals between 2 and 65 years, will have a self-limited, uncomplicated course. Symptomatic treatment is the mainstay with antipyretics, decongestants, and oral hydration. However, antiviral medications are available to help prevent disease complications and shorten the duration of symptoms. There are two types of antivirals: neuraminidase inhibitors and adamantanes. The use of a neuraminidase inhibitor, such as oseltamivir, is the recommended first-line therapy for patients requiring treatment with antivirals. Adamantane medications are active only against influenza A, and high rates of resistance have already occurred, so they are not indicated for treatment. Clinicians should use antiviral medications in any hospitalized patient with influenza or those with severe and progressive disease regardless of the patient’s age, comorbidities, or duration of illness. The Infectious Diseases Society of America also recommends treating high-risk outpatients with oseltamivir. These populations include children under age 5 but especially under age 2, adults over age 65, pregnant patients up to 2 weeks postpartum, residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities, and people with chronic asthma, chronic lung disease, coronary artery disease, congenital heart disease, diabetes, kidney insufficiency, chronic liver disease, extreme obesity with a body mass index > 40 kg/m2, and immunocompromised individuals. These patients should be started on antiviral therapy regardless of the duration of the illness. Other patients who might see some benefit from antiviral therapy but do not fall into this high-risk category include those with symptoms for < 48 hours, those with symptomatic household contacts who are at high risk for complications from influenza, and health care clinicians who routinely care for patients at high risk for complications from influenza. Keeping these indications in mind, the patient who would benefit from antiviral therapy is the 73-year-old woman with a history of arthritis who has been symptomatic for 3 days.



The 50-year-old man with a history of hypertension and high cholesterol diagnosed with influenza after 3 days of symptoms (A) would not meet high-risk criteria based on his age and chronic medical conditions, and he has had symptoms for > 48 hours. A 9-year-old healthy boy who has had symptoms for 3 days (C) also would not benefit as much from treatment with antiviral therapy because of his age and health status. He has a low risk of complications. Additionally, he has had symptoms for 3 days. Finally, an asymptomatic 35-year-old woman with two children at home with influenza for 1 day (D) would not benefit from treatment with antivirals since she is asymptomatic. She may be considered for preventative therapy instead.

Question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the ED by his parent for evaluation of a tender lump in the right axilla. His parent reports that the boy was scratched on the hand by a kitten 2 weeks ago. The scratch has healed, but he has since developed fatigue and a mild fever. On examination, there is a 2 cm tender, mobile lymph node in the right axilla without overlying erythema or fluctuance. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or rash. Which of the following is the most likely expected clinical course for this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Development of bacillary angiomatosis in 2–4 weeks
Progression to systemic toxicity with fulminant liver failure
Resolution of lymphadenopathy in 1–2 weeks, followed by chronic polyarthralgias

ExplanationEN:
Bartonella henselae is the causative organism of cat scratch disease, a zoonotic infection typically transmitted by the scratch or bite of a cat, particularly kittens. The disease most commonly affects children and adolescents. The organism is a fastidious, gram-negative bacillus that resides in feline erythrocytes and is transmitted through contaminated claws or saliva. The incubation period is usually 3–10 days for the primary inoculation lesion and 1–3 weeks for regional lymphadenopathy. Patients often present with tender, unilateral lymphadenopathy near the site of inoculation, most commonly in the axillary, cervical, or epitrochlear regions.

In the ED, the diagnosis of cat scratch disease is primarily clinical, supported by a history of cat exposure and regional lymphadenopathy. Serologic testing or PCR for B. henselae may confirm the diagnosis in atypical cases. The disease is usually self-limited, resolving within 2–4 months. Management is primarily supportive, with antipyretics and analgesics. Antibiotic therapy with oral azithromycin for 5 days can shorten the duration of lymphadenopathy, although most immunocompetent patients recover without antibiotics. Immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV infection, may develop bacillary angiomatosis, hepatic or splenic lesions, or severe systemic infection and should receive longer courses of azithromycin or doxycycline.

Complications of cat scratch disease include suppuration of lymph nodes, encephalopathy, neuroretinitis, and osteomyelitis, although these are rare. Aspiration of fluctuant lymph nodes may be necessary to relieve pain, but incision and drainage are not recommended. In immunocompromised individuals, disseminated infection can lead to severe vascular proliferative lesions due to endothelial cell invasion by B. henselae, highlighting the importance of early recognition and antimicrobial therapy in these patients.



Bacillary angiomatosis (B) is a potential complication of B. hensalae infection, but it is most commonly seen in patients with HIV. It is uncommon in patients with other forms of immunocompromisation and even more rare in immunocompetent patients.

Systemic toxicity with liver failure (C) is not a prominent clinical presentation of cat scratch disease, which typically causes a self-limited illness that resolves completely in 2–4 months. It can cause hepatic manifestations in immunocompromised patients, but this is unlikely in this patient, who has no such history.

Chronic polyarthralgias (D) occur in the setting of several infectious diseases such as chikungunya virus and reactive arthritis, but they are not a common complication of cat scratch disease. Though uncommon, potential complications of cat scratch disease include bacillary angiomatosis, suppurative lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, and neurologic disease.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED with nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. She reports the symptoms started about 2 hours after she ate at a picnic. On examination, she appears nontoxic but is actively vomiting. Her abdominal exam is notable for hyperactive bowel sounds and mild, diffuse tenderness without signs of peritonitis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Bacillus cereus is a foodborne, spore-forming bacterium that causes illness due to a preformed enterotoxin. It is a common cause of enteritis and has toxins that can lead to emesis, diarrhea, or both. It is commonly found in pasta, rice, dairy products, dried foods, meat, fruits and vegetables, and seafood. It is heat resistant and therefore can survive boiling, which makes it difficult to eliminate.

These preformed enterotoxins are present in the food prior to ingestion and stimulate the host immune system to release inflammatory cytokines, resulting in nausea, vomiting, and mild nonbloody diarrhea. Because the toxins responsible for the illness are present prior to ingestion, the onset of symptoms is rapid, often between 1–6 hours. Other foodborne bacteria that also cause illness through a preformed toxin include Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium perfringens.

B. cereus food poisoning is typically self-limited, and the treatment is supportive. Oral rehydration, if tolerated, is preferred to parenteral fluids.



Escherichia coli (B), depending on the strain, can cause foodborne disease either through toxins produced after ingestion or direct invasion of the intestinal epithelium. Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes acute watery diarrhea and is a common cause of traveler’s diarrhea. The incubation period is between 1–3 days and it is typically contracted through unsanitary water or food. Treatment is supportive.

Salmonella serotype Typhi (C) causes severe illness through invasion and destruction of the intestinal epithelium, typically resulting in diarrhea, which can be bloody, as well as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping. The incubation period is 12–24 hours, and most infections are acquired during international travel. Treatment is largely supportive. Antibiotics are typically not recommended, as the illness is self-limited. In patients with severe cases, individuals < 3 months old or > 50 years old, those who are immunocompromised, and those with sickle cell disease or prosthetic grafts, antibiotic therapy may be useful. Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin is recommended as therapy in these cases.

Vibrio vulnificus (D) is a seafood-borne bacterium that causes illness through an enterotoxin produced after ingestion. Vibrio infection can be fatal in patients with liver disease or immunosuppression. It causes acute diarrhea, often dysentery. The incubation period is 1–2 days, as the toxin is formed after ingestion. V. vulnificus infections should be treated with antibiotic therapy as soon as possible. Recommended regimens include levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus an aminoglycoside can be used in children.

A parent presents to the ED with their 6-week-old infant for evaluation of a fever. The infant was born full term and has no other symptoms. Physical exam is normal and vital signs are HR is 160 bpm, SpO2 is 99%, and a rectal T is 101.4°F (38.6°C). Blood cultures are sent and lab results from a CBC, procalcitonin, and urinalysis are as follows:

WBC: 5,300/µL

Hemoglobin: 12.2 g/dL

Platelets: 205,000/µL

Absolute neutrophil count: 2,600/µL

Procalcitonin: 0.14 ng/mL

Urinalysis

WBC: 50–100/hpf

RBC: 0–4/hpf

Nitrite: positive

Leukocyte esterase: positive

Which of the following is the most appropriate care for this patient?

Options.text: Lumbar puncture and, if results are normal, discharge home with close outpatient follow-up
Lumbar puncture, intravenous antibiotics, and hospital admission
Oral antibiotics and discharge home with close outpatient follow-up

CorrectAnswer: Oral antibiotics and discharge home with close outpatient follow-up
ExplanationEN:
This patient is an infant between 29 and 60 days of age with a temperature ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) and a urinary tract infection (UTI) evident on urinalysis. Since the patient is > 28 days of age and has normal levels of inflammatory markers, specifically absolute neutrophil count (ANC) and procalcitonin, American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines recommend oral antibiotics and discharge home. Patients at 29–60 days of age who present with a fever without an evident source of infection should all have a urinalysis, blood culture, and inflammatory markers obtained. The inflammatory markers should include an ANC and procalcitonin level, but if procalcitonin is not readily available, a C-reactive protein (CRP) should be obtained instead.

Abnormal levels of inflammatory markers include an ANC > 4,000/µL and procalcitonin > 0.5 ng/mL, or ANC > 5,200/µL and CRP > 20 mg/L. For this patient, the urinalysis is consistent with a UTI, but the inflammatory marker levels are normal. The urine should be sent for culture to ensure appropriate antibiotic therapy. The patient should be started on oral antibiotics such as cefixime (8 mg/kg per day as a single dose) or cephalexin (50–100 mg/kg four times per day). Discharge home is appropriate as long as the patient can be seen for follow-up in 12–24 hours. For patients with abnormal levels of inflammatory markers, a lumbar puncture (LP) would be considered based on the overall clinical assessment. Unless a patient in this age range has CSF results consistent with meningitis, outpatient treatment is often reasonable, as long as close follow-up is available.



Intravenous antibiotics and hospital admission (A) may be considered if the child appears ill or cannot obtain close outpatient follow-up. However, in this case, oral antibiotics are more appropriate for a well-appearing child with a UTI and otherwise normal findings.

Based on the recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics,LP (B, C) is not indicated for an infant at 29–60 days old with an abnormal urinalysis but normal inflammatory marker levels. Additionally, the patient can be sufficiently treated with oral antibiotics and discharged with close follow-up.

Question: Several individuals have presented to your ED with lesions similar to those shown above over the last 2 days. Each patient reports a prodrome of fever, malaise, and back pain. Upon further investigation, it is noted that they all travel on the same subway route at a similar time each day. Which of the following is a hallmark of this disease process?

Options.text: Lesions appear at the same stage of development
Lesions appear at various stages of development
Lesions are vesicular and develop into erosions

CorrectAnswer: Lesions appear at the same stage of development
ExplanationEN:
These patients are presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with variola, or smallpox. This disease was eradicated in 1979 as declared by the World Health Organization and routine vaccination is no longer performed. The classic rash consists of macules and papules that progress to pustules, which coalesce in a centrifugal distribution, on the face and limbs more than the trunk, often developing first on the face and oral mucosa. These pustules are deep-seated, firm, and well-circumscribed. They progress slowly with each stage lasting 1–2 days. Unlike varicella, the smallpox lesions appear at the same stage of development.

Smallpox is an airborne pathogen and is a potentially devastating biological weapon. In this scenario, it was likely deployed as part of a terrorist attack given multiple patients with a common potential exposure. Diagnosis is usually clinical but must be confirmed by a viral swab of the oral mucosa or an open pustule. Management begins with containment. These patients should be placed in immediate contact, droplet, and airborne isolation as should family members and close contacts. The CDC and local law enforcement should be contacted immediately. Vaccination and immunoglobulin during the first few days of exposure may attenuate disease severity. Supportive care is the primary therapy once the rash appears. Untreated, mortality of smallpox is approximately 30%.



With varicella (or chickenpox), lesions appear at various stages of development (B) at the time which the patient presents.

Lesions that are vesicular and develop into erosions (C) is the classic presentation and description of vesiculobullous disorders, such as erythema multiforme or Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Question: A 29-year-old previously healthy man presents to the ED with fever, myalgias, and a dry cough that began 4 days ago. He recently returned from a hiking trip in rural New Mexico, where he stayed in an old cabin and discovered a dead rodent inside. He now appears ill and is in moderate respiratory distress. His vital signs are a T of 38.3°C (100.9°F), BP of 94/60 mm Hg, HR of 118 bpm, RR of 28/min, and SpO2 of 88% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals bibasilar crackles. His chest X-ray is shown above. Laboratory evaluation reveals thrombocytopenia and hemoconcentration. What is the most appropriate treatment for the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with rapidly progressive respiratory compromise, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, bilateral pulmonary infiltrations on chest X-ray, and recent rodent exposure in an endemic region. These features are suggestive of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).

Although the diagnosis is confirmed with serologic or molecular testing, treatment should not be delayed. Supportive care, especially meticulous cardiorespiratory support, is the cornerstone of treatment. This includes oxygen supplementation, early mechanical ventilation if indicated, fluid replacement to prevent volume overload, and vasopressors if needed. Transfer to an intensive care unit with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capability is warranted early in the disease course due to a high risk of rapid decompensation.

No antiviral or disease-specific treatment has been shown to improve outcomes in HCPS. The mortality rate remains high, especially when diagnosis is delayed or when supportive care is inadequate.



Acyclovir (A) is used to treat infections caused by herpesviruses. This patient’s constellation of symptoms and environmental exposure is not consistent with any acyclovir-treatable illness. There is no role for acyclovir in the treatment of suspected HCPS.

Doxycycline (B) is effective against several zoonotic infections, including leptospirosis and rickettsial diseases, but has not been shown to benefit HCPS. This patient’s presentation, especially the severe respiratory involvement, is more consistent with HCPS.

IV corticosteroids (C) have been studied for their potential to reduce pulmonary capillary leak in HCPS, but they have not consistently shown a benefit and are not routinely recommended. Supportive care remains the mainstay, and steroids should not replace or delay definitive treatment in a critical care setting.

Ribavirin (D) has demonstrated some efficacy in certain Old World (i.e., Africa, Asia, Europe) hantavirus infections, such as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, but it has not been shown to improve outcomes in New World (i.e., Americas) hantavirus infections like HCPS. Given its limited evidence and adverse effect profile, it is not routinely used.

Question: A 37-year-old man with a known history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, human immunodeficiency virus without current antiretroviral therapy, and ongoing intravenous heroin use presents to the emergency department reporting 3 days of worsening fevers, lethargy, sinus pain, purulent nasal discharge, and facial swelling. The patient states that today he noticed that the roof of his mouth looked black, which is what prompted his presentation. His vital signs include a temperature of 101.5°F (38.6ºC), a heart rate of 124 bpm, a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/minute, a blood pressure of 102/54 mm Hg, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. The patient appears toxic, with labored breathing but clear lungs on auscultation. Physical examination is notable for left-sided periorbital and perinasal erythema and edema without crepitus, necrosis of the mucosal surfaces of the nose, and black eschars of the patient’s soft and hard palates without involvement of the patient’s dentition. Laboratory studies reveal a sodium of 128 mmol/L, potassium of 4.0 mmol/L, chloride of 92 mmol/L, bicarbonate of 8 mmol/L, glucose of 646 mg/dL, beta-hydroxybutyrate of 7.6 mmol/L, and lactate of 4.8 mmol/L. Along with beginning treatment for his uncontrolled diabetes, which of the following treatments is indicated for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Recognition and treatment of rare opportunistic infections is vital to the practice of emergency medicine, as misdiagnosis of these conditions carries a heightened risk of morbidity and mortality without proper management. This patient has multiple historical factors that make him susceptible to opportunistic infection, including intravenous drug use, untreated human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) with probable progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), and uncontrolled diabetes, the last of which notably leads to this patient’s primary pathology of rhinocerebral mucormycosis. The etiologic agent of this infection is the Rhizopus genus of fungi acquired through inhalation of spores that the cilia typically clear in immunocompetent hosts. Serum also normally inhibits the growth of Rhizopus in healthy individuals, but the serum of patients with diabetes-related ketoacidosis, like this patient, promotes Rhizopus growth due to the ketone reductase enzyme the fungus possesses, which allows it to grow vigorously in acidic, hyperglycemic environments.

Mucormycosis can manifest as pulmonary, gastrointestinal, or kidney infection, though the most common presentation of mucormycosis is rhinocerebral infection, the clinical hallmarks of which include initial signs of sinusitis such as fever, sinus pain, and purulent nasal drainage, with rapid progression to facial cellulitis and edema with nasal mucosal ulceration and necrosis, and characteristic eschar formation of the palates, nose, and orbital skin due to angioinvasion by the fungus. If untreated, the infection propagates intracranially, resulting in sinus thrombosis, obtundation, and uncal herniation. Along with the management of concomitant ketoacidosis, definitive treatment includes amphotericin B along with rapid initiation of surgical debridement, including removal of the palatal, nasal, and orbital tissue to ensure complete excision of infected tissue.



Albendazole and dexamethasone (A) is the recommended treatment for neurocysticercosis when active parasites are present. This typically presents as seizures and is the leading worldwide cause of adult-onset epilepsy.

Ganciclovir (C) is the treatment of choice for infections related to cytomegalovirus such as retinitis or encephalitis, both of which are AIDS-defining diagnoses and indicate a CD4 count < 50 cells/mm3. The soft tissue findings present in this patient are atypical of cytomegalovirus infection.

Vancomycin and clindamycin (D) would be the appropriate initial management of necrotizing fasciitis, which does have similar attributes to rhinocerebral mucormycosis. Facial necrotizing fasciitis is exceedingly rare, and cases reported have stemmed from severe odontogenic infections or recent surgical procedures of the head and neck, neither of which are noted in this patient. Necrotizing bacterial infections spread along fascial planes due to their low blood supply, as opposed to the distinctive eschar formation of rhinocerebral mucormycosis in highly vascular regions. The lack of soft tissue crepitus and lack of dental involvement further support the initiation of antifungal therapy.

Question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for a rash. His parent states the child has had a fever for the past 3 days. The fever resolved, and he appears much better today, according to the parent, but then he developed the rash, as seen above. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 95/60 mm Hg, HR is 90 bpm, RR is 15/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Roseola infantum, also known as exanthem subitum or sixth disease, is a mild illness mainly affecting children 6 months to 3 years old. It is caused by human herpesviruses 6 and 7. The virus spreads through saliva and causes a sudden high fever (39–41°C) lasting 3–4 days, followed by a rash that appears as the fever subsides. The rash consists of small pink or dark macules or maculopapules that blanch with pressure. It starts on the trunk and may spread to the neck and limbs, disappearing within 1–2 days. Despite the high fever, infants often remain well, though febrile seizures can occur. Encephalitis is rare, with the disease generally having an excellent prognosis and typically requiring no treatment.



Erythema infectiosum (A), also known as fifth disease, is caused by parvovirus B19. Unlike roseola, it often affects older children and begins with a slapped-cheek facial rash followed by a lacy rash on the body accompanied by fever, fatigue, and joint aches. In patients with hemoglobinopathies, it may cause aplastic anemia. These patients require close monitoring and possibly transfusion and admission.

Rubella (C), also known as German measles, is a viral infection characterized by a fine pink or hyperpigmented rash, mild fever, and lymphadenopathy, primarily affecting children and young adults. It is caused by the rubella virus and is preventable through vaccination. Rubella poses a significant risk to pregnant patients, as it can lead to serious congenital disorders if contracted during pregnancy.

Rubeola (D) or measles is a highly contagious viral illness notable for causing a blotchy rash, high fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and distinctive Koplik spots inside the mouth. It primarily affects children but is possible in any unvaccinated individual and can lead to serious complications like pneumonia and encephalitis.

Question: A 68-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 days of left-sided facial pain, tearing, and sensitivity to light. He reports developing a painful vesicular rash confined to the tip of his nose earlier today. Physical examination shows crusted vesicles limited to the nasal tip. What is the most common ocular complication associated with this patient's condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has herpes zoster ophthalmicus, caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic (V1) branch of the trigeminal nerve. The vesicular rash on the tip of the nose represents the Hutchinson sign, which indicates involvement of the nasociliary branch and strongly predicts ocular involvement. The associated symptoms of tearing, photophobia, and eye discomfort further support ocular surface disease related to herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

Keratitis is one of the most common ocular complications of herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Early in the disease course, patients often develop epithelial keratitis characterized by punctate epithelial erosions or pseudodendrites on fluorescein examination. Unlike herpes simplex virus dendrites, these lesions are typically smaller, lack terminal bulbs, and stain poorly with fluorescein. Keratitis may occur within days of rash onset and is a frequent cause of eye pain, photophobia, and blurred vision.

The pathophysiology of keratitis in herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves direct viral replication in corneal epithelial cells and immune-mediated inflammation. Corneal hypoesthesia is common due to trigeminal nerve involvement, which increases the risk of corneal injury and delayed healing. If not recognized and treated, keratitis can progress to stromal inflammation, scarring, and permanent vision impairment.

From an ED perspective, management priorities include early initiation of systemic antiviral therapy (famciclovir, valacyclovir, acyclovir), ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, to reduce the severity and duration of ocular disease. Patients with suspected herpes zoster ophthalmicus require urgent ophthalmology consultation, even if initial ocular findings are subtle, because keratitis and other complications may evolve rapidly. Supportive care, pain control, and avoidance of topical corticosteroids without ophthalmology guidance are also essential components of care.



Acute angle-closure glaucoma (A) is not a common ocular complication of herpes zoster ophthalmicus because varicella-zoster virus primarily affects the cornea, conjunctivae, and anterior uveal tract rather than the anatomic configuration of the anterior chamber angle. When intraocular pressure elevations occur in herpes zoster ophthalmicus, they are usually secondary to inflammatory trabeculitis or anterior uveitis rather than true pupillary block or angle-closure. These pressure changes are thus a downstream inflammatory effect rather than a primary disease manifestation. In contrast, keratitis develops frequently due to direct viral involvement of corneal epithelial cells and immune-mediated corneal inflammation, making it far more prevalent.

Optic neuritis (C) is an uncommon complication of herpes zoster ophthalmicus because optic nerve involvement requires posterior extension of inflammation beyond the structures most commonly affected by varicella-zoster virus reactivation. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus predominantly involves tissues innervated by the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve, including the cornea, conjunctiva, and anterior segment. Optic neuritis typically reflects deeper central nervous system involvement and occurs far less frequently than anterior segment disease.

Retinal detachment (D) is not a common ocular complication of herpes zoster ophthalmicus because it generally occurs only in the setting of severe posterior segment disease, such as acute retinal necrosis, which is rare. Varicella-zoster virus most often causes anterior segment pathology, including keratitis and uveitis, rather than primary retinal involvement. When retinal detachment does occur, it is typically a late complication of extensive retinal inflammation and necrosis rather than a routine manifestation of herpes zoster affecting the face and nose.

Question: A 65-year-old man presents with left leg pain. He reports progressive erythema and pain of his left lower leg after cutting it while working on his car. His examination is notable for a 5 x 5 cm area of induration and erythema with yellow purulent drainage. The area is warm to touch and tender to palpation. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication for outpatient management of this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat tissue, which manifests with localized skin erythema, edema, warmth, and pain. The most common pathogens implicated in cellulitis are beta-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA).

The treatment of cellulitis is based on whether or not there is associated purulence. Patients with purulent cellulitis should receive empiric coverage for MRSA. Oral antibiotics with MRSA coverage include doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, and linezolid. Patients with systemic symptoms requiring admission should receive parenteral antibiotics with coverage for MRSA, which include vancomycin, clindamycin, telavancin, daptomycin, and linezolid.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate (A) is a combination of penicillin and beta-lactamase inhibitor. While the addition of the beta-lactamase inhibitor extends the spectrum of amoxicillin to cover methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA), it does not cover MRSA. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is appropriate for use in cellulitis associated with human and animal bites.

Cephalexin (B) is a first-generation cephalosporin that has activity against streptococci and MSSA. It is appropriate for use in nonpurulent cellulitis but does not provide the MRSA coverage needed for the treatment of purulent cellulitis.

Levofloxacin (D) is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that, like the antibiotics mentioned above, has good streptococcal coverage but lacks coverage for MRSA. It is also associated with a variety of adverse effects, including tendon rupture and QT prolongation, so it is rarely used as a treatment for skin infections.

Question: A 12-month-old girl presents with the above rash that developed after 3 days of high fevers. The fever has subsided, and she has no other symptoms of illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to give to this family?

Options.text: She can return to daycare 14 days after disease onset
She can return to daycare 5 days after disease onset
She can return to daycare immediately
She can return to daycare when her rash resolves

CorrectAnswer: She can return to daycare immediately
ExplanationEN:
A pattern of 3–5 days of high fever followed by 1–2 days of a rash in an infant is most strongly associated with roseola. This most commonly occurs in children between 6 months and 4 years of age, with a peak at about 12 months. It is typically caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), but it can be caused by some serotypes of enterovirus, adenovirus, or parainfluenza.

Despite the high fever, children with roseola tend to lack other symptoms. Fussiness may accompany high fevers, but most children appear remarkably well despite the elevated temperatures. Cough and coryza are occasionally reported, and older children report headache and abdominal pain. Vomiting and diarrhea are rare. The rash is erythematous and macular or maculopapular, with discrete 2–5 mm macules often surrounded by a faint white or pale ring. Most children recover spontaneously with few complications.

HHV-6 spreads via asymptomatic shedding from a close family member. This theory was recently supported during the COVID-19 pandemic, as the prevalence of other viruses dropped with masking and social isolation, but HHV-6 did not. Children with sporadic cases of roseola are not considered contagious and may return to daycare immediately.



The guidelines to return to social activities for COVID-19 varied during the height of the pandemic, from up to 14 days after disease onset (A), and in some cases even up to 20 days. This is not the case for roseola.

Some sources give return-to-work guidelines for influenza as 5 days after illness onset (B), provided you are improving, not needing antipyretics, and no longer have fevers. Roseola does not have these guidelines.

Many viral exanthems are not themselves infectious and have no bearing on return-to-daycare guidelines. Roseola is similar, and return-to-daycare guidelines should depend on when the rash resolves (D).
