Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after a possible accidental ingestion. His parent states his son was playing while he was working in the garage. Suddenly the parent heard crying and noticed his son’s shirt was soaked with kerosene. The parent is concerned that the boy may have ingested kerosene. His physical exam is normal, and he is playing with his toys. Vital signs are also normal. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Obtain a chest X-ray and discharge if normal
Obtain a chest X-ray in 6 hours and discharge if normal
Obtain laboratory studies, chest X-ray, and discharge if normal

CorrectAnswer: Obtain a chest X-ray in 6 hours and discharge if normal
ExplanationEN:
Hydrocarbons are a common cause of accidental pediatric ingestions. Gasoline, motor oil, lighter fluid, kerosene, pine oil, lamp oil, and mineral spirits are the most commonly implicated hydrocarbons in accidental pediatric ingestions. Clinical manifestations of hydrocarbon ingestion involve the central nervous system as well as the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. Symptoms post-ingestion can progress rapidly. Central nervous system findings include lethargy, coma, seizures, ataxia, and visual changes. The cardiopulmonary effects of hydrocarbons are related to direct lung injury and myocardial sensitization to catecholamines. Patients can develop a necrotizing chemical pneumonitis or hemorrhagic pulmonary edema from a massive inflammatory response. The exaggerated effects of catecholamines on cardiac myocytes may result in deadly ventricular dysrhythmias.

The care of patients with potential hydrocarbon ingestion is mainly supportive. Respiratory symptoms are treated with supplemental oxygen and bronchodilators as needed. Patients with significant respiratory distress or altered mental status should undergo endotracheal intubation. Seizures are treated in a typical fashion with benzodiazepines. For asymptomatic patients, a 6-hour observation period is recommended. Patients can have delayed pulmonary findings and should have a chest X-ray performed at 6 hours post-ingestion. An asymptomatic patient can be discharged safely if their chest X-ray is normal.



Admission for observation (A) is not necessary for a patient who is asymptomatic given they remain asymptomatic and have a normal chest X-ray 6 hours post-ingestion.

Obtaining a chest X-ray and discharging if normal (B) would not be appropriate as patients can have delayed findings on chest X-ray. Patients should also be observed before obtaining a chest X-ray to assess for any delayed symptoms.

Similarly, obtaining laboratory studies, chest X-ray, and discharging if normal (D) would not be appropriate.

Question: Which of the following is a contraindication to flumazenil?
ExplanationEN:
Benzodiazepine overdose is a life-threatening condition characterized by somnolence, respiratory depression, and hypotension. It is one of the few toxicological emergencies for which an antidote exists. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that prevents binding at gamma-aminobutyric acid receptors and can even reverse benzodiazepines already bound to receptors. However, flumazenil use is not without risks. It can cause seizures, dysrhythmias, confusion, vomiting, agitation, and psychosis. The risk of precipitating seizures is of particular concern, as they can be extremely difficult to control.

Contraindications to flumazenil include mixed overdose, tricyclic antidepressant overdose, chronic benzodiazepine dependence, isoniazid overdose, head injury, and alcoholism. Large meta-analyses have determined the number needed to harm in all-comers is 6.2 for all adverse events and is 50 for serious adverse events (e.g., seizure and dysrhythmia). Accordingly, flumazenil use is a controversial decision in the overdose patient and is not recommended for routine use. Supportive care with intubation and intravenous fluids as needed for hypotension can treat many of these patients.



Age under 6 years (A) is not a contraindication to flumazenil, which can be used in patients of any age.

Iatrogenic overdose (B) is an ideal situation for flumazenil use, as the patient’s medical history is likely well-known and the presence of complicating medications is unlikely.

Prolonged QT (D) is not a contraindication to flumazenil overdose. However, it can be seen in tricyclic antidepressant overdose, which is a contraindication to flumazenil.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents after ingesting a bottle of imipramine. His ECG is shown above. What is the most appropriate treatment?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has ingested a large quantity of imipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant. Most commonly, anticholinergic symptoms predominate with tachycardia, flushed and dry skin, dilated pupils, and alteration of consciousness. Life-threatening effects are remembered by the three Cs: coma, convulsions, and cardiac dysrhythmia. Seizures are caused by several mechanisms including increased synaptic monoamines, sodium channel inhibition, and gamma-aminobutyric acid antagonism. Tricyclics also have direct alpha blockade leading to hypotension. On a cardiac level, sodium channel blockade leads to the effects seen on this ECG of QRS widening and the terminal R wave in lead aVR. The QT interval is also prolonged by blockage of potassium exit from the cell. The presence of QRS widening > 100 ms or ventricular dysrhythmia is an indication for treatment with sodium bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate may be administered in boluses of 1–2 mEq/kg until the QRS narrows. An infusion can be initiated to maintain a serum pH of 7.5–7.55. Once maximal alkalization occurs, if the QRS remains widened, hypertonic saline may be used.



Calcium gluconate (A) is not an antidote for tricyclic poisoning. It is used intravenously for cardiac membrane stability in severe hyperkalemia. Additionally, it may be used topically or as a local injection for hydrofluoric acid burns. Intravenous lipid emulsion (B) has been used successfully in cases of toxicity from lipophilic drugs including tricyclic antidepressants. However, its use is reserved for refractory cases despite traditional treatment with sodium bicarbonate. Physostigmine (C) is used in some anticholinergic toxidromes when patients manifest severe delirium. Its use is associated with asystole and it is generally considered contraindicated in tricyclic antidepressant overdose.

Question: A 51-year-old man presents to the ED in a postictal state. His vital signs include a heart rate of 98 bpm, blood pressure of 131/82 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 22/min, and oxygen saturation of 100% on 2 L nasal cannula. His fingerstick blood glucose measurement is 121 mg/dL. He is clearly postictal on examination with somnolence, a visible tongue bite, and evidence of urinary incontinence. He is unable to provide any history. However, his spouse arrives shortly after your evaluation and states that the patient has no history of seizures. She reports no trauma or substance use history, and she states that his medication list includes metoprolol, atorvastatin, tramadol, and insulin. Which of the following is the most likely explanation of his seizure?
ExplanationEN:
The synthetic analgesic tramadol has both opioid and non-opioid mechanisms responsible for its clinical effects. This drug is a reuptake inhibitor of serotonin and norepinephrine and has an active metabolite (O-desmethyltramadol) that is a mu-opioid receptor agonist.

Seizures have been described in patients using therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses of tramadol. The seizures are typically tonic clonic and last < 5 minutes. Interestingly, seizures seem to be precipitated by naloxone usage in these patients. Tramadol also confers the risk of respiratory depression typical of opiates and opioids.



The hydroxymethylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitor atorvastatin (A) is not associated with seizures. However, rhabdomyolysis is a known complication of this drug.

Cocaine (B) intoxication can cause seizures, but this patient has no history of substance use disorder, and his presentation is not consistent with cocaine intoxication, making this diagnosis less likely.

While insulin use (C) and resultant hypoglycemia are well known to cause seizures, this patient’s blood glucose measurement is within normal limits.

Metoprolol (D), a beta-blocker, has no membrane-stabilizing effect and would not be expected to cause seizures. Instead, this agent typically produces bradycardia and hypotension.

Question: A 4-year-old boy presents after spilling chemicals on himself while playing in the garage. He is confused, diaphoretic, and incontinent of urine. His temperature is 99.0°F (37.2°C), heart rate is 110 bpm, and blood pressure is 140/100 mm Hg. In addition to decontamination and supportive care, which of the following medication combinations is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has likely been poisoned by an organophosphate, a class of compounds commonly used in pesticides or chemical warfare. Exposure can occur via dermal, respiratory, or gastrointestinal routes. Organophosphates bind to acetylcholinesterase and inhibit the breakdown of acetylcholine. Muscarinic stimulation by acetylcholine causes salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, GI cramping, and emesis. Both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are stimulated, so patients can be tachycardic or bradycardic. Nicotinic stimulation of skeletal muscle causes fasciculations, muscle weakness, and paralysis. CNS effects include confusion, agitation, coma, and seizures. Mortality is caused by bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and bradycardia. Management includes decontamination, airway support, atropine, and pralidoxime. Atropine inhibits acetylcholine at muscarinic sites and should be given in repeated doses until bronchial secretions dry. Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase. Treatment should be initiated early, as organophosphate-bound acetylcholinesterase becomes “aged” with time and pralidoxime becomes ineffective.



Hydroxocobalamin (A) is part of the treatment for cyanide poisoning.

N-acetylcysteine (D) is the treatment for acetaminophen toxicity.

N-acetylcysteine and hydroxocobalamin (C) are not treatments for organophosphate poisoning.

Question: A large number of patients are presenting to the ED with varying degrees of ocular and blistering dermal burns after a chemical warfare attack in the city. Those closest to the point of attack have arrived intubated with blood-filled endotracheal tubes. Which chemical warfare agent was most likely used in this attack?
ExplanationEN:
Quick recognition of chemical warfare agent exposure is imperative to minimize the potential spread among clinicians and the community. There are four groups of chemical warfare agents: cyanide-related toxins, vesicants (e.g., mustard), choking agents (e.g., phosgene), and nerve agents (e.g., sarin). This patient’s symptoms correlate most with mustard gas exposure.

Mustard gas is a vesicant that acts as an alkylating agent, damaging anything it touches. It is the only vesicant agent that does not cause pain immediately upon exposure, allowing it to spread further within the population before decontamination attempts begin. Symptoms commonly present as a triad of ocular, dermal, and pulmonary injuries, as these organ systems are where the gas can easily come into contact. Ocular effects include pain, miosis, photophobia, lacrimation, and blepharospasm. Dermal findings often initially include erythema that turns into vesicles and bullae. Respiratory symptoms start with cough, sore throat, and chest tightness, but as membranes slough, it can lead to pulmonary hemorrhage and respiratory failure. As with all chemical warfare agents, the mainstay of treatment is immediate removal from the source of the gas, decontamination, and supportive care.



Cyanide (A) presents with primarily neurologic symptoms ranging from headaches to comas and seizures. Treatment is with hydroxycobalamin.

Phosgene (C) interferes with oxygen diffusion across the alveoli, leading to respiratory distress, often in a delayed fashion. Patients can develop pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress syndrome. While they can also develop ocular irritation and dermal symptoms, patients do not develop blisters with phosgene exposure. Although phosgene is often considered a vesicant, it technically is not, as the urticarial lesions that develop following contact are not fluid filled. Phosgene smells like freshly cut hay or grass, commonly causing individuals to inhale deeper, allowing for more widespread pulmonary effects. Treatment is supportive.

Sarin (D) is an organophosphate nerve gas that leads to a cholinergic toxidrome. Treatment is with atropine and pralidoxime.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening neurologic emergency that is associated with the use of neuroleptic agents. Medications associated with NMS are most often high-potency first-generation neuroleptic agents such as haloperidol or fluphenazine. However, all classes of neuroleptic medications have been implicated, including the low-potency and second-generation medications (risperidone, clozapine, and olanzapine). Antiemetic drugs such as metoclopramide and promethazine have also been found to cause NMS.

Clinical features classically include a tetrad of distinctive features: mental status change, muscle rigidity, fever and hyperthermia, and autonomic instability, with each feature being present in 97–100% of patients. The mental status changes are often described as agitated delirium, which can be hard to appreciate in these patients, as it is often dismissed as an exacerbation of their current psychiatric disorder. The muscular rigidity is classically described as “lead-pipe rigid.” Temperatures of 38℃ are typical but can be > 40℃. Tachycardia and labile or elevated blood pressures are the most common autonomic dysfunctions noted, with tachypnea, dysrhythmias, and diaphoresis also occurring.

Laboratory findings consistent with NMS are elevated creatine kinase (typically > 1,000 IU/L but can be as high as 10,000 IU/L), leukocytosis, mild elevations in lactate dehydrogenase and liver enzymes, myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and low iron levels. The diagnosis is clinical and is made when a patient takes associated medications and develops the clinical syndrome. Laboratory evaluation can help support the diagnosis.

Treatment focuses on stopping the causative agent, supportive care, and administering specific medications. Supportive care includes treating dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, kidney failure, dysrhythmias, hypertension, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or seizures. Specific medical therapies should also be administered in an attempt to hasten clinical response and improve outcomes. Lorazepam should be administered, followed by dantrolene, which is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant. Bromocriptine and amantadine are other medications that can be administered.



Malignant hyperthermia (A) occurs in the clinical setting in which there is use of a potent halogenated inhalational anesthetic agent and succinylcholine. The appearance of hyperthermia, dysautonomia, and muscle rigidity suggests malignant hyperthermia. Treatment includes supportive measures and the administration of dantrolene. The patient above does not have the appropriate clinical setting in order to suspect malignant hyperthermia.

Septic shock (C) occurs in the setting of bacteremia and severe infection that results in end-organ dysfunction and hypotension. Although the patient above could have an infection, the setting of muscle rigidity and being on a known antipsychotic makes infection and septic shock less likely.

Serotonin syndrome (D)] occurs in the setting of serotonin excess, usually secondary to medications that prevent serotonin uptake. This can occur with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, monoxide amine oxidase inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and herbal supplements such as St. John wort. Clinical features include clonus, hyperreflexia, shivering, and ataxia. Patients may also have rigidity, tremor, dilated pupils, and diaphoresis. The patient above does not demonstrate hyperreflexia or clonus and is not on any medications that cause serotonin syndrome, so this diagnosis is less likely.

Question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the ED via ambulance. She is actively seizing. She received several doses of IV diazepam without improvement. The patient’s parent arrives with an empty pill bottle that she recently started taking after a positive tuberculin skin test. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to administer next?
ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely ingested a large quantity of her parent’s isoniazid, which is used to treat latent tuberculosis. Isoniazid competitively interferes with pyridoxine metabolism by inhibiting the enzyme pyridoxine phosphokinase, which is required to form the active cofactor pyridoxal 5-phosphate.

This cofactor is essential for the synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid, the brain’s primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. With chronic use, pyridoxine deficiency often results in peripheral neuropathy. However, in acute overdose, the rapid depletion of gamma-aminobutyric acid results in intractable seizures refractory to conventional anticonvulsant therapy, as seen in this patient.

If the isoniazid dose is known, pyridoxine should be given IV on a gram-for-gram basis equal to the isoniazid dose, administered as a slow bolus over 3–5 minutes. If the isoniazid dose is unknown, an initial intravenous bolus of 80 mg/kg of pyridoxine should be given in children. If seizures continue, the pyridoxine dose may be repeated. It would be rare that > 10 g of pyridoxine would need to be given.



Carbamazepine (A) is a potential daily maintenance treatment for pediatric patients with a known seizure disorder that can cause seizures at toxic levels. Carbamazepine is not used to treat tuberculosis.

Magnesium sulfate (B) would be an appropriate treatment for a child in status asthmaticus with severe respiratory distress.

Pentobarbital (C) and other barbiturates work through gamma-aminobutyric acid mechanisms, but they are ineffective without adequate gamma-aminobutyric acid substrate. Pyridoxine must be given first to restore gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis.

Question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after a nearby terrorist attack. He had a minor arm injury and waited as the department cared for other critically ill patients. He is brought to a room 4 hours after arrival, with difficulty breathing. His SpO2 is 88% on room air. Physical examination reveals diffuse crackles on the chest, and a chest X-ray is shown above. Witnesses reported an odor of freshly cut grass at the scene. Which of the following agents is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
ExplanationEN:
Phosgene (COCl₂, carbonyl dichloride) is a high-production-volume industrial chemical used worldwide in the manufacture of plastics, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and dyes. It was first deployed as a chemical warfare agent during World War I, but the primary means of exposure today is via industrial accidents. However, the risk of deliberate release in a terrorist attack is a significant concern. Phosgene's toxicity is driven by its low water solubility, which allows it to bypass the upper airways without causing significant irritation and penetrate deep into the alveoli. At this level, phosgene reacts with surfactant and cellular proteins, generating hydrochloric acid and triggering a cascade of inflammatory and oxidative reactions. This leads to disruption of the alveolar-capillary barrier, increased pulmonary capillary permeability, and the development of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, which may progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Clinically, patients may initially be asymptomatic or have only a mild cough and chest tightness. However, within hours to as late as 48 hours, they develop progressive dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, diffuse crackles, and wheezing. Chest imaging commonly reveals interstitial or central pulmonary edema. The diagnosis is clinical, based on an appropriate combination of exposure history, the characteristic odor of freshly cut hay, the delayed-onset respiratory toxidrome, and imaging findings.

Management in the emergency department is primarily supportive, as no specific antidote exists. Key principles include bed rest (physical exertion exacerbates pulmonary inflammation and must be strictly avoided between exposure and symptom onset), limitation of supplemental oxygen unless overt hypoxemia is present, glucocorticoids (e.g., methylprednisolone 1g IV), and bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol) for wheezing. N-acetylcysteine and ibuprofen have shown theoretical benefit in animal models but lack robust clinical evidence. Patients requiring ventilatory support should be treated with lung-protective ventilation strategies with high PEEP, and diuretics should be avoided as they may worsen intravascular hypovolemia. Complications include progression to ARDS, bacterial superinfection, and long-term sequelae, including reactive airways dysfunction syndrome, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiolitis obliterans, bronchiectasis, and emphysema.



Chlorine (A) has intermediate water solubility and therefore causes prominent immediate upper airway irritation (e.g., burning eyes, rhinorrhea, cough, and throat pain) at the time of exposure, rather than the delayed presentation seen in this case. While high-dose chlorine exposure can cause acute lung injury, the lack of early upper airway symptoms and the characteristic "freshly cut grass" suggest against chlorine as the cause.

Cyanide (B) is a systemic asphyxiant that inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing rapid-onset cellular hypoxia with altered mental status, seizures, cardiovascular collapse, and lactic acidosis. It does not cause a delayed-onset pulmonary edema pattern.

Sarin (D) is an organophosphate nerve agent that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, producing a cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramping, emesis) along with miosis, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, fasciculations, seizures, and respiratory failure. This typically occurs within minutes of exposure, and the absence of cholinergic signs plus the delayed presentation in this case are inconsistent with sarin exposure.

Reveal Answer:
Patients exposed to a nerve agent will have bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, cyanosis, and copious nasal secretions that are not present in cyanide poisoning.

Question: A patient presents with abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea after an exposure. Vital signs are significant for an HR of 50 bpm. On exam, the patient is salivating, wheezing, and has 2 mm, round, equal, and reactive pupils. An ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient’s suspected toxidrome?
ExplanationEN:
Organophosphates are found in insecticides and nerve agents that may be used in warfare. Patients with organophosphate toxicity present similarly to those with a cholinergic crisis. Two mnemonics commonly used to remember the muscarinic effects of organophosphates are SLUDGE, which stands for salivation, lacrimation, urine incontinence, diarrhea, GI cramps, and emesis, and DUMBBELSS, which stands for diarrhea, urine incontinence, miosis, bronchospasm and bronchorrhea, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, and sweating. Nicotinic effects include fasciculations, muscle weakness, and paralysis.

Atropine and pralidoxime are used in conjunction as the antidote for organophosphate toxicity. Organophosphates inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which catalyzes the breakdown of acetylcholine, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine. Atropine competitively inhibits muscarinic receptors, while pralidoxime binds to acetylcholinesterase, restoring its activity and facilitating the breakdown of accumulated acetylcholine.



Diazepam (B) is a benzodiazepine that may be used for agitation, hypertension, and hyperthermia in patients with sympathomimetic and phencyclidine toxicity, symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, and seizures.

Physostigmine (C) is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is rarely used in anticholinergic toxicity. Patients with anticholinergic toxicity present with anhidrosis, hyperthermia, nonreactive mydriasis, vasodilation, flushing, altered mental status, and urinary retention.

Sodium bicarbonate (D) is used to treat severe metabolic acidosis and cardiac conduction abnormalities such as QRS prolongation. It is also used to alkalize serum, which increases the kidney clearance of drugs such as salicylates, methotrexate, and phenobarbital.

Question: What cofactor should be supplemented in a patient with ethylene glycol poisoning?
ExplanationEN:
All patients with ethylene glycol toxicity should have supplemental thiamine given. Ethylene glycol is a colorless, odorless, sweet-tasting liquid that is typically found in antifreeze and automobile coolant. It is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. Like methanol, ethylene glycol is minimally toxic. However, the metabolites that result from breakdown in the body are extremely toxic. Oxalic acid combines with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals in the renal tubules and other tissues. They can lead to renal tubular necrosis and eventually to kidney failure. The major metabolite is glycolic acid. Ethylene glycol can produce a profound anion gap metabolic acidosis. Fomepizole can block the metabolism of ethylene glycol reducing the toxicity. In patients with severe acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, refractory toxicity, or kidney insufficiency, dialysis can be used to remove ethylene glycol from the body. Pyridoxine and thiamine are critical cofactors in the final metabolism pathways and must be supplemented.



Folinic acid (A) is necessary for methanol toxicity. Vitamin B12 (C) and vitamin K (D) are not involved in the treatment of toxic alcohols.

Question: A 34-year-old man presents to the ED with vomiting after exposure to pesticides while working as a farmer. Which of the following would you expect to find on physical exam?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with cholinergic toxicity secondary to organophosphate poisoning. Signs and symptoms of organophosphate poisoning relate to excess acetylcholine (ACh) at the nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. This produces the cholinergic toxidrome due to high postsynaptic parasympathetic activity, resulting in the classic SLUDGE mnemonic: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, gastrointestinal cramps, and emesis. Patients will also demonstrate diaphoresis, pupillary miosis, severe bronchorrhea, bradycardia, muscular fasciculations, paralysis, agitation, seizures, or even coma.

Management of organophosphate poisoning should begin with decontamination. Organophosphates bind tightly to acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of ACh. There are two keys to definitive treatment in patients with organophosphate poisoning. The first is to temporize the life-threatening signs and symptoms of cholinergic toxicity. Atropine is a competitive inhibitor of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. The goal of treatment with atropine is to titrate to the drying of bronchial secretions. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) is the definitive antidote to organophosphate poisoning. 2-PAM forms a complex with the bound acetylcholinesterase enzyme to cause the release of the organophosphate from the enzyme. This results in regeneration of its ability to metabolize ACh. 2-PAM is only effective if given early as the organophosphate-acetylcholinesterase complex matures quickly, resulting in the inability of 2-PAM to cause regeneration of the enzyme.



Dry mucous membranes (B), mydriasis (D), and tachycardia (E) are all associated with anticholinergic toxicity. Anticholinergic toxicity is characterized by the mnemonic “hot as a hare, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, red as a beet, mad as a hatter.” This represents the associated flushing, elevated temperature, dry skin and mucous membranes, altered mental status, and mydriasis associated with the anticholinergic toxidrome.

Hyperreflexia (C) and clonus can be observed in patients with serotonin syndrome, which is associated with antidepressants, dextromethorphan, meperidine, amphetamines, and ecstasy. Organophosphate poisoning does not typically cause reflex abnormalities, though some patients may exhibit delayed deep tendon reflexes 24–96 hours after exposure.

Question: A 35-year-old man presents with hyperthermia, hypertension, and altered mental status. He was recently started on haloperidol for schizophrenia. Physical examination reveals a confused patient with muscle rigidity. Which of the following medications should be administered?
ExplanationEN:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening complication of antipsychotic drug treatment. It is most often associated with the use of first-generation antipsychotic medications, such as haloperidol and fluphenazine, but can be seen with second-generation antipsychotic medications (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) and also with antiemetic drugs (metoclopramide and promethazine). It is rare and only affects 0.02–3% of patients receiving these drugs. Symptoms typically appear within the first 2 weeks of therapy, but it can be seen at any point in treatment and has also been linked to rapid dose escalation.

NMS is characterized by muscle rigidity (leading to elevated serum creatine kinase), hyperthermia, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. It is often mistaken for serotonin syndrome because the symptoms are very similar. However, serotonin syndrome is associated with the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Additionally, patients with serotonin syndrome often have shivering, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, and ataxia, which are rarely seen in NMS.

NMS can become complicated by cardiovascular collapse, coagulopathy, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and respiratory, liver, or kidney failure. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment. Discontinuation of the offending agent and treatment of agitation and rigidity with titrated doses of benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam) is recommended. Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist, and dantrolene, a direct-acting muscle relaxant, can also be beneficial in severe cases. However, evidence of benefit for both of these medications is limited.



Benztropine (A) is an anticholinergic agent that can be used to treat acute dystonic reactions due to neuroleptic agents.

Cyproheptadine (B) is the antidote for serotonin syndrome.

Naloxone (D) is the antidote for opiate overdoses.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents to the ED reporting abdominal pain. He works at a factory using wood preservatives. The patient states that he was not wearing his face mask today and inhaled gas at the factory. Since arriving in the ED, he also reports headaches, drowsiness, nausea, and a garlic taste in his mouth. Which of the following gases was this patient exposed to?
ExplanationEN:
Arsenic is a tasteless, odorless substance. It is associated with acute gastrointestinal effects including nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, hematochezia, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Patients often report a metallic or garlicky taste within 30–60 minutes of exposure. Arsenic exposure is primarily environmental or occupational. It is found in wood preservatives, the production of glass, microcircuits, smelters, and electric power plants that burn arsenic-rich coal. The most toxic form is trivalent arsenite (As3+) which is highly lipid soluble and well absorbed by the skin but has poor gastrointestinal absorption. Absorbed arsenic binds to hemoglobin, leukocytes, and plasma proteins and concentrates in the liver, spleen, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract. Arsenic binds strongly to lactate dehydrogenase and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase inhibiting critical steps in glycolysis. Arsine gas exposure leads to severe hemolysis that is associated with renal tubular injury. Cardiovascular effects include third spacing with shock, sinus tachycardia, or ventricular tachycardia. Neurologic effects include headache, delirium, coma, and seizures.

Chloral hydrate (B) is associated with the odor of pears.

Question: Which of the following would have a strong interaction with direct thrombin inhibitors?
ExplanationEN:
Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) refer to prescribed oral medications that are rapidly effective and short acting, and they include factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban and direct thrombin inhibitors such as dabigatran. Factor Xa inhibitors work by preventing the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, whereas direct thrombin inhibitors inactivate thrombin. Several medications can interact with DOACs, making them less effective or putting patients at risk for bleeding complications.

Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that can increase the metabolism of certain medications, including direct thrombin inhibitors. This interaction can lead to decreased levels of the medication in the blood, reducing their effectiveness in preventing clot formation. Thus, careful monitoring and possible dose adjustments of a direct thrombin inhibitor may be necessary when carbamazepine is coadministered.

When considering treatment with any DOACs, clinicians should know which drugs are noted for strong cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 induction, which necessitates avoiding combinations due to major clinical significance and decreased effectiveness of the chosen DOAC. Examples include apalutamide, enzalutamide, phenytoin, and rifampin. St John’s wort, another strong inducer of CYP3A4, should be limited to < 4 g per day due to its minor significance, while grapefruit juice, a strong inhibitor, should be minimized to < 200 mL. DOACs are also substrates for the permeability glycoprotein, which is a drug efflux protein. When a medication inhibits the permeability glycoprotein, DOACs may overaccumulate. The drug ritonavir combines strong permeability glycoprotein inhibition with strong CYP3A4 inhibition, and it is recommended to avoid this combination altogether.



Amoxicillin (A) is an antibiotic with no significant effect on the enzymes that metabolize direct thrombin inhibitors. It does not interact with CYP3A4 or the permeability glycoprotein, so it would not reduce the effectiveness of direct thrombin inhibitors.

Metformin (C) is primarily used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It does not undergo extensive metabolism by liver enzymes and does not significantly affect the metabolic pathways involved with direct thrombin inhibitors.

While paracetamol (D) is metabolized in the liver, it primarily undergoes glucuronidation and sulfation rather than metabolism through the CYP system. It is not known to induce or inhibit enzymes like CYP3A4. At normal doses, it is unlikely to affect the effectiveness of direct thrombin inhibitors.

Question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after overdosing on medication. The patient is confused and refuses to answer questions. Her family reports her initial symptoms were tremors, nausea, and vomiting. She has now become progressively more confused. Her T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 95/70 mm Hg, HR is 87 bpm, RR is 15/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals a woman who is confused and intermittently vomits. Clonus is noted in the lower extremities. An ECG is performed, as seen above. Which of the following is the most likely substance ingested?
ExplanationEN:
Acute lithium toxicity is life threatening and usually results secondary to intentional overdose. It predominantly presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Patients may initially present with muscle weakness and a fine tremor. More severe presentations may include confusion, seizures, and cardiac dysrhythmias (with QT prolongation on ECG). The diagnosis can be supported with a serum lithium level. However, the degree of lithium elevation may not always correlate with symptom severity and should not be relied upon solely. Management of acute overdose may include whole bowel irrigation (for extended-release formulations), IV fluids, avoidance of nephrotoxins (to promote kidney excretion), and dialysis.



Acetaminophen (A) overdose presents with a spectrum of symptoms, ranging from asymptomatic to severe gastrointestinal symptoms with fulminant liver failure. It would be prudent to check an acetaminophen level in this patient, but her neurologic symptoms and ECG changes make this a less likely overdose. Amitriptyline (B) is a tricyclic antidepressant, and an overdose of it may present with QRS prolongation (not seen above), cardiac dysrhythmias, and an anticholinergic toxidrome. Findings in an anticholinergic toxidrome include tachycardia, dry skin, reduced bowel sounds, ileus, urinary retention, and delirium. Aspirin (C) overdose may initially cause respiratory alkalosis followed by metabolic acidosis. Tachypnea, gastrointestinal symptoms, fever, confusion, and pulmonary edema are all possible symptoms in this condition.

Question: A 26-year-old presents to the ED by EMS for altered mental status. He is minimally responsive to sternal rub and has pinpoint pupils. Vital signs include HR 68 bpm, BP 92/54 mm Hg, and RR 6/minute. He is given naloxone 0.4 mg with a return of normal mentation and improvement in vital signs. Overdose of which of the following medications requires a prolonged observation period?
ExplanationEN:
The classic presentation of a patient with an opioid overdose includes central nervous system depression, respiratory depression, and miosis. Other signs and symptoms include relative bradycardia, mild hypotension, skin flushing, nausea, and vomiting. Depending on the route used, there may also be visible needle tracks, scars from skin popping (i.e., the process of injecting opioids subcutaneously), or fentanyl patches in place. Certain opioids can also cause specific findings on electrocardiogram, such as QT prolongation with methadone or QRS widening with propoxyphene.

The goal of treatment in patients with suspected opioid toxicity includes stabilization of the airway and supporting oxygenation and ventilation. In addition to basic supportive measures, the antidote of choice is naloxone, a competitive opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses the effects of toxicity. The initial dose ranges from 0.04 mg to 0.4 mg, depending on the clinical scenario, with additional doses given as needed to alleviate respiratory depression. Patients who have toxicity secondary to long-acting opioids, such as methadone, require longer observation and admission, as the half-life of the drug greatly exceeds the half-life of naloxone.



Heroin (A), hydrocodone (B), and hydromorphone (C) all have relatively short half-lives in contrast to methadone, which has a half-life of up to 24 hours or longer. Patients with a methadone overdose will likely require repeated doses of naloxone or a naloxone drip to maintain adequate respirations. Patients who present after an overdose of a short-acting opioid, such as heroin, can be safely discharged if they do not require additional doses of naloxone within a 2–4-hour period of observation.

Question: A 57-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia presents to the ED with severe agitation. On physical exam, you note severe muscular rigidity. Vital signs are BP 190/110 mm Hg, HR 140 bpm, RR 24/min, and T 101.9°F (38.8°C). Which of the following combinations is likely responsible for this patient’s presentation?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). NMS is a combination of hyperthermia, muscular rigidity, and autonomic dysregulation associated with the use of antipsychotic medications. Some of the most commonly implicated mechanisms by which NMS occurs are via dopamine depletion from taking phenothiazines or typical antipsychotics or by withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs such as levodopa. Haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic and promethazine a phenothiazine. Treatment of NMS includes benzodiazepines, discontinuation of the offending agent(s), aggressive cooling, and fluids. Dantrolene is the classic antidote and may be useful for moderate to severe cases.



Dextromethorphan and fluoxetine (A) will likely lead to serotonin syndrome, given the combination of an antidepressant with a drug that inhibits the reuptake of serotonin. Serotonin syndrome presents with hyperthermia, myoclonus, and hyperreflexia that is often greater in the lower extremities.

Phentolamine and labetalol (D) together is the classic treatment for pheochromocytoma. Phentolamine is given first for alpha blockade, followed by a beta-blocker.

Lithium and furosemide (C) together will often lead to lithium toxicity as furosemide causes decreased lithium clearance and elevation of the drug within the serum. Lithium toxicity classically presents with early GI symptoms such as nausea and vomiting and progresses to neurologic findings such as ataxia, altered mental status, and seizures.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents to the ED after accidentally ingesting an unknown amount of gasoline while siphoning from his friend’s gas tank. He is currently asymptomatic. Vital signs are BP 118/80 mm Hg, HR 80 bpm, RR 16/min, and T 98.2°F (36.8°C). Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

Options.text: Admit to hospital for continuous pulse oximetry and telemetry
Admit to the observation unit for 24 hours
Observe in the ED for 1 hour and if remaining asymptomatic, discharge home
Observe in the ED for 6 hours and if chest X-ray is normal, discharge home

CorrectAnswer: Observe in the ED for 6 hours and if chest X-ray is normal, discharge home
ExplanationEN:
This patient had an accidental hydrocarbon ingestion. However, he is entirely asymptomatic with normal vital signs. When considering the diagnosis and management of hydrocarbon ingestions, the most important thing is to assess for clinical evidence of aspiration. If the patient is initially asymptomatic and has no clinical evidence of aspiration, it is recommended to observe the patient for 6 hours in the ED and then obtain a chest X-ray. If, after observing in the ED for 6 hours, the patient remains asymptomatic and has a normal chest X-ray, he may be discharged home. Management of symptomatic patients with hydrocarbon aspiration is mainly supportive. Antibiotics and steroids have little if any role in the absence of a documented infection. Intentional ingestions, ingestions of hydrocarbons with systemic toxicity, and all symptomatic patients should be admitted for ongoing evaluation and monitoring. Patients who ingest hydrocarbons are at high risk for aspiration, which results from the unique characteristics of hydrocarbons including their low viscosity and surface tension and significant volatility. Hydrocarbons entering the lungs can cause significant aspiration pneumonitis by destroying the alveolar lipid membranes.



Given that this patient is asymptomatic, he does not require admission (A, B) at this time.

Observing the patient in the ED for 1 hour and discharging them home if they remain asymptomatic (D) would be a disservice to the patient, as they would not receive the complete recommended observation period. Symptoms can be delayed, and the patient requires a chest X-ray before discharge, which is best performed after 6 hours of observation.

Question: A 21-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose 4 hours ago. Her family found her with an empty pill bottle that contained one of her grandparent’s medications. In the ED, her vital signs are a BP of 105/80 mm Hg, HR of 109 bpm, RR of 31/min, and SpO2 of 96%. She is lethargic and diaphoretic and is not following commands. Pupils are 4 mm and reactive bilaterally. Results from a blood gas show a pH of 7.43, pCO2 of 20 mm Hg, and bicarbonate of 15 mEq/L. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with salicylate toxicity in the setting of an acute ingestion. Salicylate ingestion commonly involves aspirin, but it is also seen with oil of wintergreen, medications containing bismuth subsalicylate, and liniments. After an acute ingestion, salicylate levels take several hours to reach peak concentration. Salicylates exist in ionized and unionized states. Acidemia increases the amount of the unionized form, which can freely cross cell membranes, increasing the severity of toxic effects. Salicylates undergo hepatic metabolism, and the primary route of excretion during an overdose is via the kidneys. Early in the course of salicylate toxicity, patients have tachypnea, resulting in respiratory alkalosis. This is followed by a concomitant elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis. Late in the disease course, neurologic toxicity may cause respiratory depression, leading to respiratory acidosis. Patients may also present with GI symptoms, diaphoresis, ototoxicity, lethargy or confusion, seizures, or acute lung injury. Initial management of salicylate toxicity involves assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation. The mainstay of management includes hydration and alkalinization. Dehydration and electrolyte disturbances are common, and intravenous fluid resuscitation and the correction of metabolic abnormalities are critical. Systemic and urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is effective at increasing kidney clearance of salicylates. In severe toxicity, hemodialysis may be considered.



Activated charcoal (A) can reduce the systemic absorption of salicylates but should not be administered to patients with reduced consciousness due to the risk of aspiration. Midazolam (B) does not have a role in treating salicylate toxicity. Psychiatry consultation (C) is not necessary until the patient is medically stabilized. Evidence does not support whole bowel irrigation (E) for acute salicylate ingestion.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a seizure. The seizure involved bilateral stiffness with eyes rolling back and lasted for 3 minutes, after which it self resolved. The patient has not had any fevers. About an hour ago, he started coughing, vomiting, and sweating. He seemed more agitated and anxious for about 30 minutes, after which he had the seizure. Now he is lethargic with a heart rate of 62 bpm, respiratory rate of 10/min, blood pressure of 74/46 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. Which of the following substances did this patient most likely ingest?
ExplanationEN:
Most nicotine ingestions are self-limited and mild, but there is an associated increase in accidental high-concentration nicotine ingestions with the widespread distribution of liquid nicotine for vape pens. Nicotine binds to the nicotinic receptors of the brain and mimics the effects of acetylcholine, altering brain and spinal cord sodium and calcium channels. Nicotine ingestions are biphasic, with a period of neurologic stimulation followed by neurologic depression. The onset of symptoms is delayed by about an hour due to the poor absorption of nicotine in the stomach. They start with signs of nicotinic excess with salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, and diaphoresis. Neurologic symptoms include agitation, confusion, anxiety, and fasciculations. Tachycardia and hypertension are early signs but are often short-lived and may not be present on arrival. This is followed by a longer period of central nervous system depression with lethargy or weakness and may be accompanied by bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoventilation. When mild ingestions have symptoms, they tend to be vomiting and agitation. Only those with high-dose nicotine ingestions will have seizures. Testing for urine or serum metabolites of nicotine can be useful to make the diagnosis. Treatment is supportive as vomiting tends to limit absorption and most patients completely recover within 12 hours of symptom onset. Respiratory support is uncommonly needed but should be used in patients such as the one above with respiratory depression and hypoxia. Atropine can be used for salivation, wheezing, and bradycardia. Seizures can be treated with benzodiazepines, and hypotension usually responds to intravenous fluids in these patients.



Colchicine (A) is used as a medication for gout and can be found in the autumn crocus (i.e., wild saffron) and gloriosa superba (i.e., glory lily) plants. Colchicine poisonings are triphasic with vomiting and diarrhea for the first 12–24 hours, organ dysfunction (especially bone marrow), and finally recovery or death. Central nervous system symptoms are uncommon. All toxic alcohols, including ethylene glycol (B), cause central nervous effects such as inebriation and may cause vomiting, but ethylene glycol tends to have little effect on heart rate and blood pressure. Ethylene glycol poisoning is associated with kidney failure. Mushroom (C) ingestion can also present with vomiting and central nervous system stimulation or depression, but it typically presents with hallucinations. Wild muscarinic mushrooms are incredibly rare and do not cause seizures.

Question: A 51-year-old woman is found somnolent in the garage after a suspected suicide attempt. An empty bottle of antifreeze is found next to her. On arrival to the ED, vital signs are significant for HR 122 bpm, BP 114/66 mm Hg, RR 38/min, SpO2 99%, and T 37.6°C. Physical exam is unremarkable except for a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 and hyperpnea. She is protecting her airway. She is empirically treated with fomepizole. What other treatment should the patient receive while awaiting dialysis?
ExplanationEN:
Thiamine and pyridoxine are administered in ethylene glycol poisoning to promote the metabolism of toxic intermediates into less harmful compounds, thereby reducing the risk of kidney injury and worsening acidosis.

This patient’s presentation, somnolence, severe metabolic acidosis, and hyperpnea after suspected antifreeze (ethylene glycol) ingestion, reflect classic ethylene glycol toxicity. She has been appropriately started on fomepizole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and prevents the formation of toxic metabolites.

Ethylene glycol is metabolized in the liver to glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and oxalic acid. These metabolites are responsible for the high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypocalcemia, and kidney injury seen in poisoning. Thiamine and pyridoxine act as cofactors that facilitate the conversion of glyoxylic acid to less toxic metabolites, rather than to oxalate, which can cause kidney damage and hypocalcemia.

Experts recommend thiamine and pyridoxine as adjuncts in the management of ethylene glycol poisoning, given their theoretical benefit and low risk, although there is no high-level evidence or randomized controlled trials demonstrating improved clinical outcomes. Typical dosing regimens are thiamine 100 mg IV every 6 hours and pyridoxine 50 mg IV every 6 hours.



Intravenous ethanol (A) is an alternative but not supplemental treatment to fomepizole. If given to this patient, it will accumulate since fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and will lead to respiratory depression, thus impairing the patient’s compensatory mechanism.

Intubation (B) should be avoided at all costs in this patient despite their depressed mental status. This patient requires a high minute ventilation for respiratory compensation, which a ventilator cannot match.

Ethylene glycol adsorbs poorly to activated charcoal (C).

Question: A 21-year-old man presents to the ED with difficulty walking due to poor balance. His symptoms began this evening. The only thing he can recall out of the ordinary is that he ate grouper at a business lunch. On physical exam, he is profoundly ataxic and unable to keep his balance. Which of the following other neurologic symptoms is pathognomonic for the most likely disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with ciguatera toxicity. This is one of the most common fish-borne toxins, along with histamine fish toxicity. It is caused by ciguatoxin, a neurotoxin, which becomes concentrated in larger fish that ingest smaller fish that feed on coral reef dinoflagellates that form the toxin. These fish include barracuda, grouper, and red snapper, which are tropical, warm-weather fish that are exported worldwide. Ciguatoxin is odorless, colorless, and tasteless. It is not deactivated by heat. Signs and symptoms are variable in onset between 2 and 30 hours from ingestion. These include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and unique neurologic symptoms such as hot-cold temperature reversal, sensation of tooth looseness, ataxia, and coma. Patients may progress to bradycardia, hypotension, and pulmonary edema. Management is supportive care, IV fluids for hypotension, antiemetics, atropine for bradydysrhythmias, and mannitol to prevent or alleviate neurologic morbidity.



The Argyll Robertson pupil (A) is a pupil that accommodates to near objects but does not react to light. It is nearly pathognomonic for neurosyphilis.

Bilateral facial nerve palsy (B) is most characteristically seen with Lyme disease.

Disconjugate gaze (C) is most often encountered with entrapment of extraocular muscles such as the inferior rectus with an orbital blowout fracture or with cranial nerve palsies due to compression of various cranial nerves, such as the abducens nerve in cavernous sinus thrombosis or the oculomotor nerve in uncal herniation syndromes.

Question: A 70-year-old woman with a history of endometrial carcinoma is brought to the emergency department with altered mental status. Her vital signs on arrival are HR 72 bpm, RR 6/min, BP 140/90 mm Hg, and T 37.4°C. The patient opens her eyes to pain, localizes to pain, and mumbles disoriented words. Her physical exam is notable for miotic pupils and decreased bowel sounds. Which of the following is most likely to improve this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
Intoxication from therapeutic or recreational opioids is becoming increasingly common in the United States and worldwide. Classic signs of opioid toxidrome include altered mental status, decreased respiratory rate and tidal volume, diminished bowel sounds, and miotic pupils. Once opioid toxicity is suspected, initial management should center on support of the patient’s airway and breathing. Patients with depressed respiratory function should receive naloxone, a short-acting opioid antagonist, which may be given intranasally, intravenously, or intramuscularly. The goal of naloxone is adequate respiratory function, not normal mental status. After the use of naloxone, patients should be monitored for signs of recurring respiratory failure, as naloxone is shorter-acting than many opioid medications. The duration of monitoring is dependent on the half-life of the specific opiate used.



Physostigmine (C) can be used in anticholinergic poisoning, which presents with tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, and dilated pupils.

Sodium bicarbonate (D) can be used in the management of salicylate overdose and tricyclic antidepressant overdose (TCA). A salicylate overdose would be recognized by hyperpnea with associated respiratory alkalosis initially and subsequent metabolic acidosis. TCA toxicity manifests with mental status changes with dilated pupils and potential cardiac dysrhythmia.

Antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone (A), are not routinely indicated in patients presenting with overdose. It might be used in sepsis, which is not this patient's clinical picture.

Question: A 16-year-old boy swallows a large volume of drain cleaner in a suicide attempt. Which of the following is most likely to be associated with this ingestion?
ExplanationEN:
Caustic ingestions are commonly encountered with suicide attempts as well as unintentional ingestions by infants. Caustic materials are categorized as acids or alkalis. Alkalis lead to liquefaction necrosis, which results in extremely rapid, deep penetration into tissues. Alkalis commonly cause severe esophageal injuries due to this rapid penetration and the partial neutralization of the substance in the stomach. This is in contrast to acids, which cause coagulative necrosis, thereby creating an eschar and preventing deeper spread into tissues. As a result, acids are more likely to injure the stomach and spare the esophagus.

Common alkalis include laundry and dishwasher detergents, drain cleaners, and bleach. Common acids include battery fluid, metal cleaner, and rust remover. A gross generalization is that acids are commonly found in the garage and alkalis under the bathroom sink. The severity of a caustic ingestion is related to the amount and concentration of the ingested substance, the duration of contact with tissue, and the corrosiveness of the substance (i.e., acid versus alkali). Importantly, symptoms may not correlate with the extent of injury, and the absence of oropharyngeal burns does not rule out esophageal injury.

Emergency department care includes aggressive airway management for any signs of airway compromise and close monitoring for signs of esophageal perforation. In general there is no role for gastric lavage, activated charcoal, or neutralization in the management of caustic ingestions. Nasogastric tubes are contraindicated secondary to the risk of esophageal perforation. Dilution with milk or water may be beneficial if done immediately at the time of ingestion. With the exception of when there is a reliable history of unintentional ingestion of a small volume of a low-concentration caustic substance (e.g., household bleach) in a patient who remains asymptomatic several hours after ingestion, all patients with caustic ingestions should be admitted for endoscopy within 24 hours.



Coagulative necrosis of the stomach (A) is associated with the ingestion of acidic substances. As noted above, coagulative necrosis from acidic ingestions creates an eschar that reduces the penetration of these substances into deeper tissues. As a result, acids tend to cause less severe injuries when encountered dermally or by ingestion. The decreased rapid penetration into esophageal tissue also allows acidic substances to move distally in the gastrointestinal tract, where they tend to cause damage to the stomach. Duodenal injury is uncommon as acid-induced pylorospasm impairs gastric emptying. The approach to management is the same as for alkali ingestion, although the prognosis tends to be better.

Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia (B) is characteristic of hydrofluoric acid burns. Hydrofluoric acid is an exception to the rule that acids cause superficial burns secondary to coagulative necrosis. The fluoride ions in hydrofluoric acid form complexes with calcium and magnesium ions leading to systemic hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Treatment of hydrofluoric acid burns is with decontamination, irrigation with copious fluids, and calcium. Local wounds are treated with calcium gel (3.5 g calcium gluconate powder in 5 oz surgical gel, applied over 60 minutes). Persistent pain or systemic toxicity is treated with IV calcium and magnesium.

No significant injury (D) would not be expected in this case. The severity of a caustic ingestion is related to the amount and concentration of the ingested substance, the duration of contact with tissue, and the corrosiveness of the substance, with alkalis being more corrosive than acids. This patient ingested a large quantity of an alkali in a suicide attempt, which is associated with both larger quantity ingestions as well as worse outcomes. Even if he remains asymptomatic while in the emergency department and has no evidence of oropharyngeal burns, he should be admitted to the hospital for observation and endoscopy within 24 hours.

Question: A 5-year-old boy presents with lethargy, bradycardia, and hypotension after he was found eating flowers from a yellow oleander plant. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
ExplanationEN:
Nerium oleander (common, pink, or white oleander) and Thevetia peruviana (yellow oleander) are common plants containing cardiac glycosides and cause a constellation of symptoms similar to that of digoxin toxicity. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, and confusion are common presenting symptoms.

Ingestions can inhibit the sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase pump, leading to hyperkalemia, bradydysrhythmias, tachydysrhythmias, atrioventricular (AV) blocks, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation.

Treatment is with digoxin-specific antigen-binding fragments (Fab), which should be administered to any patient who shows signs of toxicity (e.g., bradycardia, AV blocks, tachydysrhythmias, ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension, hyperkalemia). Serum digoxin levels are not accurate in patients with cardiac glycoside poisoning from plant ingestions and should not be used to calculate the dosing of digoxin-specific Fab. Higher doses are necessary because the binding of digoxin-specific Fab to cardiac glycosides in plants is less efficient than to digoxin. Typical dosing is 10–20 vials, regardless of age.



In patients with bradydysrhythmias following ingestion of plant species that do not contain cardiac glycosides, atropine (A) should be administered. However, atropine and beta-adrenergic agents have not been shown to be beneficial in the treatment of cardiac glycoside ingestions.

Benzodiazepines (B) are the first-line treatment for seizures associated with ingestion of Cicuta spp and Oenathe crocata, known as water hemlock. Patients often present with vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, weakness, and dizziness, followed by prolonged seizures that can be difficult to control. They do not play a role in the treatment of cardiac glycoside poisoning.

Pyridoxine (D) is used in the treatment of seizures secondary to gyromitrin-containing mushrooms, also known as false morels. Ingestion of these species can cause nausea, vomiting, hepatotoxicity, altered mental status, and seizures. The mechanism of toxicity is similar to that of isoniazid, which causes a deficiency of pyridoxine.

Supportive care (E) is recommended for various ingestions for which there is no specific antidote or treatment.

Question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the ED with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and mild jaundice. Upon further questioning, she tearfully reports she took “two bottles of pills yesterday morning.” Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of acetaminophen toxicity. The treatment for acetaminophen toxicity is N-acetylcysteine (NAC). It may be given orally or intravenously. The intravenous protocol begins with a loading dose of 150 mg/kg over 1 hour and is followed by repeated dosing for 20 hours. The oral regimen begins with a loading dose of 140 mg/kg followed by 17 doses of 70 mg/kg, each given every 4 hours for a total duration of treatment of 72 hours. If the acetaminophen level and liver function tests have not normalized at the end of the 20 hours, the process is repeated. Signs and symptoms of acetaminophen toxicity vary based on the time of presentation from the time of ingestion. If a patient presents within the first 24 hours, they may present with nausea, vomiting, and anorexia or no symptoms at all. Between 24 and 72 hours, the initial GI symptoms resolve. The patient may develop right upper quadrant abdominal pain in addition to elevated liver enzymes and prolonged INR. Between 72 and 96 hours, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, acidosis, jaundice, kidney failure, cerebral edema, and death can occur. If the patient survives, liver dysfunction may resolve over 4–14 days. A key to the treatment of acetaminophen overdoses is to predict the risk of toxicity. A reliable time of ingestion and amount ingested should be obtained. The typical toxic dose is > 150 mg/kg. A serum acetaminophen level should be obtained at 4 hours after ingestion or as soon as possible thereafter based on the time of presentation. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram can be used to determine potential toxicity and whether to treat an ingestion.



Hemodialysis (A) and sodium bicarbonate (D) are the classic treatments for salicylate toxicity. Patients who present with salicylate overdose will generally have tachypnea, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and altered mental status. They do not present with signs of liver failure.

L-carnitine (B) is the antidote associated with valproic acid toxicity.

Question: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after an intentional overdose. She has a history of depression and bipolar disorder. The patient was found altered and minimally responsive by her parent with a suicide note. On arrival, the patient is altered and making nonsensical speech. Vital signs are remarkable for an HR of 120 bpm, RR of 28/min, and BP of 180/95 mm Hg. Which physical exam feature is most supportive of a tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
ExplanationEN:
From the late 1950s to the late 1980s, tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) were used extensively in the management of psychiatric disorders and depression. At regular doses, TCAs were quite effective in the treatment of these disorders. However, in overdose, they are toxic with numerous effects on multiple organ systems. TCAs cause antagonism of sodium channels, acetylcholine receptors, peripheral alpha-1 receptors, histamine receptors, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors. It is because the antagonism presents at multiple sites that patients develop clinical features. Mental status changes, such as decreased level of consciousness or delirium, are common features of CNS toxicity and are a result of the anticholinergic effects. Sinus tachycardia, hemodynamic compromise, and cardiac conduction abnormalities are common, with mortality largely due to refractory hypotension. Prolongation of the QRS with a terminal R wave seen in aVR is a hallmark feature of cardiac toxicity. However, ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation are the terminal results of the ECG changes. Lastly, patients will demonstrate other features of anticholinergic toxicity that include dry mucous membranes, delirium, hallucinations, hyperthermia, tachycardia, flushing, urinary retention, mydriasis, and decreased bowel sounds. Fluid resuscitation and supportive care, including benzodiazepines, should be used in the treatment of TCA overdose. In the setting of a prolonged QRS or ventricular dysrhythmia, the patient should receive sodium bicarbonate.



Clonus (A) is a relatively specific finding in serotonin syndrome and is not present in isolated TCA overdose.

Diaphoresis (B) is usually observed in sympathomimetic overdoses, not a TCA overdose. Patients with a TCA overdose generally have dry, hot skin with flushing.

Urinary frequency (D) is seen in organophosphate toxicity, along with increased salivation, lacrimation, defecation, gastric emesis, bronchorrhea, and bronchospasm.

Question: A 65-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve presents with hematemesis. His vital signs are BP 95/50 mm Hg and HR 118 bpm. The patient is on warfarin and has an INR of 7.3. What is the best next step in the treatment of this patient?

Options.text: Hold reversal agents because the patient has a mechanical valve
Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

CorrectAnswer: Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
ExplanationEN:
Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K recycling, thus limiting the effectiveness of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (factors II, VII, IX, and X). The effect of warfarin can be measured using the prothrombin time or the INR. Warfarin is indicated for anticoagulation for several disorders including the presence of a mechanical valve.

Patients with mechanical valves have a higher 1-year risk of clot formation around the valve and subsequent embolic stroke. The therapeutic goal of warfarin in a patient with a metallic valve is usually an INR of 2.5–3.5 or 3–4. Despite the increased stroke risk, patients with life-threatening bleeding should always have their warfarin reversed.

Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) is the preferred first-line agent for urgent reversal of warfarin because it provides rapid, reliable correction of the INR and replenishes vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) without the need for large-volume infusions. Multiple clinical guidelines recommend the use of 4F-PCC in conjunction with intravenous vitamin K in cases of warfarin-associated major bleeding,



Fresh frozen plasma (A) was previously recommended in addition to vitamin K to reverse the effects of warfarin. However, recent recommendations indicate that 4F-PCC is more effective at normalizing the INR.

Although patients with a mechanical valve are at an increased stroke risk (increased 1-year risk), reversal should not be delayed (B), as this patient has severe GI bleeding causing hemodynamic instability.

Warfarin is not amenable to hemodialysis (C) for removal or reversal.

Question: A 55-year-old man who does not have housing presents to the ED with altered mental status. The patient has alcohol use disorder and has frequent visits to the ED. Today he was found passed out on a park bench. The patient is responsive to verbal and noxious stimuli and says he drank a bottle of an unidentified liquid with other individuals who do not have housing. He only reports having blurred vision. His vital signs are unremarkable other than a HR of 110 bpm and RR of 26/min. Physical examination is remarkable for an intoxicated but arousable man. Visual acuities are remarkable for 20/100 OD and 20/150 OS. The remainder of the exam is unremarkable. Basic metabolic panel results include sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, glucose 90 mg/dL, and calcium 9.0 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Methanol is a toxic alcohol that is most commonly found in paint products, windshield washer fluid, and antifreeze. The toxicity of methanol is derived from its metabolites. Methanol will cause an elevated osmolar gap while the toxic metabolites (formate or formic acid) produce a significant anion gap metabolic acidosis. Symptoms of toxicity may not occur for up to 12–24 hours after ingestion when the metabolites begin to accumulate. Symptoms may be further delayed if ethanol is coingested due to competitive inhibition of metabolism by ethanol. Common clinical features include visual disturbances (classically described as a snowstorm appearance), central nervous system (CNS) depression (seen as intoxication similar to ethanol), nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Funduscopic examination may reveal retinal edema and optic disc hyperemia. Treatment is focused on metabolic blockage of the parent alcohol into its more toxic metabolites as well as the removal of the toxic metabolites.

The inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase is accomplished by either fomepizole or ethanol, both of which have a higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase compared to methanol, thereby preventing its metabolism. These should be given if the methanol level is > 20 mmol/L. Folate or folic acid can be supplemented intravenously to aid in the metabolism of formate into carbon dioxide and water. Dialysis should be considered for patients with refractory metabolic acidosis, visual disturbances, kidney abnormalities, deteriorating vital signs despite aggressive therapies, refractory electrolyte abnormalities, or if methanol or ethylene glycol levels are > 50 mmol/L.



Alcohols are potentially toxic, cause inebriation, and some will cause an anion gap acidosis. Ethanol and isopropanol are the most commonly ingested alcohols. These both cause direct toxicity, whereas methanol and ethylene glycol will cause toxicity as a result of their toxic metabolites. Although ethanol (A) can cause death secondary to respiratory depression, the morbidity and mortality of ethanol are typically the results of trauma or impaired cognitive functioning. Ethanol toxicity causes central nervous system depression, altered coordination, slurred speech, and disinhibited behavior. The odor of ethanol and nystagmus may also be observed on physical exam. Ethanol toxicity will cause neither an elevated osmolar gap nor an anion gap acidosis, which helps differentiate it from isopropanol, methanol, and ethylene glycol toxicities. The treatment for ethanol intoxication is mostly observation with supportive therapies as needed.

Ethylene glycol (B) is a toxic alcohol most commonly found in polishes, coolants, and detergents. Toxicity from ethylene glycol occurs as a result of the metabolism of ethylene glycol into its toxic metabolite that results in an anion gap acidosis. Ethylene glycol will cause an elevated osmolar gap, and the toxic metabolites will produce a significant anion gap acidosis. Clinical features include tachycardia, inebriation without the odor of ethanol (unless coingestion occurs), hypertension, and tachypnea. Acute respiratory distress syndrome, congestive heart failure, and circulatory collapse can occur. Kidney effects, kidney failure, costovertebral angle tenderness, and flank pain can occur as well. Vision changes or blindness are features seen in methanol intoxication and are not classically seen with ethylene glycol unless coingestion has occurred. Classically, kidney failure is an acute tubular necrosis that is secondary to calcium oxalate deposition. Treatment for ethylene glycol toxicity is similar to that of methanol toxicity with the following exceptions. The clinician needs to closely monitor calcium levels as calcium oxalate can precipitate, causing severe hypocalcemia and dysrhythmias. Supplementation of pyridoxine and thiamine instead of folate can be used to aid in the removal of the toxic metabolite.

Isopropanol (C)is a toxic alcohol that is most commonly found in skin and hair products, solvents, paint thinners, rubbing alcohol, and antifreeze. Acetone is the primary toxic metabolite. This metabolite will cause an elevated osmolar gap without an elevated anion gap, which helps differentiate it from methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity. Clinically, isopropanol intoxication is similar to ethanol intoxication but lasts longer and has a greater degree of central nervous system depression. The smell of ketones or rubbing alcohol may be present on the patient's breath. Hemorrhagic gastritis can commonly occur and may present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Treatment is based on the patients presenting symptoms. Patients who are and remain asymptomatic for 6–8 hours can be discharged home with close follow-up, unless the patient ingested the substance in an apparent suicide attempt. Prolonged CNS depression requires admission. Hypotension should be treated aggressively with intravenous fluids or vasopressors as needed. If hemorrhagic gastritis is thought to be a cause of the hypotension, transfusion should occur. If isopropanol levels are > 400 mmol/L and refractory hypotension is present, hemodialysis should be pursued.

Question: A 63-year-old woman presents to the ED by ambulance due to a change in mental status. Her medications include glipizide, amlodipine, olanzapine, and sertraline. Her vital signs are BP 140/90 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm, RR 20/min, and T 104℉ (40°C). On physical exam, she has muscle rigidity and hyperreflexia. Her blood glucose level is 114 mg/dL. Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
ExplanationEN:
Myoclonus, which is involuntary muscle jerks or spasms, helps to distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Both conditions are diagnosed clinically, but there is significant overlap in clinical presentation. Common symptoms include fever, muscle rigidity, and altered mental status. Serotonin syndrome tends to occur more acutely with a short duration (< 24 hours) between medication use and the onset of symptoms. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are more common in serotonin syndrome but can also occur in neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome typically manifests with fever, severe stiffness, and creatinine phosphokinase elevation. Serotonin syndrome is caused by serotonin reuptake inhibitors, while neuroleptic malignant syndrome is caused by dopamine receptor antagonists. Treatment is primarily supportive in both conditions. However, benzodiazepines may improve symptoms and lead to a faster recovery. In addition, cyproheptadine can be used to treat serotonin syndrome.



Diaphoresis (A) and high-grade fevers (C) are nonspecific and can be present in both neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome.

Elevation in creatine phosphokinase (B) is more common in neuroleptic malignant syndrome and is typically four times the upper limit of normal value, although it has been described in serotonin syndrome as well.

Question: A 41-year-old man presents to the ED with cough and wheezing after an intentional ingestion of lighter fluid. What is the mechanism by which this disease process occurs?

Options.text: Air trapping due to bronchospasm and inflammation

ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with pneumonitis secondary to hydrocarbon aspiration. Aspiration results from the unique characteristics of hydrocarbons which include their low viscosity, low surface tension, and significant volatility. Large volume (> 30 mL) ingestions are at high risk for aspiration caused by regurgitation. Symptoms may result immediately or can be delayed for up to 6 hours. Signs and symptoms of aspiration in these patients may include coughing, choking, dyspnea, grunting, rales, and hypoxia. Hydrocarbons entering the lungs cause a significant aspiration pneumonitis via destruction of the alveolar lipid membranes. Further evidence of aspiration pneumonitis includes persistent cough, bronchospasm, and progressive respiratory distress. Chest X-ray will reveal diffuse infiltrates, although this finding may be delayed. Patients will commonly develop hyperthermia, leukocytosis, and potentially even respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support. Management of hydrocarbon aspiration is largely supportive.



Air trapping due to bronchospasm and inflammation (A) is the hallmark of obstructive lung disease, most commonly seen in patients with asthma or COPD.

Low intravascular oncotic pressure (C) may lead to pulmonary edema in patients with nephrotic syndrome or chronic end-stage liver disease.

Right ventricular outflow obstruction (D) is the hallmark of massive pulmonary embolism.
