Question: A 61-year-old man with alcohol use disorder presents to the ED with altered mental status and hypoxia. He has coarse bilateral breath sounds that are diminished in the right upper lobe. He has dental caries and fresh emesis on his clothes. Chest X-ray is concerning for right upper lobar pneumonia. Which of the following antibiotic regimens is most appropriate at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Aspiration pneumonia is a subtype of acute lung parenchymal infection caused by the aspiration of oropharyngeal infectious material into the lower respiratory tract. Risk factors for aspiration pneumonia include altered mental status, poor oral hygiene (e.g., decayed teeth, gingivitis, dental plaque), advanced age, prolonged supine position, neuromuscular disease, abnormal mechanisms of deglutition, abnormal airway anatomy, presence of a nasogastric or percutaneous gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube, and history of aspiration. Intoxication, seizures, or medication overdose can lead to obtundation and possible aspiration. After urinary tract infections, aspiration pneumonia is the second most common cause of infections in nursing homes.

Patients typically present with shortness of breath, hypoxia, and low-grade fever with or without bronchospasms. However, presentations may be subtle and include altered mental status, generalized weakness, and decreased appetite or oral intake.

The management of aspiration pneumonia is evolving. The most up-to-date recommendations by the IDSA and the American Thoracic Society state that for patients with suspected aspiration pneumonia, routinely adding anaerobic coverage beyond the standard empiric treatment for community-acquired pneumonia is not recommended unless lung abscess or empyema are suspected. Previously, all patients with suspected aspiration received extended anaerobic coverage, but more recent studies have shown that anaerobes are uncommon in patients admitted with suspected aspiration pneumonia.

As further studies are needed in this area, it is important for medical professionals to remain current on medical literature and expert guidelines as they continue in their practice. Therefore, treatment for nonsevere pneumonia with a beta-lactam and macrolide such as ceftriaxone and azithromycin, respectively, is considered adequate.



Although clindamycin provides anaerobic coverage and doxycycline covers atypicals, the combination of clindamycin plus doxycycline (B) is not evidence based or guideline supported for aspiration pneumonia or community-acquired pneumonia. Doxycycline adds little value here and is not part of any recommended dual therapy. Additionally, clindamycin is falling out of favor as monotherapy for aspiration due to increasing anaerobic resistance and risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

A regimen of levofloxacin plus clindamycin (C) lacks strong support for either community-acquired pneumonia or aspiration pneumonia. Levofloxacin provides broad-spectrum coverage, including atypical pathogens, but clindamycin’s role is limited due to concerns about resistance and C. difficile. Moreover, there is no evidence that this combination improves outcomes or is superior to standard community-acquired pneumonia regimens. This choice would be excessive for uncomplicated aspiration with no signs of necrotizing infection or abscess formation.

The broad-spectrum combination of vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam (D) is appropriate for health care-associated pneumonia or cases with concern for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, such as in patients with recent hospitalization or advanced structural lung disease. This patient has no risk factors for these organisms. Using this combination in an otherwise stable patient risks overtreatment, antimicrobial resistance, and nephrotoxicity, especially given the lack of sepsis or health care exposure.

Question: A 56-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-day history of progressive submandibular swelling, dysphagia, and a muffled voice. He reports worsening pain in the floor of his mouth and neck, and is unable to lie flat due to a choking sensation. On examination, he is seated upright and leaning forward, drooling, and speaking with a “hot potato” voice. Vital signs are a T of 38.5°C (101.3°F), BP of 132/88 mm Hg, HR of 108 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. Physical examination reveals bilateral, firm, indurated submandibular swelling with tenderness and elevation of the floor of the mouth. There is marked trismus. What is the recommended initial method to secure the airway in this patient?

Options.text: Flexible fiberoptic nasal intubation with topical anesthesia
Rapid sequence intubation with induction and paralysis

CorrectAnswer: Flexible fiberoptic nasal intubation with topical anesthesia
ExplanationEN:
Ludwig angina is a potentially life-threatening, rapidly progressing cellulitis involving the submandibular space. This condition is frequently caused by odontogenic infections and can result in posterior displacement of the tongue and airway obstruction due to floor-of-mouth edema. In the early stages, patients may still be able to breathe and speak, but the window for safe airway control is narrow.

Flexible fiberoptic nasal intubation with topical anesthesia is the preferred airway technique for patients with Ludwig angina who exhibit signs of impending airway obstruction but can still maintain their airway. The nasal route bypasses oral edema and trismus, allowing passage of the flexible scope. Awake intubation permits the patient to maintain spontaneous ventilation and muscle tone, minimizing the risk of complete airway collapse during the procedure. Topical anesthetics help optimize comfort and suppress reflexes without the risks associated with systemic sedation.

This approach allows controlled, visualized airway access in settings where anatomical distortion and swelling make other techniques, such as direct laryngoscopy or blind techniques, particularly hazardous. It is often performed with assistance from anesthesiology or otolaryngology in a monitored setting.



Blind nasotracheal intubation (A) avoids oral instrumentation. It may seem useful in the presence of trismus. Still, it is a blind approach with a significant risk of trauma and failure in patients with distorted airway anatomy, as seen in Ludwig angina. It can provoke airway bleeding and worsen swelling, making definitive airway access even more difficult.

Laryngeal tube airway placement (C) is a supraglottic device that may offer temporary ventilation support but does not definitively secure the airway. These devices are also less effective in patients with upper airway distortion, edema, and pharyngeal mass effect, and they do not protect against aspiration.

Rapid sequence intubation with induction and paralysis (D) is dangerous because removing airway reflexes before securing the airway risks complete obstruction in the setting of severe floor-of-mouth swelling and posterior tongue displacement.

Tracheostomy under local anesthesia (E) is an acceptable second- or third-line method if fiberoptic intubation is not feasible or has failed. However, neck swelling and distorted landmarks can complicate tracheostomy. It is reserved for cases in which intubation cannot be achieved or is contraindicated. While tracheostomy is generally preferred over cricothyroidotomy due to lower risks of dysphonia and subglottic stenosis associated with cricothyroidotomy, emergency clinicians without tracheostomy expertise should perform cricothyroidotomy as the preferred and lifesaving approach to securing the airway.

Question: A 52-year-old woman with a history of severe COPD presents to the ED in acute respiratory distress. She has hypoxia with significantly altered mental status. Initial vital signs include a heart rate of 144 bpm, blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 48/min, temperature of 97.5°F (36.4°C), and oxygen saturation of 80% on a 100% nonrebreather mask. Physical findings include a leftward deviated trachea and loss of breath sounds on the right. What is the first step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a tension pneumothorax. This needs to be converted to a simple pneumothorax emergently or it will lead to a fatal outcome. Needle decompression is the quickest way to accomplish this. This involves taking a large-bore needle, usually a 14-gauge angiocatheter, and inserting it at the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line or the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. An immediate rush of air should be elicited. Longer angiocatheters increase the likelihood of successful penetration into the pleural space. Once decompressed, a chest tube should be placed.



Albuterol and ipratropium (A) nebulized treatment will not treat the underlying problem and will delay definitive care. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (C) is absolutely contraindicated in this patient. It could result in worsening of the tension pneumothorax. In addition, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation requires the patient to be awake with normal mental status. Orotracheal intubation (D) should be performed soon after needle decompression if the mental status does not immediately improve in order to secure the patient’s airway. Tube thoracostomy (E) should be performed once the chest is decompressed to definitively manage the pneumothorax.

Question: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a stab wound to the chest. His T is 98°F (36.7°C), BP is 100/61 mm Hg, HR is 122 bpm, RR is 35/min, and SpO2 is 85% on room air. The patient is placed on oxygen via nasal cannula. Physical exam reveals a chest wall wound with air entering the wound when the patient inhales. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

Options.text: 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask and observation
Placement of a chest tube and a three-sided dressing
Placement of a four-sided dressing and transfer to the operating room

CorrectAnswer: Placement of a chest tube and a three-sided dressing
ExplanationEN:
An open pneumothorax, also called a sucking chest wound, occurs when there is an open connection between the external environment and the pleural space. This leads to the accumulation of air in the pleural space with each breath. The diagnosis can be made clinically. Management is centered on placing a three-sided dressing on the wound to prevent air inflow when the patient inhales but allow for air to leave the pleural space when the patient exhales. In addition, a chest tube must be placed to remove air from the pleural space and prevent a tension pneumothorax from occurring. Further care involves surgery of the chest wall to repair the wound.



Administering 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask and observation (A) is the appropriate management of a small (< 20% lung volume) and asymptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax, not a sucking chest wound. Placement of a chest tube (B) would be appropriate management of a tension or large pneumothorax and one will be needed in this patient eventually. A tension pneumothorax presents with a pneumothorax in addition to tension physiology, including hypotension, tachycardia, and tracheal deviation. Along with a chest tube, this patient needs a three-sided dressing. Placement of a four-sided dressing and transfer to the operating room (D) could be dangerous as this may convert a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax.

Question: What radiographic finding is most consistent with reactivation or postprimary tuberculosis?

Options.text: 1–3 mm nodules uniformly distributed throughout the lung parenchyma
Apical segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe consolidation
Reticulonodular opacities in the perihilar region
Unilateral perihilar or paratracheal lymphadenopathy with or without parenchymal infiltrate

CorrectAnswer: Apical segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe consolidation
ExplanationEN:
Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, affects one-third of the world’s population and is a leading cause of infectious death. Lack of housing, urban crowding, immigration from endemic areas, and the HIV/AIDS epidemic all contribute to the continued presence of tuberculosis in the US, though the rates have declined steadily since the 1980s. Transmission is via the respiratory route with both droplets and aerosolization of microparticles.

Reactivation or postprimary tuberculosis occurs when there is reactivation of a previous focus of infection. It most frequently involves the apical segments of the upper lobes or the superior segments of the lower lobes. Most patients develop cough, weight loss, and fatigue. Chest pain, dyspnea, and night sweats are also common. Most patients with reactivation tuberculosis will have an abnormal chest radiograph findings, with opacities most frequently seen in the apical segments of the upper lobes. Reactivation tuberculosis is also more likely to cavitate than primary disease, and hilar adenopathy is seen in one-third of cases.



Radiographic findings in miliary tuberculosis include 1–3 mm nodules uniformly distributed throughout the lung parenchyma (A), described as a millet seed pattern. Miliary tuberculosis is the result of hematogenous dissemination of infection.

Reticulonodular opacities in the perihilar region (C) can be seen in the setting of viral or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Patients with Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia often present with a nonproductive cough, malaise, fever, sore throat, and headache. Treatment is with a macrolide antibiotic.

Patients with primary tuberculosis may have unremarkable chest radiograph findings or unilateral perihilar or paratracheal lymphadenopathy with or without a parenchymal infiltrate (D). Infiltrates can occur in any lobe but are usually homogeneous in appearance and limited to one lobe.

Question: A 56-year-old man is admitted to the surgical intensive care unit following exploratory laparotomy for a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He progresses well while being weaned from the ventilator and is currently on volume control mode with a TV of 620 mL, RR of 16/min, PEEP of 5 cm H2O, and FiO2 of 40%. His vital signs are within normal limits, and his ideal body weight is 73 kg. On post-op day 2, the patient has increasing oxygen requirements with an FiO2 of 80%. A chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates concerning for acute respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the patient’s ventilation strategy?

Options.text: Continue with the current ventilator settings
Increase the PEEP to 10 cm H 2 O
Increase the TV to 700 mL and increase the PEEP to 10 cm H 2 O
Reduce the TV to 430 mL and increase the PEEP to 14 cm H 2 O

CorrectAnswer: Reduce the TV to 430 mL and increase the PEEP to 14 cm H 2 O
ExplanationEN:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) refers to an inflammatory condition of the lungs caused by varying etiologies. Roughly 1 in 10 ICU patients and 1 in 5 mechanically ventilated patients meet the criteria for ARDS, which is characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, impaired gas exchange, reduced pulmonary compliance, and elevated pulmonary arterial pressure. ARDS typically occurs 6–72 hours after a particular inciting event, which can be pulmonary or extrapulmonary in nature, though cases associated with pulmonary causes are often more severe. Sepsis is the most common cause of ARDS and should be high on the differential diagnosis in patients with ARDS that are predisposed to serious infections or with new infectious signs. Other inciting events include major trauma or surgery, transfusion complications, pancreatitis, and certain medical therapies (e.g., chemotherapeutic agents).

ARDS most commonly presents with increasing oxygen requirements, worsening dyspnea, and alveolar infiltrates on radiographic imaging 6–72 hours after the inciting event. Additional findings include tachycardia, tachypnea, and bilateral pulmonary crackles, with cyanosis, frank respiratory distress, and altered mental status in severe cases. ARDS is defined by a PaO2/FiO2 of < 300 and the exclusion of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The diagnosis of ARDS can be made when these two conditions are met, but further diagnostic evaluation is warranted to assess for the underlying trigger if not initially apparent. Exclusion of cardiogenic pulmonary edema can be achieved via a combination of clinical evaluation (e.g., presence of S3 or S4 heart sounds), serum testing for B-type natriuretic peptide, and transthoracic echocardiography.

Mechanical ventilation, both invasive and noninvasive, and supportive measures are the mainstays of treatment for ARDS. In this case, the patient is already intubated, so his current ventilator settings should be optimized for lung protection and to maximize alveolar recruitment. This includes optimization of tidal volume to target a plateau pressure of ≤ 30 cm H2O, which corresponds to an initial tidal volume of 4–8 mL/kg of ideal body weight. A value of 6 mL/kg is used initially by many clinicians, so this patient’s tidal volume can be reduced to such a level, which corresponds to approximately 430 mL. PEEP can be titrated according to the patient’s oxygen requirements. At FiO2 of 80%, a PEEP of 14 cm H2O should be used.



The current ventilator settings (A) do not reflect a lung-protective strategy and should be modified to a lower TV and higher PEEP. Furthermore, this patient has increasing oxygen requirements so adjustment to the ventilator is needed. Increasing PEEP from the current level of 5 cm H2O is warranted, but 10 cm H2O (B) is still too low, and this patient’s current TV is too high as it is > 8 mL/kg. A PEEP of 14 cm H2O should be used at FiO2 of 80%. The RR is a less impactful component of ventilator management in ARDS. So long as the patient’s minute ventilation requirements are met, modifying the PEEP and TV should be implemented prior to changing the RR (C). Further increasing the TV (D) may increase the risk of alveolar over-distention and ventilator-associated lung injury and would not be advised in this case.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents to the ED with a headache, myalgias, fever, and a nonproductive cough for the last 3 days. His temperature is 102.2°F (39°C), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, heart rate is 80 bpm, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. A physical exam reveals a well-appearing young man who is in no apparent respiratory distress and has coarse rhonchi bilaterally. His chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is a risk factor for the suspected diagnosis?

Options.text: Recent immigration to the United States

ExplanationEN:
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical bacteria that is one of the most common causes of upper respiratory tract infections and pneumonia. It is the most common cause of walking pneumonia, which occurs when the patient has relatively mild symptoms, but the chest X-ray shows significant infiltrates. Infections are often seen in children > 3 years old and adults < 40 years old. Because it is easily transmissible by respiratory droplets, individuals in close community settings, such as college dormitories, military bases, and schools, are particularly susceptible.

Typical symptoms include a nonproductive cough, sore throat, fever, chills, headache, and pleuritic chest pain. The hallmark of this disease is that the patient may not appear as ill as expected based on radiographic findings. X-ray imaging will often reveal a generalized reticulonodular pattern, patchy infiltrates in the lower lobes, or streaks of interstitial infiltrates.

Initial treatment is with azithromycin (500 mg orally on the first day and 250 mg orally daily for 4 more days) or clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily for 7 days). If regional macrolide resistance is high, treatment recommendations are a 7-day course of either doxycycline (100 mg orally twice daily), levofloxacin (500 mg orally daily), or moxifloxacin (400 mg orally once daily). If a patient requires hospitalization, treatment is with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) or a beta-lactam (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) plus a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin).



Psittacosis is a type of atypical pneumonia that should be suspected in pet shop employees (B), owners of pet birds, and veterinarians because the causative organism, Chlamydia psittaci, is harbored in birds. Typically, patients have hyperpyrexia (up to 105°F or 40.6°C), severe headache, a cough, and relative bradycardia in relation to high fever. Chest X-ray typically reveals patchy lower lung field infiltrates. Treatment is with doxycycline (100 mg orally twice daily for 2 weeks).

Patients who have recently immigrated to the United States (C) may present with diseases that are less common in the US. However, this is not an independent risk factor for Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. This organism is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia globally and is not specifically associated with recent immigration.

Although there are certainly others, coccidioidomycosis (valley fever) and hantavirus should be high on the differential diagnosis in patients with respiratory illnesses who have had recent travel to the southwestern United States (D). Hantavirus infection results from inhalation of material contaminated with rodent urine and feces. An initial period of fever and cough typically evolves into severe respiratory distress over several days. Care is supportive. Coccidioidomycosis is caused by inhalation of spores of the fungus Coccidioides, which is typically found in soil in these regions. The typical incubation period is around 2 weeks, after which time most patients develop minor respiratory symptoms, and some develop fevers and myalgias. This illness rarely causes respiratory failure. Chest X-ray findings often include infiltrates with hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy instead of a reticular pattern seen in Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Treatment is supportive.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents to the ED with shortness of breath. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes semaglutide. His vital signs show T of 97.9°F (36.6°C), BP of 144/86 mm Hg, HR of 104 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 91% on room air. Physical examination shows accessory muscle usage and diffuse crackles bilaterally. A chest X-ray is shown above. Serum B-type natriuretic peptide and troponin I are within normal limits, and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound shows no gross cardiac dysfunction. The inferior vena cava is 1.8 cm in diameter and collapses with inspiration. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia without other abnormalities. Which of the following most likely predisposed the patient to his current condition?
ExplanationEN:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a distinct pathologic entity that causes hypoxemic respiratory failure associated with a heterogeneous group of underlying conditions. Its pathogenesis involves inflammatory injury to the alveoli and subsequent alveolar hemorrhage, collapse, and deposition of proteinaceous debris. This inflammatory cascade results in impaired gas exchange, reduced alveolar compliance, and increased pulmonary arterial pressure. A wide variety of predisposing conditions and risk factors have been described as contributing to the development of ARDS, but the most common etiologies are sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, and severe trauma, including burns. Of the choices provided in this case, sepsis is the most likely risk factor.

ARDS can present similarly to acute respiratory distress from cardiac etiologies. Thus, a cardiac cause must be ruled out, as treatment differs between the two. There is no single test to achieve this, but testing to evaluate for underlying cardiac disorders, including congestive heart failure and acute coronary syndrome, may be helpful. The unremarkable B-type natriuretic peptide level, ECG, and point-of-care echocardiogram all suggest against a cardiogenic cause of this patient’s pulmonary edema. At times, the underlying cause is readily apparent, and cardiogenic pulmonary edema can be quickly ruled out by clinical evaluation alone. In these cases, further diagnostic testing to rule out cardiac causes or to identify other noncardiac causes (e.g., fungal infection) may not be necessary.



Pulmonary edema associated with acute myocardial infarction (A) and valvular heart disease (E) would be cardiogenic in origin and, by convention, would not fit the diagnostic criteria for ARDS.

ARDS is not known to be a consequence of otherwise uncomplicated hyperglycemia (B), though it has been rarely described in association with diabetes-related ketoacidosis.

Hypoxemic respiratory failure may occur as a complication of pulmonary embolism (C) but occurs via shunting and V/Q mismatch rather than inflammatory alveolar injury, as is seen in ARDS.

Question: An 11-month-old girl presents to the ED with a barking cough and noisy breathing. On physical exam, you note stridor at rest with intercostal retractions. Subglottic tracheal narrowing is seen on a frontal neck X-ray. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
ExplanationEN:
This child is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with croup, also known as laryngotracheobronchitis. Treatment of patients with severe croup, most often defined as stridor at rest, should be with racemic epinephrine. If racemic epinephrine is administered, the child should be observed for 2–3 hours after treatment to ensure there is no rebound of severe symptoms.

Care of all patients with croup includes corticosteroids regardless of symptom severity. Dexamethasone is most often used due to its excellent oral bioavailability.

Croup primarily affects children aged 6 months to 3 years. The most common causative agent is parainfluenza virus type 1. Signs and symptoms of croup include a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms for 1–3 days, followed by the development of the characteristic barking seal-like cough and stridor. Children may also present with respiratory distress and retractions. Symptoms are typically worse at night and may improve when the child is taken outside into the cool night air.

Diagnosis of croup is clinical. However, if there is diagnostic uncertainty, a chest or neck radiograph can be performed and will likely show a steeple sign caused by subglottic edema and narrowing. Children with croup should be admitted to the hospital if they have continued stridor after racemic epinephrine, if stridor returns during the 3-hour observation period, or if they require repeated dosing of racemic epinephrine.



Albuterol (A) is the first-line therapy for wheezing associated with an asthma exacerbation, not croup.

Heliox (B) is a third-line therapy for patients with asthma or other respiratory disorders.

Methylprednisolone (C) may be utilized in patients with croup. However, in this patient with stridor at rest, the initial therapy should be racemic epinephrine, and steroids may be given after the initial intervention.

Question: Which of the following would indicate that a patient with pulmonary embolism is unsafe for discharge and outpatient treatment based on the Hestia criteria?

Options.text: Current use of apixaban for atrial fibrillation
Oxygen saturation of 96% on room air

CorrectAnswer: Current use of apixaban for atrial fibrillation
ExplanationEN:
While most patients diagnosed with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) in the ED will be admitted or placed in an ED observation unit, as many as 30% can be safely discharged from the ED. Those who are deemed to be appropriate for discharge with outpatient treatment are usually prescribed a direct oral anticoagulant (e.g., apixaban, rivaroxaban) and close follow-up with a clinician in the outpatient setting. Patients who are deemed not safe for discharge and outpatient treatment should be admitted to an inpatient unit. These patients typically should be placed in a telemetry-monitored unit, though patients with low-risk PE can be in unmonitored inpatient or ED observation units.

The Hestia criteria are a set of conditions that can be used to identify patients who are low risk for complications from acute PE and may be appropriate for discharge from the ED and outpatient treatment. The criteria are shown in the image below. Of the options in this scenario, a patient’s current use of anticoagulation therapy, such as apixaban, would qualify for inpatient admission.



A threshold for systolic blood pressure < 100 mm Hg is part of the Hestia criteria, so a blood pressure of 162/92 mm Hg (A) would be well above and would not make the patient unsafe for outpatient treatment.

Creatinine clearance of 40 mL/min (B) is above the Hestia criteria threshold of 30 mL/min and appropriate for outpatient treatment.

While preexisting medical comorbidities are taken into account in some validated decision algorithms, the Hestia criteria do not consider these, and a history of COPD (D) would not make a patient unsafe for outpatient treatment.

Oxygen saturation < 94% or the need for supplemental oxygen to maintain a higher oxygen saturation would make a patient unsafe for outpatient treatment by the Hestia criteria, but a patient with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air (E) would be appropriate for outpatient treatment.

Question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and daily tobacco use presents with atraumatic right shoulder pain. On exam, he has right-sided ptosis and miosis. An X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is being compressed, causing this patient’s ptosis and miosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s chest X-ray is suspicious for a superior pulmonary sulcus tumor, also known as a Pancoast tumor. These tumors are characterized as pulmonary neoplasms adjacent to the subclavian vessels, in the apical pleuropulmonary groove. The most common initial presenting symptom is shoulder pain due to either invasion of the brachial plexus or extension to the bony surroundings. Patients are often misdiagnosed with cervical osteoarthritis or shoulder bursitis. Thus, there is typically a delay in diagnosis. Patients with a Pancoast tumor may also develop Horner syndrome, a triad consisting of ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis due to compression of the paravertebral sympathetic chain and stellate (inferior cervical) ganglion. Compression of other local structures may cause hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve) or upper extremity neurological deficits (C8 and T1). Diagnosis should be suspected on a chest X-ray showing an apical pulmonary mass. The mass can be further identified and mapped using a CT scan or an MRI of the thorax. Diagnosis is confirmed via biopsy.



Compression of the brachial plexus (A) may present as shoulder pain or upper extremity sensorimotor deficits.

Hoarseness is a manifestation of recurrent laryngeal nerve (B) compression.

Superior vena cava (D) syndrome is a medical emergency that presents as facial plethora, jugular venous distension, and upper extremity edema due to impaired superior vena cava blood drainage from the head, neck, and upper extremities. It is most often caused by the mass effect of malignancies such as mediastinal masses and Pancoast tumors.

Question: A 32-year-old previously healthy man is transferred from another facility with bilateral femur fractures. He sustained the injury the day before while skiing and was evaluated at a local clinic. Due to weather, the transfer was delayed. He was reportedly hemodynamically stable on initial evaluation and underwent a CT of his head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis yesterday, where no other injuries were noted. On arrival, his heart rate is 115 bpm, respiratory rate is 24/min, blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 90% on 6 L oxygen via nasal cannula. ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with fat embolism syndrome after sustaining long bone fractures. The incidence is 1–2% with isolated long bone fractures, rising to 5–10% when multiple fractures are present. Fat embolism syndrome should be suspected in young adults with long bone fractures (commonly tibial or femoral) or older adults with hip fractures who develop respiratory distress. Symptoms usually occur 1–2 days after an acute injury or after intramedullary nailing. Fat embolism is believed to occur due to fat globules (from the bone marrow) entering the bloodstream at the site of a long bone fracture and embolizing in the peripheral tissues and lung parenchyma. The ensuing inflammatory response in pulmonary tissues will commonly lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome and hypoxia early on. Neurological complications include altered mental status and restlessness. Other possible features include petechial rash, fever, jaundice, and kidney injury. When suspected, chest imaging should be performed. On CT scan, consolidation and ground-glass opacities are commonly noted. Management is primarily supportive.

Echocardiography demonstrating global hypokinesis (C) is suggestive of heart failure or myocarditis, which are less likely sequelae of the patient’s trauma.

X-ray demonstrating wedge-shaped consolidation (D) can suggest pulmonary embolism, a finding known as Hampton hump. The timing of this patient’s symptoms makes this diagnosis less likely, and the clinical picture of multiple, recent long-bone fractures is far more consistent with fat embolism syndrome.

Question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a cough and dyspnea. His T is 101°F (38.3°C), BP is 115/79 mm Hg, HR is 122 bpm, RR is 24/min, and SpO2 is 89% on room air and 93% on 2 L oxygen. He has no significant medical history or recent hospital admission. His chest radiograph is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), but due to his oxygen requirements and tachycardia, he should be admitted to the hospital for IV antibiotics. Pneumonia typically originates from the microaspiration of upper respiratory pathogens into the normally sterile lower respiratory tract. If the invading organisms overwhelm the host’s defenses, this triggers an immune response marked by inflammation and clinical pneumonia. Typical bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are common culprits, whereas atypical pathogens include Legionella, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydophila species. Viruses, such as influenza, also frequently contribute to the disease.

Patients may present with cough, fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, and malaise. When the diagnosis is suspected, chest imaging should be performed and will show a focal infiltrate. The inpatient treatment of CAP can include a cephalosporin (ceftriaxone is commonly used) and a macrolide (azithromycin). Alternative options include a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin). For severe CAP, particularly in patients with signs of sepsis, necrotizing pneumonia, or potential influenza coinfection, empirical coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is recommended. This may include the use of vancomycin, tigecycline, linezolid, and ceftaroline, depending on local resistance patterns and specific patient factors. Patients with risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or who have previously grown the organism in sputum or blood should receive an antibiotic with appropriate coverage (piperacillin-tazobactam). Additionally, patients admitted to intensive care units with respiratory failure should receive oseltamivir during the influenza season to cover potential viral pneumonia coinfection.



Amoxicillin (A) is used to treat CAP in healthy patients with no comorbidities and who can be treated in the outpatient setting. This patient has oxygen requirements, so he should be admitted to the hospital with IV antibiotic treatment.

Levofloxacin and vancomycin (C) might be considered if there is a high suspicion of MRSA, or the combination might be used in patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia. Levofloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone with broad-spectrum activity that covers both typical and atypical pathogens, similar to the coverage of azithromycin and ceftriaxone. Vancomycin is added to cover MRSA. This patient does not require MRSA coverage.

Piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin (D) provide broad coverage against gram-negative bacteria (including Pseudomonas), gram-positive organisms, and anaerobes, with vancomycin covering MRSA. This regimen is often used in cases of hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia or in settings in which there is a high risk of multidrug-resistant pathogens.

Question: A 56-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder is brought to the ED after passing out at a bar with his colleagues this evening. He was intubated for airway protection by EMS after being found in vomitus. Vital signs are within normal limits. Chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral patchy infiltrates, most pronounced in the dependent lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient’s current condition?

Options.text: Continue mechanical ventilation with lung-protective settings and observe without antibiotics
Perform immediate bronchoscopy to remove aspirated material

CorrectAnswer: Continue mechanical ventilation with lung-protective settings and observe without antibiotics
ExplanationEN:
This patient has aspiration pneumonitis, a chemical lung injury caused by inhalation of sterile gastric contents, most often occurring in patients with impaired consciousness due to intoxication, seizures, anesthesia, or other neurologic conditions. Epidemiologic studies suggest it accounts for a significant proportion of acute lung injury cases in hospitalized patients, particularly in critical care settings. The acidic nature and particulate matter in gastric fluid cause direct damage to alveolar epithelium, capillary endothelium, and surfactant, leading to an inflammatory cascade, alveolar flooding, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a history of a witnessed or suspected aspiration event, rapid onset of hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates in dependent lung regions. In contrast to aspiration pneumonia, which is an infectious process, aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile inflammatory reaction. Early chest imaging may reveal bilateral or unilateral opacities, but these findings are nonspecific. Laboratory testing is typically not diagnostic, and sputum cultures are generally negative in the acute phase.

The mainstay of ED care is supportive care, with attention to oxygenation and ventilation. For intubated patients, lung-protective mechanical ventilation (tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure < 30 cm H2O) is recommended. Antibiotics are not indicated initially unless there is clinical deterioration after 36–48 hours, suggesting secondary bacterial infection. Corticosteroids have no proven benefit and may increase the risk of infection. Preventive measures include early airway protection in patients with altered mental status.



Antibiotics (A) are not routinely indicated in aspiration pneumonitis because the injury is sterile chemical inflammation, not infection. Initiating antibiotics unnecessarily can lead to antimicrobial resistance and Clostridioides difficile infection. In this patient, empiric antibiotics are reserved only for aspiration pneumonia, which typically presents > 36–48 hours after the event with fever, leukocytosis, and purulent sputum.

While aspiration pneumonitis is an inflammatory condition, multiple randomized trials have failed to demonstrate benefit from corticosteroid therapy (B) in improving oxygenation or mortality. Steroids may increase the risk of secondary infection.

Bronchoscopy (D) is indicated if there is a large, obstructing foreign body or particulate matter causing lobar collapse, but it is not routinely recommended in chemical pneumonitis. Most aspirated gastric fluid disperses throughout the lung and cannot be effectively removed via bronchoscopy. This patient’s presentation and diffuse infiltrates are consistent with widespread chemical injury, making bronchoscopy unlikely to change outcomes.

Finally, the pathophysiology of aspiration pneumonitis involves inflammatory exudation and alveolar flooding, not hydrostatic pulmonary edema from volume overload. Diuretics (E) have no role in the acute management of aspiration pneumonitis unless there is concomitant heart failure or fluid overload.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the local urgent care with a cough and chest pain for 2 weeks. He reports no improvement or worsening of symptoms, and no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. ExplanationEN:
Atypical pneumonia is classified by the causative organisms, clinical course, and X-ray findings compared to classic typical pneumonia, and the etiologic organisms can cause atypical-type pneumonia in older children, young adults, and older adults.

Atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, occurs year-round and presents as a subacute respiratory illness with cough, sore throat, and headache. It is also frequently associated with retrosternal chest pain.

The diagnosis is often made clinically based on the constellation of symptoms and signs. The chest X-ray may show patchy infiltrates rather than dense lobar consolidation.

Legionella pneumonia is commonly complicated by GI symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Urinary antigen testing in the appropriate patients can confirm the diagnosis. Question: A 64-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presents for evaluation of left-sided chest pain for 3 days. His physical exam shows decreased breath sounds in the left lower lung field and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray is shown above. Initial lab results show a white blood cell count of 16,700/µL, creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, and serum protein of 7 g/dL. A thoracentesis is performed, and the pleural fluid demonstrates the following results: protein 5 g/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL, pH 7.12, and lactate dehydrogenase 1,500 IU/L. What is the most likely etiology of these findings?
ExplanationEN:
Empyema is an infection characterized by the collection of frank pus within the pleural cavity, often preceded by bacterial pneumonia and a parapneumonic effusion. Infectious culprits may include Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species, gram-negative bacilli, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Fungal organisms can be found in patients with immunosuppression. Other less common etiologies include recent thoracic surgery or procedure, trauma, esophageal perforation, and infection of preexisting pleural fluid (e.g., hemothorax, chylothorax). Clinical features include pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, cough, and fever. Physical examination will demonstrate reduced breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and occasionally, a friction rub. Imaging such as chest X-ray, ultrasound, or CT can raise suspicion for the diagnosis.

The Light criteria differentiate an exudative from a transudative effusion, with an exudative effusion defined as one of the following: a fluid protein to serum protein ratio > 0.5 (this patient’s is 0.7), a fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to serum LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH > 200 IU/L. Empyema will certainly demonstrate an exudative pattern, but the specific diagnosis is defined by a positive Gram stain or culture, pleural glucose < 40 mg/dL, pH < 7.2, or LDH > 1,000 IU/L.

The definitive treatment of empyema includes source control with drainage and antibiotics. Intrapleural fibrinolytics may aid in the drainage of loculated empyemas. Empiric antibiotic regimens should have adequate penetration into the pleural space, which can be achieved with piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, a carbapenem, or clindamycin. If patients have risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, broader antimicrobial coverage should be considered.



Acute heart failure (A) and cirrhosis (B) will exhibit a transudative pattern on pleural fluid analysis, such as a fluid protein to serum protein ratio < 0.5, a fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio < 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH < 200 IU/L. Furthermore, effusions from cirrhosis are more commonly located on the right side.

Malignancy (D) leading to a pleural effusion will demonstrate a similar inflammatory pattern on analysis of pleural fluid, with atypical cells seen on flow cytometry. Clinical features that raise suspicion of malignancy include a history of malignancy, fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats.

Rheumatoid arthritis (E) causing pleural effusion will demonstrate an exudative pattern of pleural fluid, but without a history of rheumatoid arthritis, it would be unlikely that a pleural effusion would be the presenting manifestation of the disease.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents to the ED in respiratory distress. He remembers smelling an odor of newly mown hay prior to symptom onset. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for his illness?
ExplanationEN:
Phosgene was first used in World War I as a chemical warfare agent and caused 80% of gas-related fatalities. Although no longer stockpiled by the military, it remains widely used in industry for producing plastics, pharmaceuticals, and pesticides. Phosgene can also be produced by heating chlorinated fluorocarbons, leading to poisonings in certain industries like air conditioning repair.

Phosgene exposure can be subtle due to its poor warning properties, with little to no initial irritation. It produces a white cloud with a distinct odor of newly mown hay. The gas causes acid burns in the lower airways, leading to alveolar damage, capillary leaks, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, which can be delayed by up to 24 hours.

Symptoms include dyspnea and chest tightness, and early-onset pulmonary edema suggests a poor prognosis. Treatment focuses on respiratory support, with oxygen given only when necessary to maintain saturation above 94%. Pharmacologic options include corticosteroids, nebulized beta-agonists, and NSAIDs. Rest is critical, and patients should be observed for 24 hours, even if initially asymptomatic.



Chloral hydrate (A) smells like pears and is a sedative and hypnotic medication (not a gas or industrial chemical). It does not cause respiratory distress with an odor of newly mown hay. Chloral hydrate overdose can cause CNS depression, cardiac dysrhythmias, and respiratory failure, but there is no characteristic "newly mown hay" smell or inhalation-related presentation associated with it like phosgene.

Cyanide (B) poisoning presents with symptoms like headache, dizziness, confusion, and respiratory distress due to cellular hypoxia. Cyanide exposure can cause a bitter almond smell (which not everyone can detect). Cyanide is highly toxic and rapidly lethal, but this patient’s recollection of the specific odor and the industrial context make phosgene more likely.

Hydrogen sulfide (C) has a characteristic rotten egg smell. It can cause respiratory distress, but the distinctive sulfur-like odor is a hallmark of hydrogen sulfide exposure, ruling it out in this patient.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of respiratory symptoms. He initially had a low-grade fever, mild cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, excessive tearing, and malaise that lasted about 1 week. Those symptoms improved but were followed by the onset of coughing fits, which he says are so severe he cannot catch his breath and occasionally vomits. What test is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?

Options.text: Nasopharyngeal culture and polymerase chain reaction

CorrectAnswer: Nasopharyngeal culture and polymerase chain reaction
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation is concerning for pertussis, a respiratory infection caused by the gram-negative coccobacilli Bordetella pertussis. Although it has long been an infection affecting primarily infants and children, since the introduction of the pertussis vaccine more than half of the cases of pertussis involve adolescents and adults.

There are three phases of pertussis that occur in sequence. Following an incubation period of 7–10 days, the catarrhal phase begins with nonspecific symptoms of malaise, low-grade fever, conjunctival injection, and rhinorrhea. The catarrhal phase lasts 1–2 weeks and is followed by the onset of the paroxysmal phase. During this phase, which can last 2–4 weeks, the fever subsides, and patients develop the characteristic repeated staccato cough followed by a forceful inhalation which produces the classic whoop. Paroxysms are more common at night and post-tussive vomiting may occur. The convalescent phase, which can last for weeks to months, consists of a residual cough.

Diagnosis is made via nasopharyngeal culture and polymerase chain reaction. Antibiotic therapy decreases infectivity and carriage rates but has not been shown to significantly reduce the duration or severity of illness. The antibiotic of choice is erythromycin or azithromycin.



Patients may have cyanosis and diaphoresis during the paroxysm of coughing but, between episodes, do not appear acutely ill. An arterial blood gas (A) is not likely to be abnormal and does not aid in diagnosing the condition.

A chest radiograph (B) is not indicated in cases of pertussis unless there are signs of superinfection, such as persistent high fever, hypoxia even when not coughing, or persistent dyspnea. In uncomplicated pertussis, a chest radiograph may show nonspecific peribronchial thickening and atelectasis.

During the catarrhal and paroxysmal phases, a complete blood count (C) will often show a marked leukocytosis in children. This is less commonly seen in adults and infants.

Question: What is the most common cause of an empyema?
ExplanationEN:
An empyema is a pleural space infection with pus, a positive Gram stain or culture, or a parapneumonic effusion with pleural fluid sampling. Bacterial pneumonia is the most common cause of empyema. Predisposing factors that contribute to the formation of an empyema include aspiration pneumonia, ciliary impairment, immunocompromised states, malignancy, and alcoholism. An empyema should be suspected in cases where symptoms of pneumonia do not resolve despite appropriate therapy.

Physical examination can include decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and occasionally a friction rub. Pleuritic-like chest pain may also be a symptom and may be associated with rales or rhonchi, especially if there is still an underlying pulmonary infection.

The diagnosis of empyema is based on aspiration of grossly purulent material or one of the following: positive Gram stain or culture, pleural glucose < 40 mg/dL, pH < 7.2, or LDH > 1,000 IU/L.

Treatment focuses around drainage with tube thoracostomy and antibiotics. Recommended antimicrobials are piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem, with the addition of vancomycin if methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is a concern. Fibrinolytics administered intrapleurally may be required if the empyema is loculated, in close consultation with cardiothoracic surgery if the patient is refractory to the agents stated above.



Chest surgery complication (A), esophageal perforation (B), and trauma (D) are all potential causes of empyema, however, none of them are the most common cause.

Question: A healthy 33-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for a shoulder dislocation. You decide to use procedural sedation for the shoulder reduction. During the procedure, the patient slows his breathing and becomes hypoxic for a period of time requiring bag-valve-mask ventilation. When the patient finally improves his respiratory status, he seems to inhale some oral secretions and begins coughing. You suspect that he may have aspirated during the procedure. Post-procedure, the patient is doing well and is without cough and fever. Chest radiograph does not show any infiltrates. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

Options.text: He may be discharged to have repeat chest radiograph performed in 48 hours
He may be discharged with amoxicillin-clavulanate treatment for aspiration pneumonia
He may be discharged with prednisone treatment to prevent worsening inflammation
He should be started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam treatment for aspiration pneumonia and admitted to the medicine floor for observation of worsening respiratory status

CorrectAnswer: He may be discharged to have repeat chest radiograph performed in 48 hours
ExplanationEN:
This patient may have had an acute aspiration event while he was sedated. Aspiration pneumonitis develops from exposure of the lower respiratory tract to sterile gastric contents. This results in immediate chemical irritation of the pulmonary tissues from acidic material. Risk factors for aspiration events include alcohol and drug use, drug overdose, sedative drug use, procedural sedation, general anesthesia, emergent intubation, seizures, stroke, head trauma, and chronic debilitating neurological conditions. Aspiration of small amounts of oropharyngeal contents is common, especially during sleep.

The risk of developing complicated aspiration pneumonia depends upon factors such as age, comorbid illnesses, and periodontal disease. The treatment of aspiration pneumonitis in healthy patients who may not have had a large amount of aspiration is supportive. There is no need for empiric antibiotic treatment. The patient should be reassessed and have a repeat chest radiograph performed 36–48 hours later to evaluate for development of clinically significant infiltrate.



The most common form of aspiration pneumonia is caused by bacteria that reside in the upper airways and stomach. Anaerobic bacteria are the predominant organisms. Patients with suspected aspiration pneumonia who have a cough, fever, and purulent sputum after a potential aspiration event can be treated and discharged with amoxicillin-clavulanate as treatment for aspiration pneumonia (B). This patient likely has an acute chemical pneumonitis. He does not have signs and symptoms of pneumonia and does not have comorbid illnesses to suggest worsening complications from aspiration.

Discharging the patient with prednisone treatment to prevent worsening inflammation (C) is not recommended. The use of glucocorticoids in patients with aspiration pneumonia is controversial. Human studies have generally been unsuccessful.

Patients with suspected aspiration pneumonia after a preceding aspiration event 36 hours prior and with significant comorbid illnesses, such as cancer, advanced age, and significant cardiac or respiratory illness, and any patients with hemodynamic instability should be started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam treatment for pneumonia and admitted to the medicine floor for observation of worsening respiratory status (D). This patient is healthy and without symptoms, so he does not require admission to the hospital or intravenous antibiotics.

Question: A 15-month-old boy presents with a cough, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea for 2 days. He has had decreased oral intake and only one wet diaper today. He has moderate respiratory distress with subcostal retractions and nasal flaring. Diffuse fine crackles with mild wheezing are noted on his lung exam. He is persistently hypoxic to 88% despite nasal suctioning. When 0.5 L oxygen is applied via nasal cannula, his oxygen saturation improves to 94%. ExplanationEN:
Bronchiolitis is a common lung infection generally affecting children < 2 years of age and usually attributed to respiratory syncytial virus. It can be caused by other viruses, such as rhinovirus and human metapneumovirus, and can be seen at any time of year but most commonly occurs in the winter.

Most patients start with upper respiratory symptoms progressing to lower respiratory symptoms within 2–3 days. The illness peaks on day 5 before gradually resolving, usually with a residual cough lasting for as long as 21 days. Patients with a classical presentation should be given oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation > 90%, nasal suctioning if there are signs of nasal obstruction, and methods to maintain hydration status if needed, such as IV fluids (normal saline 20 mL/kg IV) or nasogastric tube placement for feedings.



There are strong recommendations against the routine use of bronchodilators such as albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized (A), antibiotics such as ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV (B), and systemic steroids such as methylprednisolone 7.5 mg/kg IV (C) in patients with classic bronchiolitis.

Question: A 45-year-old man with a medical history of alcohol use disorder presents to the emergency department with mild confusion, fever, cough, and vomiting. He smells of alcohol and is coughing profusely. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 107/68 mm Hg, HR is 110 bpm, respiratory rate is 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Chest radiography is as seen above. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Aspiration pneumonia occurs when gastric contents are aspirated by an individual who is typically altered or unable to protect their airway. Though it can occur in healthy individuals, it commonly occurs in patients with altered mental status, such as intoxicated patients. The pathophysiology is related to both the chemical irritation from stomach acid and infectious organisms in the gastrointestinal tract including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and gram-negative rods. Anaerobic bacteria have been found to play a smaller role in the development of aspiration pneumonia than previously thought.

Radiography can support the diagnosis, and treatment involves administering antibiotics. It is no longer recommended to add empiric coverage for anaerobic pathogens in patients with aspiration pneumonia unless an abscess or empyema is found on imaging. This patient will require hospital admission for pneumonia but does not have evidence of an empyema or abscess. He should be treated with azithromycin and ceftriaxone, as is the standard for community-acquired pneumonia. Monotherapy treatment with a respiratory fluoroquinolone would also be appropriate.



Amoxicillin and metronidazole (A) provides anaerobic coverage but is not recommended unless there is evidence of abscess or empyema.

Ampicillin-sulbactam (B) would be used with a macrolide and not as monotherapy for inpatients with pneumonia.

Clindamycin (D) historically was the preferred agent for treating anaerobic pleuropulmonary infections. However, given the risk of Clostridioides difficile diarrhea and the proven efficacy of other regimens, this remains the preferred therapy only in cases of penicillin allergy when anaerobic coverage is needed.

Question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the ED with progressive exertional dyspnea and malaise over several months. She already had an unremarkable emergency department cardiac evaluation last month, including a normal stress test. She also had a normal computed tomography scan looking for a pulmonary embolism. You are considering pulmonary hypertension as a cause of her symptoms. What is the recommended initial testing modality that can help make a diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Pulmonary hypertension is a progressive disease that is defined as an elevated pulmonary arterial pressure > 25 mm Hg at rest. The World Health Organization classifies pulmonary hypertension into five different groups according to the etiology. Group 1 includes those with pulmonary arterial hypertension due to idiopathic disease, congenital pulmonary hypertension, and disease caused by drugs, connective tissue diseases, human immunodeficiency virus, or schistosomiasis. Group 2 includes those with disease caused by left heart dysfunction. Group 3 includes those with chronic lung disease and hypoxemia. Group 4 includes those with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Group 5 includes pulmonary hypertension from hematologic disorders such as sickle cell anemia, systemic disorders such as sarcoidosis, metabolic disorders such as glycogen storage diseases, and chronic kidney disease.

The diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension can be difficult because of the nonspecific symptoms and because of concomitant illnesses causing similar symptoms. An estimated 20% of patients have symptoms for 2 years before being diagnosed. The purpose of diagnostic testing for pulmonary hypertension is to confirm that the disease exists, determine the severity of the disease, and determine the etiology of pulmonary hypertension. The initial diagnostic test recommended is an echocardiogram. If pulmonary hypertension is not suspected based on an echocardiogram, then other diagnostic testing should be conducted to determine the cause of the patient’s symptoms. Patients with significant left heart disease on echocardiogram to explain the extent of pulmonary hypertension do not require further testing. If pulmonary hypertension is highly suspected but not completely explained on echocardiogram, right heart catheterization is recommended.



Pulmonary function tests (B) would be performed to determine if underlying lung disease is causing pulmonary hypertension. The tests would not help diagnose pulmonary hypertension itself.

As already mentioned, a right heart cardiac catheterization (C) is the definitive test to diagnose pulmonary hypertension. However, it may not be necessary if the initial echocardiogram shows enough left heart disease to explain the extent of pulmonary hypertension.

Ventilation-perfusion scan (D)is the preferred imaging study to evaluate patients for chronic thromboembolic disease leading to pulmonary hypertension. It is not used to diagnose pulmonary hypertension.

Question: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of congestion and cough. Earlier this evening, his parents noticed a change in the sound of his cry and cough and that he seemed to squeak when breathing. Vital signs on presentation are a BP of 104/62 mm Hg, HR of 124 bpm, RR of 26/min, and T of 101.5°F (38.6°C). On lung exam, inspiratory stridor is observed, and there are sternal retractions. An X-ray is performed, and the results are shown above. What is the most common cause of this patient’s diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Parainfluenza virus is the most common cause of croup. Croup is classically associated with a barking, seal-like cough, and inspiratory stridor. Radiographs may show subglottic narrowing (steeple sign) caused by edema. The typical age group is 6 months to 3 years, but the condition can be seen in children up to 5 years of age. The infection and inflammation are usually self-limiting, and conservative management is recommended.

Evidence supports the routine use of corticosteroids in all children with croup. Intervention at an earlier phase of the illness reduces the severity of symptoms and the rates of return to a health care practitioner for additional medical attention, ED visits, and hospital admissions. Many children respond to a single oral dose of dexamethasone. For those who do not tolerate the oral preparation, nebulized budesonide or intramuscular dexamethasone are reasonable alternatives. Mild disease can be treated with humidified oxygen. Moderate to severe disease should be treated with steroids and nebulized racemic epinephrine.



Adenovirus (A) is a common cause of upper respiratory infections but is less common than parainfluenza virus as a cause of croup.

Bordetella pertussis (B) is the most common cause of whooping cough. Patients may present with upper respiratory infection symptoms for up to 2 weeks. Coughing spells are paroxysmal and end in a high-pitched, inspiratory “whoop.”

Haemophilus influenzae type b (C) is implicated in various infections such as otitis media and epiglottitis, but it is less common as a cause of croup.

Streptococcus spp (E) infection is not a common cause of croup. Streptococcus pyogenes can cause pharyngitis, which presents with a sore throat, fever, and exudates or petechiae.

Question: Which of the following patients will benefit most from receiving tissue plasminogen activator for acute pulmonary embolism detected in the emergency department?

Options.text: 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 100 bpm, BP 80/40 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92%
55-year-old man with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 145 bpm, BP 136/86 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92%
55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus with vital signs showing HR 100 bpm, BP 116/86 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 87%
55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 110 bpm, BP 122/80 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92% with evidence of right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiogram

CorrectAnswer: 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 100 bpm, BP 80/40 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92%
ExplanationEN:
Thrombolytic therapy, such as tissue plasminogen activator, helps to form plasmin which results in accelerated lysis of thrombi. Thrombolytic agents have been used in a variety of disorders including myocardial infarction, stroke, and acute pulmonary embolism. Thrombolytic therapy for acute pulmonary embolism can lead to hemodynamic improvement but at a risk of major bleeding. The effect of thrombolytic therapy on mortality in acute pulmonary embolism remains questionable in many circumstances. Typically, only patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism are candidates for therapy, as the adverse effects of thrombolytics can be devastating. Persistent hypotension or shock due to acute pulmonary embolism is the only widely accepted indication for systemic thrombolysis. Other possible indications for thrombolytics in acute pulmonary embolism include increasing tachycardia, worsening right heart dysfunction, and significant hypoxemia. However, unless the patient is hemodynamically compromised, thrombolytics are generally not recommended at this time. Clinicians must consider on a case-by-case basis whether to use thrombolytic therapy as there is some suggestion of improved quality of life in hemodynamically stable patients with other evidence of stress from pulmonary embolism.



The 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 145 bpm, BP 136/86 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92% (B) has significant tachycardia but is otherwise hemodynamically stable. Thrombolytics would not be indicated in this situation.

The 55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus with vital signs showing HR 100 bpm, BP 116/86 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 87% (C) is hypoxic but is otherwise hemodynamically stable. Thrombolytics would also not be indicated in this situation.

Finally, the 55-year-old woman with a history of hypertension with vital signs showing HR 110 bpm, BP 122/80 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92% with evidence of right ventricular dysfunction on echocardiogram (D) is a much more controversial scenario for thrombolytic therapy. Clinicians rationalize that patients with significant right ventricular hypokinesis will have a worse prognosis than patients without right ventricular strain. However, randomized controlled trials have not shown a convincing mortality benefit in these patients, especially if there is not associated hemodynamic instability.

Question: Pneumonia secondary to Chlamydia pneumoniae is associated with which of the following complications?
ExplanationEN:
Chlamydia pneumoniae is a gram-negative bacterial pathogen that exists in two forms: as elementary bodies, which are the infectious form that survive externally to the host, and as reticulate bodies that replicate intracellularly. This pathogen is an obligate intracellular species that relies on the host cell’s adenosine triphosphate for energy. Chlamydia pneumoniae is transmitted via droplets from person to person. It leads to a form of walking pneumonia that causes milder symptoms compared to other community-acquired pneumonias.

Patients with Chlamydia pneumoniae present with low-grade fever, cough, and shortness of breath. The cough can be prolonged with a median duration of 21 days. It is not possible to distinguish a Chlamydia pneumoniae infection from other pulmonary infections based on clinical presentation. Polymerase chain reaction-based assays can confirm the diagnosis. However, treatment is typically started empirically. Treatment includes azithromycin, doxycycline, or levofloxacin. Complications from Chlamydia pneumoniae infections are rare, but there is an association with asthma and reactive arthritis.



Glomerulonephritis (A) is a disease in which there is damage to the filtration system of the kidneys, leading to loss of protein and blood through the urine. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause of glomerulonephritis in children and typically presents after a streptococcal infection. This complication occurs 1–2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis and 3–6 weeks after streptococcal skin infection.

There are a few rare reports associating Chlamydia pneumoniae with Guillain-Barré syndrome (B) and myocarditis, but this is not well established. Pathogens associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome include Campylobacter, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza-like illnesses, and human immunodeficiency virus.

Pulmonary fibrosis (C) is not a complication of Chlamydia pneumoniae infection.

Question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a cough and wheezing. His parent reports this is the fourth time he has presented with similar symptoms, but he has never needed hospitalization. She reports his symptoms are worse with season changes and upper respiratory symptoms and that he has been waking at night coughing for the last 4 days. There is no family history of a similar illness. However, multiple family members have recently had upper respiratory symptoms. The patient is well appearing, in no distress, with vital signs within normal limits for his age. He has a dry cough and diffuse wheezing with a prolonged expiratory phase to all lung fields. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Asthma is a chronic illness resulting in lower airway obstruction and air trapping due to inflammation and bronchoconstriction. It varies in severity but is often triggered by upper respiratory tract infections, inhaled allergens, exercise, and dry cold air (weather changes). Many children with asthma also have allergic rhinitis and eczema. Patients with a history of asthma or wheezing episodes that present with a dry cough, expiratory wheezing, and a prolonged expiratory phase as our patient above are having an asthma exacerbation. Immediate treatment is with inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroids. If inhaled bronchodilators are ineffective, alternative diagnoses should be considered. Continuous albuterol is used in refractory cases. Long-term treatment with inhaled corticosteroids reduces the frequency and duration of asthma exacerbations.



Allergic rhinitis (A)can mimic asthma with a nighttime cough due to postnasal drip, but patients with isolated allergic rhinitis should not have wheezing or a prolonged expiratory phase.

Most patients with pneumonia (C) will have a cough and a fever. However, the presentation may be subtle and nonspecific such as abdominal pain. Unlike our patient, there are usually focal findings on lung exam. In patients with asthma, reevaluation after bronchodilators is often helpful in ruling out focal findings concerning for pneumonia. Given his history and exam, an asthma exacerbation is more likely.

Vocal cord dysfunction (D) does not have nighttime symptoms and is more common in adolescents.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a cough, fevers, and pleuritic chest pain that began 10 days ago. He has a history of epilepsy and takes levetiracetam, but he lost his medication 3 weeks ago and has had several breakthrough seizures. He has a remote history of a Helicobacter pylori duodenal ulcer status post triple therapy. He was also treated for cellulitis 1 month ago. He smoked 1–2 cigarettes daily in his late teenage years and quit 11 years ago. He drinks 2–3 beers per week and does not use recreational drugs. On physical exam, he is well-appearing and has decreased breath sounds left side. His chest X-ray is shown above. Which one of the following factors likely predisposed this patient to developing the above radiographic findings?
ExplanationEN:
Lung abscesses are circumscribed areas of the lung parenchyma that develop necrosis and cavitation secondary to infection. The pathogenesis of lung abscesses in otherwise healthy individuals is often secondary to the aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions, which may occur in patients with reduced consciousness (e.g., medications, substance use, generalized seizures), dysphagia, upper gastrointestinal disorders (e.g., esophageal reflux), poor dental hygiene, and advancing age. Secondary lung abscesses arise from an underlying local or distant infection. Lung abscesses may be due to hematogenous spread from endocarditis, an indwelling intravascular catheter, or intravenous drug use. Direct extension from an adjacent infection (e.g., empyema), a tracheoesophageal fistula, or a nearby abscess (e.g., mediastinal abscess), may lead to a lung abscess. Bronchial obstruction arising from the mass effect of a bronchogenic lymphoma or tumor, bronchial stenosis, or airway foreign body may lead to postobstructive pneumonia and related abscess formation.

The clinical manifestations of lung abscesses mirror those of pneumonia, such as cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fatigue, malaise, and night sweats. Unlike lobar or even multifocal pneumonia, lung abscesses may have an indolent course, with symptoms gradually worsening for 2–4 weeks prior to the patient seeking evaluation. Imaging may demonstrate a dense consolidation or air-fluid level within a cavitary lesion. Infections are typically polymicrobial and consist of oral flora, as aspiration of oral contents is a common precursor to abscess formation. Monomicrobial infections and abscesses arise from pyogenic aerobic bacteria, e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and other gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus pyogenes). Opportunistic infectious agents should be considered in patients with a history of immune compromise. Empiric antimicrobial regimens include ampicillin-sulbactam, clindamycin, a carbapenem, or moxifloxacin. Image-guided percutaneous drainage, transbronchial drainage, or surgical drainage is required if patients do not experience improvement with antibiotics.



Older age at presentation (A) would increase the risk of lung abscess, not the patient’s age of 29.

Cigarette smoking (B) may impair ciliary clearance and predispose to infection, but this effect would be less likely in a patient with a remote history of tobacco use.

A history of duodenal ulcer (C), especially if it was completely treated, is less likely to predispose the patient to aspiration, unlike other upper gastrointestinal disorders, such as gastroesophageal reflux, esophageal diverticulum, and achalasia.

Recent cellulitis (E) that has been treated is not likely to result in disseminated infection, unlike patients with serious infections, such as endocarditis, bacteremia, and sepsis.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-day history of a cough with rust-colored sputum, fever, and chills. He has no significant medical history and has had no recent illnesses or hospitalizations. In the ED, vital signs are BP 120/76 mm Hg, HR 102 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, and T 102.2°F (39.0°C). A chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation. ExplanationEN:
This patient most likely has pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. The clinical presentation of pneumonia is characterized by tachypnea, tachycardia, dyspnea, chest pain, cough, fevers, and rales. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults. It is classically associated with a productive cough with rust-colored sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and high fevers. Patients are usually febrile, and a chest X-ray typically shows a lobar consolidation.

Outpatient treatment of pneumococcal pneumonia is with doxycycline, azithromycin (if community resistance is low), or high-dose amoxicillin. Those with comorbidities may need combination therapy. Inpatient treatment includes a third-generation cephalosporin and azithromycin. Monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone is an alternative treatment option.



Escherichia coli (A) is a common cause of pneumonia in neonates and older individuals.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae (B) is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia, particularly in children and young adults. These patients usually have less severe symptoms, a nonproductive cough, and diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray. This is classically referred to as walking pneumonia.

Staphylococcus aureus (C) is a common nosocomial pathogen in adults that can lead to necrotizing pneumonia. It is also associated with postinfluenza pneumonia.

Question: An unimmunized 7-year-old boy without any previous medical history presents with fever and cough. The parents report that he has been coughing for 2 weeks. The patient has sudden fits of coughing followed sometimes by post-tussive emesis. Which of the following is an appropriate treatment plan?
ExplanationEN:
Although a vaccine for pertussis was developed in the 1940s, it remains a cause of significant respiratory illness in the US each year. Decreasing immunity in adults has contributed to persistent annual cases of this disease. The disease occurs most commonly in children under age 1 who have not received the entire vaccine series and nonimmunized children. Pertussis is caused by Bordetella spp. which specifically adheres to the ciliated epithelial cells of the respiratory tract. There are three phases to the illness. The catarrhal phase lasts 1–2 weeks after an incubation period of 7–10 days. Patients are most infectious during this phase, the symptoms of which are indistinguishable from an average upper respiratory infection.

Phase two is the paroxysmal phase, characterized by the resolution of fever and increased cough. For 2–6 weeks, patients have the classic paroxysmal cough. Patients cough in fits, sometimes followed by the whoop when they forcefully inhale. Post-tussive emesis, syncope, and brief apneic episodes may occur.

The convalescent third phase lasts for weeks to months and is characterized by a residual cough. Antibiotic therapy with a macrolide is indicated to decrease the infectivity of patients in the earlier phases of the illness. The use of antibiotics does not decrease the duration of illness or severity of illness. The primary treatment is supportive care. Erythromycin is contraindicated for infants < 1 month due to increased risk for pyloric stenosis. Infants < 1 month old should receive azithromycin.
