Question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with difficulty breathing. According to his parent, he has had a fever of 102°F (38.9°C) for 2 days with a sore throat. He has not eaten anything since yesterday. Today, he will not drink anything either, and his parent says he drools a lot. He has a medical history of mild asthma and is completely unvaccinated. On examination, you find an ill-appearing child sitting straight up in bed. He grows very anxious when moved and does not want to lie down. His mouth is open slightly, and he is drooling. He has tachycardia, tachypnea, and stridor on auscultation. His oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. In this particular patient, what pathogen should the clinician be concerned about as the cause of this patient’s illness?
ExplanationEN:
Although much less common in the era of vaccines, epiglottitis is a bacterial infection characterized by rapidly progressing inflammation of and around the epiglottis. If not treated appropriately, it can progress to life-threatening airway obstruction. Symptoms include respiratory distress in a patient preferring to maintain posture in the “sniffing” or upright position with dysphagia, muffled voice, and drooling. The posterior nasopharynx is the primary source of pathogens in epiglottitis. It is caused by a number of bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens. In previously healthy children, most cases are bacterial. The most likely pathogen depends on the age of the patient and immunization status. Haemophilus influenzae type b was the most common cause in children before widespread vaccination against the pathogen. It is much less common now but is still found in unvaccinated children and would be a concern in this particular patient. This patient with presumptive epiglottitis should be kept calm and all interventions that are anxiety-provoking, including intravenous access and use of a tongue blade for examination, should be deferred until appropriate resources and assistance are in place for airway management.



Pseudomonas aeruginosa (B) is a much less common cause of epiglottitis and is usually only found in immunocompromised hosts.

Staphylococcus aureus (C) is a cause of epiglottitis but is much less common than other etiologies.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (D) is the leading cause of epiglottitis in adults. It is not uncommon that no particular pathogen is found in epiglottitis. Other etiologies include traumatic causes such as caustic or thermal injuries.

Question: A 43-year-old man presents to the ED with hemoptysis and a fever for 2 weeks. Computed tomography of his chest reveals two cavitary lesions with air-fluid levels, one in the base of the right lung and the other in the posterior left upper lobe. What is the most likely underlying cause for the development of cavitary lesions in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
A lung abscess is characterized by necrotic breakdown of the lung parenchyma. Risk factors include aspiration, intravenous drug use, pulmonary malignancies, and immunosuppression. Chest radiographs are commonly sufficient for diagnosis, though computed tomography of the chest may add further information about etiology. Radiographically, abscesses appear as well-circumscribed lesions with air-fluid levels. They commonly form in the posterior upper lobes or bases of the lower lobes.

Two specific causes will lead to abnormal lung abscess locations. Underlying malignancies commonly cause anterior abscesses, while hematogenous spread of infection (from intravenous drug use, for instance) commonly causes multilobar abscesses. Patients often present with a prolonged course of fever, productive cough with foul-smelling sputum, and night sweats. Up to 25% may have hemoptysis. The mainstay of treatment is with a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics (e.g. ampicillin-sulbactam or a carbapenem). Despite treatment, 10% of bacterial lung abscesses will require surgical intervention. Most patients are hospitalized for several weeks prior to discharge.



Alcohol misuse (A), pulmonary malignancies (C), and Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia (D)do not commonly cause multilobar lung abscesses. Alcohol misuse increases the risk of aspiration events and subsequent lung abscess formation. These commonly form in the right upper lobe due to aspiration while in the prone position. Pulmonary malignancies are associated with anterior lung abscesses. Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is not associated with a specific location of lung abscess formation.

Question: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dyspnea for 2 days. He has an extensive smoking history and has been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Current medications include albuterol, salmeterol, and tiotropium. He continues to smoke. His physical examination shows HR 104 bpm, BP 110/70 mm Hg, RR 30/min, T 37.8°C, and SpO2 93% on room air. He appears to be in moderate respiratory distress with bilateral wheezing on auscultation. Which of the following testing modalities is indicated in this patient to direct further care?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is having an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). A chest radiograph is indicated in this instance to determine whether there is an acute treatable cause for the clinical deterioration, especially pneumothorax or parenchymal consolidation consistent with pneumonia. Viral and bacterial pathogens are frequent causes of acute exacerbations of COPD. Other helpful testing modalities include pulse oximetry to monitor the severity of hypoxia, ECG to determine if cardiac ischemia is the cause of decompensation, and basic blood tests to evaluate for polycythemia, electrolyte derangements, and kidney failure.



The other testing options given are questioned or controversial in COPD. In most cases, the differentiation of COPD exacerbation from acute congestive heart failure (CHF) can be made on clinical grounds. The addition of a B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) (A) assay to the ED evaluation may identify some patients in whom a new diagnosis of CHF is suspected. Because BNP can be elevated in association with right ventricular stretch, incautious interpretation of an elevated BNP may lead a clinician to favor the diagnosis of acute left-sided heart failure and overlook cor pulmonale and pulmonary embolism, both considerations in patients with COPD. BNP may also be elevated in the setting of kidney failure. Therefore, BNP levels cannot be relied upon to “rule in” CHF or “rule out” significant pulmonary pathology. Use of the BNP may be helpful, but it should not be interpreted in isolation and must not supplant clinical judgment.

Unlike asthma, peak flow measurements (C) are relatively unchanged in an acute COPD exacerbation. Spirometric measurements are also a poor predictor of the need for admission, the likelihood of returning to the hospital, and response to therapy. Current guidelines recommend against the use of spirometric testing in patients presenting with an acute exacerbation of COPD.

Finally, although once common, sputum testing (D) has fallen out of favor. There is a low yield of useful information and sputum results rarely change clinical management.

Question: A 19-year-old man with a history of cystic fibrosis presents to the emergency department with a worsening cough, fever, and shortness of breath. Vital signs show a heart rate of 90 bpm, blood pressure of 132/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 20/min, oxygen saturation of 94% on room air, and temperature of 38°C. Diffuse rhonchi are heard on lung examination. While awaiting the chest radiograph and further laboratory testing, you review this patient’s previous sputum cultures and can see that he has grown several different organisms. Which bacterial organism will require double antibiotic coverage in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Cystic fibrosis is a hereditary disease that mainly affects the lungs and digestive system. The variant in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene produces thick mucus that obstructs the lungs and pancreatic ducts. Pulmonary disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients. Quality of life and survival for these patients depend heavily on a multifaceted treatment approach that involves antibiotics, chest physiotherapy, anti-inflammatory agents, and medications to clear respiratory secretions. These patients may present to emergency departments with an exacerbation of their chronic symptoms which may include cough, sputum production, dyspnea with exertion, fever, and fatigue.

Treatment of an acute pulmonary exacerbation is based on previous sputum culture analysis, current respiratory therapy, and changes in symptoms from the patient’s recent baseline. Some patients may have chronic shortness of breath, so it is important to only treat changes from the baseline. Most patients with cystic fibrosis have chronic respiratory bacterial infections. The most common pathogen detected in young children is Staphylococcus aureus, but Pseudomonas aeruginosa becomes more prevalent as patients age. Other common organisms include Haemophilus influenzae, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter species, Burkholderia cepacia, and nontuberculous mycobacteria. Patients with cystic fibrosis also frequently develop worsening symptoms due to viruses such as influenza, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and rhinovirus.

Treatment of any acute exacerbation includes maintenance of current medications to clear respiratory secretions, chest physiotherapy, anti-inflammatory medications such as prednisone, and optimization of nutritional status. Supplemental oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, or invasive ventilation may be required. Any patient with cystic fibrosis who presents with an exacerbation requires systemic antibiotic therapy. Antibiotic selection should be based on bacteria cultured from the most recent respiratory secretions. Sputum cultures in these patients are recommended every 3 months. The clinician should choose an antibiotic regimen that covers bacteria found in recent sputum cultures but should also include double antibiotic coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Studies have shown that patients treated adequately for Pseudomonas aeruginosa are more likely to have improved pulmonary function for at least 4 months, reduction in sputum density, less frequent pulmonary exacerbations, better quality of life, and improved survival. Therefore, it is critical to always cover for this organism. Discussing the choice of antibiotics with the patient’s pulmonologist would be ideal.



All of the other organisms, Haemophilus influenzae (A), methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (B), and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (D), are often found in patients with cystic fibrosis, but they do not require double antibiotic coverage. In fact, treatment of each of these organisms should only be based on previous sputum culture results. In general, double antibiotic coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa with combined therapy for Staphylococcus aureus is usually adequate treatment.

Question: A 56-year-old woman with a history of tobacco use, hypertension, and sigmoid colon resection for treatment of colorectal cancer 1 month ago presents to the ED with the sudden onset of dyspnea 2 hours ago. Her vital signs include a BP of 81/43 mm Hg, HR of 124 bpm, and SpO2 of 82% on room air. She is placed on high-flow nasal cannula at 10 L with improvement in her SpO2 to 92%. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with T wave inversions in leads V3–V6, and troponin I is 0.31 ng/mL. Despite 500 mL of intravenous fluids and uptitration of an intravenous epinephrine infusion, her BP is 85/40 mm Hg and HR is 128 bpm. Computed tomography with angiography of the chest shows bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Intravenous colloid fluid administration for volume expansion

ExplanationEN:
The risk stratification of pulmonary embolism is based on a patient’s hemodynamic status and cardiac function. A low-risk pulmonary embolism demonstrates hemodynamic stability and has no signs of right ventricular (RV) strain. Intermediate or submassive pulmonary emboli occur without hypotension (e.g., systolic blood pressure > 90 mm Hg) and with RV strain. Features of right heart strain include RV dysfunction or dilation on ultrasound, elevated brain natriuretic peptide, elevated troponin, and new ECG changes (e.g., right bundle branch block, anterolateral T wave inversions, or anterolateral ST segment elevation or depression). When there is hemodynamic instability (e.g., hypotension, altered mental status), the pulmonary embolism is classified as massive or high-risk.

Computed tomography with angiography of the chest definitively diagnoses pulmonary embolism. The initial resuscitation of a massive pulmonary embolism includes hemodynamic support and avoiding hypoxia and hypercapnia, as these can lead to pulmonary vasoconstriction. Gas exchange is ideally optimized by noninvasive measures (e.g., high-flow nasal cannula) and the careful avoidance of positive pressure. Positive pressure can increase intrathoracic pressure, increase RV afterload, and decrease RV output, which ultimately compromises left ventricular preload, worsens RV oxygen delivery, and precipitates biventricular failure and circulatory collapse. Early gentle hydration, vasopressors, inotropes (e.g., intravenous epinephrine infusion), and pulmonary vasodilators may be used with supportive care. Definitive treatment of massive pulmonary emboli involves intravenous thrombolytic agents. Major surgery within 3 weeks is a contraindication, but this patient is 1 month out from surgery. Catheter-directed therapies (e.g., catheter-directed thrombolytics, thrombectomy) may also be considered.



Interventional radiology consultation for thrombectomy (A) is appropriate in patients with massive pulmonary embolism who have not achieved hemodynamic improvement after intravenous thrombolysis. However, it takes a considerable amount of time to prepare the necessary equipment and staff, which may be too delayed for the initial intervention required in hemodynamically unstable patients.

Intravenous colloid fluid administration for volume expansion (B) may be considered in select patient cases, such as those with low oncotic pressure from severe hypoproteinemia or after large-volume paracentesis. This patient has already received gentle rehydration, and additional fluids may lead to increased RV metabolic demand and worsen RV function.

An intravenous heparin infusion (C) is an appropriate therapy for low-risk or intermediate-risk submassive pulmonary emboli but is inadequate in the intervention of patients with massive pulmonary embolism and persistent hypotension.

Intubation for optimization of oxygenation (E) is not required, given the patient’s improved oxygenation with noninvasive supplemental oxygenation.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the ED with a barking cough and a fever. His temperature is 100.4°F (38°C), blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 140 bpm, respiratory rate is 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. On physical exam, he exhibits inspiratory stridor and tracheal tugging. A diagnosis of croup is suspected, and you administer dexamethasone and nebulized racemic epinephrine. On repeat physical exam after 15 minutes, he does not exhibit stridor or increased work of breathing, and his oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Administer another dose of nebulized racemic epinephrine
Discharge for close follow-up with a pediatrician in 24 hours
Observe in the ED for 1 hour
Observe in the ED for 4 hours

CorrectAnswer: Observe in the ED for 4 hours
ExplanationEN:
Parainfluenza virus is the most common cause of laryngotracheobronchitis, or croup, which is a viral respiratory illness characterized by a classic barking cough and inspiratory stridor that results from inflammation in the larynx and the subglottic airway. There are many causes of upper airway obstruction, thus careful history and physical exam are necessary to rule out other causes, such as foreign body aspiration, epiglottitis, and retropharyngeal abscess. Rapid assessment of children with suspected croup is necessary to identify patients who are at risk for respiratory failure.

The Westleyscore uses inspiratory stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness to classify the severity of croup, with higher numbers indicating a worsening risk of respiratory failure. If the diagnosis is suspected, laboratory studies and radiographs are typically not needed, but if X-rays are performed, they will often reveal a classic steeple sign indicating subglottic narrowing.

Treatment of mild croup by Westley scoring involves administering warm, humidified air and a one-time dose of dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg orally, IV, or IM). As the severity increases (moderate to severe croup), the administration of nebulized racemic epinephrine (0.5 mL of a 2.25% solution diluted in 3 mL of saline) is indicated. Children receiving nebulized epinephrine should be observed for 4 hours to ensure that symptoms do not recur after the medication wears off. If the child remains symptom-free at the end of the observation period, they can safely be discharged home for close outpatient follow-up with their pediatrician. However, if symptoms are persistent or recur by the end of the observation period, a second dose of nebulized racemic epinephrine should be administered and the patient should be hospitalized.



As discussed above, administration of another dose of nebulized racemic epinephrine (A) is indicated anytime during the 4-hour observation period if symptoms have not resolved or have recurred. However, a repeat dose would not be indicated for this patient who does not have stridor or increased work of breathing.

Because of the need for continued observation after administration of racemic epinephrine, discharging the patient home for close follow-up with a pediatrician in 24 hours (B) is not recommended yet.

The need for administration of nebulized racemic epinephrine indicates moderate to severe croup. Although most patients who receive this medication improve within 15–30 minutes, patients should be observed for 4 hours because the effects can wear off after 2–3 hours and symptoms can recur. Therefore, observing the patient in the ED for 1 hour (C) would not be adequate.

Question: A 30-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents to the ED with shortness of breath and chest discomfort. He has a murmur on the cardiac exam. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral cavitary lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic to begin initially in this patient while awaiting further evaluation and consultant recommendations?
ExplanationEN:
Infective endocarditis is an infection that affects the endocardium, native or prosthetic heart valves, and indwelling cardiac devices. Its pathogenesis begins when endothelial damage or prosthetic material fosters platelet-fibrin thrombus formation, which is subsequently colonized by bacteria, leading to vegetation. While gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus predominate in resource-rich nations, Streptococcus species and other pathogens like the HACEK group (Haemophilus spp, Aggregatibacter species, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella species) are also implicated.

Risk factors include advanced age, injection drug use, prosthetic valves, and health care exposures like dialysis. IV drug use is notably associated with right-sided infections, especially involving the tricuspid valve. Left-sided infections carry a higher risk of embolic complications, including strokes and systemic abscesses.

The presentation of infective endocarditis is highly variable and often nonspecific, with fever being the most consistent feature. Other symptoms may include malaise, chills, weight loss, and complications like acute heart failure, septic emboli, or neurological deficits. Physical findings such as new or worsening heart murmurs, splinter hemorrhages, or Janeway lesions may support the diagnosis, though they are not common. Diagnostic evaluation hinges on blood cultures and echocardiography. Diagnostic criteria, like the Duke criteria, integrate clinical, microbiological, and echocardiographic findings to confirm or refute infective endocarditis.

ED management focuses on stabilization, including sepsis care and early initiation of empiric antibiotics. Vancomycin, with or without ceftriaxone, is the preferred regimen pending blood culture results to cover Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and other pathogens. In critically ill patients or those with complications such as heart failure, prompt cardiothoracic surgical consultation is crucial. Surgical intervention may be indicated for conditions like valvular insufficiency with ventricular failure, large vegetations, or recurrent embolization. Once stabilized, patients require 4–6 weeks of pathogen-specific intravenous antibiotics, often guided by infectious disease specialists.



Ceftriaxone (A) covers some organisms associated with infective endocarditis, but it is not the preferred empiric first-line therapy since these organisms cause a minority of cases.

Gentamicin (B) is not recommended for initial empiric therapy. Although it covers streptococci and enterococci, it has largely fallen out of favor as a treatment for endocarditis, mainly due to its toxic kidney effects. Gentamicin might be recommended later in the treatment course based on bacterial growth and resistance patterns, but it would not be recommended as initial empiric therapy in the ED.

Similarly, nafcillin (C) has great coverage against non-MRSA, and it might be used later in a patient’s treatment. However, it would not be recommended as initial empiric therapy due to the rising rates of MRSA-related disease.

Question: A 22-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents to the emergency department with dyspnea and wheezing. Pulmonary exam reveals poor air movement and inspiratory and expiratory wheezes. She is confused, has respiratory failure, and requires intubation. Which of the following parameters would be the most appropriate to include in her ventilator settings?

Options.text: Increased fraction of inspired oxygen to 100%

ExplanationEN:
Asthma is a chronic pulmonary condition that occurs secondary to bronchospasm and inflammation. Patients present with wheezing, dyspnea, and respiratory distress and can have absent or minimal breath sounds in severe exacerbations. Early and aggressive treatment with albuterol, ipratropium, magnesium sulfate, and steroids can reduce the need for positive pressure ventilation and intubation. However, if a patient requires intubation, managing the ventilator can be challenging.

Patients with asthma often air stack, meaning that with each inhalation, they have difficulty exhaling the same volume of air, leading to an accumulation of additional air. To prevent this, a lower respiratory rate with a prolonged expiratory phase can allow for full exhalation of air. The respiratory rate should be titrated to the patient’s acid-base status to avoid carbon dioxide accumulation.

The primary focus in ventilator settings for patients with asthma should be maintaining adequate oxygenation (targeting a PO2 > 60 mm Hg and SpO2 between 88% and 92%). This helps ensure sufficient oxygen delivery while minimizing the risk of barotrauma and volutrauma from high ventilatory pressures. Minimizing PEEP and keeping plateau pressures low is critical to avoid further exacerbation of airway pressures and the risk of pneumothorax.

Other strategies are paramount to prevent complications and improve outcomes. One of these strategies involves the concept of permissive hypercapnia. This approach accepts higher levels of PCO2 rather than striving to maintain it within a normal range, which can be detrimental if it leads to increased ventilation pressures and high volumes. The goal is to avoid aggressive ventilation that can exacerbate air trapping, increase intrathoracic pressure, and reduce venous return, potentially leading to hemodynamic instability.



Higher lung volumes (A) could cause barotrauma in this patient. Lung protective strategies include lower lung volumes.

An increased fraction of inspired oxygen to 100% (B) is inappropriate for most patients, as the goal is to maintain PO2 > 60 mm Hg, which can often be done without 100% oxygen. A patient with asthma has no automatic indication that a higher amount of oxygen is needed.

Respiratory acidosis could be improved by increasing the respiratory rate (C). However, increasing the respiratory rate automatically in a patient with asthma reduces the expiratory duration and may lead to air stacking. This increases the risk of auto-PEEP and barotrauma in a patient with obstructive lung disease.

Question: A 35-year-old nulliparous woman presents to the emergency department for a right breast mass that she has noticed for the last few months. She reports that the mass tends to increase in size and become tender right before her menses. On exam, she has nodular breast tissue bilaterally. Additionally, you palpate a cystic structure in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Which of the following is this patient’s biggest risk factor for having breast cancer?

Options.text: Cyclical changes in size and tenderness

ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting for an evaluation of a breast mass. Although most breast masses are benign, nulliparity puts the patient at a higher risk of developing breast cancer. Both benign and malignant breast masses have broad clinical manifestations, and management in the emergency department is largely based on risk stratifying patients based on history and physical exam. Examples of common benign breast masses include fibroadenomas, cysts, fibrocystic changes, galactoceles, fat necrosis, and abscesses. The most common types of malignant breast masses include infiltrating ductal carcinomas and infiltrating lobular carcinomas. Risk factors for breast cancer include increasing age, obesity, nulliparity, early menarche, and late menopause. On breast examination, careful consideration should be placed into assessing for asymmetry, skin changes, nipple retraction, lymphadenopathy, mass fixation to the chest wall, and ipsilateral arm edema. If the history and examination in the emergency department are unremarkable, then outpatient mammography and follow-up with a specialist are indicated regardless of age. If the examination is concerning for malignancy, more urgent follow-up with a breast surgeon is indicated. Of note, this patient is presenting with symptoms and findings consistent with fibrocystic changes. Fibrocystic changes are benign and reflect a manifestation of symptoms caused by breast tissue responses to hormonal cycling. Most patients present with cyclical breast pain, which may be unilateral, bilateral, or focal. The breast tissue, most often in the upper outer quadrant, may increase in size prior to the onset of menses and return to baseline after the onset of menstrual flow.



Cyclical changes in size and tenderness (A) is a reassuring finding, as it is likely referring to breast tissue responses to cyclical changes in hormones. Palpation of a cyst (B) is also reassuring, as a breast cyst is a benign fluid-filled mass that can be palpated as a component of fibrocystic changes in the breast. Nodular breast tissue (C) is also usually a benign finding, especially in young female patients, as they tend to have more dense breast tissue than older female patients.

Question: A 55-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder and coronary artery disease presents to the emergency department with epigastric pain and vomiting. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 127/77 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate is 25/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam is notable for mild bilateral pulmonary crackles and tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without guarding or rebound. Laboratory values are notable for a white blood cell count of 17,000 cells/microliter, a brain natriuretic peptide of 220 pg/mL, and a lipase of 985 U/L. While in the emergency department, the patient reports worsening dyspnea and his oxygen saturation on room air is now 88%. A chest radiograph is performed as seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a severe and diffuse inflammatory form of lung injury that can occur secondary to many etiologies including infection, aspiration, and conditions such as pancreatitis. Patients will present with severe respiratory compromise and require intubation and mechanical ventilation. Other initial findings include tachypnea, tachycardia, diffuse crackles, confusion, respiratory distress, cyanosis, and diaphoresis. Laboratory values are generally nonspecific in making the diagnosis. However, an arterial blood gas can demonstrate hypoxemia and acute respiratory alkalosis. Chest radiography can demonstrate diffuse findings including bilateral alveolar opacities, atelectasis, and pulmonary edema in the setting of a normal heart size (in contrast to patients with heart failure who typically have cardiomegaly). The treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome is management of the underlying cause and supportive measures such as intubation and ventilation while the patient recovers.



Aspiration pneumonia (B) presents in a patient with alcohol use disorder with a focal consolidation or opacity on chest radiography. Though aspiration pneumonia is certainly possible in this patient and may have predisposed him to acute respiratory distress syndrome, his current picture suggests acute respiratory distress syndrome with bilateral radiological findings.

Community-acquired pneumonia (C) presents with a fever, cough, and consolidation on chest radiography. It is unlikely to cause bilateral pulmonary edema and findings as seen in this patient.

Heart failure exacerbation (D) could present with severe pulmonary edema as is seen in this patient’s chest radiograph. However, it would also present with physical exam findings suggesting heart failure such as jugular venous distension and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. It would be less likely to be associated with an ill patient who likely has pancreatitis, given his history of alcohol use disorder, elevated lipase, and epigastric tenderness.

Question: A 2-year-old girl with mild intermittent asthma is playing in the other room when her parent hears the acute onset of choking and coughing. The episode continues for 5 minutes, and the parent brings her to the emergency department. On exam, she is awake and alert but coughing intermittently. Her respiratory rate is 30/min with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. She has mild intercostal retractions, and wheezing is present over the left lateral and posterior lung fields. Chest radiographs reveal hyperinflation of the left lobe. Which of the following is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
This child's clinical presentation is concerning for a bronchial foreign body aspiration. The classic triad of foreign body aspiration includes sudden onset of coughing, wheezing, and decreased air entry, although these symptoms are not universally present. The right mainstem bronchus is the most common location of foreign body aspiration. It is most common during the third year of life. The most commonly aspirated foreign bodies include nuts, seeds, food particles, small toys or parts of toys, and hardware.

The onset may be acute with choking and coughing. Partial obstruction of the lower airway may manifest as wheezing. On chest radiography, hyperinflation may be noted distal to the obstruction, as the object may cause partial obstruction and air trapping. Notably, only 10% of aspirated foreign bodies are radiopaque, so they will not be visualized on chest radiographs. Therefore, if a foreign body is not visualized by radiography but is suspected based on history and examination, the patient should undergo further evaluation with bronchoscopy, and this intervention is diagnostic and therapeutic.



Albuterol with ipratropium (A) can be used to relieve lower airway obstruction secondary to status asthmaticus acutely. While this child does have a history of mild intermittent asthma, the focality of her wheezing is not suggestive of status asthmaticus, which represents diffuse airway reactivity, inflammation, and obstruction. Albuterol with ipratropium would not be effective in relieving a lower airway obstruction caused by a foreign body.

Ampicillin (B) is an excellent empirical treatment for suspected bacterial community-acquired pneumonia in this child’s age group. In particular, it has excellent coverage of Streptococcus pneumoniae. However, the acute onset of this child’s symptoms, along with hyperinflation on chest radiography, is more suggestive of a foreign body aspiration than community-acquired pneumonia.

The Heimlich maneuver (D) is used for children ≥ 1 year who present with a complete airway obstruction. Since the patient is still able to cough, a complete airway obstruction is unlikely.

Intramuscular dexamethasone (E) is a glucocorticoid used to decrease airway inflammation. It is helpful in relieving upper airway obstruction in croup and lower airway obstruction in wheezing. In the case of this child’s foreign body aspiration, the obstruction is caused by an object rather than an inflammatory process.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents for evaluation of upper respiratory symptoms. Which of the following is the most common presenting symptom seen in acute bronchitis?
ExplanationEN:
Bronchitis is defined as inflammation of the lower airways and is typically caused by viral pathogens. The most common presenting symptom is cough in these patients. Other symptoms include productive sputum, nasal congestion, headache, and sore throat, often preceding the cough. In healthy adult patients, acute bronchitis is typically caused by a viral pathogen (influenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus, and parainfluenza are some of the common pathogens). As such, the condition is not amenable to antibiotic therapy, and treatment would be supportive.

In patients with chronic bronchitis or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, exacerbations of symptoms may be the result of bacterial pathogens causing acute bronchitis on top of their chronic bronchitis. Treatment with antibiotics should be considered in this subset of patients with bronchitis.



Chest pain (A) often occurs due to coughing in patients with bronchitis but is not the most common presenting concern.

Dyspnea (C) is rarely seen with acute bronchitis and should be concerning for other underlying conditions like pneumonia or asthma.

Fever (D) may or may not be present and does not indicate a higher likelihood of bacterial infection.

Sputum production (E) is present in about half of patients with acute bronchitis.

Question: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department reporting chest pain for 3 days. He says that the pain is slightly to the left of his sternum and worse with inspiration and while playing basketball. It is a dull pain that can sometimes feel like a stinging sensation. He reports no shortness of breath, cough, nausea, diaphoresis, and fever. His blood pressure is 139/74 mm Hg, heart rate is 82 bpm, temperature is 98.5°F (37°C), and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On exam, he has normal heart and lung sounds, but he winces when leaning forward. There is distinct pain noted with palpation over the left anterior medial third rib. His ECG is as shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Costochondritis is caused by inflammation of the costal cartilages or their articulation with the sternum. Pain is often made worse with breathing, movement, and particularly, horizontal arm flexion (e.g., crowing rooster maneuver). The pain may be intermittently sharp or dull. The upper costal cartilages are the most frequent site of inflammation. Diagnosis is made during the physical exam when the pain is reproduced by palpating the specific area over the costochondral junction(s) involved. Findings of at least two of the following are 63% sensitive and 79% specific for a diagnosis of costochondritis: localized muscle tension, stinging pain, lack of cough, and pain reproduced by palpation.



Acute pericarditis (A)is caused by inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart. The associated pain is typically substernal, sharp, constant, improved with leaning forward, and worsened with laying back. The exam may reveal a pericardial friction rub, and ECG will sometimes show diffuse ST segment elevation with PR depression. While pulmonary embolism (C) also presents with sharp chest pain made worse with inspiration, it often presents with other signs and symptoms such as dyspnea, hypoxemia, syncope, shock, fever, cough, hemoptysis, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Xiphodynia (D) is caused by inflammation of the xiphoid process. It may present with sharp chest pain that is worse with breathing. However, the pain is reproduced by palpation of the xiphoid specifically.

Question: Which characteristic of a chest wall wound most influences the airflow physiology of an open pneumothorax?

Options.text: Location of the wound on the anterior or posterior chest

ExplanationEN:
The size of the wound most influences the physiology of an open pneumothorax, specifically determining whether air preferentially enters through the chest wall defect versus the trachea and the degree of resulting ventilation impairment and respiratory compromise.

For stab wounds, most handgun wounds, and many rifle wounds, a small wound does not lead to enough air leak to impair respirations, while for larger chest wall defects such as those caused by high-velocity rifle wounds, shotgun wounds, and blast injuries, first aid interventions designed to reduce air entry through the wound are theoretically beneficial. This size-dependent effect directly determines the pathophysiology.

The fundamental principle is that air follows the path of least resistance during inspiration. The goal of sealing an open chest wound is to increase airflow resistance through the chest wall defect so that it exceeds resistance through the trachea, allowing proper lung ventilation. When a chest wall defect is large enough that its airflow resistance is lower than tracheal resistance, air preferentially enters the pleural space rather than ventilating the lungs, creating the classic sucking chest wound with impaired gas exchange, decreased vital capacity, increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, and hypoxemia.



Bleeding from the wound edge (A) can be concerning for associated vascular injury but does not affect the air dynamics of an open pneumothorax. It may complicate wound care, but it does not affect how air enters the chest.

Location of the wound on the anterior or posterior chest (B) may affect clinical detection or associated injuries, but it does not determine the physiologic behavior of airflow in an open pneumothorax. Air entry is primarily governed by wound size and pressure gradients rather than by specific chest wall location.

The presence of subcutaneous emphysema (C) is a secondary finding that may suggest air leakage into soft tissues but does not directly determine how air enters the pleural space. It is a clinical clue, not a driving factor in the physiology of open pneumothorax.

The shape of the wound (D) (e.g., round, linear, jagged) does not significantly influence airflow or pleural pressure changes. What matters is whether the opening is large enough to allow air to bypass the trachea during respiration.

Question: A 19-year-old man is found unconscious in a park and is brought into the ED by paramedics for altered mental status. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 5 on arrival with sonorous respirations. He has asymmetric wheezes on exam. He is intubated for airway protection. CT of the chest demonstrates an occlusive foreign object located in the bronchus intermedius with distal atelectasis. Which of the following lobes is most affected by this airway obstruction?
ExplanationEN:
The trachea bifurcates at the carina and gives rise to the right and left mainstem bronchi. The mainstem bronchi then divide into secondary bronchi (or lobar bronchi). The right mainstem bronchus gives rise to the superior lobar bronchus and the bronchus intermedius. The bronchus intermedius is the continuation of the right main bronchus after its bifurcation. It continues distally and gives rise to the middle lobar bronchus and the lower lobar bronchus. The left mainstem bronchus bifurcates into the upper and lower lobar bronchi that supply the left upper and lower lobes, respectively. The right mainstem bronchus continues in a more direct trajectory from the carina as opposed to the left mainstem bronchus, which takes a more acute angle after its origin. This is why foreign bodies are more likely to settle in the right bronchial tree than the left. An occlusive foreign object will prevent effective aeration and gas exchange within the distal pulmonary segments. Therefore, occlusion of the bronchus intermedius would cause decreased aeration of the right middle lobe and right lower lobe.



The left upper lobe (A) is supplied by the upper lobar bronchus.

The lingula (B) is part of the left upper lobe.

The right upper lobe (D) is supplied by the upper lobar bronchus before the right main bronchus gives rise to the bronchus intermedius.

Question: A 56-year-old man presents to the ED with dyspnea. His medical history includes hypertension, for which he takes no medications. Chest X-ray shows a small pleural effusion on the right. Pleural fluid analysis shows a total protein of 2.0 g/dL and lactate dehydrogenase of 62 U/L. Serum analysis shows a total protein of 6.2 g/dL and lactate dehydrogenase of 194 U/L. Which of the following is most likely to be present on physical examination of this patient?

Options.text: Pericardial friction rub and muffled heart sounds
Unilateral crackles in the mid lung

ExplanationEN:
Pleural effusion refers to an abnormal collection of fluid within the pleural space between the visceral and parietal pleura that results from a variety of associated conditions. In the United States, the most common associated causes are malignancy, bacterial pneumonia, congestive heart failure, and pulmonary embolism. Under normal circumstances, there is a continuous flow of fluid across the pleural space with influx and efflux in equilibrium. Effusion occurs if the equilibrium is disrupted. The underlying pathophysiology involves one of two mechanisms: increased capillary permeability or changes in hydrostatic or osmotic pressure. Effusions associated with the latter mechanism are transudative, while the former causes exudative effusions.

Many patients with new-onset pleural effusion will require thoracentesis and pleural fluid analysis to aid in the evaluation of the underlying cause. While this does not always need to occur emergently in the ED, it may be done to aid in the diagnosis of life-threatening causes or to provide urgent symptom relief. Pleural fluid analysis helps to differentiate transudates from exudates via the application of Light criteria, which are pleural fluid protein to serum protein > 0.5, pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to serum LDH > 0.6, and pleural fluid LDH more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH. Only one of these conditions needs to be met for an effusion to be considered exudative. In this scenario, none of these conditions are met, so the patient’s pleural effusion can be said to be transudative.

Conditions that cause transudative effusions are often those that cause edema in other locations, whether due to increased plasma hydrostatic or decreased plasma oncotic pressure, and may have other associated clinical features. Such conditions include congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and pulmonary embolism. In the case of pleural effusions associated with congestive heart failure, clinical evidence of pulmonary edema, such as crackles, may be present. Ultimately, management is typically not targeted at a pleural effusion itself but at the underlying condition. In some cases (e.g., empyema), primarily with exudative effusions, tube thoracostomy is required to achieve source control of infection and reduce the risk of complications.



Esophageal rupture may present with crepitus on palpation of the neck (B) or chest wall and is a life-threatening cause of exudative effusions rather than transudative ones.

Pancreatitis is a cause of exudative effusions and classically presents clinically with epigastric tenderness, often with guarding (C).

A pericardial friction rub and muffled heart sounds (D) are signs of effusive pericarditis, which does not cause pleural effusions by itself.

Unilateral crackles in the mid lung (E) may be present with acute infectious pneumonia, which would be associated with exudative effusion rather than transudative.

Question: A 51-year-old woman presents to the ED with leg pain and swelling. Physical examination shows asymmetric calf swelling and tenderness on the right leg, and based on her history, her Wells score is 4. Which of the following, if negative, sufficiently excludes deep vein thrombosis in this patient?

Options.text: Three-point venous ultrasound now and in 48 hours

ExplanationEN:
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) results from the interplay of the Virchow triad: hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury, with prominent risk factors including major surgery (especially orthopedic), prolonged immobilization, active malignancy, pregnancy, and inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden. However, roughly up to half of DVT cases are unprovoked, occurring without an identifiable transient risk factor. The classic clinical features of DVT consist of unilateral leg pain and swelling, with heightened suspicion in patients with identifiable triggers or risk factors. Patients may also present with symptoms of pulmonary embolism (chest pain, dyspnea) in cases complicated by such.

The diagnostic evaluation of suspected DVT is complex and begins with the estimation of pretest probability, classically by calculating a Wells score. The Wells score stratifies patients based on risk factors, including active malignancy, recent immobilization, and exam findings (e.g., unilateral swelling, localized tenderness). The score ranges from –2 to 9, with a score ≥ 3 indicating high probability, 1–2 indicating moderate probability, and ≤ 0 indicating low probability. Alternatively, a two-level system uses a score of ≤ 1 for unlikely and ≥ 2 for likely of having DVT.

Patients with a low pretest probability (i.e., Wells score ≤ 0) can have DVT excluded with a negative serum D-dimer, three-point compression ultrasound, or whole-leg compression ultrasound. Patients with a moderate pretest probability are more challenging to evaluate, as recommendations vary on whether the diagnosis can be ruled out with a negative serum D-dimer or whether further imaging is required or should be used instead. However, patients with high pretest probability cannot have DVT ruled out without imaging, though a single negative whole-leg compression ultrasound is sufficient to rule out DVT regardless of pretest probability. If three-point (rather than whole-leg) compression ultrasound is used, then a negative serum D-dimer is also required for patients with high pretest probability.



Clinical assessment (i.e., Wells score) alone (A) cannot exclude DVT, as even patients with the lowest Wells score of –2 have approximately 5% prevalence of DVT. Clinical decision rules must be combined with D-dimer testing or imaging for safe exclusion.

In patients with a high pretest probability (Wells score ≥ 3 or ≥ 2, depending on the scoring system), a negative D-dimer test (B) has only a 92% negative predictive value, which is insufficient to safely exclude DVT. These patients require direct imaging regardless of the D-dimer result.

While a negative proximal (i.e., three-point) compression ultrasound (C) in patients with low pretest probability can exclude DVT, this patient has a high probability (Wells score of 4), which requires either serial ultrasound at 1 week or whole-leg ultrasound to safely exclude DVT. A single proximal ultrasound may miss distal DVT that could extend proximally.

Serial ultrasound is typically performed at 1 week after an initial negative proximal ultrasound in patients with high pretest probability. A 48-hour time frame (D) is too short for clinically significant proximal extension to occur.

Question: A 9-year-old boy with a history of asthma presents to the emergency department with chest pain that started a few hours ago after swimming. He reports pleuritic chest pain but no real shortness of breath. He reports no other symptoms, such as coughing or vomiting. Vital signs show HR 85 bpm, RR 16/min, and T 98.4°F (36.9°C). Lung examination reveals clear lungs. Utilizing the chest radiograph above, what is the diagnosis to explain this patient's pain?
ExplanationEN:
This chest radiograph shows pneumomediastinum. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum is uncommon in children, but when it occurs, it is often associated with asthma. Pneumomediastinum occurs when air escapes from the upper respiratory tract, intrathoracic airways, or gastrointestinal tract. Other causes of pneumomediastinum include the Valsalva maneuver, often related to sporting activities or coughing, vomiting, diabetes-related ketoacidosis, esophageal rupture, choking or foreign body aspiration, inhalation of gas from helium balloons, and barotrauma from diving or flying. A chest radiograph in pneumomediastinum demonstrates gas outlining the mediastinal structures with a lucent streak, usually most clear above the heart on the left side. Blood tests are not useful in making the diagnosis. Uncomplicated spontaneous pneumomediastinum can usually be treated conservatively with analgesics, rest, and avoidance of maneuvers that increase pulmonary pressure.



Chest radiograph findings in pneumonia (B) would include airspace opacity or lobar consolidation. This chest radiograph does not show an opacity. Patients with pneumonia also typically present with cough, shortness of breath, and fever.

Chest radiograph findings in pneumothorax (C)include the outer margin of the visceral pleura, or lung, separated from the chest wall by a lucent gas space without pulmonary vessels. This chest radiograph is not consistent with pneumothorax.

Chest radiograph findings in viral bronchitis (D) usually include peribronchial cuffing. Patients present with cough and upper respiratory symptoms.

Question: Which of the following medications should be part of standard care in a patient presenting to the emergency department with a moderate asthma exacerbation?
ExplanationEN:
Patients with moderate to severe asthma exacerbations should be started on systemic corticosteroids in the emergency department. Systemic corticosteroids inhibit the activation of inflammatory cells and decrease airflow obstruction. They should be given to any patient who has an incomplete response to initial beta-agonist therapy. In patients with acute asthma, corticosteroid effects begin within hours and peak at 24 hours. The use of steroids in asthma exacerbations has been shown to reduce the relapse rate and decrease admissions in severe asthma exacerbations. For this reason, corticosteroids should be offered to all patients with moderate to severe exacerbations. There is no difference in efficacy between oral and parenteral corticosteroids.



Inhaled magnesium (A) has not consistently been shown to improve symptoms of asthma and is typically reserved for severe asthma exacerbations.

Inhaled steroids (B) are useful in the chronic management of asthma and the prevention of exacerbations. There is some evidence that suggests that treating with both systemic and inhaled steroids in acute exacerbations is more effective than either method alone.

Intravenous ketamine (C) is frequently used as an induction agent prior to intubation in patients with asthma as it can bronchodilate.

Question: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath. He reports no significant medical history but performs heavy lifting at work. His chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following physical exam findings is most suggestive of the diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Pneumomediastinum means air in the mediastinum and may occur spontaneously or due to trauma. Pneumomediastinum that occurs spontaneously is typically associated with asthma, respiratory infections, retching, coughing, drug use (e.g., cocaine), choking, and foreign bodies (e.g., in children). When associated with blunt chest trauma, the most common cause is alveolar rupture, which allows air to dissect along the bronchoalveolar sheath and track into the mediastinum. Mechanical ventilation and medical procedures are also potential culprits. Pneumomediastinum is caused by perforation of the larynx, pharynx, esophagus, trachea, major bronchi, or alveoli. The air may sometimes be palpated as subcutaneous emphysema in the neck or heard on auscultation as a crunching sound over the heart (Hamman sign). The air in the mediastinum can be seen on a chest radiograph as streaking or bubbling along mediastinal structures, which is seen on this patient’s radiograph along the left heart border. When a radiograph is ambiguous, a chest CT scan confirms the diagnosis. Symptoms may include chest pain, neck pain, dyspnea, voice change, stridor, and cough, though a patient may also be asymptomatic. Further treatment, testing, and intervention are not required in an asymptomatic patient without other concerns for serious injury. Analgesia, rest, and avoidance of activities that increase pulmonary pressure (e.g., Valsalva maneuvers, scuba diving) are advised.



Deviated trachea (A), diminished breath sounds (B), and distended neck veins (C) are all signs of tension pneumothorax, which may co-occur with pneumomediastinum in patients with chest trauma but are not typically present in patients with spontaneous pneumomediastinum, as in this patient.

Tachycardia (E) is a nonspecific finding in tension pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism and does not specifically suggest pneumomediastinum. Patients with spontaneous pneumomediastinum often will have no or mild symptoms without a change in vital signs.

Question: A 52-year-old farmer presents to the ED with dyspnea, cough, and chest tightness that began several hours after working inside a freshly filled silo. He initially noticed a harsh, bleach-like odor but continued working without a respirator. He reports transient improvement after leaving the silo, but his symptoms have worsened. On examination, he is tachypneic with mild hypoxia (SpO2 91% on room air). Chest X-ray is unremarkable. Which of the following gases has the patient most likely been exposed to?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has silo filler’s disease, a toxic pneumonitis caused by inhalation of nitrogen dioxide, which is produced by fermenting silage. Nitrogen dioxide is a reddish-brown gas with a characteristic bleach-like odor, but exposure often occurs before workers recognize the danger. It is heavier than air, accumulating in low-lying areas such as freshly filled silos. Agricultural workers are particularly at risk, especially those entering silos shortly after filling. Exposure can lead to immediate mucosal irritation, followed by a delayed onset of dyspnea, cough, and chest tightness, with potential progression to acute lung injury or delayed-onset pulmonary edema (acute respiratory distress syndrome-like presentation within 24 hours).

Diagnosis is clinical, based on history of exposure and characteristic symptoms. Chest X-ray may initially be normal but can later show interstitial or alveolar infiltrates if pulmonary edema develops. Pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas may reveal hypoxemia, and pulmonary function tests in subacute cases may show obstructive or restrictive patterns. The mainstay of treatment is oxygen therapy, and patients should be admitted for observation due to the risk of delayed pulmonary edema. Steroids may be considered in severe cases, but evidence is limited. Inhaled beta-agonists can be used for bronchospasm, though they do not address the underlying lung injury. Mechanical ventilation may be required for respiratory failure. Preventive measures include avoiding freshly filled silos or using self-contained respirators when entering them.



Ammonia (A) is a highly water-soluble gas that primarily causes upper airway irritation, including cough, laryngospasm, and eye irritation. It is commonly found in fertilizers and cleaning products, not silo environments. Unlike nitrogen dioxide, ammonia does not typically cause delayed-onset pulmonary edema. Treatment involves airway protection and supportive care.

Carbon monoxide (CO) (B) poisoning presents with headache, dizziness, confusion, and cherry-red skin rather than respiratory distress. CO exposure is common in enclosed spaces with combustion, such as homes with faulty furnaces, not silos. Additionally, pulse oximetry is unreliable in CO poisoning because carboxyhemoglobin falsely normalizes SpO2 readings. Diagnosis requires co-oximetry, and treatment is high-flow oxygen or hyperbaric therapy.

Hydrogen sulfide (C) exposure occurs in sewers, manure pits, and oil refineries, not silos. It causes rapid unconsciousness and respiratory paralysis at high concentrations rather than delayed-onset pulmonary edema. It has a characteristic rotten egg odor, but olfactory fatigue can quickly render it undetectable. Management includes removal from exposure, supportive care, and high-flow oxygen.

Methane (D) is a colorless, odorless, and nonirritating gas that primarily causes asphyxiation by displacing oxygen rather than direct lung injury. It is a major component of natural gas and manure pit gases but does not produce toxic pulmonary effects like nitrogen dioxide. Treatment focuses on removing the patient from the environment and providing supplemental oxygen if hypoxic.

Question: Which of the following values would be concerning for an empyema in pleural fluid analysis?

Options.text: Pleural albumin 2 g/L, serum albumin 5 g/dL
Pleural glucose 65 g/dL, serum glucose 90 g/dL
Pleural lactate dehydrogenase 150 IU/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase 225 IU/L
Pleural protein 3 g/dL, serum protein 7 g/dL

CorrectAnswer: Pleural lactate dehydrogenase 150 IU/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase 225 IU/L
ExplanationEN:
A thoracic empyema occurs when a pleural effusion becomes infected with bacteria, resulting in pus in the pleural space. Patients with empyema generally present later, such as when bacteria are left untreated from pneumonia and are given time to colonize the pleural space. The less virulent the bacteria are, the later the presentation. Therefore, indolent anaerobic cases of pneumonia (aspiration) are often the type of pneumonia complicated by empyemas. Common clinical features include cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and sputum production. Duration of fever and pleuritic chest pain are the only two presenting symptoms that differentiate pneumonia from pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion or empyema.

Patients with empyema will often report several days of malaise and fever compared to hours for pneumonia. Physical examination may reveal coarse crackles, egophony, and increased tactile fremitus. The appearance of an effusion or empyema is first suspected based on imaging, which is commonly a chest X-ray. Optimal evaluation of an empyema or loculated effusion, especially in adults, is best done with a CT scan of the chest with intravenous contrast. Ultimately, in order to diagnose an empyema, a thoracentesis with fluid analysis must be performed.

Pleural fluid should undergo microscopic analysis, Gram stain, and cultures. Differentiating between a transudative and exudative effusion is the initial step in the management of effusions. Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusions, complicated parapneumonic effusions, and empyemas are all classified as exudative effusions. Light criteria helps distinguish transudative from exudative effusions, as it defines an exudative effusion as a pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio > 0.5, pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to serum LDH ratio > 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper limits of the laboratory’s normal serum LDH. When pus is present, the diagnosis of empyema is made versus an uncomplicated or complicated parapneumonic effusion.

Treatment is focused on antibiotics and drainage. The antibiotic of choice should be focused on which agent will treat the pneumonia causing the empyema or the bacteria that were isolated from the thoracentesis. However, aminoglycoside use should be avoided due to inactivation secondary to the empyema’s low pH. Anaerobic bacteria are common and appropriate anaerobic antibiotic coverage is warranted. Drainage is commonly required with tube thoracostomy, which is guided by ultrasound or CT scan due to loculations. More invasive procedures such as fibrinolytic agents, thoracoscopic debridement, decortication, and open thoracotomy are sometimes required.



Pleural albumin 2 g/L, serum albumin 5 g/dL (A) is not a ratio used to help determine if a pleural effusion is transudative or exudative. Albumin is more often used as part of the serum-ascites albumin gradient, which helps determine if the source of the ascites is due to portal hypertension or not.

Pleural glucose 65 g/dL, serum glucose 90 g/dL (B) is not a ratio used for pleural effusions.

A pleural protein 3 g/dL to serum protein 7 g/dL (D) ratio is < 0.5 and thus is more associated with a transudative effusion than an exudative effusion. Empyemas are classified as exudative effusions.

Question: A 56-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to the ED for dyspnea. Vital signs show a T of 37.0°C (98.6°F), BP of 134/80 mm Hg, HR of 115 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. Physical examination is unremarkable. CTA of the chest is shown above. Which of the following, if present, most likely contributed to this patient’s current condition?
ExplanationEN:
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a relatively common cause of chest pain and dyspnea in the ED and may be life-threatening when complicated by shock, respiratory failure, or cardiac arrest. Most PEs arise from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the lower extremities and subsequently embolize to the pulmonary arterial circulation. Proximal DVTs, particularly those involving the popliteal, femoral, or iliac veins, account for the greatest risk of clinically significant embolization due to their larger clot burden and direct venous drainage into the inferior vena cava. Distal DVTs, such as those in veins below the knee, carry a significantly lower risk of embolization.

The pathogenesis of PE is typically explained by the Virchow triad, which comprises venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Upon embolization, the clots lodge in the pulmonary arteries, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxemia, and right ventricular strain or failure. This patient’s tachycardia and tachypnea with otherwise normal lung examination findings are classic for PE, and CTA showing multiple vascular filling defects confirms the diagnosis.

Clinical presentation of PE is variable and ranges from mild dyspnea to syncope or shock. Common findings include tachycardia, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, and unexplained dyspnea, with physical examination often unremarkable. Pulmonary CTA is the diagnostic test of choice in hemodynamically stable patients. Initial treatment focuses on prompt anticoagulation, typically with unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, or direct oral anticoagulants. Patients with hemodynamic instability may require systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapy, or surgical embolectomy. Complications include right ventricular failure, recurrent venous thromboembolism, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and death if untreated.



Atrial fibrillation (A) predisposes patients to thrombus formation in the left atrium, which can embolize to the systemic circulation and cause stroke, not PE. PEs arise from the venous system or right-sided cardiac sources.

Chronic pulmonary disease (B) may cause dyspnea and hypoxemia but does not directly lead to venous thromboembolism. It does not explain the presence of bilateral pulmonary emboli on this patient’s CT imaging.

Thrombosis in distal veins such as the peroneal vein (C) is less likely to embolize to the lungs compared with proximal deep veins. While distal thrombosis can extend proximally, proximal vein involvement is more strongly associated with PE.

Tricuspid valve endocarditis (E) can cause septic pulmonary emboli, typically associated with fever, bacteremia, and peripheral cavitary lung lesions. This patient is afebrile with imaging consistent with thrombotic, not septic, pulmonary emboli.

Question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the ED for difficulty breathing. His parent reports that he was diagnosed with croup 4 days ago at his pediatrician’s office and was treated as an outpatient with racemic epinephrine and dexamethasone. His parent states that he improved with the treatment and had been doing well until last night when he started to have stridor. He has no other significant medical history and is up-to-date with his immunizations. In the ED, his vital signs include T 40°C, HR 140 bpm, RR 40/min, BP 90/60 mm Hg, and SpO2 94% on room air. On physical examination, the child has full range of motion of his neck and is lying limp in his parent's arms. Audible inspiratory and expiratory stridor is noted, but no drooling. He receives a treatment of racemic epinephrine with no change in status. In addition to starting the patient on appropriate medications, which of the following would you do next?

Options.text: Consult otolaryngology for an emergent laryngoscopy
Nothing is needed because it is a clinical diagnosis
Perform a CT scan of the neck with IV contrast

CorrectAnswer: Consult otolaryngology for an emergent laryngoscopy
ExplanationEN:
This patient has bacterial tracheitis. Patients with bacterial tracheitis usually present with a history of a recent upper respiratory tract infection or croup that improves initially and then worsens. Definitive diagnosis of bacterial tracheitis requires direct visualization with bronchoscopy or laryngoscopy showing laryngotracheal erythema, edema, and thick purulent secretions. Antibiotic therapy should be directed at Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. Vancomycin in combination with a third-generation cephalosporin or ampicillin-sulbactam is appropriate as first-line therapy. Antibiotics can be tailored once cultures and sensitivities are available.



Croup, not bacterial tracheitis, is a clinical diagnosis (B). An anteroposterior neck radiograph (C) can show a steeple sign consistent with croup. A lateral radiograph may show the thumbprint sign consistent with epiglottitis. Given that this child’s clinical status is worsening after the treatment for croup (steroids and racemic epinephrine), this is unlikely a recurrence of croup. A lateral neck X-ray would be needed (not AP) and presents as subglottic narrowing that may be irregular as opposed to the symmetric tapering typical of croup. A neck CT scan with IV contrast (D) is helpful for deep neck infections such as retropharyngeal abscesses. A retropharyngeal abscess usually presents with a sore throat and decreased range of motion of the neck rather than stridor, making the diagnosis less likely.

Question: A 67-year-old man with a history of seizure disorder, COPD, coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and associated cough, sputum production, and a fever for 3 days. He states he had an increased frequency of breakthrough seizures in the week preceding these symptoms after he ran out of his levetiracetam. He has no chest pain, orthopnea, or leg swelling. His vital signs include an HR of 98 bpm, a BP of 105/78 mm Hg, an RR of 18/min, and an SpO2 of 87% on room air. He is placed on 3 L supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula with improvement. His X-ray is shown above. What is the most likely etiology of his symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Aspiration pneumonia occurs when gastric or oropharyngeal contents enter the lower respiratory tract and cause infection in the alveolar space. The risk of aspiration pneumonia is increased in patients with abnormal upper airway anatomy, compromised swallow coordination (e.g., neuromuscular disease), older age, altered consciousness, gastroesophageal disorders (e.g., gastroesophageal reflux, retained gastric contents), and poor oral hygiene. Patients may initially develop aspiration pneumonitis, which is a chemical injury and secondary inflammation, which can progress to pneumonia and should be suspected if symptoms persist beyond 48 hours. The diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia is based on a combination of risk factors and chest X-ray findings (e.g., opacification of dependent lung segments, most often the right lower lobe, as demonstrated above). The treatment of aspiration pneumonia is similar to that of community-acquired pneumonia. Example inpatient treatment regimens include a beta-lactam (e.g., ceftriaxone) and a macrolide (e.g., azithromycin) or doxycycline. Single-agent treatment with levofloxacin or moxifloxacin is also appropriate. Anaerobic coverage is not routinely recommended unless there is a concomitant abscess or empyema.



Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (B) often demonstrates bilateral interstitial opacities, though asymmetric pulmonary edema can be seen in some specific instances (e.g., mitral insufficiency). Chest X-ray findings in COPD (C) include hyperinflated lungs and flattening of the diaphragm, secondary to the air trapping that arises with bronchoconstriction. Empyema (D) is an infection of the pleural space arising from underlying pneumonia, an extension of an adjacent lung abscess, inoculation of an existing pleural fluid collection (e.g., hemothorax, hydrothorax, or chylothorax), or can be secondary to thoracic trauma. Empyema should be suspected if a pleural air-fluid level is visualized on a chest X-ray or CT. Viral pneumonia (E) presents with similar symptoms to bacterial pneumonia (e.g., cough, fever, dyspnea), though it is more gradual in onset. Chest X-ray characteristics include perihilar infiltrates, bronchial thickening, and interstitial infiltrates.

Question: A 33-year-old woman presents in respiratory distress. She is known to the emergency department for multiple overdoses with IV heroin requiring naloxone. She states her symptoms started over the past 3 days and began with a nonproductive cough. Her vital signs are remarkable for a temperature of 40°C, HR of 140 bpm, RR of 31/min, BP of 100/40 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 89% on room air. Physical exam reveals diminished and coarse breath sounds and a high-pitched holosystolic heart murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border. Chest X-ray is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Septic emboli cause two insults, an embolic or ischemic insult due to the vascular occlusion and an infectious insult due to a deep-seated nidus of infection. The causes of septic emboli include infectious endocarditis, infected intravascular device, septic thrombophlebitis, periodontal disease, perivascular infection, myxoma, and vascular fistulae. This patient is presenting with concerning features for infectious endocarditis. Patients at risk for infectious endocarditis are usually male, > 60 years of age, use injection drugs, or have poor dentition or dental infections. Other risk factors include the presence of structural heart disease, prosthetic heart valves, intravascular devices, or a history of infective endocarditis. Clinical features can range from asymptomatic with incidental findings to devastating cardiovascular or cerebral events. Patients may develop respiratory symptoms of cough, shortness of breath, and even hemoptysis as a result of pulmonary embolic disease. Patients may also present with an acute or new heart murmur. In the setting of IV drug use, the most likely culprit is tricuspid valve endocarditis, which presents with a holosystolic murmur best auscultated along the left lower sternal border. Complications are related to the location of the insult. Respiratory complications include nodules, abscesses, and empyemas. Emboli can cause central nervous system dysfunction, gastrointestinal dysfunction, musculoskeletal dysfunction, or other cardiovascular dysfunction. Treatment focuses on source control, treating the underlying cause, giving antibiotics, and treating specific complications of septic embolization.



A patient with acute mitral regurgitation (A) typically presents in acute respiratory distress with acute heart failure. Etiologies can include infective endocarditis, acute myocardial infarction, papillary muscle displacement, trauma, rheumatic heart disease, and other causes that are generally classified as either ischemic or nonischemic. The murmur in mitral regurgitation is typically an early systolic, midsystolic, or holosystolic murmur. This murmur is best auscultated at the apex of the heart. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (B), or ARDS, is characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and has a wide spectrum of etiologies. ARDS is classified as mild, moderate, and severe based on the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of > 200 but ≤ 300 mm Hg, > 100 but ≤ 200 mm Hg, and < 100 mm Hg, respectively. Treatment focuses on lung-protective ventilatory settings, treating the underlying cause, and supportive care. Community-acquired pneumonia (C) is within the differential for this patient. However, given the appearance of the chest X-ray along with the risk factors and new murmur, the most likely and most concerning diagnosis is septic emboli affecting the pulmonary system.

Question: A 36-year-old man with a prior history of intravenous drug use presents with symptoms of a dry cough, fever, and exertional dyspnea over the past 10 days. He also reports a 15-pound weight loss in the last 4 months. On examination, he has a temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F), heart rate of 102 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/minute, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Lung auscultation is unremarkable. His chest radiograph reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly carinii) pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic fungal infection that primarily affects immunocompromised patients including those with HIV/AIDS, as well as cancer and organ transplant patients who take immunosuppressants. PCP is one of the most common AIDS-defining opportunistic infections. Patients present with a gradual onset of nonproductive cough, fever, dyspnea, and decreased exercise tolerance. Patients with previously undiagnosed HIV/AIDS may also present with symptoms such as weight loss and oral candidiasis. Lung auscultation is often normal, although rales or rhonchi may be present. Chest X-ray often shows bilateral diffuse interstitial perihilar infiltrates that extend in a bat-wing pattern. However, atypical findings, such as a normal chest X-ray or apical infiltrates, can be seen. Spontaneous pneumothorax is also seen in about 10% of patients. Arterial blood gases are often abnormal, with decreased pO2 and respiratory alkalosis. Lactate dehydrogenase is increased, with the degree of elevation used as a marker for a worse prognosis. In patients with HIV, CD4 counts are typically < 200 cells/mm3.

Intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the antibiotic of choice. It should be administered for a total of 21 days. Alternative regimens include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus dapsone, primaquine plus clindamycin, or pentamidine. Steroids are indicated in patients with moderate to severe disease as indicated by pO2 < 70 mm Hg. Steroids have been found to decrease mortality and accelerate recovery and should also be administered for 21 days with a tapering regimen.



Cefepime and levofloxacin (A) would be a good choice for a patient with multi-drug-resistant pneumonia, which would be indicated by risk factors for a resistant organism and a focal consolidation on imaging.

An 8-week course of isoniazid and rifampin (B) can be prescribed for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. Tuberculosis can also present with a gradual onset of symptoms, although these patients also may have night sweats and hemoptysis. However, chest X-ray findings would show a cavitary lesion instead of bilateral interstitial infiltrates.

Levofloxacin (C) alone would provide adequate coverage for a patient with community-acquired pneumonia. These patients typically have a more acute onset of symptoms, including a cough productive of purulent sputum, fever, and chills. Chest radiograph often shows a focal consolidation.
