Question: A 45-year-old man presents to the ED for evaluation of a fever and productive cough with hemoptysis ongoing for 2 weeks. He has lost approximately 10 pounds since symptom onset. Over the last 2 days, his temperature has been consistently 39–40°C despite regular use of ibuprofen and acetaminophen. He has a history of diabetes mellitus status post pancreatic transplantation and previous end-stage kidney disease status post kidney transplantation, along with hypertension and coronary artery disease. He has tachypnea, speaks in full sentences, and has coarse rales throughout the right lung fields. His SpO2 is 98% at rest and 90% with speaking and exertion. His abdomen is soft, with no organomegaly noted. He has superficial cervical lymphadenopathy, and there is no peripheral edema. A chest X-ray is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an important cause of fever and respiratory symptoms in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., patients with HIV infection, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, or autoimmune disease), people with occupational or close contact exposure (e.g., incarcerated individuals, health care workers), and travelers returning from or residents living in endemic regions. In primary tuberculosis, most patients are asymptomatic, and the disease is not identified unless testing is performed. In immunocompromised patients, rapidly progressive reactivated or fulminant disease may arise with fever, malaise, pleuritic chest pain, and a cough. Chest X-ray often demonstrates an infiltrate in the upper lobes with hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, sometimes with cavitation. However, lymphadenopathy may be the only finding in primary tuberculosis. Development of a pleural effusion occurs when subpleural lymph nodes rupture into the pleural space. Fluid sampling will demonstrate an exudative fluid. Diagnosis is aided by acid-fast staining and PCR testing of sputum or any pulmonary or pleural fluid samples. Patients will require multidrug therapy with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.



Community-acquired pneumonia (A) most often arises from Streptococcus pneumoniae and presents with usual symptoms of pneumonia (e.g., cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fever) and a lobar infiltrate on chest X-ray. This patient has risk factors for other pulmonary organisms, and the chest X-ray shows an upper lobe infiltrate more consistent with tuberculosis. Coxiella burnetii infection (B) causes Q fever weeks after exposure, presenting with high fever (up to 40°C), malaise, headache, cough, and gastrointestinal distress. Pneumonia with bilateral alveolar opacities is a common complication in addition to hepatitis and myocarditis. Influenza pneumonia (C) causes patchy bilateral opacities and often presents seasonally with cough, congestion, fever, malaise, and gastrointestinal distress. Loeffler syndrome (D) secondary to Ascaris lumbricoides infection can mimic community-acquired pneumonia or asthma, particularly in pediatric patients. It causes postobstructive pneumonia with associated eosinophilic inflammation, often presenting with lobar infiltrates on chest X-ray.

Question: A previously healthy 21-year-old man presents to the ED with sudden onset chest pain and shortness of breath. On physical exam, you note diminished breath sounds on the right. His chest radiograph is shown above. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with a simple spontaneous pneumothorax. He has no underlying lung disease. The single greatest risk factor for a spontaneous pneumothorax is smoking as this portends a twenty-fold increase in risk. Secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are seen in patients with asthma, COPD, pulmonary neoplasm, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, or cystic fibrosis. Tension pneumothorax occurs when there is a pleural defect that creates a one-way valve leading to increased pleural pressure, mediastinal shift, and decreased venous return to the heart via increased intrathoracic pressure. Signs and symptoms of a simple pneumothorax include pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Tension pneumothorax presents with decreased breath sounds on one side, hyperresonance to percussion, jugular venous distension, hypotension, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

Diagnosis is via chest radiography or ultrasound for simple pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax should be diagnosed clinically and immediately decompressed with needle thoracostomy followed by definitive management with tube thoracostomy. Small, stable spontaneous pneumothoraces may be treated with 100% oxygen and will reabsorb 5–7% per day. Larger spontaneous pneumothoraces also warrant tube thoracostomy. Reexpansion pulmonary edema should be a concern if the pneumothorax has been present for > 3 days.



While tall height (A), thin stature, male sex (B), and recent pneumonia (C), especially with cavitation or abscess, are risk factors for spontaneous pneumothorax, they portend significantly less risk than smoking. The second greatest risk factor is male sex and this only results in a six-fold increase in risk.

Question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ED with a 2-day history of worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. She has a history of asthma and ran out of her maintenance inhaler 2 weeks ago. Her vital signs show a respiratory rate of 24/min, heart rate of 110 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. On examination, she has diffuse expiratory wheezes and accessory muscle use. After initial treatment with oxygen and nebulized albuterol and ipratropium, what is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Discharge home with a refill for her inhaler

ExplanationEN:
Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterized by reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Key features include episodic symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough, often triggered by allergens, infections, or exercise. Asthma is diagnosed based on a combination of clinical history, physical exam findings (e.g., wheezing), and objective measures like spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction.

The cornerstone of acute asthma care involves addressing bronchospasm, airway inflammation, and hypoxemia. In this case, the patient’s symptoms and physical findings indicate a moderate to severe exacerbation requiring bronchodilators such as albuterol and ipratropium. However, systemic corticosteroids are also indicated to reduce airway inflammation and should be administered within 1 hour of presentation. Methylprednisolone is the preferred intravenous agent in the emergency setting due to its rapid onset of action, particularly in patients with moderate to severe exacerbations. Current evidence suggests that the intravenous and oral routes have equivalent bioavailability and efficacy in the ED. Steroids help prevent relapse and reduce the need for hospitalization.

In addition to corticosteroids, acute management can include adjunctive therapies like magnesium sulfate for severe cases. Addressing underlying triggers, educating the patient on maintenance therapy adherence, and ensuring follow-up are critical to preventing future exacerbations. Patients who improve in the ED can often be discharged with oral steroid therapy along with refills of bronchodilator inhalers. Inhaled steroids are also an integral component of the outpatient management of chronic asthma and should be considered upon discharge for use as a controller medication.



Asthma exacerbations are most commonly triggered by viral infections or environmental factors rather than bacterial infections. Unless there is evidence of a concurrent bacterial infection, such as fever and focal lung findings consistent with pneumonia, antibiotics (A) are not indicated and may contribute to antibiotic resistance.

Magnesium sulfate (B) is a bronchodilator used as adjunctive therapy for severe asthma exacerbations that fail to respond to initial treatment with bronchodilators and corticosteroids. This patient just started initial bronchodilator therapy and has not been given corticosteroids or been monitored for improvement yet. She does not yet meet the criteria for magnesium sulfate administration.

Discharging (C) this patient without addressing the acute inflammation and ensuring stabilization would be inappropriate. Patients presenting with moderate to severe exacerbations require systemic corticosteroids and observation for clinical improvement before being discharged. Additionally, follow-up and education on maintenance therapy are crucial to prevent recurrence.

Intubation (E) is reserved for patients with impending respiratory failure, evidenced by severe hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or altered mental status. This patient, while showing signs of a moderate exacerbation, does not exhibit these critical findings. Early intubation without clear need exposes the patient to unnecessary risks, including barotrauma and ventilator-associated complications.

Question: A 14-month-old girl presents to the emergency department with difficulty breathing. Your history and examination suggest moderate viral bronchiolitis, and she is placed on 1 L of supplemental oxygen via a nasal cannula for mild hypoxia as you prepare for hospital admission. Which of the following would be the strongest indicator that this patient is in danger of impending respiratory failure if it happens?

Options.text: She has persistent wheezing after albuterol administration

ExplanationEN:
Viral bronchiolitis is an incredibly common lower respiratory tract infection in children. It is caused by respiratory syncytial virus about half of the time in most studies but can be triggered by any upper respiratory virus. Viral bronchiolitis can occur at any time of the year but is very seasonal, affecting most areas in the United States in the first few months of the year. Children present with cough, nasal congestion, and copious rhinorrhea, and many of them will have some degree of difficulty breathing. Wheezing is common. Fevers are not uncommon but also usually not severe. The difficulty breathing tends to worsen over the first 5 days of illness before improving. At the peak of the illness, the difficulty breathing can vary from one minute to the next, so multiple assessments are recommended during a patient encounter.

Treatment is supportive, with nasal suctioning and oxygen support as needed. Patients should be hospitalized if they have persistent hypoxemia, retractions (intercostal, subcostal, or suprasternal), a respiratory rate > 70 breaths/minute, apnea (more common in infants < 38 weeks gestational age), or are not feeding well enough to maintain hydration. Infants with viral bronchiolitis needing hospitalization are at the highest risk of progressing to respiratory failure within the first 72 hours of symptoms. The strongest indicators that infants with bronchiolitis are progressing to respiratory failure are marked retractions, decreased breath sounds, and poor responsiveness.



Infants with viral bronchiolitis whose respiratory rate slows (A) may either be responding to treatment or progressing to respiratory failure, which can be determined by the infant’s level of alertness, breath sounds, and work of breathing.

Albuterol is not recommended in patients with viral bronchiolitis, but as there is symptom overlap with reactive airway disease, albuterol is sometimes used to differentiate the two. Infants who have persistent wheezing after albuterol administration (C) are simply less likely to have any component of reactive airway disease.

Hypoxia is actually a poor indicator of impending respiratory failure, especially while on supplemental oxygen. Infants who require more oxygen flow (D) are not uncommon, and this would be less likely to indicate respiratory failure than patient alertness, worsening retractions, or decreased breath sounds.

Question: Which of the following is the most common sign seen in patients presenting with a pulmonary embolism?
ExplanationEN:
Tachypnea is the most common sign seen in acute pulmonary embolism (PE). PE is a common, life-threatening disease caused by the occlusion of pulmonary arteries by blood clots. Most of these clots originate in the deep venous system (more commonly in the legs than in the upper body).

Patients can present with various symptoms, including weakness, shortness of breath, malaise, syncope, dizziness, and chest pain. In addition, PE can cause changes to all of the major vital signs. Sinus tachycardia is the most common abnormality found on ECG.



The fever (A) observed in PE is typically low grade and occurs when the PE leads to pulmonary infarction.

Hypoxia (C) and hemoptysis (B) are common in larger PEs but are frequently not seen in smaller ones.

While a swollen calf (D) may indicate a possible PE, it is not the most common finding.

Question: A 44-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents with a productive cough and shortness of breath. His oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Physical examination is significant for bilateral expiratory wheezes. A chest X-ray is obtained and shows chronic emphysematous changes but no acute pulmonary process. He is treated with nebulized albuterol and glycopyrrolate. What is a side effect of glycopyrrolate?
ExplanationEN:
Glycopyrrolate is an anticholinergic used to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Patients with COPD often have acute exacerbations from inhaled irritants (e.g., cigarette smoke) that cause respiratory symptoms that are worse than their baseline, causing them to seek emergency care for treatment. Most patients with acute exacerbations have an underlying viral or bacterial infection. During acute exacerbations, inflammatory mediators are released, and this leads to bronchoconstriction, pulmonary vasoconstriction, and mucus secretion. Patients may present with hypoxemia (arterial oxygen saturation < 90%), which may be accompanied by tachycardia, tachypnea, cyanosis, or mental status change. Management of acute exacerbations of COPD is aimed at correcting oxygenation, reversing bronchospasm, and identifying and treating the underlying cause (e.g., pneumonia). Therapies include oxygen, beta-adrenergic agonists, and anticholinergics. The latter two are given in nebulized form and act as bronchodilators to improve air movement and gas exchange at the alveolar-arterial level. Side effects of beta-agonists include tremors, palpitations, and anxiety. Anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium bromide, glycopyrrolate) are best used with beta-agonists. Side effects are limited to dry mouth and metallic taste. A short course of corticosteroids (e.g., 5–7 days) has been shown to improve lung function, shorten recovery time, and decrease the number of return ED visits. Antibiotics may be given for a change in purulence or frequency of sputum production and in patients with respiratory failure and should cover common pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation or invasive ventilation may be required for hypoxic or hypercapnic respiratory failure.



Anticholinergic medications do not cause bradycardia (A) or pruritus (D) as side effects. Anticholinergics are more likely to cause drying of secretions and decreased bowel motility, so diarrhea (B) is less likely to be a side effect.

Question: A 1-year-old boy presents to the ED with shortness of breath and cough. Vital signs are BP 90/60 mm Hg, HR 110 bpm, RR 40/minute, SpO2 91% on room air, and T 97.5°F (36.4ºC). Physical exam reveals intercostal retractions, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?
ExplanationEN:
Nasal suctioning is the first step in care for a child presenting with bronchiolitis. Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the lower airways most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus. Inflammation of the lower respiratory tracts leads to edema, bronchospasm, and increased mucus production within the bronchioles. The resulting increase in airway resistance leads to respiratory distress and increased work of breathing. Since infants are obligate nasal breathers, and the nasal passages account for 50% of airway resistance, nasal suctioning is essential in helping decrease the work of breathing. In addition to nasal suctioning, supplemental oxygen should be administered for oxygen saturation < 91%.



Nebulized albuterol (A) would be an appropriate treatment option for a child presenting with an asthma exacerbation. In a child < 2 years old with tachypnea, cough, rhinorrhea, crackles, and wheezing, the most likely diagnosis is bronchiolitis. Although wheezing is common in children with bronchiolitis, albuterol has not been shown to improve oxygen saturation, rates of hospitalization, or duration of hospitalization in a child with severe bronchiolitis. The routine use of nebulized albuterol is not recommended in the treatment of bronchiolitis.

Racemic epinephrine (B) in combination with dexamethasone may help decrease inflammation and edema in the lower respiratory tract. This is generally considered the standard therapy for patients present with croup. Symptoms of croup include upper respiratory symptoms with stridor and a barking cough, which are not present in this patient.

Endotracheal intubation (C) would be appropriate after failure of standard therapy with nasal suctioning, supplemental oxygen, and positive pressure ventilation. Noninvasive ventilation with nasal continuous positive airway pressure. bi-level ventilation, and high-flow nasal cannula therapy may help to avoid endotracheal intubation and should be considered prior to endotracheal intubation.

Question: You are caring for a 66-year-old man with a history of lung cancer who presented to the ED with massive hemoptysis. You obtain the chest radiograph seen above. His condition continues to deteriorate, so you decide to perform endotracheal intubation. While you prepare for intubation, what is the best position to place the patient in to optimize gas exchange?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has complete “white-out” of his right lung, which is related to his history of lung cancer. It appears that there is a large pleural effusion on the chest radiograph. In most cases, the "good lung" should be placed "down" (Good to Ground) to improve V/Q mismatch. However, exceptions where the patient should be placed so the "bad lung" is down (in the dependent position) include massive hemoptysis, severe pleural effusions, and large pulmonary abscesses. This position will help to optimize gas exchange in those cases. Therefore, this patient with a significant right pleural effusion should be placed in the right lateral decubitus position so that the white-out lung is in the dependent position, and the good lung is up.



If the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position (A), gravity will cause fluid to enter the left hemithorax and compromise his good lung.

Placing the patient in supine (C) or Trendelenburg (D) position increases the likelihood of aspiration.

Question: A 9-year-old girl with a history of prematurity at 25 weeks gestational age, cerebral palsy, gastrostomy tube dependence, and tracheostomy and ventilator dependence presents to the ED with a fever. Her parents state that for the last 2 days, they have noticed thick, malodorous secretions around her tracheostomy site, and today, they increased her oxygen supplementation. On examination, she is ill-appearing with a delayed capillary refill. Her temperature is 102.2°F (39°C). Her laboratory workup demonstrates leukocytosis with a left shift. Upon chart review, you notice that she has been infected previously with pan-sensitive gram-negative bacilli. Which of the following represents the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms that are concerning for bacterial tracheitis. Given advances in neonatology and critical care, many children with extreme prematurity are able to survive. Chronic respiratory support may be necessary secondary to neurologic and neuromuscular disorders, central hypoventilation syndromes, obstructive apnea, or congenital facial and airway anomalies. Many children are able to be cared for at home with tracheostomies and mechanical ventilation. However, technology-assisted pediatric patients are at higher risk for complications, including tracheitis, pneumonia, and peristomal cellulitis.

Bacterial colonization of the trachea often occurs in children with tracheostomies, so it is important to review any available medical records for prior tracheal cultures, and it is also important to distinguish colonization from true infection. Culture samples from this patient have previously grown gram-negative bacilli that could include Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli, Serratia marcescens, and Haemophilus influenzae species. Pseudomonas is also particularly important to consider in children who are ventilator dependent. This patient is febrile and ill-appearing, and she also has changes in tracheal secretions, leukocytosis, and an increase in oxygen requirements, so she should be admitted and treated empirically for bacterial tracheitis. Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam will cover the most likely etiology of her symptoms, including Pseudomonas.



Admission with ceftriaxone (A) will not provide adequate coverage against Pseudomonas species.

Discharging home with cephalexin (C) or ciprofloxacin (D) is not appropriate for this patient.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the ED with a cough. Vital signs are BP 100/60 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm, RR 30/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and T 100.5°F (38.1°C). Physical exam reveals rhinorrhea, subcostal retractions, and inspiratory stridor. X-ray shows narrowing of the subglottic space. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
ExplanationEN:
Croup is a clinical diagnosis, but radiographs may be ordered to assess for other causes of upper airway obstruction such as foreign body aspiration, retropharyngeal abscess, or epiglottis. Neck radiographs may reveal upper airway edema demonstrated by subglottic narrowing known as the steeple sign.

Racemic epinephrine is the most appropriate initial treatment for children presenting with moderate to severe croup, also known as viral laryngotracheobronchitis. Croup is a viral upper respiratory infection that leads to edema of the subglottic space. Children typically present with a harsh barking cough, rhinorrhea, and stridor. Stridor is a sign of significant airway obstruction and should be treated rapidly. The effects of racemic epinephrine are rapid, seen within 10 minutes of administration, and last up to 1 hour. Racemic epinephrine is effective in decreasing upper airway edema through alpha-1 receptor stimulation, resulting in vasoconstriction.

All patients with croup benefit from a one-time dose of oral steroids, such as dexamethasone, which reduces symptom severity, duration, and return visits. Dexamethasone is effective orally or parenterally, with a recommended dose of 0.6 mg/kg PO. For children who are vomiting, alternatives include nebulized budesonide or IM dexamethasone.



Endotracheal intubation (A) may be necessary in children presenting with severe croup if all other treatment options have failed. A more appropriate therapy in this child would be racemic epinephrine. The effects of racemic epinephrine are rapid and have been shown to decrease the number of children requiring intubation.

Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam (B) would be the treatment for a child with epiglottitis. Children with epiglottis will typically appear toxic with high fevers and will have the classic thumbprint sign on neck radiographs. In a patient with stridor, treatment should be targeted towards rapid improvement of upper airway edema, and antibiotics should not take priority in the immediate resuscitation of these patients.

Nebulized salbutamol (C) is a bronchodilator primarily used to treat bronchospasm in conditions like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Croup, on the other hand, involves inflammation and swelling of the upper airway, specifically the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, typically due to a viral infection. Salbutamol does not address the primary pathology of croup and thus is not effective for this condition.

Question: A 36-year-old man is brought to the ED after being found unresponsive in an alley. Vital signs show a T of 93.4°F (34.1°C), BP of 100/64 mm Hg, HR of 98 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 82% on room air. Physical exam reveals obtundation with ecchymoses over the chest and abdomen and deformities of the right arm and left leg. Chest X-ray shows diffuse, bilateral patchy opacities. He is intubated for hypoxemic respiratory failure and airway protection. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his respiratory status?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has profound hypoxemia with diffuse, bilateral patchy opacities on chest X-ray after an apparent unwitnessed traumatic event, given that he has objective findings of significant trauma (e.g., bony deformities, ecchymosis on trunk). This combination should trigger concern for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) from trauma-associated lung injury, likely related to multiple fractures (especially long bone and pelvic fractures) and associated systemic inflammation. Even when the patient cannot provide a history, the physical exam strongly supports significant trauma, and trauma is a well-established ARDS risk factor. Other traumatic conditions associated with ARDS include pulmonary contusion (most common), burns, and head trauma, though the latter are rarer. Common nontraumatic causes include sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, and pancreatitis.

ARDS is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, which increases alveolar-capillary permeability, leads to protein-rich pulmonary edema, reduces lung compliance, causes V/Q mismatch, and results in hypoxemia. The Berlin definition requires acute onset (within 1 week of a clinical insult), bilateral opacities on imaging not fully explained by effusions or lobar collapse, and respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, with hypoxemia quantified by the PO2/FiO2 ratio. Trauma can precipitate ARDS through systemic cytokine release and endothelial injury, and it can present early with severe hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates, as seen here.

In the ED, management is primarily supportive while treating contributory injury patterns. Key steps include lung-protective ventilation with a low tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, limiting plateau pressure to < 30 cm H2O, titrating positive end-expiratory pressure and FiO2 to maintain adequate oxygenation, and avoiding iatrogenic over-resuscitation when feasible. Adjuncts for moderate to severe ARDS include prone positioning and consideration of neuromuscular blockade in select patients with ventilator dyssynchrony. However, these measures are unlikely to occur in the ED and are more within the purview of critical care medicine. Complications include ventilator-associated pneumonia, barotrauma, right ventricular strain, and long-term functional impairment.



Diffuse axonal injury (A) can explain obtundation after trauma, but it does not directly cause diffuse bilateral opacities and severe hypoxemia. The chest X-ray and SpO2 of 82% point to primary lung pathology such as ARDS rather than isolated traumatic brain injury.

Fat embolism syndrome (B) is associated with long bone fractures and can cause ARDS-like hypoxemia, but it classically develops 24–72 hours after injury and often includes petechiae and disproportionate neurologic changes. This patient’s presentation is immediately severe on ED arrival, with no described petechial rash, making fat embolism less likely than trauma-associated ARDS from the overall injury burden.

Hemorrhagic shock (C) would be expected to cause more pronounced hypotension and signs of poor perfusion, and while severe shock can contribute to lung injury indirectly, this patient’s BP is 100/64 mm Hg with HR 98 bpm, which is not strongly supportive of shock as the primary driver of respiratory failure. Diffuse bilateral opacities and profound hypoxemia in this context fit better with trauma-associated ARDS than with hemorrhagic shock alone.

Pancreatitis (E) is associated with ARDS, but there is nothing in this scenario to suggest that this patient has this condition, such as vomiting or abdominal pain. The clear evidence of severe trauma on exam suggests trauma-related ARDS as the cause.

Question: A 47-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with fever, dysphagia, and voice changes. He reports progressive neck swelling and trismus for the past 2 days. On examination, he appears ill, with a T of 39.2°C (102.6°F), HR of 112 bpm, BP of 132/86 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 95% on room air. He has a firm, tender swelling in the submandibular region bilaterally with elevation of the tongue and drooling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s current condition?

Options.text: Bedside incision and drainage of the submandibular space
Needle aspiration of the submandibular space

ExplanationEN:
Ludwig angina is a life-threatening cellulitis of the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. It most commonly originates from odontogenic infections, particularly of the second or third mandibular molars, and spreads through fascial planes. It causes progressive soft tissue swelling, tongue elevation, and potential airway compromise. Patients frequently present with fever, trismus, dysphagia, odynophagia, and voice changes. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, and recent dental procedures.

In the emergency department, the primary concern is control of the patient’s airway. Ludwig angina can rapidly progress to airway obstruction due to soft tissue edema and tongue displacement. Thus, when appropriate, evaluating and securing the airway is the most important immediate step. Fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation is often preferred to visualize the distorted anatomy, and it should be performed by the most experienced clinician available. Concomitantly, empiric IV antibiotics should be initiated immediately to target the typical polymicrobial flora, including Streptococcus species, anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Ampicillin-sulbactam is a first-line option, with clindamycin or metronidazole-based regimens reserved for those with penicillin allergy.

Although imaging and surgical consultation are part of the overall management, airway stabilization and empiric antibiotics must come first when clinical signs indicate impending obstruction. Delaying intervention for diagnostic imaging can be fatal. An otolaryngology consultation should be obtained for potential operative management, based on the clinical and imaging findings, once the airway is secured. For patients early in the disease course without evidence of airway compromise, immediate airway intervention may not be indicated, and further diagnostic evaluation may be pursued. However, this patient has clear evidence of airway obstruction, as he is reporting dysphagia and voice changes and has drooling.



Ludwig angina typically involves cellulitis without a localized abscess, making incision and drainage at the bedside (A) ineffective and potentially hazardous. Attempting drainage in a patient with distorted anatomy and no secured airway can worsen edema and lead to rapid airway collapse.

While CT imaging (B) is useful for evaluating the extent of deep neck space infections, it should not precede airway management in patients with clinical signs of airway compromise. This patient’s presentation with trismus, drooling, and tongue elevation signals impending obstruction, making airway protection the immediate priority.

Corticosteroids may be used as adjunct therapy with antibiotics (C) to reduce edema, but this regimen does not adequately address the threat of airway obstruction. Furthermore, ceftriaxone alone does not provide adequate coverage against polymicrobial pathogens. Anaerobic coverage (e.g., metronidazole) should be added to ceftriaxone.

Needle aspiration (E) is unlikely to be helpful in Ludwig angina, which is a diffuse cellulitis. It neither relieves airway obstruction nor supplants antibiotics or definitive airway protection.

Question: A 42-year-old woman with no previous medical history presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. She was shopping when she developed exertional dyspnea and had one episode of hemoptysis. She reports a mild dry cough over 1 week but reports no fever, congestion, or chest pain. She used to smoke tobacco but now uses vaping devices instead. She occasionally smokes marijuana, and she last used cocaine 1 year ago. Vital signs show HR 143 bpm, BP 162/88 mm Hg, RR 32/min, T 37.8°C, and SpO2 85% on room air. She is speaking short sentences, and lung auscultation reveals fine crackles bilaterally. Her examination is unremarkable otherwise. What will this patient’s chest radiograph most likely show based on her story and background?

Options.text: Pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions

ExplanationEN:
It is important to recognize in this patient’s social history that she uses vaping devices and occasionally smokes marijuana. More than 2,000 cases of e-cigarette and vaping product use associated lung injury (EVALI) were reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 2019. Vaping-associated lung injury is becoming more prominent and needs to be recognized by the emergency physician. The precise pathogenesis is not yet known, but it appears that EVALI is associated with the inhalation of unlicensed vaping products such as tetrahydrocannabinol, cannabinoid oils, and other substances and additives. Lung injury associated with vaping reflects a spectrum of disease processes, including fibrinous pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, and eosinophilic or lipoid pneumonia. The majority of patients present with shortness of breath, cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Some patients may present with a relatively benign-looking illness, while many others present as acutely ill with signs of acute respiratory distress syndrome and hypoxemia. Most patients presenting with EVALI have chest radiograph findings of diffuse bilateral hazy opacities. A formal diagnosis of EVALI can be difficult to make, particularly in the emergency department. Current criteria include the use of e-cigarette or vaping-related products, lung opacities on chest radiographs, exclusion of other lung infections such as influenza and bacterial pneumonia, and absence of an alternative diagnosis such as a neoplastic cause. Treatment in the emergency department includes empiric antibiotic coverage for potential bacterial pneumonia. Systemic glucocorticoids have typically been added in patients with EVALI, but the efficacy of the treatment has not been formally studied. The mainstay of treatment at this time is supportive care, which often requires oxygen supplementation with or without mechanical ventilation.



Atelectasis (A) is defined as lobar collapse, and it is generally considered a nonspecific chest radiograph finding. It usually does not cause significant symptoms unless associated with other findings. It is often found in patients with underlying asthma. Pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions (C) is found in patients presenting with acute decompensated congestive heart failure. This patient’s presentation and history are not consistent with congestive heart failure. Right lower lobar consolidation (D) is typical in a patient presenting with pneumonia, particularly aspiration pneumonia. Although this patient could be presenting with signs and symptoms of pneumonia, the clinician should pay attention to her history of vaping and marijuana use, which are suggestive of e-cigarette and vaping product use associated lung injury.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with chest pain that is worsened with deep breaths. She has no significant medical history and is currently taking oral contraceptive pills. She recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 127/68 mm Hg, heart rate is 115 bpm, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. An initial ECG is notable for sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation. Physical exam is notable for tachypnea and a rapid and regular heart rate. A chest radiograph reveals localized oligemia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Pulmonary embolism occurs when a clot, typically from the deep veins, dislodges and travels to the pulmonary vasculature, impairing perfusion to a portion of the lung. Risk factors include hypercoagulable state (such as hereditary clotting disorders or malignancy), stasis (common after surgery), and medications (such as oral contraceptive pills). Presenting findings can include pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and hypoxia. ECG can demonstrate sinus tachycardia (the most common finding) or the S1Q3T3 finding (which is less common but more specific). Imaging can include a chest radiograph and CT angiography. Chest radiography is insensitive. However, specific findings include a Hampton hump and the Westermark sign. A Hampton hump is a wedge-shaped infarct that can be seen on chest radiograph secondary to occlusion of the perfusing vessel and subsequent ischemia and injury to the region of the lung supplied. The Westermark sign (seen in this case) is when there is proximal engorgement of vessels (behind the clot) and distal loss of vascular markings (after the clot). A CT angiogram is a more sensitive and specific test that will demonstrate a clot in the pulmonary vasculature. The treatment of a pulmonary embolism includes anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin as an appropriate initial measure. Thrombolytics and surgical thrombectomy are reserved for massive pulmonary embolism in patients with hemodynamic instability.



Angina (A) presents with chest pain that is exertional and may be described as pressure or squeezing pain. It is typically seen in older patients with risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, and diabetes. A chest radiograph would be normal, and ECG and troponins would likely be normal as well.

Costochondritis (B) presents with chest pain that may be pleuritic and worsened with palpation and is associated with pain along the costochondral joints.

Pericarditis (C) presents with positional chest pain and is often associated with ECG changes such as diffuse ST elevations and PR depressions, which are not seen on this patient's ECG.

Pleurisy (D) is irritation of the pleural lining of the lung and is common after a pulmonary infection secondary to inflammation and irritation from coughing. This diagnosis would be more likely were it not for the radiological findings suggestive of a pulmonary embolism.

Question: A 29-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 weeks of fatigue and shortness of breath. He says he has spent the last 2 days in bed, unable to leave the house due to his symptoms. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. He reports numerous sexual partners in the past year and does not use barrier contraception. He has no medication allergies. Vital signs show a T of 98.0°F (36.7°C), BP of 114/70 mm Hg, HR of 96 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 88% on room air. An arterial blood gas reveals a PaO2 of 65 mm Hg, and other serum laboratory results are significant for a CD4 count of 185/µL, lactate dehydrogenase of 430 U/L, and creatinine of 0.7 mg/dL. His chest radiograph is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s clinical history, laboratory results, and imaging findings are highly indicative of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), which is the most common opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS and affects approximately 70% of patients with HIV at some point in the course of their illness. P. jirovecii was previously classified as a protozoa, but it has since been reclassified as a fungus and typically causes infection in patients with a CD4 count < 200/µL. In patients without AIDS, risk factors include cancer, solid organ transplantation, hematopoeitic stem cell transplantation, rheumatologic disease, and primary immunodeficiencies. Many of these patients are on chronic glucocorticoid therapy or have hereditary or acquired defects in cell-mediated immunity. Other risk factors include previous PJP infection, oral thrush, bacterial pneumonia, unintentional weight loss, and higher HIV viral load.

The most common symptoms of PJP are fever, nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and significant fatigue, and these are present in > 80% of patients. Symptoms typically develop insidiously and are first present on exertion, but they progress to manifesting at rest as well. While this patient’s hypoxemia is present at rest, exertional hypoxemia is a common finding and can quickly be demonstrated in the ED via ambulatory pulse oximetry.

This patient’s X-ray is characteristic of PJP, showing diffuse, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, though up to 25% of patients with PJP will initially have a normal chest radiograph. Laboratory findings may include low PO2 and elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels, though the latter has fairly low sensitivity and specificity. Definitive diagnosis usually includes inpatient bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain specimens for analysis, but a presumptive diagnosis can be made in the ED in the appropriate clinical scenario without other explanations for hypoxemia.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (15–20 mg/kg/day orally in three or four divided doses for a total of 21 days) is the first-line therapy. Intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indicated for patients with severe disease (defined as an alveolar-arterial [A-a] oxygen gradient ≥ 45 mm Hg, PaO2 < 60 mm Hg) or increased work of breathing with potential for respiratory failure. Patients can be transitioned to oral therapy after improvement in clinical status. For patients with allergies or other contraindications to sulfa, alternative agents include trimethoprim-dapsone, clindamycin-primaquine, atovaquone, and pentamidine.

Systemic corticosteroids are indicated for patients with a PO2 < 70 mm Hg or an A-a oxygen gradient ≥ 35 mm Hg. A typical regimen is oral prednisone (40 mg twice daily) tapering over 21 days. If a patient has resting hypoxia (SpO2 < 92% on room air), an arterial blood gas is not necessarily needed to determine the need for corticosteroid therapy. Intravenous methylprednisolone can be used at 75% of the oral prednisone dose if intravenous therapy is necessary.

Patients diagnosed with HIV should be started or continued on antiretroviral therapy, though this should be done in consultation with an infectious disease specialist. Nearly 70% of patients will experience re-infection within 18 months, so all patients with a CD4 count < 200/µL should be started on prophylaxis with one tablet of double-strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily or atovaquone as an alternate prophylactic agent.



Intravenous clindamycin and methylprednisolone (A) may be warranted in cases of severe disease. Indications for intravenous antibiotic therapy include an A-a oxygen gradient ≥ 45 mm Hg, PO2 < 60 mm Hg, or increased work of breathing with the potential for respiratory failure. Indications for corticosteroid therapy are a PO2 < 70 mm Hg or an A-a oxygen gradient ≥ 35 mm Hg. For this patient with a PO2 of 65 mm Hg and no signs of respiratory distress, intravenous antibiotics are not indicated, and clindamycin alone is not a recommended treatment regimen.

Intravenous clindamycin and oral primaquine (B) is an acceptable treatment regimen. However, as discussed above, intravenous medications are reserved for patients with severe disease. Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for patients without severe disease and without allergies precluding its use.

Intravenous pentamidine (C) is a parenteral agent available for patients with contraindications to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or those who cannot tolerate oral agents, but there is nothing in this case to suggest that first-line therapy should not be used.

Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) should be used for this patient, but patients with a PO2 < 70 mm Hg should also receive systemic glucocorticoid therapy with prednisone.

Question: What is the primary mechanism of action of the best medication to use in a 36-year-old man with a history of moderate persistent asthma who presents with respiratory failure despite treatment with inhaled albuterol and ipratropium, systemic corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate, and BPAP?

Options.text: Binds to GABA-A receptors to enhance inhibitory neurotransmission
Blocks histamine H1 receptors centrally and peripherally
Stimulates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem

ExplanationEN:
Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for patients with severe asthma who require endotracheal intubation. Its bronchodilatory properties make it particularly advantageous in this setting. Ketamine primarily antagonizes NMDA receptors in the central nervous system, leading to dissociative anesthesia and analgesia. This mechanism also contributes to increased sympathetic tone, which can help support blood pressure in critically ill patients. The typical induction dose is 1–2 mg/kg IV. In addition to its favorable hemodynamic profile, ketamine is unique among induction agents for its ability to cause smooth muscle relaxation in the lower airways, reducing airway resistance and improving ventilation.

In patients with asthma, especially those with life-threatening bronchospasm, ketamine has been shown to reduce airway resistance and enhance oxygenation. Its bronchodilatory effects are thought to stem not only from direct smooth muscle relaxation but also from suppression of airway reflexes and reduction of vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. These characteristics make ketamine an ideal induction agent for patients with reactive airway disease who are at risk of worsening bronchospasm during intubation. Furthermore, ketamine preserves respiratory drive at lower doses and does not significantly depress ventilation compared with other agents, which may be beneficial in patients with marginal respiratory reserve.

While ketamine does have some limitations, including the potential to increase secretions, which may necessitate coadministration of an anticholinergic such as atropine or glycopyrrolate, it remains the agent of choice for induction in patients with asthma. Caution should be exercised in patients with known coronary artery disease or those at risk of increased intracranial pressure, although recent evidence has challenged the clinical significance of these concerns. In hemodynamically unstable patients with reactive airway disease, ketamine provides both cardiovascular support and respiratory benefit.



Etomidate binds to GABA-A receptors to enhance inhibitory neurotransmission (A). While etomidate is commonly used for its hemodynamic stability and is appropriate in many critically ill patients, it does not provide bronchodilation and may worsen bronchospasm in patients with reactive airway disease.

Antihistamines like diphenhydramine block histamine H1 receptors centrally and peripherally (B). These agents may be helpful for allergic reactions or sedation but are not appropriate for induction in airway management. They do not provide the depth of anesthesia or bronchodilatory effects needed for intubating a patient with status asthmaticus.

Dexmedetomidine stimulates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem (D). While dexmedetomidine provides sedation and has some sympatholytic effects, it is not suitable for induction in the emergency airway setting due to its slower onset and potential for bradycardia and hypotension. It does not offer bronchodilation or sufficient anesthesia for rapid sequence intubation.

Question: A 51-year-old man presents to the ED with retrosternal chest pain beginning this morning when he woke up after a night of heavy drinking. Vital signs are a T of 37.0°C (98.6°F), BP of 128/76 mm Hg, HR of 104 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. On physical examination, he is in mild distress due to pain, and the lungs are clear to auscultation. A chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following, if present, most likely contributed to this patient’s current condition?
ExplanationEN:
Esophageal perforation, particularly in the context of forceful vomiting, is the most concerning cause of pneumomediastinum in this clinical scenario. This condition, also known as Boerhaave syndrome, results from a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed cricopharyngeus muscle, leading to full-thickness esophageal rupture. The leaked air and gastric contents can enter the mediastinum, causing retrosternal chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and systemic signs if mediastinitis develops. While not noted in this case, the presence of crepitus over the suprasternal notch is highly suggestive of subcutaneous air tracking from the mediastinum. Hamman sign refers to a “crunching” sound heard during auscultation that is considered pathognomonic for pneumomediastinum.

Pneumomediastinum can be spontaneous or secondary to trauma, esophageal rupture, pulmonary conditions, or iatrogenic injury (e.g., endoscopy). Among young adults, spontaneous pneumomediastinum is often associated with barotrauma from activities such as vomiting, coughing, or illicit drug inhalation. Esophageal perforation necessitates rapid identification due to the risk of septic shock and death. Diagnostic evaluation includes upright chest radiography, which may show mediastinal air, and confirmation with chest CT or water-soluble contrast esophagography.

Management of esophageal perforation includes restricting oral intake, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics, and obtaining urgent surgical consultation. Vancomycin and pipericillin-tazobactam is a commonly recommended regimen, while antifungal coverage (e.g., fluconazole) should be considered in patients with risk factors for fungal colonization. In contrast, spontaneous pneumomediastinum without esophageal perforation may be treated conservatively, whereas esophageal perforation requires aggressive intervention due to the risk of mediastinitis and sepsis.



Aspiration of gastric contents (A) can cause chemical pneumonitis or aspiration pneumonia, leading to hypoxia, wheezing, or rales, but it does not result in pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema.

While intravenous drug use (C) is associated with numerous cardiopulmonary complications, including septic emboli and endocarditis, it does not cause pneumomediastinum. This patient’s acute presentation after a night of drinking that may have involved vomiting, combined with the chest X-ray, strongly suggests a gastrointestinal origin rather than hematogenous spread of infection.

A recent upper respiratory infection (D) might lead to acute pericarditis or pneumonia, neither of which is depicted in this patient’s evaluation. Pericarditis typically presents with pleuritic chest pain that improves with sitting forward and may show diffuse ST segment elevations on ECG. It does not cause pneumomediastinum. This patient’s chest X-ray also does not show pneumonia.

Question: In which of the following scenarios is it most appropriate to apply the pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria to exclude the disease in a patient?

Options.text: High pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on clinician gestalt
High pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on Wells criteria
Low pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on clinician gestalt
Low pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on Geneva criteria
Moderate pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on Wells criteria

CorrectAnswer: Low pretest probability of pulmonary embolism based on clinician gestalt
ExplanationEN:
The diagnostic evaluation for pulmonary embolism (PE) begins with the clinician’s determination of whether objective testing is indicated. If clinical suspicion for PE is high enough to warrant evaluation, the next step is the estimation of the patient’s pretest probability of PE. The three well-validated methods of achieving this are the application of clinician gestalt, the Wells score, and the revised Geneva score. While the latter two provide a more explicit quantitative assessment of pretest probability than gestalt alone, clinician gestalt has been shown to be the most effective assessment of pretest probability. However, none of these three methods reliably identify patients at very low risk whose pretest probability of PE is below the test threshold of 2%, which is below the risk of harm from diagnostic testing for PE that outweighs the benefit of potential testing.

The PE rule-out criteria (PERC) are a set of eight criteria that, when completely satisfied and applied properly, identify patients who have a very low risk for PE with a pretest probability < 2%. The criteria are age < 50 years, HR < 100 bpm, SpO2 > 95%, and the absence of unilateral leg swelling, hemoptysis, recent trauma or surgery, prior deep vein thrombosis or PE, and systemic hormone use. However, these criteria should only be applied to patients in whom the pretest probability is low, as determined by clinician gestalt. There is some overlap between the PERC and the Wells and Geneva scores, and estimation of pretest probability for application of the PERC has only been validated when done with clinician gestalt rather than the other scoring metrics.



A patient determined to have a high pretest probability of PE (A, B), regardless of the method used for estimation, is not appropriate for the application of the PERC.

For application of the PERC, pretest probability should be estimated using clinician gestalt as the most effective method, so using the Geneva criteria (D) would not be the best option.

Using the Wells score (E) can be done before applying the PERC criteria. However, this also is not the most effective assessment of pretest probability, and use of the PERC should commence if a patient has low pretest probability for PE based on the Wells criteria, not moderate pretest probability.

Question: A 12-month-old boy presents to the emergency department accompanied by his parents with 3 days of cough and congestion. His older sibling has a history of asthma and was recently sick with similar symptoms. Upon waking today, his parents noticed the patient had tachypnea and prominence of his clavicles and rib outlines with breathing. His parents tried the patient’s sibling’s inhaler without relief. On exam, he has scattered rales and wheezing bilaterally. His SpO2 is 91% on room air. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Administer an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist

ExplanationEN:
Bronchiolitis is a common diagnosis in pediatric patients, particularly those who are < 2 years old or who have a history of prematurity, chronic lung disease (e.g., reactive airway disease, asthma, bronchopulmonary dysplasia), or congenital heart disease. The disease is associated with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, which peaks in the winter months. Bronchiole inflammation, necrosis, and sloughing may lead to debris accumulation in smaller conducting airways and subsequent obstructive lung disease. Manifestations include prodromal upper respiratory symptoms (e.g., cough, congestion, fever), variable increased respiratory effort (e.g., retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing), variable adventitious breath sounds (e.g., rales, wheezing), hypoxia, cyanosis, and even respiratory failure when severe. The diagnosis is clinical, though viral testing may aid in confirming the diagnosis. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment and includes as-needed suctioning and supplemental oxygen, including high-flow nasal cannula. Adjuvants such as bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol) and nebulized racemic epinephrine are not routinely recommended.



In bronchiolitis, the evidence does not support the routine practice of administering an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist (A). In patients with underlying reactive airway disease or asthma, a short-acting beta-2 agonist (e.g., albuterol) can be considered if a component of wheezing is thought to be secondary to the patient’s underlying native lung disease. In patients with a diagnosis of moderate to severe croup, it is reasonable to administer nebulized racemic epinephrine (B), but evidence of benefit in bronchiolitis has not been demonstrated. If a superimposed bacterial infection or other cardiopulmonary process is suspected, it is reasonable to obtain a chest X-ray (D), though the diagnosis of bronchiolitis can otherwise be made clinically.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the ED for a wrist injury after slipping on ice. During her evaluation, the patient is found to have a distal radius fracture that requires reduction. The reduction is performed under moderate sedation without any initial complications. While the patient is recovering, she starts vomiting and coughing, requiring oxygen supplementation due to becoming hypoxic, with an oxygen saturation of 87%. Chest X-ray reveals an infiltrate located in the posterior right upper lobe. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with aspiration pneumonitis, an inflammatory chemical injury to the lungs caused by inhalation of sterile gastric contents. It commonly occurs in the setting of altered mental status or sedation, or during procedures where airway protection is compromised, such as with procedural sedation in this case. Aspiration pneumonitis typically develops within hours, presenting with sudden hypoxia, coughing, and possible fever. The posterior segment of the right upper lobe is a common location for aspiration during recumbency.

The key distinction is that aspiration pneumonitis is an inflammatory process, not an infection. Therefore, antibiotics are not indicated initially unless the clinical picture evolves or signs of infection (e.g., fever, leukocytosis, purulent sputum, worsening infiltrates) develop after 48–72 hours.

Management in the ED should focus on supportive care, including oxygen therapy, monitoring, and potentially airway protection if respiratory status worsens. Most patients recover with conservative management.



Ampicillin-sulbactam and intubation (A) may be warranted in patients with aspiration pneumonia and significant respiratory compromise or those who do not benefit from conservative treatment. However, this patient’s presentation is more consistent with early aspiration pneumonitis, in which inflammation, not infection, is the primary issue. Intubation is not indicated unless the patient’s mental status or respiratory effort worsens significantly, and empiric antibiotics at this stage are premature. Additionally, ampicillin-sulbactam is not recommended as a first-line treatment of aspiration pneumonia unless abscess or empyema are present.

A combination of ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (B) is standard therapy for community-acquired pneumonia and for aspiration pneumonia without abscess or empyema and is unnecessary for aspiration pneumonitis without superimposed infection. Using antibiotics in the absence of infection increases the risk of resistance and other complications.

A regimen of ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (C) targets aerobic and anaerobic bacteria and would be appropriate for aspiration pneumonia with lung abscess or empyema, particularly in patients with risk factors like poor dentition or alcohol use disorder. However, this patient has no signs of infection and no foul-smelling sputum, and the timing suggests a chemical pneumonitis, making antibiotics unnecessary at this stage.

Clindamycin (D) was historically used for aspiration pneumonia due to its anaerobic coverage, but resistance and Clostridioides difficile concerns have limited its use. More importantly, it is not indicated in aspiration pneumonitis, when the pathophysiology is sterile chemical injury. Starting clindamycin would be overtreatment without supporting evidence of infection.

Question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the ED for severe chest pain that began 1 day after an outpatient endoscopy. She has crepitus on examination of her chest wall. Which of the following is the most likely complication of her condition?
ExplanationEN:
Esophageal perforation can occur iatrogenically from procedures such as esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), esophageal dilation, variceal management, or operative procedures. It can also occur from forceful vomiting (Boerhaave syndrome), trauma, foreign body ingestion, malignancy, aortic disease, or erosive esophagitis. Esophageal rupture from any cause can lead to fulminant, necrotizing mediastinitis due to leakage of esophageal contents into the mediastinal space. Contents can also leak into the pleural and peritoneal space, leading to pneumonitis or peritonitis, respectively. Patients may present in shock with hemodynamic instability and multisystem organ failure. The left posterolateral distal esophagus is the most common location for spontaneous perforations. Instrumentation-induced perforations are mostly proximal.

Patients may present with chest pain, back pain, dysphagia or odynophagia, emesis, or hematemesis. Mediastinal emphysema may develop after a period of time in about 30% of patients and is palpated on examination of the chest wall. Its absence does not rule out perforation. Auscultation of mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign) may be present. CT or esophagram with water-soluble contrast can detect perforations, and timely diagnosis is key to prevent delay in definitive management, which is emergent surgical repair. Stabilizing the patient and managing sepsis or septic shock with IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics is critical in the acute setting.



Aspiration pneumonia (A) is not a commonly observed or expected complication of iatrogenic esophageal perforation.

Cardiac tamponade (B)should not result from esophageal perforation or rupture. If the pericardium is penetrated somehow during esophageal instrumentation, this would create an opening for any pericardial fluid, thus preventing a rapidly developing pericardial effusion from developing. The classic Beck triad of cardiac tamponade is muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension, and hypotension.

Tension pneumothorax (D) is a type of obstructive shock caused by lung parenchymal injury that leads to air entering the space between the visceral pleura and the chest wall that is not able to escape. This can result in hypotension, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, and cardiopulmonary failure.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents with a sore throat and difficulty swallowing. He has had 4 days of worsening sore throat and fever, but today, he was unable to swallow any liquids. Physical examination reveals a muffled voice, difficulty tolerating saliva, and minimal pharyngeal erythema with a midline uvula. There is no neck stiffness, but he has tenderness over the hyoid bone. Which of the following is the best management?

Options.text: Airway management, intravenous antibiotics, and admission
Inhaled racemic epinephrine and discharge home
Otolaryngology consultation for CT-guided surgical drainage

CorrectAnswer: Airway management, intravenous antibiotics, and admission
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with symptoms and signs concerning for epiglottitis. He should be started on antibiotics and admitted for further monitoring. Epiglottitis is a localized cellulitis of the supraglottic structures, including the aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, lingual tonsils, epiglottis, and base of the tongue. It may be caused by viral or bacterial agents (Haemophilus influenzae type b is the most common). Although incidence in pediatric populations has decreased with the H. influenzae vaccine, it is becoming more common in adults and can lead to rapid airway obstruction.

Patients usually present with dysphagia, odynophagia, and sore throat. Pain may be severe in relation to physical exam findings. Additionally, patients frequently have a muffled voice. Fever is present in half of cases. Physical examination typically reveals mild inflammation in the oropharynx and may reveal tenderness to the neck over the hyoid bone.

Epiglottitis is a clinical diagnosis but may be aided by plain radiographs of the neck, which show edema of the epiglottis (thumb sign). An epiglottic width > 8 mm or an aryepiglottic fold > 7 mm suggests epiglottitis. A definitive diagnosis can be made with indirect laryngoscopy. Treatment focuses on protecting the airway when necessary, starting intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and ampicillin-sulbactam are first-line), and admitting for monitoring. Supportive care with hydration is important as well.



Inhaled racemic epinephrine (B) is a measure that should be instituted for pediatric patients with cough and stridor due to croup, which is not present in this patient. Patients who improve after inhaled epinephrine should be monitored, as a rebound phenomenon has been described.

Intravenous corticosteroids (C) have not been shown to be efficacious for epiglottitis.

Needle aspiration of the peritonsillar area (D) is the treatment of choice in peritonsillar abscess. A patient with a peritonsillar abscess would have an asymmetrically enlarged tonsil and uvula deviation.

CT-guided surgical drainage (E) is appropriate in severe retropharyngeal abscesses (RPA). Patients with an RPA often have neck stiffness. Initial management may be similar to that of epiglottitis (i.e., hospital admission, intravenous antibiotics, and admission).

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the ED with a persistent cough. Last week he had a low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and fatigue, which has now developed into repeated episodes of coughing. The coughing is so forceful and persistent that he has trouble catching his breath and has even vomited. Given his likely diagnosis, during which stage of the disease is infectivity the highest?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s presentation is concerning for pertussis, a respiratory infection caused by the gram-negative coccobacilli Bordetella pertussis. Although it has long been an infection affecting primarily infants and children, since the introduction of the pertussis vaccine, more than half of the cases of pertussis involve adolescents and adults. There are three phases of pertussis that occur in sequence. Following an incubation period of ≥ 7–10 days, the catarrhal phase begins with nonspecific symptoms of malaise, low-grade fever, conjunctival injection, and rhinorrhea. Infectivity is highest during this stage which lasts 1–2 weeks. During the paroxysmal phase, which can last 2–8 weeks, the fever subsides and patients develop the characteristic repeated staccato cough followed by a forceful inhalation, which produces the classic whoop. Paroxysms are more common at night and post-tussive vomiting may occur.

The convalescent phase, which can last for weeks, consists of a residual cough. Diagnosis is made via nasopharyngeal culture and polymerase chain reaction. Antibiotic therapy decreases infectivity and carriage rates but has not been shown to significantly reduce the duration or severity of illness. The antibiotic of choice is erythromycin or azithromycin.



The convalescent phase (B) may last weeks. Recurrent paroxysms of cough may be triggered by an unrelated respiratory infection. The cough during this period is typically not as severe or frequent as during the paroxysmal phase, and infectivity is low during this period.

The incubation period (C) of B. pertussis can last weeks, which is considerably longer than the incubation periods of most common infections. Patients are not generally spreading infection during this time.

The paroxysmal phase (D) often lasts the longest. Although the symptoms during this phase are the most dramatic, infectivity rates during this phase are lower than during the catarrhal phase.

Question: A 20-year-old man presents with sharp, sudden chest pain while playing football. States it happened when running and denies being hit prior to the onset. A spontaneous pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space causing lung collapse. It is associated with smoking, asthma, cystic fibrosis, a tall, thin body habitus, and connective tissue disease. Patients may present with pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, and reduced unilateral breath sounds, though breath sounds should not be relied upon to make the diagnosis. The diagnosis can be made with a chest radiograph or chest CT for improved sensitivity. The management of a spontaneous pneumothorax is dependent on several factors. Small (< 20% lung volume) asymptomatic pneumothoraces can be managed with observation, 100% supplemental oxygen to increase the rate of resolution, and a repeat chest radiograph in 24 hours. Large (> 2–3 cm), symptomatic, or bilateral pneumothoraces require drainage with a chest tube.



Placement of a 28 French chest tube (B) or pigtail catheter (C) would be appropriate for a larger or symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax. Reassurance and observation (D) is not optimal management of a small asymptomatic pneumothorax. Rather, placing the patient on oxygen and monitoring for a reduction in the size of the pneumothorax is preferred.

Question: Which of the following represents an absolute contraindication to the use of systemic thrombolytic therapy in patients with acute massive pulmonary embolism?

Options.text: History of ischemic stroke 1 year ago

ExplanationEN:
Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is classified as high-risk or massive based on the presence of hemodynamic instability (including cardiac arrest) that persists despite initial fluid resuscitation. The term “massive” refers to the hemodynamic consequences rather than the size of the clot, though radiologists’ use of the term may differ. As with lower-risk PEs, the majority arise from deep vein thrombi in the lower extremities or pelvis due to a combination of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury. The hemodynamic consequences of massive PEs result from increased pulmonary vascular resistance due to vascular occlusion, which increases right ventricular afterload, left ventricular preload, and cardiac output.

The mainstay of treatment in PE is prompt initiation of anticoagulation, typically with unfractionated heparin, along with respiratory and hemodynamic supportive care (e.g., supplemental oxygen, fluids, vasopressors). However, patients with massive PE will often require additional intervention due to a high risk of clinical deterioration. Reperfusion therapy, either systemic or catheter-based, is indicated in these patients, with systemic thrombolysis (e.g., alteplase, tenecteplase) preferred in patients without contraindications. However, there are numerous absolute and relative contraindications that may necessitate other procedural treatments when the bleeding risk of systemic therapy outweighs the potential benefit.

Absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis include known intracranial lesions (malignant, vascular abnormality), suspected aortic dissection, prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding (excluding menstrual bleeding) or bleeding diathesis, ischemic stroke within 3 months prior, and significant head or facial trauma within the past 3 months. Relative contraindications include ischemic stroke > 3 months prior, history of severe uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy, age > 75 years, and active peptic ulcer disease. Notably, a patient’s use of aspirin and dual antiplatelet therapy is not a contraindication to using systemic thrombolysis, though they do increase the risk of bleeding.



While bleeding diathesis is an absolute contraindication, normal menstrual bleeding (A) alone does not preclude thrombolysis if the clinical benefit outweighs the risk.

Ischemic stroke 1 year ago (B) is a relative contraindication, not an absolute contraindication, to systemic thrombolysis. According to the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines, ischemic stroke within 3 months is an absolute contraindication, but a history of ischemic stroke > 3 months prior (such as 1 year) is considered only a relative contraindication.

Uncontrolled hypertension (C), whether acute or chronic, represents a relative contraindication rather than an absolute one. Thus, systemic thrombolysis may still be given if the perceived benefit outweighs the risk.

Pregnancy (D) is a relative contraindication, not an absolute contraindication to thrombolytic therapy. Current guidelines support the use of thrombolysis in pregnancy for life-threatening conditions like massive PE when anticipated benefits outweigh risks, as thrombolytic agents do not cross the placenta.

Question: A 74-year-old woman presents to the ED with progressive dyspnea. Her chest radiograph is shown above. Fluid analysis shows protein of 9 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase of 280 U/L, and glucose of 42 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has evidence of a pleural effusion. A pleural effusion is defined as a collection of fluid within the pleural space. The Light criteria are used to differentiate between transudative and exudative effusions. A single positive criterion is enough to classify an effusion as an exudative effusion. Transudative effusions have a pleural to serum protein ratio < 0.5 and a pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio < 0.6. Additionally, the pleural LDH is less than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal. Congestive heart failure (CHF), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and pulmonary embolism typically cause transudative effusions. Exudative effusions have a higher pleural to serum protein and LDH ratio and a pleural LDH greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal. Examples of causes of exudative effusions include malignancy, infectious causes such as empyema or tuberculosis, inflammatory etiologies such as lupus or pancreatitis, and pulmonary embolism, which may be either transudative or exudative.

Empyemas additionally will have a pH < 7.2, glucose < 60 mg/dL, WBC count > 50,000 cells/hpf, and may have grossly purulent fluid. A low pH can also be seen with inflammatory processes such as malignancies, collagen vascular disease, tuberculosis, and esophageal rupture. Signs and symptoms of pleural effusion include dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and dullness to percussion of the chest wall. Diagnosis is via chest radiography. A pleural effusion can be visualized when pleural fluid volume approaches 150 mL. Thoracentesis is required to determine the etiology of the effusion. Treatment is via therapeutic thoracentesis if symptomatic and identifying and treating the underlying cause. If the fluid is an empyema, tube thoracostomy will be required to evacuate the thick fluid.



Congestive heart failure (A) causes a transudative effusion, which is inconsistent with the fluid analysis provided above. CHF is the most common cause of pleural effusion, followed by malignancy, bacterial pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. Tuberculosis is the most common etiology of pleural effusion in resource-poor countries.

Nephrotic syndrome (C) will also produce a transudative effusion.

While pulmonary embolism (D) can produce a transudative or exudative effusion, the pleural fluid will not have a low glucose level.

Question: A thin 26-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and a productive cough for 5 days. He has a history of cystic fibrosis and multiple hospital admissions over the last 9 months. His vital signs are T 101.6°F (38.7°C), HR 111 bpm, RR 22/min, BP 100/70 mm Hg, and SpO2 92% on room air. He has bilateral diffuse crackles and rhonchi on exam with increased tactile fremitus. His chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral alveolar consolidation concerning for pneumonia. Which of the following is the most appropriate component of this patient's therapy at this time?
ExplanationEN:
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive pulmonary process affecting 1 in 2,500 children, most commonly seen in Europeans and those of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. It leads to abnormal chloride transport in various tissues (e.g, lungs, pancreas, GI tract), leading to thick, viscous secretions. Infection is common, especially pneumonia. Patients with cystic fibrosis require broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage as they develop chronic colonization with pathologic bacteria, leading to recurrent bouts of infection and antibiotic use. This creates resistant organisms and special antibiotic considerations. Antibiotics should cover Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenza, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin that has appropriate coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Other options for anti-pseudomonal coverage include ceftazidime (the only third-generation cephalosporin with antipseudomonal coverage), piperacillin-tazobactam, fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin), carbapenems (e.g., meropenem, imipenem), aztreonam, amikacin, and tobramycin. Double coverage for pseudomonas is typically recommended.



Cefdinir (A), cefpodoxime (C), and ceftriaxone (D) are all third-generation cephalosporins that do not have antipseudomonal coverage. They have good potency against other gram-negative rods and reduced potency towards gram-positive cocci.
