Question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the ED 4 days after being involved in a head-on motor vehicle collision, and a contrasted abdominal computed tomography scan demonstrates a duodenal hematoma in the descending portion of the duodenum. Which of the following is a common secondary outcome of this condition?
ExplanationEN:
Intramural duodenal hematomas are relatively uncommon but occur most frequently in children secondary to some traumatic event (e.g., motor vehicle collision with seatbelt injury, endoscopy) when the duodenum is compressed against the spine. Intestinal hematomas can occur from the shearing of intramural vessels, or an extraintestinal hematoma may develop in the retroperitoneum, creating extrinsic pressure on the bowel lumen. Morbidity is related to delay in diagnosis and occult injuries to surrounding structures. This may be due, in part, to little or no external signs of injury at the time of initial presentation. The prognosis is usually favorable, with most resolving spontaneously with conservative management.

One of the complications of duodenal hematomas is partial or complete intestinal or gastric outlet obstruction. A secondary complication can include acute pancreatitis. Delayed onset of abdominal pain, distension, vomiting or hematemesis, and diminished bowel sounds following a recent history of blunt abdominal trauma or endoscopic procedure should raise suspicion for duodenal hematoma. Initial diagnostic evaluation can be performed with an abdominal CT with intravenous and oral contrast. Minimal contrast observed in the small bowel suggests gastric outlet obstruction. Further diagnosis can be continued with a contrast swallow study to assess gastric emptying. Management includes nasogastric decompression, enteral rest, intravenous hydration, pain control, and (in severe cases) total parenteral nutrition for up to 3 weeks.



Duodenal hematoma is not associated with acalculous cholecystitis (A).

Acute rather than chronic pancreatitis (B) has been reported in cases of duodenal hematoma.

Eosinophilic duodenitis (C) is not a cause or complication of duodenal hematomas.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the ED after falling from a barstool onto a tile floor 1 hour ago. She had no loss of consciousness or vomiting. She is very playful and interactive on exam without any bruising behind the ears or around the eyes. Her ear exam finding is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Monitor in the ED for 3 more hours

ExplanationEN:
An ear examination is an important part of an evaluation of a child with a closed head injury because the most common sign of a basilar skull fracture in children is hemotympanum. Basilar skull fractures in children are strongly associated with intracranial injury, many of which have significant morbidity and mortality and may include apnea and altered mental status on presentation. Other presentations include a CSF leak seen as otorrhea or rhinorrhea, bleeding into the mastoid air cells seen as retroauricular bruising (i.e., Battle sign), and bleeding from a cribriform plate fracture seen as periorbital bruising (i.e., raccoon eyes).

Basilar skull fractures are commonly associated with cranial nerve VI, VII, or VIII impairment and present as an inability to abduct an eye, facial weakness or numbness, and hearing loss. Hearing loss is very common, which can be from cranial nerve dysfunction, hemotympanum, tympanic membrane perforation, or ossicular injury. Children may also express dizziness or vertigo.

A CT scan of the brain should be performed in children with physical exam findings of a basilar skull fracture to evaluate for intracranial injury. A basilar skull fracture may be difficult to see on a CT scan, so children with exam findings but a normal CT should still be presumed to have a basilar skull fracture. Treatment is as directed by a pediatric neurosurgeon or otolaryngologist. Bacterial meningitis is a late complication of a CSF leak from a basilar skull fracture, but prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.



Amoxicillin (A) is the appropriate treatment for a child with uncomplicated otitis media, not hemotympanum.

Monitoring for worsening (C) is a common practice in children with a head injury from a significant mechanism or those with loss of consciousness or vomiting but who appear well, but it does not replace a CT scan in children with signs of a basilar skull fracture.

Reassurance and discharge (D) would be appropriate for this patient should the signs of a basilar skull fracture be missing.

A TEE can be performed at the bedside or in the operating room prior to emergent surgical exploration.

Question: A 65-year-old man is an unrestrained rear passenger in a motor vehicle collision. After intubation and central line placement, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on the chest X-ray seen above?
ExplanationEN:
The deep sulcus sign is a radiographic sign of pneumothorax. A pneumothorax occurs when air escapes into the pleural space either spontaneously or as a result of chest trauma. As patients continue to breathe normally, each inspiration causes additional air to accumulate in the pleural space due to the traumatic injury. Most commonly, patients report shortness of breath and chest pain. Air in the pleural space most commonly collects at the apex of the lung and an upright chest X-ray is the imaging study of choice. More recently, an ultrasound performed in the context of an E-FAST is increasingly used in the evaluation of pneumothorax. When evaluating a patient in the setting of trauma, an upright film may not be possible. The chest X-ray may be a supine film in which case detection of a pneumothorax is more challenging. In this position, air accumulates anteriorly and basally and deepens the costophrenic angle on that side. This is referred to as the deep sulcus sign.



A chest wall contusion (A) is not visible on plain radiographs. Diaphragmatic rupture (B) may occur in the setting of trauma and is sometimes a difficult diagnosis to make because of the unreliability of radiographic imaging. In some instances, the injury is not visible, but in other cases, findings may have a similar appearance to other pathologies (e.g., hemothorax). On plain X-ray, several findings are possible including the presence of bowel or other intra-abdominal contents in the thoracic cavity. Additionally, the hemidiaphragm on that side may be elevated. Pneumomediastinum (C) is a collection of air in the mediastinal cavity. This may also occur in the setting of a pneumothorax. Pneumomediastinum may occur spontaneously, in asthma, in COPD, or in the setting of severe mediastinitis. Additionally, esophageal or tracheal injuries may lead to the accumulation of air in this space.

Question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after hitting his head 5 hours ago on a coffee table at home. ExplanationEN:
A concussion occurs when there is blunt trauma to the head. Patients may present with headache, nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, grogginess, amnesia to the inciting event, and irritability. The decision to perform a head CT scan on a pediatric patient can be aided by the PECARN rule. In this patient, the risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury is < 0.8% based on the PECARN study. Trauma or spontaneous rupture of a berry aneurysm are common etiologies. Trauma results in the tearing of the bridging veins, leading to a slower accumulation of blood when compared to epidural hematomas.

Question: A 52-year-old man presents with acute left-sided chest pain after falling from a ladder 5 feet in height. He fell onto his left chest and now has pain, particularly with taking deep breaths and movement. Vital signs show HR 96 bpm, BP 131/79 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and SpO2 90% on room air. The patient is splinting when he breathes. Examination findings include tenderness over the lateral left chest wall and left lateral back with a small abrasion over the back. Lung sounds are evident bilaterally, but splinting limits the exam. No crepitus is palpable. What is the best next step to screen for traumatic pneumothorax?

Options.text: Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography with angiography

ExplanationEN:
Pneumothorax is a common complication of blunt chest trauma and is often sustained when a rib fracture is present. Patients often manifest with chest pain, rib pain, tachypnea, diminished or absent breath sounds, and hypoxia. Patients presenting with any trauma, including blunt chest trauma, should be evaluated through a typical advanced trauma life support algorithm. Hemodynamically unstable patients and those with a high-risk injury or with significant examination findings to suggest trauma pathology should have fast and reliable initial screening tests performed to evaluate for abnormalities such as pneumothorax. These tests usually include the focused assessment with sonography in trauma, chest radiography, and ECG. Ultrasonography has become an integral part of the trauma assessment and is commonly performed to evaluate for pneumothoraces or hemothoraces. Many studies suggest that ultrasonography is a very effective screening tool for the evaluation of traumatic pneumothoraces but is less sensitive for hemothoraces. For the evaluation of pneumothorax, ultrasonography has been found to be significantly more sensitive than supine chest radiography with similar specificity. Thus, in this patient, ultrasonography would be the most sensitive screening test and should be performed to rapidly diagnose traumatic pneumothorax.

Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography with angiography (B) is used to diagnose blunt aortic injury and is theoretically more sensitive than noncontrast computed tomography. However, it is time-consuming and invasive, and it rarely improves upon noncontrast computed tomography for evaluation of other injuries.

Supine chest radiography (C) is generally the initial screening study in all blunt chest trauma patients. It is inexpensive, easy to obtain, and noninvasive. It should be performed in all patients unless there is a need for immediate surgery or emergent computed tomography. However, as already discussed, specifically for pneumothorax, supine chest radiography has been found to be less sensitive than ultrasonography. Therefore, in this patient, ultrasonography would be the better study.

Question: Which of the following radiographic signs supports the diagnosis of a Galeazzi fracture?
ExplanationEN:
Galeazzi fractures are relatively uncommon injuries that occur more frequently in adults than children, with an average patient age of 34 years. The typical mechanism involves forceful axial loading and torsion of the forearm, commonly from a fall onto an outstretched hand. The injury results from ligamentous disruption at the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ), including the triangular fibrocartilage complex and interosseous membrane. In pediatrics, a Galeazzi-equivalent fracture may occur, involving a distal radial fracture with distal ulnar physeal separation rather than true DRUJ dislocation.

Patients present with forearm and wrist pain following trauma, with visible deformity, swelling, and tenderness over the distal radius and wrist. Diagnosis is established through radiographic evaluation with anteroposterior and lateral views of the forearm and wrist. However, underdiagnosis is common because DRUJ disruption may be subtle or overlooked. Radiographic signs suggesting DRUJ injury include radial shortening, fracture within 7.5 cm of the lunate facet, and the presence of ulnar styloid fracture, with ulnar styloid fracture carrying the highest predictive value for DRUJ injury.

Initial management includes analgesia, neurovascular assessment, and splinting with prompt orthopedic consultation. Children may be successfully treated with closed reduction and long-arm cast immobilization. However, in adults, nonsurgical treatment fails in a significant majority of cases due to deforming forces on the distal radius and DRUJ instability. Thus, open reduction and internal fixation of the radius is the preferred treatment in adults. Complications from misdiagnosis or inadequate management include DRUJ instability, malunion, limited forearm range of motion, chronic wrist pain, and post-traumatic osteoarthritis.



A midshaft ulna fracture (B) is a component of a Monteggia fracture, not a Galeazzi fracture. A Monteggia fracture consists of an ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation, which is the opposite pattern from Galeazzi.

Radial head dislocation (C) is the hallmark finding of a Monteggia fracture, not a Galeazzi fracture. The Galeazzi injury involves the wrist joint (DRUJ) rather than the elbow.

While radial head fractures (D) can occur with elbow trauma, they are not associated with Galeazzi fractures. A Galeazzi fracture involves the radial shaft or diaphysis, not the radial head, and the associated joint injury is at the wrist (DRUJ), not the elbow.

Question: A 22-year-old man presents after being punched in the face while at a bar. He spent the night in the ED because he was too intoxicated and uncooperative with a full exam. On reevaluation, he has blurry vision, photophobia, pain in his left eye, nausea, and headache. A limited exam reveals left periorbital edema and ecchymosis. His neurological exam is unremarkable. A CT scan of the head from the previous night was unremarkable. Which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Slit lamp examination of the eye

CorrectAnswer: Slit lamp examination of the eye
ExplanationEN:
These symptoms and signs suggest traumatic hyphema. Hyphema is caused by bleeding into the anterior chamber of the eye from a damaged iris or ciliary body. The most common cause is trauma to the eye, but it can also occur spontaneously in the setting of diabetes mellitus or anticoagulation. While a large hyphema may be noted with just pen-light examination, a microhyphema or low-grade hyphema may only be visible on slit-lamp examination. Symptoms include decreased visual acuity and photophobia. Signs include anisocoria (i.e., asymmetrically sized pupils), visualized blood in the anterior chamber, and ciliary flush (i.e., conjunctival injection adjacent to the iris). Open globe injury should be considered in the setting of traumatic hyphema. The management depends on the volume of bleeding. Admission is recommended if ≥ 50% of the anterior chamber is filled with blood. If < 50% of the anterior chamber is occupied by blood, outpatient management with ophthalmology follow-up is indicated.



In cases of traumatic eye injury, globe rupture should be ruled out prior to measuring intraocular pressure (A).

An ophthalmology consult (B) is appropriate for gross hyphema involving ≥ 50% of the anterior chamber or if an open globe is suspected. However, a thorough physical exam should be performed before consulting the specialist.

Repeating a head CT (C) is unlikely to reveal new findings in the absence of focal neurological deficits or altered mental status.

Question: A 23-year-old man with a history of morbid obesity presents to the ED after injuring his left index finger 3 hours ago while injecting sealant with a high-pressure nozzle. He is in severe pain and intravenous access cannot be obtained due to his habitus. Exam shows his left index finger is similar in size to other digits, with a nonbleeding 0.5 cm laceration on the lateral middle phalanx. He refuses range of motion testing due to pain but is neurovascularly intact distal to the injury. Which of the following is contraindicated in this patient?

Options.text: Passive and active range of motion testing

ExplanationEN:
This patient has sustained a high-pressure injection injury. The most common cause of high-pressure injection injuries is with trigger-activated tools (e.g., portable epinephrine pens), and they usually occur in the nondominant hand. Diagnosis is primarily made clinically. Radiographs may supplement the diagnosis as they often show the dissemination of fluid or air beneath the injury and across fascial planes. Fractures are not uncommon, due to the high localized pressure. Upon arrival, the patient’s high-pressure injection injury commonly seems innocuous. However, underlying ischemia may be ongoing. As little as 6 hours of delay to treatment increases the already high amputation rates of 30–48%. Patients will present with a history of high-pressure injection tool use and delayed onset of a myriad of symptoms such as pain, swelling, discoloration, and neurologic deficits.

Treatment depends on the composition of the injection injury. If only water is injected, most patients can be observed for signs and symptoms of ischemia and compartment syndrome. For epinephrine auto-injector injuries, ischemia and pain result and can be treated with either subcutaneous phentolamine or close observation. Digital blocks for pain control can increase the pressure within the injured finger leading to further neurovascular compromise. Therefore, they are contraindicated in these injuries. For any other compositions, treatment includes immediate hand surgery consultation, parenteral pain control, elevation of the extremity, intravenous antibiotics with skin flora coverage, and radiographs. Notably, imaging and further workup should not delay immediate hand surgery evaluation and likely emergent operative debridement.



As noted above, treatment of high-pressure injection injuries includes elevation of the extremity (B) to help reduce swelling and further increases in intra-digital pressure and intravenous ceftriaxone (C) or another antibiotic that covers skin flora.

A full physical exam, including passive and active range of motion testing (D), despite the pain, should be done to exclude tendinous injuries.

Question: A 53-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain after a motor vehicle collision. He is having shortness of breath and severe diffuse chest pain. He is tachycardic, but his vital signs are otherwise normal. His chest X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the midsternum on the lateral view. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

Options.text: ECG and computed tomography of the chest

CorrectAnswer: ECG and computed tomography of the chest
ExplanationEN:
Sternal fractures are high-mechanism injuries that tend to occur across the body of the sternum. They are more common in restrained passengers due to compression from the chest portion of the seatbelt restricting forward movement. Imaging is required for diagnosis, particularly a lateral chest X-ray. Patients with a high likelihood of a sternal injury should have a helical chest CT performed, as small fractures may be missed on X-ray. Any patient with a known sternal fracture should have a helical chest CT to rule out intrathoracic injuries that can be associated with high-mechanism blunt trauma. Given the risk of cardiac contusions in the setting of sternal fractures, all patients should at least have an ECG performed and may need a troponin checked as well. In the setting of an isolated sternal fracture, if the helical chest CT, ECG, troponin, and vital signs are normal and the pain is well-controlled, the patient can be discharged home safely after an observation period of 6 hours. If any of this workup is abnormal, strong consideration should be given for admission and close telemonitoring.



A chest CT (A) is indicated to rule out other intrathoracic injuries given the high-mechanism injury. However, conservative management of sternal fractures should also always include at least an ECG. Almost all sternal fractures are treated conservatively with close follow-up.

Unless there are other traumatic injuries requiring surgical intervention, immediate consultation with trauma surgery (C) is not indicated.

Question: Which of the following appropriately describes neurogenic shock?

Options.text: Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload
Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; increased preload
Warm, dry distal extremities; normal sinus rhythm; decreased preload
Warm, dry distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload

CorrectAnswer: Warm, dry distal extremities; normal sinus rhythm; decreased preload
ExplanationEN:
Neurogenic shock is a type of distributive shock that occurs with a central nervous system or spinal cord injury. It occurs in < 20% of patients with spinal cord injuries and is secondary to a loss of peripheral sympathetic innervation resulting in vasodilation. If the injury occurs through the T1–T4 cord levels, loss of sympathetic innervation to the heart leaves unopposed vagal stimulation, resulting in bradycardia or absence of reflex tachycardia. Therefore, in general, patients with neurogenic shock are warm, peripherally vasodilated, and hypotensive with a relative bradycardia and decreased preload. Treatment of neurogenic shock focuses on fixing any underlying hypovolemia with either blood products (in the setting of hemorrhage) or fluids (if fluid depleted). If IV fluids are not adequate to maintain organ perfusion, positive inotropic or vasopressor agents may be beneficial adjuncts to improve cardiac output and raise perfusion pressure. The recommendation is to maintain a higher MAP than in other traumatic injuries, with pressures close to 85–90 mm Hg.



Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload (A) is the description of hypovolemic shock. Cool, clammy distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; increased preload (B) is the description of cardiogenic shock. Warm, dry distal extremities; sinus tachycardia; decreased preload (D) is the description of septic shock, which is another form of distributive shock. The key difference between the two types is the relative bradycardia that is seen in neurogenic shock.

Question: A 69-year-old man presents with neck pain after a fall. An X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
The radiograph provided is suggestive of a flexion teardrop fracture, which is an unstable fracture of the anteroinferior aspect of the vertebral body that occurs due to hyperflexion. The three-column concept of spine stability proposed by Denis is a concept commonly used to distinguish between stable and unstable vertebral injuries. The vertebral body is divided into three columns: the anterior, middle, and posterior columns. The anterior column consists of the anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior half of the vertebral body and disc, the middle column consists of the posterior half of the vertebral body and disk as well as the posterior longitudinal ligament, and the posterior column consists of the facet joints, ligamentum flavum, and posterior elements. A flexion teardrop fracture is considered an unstable fracture due to disruption of the anterior, middle, and posterior columns. Other unstable cervical spinal injuries include hangman fracture, type II and III odontoid fractures, Jefferson fracture, bilateral facet dislocation, atlantoaxial subluxation, and atlanto-occipital dislocation.



Bilateral facet dislocation (A) is an unstable cervical spine injury defined as anterior displacement of more than half of the anteroposterior diameter of the vertebral body. A clay-shoveler fracture (B) is a stable cervical spine injury defined as a spinous process fracture. A Jefferson fracture (D) is an unstable cervical spine injury caused by axial forces causing fractures of the anterior and posterior arches of C1, with possible disruption of the transverse ligament.

Question: A 17-year-old girl presents to the ED with bilateral eye pain. The patient woke up with pain and photophobia. She notes that yesterday she was skiing at a resort in Colorado and forgot to wear her ski goggles but did apply sunscreen to her face. She initially thought the pain might be some dust or something irritating her eyes, but the pain continues to intensify. On exam, her pupillary reflexes and cranial nerves are intact. Her visual acuity is 20/40 bilaterally, and she has no history of vision correction. She has conjunctival injection, and an example of a fluorescein stain of her eye is shown in the image above. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with bilateral eye pain and conjunctival injection after skiing at high altitude without goggles, most consistent with ultraviolet keratitis, the most common cause of radiation damage to the eye. The epithelial layer of the cornea absorbs the majority of ultraviolet radiation, and prolonged exposure can cause desquamation of the epithelium. Tanning beds, welding torches, and sun exposure (including ultraviolet rays reflected off of snow, snow blindness) are risk factors if patients do not wear appropriate eye protection. Similar to cutaneous sunburn, pain develops between 8 and 12 hours after exposure. Patients may have conjunctival injection, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Fluorescein dye shows diffuse punctate corneal uptake and can help rule out corneal abrasion. Patients are generally treated supportively, with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and lubricating eye drops or ointments. Topical antibiotics are often administered but have no proven benefit.



Contact dermatitis (A) could present with conjunctival or facial irritation after a new exposure (such as sunscreen). However, this patient has decreased visual acuity and diffuse fluorescein uptake on exam, which is more consistent with ultraviolet keratitis.

Corneal abrasions (B) could also cause intense discomfort, and skiing without goggles would be a risk factor. However, corneal abrasions are generally rapid in onset and unilateral. This patient also has no distinct areas of fluorescein uptake on exam.

Disciform keratitis (C) is an ocular reactivation of herpes simplex virus that manifests itself in pain, decreased visual acuity, and a distinct disciform distribution of keratic precipitates. It is usually unilateral and gradual in onset.

Her visual acuity is 20/40 bilaterally, and she has no history of vision correction. She has conjunctival injection, and an example of a fluorescein stain of her eye is shown in the image above. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

Question: Which of the following tests is the most sensitive physical examination maneuver to identify an injury to the anterior cruciate ligament?
ExplanationEN:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the four major ligaments of the knee (anterior cruciate, posterior cruciate, medial collateral, and lateral collateral). It provides anterior stability to the knee joint and is the most commonly injured ligament of the knee. A tear results from deceleration, hyperextension, or marked internal rotation of the tibia on the femur. Most ACL tears occur during sporting activities such as skiing, football, soccer, and basketball. Clinically, there is usually rapid development of hemarthroses, causing significant swelling. Almost half of individuals report feeling or hearing a pop, which is the most reliable indicator. There is usually instability of the knee or a wobbly feeling.

The Lachman test is the most sensitive test (approximately 98% sensitivity) for an ACL tear. This is performed by placing the knee in 20–30° of flexion with the leg slightly externally rotated. One hand is placed behind the tibia with the thumb on the tibial tuberosity, and one hand is placed on the thigh while the examiner pulls the tibia anteriorly. In a patient with an intact ACL, a firm end point should be elicited. With a positive test, the examiner feels a soft end point at the end of the motion, indicating an ACL tear.

X-rays are often performed in acute knee injuries but are not helpful in making a diagnosis of an ACL tear. However, they may be helpful in ruling out other associated injuries or causes of knee pain. A Segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the lateral tibial condyle that is indicative of disruption of the lateral capsule and associated ACL injury. MRI is rarely necessary to make a diagnosis. Rest, ice, crutches, immobilization, and NSAIDs are common initial treatment options. Patients should be referred to orthopedic surgery. Management options are often surgical, but nonoperative management can be pursued depending on the patient’s age, functional status, and medical comorbidities.



While the anterior drawer test (A) is used to assess the integrity of the ACL, it is less sensitive than the Lachman test with a sensitivity of approximately 48%. The anterior drawer test can be affected by hamstring muscle tension and may not reveal subtle laxity present in ACL injuries.

McMurray test (C) is used to identify meniscal tears. It is performed with the patient lying supine on a stretcher, at which time the examiner flexes the foot and extends the knee while internally and externally rotating the tibia on the femur. A clicking indicates a positive test.

The Thompson test (D) is performed to evaluate the integrity of the Achilles tendon. With the patient lying prone, the calf is squeezed, which causes plantar flexion of the ankle joint. If flexion does not occur with the squeezing, the Achilles tendon is injured.

Valgus stress (E) applied to the knee joint assesses the integrity of the medial aspect of the joint, including the medial collateral ligament.

Reveal Answer:
Anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament, and medial meniscus.

Question: Which of the following is the most reliable indication of an Achilles tendon rupture?

Options.text: Inability to plantar flex the foot

ExplanationEN:
The Achilles tendon is formed by the convergence of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles and attaches to the posterior calcaneus. Achilles tendon ruptures tend to occur when sudden force is placed on the Achilles tendon during physical activity that involves pivoting on the foot or sudden acceleration. Most ruptures occur in tendons that are already weakened from previous injury or degeneration. Both partial and complete ruptures can occur. Men, typically those in their 30s and 40s, are significantly more likely to have an Achilles tendon rupture.

Patients often present with a history of sudden pain and a popping sensation in the posterior ankle during physical activity. On examination, there may be edema and ecchymosis over the Achilles tendon, and a palpable defect may be appreciated. The calf squeeze test, or Thompson test, is the most reliable indicator of an Achilles tendon rupture, with a sensitivity of 96%. With the patient prone or kneeling on a chair, the posterior calf is squeezed at its widest point. The absence of plantar flexion indicates a rupture of the tendon. Management includes immobilization with a short leg cast with the ankle in slight plantar flexion, known as the equinus position, and orthopedic consultation.



A tendon rupture can result in a decreased Achilles reflex due to the structural integrity of the tendon being impaired. However, the Achilles reflex (A) primarily assesses the S1 and S2 nerve roots. A diminished reflex is not a specific or reliable indicator for an Achilles tendon rupture and can be seen in other conditions, including peripheral nerve disorders such as neuropathy and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Because of the multiple muscles involved in plantar flexion of the foot that remain intact and functional even with an Achilles tendon rupture, the ability or inability to ambulate (B) and plantar flex the foot (C) does not reliably exclude or diagnose an Achilles tendon rupture.

Pain along the posterior ankle (D) is typical. However, one study showed that up to one-third of patients with tendon rupture report no pain.

Question: A 29-year-old man is brought to the ED with a gunshot wound to the abdomen. Vital signs are BP 110/65 mm Hg, HR 90 bpm, RR 19/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and T 37.7°C (99.9°F). The bedside focused assessment with sonography in trauma exam is positive. What is the best next step in diagnostic management?
ExplanationEN:
Penetrating abdominal trauma is defined as the violation of the abdominal cavity by stab or gunshot wounds or impalement. Clinical signs may be obvious and dramatic or may be occult. When evaluating gunshot wounds, it is important to keep in mind that additional injury is possible from transmitted energy and from secondary missiles in the form of fragmented bone. Abdominal gunshot wounds penetrate the peritoneal cavity in about 80% of cases, causing intraperitoneal damage in > 90% of those cases. The most commonly injured organ in abdominal gunshot wounds is the small bowel, followed by the colon and liver. It is often difficult to assess the exact trajectory of the object during initial evaluation, and thus it is best assumed that any penetrating injury to the lower chest, pelvis, flank, or back may also have penetrated the abdominal cavity. The focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) examination is the current primary diagnostic study at the bedside of patients with trauma, and a massive hemoperitoneum can be detected within seconds of performing a single view of the Morison pouch in a hypotensive patient.

Patients who are hemodynamically unstable or have peritonitis or unreliable abdominal exams require emergent laparotomy. Patients who are stable can benefit from a CT scan with IV contrast to assess injury severity and active bleeding. If peritoneal violation is absent or unclear, serial examinations are indicated. Previously, almost all patients with peritoneal violation from a gunshot wound underwent emergent laparotomy.

Advances in CT technology and increasing use of selective nonoperative management (SNOM) for abdominal injuries have led to a growing trend toward SNOM for isolated solid organ injuries from gunshot wounds. This approach includes intensive monitoring by a trauma surgeon and possibly therapeutic angiography. Data suggest SNOM is used in up to 35% of kidney injuries and nearly 40% of liver injuries from gunshot wounds, with increased survival and fewer postoperative complications. The failure rate of SNOM is around 10%, but it is not linked to adverse outcomes. SNOM has been used for all grades of kidney and liver injuries. Patient selection is critical, considering hemodynamic status, mental status, abdominal exam, and CT findings. Patients not undergoing surgery should be admitted for monitoring and observation.



A high suspicion for a transabdominal trajectory after a gunshot wound used to be an absolute indication for immediate laparotomy (B). However, performing a CT first is currently preferred in a patient who is stable to better delineate the precise nature of the injuries prior to taking the patient to the operating room.

MRI (C) does not usually play a prominent role in the treatment of patients with trauma unless the patient is stable and has trauma to the spinal contents.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (D), which requires time and expertise, is only currently used in resource-poor settings. This patient already has a positive FAST exam finding, making a diagnostic peritoneal lavage unnecessary.

Reveal Answer:
Anterior abdominal stab wounds.

Question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the ED after being struck by a car. A FAST exam is performed with one of the images shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the findings shown? What does the ultrasound image shown above, obtained on a 5-year-old boy who presented after being struck by a motorized vehicle, show?
ExplanationEN:
Blunt abdominal trauma (BAT) is the most common form of trauma in children, with motor vehicle collisions being the leading mechanism, though non-accidental trauma is the leading cause in children ≤4 years old. The spleen is the most commonly injured solid organ, followed by the liver and the kidney.

The pathogenesis of intra-abdominal hemorrhage in pediatric blunt trauma involves direct force transmission to solid organs (spleen, liver, kidney), which causes parenchymal disruption and bleeding into the peritoneal cavity. Children are particularly vulnerable because of their relatively larger solid organs, thinner abdominal wall, and less protective musculature and fat compared to adults.

Clinically, children with intra-abdominal hemorrhage may present with abdominal pain, tenderness, distension, and abdominal wall ecchymosis (e.g., seatbelt sign). Hemodynamic instability may be present, though many initially appear stable, as children have robust compensatory mechanisms that maintain hemodynamics longer, even with significant blood loss. The FAST exam is a rapid bedside ultrasound that evaluates four windows (subxiphoid/cardiac, right upper quadrant/Morison's pouch, left upper quadrant/splenorenal recess, and suprapubic/pelvis) for free fluid. The eFAST expands this to include views of both lungs to evaluate for pneumothorax. While still used in children, it is poorly sensitive and less reliable than in adults and is not appropriate to rule out intra-abdominal injury. However, a positive FAST exam in an unstable child may obviate the need for CT and prompt direct operative intervention.

Treatment in the ED follows ATLS principles beginning with the primary survey, IV access, fluid resuscitation, and blood product administration as needed. The vast majority of pediatric solid organ injuries are managed nonoperatively with observation, with intervention (e.g., laparotomy, angiography) needed in rare cases. Indications for operative intervention include hemodynamic instability unresponsive to resuscitation with a positive FAST, peritonitis, or hollow viscus injury. Transfusion of >40 mL/kg of blood products is strongly associated with the need for intervention or death. Complications include delayed hemorrhage, missed injuries (especially hollow viscous, pancreas), and the risks of unnecessary CT radiation exposure in the pediatric population.



While ascites (A) can appear as anechoic fluid in Morison's pouch, in the acute setting of a pediatric trauma patient struck by a car, free fluid is presumed to represent hemoperitoneum, not iatrogenic ascites from fluid resuscitation. This would be an unlikely finding this early in the clinical course.

The gallbladder (C) is an anechoic fluid-filled structure, but it is located anteriorly within the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the liver, not in the hepatorenal recess posteriorly between the liver and kidney. A band-like collection in Morison's pouch is anatomically distinct from the gallbladder. [1-2]

Pericardial effusion (D) is assessed on the subxiphoid (cardiac) view of the FAST exam, not the right upper quadrant/hepatorenal view. Pericardial fluid appears as an anechoic stripe surrounding the heart, not in Morison's pouch.

While perihepatic fat (E) can occasionally create echogenic or hypoechoic artifacts near the liver, it does not produce a discrete anechoic band-like collection in the hepatorenal recess. Free fluid in Morison's pouch collects with sharp angles in the most gravity-dependent areas, distinguishing it from fat or edge artifact.

Question: Which of the following age group is at highest risk of the finding seen on the image above?
ExplanationEN:
The coronal reconstruction from a cervical spine CT scan pictured above reveals a type III fracture of the second cervical vertebra. There are three common varieties of fractures of the second cervical vertebra involving the dens, or odontoid process, which articulates with the ring of the first cervical vertebra. The fractures are most commonly seen in older patients (> 65 years). The characteristic appearance of the fracture, which involves the body of the second cervical vertebra, is typical for type III fractures. Type II fractures present at the junction of the odontoid process and the vertebral body. Type I fractures involve the tip of the odontoid process. In neurologically intact patients, these fractures are often initially treated nonoperatively with a trial of cervical immobilization in a hard collar.



It is thought that odontoid fractures are more common in older individuals due to age-related bone loss coupled with the fact that there is disproportionate bone loss in the second cervical vertebra at the base of the odontoid process. Since patients who are 1–20 years of age (B), 21–40 years of age (C), and 41–65 years of age (D) are at lower risk of osteoporosis, they are at less risk for a type III odontoid fracture as compared individuals > 65 years of age.

Question: A 7-year-old girl resents to the ED via EMS after being struck by a car as a pedestrian. She has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 5 and has multiple areas of ecchymosis on her chest wall. Which of the following conditions is most likely to occur in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Pulmonary contusion is the most common intrathoracic injury in pediatric blunt chest trauma, with motor vehicle crashes being the most common mechanism. Multiple studies have affirmed this pattern, with rib fractures, pneumothorax, and hemothorax all occurring less frequently than pulmonary contusions in pediatric patients with blunt chest trauma. This is the case because the pediatric chest wall is highly compliant and elastic, meaning kinetic energy is transmitted directly to the underlying lung parenchyma without necessarily fracturing the ribs. The pathogenesis involves direct mechanical disruption of the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing alveolar hemorrhage and parenchymal destruction that is followed by further inflammatory and oxidative injury. Importantly, the contralateral uninjured lung also develops delayed capillary leak, thickened alveolar septa, and neutrophilic infiltration, indicating a systemic inflammatory component beyond the direct injury site.

Clinical symptoms include increased work of breathing, dyspnea, chest wall tenderness, and occasional hemoptysis, which may progress to respiratory insufficiency (i.e., hypoxemia, hypercapnia) and failure. Symptoms typically manifest within hours of injury and peak at approximately 72 hours. Chest radiograph is the initial imaging modality of choice in pediatric blunt thoracic trauma. CT is far more sensitive for identifying pulmonary contusion and is highly predictive of the need for subsequent mechanical ventilation, and is useful in assessing for associated injuries, but often does not change the management of pulmonary contusions themselves.

Management is primarily supportive, predominantly of the airway, respiratory status, and hemodynamics. This patient's Glasgow Coma Scale of 5 suggests the need for endotracheal intubation, but supplemental oxygen (targeting normoxia and avoiding hyperoxia) and judicious fluid resuscitation targeting euvolemia should be administered. Patients should be given appropriate analgesia to facilitate deep breathing and coughing, while lung-protective ventilation strategies should be employed in patients who receive positive pressure ventilation. Steroids are not recommended, and routine antibiotic prophylaxis should not be given in the absence of penetrating injuries. Prominent complications include pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and long-term pulmonary impairment.



Hemothorax (A) is far less common of the major pediatric chest injuries, occurring in roughly 1/10 of cases, and is more frequently associated with penetrating trauma, rib/sternal fractures, or high-energy mechanisms causing vascular injury rather. Pulmonary contusions are far more likely in pediatric blunt chest trauma.

While pneumothorax (B) occurs in a fair number of pediatric chest trauma cases, it is less common than pulmonary contusion and is typically associated with rib fractures that lacerate the visceral pleura or with alveolar rupture from increased pressure. Primary parenchymal injury leading to pulmonary contusions is more common.

Pulmonary laceration (D) represents a more severe, focal disruption of lung tissue and is far less common than pulmonary contusion in pediatric blunt trauma. The compliant pediatric chest wall tends to produce diffuse contusion rather than discrete laceration.

Rib fractures (E) are notably less common in children than in adults because the pediatric rib cage is highly elastic and pliable. The incidence of rib fractures increases with age, particularly around puberty when ossification is completed.

Question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after he jumped on the bed and fell onto his hands. It was witnessed by his parent, who reports he began crying immediately and did not hit his head. The patient only has arm pain. An X-ray of his forearm is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s X-ray is consistent with a torus fracture. They are most commonly seen in children’s extremities secondary to an axial loading force. This axial loading force leads to buckling of the cortex and underlying periosteum. They may appear subtle on plain radiography. However, more advanced imaging (e.g., computed tomography) is not indicated purely for the evaluation of torus fractures. Patients commonly present with point tenderness over the fracture site with or without overlying swelling. A firm ridge across the fracture line may be palpable, but lack of this does not preclude the diagnosis. The injured extremity should be splinted, and the patient should be given close follow-up within 1 week. In cases of distal radius torus fractures, follow-up can be made with the pediatrician alone. Otherwise, orthopedic follow-up should be recommended.



Greenstick fractures (A) are characterized by cortical rupture on one side with an intact cortex on the other side. The bone will be bowed away from the disrupted cortex.

Plastic deformation injuries (B) result from trauma that is forceful enough to create a bend in the bone without causing any cortical disruption.

Salter-Harris type I fracture (C) is a transverse fracture through the physis. Radiographs may appear normal, but patients will have point tenderness over the growth plate.

Question: A 17-year-old boy presents with dizziness, nausea, and headache after falling off a trampoline this evening. He thinks he lost consciousness for a second but otherwise was awake shortly after the incident. He vomited once after the fall but has not since. There are no focal findings on neurologic examination, and he is ambulatory. After 6 hours of observation, he remains neurologically intact, has not had further vomiting, and appears well. What are the most appropriate disposition recommendations to give this patient?

Options.text: No sports activity but may return to other activities immediately
Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 1 week, with a gradual return to physical activity
Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 24–48 hours, with gradual return to physical activity

CorrectAnswer: Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 24–48 hours, with gradual return to physical activity
ExplanationEN:
The term concussion is often used synonymously with mild traumatic brain injury, but, more specifically, it describes a pathophysiological state resulting in symptoms and signs experienced by patients after a mild traumatic brain injury. A concussion typically results in short-lived impairment of neurologic function after a direct blow to the head or face that spontaneously resolves. Clinical signs and symptoms of a concussion reflect a functional disturbance rather than structural injury to the brain. No abnormalities are seen on neuroimaging. The incidence of concussion is highest among boys playing collision sports, such as rugby, football, hockey, and lacrosse. In girls, those who participate in soccer, lacrosse, and hockey have the highest incidence of concussion. Children with a concussion may manifest headaches, confusion or disorientation, difficulties with memory, inattentiveness, slow speech, dizziness, gait abnormalities, vomiting, and emotional lability. Patients may or may not have experienced loss of consciousness.

A diagnosis of concussion is determined clinically based on the mechanism of injury, symptoms, and examination findings. Management of concussion includes removal from competitive sports, restriction of physical activity, and neurocognitive rest. Observational studies have suggested that strict physical rest for more than a few days after a concussion may prolong symptoms. Therefore, the recommendation is brief cognitive rest for 24–48 hours after concussion, followed by a gradual return to noncontact physical activity. Patients with worsening or persistent symptoms for > 21 days should be referred for specialty evaluation. Patients with persistent neurological symptoms in the acute setting (e.g., drowsiness, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 15, persistent vomiting) should be admitted for observation. Potential long-term complications related to repeated concussions include permanent changes in mood, behavior, cognition, somatic symptoms, and, in severe cases, dementia or Parkinsonian-like symptoms.



Inpatient admission for 24-hour observation (A) would only be recommended for patients with immediate complications from a head injury, including those with a GCS < 15, seizures, recurrent vomiting, or abnormalities on CT imaging.

All patients should have a period of cognitive rest for at least 24–48 hours before returning to normal activities (B).

Outpatient cognitive and physical rest for 1 week with a gradual return to physical activity (C) is not recommended as these adolescents become deconditioned and a prolonged period of rest does not improve outcomes.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents after being the unrestrained driver in a motor vehicle collision with ejection through the windshield. He was found approximately 10 feet from the vehicle. On arrival, he is alert and screaming in pain. His vital signs are HR 38 bpm, BP 62/40 mm Hg, T 36.2°C, and RR 25/min. His exam is notable for diffuse road rash and thoracic and lumbar vertebral tenderness. His extremities are warm, well-perfused, and without obvious deformity. He is unable to move his bilateral lower extremities and is noted to have an erection. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s hypotension?
ExplanationEN:
Shock is defined as a state of circulatory insufficiency that results in an imbalance of oxygen delivery and metabolic demand. By definition, it results in tissue underperfusion and end-organ dysfunction. The four broad categories of shock are hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive. The presentation above is most consistent with neurogenic shock in the setting of spinal cord injury. Neurogenic shock is a type of distributive shock that occurs due to loss of sympathetic innervation, leading to extreme vasodilation from loss of sympathetic arterial tone. If spinal cord levels T1–T4 are damaged, loss of sympathetic innervation to the heart leads to bradycardia from unopposed vagal tone. This blocks the reflex tachycardia that would otherwise compensate for hypotension. Patients in neurogenic shock are typically hypotensive, bradycardic, and peripherally vasodilated, with well-perfused, warm extremities, and good capillary refill. Neurogenic shock occurs in < 20% of traumatic spine injuries.



Cardiogenic shock (A) occurs secondary to decreased cardiac output, leading to underperfusion of the tissues. This may occur in the setting of decreased preload, increased afterload, or impaired myocardial contractility. Patients with cardiogenic shock may show symptoms of total body fluid overload, including lower extremity edema or jugular venous distention, though these are not required for the diagnosis. These patients show symptoms of poor circulatory flow, such as cool, pale extremities and slowed capillary refill.

Hypovolemic shock (C) occurs when decreased intravascular volume, either through hemorrhage or nonhemorrhagic fluid loss, causes decreased cardiac output, imbalance in oxygen supply and demand, and organ hypoperfusion. This decreased cardiac output leads to compensatory tachycardia in an attempt to maintain stroke volume and an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Arterial and venous vasoconstriction lead to a narrowing of pulse pressure, a sign that is present well before the onset of hypotension. Patients with hemorrhagic shock present with signs of poor peripheral perfusion, such as weak peripheral pulses, paleness, poor capillary refill, and cool extremities. Cerebral hypoperfusion may lead to subtle mental status changes including anxiety and confusion.

Obstructive shock (D) results from a decrease in venous return or cardiac compliance due to left ventricular outflow obstruction or a significant decrease in preload, as seen in cardiac tamponade or a massive pulmonary embolism.

Question: A 19-year-old man presents to the ED in respiratory distress. He has a penetrating wound to the left of his sternum where his partner stabbed him with a screwdriver during an altercation. His vital signs are T 98.6°F (37°C), BP 80/46 mm Hg, HR 124 bpm, RR 24/min, and SpO2 92% on room air. He has distended neck veins and symmetric breath sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Pericardial tamponade is a condition caused by the rapid accumulation of fluid within the pericardial space, leading to hypotension. Pericardial tamponade can be seen in 2% of patients with penetrating thoracoabdominal trauma, and up to 80% of cardiac stab wounds develop pericardial tamponade. Gunshot wounds are less likely to cause tamponade because the large defect caused by the ballistic injury does not allow the pericardial defect to seal as easily. Bedside ultrasound can detect fluid in the pericardial space, but without ultrasound, it can be clinically difficult to diagnose pericardial tamponade.

Beck triad of hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds are classic but seen only in a minority (< 10%) of cases. Sinus tachycardia may be the only clinical finding. As the intrapericardial fluid accumulates, intrapericardial pressure rises and decreases right and left ventricular filling. Patients can rapidly decompensate from obstructive shock.

The treatment for pericardial tamponade is emergent pericardiocentesis, as needed, and surgical repair. It is important for emergency clinicians to remember that pericardial tamponade is a potential cause of pulseless electrical activity and to manage this accordingly during cardiac arrest. Medical causes of pericardial effusions exist (e.g., uremia, radiation therapy, viral pericarditis, malignancy) but typically do not cause tamponade physiology due to the slow accumulation of fluid over time.



Pulmonary embolism (B) can cause hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia as seen in this patient. However, a history of penetrating chest trauma is more suggestive of pericardial tamponade as the cause of this patient’s clinical condition.

Tension pneumomediastinum (C) is a phenomenon in which free air in the mediastinum creates pressure on the mediastinal structures. Pneumomediastinum can be spontaneous (e.g., from Valsalva maneuvers) or iatrogenic (e.g., upper endoscopy, transesophageal echocardiography). Subcutaneous emphysema with crepitus and Hamman crunch on auscultation are likely to be present.

Tension pneumothorax (D) is a life-threatening emergency that can be caused by penetrating chest trauma. It is a clinical diagnosis that should be made prior to imaging. Diminished or absent breath sounds help distinguish this from pericardial tamponade.

Question: An 8-year-old boy presents by private vehicle after being impaled by a rod after a fall from a fence. He is struggling to breathe, with a sucking upper left chest wound. He has no lung sounds on the left. He is placed on monitors and a nonrebreather facemask. Which of the following is the best next step?

Options.text: Put a three-sided occlusive dressing over the wound

CorrectAnswer: Put a three-sided occlusive dressing over the wound
ExplanationEN:
Blast injuries, severe avulsion, and impalement are the most common causes of an open pneumothorax. During an open pneumothorax, spontaneous breathing causes air to be sucked from the room into the chest because of the decrease in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration. Not only does the lung collapse, but air trapping can result in a tension pneumothorax, shifting mediastinal structures away from the wound. Placing a three-sided, tight occlusive dressing over the wound prevents air from entering from the environment and prevents tension within the chest from developing and from worsening while the patient is still spontaneously breathing. A thoracostomy tube should then be rapidly placed on the affected side to drain the hemothorax or pneumothorax and reinflate the patient’s lung.



Performing a needle thoracostomy (A) would relieve pressure in the chest but would not prevent further accumulation during spontaneous ventilation. While this is clearly an important early step in this patient’s care, a three-sided occlusive dressing should be placed first.

Endotracheal intubation (B) in a patient with a pneumothorax is physiologically difficult. Such a patient is more likely to develop cardiopulmonary collapse than one whose pneumothorax has been drained. It is best first to place a three-sided occlusive dressing and a thoracostomy tube to optimize intubation conditions or, altogether, prevent the need for intubation in this patient.

Alternatively, performing a needle thoracostomy and using a syringe to actively pull air from the intrathoracic space or first placing a thoracostomy tube (C) could temporize the situation. Still, the air will reaccumulate without the three-sided occlusive dressing.

Reveal Answer:

Question: What function is significantly impaired by rupture of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon?

Options.text: Flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint
Flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint

CorrectAnswer: Flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint
ExplanationEN:
Injuries to the flexor tendons in the hand are typically the result of lacerations, but closed traumatic disruption (e.g., avulsion fractures) can also occur. Careful examination of the hand with specific knowledge about the function of various tendons is essential, as presentations can be subtle.

The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and travels distally through the anterior compartment of the forearm. At the wrist, four tendons come off the muscle and travel through the carpal tunnel. The tendons insert at the proximal aspect of the middle phalanx of each of the four fingers. The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon passes deep to the split of the distal FDS tendon and inserts at the base of the distal phalanx. The primary function of the FDS is flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, but it also assists with flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. On examination, the patient should be asked to flex at the PIP joint against resistance while the other three fingers are held in extension.

Injuries to flexor tendons should be referred to a hand specialist for definitive care. If one is not immediately available, open wounds should be irrigated and approximated, the hand should be splinted in partial flexion at the MCP, PIP, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, and the patient should be referred for urgent outpatient care.



The FDP is primarily responsible for flexion at the DIP joint (A), but the FDS is responsible for PIP flexion.

The FDS and FDP together assist with flexion at the MCP joint (B), but rupture of the FDS would not significantly impair MCP joint flexion.

The pincer function (D) also requires an intact FDP in the finger. To test the function of the FDP, the patient should attempt to flex the DIP joint against resistance while holding the MCP and PIP joints in extension.

Thumb flexion (E) is controlled by the flexor pollicis longus, not the FDS.

Question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being burned while an adult was lighting a bonfire with gasoline. He weighs 20 kg, has 10% full-thickness burns, 10% partial-thickness burns, and 10% superficial burns. How much IV lactated Ringer should the patient receive in the first 8 hours after injury according to the Parkland formula?
ExplanationEN:
Resuscitation of a patient with severe burns is similar to any other resuscitation, focusing on the airway, breathing, and circulation. Early intubation should be performed in patients with signs of pharyngeal or airway swelling. Other concerning signs include full-thickness burns, large (> 15%) partial-thickness burns, burns to the face or genitals, chemical burns to the eyes, circumferential burns, significant burns to the hands or feet, and electrical burns with loss of consciousness or entrance and exit wounds. Clinicians should also be aware that an estimated 10–20% of children’s burns result from nonaccidental trauma. Determining the percentage of burned body surface area is challenging in children due to their different proportions, so an appropriate diagram should be used instead of the adult rule of nines. Formulas such as the Parkland formula and the Galveston formula should be used to determine the amount of fluid needed for resuscitation. Areas of superficial burns should not be included in the calculation of the total area burned for these formulas. For the Parkland formula, 4 mL/kg/% of body surface area burned should be given over 24 hours, with the first half given in 8 hours after the burn. So for our patient, 4 mL × 20 kg × 20% body surface area is 1,600 mL, and half of that, or 800 mL, should be given in the first 8 hours.



If the patient had 30% body surface area of full- and partial-thickness burns, 1,200 mL (A) would be appropriate. Remember that areas of superficial burns should not be included in the formula calculations. This patient should receive 1,600 mL (B) of fluid in 24 hours. If this patient had 30% body surface area burned, 2,400 mL (C) is the amount of fluid they should receive in 24 hours.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents to the ED with facial and mouth pain after being kicked in the face. On physical exam, you note significant swelling and deformity of the left inferior face, misalignment of the inferior premolars, and an associated intraoral laceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate care for this patient?

Options.text: Discharge with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and close dental follow-up
Discharge with oxycodone and close dental follow-up

ExplanationEN:
This patient has signs and symptoms consistent with an open mandibular fracture. Management of mandibular fractures is variable depending on location and whether the fracture is open or closed. Open fractures require admission and administration of intravenous antibiotics, such as a cephalosporin. Patients with closed fractures may be discharged with dental follow-up. Many fractures will require open reduction and internal fixation. This patient will require early operative intervention, and depending upon your institutional practice, otolaryngology, oromaxillofacial, or plastic surgery will need to be consulted to care for his injury.

The mandible is the second most commonly fractured facial bone behind the nasal bone. Signs and symptoms of a mandibular fracture include trismus, tooth misalignment, malocclusion of the bite, intraoral lacerations, and missing teeth. The tongue blade test is a way of detecting even subtle mandibular fractures. The patient bites the blade while the examiner attempts to break it. The inability to stabilize the blade is an indication that the patient may have a mandibular fracture and should undergo imaging. Plain mandibular X-rays and panoramic radiographs are appropriate screening tests for mandibular fractures. However, CT of the facial bones is the gold diagnostic standard for this injury.



Admission and intravenous metronidazole (B) would be an appropriate component of therapy for a serious anaerobic infection below the diaphragm as opposed to prophylaxis against skin and oral flora for an open facial fracture.

Discharge with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (C) would be inappropriate management of an open fracture of the mandible.

Discharge with oxycodone and close dental follow-up (D) would be an appropriate plan for a closed fracture of the mandible. However, this patient has an open fracture.

Question: A 32-year-old man without a significant medical history presents to the ED for knee pain. He was playing football and was tackled, falling onto his knee. He has severe pain, making it difficult to move his knee, and cannot perform a straight leg raise. An image of his affected knee is shown above. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee
Placement in a knee immobilizer and urgent orthopedic follow-up

CorrectAnswer: Placement in a knee immobilizer and urgent orthopedic follow-up
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a high-riding patella, which indicates a patellar tendon rupture. These injuries are more common in patients under the age of 40 who have direct trauma to a flexed knee. Risk factors include contact sports, chronic steroid use, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis is made with X-ray imaging showing a high-riding patella along with clinical signs of disruption of the knee extension system.

Patients will commonly present with a history of trauma to the knee, immediate pain, difficulty extending the knee, soft tissue swelling, and likely a palpable mass across the inferior quadriceps region (i.e., the patella itself). The typical mechanism for this injury is landing from a high jump or a sudden change in direction when the quadriceps is forcefully contracted.

The diagnosis is often made clinically, but X-rays may be helpful in ruling out other potential diagnoses or any associated injuries. Patients with partial or full patellar tendon tears should be placed in a knee immobilizer, instructed to be non-weight-bearing, and given urgent orthopedic follow-up, as delay in care can lead to poor functional outcomes.



This patient has a clear history of trauma and evidence of patellar tendon rupture on imaging, so an arthrocentesis (A) to rule out infectious or rheumatologic etiologies of his pain is unnecessary.

An emergent orthopedics consultation (B) in the emergency department is not necessary. However, urgent follow-up is indicated, as delays in management can lead to quadriceps contractures and adhesions and poor final range of motion outcomes.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (C) is rarely indicated in the emergent setting, especially for joint pain. MRI is reserved for patients with unclear partial thickness injuries or significant intra-articular changes and can be performed nonemergently.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department unresponsive after being backed over by a vehicle. His abdomen is distended and has wheel marks crossing it transversely. Bilateral tibial intraosseous access is obtained, and he is rapidly intubated and given isotonic boluses while blood is prepared. An e-FAST exam is negative. After the first two units of blood, his heart rate is still 190 bpm, with blood pressure unchanged at 64/32 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN:
An e-FAST is an excellent adjunct in hemodynamically unstable patients. This approach uses ultrasound to rapidly evaluate for free abdominal fluid, fluid in the pericardial sac, and pneumothoraces. Unfortunately, due to the increased organ-to-body mass ratio, children with severe intra-abdominal trauma are more likely to sustain a solid organ laceration than free intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Solid organ lacerations are less visible on an e-FAST evaluation. Due to the low sensitivity, a negative e-FAST does not rule out serious intra-abdominal injuries in children after multisystem trauma. An e-FAST should still be used in hemodynamically unstable children since it helps surgeons assess the location of necessary interventions (e.g., chest or abdomen) when positive. When children require an emergent craniotomy, it also can give an indication of the need for laparotomy when positive. An e-FAST should not be performed to limit abdominal CT use in children with blunt abdominal trauma. Hemodynamically unstable children with evidence of severe abdominal trauma and who are unresponsive to resuscitation should be taken to the operating room for a diagnostic laparotomy in an attempt to stop the bleeding and repair internal injuries. The only exception to this is when a patient requires a thoracotomy, in which case cross-clamping the aorta should prevent additional intra-abdominal hemorrhage.



While useful in resuscitation, central line placement (A) takes time and will delay operative intervention needed to stabilize a critically ill patient.

A computed tomography scan (B) of the abdomen is the diagnostic modality of choice in hemodynamically stable children with severe abdominal trauma. Children who are hemodynamically unstable, like this patient, should not be taken to CT scan.

An epinephrine infusion (D) is most likely to be futile early in hypovolemic shock due to endogenous secretion.

Question: A 22-year-old man presents to the ED after injuring his lower leg while playing soccer. He is found to have a comminuted tibia fracture on X-ray. He reports progressively worsening severe pain in the calf. He continues to scream in pain despite repeated doses of hydromorphone. On examination, he is afebrile with a heart rate of 110 bpm and blood pressure of 117/63 mm Hg. There is swelling of the midcalf with intact distal pulses and weakness with dorsiflexion of the foot. Based on your clinical suspicion, compartment pressure is measured and found to be 36 mm Hg. What is the delta pressure of the compartment?
ExplanationEN:
Occurring in the presence of increased pressure within a nonexpandable space, compartment syndrome results in decreased venous blood flow, worsening congestion, and eventual arterial compromise if left untreated. Most often associated with long bone fractures, compartment syndrome can also occur in the setting of soft tissue injury, crush injuries, and spontaneous hemorrhage. Clinically, patients present with pain out of proportion to the injury, pain with passive stretching of the muscles in the compartment, and paresthesias.

Pallor and loss of pulses are late and ominous findings. While compartment syndrome is diagnosed clinically, measurement of the pressure within the compartment can provide confirmation of the diagnosis. While compartment pressures < 30 mm Hg generally do not cause compartment syndrome, tolerance to tissue ischemia varies between individuals. Because of this, many sources advocate using the delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure - compartment pressure) as a more reliable indicator of compartment syndrome. A delta pressure < 30 mm Hg indicates the need for a fasciotomy. In this patient, the delta pressure is 63 - 36, or 27 mm Hg.



The delta pressure is calculated by subtracting the direct pressure of the compartment from the diastolic blood pressure. In this case, the delta pressure is 27 mm Hg, not 35 mm Hg (B).

The systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure (i.e., 54 mm Hg (C)) is not correct. Likewise, the systolic pressure minus the direct compartment pressure (i.e., 81 mm Hg (D)) is also not correct. While a single elevated pressure is concerning, rising or persistently elevated pressures are superior to a single measurement when confirming the diagnosis.

Question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle collision in which he was the front-seat passenger and hit a wall. His vital signs are within normal limits, and there is no evidence of open wounds or bleeding. Upon examination, the right leg is internally rotated and shortened. He reports severe pain with any attempts at hip movement. A pelvis X-ray is presented above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
A posterior hip dislocation takes a tremendous amount of force to occur. High-energy trauma typically precedes this injury, and patients often present with pain and a shortened, internally rotated lower extremity. This is an orthopedic emergency, as arterial injury and avascular necrosis may occur if not treated rapidly. Most native hip dislocations are posterior, though some can be anterior. A posterior dislocation presents on radiography with a femoral head posterior and superior to the acetabulum. If there is no fracture, closed reduction early can improve outcomes. Patients will need procedural sedation prior to reduction. After reduction, a thorough neurovascular exam must occur. The patient should be placed in a knee immobilizer and given hip precautions. The inability to reduce the hip requires orthopedic consultation and reduction in the operating room. Complications of posterior hip dislocation can include sciatic nerve injury, leading to motor and sensory deficits in the lower extremity. There is also a risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head due to disrupted blood supply. Additionally, patients may experience recurrent dislocations or develop post-traumatic arthritis, impacting long-term joint function and mobility.



In anterior hip dislocation (A), the affected leg is often externally rotated, contrary to the findings in this case. Native hip anterior dislocations are less common than posterior dislocations and occur when the hip is forced into hyperextension and external rotation.

Femoral neck fractures (B) typically present with external rotation of the leg, which contrasts with the internal rotation seen in this case. Additionally, femur neck fractures are more common in older adults with low bone density, unlike young patients involved in high-energy trauma. Movement and leg manipulation might still be possible, albeit painful, in femoral neck fractures, unlike the severe restriction typically observed in hip dislocations. Furthermore, there is no femoral neck fracture identified on imaging in this patient.

Intertrochanteric fractures (C) typically present with external leg rotation. The mechanism of injury for hip dislocations often involves direct, high-energy trauma that forces the thigh backward, common in vehicle collisions, contrasting with the more indirect impacts or falls associated with intertrochanteric fractures. Additionally, hip dislocations are more prevalent in younger patients due to traumatic events, whereas intertrochanteric fractures frequently occur in older adults due to osteoporosis and falls.

Open book pelvic fracture (D) generally presents with significant pelvic instability and pain, particularly upon compression or spreading of the hips, which differs from the internal rotation and shortening indicative of a hip dislocation. These fractures are also associated with potentially severe hemorrhage and signs of shock, which are not indicated in this scenario. Furthermore, the specific leg deformity and the mechanics of the injury align more closely with posterior hip dislocation rather than the broader pelvic instability seen in open book fractures.

Question: A 7-year-old boy is a restrained back seat passenger in a high-speed, frontal motor vehicle collision. He presents to the hospital with minimal sensation and 3/5 strength of his bilateral lower extremities. CT and MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord do not reveal any detectable abnormalities. Plain films of the legs do not reveal any fractures or other acute injuries. What is the expected long-term clinical course of this patient?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has neurologic deficits concerning for spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality, which typically resolves without any permanent neurologic deficits. Children are at highest risk for spinal cord injuries from falls, car crashes, and intentional trauma. Patients can present with symptoms of spinal cord damage, such as weakness, paresthesias, decreased reflexes, and urinary retention. Pediatric patients with neurologic deficits should have initial imaging with either plain radiographs or CT. If initial imaging does not reveal an abnormality and neurologic deficits persist, the patient should have an MRI to assess for intrinsic cord damage (such as edema). Many patients with normal CT scans will have MRI abnormalities, which indicate a higher likelihood of persistent neurologic deficits. Patients with no evidence of spinal cord change on MRI have an excellent prognosis, with nearly all patients having full recovery of function at 6 months. Patients are often treated with cervical bracing, though the practice is controversial, and the decision should be made in conjunction with a pediatric neurosurgeon.



Incomplete recovery (B) can occur in the setting of visualized damage to the spinal cord on MRI. Patients benefit from physical therapy regardless of the degree of partial damage.

No recovery (C) is expected from a complete transection of the spinal cord.

Patients with spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality can present late (up to 4 days after the injury), and initial deficits may transiently worsen (D) before improving.
