Question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling from a tree while trimming branches. The patient reports that prior to landing she grabbed onto a branch with her right hand, but lost her grasp and then fell to the ground. Upon arrival, the patient’s arm is held in the position shown above. Physical examination is notable for numbness along the patient’s right deltoid, a nontender humerus, intact radial and ulnar pulses, and the inability to move her right arm from above her head. Which of the following techniques is the appropriate management of this condition?
ExplanationEN:
Luxatio erecta (inferior shoulder dislocation) is the rarest type of glenohumeral dislocation, representing only 0.5% of all shoulder dislocations. The mechanism of injury is typically a high-energy axial load applied directly to the shoulder joint, or a forceful hyperabduction of the arm, such as a person suddenly grasping an object above their head while falling, as in the case with this patient. On examination, the classic appearance of an inferiorly dislocated shoulder is an arm locked in marked abduction with the forearm flexed and pronated. Thorough evaluation of the extremity is vital, as luxatio erecta carries the highest risk of neurovascular, fracture, and soft tissue injury of any shoulder dislocation.

Axillary nerve injuries are noted in up to 60% of cases, as seen with this patient reporting numbness along her deltoid, though most resolve after successful reduction. Up to one-third of patients have concomitant humeral fractures, approximately 10% sustain rotator cuff tears, and 3% develop axillary artery injuries. In cases of humeral neck or shaft fractures or vascular compromise, open reduction should be pursued to hasten repair of arterial injuries and reduce the risk of avascular necrosis, as closed reduction of an inferiorly dislocated shoulder with a fractured proximal humerus can worsen existing displacement.

When closed reduction is indicated, traction-countertraction is the preferred method, which involves overhead traction in the longitudinal tract of the abducted arm with simultaneous cephalad pressure on the humeral head by one provider, and countertraction directed toward the patient’s feet with a sheet wrapped around the shoulder by another provider. A second approach, called the “two-step” maneuver, would also be an appropriate technique for closed reduction. This involves first converting the inferior dislocation to an anterior one by applying stabilizing pressure to the medial epicondyle of the elbow, and then pushing on the humeral shaft and rotating the humeral head from an inferior to anterior location, followed by reduction of the anterior dislocation.



The Allis maneuver (A) is a method for reducing posterior hip dislocations involving one provider providing pelvis stabilization and another holding the extremity with the knee flexed and applying in-line longitudinal traction with the femur while gently adducting and flexing the hip until reduction is achieved.

Scapular manipulation (B) involves rotation of the scapula with medial and inferior traction with concurrent downward traction on the injured arm to allow the humeral head to relocate into the glenoid. This technique is used for anterior shoulder dislocations and is not a useful maneuver for luxatio erecta.

Similarly, the Stimson technique (C) is also utilized for anterior shoulder dislocations and involves a prone patient hanging the injured arm off of the stretcher with a 10–15 lb weight attached to the arm, with reduction taking approximately thirty minutes to achieve.

Reveal Answer:

Question: An 18-year-old hurdler tripped and fell, contacting the running track through his hyperextended left wrist. He presents to the ED with dorsolateral wrist pain, erythema, edema, and anatomic snuffbox tenderness. Initial anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique radiographs are negative for fracture. He is splinted and discharged. Which of the following should be recommended on his discharge paperwork?

Options.text: MRI in 4 weeks if pain persists
Primary care medical clearance examination for upcoming orthopedic surgery

ExplanationEN:
A fall onto an outstretched hand injury (outstretched refers to wrist hyperextension) is a common cause of scaphoid fracture, which represents the most common fractured carpal bone. The most common fracture site on the scaphoid is the waist. Since the blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally, any fracture or displacement > 1 mm is worrisome for complications of osteonecrosis and nonunion.

A scaphoid fracture should be suspected any time there is snuffbox tenderness. Wrist and scaphoid X-rays may be negative in the setting of acute fracture. Therefore, patients with snuffbox tenderness or suspicion of scaphoid fracture should be placed in a thumb spica splint with repeat radiographs or MRI in 10–14 days.



Bone scans (A) are sensitive for detecting occult fractures but are not the first-line follow-up since they expose patients to radiation, and repeat radiographs in 2 weeks are usually sufficient.

Waiting 4 weeks for repeat MRI (B) or plain radiographs is too long. Repeat imaging should occur within 10–14 days.

It is unknown if a true fracture is present at this time, so surgery (C) would not be arranged at discharge.

This wrist erythema and edema are related to trauma and not to an underlying rheumatologic condition (E).

One Step Further

Is osteonecrosis more likely with fractures of the scaphoid in the proximal or distal pole?

Reveal Answer:
The more proximal the fracture, the greater the likelihood of osteonecrosis.

Question: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver and his abdomen struck the steering wheel. Which of the following is most likely injured in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
One of the most common organs injured in blunt abdominal trauma is the spleen. The liver and spleen are the most commonly injured organs in the setting of a motor vehicle collision in which the patient hits the steering wheel. An injury to the spleen can cause bleeding, leading to hypotension, tachycardia, and a positive FAST exam that demonstrates free intraperitoneal fluid. However, the most common physical exam finding is abdominal tenderness with referred left shoulder pain. This is a specific finding in a splenic injury.

Any hemodynamically unstable patient presenting with abdominal pain and a positive FAST exam should be taken to the operating room for exploration and to stop the bleeding. Radiography that demonstrates left-sided lower rib fractures should increase suspicion of a splenic laceration. In uncertain cases of a visceral injury in a hemodynamically stable patient, an abdominal CT scan can further characterize potential injuries and helps plan operative care. Conditions that can predispose the spleen to rupture include infectious mononucleosis, which causes splenic enlargement, increasing the risk of injury with even minor abdominal trauma.



Colon (A) injury presents with abdominal pain and peritoneal signs with infection from colonic flora. The colon is less likely to be injured with blunt trauma and more likely to be injured with penetrating trauma.

The pancreas (B) can be injured in blunt abdominal trauma but is not nearly as commonly injured as the spleen and liver.

Small intestine (C) is less likely to be injured in blunt abdominal trauma. However, blunt abdominal trauma can cause pathologies such as a duodenal hematoma, which would present with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and obstruction of the duodenum on a CT scan.

Question: A 34-year-old, right-hand dominant man presents with pain and swelling of his left index finger. The patient is a painter and was using an industrial paint sprayer when he accidentally punctured his left index finger with the sprayer. At first, his finger was not painful but he has developed increasing pain and swelling. The finger is mildly swollen but no laceration, erythema, or warmth is noted. Range of motion is full and sensation and capillary refill are normal. In addition to splinting and elevation, which of the following represents the most appropriate management course?

Options.text: Admission to medical service for intravenous antibiotics
Discharge with urgent orthopedics follow up within 72 hours
Performance of bedside incision and drainage

ExplanationEN:
High pressure injection injuries are associated with high morbidity. Devices which spray liquids at high pressure can inject foreign material deep into soft tissue. This causes an inflammatory response and fibrosis which varies based upon the material injected. Paint and paint thinner cause an earlier, more intense inflammatory response and result in a high number of amputations. Grease injuries, on the other hand, cause a less intense inflammatory response and fewer amputations, but more often cause granuloma and fistula formation with loss of function.

Symptoms may be minimal immediately after the injury but swelling, vascular compromise and tissue necrosis develop in a matter of hours. X-rays may reveal the extent of spread of radio-opaque material and can show subcutaneous edema. Patients with these injuries should be splinted, given tetanus prophylaxis and broad spectrum antibiotics. The affected extremity should be elevated. Emergent hand surgery consultation is necessary as most cases require extensive surgical decompression and debridement.



This patient should not be admitted to a medical service for intravenous antibiotics (A) without hand surgery consultation as he will likely require surgical debridement.

Discharge with urgent orthopedics follow up within 72 hours (B) is inappropriate, as the inflammatory response is likely to progress in a matter of hours. A delay in treatment would likely lead to significant morbidity.

Performance of bedside incision and drainage (D) is inappropriate as this patient will require surgical exposure of the deep tissues of the hand to ensure adequate washout.

Question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a left ring finger injury after being kicked in the fingertips while sparring. On exam, the patient is unable to straighten the distal joint of the affected finger. The fingertip remains flexed when the fingers of the left hand are extended. There is pain and swelling around the distal interphalangeal joint. Which specific complication can be prevented if this injury is recognized early?
ExplanationEN:
The exam findings are indicative of mallet finger, an injury to the extensor tendon of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Improper or delayed treatment may lead to the complication of swan-neck deformity. This results in a permanent abnormal flexion of the DIP and involves the central slip. Symptoms often include pain, decreased grip strength, and difficulty with fine motor tasks. Conservative approaches may involve splinting and exercises to strengthen surrounding muscles. Immobilization of the DIP in full extension or 5–15 degrees of hyperextension is recommended. An aluminum splint can be applied, or a custom-made splint may be used. The metal ring splints are generally not recommended due to patient discomfort. In more severe cases or cases that are refractory to conservative measures, surgical intervention may be required. Given the high incidence of complications from mallet finger, referral to hand surgery is recommended.



Boutonniere deformity (A) involves flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint and hyperextension of the DIP, not hyperflexion of the DIP. This is the result of a rupture to the insertion of the extensor expansion into the base of the phalanx. Dupuytren contracture (B) is a progressive thickening of the palmar fascia of the hand, leading to contracture of the fingers. While post-traumatic arthritis (C) may be a common complication from any injury, it is not specific to injuries of the extensor tendon of the distal interphalangeal joint of the finger.

Question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the ED for bilateral eye pain. She was sitting by a fire for a few hours after a full day of skiing when she noticed gradually worsening bilateral eye pain, tearing, and photophobia. An example of her fluorescein exam is shown above. What is this patient’s most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Radiation burn, or ultraviolet keratitis, is characterized by diffuse corneal injury due to the direct effects of ultraviolet radiation. The classic fluorescein exam finding is diffuse punctate uptake due to the ultraviolet light causing corneal epithelial damage. Risk factors include snow sports, welding, and tanning bed use in patients who do not use or improperly use eye protection. Diagnosis is made with a fluorescein exam. Patients commonly have a delayed onset, of up to 10 hours, of symptoms from initial injury. Symptoms include bilateral eye pain, photophobia, and tearing. Physical exam may reveal conjunctival injection and decreased visual acuity. Treatment is with ophthalmic antibiotics and cycloplegics, although the benefit of antibiotics is weak. Patients should have ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours if their symptoms have not resolved. Ultraviolet keratitis often resolves within 24 hours.



Herpes keratitis (A) presents on fluorescein exam with dendritic lesions with or without the classic clear vesicles on the eyelid or conjunctiva. It is treated with a topical antiviral, like trifluridine, cycloplegics, and an emergent ophthalmologic evaluation.

Smoke irritation (C) will commonly present with bilateral conjunctival injection and a normal fluorescein exam. Avoidance of the source of irritation is the first-line treatment.

Thermal burns (D) more commonly present as eyelid injuries due to the Bell phenomenon. If there is a thermal burn to the globe, patients most commonly present with superficial corneal lesions that are treated as corneal abrasions.

Reveal Answer:

Question: What organ is the most common site of injury for gunshots to the abdomen?
ExplanationEN:
Traumatic injury remains the leading cause of death for individuals under the age of 45 years, with abdominal trauma accounting for up to 20% of deaths. The vast majority of the mortality associated with abdominal injuries is related to penetrating trauma, most commonly from stabbing and gunshot injuries. Gunshot wounds represent 90% of deaths in patients with traumatic abdominal injuries due to the concomitant physical tissue injury from the projectile and the transmission of energy from the blast. The extent of trauma from gunshots widely varies based on the caliber, trajectory, fragmentation, and spread of bullets. The trauma carries the potential for injury to all intra-abdominal viscera including the liver, colon, and abdominal vasculature. The small intestine is the organ most commonly injured by abdominal gunshots and is seen in approximately 50% of cases. With the advent of advanced diagnostic imaging including bedside ultrasound and high-resolution CT scanning, a rise in rapid and accurate identification of solid and hollow viscus injuries and particularly small bowel injuries has resulted in decreased emergent laparotomies, selective nonoperative management of appropriate patients, and improved overall morbidity and mortality rates.



The liver (A) is the most common site of injury for abdominal stab wounds, and though it is a common site of trauma from gunshots, it is less frequently injured than the small intestine.

Injuries to the pancreas (B) are seen with both blunt and penetrating abdominal injuries but to a lesser extent than other structures.

The spleen (D) is the most common organ injured in sports-related blunt abdominal trauma and is noted more frequently in patients with blunt traumatic injury as opposed to penetrating abdominal trauma.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED after being stabbed in his left precordium. Vital signs are BP 85/42 mm Hg, HR 125 bpm, RR 14/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. On exam, he is awake and alert. You hear bilateral breath sounds and his abdomen is soft and nontender. You perform a FAST exam as seen above. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Admit to floor and obtain echocardiogram in the morning
Obtain surgical consultation for emergent thoracotomy in the operating room

CorrectAnswer: Obtain surgical consultation for emergent thoracotomy in the operating room
ExplanationEN:
In patients with suspected penetrating cardiac injury, the FAST exam can be a very useful test to guide patient management. Echocardiography is very sensitive for detecting even small amounts of pericardial fluid. Studies show that the pericardial window of the FAST exam is highly accurate and should be the initial modality for the evaluation of the patient with suspected penetrating cardiac injury. It is currently recommended that patients with penetrating torso trauma who are found to have hemopericardium, regardless of hemodynamic stability, should undergo emergent operative intervention and it should be noted that this recommendation is not influenced by the size of the pericardial effusion or absence of tamponade physiology.



Admitting the patient to the floor (A) for observation and echocardiogram in the morning is dangerous since the patient has hemopericardium on the FAST exam and is at great risk of sudden deterioration.

An emergency department thoracotomy (C) is contraindicated in the awake, alert patient with vital signs. This procedure is reserved for those patients with penetrating chest trauma who lose their vital signs enroute to the ED or in the ED.

Bilateral tube thoracostomies (D) is indicated when there is suspicion for bilateral pneumothoraces. This patient has bilateral breath sounds.

Question: In patients with displaced fractures of the proximal humerus, which of the following are they most at increased risk of developing?
ExplanationEN:
Fractures of the humerus can occur distally, mid-shaft, or proximally. The incidence of the latter is increasing, accounting for approximately 5% of all fractures. Incidence increases with age, and nearly three-quarters occur in patients > 60 years. Major risk factors include frequent falls and low bone mineral density, as falls are known to be the most common associated mechanism of injury. Concomitant glenohumeral dislocations are sometimes seen. Most proximal and mid-shaft fractures are nondisplaced, but those that are displaced pose greater challenges in terms of both potential complications and management.

Clinically, proximal humerus fractures usually cause significant shoulder pain that increases with shoulder movement. Patients often hold their arm in adduction, and swelling and ecchymosis may be present. There are no physical examination maneuvers specific for proximal humerus fractures, but distal neurovascular function must be evaluated to assess for associated nerve or vascular injury. The axillary and suprascapular nerves are the most commonly injured in cases of proximal humeral fracture. Plain X-rays should be obtained, including anteroposterior, axillary, and scapular Y views, to evaluate the humerus and glenohumeral joint. CT is recommended if the initial X-rays are nondiagnostic or if further information regarding the anatomy of the fracture is needed.

Most proximal humerus fractures are nondisplaced and can be treated nonsurgically, but those with significant displacement or involvement of the humeral neck should be referred for orthopedic evaluation. The most common complication of proximal humeral fracture is impaired shoulder mobility, ranging from clinically insignificant to adhesive capsulitis. This is more likely to occur in patients who do not perform proper range of motion exercises during the recovery period from the acute injury. Other complications include axillary or suprascapular nerve injury, circumflex artery injury, rotator cuff tear, glenohumeral dislocation, and avascular necrosis, though the latter is uncommon.



Avascular necrosis (A) and brachial plexus injury (D) are possible complications of proximal humeral fracture but occur less frequently compared to axillary nerve injury.

The brachial artery (C) is typically located too distally to be injured with an isolated proximal humerus fracture.

Mid-shaft humerus fractures rather than proximal humerus fractures are classically associated with radial nerve injury (E).

Question: A 73-year-old man presents after a fall. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14, and his vital signs are within normal limits for his age. An image of his ear canal is shown above. What other physical examination finding is associated with this injury?
ExplanationEN:
Basilar skull fractures are often diagnosed clinically based on characteristic findings on the physical examination. Basilar fractures are linear breaks in the base of the skull, most commonly through the temporal bone. The injury may also cause a dural tear. The presence of a basilar skull fracture implies significant force in the traumatic injury although does not necessarily predict significant intracranial pathology. The image above demonstrates hemotympanum, a collection of blood behind the tympanic membrane visualized on inspection of the ear canal. Periorbital ecchymosis is also known as the Raccoon sign. Other physical examination findings associated with a basilar skull fracture include blood in the ear canal, rhinorrhea, otorrhea, retroauricular hematoma (Battle sign), cranial nerve deficits (facial paralysis, tinnitus, impaired hearing, nystagmus). Rhinorrhea and otorrhea with clear liquid suggest a CSF leak secondary to the basilar skull fracture. Patients with a CSF leak are at risk of developing meningitis and some suggest administering prophylactic antibiotics. Depending on the location of the injury, cranial nerves may become entrapped if they pass through the basal foramina. The fracture is diagnosed definitively on a CT scan of the head, often ordered with thin cuts through the temporal bone.



Crepitus over the parietal bone (A) is not associated with a basilar skull fracture. Crepitus implies subcutaneous air or possibly the sensation when broken pieces of bone rub together. The parietal skull is not the location of a basilar skull injury. A scalp hematoma (C) is often associated with an underlying skull fracture. In children < 2 years, the presence of a scalp hematoma anywhere on the skull with the exception of the forehead is an indication to perform imaging to rule out a fracture or intracranial injury. A scalp hematoma is not necessarily a marker for basilar skull fracture. A septal hematoma (D) is seen on inspection of the nasal cavity with nasal injuries. Patients with nasal trauma need the nares inspected to identify a septal hematoma. In order to prevent necrosis of the septum, the hematoma must be drained.

Reveal Answer:
Most heal spontaneously in one week.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents after a high-speed, rollover motor vehicle collision. Vital signs are a T of 98.5°F (36.9°C), BP of 89/50 mm Hg, HR of 145 bpm, RR of 22/min, and SpO2 of 96% on room air. On physical exam, he is anxious and clammy but is awake and alert. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally, and his abdomen is nontender. There is ecchymosis above the right inguinal ligament, and his pelvis is unstable. Pelvic X-ray shows an open-book pelvic fracture. The eFAST exam is negative for free fluid in all views. A pelvic binder is placed, and a massive transfusion protocol is initiated. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis

ExplanationEN:
Pelvic ring fractures result from high-energy blunt trauma. Motor vehicle collisions, motorcycle injuries, and pedestrians struck by vehicles are the most common mechanisms of injury. Pelvic fractures can lead to significant hemorrhage, and the presence of a pelvic fracture is an independent risk factor for death in the trauma patient. The pelvic ring is composed of the sacrum and paired innominate bones, which include the pubis, ischium, and ilium. These bones are held together by several strong ligaments, and ligamentous disruption can lead to pelvic instability. Vertical shear, lateral compression, and anterior-posterior compression forces produce characteristic fracture patterns, which are further classified as stable or unstable based on the degree of ligamentous disruption, bony injury, and displacement. An open-book fracture refers to an anterior-posterior compression injury with widening of the pubic symphysis and is unstable if there is > 2.5 cm of widening. The thin-walled pelvic veins are easily sheared by blunt force and are the source of most pelvic bleeding. The initial treatment of the hemodynamically unstable patient with a suspected or confirmed pelvic fracture includes external stabilization with a commercial pelvic binder or sheet to decrease pelvic volume and tamponade bleeding and resuscitation with blood products. Due to the significant force required to break the pelvic ring, pelvic fractures often occur in conjunction with other life-threatening injuries, most commonly intra-abdominal injuries. Thus, an important part of management includes excluding other significant injuries that require emergent intervention, mainly intraperitoneal and intrathoracic hemorrhage.

The eFAST exam is a reliable bedside tool for excluding intraperitoneal hemorrhage in the patient in shock. The hemodynamically unstable patient with a suspected or confirmed pelvic fracture who has an eFAST exam positive for intraperitoneal free fluid should go immediately to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy. This is also true of patients with significant thoracic bleeding, which may be identified on chest X-ray or by chest tube output. Preperitoneal packing to control pelvic hemorrhage can be performed concomitantly in the operating room. If the eFAST exam is negative and there are no other obvious sources of bleeding, controlling pelvic hemorrhage is the priority. Definitive treatment of pelvic bleeding will depend on institutional protocols and resource availability. Angiography and embolization of pelvic vessels is often the preferred initial treatment. However, given that most pelvic bleeding is venous, this is not always effective. Other potential treatment options include preperitoneal packing, resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta, and external stabilization. Some institutions have hybrid surgical suites allowing for operative intervention and angiography to occur simultaneously. Treatment decisions should be made in conjunction with a trauma surgeon, orthopedic surgeon, and interventional radiologist. The patient above, who is hemodynamically unstable with an open-book pelvic fracture and a negative eFAST exam, should be treated with angiographic embolization.



CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis (B) is useful in hemodynamically stable patients to further characterize the pelvic fracture, identify arterial bleeding amenable to embolization, and evaluate for other injuries. However, CT will delay definitive treatment and is not appropriate in the hemodynamically unstable patient.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) (C) may be performed in hemodynamically unstable patients with a negative eFAST exam and no other obvious source of bleeding to further evaluate for intraperitoneal hemorrhage. However, in this patient with an unstable pelvic fracture and a negative eFAST exam, the pelvic fracture can be presumed to be the source of bleeding and performing a DPL is unnecessary.

Exploratory laparotomy (D) is indicated in the hemodynamically unstable patient with a pelvic fracture if the eFAST exam is positive for intraperitoneal fluid.

Question: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle collision, and she has a large hematoma on her forehead and a tourniquet on her left arm to slow an arterial bleed. She has a blood pressure of 87/52 mm Hg and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7. What is the best initial fluid resuscitation strategy in this patient?

Options.text: Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells to restore normal blood pressure
Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells with permissive hypotension
Crystalloid infusion to restore normal blood pressure, up to 6 L

CorrectAnswer: Crystalloid infusion and packed red blood cells to restore normal blood pressure
ExplanationEN:
This patient has hemorrhagic shock from an arterial bleed and has signs concerning for intracranial hemorrhage (blunt trauma to the forehead and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7). Fluid resuscitation is a critical and time-sensitive intervention in hemorrhagic shock. Although crystalloid products are often used initially, hemorrhagic shock should be treated with blood transfusion. Permissive hypotension can be an acceptable strategy in the case of isolated hemorrhage but is contraindicated in the setting of severe head trauma. Intracranial hemorrhage increases intracranial pressure. If mean arterial pressure is decreased while intracranial pressure is increased, cerebral perfusion pressure may diminish dramatically leading to irreversible brain damage.



Colloids (A), such as albumin, are not superior to crystalloids for resuscitation in hemorrhage and should be avoided because of their relative expense.

Permissive hypotension (C) is contraindicated in those with suspected intracranial hemorrhage.

Crystalloids (D), such as normal saline or Ringer lactate, can be used initially for resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock, but blood is the preferred resuscitative product. As a general rule, patients with hemorrhagic shock should receive no more than 2 L of crystalloid before blood products are also administered.

Question: A 15-year-old girl presents to the ED with a gunshot wound to the upper right chest. She is confused and agitated but cooperative with instructions. Her heart rate is 165 bpm, blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 84% with a nonrebreather facemask. She has diminished lung sounds on the right and is struggling to breathe. Two large bore intravenous lines are being placed, and uncrossmatched whole blood is hung. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient's care?

Options.text: Endotracheal intubation with etomidate and rocuronium
Thoracostomy tube placement on the right

CorrectAnswer: Thoracostomy tube placement on the right
ExplanationEN:
The advanced trauma life support (ATLS) system was designed by the American College of Surgeons to standardize the care of trauma patients. The primary survey has historically been a rapid evaluation of the airway, breathing, circulation, and disability, and ends with exposure of the patient. This assessment is considered the ABCs of trauma, each step occurring in rapid succession with the goal of completing a primary survey within moments of the patient’s arrival. A change adopted in 2025 by the ATLS system is the xABCDE approach, which involves first finding and controlling catastrophic hemorrhage (e.g., with the application of a tourniquet or compression) to prevent exsanguination before evaluating the airway.

Previous training emphasized securing an airway with an endotracheal tube as soon as possible in hemodynamically unstable patients. Newer training encourages running processes in parallel with goal endpoints of endotracheal intubation, venous access, and stabilizing hemodynamics. Medically optimizing a patient for endotracheal intubation can reduce the risk of hemodynamic collapse and enhance success rates by improving intubation conditions. This patient is showing signs of severe hypovolemic shock and is at risk of cardiovascular collapse from loss of sympathetic tone or worsening hypoxia, both of which could occur with immediate rapid sequence intubation.

This patient has diminished lung sounds on the right, and the placement of a thoracostomy tube on the right is both diagnostic and therapeutic for either pneumothorax or hemothorax. Most patients will need some amount of sedation to tolerate a thoracostomy tube, so delayed sequence intubation using ketamine is most appropriate. This would also allow bag-mask ventilation in this confused patient. The thoracostomy tube would result in lung reexpansion and should improve oxygenation. This and the addition of a blood transfusion could normalize her hemodynamics for endotracheal intubation. This would allow the patient to tolerate a longer period of apnea during intubation without cardiopulmonary collapse.



Patients who are somewhat aware are less likely to tolerate bag-mask ventilation (A), and while this may improve the hypoxia, it is less likely to optimize moving toward endotracheal intubation when done without sedation.

Directly moving to rapid sequence endotracheal intubation (B) before optimizing hemodynamics will give a shorter period of time to perform the intubation without cardiopulmonary collapse.

An eFAST exam (C) would confirm the diagnosis of either a pneumothorax or a hemothorax, but a thoracostomy tube would also treat the problem and could improve hemodynamics.

Question: Which of the following tests evaluates for a meniscal injury of the knee?
ExplanationEN:
The knee is a complex modified hinge joint consisting of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints. The medial and lateral menisci are cushions that reduce friction between the femoral and tibial condyles. Meniscal tears can result from trauma or age-related degenerative changes. Clinical features pointing to a meniscal injury include pain and tenderness along the joint line or a clicking or popping felt with flexion and extension. Patients may be unable to fully extend the knee.

The McMurray test is used to screen for a meniscal tear. In this test, the patient lies supine with the knee hyperflexed. To perform the test, the examiner uses one hand to stabilize the knee while using the other hand to internally and externally rotate the tibia on the femur, providing varus and valgus stress. A positive test result is a palpable clicking along the joint line or locking of the knee. Internal rotation assesses the lateral meniscus, while external rotation tests the medial meniscus. This test can be difficult to perform in the acute setting because swelling and pain preclude sufficient hyperflexion to perform the test.



The anterior drawer test (A) and Lachman test (B) both assess for anterior cruciate ligament injury.

The posterior drawer test (D) assesses for posterior cruciate ligament injury.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe burns after his clothes caught fire when he fell into a large fire pit. You estimate that 5% of his body surface area has third-degree or full-thickness burns, 15% has second-degree or deep partial-thickness burns, and 10% has superficial burns involving the entire left leg and a large part of the lower left trunk. He weighs 12.5 kg. Which of the following is the most appropriate amount and type of fluid to give to this patient over the first 8 hours, in addition to dextrose-containing maintenance fluids, based on the Parkland formula?
ExplanationEN:
Dehydration after severe burns is extremely common in children due to the loss of the skin’s function to retain moisture. Appropriate initial fluid resuscitation is important, as inadequate resuscitation leads to organ failure and death, and fluid over resuscitation leads to pulmonary edema. The Parkland formula and the Galveston Shriner formula are good starting guidelines, of which the Parkland formula is more commonly used for its easy application. The Parkland formula recommends giving 4 mL/kg multiplied by the percentage of body surface area burned over 24 hours. Half of the fluid is given over the first 8 hours, and the second half is given within the next 16 hours. Only second- and third-degree burns or partial- and full-thickness burns should be included in the percentage of body surface area calculation.

In this patient, the recommended fluid volume in the first 24 hours is 4 mL × 12.5 kg × 20% body surface area, which is 1,000 mL. Half of this should be given in the first 8 hours, or 500 mL. This fluid is in addition to dextrose-containing intravenous maintenance fluids. Lactate Ringer solution is the typical recommended fluid choice in these patients to prevent hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and is preferred by many burn centers, but the choice of fluid and formula used should depend on the preference of the burn center that will be providing further care.



1,000 mL of normal saline (A) is the recommended amount of fluid over the first 24 hours when using the Parkland formula, which should be halved for the first 8 hours.

A 20 mL/kg bolus, 250 mL of normal saline (B) in this patient, is often used while performing an initial evaluation but frequently underestimates the amount needed over the first 8 hours in severely burned patients.

750 mL of lactate Ringer solution (D) is more fluid than recommended in the first 8 hours but is a common mistake when superficial burns are included in the calculation.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being stabbed in the chest. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 97/58 mm Hg, heart rate is 120 bpm, respiratory rate is 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a large right chest wall wound with audible air movement through the wound upon inspiration and expiration. Which of the following is the best initial step in management?
ExplanationEN:
An open or communicating pneumothorax occurs when a traumatic chest wall defect allows ambient air to enter the pleural space during inspiration and expiration. This causes tension physiology, a mediastinal shift, and persistent collapse of the ipsilateral lung. During expiration, when pressure in the thoracic cavity increases, air leaves via the wound, and tension physiology is somewhat relieved (in contrast to a tension pneumothorax in which there is communication via the wound that primarily allows air to enter the chest but not to leave). Given the open communication of the wound with the external environment, an appropriate initial stabilization method is to place a vented dressing over the wound, which allows air to leave the chest and minimizes air entry back into the chest during inspiration. Subsequent management of this sealed-off open pneumothorax may involve chest tube placement and operative repair.



Needle decompression (A) would be a good initial step in the management of a tension pneumothorax which would present with unilateral absent breath sounds, jugular venous distension, hypotension, tachycardia, and tracheal shift. In the case of open pneumothorax, there is already open communication with the external environment via the sucking chest wound, and it is less likely to be effective to place another hole in the chest wall to relieve pressure when there is a large wound already present in this patient’s chest wall.

Placement of a chest tube (B) would be indicated for treatment of a large spontaneous pneumothorax or as an immediate intervention in a patient with a traumatic tension pneumothorax. It would also be indicated after initial management and stabilization of an open pneumothorax with a vented dressing. However, it should not be performed until the opening in the chest wall has been addressed.

Performing a thoracotomy (D) would be indicated for a pericardiotomy (for cardiac tamponade), for temporary repair of myocardial wounds, and for cross-clamping of the aorta to reduce exsanguination in the abdomen and improve perfusion of vital organs during traumatic cardiac arrest.

Question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after being involved in a head-on motor vehicle collision. Which of the following is the most appropriate reason to perform a computed tomography scan of his abdomen?

Options.text: He has 4 RBCs/hpf in a catheterized urine sample
He was restrained in a 5-point child harness car seat
His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 9

CorrectAnswer: His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 9
ExplanationEN:
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan is an important test for the evaluation of pediatric trauma patients. In general, abdominal CT should be considered for patients with a severe trauma mechanism and abdominal tenderness, elevations in liver function tests, a hematocrit < 30% (hemoglobin < 10 g/dL), and a urinalysis with > 5 RBCs/hpf. Neurologic impairment in the face of probable multisystem trauma is also a reason to perform a CT scan of the abdomen in a pediatric patient. Vehicle collision is a major cause of blunt trauma, but abdominal trauma accounts for only 10% of injuries in children. In blunt abdominal trauma, the most commonly injured organs are the spleen and liver. Most injuries are managed conservatively, healing without surgical intervention. In the setting of an inability to complete a physical examination due to mental status, a CT scan is the most appropriate choice to aid the clinician in the immediate assessment of the patient. Generally, a CT scan can be considered sensitive enough to diagnose solid organ injury, but this is not the case for hollow viscus injury.



A hematocrit of 37% (D) is normal for a child this age, and while it may serve as a baseline to monitor for a downward trend alone, it is not a reason to perform a CT scan.

A 5-point harness (B) is the safest manner of restraining a passenger in a motorized vehicle. It decreases the risk of major injury in patients involved in a motor vehicle collision.

Any number of red blood cells in a catheterized urine sample (A) may be a reason to perform a CT scan, although there is debate as to the cut-off value. Most recommend that any number between 5 and 50 RBCs/hpf should lead a clinician to suspect intraabdominal injury.

Question: A 46-year-old woman presents as a restrained driver who required prolonged extraction from a high-speed motor vehicle collision. In the ED, her HR is 125 bpm, BP is 80/50 mm Hg, RR is 22/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. The exam reveals mobility of her right iliac crest and a large volume of fluid in Morison pouch on the FAST exam. A chest radiograph is normal. Two large-bore IVs are placed and blood products are ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Activation of the interventional radiology suite
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Immediate placement of an external fixation device by an orthopedic surgeon
Transfer to the operating room for laparotomy

CorrectAnswer: Transfer to the operating room for laparotomy
ExplanationEN:
This patient has sustained blunt abdominal trauma, a management challenge to both emergency medicine physicians and trauma surgeons. Motor vehicle collisions are the most common cause of blunt abdominal trauma. The spleen is the solid organ most likely to be injured. In patients who are hemodynamically unstable, the source of bleeding is usually from the abdomen, pelvis, or thorax. Chest and pelvis radiographs are performed to evaluate for injury to the thorax and pelvis, respectively. A FAST ultrasound is highly sensitive for intraperitoneal bleeding. This patient is hypotensive and has a positive FAST ultrasound. Consequently, the most appropriate next step is exploratory laparotomy.



Interventional radiology (A) is a critical component in the management of pelvic injuries with suspected arterial bleeding and hemodynamically stable liver or spleen injuries that can benefit from angioembolization. However, when hypotension is present with blunt abdominal trauma and free intraperitoneal fluid, immediate exploratory laparotomy is needed. In some trauma centers, arterial embolization can be performed in the operating room concurrent with exploratory laparotomy. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (B) is appropriate in the normotensive patient or the hypotensive patient who responds to resuscitation and has a negative FAST exam. Placement of an external fixation device (C) is necessary for patients with disruption of the pelvis, most commonly from an open-book fracture. However, this procedure should not delay the transfer of the patient to the operating room and can be performed alongside the trauma surgeon.

Question: A 54-year-old man who takes an anticoagulant for a relatively recent deep vein thrombosis presents for evaluation of back pain that began after lifting weights at the gym today. He has been unable to ambulate due to profound lower extremity weakness. On examination, his cranial nerves are intact. He exhibits intact strength against an opposed force in his bilateral upper extremities proximally and distally. He is unable to flex or extend at the hips, knees, or ankles. He has diminished pain sensation below the umbilicus with intact position sense in his bilateral lower extremities. What is the likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Anterior cord syndrome can arise from a hyperflexion injury that causes contusion of the anterior spinal cord and can be related to hematoma formation, which could be a risk in this patient taking an anticoagulant. The spinothalamic tracts responsible for pain and temperature sensation and corticospinal tracts responsible for motor function are the anterior most cord structures often affected. Injury to these tracts leads to bilateral motor weakness and reduced sensation below the level of the injury. Sensation to vibration, position, and light touch remains intact. Magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine can aid in the diagnosis. Prompt evaluation for surgical correction should be considered to evaluate for a reversible underlying cause (e.g., fracture fragment compressing the spinal cord).



Cauda equina syndrome (B) involves lower extremity weakness, impaired bowel and bladder function (e.g., urinary retention, bowel or bladder incontinence), perianal anesthesia, diminished rectal tone, and hyporeflexia in the lower extremities, which can result from nerve root injury below L2. This patient’s injury appears to be higher than L2.

Central cord syndrome (C) manifests with loss of pain and temperature sensation and with bilateral upper extremity weakness that is more prominent than lower extremity weakness.

Conus medullaris syndrome (D) shares clinical findings seen in cauda equina syndrome but involves the spinal cord at the level of L2 and affects upper motor neurons to cause hyperreflexia of the lower extremities.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the ED after falling from a 10 ft ladder. On examination, he has an open, displaced tibia fracture with 1 cm overlying laceration and minimal active bleeding. Which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate for initial prophylaxis?
ExplanationEN:
A fracture that communicates with the skin surface is defined as an open fracture and represents a true time-dependent orthopedic emergency because of the risk of osteomyelitis. The high morbidity associated with bone infection requires rapid initiation of treatment, including early parenteral antibiotics, coverage of the wound with a moist sterile dressing, and urgent surgical washout and debridement.

Open fractures are commonly described using the Gustilo-Anderson classification, which stratifies injuries based on wound size, degree of contamination, soft tissue damage, and the presence of vascular injury.

Initial ED management focuses on hemorrhage control with a sterile pressure dressing after removal of gross debris, splinting of the extremity without reduction unless vascular compromise is present, and irrigation with saline, followed by coverage with saline-soaked dressings.

Antibiotic strategies include cefazolin for all open fractures, with gentamicin added for higher-grade injuries, while broad-spectrum beta-lactams such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam may provide equivalent coverage.

In cases involving farm injuries or potential fecal contamination, additional coverage with penicillin or ampicillin is recommended to address clostridial organisms.

Open distal tuft fractures of the fingers and toes are an important exception, as these injuries commonly result from crush mechanisms with an overlying skin wound and can usually be managed by the emergency clinician alone. Vigorous irrigation and debridement are sufficient treatment for these injuries when digital arterial flow is intact, and infections of the distal tuft are uncommon.



Doxycycline (B) has activity against atypical organisms and some gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens. However, it is not the first-line antibiotic for prophylaxis in open fractures. It lacks consistent coverage of Staphylococcus aureus and does not provide the same efficacy as cefazolin in this clinical context. Doxycyline may be used as part of a regimen for specific indications such as marine injuries or when unusual pathogens are suspected, but it is not for routine open fracture prophylaxis.

Gentamicin (C) is an aminoglycoside used for coverage of gram-negative organisms. It is not appropriate as monotherapy for open fracture prophylaxis. In type III open fractures (extensive soft tissue damage, high contamination), gentamicin is used in addition to cefazolin. For this patient with a type I open fracture, cefazolin alone is sufficient.

Penicillin (D) is reserved for specific situations, such as prophylaxis against Clostridium perfringens in farm-related injuries or when anaerobic contamination is a concern. It is not the appropriate first-line agent for prophylaxis in a routine open tibial fracture without gross contamination. As monotherapy, it would inadequately cover the most common skin flora implicated in infection.

Question: A 23-year-old G1P0 woman at 27 weeks gestation presents to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. She reports abdominal cramping without associated vaginal bleeding. Physical examination is unremarkable, with the exception of a tender uterine fundus that is palpated just superior to the umbilicus. What is the minimum amount of time that fetal monitoring should be performed to adequately rule out uterine or fetal traumatic injuries?
ExplanationEN:
Trauma during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of preterm labor, placental abruption, fetomaternal hemorrhage, and pregnancy loss. Gestational age 22–24 weeks is generally considered compatible with fetal viability, and rapid assessment should occur on arrival to estimate the gestational age. A 20-week uterine fundus roughly reaches the level of the umbilicus. Placental abruption can occur in the setting of trauma and is the second leading cause of fetal demise. It occurs in approximately 1% of pregnancies. Direct abdominal blows or decelerating injuries are the most common etiology, and even injuries that were initially perceived as minor are associated with placental abruption.

Placental abruption can present with a rigid, boardlike uterus or no signs may be evident at all. The most sensitive clinical finding, after trauma, is uterine irritability that may require monitoring to identify, as it might not be evident clinically. External tocodynamometry monitoring of a potentially viable fetus for 4–6 hours appears sufficient to predict immediate adverse pregnancy outcomes and is indicated for all pregnant patients evaluated for trauma, even without obvious signs of abdominal trauma. If during this time, uterine irritability is identified, the patient warrants admission and consultation with OB/GYN. After this observational period, if the patient remains symptom-free without any evidence of uterine irritability, the patient can be discharged with close follow-up.



Monitoring for 1 hour (A) or 2–3 hours (B) is not sufficient time to identify any uterine irritability.

Although monitoring for 7–9 hours (D) is sufficient to identify any uterine irritability, it is not the minimum amount of time to rule out injury.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED after getting punched in the eye in a bar fight. On physical exam, his affected eye does not look upward with upward gaze. CT imaging is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle on exam, and the CT scan shows a left orbital blowout fracture with disruption of the orbital floor and herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus. Orbital wall fractures are often suspected based on clinical examination and confirmed via CT scan. Approximately one-third of blowout fractures coincide with ocular injuries, such as abrasion, traumatic iritis, hyphema, lens dislocation or subluxation, retinal tear, or detachment. Thus, a thorough eye examination is essential. The most common sites for orbital blowout fractures are the inferior wall (maxillary sinus) and the medial wall (ethmoid sinus via the lamina papyracea). Medial wall fractures may lead to subcutaneous emphysema, which can worsen with sneezing or nose blowing.

Fractures of the inferior wall may trap the inferior rectus muscle, resulting in restricted upward gaze and diplopia. Other physical exam findings suggestive of this condition include enophthalmos, crepitus, and possible paresthesias inferior to the orbit (from infraorbital nerve injury). Other injuries, including ocular injuries such as an open globe, may be present. The diagnosis can be supported with a CT scan. Treatment may involve antibiotics, plastic surgery or otolaryngology consultation, sinus precautions, and possible surgical repair, though this can often occur outpatient at a later time. Surgery is generally indicated if there is muscle entrapment that affects ocular mobility and causes diplopia or significant cosmetic deformity. The timing of surgery is crucial and often performed within 2 weeks from injury to prevent fibrosis of the entrapped muscle. Patients with blowout fractures and normal initial eye exams should be referred to an ophthalmologist for a dilated exam to exclude any undetected retinal issues.



Le Fort fractures (A) are broken up into several types. These are complex fractures that involve the maxilla and surrounding facial bones but typically do not specifically impact eye movement unless there is extensive damage.

An open globe (B) is possible and should be worked up in patients with eye trauma. A teardrop-shaped pupil and Seidel sign on fluorescein stain may be seen on exam. While serious and needing immediate care, it does not usually cause restricted eye movement without other visible signs of globe injury like severe eye pain and visual loss.

Retrobulbar hematoma (D) is also possible in the setting of an orbital floor fracture. It would present with eye pain, proptosis (rather than enophthalmos), reduced visual acuity, and elevated intraocular pressure. It typically would not selectively affect upward gaze without other signs of elevated eye pressure.

Question: A patient presents with epistaxis following blunt trauma to the nose. Which of the following characterizations of an intra-nasal mass is most suggestive of a nasal septal hematoma?

Options.text: Complete blockage of the nasal cavity
No change in the size of the swelling with oxymetazoline
Presence of associated nasal bone fracture

CorrectAnswer: No change in the size of the swelling with oxymetazoline
ExplanationEN:
In any situation of nasal trauma, the examiner must inspect the inside of the nares for a septal hematoma. A septal hematoma looks like a large purple mass extending from the septum. In the setting of blunt trauma, submucosal blood vessels are torn and blood accumulates between the perichondrium and the cartilage of the septum leading to the hematoma. Within days, the hematoma can become infected and drainage is indicated. Additionally, the pressure of the hematoma on the septum may lead to necrosis and septal perforation. On physical examination, it is often difficult to distinguish between soft tissue edema as a result of blunt trauma or an actual hematoma. A septal hematoma should not change size with the administration of oxymetazoline.



Typically, a septal hematoma does not have a bright red discoloration (A) but is more purple in color due to the accumulation of blood under the perichondrium.

Both regular soft tissue swelling as well as a hematoma may cause complete blockage of the nasal cavity (B), so this cannot be used as a discriminatory criterion.

While septal hematomas are often associated with the presence of an associated nasal bone fracture (D), it is common to have significant soft tissue swelling without the development of a hematoma.

Question: A 30-year-old man presents with altered mental status after being struck in the head with a line drive while playing baseball. A computed tomography image is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
An epidural hematoma occurs due to accumulation of blood in the potential space between the dura mater and the skull. The most common primary mechanism of injury is blunt trauma to the temporal or temporoparietal area that causes a skull fracture and disruption of the middle meningeal artery. The classic progression of disease involves blunt head trauma that results in a loss of consciousness or altered mental status, followed by a period of lucidity and subsequent rapid neurologic deterioration. Diagnosis of an epidural hematoma is made via computed tomography, showing a hyperechoic biconvex-shaped hemorrhage in the temporal region that does not cross suture lines. This is in contrast to a subdural hematoma, which is crescent-shaped, may cross suture lines, and may occur anywhere in the brain. Patients with epidural hematomas are at risk for rapid herniation due to high-pressured arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery. Ideal treatment is neurosurgical evacuation. However, Burr hole placement in the emergency department is indicated in patients with midline shift, unequal pupils, a Glasgow Coma Scale score < 8, and anticipation of extended time to treatment by a neurosurgeon. Temporizing measures to reduce intracranial pressure (elevation of the head of the bed to 30°, mannitol, and hypertonic saline), maintenance of cerebral perfusion, prevention of cerebral vasoconstriction, and seizure prophylaxis (phenytoin, fosphenytoin) are also indicated.



Disruption of an arteriovenous malformation (A) is one of the mechanisms of subarachnoid hemorrhage in addition to the rupture of a cerebral aneurysm. Shearing of bridging veins (B) is the mechanism causing a subdural hematoma. Inflammation of the temporal artery (D) is the pathogenesis behind temporal arteritis, also known as giant cell arteritis.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents by EMS after being the unhelmeted operator of a motorcycle involved in a collision with a truck. He was found approximately 15 feet from where his motorcycle was found and was intubated at the scene for depressed mental status. His vital signs on arrival are HR 38 bpm, BP 62/40 mm Hg, T 36.2°C, and RR 14/min on mechanical ventilation. His extremities are warm, well-perfused, and without obvious deformity. His exam is otherwise significant only for widespread road rash. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s hypotension?
ExplanationEN:
Shock is a state of circulatory insufficiency that results in an imbalance of oxygen delivery and metabolic demand. It results in tissue underperfusion and end-organ dysfunction. The four broad categories of shock are hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive. The presentation above is most consistent with neurogenic shock in the setting of spinal cord injury.

Neurogenic shock is a type of distributive shock that occurs due to loss of sympathetic innervation, leading to extreme vasodilation from loss of sympathetic arterial tone. If spinal cord levels T1–T4 are damaged, loss of sympathetic innervation to the heart leads to bradycardia from unopposed vagal tone. This blocks the reflex tachycardia that would otherwise compensate for hypotension. Patients in neurogenic shock are typically hypotensive, bradycardic, and peripherally vasodilated, with well-perfused, warm extremities and good capillary refill. Neurogenic shock occurs in < 20% of traumatic spine injuries.



Cardiogenic shock (A) occurs secondary to decreased cardiac output, leading to underperfusion of the tissues. Cardiogenic shock may occur in the setting of decreased preload, increased afterload, or impaired myocardial contractility. Patients with cardiogenic shock may show symptoms of total body fluid overload, including lower extremity edema or jugular venous distention, though these are not required for the diagnosis. These patients show symptoms of poor circulatory flow, such as cool, pale extremities and slowed capillary refill.

Hypovolemic shock (C) occurs when decreased intravascular volume, either through hemorrhage or nonhemorrhagic fluid loss, causes decreased cardiac output, imbalance in oxygen supply and demand, and organ hypoperfusion. This decreased cardiac output leads to compensatory tachycardia to try to maintain stroke volume and an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Arterial and venous vasoconstriction lead to a narrowing of pulse pressure, a sign that is present well before the onset of hypotension. Patients with hemorrhagic shock present with signs of poor peripheral perfusion, such as weak peripheral pulses, paleness, poor capillary refill, and cool extremities. Cerebral hypoperfusion may lead to subtle mental status changes including anxiety and confusion.

Obstructive shock (D) results from a decrease in venous return or cardiac compliance due to a left ventricular outflow obstruction or a significant decrease in preload, as seen in cardiac tamponade or a massive pulmonary embolism. This, too, would present with tachycardia rather than bradycardia.

Question: A 37-year-old woman presents with a stab wound to the abdomen. Her vital signs are HR 157 bpm, BP 92/50 mm Hg, RR 22/min, and SpO2 96%. Physical examination reveals a single stab wound to the left upper quadrant and is otherwise unremarkable. The FAST exam is positive for fluid in the splenorenal space. What management should be pursued at this time?

Options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Transport to the operating room to undergo explorative laparotomy

CorrectAnswer: Transport to the operating room to undergo explorative laparotomy
ExplanationEN:
This patient has hemorrhagic shock from a penetrating abdominal injury and requires immediate operative management. Hemorrhagic shock in this patient is evidenced by a marked tachycardia. In young patients, a fall in blood pressure can be a late finding of hemorrhagic shock, as these patients are able to maximally vasoconstrict their peripheral vasculature in an effort to maintain perfusion. Heart rate, however, will rise earlier in the course. The assessment of a trauma patient with hemorrhagic shock should focus first on stabilizing the airway and breathing and then on reversible causes of circulatory collapse. These reversible causes include hemopneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, displaced long bone fractures, and in some cases, pelvic bleeding from the fracture. This patient does not exhibit any of these reversible causes. The FAST exam demonstrates free peritoneal fluid in the splenorenal space. FAST exam has a sensitivity of 60–95% for detecting as little as 100 mL of free fluid and an excellent specificity. As a result of the high specificity, a positive study should be immediately acted upon without delay and the patient should be brought to the operating room to undergo an explorative laparotomy. In the image below, the patient has free fluid in the presplenic space, which is another possible location for fluid to accumulate in the left upper quadrant.



A CT scan (A) of the abdomen and pelvis represents the optimal imaging modality for delineating all injuries in an abdominal trauma. CT is very sensitive for detecting vascular, solid, and hollow organ pathology. However, CT scan takes time, and delaying operative management in a patient with penetrating trauma and hemorrhagic shock can result in increased morbidity and mortality. Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) (B) consists of two procedures. The first is aspiration, and if negative, the clinician should proceed to lavage. DPL has been supplanted in recent years for the diagnosis of intra-abdominal injuries after trauma by FAST examination, as bedside ultrasound is faster and less invasive. However, in patients with multiple trauma and hemodynamic instability and an equivocal FAST, DPL can be used to differentiate an abdominal injury from a pelvic injury (which will have a negative DPL). In the presence of a clearly positive FAST exam, DPL is not necessary. A tube thoracostomy (C) is not indicated for this patient, as there are no signs of hemo- or pneumothorax.

Question: An 11-year-old girl presents after getting hit in the eye with a golf ball. She reports right eye pain and decreased vision. Examination reveals moderate periorbital swelling, conjunctival hemorrhage, and a teardrop-shaped pupil. Visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye, and she has light perception only in the right eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

Options.text: Eye shield, CT scan of the orbit, and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Measure intraocular pressure and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Ocular ultrasound and emergent ophthalmology consultation
Timolol drops, intravenous acetazolamide, and emergent ophthalmology consultation

CorrectAnswer: Eye shield, CT scan of the orbit, and emergent ophthalmology consultation
ExplanationEN:
This patient has a ruptured globe resulting from direct trauma to the eye. Blunt trauma to the eye causes a sudden elevation in intraocular pressure, leading to scleral rupture. Patients will present with ocular pain and decreased vision. Examination often reveals chemosis or subconjunctival hemorrhage overlying the scleral defect. If rupture occurs at the limbus, an irregularly shaped (teardrop) pupil may be seen.

Management of suspected globe rupture involves protection of the eye (optimally with a curved eye shield that does not touch the globe), CT scan of the orbit, 30-degree head-of-bed elevation, and emergent ophthalmology consultation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics should be administered, as well, to reduce the development of endophthalmitis. Historically, succinylcholine was contraindicated as a paralytic agent if the patient required intubation because it was believed that increasing intraocular pressure could lead to ocular extrusion. Recent studies have demonstrated a lack of increased poor outcomes with succinylcholine.



Although a decreased intraocular pressure (< 10 mm Hg) supports the diagnosis of a globe rupture, tonometry (B) should not be performed in patients with a high suspicion of a globe rupture, as any increase in pressure can worsen the defect or lead to extrusion of intraocular materials.

Ocular ultrasound (C) should be avoided for the same reason as avoiding tonometry as it will increase ocular pressure and cause extrusion of intraocular material..

Timolol drops and acetazolamide (D) are two treatments directed at reducing intraocular pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Question: An 8-year-old girl presents after falling from the monkey bars onto an outstretched arm at recess. She reports pain over her distal forearm proximal to the wrist. A plain radiograph of the forearm is shown above. What type of bony injury is most consistent with this patient’s X-ray?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with bony tenderness after a fall. An X-ray of her forearm shows a transverse disruption of a single cortex without deformity of the opposite cortex, consistent with a greenstick fracture. During childhood, pediatric bones undergo remodeling and calcification of the cortices. While bones undergo ossification, they retain some plasticity that allows more resistance to fracturing under stress. Greenstick fractures occur when a force is strong enough to disrupt the cortex on the side of the force but does not penetrate the cortex on the side opposite to the force. The fracture is stable, as the periosteum and one cortex remain intact. The prognosis is good, with a minimal risk of bony deformity. Patients present with pain and swelling at the location of the fracture. Treatment generally involves immobilization and pain management.



Abuckle (torus) fracture is similar to a greenstick fracture and occurs in pediatric patients as a result of traumatic force. However, in a buckle fracture, the bony cortex on the side opposite the force is compressed and buckles outward without true cortical disruption. They are treated with a removable splint.

A bowing fracture (A) is a plastic deformation and bowing of a bone due to an external force without evidence of focal cortical compression or disruption.

Physeal fractures (D) affect the growth plate and are generally classified by the Salter-Harris classification based on which portion is involved. While a concomitant physeal fracture is possible with greenstick fractures, the patient’s pain is located proximal to her growth plate and the X-ray shows a greenstick fracture.

Question: A 16-month-old boy presents to the emergency department after a fall, not moving his left arm. His parent was in the bathroom when he heard a thump and a cry and found his son on the ground near a couch. He tried acetaminophen without effect and waited an hour before presenting to the ED. The exam is challenging as the patient is crying and anxious, but you do not find any obvious swelling or tenderness along the left forearm or elbow. His left shoulder has an appropriate contour. He cries excessively when picked up beneath his arms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Contact social services to report suspected child abuse
Obtain X-rays of the entire left arm and clavicle

CorrectAnswer: Obtain X-rays of the entire left arm and clavicle
ExplanationEN:
One of the most commonly fractured bones in children is the clavicle. This fracture can occur due to birth trauma, short falls onto the shoulder or outstretched hand, or a direct blow to the clavicle. This usually presents with pain on palpation of the clavicle or movement of the arm, occasionally with palpable movement of the bone fragments or a visible overlying hematoma. In nonverbal children, pain can sometimes be elicited by picking the child up beneath the arms. Clavicle fractures are confirmed by plain radiographs. Any child not moving their arm appropriately after a fall should have radiographs of the entire extremity to identify injury, even when the exam is unremarkable. This can be completed with an X-ray of the hand, forearm, humerus, and clavicle. In skeletally immature children, specific joint X-rays (e.g., wrist, shoulder) are less helpful in identifying fractures, with the exception of elbow films used to identify an occult supracondylar fracture commonly seen between 2 and 7 years of age.

Clavicle fractures are treated based on age and location of the fracture (medial, shaft, or distal), but most infants and young children can be treated conservatively with a sling and swath due to excellent fracture healing and remodeling. Fractures that require orthopedic intervention are open, tenting, have neurovascular compromise, or have suspected shoulder ligament injury. Proximal clavicle fractures typically occur in cases of major multisystem trauma, such as high-speed motor vehicle collisions. They are associated with head, neck, chest, and visceral injuries, and patients should undergo an additional trauma evaluation.



Contacting social services to report suspected abuse (A) is recommended whenever abuse is on the differential diagnosis. However, a midshaft clavicle fracture is common in this age group and easily plausible after a short fall.

Drawing serum inflammatory markers (B) is used to increase or decrease suspicion of a septic joint, which typically presents with a warm, red, and swollen joint. These patients often have fevers.

Performing pulled elbow reduction maneuvers (D) is only appropriate before X-rays in patients with a history of longitudinal traction on the arm and when there is no swelling or tenderness on exam.

Question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with eye pain, a hoarse voice, and a blistering rash. A few hours ago, he was with a parent on the outskirts of a riot, and they had to walk through a cloud of foul-smelling gas that tasted like onions. He initially seemed fine but now has severe photophobia and a cough. His parent reports similar but less severe symptoms. On exam, he has miosis, conjunctival injection, diffuse erythema of the skin, and developing bullae of the scrotum, axillae, and neck. Which of the following was the patient most likely exposed to?
ExplanationEN:
Skin erythema and blistering are unusual after an aerosolized chemical exposure but can be seen in vesicants, which are also known as blistering agents. These agents include sulfur mustard and lewisite. A type of phosgene is sometimes included in this group, as there is one that can cause skin pain but does not cause blistering.

Mustard gas rapidly depletes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and inhibits glycolysis, leading to cellular necrosis from adenosine triphosphate depletion. This presents with skin erythema, vesicles, and bullae after a short latent period. Eye involvement is common and manifests as photophobia, lacrimation, and blepharospasm. Serious lung injury is rare, but it can present with tracheobronchitis with hoarseness and sore throat. While exposure to this gas has a low fatality rate, it can be severely debilitating and frequently results in chronic bronchitis, emphysema, keratitis, skin scarring, neuropathic pain, and chronic pruritus.

Mustard gas was used most significantly in World War I but has been deployed in a number of conflicts since, including the Iran-Iraq War (1984–1988). Most injuries are caused by vapor exposure, but direct contact with the oily liquid will cause full-thickness burns. Clothes do not protect the individual, as the agent seeps through clothing and will affect skin that is warm, moist, and thin. As such, it is more likely to involve the perineum, scrotum, axillae, antecubital fossae, and neck. The vapor can also land on nearby objects and cause gluteal or perineal burns from someone sitting on a contaminated surface.

The chemical reaction is complete within minutes, so early decontamination is the most effective for preventing burns. Decontamination after a few hours can still help reduce the severity of illness, so it should be performed whenever exposure is suspected. As the chemical reaction is complete, the fluid inside the bullae will not contain any mustard gas. Treatment is otherwise supportive care. Eye injuries can be treated with mydriatic and antibiotic eye drops and petroleum jelly, and the blistering can be treated like a burn.



Phosgene (A) is a colorless gas described as smelling like sweet grass or newly mown hay. It is primarily a pulmonary irritant, and patients present with a cough, difficulty breathing, and chest tightness. Initially, they may be well-appearing but return a few hours later with severe respiratory distress from pulmonary edema. It does not affect the skin, although there is a type of phosgene that can cause skin pain but not blistering.

Patients exposed to a riot control agent (B) such as tear gas present with burning irritation of the eyes and a burning sensation over the skin and throat. They can also develop chest tightness, cough, and increased secretions. Although these agents can cause a burning sensation to the skin, they do not cause blisters as seen in this patient. Removal from exposure to the agent is usually sufficient treatment because it is primarily an irritant.

Tabun (D) is a nerve agent described as having a faint fruity odor that, when inhaled, causes rapid weakness, headache, bronchoconstriction, dyspnea, eye pain, and blurry vision. In large exposures, one or two breaths are all that is needed to cause rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, paralysis, and apnea. It does not cause the blisters seen in this patient.

Question: A healthy 33-year-old woman who has no medical history and does not take any medications presents to the ED due to concern for facial asymmetry in her forehead. She noticed this following a motor vehicle collision she was involved in several months prior. Following her collision, she was thoroughly evaluated with CT brain, facial bones, and cervical spine, all of which resulted without acute injuries. She was ultimately discharged from the ED after having a large forehead and scalp laceration repaired in the trauma bay. Assuming her new facial asymmetry is a direct result of her recent traumatic injury, which of the following is most likely responsible for her concern?

Options.text: Facial muscle paralysis following traumatic injury
Failure to identify a galeal defect
Laceration to a distal branch of the trigeminal nerve

CorrectAnswer: Failure to identify a galeal defect
ExplanationEN:
When evaluating scalp lacerations, care must be taken to perform a thorough wound exploration to identify defects of the galea. Failure to identify a galeal defect can result in facial asymmetry and deformities in facial expression. The galea is a thick fibrous layer just superficial to the periosteum and deep to the skin and connective tissue. It is the anchoring structure for the frontalis muscle. If the frontalis muscle loses its anchoring point, contraction can result in visible asymmetry. Furthermore, galeal repair after laceration prevents the spread of deep infection as well as subgaleal hematomas.

The galea should be repaired if the lesion is > 0.5 cm and can be done so in a simple interrupted fashion with your choice of absorbable sutures sized 3.0 or 4.0. Most scalp lacerations require repair, as the scalp is highly vascular, and closure may be required to prevent bleeding. Frontal scalp lacerations (covered by hair) in young men are considered cosmetic, as men are likely to bald later in life.



Though facial muscle paralysis following traumatic injury (A) is possible, this is less likely in this clinical scenario. The insulting injury is located on the scalp and forehead, not near the maxilla or ear, where one would expect the facial nerve. Given the location of the wound, only a small distal branch of the facial nerve could potentially be affected, which would be less likely to result in facial asymmetry.

In a woman who is not on anticoagulation, delayed intracranial hemorrhage is exceedingly unlikely. Furthermore, an indolent epidural hematoma (C) does not occur, as they are classically caused by the middle meningeal artery.

Though laceration of a distal branch of the trigeminal nerve (D) is theoretically possible, this would result in sensory deficit rather than muscular atrophy.
