Question: A 23-year-old man presents with left leg pain after being trapped in a collapsed building. Physical examination reveals abrasions, numbness, pain with passive range of motion of the ankle and foot, and weakness to dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. An X-ray is negative for fracture. Which of the following is most likely indicated?

Options.text: CT scan of the lower extremity
Discharge home to follow-up with orthopedics

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms highly concerning for compartment syndrome and should be taken emergently to the operating room for fasciotomy. Compartment syndrome results from increased pressure within a confined space leading to compromised tissue perfusion. Ultimately, hypoperfusion causes necrosis of muscle, nerves, and bone. Compartment syndrome often develops after major trauma but can also occur after relatively minor injuries. Both the amount of external pressure applied to the body part as well as the duration that force was applied are important factors in development of increased compartment pressures.

The clinical hallmarks of the disease are the 6 Ps – paresthesias, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, and pain out of proportion to exam. The most common early sign of a compartment syndrome is pain with passive stretch of the muscle contained within the compartment. Patients with suspected compartment syndrome and unequivocally positive clinical findings should immediately be taken to the operating room for fasciotomies. Any delay in treatment can result in increased tissue loss and potentially irreversible nerve damage.



CT scan of the lower extremity (A) may reveal tissue damage or subtle fractures but does not give information about the presence or absence of compartment syndrome.

Discharging home to follow-up with orthopedics (B) would be inappropriate as the patient needs to be taken to the operating room for a fasciotomy due to his physical exam findings.

Pain medications (C) should be given but observing a patient with compartment syndrome leads to increased morbidity.

Question: A 35-year-old man is brought in by EMS after being the restrained driver in a high-speed vehicle collision. On examination, he is noted to have malocclusion. When the forehead is held stationary and the upper teeth are grasped, there is movement of the maxilla without any movement of the nasal bridge. Which of the following best classifies the likely fracture pattern in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
The LeFort fractures are midface fractures that involve either complete or partial detachment of the maxilla from the skull. They are classified by their location and the bones involved in the fracture pattern. LeFort I fractures involve a transverse fracture line through the maxilla, separating the maxilla from the pterygoid plate and the nasal septum and detaching the hard palate from the skull. On examination, patients will exhibit maxillary movement when the upper teeth are rocked while the forehead is held steady. Other physical examination findings include facial swelling and ecchymosis. Unlike LeFort II and III fractures, LeFort I fractures are rarely associated with cerebrovascular involvement. Maxillofacial CT is the imaging modality of choice. Management is surgical.



A LeFort II (B) fracture is a pyramidal fracture pattern that includes the nasal bridge, maxilla, lacrimal bones, orbital floor, and orbital rim. In this fracture pattern, the entire nasal complex will move when the maxilla is rocked with the forehead held steady.

A LeFort III (C) fracture, also known as craniofacial dislocation, is characterized by a fracture line that travels transversely through the midface at the level of the nasal bridge and extends through the zygomatic arches. On examination, there is complete dissociation with motion of the entire midface from the cranium when the maxilla is rocked while the forehead is held steady.

While not universally used, some modern surgeons and texts use the term LeFort IV (D) to describe an even more severe injury that involves the same fracture pattern as LeFort III fractures but also involves the frontal bone.

Question: A 26-year-old professional football player presents to the ED for a knee injury. He was hit in the left leg while planted and immediately felt severe pain. It has subsided somewhat but is still present. He has no medical history. Vital signs are a T of 99°F (37.2°C), BP of 144/85 mm Hg, HR of 102 bpm, and RR of 20/min. X-ray of his knee is shown above. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ on the right and absent on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

Options.text: Closed reduction with repeat neurovascular exam
CT angiography of the lower extremity
Transfer to the operating room for open reduction

CorrectAnswer: Closed reduction with repeat neurovascular exam
ExplanationEN:
Tibiofemoral (knee) dislocations are true limb-threatening orthopedic emergencies due to the high frequency of associated neurovascular injury. They most commonly occur in cases of high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions and sports injuries, though they are relatively uncommon. By nature, they are always associated with significant ligamentous injury due to the degree of ligamentous destabilization required to displace the tibia and femur from each other.

Some tibiofemoral dislocations will reduce spontaneously prior to arrival to the hospital, but those that do not are typically obvious on physical exam. There is often significant hemarthrosis and ecchymosis, and deformities of the joint itself may be apparent. Plain radiographs of the knee will typically confirm the diagnosis and provide better detail regarding the specific anatomic deformity in each patient, thus guiding subsequent reduction. In situations in which there is an unclear presence of popliteal artery injury, vascular imaging in the form of duplex ultrasound, ankle-brachial indices, or CT angiography is indicated.

Reduction should occur at the earliest opportunity within the secondary trauma survey, with neurovascular status documented afterward. So-called “hard” signs of vascular injury include absent pedal pulses, expanding popliteal hematoma, audible bruit or palpable thrill, and popliteal hemorrhage and warrant immediate consultation with a surgeon and transfer to the operating room for repair. “Soft” signs warranting further investigation include asymmetric pedal pulses, nonexpanding hematoma, significant hemorrhage at the scene, proximate bony injury or penetrating wound, and paresthesias in the leg or foot. In the absence of popliteal artery injury, patients with tibiofemoral dislocation can be observed for 24 hours post-injury, with ankle-brachial indices performed every 4 hours to assess for developing vascular compromise.



Ankle-brachial indices (A) and CT angiography (C) can be used in patients with soft signs of vascular injury, while this patient has absent pulses, requiring immediate intervention.

IV heparin (D) is indicated in cases of acute limb ischemia due to thrombotic or embolic events rather than the mechanical injury present here. Heparin may actually worsen an associated hematoma or external hemorrhage from the popliteal artery.

Closed reduction with repeat neurovascular exam should occur to determine whether emergent operative intervention (E) is needed. If the patient is neurovascularly intact following reduction or only soft signs of vascular injury are present, immediate operative intervention is not indicated.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents with a partial thickness burn to his forearm from a grease fire. Which of the following topical agents has been shown to delay wound healing?
ExplanationEN:
Burn injuries result in approximately 450,000 patients seeking medical attention in the United States each year, with 10% of these patients requiring hospitalization. Burn severity is subdivided into four categories: superficial (first-degree), partial thickness (second-degree), full thickness (third-degree), and fourth-degree. First-degree burns are characterized by injury to the epidermis alone and appear erythematous with extreme tenderness to palpation. Second-degree burns are also very painful and are further divided into superficial partial-thickness burns (blanching erythema and exhibiting weeping or blisters) and deep partial-thickness burns (white or yellow coloration and dry). Third-degree or full thickness burns are black or white in coloration, nonblanching, feel leathery and dry, and exhibit loss of sensation. Fourth-degree burns extend to the bone.

Circumferential burns resulting in neurovascular compromise require escharotomy. Airway management is paramount in burn patients. Airway compromise can result in the immediate term from inhalation injury, leading to airway edema or lung injury, but can also present in a delayed fashion owing to airway edema from large volume resuscitation. Airway edema should be evaluated via laryngoscopy, and patients with edematous airways should receive awake intubation. Inhalation injury is suggested by large total body surface area (TBSA) burns, carbonaceous sputum, and facial burns. Patients with suspected inhalation injury should also be evaluated for carbon monoxide poisoning, which is treated with 100% oxygen via a nonrebreather mask.

Fluid resuscitation should be initiated for burns ≥ 20% TBSA using guidelines such as the Parkland formula with a goal urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Superficial epidermal burns require no dressing and can be treated with topical therapy such as aloe vera. Partial- and full-thickness burns should be cleaned with antiseptic and covered with antimicrobial dressings such as bacitracin. Silver sulfadiazine has been shown to delay wound healing and is no longer routinely recommended. Tetanus should be updated if the patient has not been immunized in the last 5 years. Criteria for referral to a burn center include partial-thickness burns > 10% TBSA, any full-thickness burn, and burns to the face, hands, feet, major joints, or genitals.



Bacitracin (A) does not penetrate eschar but otherwise has no negative effects on wound healing.

Bismuth tribromophenate (B) has good antimicrobial properties and no negative wound healing effects.

Mafenide acetate (C) can result in metabolic acidosis but has no negative effect on wound healing.

Question: A 22-year-old woman presents to the ED with abdominal pain after tripping and falling down five stairs. She struck the left side of her abdomen during the fall. She is 31 weeks pregnant. Her laboratory testing results include blood type A and Rh status negative. Which of the following is the next step in treatment?

Options.text: Anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection
Two units of type O blood transfusion

CorrectAnswer: Anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection
ExplanationEN:
Trauma is the cause of the majority of maternal deaths during pregnancy. Approximately 5–10% of women experience some form of trauma during their pregnancy, with the majority occurring during the third trimester. The best care for the fetus is caring appropriately for the mother. Maternal Rh status needs to be determined and anti-D immune globulin should be administered if indicated. Given that this patient is Rh negative, she will require anti-D immune globulin 300 mcg intramuscular injection since she sustained direct abdominal trauma and is at risk for maternal-fetal hemorrhage. If untreated, this could lead to Rh sensitization and fetal hydrops. If there is evidence of, or concern for, significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, the Kleihauer-Betke test can be performed. Positive testing may indicate severe trauma and significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, requiring additional anti-D immune globulin as the standard dose clears only 15 mL of fetal red blood cells. Additional monitoring should include assessing fetal heart rate with Doppler and placing the patient on fetal cardiotocographic monitoring if the fetus is > 20 weeks gestation. These patients should be monitored for a minimum of 4 hours before discharge home if no injuries are identified, maternal vital signs remain stable, and cardiotocographic tracing is unremarkable.



Betamethasone 12 mg IM (B) is the appropriate therapy for preterm labor to encourage fetal lung maturation before delivery. It is given twice, 24 hours apart.

Nifedipine 20 mg PO (C) is a tocolytic that will help ease uterine contractions in preterm labor to attempt to delay delivery.

Two units of type O blood transfusion (D) would be appropriate if the patient exhibited unstable vital signs or evidence of significant hemorrhage. However, this is not indicated in this patient.

Question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the ED via EMS after a physical altercation. He was thrown to the ground and choked for several minutes. He has shortness of breath and a sensation of pressure in his neck. He reports no loss of consciousness and has a hoarse voice on exam. There is no evidence of neurological deficits or airway compromise. What is the most appropriate imaging study for this patient?

Options.text: CT of the head and cervical spine without contrast
CT of the head and neck with intravenous contrast
MRI of the head and neck

ExplanationEN:
Strangulation is a serious form of trauma that may result in injury to the airway, soft tissue, and vascular structures of the neck. Initial management of strangulation cases begins with the trauma ABCs: airway, breathing, and circulation. Ensure the airway is patent, assessing for edema or soft tissue swelling that might suggest impending airway compromise. Monitoring for respiratory distress or hypoxia should also be performed. Evaluate for signs of shock, such as hypotension, tachycardia, or cool extremities, that may suggest severe vascular injury. Exam findings that suggest more serious injuries should then be performed. Hoarseness and difficulty swallowing may suggest laryngeal injury. Neck pain, ecchymosis, and swelling indicate soft tissue injury and should raise concern for underlying vascular injury. Neurologic deficits, seizure, and loss of consciousness may suggest cerebral hypoxia or vascular compromise.

CT angiogram of the neck is the best imaging modality when there is concern for vascular injury (pressure in the neck and hoarseness). This study provides detailed views of the carotid arteries, vertebral arteries, and jugular venous systems. It will identify vascular occlusion, thrombosis, dissection, and hematoma and can guide management. If the patient has altered mental status, neurologic deficits, or loss of consciousness, a noncontrast head CT should also be performed to evaluate for cerebral edema or hemorrhage. X-ray or CT of the cervical spine may be performed if there is midline cervical spine tenderness or other concerns for a spinal fracture.

Patients with significant strangulation should be monitored for several hours for serial evaluations, even when initial imaging is unremarkable, as delayed complications may occur. Vascular occlusion, airway obstruction, or neurologic changes may occur due to delayed vascular or airway inflammation. Delayed complications of stroke and hypoxia may occur.



While CT of the head and cervical spine without contrast (B) may be important in evaluating head and cervical spine injuries in this patient, it fails to assess the life-threatening vascular injuries that may occur with strangulation.

CT of the head and neck with intravenous contrast (C) may identify trauma to the airway or soft tissue and provide more information than a noncontrast CT scan but is not the best choice for evaluating vascular injury in strangulation. It is less specialized than CT angiogram and is not as effective at detecting vascular injuries that may result from strangulation.

MRI of the head and neck (D) is not the first-line imaging for acute trauma or assessment of vascular injury from strangulation. CT angiogram is faster, more accessible in the ED setting, and more effective at evaluating vascular injuries or dissections than MRI.

Question: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by EMS after being struck by a vehicle traveling approximately 30 mph. He was given 100 mcg of fentanyl prehospital for an open lower leg fracture without active bleeding. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14. His vital signs are HR 112 bpm, BP 85/55 mm Hg, RR 18/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. One unit of whole blood is ordered and transfused for his hypotension with improvement to 92/58 mm Hg. His exam is positive for diffuse abrasions, superficial scrapes, the obvious right lower leg deformity, and pain with pelvic rocking. FAST exam and pelvis radiograph are negative. As such, the patient was sent to CT with a physician. CT of his head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows a blush in the area of his right internal iliac artery with right and left pubic rami fractures in the pattern of a lateral compression fracture. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate for this patient?

Options.text: Immediate application of a pelvic binder

ExplanationEN:
Pelvic fractures are associated with approximately 5% mortality and should be considered in all serious blunt trauma, especially in trauma patients demonstrating signs of shock on arrival. CT scan is more sensitive than a plain radiograph in diagnosing a pelvic fracture. Plain radiographs can miss up to 15% of pelvic fractures. Additionally, contrast-enhanced CT imaging provides information regarding complications of pelvic fracture such as pelvic ring ligamentous injuries, contrast extravasation, pelvic hematoma, and retroperitoneal bleeding. Most bleeding associated with pelvic fractures is associated with venous bleeding or bleeding from mobile bone edges. However, arterial bleeding is a possibility. If a patient is hemodynamically unstable and other sources of bleeding have been excluded on CT scan, the treatment of choice is angiography with embolization.



An alternative method of hemorrhage control is laparotomy with pelvic packing (D). This treatment option should be considered when angiography is not available or when laparotomy is indicated prior to angiography, such as with a positive FAST. Particularly in hemodynamically unstable pelvic fractures, pelvic binding stabilizes the pelvis and decreases pelvic volume. A bed sheet, pelvic binding device, or both are applied properly across the greater trochanters. This is appropriate in open-book fractures and vertical shear fractures. However, lateral compression fractures do not benefit from pelvic binders and can result in further lateral compression. Thus, the immediate application of a pelvic binder (C) is incorrect in this clinical scenario. All pelvic fractures require admission and orthopedics consultation (A), but given this patient’s vital signs, this is not the most appropriate action to be taken.

Question: A 41-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after being struck by a golf ball. She reports blurry vision in the left eye. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism, sickle cell disease, and irritable bowel syndrome. She reports no neck pain, loss of consciousness, or diplopia. On physical examination, you note the above finding. Her cranial nerves III through XII are grossly intact. Which of the following agents should be avoided at this time?
ExplanationEN:
A hyphema is the presence of blood in the anterior chamber from ruptured blood vessels in the iris or ciliary body. It may be caused by trauma or may occur spontaneously. Patients with sickle cell disease are at risk for spontaneous hyphemas. Symptoms include pain, vision impairment, photophobia, and tearing. Management involves elevating the head of the bed to prevent occlusion of the trabecular meshwork (which leads to elevated intraocular pressure), consulting an ophthalmologist, controlling pain, and lowering intraocular pressure. The latter may be accomplished with topical beta-blockers (e.g., betaxolol hydrochloride), topical alpha-agonists (e.g., apraclonidine), intravenous mannitol, and topical, oral, or intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide). However, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are contraindicated in patients with sickle cell disease because the lower aqueous pH induces sickling of red blood cells, occludes the trabecular meshwork, and leads to increased intraocular pressure. Complications include increased intraocular pressure, vision impairment, corneal staining, accommodative impairment, optic nerve atrophy, and rebleeding. Vision loss is more likely in patients with large hyphemas, sickle cell disease, or bleeding tendencies (including those taking anticoagulants).

Question: An 18-year-old college pitcher presents to the ED after being struck in the eye by a baseball. He has severe eye pain and proptosis of the right eye. Visual acuity is 20/25 on the left and hand waving on the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Obtain computed tomography of the orbits

ExplanationEN:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of a retrobulbar hematoma, a condition in which blood accumulates behind the eye (globe), leading to orbital compartment syndrome. The expanding hematoma increases pressure on critical structures such as the optic nerve, globe, and central retinal artery, causing ischemia. Retrobulbar hematoma is most commonly caused by trauma, as in this case, and can lead to irreversible vision loss if not addressed promptly.

Signs and symptoms of a retrobulbar hematoma include severe pain, vision loss (such as this patient’s vision limited to hand waving), proptosis (protrusion of the globe), afferent pupillary defect, and ophthalmoplegia (paralysis or limited movement of the extraocular muscles). There may also be evidence of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), further supporting the diagnosis.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, given the combination of proptosis, vision loss, and pain following trauma. Although CT of the orbits can be obtained to confirm the diagnosis or assess for associated fractures, definitive treatment should not be delayed if the diagnosis is clear. The key to preventing permanent vision loss is to promptly relieve orbital pressure. This is done through an emergent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis, a procedure that releases the pressure within the orbit.

The goal is to relieve orbital pressure and restore blood flow to the optic nerve and globe. Improvement in proptosis and ocular tension should be observed immediately after the procedure. If the globe remains tense or if vision does not improve, further intervention may be required. Throughout the process, ophthalmology should be consulted immediately to manage ongoing care and potential complications. Vision loss can become permanent after 90 to 120 minutes of ischemia, so rapid recognition and intervention are essential. Lateral canthotomy is a sight-saving procedure that buys time while awaiting specialized care.



Acetazolamide (A) can reduce IOP in conditions like acute angle-closure glaucoma, but it is not the best treatment for orbital compartment syndrome, in which surgical decompression is required urgently. IOP-lowering agents should be administered to temporarily reduce compartment pressure until surgical decompression can be performed. These agents include intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, and in some cases, intravenous mannitol at a dose of 1 to 2 g/kg. Once ischemia and vision loss occur, timely canthotomy becomes critical.

While measuring IOP (B) could help confirm the diagnosis of increased pressure within the eye, immediate intervention (lateral canthotomy) is prioritized over diagnostic testing in a situation with such obvious signs of orbital compartment syndrome and impending vision loss.

A CT scan (C) can help visualize fractures or hematomas, but in a patient with clear signs of orbital compartment syndrome, imaging should not delay the necessary emergent treatment (lateral canthotomy) to prevent permanent vision loss.

Question: A patient presents to the emergency department after a skiing collision and is diagnosed with a fibular head fracture. Which of the following findings on neurovascular examination would most likely be seen with this injury?

Options.text: Decreased sensation between the first and second toes
Weakness with plantar flexion of the ankle

CorrectAnswer: Decreased sensation between the first and second toes
ExplanationEN:
Many orthopedic injuries may also cause nerve or vascular injuries due to the close proximity of these structures and the force required to break bones. A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed to evaluate strength, sensation, and blood flow of the major muscles and nerves distal to any suspected injury. Knowledge of anatomy and function can also help assess which nerves are most at risk, given a suspected or known fracture. The common peroneal nerve courses around the fibular head prior to bifurcating into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves. It is susceptible to injury here from fibular head fractures as well as from excess pressure with casting or during operative procedures. These branches of the peroneal nerve continue to the foot, where the deep peroneal nerve provides sensation between the first and second toes and motor function to the tibialis anterior (dorsiflexion and inversion of the ankle) and extensor hallucis longus (extension of the great toe). The superficial peroneal nerve innervates the peroneus longus, which aids in ankle eversion and provides sensory innervation to much of the dorsum of the foot. Fractures with neurovascular compromise should be emergently reduced and referred to orthopedics.



The tibial nerve provides sensation to the calf (B) after passing through the popliteal fossa and is unlikely to be affected by a fibular head fracture.

A weakened dorsalis pedis pulse (C) would more likely be seen after injury to the tibia or knee. The popliteal artery passes through the popliteal fossa and then gives rise to the anterior tibial artery, which ultimately becomes the dorsalis pedis artery.

Weakness with plantar flexion of the ankle (D) would be caused by injury to the tibial nerve, which also passes through the popliteal fossa. Injuries to all of these structures may be seen with knee dislocations.

Question: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED after a gunshot wound to the leg. His airway is intact and vital signs are normal. An entry wound is observed in the right lower extremity just medial to the femur, one-fourth of the way down the thigh. There is no observed exit wound. Strength and sensation are intact. A nonpulsatile, stable hematoma is noted on exam near the wound. Ankle-brachial index is 0.85. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the care of this patient?

Options.text: Administer tetanus prophylaxis and admit for observation and serial blood pressures in the affected extremity
Order a CTA of the extremity

CorrectAnswer: Order a CTA of the extremity
ExplanationEN:
The appropriate next step is CTA of the extremity, as this patient exhibits a sign of vascular injury based on an ankle-brachial index (ABI) of 0.85 following penetrating trauma. CTA is a noninvasive, highly sensitive modality for identifying vascular injuries and determining the need for operative or interventional management. This patient’s stable hematoma, absence of hard signs (e.g., pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, bruit or thrill), and intact neurovascular status indicate that emergent surgical exploration is not warranted at this time. CTA offers definitive vascular imaging to assess for potential injury, such as pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, or partial vessel transection.

Penetrating extremity trauma requires prompt assessment for vascular compromise. Hard signs of vascular injury (e.g., active expanding hematoma, absent distal pulses, pulsatile bleeding, bruit or thrill) typically necessitate immediate surgical intervention, bypassing imaging. In contrast, soft signs (e.g., stable hematoma, a decreased pulse compared to the other extremity, neurologic findings, or proximity injury to major vessels) or an abnormal ABI suggest a lower likelihood of severe vascular injury but still warrant further diagnostic evaluation. An ABI < 0.9 is a validated threshold indicating the need for vascular imaging, as its sensitivity for vascular injury exceeds 95%.

In the ED, care for penetrating extremity trauma includes initial stabilization (airway, breathing, circulation), thorough neurovascular examination, and consideration of imaging or intervention based on clinical findings. Following CTA, vascular injuries may be managed operatively or endovascularly, depending on the lesion. Patients without significant vascular compromise and reassuring imaging can often be safely observed or discharged with outpatient follow-up.



Administering tetanus prophylaxis and admitting the patient for observation (A) covers standard wound care but does not address the abnormal ABI or the potential vascular injury suggested by the stable hematoma. Observation without imaging could delay the diagnosis and treatment of a clinically significant vascular injury.

Discharging (B) this patient without further evaluation is inappropriate because an ABI of 0.85 is abnormal, indicating potential vascular injury. Relying solely on clinical examination risks missing injuries like partial vessel transection or pseudoaneurysms, which can have delayed complications. This patient requires vascular imaging before disposition decisions are made.

Emergent operative exploration (D) is reserved for patients with hard signs of vascular injury (e.g., pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, bruit, loss of pulse). This patient has no hard signs and is hemodynamically stable, making operative exploration unnecessary without further imaging to confirm significant vascular injury.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to a community emergency department reporting severe pain in his left hand after spilling an unknown liquid on himself while at work, where he transports waste products at a semiconductor fabrication plant. After irrigating the affected area with water, he notified his supervisor about the incident and was instructed to go to the hospital due to “very harmful chemicals” in the liquid. Physical exam is notable for injuries to the patient’s left hand pictured above and is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is consistent with systemic toxicity related to this chemical exposure?
ExplanationEN:
Used primarily for industrial purposes such as glass etching, metal cleaning, and semiconductor production, hydrofluoric acid is a highly potent inorganic acid, capable of producing lethal systemic toxicity from even trace exposure. Aside from the corrosive effect of direct skin exposure that results in burns from free hydrogen ions, the fluoride ions penetrate deeper into the tissue, forming insoluble salts with calcium and magnesium and rapidly dissociating soluble salts with other cations, which leads to deeper tissue destruction. Without treatment, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia result from the consumptive process initiated by free fluoride ions, along with hyperkalemia, which is initiated by the efflux of potassium from cells initiated by hypocalcemia. Along with intravascular volume losses from the tissue destruction, mortality is attributable to the resultant electrolyte abnormalities and the directly cardiotoxic effect of fluoride ions, which trigger cardiac dysrhythmias, the primary cause of death from hydrofluoric acid exposure. Immediate decontamination is vital, along with the administration of topical calcium gluconate gel to exposed areas, which forms complexes with free fluoride ions prior to deeper tissue penetration. If pain persists, or if there is a delay in presentation with severe tissue destruction prior to evaluation, intravascular calcium gluconate should also be administered either intra-arterially through the brachial artery or intravenously with the use of a Bier block.



Hydrofluoric acid toxicity does not result in hypercalcemia, hypermagnesemia, and hypokalemia (A), hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyperkalemia (B), or hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia, and hypokalemia (C), as systemic fluoride consumes calcium and magnesium that lowers these levels and secondarily causes hyperkalemia through intracellular shifting brought about by hypocalcemia.

Question: A 4-year-old boy presents with knee pain after a fall while running. His X-ray is shown above. What is the Salter-Harris classification of this fracture?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a fracture through the epiphysis, physis (growth plate), and metaphysis, representing a Salter-Harris type IV fracture. The Salter-Harris classification is used for physeal injuries only. Type II fractures are the most common and, along with type I, have the best prognosis. Tenderness over a physis, even with normal findings on radiograph, should be treated as a Salter-Harris I fracture.

Salter-Harris type IV fractures require orthopedic consultation and prompt follow-up and potential operative repair. This patient should be placed in a long leg posterior mold splint and should be non-weight-bearing.





Salter-Harris I fractures (A) are rarely visible on radiography and are described as an epiphyseal slip.

Salter-Harris II fractures (B) occur through a portion of the physis and extend through the metaphysis.

Salter-Harris III fractures (C) occur through a portion of the physis and extend through the epiphysis and into the joint. In general, type I and II injuries can be managed with closed reduction and splinting, but type III, IV, and V injuries typically require open reduction.

Question: A 38-year-old man presents to the ED with a posterior hip dislocation after striking his left knee on the dashboard during a motor vehicle crash. He has weakness with dorsiflexion of the left foot. Which nerve has likely been damaged?
ExplanationEN:
Hip dislocations are true orthopedic emergencies. Because of the considerable force required to cause these injuries, patients often have other injuries, and a thorough physical exam is required. Up to 70% of patients with a hip dislocation have an associated fracture of the acetabulum. The force required to dislocate a pediatric hip is less than that of an adult because the acetabulum is not completely developed. Because of this, minor trauma can dislocate the hip in a young child, and in school-aged children, athletic injuries are the most common cause of traumatic hip dislocation. In the teenage years and beyond, motor vehicle collisions are the predominant cause.

Posterior hip dislocations are almost always the result of motor vehicle collisions. A seated vehicle occupant typically has the hip adducted, flexed, and internally rotated at the time of impact. The force is transmitted through the femoral shaft to the femoral head as the knee strikes the dashboard, and the femoral shaft dislocates posteriorly. These dislocations account for 80–90% of hip dislocations. Anterior hip dislocations are seen in 10–15% of patients and include pubic, obturator, and iliac crest dislocations. Less commonly, central and inferior dislocations can occur.

Patients with posterior hip dislocations typically hold the hip flexed, adducted, and internally rotated, and the leg generally appears shortened. In contrast, patients with anterior hip dislocations hold the hip in abduction, slight flexion, and external rotation, and the leg may appear lengthened. The neurovascular exam should focus on the sciatic nerve and femoral vessels. Sciatic palsy occurs in approximately 10% of patients with hip dislocations. The peroneal nerve is most commonly involved, as manifested by weakness of the extensor hallucis longus, weakness of dorsiflexion, and numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

An anteroposterior pelvis X-ray should be obtained in all trauma patients and will identify the majority of hip dislocations. A lateral view of the hip is recommended if a dislocation is noted. Associated fractures are important to diagnose because these (especially acetabular fractures) may impede attempts at closed reduction.

Reduction of hip dislocations should be performed within 6 hours. The incidence of avascular necrosis (AVN), traumatic arthritis, and permanent sciatic nerve palsy increase exponentially with the length of time the hip remains dislocated. Up to 15% of patients with hip dislocations develop AVN. Other risk factors for the development of AVN include total dislocation time, severity of the injury, number of reduction attempts, and underlying comorbid conditions.

In the case of simple dislocations, closed reduction should be attempted in the ED, typically with the use of procedural sedation. The Allis technique is the most commonly used technique for reducing posterior hip dislocations. The patient is placed in a supine position with the pelvis stabilized by an assistant. The knee of the affected extremity is flexed, and steady traction is applied in line with the deformity. The hip is slowly brought to 90° of flexion while upward traction is applied. The assistant then pushes the greater trochanter forward, toward the acetabulum. Other techniques often used are the Stimson, Whistler, and Captain Morgan techniques. If closed reduction is unsuccessful, the patient should be taken to the operating room for open or closed reduction under general anesthesia.

After reduction, postreduction anteroposterior pelvis X-rays should be obtained to verify adequacy of reduction. Most patients with a native hip dislocation will require admission to the hospital for serial exams and orthopedic surgery evaluation.



The femoral nerve (A) innervates the muscles of the anterior thigh and allows hip flexion and knee extension.

The obturator nerve (B) innervates the medial thigh and allows adduction of the thigh.

Once it reaches the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve bifurcates into the common peroneal nerve (which innervates the anterior lower leg and allows dorsiflexion of the foot) and the tibial nerve (D) (which innervates the posterior lower leg and allows plantar flexion of the foot).

Question: A 3-year-old boy presents after biting through a television power cord 20 minutes prior to arrival. The parents note that the child cried immediately and did not lose consciousness. He has since been acting normally and is tolerating oral fluids. On physical exam, there is an eschar over the left oral commissure without bleeding. There are no other burns to the tongue or oropharynx. What is the most serious complication of this injury?
ExplanationEN:
Electrical burns in children most commonly involve the lips, mouth, and tongue. These injuries typically result after a child, usually under the age of 3, chews or sucks on an electrical cord. Electrolyte-rich saliva conducts electricity to the mucous membranes, which have a high risk of thermal injury due to their relatively low resistance. The oral commissure is the most common site for an oral burn after electrical injury. Oral commissure burns usually appear gray or white and are typically painless due to underlying nerve injury. Initial evaluation of any patient with facial burns requires careful inspection of the mouth and oropharynx for signs of airway involvement. The presence of soot in the mouth, singed nasal hairs, wheezing, voice changes, or respiratory distress should heighten the suspicion for airway burns and prompt consideration for early endotracheal intubation.

Patients with isolated oral commissure burns do not usually require workup or admission to the hospital. Emergency management includes providing tetanus vaccination for those who are unvaccinated, arranging expedited follow-up with an oral or plastic surgeon, and educating parents about the most serious potential complication of delayed bleeding. Bleeding from an oral commissure wound is rare in the immediate setting, as the blood vessels are cauterized by thermal injury. However, as the eschar sloughs, there can be massive bleeding from the labial artery, usually within the first 2 weeks of injury. In the event of bleeding, parents should be instructed to apply direct compression of the commissure with two fingers and to seek immediate emergency care. Patients with oral commissure burns often require reconstructive surgery or splinting to ensure adequate cosmetic and functional outcomes, but this is not done emergently.



Cardiac dysrhythmias (A) are uncommon after household electrical injuries. Standard household current in the United States is 110 V. Cardiac dysrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, and other sequelae of electrical injuries are typically observed after high voltage injuries, defined by a current > 1,000 V. Patients with low voltage injuries who have no cardiac symptoms, who had no loss of consciousness, and who have a normal screening ECG are considered low-risk for dysrhythmias and do not require prolonged monitoring on telemetry. Additionally, oral commissure burns result from a local arc of electrical current that does not typically reach the myocardium. While infection (C) is possible after any burn, it is not immediately life-threatening. Delayed labial artery bleeding can lead to exsanguination and death and is the most important complication to educate parents about prior to discharge. Microstomia (D), or decreased mouth size from perioral contracture, is a potential complication of oral commissure burns that can lead to morbidity, but it is not immediately life-threatening.

Question: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. Paramedics report the patient had a brief loss of consciousness following the collision. En route to the hospital, he sustained a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which was treated with lorazepam. He arrives in a postictal state with normal vital signs, protecting his airway. Generally, patients who sustain head trauma and a loss of consciousness should undergo CT imaging of the head. Alcohol use is also predictive of the need for CT imaging in patients with head trauma. This patient’s CT scan shows a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Trauma-related seizures are more likely in patients with more severe head injuries (e.g., those with intracranial bleeding or depressed skull fractures) but can be seen in patients with minor traumatic injuries and normal head CTs. About half of trauma-related seizures occur in the first 24 hours postinjury and one-quarter occur in the first hour. Trauma-associated seizures may be treated with benzodiazepines, such as lorazepam. Approximately 25% of patients with post-traumatic seizures will have recurrent seizures within 7 days. First-line treatment for trauma-associated seizure prophylaxis is phenytoin, fosphenytoin, or levetiracetam.

Midazolam (B) is a benzodiazepine used to abort active seizures. It is not a first-line agent for seizure prophylaxis.

Tranexamic acid (D) is an antifibrinolytic agent indicated in patients with intracranial bleeding within 3 hours of injury. This medication is not used for trauma-associated seizure prophylaxis.

Question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling from a roof. She reports tingling in her fingers and toes. She is immobilized in a cervical collar. An image of her vertebra is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the lateral masses of C1. It is caused by axial loading or a vertical compression force that is transmitted through the occipital condyles and causes displacement of the lateral masses from their articulation with the facets of the axis (C2). The anterior and posterior arches of C1 are often fractured as well. This is an unstable cervical spine fracture. On X-ray, the lateral masses can be viewed as laterally displaced from the atlantoaxial unit. Further imaging should be obtained to evaluate for other spinal injuries, especially in the presence of neurological deficits.



A hangman fracture (A) is caused by extreme hyperextension and creates fractures of the bilateral pedicles of C2. It is also an unstable injury. Odontoid fractures (C) can occur from a variety of mechanisms, including shearing force or extreme flexion. Type I odontoid fractures are stable; types II and III are unstable. Teardrop fractures (D) are unstable and may occur at any vertebral level, although the cervical spine is the most common location. They result from extreme flexion that causes an anterior displacement of a wedge-shaped vertebral body fragment that resembles a teardrop.

Question: A 38-year-old man is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. He reports chest pain and was not wearing his seat belt. He has no known medical problems. Vital signs are normal. Exam shows ecchymosis over the sternum. Lateral chest imaging is shown above. Which of the following should be included in his evaluation?
ExplanationEN:
Chest trauma with rapid deceleration is the most common mechanism for blunt cardiac trauma, followed by a direct blow to the precordium. Blunt cardiac trauma often presents with the chief concern of chest pain and can be described on a spectrum from pleuritic to pressure-like chest pain. Even the classic crushing retrosternal chest pain of myocardial ischemia can be described, especially if the coronary arteries are involved. Symptoms of dyspnea, lightheadedness, or palpitations may also occur and may be related to pulmonary or cardiac dysfunction.

Patients with a concerning history and presentation should be evaluated for blunt cardiac trauma and cardiac contusion. This patient has a transverse sternal fracture on his CT imaging, which puts him at risk for other thoracic trauma like cardiac contusion. While there is no gold standard for the diagnosis of cardiac contusion in the ED, patients with a normal ECG and negative cardiac biomarkers (specifically troponin T or I) are unlikely to have a significant injury and can be discharged. Those with significant symptoms, abnormal ECG, or abnormal troponin should be admitted for continuous cardiac monitoring and echocardiography.



Cardiac monitoring for 24 hours (A) is not indicated unless the patient is significantly symptomatic or has an abnormal ECG or cardiac biomarkers.

ECG alone (B) is not correct as it does not have sufficient sensitivity to rule out a cardiac contusion.

Troponin alone (D) is also incorrect. Patients should also have an ECG as part of the initial evaluation for cardiac contusion.

Question: A 36-year-old man presents after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. EMS reports significant intrusion into the driver’s side door. He reports left chest wall and abdominal pain. Vitals signs include heart rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 112/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. His initial chest radiograph is shown above. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Computed tomographic scan of the chest and abdomen
Needle decompression of the left chest
Placement of a left thoracostomy tube

CorrectAnswer: Computed tomographic scan of the chest and abdomen
ExplanationEN:
Diaphragmatic rupture is uncommon, but associated with significant mortality, especially if the diagnosis is delayed. Most often caused by blunt force trauma to the chest or abdominal wall, rupture of the diaphragm can result in herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity. The most common site of rupture is the left hemidiaphragm, often the posterolateral aspect, which accounts for > 70% of cases. The right hemidiaphragm is less frequently involved, likely due to the protective effect of the liver. However, right-sided injuries are associated with a greater severity of injury to adjacent organs. Signs of diaphragmatic injury on the chest radiograph include elevation or discontinuity of the hemidiaphragm, presence of bowel contents in the thoracic cavity, and abnormal positioning of the nasogastric tube. In hemodynamically stable patients with suspicion of diaphragmatic injury, CT of the chest and abdomen can confirm the diagnosis and provide additional information regarding the extent of the rupture and associated injuries.



Exploratory laparotomy (B) is not indicated emergently as the patient is hemodynamically stable. Further evaluation with a CT is warranted first.

Needle decompression (C) is indicated when there are signs of tension pneumothorax (e.g., unilateral decreased breath sounds, hypotension, mediastinal shift). This patient does not have evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax on the chest radiograph, making placement of left thoracostomy tube (D) also unnecessary.

Question: A 30-year-old man presents to the ED after a high-speed single-vehicle collision in which he swerved to miss a deer and hit a bridge head-on. He appears in acute distress and has asymmetric radial pulses and chest wall ecchymosis. A chest X-ray is obtained and shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most common location for this type of injury?
ExplanationEN:
Blunt aortic injury usually occurs when high-energy compression, shearing, or torsional forces are applied to the chest. Common mechanisms include fall from a height greater than 10 feet and motor vehicle collisions at speeds greater than 30 miles per hour. In motor vehicle collisions in which there is front-end impact, the chest impacts the steering wheel, allowing inertia to carry the intrathoracic contents forward. However, the aorta is anatomically fixed at the left subclavian artery origin by the ligamentum arteriosum. This causes the proximal descending aorta to decelerate with the chest wall while the ascending aorta is mobile and continues forward at impact. This can cause aortic rupture or tears in the intima or media, creating dissection or pseudoaneurysm formation that may predispose to aortic rupture. The aorta may also become compressed between the sternum and the vertebral bodies, increasing intraluminal pressure and causing rupture. Aortic rupture is usually rapidly fatal, and many patients do not survive to ED evaluation.

Patients with blunt aortic injury may be asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms such as back pain, chest pain, or dyspnea. However, these injuries may be clinically occult, and providers should consider aortic trauma in any patient with high-energy mechanisms. Clinical clues that might suggest blunt aortic injury include asymmetric pulses or blood pressures in extremities, hypotension, interscapular murmurs or bruits, palpable rib fractures, flail chest, chest wall contusions (e.g., seat belt markings), or expanding thoracic outlet hematoma. Mediastinal widening on chest radiography is suggestive of great vessel injury. CT angiography is the diagnostic modality of choice to evaluate for aortic injury. Trauma or vascular surgery consultation is needed upon initial suspicion or at diagnosis.



Ascending aortic injuries and traumatic rupture at the aortic root (A) are less common than tears at the ligamentum arteriosum and are almost always fatal.

The brachiocephalic artery origin (B) and right subclavian artery origin (D) are not tethered, therefore, they are not as common as the left subclavian artery origin for aortic injuries.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents to the ED after a fall from a bicycle. He reports left shoulder pain and has a visible deformity. A chest radiograph confirms a clavicle fracture. Which of the following is an indication for surgical repair of this patient’s fracture?

Options.text: Comminuted fracture without skin tenting, significant displacement, or neurovascular compromise
Midshaft fracture with > 2 cm of shortening
Nondisplaced midshaft fracture with pain during overhead motion

CorrectAnswer: Midshaft fracture with > 2 cm of shortening
ExplanationEN:
Clavicle fractures are common injuries, particularly in younger adults and athletes, accounting for approximately 2–5% of all fractures and almost half of shoulder girdle fractures. The majority occur in the midshaft, typically from direct trauma such as a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand. Midshaft fractures often present with visible deformity, pain with arm movement, and localized swelling. Most cases can be managed nonoperatively with a sling and outpatient orthopedic follow-up. However, there are certain features that suggest a higher risk of nonunion or functional impairment, prompting consideration for surgical management.

Surgical repair, typically with open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), is indicated for specific patterns of midshaft fractures. One major indication is > 1.8–2 cm of shortening or displacement. Such fractures are associated with a higher risk of malunion and long-term functional deficits, including strength loss and reduced shoulder endurance. Other surgical indications include open fractures, skin tenting (suggesting impending skin compromise), neurovascular injury, severely comminuted and displaced fractures, and a floating shoulder (clavicle fracture with scapular neck fracture). ORIF improves union rates, restores anatomic alignment, and typically results in better cosmetic and functional outcomes in select patients.



Although comminution is a risk factor for nonunion, isolated comminution without skin tenting, significant displacement, neurovascular injury, or skin compromise (A) does not by itself necessitate surgical repair. In the absence of significant shortening, open fracture, or other complications, conservative management remains appropriate.

Most nondisplaced distal third fractures (C) are treated conservatively. While certain distal third fracture types (Neer type II or V) are at higher risk of nonunion and may warrant surgery, this requires displacement or ligamentous instability. The key descriptor here is “nondisplaced,” which strongly favors nonsurgical management.

Pain with motion is common in clavicle fractures, especially early after injury. A nondisplaced midshaft fracture without other risk features (shortening, displacement, skin compromise) is typically treated conservatively. Functional symptoms alone, such as pain during overhead motion (D), especially in the acute setting, are not a surgical indication. Thus, this patient needs to have other factors describing the fracture that would necessitate surgical care, rather than pain alone.

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a stab wound to the abdomen. He is agitated due to severe pain. Vital signs show tachycardia but are otherwise within normal limits. Physical examination shows two stab wounds to the left lower quadrant with diffuse abdominal tenderness and guarding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation and management of this patient's condition?

Options.text: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast
Upper GI series with small bowel follow-through

ExplanationEN:
Penetrating abdominal trauma in children is relatively rare compared to adults, with stab wounds and gunshot wounds being the most common mechanisms. The majority of patients with pediatric abdominal trauma are boys, with a median age of 14 years. The pathogenesis of injury depends on the mechanism, as stab wounds cause damage along a relatively predictable wound tract with lower kinetic energy transfer, while gunshot wounds produce greater tissue destruction through cavitation and fragmentation. The most commonly injured organs in pediatric abdominal trauma overall are the liver and spleen, though hollow viscus injuries carry the highest risk of subsequent infectious complications.

Children with penetrating abdominal trauma may present with localized or diffuse abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, rigidity, or signs of hemorrhagic shock, depending on the severity and organs involved. The initial evaluation should follow standard ATLS principles, with hemodynamic status being the most critical determinant of the diagnostic and management pathway. Patients with penetrating trauma and hemodynamic instability should receive appropriate resuscitation with crystalloid fluids and blood products, and should generally be taken for emergent laparotomy without imaging. Additional indications for immediate laparotomy include clinical evidence of peritonitis (e.g., diffuse tenderness, guarding), evisceration of abdominal contents, impalement, and frank blood in a nasogastric tube or on rectal examination. This patient's clinical findings that suggest peritonitis represent an indication for immediate transfer to the operating room for laparotomy.

In hemodynamically stable patients without peritonitis, it must be determined whether the peritoneum has been violated to guide further evaluation and treatment decisions. Local wound exploration is recommended for this purpose, with contrast-enhanced CT used when there is suspicion for associated solid organ or hollow viscous injury. However, in pediatrics, routine CT is not universally recommended for stab wounds, given the lower rate of significant intra-abdominal injury and the desire to minimize radiation exposure. Thus, serial clinical examinations are preferred when feasible. Prophylactic antibiotics should be given when peritoneal violation is suspected to preempt infectious complications (e.g., abscess, peritonitis), while other complications include bowel ischemia, ileus, and obstruction. In the pediatric population, outcomes are generally favorable, with the majority of stab wound victims sustaining minor injuries and minimal to no mortality in registry studies.



While CT (A) is useful for identifying organ injury in hemodynamically stable patients with stab wounds that violate the peritoneum, this patient has clinical peritonitis (diffuse tenderness and guarding), which is an indication for immediate surgical exploration rather than further imaging that would delay definitive treatment.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (B) has a very limited role in modern trauma management and has been largely supplanted by FAST and CT. It is overly sensitive, leading to unnecessary laparotomies, and is not indicated when clinical peritonitis already establishes the need for operative intervention.

Serial examinations (D) are appropriate for hemodynamically stable patients with penetrating abdominal trauma who do not have peritonitis, evisceration, or hemodynamic instability. This patient's diffuse tenderness and guarding constitute peritonitis, making observation alone inappropriate and potentially dangerous.

Upper GI series with small bowel follow-through (E) is a fluoroscopic study that has no established role in the acute evaluation of penetrating abdominal trauma. It is time-consuming, insensitive for the injuries of concern, and would inappropriately delay surgical management in a patient with peritonitis.

Question: A 28-year-old man was involved in a bar fight yesterday and presents to the emergency department with right hand pain. He has a laceration over the third metacarpophalangeal joint as shown above. Which of the following is most appropriate at this time?

Options.text: Healing by secondary intention and amoxicillin-clavulanate

CorrectAnswer: Healing by secondary intention and amoxicillin-clavulanate
ExplanationEN:
Fight bites are lacerations that involve the hand, usually over the metacarpophalangeal joints, and are incurred from punching someone in the mouth. They should be treated as human bites. Human bites are highly infectious and should not be closed primarily. Healing by secondary intention is preferred. It is important to examine the entire hand for signs of infection or extensor tendon involvement. It may also be appropriate to obtain plain radiographs of the hand to assess for retained foreign bodies (e.g., teeth) and associated fractures. An antibiotic that covers gram-positive organisms, gram-negative organisms, and anaerobes (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) should be given. Other bites at high risk for infection include bites from cats, livestock, or monkeys; bites in immunosuppressed patients or those with diabetes; bites with heavy contamination or signs of infection at the time of initial presentation; hand or foot wounds; and puncture wounds. Patients may be at risk for communicable diseases (e.g., HIV). They should also be provided with a tetanus update. Depending on social factors or the severity of the infection, patients may require a period of observation to ensure the infection is not worsening, or they may require admission for parenteral antibiotics.



Macrolide antibiotic therapy (B) alone would insufficiently cover the range of organisms associated with the human oral cavity.

Primary closure with absorbable sutures (C) or any primary closure is contraindicated for human bites, especially after a delayed presentation.

Topical antibiotic therapy and reassurance (D) is inadequate management as it does not address the deep tissue infection caused by many human bite wounds. Furthermore, patients may require a period of observation or admission for parenteral antibiotics or specialist consultation and management, depending on the severity of infection.

Question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department in cardiac arrest with high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation underway. Emergency medical personnel report that she is currently 27 weeks pregnant. Which of the following is the most common cause of death in this patient population?
ExplanationEN:
Trauma is the cause of most maternal deaths during pregnancy. Approximately 5–10% of women experience some form of trauma during their pregnancy, with the majority occurring during the third trimester. Motor vehicle collisions are the most common, followed by domestic violence and accidental falls. Signs and symptoms of trauma during pregnancy include vaginal bleeding, which may be a sign of placental abruption, premature rupture of membranes, uterine contractions or tenderness, and absent or decreased fetal movement. Uterine tenderness and pain are much more common than true abdominal pain in traumatic injuries in pregnant patients, as peritoneal stretching results in decreased nerve density per area during pregnancy.

Diagnosis of injuries includes the characteristic trauma panel of laboratory testing and consideration of imaging in a manner similar to nonpregnant patients, with the risk-benefit analysis of radiation exposure taken into consideration. The best care for the fetus is caring appropriately for the mother. Additionally, maternal Rh status needs to be determined and Rhogam administered if indicated. If there is evidence of, or concern for, significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, the Kleihauer-Betke test can be performed to further assess. Positive testing may indicate severe trauma and significant maternal-fetal hemorrhage, requiring additional Rhogam as the standard dose clears only 15 mL of fetal red blood cells. Additional monitoring should include assessing fetal heart rate with Doppler and placing the patient on fetal cardiotocographic monitoring if the fetus is > 20 weeks gestation. These patients should be monitored for a minimum of 4 hours prior to discharge home if no injuries are identified, maternal vital signs remain stable, and cardiotocographic tracing is unremarkable. If the patient remains in cardiac arrest, a perimortem cesarean section may be considered.



Infection (A) and suicide (B) are possible, albeit less common, causes of maternal death during pregnancy.

Vaginal bleeding (D) is a rare cause of maternal death during pregnancy.

Question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the ED by her parent, who reports she placed her finger in a wall electrical socket. In the ED, the child is easily consolable but holds her right index finger in the air. Visual inspection reveals localized erythema at the distal tip but good capillary refill. There are no other signs of trauma. Which diagnostic test should be performed next?
ExplanationEN:
There are two basic types of electrical current: alternating (AC) and direct (DC). This child sustained a low-voltage (< 1,000 volts) electrical injury from an unprotected wall socket. In the United States, household wiring has 120 volts of alternating current with a frequency of 60 Hz. Alternating current causes continuous tetanic muscle contraction between 8 and 22 mA that does not allow the individual to release the electrical source. This child sustained a superficial thermal burn and most likely did not become part of the circuit, given that there are no clear entry or exit wounds. However, patients sustaining such an injury still warrant an ECG and cardiac monitoring in the ED. The most common ECG abnormality is sinus tachycardia and nonspecific ST-T wave changes that resolve spontaneously. Atrial or ventricular ectopy, fibrillation, interval prolongations, or blocks may also be seen. Asystole and ventricular fibrillation are more commonly seen in higher-voltage exposures.



Although a urinalysis (D) to screen for myoglobin and a basic metabolic panel (A) to check kidney function might be performed, it is not necessary given the nature of this child’s injury. Creatine phosphokinase and serial cardiac-specific troponins may be obtained if significant skeletal muscle or cardiomyocyte damage is suspected.

A chest radiograph (B) will provide no useful information, given the clinical exam.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the emergency department after a high-speed front-end motor vehicle collision. She is obtunded and has no purposeful movements. She has paradoxical respirations, for which she is sedated and intubated. There are no external signs of injury or bleeding. Her chest X-ray, lateral neck X-ray, and head CT do not show any fractures or hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Children < 9 years old have a larger head and weaker neck muscles than adults, so spinal injuries tend to occur in the C1–C4 region. Spinal cord injuries in children have various presentations, from as mild as transient neurapraxia to as severe as sudden cardiopulmonary arrest.

A traumatic atlanto-occipital dislocation usually causes a brain stem and upper cervical cord injury. This can cause significant transient or permanent neurologic dysfunction, and many of these children die from respiratory dysfunction or apnea before reaching the hospital. Those with a high spinal cord injury often have a paradoxical respiratory pattern from a functioning diaphragm but paralyzed intercostal muscles. Another condition that presents with a paradoxical respiratory pattern is an airway foreign body, when the muscles of the diaphragm are working but no air is moving.

Patients with a traumatic atlanto-occipital dislocation sometimes present with limb paralysis or high cervical cord motor deficits (e.g., inability to cough or control bladder movements). Rarely, it presents as an alert patient with lower cranial nerve paresis, including cranial nerves VI, X, or XII. Findings on cervical spine X-rays of patients with a traumatic atlanto-occipital dislocation are usually normal. The diagnosis is made by a CT or MRI of the C-spine.



A cervical artery dissection (B) is another rare catastrophic event that must be considered in patients with a severely depressed mental status after a motor vehicle collision. But it usually presents with a stroke-like pattern, a sudden change in mental status, cranial or cervical neuropathies, Horner syndrome, or, in older patients, head or neck pain. They do not have a paradoxical respiratory pattern.

Diffuse axonal injury (C) results from high-velocity rotational trauma and typically presents with coma and minimal findings on CT. Although it shares similarities with the patient’s presentation, diffuse axonal injury originates from shearing forces affecting white matter tracts, not the craniovertebral junction. It does not typically cause abnormal respiratory patterns such as paradoxical respirations, which suggest involvement of the medulla and lower cranial nerves, making atlanto-occipital dislocation more likely.

Patients with a concussion (D) usually have confusion, disorientation, slow speech, gait abnormalities, and vomiting, but even those with severe isolated concussions maintain their respiratory drive.

Question: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with ankle pain. He states that he was jumping to grab a ball when he was playing basketball and felt a “pop” at the back of his ankle. On exam, he has a positive Thompson test. What is the most appropriate next step in care?

Options.text: Apply a splint with the ankle in slight plantarflexion
Obtain CT angiography of the extremity to rule out vascular compromise
Place the patient in a controlled ankle movement boot

CorrectAnswer: Apply a splint with the ankle in slight plantarflexion
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with an Achilles tendon rupture. These usually occur when sudden forces are exerted on the Achilles tendon. They often occur during strenuous activities that involve rapid acceleration or pivoting on a foot. Many patients will report feeling a pop or feel like they were struck at the back of their ankle. Patients often present with significant pain, and a defect is often easily identified and palpated. However, a small percentage of patients may present without pain or significant difficulty ambulating. Certain tests, such as the Thompson test, can help provide a more accurate means for diagnosing Achilles tendon ruptures on exam.

For this test, the patient lies prone with their knee flexed at 90°. The examiner squeezes the patient’s calf muscles which should cause contraction of an intact Achilles tendon, leading to plantar flexion. If the tendon is completely ruptured, no plantar flexion would be seen, leading to a positive finding. MRI may help differentiate the extent of the tear and could potentially differentiate between partial and complete tears, but this can be performed in the outpatient setting.

Initial care of Achilles tendon ruptures consists of conservative management, analgesics (anti-inflammatories), and immobilization with the ankle in slight plantarflexion. All patients should be discharged with close follow-up with orthopedic surgery, as many of these patients will be treated operatively.



Consulting orthopedic surgery in the emergency department (B) would be inappropriate, as an isolated Achilles tendon rupture is not an indication for emergency surgery.

Obtaining CT angiography of the extremity to rule out vascular compromise (C) is also inappropriate, as most Achilles tendon injuries caused by running and jumping are not significant enough to lead to vascular injury. Assessment for such should start with a physical exam, not imaging.

Placing the patient in a controlled ankle movement boot (D) would still allow some movement in the ankle. These patients should be immobilized in slight plantarflexion and placed in non-weight-bearing status when discharged from the emergency department.

Question: A 21-year-old man presents to the ED with pelvic pain. He was pitching in a baseball game 8 hours ago when a ball was hit directly back at him and struck him in the groin. He was not wearing guard protection. The patient has no significant medical history and takes no medications. ExplanationEN:
Blunt trauma to the external male genitalia can produce a variety of injuries, ranging from testicular hematomas to penile fractures. Scrotal injuries may present with concomitant penile or urethral injuries or may be isolated. Patients may present with symptoms immediately after injury but more commonly seek care later, with a median symptom duration of 3 days at presentation. Patients typically report pain with varying degrees of swelling, tenderness, and ecchymosis noted objectively on exam, which can make clinical differentiation of testicular injuries challenging.

Due to the relative ambiguity of the clinical features of different testicular injuries, imaging is usually warranted in the form of scrotal ultrasound. If there is clinical concern for a concomitant pelvic fracture or alternate abdominopelvic injury, CT of the abdomen should be considered. Ultrasound findings that suggest testicular rupture include irregularity of the tunica albuginea, heterogeneous echogenicity of the testicular parenchyma, and extrusion of the seminiferous tubules. Because the presence of testicular rupture, hematocele, or testicular hematoma can result in ischemic atrophy of the testes with subsequent orchialgia or infection requiring orchiectomy, any of these findings warrants surgical exploration with repair of the injuries performed by urology.



A scrotal hematocele (A) may be present in the setting of blunt scrotal trauma but will present on ultrasound with an area of increased echogenicity with septations within the scrotum but outside the testis itself. This is shown on the patient’s left side but not the right side.

Penile fractures (B) most commonly result from inadvertent thrusting of an erect penis against a sexual partner’s perineum or pubic symphysis during intercourse. These fractures present with sudden detumescence and pain associated with an audible popping noise.

Ultrasound of a testicular hematoma (C) most commonly shows a focal area of increased echogenicity within the testis.

Ultrasound findings of testicular torsion (E) include the whirlpool sign (twisting of the spermatic cord within the scrotum or inguinal ring), increased size, heterogeneous echotexture, and changes in Doppler flow.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents to the ED after electrocution while at work. He has experienced muscle spasms, cramping, and pain since the episode. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 125/80 mm Hg, HR is 112 bpm, RR is 19/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical examination reveals diffuse muscle tenderness. Laboratory values are notable for a potassium of 6.0 mEq/L, calcium of 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL, and phosphorus of 5.1 mg/dL, while other results are still pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

Options.text: Ringer lactate bolus and sodium bicarbonate ampule

ExplanationEN:
Electrical injuries can be life-threatening and can cause deep injury to underlying tissues and cardiac dysrhythmias. One possible complication of electrical injury is rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when skeletal muscle breakdown causes the release of intracellular contents. Laboratory findings suggestive of rhabdomyolysis include a creatine kinase over five times the upper limit of normal, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Acute kidney injury is a possible complication of rhabdomyolysis and is caused by myoglobin accumulation.

The best treatment and prevention of acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis is fluid administration to ensure adequate urinary output. Start administering IV normal saline at 1 L/hr or other appropriate fluid to maintain urine output. Continue aggressive IV rehydration for the next 24–72 hours. One approach is to quickly correct the fluid deficit using IV crystalloids, followed by an infusion rate of 4 mL/kg/h, aiming to maintain a urine output of at least 3–4 mL/kg/h. Alternatively, target a urine output of 200–300 mL/hr. Electrolyte derangements should be addressed, as they are common in this condition.



Furosemide (A) might be an appropriate treatment for hyperkalemia. However, it could potentially worsen kidney function without proper hydration. To prevent kidney injury and hyperkalemia, giving IV fluids first is more appropriate and will likely prevent the need for loop diuretic administration.

A nephrology consult to initiate dialysis (B) would be warranted in a patient with acute kidney failure with an emergent need for dialysis, such as hyperkalemia, acidosis, or fluid overload. It is generally more appropriate after initial measures to stabilize electrolyte imbalances have failed and after reassessing kidney function following initial treatment.

Ringer lactate and sodium bicarbonate (D) would not be the best treatment. While some older sources might recommend sodium bicarbonate treatment for severe rhabdomyolysis, more recent evidence does not suggest a benefit to bicarbonate administration. IV crystalloid alone is preferred to manage fluid balance and facilitate kidney excretion of myoglobin.

Question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the ED after being ejected from a motor vehicle. He arrives with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3, ashen skin, and is hypotensive. Injuries identified on a primary and secondary survey include a boggy scalp hematoma, abdominal bruising, and an open femur fracture. During the resuscitation, he is given packed red blood cells and rapidly intubated with normalizing vital signs. During a FAST exam, the patient again becomes tachycardic and hypotensive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Administer additional packed red blood cells

ExplanationEN:
Rapid assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of life-threatening injuries is critical to preventing morbidity and mortality after major trauma. The initial approach to trauma in children is nearly identical to that of adults, using the systemic approach of Advanced Trauma Life Support. Systems should be in place to allow team members to be notified and present upon arrival of critically injured children. The primary survey includes rapid evaluation of airway, breathing, circulation, and disability, with complete exposure of the patient to facilitate diagnosis and hemorrhage control while maintaining cervical spine immobilization.

Any immediately identified life threats must be dealt with as they are found (e.g., tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade). The secondary survey includes a head-to-toe evaluation, including perineum and back, with a brief history. Adjuncts such as CT, X-ray, and ultrasound are useful to confirm suspected findings based on exam. The only significant difference in trauma management compared to adults is the size of equipment (e.g., 22–24 gauge IV) and dosing (e.g., 20 mL/kg bolus).

Similarly, if a patient deteriorates during the trauma evaluation, the first step is to repeat the primary survey to identify and treat any new problems that may have arisen.



While it is important to prepare to administer additional packed red blood cells (A) as this patient has continued to decline, repeating the primary survey is rapid and may identify a different cause such as a pneumothorax.

Performing extubation and bag valve mask (B) may be necessary but will not help in a patient with a pneumothorax or bleeding. An intubated patient who develops hypoxia most commonly has a dislodged endotracheal tube, an obstructed endotracheal tube, a pneumothorax, or equipment failure.

Performing an open thoracotomy (C) is only recommended in the case of last resort, when a trauma patient completely loses vital signs in the emergency department, not in one with vital sign changes.
