Question: A 26-year-old man presents to the emergency department via ambulance following a motorcycle collision. EMS reports the patient was a single rider on his motorcycle traveling an estimated 70 mph when he lost control of the vehicle and hit a guardrail before stopping abruptly after hitting a concrete barrier. Vital signs show T of 97.9°F (36.6°C), BP of 155/90 mm Hg, HR of 104 bpm, RR of 24/min, and SpO2 of 95% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 6, and the patient is intubated for airway protection. Further examination reveals decreased breath sounds on the left and ecchymosis over the anterior chest wall and upper abdomen. His chest X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Rupture of the diaphragm is a relatively uncommon complication of trauma. Diaphragmatic injury can occur in both blunt and penetrating trauma and most commonly occurs with concomitant injuries to other organs. The pathophysiology varies by injury mechanism. Penetrating trauma typically causes direct injury to the diaphragm, while blunt trauma produces a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure. This pressure causes a tear in the diaphragm that allows for the herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity.

Presentation of diaphragm injuries on clinical and diagnostic evaluation can vary widely and range from readily discernible to subtle. Subjective reports from the patient can range from no symptoms to vomiting, pain, or shortness of breath. Contusions or ecchymosis on the chest or abdomen may be present and suggest significant blunt injuries. Reduced breath sounds due to herniation of abdominal contents into the chest or associated pneumothorax may also be present. In the case of penetrating injuries, a high level of suspicion for diaphragmatic injury should be maintained for injuries between the T4 and T12 dermatomes, especially with wounds on both sides of the midline. Chest X-ray is the most commonly performed imaging study in patients with trauma. Findings can range from as obvious as the stomach presenting within the thoracic cavity or as subtle as basilar atelectasis or hemidiaphragm elevation. Many of these patients will undergo CT imaging, which is more sensitive and may show a discontinuous or thickened diaphragm at the injury site or organ herniation into the chest.

Surgical repair of the injured diaphragm is indicated with these findings. Laparoscopy and thoracoscopy may be used when injuries are amenable, though open repair may be required both for the diaphragmatic injuries themselves and associated organ injuries. The morbidity of diaphragmatic trauma can be high and largely results from associated organ injury. Complications include organ herniation, diaphragm paralysis, pulmonary pathology (e.g., pleural effusion, atelectasis), and biliary fistulae. Diaphragmatic trauma is commonly missed at the time of the initial traumatic injury, and patients with a history of significant trauma presenting with clinical signs consistent with bowel obstruction should be evaluated for a possible missed diaphragm injury.



Traumatic aortic rupture (A) is a serious complication of blunt trauma and should be ruled out in this patient. His abnormal breath sounds and herniation of abdominal contents into the chest suggest diaphragm rupture instead.

Noniatrogenic injury of the esophagus (C) is an exceedingly rare complication of trauma and may show pneumomediastinum on X-ray rather than abdominal contents within the thoracic cavity.

Gastric perforation (D) is another rare complication of trauma. Rather than herniation of the stomach into the thoracic cavity, free air under the diaphragm (i.e., pneumoperitoneum) would be expected.

Pneumothorax (E) is a potential concomitant condition with diaphragm injury but is not seen on this patient’s X-ray. The patient’s abnormal breath sounds are caused by lung collapse due to herniation of abdominal contents into the chest.

Question: A 37-year-old man presents with severe pain in his forearm. He works in a glass etching factory, and a high-concentration chemical solution spilled onto his arm. He reports severe pain in the area of his injury, diffuse abdominal pain, and intermittent twitching of several different muscles. On physical examination, there is destruction of the skin tissue in the area of exposure and the beginning of tissue necrosis. The nurse has initiated irrigation with tap water. Which of the following is the next appropriate action?

Options.text: Irrigation with an alkaline neutralizing solution

ExplanationEN:
This patient has a hydrofluoric acid burn. Hydrofluoric acid is an acidic solution used in several areas, such as the petroleum industry for high-octane gasoline, the production of microelectronics, etching glass, removing rust, and cleaning cement and bricks. The most common exposure is dermal causing tissue destruction locally. Untreated skin will eventually become coagulated and may form an eschar. Severe pain is often present. The fluoride ion binds to calcium and magnesium ions. If irrigation is not successful, infiltration of calcium gluconate can be considered. Additionally, a topical calcium gluconate gel can be applied. In severe cases, calcium gluconate in lactated Ringers can be injected intra-arterially. Systemic toxicity may occur leading to hypocalcemia demonstrated in this patient by his muscle fasciculations and abdominal pain. Of note, when caring for a patient with hydrofluoric acid exposure, health care workers should use proper precaution which includes nitrile gloves. Regular latex gloves will not provide adequate protection.



The first step in detoxifying patients with chemical burns involves removing the offending agent typically through low-pressure water irrigation. High-pressure irrigation (A) is not used because of the possibility of pushing the chemical deeper into the skin or wound. Multiple animal studies have not demonstrated improvement with neutralizing solutions (C), as irrigation with water had better outcomes. Polyethylene glycol therapy (D) is the treatment of choice for exposures to phenols used in the production of organic polymers and plastics.

Question: A 9-year-old boy presents to the emergency department for severe ankle pain. He was jumping on a trampoline and landed feet first on the concrete from a high height. On exam, his ankle does not appear deformed and he is neurovascularly intact. He has significant bony tenderness over the tibia just proximal to the ankle joint. His X-ray is shown above. What is the most appropriate next treatment?

Options.text: Orthopedic consultation in the emergency department
Placing in a walking boot and facilitating follow-up with orthopedics as an outpatient
Strict non-weight bearing instructions and giving crutches until general outpatient follow-up

CorrectAnswer: Orthopedic consultation in the emergency department
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s fracture is through the metaphysis, growth plate, and epiphysis, and thus is a Salter-Harris type IV fracture. Salter-Harris fractures are more common than sprains and strains in childhood because children’s cartilaginous growth zones are weaker than the adjacent ligaments and bones. Type II, a fracture through a portion of the growth plate and into the metaphysis, is the most common. Types I and II can be treated conservatively with splinting and close orthopedic follow-up. Type I fractures often have normal-appearing radiographs. Thus, patients with continued pain and growth plate tenderness should be treated as a type I fracture. Types III, IV, and V fractures require an orthopedic consultation in the ED. Type III fractures may lead to limb length discrepancies and should be followed closely by orthopedics. Type IV and V fractures almost always lead to limb length discrepancies and require surgical fixation.



All patients with Salter-Harris fractures should be non-weightbearing and should not be given a walking boot (B).

Type III, IV, and V fractures are associated with limb length discrepancies and should be seen by orthopedics in the emergency department prior to discharge. Thus, discharge with orthopedics or general medicine outpatient follow-up (B, D) is incorrect.

Rest, ice, compression, and elevation (C) would be appropriate if this patient had an uncomplicated ankle sprain.

Question: A 24-year-old man presents after a rollover motor vehicle collision. Vital signs are notable for a BP of 89/50 mm Hg, HR of 130 bpm, RR of 18/min, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. The patient is awake and alert and reports abdominal pain. He has bruising over the abdomen and is diffusely tender with involuntary guarding. No other injuries are noted on the exam. eFAST shows free fluid in the hepatorenal space. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Transfer to the OR for exploratory laparotomy

CorrectAnswer: Transfer to the OR for exploratory laparotomy
ExplanationEN:
This patient is in shock with peritonitis after blunt trauma. The hemodynamically unstable trauma patient should be assumed to be in hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. However, patients with blunt trauma often have multiple thoracoabdominal injuries, and evaluation for obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax or pericardial tamponade is critical, as these conditions are managed differently. In addition to a thorough primary and secondary survey, the eFAST examination should be performed on all trauma patients. Cardiac and lung windows allow for rapid assessment of pericardial tamponade, pneumothorax, and hemothorax, and the three abdominal windows (the hepatorenal space, splenorenal space, and pelvis) allow for assessment of hemoperitoneum.

In the hemodynamically unstable patient with an eFAST exam positive for intra-abdominal free fluid, the best next step after basic supportive measures is to transfer to the OR for exploratory laparotomy. Immediate surgical intervention is also indicated in the patient with peritoneal signs and a positive eFAST. Further diagnostic imaging should not delay definitive operative management. In the hemodynamically stable patient with a positive eFAST exam, CT of the abdomen and pelvis is indicated, as CT can identify the source of bleeding and guide the need for operative management. Finally, the eFAST exam should not be used to rule out significant abdominal injury, as CT is more sensitive for detecting retroperitoneal, diaphragmatic, and solid organ injury.



This patient is awake and protecting his airway, so intubation (A) is unnecessary. Additionally, he should be resuscitated prior to intubation to avoid peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse.

CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (B) is indicated in the hemodynamically stable patient but should not delay definitive operative care in the hemodynamically unstable patient.

Performing serial abdominal exams (C) is appropriate in a patient with negative CT imaging if there is an ongoing concern for hollow viscus injury, but it is not appropriate in an unstable patient with peritonitis.

Question: An 18-year-old woman presents with a stab wound to the anterior neck. Which sign requires immediate operative management?
ExplanationEN:
A patient with an expanding or pulsatile hematoma is at high risk for a serious vascular injury and should immediately be transported for surgical intervention after initial resuscitation. There are a number of hard signs of vascular injury in penetrating neck injuries. These include active hemorrhage, expanding or pulsatile hematoma, bruit, thrill, massive hemoptysis, shock, major hematemesis, or aerodigestive tract injury. Patients with these signs require surgical intervention regardless of imaging findings. Control of the patient’s airway should be undertaken early as many of these injuries can lead to precipitous decompensation and airway obstruction. Patients with soft signs of vascular injuries should have further diagnostic testing done to confirm the presence or absence of a surgical lesion.



Soft signs of vascular injury include minor hemoptysis (B), subcutaneous emphysema (C), venous oozing from the neck (D), and nonpulsatile, nonexpanding hematomas.

Question: A 21-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bleeding from his nose after he was in an altercation at the bar tonight. The initial examination is remarkable for swelling and slight deformity to the bridge of the nose without any lacerations. The man is bleeding from his right naris. You attempt to stop the bleeding with compression, the use of an intranasal vasoconstrictor, and cautery without success. You decide to place anterior packing, which controls the bleeding. No other facial injuries are noted on examination or imaging. What is the most appropriate management?

Options.text: Begin prophylactic antibiotics and discharge the patient to follow up with otolaryngology in 2 days
Consult interventional radiology for embolization of a bleeding anterior nasal artery
Consult otolaryngology to evaluate the patient in the emergency department as the patient will need emergent surgery
No further emergency department intervention; discharge the patient to follow up with otolaryngology in 2 days

CorrectAnswer: No further emergency department intervention; discharge the patient to follow up with otolaryngology in 2 days
ExplanationEN:
Treatment of nasal injuries begins with the same management as any soft-tissue injury and includes compression to control bleeding. Irrigation is necessary for contaminated wounds. Many nasal fractures can be diagnosed clinically, and the care is conservative with pain medicine, rest, ice, and head elevation. If nasal bleeding continues, identification of the source of bleeding is advisable. Treatment of continued epistaxis may include silver nitrate cautery, which is successful in most cases. If bleeding continues, anterior nasal packing may be required. It is recommended that the packing be removed in approximately 3–4 days. The use of prophylactic antibiotics in the setting of nasal packing is controversial, and the recommendation at this time is to discharge the patient without antibiotics to see otolaryngology in 2–3 days.



It has been previously recommended that all patients with nasal packing receive prophylactic antibiotics upon discharge from the emergency department due to concern for toxic shock syndrome. However, the incidence of toxic shock syndrome after packing for epistaxis is unknown, and in one study of patients who underwent nasal surgery and had packing placed, the incidence was as low as 16 cases per 100,000 patients. No data exists to indicate that the use of prophylactic antibiotics will reduce the incidence of toxic shock syndrome. In fact, there are likely more complications from the use of antibiotics in this setting. Thus, beginning prophylactic antibiotics and discharging the patient to follow up with otolaryngology in 2 days (A) is incorrect.

No evidence currently exists to support early nasal fracture reduction and management. Treatment is conservative and includes rest, ice, pain control, and head elevation. Even if nasal packing is required to control hemorrhage, consulting otolaryngology to evaluate the patient in the emergency department (C) is not needed. A follow-up evaluation with an otolaryngologist is recommended after the swelling has subsided.

If bleeding in the nose continues after compression, cautery, and anterior nasal packing attempts, then one must consider a posterior bleed. Posterior packing may need to be placed, and the patient should be admitted because patients with posterior packing in place are at higher risk for hypoxia, hypoventilation, and dysrhythmias. If posterior packing strategies fail, a consult with interventional radiology may be necessary for embolization. However, in this case, consulting interventional radiology for embolizing a bleeding anterior nasal artery (B) is inappropriate.

Question: Which of the following is most likely in blunt trauma to the cricoid cartilage?
ExplanationEN:
Cricoid cartilage fractures are uncommon but clinically significant injuries associated with high-energy blunt neck trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions or strangulation. The cricoid is a complete ring of cartilage, unlike the open C-shaped tracheal cartilages, which makes it more susceptible to specific fracture patterns under compressive force.

The most common location for cricoid fractures is through the anterior and posterior portions of the cartilage. This pattern results from anterior-posterior compression of the neck, where force applied to the front of the neck causes the cricoid ring to fracture both anteriorly and posteriorly in a two-point pattern.

These fractures often lead to airway compromise due to associated mucosal laceration, soft tissue swelling, or hematoma formation. Patients may present with hoarseness, stridor, subcutaneous emphysema, or signs of upper airway obstruction. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy and CT imaging of the neck are useful diagnostic tools. Treatment depends on the degree of airway compromise and may range from observation to tracheostomy and surgical repair.



Arytenoid (B) cartilages are separate paired cartilages located posteriorly on the superior surface of the cricoid cartilage and play a key role in vocal cord motion. While arytenoid dislocation can occur with laryngeal trauma or endotracheal intubation, this injury is distinct from cricoid cartilage fracture. It affects phonation rather than airway patency and is not the most common cricoid-related injury.

Comminuted fracture (C) implies fragmentation of the cartilage into multiple pieces, which is possible but uncommon and reflects severe trauma. The usual fracture pattern is a two-point break (anterior and posterior) rather than multiple fragmented segments.

Complete dislocation (D) of the cricoid cartilage from the surrounding laryngeal framework is exceedingly rare and represents a catastrophic airway injury. This is not the typical presentation of a cricoid fracture, which usually involves a break in the cartilage rather than disarticulation.

Question: In patients with a presumed tripod fracture, which imaging study is the mainstay of emergent evaluation?
ExplanationEN:
A tripod fracture is a triple fracture pattern made up of fractures of the three main processes of the zygoma: zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomaticotemporal suture, and infraorbital rim. This leads to free movement of the zygoma. All forms of zygomatic fractures are most commonly due to direct and forceful trauma. Diagnosis is confirmed with computed tomography of the face. Tripod fractures are associated with vision loss and poor cosmetic outcomes without timely operative repair. Patients commonly present with cheek swelling, ecchymosis, and severe tenderness to palpation. Crepitus and mobility of the cheek may be present. Epistaxis may indicate concomitant sinus fractures. Those with isolated zygomatic arch fractures can be discharged with pain control and close plastic surgery follow-up. Zygomatic fractures involving the sinuses should receive antibiotics. Tripod fractures with significant malar eminence flattening or vision changes should be given intravenous antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam) and admitted after emergent plastic or oral maxillofacial surgery consultation.



A tripod fracture is a facial fracture and does not require extremity or mandibular imaging. Trimalleolar ankle fractures, a fracture pattern made up of fractures of the lateral and medial malleoli and the distal posterior tibia, should be evaluated by computed tomography of the ankle (A).

Hip fractures do not commonly need computed tomography evaluation (C) emergently. However, computed tomography is commonly preferred over plain radiographs in patients with a prosthesis being evaluated for hip fractures.

Evaluation of isolated mandibular injuries may warrant dedicated computed tomography of the mandible (D). Occasionally, triple fractures involving the bilateral condyles and symphysis may be noted.

Question: Which of the patients described below is most likely to have an acute radial head subluxation?

Options.text: A 2-year-old boy who reports right arm pain of unknown origin holds his right arm in slight flexion at the elbow with a pronated wrist and has no edema, bruising, or deformity of the elbow
A 3-year-old boy who reports right arm pain near the elbow after his babysitter picked him up by that arm and has swelling and tenderness at the elbow and severe pain with range of motion
A 5-year-old girl who reports left wrist pain after a fall at school cradles her left arm against her chest and has swelling and tenderness on the radial side of the wrist
A 7-year-old girl who reports left arm pain after falling on an outstretched hand holds her left arm in flexion at the elbow and has swelling and tenderness at the elbow

CorrectAnswer: A 2-year-old boy who reports right arm pain of unknown origin holds his right arm in slight flexion at the elbow with a pronated wrist and has no edema, bruising, or deformity of the elbow
ExplanationEN:
A 2-year-old boy who reports right arm pain of unknown origin holds his right arm in slight flexion at the elbow with a pronated wrist and has no edema, bruising, or deformity at the elbow is correct. Radial head subluxation, also known as pulled elbow, occurs most commonly in the 2- to 3-year-old age group but can be found from several months to 6–7 years of age when the annular ligament is stiffer. It is most commonly the result of axial traction with a pronated wrist but can also occur due to a fall onto an outstretched hand or direct trauma to the elbow. The head of the radius slips out of the annular ligament that usually stabilizes the bone in the radiohumeral joint, causing pain with arm manipulation and reluctance to try to move the elbow. Pain does not always localize to the elbow. There is usually no swelling, bruising, or deformity and distal neurovascular function is normal. These features are very consistent, usually allowing for a clinical diagnosis without the need for radiological studies. The subluxation can usually be reduced with either of two maneuvers: hyperpronation-extension or supination-flexion. The patient usually has complete resolution of symptoms within several minutes of reduction. Approximately 90% of patients are completely recovered within 30 minutes. Splints and slings are usually not necessary, but caregivers should be counseled to try to avoid activities that involve axial traction on the arm to reduce the chances of recurrence.



A 3-year-old boy who reports right arm pain near the elbow after his babysitter picked him up by the right arm has swelling and tenderness at the elbow and severe pain with range of motion (B) is incorrect. Although the mechanism of injury is typical and pulled elbow may cause severe pain upon movement, there is typically no swelling, bruising, or deformity.

A 5-year-old girl who reports left wrist pain after a fall at school cradles her left arm against her chest and has swelling and tenderness on the radial side of the wrist (C) is incorrect. Although the mechanism of injury is consistent with pulled elbow, wrist pain with other signs of wrist injury is not.

A 7-year-old girl who reports left arm pain after falling on an outstretched hand holds her left arm in flexion at the elbow and has swelling and tenderness at the elbow (D) is also incorrect. The position of comfort with a pulled elbow is usually arm flexion with pronation. However, swelling, bruising, or deformity at the elbow are usually not present.

Question: A 50-year-old man presents to the ED with severe swelling and pain in his left forearm. He sustained a puncture wound to this area 3 days ago while working on a construction site. He has a diminished left radial pulse and severe pain with passive extension of his fingers. Which muscle in the deep volar compartment is at risk for ischemia?
ExplanationEN:
Compartment syndrome is a musculoskeletal emergency characterized by increased pressure within a confined space outlined by fascial planes that leads to tissue death and neurovascular compromise if not managed in a timely manner. Trauma is a common cause, including penetrating injuries, fractures, or crush injuries. However, external forces such as a tight dressing or cast may also precipitate compartment syndrome. Envenomation and high-pressure injection injuries are other causes. Intracompartmental hemorrhage or edema may lead to compression of neurovascular structures, leading to limb ischemia and necrosis. This occurs when tissue pressure or pressure from an external source exceeds perfusion pressure.

Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, characterized by pain out of proportion to exam findings, pulselessness, pallor, poikilothermia (coolness to touch), paresthesias, and exacerbation of pain with passive extension of the digits. Compartment pressures may be measured directly to aid in the diagnosis. Normal compartment pressure is 0–10 mm Hg. Compartment syndrome occurs when intracompartmental pressure exceeds 30 mm Hg or when the difference in the diastolic blood pressure and intracompartmental pressure (called the delta pressure) is < 30 mm Hg.

Most cases of compartment syndrome occur in the lower leg, followed by the forearm. The forearm is divided into four fascial compartments. The superficial volar compartment contains the flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor carpi radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis, palmaris longus, and pronator teres muscle. The deep volar compartment contains the flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus, and pronator quadratus muscles. The lateral compartment, or mobile wad of Henry, contains the brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis brevis, and extensor carpi radialis longus muscles. The dorsal compartment contains the extensor muscles, including the extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor pollicis longus, extensor digitorum, and supinator muscles. The treatment of choice for compartment syndrome is early decompression. This can occur by way of emergent fasciotomy or cast cutting or removal.



The flexor carpi ulnaris (A) and the palmaris longus (C) muscles are located in the superficial volar compartment of the forearm.

The supinator (D) muscle is located in the dorsal (extensor) compartment.

Question: Which of the following exam findings is most characteristic of a penile fracture?

Options.text: Gradual swelling and ecchymosis without deformity
Penile swelling with an upward curvature to the shaft

ExplanationEN:
Penile fractures are caused by a rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum. They occur as the result of blunt trauma to an erect penis. The classic signs include immediate detumescence, severe swelling, and ecchymosis. Patients note an audible snap before symptom onset.

The corpus spongiosum is involved in one-third of cases, and urethral involvement may occur in up to 20% of cases. Penile fractures occur in an erect penis when the tunica albuginea fibers are stretched and thinned. This increases the risk of injury or rupture due to any forced or aggressive downward bending of the penis. A tunica defect may be palpated.

Emergent urological consultation for surgical repair is the gold standard of treatment. Imaging is not necessary, as this is a clinical diagnosis. If there is blood at the urethral meatus, hematuria, or suspicion of urethral injury, a retrograde urethrogram may be performed. When the diagnosis is in question, a penile ultrasound will identify a disruption of the tunica albuginea. While less cost-effective, a T1-weighted MRI may also be obtained to confirm the diagnosis.



Edematous foreskin with dusky glans (B) describes paraphimosis, which occurs when the edematous foreskin retracts behind the glans, causing swelling and possible ischemia to the glans.

Gradual swelling and ecchymosis without deformity (C) is more suggestive of a penile contusion or soft tissue injury and not a tunical rupture.

Penile swelling with an upward curvature to the shaft (D) describes Peyronie disease, which is a fibrotic plaque formation in the tunica albuginea that leads to penile curvature. This does not describe penile fracture exam findings.

Question: A 35-year-old man is brought in via ambulance after being stabbed in the chest. On exam, there is a 1.5 cm linear laceration in the fourth intercostal space. Lung sounds are diminished on that side, and no tracheal deviation is noted. His vital signs are HR 131 bpm, BP 80/45 mm Hg, RR 28/min, and SpO2 90% on a nonrebreather mask. A single-view chest X-ray is obtained. What is the minimum volume of blood required to diagnose hemothorax on the image?
ExplanationEN:
Injuries leading to massive hemothorax include aortic rupture, myocardial rupture, injuries to hilar structures, lung parenchymal injuries, or intercostal mammary blood vessel injuries. Intercostal vessel injury can also cause hemothorax but rarely massive hemothorax. Significant hemothorax is most likely caused by direct lung injury. A volume of 300 mL is needed to identify hemothorax on an upright chest X-ray. When the patient is supine, volumes > 1,000 mL may be missed due to posterior layering of blood.

Treatment focuses on initial resuscitation and airway management. Care should include pain control, oxygen, blood volume support, and tube thoracostomy. Indications for surgery include an immediate return of ≥ 20 mL/kg (approximately 1,500 mL) of blood or ongoing bleeding of 150–200 mL/h for 2–4 hours. Consider blood transfusion or heparinized autotransfusion device if massive hemothorax is suspected. Patients with penetrating chest injuries with signs of life in the field who become pulseless may be candidates for emergent thoracotomy in the emergency department. Stab wounds to the heart are more amenable to repair than gunshot wounds. Relieving cardiac tamponade, controlling hilar bleeding, cross-clamping the aorta, and repairing myocardial lacerations with staples, sutures, or an inflated Foley catheter may be lifesaving techniques and can temporize bleeding until definitive repair in the operating room can be performed.



100 mL (A) is an insufficient amount of blood to accurately diagnose a hemothorax on X-ray.

While 500 mL (C) and 700 mL (D) of blood would both be visible on X-ray, they are not the minimum amounts required.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department via EMS for a gunshot wound to his abdomen. EMS reports the patient was shot once in the abdomen approximately 1 hour prior to arrival. He was found on scene anxious and was in severe pain but otherwise showed no acute distress. ExplanationEN:
Penetrating abdominal trauma most commonly occurs by stab or gunshot wound but can result from a variety of mechanisms ranging from weapons to building materials. The severity of injury is directly related to the depth and velocity of penetration, and the liver, colon, and small bowel are the most commonly injured organs.

The initial evaluation of a trauma patient consists of the primary survey to assess airway integrity and hemodynamic stability, followed by the secondary survey with adjunctive diagnostic testing. This patient’s abdominal distention and tenderness suggest some degree of intra-abdominal injury, but these findings are not specific to any one particular injury. Because this patient is hemodynamically stable, the suspicion of intra-abdominal injury can be further explored via CT scanning with IV contrast.

Question: A 51-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He reports abdominal pain and lightheadedness. His vital signs on arrival are T of 98.4°F (36.9°C), BP of 96/55 mm Hg, RR of 20/min, HR of 122 bpm and irregular, and SpO2 of 96% on room air. ExplanationEN:
A FAST examination offers rapid identification of free intraperitoneal fluid in the setting of trauma and hypotension. Massive hemoperitoneum can be quickly detected with a view of the Morison pouch in the right upper quadrant. This appears as an anechoic (i.e., black) stripe between the right kidney and the liver. FAST examination is rapid, noninvasive, repeatable, and portable, making it superior in many ways to computed tomography in the immediate evaluation of the trauma patient. However, it is not without limitations. It is not as good at evaluating for retroperitoneal bleeding as computed tomography. In the presence of clinical instability and a negative FAST examination, patients should be hemodynamically resuscitated and computed tomography imaging obtained to evaluate for traumatic causes of hypotension. Other causes of hypotension may be present (e.g., myocardial infarction, spinal shock), but computed tomography should be obtained to evaluate for operative causes concurrently with resuscitation.

Calculating the patient’s initial fluid requirements first requires estimating the extent of the burn. In this patient, the upper and lower back and the back of both arms are involved giving a BSA of 27%. The fluid requirement over the next 24 hours = 4 mL/kg x 70 kg x 27 ≅ 7,560 mL of fluid. One-half of this number (3,780 mL) should be given over the first 8 hours, and the rest should be given over the subsequent 16 hours.

Question: Which of the following is most likely to be affected by a primary blast injury?
ExplanationEN:
Injuries from blasts can be subdivided into several different categories. Primary blast injuries are caused by direct overpressure from blast waves on the body and, as such, primarily affect air-filled structures such as the lungs, auditory system, and gastrointestinal tract. Secondary blast injuries are caused by impact from debris created by the explosion, such as shrapnel. Tertiary blast injuries are caused by the patient being thrown by the force of the blast into stationary objects. Quaternary blast injuries result from burns, smoke inhalation, or chemical exposure caused by the blast. Finally, quinary injuries include the clinical effects from absorption of toxic material released into the environment.



Since primary blast injuries result from direct overpressure on structures, non-air-filled structures such as the heart (A), liver (B), and lymphocytes (D) are not typically affected.

Injury to which of the following structures could result in his examination findings?
ExplanationEN:
Grey-Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) in the setting of trauma with flank pain suggests retroperitoneal hemorrhage, most commonly from injury to the kidney or other retroperitoneal structures. The Grey-Turner sign is a subcutaneous manifestation of retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal hemorrhage, appearing as flank ecchymosis. In this patient with a history of falling down multiple steps, the unilateral left-sided Grey-Turner sign, combined with left flank pain and mild tachycardia, points toward kidney trauma with retroperitoneal bleeding.

The retroperitoneal location of the kidneys allows blood from kidney injury to track along tissue planes, manifesting as flank ecchymosis. Other retroperitoneal structures that could produce similar findings include the pancreas (though typically associated with pancreatitis rather than trauma), major vessels, and the duodenum. However, given the traumatic mechanism and unilateral left-sided presentation, kidney injury is the most likely source.

Kidney trauma occurs in approximately 10% of all blunt abdominal trauma cases and is the most commonly injured genitourinary organ. Patients may present with flank pain, hematuria, costovertebral angle tenderness, or signs of internal bleeding such as tachycardia and hypotension. However, hematuria is not a reliable predictor of injury severity, and significant kidney injury may occur even in its absence. In a hemodynamically stable patient, the preferred diagnostic test is a contrast-enhanced CT scan, which provides information on kidney parenchymal injury, collecting system disruption, and the presence of hematoma.

Most kidney injuries are low-grade and treated conservatively with fluid resuscitation, close observation, and serial hemoglobin monitoring. Interventional radiology may be used for angioembolization in select cases with active bleeding. Surgery is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients or those with high-grade injuries and associated complications. Long-term complications may include hypertension, urinoma, or loss of kidney function, highlighting the need for timely diagnosis and appropriate management in the ED.



The ileum (A) is an intraperitoneal segment of the small intestine and is not located in the retroperitoneal space. Injuries to the ileum typically result in intraperitoneal air or free fluid on imaging and are more likely to cause diffuse peritonitis if perforated. It is not associated with flank ecchymosis or retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

The spleen (C) is an intraperitoneal organ and the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Splenic injury typically results in intraperitoneal bleeding and may cause Kehr sign (referred left shoulder pain) or left upper quadrant tenderness. It does not usually result in flank ecchymosis unless hemorrhage is extensive enough to track into the retroperitoneum, which is less typical.

The stomach (D) is also an intraperitoneal organ. Injury to the stomach from blunt trauma may result in free air under the diaphragm if perforated or signs of peritonitis, but not retroperitoneal hemorrhage or flank ecchymosis.

Question: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a chin laceration. She was running at home and tripped, striking her chin on a brick fireplace just prior to arrival. On your exam, she is well-appearing with vital signs within normal limits for her age. She has a 2 cm laceration and a superficial abrasion just underneath the center of her chin. You notice that she also has a limited mandibular range of motion and malocclusion of the teeth. She reports tenderness on palpation of her right temporomandibular joint. You perform wound care and skin closure. Which of the following is the most preferred next step in her care?
ExplanationEN:
Chin lacerations in children are uncommonly associated with temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dislocation or a mandibular fracture. The mandible in children is smaller and more elastic than in adults, growing downward, forward, and laterally as the child ages. The mandible is extremely stable in infants and toddlers, so fractures in children < 5 years of age are rare without significant additional injury. The diagnosis of TMJ dislocation or fracture should be suspected in patients with limited mandibular range of motion and teeth malocclusion, as seen in this patient. In some cases, the injury results in a fixed open jaw that causes unclear speech and drooling. TMJ dislocation in children is commonly associated with a mandibular fracture regardless of the mechanism. Children who present with TMJ dislocation require imaging to rule out an associated fracture before reduction attempts. Children with nontraumatic TMJ dislocation who are skeletally mature may be treated similarly to adults and undergo reduction and treatment without imaging. A maxillofacial CT scan is the preferred method of evaluation in children with traumatic TMJ dislocation as it is the most sensitive test to rule out a mandibular fracture. A panoramic jaw radiograph is preferred in nontraumatic cases due to the lower radiation risk. The most common site of mandibular fracture in children is the condyle. TMJ reduction attempts in children are similar to those performed in adults involving a syringe method, intraoral technique, or extraoral technique. All children with a mandibular fracture should be evaluated and treated by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon. Complications can include growth disturbance, facial asymmetry, malocclusion, tooth bud damage, joint dysfunction, sleep apnea, chronic pain, and salivary disorders.



Attempting a closed reduction (A) is appropriate in an adolescent with a nontraumatic TMJ dislocation but not in a skeletally immature child after trauma.

A lateral neck radiograph (B) is appropriate when there is concern for a retropharyngeal abscess that usually presents with trismus, throat pain, and fever.

A panoramic jaw radiograph (D) is preferred in the setting of a nontraumatic TMJ dislocation in a skeletally immature child due to the lower amount of radiation, but it is less sensitive when evaluating for fractures after trauma.

Question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after being stabbed in the neck. She does not remember what she was stabbed with. On exam, you notice a puncture wound to the anterior aspect of her neck that appears to violate the platysma. Which of the following physical exam findings is considered a soft sign of injury in this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Although the mechanism of the injury is not clear in this case, any wound that appears to penetrate the platysma should raise concern for structural injury to the neck. Specifically, particular attention should be paid to assessing for signs of aerodigestive or vascular injuries. The patient should be assessed for hard and soft signs of injury. If a patient has a hard sign, they will likely have an injury requiring repair and should be transferred emergently to an operating room or an angiography suite. If a patient has a soft sign, it indicates a need for further diagnostic evaluation to rule out a surgical emergency. Hard signs of neck injury include shock, unresponsiveness to fluids, active arterial bleeding, pulse defect, pulsatile or expanding hematoma, vascular thrill or bruit, stridor, major hemoptysis, air bubbling in the wound, extensive subcutaneous emphysema, and airway obstruction. Soft signs of injury include nonexpanding hematoma, mild subcutaneous emphysema, cervical ecchymosis, dysphagia, and mild hematemesis.



Audible stridor (A), decreased radial pulse (B), and vascular bruit (D) are all considered hard signs of penetrating neck trauma. These findings suggest a significant aerodigestive or vascular injury that requires emergent definitive repair, and the patient should be transferred to the operating room without further workup in the emergency department.

Question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the ED after being hit in the face by a soccer ball. He has eye pain and redness, with the above exam finding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
A blunt injury to the eye can result in bleeding within the orbit. Red blood cells within the aqueous humor cause a decrease in available light to the retina, which results in blurry vision. Findings of a hyphema on exam include haziness within the pupil and an afferent pupillary defect. Red blood cells layering out within the iris suggest a significant injury. Patients with a hyphema are at risk of spontaneous rebleeding within the next 5 days, which can increase intraocular pressure and result in blindness.

Initial treatment involves measuring intraocular pressure, an eye shield, and having the patient sit upright to prevent blood from layering along the retina. Cases that require emergent bedside evaluation by an ophthalmologist include those with severe pain, elevated intraocular pressure, a hyphema that covers > 50% of the pupil, visual acuity worse than 20/200, and patients with sickle cell disease, as they are at particular risk of ocular complications of a hyphema. All children with a hyphema should receive prompt ophthalmology follow-up. Further care is as directed by an ophthalmologist and typically includes topical corticosteroids and cycloplegic eye drops.



A corneal abrasion (A) is a scratch across the cornea that is visible using fluorescein and is not visible on this patient’s exam.

A ruptured globe (C) presents with a circumferential subconjunctival hematoma, a teardrop pupil, or signs of leakage of aqueous humor on fluorescein stain, which is not visible above.

A subconjunctival hemorrhage (D) is superficial bleeding along the surface of the conjunctivae but not the pupil.

Question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off his skateboard. He reports that he had a straddle injury on a handrail. His genitourinary exam is remarkable for mild perineal ecchymosis. He is unable to urinate despite adequate hydration and normal plain radiographs. What is the appropriate next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
The patient presents with the inability to urinate after a straddle injury concerning for urethral injury, which requires retrograde urethrography. Other findings consistent with urethral disruption include blood at the meatus, gross hematuria, and marked periurethral or perineal swelling. Question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation is brought to the ED after a motor vehicle collision. She was an unrestrained driver and is reporting neck and abdominal pain. Vital signs show BP 90/55 mm Hg, HR 118 bpm, RR 22/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Initial trauma survey is significant for a distended, tender abdomen with a palpable fetal leg above the level of the umbilicus and no vaginal bleeding or discharge. FAST exam shows free fluid in the right upper quadrant. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient’s clinical presentation is most consistent with uterine rupture. Traumatic uterine rupture classically presents with a triad of shock, palpable fetal parts, and abdominal pain. Blunt abdominal trauma is a primary cause in second and third trimester patients as the uterus rises and becomes more exposed in the abdomen. Additional findings to support this diagnosis include a positive FAST scan or uterine atony and fetal distress on tocodynamometry. Fetal bradycardia or late decelerations (heart rate decelerations just after contractions) on tocodynamometry suggest uterine rupture in the correct clinical scenario.

The most common cause of nontraumatic uterine rupture is a previous cesarean section. Treatment for this patient requires emergent delivery of the fetus in addition to fluid resuscitation, stabilization, and standard trauma evaluation and treatment.



Kidney laceration (A) would also cause free fluid and hypotension or shock, but would not present with palpable fetal parts and is less likely in a gravid patient due to the size and position of the uterus.

Placental abruption (B), separation of the placenta from the wall of the uterus, most commonly presents as painful vaginal bleeding. On ultrasonography, there may be an anechoic stripe in the uterus but there would not be any abdominal free fluid. Treatment for abruption typically requires immediate surgery.

Placenta previa (C) is placental implantation over the cervical os and typically presents with painless vaginal bleeding without palpable fetal parts.

Question: A 19-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks gestation presents to the ED following a motor vehicle collision in which she was the restrained driver. She reports severe abdominal pain and decreased fetal movement. She has had no vaginal bleeding or rush of water. Her vital signs upon arrival are a T of 37.2°C (98.96°F), BP of 80/50 mm Hg, HR of 130 bpm, and RR of 30/min. Fibrinogen is 190 mg/dL. A fetal heart rate by bedside Doppler is 100 bpm. Physical exam reveals a rigid, tender uterus. An ultrasound shows a normally implanted posterior placenta with diffuse thickening. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with severe abdominal pain, a rigid and tender uterus, hypotension, tachycardia, decreased fetal movement, and a low fibrinogen level after trauma, all classic signs of placental abruption, which is the most likely diagnosis in this context.

Placental abruption, also known as abruptio placentae, refers to bleeding at the interface between the placenta and the uterine decidua, leading to partial or complete detachment of the placenta from the uterine wall before birth. It is the second most common cause of vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks of gestation. Risk factors include maternal trauma, cocaine use, multiple gestation, antiphospholipid syndrome, chronic hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, tobacco use, and a history of previous placental abruption.

Placental abruption presents with third-trimester bleeding accompanied by abdominal pain or uterine contractions. However, up to 20% of cases may not present with visible vaginal bleeding, as blood can accumulate behind the placenta (concealed abruption).

On physical examination, the uterus may be firm, tender, and larger than expected for gestational age. A fibrinogen level < 200 mg/dL is highly predictive of severe maternal hemorrhage and may signal impending disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

Ultrasound may show a retroplacental hematoma, the most classic finding. Other sonographic findings include placental thickening and echogenic debris in the amniotic fluid. However, despite its specificity, ultrasound has low sensitivity for placental abruption, and a normal scan does not rule out the diagnosis. Ultimately, the diagnosis is clinical and should be suspected in any pregnant patient with late-pregnancy bleeding or unexplained abdominal pain. Complications of placental abruption include fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, fetal demise, maternal coagulopathy, DIC, and hemorrhagic shock.

Management depends on both maternal and fetal status. If both the parent and fetus are hemodynamically stable with reassuring findings, vaginal birth may be attempted with close monitoring. However, if there are signs of maternal hemodynamic instability or nonreassuring fetal status, emergent cesarean section is indicated.



Chorioamnionitis (A)presents with fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling amniotic fluid. It is an infectious process and not related to trauma. The absence of fever and the presence of fetal bradycardia and hypotension make this unlikely.

Placenta accreta (B) involves abnormal placental adherence to the myometrium, usually diagnosed antepartum via imaging or intrapartum due to retained placenta. It does not typically present with acute abdominal pain, uterine rigidity, or fetal distress in a trauma setting.

Uterine rupture (D)can present with sudden pain and fetal distress, but it is more commonly associated with previous uterine surgery (e.g., cesarean section). This patient has no history of uterine surgery and has a normally implanted posterior placenta, making rupture less likely. Also, uterine rupture often shows loss of fetal station and palpable fetal parts on exam.

Question: A 24-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the ED in respiratory distress. He has no previous medical problems and states his symptoms started 30 minutes prior to arrival after falling off his moped. At first, his respiratory symptoms were mild but they rapidly progressed, prompting him to call 911. Vital signs are remarkable for HR 135 bpm, BP 88/50 mm Hg, RR 30/min, and SpO2 85%. On exam, you see a young, tall, and thin male patient in severe respiratory distress. Jugular venous distention, tachypnea, and decreased breath sounds on the right are notable. What is the best next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
A pneumothorax occurs when air accumulates in the pleural space secondary to lung injury or due to chest wall penetration. The majority are secondary to trauma representing the most common cause of all pneumothoraces. They can also occur spontaneously, and male patients between the ages of 10 and 30 years who are tall and thin have classically been described as having a risk for pneumothorax, secondary to subpleural blebs. A tension pneumothorax occurs when air in the pleural space causes displacement of mediastinal structures resulting in the characteristic clinical features that include tachypnea, chest pain, hypoxia, unilateral diminished or absent breath sounds, subcutaneous air, and unilateral hyperresonance to percussion. These findings, in association with shock, hypotension, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side should prompt the clinician to treat with immediate needle decompression or tube thoracostomy. Acceptable sites for needle decompression include the second or third intercostal space in the midclavicular line or the fifth intercostal space in the anterior or mid-axillary line. Needle decompression, when performed, should be followed promptly by tube thoracostomy.



A bolus of normal saline (A) is the initial treatment for septic shock, hypovolemic shock, and hemorrhagic shock. The patient above has obstructive shock due to tension pneumothorax and a rapid infusion of intravascular volume is not the appropriate treatment.

Obtaining a chest X-ray (B) is often how a pneumothorax, whether immediately evident or occult, is identified and diagnosed. However, a chest X-ray is not required to make the diagnosis of a tension pneumothorax, which can be diagnosed clinically and should prompt immediate treatment.

Pericardiocentesis (D) is the treatment of choice for cardiac tamponade, which classically presents with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and hypotension. Although this patient has two of the above findings, the unilateral absence of breath sounds makes a tension pneumothorax more likely.

Question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the ED after getting acid splashed in her eyes. What is the most appropriate end point to guide when eye irrigation should be stopped?

Options.text: Once the ocular pH normalizes to 7.4
When the patient reports resolution of eye pain

CorrectAnswer: Once the ocular pH normalizes to 7.4
ExplanationEN:
Chemical burns to the eye are true ophthalmologic emergencies requiring immediate and aggressive treatment. The cornerstone of therapy is copious, continuous irrigation initiated as soon as possible, ideally in the prehospital setting. Although tap water is appropriate for initial irrigation, balanced solutions such as lactated Ringer, normal saline, or commercially available amphoteric solutions are preferred in the ED due to their isotonicity and lower risk of inducing corneal edema.

The goal of irrigation is to normalize the ocular surface pH to physiologic levels, ideally 7.4, which helps limit further tissue injury and supports re-epithelialization. To determine when irrigation can be safely discontinued, pH should be checked using litmus paper placed in the lower conjunctival fornix. Irrigation should continue until serial pH measurements confirm a stable reading at or near 7.4.

Acidic and alkali injuries may differ in the volume of fluid required to achieve this end point, with alkali exposures often requiring more prolonged irrigation due to deeper penetration and ongoing tissue damage.



Reaching 30 minutes of continuous irrigation (A) is not a reliable end point. The volume and duration of irrigation required depend on the substance involved, the degree of exposure, and the measured pH.

Reaching 60 minutes of continuous irrigation (B) may be required for many injuries, but the definitive marker for stopping is normalization of ocular pH.

Symptom improvement (D) may lag behind tissue recovery or may occur prematurely despite ongoing injury. Reliance on subjective pain alone is not a safe or evidence-based method for assessing irrigation adequacy.

Question: A 32-year-old man presents to the ED with a deformity of the forearm after a fall on an outstretched hand. An X-ray is obtained and seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the distal radius paired with a dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. The fracture pattern is most often seen in men and is usually the result of a fall on an outstretched arm. Another common clinical scenario leading to this fracture is the patient in a motor vehicle collision who attempts to brace for impact with an arm against the dashboard. In adults, nonsurgical treatment is ineffective due to muscular forces that stress the injury and lead to radioulnar joint malunion. Therefore, open surgical repair is required. For this reason, Galeazzi fractures are sometimes called “fractures of necessity.” In children, the fracture is treated via closed reduction. A Galeazzi fracture is much more common than its counterpart, the Monteggia fracture.



A boxer fracture (A) is a transverse fracture of the fourth metacarpal, fifth metacarpal, or both after an axial loading trauma, such as punching a hard object. A Colles fracture (B) is a distal radius fracture with dorsal and radial displacement of the distal segment. A Jefferson fracture (D) is a fracture of the anterior and posterior arches of the C1 vertebrae after hyperextension injury to the neck or a severe axial load on the cervical spine.

Question: A 27-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver. He presents to the ED with significant facial trauma. A CT of his face shows a Le Fort type III fracture. Which of the following structures is directly affected?
ExplanationEN:
Complex facial fractures can be classified using the Le Fort classification system, which is divided into three types. A type I Le Fort fracture is a transverse fracture through the base of the maxilla and often involves the roots of the teeth. It may be unilateral or bilateral. The upper teeth may be grasped and rocked independently of the midface, indicating discontinuity with the maxilla. A type II Le Fort fracture is often bilateral and is characterized by pyramidal fractures that extend through the body of maxilla, orbital floor, nasal bones, hard palate, and lacrimal bones. The nasal unit and maxilla may be grasped and move as a unit relative to the orbital complexes and lower face.

Type III Le Fort fractures are considered complete craniofacial disjunction as the fracture extends from the nasal bridge, traveling posteriorly along the ethmoid bone, which comprises the medial orbital wall, and continues through the inferior and lateral orbital walls and frontozygomatic suture. The sphenoid bone is often involved with type III fractures, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak may occur. CSF may also leak from involvement of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bones. Le Fort fractures are best diagnosed with CT imaging. Depending on the extent of the injury, these often require management with a multidisciplinary team and may necessitate consultation with otolaryngology, plastic and reconstructive surgery, dentistry, and neurosurgery if a CSF leak is present.



A type II Le Fort fracture involves the central maxilla (A), nasal bridge, lacrimal bones, hard palate (C), and orbital floor. It often occurs bilaterally and in a pyramidal pattern.

Fractures of the mandibular condyle (D) are not included in the Le Fort classification of midface fractures.

Question: A 36-year-old woman presents to the ED 1 day after falling off a barstool and striking her head on the floor. She reports no loss of consciousness. Her exam is shown above. What is the most appropriate diagnostic study to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

Options.text: CT angiography of the head and neck
CT of the head without contrast
MRI of the brain with contrast

CorrectAnswer: CT of the head without contrast
ExplanationEN:
A basilar skull fracture is a traumatic injury involving the bones at the base of the skull, including the temporal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones. These fractures account for approximately 4% of severe head injuries and are commonly associated with high-energy trauma. They often result in communication between the intracranial space and air-filled sinuses or the middle ear, creating risk for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak and infection. Characteristic clinical signs include periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), retroauricular hematoma (Battle sign) as seen in this patient, hemotympanum, and clear otorrhea or rhinorrhea consistent with CSF leak.

The best initial imaging study for suspected basilar skull fracture is a noncontrast CT of the head, which is highly sensitive for detecting acute fractures and associated intracranial hemorrhage. Thin-cut bone windows increase detection rates, especially in the temporal bone and skull base. MRI has limited utility in acute trauma because it is less sensitive for fractures, though it may detect subtle intracranial injury. Skull radiographs lack sensitivity and specificity and should not be used.

In the ED, management of basilar skull fracture is largely supportive and focused on preventing secondary complications. Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely indicated for isolated CSF leaks, though patients should be monitored closely for meningitis. Neurosurgical consultation is recommended if there is a persistent CSF leak, intracranial hemorrhage, or vascular injury. Potential complications include meningitis, cranial nerve injury (particularly cranial nerves VII and VIII), vascular injury, and long-term CSF leak.



CT angiography of the head and neck (A) evaluates vascular injuries such as carotid or vertebral artery dissection. Vascular imaging may be indicated in severe trauma with neurologic deficits or an expanding hematoma. However, this patient has a Battle sign, a classic finding of basilar skull fracture, without focal neurologic symptoms. The appropriate first-line study is noncontrast CT of the head, not angiography.

Lumbar puncture (C) is often contraindicated in acute head trauma because of the risk of cerebral herniation in patients with elevated intracranial pressure. In addition, CSF testing is not required for the diagnosis of basilar skull fracture, which is made clinically with confirmatory imaging. In this patient, the physical examination finding of retroauricular hematoma should prompt CT imaging rather than invasive testing.

MRI of the brain with contrast (D) is superior to CT for evaluating parenchymal brain injury, demyelination, or tumors, but it is not the test of choice in acute trauma. MRI lacks sensitivity for detecting bone fractures, particularly in the skull base. Given the mechanism of injury and the pathognomonic physical examination finding, noncontrast CT of the head is more appropriate.

Skull radiographs (E) have poor sensitivity for detecting basilar skull fractures and cannot reliably exclude intracranial complications. Although historically used, they have been replaced by CT imaging, which provides rapid, high-resolution images of bone and brain tissue. In this patient with a posterior auricular hematoma, noncontrast CT of the head is the best next step.

Question: A 33-year-old man presents with right shoulder and upper arm pain after a fall. Physical examination reveals a “squared-off” appearance of the shoulder. Which nerve is most commonly affected in this injury?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with an anterior shoulder (glenohumeral) dislocation and the axillary nerve is a common concomitant injury. The glenohumeral joint represents the most commonly dislocated major joint. The joint may dislocate anteriorly (most common), posteriorly, or inferiorly. The injury is most commonly sustained in young patients during athletic activities involving rapid movements and in older people with axial trauma (e.g., fall on an outstretched arm). Patients present with severe pain and the arm is typically held in slight abduction and external rotation. The acromion becomes prominent and the shoulder appears “squared-off” as opposed to the typical rounded appearance. A complete neurovascular examination should be performed on all patients with glenohumeral dislocations. Due to its location, injury to the axillary nerve is common, occurring in up to 54% of patients (but may be as low as 5%). The axillary nerve provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the shoulder. Motor function of this nerve can be tested by examining the function of the deltoid muscle. The majority of patients with axillary nerve injury have neuropraxia, which typically recovers over time without specific intervention.



The median nerve (B) may be injured during a posterior elbow dislocation.

Radial nerve injuries (C) should be suspected in humeral fractures.

Ulnar nerve injuries (D) are uncommonly seen in anterior elbow dislocations.

Question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a linear 2 cm forehead laceration after a fall. While you are suturing the wound, her parent expresses concern about the cosmetic result and asks which cream can be applied to improve the appearance of the scar. Which of the following topical treatments has been shown to most reduce scar formation?
ExplanationEN:
The primary goals of wound care and subsequent closure are to achieve hemostasis, prevent infection, and optimize the cosmetic result. Before closure, the wound needs to be thoroughly assessed for retained foreign bodies, nerve injury, and tendon injury. Contrary to some parental perceptions, all wounds will scar. The risk of scarring increases for wounds with greater tissue damage (e.g., crush injury compared to a cut with a knife), increased tension (e.g., injuries over a joint or perpendicular to skin tension lines), and if the wound becomes infected.

Factors that increase the risk of infection include wounds caused by a blunt object (i.e., more tissue damage, devitalized tissue), those with > 6 hours between injury and repair, heavily contaminated wounds, and animal bites. Copious wound irrigation reduces the risk of infection with care taken not to soak the wound or cause local edema. Wound healing begins with hemostasis followed rapidly by an inflammatory response and epithelial cell growth.

Neovascularization begins within 24 hours and is followed by collagen synthesis, which peaks about 7 days after the injury and lasts for months. The wound then contracts and remodels over a year, during which less sun exposure is shown to reduce scar formation and hyperpigmentation. Prolonged daily sunscreen application is most likely to result in optimal wound healing and scar appearance.



Topical antibiotics (A) are recommended initially, as they can help with epithelialization and decrease crust formation allowing for easier suture removal. However, the do not work as well for preventing scar formation.

Corticosteroids (B) have been shown to benefit patients with chronic wounds but should not be used in acute wounds as they can interfere with the inflammatory response and wound healing.

Emollients (C) have not been shown to affect scar formation.

Question: A 16-year-old girl presents with pain in the right index finger after slamming it in a car door. Physical examination reveals a 50% subungual hematoma and intact nail folds. An X-ray shows a nondisplaced distal tuft fracture. What treatment is indicated?

Options.text: Pain management, application of ice, and follow-up
Trephination, splinting, oral antibiotics, and follow-up

ExplanationEN:
This patient should undergo trephination to relieve pain from the subungual hematoma, be splinted in extension, and follow up with a hand surgeon. Subungual hematomas are common after crush injuries to the digits. They are often associated with distal phalanx fractures. Pain associated with these hematomas can be severe as pressure increases under the nail. Management focuses on diagnosing associated injuries and providing pain relief.

Subungual hematomas can be simple (involving only the nail) or more complex (with injuries to the nail fold and digit). The nail matrix, which begins 7–8 mm under the proximal fold and ends at the lunula, is crucial for nail growth. Trauma to this area can cause scarring, leading to nail deformity or loss. When assessing subungual hematomas, the affected nail bed percentage is estimated, and any associated trauma is noted. The extensor and flexor tendons, capillary refill, and sensitivity should be examined. If a distal phalanx fracture is suspected, anteroposterior and lateral X-rays should be obtained. Referral to a hand surgeon is necessary for angulated, displaced, unstable, intra-articular fractures or those involving a significant portion of the articular surface.

Trephination is recommended for subungual hematomas that are acute (< 24–48 hours old), painful, or not spontaneously draining, provided the nail folds are intact. After 48 hours, trephination is usually ineffective, as the hematoma has clotted. Nail removal is unnecessary if the nail and margins are intact, even with an underlying distal phalanx fracture. Simple trephination generally results in good functional and cosmetic outcomes, especially if the hematoma covers more than half the nail or is painful.

The easiest way to relieve pain in the digit is by relieving the pressure building under the nail. This can be accomplished with trephination of the nail. Typically, an 18-gauge needle or electrocautery device is placed over the center of the hematoma. Gentle pressure is applied until the nail is penetrated. This typically results in a drop or two of blood exiting through the hole that has been created. The patient typically experiences immediate pain relief. Nail removal is typically unnecessary.



Antibiotics (A, E) are not needed for uncomplicated subungual hematomas, even with an underlying tuft fracture, as thorough cleaning and soft tissue repair are usually sufficient.

Pain management and icing (B) are helpful for immediate relief of acute pain and swelling, but alone, it does not address the subungual hematoma’s pressure. Trephination is needed to relieve pain caused by the hematoma.

Splinting and follow-up (C) are appropriate after trephination. Even though trephination in the presence of a distal phalanx fracture technically converts a closed fracture into an open one, drainage of the blood is not contraindicated.

Question: A 28-year-old man presents after a motor vehicle collision. He is conscious and reports severe pain shooting down the back of his legs. On exam, you note bilateral leg weakness and decreased lower extremity reflexes, decreased rectal tone, decreased sensation over the inner thighs, and pain on gentle compression of the pelvis. You obtain an X-ray, which shows a sacral fracture. What is the most critical next step in the management of this patient’s condition, along with appropriate further imaging?

Options.text: Physical therapy consultation for sacral fracture

ExplanationEN:
Traumatic cauda equina syndrome is not a spinal cord injury since the cauda equina (Latin for “horse’s tail”) is a bundle of nerve roots distal to the conus medullaris. Since injury to or compression of any of these nerve roots is possible, there is no single finding that is 100% predictive of the diagnosis, and the presentation may be variable. Symptoms and signs may include a sensory deficit over the buttocks, perineal area, and inner thighs (saddle anesthesia), decreased rectal tone, severe sciatica, variable sensory and motor loss in one or both lower extremities, and decreased lower extremity reflexes. Variable bladder or bowel dysfunction, including overflow incontinence, is possible but often not present when presenting acutely. Likewise, rectal tone may be spared. In contrast, lesions that affect only the conus medullaris present with early bladder and bowel dysfunction. When trauma is the cause of cauda equina syndrome, trauma protocols should be adhered to, and pelvic X-rays may reveal a sacral fracture. Magnetic resonance imaging is the study of choice to assist in the diagnosis, although computed tomography or myelography may help delineate the injury. Neurosurgical consultation is critical since acute traumatic cauda equina syndrome presents as a surgical emergency with decompression, preferably within 6 hours, traditionally regarded as the treatment of choice.



Catheterization of the bladder (A) may become necessary in this patient, as bladder dysfunction is a common part of the presentation. However, classic signs such as overflow incontinence tend to present late, and this would not be the most critical next step in management.

Methylprednisolone administration (B) is recommended within 8 hours of presentation in cases in which cauda equina syndrome was caused by an inflammatory condition, but it has not been shown to be of any benefit in cases caused by acute trauma.

Physical therapy consultation for sacral fracture (D) is not the most critical next step. The main concerns with a fracture of the sacrum are neurological injuries and a keen awareness of the amount of force necessary to cause this fracture. Unstable and displaced fractures may need surgery even in the absence of nerve injury. It is prudent to carefully look for associated injuries. Physical therapy may be needed later in the patient’s hospital or outpatient course.

Question: A 38-year-old man presents to the ED with facial and mouth pain after being punched in the face multiple times. On physical exam, you note significant swelling over the left inferior and lateral face, as well as misalignment of the inferior premolars. Which of the following is another common physical exam finding in patients with this injury?
ExplanationEN:
This patient has signs and symptoms consistent with a mandibular fracture. Signs and symptoms of a mandibular fracture include trismus, tooth misalignment, bite malocclusion, intraoral lacerations, and missing teeth. The tongue blade test is a way of detecting even subtle mandibular fractures. The patient bites the blade while the examiner attempts to break it. The inability to stabilize the blade is an indication that the patient may have a mandibular fracture and should undergo imaging. Plain mandibular X-rays and panoramic radiographs are screening tests for mandibular fractures. However, CT of the facial bones is the gold standard diagnostic test.

The mandible is the second most commonly fractured facial bone behind the nasal bone. The body of the mandible, the angle of the mandible, and the condyle are most often fractured. Management depends on location and whether the fracture is open or closed. Open fractures require IV antibiotics, such as penicillin or clindamycin, and hospital admission. Patients with closed fractures may be discharged with dental follow-up. The patient should be given adequate oral analgesics and be instructed to observe a soft diet and chew on the nonfractured side. Many fractures will require open reduction and internal fixation but do not require admission initially if not open fractures.

Midface instability (C) is a common finding with Le Fort fractures of the midface.

Question: A healthy 40-year-old man presents to the ED with a chemical burn to his right foot. He spilled an industrial cleaning solution containing hydrofluoric acid on the dorsum of the foot 15 minutes prior to arrival and has not performed any treatment. Exam is significant for tachycardia to 105 bpm, and a 1% body surface area lesion with white tissue surrounded by erythema on his right foot. In addition to copious irrigation and tetanus assessment, which of the following is the best next treatment option?

Options.text: Calcium gluconate gel topically to the burned area
Petroleum jelly topically to the burned area

CorrectAnswer: Calcium gluconate gel topically to the burned area
ExplanationEN:
Hydrofluoric acid is a highly corrosive acid that can cause systemic electrolyte disturbances and cardiotoxicity in addition to local damage like most other chemical burns. It quickly dissociates into hydrogen and fluoride ions after penetrating the skin. These free fluoride ions can complex with calcium and magnesium, causing hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Additionally, hypocalcemia will cause potassium efflux from cells, causing severe hyperkalemia. This combination of electrolyte abnormalities, in addition to the cardiotoxic effects of fluoride, can cause severe dysrhythmias such as prolonged QT interval.

Calcium gluconate gel topically can help complex the free fluoride ions, decreasing systemic effects. This should be applied consistently for 1 hour or until the pain is resolved. Large areas of burn may require intradermal or intra-arterial calcium gluconate. After initial stabilization and correction of electrolyte abnormalities, patients should receive tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotic ointment.



Intravenous calcium gluconate (B) is not the initial treatment for hydrofluoric acid but is an option if local application fails to correct the insult. It is also used for cardioprotective effects in those with hyperkalemia.

Intravenous potassium chloride (C) would not be indicated, as the damage from hydrofluoric acid will cause hyperkalemia. IV potassium can be given to correct hypokalemia, which can result from GI losses, rapid insulin infusion, or drug side effects including diuretics or antipsychotics.

Petroleum jelly topically to the burned area (D) is used in tar or asphalt burns. The treatment for these burns calls for rapid cooling of the tar to reduce thermal injury, and then the application of a solubilizing agent such as petroleum jelly to remove the tar.

What ECG changes will be seen in hyperkalemia?

Reveal Answer:
Progressive changes start with peaked T waves, followed by lengthening of the PR and QRS, and lastly, a sinusoidal pattern is seen with increasing potassium concentration.

Question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the ED with left ear pain after wrestling with his friends in his backyard 3 days ago. On exam, you note the finding in the image above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: CT imaging of the head with thin cuts of the temporal bone
Incision and drainage followed by pressure dressing with next-day follow-up
Needle aspiration followed by loose dressing application and next-day follow-up
Symptomatic care with analgesia, ice packs, and urgent referral to plastic surgery

CorrectAnswer: Incision and drainage followed by pressure dressing with next-day follow-up
ExplanationEN:
Auricular hematomas in the subperichondrial potential space can occur after blunt trauma to the ear. This is a common injury that occurs in wrestlers. Without proper treatment, the cartilaginous structures of the ear can become permanently deformed, resulting in a cauliflower ear. The recommended treatment modality is drainage of the hematoma, especially for large hematomas and for those > 2 days after the injury. The procedure is performed by making a small incision in the helix or antihelix, followed by the application of a pressure dressing to maintain the contours of the ear. Next-day follow-up to ensure hematoma reaccumulation has not occurred is also encouraged. The use of prophylactic antibiotics after incision and drainage is controversial. Needle aspiration (C) may result in less cosmetic deformity than incision and drainage and may be used for acute hematomas (< 48 hours) that are < 2 cm in size. It is often ineffective or insufficient in fully draining a larger hematoma. Improved cosmesis with incision and drainage can be achieved by positioning the incision at the helix or antihelix of the auricle, where scarring is less likely to be noticeable.

In very small hematomas, symptomatic care (D) might be advisable. Since auricular hematomas are the prelude to the development of cauliflower ear, it is important to have a low threshold for draining the hematoma.
