This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with a high-pressure injection injury. The chemical properties of the injectant, and the resultant irritation, it causes is the primary determinant of the damage caused. Air and clean water generally have a relatively benign course, while paint solvents cause the most severe inflammation. Injuries to the nondominant index finger and other nondominant digits are most common.

The initial external examination may look deceptively innocuous. However, there is typically delayed pain, distension and swelling of the digit, and finally vascular involvement that results in digital ischemia as the inflammation progresses. Tracking among tendon sheaths allows the inflammation to progress more proximally on the flexor surface of the hand, which may result in loss of function and significant morbidity. These injuries often come from grease guns, paint sprayers, fuel injectors, air guns, and other industrial equipment. The injectant distributes along fascial planes, tendon sheaths, and neurovascular bundles and causes chemical irritation over time, leading to digit ischemia.

High-pressure injection injuries are a surgical emergency, thus management of these injuries is by immediate surgical debridement and exploration by a hand surgeon. While in the ED, tetanus prophylaxis should be updated, analgesia provided, and intravenous antibiotics started.



Grease (A) generally causes the second-most tissue destruction after paint solvents.

Pressurized air (C) and warm water (D) generally cause less tissue damage overall but may still result in significant damage if not addressed early in the course.

Question: What is the maximum volume of intrathoracic blood that may be missed on a supine chest X-ray?
ExplanationEN:
A hemothorax is defined as the presence of blood in the pleural space, which may originate from the lung, chest wall, diaphragm, heart, or the great vessels. The most common is direct bleeding from the lung or the intercostal arteries. If the bleeding is venous in origin, it may tamponade itself without intervention, while arterial bleeding almost always requires aggressive invasive management. Both blunt and penetrating trauma can result in a hemothorax. It is important to keep in mind that each hemithorax can hold about 40% of a patient’s circulating blood volume. An upright chest radiograph is the ideal initial diagnostic study. Up to 1,000 mL of blood may be missed on a chest radiograph of a supine patient due to posterior layering of the blood, which produces only a subtle diffuse haziness on the film on the affected side. A point-of-care ultrasound may be the preferred initial study in a critically ill patient who cannot tolerate an upright chest film. A computed tomography scan has the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting a hemothorax in a hemodynamically stable patient. If the hemothorax is large enough to be seen on an upright chest film, the standard of care remains to perform a tube thoracostomy on the affected site.



Up to 200 mL (B) of blood can be easily missed on an upright chest radiograph. 200 mL and up to 500 mL (C) of blood should be identifiable on an upright chest radiograph as blunting of the costophrenic angle, as well as lateral layering on a decubitus film. This amount of blood needs to be evacuated via tube thoracostomy. 500 mL and up to 700 mL (D) of blood should be easily identifiable on upright and decubitus chest films.

Question: A 55-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia presents to the ED with leg pain and swelling with blisters. The patient indicates she jumped out of a truck bed landing on her feet but hurt her leg in some way. She limped into the house, tied a few bandanas around her leg because she had seen that in the movies, and then took a nap. She awoke unable to walk and noticed swelling and blisters as pictured above. She has tenderness to her entire lower leg. She has a strong palpable posterior tibialis pulse. She has difficulty dorsiflexing at the ankle. Which compartment of the lower leg is most likely affected by this disease process?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with a story and exam that is concerning for compartment syndrome. Acute compartment syndrome most often occurs after trauma but can occur after extreme exertion in athletes or from thrombosis, reperfusion injury, vascular disorders, certain envenomations, or prolonged limb compression. This patient had a traumatic injury and then likely prolonged limb ischemia and reperfusion injury after placing makeshift tourniquets on her leg.

Compartment syndrome in the lower leg can occur in a distinct anatomic compartment bound by fascial membranes. The anterior compartment is the most common site for compartment syndrome in the lower leg. It contains the foot extensor muscles, so patients with compartment syndrome in this area may have difficulty dorsiflexing at the ankle. Patients may also report a loss of sensation between the first and second toes. Late complications, if not recognized and treated, include drop foot and claw foot. Based on this patient’s presentation, she most likely has, at a minimum, compartment syndrome of her anterior compartment in the lower leg. It is important to have a high index of suspicion for this disease process and to act quickly when the diagnosis is suspected. Treatment is surgical fasciotomy.



The deep posterior compartment (B) contains muscles that aid in plantar flexion, the tibial artery, the peroneal artery, and the tibial nerve. Along with difficulty flexing the toes, patients may have plantar hyperesthesia.

The lateral compartment (C) of the lower leg contains the muscles responsible for foot eversion and some plantar flexion. Patients with lateral compartment syndrome may report sensory loss to the lower leg and dorsum of the foot due to compression of the superficial peroneal nerve.

The superficial posterior compartment (D) is the least likely to develop compartment syndrome since there are no major vessels or nerves that travel through this compartment. Patients may have difficulty with plantar flexion if this area is affected.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents after a fall down two stairs. He has a headache and a small scalp hematoma. Which of the following abnormalities is seen on his CT scan of the brain?
ExplanationEN:
A subdural hematoma is a collection of blood between the dura and arachnoid mater. Most commonly, this occurs from shear force causing an injury of the bridging veins. Older patients are at higher risk because as the brain atrophies with age, the bridging veins are under more tension. On a CT scan, the blood is crescent-shaped and does not cross the midline, although it can cross suture lines. Surgical management is determined by the size of the hematoma, the presence of midline shift (typically > 5 mm), and neurologic deterioration.



An epidural hematoma (A) is bleeding outside of the dura below the skull. A common cause of an epidural hematoma is direct trauma to the temporoparietal region of the head, injuring the middle meningeal artery. As a result of arterial bleeding, epidural hematomas progress rapidly and carry significant risk for morbidity and mortality. On a CT scan, an epidural hematoma does not cross suture lines.

A subarachnoid hemorrhage (B) may result from trauma, and on a CT scan, blood is present within the cerebrospinal fluid. A subarachnoid hemorrhage is caused by injury to the small subarachnoid vessels. It is the most common abnormality seen on CT scan after a head injury.

A subdural hygroma (D) appears as a fluid collection in the same location as a subdural hematoma on CT scan but has the same density as cerebrospinal fluid. It is unclear whether a tear in the dura allows cerebrospinal fluid to escape into this area or whether it is an effusion from an injured vessel.

Question: A 23-year-old G1P0 woman at 28 weeks gestation presents to the ED after a minor motor vehicle collision with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She states she was a belted, front-seat passenger, and the car was hit from behind. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Her physical exam reveals a well-appearing woman with a gravid uterus and a nontender abdominal examination. A transabdominal ultrasound shows a fetus of approximately 28 weeks gestational age with a fetal heart rate of 160 bpm and a negative focused assessment with sonography in trauma examination. A sterile speculum exam reveals a closed cervix with a small amount of dark blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Discharge home with obstetrics follow-up the next day
Immediate transfer to obstetrics service for fetal monitoring
Repeat abdominal examination and ultrasound in 6 hours

CorrectAnswer: Immediate transfer to obstetrics service for fetal monitoring
ExplanationEN:
In any pregnant patient ≥ 20 weeks gestation involved in a motor vehicle collision, even one that is minor, the standard of care includes continuous external fetal monitoring for at least 4–6 hours, regardless of maternal symptoms or reassuring initial findings.

This patient at 28 weeks gestation presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, both of which are potential signs of placental abruption, even in the absence of uterine tenderness or ultrasound findings. A negative FAST exam rules out hemoperitoneum but does not exclude placental injury or uterine irritability. The combination of blunt trauma, gestational age ≥ 20 weeks, and vaginal bleeding necessitates immediate obstetric evaluation and fetal monitoring to assess for fetal distress and uterine contractions.

Trauma is a leading cause of maternal and fetal morbidity. The placenta can shear from the uterine wall with acceleration-deceleration injuries, and clinical signs of abruption (e.g., bleeding, pain, contractions) may not be immediate. Furthermore, fetal distress may be the first sign of significant maternal-fetal compromise. Timely cardiotocographic monitoring is essential to detect subtle changes in fetal heart rate or uterine activity that could indicate abruption, preterm labor, or uterine rupture.

Close monitoring in a setting with obstetric capability allows for rapid intervention, including corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm delivery becomes necessary, or urgent delivery in the setting of fetal compromise.



Discharging (A) a pregnant patient with vaginal bleeding after trauma without a period of fetal monitoring is inappropriate. Despite reassuring initial findings, the risk of delayed complications such as placental abruption or preterm labor necessitates observation. Discharge would ignore the standard protocols for trauma in pregnancy and risk missing time-sensitive complications.

Emergent C-section (C) is not indicated when there is no evidence of fetal distress, maternal instability, or uterine rupture that would necessitate emergent cesarean delivery. The fetal heart rate is reassuring, and the patient is hemodynamically stable.

Serial assessment (D) may be appropriate in some cases, but this approach alone is inadequate. Fetal monitoring (not repeated imaging) is the cornerstone of trauma evaluation in pregnancy ≥ 20 weeks gestation. Ultrasound is not sensitive for detecting placental abruption, and physical examination alone cannot reliably assess uterine activity or fetal well-being.

Question: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after a fight. He was stabbed in the abdomen with a knife. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 85/40 mm Hg, HR is 162 bpm, RR is 25/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals a stab wound in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. A FAST exam is notable for the findings above. The patient remains hypotensive despite bolus saline infusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a stab wound, and the video shows the Morison pouch view with an anechoic stripe indicative of a fluid collection between the liver and kidney. The extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (e-FAST) examination is recommended for all patients with significant trauma and for those with suspected abdominal injuries, regardless of whether the injuries are blunt or penetrating. Due to anatomical and physiological differences between children and adults, up to 30% of children with solid organ injuries may not show free fluid on a FAST exam. Thus, there is reduced test sensitivity for detecting such injuries and more limited negative predictive value, especially in hemodynamically stable children. FAST might miss injuries that require surgical intervention, and CT imaging is recommended if injuries are suspected clinically, regardless of ultrasound results. Additionally, unlike adults, in whom the presence of free fluid often leads to surgery, many children with hemoperitoneum and stable vital signs are cared for nonoperatively, meaning a positive FAST result sometimes does not alter the management approach.

In penetrating abdominal trauma, the small intestine (most common in gunshot wounds), colon, and liver (most common in stab wounds) are the organs most frequently damaged. Signs of abdominal trauma vary from subtle to severe, including shock and coma. Intraperitoneal injuries might cause abdominal tenderness, gastrointestinal bleeding, or hypovolemia not linked to external causes. These signs can be initially elusive but may become apparent in subsequent examinations.

When managing stab wounds to the anterior abdomen, clinicians must address three key tasks. First, assess if emergent laparotomy is needed (indications of hemodynamic compromise, peritoneal signs, viscus evisceration, left-sided diaphragmatic injuries, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and intraperitoneal air), especially if the patient is hemodynamically unstable. Patients who are hypotensive and tachycardic should be resuscitated. Blood products and crystalloids can be given. However, if the patient has ongoing hypotension or is in hemorrhagic shock, a massive transfusion protocol should be activated. An unstable patient with a positive FAST examination should go to the operating room.

If laparotomy is not immediately indicated, the second task is to determine whether the peritoneal cavity has been breached (using local wound exploration, e-FAST, CT scan, and laparoscopy). If not, the patient can sometimes be discharged after proper wound care. If the peritoneal cavity has been breached or if it is unclear, the third task is to establish the presence of an intraperitoneal injury (using serial physical examination, CT scan, and laparoscopy) and decide if further intervention is necessary.



CT scan with IV contrast (A) is appropriate care for a patient with a positive FAST exam who is hemodynamically stable. Patients should not be sent for CT imaging when they are hemodynamically unstable.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) (B) is an invasive procedure used to detect intra-abdominal bleeding by inserting a catheter into the peritoneal cavity. While it can provide information on internal bleeding, the FAST exam has already indicated positive findings for internal bleeding in this patient, making DPL unnecessary and redundant.

Serial abdominal and FAST exams (C) are appropriate care for a stable patient with penetrating abdominal trauma with negative imaging studies. However, this approach is too slow and risky for a patient showing clear signs of instability and a positive FAST exam indicating internal bleeding. Immediate surgery is required instead of waiting and watching.

Question: A 34-year-old man presents to the ED after he spilled a liquid chemical on his hands while etching glass. He reports intense hand pain, which appears out of proportion to physical exam. His fingertips are white but without ulceration. What is the most appropriate therapy for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
The most commonly used glass-etching chemical is hydrofluoric acid. Fluoride ions can bind calcium and cause profound hypocalcemia, thus topical calcium gluconate application is the treatment of choice. If commercial 2.5% calcium gluconate gel is unavailable, a gel can be created by mixing 3.5 g of calcium gluconate powder with 5 oz of water-soluble lubricant, or by combining 25 mL of 10% calcium gluconate with 75 mL of water-soluble lubricant. If calcium gluconate is not accessible, calcium chloride or calcium carbonate can be used as substitutes. This mixture should be applied generously to the affected skin. However, the main limitation of this topical therapy is that the skin is relatively impermeable to calcium, so it should only be used for mild, superficial burns. Most importantly, the use of topical therapy should not delay the administration of intradermal or intra-arterial injections for severe burns.

Hypocalcemia can cause QTc prolongation and precipitate ventricular dysrhythmias, which is the most common cause of death from hydrofluoric acid exposure. Calcium can be administered topically, intradermally, or systemically.

Hydrofluoric acid also penetrates deeply into tissue and can cause severe pain out of proportion to physical exam findings. Onset of symptoms from dermal exposure to low concentrations of hydrofluoric acid may be delayed up to 24 hours. Deaths due to cardiac arrest have been reported with hydrofluoric acid exposures involving < 5% of the body surface area.



Irrigation (A) should be performed to decontaminate the area, but neutralization should be avoided because it may create an exothermic reaction that can worsen tissue damage.

Surgical consultation (B) is not required for patients with hydrofluoric acid exposure unless significant tissue necrosis is present. This patient had no evidence of tissue necrosis or chemical burns that required debridement.

Prophylactic antibiotics (C) are not needed for this patient, but they should be considered if subsequent infection develops. However, wound care and tetanus prophylaxis are indicated.

Topical nitroglycerin (E) is a vasodilator and may be useful for digital ischemia due to vasoconstriction from epinephrine, but calcium is the treatment of choice for hydrofluoric acid exposure.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents to the ED reporting severe dental pain following an assault. In addition to ecchymosis and swelling to his right upper lip with a small lip laceration, he has a fracture of his right upper central incisor. You note blood coming from the central aspect of the fractured tooth. What type of dental fracture has the patient sustained?
ExplanationEN:
Dental fractures can be classified by the Ellis system, which considers the depth of the injury. An Ellis III fracture is a true dental emergency consisting of a fracture of the enamel, dentin, and pulp. The pulp has a reddish-pink color and will bleed. Pain and a drop of blood at the fracture site are common. The pulp should be covered to prevent infection. A calcium hydroxide paste or Coe-Pak is ideal, but if unavailable, a piece of moist cotton covered by a piece of aluminum foil can be placed over the exposed pulp. The patient should have prompt dental follow-up within 24 hours.



An Ellis I fracture (A) is an enamel fracture with no exposed dentin. There should be no color change, no sensitivity to hot or cold, and the tooth should not be painful. The patient should have routine follow-up with a dentist for cosmetic reasons only.

An Ellis II fracture (B) is a fracture of the enamel and the yellow dentin of the tooth. Hot and cold sensitivity are often present. The pulp is prone to infection and should be covered to prevent pulpitis. A dressing of calcium hydroxide should be applied to the tooth. If unavailable, a moist gauze dressing can be placed, and the tooth should be covered with aluminum foil. Patients should be referred for dental follow-up in 24 hours.

The Ellis classification system is divided into three categories, and an Ellis IV fracture (D) does not exist.

Question: A 64 year-old woman presents to the emergency department due to facial pain. She was at a major league baseball game and was struck in the face with a foul ball. She is awake and alert and able to provide you with the history. On physical exam she has extensive swelling and ecchymosis to the nasal bridge and upper lip region. Upon grasping her upper teeth, the nasal complex and maxilla move together as a unit. A CT of the facial bones reveals a fracture extending from the maxilla superiorly to the nasal bridge in a pyramidal shape. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
A Le Fort II fracture is a complex fracture of the midface. It is typically bilateral and pyramidal in shape. The fracture extends from the maxilla superiorly to the nasal bridge, including the lacrimal bones, orbital floor, and rim. On physical exam the nasal complex moves with the maxilla when the upper teeth are grasped and rocked. CT of the facial bones confirms the diagnosis. Management includes pain control and facial trauma consultation for operative repair.



A Le Fort I fracture (A) involves a transverse fracture through the maxilla above the roots of the teeth. It may be unilateral or bilateral. Patients often report malocclusion. On physical exam the maxilla may be mobile when the upper teeth are grasped and rocked.

A Le Fort III fracture (C) is rare and results in a craniofacial disjunction. These fractures start at the bridge of the nose and extend posteriorly along the medial wall of the orbit, along the orbital floor, through the lateral wall of the orbit, and through the zygomatic arch. They are often associated with a CSF leak due to fracture extension through the base of the sphenoid.

A Le Fort-Wagstaffe fracture (D) is an avulsion fracture of the anterior cortex of the lateral malleolus.

Question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being assaulted 6 hours ago. He was hit in the face multiple times but did not lose consciousness. His review of systems is negative other than nose pain. The bridge of his nose is swollen with mild tenderness. There is dried blood in his nares with an intact, pink septum. He has no other bony tenderness or evidence of trauma on his exam. What is the appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Attempt closed reduction of the presumed nasal fracture
Discharge with otolaryngology follow-up in 7–10 days

CorrectAnswer: Discharge with otolaryngology follow-up in 7–10 days
ExplanationEN:
Nasal fractures are common, given the protruding midface location and the thin bones that make up the nasal pyramid and bridge. Fractures are most commonly due to direct trauma. Diagnosis of an isolated nasal fracture is clinical and confirmation with imaging is not required. Instead, imaging should be obtained if there is evidence of other presumed fractures or injuries, or evidence of septal deviation or septal hematoma. Most nasal fractures will heal without medical complications. However, cosmetic outcomes will vary depending on the severity of displacement and angulation. These outcomes can be improved with close otolaryngology follow-up. Patients commonly present with nasal swelling, nasal deformity, and epistaxis. Fractures may be associated with septal hematomas and Le Fort fracture patterns. All patients should be evaluated for these injuries as they require more aggressive and different management than isolated nasal fractures. Treatment is primarily supportive with pain control and close otolaryngology follow-up. Adults should be seen within 10 days and children within 4 days. This is to avoid fibrous scar tissue development that leads to cosmetically poor outcomes and an increased need for corrective rhinoseptoplasty.



Closed reduction (A) of nasal fractures is best left to otolaryngologists. It is best attempted in the emergency department when patients present before the onset of swelling, making anatomical alignment easier.

Diagnosis of an isolated nasal fracture is clinical and confirmation with imaging, like computed tomography of facial bones (B) and lateral facial bones X-ray (D), is not required.

Question: Which type of clavicle fracture is most prone to nonunion complication and, therefore, should always be referred to an outpatient orthopedic surgeon after evaluation in the emergency department?
ExplanationEN:
Clavicle fractures are common injuries encountered in the emergency department, particularly in children and young adults, and usually result from direct trauma to the shoulder. Clavicle fractures are classified into three groups based on the fracture location. The majority of fractures occur in the middle third of the clavicle. The least commonly encountered fracture is a proximal injury. While the majority of clavicle fractures do not require orthopedic evaluation, it is still important to know the indications for emergent surgical intervention and to know the long-term outcomes of certain fractures so the patient may be appropriately referred to an orthopedic surgeon on an outpatient basis. Emergent evaluation by an orthopedic surgeon is required for open fractures, neurovascular compromise, and tenting of the skin. Among these criteria, tenting of the skin is more common and should not be ignored, as lack of intervention can lead to skin necrosis and development of an open fracture. All other clavicle fractures can either be treated conservatively with a sling or, depending on the type of fracture, referred to an orthopedic surgeon on an outpatient basis. Among the fracture options above, all type II distal clavicle fractures, or those with superior displacement, should be referred to an orthopedic surgeon because they are prone to nonunion complications. Complications develop with these fractures because they are associated with a ligamentous injury that requires operative repair.



There is wide variability regarding the appropriate treatment of a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture (A). Historically, nonoperative treatment has been recommended, even if considerable displacement of the bone fragments exists. However, some fractures, including comminuted fractures and those with significant shortening, do not heal as well when treated conservatively. The decision for surgical intervention is based on the degree of fracture displacement, the patient’s needs, the patient’s preferences, and the risks associated with surgery. Not all of these fractures require orthopedic intervention.

An intra-articular distal clavicle fracture (B) is a type III distal injury that extends into the acromioclavicular joint. Type I distal clavicle fractures are those in which the fracture fragments remain aligned. Both of these types of distal clavicle fractures heal well with conservative therapy alone and do not require orthopedic evaluation or surgery.

While a proximal clavicle fracture (C) should motivate the clinician to evaluate for other injuries associated with the head, neck, and chest, unless other injuries are found, these fractures may not require orthopedic consultation and can typically be followed on an outpatient basis. Nondisplaced proximal clavicle fractures are managed conservatively. Only patients with significant displacement of the fracture require urgent orthopedic evaluation.

Question: A 14-year-old boy presents after being hit in the head with a baseball bat several times in an altercation. He initially had a brief loss of consciousness but had been acting normally for the past few hours. His family states that he is now acting more confused and less responsive. His CT scan is shown above. An injury to what vessel(s) is most likely?
ExplanationEN:
The image depicts an example of an epidural hematoma, which results most commonly as an injury to the middle meningeal artery. Epidural hematoma is typically an injury that occurs in the younger population. This patient’s presentation is classic, with a history of decreased level of consciousness followed by a lucid interval. About half of patients with epidural hematoma present in this manner. They will have a severe headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and sleepiness. On CT scan, epidural hematoma presents as a biconvex, ovoid hyperdensity. It usually does not extend beyond suture lines and usually bulges inward toward the brain.



Deep arterioles (A) are damaged by shear or tensile forces and may result in intracerebral hematomas. Most such injuries occur in the frontal and temporal lobes.

Injury to superficial bridging vessels (B) causes a subdural hematoma. This is more commonly seen in older patients and those with alcohol misuse disorder with brain atrophy, who typically have bridging vessels traversing longer distances, making them more prone to injury. Unlike epidural hematoma, subdural hematomas will often cross suture lines and patients may have intracerebral lesions on the contralateral side.

The middle cerebral artery (C) is rarely injured in blunt cerebral injuries. It is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery and occlusion results in stroke symptoms.

Question: A 10-year-old boy presents to the ED after slamming his finger in a car door. Physical exam reveals a near-complete avulsion of the right thumbnail with associated subungual hematoma and visible nail bed laceration. The distal phalanx is tender but without gross deformity. X-rays show a nondisplaced tuft fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this injury?

Options.text: Administer tetanus booster and refer for outpatient hand surgery follow-up
Discharge with topical antibiotic ointment and return precautions
Irrigate and dress the wound and refer for outpatient reassessment
Perform trephination of the nail for hematoma drainage and dress the wound
Remove the nail, repair the nail bed, and replace the nail as a splint

CorrectAnswer: Remove the nail, repair the nail bed, and replace the nail as a splint
ExplanationEN:
Fingernail avulsion injuries are common in pediatric and adult populations, particularly due to crush injuries such as door slams. This patient has a near-complete nail avulsion with a visible nail bed laceration and nondisplaced tuft fracture, which represents a type of open fracture. Proper management in the ED requires removal of the nail plate, thorough irrigation, precise nail bed repair with absorbable suture, and replacement of the nail (or a substitute such as foil) to serve as a splint for the eponychial fold. Failure to repair the nail bed can result in permanent nail deformity, such as ridging or nonadherence.

The nail bed (germinal matrix) is responsible for nail growth and lies beneath the proximal nail. Injuries to this structure, especially when associated with distal phalanx fractures, must be considered open fractures and treated with proper irrigation and primary repair. The avulsed nail acts as a natural splint and should be cleansed and reinserted under the eponychial fold to maintain space for future nail regrowth. Patients may require a digital nerve block or procedural sedation for comfort during repair. The use of routine prophylactic antibiotics in the setting of a tuft fracture is not necessary. The focus should be on thorough irrigation and debridement rather than routine antibiotic administration.

In the ED, management includes digital block anesthesia, sterile technique, and referral to hand surgery if the injury is complex or involves tendon or bone. Most uncomplicated injuries can be managed in the ED and followed up as an outpatient. Complications of inadequate treatment include chronic pain and nail dystrophy.



While tetanus prophylaxis is indicated, delaying nail bed repair (A) risks poor cosmetic and functional outcomes. This procedure should be performed in the ED during the initial visit.

While superficial nail injuries without fracture or exposed nail bed may be treated conservatively, this case involves an open fracture and nail bed laceration, both of which require surgical repair and splinting. Discharge without repair (B) risks poor healing and deformity.

Leaving the avulsed nail in place after irrigation and wound care (C) when there is a visible nail bed laceration prevents proper visualization and repair. The nail must be removed to allow adequate inspection and precise closure of the matrix.

Trephination (D) is appropriate for intact nails with subungual hematoma and no nail avulsion or fracture. In this case, there is a near-complete avulsion and a tuft fracture, making trephination alone inappropriate.

Question: A 54-year-old woman is brought to the ED as a pedestrian struck by a motor vehicle. She arrives unresponsive, intubated, collared, and on a backboard. Initial vital signs reveal a BP of 72/41 mm Hg, HR of 54 bpm, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. ECG shows sinus bradycardia, which improves with atropine. CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no signs of internal bleeding. Extremities are warm to the touch without obvious deformities. A bedside echocardiogram shows a grossly intact ejection fraction. Her BP does not improve despite fluid boluses, so norepinephrine is started. What should be the minimum goal mean arterial pressure for this patient?
ExplanationEN:
Neurogenic shock occurs when the autonomic pathways of the spinal cord are disrupted by trauma, resulting in poor vascular tone and consequent hypotension. Due to vasodilation, patients are often warm to the touch but exhibit low internal temperature, which must be treated. Bradycardia is often also seen but is not universally present. Bradycardia should be treated with atropine to maintain a heart rate > 60 bpm, and refractory cases may require pacing. Neurogenic shock is a diagnosis of exclusion in patients who have experienced trauma, and other causes of shock such as cardiogenic (e.g., acute coronary syndrome and myocardial contusion), obstructive (e.g., tension pneumothorax), and hypovolemic shock should be ruled out first.

Hypotension should initially be treated with fluid boluses, taking care not to fluid overload the patient, as excessive boluses can worsen spinal cord swelling. After the patient has been adequately volume resuscitated, norepinephrine should be initiated to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) to at least 85–90 mm Hg. This goal is set higher than the typical MAP of 65 mm Hg because the injured spinal cord is especially vulnerable to ischemic injury.

Patients with refractory hypotension despite norepinephrine should receive phenylephrine as well. Phenylephrine should not be given as a single agent, as its isolated alpha-agonism can result in reflex bradycardia. Neurogenic shock lasts 1 to 3 weeks but has been shown to last as long as 5 weeks.



A MAP goal of 55 mm Hg (A) is not appropriate for a patient with shock when hypoperfusion can cause organ damage and death.

A MAP goal of 65 mm Hg (B) is appropriate for most patients in shock. However, patients with spinal cord injuries are at high risk for secondary injury from ischemia and thus require a higher MAP goal.

A MAP goal of 75 mm Hg (C) is not high enough to ensure adequate perfusion to the spinal cord.

Question: An 18-year-old man is brought in by EMS 26 hours after a motor vehicle collision with prolonged extrication in a remote area. His vital signs on arrival are HR 110 bpm, BP 100/60 mm Hg, and RR 20/min. He is noted to have periorbital ecchymosis with tarsal plate sparing on physical examination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Basilar skull fractures are those that involve any of the five bones comprising the skull base, including the cribriform plate, the occipital bones, the sphenoid bones, the squamous and petrous portions of the temporal bones, and the orbital plate of the frontal bones. Basilar skull fractures are often associated with extra-axial hematomas, especially epidural hematomas, due to the involvement of the middle meningeal artery. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks are also possible due to dural tears. Physical examination findings include mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign) (typically appears 1–3 days post-trauma), hemotympanum, CSF leaks (presenting as otorrhea or rhinorrhea), and periorbital ecchymosis with tarsal plate sparing (“raccoon eyes”, typically appears 1–3 days post-trauma). Basilar skull fractures may be suspected clinically, but diagnosis needs to be confirmed with imaging. Any patient with a suspected basilar skull fracture should undergo a head CT to look for extra-axial hematoma formation as well as cerebral damage, which is common. Management of basilar skull fractures is dependent on presentation and involved structures. Extra-axial hematomas associated with a basilar skull fracture are a neurosurgical emergency. CSF leaks in the setting of basilar skull fractures are typically self-limited. Meningitis prophylaxis in this setting is controversial.



Globe rupture (B) is a traumatic vision-threatening emergency that can present with corneal or scleral lacerations, bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage, iris abnormalities (“teardrop pupil”), or uveal prolapse. Periorbital ecchymosis with tarsal plate sparing is not typical of this injury.

Orbital floor fractures (C), also known as “blowout fractures,” most often occur due to direct trauma to the eye. Periorbital ecchymosis in this setting will also not show tarsal plate sparing as seen with basilar skull fractures.

Subdural hematomas (D) occur due to the tearing of the bridging veins that cross the subdural space. Unlike epidural hematomas, subdural hematomas are not typically associated with basilar skull fractures.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe perineal pain after he fell while attempting to skateboard down a railing. He has been unable to urinate since this occurred 2 hours ago. His examination is notable for moderate ecchymosis in the perineal area. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
This patient is presenting with symptoms of an anterior urethral injury, a type of lower urinary tract injury. The urethra can be divided anatomically into two portions separated by the urogenital diaphragm: the anterior portion, which includes the bulbar and penile segments of the urethra, and the posterior portion, which includes prostatic and membranous segments. Anterior urethral injuries most commonly occur as a result of direct trauma to the perineum. Straddle injuries are a classic mechanism, although anterior urethral injuries are also seen with penile fractures. Symptoms of urethral injury include blood at the penile meatus and inability to void. Hematuria is neither sensitive nor specific for lower urinary tract injury. Whereas physical examination in the setting of posterior urethral injuries typically demonstrates a grossly normal penis and perineum, anterior urethral injuries are associated with abnormal findings on examination, including perineal hematoma or penile swelling. Diagnosis of urethral injuries is made by retrograde urethrogram. In cases of suspected urethral injury, the insertion of a foley catheter should be avoided until urethral and bladder integrity are ascertained. Treatment of urethral injuries is surgical. Failure to diagnose and appropriately treat these injuries can result in strictures, impotence, urinary retention, or incontinence.



Bladder rupture is another type of lower urinary tract injury; these injuries can result in urinary extravasation into either the peritoneal or extraperitoneal portions of the abdomen. Bladder injuries typically occur in the setting of penetrating trauma or blunt trauma with associated pelvic fractures. Abdominal wall bruising, abdominal distention, and perineal edema may be seen in either extraperitoneal (B) or intraperitoneal (C) bladder rupture. Perineal ecchymosis, as seen above, is not typically seen in isolated bladder rupture. Posterior urethral injuries (D) can present similarly to injuries of the anterior urethra, with blood at the meatus and inability to void. However, perineal hematomas are more likely to be associated with anterior urethral injuries rather than posterior. A high-riding prostate is the classic examination finding associated with injury to the posterior urethra.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being shocked when he was using a pair of old pliers to remove a broken plug from an outlet in his home. He states his hand cramped up and he felt a shock travel up his arm to his shoulder. He reports no burns to the hand, shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, numbness, tingling, or weakness. On exam, the patient has no wounds, palpitations, or irregular heart rhythm. When treating patients with this injury, what initial testing should be performed to evaluate the severity of the injury?

Options.text: ECG and cardiac monitoring for 6 hours
ECG, serial creatine kinase, and cardiac monitoring for 12–24 hours
No testing is required for this patient’s injuries
Wound debridement and hand surgery consultation

CorrectAnswer: No testing is required for this patient’s injuries
ExplanationEN:
There are no specific evidence-based guidelines regarding the required testing of patients who have experienced electrical injury. However, consensus states that testing is not required for patients with low-voltage electrical injuries, which includes a household electrical current. This is especially the case in those who are asymptomatic or have minimal localized symptoms. Asymptomatic patients include those who present with no symptoms or those whose symptoms have resolved, those who did not lose consciousness, and those who have a normal physical exam with no burns or contact points. Patients with mild persistent symptoms or minor cutaneous burns should have an ECG and urinalysis to include myoglobin, and they should be observed on a cardiac monitor for 6 hours. If the initial ECG is unremarkable and there is no myoglobinuria or dysrhythmias during the observation period, the patient may be discharged home. The patient in this case is asymptomatic with an unremarkable physical exam. No further testing is required.



ECG and cardiac monitoring for 6 hours (A) are required for symptomatic patients only. Serial creatine kinase measurements and monitoring for 12–24 hours (B) is recommended for patients who have abnormal initial testing (dysrhythmias or myoglobinuria) or who have severe symptoms (loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, entrance and exit wounds, or more than superficial partial-thickness burns). Wound debridement and hand surgery consultation (D) are indicated for severe burns to the hand or nerve injuries and are not indicated for this patient.

Question: A 43-year-old man presents to the ED after an explosion at a nearby nuclear energy plant. He is found to have bleeding in his right ear canal, second-degree burns to his anterior chest, and a fractured right humerus. What type of blast injury is the humerus fracture?
ExplanationEN:
Blast injuries vary immensely, depending on several variables, including the type of explosive, distance from the explosion, the area surrounding the detonation, and associated chemical or biological exposures. There are four main types of blast injuries. Tertiary injuries are caused by the patient being thrown or pushed into surrounding stationary objects. The force behind this phase of the blast can cause several injuries, including extremity fractures, traumatic amputations, severe contusions, and open and closed head injuries.



Primary injuries (A) are those caused by the initial blast wave of the explosion, which results in over-pressurization of gas-filled structures of the body. Examples of this are rupturing of the tympanic membranes, bowel perforation, and pulmonary barotrauma.

Secondary blast injuries (C) are caused by flying debris and shrapnel from the explosion. Common examples are impaled extremities as well as penetrating trauma to the torso and eyes.

Lastly, quaternary blast injuries (B) are a result of the exposures created by the blast, such as fire, smoke, and chemical agents. Burns, crush injuries, smoke inhalation, and toxic chemical exposures are the typical injuries seen with this type of blast injury.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents after acute onset of right leg pain while playing soccer. The patient was sprinting toward the ball when he felt something “pop” in his right hip and fell. He reports no loss of consciousness or head trauma but needed assistance to ambulate to the sideline. He has 3/5 strength with right hip flexion and 4/5 strength with right hip abduction, both movements limited by pain. He also reports pain with lateral compression of the pelvis. The patient is able to ambulate with an antalgic gait. An anterior-posterior X-ray of the pelvis is obtained and shown above. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Discharging the patient with crutches and symptomatic treatment
Extremity traction and emergent orthopedic surgery consult for repair
Frog-leg X-ray to visualize possible femoral head fracture
Pelvic binding for 2 weeks with gradual return to activity

CorrectAnswer: Discharging the patient with crutches and symptomatic treatment
ExplanationEN:
Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) avulsion fractures usually occur in young athletes as a result of a sudden hip extension, usually in the context of jumping or running (e.g., pole vaulting, sprinting, or soccer). In adolescents, the tendons of the sartorius and tensor fascia are often stronger than the developing bone and can avulse from the pelvic brim when subjected to high stress. Patients report substantial pain with hip flexion and knee flexion, but can often bear weight on the affected extremity. X-ray findings are often subtle and patients can be misdiagnosed as having an acute muscular strain. MRI can also be used to distinguish between musculo-ligamentous injury and fracture.

Most ASIS avulsion fractures can be managed conservatively, with crutches and partial weight bearing followed by physical therapy. Patients should have a referral to orthopedic surgery to monitor for malunion. Indications for surgery include neurologic symptoms (e.g., paresthesias over the lateral hip), large avulsions, and bony separation > 3 cm. Such injuries may require internal screw fixation. The prognosis is very good in both surgically and nonsurgically treated patients. Surgical intervention allows for earlier mobility and weight bearing, but functional status is identical at 1 year regardless of treatment.



Orthopedic repair (B) can be indicated if the ASIS avulsion is > 3 cm or patients have ongoing non-union, but surgery is nonurgent and extremity traction could potentially worsen the avulsion. This fracture is minimally displaced and could likely be managed nonoperatively.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) (C) is an acute fracture of the femoral head that can be visualized on frog-leg X-ray. SCFE is usually atraumatic and presents as gradually worsening hip or knee pain in younger adolescents. This radiograph shows no evidence of femoral pathology.

Pelvic binding (D) can be used in acute, unstable pelvic fractures to attain a tamponade of bleeding from a pelvic fracture. However, binding is a temporizing measure and is not indicated for small fractures that do not compromise the structural integrity of the pelvis.

Question: A 21-year-old man presents after falling from standing while intoxicated 2 days ago. He has tenderness to palpation of the nasal bridge and bilateral periorbital ecchymosis. There is no rhinorrhea, mastoid ecchymosis, or hemotympanum. Computed tomography of the face reveals bilateral nondisplaced nasal bone fractures. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options.text: Discharge home with pain control and antibiotics
Discharge home with pain control and nasal decongestants

CorrectAnswer: Discharge home with pain control and nasal decongestants
ExplanationEN:
Discharging with pain control and nasal decongestants is appropriate management for isolated, uncomplicated nasal bone fractures. Nasal bone fractures are common and may be associated with other facial injuries, including orbital or midface fractures, so careful examination of the orbits and midface is essential. Nasal septal hematomas, which appear as a grape-like mass in the naris, can cause septal necrosis leading to perforation and should be drained emergently. Imaging is often unnecessary for the diagnosis of nasal bone fractures. Indications for imaging include if the patient is unable to breathe from the nose, a septal hematoma is present, septal deviation exists, or if there is tenderness that is not isolated to the nasal bridge. Plain films may be obtained, but CT is preferred, especially if there is a concern for other facial trauma. Management of isolated, nondisplaced fractures involves head elevation, ice, and pain control. Displaced fractures that are evaluated within 6 hours of the injury may be reduced immediately. Fractures > 10 days old can be managed by an otolaryngologist in an outpatient setting.



Consultation to otolaryngology (A) is not indicated in isolated nasal bone fractures, but follow-up may be arranged if cosmesis is a concern. Discharging home with pain control and antibiotics (B) is not indicated because simple facial injuries rarely become infected. There is no indication to perform closed reduction under sedation (D) in nondisplaced fractures.

Question: A 16-year-old girl presents with knee pain. The patient was dancing when she suddenly developed pain in the right knee and was unable to walk. Physical examination reveals the above image. What care is indicated?
ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with a lateral patellar dislocation and should have closed reduction attempted. Patellar dislocations are common in adolescents. They typically occur with quadriceps contraction combined with valgus and external rotation. They are frequently seen in dancing and in sports where players perform “cut” moves. Lateral dislocations are the most common, are obvious on physical examination, and are amenable to closed reduction. In lateral dislocations, the knee is held in moderate flexion, and the patella can be seen and palpated lateral to the joint. Closed reduction is performed by gently extending the knee and applying medial pressure to the lateral edge of the patella.



Operative repair (A) is often necessary for intercondylar and superior dislocations but not for lateral dislocations.

CT scan of the knee (C) is usually unnecessary.

Joint aspiration (D) is indicated in the workup of a septic joint, which is not this patient's presentation.

Question: A 13-year-old boy presents after falling on his outstretched hand. Physical examination shows dorsal wrist pain and swelling, with localized tenderness on palpation of the capitate. An X-ray is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Perilunate and lunate dislocations represent different stages of the same progressive injury pattern, accounting for approximately 10% of all carpal injuries. These injuries predominantly affect young male patients following high-energy trauma such as motor vehicle collisions or falls from height. The mechanism involves hyperextension, ulnar deviation, and intercarpal supination, leading to sequential ligamentous failure. In perilunate dislocation, the capitate and remaining carpal bones displace dorsally while the lunate maintains normal alignment with the radius. With further energy, complete disruption occurs, and the lunate dislocates volarly into the carpal tunnel.

Clinical presentation typically includes severe wrist pain, swelling, and deformity following trauma, with median nerve compression symptoms present in many cases. Physical examination reveals dorsal prominence, limited range of motion, and point tenderness over the carpus. However, diagnosis requires careful evaluation of posteroanterior (PA) and lateral radiographs, with the lateral view being the most critical, showing loss of normal radiocarpal and intercarpal colinearity. CT with multiplanar reformations helps delineate associated fractures, while MRI can identify ligamentous injuries and cartilage damage, though these studies are typically not necessary in the ED.

Acute management begins with closed reduction to restore carpal alignment and decompress the median nerve, often under procedural sedation using traction, wrist flexion, and direct pressure. Following reduction, the wrist is immobilized in slight flexion, and the patient requires urgent orthopedic consultation for definitive operative management within 24–48 hours. Despite optimal treatment, these injuries carry significant long-term morbidity, as patients commonly experience persistent pain, reduced grip strength, loss of wrist motion, and post-traumatic arthritis. Additional complications include avascular necrosis, carpal instability, complex regional pain syndrome, and median nerve dysfunction.



In a lunate dislocation (A), the lunate is displaced volarly into the carpal tunnel while the capitate maintains alignment with the radius on a lateral radiograph. However, this patient's X-ray shows dorsal displacement of the capitate, indicating the lunate remains in its normal position.

Radiocarpal dislocations (C) involve complete disruption between the carpus and the radius, representing an even higher-energy injury than perilunate dislocations. They are extremely rare and would show displacement of all carpal bones including the lunate relative to the radius.

Scapholunate dissociation (D) presents with scapholunate widening on PA radiographs and rotary subluxation of the scaphoid, but would not cause isolated dorsal displacement of the capitate. This represents an earlier, less severe stage of the same injury spectrum.

She states her partner grabbed the back of her head, slamming it onto the table, resulting in a significant laceration to her forehead and scalp. She has no sensation to the forehead, she is unable to raise her eyebrows, and there is visible galeal disruption, with exposed bone. CT of the head is negative for fracture and intracranial bleeding. What is the best next step in the care of this patient?

Options.text: Intravenous antibiotics and admission for head injury monitoring
Primary closure of the wound with absorbable suture in the emergency department
Staple closure of the scalp laceration with close follow-up
Urgent expert surgery consultation for layered repair

CorrectAnswer: Urgent expert surgery consultation for layered repair
ExplanationEN:
The principles of wound care for facial and scalp lacerations in the emergency department are to restore function, minimize infection risk, and improve cosmetic outcomes. Crush injuries, wounds > 5 cm in length, deep wounds, contamination, and extended time from initial injury are risk factors for poor wound outcomes. Prior recommendations suggested that wounds should be closed within 12 hours of injury to reduce infection risk. However, recent data suggest the other risk factors are more predictive of infection than timing alone. Face and scalp lacerations have a < 4% risk of infection due to their high vascularity and thus may be closed ≥ 24 hours from the time of injury.

Initial management begins with a careful exam of the injury and its underlying structures. Bleeding should be controlled with direct pressure for approximately 15 minutes before in-depth examination. Additionally, the use of intradermal lidocaine with epinephrine may provide sufficient hemostasis. Removal of all foreign bodies is imperative to allow for proper assessment. Documentation should include the presence of foreign bodies, tissue loss, and length, shape, and depth of the wound. Specifics for the depth should include the layers of tissue affected (epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous, muscle, galea aponeurosis, connective tissue, and periosteum).

Imaging may include plain radiographs to assess for radiopaque foreign bodies and CT scans to assess for skull fractures and intracranial injuries. Antibiotics are reserved for wounds with obvious signs of infection, wounds that require delayed closure, and animal and human bites. Tetanus should be updated, if needed.

Facial and scalp wounds with significant skin loss that may require grafting, complex wounds that require extensive revision, penetration into the cranial vault, underlying fractures, and suspicion of neurologic or vascular injury require expert consultation for surgical repair. This patient has an extensive multilayer wound with altered motor and sensory function and requires expert consultation for definitive repair.



Intravenous antibiotics (A) are an important part of the care of this patient due to bone exposure. Monitoring for head injury is also an important part of the care of this patient, but neither address the primary issue of the complex laceration that requires immediate surgical intervention.

Primary closure of the wound with absorbable suture in the emergency department (B) could be appropriate for a single-layer closure. Complex lacerations with galeal involvement require meticulous layered repair by a specialist.

Staple closure of the scalp laceration with close follow-up (C) would not address the galeal disruption or potential nerve injury. Additionally, staples to the face may leave track mark scars, provide less precise wound approximation than sutures, leave wider wound margins and a more noticeable scar, and result in poor cosmetic outcomes.

Question: An 18-year-old man presents after being stabbed in the back. His vital signs are within normal limits, and his focused assessment with sonography in trauma examination is negative. Physical examination demonstrates a stab wound to the lower back located just to the left of the midline. The patient is unable to move his left leg and reports that his right leg is numb. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Brown-Séquard syndrome is a neurological condition resulting from a hemisection of the spinal cord, most commonly occurring after a penetrating injury. It is characterized by ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception and vibratory sensation deficit, owing to damage to the corticospinal tract and dorsal columns, respectively.

Contralaterally, there is a loss of pain and temperature sensation due to disruption of the spinothalamic tract since these fibers cross the spinal cord at the level of their nerve roots. This dissociative sensory loss provides a distinct clinical presentation that aids in diagnosis. Treatment primarily focuses on addressing the underlying cause, such as surgical intervention for decompression, along with rehabilitation to maximize recovery and manage symptoms.



Anterior cord syndrome (A) most commonly occurs from a contusion of the spinal cord after a hyperflexion injury. It may also be caused by injury or occlusion of the anterior spinal artery. In this syndrome, patients lose motor function and have decreased pain and temperature distal to the lesion. The components of the posterior cord (position, touch, and vibratory sensation) are maintained.

Central cord syndrome (C) is the most common incomplete spinal cord syndrome seen after hyperextension injuries. The central area of the cord contains components of the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts that transmit motor and sensory signals. The upper extremities are affected more than the lower extremities because distal parts of the body are located more peripherally in the cord.

Posterior cord syndrome (D) is a rare type of incomplete spinal cord injury characterized by damage to the posterior columns, leading to a loss of proprioception and vibratory sensation below the level of injury. Patients typically retain motor function, pain, and temperature sensation, as these are mediated by other pathways. Causes include trauma, ischemia, and diseases such as multiple sclerosis or vitamin B12 deficiency.

Spinal shock (E) involves total loss of function distal to the point of injury due to a contusion or concussive injury to the entire spinal cord.

Question: A 48-year-old man presents with nontraumatic lower back pain radiating to the right leg and bilateral leg weakness. He has a history of chronic back pain, exacerbated 1 week ago when he lifted a heavy box. He reports a new onset of numbness in his groin and difficulty with urination 2 days prior. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg, heart rate is 104 bpm, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. On physical exam, he has decreased deep tendon reflexes in his knees and ankles bilaterally, symmetric bilateral lower extremity weakness, decreased sensation in the perineum, suprapubic fullness, and right foot drop. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN:
Five lumbar vertebrae and five fused sacral vertebrae make up the lumbosacral spine. The spinal cord typically terminates at the conus medullaris, within the spinal canal between the T12 and L2 vertebral levels. The lumbosacral nerve roots, L2–S5, extend distally through the spinal canal as the cauda equina, and these nerve roots provide motor and sensory innervation to the legs, anus, perineum, and bladder. Cauda equina syndrome occurs when these nerve roots are compressed, most commonly from lumbar disc herniation.

Typical symptoms include back pain, leg weakness (most often bilateral), urinary retention or incontinence, constipation, fecal incontinence, and perineal (or saddle) anesthesia. If cauda equina syndrome is suspected, an emergent MRI of the lumbar spine should be ordered, and a neurosurgical consultation should be performed. Delay in diagnosis can lead to permanent disability. The definitive treatment is surgical decompression.



Discitis (B) is an infection of the intervertebral disc space that should be suspected in any patient with new-onset back pain and fevers, particularly in patients with a history of IV drug use. It is typically caused by the hematogenous spread of bacteria, and if left untreated, can lead to serious complications such as epidural abscess and resultant paralysis. Diagnosis is made by emergent MRI imaging, and treatment is long-term IV antibiotic therapy and surgical debridement in some cases.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) (C) is a chronic autoimmune disease that destroys the myelin sheaths surrounding motor and sensory neurons. Neurologic symptoms vary greatly and can include visual disturbances, muscle weakness, bowel and bladder dysfunction, and sensory and cognitive deficits. Most commonly, MS occurs in young female individuals and follows a relapsing and remitting course of various symptoms. Many different immunomodulatory medications, and often steroids, are used in treatment. However, no cure exists.

The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body and comprises the L4–S2 nerve roots. It provides motor innervation to the hamstrings, adductors, and portions of the calf and foot musculature and sensation to the posterior and lateral lower leg and plantar foot. Sciatica (D) is caused by inflammation or compression of this nerve anywhere along its course, often by intervertebral disc disease, and is typically unilateral. Diagnosis is made by nonemergent MRI of the lumbar spine. Treatment options include analgesics, physical therapy, and, less often, neurosurgical intervention.

Question: An 8-year-old boy falls onto his outstretched right arm at a local playground. He develops right posterior elbow and forearm swelling and pain, limiting his range of motion at the elbow. The skin is intact. He exhibits weakness with attempts to extend the right thumb. An X-ray of the elbow and forearm is shown above. Which of the following is the most common nerve injury associated with this fracture?
ExplanationEN:
The X-ray demonstrates a displaced midshaft ulna fracture with apex anterior angulation along with anterior dislocation of the radial head consistent with Monteggia Bado type 1 fracture. An acute injury to the posterior interosseous nerve will occur in 10% of these fractures. The posterior interosseous nerve arises from the deep branch of the radial nerve and spirals laterally around the head of the radius running along the fascial plane between the superficial and deep forearm extensor muscles, eventually reaching the interosseous membrane. Acute posterior interosseous nerve neuropathy may be indicated on physical exam by radial deviation of the hand during wrist extension or weakness with thumb or metacarpophalangeal extension.

Most Monteggia fractures in children can be treated with closed reductions of the ulnar fracture and radial head dislocation followed by casting in supination with a bivalve. Open reduction and internal fixation are reserved for fractures that cannot be reduced. Monteggia fractures in adults are typically managed surgically.



Injury to the anterior interosseous nerve (A) is associated with a Galeazzi fracture.

Median nerve injury (B) is associated with fractures of the distal humerus, especially supracondylar fractures.

The musculocutaneous nerve (C) can be acutely injured with glenohumeral trauma.

Question: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a fall in which he hit his head, causing severe neck flexion. On examination, he has 4/5 strength and normal sensation of his upper extremities but has 0/5 strength of his lower extremities and absent sensation to pain below his clavicles, but he is able to sense vibration and tell which direction his toes are pointed. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
ExplanationEN:
Patients presenting with neurologic symptoms following trauma should be stabilized according to standard trauma guidelines, with special considerations for immobilization of the neck and spine, including cervical collars, flattened bed position, and stabilization when moving. These patients should undergo a thorough evaluation of their neurologic function, including detailed physical exam of strength, sensation, and reflexes.

This patient’s presentation is consistent with anterior cord syndrome, an incomplete spinal cord syndrome caused by hyperflexion of the spine or thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery. This presentation leads to damage to the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts while not damaging the posterior columns. Findings on examination include loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the level of the injury with preservation of position and vibratory sensation. Neuroimaging should be used to diagnose any associated fractures, although most incomplete cord injuries will not be apparent on computed tomography scans. Magnetic resonance imaging and neurosurgical evaluation will be required in these patients.



Brown-Séquard syndrome (B) most often presents following penetrating trauma that causes hemisection of the spinal cord. This injury leads to loss of motor function and vibratory sensation on the affected side and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral side.

Central cord syndrome (C) presents after hyperextension of the spine, causing decreased strength and sensation that is more pronounced in the upper extremities than the lower extremities.

Spinal shock (D) is a temporary loss of spinal reflexes below the level of a spinal injury. These patients will present with flaccid paralysis and loss of reflexes below the affected level that will improve over weeks to months.

Question: A 45-year-old man with no medical history presents with chest wall pain after slipping on ice and landing on his left side. His vital signs are BP 120/80 mm Hg, HR 75 bpm, RR 16/min, T 98.0°F (36.7°C), and SpO2 98% on room air. He appears comfortable, is not in respiratory distress. Physical exam shows point tenderness to palpation over the left eighth rib with bony crepitus , and has equal breath sounds. Posteroanterior and lateral chest X-rays are normal. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Obtain a chest CT with contrast
Repeat the chest X-ray in 6 hours

ExplanationEN:
This patient presents with isolated chest trauma and point tenderness over the rib cage, suggestive of a rib fracture. Rib fractures occur most commonly in the setting of blunt chest trauma. Patients present with localized chest wall pain and may have pain with breathing, coughing, and movement. On physical exam, there is often point tenderness, bony crepitus, and ecchymosis at the fracture site. Rib fractures are a concern not due to the fractures themselves, which are managed conservatively, but because of the potential for injury to the underlying lung parenchyma and abdominal organs. These injuries may be suggested by abnormal vital signs, a severe mechanism of trauma, three or more adjacent ribs fractured in two places causing paradoxical chest wall movement, and the location of the rib fracture. Ribs one through three require significant force to fracture and are associated with mediastinal injuries, particularly of the aorta. Due to their location, ribs nine through twelve are associated with injury to the spleen and liver.

The diagnosis of rib fractures is largely clinical. Patients with minor trauma can be treated without imaging, and this patient likely did not need the original chest X-ray. If there is any concern for more serious injury, chest X-ray is the initial diagnostic test of choice. However, chest X-ray is only about 50% sensitive for the diagnosis of a single rib fracture and often misses fractures that are nondisplaced. Still, the value of the chest X-ray is to rule out underlying injury to the lung, including pneumothorax, hemothorax, and contusion. While CT is more sensitive than chest X-ray in detecting rib fractures, no further imaging is indicated to confirm an isolated rib fracture, as the imaging does not change management in this particular patient.

Patients with isolated rib fractures diagnosed clinically or by imaging who are hemodynamically stable and have adequate pain control can be discharged with oral analgesia. Patients with rib fractures for whom admission for IV analgesia should be considered include patients > 65 years, those with underlying lung disease, and those with multiple rib fractures, as they are more likely to develop atelectasis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure. This patient's history and physical exam are suggestive of a rib fracture despite it not being seen on chest X-ray. He has normal vital signs, appears comfortable, and has no other injuries identified on imaging. Thus, he can be discharged with oral analgesia.



Admission for IV analgesia (A) may be necessary for patients > 65 years or those with underlying lung disease who are at higher risk of morbidity and mortality from rib fractures. This patient is otherwise healthy and can be discharged.

Obtaining a chest CT (C) is not necessary, as there is no concern for more serious injury given the minor mechanism, reassuring exam, normal vital signs, and lack of other injuries identified on chest X-ray.

Repeating the chest X-ray in 6 hours (D) is of minimal utility unless the patient has a change in clinical status.

Question: A 42-year-old man presents to the ED after falling directly onto his knee while stepping off a curb. He reports immediate swelling and pain and is unable to extend the knee or perform a straight leg raise. On exam, there is significant prepatellar swelling and tenderness, with a palpable gap over the inferior patella. Radiographs are obtained and shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

Options.text: Apply a compression wrap and encourage early range of motion
Aspirate the hemarthrosis and discharge with crutches
Consult orthopedic surgery for possible surgical fixation
Discharge with knee immobilizer and follow-up in 1 week
Initiate physical therapy and prescribe NSAIDs

CorrectAnswer: Consult orthopedic surgery for possible surgical fixation
ExplanationEN:
Patella fractures account for approximately 1% of all skeletal injuries and are most commonly caused by either direct trauma to the anterior knee (e.g., falls onto the knee or dashboard injuries) or indirect forces such as sudden, forceful quadriceps contraction (e.g., during rapid deceleration or jumping). The patella functions to increase the leverage of the quadriceps tendon, and its integrity is essential for knee extension. Patellar fractures are classified based on their morphology: transverse, vertical, stellate, comminuted, marginal, or osteochondral. Transverse fractures are particularly important to identify because they can disrupt the extensor mechanism.

Patients with a patellar fracture typically present with anterior knee pain, swelling, inability to extend the knee, and sometimes a palpable defect. If the extensor mechanism is disrupted, the patient will not be able to perform a straight leg raise. Imaging should begin with anteroposterior, lateral, and sunrise (axial) knee radiographs. A transverse fracture with significant displacement (> 3 mm), step-off (> 2 mm), or inability to extend the knee suggests disruption of the extensor mechanism and warrants orthopedic evaluation for surgical fixation, typically with tension band wiring or screw fixation. Nondisplaced fractures with an intact extensor mechanism can often be treated conservatively with immobilization and orthopedic follow-up.

Complications of patellar fractures include post-traumatic osteoarthritis, loss of knee range of motion, patella baja or alta, chronic pain, and quadriceps weakness. ED management includes immobilization in extension, analgesia, and prompt orthopedic consultation when the extensor mechanism is disrupted or the fracture is displaced. Early surgical intervention in these cases can significantly improve functional outcomes and reduce long-term complications.



Applying a compression wrap and encouraging early range of motion (A) is contraindicated in acute patellar fractures, especially those with extensor mechanism disruption. Encouraging movement in this context could exacerbate displacement and lead to poor healing or permanent loss of function. Compression wraps may be used for mild soft tissue injuries or in combination with immobilization for conservative fracture management, but in this clinical scenario, the priority is stabilization and surgical planning, not mobilization.

While aspiration (B) may provide some symptomatic relief in cases of hemarthrosis, it is not standard care in the acute setting of a patellar fracture and does not address the underlying mechanical instability if the extensor mechanism is disrupted. Additionally, joint aspiration may introduce infection and is contraindicated in open fractures or when surgical intervention is likely. This patient’s inability to extend the knee signals a more serious injury requiring surgical evaluation, not just symptomatic management and crutches.

Discharging with a knee immobilizer (D) may be appropriate for nondisplaced patellar fractures with intact extensor mechanism function, confirmed on physical exam (i.e., ability to perform a straight leg raise) and imaging. However, in this case, the patient cannot extend the knee or perform a straight leg raise, indicating extensor mechanism disruption. This finding mandates urgent orthopedic consultation for possible surgical repair rather than delayed outpatient follow-up.

Physical therapy (E) is not indicated in the acute management of a patellar fracture with extensor mechanism disruption. NSAIDs may be used for pain control, but they are insufficient as monotherapy. Initiating physical therapy before surgical stabilization could worsen the injury and increase the risk of long-term disability. Rehabilitation is appropriate only after the fracture has been stabilized and healing is underway under orthopedic supervision.

Question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the ED via EMS from the scene of a motor vehicle collision where she was the unrestrained driver of a vehicle that was struck on the driver’s side. She is moaning in pain and appears to be in acute distress. Her vital signs are HR of 145 bpm, BP of 80/40 mm Hg, RR of 28/min, and SpO2 of 99%. Her airway is intact, and there are bilateral breath sounds. She has palpable but weak femoral pulses bilaterally. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13. She has a large ecchymosis over the left flank and upper abdomen. What is the approximate amount of blood volume lost?
ExplanationEN:
Blunt or penetrating trauma can potentially cause hemorrhagic shock if enough blood loss and related end-organ ischemia develop. A patient’s vital signs and mental status provide valuable information regarding the degree of blood loss. These clinical features can be categorized into classes I–IV. Class I hemorrhage describes the findings of a normal HR, normal systolic BP, and normal or increased pulse pressure, with preserved mentation. The blood loss is estimated to be 15%. When blood loss continues to 15–30% of total blood volume, class II hemorrhage is present. Symptoms include mild tachycardia and a narrowed pulse pressure, but systolic BP remains normal. In class III hemorrhage, with 30–40% blood loss, there will be a further increase in HR, reduced systolic BP, decreased pulse pressure, and preserved mentation. In class IV hemorrhage, 40% or more of blood volume is lost due to hemorrhage, with signs such as marked tachycardia, decreased systolic BP, very narrowed pulse pressure, and marked confusion or diminished mental status. In a patient weighing approximately 70 kg with an estimated circulating blood volume of 5 L, class IV hemorrhage would present after 2,000 mL of blood loss.



A patient who has lost 500 mL (D) of blood would present with class I hemorrhage, which includes a normal HR, systolic BP, pulse pressure, and RR, with the earliest sign being slight anxiety. A patient who has lost 1,000 mL (A) of blood will display features of class II hemorrhage when tachycardia and a narrowed pulse pressure develop, with the maintenance of a normal BP. Patients with 1,500 mL (B) of blood loss may start to demonstrate early signs of class III shock, including hypotension, narrowed pulse pressure, progressive tachycardia, and marked anxiety.
